Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Priya, one of the nurses. Can I get the patient's first and last name, please?
Caller -> Hi, yes. It's for my mom. Um, Dorothy. Dorothy Lindqvist.
Nurse -> Okay, Dorothy Lindqvist. And her date of birth?
Caller -> And I'm Karen, I'm her daughter.
Caller -> Oh, sorry, her birthday. March twenty second, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Thank you, Karen. March twenty second, forty one. And I have a callback number here of three one two, five five five, zero one one zero. Is that still good?
Caller -> Yes, that's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect. How can I help you this morning?
Caller -> So, um, she hasn't had a bowel movement in, it's been three days now.
Caller -> And I'm, I'm starting to worry about it.
Nurse -> Okay. Three days. Is she on anything for her bowels right now?
Caller -> She has the senna. She takes the two tablets at night, every night.
Caller -> And we've been doing that.
Nurse -> Okay, good. And is she having any nausea or throwing up at all?
Caller -> No. No nausea.
Nurse -> Any belly pain, or does her belly feel hard or swollen to you?
Caller -> Um, no, she says her belly isn't hurting her. It feels soft. She's passing gas, so.
Nurse -> Okay, that's good to hear.
Caller -> Uh huh.
Nurse -> Let me just look at her orders here. Okay. So she does have the MiraLAX ordered as needed. Do you have that in the house?
Caller -> We do. We have the the big bottle, but we haven't used it yet.
Nurse -> Okay. So what I would do is go ahead and give her one capful of the MiraLAX today. That's seventeen grams, mixed in about eight ounces of water or juice.
Caller -> One capful. Okay. In juice is fine?
Nurse -> Juice is fine. And keep up with the senna at night like you've been doing.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And try to get some fluids in her, prune juice if she likes it, and, you know, some fruit if she's eating.
Caller -> She does like prune juice, actually.
Nurse -> Oh good. Now, I've put a note in her chart so Shannon sees it. And Shannon is scheduled to come out tomorrow at ten for her visit, so she'll check on her.
Caller -> Oh good, okay. Ten o'clock.
Nurse -> Mm hmm. But if she starts throwing up, or her belly gets hard or swollen, or she hasn't gone by tomorrow evening after the MiraLAX, please call us back right away.
Caller -> Okay. Throwing up, belly hard, or nothing by tomorrow night. Got it.
Nurse -> You got it. Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No, that's it. Thank you so much, Priya.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Karen. Have a good day.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Marcus. Who am I speaking with?
Caller -> Hi, Marcus. This is Angela Ruiz. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Angela. Can you give me your date of birth?
Caller -> November eighth, nineteen seventy nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I've got four one five, five five five, zero one one one as your number. Still good?
Caller -> Yep, that's me.
Nurse -> Great. What's going on today?
Caller -> So I had my hernia repair, um, nine days ago now, and I still have the dressing on my belly.
Caller -> And I just want to know if I can take a shower with it. Like an actual shower.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good question. How's the incision feeling?
Caller -> Honestly not bad. It's sore when I sit up, but I'd say like a two.
Nurse -> Okay, a two. Any fever at all?
Caller -> No, no fever. I've been checking.
Nurse -> Any drainage coming through the dressing, or any redness around the edges?
Caller -> No drainage. And it's not red, it looks, it looks fine.
Nurse -> Good. So the order I'm looking at says to keep the dressing dry until the wound nurse changes it.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> So you can shower, but cover it. Plastic wrap over the dressing, tape it down on all the edges, and keep your back to the water. No baths, no soaking, no hot tub.
Caller -> Got it. Plastic wrap and tape.
Nurse -> And I'll send a message to our wound nurse, Tasha, to ask if we can switch you to a waterproof dressing. That would make life easier.
Caller -> Oh, that would be great.
Nurse -> She's usually quick. I'll call you back this afternoon with what she says.
Caller -> Okay, perfect.
Nurse -> In the meantime, if you see redness, if it feels warm, if there's any pus or drainage, or you get a fever of one hundred point four or higher, you call us.
Caller -> Okay. Redness, warmth, pus, fever. I can remember that.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No, that's everything. Thanks, Marcus.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk to you this afternoon.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise speaking.
Caller -> Hey Denise. Um, this is Mike, I'm calling about my dad.
Nurse -> Hi Mike. What's your dad's name?
Caller -> Walter. Walter Brzezinski.
Nurse -> And his birthday?
Caller -> Hang on. Dad, it's the nurse. No, no, you don't have to talk, I got it.
Caller -> Sorry. January seventeenth, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> No problem. And the best number for you, Mike?
Caller -> Six one four, five five five, zero one one three.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's going on?
Caller -> So, the nurse came out Tuesday, which, she was great, by the way.
Nurse -> Oh good, I'll tell her.
Caller -> Yeah. But since then, I mean, even before that, he's just not eating like he was.
Caller -> I'd say maybe half of what he used to eat. Maybe. I'd say.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has that been going on, would you say?
Caller -> Um, about a week? About a week, I think.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he drinking okay?
Caller -> Drinking, yeah. He drinks his water. And his coffee, he will not give up the coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, that's good, actually. Fluids are fluids.
Caller -> Right.
Nurse -> And how's his energy?
Caller -> He's tired. He's napping, like, most of the afternoon now.
Caller -> He'll fall asleep in the chair right after lunch and that's it till dinner.
Nurse -> Okay. Did the nurse check his weight on Tuesday?
Caller -> She did. She said he was down, I think three pounds? I think that's what she said.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look. I'm just pulling up her note here.
Caller -> Sure. Dad, you want the TV down? Okay. He says no.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine.
Caller -> He's watching the, the game replay. My son, his grandson, he plays football for the high school, so.
Nurse -> Oh, how fun. What position?
Caller -> He's a lineman. He's a big kid. Dad never misses a game, he goes in the wheelchair and everything.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. That's so good for him.
Caller -> Yeah, it really is. Anyway. Sorry.
Nurse -> No, no, don't be sorry.
Caller -> So, my question was, um, should we be giving him those shakes? Like Ensure or something?
Caller -> My wife picked some up but we didn't know if that's okay for him.
Nurse -> Yeah, Ensure is fine. One or two a day is fine, in between meals, so it doesn't fill him up before he eats.
Caller -> Okay. One or two a day.
Nurse -> And instead of three big meals, try small meals more often. Little plates. Whatever he likes, his favorite things, even if it's not perfectly healthy.
Caller -> He likes those little powdered donuts.
Nurse -> Then give him a donut. Honestly, at this point we want him to enjoy eating.
Caller -> Okay, he'll like that.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a message to our dietitian, so she can give you some ideas for supplements and things that are easy for him.
Caller -> Oh, that would be helpful.
Nurse -> And I'll ask the nurse to recheck his weight at his visit next Tuesday.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Now, if he stops drinking, or he gets confused, or he goes two whole days without eating anything, you call us. Don't wait for Tuesday.
Caller -> Okay. Can I ask you something else? Is it normal, him being this tired? Like, is that the disease, or is it something we're doing?
Nurse -> It's not anything you're doing. When people eat less, they have less energy, and sometimes it's the illness itself moving along. The nurse can look at that more closely on Tuesday too.
Caller -> Okay. That, yeah. That makes me feel a little better, honestly.
Nurse -> Just keep an eye on how much he's sleeping. If it's suddenly a lot more, or he's hard to wake up, that's a call right away, day or night.
Caller -> Hard to wake up. Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> And how are you doing with all this? It's a lot.
Caller -> I'm okay. My wife and I are splitting it, and my sister comes on weekends. We're managing.
Nurse -> Good. Make sure you're taking breaks too.
Caller -> Ha, I'll try. Friday night's the big game, so that's our break. The whole family goes.
Nurse -> That sounds perfect. Is it supposed to rain?
Caller -> They said maybe. We'll bring the big blanket for Dad and the umbrella. He'll sit through anything for that kid.
Nurse -> Ha. My dad was the same way with my brother's baseball. Rain or shine, front row, with a thermos.
Caller -> That's exactly him. Thermos of coffee. Of course.
Nurse -> I love that. Alright, anything else for him or for you?
Caller -> No. No, I think that's it. Thank you, Denise.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Mike. Good luck to your son this week.
Caller -> Ha, thanks. I'll tell him. Bye.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hi, Ana. I'm calling for my son. His name is Mateo Alvarez.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you spell the last name for me?
Caller -> A L V A R E Z.
Nurse -> Thank you. And his date of birth?
Caller -> Mateo, put that down, please. Put it down.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Sorry. February eleventh, twenty twenty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And who am I talking to?
Caller -> I'm Lucia, his mom.
Nurse -> Hi Lucia. What's the best number for you?
Caller -> Seven zero two, five five five, zero one one four.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on with Mateo today?
Caller -> So, his G-tube, around the button, it's a little red. It started yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. How big is the red area, would you say?
Caller -> Um, about the size of a nickel? Like right around it.
Nurse -> Okay. Any pus, any thick yellow or green stuff coming out?
Caller -> No, no pus. There's like a little bit of clear crusty stuff, that's all.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had a fever?

Nurse -> Good. And he's taking his feeds okay? No leaking around the tube?
Caller -> Yeah, feeds are fine. He's eating fine. No leaking.
Nurse -> Okay, perfect. So for now, clean around the site with soap and water twice a day, pat it dry really well, and keep the split gauze under the button dry.
Caller -> Twice a day. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm going to come out tomorrow morning and take a look at it myself.
Caller -> Oh, okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> If he gets a fever of one hundred point four or more, or the redness spreads, or you see pus, or it's leaking feeds, or the tube comes out, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call.
Nurse -> Alright. See you tomorrow, Lucia.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, um, this is Tanya, I'm the aide for Mr. Pruitt?
Nurse -> Okay, Tanya. What's his first and last name?
Caller -> Eugene. Eugene Pruitt.
Nurse -> Eugene Prewitt, P R E W I T T?
Caller -> No, no. P R U I T T.
Nurse -> Got it, Pruitt. Okay. And his birthday?
Caller -> September third, forty six. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. I have a number on file, four oh four, five five five, zero one one five. Is that you?
Caller -> That's the agency cell, yeah. That's me.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on, Tanya?
Caller -> So I took his blood pressure just now, and it's one fifty two over eighty eight.
Caller -> I just, I wanted to ask if that's okay. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. What's his usual run, do you know?
Caller -> Usually it's like one thirty something. One thirty over eighty. Something like that.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a headache?
Caller -> No.
Nurse -> Any dizziness? Anything blurry in his eyes?
Caller -> No. He's sitting in his chair, he's fine. He's talking about the game.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he take his blood pressure medicine today?
Caller -> Yes. He took it at eight, I gave it to him. And he just finished lunch.
Caller -> Maybe that's why? I don't know.
Nurse -> It could be part of it. Sometimes it runs up a little after a meal, or if he's been up and moving around. So, what I want you to do is have him sit quietly, feet flat on the floor, arm resting at heart level, and take it again in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thirty minutes.
Nurse -> Right. If the top number is over one eighty, or he gets a headache or dizzy or his vision changes, you call us right back.
Caller -> Over one eighty. Okay.
Nurse -> And if he has chest pain, or weakness on one side, or trouble talking, that's nine one one, don't call us first.
Caller -> Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> I'm going to send a note to his doctor's office about the reading so they have it.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Sure. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Rhonda.
Nurse -> Bye now.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom, how can I help you?
Caller -> Hi, Tom. Um, hi. This is Gina, I'm calling about my mother.
Nurse -> Hi, Gina. What's your mother's name?
Caller -> Eleanor Castellano.
Nurse -> Okay, Eleanor Castellano. And her date of birth?
Caller -> Februar. Sorry. February fourteenth, nineteen thirty two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a good call back number for you?
Caller -> Um, eight four five, five five five, oh one one seven.
Nurse -> Okay, eight four five, five five five, zero one one seven.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> Alright. So, what's going on with your mom today?
Caller -> Well, I, I don't know if this is a big deal or not.
Caller -> She's just been sleeping so much. Like, most of the day. For about four days now.
Nurse -> Okay. Four days.
Caller -> Yeah. And she's not eating. Hardly anything.
Nurse -> Okay. When you say hardly anything, what has she had today?
Caller -> Um. A few spoonfuls of pudding this morning. And she'll take a sip of water if I put the straw up.
Caller -> That's about it. It's been like that since the weekend.
Nurse -> Okay, since the weekend. I'm sorry, Gina. That's hard to see.
Caller -> It is. Thank you.
Caller -> Mom? Mom, can you hear me? No. She's just sleeping. Sorry.
Nurse -> That's okay. You take your time.
Caller -> And then today, when I was changing her socks, I saw her heel.
Caller -> The left one. It's red. A red spot, about the size of a quarter, I'd say.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the skin open, or is it just red?
Caller -> It's just red. It's not open. No blister or anything.
Nurse -> Okay. And does she seem uncomfortable when you touch it? Is she grimacing, or moaning?
Caller -> No. She doesn't, she doesn't make a face or anything. She's just sleeping.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Caller -> Is that what it is? Is that, like, a bed sore?
Nurse -> It could be the beginning of a pressure area, yes. Especially with her being in bed more. The good news is it's not open, so we can really help with that.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Let me get her medication list up here so I can see everything she's on.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. So, I'm looking at her list. I see furosemide, that's her water pill. Metoprolol. Atorvastatin. Famotidine.
Caller -> Yeah, we stopped those. The hospice nurse who came last week said we could stop all the pills she can't swallow anymore.
Nurse -> Okay, that makes sense. So those are all off. Now what I'm showing for comfort is lorazepam, point five milligrams, under the tongue every six hours as needed.
Caller -> Mhm. Yes. I have that.
Nurse -> And she also has the morphine liquid, but that's for pain or breathing. Has she needed any of that?
Caller -> No. No, she hasn't needed the morphine. She's not in pain, I don't think.
Caller -> I gave her the lorazepam once. Last night around nine. She was kind of restless, picking at the blanket.
Nurse -> Okay. And did that help?
Caller -> Yes, she settled down and slept.
Nurse -> Good. So that's the right use for it. If she gets restless like that again, go ahead and give her the lorazepam, point five milligrams under the tongue, like you did.
Caller -> Okay. Even if it's been less than six hours? Because it was last night.
Nurse -> It's been way more than six hours, so you're fine. Just don't give it more often than every six hours.
Caller -> Okay. Got it. Thank you.
Caller -> Oh, my sister's here. Hi, Maria. It's the hospice nurse. I'm asking about Mom's heel. Yes. Okay, I'll ask.
Caller -> Maria wants to know if she should stop trying to feed her.
Nurse -> That's a really good question. What I'd tell you both is, it's normal, at this stage, for her to sleep more and eat less. Her body is slowing down, and it doesn't need the same amount. So please don't push food. If she wants a spoonful of pudding or a sip, great. But don't force it.
Caller -> Okay. So we're not starving her.
Nurse -> No, no. You're not. Not at all. It's really the opposite. Forcing it can make her uncomfortable. You can offer sips, and you can use a little mouth swab to keep her lips and mouth moist. That feels good to people.
Caller -> Mouth swabs. Okay, we have those pink sponge things in the kit.
Nurse -> Yes, exactly those.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell Maria.
Caller -> She says thank you. She said she's been so worried.
Nurse -> Of course. Is anybody else with you today?
Caller -> Yeah, we're all here. My brother flew in from Phoenix last night, and my sister from Tampa. And the grandkids are coming this weekend. Mom has nine grandkids. She'd be thrilled, if she were awake.
Nurse -> Nine! That's wonderful. I bet she knows they're there, even sleeping.
Caller -> I hope so. We keep talking to her. We play her old records, the Sinatra.
Nurse -> Oh, I love that. Hearing is the last thing to go, so please keep doing that. Keep talking to her.
Caller -> We will. My brother reads her the newspaper. The sports page. She never cared about sports, ha, but he does it anyway.
Nurse -> Ha. That's sweet.
Caller -> Okay. So. What do we do about the heel?
Nurse -> Okay. So, a few things. First, we want to take the pressure off that heel. Put a pillow under her calves, so the heels are floating, not touching the mattress.
Caller -> A pillow under her calves. Okay.
Nurse -> Right. And turn her every two hours, side to side, with a pillow between the knees.
Caller -> Every two hours. Okay. We can do that. We have enough people.
Nurse -> That's perfect. And please don't rub or massage the red spot. That can actually hurt the skin. Just leave it alone.
Caller -> Don't rub it. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm also going to order heel protector boots for her. They're soft foam boots that keep the heels off the bed. We can usually get those out the same day or the next day.
Caller -> Oh, that would be great. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'm going to send our nurse out tomorrow morning to take a look at the heel, and to check on her comfort.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Mm hmm. Now, if the skin opens up, or blisters, or if she starts to groan or grimace, or if her breathing gets noisy or hard, you call us right away. Okay?
Caller -> Skin opens, groaning, breathing. Okay.
Nurse -> Right. And you can call us any time, day or night. You don't have to wait.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I feel better, honestly.
Caller -> Oh, one more thing. Is it possible to have the chaplain come? Our mother's very religious, and we'd love to have somebody come and pray with her.
Nurse -> Absolutely. I'll send a message to our chaplain and ask him to reach out to you today or tomorrow.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Thank you so much. That would mean a lot.
Caller -> Sorry, my brother just walked in. Dave, shh, I'm on with hospice. He wants to know if he can sit with her tonight.
Nurse -> Of course. Tell him he can sit with her as long as he likes. Hold her hand, talk to her. She'll know he's there.
Caller -> He says okay. He's such a softie. He's been crying out in the garage all morning, and he thinks nobody knows.
Nurse -> That's very normal. Everybody grieves in their own way, and that's okay.
Caller -> Yeah. And the neighbors keep dropping off food, we have like four casseroles. We can't possibly eat it all.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what people do when they care. Freeze what you can, you'll be glad to have it later this week.
Caller -> That's a good idea. Okay. I'll tell Maria to start labeling things.
Nurse -> Of course, Gina. Is there anything else I can do for you?
Caller -> No, I think that's it. You've been so kind.
Nurse -> You're very welcome. Take care of yourself, too. And give your mom a kiss from me.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye now.

Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi Beth. Um, this is Sandra Whitfield. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi Sandra. Date of birth?
Caller -> May nineteenth, nineteen seventy one. Oh, no, nineteen seventy two. Seventy two, sorry.
Nurse -> Seventy two. Okay. And your callback number is nine one nine, five five five, zero one one six?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> What can I help you with?
Caller -> I started the, the antibiotic, the amoxicillin, for the bladder thing.
Caller -> And I've been kind of nauseous. Not terrible. Just, like, a queasy feeling.
Nurse -> Okay. When did that start, do you know?
Caller -> I think Monday. Yeah, I think it was Monday. Or maybe Sunday night.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you throwing up?
Caller -> No, no, nothing like that.
Nurse -> How often do you take the amoxicillin?
Caller -> Twice a day. Morning and night.
Nurse -> Okay. And I see here you have ondansetron ordered for nausea, as needed. Do you have that at home?
Caller -> I do. I just haven't taken it. I didn't know if I should.
Nurse -> Yes, go ahead and take the ondansetron, as it's ordered, when you feel queasy. It shouldn't interfere with the antibiotic.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And make sure you're taking the amoxicillin with some food, not on an empty stomach. Even toast or crackers.
Caller -> Oh. I've been taking it first thing, before I eat. That might be it.
Nurse -> It might be. Try it with food tonight and see.
Caller -> Okay, I will.
Nurse -> Also, small bland meals, sip fluids during the day, and stay away from greasy or spicy food for now.
Caller -> Okay. Bland. Got it.
Nurse -> If you can't keep fluids down, or you start throwing up, or you get a rash or any swelling, call us.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No, that's all. Thanks, Beth.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Feel better.

Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi, yeah, hi. This is Victor. I'm calling about my mom. Rosa Delgado.
Nurse -> Hi, Victor. And Rosa's date of birth?
Caller -> October twenty fifth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. And I've got three oh five, five five five, zero one one eight on file for you.
Caller -> That's me.
Nurse -> What's going on tonight?
Caller -> So my sister just left. She was here all day. And I took over for the night.
Caller -> And my mom's, she's kind of moaning, a little. Like she's hurting.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad do you think the pain is?
Caller -> I'd say maybe a five? I don't know. A five.
Nurse -> Okay. What's she taking for pain?
Caller -> The oxycodone. The five milligram pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull up her orders. So the oxycodone five milligrams, by mouth, every four hours as needed.
Caller -> Right. That's the one.
Nurse -> And when was her last dose?
Caller -> That's the thing. I'm not sure.
Caller -> My sister said she'd give her one at eight. But she left at like, quarter after eight, so, I don't know if she did it before she left or not.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a note, or anything written down?
Caller -> I looked. There's nothing on the, there's a pad here, but she didn't write anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you call your sister?
Caller -> I tried. It went to voicemail. She's probably driving.
Nurse -> Okay. So here's what I'd like you to do. Hold off on giving another dose of the oxycodone until you've reached her, so we know it's safe. It's not safe to guess.
Caller -> Okay. But she's in pain.
Nurse -> I understand. It's just after three in the morning, so if your sister gave it at eight, she's overdue. But if she gave it later, that's different. I want to be sure first. Try her again in ten minutes, and keep trying.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll try her again.
Nurse -> I'm going to put a note in the chart about this.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in thirty minutes to see where things are. If you reach her sooner and she says no dose was given, go ahead and give the oxycodone and then call me.
Caller -> Okay. Thirty minutes. Got it.
Nurse -> Also, from now on, write every dose and the time on a sheet, right by the bed, so whoever is there knows.
Caller -> Yeah, that's a good idea. I'll start tonight.
Nurse -> And if she gets really sleepy, hard to wake, or the pain isn't settling at all, call me right away.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Alright, Victor. Talk to you soon.
Caller -> Thanks, Carla. Bye.

Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi Marcus. This is Irene Moretti. It's about my husband.
Nurse -> Hi, Irene. What's your husband's first name?
Caller -> Frank. Frank Moretti. Same as mine, ha.
Nurse -> And his birthday?
Caller -> June twelfth, nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> Thank you. Is six one seven, five five five, zero one two one still the best number?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house phone.
Nurse -> What's going on with Frank?
Caller -> Okay, so, I want to start by saying he did not fall.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I mean, I wasn't, I didn't see him fall. But I found him this morning, on the floor. By his recliner.
Nurse -> Okay. So you found him on the floor.
Caller -> Yes. But he didn't fall. He says he, he slid. He slid down out of the chair.
Nurse -> Okay. So he slid out of the recliner and ended up on the floor.
Caller -> Right. Right. But that's not a fall, is it?
Nurse -> It sounds like a fall to me, Irene, and that's okay. It's good that you called. When did this happen, do you know?
Caller -> He says it was last night. After I went to bed. But I didn't find him until this morning.
Caller -> Which, I don't, I don't know. He might've been down there all night. I feel terrible.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't feel terrible. Is he saying he was on the floor all night?
Caller -> He says no. He says he was in the chair and then he slid in the morning. Early. Before I got up. So I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. So the timing isn't clear. That's alright. Did he hit his head?
Caller -> No. He says no. And I looked, there's nothing on his head. No bump.
Nurse -> Okay, good. Is he complaining of any pain? His hip, his back, his wrist?
Caller -> No. He's not complaining of anything. He's actually fine. I looked him over and I don't see any bruises.
Nurse -> Okay. How did he get up off the floor?
Caller -> My son was here. He came over for the morning. He and I got him up. And Frank walked to the bathroom with the walker.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's good to hear.
Caller -> Yeah. And I don't want to make a big deal. But there's something else.
Nurse -> Sure. Go ahead.
Caller -> He's been so forgetful. The last couple of weeks. Like, he asks me the same thing three times. And this morning he didn't know why he was on the floor.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important, Irene. Has anything changed? New medications, or a fever, or any burning when he urinates?
Caller -> No. No new medicines. And no fever. He's just, forgetful.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to write this up as a fall, so it's in his record and the team knows. I've got that started now.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll have a nurse come out tomorrow morning to check him over for bruising, and do a proper assessment. Sometimes the bruises show up the next day.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a message to his physical therapist. She can come out and look at the house, the chair, the walker, and see what we can do to make it safer.
Caller -> Oh, that'd be wonderful. She's so nice.
Nurse -> What's he wearing on his feet when he's walking around the house?
Caller -> His slippers. The old leather ones. They're pretty worn out, honestly.
Nurse -> Those can be slippery. Non-skid socks, or shoes with a back on them, are much safer, even indoors.
Caller -> I have those grippy socks from the hospital. I'll find them and put them on him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is the recliner a power one, or manual?
Caller -> Manual. He pops it up and down himself. And sometimes it kind of kicks when it comes up.
Nurse -> That can throw somebody off balance. For now, have him scoot to the edge of the seat first, and wait a moment before standing.
Caller -> Okay. Scoot forward and wait. I'll remind him.
Nurse -> In the meantime, he needs to use the walker every time he gets up. Even for a short walk. And try to clear the floor of rugs and cords.
Caller -> Okay. I took the throw rug out already.
Nurse -> Good. And please don't try to lift him by yourself if it happens again. Call us or call nine one one for help getting him up.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll call.
Nurse -> Now, if he gets a headache, or he's throwing up, or he's more confused than usual, or any new pain or bruising, call us. If he ever hits his head and he's drowsy or confused, call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Headache, throwing up, more confused. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll mention the forgetfulness to the nurse and to his doctor, too.
Caller -> Thank you, Marcus. I really appreciate it.
Nurse -> Of course. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I think that's all.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll see you tomorrow. Take care, Irene.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Hi Joanne, my name is Shari. I'm calling about my mother.
Nurse -> Okay, Shari. What's your mom's name?
Caller -> Lorraine Kowalczyk. That's K O W A L C Z Y K.
Nurse -> Thank you. And her date of birth?
Caller -> December second, nineteen forty five. No, wait. Forty four. Nineteen forty four. Sorry, she'd kill me.
Nurse -> Ha. Forty four. And a good number for you?
Caller -> Two one six, five five five, oh one one nine.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> It's her knee. The right one. It's been bothering her a couple of weeks.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad is it?
Caller -> She says maybe a four. A four out of ten. But it's stiff in the morning, like, really stiff.
Nurse -> How long does the stiffness last?
Caller -> About an hour. She can't get going until she's been up for an hour.
Nurse -> Okay. What is she taking for it?
Caller -> The Tylenol. Well, the acetaminophen, the five hundred milligram.
Caller -> I gave her two tablets this morning. No, one. One tablet.
Nurse -> So one tablet. Okay. How often is she taking it?
Caller -> Every six hours, if she needs it. She's pretty good about it.
Nurse -> Okay. So that's fine. I just want to be sure she doesn't go over the daily maximum of acetaminophen. With the five hundred milligram tablets, no more than six in twenty four hours.
Caller -> Six. Okay. That's what I thought.
Nurse -> And check the other things she takes, because some cold medicines and sleep aids have acetaminophen in them too.
Caller -> Oh. Oh, I didn't think of that. She takes a night time one sometimes.
Nurse -> Check the label. If it says acetaminophen, count it in the total.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> For the stiffness, a warm shower in the morning helps a lot of people. Or a heating pad on low. Then some gentle movement, nothing hard.
Caller -> Okay. We have a heating pad.
Nurse -> And I'm going to send a message to her doctor about the knee pain and the stiffness, since it's been a couple of weeks. They might want to take a look.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Anything else, Shari?
Caller -> No, that's it. Thank you, Joanne.
Nurse -> You're welcome.

assessment.explanation: Documents the dose with the caller's self-correction.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi. Um, I don't know if I'm calling the right place. I'm calling about my neighbor.
Nurse -> Okay. Can I get your neighbor's name?
Caller -> Carol. Carol Whitaker. Or Whitacre? Something like that. I think it's Whitaker.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> Oh gosh, no. She's, I want to say late fifties? I don't know.
Nurse -> That's okay. And what's your name?
Caller -> I'm Dana. Dana from next door.
Nurse -> Hi, Dana. What's a good callback number for you?
Caller -> Actually I'm on my cell and I'm going to lose signal in the garage. Could you just call her daughter? You should have the number.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll check. What's going on with Carol?
Caller -> So I stopped by to check on her this morning, and her ankle's all swollen.
Nurse -> Okay. Which ankle?
Caller -> The left one. I think. Maybe the left.
Nurse -> And how long has it been like that?
Caller -> She said a few days. Maybe a week? She wasn't sure either.
Nurse -> Okay. Does it hurt?
Caller -> She says it doesn't hurt much. She's not complaining.
Nurse -> Okay. Any shortness of breath, chest pain, anything like that, that you've noticed?
Caller -> I didn't notice anything. But I wasn't there long.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she taking a water pill, do you know?
Caller -> I really don't know. I don't know what she takes. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's alright. I have her chart pulled up. I do see her daughter on the contact list. I'll call her this evening, and let her know about the ankle.
Caller -> Oh good. That'd be great.
Nurse -> And I'm going to see about getting a nurse out there tomorrow to take a look at it.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> In the meantime, if you're able to, have her sit with that foot up on a pillow.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> And if she has chest pain, or trouble breathing, or the leg turns red, hot, or really painful, call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Nine one one. Got it.
Nurse -> Thank you so much for checking on her, Dana. That's really helpful.
Caller -> Of course. She's a sweetheart.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom, this is Shanice, I'm one of the med aides over at Oak Terrace Assisted Living.
Nurse -> Hi, Shanice. What can I do for you?
Caller -> I'm calling about one of your residents. Ernestine Kowalewski.
Nurse -> Can you spell that last name?
Caller -> K O W A L E W S K I.
Nurse -> Thanks. And do you have her date of birth?
Caller -> Um. Hang on. I have it right here on the face sheet. March eighth, nineteen thirty five.
Nurse -> Okay. And a number for you, Shanice?
Caller -> The main desk. It's two one five, five five five, zero one five zero.
Nurse -> Okay, got it. Two one five, five five five, zero one five zero.
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's it.
Nurse -> So what's going on with Ernestine?
Caller -> Okay, so, I just came on at seven this morning. And the night girls told me she was up. Most of the night.
Caller -> They said she was confused, and walking in the hallway, and she didn't know where she was.
Nurse -> Okay. So you weren't there overnight.
Caller -> No, no, I was not. I'm just giving you what they told me. Sorry. I wish I had more.
Nurse -> No, that's fine. Did they say what time it started?
Caller -> I think around, what did she say, maybe two? Two or three in the morning. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> Okay. And is she still confused now?
Caller -> No. She's sleeping now. She's calm. I just checked on her.
Nurse -> Okay, good. Did she fall, or did the staff say anything about a fall?
Caller -> No. I don't think so. They didn't say anything about a fall. I'd have heard.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> I took her temperature when I checked on her. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> Okay. That's normal. How's she been eating?
Caller -> She hardly touched breakfast. I'd say a quarter, maybe. She ate the applesauce and a few bites of toast.
Nurse -> Okay. Okay. Let me pull up her orders. Hang on a second.
Caller -> Sure.
Nurse -> I'm just going to read through. Metoprolol. Atorvastatin. Famotidine. Levothyroxine.
Caller -> Yeah, those are the morning pills. We gave those at seven thirty. She took them with the applesauce.
Nurse -> Okay. And for comfort, I'm seeing haloperidol, point five milligram, by mouth, every six hours as needed for agitation or restlessness.
Caller -> Mm hmm. Yes. That's on her list.
Nurse -> Do you know if any was given overnight?
Caller -> I, I don't know. I'm not sure. The night girls didn't say. I'd have to look at the, the book.
Nurse -> Okay. The MAR, the medication record?
Caller -> Yes. The MAR. It's in the office. I can go get it. Hang on.
Caller -> Marcy? Marcy, can you check the MAR for Mrs. Kowalewski, whether they gave the haloperidol last night? Okay. She's looking.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> Sorry, it's a little crazy here. We've got a new resident moving in today, and there's boxes everywhere.
Nurse -> Oh, that sounds busy. Is this a new move in on the first floor?
Caller -> Second floor. A gentleman. His son's been here since eight, hauling furniture. A recliner the size of a car.
Nurse -> Ha. Those always take forever.
Caller -> Tell me about it. The elevator has been out since Tuesday, so everything has to go up the stairs lift, one at a time.
Nurse -> Oh no. That's rough. Hopefully they fix it soon.
Caller -> They said Friday. We'll see.
Nurse -> Is Ernestine usually like this at night? Or is this new?
Caller -> It's new, I think. She's usually a very sweet lady. She loves her soap operas. She'll tell you the whole plot of what happened yesterday, even though she can't remember what she had for breakfast.
Nurse -> Ha. That's how it goes. Does she have any friends in the building?
Caller -> She has Dolores down the hall. They play cards on Tuesdays. Dolores was asking about her this morning, actually, because Ernestine wasn't at the table.
Nurse -> That's sweet. It sounds like she has a good community there.
Caller -> She does. We all love her. That's why it worried me.
Caller -> Okay, Marcy's back. She says, it just says, there's no initials for last night. For the haloperidol.
Nurse -> Okay. No initials. So it looks like it wasn't given, or it wasn't documented.
Caller -> Right. We don't know which. The night nurse isn't here, she went home. She'll be back at eleven tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. So we can't be sure. That's all I need to know for now. Shanice, I think I should have a nurse come see her. Today.
Caller -> Oh, okay. That'd be good. When would that be?
Nurse -> I'm going to try for before noon. She'll look at Ernestine, and go over the medications, and the whole picture.
Caller -> Before noon. Okay. I'll tell the family.
Nurse -> Is the family involved? Who's her contact?
Caller -> Her daughter. She lives in Florida. She calls every Sunday. I'll call her today.
Nurse -> Good. Please do. And in the meantime, could you fax me the MAR for the last week? That helps the nurse a lot.
Caller -> Sure. I can do that. What's your fax number?
Nurse -> It's on your hospice contact sheet, the one at the front of her binder. Or Marcy can call the main line and ask the front desk.
Caller -> Okay. I'll have Marcy do that, she's good at that stuff.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to let our hospice doctor know about the new confusion at night.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Shanice, for the haloperidol, please don't give any more until the nurse has looked at the MAR and talked with the doctor.
Caller -> Okay. Not until the nurse says. Got it. I'll tell the other aides.
Nurse -> Thank you. And for tonight, ask the night staff to write down every time she's up, what time, and if anyone gave her any medication. That'll help us figure out a pattern.
Caller -> I'll write a note for them. A note on her door.
Nurse -> Good. And ask them to check if she might be in pain, or constipated, or needs to use the bathroom. Sometimes that looks like confusion.
Caller -> That makes sense. Honestly, I wonder if she needs to go. She was a bit like that a few weeks ago, and it turned out she had a UTI.
Nurse -> That's good to remember. I'll mention that to the nurse so she can ask about urinary symptoms. We can check.
Caller -> Okay. I'd feel better if somebody looked.
Nurse -> Totally. Also, keep a night light on, keep her bed low if you can, and call the hospice line for any fall at all, even a small one.
Caller -> We have the low bed. And the night light. Yes.
Nurse -> If she gets hard to wake up, or agitated, or combative, or she falls, or has trouble breathing, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Hard to wake, agitated, falls, breathing. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Thank you. You're doing a good job, Shanice, thinking to call.
Caller -> Thanks. I just felt like something wasn't right.
Nurse -> That's what we want. Always call when something doesn't feel right.
Caller -> Okay. Oh, hold on one second. Yes? Okay. Marcy says the fax number is on the second page. Got it.
Nurse -> Perfect. So you've got that covered.
Caller -> I do. Marcy is a lifesaver. She's been here eleven years. She knows where every single thing is.
Nurse -> Those people are gold. Hold on to her.
Caller -> Oh, believe me. We try.
Caller -> I do. Okay, I'll let you go. Thank you, Tom.
Nurse -> Thank you. Take care. Good luck with the move in.
Caller -> Ha. Thanks. We'll need it. Oh, wait. One more thing. The son just asked me if there's a good place to park a moving truck, and I have no idea.
Nurse -> Ha. I don't think I can help with that one. The front loading zone, maybe?
Caller -> That's what I told him. The front loading zone. Okay. Thank you again, Tom. Bye.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. This is Patricia Nwosu. I'm a patient of yours.
Nurse -> Hi, Patricia. Can you give me your date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty seventh, nineteen sixty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number is seven one three, five five five, zero one two two?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> What can I do for you?
Caller -> So, I'm confused about my insulin. The long acting one. The glargine.
Caller -> I think I take ten units at night. But my sister told me twelve. And now I'm, I'm second guessing.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull up your orders. Hang on one second.
Caller -> Sure.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm showing insulin glargine, ten units, injection at bedtime.
Caller -> Ten. Okay. So I've been right. I was doing ten.
Nurse -> Yes. Ten units at bedtime. That's what your doctor ordered.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Why are you asking today? Is something going on with your sugars?
Caller -> Well, yeah. This morning, before breakfast, I was two ten. And yesterday it was two oh five, I think.
Nurse -> Okay. So two ten this morning. Is that higher than usual for you?
Caller -> Yeah. I'm usually like, a hundred forty, hundred fifty.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you throwing up, or feeling sick to your stomach?
Caller -> No, nothing like that.
Nurse -> Any extra thirst, or going to the bathroom a lot?
Caller -> A little more thirsty. The last few days.
Nurse -> Okay. So, here's the plan. Don't change the dose on your own. Keep taking ten units at bedtime, like it's ordered.
Caller -> Okay. Ten.
Nurse -> And I'm going to send a message to your doctor about the morning numbers, since they've been in the two hundreds. They may want to adjust it.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense.
Nurse -> Keep checking every morning, before you eat, and write it down. So when the doctor calls, you have the numbers.
Caller -> I do write them down.
Nurse -> Good. And call us if it goes over three hundred, or if you start vomiting, or you feel confused, or you're really thirsty.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Also, if it ever drops under seventy and you feel shaky or sweaty, drink half a cup of juice and recheck in fifteen minutes. And if you ever pass out, that's nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Juice, recheck, nine one one if I pass out. I got it.
Nurse -> Alright, Patricia. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.

assessment.explanation: Documents the dose clarified against the order in the chart.

assessment.explanation: Documents a pertinent negative for gastrointestinal symptoms.

assessment.speaker: Caller

assessment.explanation: Documents a symptom associated with elevated glucose.

response.text: Advised continuing insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime as ordered without changing the dose.
response.speaker: Nurse
response.quote: Don't change the dose on your own. Keep taking ten units at bedtime, like it's ordered.

response.speaker: Nurse

Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi Carla, it's Colleen. I'm calling about my mom, Hattie. Hattie Brennan.
Nurse -> Hi Colleen. And Hattie's birthday?
Caller -> August thirtieth. Nineteen thirty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I have seven two seven, five five five, zero one two three for you.
Caller -> Mhm. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Alright. What's going on?
Caller -> She's been throwing up. Twice this morning.
Caller -> And it's just, she just can't, she's so nauseous.
Nurse -> Okay. Twice since this morning. Is she able to keep any fluids down?
Caller -> Yeah. She's keeping little sips of water down. It's just the food she doesn't want.
Nurse -> Okay. Any blood in the vomit, or anything dark, like coffee grounds?
Caller -> No. No, nothing like that. It's just, it's clear and some of her breakfast.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she taking anything for the nausea?
Caller -> Yes. She has the Zofrin. The four milligram, the one that melts on her tongue.
Nurse -> Okay. And when was her last one?
Caller -> I gave her one at seven. Seven this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. So the Zofrin can be given every eight hours as needed. So she can have another one around three this afternoon.
Caller -> Oh, okay. Three o'clock. Okay.
Nurse -> And how many do you have left?
Caller -> Um. Let me look. I have, one, two, three. Three. There's three left.
Nurse -> Okay. Three. I'm going to put in a refill request for the Zofrin for you, so that you don't run out.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. I was just about to ask.
Nurse -> Sure. In the meantime, just small sips of clear liquids. Ice chips if she likes them. Hold off on solid food until the nausea settles down.
Caller -> Okay. Sips and ice chips. No food.
Nurse -> If she vomits blood, or anything that looks like coffee grounds, or she can't keep any fluids down for eight hours, or she has belly pain or a fever, call us.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Alright, Colleen. Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. It's Brandon. I'm calling for my dad. Alvin Castellanos.
Nurse -> Hi, Brandon. Can you spell the last name for me?
Caller -> C A S T E L L A N O S.
Nurse -> Thank you. And his date of birth?
Caller -> April twenty sixth, nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And your number, Brandon?
Caller -> Two four eight, five five five, zero one five one.
Nurse -> Okay. Two four eight, five five five, zero one five one.
Caller -> Yep.
Nurse -> What can I do for you tonight?
Caller -> Okay, so, a couple things. First, my dad hasn't had a bowel movement in four days.
Caller -> And he's, he's really uncomfortable. And he's not sleeping. He's up until three in the morning. Every night this week.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take one at a time. The bowels first. Four days. Is he eating?
Caller -> He's eating. Not a lot. But he's eating.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he nauseous? Throwing up?
Caller -> No. No nausea. No throwing up.
Nurse -> Okay. Is his belly hard or swollen?
Caller -> I don't think so. It's soft. He says it feels full though.
Nurse -> Okay. What is he taking for his bowels?
Caller -> He takes the doc you sate. Twice a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> That's it, I think. Just that one.
Nurse -> Okay. And I know he's on pain medicine too, that can cause constipation. What's he taking for pain?
Caller -> He takes the, hold on, I want to say it right. The trauma doll.
Nurse -> Trauma doll? Let me look at the chart. I'm going to read what I see, and you tell me if it's the same. I see tramadol, fifty milligrams, every six hours as needed.
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's it. Tramadol. That's what's on the bottle.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I keep mixing up the names.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. They're not easy names. How often is he taking it?
Caller -> About three or four times a day. It depends on how his back is.
Nurse -> Okay. And how bad is his back pain right now?
Caller -> He says it's a five. Right now. Lower back.
Nurse -> Okay, a five. Okay. While I have the chart open, I'm going to just go through what else I see, so I know the full picture. Lisinopril. Atorvastatin. Metformin. Furosemide.
Caller -> Yeah, he takes those. In the morning. All together. He doesn't have any problems with them.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Those are his regular morning ones.
Nurse -> Dad, can you hear me? No? Okay.
Caller -> Dad! Dad, turn the TV down, I'm on with the nurse! Sorry. He's watching his show and he can't hear anything.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine. What's he watching?
Caller -> Some baking competition. He doesn't bake. He just likes to yell at the TV when somebody's cake falls.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best. My husband does the same thing with the cooking shows.
Caller -> It's the highlight of his week, honestly. Okay.
Nurse -> How's the physical therapy going, since the surgery?
Caller -> He did two sessions last week. The therapist, Kelly, is great. She's got him doing leg lifts and walking with the walker. But then she leaves and he just sits.
Nurse -> That's very common. The home exercises make a big difference. Does she give him a sheet?
Caller -> Yes, it's on the fridge. He does maybe half of it. Or none of it, if I'm not here to nag him.
Nurse -> Ha. Nagging is part of the job. Could you nag him a little more? Even five minutes, a couple of times a day.
Caller -> I'll set an alarm on my phone. I'll call him from work.
Nurse -> That's smart. Movement helps the bowels, the back, and the sleep.
Caller -> Everything. I know. And honestly, the dog helps. Biscuit. He has to let him out, so that's a few trips to the door a day.
Nurse -> Oh, that's great. What kind of dog?
Caller -> A beagle mix. Eleven years old. They're a pair, the two of them.
Nurse -> Aw. A walking buddy. Even short trips to the yard count.
Caller -> Yes. Okay. I'll count the dog trips.
Nurse -> Alright. Back to the bowels. Has he been walking?
Caller -> Not much. He's mostly in the recliner. Since the surgery he's been pretty stiff, and he's scared to move around too much.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he drinking enough water?
Caller -> I don't think so. He drinks coffee, mostly. Like four cups a day. And some juice.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something we can work on.
Caller -> Yeah. He's stubborn. He won't drink water. He says it tastes like nothing.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people say that. Maybe add a squeeze of lemon, or some flavor.
Caller -> I'll try that.
Nurse -> Okay. So here's what I'd like him to do for the constipation tonight. Take two senna tablets at bedtime. I see he has it on his list, as needed.
Caller -> Okay. Two senna tablets at bedtime. We have that. It's in the cabinet.
Nurse -> And keep taking the stool softener he's already on, twice a day.
Caller -> Okay. The doc you sate. Yes.
Nurse -> And during the day, more fluids. Prune juice is great. Some fiber, fruit, oatmeal. And short walks, a few times a day. Even just to the kitchen and back.
Caller -> Okay. Prune juice. We have some. We'll do walks.
Nurse -> Right. And if he starts throwing up, or his belly gets hard or swollen, or he has severe pain, or he hasn't had a bowel movement within twenty four hours after the senna, call us.
Caller -> Okay. Throwing up, swollen belly, severe pain, no movement in twenty four hours. Got it.
Nurse -> Now. The sleep.
Caller -> Yeah. He's up until three. Like, every night this week.
Caller -> I think it's the pain. And maybe he naps too much in the afternoon.
Nurse -> Possibly. Does he drink coffee late in the day?
Nurse -> I'd say the last cup is around four or five.
Caller -> Oh. It's the last cup around four or five, yeah. I answered like, wait. I think it got switched. Sorry, I'm the caller. Yeah, four or five.
Nurse -> Okay. Ha. No problem, I understand. So four or five o'clock is too late. Try to have the last coffee by noon.
Caller -> By noon. He's going to hate that.
Nurse -> I know. Maybe decaf in the afternoon. And dim the lights in the evening, turn off the TV an hour before bed, and no screens.
Caller -> He'll fight me on the TV.
Nurse -> Maybe the baking show can be the wind down. But low volume.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm going to send a message to his doctor about the constipation and the sleep, so they know.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll send a nurse out tomorrow to see him, and check how the bowels are doing, and his pain.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time?
Nurse -> In the afternoon, probably. She'll call you before she comes.
Caller -> Okay. I'll make sure Dad's up. And I'll be there too. I work from home on Wednesdays.
Nurse -> Perfect. And how are you holding up, Brandon? You sound tired.
Caller -> I'm okay. I just do a lot. Work, and then him, and my own kids. But my wife helps.
Nurse -> It's a lot. Make sure you take care of you, too.
Caller -> Thanks. I'm trying. My daughter has a recital next week and I really don't want to miss it.
Nurse -> Oh, what does she play?
Caller -> The cello. She's nine. She's still at the screeching stage, but she's proud of it.
Nurse -> Ha. The screeching stage is the best stage. Don't miss it.
Caller -> I won't. My dad's coming, too. He wouldn't miss it, even with his back.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. That gives him something to work toward.
Caller -> Exactly. That's my motivation speech for him.
Nurse -> Anything else I can help you with tonight, Brandon?
Caller -> No. I think that's everything. Oh, wait. Is it okay if he takes the tramadol with the senna?
Nurse -> Yes. They're fine together. The senna helps the constipation from the tramadol.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I wanted to ask. Thanks, Rhonda.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Have a good night.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Hi, Joanne. It's Raymond. I'm calling about my dad. Lionel Achebe.

Nurse -> Okay. And I have seven seven three, five five five, zero one three two for you. Still good?
Caller -> Yes, that's me.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> So, it's a medication thing. My dad took his metoprolol twice this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Twice. Tell me how that happened.
Caller -> He took it at seven, with his breakfast. Like he does. And then at nine, he took it again. He totally forgot he'd taken it.
Nurse -> Okay. And how much is the dose?
Caller -> Twenty five milligrams. It's twice a day, normally. So he's had his morning one, and then another.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's had fifty milligrams in two hours. How's he feeling?
Caller -> He says he's a little dizzy. Kind of lightheaded. It started around ten, I think.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he passed out, or almost passed out?
Caller -> No. No, he hasn't passed out.
Nurse -> Any chest pain, or trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. None of that.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff there?
Caller -> Yes. We have it. Hang on.
Caller -> Okay. It's, it says one oh four over sixty two.
Nurse -> Okay. And a pulse?
Caller -> The pulse is fifty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Fifty eight. That's lower than I'd like. That's the metoprolol working, it slows the heart. Where is he right now?
Caller -> He's in the kitchen. He's sitting at the table.
Nurse -> Okay. I want him to lie down, or at least sit in a good chair, and take it easy. Not walk around alone. If he gets up, he should get up slowly.
Caller -> Okay. I'll get him to the couch.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call doctor right now. I've already paged her actually, while we were talking. She'll call us back.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Don't give him any more metoprolol today, not the evening dose, not until the doctor tells you what to do.
Caller -> Okay. No more metoprolol. Got it.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in fifteen minutes either way, to see how he's doing.
Caller -> Okay. Fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> Check his pulse and blood pressure every thirty minutes, and write them down so we have the numbers.
Caller -> Yeah. I'll write them on the pad.
Nurse -> If he faints, or has chest pain, or trouble breathing, or the pulse goes under fifty, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for us.
Caller -> Under fifty. Okay.
Nurse -> Raymond, how is he with his pills usually? Does he manage them himself?
Caller -> Yeah, he does his own. He's very stubborn about it. But he's been forgetting more lately. Like last week he missed his water pill.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful to know. A pill organizer with the days on it can help a lot. And a little log where he checks off each dose.
Caller -> I have one of those organizers in my car, actually. I got it for him a month ago and he said he didn't need it.
Nurse -> Ha. Maybe he needs it now. Put it on the table where he can't miss it.
Caller -> Yeah. I'll bring it in right now.
Caller -> I work nights, so I'm not here in the mornings. My sister Ngozi checks in on him, but she had a double shift today.
Nurse -> So he's alone a lot of the morning.
Caller -> A little. Mostly in the mornings. He doesn't like anybody hovering over him, you know? He's a proud man.
Nurse -> I understand. Would it help if one of our aides came in a couple of mornings a week? Even just to set out his pills and make sure he eats.
Caller -> Honestly, yes. He'd complain, but I think it would really help.
Nurse -> I'll ask our scheduler to look at that and give you a call. I can't promise the timing, but I'll put the request in today.
Caller -> Okay. That's great. Thank you.
Nurse -> Is there anything else going on with him, besides the forgetting? His appetite, or sleep?
Caller -> He's eating okay. He's sleeping okay. It's just the memory.
Nurse -> Okay, good. I'll let the doctor know that, too.
Nurse -> And I'll mention the forgetfulness to the doctor when she calls. They may want to look at how he's managing at home.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I really appreciate it.
Nurse -> Of course. Talk to you in fifteen.
Caller -> Joanne, thank you. I panicked a little when I saw the two pill bottles on the table and he didn't remember. I'm glad I called right away.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing, Raymond. Calling right away is always the right move with a medicine mix-up.
Caller -> Okay. I'll go sit with him. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

Caller -> Okay. I will.

Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, um, hi. I need help with a medicine. It's my grandpa.
Nurse -> Okay. What's his name?
Caller -> Cornelius Bell.
Nurse -> And his date of birth?
Caller -> December first. Nineteen thirty three.
Nurse -> Okay. And who am I speaking with?
Caller -> I'm Keisha. I'm his granddaughter. I'm staying the night with him.
Nurse -> Okay, Keisha. A good number for you?
Caller -> Three one three. Five five five. Oh one three four.
Nurse -> Three one three, five five five, zero one three four. Got it.
Caller -> Mhm.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> So what's going on tonight?
Caller -> Okay, so, he's moaning. Kind of moaning. And I think he's in pain.
Caller -> I'd say maybe a six? I don't, I don't really know how to tell.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he able to tell you?
Caller -> No, he's mostly sleeping. He woke up for a second and he just kind of frowned.
Nurse -> Okay. What's he got for pain?
Caller -> The, um, the morphine. The liquid one. In the little brown bottle.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you read me the label?
Caller -> Okay. Hang on. It says, morphine sulfate. Oral solution. And then it says, twenty milligrams per, and then it's torn.
Nurse -> Torn?
Caller -> Yeah. The label's ripped right there. It was in the kit and the box got wet, I think. So I can't see the rest.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anything else on the box, or a pharmacy sticker?
Caller -> I'm looking. The box is, it's all soggy. There's a sticker but it's smeared. I can't read it.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you know how much the nurse told you to give him?
Caller -> The aide said, um, half a milliliter. Half a mil. But I'm not sure. I wasn't there when she said it.
Nurse -> Okay. So you've got a torn label, and you're not certain of the dose.
Caller -> Right. Right. And I don't want to give him too much. But I don't want him hurting.
Nurse -> I completely understand. And I'm glad you called. Here's the thing. I'm trying to pull up his medication list, but our system is running slow tonight.
Caller -> Oh no.
Nurse -> It's okay. I'm going to call our pharmacist on call to verify exactly what's on that bottle. I want to be one hundred percent sure before I tell you to give anything.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> So please don't give him the morphine yet. Hold off until I call you back.
Caller -> But he's in pain.
Nurse -> I know. It shouldn't be long. I'll call you back in ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, can you reposition him? Maybe a pillow under his knees, or turn him a little. And loosen the blanket if he's hot.
Caller -> Okay. I can do that.
Nurse -> And hold his hand, talk to him quietly. A lot of times that helps.
Caller -> Okay. I'm doing that now. He's, he's holding my hand.
Nurse -> That's good. That's really good.
Caller -> He was a city bus driver for thirty four years. Route nineteen. He still hums when he's comfortable.
Nurse -> Oh, I love that. Does he hum now?
Caller -> A little, earlier tonight. That's how I knew he was okay. And then the moaning started.
Nurse -> That's helpful to know. When he's comfortable, we'll hope to hear the humming again.
Caller -> Yeah. I hope so. He's got a great voice.
Nurse -> I bet he does.
Caller -> Mhm.
Caller -> He used to sing in the church choir, too. My grandma always said that's why she married him.
Nurse -> That's a lovely story. I hope he'll be humming again soon.
Caller -> Is it okay if I ask something else?
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> He's been having trouble with his pills. The last couple of days. He coughs when he swallows them. Like, he chokes.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pills is he taking?
Caller -> I don't know. Several. I just know he coughs.
Nurse -> Okay. That's an important thing to tell us. When the nurse comes, she'll look at which pills can be stopped or switched to liquid. For tonight, don't force any pills.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> In general, when the label isn't clear, don't guess the concentration. Keep the bottle and the box together, and read the pharmacy sticker. That's the safest way.
Caller -> I'll keep it all together. I'm going to take a picture of the sticker, too. Maybe the camera can read it better.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Send it to us, or read it to me when I call.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try.
Nurse -> If he starts groaning more, or grimacing, or his breathing gets noisy or fast, call me right away, even before the ten minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Alright. Talk to you in a few minutes, Keisha.
Caller -> Thank you so much, Carla.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Tom, hi. This is Eduardo Soto. My wife, Margarita.
Nurse -> Hi, Eduardo. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty fifth, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> Okay. And I have nine five six, five five five, zero one three five for you.
Caller -> Yeah, that's the house.
Nurse -> Alright. What's going on?
Caller -> Her patch fell off. The pain patch. In the shower this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Which patch is it?
Caller -> The fentanyl. The twenty five. Twenty five micrograms.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you put that one on?
Caller -> Sunday morning. So, three days ago.
Nurse -> Okay. So she's due to change it today anyway. Where's the patch now?
Caller -> It was in the tub. When she got out, it was in the tub, stuck to the side.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't put that one back on. Once it's come off, you can't reuse it.
Caller -> Yeah, I figured. It's all wet anyway.
Nurse -> Right. How many new patches do you have?
Caller -> Three. I have three left in the box.
Nurse -> Okay, good. So, put a new fentanyl patch on her now. Clean, dry skin, upper back or chest, somewhere with no hair. Press it down with your hand for thirty seconds.
Caller -> Thirty seconds. Okay.
Caller -> Do I write on it?
Nurse -> Yes. Write the date and the time right on the patch. And that's the new change day, seventy two hours from now.
Caller -> Okay. So that'd be Friday.
Nurse -> Right. I've got the chart open, I'll note the new change day right now.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And fold the old patch in half, sticky sides together, and dispose of it the way the hospice nurse showed you. Keep it where the dog can't get it.
Caller -> We don't have a dog. But yes. I'll throw it out.
Nurse -> How's her pain right now?
Caller -> It's not bad. She says a three. Mostly because it's been three days.
Nurse -> Okay. It might creep up a little until the new patch starts working. If she needs it, she can have her as needed medicine too.
Caller -> Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> And if she gets very sleepy, hard to wake, or her breathing gets slow, call us right away. If you can't wake her, nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Tom.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. This is Esther Park. I'm calling about my dad, Wendell.
Nurse -> Hi, Esther. Can you spell his last name?
Caller -> P A R K. Park. Like the park.
Nurse -> And his date of birth?
Caller -> January fourteenth, nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> Okay. And your phone number, Esther?
Caller -> Eight one three, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Okay, eight one three, five five five, zero one five two.
Caller -> Yes. That's me.
Nurse -> Thank you. And you said you drove in to see him? From where?
Caller -> From Orlando. It's about three hours on a good day. I try to come every other weekend, but work has been crazy.
Nurse -> It's great that you make the trip. A lot of folks can't.
Caller -> I feel guilty that I'm not closer. That's partly why this bothers me.
Nurse -> You caught it, that's what matters. What's going on with your dad?
Caller -> So, I came to visit him this weekend. I live about three hours away. And I found out something that's really bothering me.
Caller -> He stopped taking his lisinopril and his metformin. His blood pressure pill and his diabetes pill. About two weeks ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Two weeks. Did he tell you why?
Caller -> He said he felt fine. And that he's tired of taking so many pills. He takes like eight a day. He said, why do I need all this, I feel great.
Caller -> He lives alone, so nobody was checking.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very common, Esther, and I'm glad you caught it. Let me pull up his chart so I can see what he's supposed to be taking.
Caller -> Sure. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. So I'm seeing lisinopril, twenty milligrams, once a day. Metformin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day. Is that what he stopped?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Those two. The twenty and the five hundred.
Nurse -> Okay. And I also see amlodipine, five milligrams, once a day. Atorvastatin. And a baby aspirin.
Caller -> He's still taking the amlodipine. I counted the pills. That one is going down. The other ones are just sitting there.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And the atorvastatin and the aspirin?
Caller -> I think so. They're in the little organizer. I didn't check those, I was focused on the other two.
Nurse -> That's fine. Okay. Do you have any numbers? A blood sugar, or a blood pressure?
Caller -> I do. Well, he has a meter. I checked it this morning, before breakfast. It was two forty.
Nurse -> Okay. Two forty, fasting. And a blood pressure?
Caller -> We went to the pharmacy yesterday and used the machine. It was one sixty eight over ninety four.
Nurse -> Okay. One sixty eight over ninety four. Those are both higher than I'd like.
Caller -> I figured. That's why I'm calling.
Nurse -> Is he having any symptoms? Headache, chest pain, vision changes?
Caller -> No. No headache, no chest pain. His vision's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Any extra thirst, or going to the bathroom a lot?
Caller -> Yeah. That I noticed. He's been drinking a lot of water. And he's up in the night to go. He said it's been about a week.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits with the higher sugar. Okay.
Caller -> Dad, I'm on the phone with the nurse. Hang on. He's asking me what I'm telling you. He's not happy.
Nurse -> Ha. That's okay. Is he nearby?
Caller -> He's in the garden. He's been out there since breakfast. He grows tomatoes. He's got like forty plants.
Nurse -> Forty tomato plants! That's a lot.
Caller -> Right? He gives them away to the whole neighborhood. It's his thing. He says it keeps him alive.
Nurse -> It sounds like he's very active. That's a good thing.
Caller -> He is. He's stubborn, but he's active. He walks the dog every morning.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Okay. Esther, here's what I'm going to do. First, I'm going to document all of this in his chart, right now. I've started a note.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to send a message to his primary care doctor today, about the stopped medications, and those numbers. They'll decide how to restart things safely.
Caller -> Okay. Should he just start taking them again?
Nurse -> Not on his own. I'd rather he not restart the lisinopril and metformin until the doctor tells us how. Sometimes restarting at the full dose after a break isn't the right move.
Caller -> Okay. So just wait.
Nurse -> Just wait for the doctor's guidance. It shouldn't be long. I'll call you back this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. I'll be here until five. Then I have to drive home.
Nurse -> That works. I'll call before then.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, have him check his sugar every morning and evening, and his blood pressure once a day, and write the numbers down.
Caller -> I'll set it up for him. He has a little notebook. I'll put it next to the meter.
Nurse -> Perfect. And encourage water, no sweet drinks and no juice, and regular meals.
Caller -> He drinks sweet tea. All day. I'll swap it out.
Nurse -> Ha. Good luck with that.
Caller -> I know. That's going to be a fight.
Caller -> Should I take him to the doctor, like tomorrow? Or is that overkill?
Nurse -> Not overkill at all. I'll ask the doctor's office to get him in this week, since his numbers are up and the medicines have been off for two weeks. I'll put that in my message.
Caller -> Oh good. Because he won't go on his own.
Nurse -> If the office calls him, they'll probably call you too, if I note you as the contact. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Please. Put me down.
Nurse -> Done. I'll note it.
Caller -> Thank you. And, can I ask, is there anyone who could check on him more often? Like a nurse, or an aide?
Nurse -> We do have a nurse who visits him. She's due this Thursday. I can ask her to do a medication check and set up the organizer with him, so it's easier for him.
Caller -> That would be a huge help. He listens to her more than he listens to me.
Nurse -> Ha. That happens. I'll make sure she knows.
Caller -> And the neighbor, Mrs. Alvarez, she checks on him in the afternoons. I'll let her know to watch out for things.
Nurse -> That's great. A neighbor who checks in is gold.
Nurse -> Call us if his sugar goes over three hundred, or he's throwing up, or he's confused, or the blood pressure is over one eighty, or he gets a bad headache.
Caller -> Over three hundred. Over one eighty. Okay.
Nurse -> And if he has chest pain, or weakness on one side, or trouble talking, that's nine one one.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> I'd also like to talk to him, if he's willing. Just a quick word. Is that okay?
Caller -> Let me see. He's coming in. Dad, the nurse wants to talk. Dad. Okay. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> He says he doesn't want to talk. He says he's fine.
Nurse -> That's alright. Please tell him that I said it's his choice, but that it's important to take the medicines the doctor ordered, and never stop them without talking to us first.
Caller -> I'll tell him. He'll listen to me, eventually.
Nurse -> I'm sure he will. He raised you. Ha.
Caller -> Ha. That's what I tell him.
Nurse -> Anything else I can help with, Esther?
Caller -> No, that's it. Thank you so much, Rhonda. I really appreciate you taking this seriously.
Nurse -> Of course. It's what we're here for. I'll call you this afternoon.
Caller -> He'll probably try to give your nurse a bag of tomatoes on Thursday. He does that to everyone.
Nurse -> Ha. We're not allowed to accept gifts, but I'll let her know it's coming.
Caller -> He'll insist. You'll see.
Nurse -> I believe it. Take care, Esther.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.

Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth. It's Colin Fraser. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Colin. Your date of birth?
Caller -> August twelfth, nineteen eighty one.
Nurse -> Okay. And I've got six oh two, five five five, zero one three six for you.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> It's pretty early. What's going on?
Caller -> I can't sleep. I haven't been able to sleep, I don't know, maybe three weeks? Something like that.
Caller -> I'm up until like three or four in the morning. Every night.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you in pain, is that what's keeping you up?
Caller -> No, no, the pain's fine. It's not that.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you tried anything?
Caller -> I took the melatonin. Three milligrams. It didn't do anything.
Caller -> So I was wondering if the doctor could give me something. Like a real sleeping pill.
Nurse -> Okay. I can ask. Can I ask you a couple of questions first? Just so I give them the full picture.
Caller -> Sure.
Nurse -> How's your mood been? Have you been feeling down, or hopeless?
Caller -> No. No, not at all. I'm not depressed or anything. I'm just tired.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you have any thoughts of hurting yourself?
Caller -> No. Absolutely not.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for answering. I ask everyone.
Caller -> No, that's fine. I get it.
Nurse -> So, I'll send a message to your provider about the sleeping medication. I can't promise what they'll say, but I'll ask.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back later today once I hear.
Caller -> Great.
Nurse -> Until then, don't take any over the counter sleep aids, like Benadryl, or anything with diphenhydramine in it, until the provider replies. They can interact.
Caller -> Okay. I wasn't going to. Okay.
Nurse -> And a few things that help. Same bedtime, same wake time, even on weekends. No screens for an hour before bed. No caffeine after noon. And keep the room cool and dark.
Caller -> I do look at my phone a lot. In bed.
Nurse -> That's probably part of it.
Caller -> Yeah. Okay. I'll try the no phone thing.
Nurse -> If you start feeling hopeless, or you have any thoughts of hurting yourself, or you go a few days with no sleep at all, call us. And in a crisis, you can call or text nine eight eight, or call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thanks, Beth.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Tom, it's Gerald. Gerald Fitzgerald. My wife is Opal.
Nurse -> Hi, Gerald. Opal's date of birth?
Caller -> April third, nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> And a number for you is nine oh one, five five five, zero one three eight?
Caller -> Yep, that's me.
Nurse -> What's going on this morning?
Caller -> The oxygen machine. The concentrator. It's beeping. It's been going about an hour.
Caller -> I turned it off and on, it just keeps going.
Nurse -> Okay. Is Opal okay? Is she breathing alright?
Caller -> She's fine. She's breathing fine. I put her on one of the tanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Do you have a finger oxygen meter?
Caller -> Yeah. Hang on. She's, it says ninety four.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety four. That's good. How many backup tanks do you have?
Caller -> I have, one, two. Two. The little ones.
Nurse -> Okay. And what flow is she on?
Caller -> Two liters.
Nurse -> Okay. So here's what I'll do. I'm placing an order for more tanks right now. I've got the form open.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Done. I've ordered the tanks. They'll deliver them this morning.
Caller -> Oh good. That was fast.
