Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi, Marcus. This is Natalia Voss. V O S S. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Natalia. Your date of birth?
Caller -> November thirtieth, nineteen seventy six.
Nurse -> Okay. And I have seven two oh, five five five, zero one four oh for you. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What do you need today?
Caller -> Two things. First, I'm almost out of dressings. For my incision.
Caller -> I have two left. The foam ones. I change them every three days, so that's like six days. But I would feel better with more.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. I'll order those for you. How's the incision looking?
Caller -> It's okay. There's a little drainage. It's clear. A small amount on the dressing when I take it off.
Nurse -> Okay. Any redness around it? Does it feel warm?
Caller -> No. No redness, and it doesn't feel warm.
Nurse -> Any fever?
Caller -> No. I took my temperature this morning. It was ninety eight point two.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all reassuring. Let me get the order in. Foam dressings, the same size you've been using?
Caller -> Yes. The four by four.
Nurse -> Okay. One moment. Alright. I've put the order in now. They'll deliver tomorrow.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And the wound nurse is scheduled to see you Friday morning, to change the dressing and look at everything.
Caller -> Okay. Friday. Good.
Nurse -> You said two things. What's the other one?
Caller -> Oh. This is kind of embarrassing. I'm constipated. I haven't gone in two days.
Nurse -> It's not embarrassing, it's really common after surgery, especially with pain medicine. Are you in pain? Is your belly hard?
Caller -> No, my belly's okay. I just feel backed up.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have anything at home?
Caller -> The doctor sent me home with some senna. But I haven't taken any, because I didn't know if I should.
Nurse -> Yes, go ahead and take the senna. Two tablets at bedtime tonight.
Caller -> Two tablets at bedtime. Okay.
Nurse -> And drink more water than you think you need. Eat some fiber, like fruit, oatmeal, prunes. And walk a little several times a day. Walking really helps.
Caller -> I've been mostly on the couch. I'll walk more.
Nurse -> Even short walks. Around the house is fine. But no heavy lifting, remember. Nothing over ten pounds.
Caller -> I know. I haven't been lifting anything. My sister has been doing the laundry.
Nurse -> Good. How are you feeling overall? Energy, appetite?
Caller -> Pretty good, actually. I've been eating okay. My appetite is back.
Nurse -> That's great. That's a good sign.
Caller -> I have a question about showering. Can I get the dressing wet?
Nurse -> Foam dressings are usually okay in a quick shower, but don't let the water hit it directly. If it does get soaked, change it right away.
Caller -> Okay. So quick showers, with my back to the water.
Nurse -> Exactly. And no baths or swimming until the surgeon says so.
Caller -> My surgeon said six weeks. I haven't been in the pool since.
Nurse -> Right, so you're following that. When's your follow up with the surgeon?
Caller -> Next Wednesday. My sister is driving me.
Nurse -> Good. Bring a list of questions, and mention the constipation if it hasn't resolved.
Caller -> I will. I'm writing everything down in a notebook.
Caller -> Oh, can I drive yet?
Nurse -> Not while you're taking pain medicine, and not until your surgeon clears you. You need to be able to slam on the brakes if you have to.
Caller -> Makes sense. I'm not ready anyway.
Nurse -> Is somebody staying with you at night, in case you need anything?
Caller -> My sister sleeps over most nights. And my neighbor checks on me in the morning. I'm really lucky.
Nurse -> You are. That kind of support makes a big difference when you're healing.
Caller -> I know. I made her a big pot of soup yesterday, well, I supervised. She did the lifting.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the right way to do it.
Caller -> Yeah. I just want to be sure I'm doing this right.
Nurse -> You're doing great. When you change the dressing, wash your hands first, and change it sooner if it gets soaked or starts peeling. Keep the area dry.
Caller -> Okay. Wash hands, and change it if it's soaked.
Nurse -> Right. And if you see redness, or it feels warm, or you notice pus, or a bad smell, or any bleeding, or you get a fever of one hundred point four or higher, call us right away.
Caller -> Okay. Redness, warmth, pus, smell, bleeding, fever. I'll write it on the fridge.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Anything else, Natalia?
Caller -> No. That's everything. Thank you so much, Marcus.
Nurse -> You're welcome. See you Friday, well, the wound nurse will.
Caller -> Ha. Right. Thank you. Bye.

Caller -> Hey. Hi. My name is Tyler. I'm calling about my grandma. Ruth Abernathy.
Nurse -> Hi, Tyler. And Ruth's date of birth?
Caller -> September twenty first, nineteen forty four. No, forty five. Nineteen forty five.
Nurse -> Forty five. Okay. And a number for you?
Caller -> Five one two, five five five, zero one four one.
Nurse -> Got it. What can I help with?
Caller -> We're running out of her briefs. And the pads, the underpads. We have about a day's worth.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me put that in. Is there anything else you need?
Caller -> Um, no. Just those. Oh, and, there's one other thing. Is this okay to ask now?
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> I noticed a red spot on her, um, her tailbone. When I was changing her.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has it been there?

Nurse -> Okay. Is the skin open at all? Is there a sore or any drainage?

Nurse -> Okay. So here's what I'm going to do. I'll order the briefs and underpads for you. You'll have them tomorrow.

Caller -> No rubbing. Every two hours. We have barrier cream. Okay.

Caller -> Okay. I will.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, hello? Is this the home health?
Nurse -> It is. This is Rhonda. How can I help you?
Caller -> Oh, thank goodness. I've been on hold, I think. Or I got transferred. I've been trying to reach somebody all afternoon.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about that. I'm here now. Who am I speaking with?
Caller -> My name's Patsy. Patsy Dunleavy. I'm his neighbor. I live next door to Clarence.
Nurse -> Okay, Patsy. What's Clarence's last name?
Caller -> Whitmore. Clarence Whitmore.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you know his date of birth?
Caller -> I do, actually. I wrote it down. Hang on. October thirtieth, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Thank you. And can I get a number for you, Patsy?
Caller -> Oh, I'm at his house. I'm on his landline. You'll have that number, it's right on his chart. I don't want to give you mine, I'm hopeless with my cell, it never has a signal in his kitchen.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'll use the number on file.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> So what's going on?
Caller -> Well, the bed never came. The hospital bed. They told us yesterday between one and five. And I sat here all day. Nobody came. Nobody called.
Caller -> And he still needs the commode. The one next to the bed. We haven't gotten that either.
Nurse -> Okay. So the bed and the commode.
Caller -> Right. And he's been sleeping in his chair. In the recliner. For three nights.
Nurse -> Okay. Why is he in the recliner, not his own bed?
Caller -> His bed is too low. And it hurts his hip to get up. He just can't do it. So he just sleeps in the chair.
Nurse -> Okay. Which hip?
Caller -> The right one, I think. Right.
Nurse -> And how bad is the pain?
Caller -> He says it's, I don't know, maybe a four? When he gets up. Otherwise he says it's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he fallen?
Caller -> Well. Last week. He slid off the couch. Onto the floor.
Nurse -> Okay. Was he hurt?
Caller -> No. No, he wasn't hurt. He said he was fine. I got him up. I called my husband to come help, and between us, we got him up.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that he wasn't hurt. And you didn't call us at the time?
Caller -> No. I didn't think to. I didn't want to bother anybody.
Nurse -> Please don't ever hesitate to call about a fall, Patsy. Even if no one's hurt.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> No, no apology needed. I'm glad you're calling now.
Caller -> Thank you. It's just, I'm trying to help, but I'm not family. His daughter's in Arizona and his son's in Germany. They're doing what they can on the phone.
Nurse -> It sounds like you're doing a lot.
Caller -> I'm trying. He's a sweetheart. He fixed my fence last spring. Wouldn't take a dime.
Nurse -> Aw. That's how neighbors should be.
Caller -> My husband says the same. He's always talking about how Clarence taught him how to prune the roses.
Nurse -> Ha. A good neighbor and a gardener.
Caller -> Oh yes. His roses are the best on the street. Prize winners, I'd say. He won a ribbon at the county fair three years in a row.
Nurse -> Three years in a row! That's impressive.
Caller -> He had a rose named after his late wife. A pink one. Every June it blooms and he just sits and looks at it.
Nurse -> That's so sweet.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Okay. Let me look at the equipment orders. Hold on a moment.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time.
Caller -> Oh, hello! Sorry, my husband's at the door. He's got a casserole for Clarence. Yes, honey, in the kitchen. Sorry.
Nurse -> Ha. No problem. Okay, I'm seeing the hospital bed order. It shows it was scheduled for yesterday, and it was marked as "not delivered, customer unavailable."
Caller -> Unavailable! I was here all day. I never left the house. I even skipped my bridge game.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's frustrating. That must be a mistake by the company.
Caller -> I'd say so.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to call the equipment company myself, and see about rescheduling the bed. I'll try for tomorrow.
Caller -> Oh, that would be wonderful. Thank you.
Nurse -> And the commode, I'm seeing it wasn't ordered. It looks like it was never put in.
Caller -> Oh no. That's why.
Nurse -> Let me fix that now. I'm placing the order for the commode right now. Okay. I've just submitted it. They'll deliver it tomorrow, too.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Thank you so much. I thought maybe I was losing my mind.
Nurse -> No, no. It was just a missed step on our end. I'm sorry.
Caller -> That's okay. It happens.
Nurse -> In the meantime, what is he using at night, for the bathroom?
Caller -> He gets up and goes to the bathroom. With the walker. It's about twelve steps. And, well. Sometimes he uses a bucket. A bucket we put next to the chair.
Nurse -> Okay. I understand. For now, make sure he always uses the walker when he stands, even for a few steps. And have the floor clear, no rugs, no cords.
Caller -> I took the rug out last week. After the fall.
Nurse -> Good. And if you can, have someone nearby when he gets up at night.
Caller -> My husband is going to sleep on the couch tonight. We discussed it.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Thank you both.
Caller -> It's no trouble. Honestly.
Nurse -> Patsy, who's helping him with meals?
Caller -> Meals on Wheels brings his lunch at noon, and I bring dinner. Or the church ladies do. We have a schedule on the fridge.
Nurse -> That's a good system. And is he eating okay?
Caller -> Pretty well. He cleans his plate, mostly. He's lost a bit of weight, but he says that's from the hip.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll mention that to the nurse who sees him.
Caller -> His daughter calls every evening, around six her time. That's nine here. She asks me to put the phone on speaker so he can't hang up on her.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like a daughter.
Caller -> And his son calls on Sundays. The time difference is hard. He's in Munich, so it's the middle of the night for one of them.
Nurse -> That's tough. At least they're checking in.
Caller -> They are. They're good kids. They'd come if they could. They've both asked about flying in.
Nurse -> When the commode comes, put it right next to his chair, with the brakes locked, and raise the seat so it's easier to stand.
Caller -> Raise the seat. Okay. Brakes on. Got it.
Nurse -> And I'd like our physical therapist to take a look at his home. The bed height, the chair, the walker. She can help prevent another fall. I'll send her a message today.
Caller -> That would be so helpful.
Nurse -> I'll also call Clarence directly at his number on file, within the hour, to give you both an update about the bed and the commode.
Caller -> Oh, perfect. I'll stay here until you call. I'll make some coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. Don't stay if you have other things to do. I'll leave a message if he doesn't pick up.
Caller -> No, no. I'll be here. Clarence is in his chair. He'll be glad to hear from you.
Nurse -> If he has another fall, or the hip pain gets worse, or he has trouble standing, or he seems confused, call us right away. And if he ever hits his head or can't get up, call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine one one if he hits his head. Okay. I'll tell my husband too.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else, Patsy?
Caller -> No, I think that's it. You've been very kind.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Thank you for looking out for him.
Caller -> He'd do the same for me. Thank you, Rhonda.
Nurse -> One last thing. When the delivery people come, they'll need to bring the bed into the bedroom and take the old one apart. Is there a clear path through the hall?
Caller -> I think so. There's a little table I can move. And the dog bed. Clarence doesn't have a dog, it's mine. I was bringing her over to keep him company.
Nurse -> Ha. That's sweet. Just move the table and the dog bed, and it should be fine.
Caller -> I will. Her name's Biscuit. She's a terrible watchdog.
Nurse -> Take care, Patsy. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye now.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Ana, hi. It's Wen. I'm calling about my daughter. Mei Lin.
Nurse -> Hi, Wen. Can you spell the name for me?
Caller -> M E I, space, L I N. Chen, C H E N.
Nurse -> Mei Lin Chen. And her date of birth?
Caller -> May nineteenth, twenty twenty three.
Nurse -> Okay. And your number, Wen? Is it six five oh, five five five, zero one four eight?
Caller -> Yes. Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> She's been throwing up. Since this morning, since like six. Six times. Maybe seven.
Caller -> And she can't, she can't keep anything down. Even water.
Nurse -> Okay. Even sips of water?
Caller -> I gave her a few sips about an hour ago and she threw it up in like ten minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. How many wet diapers has she had today?
Caller -> One. Just one. Since last night. That's twelve hours.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake? How is she acting?
Caller -> She's, she's sleepy. More than normal. She wakes up when I call her, but she just wants to lie down.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a fever?
Caller -> A little. I just took it. A hundred point two.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she vomited any blood, or anything green?
Caller -> No. No blood. No green. It's just whatever she drinks. And she has no diarrhea.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you, Wen. I'm glad you called. Let me tell you what I think.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> A three year old who's vomited six or seven times, can't keep fluids down, and has had one wet diaper in twelve hours is at risk of getting dehydrated. And she's sleepier than usual. I'd like you to take her to the emergency room now.
Caller -> Now? Like, tonight?
Nurse -> Yes. Tonight. Now. She needs to be checked and probably have some fluids.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I was afraid you'd say that. I just didn't want to overreact.
Nurse -> You're not overreacting. It's the right call. Do you have a car and someone who can drive, so you can sit with her in the back?
Caller -> My husband is home. He can drive.
Nurse -> Good. In the car seat, if she's sleepy, keep an eye on her. If she vomits, turn her head to the side.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> On the way, you can offer her one teaspoon of fluid every few minutes. Pedialyte, or water. Just a teaspoon. Don't force it.
Caller -> A teaspoon. Okay.
Nurse -> And bring her medicine list, a diaper if she has one, and if you can, a little of what she's vomited, in a bag. They sometimes want to see it.
Caller -> Okay. I'll bring the medicine list.
Nurse -> Before you go, I need a few things for the ER. Does she have any allergies?
Caller -> No allergies. Just the stuff with her swallowing, which they know about.
Nurse -> Okay. And what medicines does she take?
Caller -> A daily vitamin and a reflux medicine. I gave the vitamin this morning. She threw up the reflux one right away, so I don't think she got it.
Nurse -> Okay. When was the last time she ate anything?
Caller -> Dinner last night. Some rice and chicken. She wouldn't eat breakfast.
Nurse -> Okay. Has anyone else at home been sick?
Caller -> My son had a stomach bug last week. He's six. He was throwing up for a day and then he was fine.
Nurse -> That could be the same bug. Has she been around anyone else?
Caller -> Daycare, Monday and Tuesday. Maybe somebody there was sick.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the ER know about the exposure, too.
Caller -> I'm really nervous. She's never been to the ER.
Nurse -> It's okay to be nervous. They'll see her quickly because she's so little and sleepy. Tell the front desk right away that she's vomiting, dehydrated, and sleepier than usual.
Caller -> Vomiting, dehydrated, sleepy. Okay. I'll say it.
Nurse -> And bring her favorite blanket or toy. It helps a lot when they're scared.
Caller -> She has a stuffed rabbit. She won't go anywhere without it. I'll grab it.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a phone charger for you, because ER waits can be long.
Caller -> Good point. My husband will bring the charger.
Nurse -> Does she have a car seat ready?
Caller -> Yes. It's already in the car. We came back from daycare in it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Which hospital will you go to?
Caller -> The children's one. Mercy Children's.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to call the emergency room ahead of you, so they know she's coming.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That helps.
Nurse -> If she gets hard to wake up, or limp, or has a seizure, or turns blue or gray, don't drive. Call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hard to wake, limp. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow morning to see how she's doing.
Caller -> Thank you so much, Ana.
Nurse -> Go. Get her to the ER. Take care.

Caller -> Marcus, I need help. It's Janelle. It's my mom, Odessa Marlowe.

Nurse -> And your number, is it four seven oh, five five five, zero one four three?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's me.
Nurse -> What's going on?
Caller -> I think my mom took too many of her hydromorphone pills.
Nurse -> Okay. How many do you think she took?
Caller -> I don't know exactly. I counted what's left in the bottle and I think she took about four. In the last two hours.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's the strength of the tablet?
Caller -> Two milligrams. The two milligram ones.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's she supposed to take?
Caller -> One. One every four hours, if she needs it. She did it herself, she was in pain and I think she just kept taking them.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she right now? Is she awake?

Nurse -> Okay. Is she hard to wake up?
Caller -> No. She's sleepy, but she, she's, she answers. She's talking.
Nurse -> Okay. What does her breathing look like? Is it slow, or shallow?
Caller -> I think it's regular. It looks regular. I think. I'm not sure what slow would look like.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she throwing up?
Caller -> No, no throwing up at all.
Nurse -> Okay, Janelle. Here's what I need you to do. Stay right with her. Talk to her, keep her awake. Keep her sitting up, or on her side, not flat on her back.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Tom.
Caller -> Tom, thank God. It's Oscar Rasmussen. I'm calling about my wife, Thelma.
Nurse -> Hi, Oscar. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> December nineteenth, nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And I have two one four, five five five, zero one five four on file for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house. That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on tonight, Oscar?
Caller -> We ran out of the morphine. Yesterday. And she's in terrible pain. I've been trying to get it refilled since yesterday afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm sorry. Let's get this sorted. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> Okay. So, the bottle was almost empty. Yesterday around lunchtime. So I called the pharmacy, the one on Main. And they said, they can't refill it. They need a new prescription from the doctor.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I said, but she's on hospice. They said, it's a controlled substance. They need a new script. I said, who do I call? They said, the doctor.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you call the doctor's office?
Caller -> I did. But it was after four by then, and they were closed. I got the answering machine.
Nurse -> Okay. And you didn't call us?
Caller -> I thought the doctor's office was the right place. I didn't want to bother you. I know how busy you are.
Nurse -> Oscar, you're never bothering us. We're here twenty four hours a day, for exactly this.
Caller -> I know. I know that now. I'm sorry. I just, I wasn't thinking straight.
Nurse -> Okay. It's okay. When did she last get a dose?
Caller -> Yesterday. About three in the afternoon. I gave her the last little bit. Half a milliliter.
Nurse -> Okay. And that was the twenty milligram per milliliter?
Caller -> Yes. Twenty milligrams per milliliter. Half a milliliter, under the tongue.
Nurse -> Okay. So she's been without it for about, what, thirty one hours?
Caller -> Something like that. A day and a half, almost.
Nurse -> Okay. How's her pain right now?
Caller -> It's bad. It's a seven. She says it's a seven. She's crying. She's moaning.
Nurse -> Okay. Where does it hurt?
Caller -> Her belly. And her back. It's been getting worse since this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she throwing up?
Caller -> No. She hasn't thrown up.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had anything else for comfort?
Caller -> She has the lorazepam. I gave her one, this morning. The point five. It helped her rest a little. But it doesn't do anything for the pain.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense.
Caller -> Oscar? Oscar! Is Mom okay? Yes, honey. I'm on with the nurse. Go sit with her. Sorry. That's my daughter.
Nurse -> No problem. She's there too?
Caller -> Yes, she drove in tonight. Karen. She's sitting with her mother. She's the one who told me to call you. She said, Dad, call hospice, right now.
Nurse -> Karen sounds like a smart woman. I'm glad she's there.
Caller -> She's a nurse herself. A pediatric nurse. She's been so upset.
Nurse -> I understand. Okay, Oscar. Here's what we're going to do. I'm going to page our on-call doctor right now, for a new prescription tonight. Hold on. Okay. I've sent the page.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> And then I'm going to call our emergency pharmacy, the twenty four hour one, and have them fill it as soon as the doctor signs.
Caller -> Okay. How long will that take?
Nurse -> Usually the doctor calls back within ten or fifteen minutes. Then the pharmacy fills it, and they deliver. I'm going to ask for delivery tonight, within two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> I know that feels long when she's in pain. But that's the fastest safe way.
Caller -> I understand. It's just, it's so hard to watch.
Nurse -> I know. I know it is. I'll call you back in twenty minutes with an update.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, there are some things we can try for comfort. Can you put a pillow between her knees, and one under her back? And a warm pack on her belly, on low.
Caller -> I think we have a heating pad. Karen, get the heating pad. The one in the hall closet.
Nurse -> On low, wrapped in a towel. And a cool cloth on her forehead can feel good. And keep the room quiet.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Karen's getting it.
Nurse -> And you can give her another lorazepam, if it's been at least six hours since the last one. It won't help the pain, but it can help her feel calmer.
Caller -> It's been about, since seven this morning, so more than six. Okay. I'll give her another one.
Nurse -> Good. Give it under the tongue, like before.
Caller -> Okay. Karen has it. She's doing it now.
Nurse -> Perfect. How are you doing, Oscar? Are you holding up?
Caller -> Honestly? Not great. I haven't slept. I've been up since five. I just feel like I failed her.
Nurse -> You didn't fail her. Oscar. You did what a lot of people would do. You called the pharmacy and the doctor. The system made it hard. That's on us, not you.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot.
Nurse -> Has she been eating or drinking today?
Caller -> Just sips of water. A little ice. She didn't touch her breakfast or her dinner.
Nurse -> Okay. Is her mouth dry?
Caller -> Very. Her lips are cracked. She keeps asking for ice.
Nurse -> Ice chips are fine. And mouth swabs can help, the pink sponges, dipped in water. Does she have those?
Caller -> We have a pack. Karen, can you get the mouth swabs? She's on it. Okay.
Nurse -> And a little lip balm feels good too.
Caller -> Okay. Chapstick. We have that. I'll put some on her.
Caller -> I still don't understand why the pharmacy wouldn't give me a few days' worth, just to get us through. Nobody told me any of this.
Nurse -> Medicines like morphine can't be refilled the way other prescriptions are. The pharmacy needs a new signed prescription each time, and it's a rule they can't bend. That's why we usually send it to them ahead of time, before it runs low.
Caller -> I understand. Nobody explained that to me.
Nurse -> That's on us. I'll make sure the nurse reviews the plan with you at the next visit.
Caller -> Thank you. Karen says to tell you she's grateful. She's been the one calling around all day.
Nurse -> Tell her thank you from me. How many kids does she have?
Caller -> Two. A boy and a girl. They're with her husband tonight. They wanted to come, but it's a school night.
Nurse -> That makes sense. It's good that she has help at home.
Caller -> She does. And they call every hour to ask about their grandma. They love her so much.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. She'll feel that.
Caller -> I tell her. I say, the kids called, they love you. She squeezes my hand. I think she hears.
Nurse -> I'm sure she does. Hearing is the last sense to go. Keep talking to her.
Caller -> I will. I read her the cards the kids made. She had a pile of them on the table.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> And going forward, I want to make sure this never happens again. We'll set up automatic refills, and when you get down to three doses, you call us. Not the pharmacy. Us.
Caller -> Three doses. Okay. I'll write that on the bottle.
Nurse -> Perfect. When the morphine arrives, give her half a milliliter under the tongue, and write the time down.
Caller -> Half a milliliter. And write the time. Okay.
Nurse -> And if the pain becomes unbearable before it comes, or she's very hard to wake, or her breathing slows down, call me right away.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Do you have any questions, Oscar?
Caller -> No. Just, thank you. Thank you for taking care of this.
Nurse -> Of course. I'm going to go make the calls now. Twenty minutes.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Karen, they're getting it. Yes, tonight. Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Denise. This is Nate Szabo. I'm calling about my dad. Everett.
Nurse -> Hi, Nate. Everett's date of birth?
Caller -> August eighth, nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And your number, Nate?
Caller -> Seven one nine, five five five, zero one four four.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on tonight?
Caller -> I'm worried about him. He said something, a couple of hours ago, and it's really bothering me.
Nurse -> Okay. Take your time. What did he say?
Caller -> He said, he said I'd be better off gone. And that he doesn't want to be here anymore.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me, Nate. That sounds scary.
Caller -> It was. It is. He's never said anything like that.
Nurse -> Okay. Is your dad with you right now?
Caller -> Yes. He's in the living room. I'm in the kitchen, with the phone. I'm staying here tonight.

Nurse -> Okay. That's very good. And what about his medications, are they locked?
Caller -> No, they're just in the cabinet. I can lock them up.
Nurse -> I'd do that tonight. How has his mood been the last few days?

Caller -> Okay. Today. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm going to let our doctor know about this tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll call you back within the hour to check on how things are.

Caller -> Nine eight eight. Nine one one if he has a plan. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> You did the right thing by calling. Talk to you within the hour.
Caller -> Thank you.

transcript:
Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth. It's Rosalind Teague. I'm a patient. I'm sorry for calling so late.
Nurse -> Hi, Rosalind. Don't apologize. We're here all night. Can I get your date of birth?
Caller -> July fourth, nineteen seventy five.
Nurse -> Okay. And a number for you? I have four eight oh, five five five, zero one five five.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on tonight?
Caller -> It's my back. It's really bad tonight. I can't, I can't get comfortable. This pain is killing me.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. Tell me about the pain. How bad is it, zero to ten?
Caller -> An eight. An eight. It's been bad for months, but tonight is worse.
Nurse -> Okay. Where is it?
Caller -> Lower back. Right here. It goes down my leg sometimes.
Nurse -> Okay. What are you taking for it?
Caller -> The tramadol. The fifty milligram. Twice a day. And it isn't enough. It's not even close.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you taken extra tonight?
Caller -> No. No, I took what I'm supposed to. I took it at nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. Have you been sleeping?
Caller -> Barely. Maybe three hours a night. I just lie there.
Nurse -> That sounds exhausting.
Caller -> It is. I'm so tired, Beth. I'm so tired of this.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you. Rosalind, how has your mood been?
Caller -> Not good. Some days I feel like it's never going to get better. The pain. Like, this is just my life now.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being honest. Have you been having any thoughts of hurting yourself, or ending your life?
Caller -> Some days, I do think about ending it.
Caller -> I mean, not like, I'm not going to. Not like I have a plan. It's just a thought. It comes and goes.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That took courage. I'm really glad you did.
Caller -> I didn't mean to say it. It just came out.
Nurse -> I'm glad it did. I want to ask you a few more questions, so I can understand and help. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yeah. Okay.
Nurse -> Do you have a plan? Have you thought about how you might do it?
Caller -> No. No plan. I don't have a plan.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have any guns in the house?
Caller -> No. No guns. I've never had a gun.
Nurse -> Okay. What about your medications? Do you keep a lot of them?
Caller -> No. Just what I take. The tramadol, and my vitamin. I don't have a stockpile or anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you thinking of doing anything tonight?
Caller -> No. I'm not going to do anything tonight. I just needed to talk to somebody.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called. Who's with you tonight?
Caller -> Nobody. I live alone. My sister, Dana, she lives about fifteen minutes away.
Nurse -> Okay. Is Dana someone you trust?
Caller -> Yes. She's my best friend. She's the only one who really gets it.
Nurse -> Would it be okay if I called Dana, with your permission, and asked her to come over?
Caller -> I don't want to wake her. She has work in the morning.
Nurse -> I understand. But I think it would help to have someone with you tonight. And I think she'd want to be there. Would you let me call her?
Caller -> Okay. Yeah. Okay. You can call her. Her number is on my file.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll call her right after we talk. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Okay.
Nurse -> Rosalind, I want you to know something. What you're feeling is real, and it matters. And there are people who can help, both with the pain and with how you're feeling. You don't have to carry this alone.
Caller -> I feel like I'm a burden. To Dana. To everyone.
Nurse -> You're not a burden. You called because you're reaching out, and that's strength, not weakness.
Caller -> I haven't worked in two years. I lost my job after the accident. I used to be a physical therapist assistant. I used to help people with exactly this kind of pain.
Nurse -> Oh, Rosalind. That must feel so painful. To be on the other side of it now.
Caller -> It is. It's really hard. I just, I feel like I lost myself.
Nurse -> That makes sense. A lot of people feel that way when chronic pain changes their life. It's not a failing.
Caller -> Thank you. I haven't told anyone that.
Nurse -> Have you talked with anyone about how you've been feeling? A counselor, or your doctor?
Caller -> I saw a therapist for a while, about a year ago. Then my insurance changed and I stopped going. And I never started again.
Nurse -> Would you be open to seeing someone again?
Caller -> I think so. I think I need to. I just didn't know where to start.
Nurse -> That's exactly what our counselor can help with. She'll work with you to find the right person.
Caller -> Okay. That actually makes me feel a little hopeful.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Hold on to that little bit.
Caller -> I will. I have my cat, too. Mochi. She sleeps on my feet every night. She's the reason I get out of bed some mornings.
Nurse -> Aw. Pets can be wonderful that way. How old is Mochi?
Caller -> She's six. She was a rescue. She was scared of everything when I got her, and now she follows me around the apartment.
Nurse -> That sounds like she's been good for you.
Caller -> She has. She's my little shadow.
Nurse -> I'm glad you have her. Is there anything else that helps you on the hard days? Music, a show, a walk?
Caller -> Music, a little. I used to play guitar. I haven't picked it up since the accident. My fingers go numb.
Nurse -> That's a loss too. Maybe we can talk about it with the counselor, there might be a way to ease back into it.
Caller -> Maybe. I'd like that. I miss it.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'd like to do. First, I'm going to stay on the line with you while we figure out the next steps. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to ask our counselor to call you today. She'll call within two hours. She's wonderful, she specializes in chronic pain and mood.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds good.
Nurse -> Third, I'm going to let your provider know tonight, about the pain, and how you've been feeling. We may need to change your pain plan.
Caller -> I'd like that. I really would.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in thirty minutes to check on you, either way.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Rosalind, I want to give you a number. It's nine eight eight. It's a crisis line. You can call or text it any time, day or night. Even if you're not sure it's an emergency.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay. I know that one.
Nurse -> And if you ever have a plan, or you feel like you might act on the thoughts, or you've taken something, call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> For the pain tonight, can you put a heating pad on low on your back? Change position every half hour or so. And a warm shower might help, if you feel steady.
Caller -> I have a heating pad. I'll try that.
Nurse -> Good. And with Dana coming, ask her to stay the night.
Caller -> I will. Okay.
Nurse -> And keep your medication to just the daily amounts, nothing extra.
Caller -> I will. I only have a few days' worth anyway.
Nurse -> Perfect. And you can call us again tonight, at any time, if the thoughts get stronger, or you start to think about a plan.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> How are you feeling right now, compared to when we started talking?
Caller -> A little better. A little calmer. Just talking helped.
Nurse -> I'm glad. That matters. Okay. I'm going to call Dana now. I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Beth. I mean it.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Rosalind. You did a brave thing tonight.
Caller -> Bye.

Caller -> Priya, it's Beatriz Pereira. It's my father, Augustin. Please.
Nurse -> Hi, Beatriz. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> February second, nineteen thirty four.
Nurse -> And your number, Beatriz?
Caller -> Five oh eight, five five five, oh one four five.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's happening.
Caller -> He's working so hard to breathe. And it's making this noise, a gurgling. Like a rattle.
Caller -> It started about a half hour ago. He's been sleeping, he hasn't eaten or had anything to drink in three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he awake?
Caller -> No. He's sleeping. But his breathing, it sounds so hard. Can somebody please come out? I don't want him to suffer.
Caller -> My sister's here too. She wants somebody to come.
Nurse -> Okay, Beatriz. I'm going to send a nurse to you. But first, let's help him right now. Do you have the comfort kit?
Caller -> Yes. It's in the fridge. In the little box.
Nurse -> Okay. Take out the morphine. It's the liquid, and the label should say twenty milligrams per milliliter.
Caller -> Twenty milligrams per milliliter. Yes. That's what it says.
Nurse -> Okay. Draw up point two five milliliters. That's a quarter of a milliliter, the very small amount. And put it under his tongue, in the cheek, gently.
Caller -> Okay. A quarter. Point two five. Under the tongue.
Nurse -> Yes. Take your time. It helps with the work of breathing, and with the discomfort.
Caller -> Okay. I'm doing it. I'm doing it. Okay. It's in.
Nurse -> Good. That was perfect. Now, put extra pillows behind his head and shoulders, so he's raised up. Or turn him gently on his side. That helps the gurgling.
Caller -> Okay. Maria, help me with the pillows. Okay. Got him up.
Nurse -> Good. And you can use a mouth swab to keep his lips and mouth moist.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Beatriz, I want you to know that the gurgling sound is from secretions he can't clear anymore. It sounds worse to us than it feels to him. Usually it doesn't bother him.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That helps. That helps, to hear that.
Nurse -> I'm sending the nurse right now. She should be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And call me back any time before she gets there, if you need me.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Priya.
Nurse -> You're doing great. You're doing everything right.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Rhonda, please help me. It's my husband. He can't breathe. This is Ngozi Okonkwo.
Nurse -> Okay, Nozzy. I'm here. Tell me what's happening.
Caller -> It's Ngozi. N G O Z I. Please. It's my husband, Raymond Okonkwo. He can hardly breathe.
Nurse -> Okay, Ngozi. Sorry about that. Stay with me. What's Raymond's date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty fourth, nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. And your phone number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Three oh two, five five five, zero one five six.
Nurse -> Got it. Three oh two, five five five, zero one five six.
Caller -> Yes. Yes.
Nurse -> Alright. Tell me about his breathing. When did this start?
Caller -> It's been getting worse since last night. But the last hour is so much worse. He's working so hard. His shoulders are going up and down.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he able to talk to you?
Caller -> Only a few words. He can't finish a sentence. He says a word, and then he has to stop.
Nurse -> Okay. What color are his lips?
Caller -> They look blue. A little blue. Maybe purple. I noticed in the last hour.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have an oxygen meter?
Caller -> Yes. The little one on his finger. It says eighty four.
Nurse -> Okay. Eighty four. Is he wearing his oxygen?
Caller -> Yes. The nose tube. At two liters. It's on. And he still is eighty four.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he used his nebulizer?
Caller -> Yes. The albuterol. I gave him a treatment thirty minutes ago.
Nurse -> Okay. How much?
Caller -> The two point five. In the machine. He's had one every two hours since last night. Like the doctor said, if he needs it.
Nurse -> And did it help?
Caller -> A little. Just a little. It doesn't last.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have chest pain?
Caller -> No. He says no chest pain. It's just his breathing.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he coughing?
Caller -> A lot. And more phlegm than usual. Yellow. Since yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> He says he can't talk. He doesn't want to go to the hospital.
Caller -> Raymond, please. Shh. Don't try to talk. Rhonda, he says he hates the hospital. He says he's not going.
Nurse -> Okay. Ngozi, listen to me carefully. I understand that. But Raymond's oxygen is at eighty four, even with his oxygen on, his lips are blue, and he can't speak a full sentence. This is an emergency. I need you to call nine one one right now.
Caller -> But he said no. He's so stubborn.
Nurse -> I know. And this is your decision to make, along with him. But I would be doing you a disservice if I didn't tell you plainly: he needs to go. Now. Please call nine one one.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll call. I'll call them. Raymond, honey, I'm calling the ambulance. I know, I know.
Nurse -> Ngozi, can you put me on speaker, and call nine one one on another phone? Or do you have a cell phone nearby?
Caller -> I have my cell. Hang on. I'll put you down.
Caller -> Okay. I'm calling. Hello? Yes, I need an ambulance. My husband can't breathe. Three twelve Maple Court. Yes. Yes. He has COPD. Okay.
Caller -> They're sending someone. They said about eight minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's good. Now, while you wait. Is he sitting up?
Caller -> He's in his chair. The recliner. But he's leaning back.
Nurse -> Okay. I want him sitting upright, leaning forward a little, with his elbows on his knees or on a pillow on a table. That helps the breathing.
Caller -> Okay. Raymond, sit up. Lean forward. Here, put your arms on the pillow. There.
Nurse -> Good. And coach him to breathe in slowly through his nose, and out slowly through pursed lips, like he's blowing out a candle.
Caller -> In through the nose. Out like a candle. Raymond, like this. Like this. Good.
Nurse -> Keep his oxygen on. Don't take it off.
Caller -> It's on. It's on.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the front door unlocked? And can you turn on the porch light?
Caller -> No, I'll do that. Wait. Okay. Unlocked. The light is on.
Nurse -> Good. Now, can you get his medication list, or the pill bottles, and put them in a bag for the paramedics?
Caller -> Yes. They're on the kitchen counter. I'll grab them. I have the list on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. And his inhaler and the nebulizer medicine, bring those too.
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting a bag.
Nurse -> I'll stay on the line. Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I have it. It's all in the bag.
Nurse -> Is anyone else with you in the house?
Caller -> No, it's just us. Our son lives in Houston. I'll call him once we're in the ambulance.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good plan.
Caller -> He's going to be upset that I didn't call him sooner. He always says, Mom, call me first.
Nurse -> You called for help, and that's what matters.
Caller -> I know. I keep thinking, did I wait too long? Last night I thought it would pass.
Nurse -> You didn't wait too long. You're calling now, and help is on the way.
Caller -> He had pneumonia last winter. Two weeks in the hospital. He hated every minute.
Nurse -> That's probably why he's reluctant. It's understandable.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla. How can I help?
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Carla. It's, um, it's Dennis. My dad's a patient. Marvin. Marvin Fitzwater.
Nurse -> Hi, Dennis. Can you spell that last name for me?
Caller -> F I T Z W A T E R.
Nurse -> Thank you. And his birthday?
Caller -> September fourteenth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. And I have a number here, four oh seven, five five five, zero one two two.
Caller -> That's the house. That's the house phone.
Nurse -> Is there a better one?
Caller -> Yeah, use my cell. Four oh seven, five five five, zero one one three.
Nurse -> Four oh seven, five five five, zero one one three. Okay. So what's going on tonight, Dennis?
Caller -> Okay. So. It's kind of a lot. His, his breathing sounds really wet. Like a rattle.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Since when?
Caller -> Since this afternoon. Like three? Maybe three. And it keeps getting louder.
Nurse -> Does he look like he's struggling to breathe? Is he working hard, gasping?
Caller -> No. No, I don't, I don't think so. It just sounds bad. He's not gasping or anything.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> But he's also been really restless tonight. Picking at the sheets. Pulling at his gown.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had anything for that?
Caller -> I gave him the lorazepam. The little tablet, under his tongue. At nine.
Caller -> Nine o'clock.
Nurse -> Do you remember the dose?
Caller -> Point five. Half a milligram. It's on the bottle.
Nurse -> Okay. Did it help?
Caller -> For an hour. Maybe an hour. And then he started up again.
Nurse -> Okay. What about the morphine? Has he had any of that?
Caller -> The liquid? Yeah. At six. For the breathing. I gave him the point two five.
Nurse -> The point two five milliliters. Okay, good. That's his dose.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Is he eating or drinking anything?
Caller -> No. Not since Sunday. He hasn't had anything since Sunday. Maybe a sip. He just turns his head away.
Nurse -> That's very common at this stage. How does his mouth look?
Caller -> Dry. It's really dry. His lips are all cracked.
Nurse -> And is he making any urine?
Caller -> A little. Just a little today. And it was dark. Like tea.
Nurse -> Okay. And his last bowel movement?
Caller -> Oh gosh. Thursday? So that's, that's four days.
Nurse -> Alright. And his skin. Do you see any color changes? His hands, his knees?
Caller -> His knees. They look kind of blotchy. Purple-ish. And his feet are cold. They're really cold.
Nurse -> Mm-hm.
Caller -> Is that bad? Is that, is that the end?
Nurse -> It's a sign that his body is slowing down, Dennis. And I want to walk you through what you're seeing, because it's scary when you don't know what it means.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> That wet, rattly sound is from the little bit of saliva at the back of his throat that he can't swallow anymore. It sounds a lot worse to us than it feels to him. It doesn't mean he's in pain, and it doesn't mean he's suffocating.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> The blotchy knees and the cold feet are because his blood flow is going to the most important organs. The dark urine, not much of it, that's the same thing. And not eating or drinking is his body telling us he doesn't need it anymore.
Caller -> Okay. I just. I don't want him to be, I don't want him to feel anything.
Nurse -> I know. That's what we're here for. Does he look like he's in pain? Is he grimacing, moaning?
Caller -> No. Not really. He just, he's just restless. He doesn't look like he's hurting.
Caller -> Dad, it's okay. It's okay, Dad. Sorry. He's trying to sit up.
Nurse -> That's okay. You go ahead. I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. He's okay. He's back down.
Caller -> Sorry. The dog is going crazy. Hang on. Bailey, no. Bailey, quiet. Sorry.
Nurse -> It's fine. Dogs know when something's different. Is he settled for a second?
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, he's lying there. His eyes are kind of half open.
Nurse -> That's okay. That's common too.
Nurse -> Good. Dennis, let's take care of the restlessness first. It's been a few hours since the lorazepam, so you can give him another one. Same dose, the half a milligram under his tongue. Go ahead and do that right now.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Let me get it. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I'm. It's, okay, I got it. I'm putting it under his tongue. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, for the wet sound, do you have a little bottle of drops? Atropine, with the blue cap? It should be in the comfort kit.
Caller -> The blue one? Yes. Yeah, I see it. The atropine.
Nurse -> Okay. Two drops under his tongue. You can repeat that every four hours if the sound is bothering him.
Caller -> Two drops. Every four hours. Okay. Do I do that now?
Nurse -> Yes, do that now too. And then turn him onto his side, with the head of the bed raised, or a few pillows under his head. That helps the secretions drain.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. On his side. I'll get my brother to help me, he's down the hall.
Nurse -> That's good. And another thing, his mouth. Take one of the little pink sponge swabs, dip it in water, and wipe his mouth and lips every hour. Then put some lip balm on his lips so they don't crack.
Caller -> We, we have the lip balm. I don't think we have the swabs. I think we ran out.
Nurse -> Okay. Then use a clean damp washcloth for now. I'll order more swabs for you.
Caller -> Okay. A washcloth. Thank you.
Nurse -> And you don't need to push food or drinks. If he's awake and he asks, you can give him an ice chip or a tiny sip. But don't force anything.
Caller -> Okay. That's. That's good. My sister keeps trying to get him to drink. She's got the, the little cup.
Nurse -> It's okay to tell her. It comes from love, but it's not going to help him right now, and it could make him choke.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, she's, honestly that's the other thing. That's what I wanted to say.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Go ahead.
Caller -> So my sister, Joanna, she wants to call 911. She wants to take him to the hospital. She keeps saying we're not doing enough. And my brother and I, we're saying no. Dad said no hospital. He said it. He said it a hundred times.
Nurse -> I understand. And I want you to know, your dad's wishes are written in his plan. He wants to stay home and be comfortable. You're doing exactly what he asked.
Caller -> I know. I know that. I just. She's. She's screaming at us. She's crying and she's.
Nurse -> It sounds like everybody is hurting right now.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, we are. Can somebody come? Can somebody come out here tonight? Please. I don't, I can't do this by myself.
Nurse -> Yes. Yes, Dennis. I'm sending our on-call nurse out to you. She'll be there within ninety minutes. She can check him, and she can sit down with your sister too.
Caller -> Ninety minutes. Okay. Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> And I'm going to call you back in an hour, to see how he's doing after the medicine.
Caller -> Okay. In an hour.
Nurse -> I'd also like our social worker to call your family tomorrow, and our chaplain, if you'd want that. It helps with the hard parts, like this.
Caller -> Yeah. I think, yeah. Joanna would probably, yeah. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Good. Dennis, if anything changes, if he's in pain, if his breathing gets hard, if you're just scared, call us. Any hour tonight. You don't have to wait for me to call you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Is there anything else, before we hang up?
Caller -> No. I think, um, no. That's it. Thank you, Carla.
Nurse -> You're doing a good job, Dennis. Okay.
Caller -> Okay.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. It's Renata Voskuijlen. I'm a patient. Um, sorry, it's V O S K U I J L E N.
Nurse -> No problem, Renata. Date of birth?
Caller -> May thirtieth, nineteen eighty three.
Nurse -> Okay. And is two oh six, five five five, zero one nine four still your cell?
Caller -> Yes. That's me.
Nurse -> What can I help with?
Caller -> I'm trying to figure out when I can take my next pain pill and I, I lost track. I honestly lost track of what I took today.
Nurse -> Okay. That's okay, let's sort it out. How's your knee?
Caller -> It hurts. It's like a five right now. I had the replacement six days ago.
Nurse -> Okay. So you have the oxycodone, five milligrams, every four hours as needed. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. The oxycodone.
Nurse -> How many have you had today?
Caller -> Um. Three? Maybe four. I think three.
Nurse -> And when was the last one?
Caller -> I think it was around eleven. Eleven-ish. I fell asleep after. I really don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. And the Tylenol, the thousand milligrams every eight hours?
Caller -> Yes, the Tylenol. And I took that at eight this morning. I know that one because I set an alarm.
Nurse -> Good. So the Tylenol is due at four. Take that at four. For the oxycodone, if it's been at least four hours since your last one, and it has, since it's after two now, you can take one. Just one.
Caller -> One. Okay.
Nurse -> And don't take anything else with Tylenol in it. A lot of cold medicines and sleep aids have it hidden in there.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. I didn't know that. I do have some of the, the nighttime stuff.
Nurse -> Skip those for now. And from here on, grab a piece of paper and write down every dose and the time. Then we're not guessing.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, I should do that.
Nurse -> I'll make a note in your chart that you weren't sure about today's count.
Caller -> Okay. Is that bad?

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi, Denise. Hi. It's Abena Boateng. I'm calling about my husband. Ignatius. Ignatius Boateng.
Nurse -> Hi, Mrs. Boateng. How do you spell the last name?
Caller -> B O A T E N G.
Nurse -> Perfect. And his birthday?
Caller -> March eighteenth. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> Okay. And I have two oh two, five five five, zero one seven one for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. So how are things going?
Caller -> Okay. Um. Okay, so, it's a few things. I wrote them down, I'm sorry, it's a list.
Nurse -> No, that's perfect. Go ahead.
Caller -> So the first thing is his blood pressure. I've been taking it like you showed me. And this morning it was one forty eight over ninety. And last night it was one thirty eight over eighty four.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Is that okay? Is that too high?
Nurse -> Those are a little high but not alarming, especially a few weeks after a stroke. I'm going to pass them along to his doctor. Do you take it sitting down?
Caller -> Yes. Sitting, with the arm on the table. Like you showed.
Nurse -> Good. Okay. What's next?
Caller -> The bruise. So on Sunday I saw this big purple bruise. On his left forearm. It's like, um, as big as my palm. And he doesn't remember hitting anything.
Nurse -> Hm. Okay. Is it tender? Is it swollen?
Caller -> A little tender. Not swollen. It's just really dark. It's ugly.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Let me look at his medicines. I'm looking at his list. I see aspirin, eighty one milligrams, once a day. And clopidogrel, seventy five milligrams, once a day. Is he taking both of those?
Caller -> Yes. Every morning. The baby aspirin and the, the Plavix one. The clopidogrel.
Nurse -> Yes. Okay. So those two together can make him bruise more easily. That's likely what this is. But I want his doctor to know.
Caller -> So he should keep taking them?
Nurse -> Yes. Don't stop either of them. They're protecting him from another stroke. I'll ask the doctor about the bruise, though.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Good.
Caller -> And then he almost fell yesterday.
Nurse -> Oh. Tell me about that.
Caller -> We were going to the bedroom, he was using the walker, and his right leg just, it kind of gave out. I caught him. I caught him by the belt.
Nurse -> Oh my goodness. Okay. Did he hit anything? Did he go down?
Caller -> No. No, he didn't hit anything. He didn't go down. I just held him up. I'm still sore, honestly.
Nurse -> Mm. Okay. Yeah. You need to be careful with your back too.
Caller -> I know. I know.
Nurse -> Was it the right leg that gave out?
Caller -> Yes. The right. It's the weak side.
Nurse -> Okay. Any new weakness? Any change in his face, or his speech, since the stroke?
Caller -> No. No change. His face is the same. His talking is the same, a little slow, but the same.
Nurse -> And the right arm?
Caller -> The right arm is the same. It's no better and no worse. He can lift it a little. He can't make a fist.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Caller -> Mm.
Nurse -> Okay. What else is on the list?
Caller -> So, he's been really, I don't know. Sad. Crying. Like yesterday he was crying at the TV. He was watching a cooking show and he started crying.
Nurse -> Mm-hm.
Caller -> And he gets so frustrated. He says why can't I do it, why can't I do it. He throws the, he threw the spoon.
Nurse -> That's very common after a stroke, Mrs. Boateng. The emotions can be big. It's partly the brain healing and it's partly, you know, it's a lot to go through.
Caller -> I know. I just don't know what to say to him.
Nurse -> I think our social worker can help with that. I'd like her to call you, and talk to both of you.
Caller -> Yes. I'd like that. That would be really good.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll put that in.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Is there anything else on your list?
Caller -> The shower chair. The, the plastic one. It cracked. There's a big crack in the seat. I don't want him on it. So we don't have one now.
Nurse -> Oh no. Okay. Definitely don't use that. I'll order you a new one.
Caller -> Oh, thank you.
Nurse -> Until it comes, just sponge bathe him. Sitting at the edge of the bed or at the sink. Not the shower.
Caller -> Okay. Sponge bath. He'll like that, he doesn't like the shower anyway.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. What else?
Caller -> Oh, and he's sleeping okay. Mostly. He wakes up once or twice, to use the urinal. But then he goes right back.
Nurse -> That's good. And eating?
Caller -> He eats fine. He likes the rice and the stew. I make it soft for him.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Therapy. His physical therapist is supposed to come Thursday but my daughter's flying in Thursday and I wanted her to meet the therapist. Could it be Friday instead?
Nurse -> Let me ask the scheduler. I'll message her to try to move Thursday to Friday.
Caller -> Okay. Oh, thank you.
Nurse -> I can't promise Friday, but I'll ask. They'll call you to confirm.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine.
Nurse -> And I'm going to come see him myself Thursday, so I can look at that arm and check his blood pressure and look at everything.
Caller -> Oh, you're coming? Okay. Good. That's good.
Caller -> My daughter is a nurse too, in Atlanta. She's been telling me for weeks to call you about everything. She says I wait too long.
Nurse -> Ha. She's right. You can call us for any of this, any time. It's never too small.
Caller -> I know. I just don't like to bother people. I feel like, you have so many patients.
Nurse -> You're not bothering anybody. That's literally what we're here for.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Denise. You are very kind.
Nurse -> Now let's talk about the falls, because that near fall worries me. Make sure the walker is right next to him any time he's sitting. And please don't let him stand up by himself. Even for a minute.
Caller -> I try. But he gets up. He doesn't wait for me.
Nurse -> I know. It's hard. Put a chair alarm, or a little bell by his chair, if he'll go for it. And clear anything on the floor between his chair and the bathroom. Rugs, cords.
Caller -> The rugs. We have a runner in the hall. I'll take that up.
Nurse -> That would help a lot.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. And for the blood pressure, keep checking it every morning and every evening. Sit him quietly for five minutes first, and write the numbers down so I can see them Thursday.
Caller -> I've got the notebook. I write them all.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, important. If you see his face droop, if the arm weakness gets worse, if his speech gets slurred or he can't get words out, or he's suddenly confused, call nine one one. Don't wait.
Caller -> Face, arm, talking, confused. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if the bruise gets bigger, if he has any bleeding that won't stop, or if his stool turns black.
Caller -> Black. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Mrs. Boateng, how are you doing? Honestly.
Caller -> Me? Oh. I'm okay. I'm tired. I'm, I do everything. My daughter can't come most days, she's far. I'm up at night with him.
Nurse -> That's a lot.
Caller -> It's okay. It's what you do.
Nurse -> It is. But you have to take care of you too. The social worker will talk to you about that, about respite, about some help. Okay?
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That's very kind.
Nurse -> Alright. Anything else before I let you go?
Caller -> No, I think that's everything. Oh, wait. Should he still take the amlodipine? I forgot to ask. Or is that, that's the blood pressure one?

Caller -> Okay.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi, Denise. It's Karin. I'm Ottilie's daughter. Ottilie Brandvold.
Nurse -> Hi, Karin. How do you spell her last name?
Caller -> B R A N D V O L D.
Nurse -> Thanks. Her birthday?
Caller -> February eighth. Nineteen fifty four.
Nurse -> And I've got six one two, five five five, zero one four two for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's my number.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on tonight?
Caller -> Okay. So. It's a lot. She's been throwing up. Twice today.
Nurse -> Okay. Twice.
Caller -> Once this morning and once just now. About an hour ago.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. What did she throw up?
Caller -> Mostly water. And some, like, yellow. Bile or something. Not blood. I checked.
Nurse -> Okay. Good that you checked.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Has she had anything for the nausea?
Caller -> The ondansetron. The little dissolving one. She took one at eight this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. The four milligram?
Caller -> Yeah, I think so. Four. And it helped a little but then it came back this afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> And I'm almost out. I have three left. I counted.
Nurse -> Okay, good to know. Let me write that down.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> What about pain? How is she?
Caller -> She says about a five. Up here. In her upper belly and it goes through to her back.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's she taking for that?
Caller -> She has the patch. The fentanyl patch. We changed it yesterday. Twenty five.
Nurse -> Okay. The twenty five microgram.
Caller -> Yes. And she's had the oxycodone twice today. The five milligram.
Nurse -> When was the last one?
Caller -> Um. Noon. Maybe one. Something like that. Around lunch.
Nurse -> Okay. Has it been helping?
Caller -> Some. It takes the edge off. It doesn't get rid of it.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Okay. And her bowels? When was the last time she went?
Caller -> Oh gosh. Three days. It's been three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she taking anything for it?
Caller -> The senna. At night. But she hasn't been taking it the last two nights because she's been too sick.
Nurse -> Okay. That would do it. Is her belly swollen? Hard?
Caller -> A little. It's, I don't know. It's a little puffy. It's not hard.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> And there's something else. Her tongue. It's got a, like a white coating. Like milk. All over.
Nurse -> Okay. Does it hurt?
Caller -> She says it feels kind of, it burns a little when she eats. Or drinks.
Nurse -> Has she been sleeping a lot today, or is she awake and talking with you?
Caller -> Both. She slept most of the afternoon. But when she's up she's herself. She asked about my kids. She asked what we're having for dinner, which, I mean, she can't eat any of it, but she asked.
Nurse -> That's a good sign, that she's herself.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, it is.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Okay. And what is she eating and drinking?
Caller -> Nothing. Almost nothing. Sips. Like, she'll take a sip of water and that's it. Tea, a little bit of tea this morning.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I tried some applesauce and she wouldn't. She said it hurt.
Nurse -> Mm.
Caller -> I'm just. I don't know, Denise. I'm scared. I want to keep her home. That's what she wants. She's always said it. But I feel like she's getting worse and I don't know what I'm supposed to do.
Nurse -> I hear you, Karin. And you're doing a good job. What you're describing is what we can help with here at home. Okay?
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> So let's take it one thing at a time. First, the nausea. It's been about twelve hours since the ondansetron, right? Eight in the morning?
Caller -> Yes. Yeah. Eight.
Nurse -> It's every eight hours as needed. So she can have another one at four. If it's already after four, she can have it now.
Caller -> It's after four. It's like eight at night. Oh. I should've given it earlier, huh?
Nurse -> No, no. It's okay. Give her one now. It dissolves on her tongue, so she doesn't have to swallow it.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Let me get it. Mom. Mom, open your mouth. Okay. Under the tongue. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Good. Good job.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And since you're down to three, I'm going to send in a refill for the ondansetron tonight.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Thank you. That's one thing I was worried about.
Nurse -> Next, the white tongue. That sounds like thrush, which is a yeast infection in the mouth. It's common. I'm going to message her doctor about it, along with the vomiting and the constipation. They may want to prescribe something.
Caller -> Okay. Is that from the, the cancer?
Nurse -> More from being sick and not eating much. Her mouth gets dry. Nothing you did.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief.
Nurse -> In the meantime, rinse her mouth gently with a little water and baking soda. A quarter teaspoon in a cup of warm water. And you can wipe her tongue with a soft swab.
Caller -> Water and baking soda. Okay. A soft swab. I have those pink ones.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> For drinks, tiny sips only. Flat ginger ale, ice chips, popsicles if she'll take them. Don't push food.
Caller -> Popsicles. Okay. She likes the cherry ones.
Nurse -> Cherry is great.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> About the patch, make sure no heating pads or hot water bottles near it. Heat makes the medicine absorb faster and that can be dangerous.
Caller -> No heating pad. We had one on her back yesterday! I'll take it off.
Nurse -> Yes, take it off, please. Not on or near the patch. Thank you for telling me.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Sorry.
Nurse -> No, it's good you asked. And leave the patch on. Don't take it off. It stays on until we change it.
Caller -> Okay. It stays on.
Nurse -> I'm going to send a nurse to see her tomorrow. We'll look at her belly, her mouth, and go over everything.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you this evening, after I hear from the doctor.
Caller -> Okay. That would be good.
Nurse -> Any fever? Has she felt hot, or had chills?
Caller -> No. I took it at dinner. Ninety eight something. She's cool, if anything. Her hands are cold.
Nurse -> Okay. And is she peeing?
Caller -> Some. Not a lot. It's dark-ish.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. That's from not drinking enough, so we'll work on that. And I see her pantoprazole on the list, the stomach pill. Is she still taking that one?
Caller -> Yes, that one she keeps down. She takes it first thing in the morning with a sip. That one's fine.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing that.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Who else is at the house with you tonight?
Caller -> Just me and my husband. Our kids are at college. My brother's coming this weekend from Duluth.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. You'll have some help.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, I really need it. I've been sleeping on the couch next to her bed.
Nurse -> I'm glad you're close by. Just make sure you rest when you can, too.
Caller -> I'm trying.
Nurse -> Now, here's what I want you to watch for. If she can't keep her pills down for a whole day. Or if she throws up blood, or something black like coffee grounds. Or if the pain gets really bad. Or she's too drowsy to wake up. Call us.
Caller -> Pills down. Blood. Black. Pain. Drowsy. Okay. I wrote it down.
Nurse -> Good. Karin, you can call us any time tonight.
Caller -> I know. I will. Thank you.
Nurse -> Is your mom comfortable right now? Is she awake?
Caller -> She's resting. She's kind of dozing. She said thank you. She says hi, Denise.
Nurse -> Aw. Tell her hi back.
Caller -> I will.

Caller -> Okay, good. I wasn't sure about the dose.

Caller -> He's drinking. He's had, let me think, four bottles today. Small ones. Four. Not a lot but he's taking them.
Nurse -> Okay. And wet diapers?
Caller -> Four. In the last twenty four hours. I counted. I've been counting because the other nurse told me to.
Nurse -> Good, that's exactly right. That's a good number. Four is fine.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Now, how's his breathing? Is he breathing fast? Do you see his belly or his ribs pulling in with each breath?
Caller -> No. No, I don't think so. I watched him. His breathing is noisy, from the stuffy nose, but it isn't fast. His belly isn't sucking in.
Nurse -> Okay. Any blue color around his lips?
Caller -> No. His lips are pink.

Caller -> Yes, I put it on his foot. It says ninety six.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety six is good.
Caller -> Okay. I was worried about that number.
Nurse -> It's a good number. Okay.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> And how's he acting? Is he playing, smiling?

Nurse -> Ha. That's good.
Caller -> Yeah. His dad does the dinosaur thing. It always works.

Caller -> He wakes up a lot. Every hour or two, coughing, and then he can't breathe through his nose so he cries. I'm up with him. We're taking turns.
Nurse -> That's rough. Is his dad able to help at night?
Caller -> Yeah, he does the first half. I do the second. We're tired, but we're managing.
Nurse -> Good. That sounds like a plan that works.

Nurse -> That's a great sign. Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'll message his pediatrician about day five and the fever.

Nurse -> And I'm going to come see him tomorrow myself, to listen to his lungs.
Caller -> Oh good. Tomorrow. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow morning before that, to see how the night went.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> You can give the Tylenol again, the same three point seven five, as long as it's been six hours since the last one.
Caller -> Okay. Six hours. So like, in an hour.

Caller -> I will.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. It's Verna Prentiss. I'm calling about my husband. Hollis. Hollis Prentiss.
Nurse -> Hi, Verna. How do you spell Prentiss?
Caller -> P R E N T I S S.
Nurse -> Thanks. His date of birth?
Caller -> February sixteenth. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And I have four oh four, five five five, zero one three nine.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on this morning?
Caller -> He's more short of breath than usual. Since this morning. He woke up like that.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. How much more?
Caller -> Um. It's hard to say. He's, he's winded just going to the bathroom. And that's like ten feet.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he used his inhaler?
Caller -> The albuterol. Yes. Two puffs. He's had it three times since he woke up.
Nurse -> Three times. And does it help?
Caller -> A little. For maybe a half hour. And then it's back.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Is he coughing?
Caller -> Yes. It's wet. Since yesterday. And it's yellow. What comes up. It's yellow.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had a fever?
Caller -> I took it. Ninety nine point eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. He says no chest pain. I asked him twice.
Nurse -> Has he had any swelling in his legs? Any weight gain lately?
Caller -> No. His legs are the same. They're thin, honestly. He's lost weight.
Nurse -> Okay. And did he sleep at all last night?
Caller -> Not much. He was up coughing. I heard him at one and at four. And he was wheezing a little. I could hear it from the bedroom.
Nurse -> Has he been using a spacer with the inhaler, or just the inhaler by itself?
Caller -> Just the inhaler. He doesn't like the spacer. He says it's a pain.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll talk to him about that another time. It does help it work better.
Caller -> Okay. Yeah, I keep telling him that. He never listens to me.
Nurse -> Ha. Husbands. They never do. Alright.
Caller -> Ha. No. They don't.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Does he have a nebulizer machine at home, or just the inhaler?
Caller -> Just the inhaler. The nebulizer broke last year. We never replaced it. I should have said something.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll deal with that later. Okay, Verna, do you have the pulse oximeter on him?
Caller -> I do. Hold on. Hollis, give me your finger. Hold still. Okay. It says eighty nine.
Nurse -> Eighty nine. And he's on how many liters right now?
Caller -> Two. It's on two. The usual.
Nurse -> Okay. His order lets us go up to three. I want you to turn it up to three liters.
Caller -> Three. Okay. The knob. Okay. It's on three.
Nurse -> Good. Now, Hollis, if you can hear me, I want him sitting up, leaning forward a little. Elbows on his knees if he can.
Caller -> He's in the recliner. Hollis, lean forward. Lean forward, honey. Okay.
Nurse -> And I want him breathing in through his nose, and then out slowly through pursed lips. Like blowing out a candle.
Caller -> Like a candle. Hollis, like blowing out a candle. In through the nose. Okay. He's doing it.
Nurse -> Good. Let's give that ten minutes and recheck. Stay on with me, I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> While we wait, let me ask you a few things. Has anyone been sick at the house? A grandchild, anyone with a cold?
Caller -> Our grandson was here Sunday. He had a runny nose. He was sneezing. I should have, I didn't think anything of it.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. These things happen. Has Hollis been eating and drinking okay?
Caller -> He had half a piece of toast. A little coffee. He didn't want breakfast. He just wanted to sit.
Nurse -> Okay. And did he sleep in the bed or the recliner last night?
Caller -> The recliner. He's been sleeping there for three weeks. He says he breathes better sitting up.
Nurse -> That makes sense.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Is he on any steroids right now, like prednisone, that you know of? Anything new from the doctor?
Caller -> No. Nothing new. Not since September. The doctor was going to see him this week, Thursday I think. For a check.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anyone else at the house with you?
Caller -> No. It's just me. Our son is forty minutes away. He keeps calling. He's very worried.
Nurse -> I understand. You're doing great, Verna. You're watching him closely and that's what counts.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm trying to stay calm. It's hard.
Nurse -> I know. Is he still sitting forward? Still doing the candle breathing?
Caller -> He's trying. He keeps leaning back.
Nurse -> Gently remind him. Forward. Elbows on his knees.
Caller -> Hollis, forward. Elbows. There you go. Yes.
Nurse -> Verna, does Hollis have a living will, or any papers about what he wants if he gets very sick?
Caller -> He does. It's in the blue folder. It says he doesn't want to be on a machine, a breathing machine, for a long time. But he does want to be treated for things like this. Pneumonia and so on.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful to know. If we do need to send him in, they'll want that folder.
Caller -> I'll get it. It's in the kitchen drawer.
Nurse -> Maybe grab it now, while he's sitting. I'm still here.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm just walking to the kitchen. Hollis, I'm right here, I'm just in the kitchen. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Put it by the door.
Caller -> Okay. By the door. Done.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing, Verna?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm nervous. He doesn't want to go to the hospital. He's said that a hundred times. He hates it there.
Nurse -> I understand. Let's see how he does on the higher oxygen.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Dad, you're okay. It's fine. Oh, sorry. That's my son on the other line. He's calling from work.
Nurse -> That's okay. Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I told him I'd call back. Okay. How's it been, ten minutes?
Nurse -> About that. Check the oxygen again.
Caller -> Hold on. Hollis, finger. Okay. Hmm. It says eighty six. On three.
Nurse -> Eighty six. On three liters?
Caller -> Yes. On three. And he's, he's not good. He's breathing really fast. He can't talk, he tried to say something and he couldn't get a sentence out.
Nurse -> Okay. Look at his lips for me. What color are they?
Caller -> They're, I don't know. They look a little blue. Purple-ish. Oh God.
Nurse -> Okay, Verna, listen to me. I want you to call 911 right now. He needs an ambulance.
Caller -> But he doesn't want to. He said he doesn't want to go.
Nurse -> I know. But his oxygen is dropping even with more oxygen, and he can't speak. This is more than we can fix at home. He needs to be seen.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hollis. Hollis, honey, I'm calling the ambulance. I'm calling. I know. I know you don't want to. Okay.
Nurse -> Tell him it's just to get him breathing better. He can come home.
Caller -> I'll tell him. Hollis, it's just to get your breathing better. You're coming home. I promise. Okay.
Nurse -> Is he still awake? Is he still responding to you?
Caller -> Yes. He's looking at me. He nodded. He's squeezing my hand. He's scared. He's just scared.
Nurse -> Of course. Keep talking to him, keep holding his hand.
Caller -> I will.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him. Okay. I'm hanging up and calling.
Nurse -> One more thing. Leave the oxygen on three liters. Unlock the front door. Don't try to drive him yourself. And have his medication list ready for the paramedics.
Caller -> Three liters. Door. List. Okay. It's on the fridge.
Nurse -> I'm going to call his lung doctor and the emergency department so they know he's coming.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Tom.
Nurse -> Go ahead, Verna. Go now.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> And his date of birth?
Caller -> June sixth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And I have three one oh, five five five, zero one one eight for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have the discharge papers in front of you?
Caller -> I do. I have the list. And I have all the bottles on the kitchen table. There's like twelve of them.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through it one at a time. Start with whatever's first on the list.
Caller -> Okay. So the first one is metoprolol. Succinate. Twenty five milligrams. Once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. In the morning?
Caller -> Yes. In the morning. Yes.
Nurse -> Good. Next.
Caller -> Furosemide. Forty milligrams. Once a day. It says increased. Before it was twenty.
Nurse -> Right. That's the water pill. They doubled it in the hospital.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Next.
Caller -> Apixaban. Five milligrams. Twice a day. Morning and night.
Nurse -> That's the Eliquis. The blood thinner. Good.
Caller -> Yeah. That one I'm very careful with. I give it at eight and eight.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep doing that.
Caller -> Okay. Next is atorvastatin. Forty milligrams. At night.
Nurse -> Okay. Cholesterol pill. Good.
Caller -> Then levothyroxine. Fifty micrograms. Every morning. Empty stomach.
Nurse -> Right. And donepezil?
Caller -> Yes. Donepezil. Five milligrams. At night. For his memory.
Nurse -> Good. That's seven. And what about his blood pressure pill?
Caller -> Okay. This is where I'm confused. This is the thing.
Nurse -> Go ahead.
Caller -> The list says losartan. Twenty five milligrams. Once a day. And it says NEW next to it. And then it says STOP lisinopril. In capital letters.
Nurse -> Right. They switched him. Lisinopril is out. Losartan is in.

Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?

Caller -> Is that bad? Is that dangerous?
