Caller -> Nothing more. Okay.
Nurse -> And from tomorrow on, lisinopril is stopped for good. Only the losartan. That's what the hospital wants.
Caller -> Only losartan. Lisinopril is done. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm going to message his prescriber and the pharmacist right now, and tell them he got both this morning.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll call you this evening with what they say.
Caller -> This evening. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm coming tomorrow to go through every bottle with you. We'll set up a pill box.
Caller -> Oh, good. That would be so helpful. Thank you.
Nurse -> For now, take that lisinopril bottle and put it in a bag, away from the others. Out of sight.
Caller -> A bag. Yes. I'll put it in the garage. Okay.
Nurse -> And a weekly pill box would help a lot. They're a couple dollars at the drugstore.
Caller -> I'll get one tonight. I'll run out. My wife can stay with him.
Nurse -> Good. Now, blood pressure. Check it twice a day, sitting and then again after he stands for a minute. Write both down.
Caller -> Sitting and standing. Twice a day. Okay.
Nurse -> And help him up slowly. Have him sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before he stands. Walk with him.
Caller -> Slowly. Edge of the bed. Okay.
Nurse -> Julian, call me if the top number is under ninety. Or if he faints, or he's very weak and can't stand. Or if he gets chest pain, that's nine one one.
Caller -> Under ninety. Faint. Weak. Chest pain, nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Has he eaten today? Any nausea, any trouble with his stomach since the pills?
Caller -> He ate breakfast. Eggs and toast. No nausea. He's been fine with food. He had a little soup at lunch.
Nurse -> Okay, good. And is he making urine normally, with the new water pill dose?
Caller -> Yes. A lot, actually. He's up and down to the bathroom. Which is why I'm watching him on his feet.
Nurse -> That's what the higher dose does. That's expected.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And one thing, Julian, make sure he isn't taking any over-the-counter pain pills or cold medicine from the drugstore. Those can strain the heart and the kidneys, and add to his pills.
Caller -> No. I don't think so. I'll check the cabinet though. I'll take them out.
Nurse -> That would be good.
Nurse -> Is he sitting right now?
Caller -> Yes. He's in the recliner. He's watching the news. He's fine. He says what's the fuss.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Tell him the fuss is that we want him to be safe.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> Did you give the apixaban this morning, too?
Caller -> Yes. At eight. And I'll give the evening one at eight.
Nurse -> Perfect. That one stays on schedule.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> One more thing. Did they give you any other instructions at discharge? Diet, fluids, weights?
Caller -> Yes. They said low salt. And to weigh him every morning. And to limit fluids, I think it was like two liters a day. Let me look. Yes, two liters.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Are you doing the daily weights?
Caller -> I did this morning. He was one seventy four. They told us his dry weight is one seventy. So he's still a little over.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that you have that number. Keep writing it down with the blood pressure.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I have a notebook and a pen right on the table.
Nurse -> Perfect. Does he have a follow-up appointment with the heart doctor?
Caller -> Friday. At ten. Dr. Mendez. I'm taking off work to drive him.
Nurse -> Good. Bring all the bottles and the notebook with you.
Caller -> Okay. All twelve bottles. Ha. And the notebook.
Nurse -> Does he have any trouble with stairs at the house, or is everything on one floor?
Caller -> One floor. Thank God. There's one step at the front door, with a rail. He does okay with that.
Nurse -> Good. And is he using a walker, a cane?
Caller -> A walker. The hospital gave him one. He doesn't love it, but he uses it.
Nurse -> And what about at night? Who's staying with him?
Caller -> I'm staying here. I'm in my old room. My wife comes in the day and I go to work, then switch. We're making it work.
Nurse -> That's a lot of juggling. How are you holding up?
Caller -> I'm okay. It was a scare. He was in the hospital six days. I've been a mess.
Nurse -> I'm sure. It's good that you're all pitching in.
Caller -> Yeah. My sister's coming in from Phoenix next week.
Nurse -> That will help. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else before we hang up?
Caller -> No. I feel a lot better. I was really freaking out.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling. Talk to you tonight.
Caller -> Thanks, Marcus.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. It's Agatha Fenwick. I'm calling about my husband, Lucius. Lucius Fenwick.
Nurse -> Hi, Agatha. His birthday?
Caller -> July twenty fifth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> And I have eight six four, five five five, zero one six two.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> What can I do for you?
Caller -> It's his blood thinner. The warfarin. They checked his INR yesterday. And the clinic called and said it was high. Three point eight.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> And they told me something about tonight's pill. But I was cooking, and I, I wrote it down wrong. I think they said skip it. Or was it half? I don't know.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. What does he normally take?
Caller -> Five milligrams. Every evening. At six.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at the clinic note in his chart. I'm seeing warfarin five milligrams. And the note from yesterday says, hold tonight's dose. Then two and a half milligrams tomorrow evening. And recheck the INR Friday.
Caller -> Hold tonight's. So skip it.
Nurse -> Skip it tonight, yes. Half a pill tomorrow.
Caller -> Skip tonight. Half tomorrow. Okay. Oh, thank goodness. I almost gave it to him.
Nurse -> Good thing you called. Has he had any bleeding? Gums, nose, bruising?
Caller -> His gums. A little. When he brushes. There's a little pink on the toothbrush.
Nurse -> Okay. Any nosebleeds, black stools, anything like that?
Caller -> No. No. Just the gums. A little.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to call the anticoagulation clinic and make sure that plan is right, and tell them about the gums.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And the Friday INR is on the schedule. I'll make sure someone comes to draw it.
Caller -> Okay. Friday. Good.
Nurse -> Use a soft toothbrush, and if he shaves, an electric razor.
Caller -> He has an electric. And a soft brush. I'll get a softer one.
Nurse -> And call nine one one if the bleeding doesn't stop, if his stool is black or bloody, if he throws up blood, or if he hits his head. Call us for more gum or nose bleeding.
Caller -> Black stool, throws up blood, hits his head. Nine one one. Okay.

Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Marguerite Tillman. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Marguerite. Can I get your birthday?
Caller -> February second, nineteen sixty three. Groundhog Day. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Easy to remember. And I have nine one nine, five five five, zero one eight four.
Caller -> That's me.
Nurse -> What do you need today?
Caller -> Supplies. Diabetes stuff. I'm running out of things. The test strips, I have like ten. Ten left.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> And the pen needles. I have five. And I'm completely out of the lancets.
Nurse -> Okay. Out of lancets. How many times a day are you checking?
Caller -> Four. Before meals and at bedtime. So the ten strips is, what, two days.
Nurse -> Right. Okay. We'll get that fixed. Anything else going on with your sugars?
Caller -> Well, yesterday I had a low. It was fifty eight. In the afternoon. I felt shaky and sweaty.
Nurse -> Oh. Okay. What did you do?
Caller -> I drank juice. Orange juice. Half a glass. And I felt better in like fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> Good. That's the right thing. Did you recheck?
Caller -> I did. It came up to ninety something. So I was okay.
Nurse -> Okay. And what insulin are you on?
Caller -> The Lantus. Twenty units at bedtime.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Okay. And had you eaten that day?
Caller -> I had a late lunch. I skipped my morning snack. I was busy. I was watching my niece. She's, she's three, she's a handful.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet. Okay.
Caller -> Yeah. She had me running. We were at the park.
Nurse -> That'll do it. More activity and less food. Okay.
Caller -> Yeah. That's probably what it was.
Nurse -> How have your fasting numbers been, the morning ones, this week?
Caller -> Pretty good. One ten, one twenty. A hundred and thirty one day. Nothing crazy.
Nurse -> That's good. And have you noticed any of those shaky feelings at night? Waking up sweaty?
Caller -> No. Not at night. Just that once, at the park.
Nurse -> Okay. How are your feet? Any sores, numbness, tingling?
Caller -> My feet are okay. A little tingling sometimes, in the toes. It's been like that for a year. I look at them every night like they told me.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing that. And your eyes, are you seeing okay?
Caller -> I have an appointment next month. I'm okay, I think. Reading glasses.
Nurse -> Good. Keep that appointment.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> I'm going to let your prescriber know about the fifty eight, in case she wants to adjust anything.
Caller -> Okay. I don't want to go lower on it. I mean I don't want lows.
Nurse -> Right. Nobody does. Now, what about your injection sites? How do those look?
Caller -> That's the other thing. My belly is all bruised. I always use my belly. I don't know where else to go.
Nurse -> Okay. So you can rotate. Use the thighs, the back of your upper arms, and the belly, but move around. Stay at least an inch away from the last spot.
Caller -> An inch. Thighs. Back of the arms. Okay.
Nurse -> And a new needle every time. That will help with bruising too.
Caller -> I do use a new one. I think. Most of the time. I stretch them sometimes.
Nurse -> That's why we're ordering more. Don't stretch them.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll put in the order for test strips, pen needles and lancets.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> It'll be delivered Thursday. Is somebody home?
Caller -> I'm home. I work from home.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now one more time on the lows. If your sugar is under seventy, take fifteen grams of fast sugar. Half a cup of juice is about right. Wait fifteen minutes, recheck, and repeat if it's still low.
Caller -> Under seventy. Half a cup. Fifteen minutes. Recheck. Okay.
Nurse -> And call nine one one if you're too confused or sleepy to swallow. Call us for any sugar under seventy, even if you fixed it.
Caller -> Confused, sleepy, nine one one. Under seventy, call you. Okay.
Nurse -> And who helps if you do have a bad low and you're alone?
Caller -> My sister lives two doors down. She has a key. And I wear my medical bracelet, always. It says diabetic, and it has my sister's phone number on the back.
Nurse -> That's great. Good planning.
Caller -> Thanks. After the low I made her promise to check on me more.
Nurse -> Do you keep juice or glucose tabs by your bed?
Caller -> Juice in the fridge, and crackers in the nightstand drawer too, for emergencies.
Caller -> Juice in the fridge. I'll put some glucose tabs in my purse and by the bed.
Nurse -> Good idea. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thanks so much, Gwen.
Nurse -> Take care, Marguerite.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hi, Priya. It's Thandiwe Mbeki. I'm Zuri's mom. Zuri Mbeki.
Nurse -> Hi, Thandiwe. How do you spell Zuri's last name?
Caller -> M B E K I.
Nurse -> Thanks. Her birthday?
Caller -> April ninth. Twenty nineteen.
Nurse -> And I've got six seven eight, five five five, zero one nine three.
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on?
Caller -> Okay, so it's several things. I made a list. I'm sorry. It's been a week.
Nurse -> No, go ahead. I'm listening.
Caller -> Number one is the spasms. At night. They're worse. Three nights now. She's all stiff, and her legs are crossing, and she cries.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Three nights.
Caller -> Yeah. She wakes up around two and she's arched and she can't settle. I've been up with her.
Nurse -> Okay. And what is she taking for the spasms?
Caller -> The baclofen. Five milligrams. Three times a day.
Nurse -> Okay. And you've been giving it on time?
Caller -> Every time. Eight, two, and eight. I have an alarm.
Nurse -> Good. Okay.
Caller -> I was wondering if we could bump it up. The dose. Just a little. Or give her an extra one at night.
Nurse -> I understand why you're asking. But I don't want to change that on my own. Baclofen has to be adjusted carefully by her doctor. I'll ask them.
Caller -> Okay. That's fair.
Nurse -> Don't stop it or skip any doses either. That can make the spasms a lot worse.
Caller -> No. I wouldn't. I know that one.
Nurse -> Okay. What's number two?
Caller -> The bowels. She hasn't gone in three days.
Nurse -> Three days. And is she on anything?
Caller -> The MiraLAX. One capful, once a day, in her feeds. I gave it yesterday and today.
Nurse -> Okay. And is her belly hard? Swollen?
Caller -> A little round. It's not hard. She's not crying when I touch it. It's just kind of full.
Nurse -> Okay. Any vomiting?
Caller -> No. No vomiting. She's tolerating everything. She's getting four cans a day. Every one of them.
Nurse -> Good. That's good news. Okay.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> What's number three?
Caller -> Her mouth. She's drooling more than usual. And she has a little cough. A wet one. Since the cold last week.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Any fever?
Caller -> I took it before I called. Ninety eight point nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. How's her breathing? Is she working hard?
Caller -> No. She's breathing normal. The cough is just in the morning. It sounds like she needs to clear her throat. A little rattly.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something to watch with her. I'll look at that Friday.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And four?
Caller -> Her wheelchair cushion. It's totally flat. It's been flat for months. She's sliding and I think it's hurting her. And the company hasn't come.
Nurse -> Okay. Is her skin okay, around her bottom? Any red spots?
Caller -> No. Her skin's fine. I check it every night. It's just, it's not supporting her.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order a new one. I'll follow up with the equipment company too.
Caller -> Oh, thank you.
Nurse -> And five?
Caller -> The school nurse. She needs an updated medication form. By Monday. The doctor has to sign it and I don't know where to start.
Nurse -> I can help with that. I'll fill out the nursing part of the form and have it ready by Friday when I come, and then we'll get the doctor to sign.
Caller -> Oh my gosh. That would be a huge help. Thank you.
Nurse -> Of course. That's what I'm here for. Is that all the list?
Caller -> That's the list. But, I also just, I'm tired. I'm so tired, Priya.
Nurse -> I hear you.
Caller -> I haven't slept more than three hours in a row this whole week. My husband works nights. It's just me.
Nurse -> That's really hard. You are doing so much.
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm okay. I just wanted to say it out loud.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. Let's see what we can do to give you some relief. Let me start with what we can fix tonight.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> For the constipation, give her another capful of MiraLAX tonight in her feed, and do an extra water flush after each feed. That helps the stool move.
Caller -> An extra flush after every feed. Okay. How much?
Caller -> Is sixty enough?
Nurse -> Sixty milliliters is good.
Caller -> Okay. Sixty after each one.
Nurse -> For the spasms tonight, a warm bath before bed, and some gentle stretching. Nice and slow. And put pillows between her knees and under her legs so she's supported and her legs aren't crossing.
Caller -> A warm bath. Okay. We do that sometimes. I'll do it tonight. And the pillows.
Nurse -> And I'm going to message her doctor tonight about the spasms and the constipation.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow and tell you what they say.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm coming Friday. We'll check her belly, listen to her chest, and go over the form.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Perfect.
Nurse -> How is she in the daytime, besides the nights? Is she smiling, engaging with you?
Caller -> She's great in the daytime. She's laughing. She loves her tablet, she's watching the animal videos. She smiles when her brother comes home.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. And therapy, is she still getting her physical therapy?
Caller -> Tuesdays and Fridays. The therapist is great. She said Zuri's tone has been a little tighter though. That's why I think it's all connected.
Nurse -> It might be. I'll pass that along to the doctor too.
Caller -> Thank you. That'd be good.
Nurse -> Does Zuri have any pain that you can tell? Any grimacing, a certain place she holds?
Caller -> At night when she arches, yes. She cries out. In the daytime, no. She's comfortable.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits with the spasms.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> And how's her sleep position? What does she sleep in?
Caller -> On her side, with the wedge. But she keeps rolling out of it when she's stiff. I put her back four or five times a night.
Nurse -> That's exhausting. The pillows between her knees should help her stay put a little better.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try the pillows and the wedge both.
Nurse -> Now call us if she starts vomiting, if her belly gets hard or really swollen, if her fever gets to a hundred point four, or if the cough gets wet and noisy with fast breathing.
Caller -> Vomiting. Belly. Fever. Cough and fast breathing. Okay.
Nurse -> And call nine one one if she's choking or her lips turn blue.
Caller -> Choking. Blue. Okay.
Nurse -> And how is her brother handling all this? You said he's around.
Caller -> He's ten. He's good. He helps with her. He puts her socks on and reads her stories. He's honestly my best helper. But he gets woken up too, when she cries, and he has school.
Nurse -> That's a lot for a ten year old.
Caller -> It is. He doesn't say much about it, but I think he worries. He asked me last week if Zuri's going to be okay, and I didn't know what to say.
Nurse -> That's such a hard question to answer.
Nurse -> Is she due for her seizure medicine tonight? I just want to make sure nothing's been missed.
Caller -> She got the levetiracetam at seven. That's all done.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Is there someone who can sit with her so you can take a nap tomorrow?

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hi, Ana. It's Henrietta Calloway. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Henrietta. Can you spell the last name?
Caller -> C A L L O W A Y.
Nurse -> And your birthday?
Caller -> November thirtieth. Nineteen fifty six.
Nurse -> And I've got two one four, five five five, zero one seven one.
Caller -> Yes. That's my number.
Nurse -> What can I do for you?
Caller -> I'm on the, the steroid. The prednisone. And it's a taper. And I lost count. I don't know what day I'm on.
Nurse -> Okay. That's easy to do. Let me pull up the taper in your chart. Hold on one second.
Caller -> Okay. Take your time.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Okay. I'm looking at it. So it says twenty milligrams for three days. Then ten milligrams for three days. Then five milligrams for three days. And stop.
Caller -> Right. That's what I have on the paper too. Twenty, ten, five.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you start?
Caller -> Saturday. I started Saturday.
Nurse -> So Saturday, Sunday, Monday was the twenty. Then Tuesday would be the first ten. Is that right?
Caller -> That's what I thought. But, here's the thing. I think I took the ten on Monday. Because I got confused and I looked at the pill box.
Nurse -> Mm. Okay. So you might have started the ten a day early.
Caller -> Maybe. I don't know. I think. Or maybe I took the twenty twice on Sunday. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. Henrietta, what does your pill box show? Which slots are empty?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me look. It's the, it's the one with the days on it. Saturday, empty. Sunday, empty. Monday, empty. Tuesday, empty. And Wednesday. That's today. Is empty too. I took it this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So five days. Saturday through today.
Caller -> Yes. Five days. But I only put in what the box tells me, and I don't know if I put in the right ones.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let's go by the calendar. If you started Saturday, then today is day five. Days one through three were twenty. Days four through six are ten. So today's dose is ten.
Caller -> Okay. So I'm on the ten. And I took the ten today?
Nurse -> What did you take this morning?
Caller -> I took the ten. I'm pretty sure it was the ten. Two of the five. Or one of the ten. One of those.
Nurse -> Okay. Either way, that's ten. Good.
Caller -> Oh good. Okay.
Nurse -> So, today and tomorrow are ten. Then five milligrams for three days. Then you stop.
Caller -> Ten, ten. Then five, five, five. Then stop.
Nurse -> Right. I'm going to message your prescriber to confirm that, since you were a little unsure about the first few days.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I don't want to mess it up.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. How are your joints? How's the pain?
Caller -> Better. They're better than last week. I'd say a three. My hands and my knees. It was an eight before the steroid.
Nurse -> That's good. That's what we want. And have you been checking your sugar?
Caller -> This morning it was one sixty eight. Which is high for me. Usually I'm about one ten.
Nurse -> Okay. The steroid can raise it. I'll pass that along too.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And you're taking this with food, in the morning?
Caller -> Yes. With my breakfast. And my stomach pill. The omeprazole. They told me to take that too.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing that.
Caller -> Okay. I'm so sorry about all this. I feel silly.
Nurse -> Not at all. A taper is confusing. Henrietta, let's do this. Get a calendar and write the date every time you take a dose. Don't count on the pill box.
Caller -> I have a calendar. From the church. I'll use that. It has big squares.
Nurse -> Perfect. And don't stop it suddenly. Finish the taper just as written.
Caller -> I won't.
Nurse -> I'll call you this afternoon after I hear from the prescriber.
Caller -> Okay. This afternoon.
Nurse -> And call us if your sugar goes over three hundred, if you see black stools, have bad stomach pain, or the joint pain comes roaring back.
Caller -> Over three hundred. Black stools. Stomach pain. Pain back. Okay.
Nurse -> Have you noticed any swelling in your face or your ankles, or trouble sleeping on the steroid?
Caller -> My sleep is terrible. I'm awake at three, wide awake, and my mind is running. My face is a little puffy. My daughter said I look like a chipmunk. Ha.
Nurse -> That's common on this medicine. It gets better as the dose comes down.
Caller -> That's what I figured. I just wanted to hear it.
Nurse -> And are you eating okay? Any heartburn?
Caller -> I'm eating everything. I'm starving all the time. That's the steroid too, right?
Nurse -> Yes, it can make you very hungry. Try to choose lower sugar snacks while your sugars are up.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stay away from the cookies. My neighbor keeps bringing cookies, though. Lemon ones.
Nurse -> Ha. A little at a time.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you so much, Ana. You are a lifesaver.
Nurse -> Anytime.

Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi. Yes. Hello. My name is Pete Granger. I'm a neighbor. I'm calling about Alma next door. Alma Sutherland.
Nurse -> Hi, Pete. Thanks for calling. Do you know Alma's date of birth?
Caller -> Oh, gosh. No. I know she turned eighty seven last spring, her daughter told me. But the date, no. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's alright. We can work around it. Is Alma okay right now?
Caller -> She's awake. She's in her chair by the window. She's okay. It's just that she told me this morning she hasn't gone, you know, number two, in four days. And she's embarrassed. I could tell.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me, Pete. It's very common and we can help with it. What's a good number for you?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, oh one eight three.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, zero one eight three.
Caller -> That's it. That's my house phone.
Nurse -> Okay. So four days with no bowel movement. Does she have any belly pain?
Caller -> She said some cramps. On and off. She said it's, what did she say, a three? A three out of ten.
Nurse -> Okay. And does her belly look swollen or tight to you?
Caller -> It does, actually. It looks puffy. Kind of tight. She keeps pressing on it with her hand.
Nurse -> Okay. Any nausea? Has she thrown up?
Caller -> No. No throwing up. She ate some toast this morning. And half a banana.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. And how much has she been drinking?
Caller -> Not much. She says she's not thirsty. A cup of tea this morning, that's about it.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she take anything for constipation?
Caller -> Yes, there's a box on the counter. Senna. The purple box. She told me she takes two at bedtime.
Nurse -> Okay. Senna, two at bedtime. And is she on any pain medicine? Like oxycodone?
Caller -> Yeah, I see the oxycodone bottle on the counter too. She takes it for her back. Five milligrams, it says on the label. Every four hours if she needs it.
Nurse -> Okay. That can slow things down. Pete, are you with her during the day?
Caller -> No, no. I'm next door. I check on her every morning and again in the evening. Her daughter lives in Oregon, so I'm kind of, you know, the person.
Nurse -> That's really kind of you. It means a lot.
Caller -> Oh, it's nothing. She makes me banana bread. And the dog loves her. He's sitting right on her feet now, he followed me over.
Nurse -> Ha. Dogs know. What kind of dog?
Caller -> A beagle. Well, half beagle. Mostly he's a, he's a couch. He doesn't do anything.
Nurse -> That sounds like good company for her.
Caller -> It is. It really is. She talks to him. She tells him all about her day, even when nothing happened.
Nurse -> How long have you two been neighbors?
Caller -> Thirty one years. We moved in the same spring. Her husband, Walt, he and I used to do the gutters together every fall. He passed a while back. So now I do hers.
Nurse -> Oh, Pete. That's lovely.
Caller -> Well. It's what you do. You know. Anyway. Okay, sorry. Back to Alma.
Nurse -> No, it's fine. I'm glad she has you. Will you be around to let the nurse in tomorrow?
Caller -> Yes. I have her spare key. I'm retired. I'm over there every morning at eight, so I can just stay till they come.
Nurse -> No, it's fine. Okay, Pete. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message her hospice provider about a stronger plan for her bowels.
Caller -> Okay. A stronger plan. Good.
Nurse -> And one of our nurses will come see her tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I'll make sure she's up and I'll let them in.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I'll call you back tonight to let you know what the provider says.
Caller -> Tonight. Okay. Same number.
Nurse -> Yes. Meanwhile, see if she'll drink some fluids. Water, prune juice, warm tea, whatever she likes. And small meals, a little fruit if she can.
Caller -> Prune juice. She hates it. But I'll tell her it's medicine. I'll bring her some tonight.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. And Pete, if she starts vomiting, if the belly pain gets bad, or she can't pass gas, call us right away.
Caller -> Vomiting. Pain. No gas. Okay. Should I write that down?
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> Okay, I have a pen. Vomiting, belly pain, no gas. Call Cedar Point.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else I can help you with?
Caller -> No. No, that's everything. Thank you so much, Beth. She'll be glad someone's coming.
Nurse -> We'll take good care of her. Thanks for looking out for her.
Caller -> Of course. I'll tell her you called. She'll pretend she's annoyed, but she'll be glad.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her Beth says hello.
Caller -> Will do. Bye now.

Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Gwen, it's Dolores Pennington. It's my husband, Orville. He can't breathe right.
Nurse -> Okay, Dolores, I'm right here. Slow down for me. First, what is Orville's date of birth, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> September twenty seventh. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And the number you're calling from, is it five seven three, five five five, zero one four eight?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's the house phone.
Nurse -> Okay. Now tell me how he's breathing right now.
Caller -> Fast. And shallow. He's sitting up in the recliner, he's gripping the arms. He can only say a few words at a time. Like three words and then he has to stop.
Nurse -> Okay. When did this start?
Caller -> Last night. It got worse around dinner. But then in the last hour it's gotten really, really bad. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> You're doing the right thing by calling. Let's go step by step. Is his oxygen on?
Caller -> Yes. It's on. It's on three liters, like always, for his COPD. The machine is humming, I checked.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Do you have the little finger meter? The pulse oximeter?
Caller -> Yes. Hold on. Let me, hold on. Orville, give me your finger. Orville. Okay. It says eighty four. Eighty four.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. And what is it usually?
Caller -> Ninety. Ninety one, ninety two. It's never this low. Never.
Nurse -> Okay. Dolores, what color are his lips?
Caller -> They look, they look kind of gray. Bluish gray. Around the mouth, too.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he used his albuterol?
Caller -> Yes. I did the breathing treatment twice. The nebulizer with the albuterol. Once about an hour ago, and again about twenty minutes ago. And it's not helping. It's not helping at all.
Nurse -> Okay. On a scale of one to ten, how hard is it to breathe? Can you ask him?
Caller -> Orville. Honey. How hard is it to breathe, one to ten? He's holding up nine fingers. Nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have any chest pain, that you know of?
Caller -> He says no. He shook his head. He said no chest, no pain, when I asked.
Nurse -> Any fever? Any new cough or colored phlegm?
Caller -> No fever. I took it this morning. It was normal. And it's the same cough as always. White. Nothing new.
Nurse -> Okay. And his legs, any swelling in his ankles or legs?
Caller -> No. They look the same. Skinny, honestly. He's lost so much weight. No swelling.
Nurse -> Okay. Has anyone been sick around him? Anybody with a cold?
Caller -> Well. Our grandson was here last weekend. He had a cold. A runny nose. I told him to stay home but his mother brought him anyway.
Nurse -> Okay. That could be part of it. Dolores, I want to check something with you. Can you follow the oxygen tubing from the machine all the way to his nose? Is there a kink, or is it pinched under the chair?
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm looking. The tubing goes behind the chair, and, hold on. No. No, it's straight. It's not kinked. The cannula is in his nose.
Nurse -> Good. And is there a backup tank in the house?
Caller -> Yes. In the hall. It's full. The man from the oxygen company checked it on Tuesday.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. If the machine stops or you hear it alarm, switch him to the tank right away.
Caller -> Switch to the tank. Okay. The machine is fine. It's still going.
Nurse -> Okay. Now help him sit as upright as he can, leaning a little forward, with his arms resting on a table or a pillow. And turn a fan on, pointing toward his face.
Caller -> He's already sitting up. Let me get a pillow. Okay. Putting a pillow on the tray table. Orville, lean on it. Lean forward. Okay. There. And the fan. I have the little fan from the bedroom. Okay. It's on.
Nurse -> Good. And tell him to breathe in through his nose, and out slowly through pursed lips, like he's blowing out a candle.
Caller -> Orville, like a candle. In the nose. Out like a candle. He's trying. He's trying so hard.
Nurse -> I know. You're doing great, Dolores. Both of you. Dolores, I'm going to page our on-call nurse right now.
Caller -> Please. Please hurry. He's really struggling to breathe. Can someone come now? Please.
Nurse -> Yes. A nurse will come to the house, and she'll be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Okay. That's so long, though.
Nurse -> I know it feels long. We'll do everything we can to get her there faster. While I have you, can you turn on the porch light and unlock the front door so she can come right in?
Caller -> The porch light. Yes. Hold on. I can reach the switch from here. Okay. It's on. And the door, I'll, hold on, I'll go unlock it. Orville, I'm just going to the door. I'll be right back. I'm right back.
Nurse -> Take your time, I'm here. Don't go far from him.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. It's unlocked. The dog is going crazy, he knows something is wrong.
Nurse -> Is the dog a big one? The nurse will need to get in without being knocked over.
Caller -> Oh, no, no. Little. He's a little terrier. I'll put him in the bedroom. Hold on. Okay, he's in. He's barking but he's in.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're thinking of everything, Dolores.
Caller -> I don't feel like it. I feel like I'm shaking.
Nurse -> That's normal. Take a breath yourself. In through your nose, slowly.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. In. Out. Okay.
Nurse -> Is there anything in the way at the front, steps, a gate, anything the nurse should know about?
Caller -> Three steps up to the porch. No gate. Our son put a rail in last year. The house number is on the mailbox, it's a big one, you can see it from the street.
Nurse -> Great. That's helpful.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I'm sorry I'm so, I'm not usually like this.
Nurse -> You don't have to apologize. You are doing exactly what he needs.
Nurse -> Okay. In the meantime, I need to ask you something important. Has Orville signed a DNR? Does he have his wishes written down?
Caller -> Yes. We signed it in the spring. He doesn't want to go back to the hospital. He told me that, he told the doctor, he told everybody. He wants to stay home.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. I understand. Then we'll focus on keeping him as comfortable as we can and getting the nurse to you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you for understanding.
Nurse -> Of course. Dolores, check his finger meter again now that he's leaning forward.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. It's, it says eighty six. Eighty six now.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a little better. Keep him leaning forward, and keep the fan on his face.
Caller -> Okay. His breathing is, I think it's a little slower. Maybe. A little.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anyone else in the house with you?
Caller -> No. Just us. Our son is in Springfield, that's an hour away. I'll call him after this.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good idea. Do that once we hang up. Dolores, I'm going to hang up so I can reach the on-call nurse, and I'll call you back in ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay. Please call. I'll keep the phone right next to me.
Nurse -> I will. And if his lips get darker, if he can't say anything at all, or if you can't wake him, call me right back.
Caller -> Darker. Can't talk. Can't wake him. Okay. Okay, I will.
Nurse -> And don't give him anything from the comfort kit until the on-call nurse tells you what to give.
Caller -> Okay. Nothing from the kit. Okay.
Nurse -> You are doing everything right, Dolores. Hang in there.
Caller -> Thank you, Gwen. Thank you so much. Please call. I'll keep my hand on his back and watch him.
Nurse -> That's perfect. He knows you're there. Just talk to him, tell him the nurse is on the way.
Caller -> I will. Orville, the nurse is coming. Gwen is sending her. Okay. Okay, I'm going to hang up now.
Nurse -> Ten minutes.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. It's Adaeze Oyelowo. I'm calling about my father, Bertram Oyelowo. He came home from the hospital a few days ago, and I have a whole bag of pills, and I think I messed something up.
Nurse -> Okay, Adaeze. Take a breath. We'll go through it together. Can I get his date of birth first?
Caller -> May sixteenth. Nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And the best number for you, is it three oh one, five five five, zero one six eight?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What was the hospital stay for?
Caller -> His heart. Heart failure. Five days in. They sent him home four days ago.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's worrying you?
Caller -> The pills. They gave me a new list when he left. But we also had his old pillbox from before. And I filled the box from the old bottles, and then tonight I looked at the paper and I think I gave him something I shouldn't have.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's sort it out. Do you have the discharge paper and the bottles in front of you?
Caller -> Yes. All of them. They're on the kitchen table. Hold on, let me sit down.
Nurse -> Take your time. Let's start with the paper. What does it list?
Caller -> Okay. Metoprolol succinate. Fifty milligrams. Once a day in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Metoprolol succinate, fifty milligrams, once a day in the morning. Is he taking that?
Caller -> Yes. Every morning since he's been home.
Nurse -> Good. Next one.
Caller -> Um. Eliquis. No, wait. Apixaban. Five milligrams, twice a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Apixaban, five milligrams, twice a day. That's his blood thinner. Is he taking it?
Caller -> Yes. Morning and night. I set an alarm on my phone so I don't forget.
Nurse -> Great. Next.
Caller -> Furosemide. Forty milligrams. Morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Furosemide, forty, every morning. Taking that?
Caller -> Yes. Every morning. He complains because he has to keep going to the bathroom.
Nurse -> That's what it's for. Next.
Caller -> Potassium chloride. Twenty. Milliequivalents? M E Q. Once a day. It's new. I picked it up yesterday. But I haven't started it, because I wasn't sure. The paper says start, but the pharmacist said maybe ask.
Nurse -> Okay. Potassium chloride, twenty milliequivalents, once a day. So he hasn't taken any yet?
Caller -> No. None. It's still sealed in the bag.
Nurse -> Okay. Hold off on the potassium until I hear back from his cardiologist. I'll explain in a second.
Caller -> Okay. Hold off. Okay.
Nurse -> Is there anything else on the paper?
Caller -> Atorvastatin at night. That's on the list too. And then under it there's a section that says stopped.
Nurse -> Okay. What's under stopped?
Caller -> Aspirin. Eighty one milligrams. It says discontinue. And, oh no. Oh no. Tom, I gave him the aspirin.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you give him the aspirin?
Caller -> Every morning since he came home. This morning too. It was in the old pillbox. I filled the box from the old bottles, and the aspirin was one of them. I gave him the aspirin the last three mornings.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you caught it, Adaeze. I need to ask a few things. He's on the apixaban, and aspirin on top of that can raise the risk of bleeding. Has he had any bleeding? Nosebleeds, blood in his stool or urine?
Caller -> No. None of that. No blood in his stool, I check. No blood in his urine. And no nosebleeds.
Nurse -> Any new bruises?
Caller -> Actually, yes. On his forearms. A couple of purple ones. I thought it was from the hospital IV, but I think they're new. They weren't there when he came home.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. How is he feeling today? Dizzy? Short of breath?
Caller -> He gets a little dizzy when he stands up. Since he got home. Not falling or anything. Just a little woozy. And his breathing is okay.
Nurse -> Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> Yes. I took it this morning. One eighteen over seventy.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reasonable. Adaeze, here's what I'm going to do. First, stop the aspirin completely. Take it out of the pillbox today and put the bottle away.
Caller -> Okay. Out of the box. Bottle away. Okay.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to call his cardiologist about the three days of aspirin with the apixaban, and about the new bruises, and ask about the potassium.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Can I ask something? My brother says I should have just left the aspirin in because it's good for the heart. Is he right?
Nurse -> The hospital stopped the aspirin for a reason, and a big part of that is the apixaban. Let the cardiologist decide, not your brother.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him. He's going to argue, but I'll tell him.
Nurse -> Third, I'm going to ask his pharmacy to print a clean medication list and check that there's nothing else left over from the old prescriptions.
Caller -> Oh, that would help. Because the old bottles are the problem. I can bring them all to you.
Nurse -> You can, actually. A nurse will come out Thursday and sit down with you and set up the pillbox from scratch.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. Good. Thank you. I feel so stupid.
Nurse -> You shouldn't. This happens a lot after a hospital stay. The paperwork is confusing, and you caught it.
Caller -> I caught it because I got curious about the list. If I hadn't, he'd have gotten it tomorrow too.
Nurse -> Well, you did look. Adaeze, is he taking anything else? Anything over the counter, for pain, or a sleep aid?
Caller -> Just Tylenol at night sometimes. For his knee. Five hundred milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol is fine. But don't give him ibuprofen or naproxen, like Advil or Aleve. Those can cause bleeding and also hurt the heart.
Caller -> Okay. Tylenol is okay. No Advil. No Aleve. I think there's a bottle of Advil in the cabinet. I'll throw it out.
Nurse -> Good. And I'll call you back tomorrow morning once I hear from the cardiologist.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I work from nine but I'll have my phone on me.
Nurse -> That's fine. Now, here are the things to watch for. Black or bloody stools, blood in his urine, a nosebleed that won't stop, or if he falls and hits his head, call nine one one.
Caller -> Black stools, blood in urine, nosebleed that won't stop, fall and hit his head. Okay. I'm writing it on the paper.
Nurse -> Good. Also, weigh him every morning, same scale, after he uses the bathroom. Call us if he's up three pounds in a day or five in a week.
Caller -> Okay. Three in a day, five in a week. We have a scale. I wrote down his weight from the hospital on the paper.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the atorvastatin at night stays the same. No changes there.
Caller -> Okay. I thought so.
Nurse -> How is he doing otherwise? Is he eating?
Caller -> He's eating okay. He's grumpy. He hates the low salt food. He keeps asking for his soup from the can.
Nurse -> Ha. Yes, that's a hard one. Canned soup is very salty. Maybe try making a batch yourself without added salt.
Caller -> I could do that. My mother used to make a pepper soup, with the chicken, and the little peppers, and ginger. I'll try to remember how she made it. He'd love that. He grew up on it.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful. Anything else you want to go over tonight?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you, Tom. Really. I was panicking. My hands were shaking when I read the word stopped.
Nurse -> I'd have been the same. Honestly, the fact that you read the whole paper is why we caught this.
Caller -> My husband keeps saying I read too much. Tonight I'm telling him he's wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him I said so.
Nurse -> You did the right thing by calling. We'll talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Palliative Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Gianna Santoro. I'm calling about my mom. Imelda Santoro. She's been throwing up.
Nurse -> Oh no. Okay, Gianna. I'm here. What's your mom's date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty fourth. Nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> And is six one oh, five five five, zero one seven seven a good number for you?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's been happening.
Caller -> She's been nauseous for two days. Really queasy. And yesterday she threw up twice. Once in the morning and once in the evening.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she vomited today?
Caller -> Not today. Not yet. But she says she feels like she's going to. All the time. She just lies there with her eyes closed.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have anything for nausea?
Caller -> Yes, the ondansetron. The little melt-in-your-mouth ones. Four milligrams. She can have one every eight hours if she needs it.
Nurse -> Okay. When did she last take the ondansetron?
Caller -> This morning. About eight. It helps a little. It takes the edge off for a few hours, but it doesn't make it go away.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating anything?
Caller -> A few bites. That's it. A bite of toast, a couple of crackers. Nothing else. She says the smell of food makes it worse.
Nurse -> Okay. And how about drinking?
Caller -> Sips. Very small. I keep offering water and she keeps pushing it away. And her urine is dark. Dark yellow, almost brown.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?
Caller -> No. I checked this morning. She was normal.
Nurse -> Any belly pain, or cramping?
Caller -> No. No pain in her belly. She says it's just the nausea.
Nurse -> Okay. Gianna, did anything change with her medicines recently?
Caller -> Well. Yes. She started the patch last Thursday. The fentanyl patch. The twelve one. For her back. We put one on and it's supposed to last three days.
Nurse -> Okay. So the fentanyl patch, twelve micrograms an hour, changed every seventy two hours. That's useful to know, because nausea can be a side effect when we start one.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't think of that. She's been on the other pain medicine for months and never got sick. I thought it was a stomach bug. Her neighbor's grandson had one.
Nurse -> It could be. I can't say for sure. I'll message her palliative provider about the nausea and the patch together.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I just want her to stop feeling sick.
Nurse -> I know. I'll call you back this afternoon after I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. I'll be here. I'm working from home today so I'm right next to her.
Nurse -> That's good. And a nurse will come see her tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time, do you know?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time window. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. That's fine. Thank you.
Nurse -> Now, in the meantime, offer very small amounts of fluid. A sip, or an ice chip, or a bite of a popsicle every few minutes. Crackers or dry toast if she wants something.
Caller -> Ice chips. Popsicles. She might like that. She likes the orange ones.
Nurse -> Orange is a good choice. Cold things often go down easier than warm ones when she's queasy.
Caller -> That makes sense. She won't touch her tea anymore. She used to have it with honey, three times a day. Now she says the smell turns her stomach.
Nurse -> That's very common. Smells can be the worst part. If you can, keep cooking smells away from her room, and maybe let the food cool down before you bring it in.
Caller -> Okay. I made soup yesterday and the whole house smelled. I think that didn't help. I'll stop. I'll just do cold things.
Nurse -> Perfect. And keep the room cool with a little fresh air, a cool cloth on her forehead, and keep her head raised after she drinks.
Caller -> Cool cloth. Head up. Okay. I'll open the window.
Nurse -> And Gianna, take care of yourself too. Are you eating, are you sleeping a little?
Caller -> Sort of. I keep waking up to check on her. My brother lives in Phoenix so it's mostly me. It's fine. I just worry.
Nurse -> It's a lot to carry. You're allowed to call us just to ask a question, you don't need a crisis to call.
Caller -> Thank you. That really helps. I always feel like I'm bothering somebody.
Nurse -> Good. Gianna, I want you to call us if she can't keep any fluids down for twelve hours, if she hasn't passed urine in eight hours, if she gets belly pain, or if she seems confused.
Caller -> Twelve hours. Eight hours. Belly pain. Confused. Okay. I'm writing it on a sticky note.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else I can help you with?
Caller -> No. I don't think so. Thank you, Naomi. It helps just to talk to someone.
Nurse -> Of course. Hang in there. We'll talk this afternoon.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Caller -> The morphine. The liquid. I gave her the dose, the five milligrams, and then I forgot I did it. And I gave her another one. About ten minutes later. Two doses. I gave her two.

Nurse -> Okay. How is she right now? Is she awake?

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Lorraine.
Caller -> Hi, Lorraine. This is Francesca Marchetti. My mother is Estelle Marchetti. I think, I think it's getting close.
Nurse -> Okay, Francesca. I'm so glad you called. I'm here with you. Let me get her date of birth first.
Caller -> December second. Nineteen thirty two.
Nurse -> And the best number for you, is it seven eight one, five five five, zero one six two?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm at her house.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> She's sleeping. All the time now. Since Sunday she's mostly asleep. And today I can barely wake her. I say her name and she opens her eyes a little and then she's gone again.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating or drinking anything?
Caller -> No. Nothing. Three days. Not even water. I put a little spoon of applesauce to her lips yesterday and she turned her head away.
Nurse -> Okay. That is very common at this stage. What else have you noticed?
Caller -> Her knees. They're purple. Kind of blotchy. Like a bruise, but all over, lacy. And her feet are cold. Her hands too.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. And her breathing?
Caller -> It's loud. It sounds wet, like a rattle in her chest. And then sometimes she stops. For a few seconds. And then she takes a big breath. I counted ten seconds once.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she look like she's in pain? Is she grimacing, or moaning?
Caller -> No. No, she looks peaceful. Her face is relaxed. It's just the sound. The sound is hard.
Nurse -> I'm glad she looks comfortable. That sound comes from secretions she can't clear anymore, and it usually bothers the family more than the patient.
Caller -> That's what the pamphlet said. But hearing it is different.
Nurse -> I know. It is different.
Caller -> Lorraine. How long does this last? I don't know if I should call my brother. He's flying in tomorrow, but if it's tonight. I don't know. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> I can't tell you exactly. Everyone is different. But the changes you're describing, the sleeping, no eating or drinking, the mottling, the pauses in her breathing, they tell us she is very close. It could be hours. It could be a few days.
Caller -> Hours or days. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Francesca, are you there by yourself right now?
Caller -> Yes. I mean, my husband is on his way, but he's an hour out. He's coming from work. And my brother's flight lands tomorrow morning. So it's just me tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. I don't want you to do this alone. I'm going to send a nurse to the house now, and she'll be there within two hours.
Caller -> Thank you. Oh, thank you. I didn't want to ask, I didn't want to be a bother.
Nurse -> You're not. This is exactly what we're here for.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Has she had any medicine today? Anything for comfort, for the breathing?
Caller -> Yes. The morphine, the liquid, under her tongue. I gave her some at four. From the comfort kit.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. I'm also going to message her provider about something for the rattle in her breathing. There's a medicine that can dry up the secretions.
Caller -> Okay. That would be good. That would help me, honestly.
Nurse -> And our social worker will give you a call this evening. She can help with anything you need, including the family.
Caller -> Okay. That'd be nice. Thank you.
Caller -> Her priest wanted to know when it was time. Should I call him?
Nurse -> Yes. Please call him now. If he can come tonight, that's wonderful.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call him after we hang up. Father Dominic. He's known her thirty years.
Nurse -> That will mean a lot to her, and to you. Now, while we wait, here are some things that will keep her comfortable. Wet her lips and mouth with a damp swab every hour or so, and put a little lip balm on.
Caller -> Swab. Lip balm. Okay. We have the pink sponge sticks from the kit.
Nurse -> Perfect. And turn her gently from side to side every couple of hours, with pillows behind her back. Turning her on her side can help the rattle, too.
Caller -> Side. Pillows. Okay. She's so light. She weighs nothing now.
Nurse -> I know. Move slowly, and if it's too much, wait for the nurse. You can use lotion on her hands and feet. Keep a light blanket on her, not heavy ones. The cold hands and feet are part of this.
Caller -> Okay. I put the pink blanket on her this morning. The crocheted one. She loved that blanket.
Nurse -> That's lovely. And keep talking to her. Hearing is the last sense to go. She can still hear you.
Caller -> I've been talking to her all day. I read her the psalm she liked. And I played her Sinatra. She used to dance in the kitchen to Sinatra.
Nurse -> That is exactly right. What was she like, your mom?
Caller -> Oh. Stubborn. Funny. She raised four of us by herself after my dad died. She worked nights at the bakery for twenty years. She'd come home at six in the morning smelling like bread and make us eggs before school.
Nurse -> That sounds like a woman who gave you everything.
Caller -> She did. She really did. I don't know how she did it. And now she's so small. I keep looking at her hands. They were always flour and strong hands.
Nurse -> Take your time with her. There's no rush tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Is it okay if I get in the bed with her? Is that allowed?
Nurse -> Of course. Whatever feels right.
Caller -> Okay. I wasn't sure. I didn't want to hurt her. Okay.
Nurse -> Lie next to her, hold her hand, put your head by hers if you want to. Some people find it quiets the room.
Caller -> I think I'd like that. I'm so tired. I haven't really slept since Saturday. I kept thinking if I fell asleep I'd miss something.
Nurse -> That is so common. The nurse who is coming can sit with her so you can rest a little, if you want.
Caller -> I don't think I could rest. But it's nice to know. Thank you.
Nurse -> You won't hurt her. Francesca, if she seems uncomfortable, if she's restless, if she's grimacing, or if anything at all worries you, call us right away. Day or night.
Caller -> Day or night. Okay.
Nurse -> And one more thing. If she stops breathing, you don't need to call nine one one. You call us, and we'll come.
Caller -> Not nine one one. Call you. Okay. That's what the paper on the fridge says too.
Nurse -> Right. The number on the paper reaches us any hour, and one of the nurses will pick up.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I have it. I have the number.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anyone who can sit with you until the nurse comes?
Caller -> My neighbor, Mrs. Pellegrino, she offered. I'll call her. She's right next door.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Call her now, and then call Father Dominic. I'll stay on if you want me to while you do.
Caller -> No, no, I'm okay. I'll call them from the other phone. Thank you. Thank you for talking to me.
Nurse -> Of course. You're doing a beautiful thing for your mother.
Caller -> I don't feel like it. I feel like I'm falling apart.
Nurse -> That is what doing a beautiful thing feels like, most of the time.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you, Lorraine.
Nurse -> One more thing, Francesca. Is the front door unlocked, or will you be able to let the nurse in?
Caller -> I'll unlock it. And I'll turn on the porch light. It's getting dark. The house is on Birchwood, the blue one with the white shutters. The number's on the mailbox.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's all she needs.
Caller -> Okay. I'm going to go sit with Mom. I'll call the priest, and the neighbor, and then I'll sit with her.
Nurse -> That sounds like exactly the right plan. The nurse will be there soon.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Dennis.
Caller -> Hi, Dennis. It's Thandi Mbatha. I'm calling about my father, Alistair Mbatha. It's his sugar. It's been high two days and I'm not sure I'm doing his shots right.
Nurse -> Okay, Thandi. We'll go through it together. First, his date of birth?
Caller -> September ninth. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And for you, seven oh six, five five five, zero one seven three?
Caller -> That's right. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What was his sugar this morning?
Caller -> Three twelve. Before breakfast. Yesterday morning it was two ninety something. I didn't write it down.
Nurse -> Okay. And what did you give him this morning?
Caller -> The lispro. Okay, I have the sheet right here. The sliding scale. It says two fifty one to three hundred is six units. Three oh one to three fifty is eight units. So I gave him eight.
Nurse -> Okay. So eight units of lispro at three twelve. That matches the scale you just read me. What about his long-acting one?
Caller -> The glargine. Twenty units at bedtime. Every night. I gave it last night at ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Glargine, twenty units at bedtime. Let me pull up his chart so we're looking at the same orders.
Caller -> Okay. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay, I have it. Glargine twenty units at bedtime, and the lispro sliding scale before meals. I also see metformin on his list, and we're not changing that today.
Caller -> Okay. Fine. That's the one he takes with breakfast and dinner.
Nurse -> Right. What was his sugar before lunch today?
Caller -> Two forty five. I gave him four units. That's what the scale says for two oh one to two fifty.
Nurse -> Okay. Is that four units of the lispro?
Caller -> Yes. The lispro. Four.
Nurse -> Okay. Thandi, are you giving the lispro before he eats or after?
Caller -> Before. I check the sugar, then I do the shot, then I make the food. But sometimes he doesn't want to eat after. He says he isn't hungry. Like this morning, he only ate half his oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a really good question to ask. We'll talk about it in a second. First, has he been thirsty, or going to the bathroom a lot?
Caller -> Yes. Both. He's drinking and drinking. Juice, mostly. And sweet tea, the way my mother used to make it. And he was up three times last night to pee.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had any shaky, sweaty spells? Any low sugars?
Caller -> No. None. His lowest this week was one forty. No shaking. No sweating. He's fine that way.
Nurse -> Okay. So the sugars are running high, but there are no lows. That's helpful. Here's what I'd like you to do. Keep giving the lispro exactly by the scale. Don't give extra.
Caller -> Okay. No extra. I was tempted to give more this morning. I looked at the number and I thought, it's too high, I'll add two.
Nurse -> I understand the instinct. But extra insulin on top of the scale can drop him low, especially if he doesn't eat much.
Caller -> That's what I was afraid of. That's why I called.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Now, your question about eating. If he says he's not going to eat at least half of the meal, check with me before you give the lispro.
Caller -> Check with you. Okay. At any hour?
Nurse -> During the day, call us. After hours, the on-call nurse will pick up the same number.
Caller -> Okay. I'll put that on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. Thandi, tell me about how you give it. Do you use the pen?
Caller -> Yes. The pen. I prime it, two units, to make sure it comes out. Then I dial the dose. Then I put it in his belly, I hold it for ten seconds. And I move around so it's not the same spot. My cousin is a nurse and she showed me over video, which helped a lot.
Nurse -> That's right. You're doing the technique well, and a video lesson from a nurse in the family is a real help. We'll watch you do it when the nurse visits so you can feel sure.
Caller -> Okay. That would help.
Nurse -> I'm going to message his provider about the high numbers and ask if the scale needs to change.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Do you think it will change?
Nurse -> I can't say. That's up to the provider. I'll call you back this evening to tell you what they say.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. I'm home by six.
Nurse -> Good. And a nurse will come out Friday to go over the shot technique and the scale with you.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Can it be after five? I work till four thirty.
Nurse -> I'll ask the scheduler to give you a late window.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps a lot.
Nurse -> Now, a few things until then. Check his sugar before every meal and at bedtime, and write every number down, even the ones you don't like. That way the provider can see the whole picture.
Caller -> Before every meal and bedtime. Write them down. I'll get a notebook.
Nurse -> And about the drinks. Try to swap the juice and the sweet tea for water or unsweetened tea. Those drinks push his sugar up a lot.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. He's not going to like that. He loves his sweet tea. He says it's the one thing he has left.
Nurse -> I hear you. Maybe a small glass with a meal, and water the rest of the time. We can talk about it when we visit.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try. I'll tell him the nurse said so. He listens to nurses more than he listens to me.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine with me. Does he eat the same things every day, or does it change?
Caller -> Mostly the same. Oatmeal in the morning with brown sugar. Rice and stew for lunch, he loves rice. And at night whatever I cook, usually chicken. I've been trying less salt too, because of his pressure.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good base. The brown sugar and the big portions of rice are things we can look at together when we visit.
Caller -> Okay. I never thought about the brown sugar. I thought oatmeal was healthy.
Nurse -> It is. It's just the sugar on top. A little cinnamon is a nice swap.
Caller -> Cinnamon. He might go for that. He used to put it on his toast.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine with me. And Thandi, I want you to call us if his sugar goes over four hundred or under seventy, or if he gets shaky, sweaty, very sleepy, or confused. And if you can't wake him, call nine one one.
Caller -> Over four hundred. Under seventy. Shaky, sweaty, sleepy, confused. Can't wake him, nine one one. Okay. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Good. If he's under seventy, give him half a cup of juice and recheck in fifteen minutes, then call us.
Caller -> Juice. Half a cup. Recheck. That's a good use for the juice, then.
Nurse -> Exactly. Keep a little bit in the house for that.
Caller -> I will. Okay.
Nurse -> How are you holding up? This is a lot to manage.
Caller -> I'm okay. It's a lot. He moved in with me in the spring after my mother passed. I'm learning as I go. Honestly, I didn't know anything about diabetes in March.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job. Most people would not have noticed the numbers or called.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot. I just don't want to get it wrong.
Nurse -> You're not getting it wrong. You're asking questions, and that's what keeps people safe.
Caller -> My brother says I'm overdoing it. He says Dad should just eat what he wants at his age. But I can't do that. I can't watch him get sick.
Nurse -> That's a hard place to be. It's your call as the one helping him every day, and the plan we're making is a good one.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll tell my brother you said that too.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Dennis.
Nurse -> Anything else tonight?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. I'll be waiting for your call this evening.
Nurse -> I'll call you.

Caller -> Yes. He's awake. He's sitting on the bathroom floor. He's holding a towel on it.

Caller -> January seventeenth, nineteen thirty eight. And four two three, five five five, zero one five six.

Nurse -> Yes. Call nine one one. Press a clean cloth firmly on the cut, and don't let him get up or move around. Unlock the front door.
Caller -> Nine one one. Press. Don't move him. Door. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll let the team know. Go ahead and call.

Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Samantha.
Caller -> Hi. This is Juanita Espinoza. I'm one of your patients. I have a question about my pills.
Nurse -> Hi, Juanita. Could I have your date of birth?
Caller -> March third. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> And is five oh five, five five five, zero one one nine a good number?
Caller -> Yes. The cell.
Nurse -> Great. What's your question?
Caller -> I take my thyroid pill every morning. The levothyroxine. Seventy five micrograms. And I take it with my coffee. And my calcium. All together at breakfast. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for asking. Let me check the chart. Levothyroxine, seventy five micrograms in the morning. That's what you're taking?
Caller -> Yes. That's the one. Every morning.
Nurse -> And the calcium. Is that a tablet, a chew?
Caller -> A tablet. A big one. I take it with the thyroid one so I don't forget either of them.
Nurse -> I understand. It makes sense to pair them. But the thyroid medicine doesn't work as well when it's taken with coffee or with calcium.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't know that. Is that why I'm still so tired?
Nurse -> It could be part of it. I can't say for sure. I'm going to message your prescriber to confirm the dose, because they may want to check your levels.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, take the levothyroxine first thing with a glass of water. Wait thirty to sixty minutes before you have coffee or breakfast. And take your calcium at least four hours later, with lunch or dinner.
Caller -> Thirty to sixty minutes. Water only. Calcium at lunch. Okay. I can do that. I'll put the calcium next to my lunch plate so I don't forget.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's all. Thank you for explaining it. Nobody ever told me.
Nurse -> You're welcome. We're glad you asked.

Caller -> Yes. The cell. I keep it with me because I can't get up and down fast.
Nurse -> I understand. What's going on with the knee?
Caller -> The incision. At the top end of it, there's a spot that's red. About the size of a dime. I noticed it when I changed the dressing this morning. I don't remember it being there yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the redness spreading, or does it stay in that one spot?
Caller -> I think it's the same since this morning. I looked again an hour ago. I'm not sure, honestly. I keep staring at it.
Nurse -> That's okay. Is there any drainage? Any fluid, pus, anything on the dressing?
Caller -> No. The dressing was dry. Clean. No stains.
Nurse -> Good. Any smell?
Caller -> No smell. Nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you checked your temperature?
Caller -> I did, just now. Ninety nine point one.
Nurse -> Okay. That's slightly warm but not a fever. How is your pain?
Caller -> About a four. It's been about a four most of the day. It gets better when I'm sitting with my foot up.
Nurse -> Okay. And what are you taking for it?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams. Every six hours is what the bottle says. I've taken two today. One at seven and one at one.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And is there any swelling?
Caller -> A little. The whole knee is puffy, but the surgeon said it would be for weeks. It's not worse than yesterday, I don't think. It's about the same.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like expected swelling. Lucille, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message your surgeon's office about the redness at the incision.
Caller -> Okay. Do you think it's an infection?
Nurse -> I can't say from the phone. A small spot that isn't draining and no fever is reassuring. But we want the surgeon's office to know, and we want to look at it in person.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. I just didn't want to wait and have it get worse.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling. A nurse will come see you tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. In the morning or afternoon, do you know?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. Is there a time that works better?
Caller -> Morning is better. My neighbor takes me to physical therapy at one, so before noon.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along to the scheduler.
Caller -> Thank you. That's very helpful.
Nurse -> Now, in the meantime, ice your knee for twenty minutes at a time, with a cloth between the ice and your skin. And keep your leg raised above your heart when you're resting.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Cloth. Leg up above my heart. Okay. I have a bag of frozen peas. They work great.
Nurse -> Frozen peas are perfect. And Lucille, call us right away if the redness spreads, if you see pus or smell something, if your temperature goes over one oh one, or if you get a sudden pain in your calf. If you get chest pain or trouble breathing, call nine one one.
Caller -> Spreads, pus, smell, over one oh one, calf pain. Chest pain or can't breathe, nine one one. Okay. Let me write that down.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Done. I have it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. How are you managing otherwise? Getting around the house okay?
Caller -> With the walker. It's slow, but I'm doing it. My daughter lives in Hartford and she's coming Saturday to help for a week. So I just have to get through till Saturday.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. A little help will make a big difference.
Nurse -> And are you sleeping okay with the knee?
Caller -> In pieces. An hour here, an hour there. I keep waking up when I roll over and bump it. My cat doesn't help. She sleeps right on the bad leg, I have to move her every time.
Nurse -> Ha. Cats find the one spot you can't have them. Try a pillow under the knee and one between your legs if you can.
Caller -> I'll try that tonight. The pillow thing. Thank you. I didn't think to ask anyone about sleeping, I figured it was just part of it.
Nurse -> Mention it to the nurse tomorrow too. Sleep matters for healing.
Caller -> I will.
Caller -> It really does. I miss my own bed, honestly, and the whole routine. The recliner is okay but my back is killing me, ha. Just kidding. It's fine.
Nurse -> Ha. If your back really bothers you, tell the nurse tomorrow too.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Naomi. You're always so patient with me.
Nurse -> It's my pleasure, Lucille. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Hector.
Caller -> Hello, Hector. It's Halina Dobrowolski. I'm calling about my husband, Casimir. Casimir Dobrowolski. I think his heart is acting up again. His legs are swollen and he's gained weight.
Nurse -> Okay, Halina. I'm glad you called. Let me get his date of birth.
Caller -> July nineteenth. Nineteen forty.
Nurse -> And is five eight five, five five five, zero one three one the best number for you?
Caller -> Yes. The house phone. I'm always here.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the weight. How much has he gained?
Caller -> We weigh him every morning, like you told us. Monday he was one eighty two. This morning he's one eighty six. So four pounds. In two days.
Nurse -> Okay. That's more than I'd like to see. And the swelling, where is it?
Caller -> His ankles. Both of them. They were a little puffy on Sunday, but now they're really puffy. I press with my thumb and it leaves a dent. It stays a few seconds.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he short of breath at all?
Caller -> Yes. A little. When he walks to the bathroom. Just to the bathroom, it's ten steps. He has to stop and catch his breath. That's new. Last week he could walk to the mailbox.
Nurse -> Okay. And at night, how is he sleeping?
Caller -> Not good. He's using two pillows. Before it was one. And he coughs. A dry cough, mostly when he lies back. I put an extra pillow under him last night and it helped a little.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have any chest pain?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. He says no. I ask him every day.
Nurse -> Any fever, chills?
Caller -> No. No fever. I took it this morning. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> Good. Have you taken his blood pressure and oxygen today?
Caller -> Yes. I have the machine. Blood pressure is one twenty eight over seventy six. And the oxygen on the finger thing says ninety four.
Nurse -> Is that the same machine and the same arm you've been using?
Caller -> The same one. The left arm. The nurse showed me how, with the cuff right at the heart, and his arm on the table. I do it sitting down, after he has rested five minutes. I'm very careful.
Nurse -> That's exactly right. You've been doing a great job with the log.
Caller -> Thank you. I keep everything in the notebook, the weights, the pressures, the pills. If the doctor asks, I can read it all to him.
Nurse -> Okay. Those are reasonable numbers. Halina, has he taken his water pill?
Caller -> The furosemide. Yes. Forty milligrams, every morning. He took it this morning at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Furosemide forty this morning. Did anything change this weekend, with food or anything else?
Caller -> Well. Maybe. Saturday our grandson was here, and I made ham sandwiches. And Sunday I made soup, from the can. I didn't think. It was an easy lunch. Casimir ate two sandwiches.
Nurse -> Okay. That can do it. Canned soup and ham are very salty, and salt makes the body hold on to water.
Caller -> I know. I know. I knew it while I was opening the can. You tell yourself it's one time. Our grandson was here and he wanted something quick, and Casimir was so happy to have him, and I just wanted everyone to be happy.
Nurse -> That makes total sense. A weekend with family is hard to turn into a diet. The important thing is we caught it in two days and not two weeks.
Caller -> That's true. Last time, I waited a week, and he ended up in the hospital. I didn't want that again.
Nurse -> That's why I'm so glad you called today.
Nurse -> It happens to everybody. It's good that you're telling me. Halina, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message his provider about the weight gain and the swelling, because they may want to adjust the water pill.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Do you think he needs to go to the hospital?
Nurse -> From what you're telling me, I don't think he needs the emergency room right now. His breathing is only short with walking, his oxygen is fine, and he has no chest pain. But we want to act quickly so it doesn't get worse.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel better.
Nurse -> A nurse will come see him tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a window. I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Morning is good. He has a doctor's appointment Tuesday, but that's another day. His cardiologist is in the city, and my daughter drives us, because I don't like the highway anymore.
Nurse -> That's helpful for the visit. The nurse can look at his legs, listen to his lungs, and check his weight on your scale and ours.
Caller -> Good. I'll make sure the scale is out where she can see it. And I'll make coffee. Do the nurses drink coffee? I never know.
Nurse -> Ha. Some do. Don't go to any trouble.
Nurse -> Good. And I'll call you back this evening once I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. I'll keep the phone near me.
Nurse -> Now, a few things until then. Keep weighing him every morning, after he uses the bathroom and before breakfast, same scale, and write it down.
Caller -> Every morning. After the bathroom, before breakfast. Same scale. Okay. I have a notebook on the table.
Nurse -> Perfect. And for food, no canned soup, no ham, no other salty things for now. Cook with herbs and lemon, not salt.
Caller -> No salt. Herbs and lemon. Okay. He is going to complain. He loves my sausage soup. My mother's recipe, from the old country, with the cabbage and the caraway.
Nurse -> That sounds delicious. Maybe we can find a version with much less salt and a lot of caraway, when he's feeling better.
Caller -> I'll try it. I'll leave out the sausage and use a little chicken. He won't know the difference. Or he will, but he won't say.
Nurse -> I know. We can find a way to do a lower salt version later. For now, keep it simple.
Caller -> Okay. Fresh vegetables. A little chicken. I can do that.
Nurse -> That sounds great. And when he's sitting, keep his feet up on a stool, higher than his hips if he can. And use extra pillows at night.
Caller -> Feet up. Extra pillows. I'll get the footstool from the bedroom.
Nurse -> Good. Halina, I also want you to call us if his breathing gets worse, if he can't lie flat at all, if he gains another two pounds overnight, or if the cough gets worse. If he has chest pain, or if he is struggling to breathe, call nine one one.
Caller -> Worse breathing, can't lie flat, two more pounds, worse cough. Chest pain or struggling, nine one one. Okay. I'm writing it on the notebook.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> How are you doing, Halina? You've been caring for him for a long time.
Caller -> I'm okay. It's seven years since his first heart attack. I'm tired, but he's my husband. We did our fiftieth anniversary in March. The kids came from Chicago. He danced one dance with me, he was so proud.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Keep that in mind. You're doing a great job.
Caller -> Thank you. You always make me feel better, Hector.
Nurse -> Anything else tonight?
Caller -> No, I think that's everything. Thank you. Thank you so much. I feel better just having a plan. When it gets quiet at night, that's when I start worrying.
Nurse -> That's very normal. If you wake up at night and something doesn't feel right, you can call the same number, any hour, and the on-call nurse will pick up.
Caller -> I didn't know that. I thought it was only for the daytime. Okay. I'll remember. I'll put the number on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. You've got a good system going, Halina.
Nurse -> I'll call you this evening.
Caller -> Okay. Goodbye.
