Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Declan Fitzsimmons. My mother is Maude Fitzsimmons, she's on your service. My sister went home tonight, so it's just me, and I don't know what I'm doing.
Nurse -> Okay, Declan. You called the right place. Let me start with your mom's date of birth.
Caller -> February fourteenth. Nineteen thirty five. Valentine's Day.
Nurse -> And is six oh three, five five five, zero one seven seven your number?
Caller -> Yes. My cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What's happening with Mom tonight?
Caller -> She's restless. She keeps picking at the sheets. She was sleeping all day and now she's, I don't know, agitated. She's moving her legs. And when I try to turn her, she moans.
Nurse -> Okay. Can she tell you if she's in pain?
Caller -> No. She can't talk anymore. I guess it's a five? If I had to guess. That's just my guess, from her face.
Nurse -> That's a good guess. We read faces when people can't speak. Anything else?
Caller -> Her breathing is starting to sound wet. A rattle. Not loud yet, but it's starting.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she feel warm?
Caller -> A little. I took her temperature under the arm. One hundred point two.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Declan, you have a comfort kit in the refrigerator. Have you opened it?
Caller -> Yes. It's on the kitchen counter now. I took it out. There are a bunch of little bottles. And I don't know what any of them are for. I'm afraid to give her the wrong one.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll go through them one by one. I have her orders in front of me. Pick up the bottle that says morphine.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Here. It says morphine concentrate, twenty milligrams per milliliter. There's a little syringe with it.
Nurse -> Right. The order is point two five milliliters, which is five milligrams, under the tongue every two hours if needed, for pain or for labored breathing. That's the morphine concentrate.
Caller -> Point two five. On the syringe it's the line, the first line. Okay. Every two hours.
Nurse -> Yes. And Declan, can I ask what you're most worried about with that one?
Caller -> That I'll give her too much. That it'll, you know. That I'll be the one who makes it happen.
Nurse -> I'm so glad you said that. The dose we gave you is a comfort dose. It is meant to treat pain and the struggle to breathe. Given as ordered, it eases her. It does not cause her to die sooner. Her illness is what's happening.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's what I needed to hear. I think I've been carrying that all day.
Nurse -> I know. You're doing exactly what she needs. So, for the moaning when you turn her, I'd give the morphine about twenty minutes before you turn her, and use pillows to turn her slowly.
Caller -> Twenty minutes before. Pillows. Slowly. Okay. Should I give it now?
Nurse -> Yes. She's moaning and restless, and it's been at least two hours since she's had anything, hasn't it?
Caller -> My sister gave her the last dose at ten. It's two now.
Nurse -> Perfect. Give point two five of the morphine under her tongue now. And write down the dose and the time every time.
Caller -> Okay. I'm doing it. Mom. Mom, it's Declan. Under your tongue. Okay. Done. It's two fifteen. I'm writing it.
Nurse -> Good. Tell her what you're doing as you go. Even when she can't answer, she hears you and it helps.
Caller -> I do. I told her it's me, and that she's okay. She squeezed my hand a little. I think that was her. Or I hope so.
Nurse -> I think so too.
Nurse -> Good. Thank you. Now pick up the one that says lorazepam.
Caller -> Lorazepam. Okay. Point five milligrams, little tablets.
Nurse -> Right. Lorazepam point five milligrams, one tablet under the tongue every four hours if needed. That one is for anxiety or restlessness. If she's still picking at the sheets after the morphine has had time to work, you can give the lorazepam.
Caller -> After the morphine. Not at the same time. Okay.
Nurse -> You can give both. But give the morphine first and see how she settles. And don't give the lorazepam more often than every four hours.
Caller -> Four hours. Okay. I'll watch the clock. I set an alarm on my phone for the morphine. Two hours from now. Four for the other one.
Nurse -> That's a smart idea. Label the alarms so you don't mix them up at three in the morning.
Caller -> Good point. Morphine, Mom one. Other, Mom two.
Nurse -> Now the little dropper bottle. It says atropine drops.
Caller -> Atropine drops. Here.
Nurse -> The order for the atropine drops is two drops under the tongue every four hours if needed, for the rattle. It dries up the secretions.
Caller -> Two drops. For the rattle. Her breathing isn't very loud yet. Do I give it now?
Nurse -> Not yet. Wait until the rattle is clearly there and bothers her, or you. It's fine to hold off for now.
Caller -> Okay. Hold off. I'll listen.
Nurse -> Next. Haloperidol. It's a small bottle of tablets, point five milligram.
Caller -> Haloperidol. Yes. Tablets. It says point five. Every six hours, as needed.
Nurse -> Yes. Haloperidol, point five milligrams, every six hours if needed. That's for severe agitation or confusion, or nausea. Don't use it unless the lorazepam doesn't settle her. If that happens, call me first.
Caller -> Call you first. Okay. I won't use it on my own.
Nurse -> Right. And the last one, the acetaminophen suppositories, six fifty milligrams.
Caller -> Acetaminophen. A box of suppositories. Six fifty.
Nurse -> The acetaminophen suppository, six fifty milligrams every six hours if needed, is for the fever. Her temperature of one hundred point two is only slightly high. I wouldn't give it yet. If it goes above one oh one, or if she looks hot and uncomfortable, give one suppository, and don't repeat it for six hours.
Caller -> Over one oh one. One suppository. Not again for six hours. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's all five. You've got it. Do you want me to repeat any of them?
Caller -> Can you say it one more time quick? Which one is for pain?
Nurse -> Morphine is for pain and for labored breathing. Lorazepam is for anxiety and restlessness. Atropine drops are for the rattle. Haloperidol is for severe agitation, call me first. Acetaminophen suppository is for fever.
Caller -> Okay. Morphine, pain and breathing. Lorazepam, restless. Atropine, rattle. Haloperidol, call you. Acetaminophen, fever. I wrote it on the back of an envelope.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Tape the envelope to the counter.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> I'm going to message her provider about the restlessness, the pain with turning, and the fever, so they know what's going on tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And a nurse will come out tomorrow morning to see her and go over this with you again.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. My sister will be back by then too, I think.
Nurse -> Good. And I'll call you back at nine tonight to see how she's doing.
Caller -> At nine. Okay. I'll have the phone on.
Nurse -> Declan, call me at any hour if you have questions or if she seems uncomfortable. You don't have to wait for nine.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. Even three in the morning?
Nurse -> Even three in the morning.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief. I was afraid I'd be bothering you.
Nurse -> You will never be bothering us. This is exactly what we're here for.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Gwen. I think I can do this.
Nurse -> You can. And you're already doing it.
Caller -> I'm going to sit with her. I'll hold her hand. She's calmer already. Maybe it's just me being here.
Nurse -> It's probably both. Talk to her. She knows your voice.
Caller -> I will. Okay. Thank you again.

Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's right.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Samira.
Caller -> Hi, Samira. It's Chidinma Okonkwo-Hart. I'm calling about my daughter, Mila. Mila Okonkwo-Hart. That's O K O N K W O, dash, H A R T.
Nurse -> Hi, Chidinma. Thank you for spelling it. Mila's date of birth?
Caller -> April second, twenty twenty three.
Nurse -> And is six seven eight, five five five, zero one zero nine still your number?
Caller -> Still the same. Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. What can I do for you today?
Caller -> I'm getting low on her feeding supplies. I wanted to get an order in before the weekend, since last time the delivery took forever.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Tell me what you have. Let's start with the formula.
Caller -> The formula. Okay. I have six cans. The big ones. We use about a can and a half a day, so that's about four days. Not enough for a week.
Nurse -> Okay. And the syringes?
Caller -> The big syringes, the sixty mil ones. I have two. Just two. One of them is getting kind of cloudy, I think it's old.
Nurse -> Okay. And the extension sets?
Caller -> The little tube that connects to her button. One spare. One. And the one on her now is from, I don't know, last Sunday.
Nurse -> Okay. How many feeds a day is she getting?
Caller -> Four. Morning, noon, afternoon, bedtime. She likes the noon one because I give it while she's watching her show.
Nurse -> That's a great routine. Any vomiting or diarrhea lately?
Caller -> No. None. She's been really good. Her tummy has been fine. No diarrhea either.
Nurse -> Good. And how is the skin around the tube? Any redness or leaking?
Caller -> No leaking. It's clean. A little dry sometimes but no redness. I check it every time I clean it.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order the formula, the sixty mil syringes, and the extension sets.
Caller -> Thank you. How many extension sets will you send? Last time it was just two.
Nurse -> I'll ask for a box so you have enough for a month.
Caller -> That would be amazing. Thank you.
Nurse -> They'll deliver Tuesday.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. Is it a window? I have to be home for it, right?
Nurse -> Someone needs to sign. You'll get a window from the delivery company. Is there a time that's better for you?
Caller -> After lunch is best. She naps from one to three and she's happier when she's sleeping through the knock on the door.
Nurse -> I'll note that. Is there anything else on your mind?
Caller -> Actually, yes. A question. A friend of mine, her son has a tube too, and she blends real food for him. Like sweet potato and chicken. Could I do that for Mila? I'd love for her to have real food.
Nurse -> That's a really good question, and a lot of families ask. I want our dietitian to answer it, because it depends on the size of her tube and what formula she's on. I'll message the dietitian for you.
Caller -> Okay. I won't do anything until I hear. I just wondered.
Nurse -> That's the right approach. Please don't put blended foods through the tube until the dietitian says it's safe. And keep flushing the tube with water after every feed.
Caller -> Flush with water after every feed. I do. Five mil. And no blended food until I hear. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a few notes on the supplies. After each use, rinse the syringes in warm, soapy water and let them air dry. And change the extension set once a week, or sooner if it looks cloudy.
Caller -> Warm soapy water. Air dry. Extension set weekly. Okay. I think I've been rinsing but not with soap. Is that bad?
Nurse -> Not terrible, but soap helps. Just rinse the soap out well.
Caller -> Okay. Good to know. I've been doing it wrong for a month, ha.
Nurse -> No, you've been doing a great job. Mila is lucky to have you.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot. Some days I'm not so sure. Last week she pulled the extension set right off in the middle of a feed and formula went everywhere. All over the carpet, all over me, and she thought it was hilarious.
Nurse -> Oh no. That happens to everybody at some point. Did you have to restart the feed?
Caller -> I just cleaned her up and gave her the rest with a new set. That's actually why I'm down to one spare. I used one that day.
Nurse -> That makes sense. That's why I'm asking for a whole box.
Caller -> Perfect. And I'm going to try one of those little onesies that snaps over the button. My friend says it keeps their hands off.
Nurse -> Those work well. It's a good idea.
Nurse -> You're doing great. How is she doing overall?
Caller -> She's wonderful. She just learned to say my name. Mama. Well, Mamma-ma. She walks around holding the couch. She's so determined.
Nurse -> That's fantastic. Give her a hug from us.
Caller -> I will. Okay, that's everything. Thank you, Samira.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Dennis.
Caller -> Hello, Dennis. It's Folasade Oduya. I'm calling about my husband, Barnabas Oduya. He's the one who had the stroke last month. I wanted to give an update and ask about a few things.
Nurse -> Hi, Folasade. I remember Barnabas. I'm glad you called. Let me confirm his date of birth.
Caller -> December fourteenth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> And your number, is it four six nine, five five five, zero one four four?
Caller -> Yes. The cell. I keep it on me.
Nurse -> Great. So how is he doing overall? It's been about three weeks.
Caller -> Three weeks on Tuesday. He's doing better, I think. In the first week, he couldn't lift his right arm at all. It was just hanging there. Now he can lift it up to his shoulder. Not above. But up to the shoulder. He was so happy when he did it, he cried.
Nurse -> That's wonderful progress. Is the therapist giving him exercises to do between visits?
Caller -> Yes. A sheet with pictures. Squeezing a soft ball, lifting his arm with the other hand helping, and standing up from the chair ten times. He does it twice a day when he feels like it. When he doesn't feel like it, I bribe him with pound cake.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works. Is his grip getting stronger?
Caller -> A little. He can hold a cup now with the right hand if it's not too full. He still uses the left for his fork. But the physical therapist says it's coming. She says everything comes back in its own order. First the shoulder, then the elbow, then the hand.
Nurse -> That's right, that's often how it goes. It takes patience.
Caller -> Patience I have. After fifty one years of marriage I have plenty of it. It's him that doesn't have any. He was a school principal for thirty years. He doesn't like waiting for anything.
Nurse -> I can imagine. That's a lot of schedule to give up.
Caller -> He still tells the nurses when to be on time. He told the physical therapist she was four minutes late.
Nurse -> That's good to hear. Any new weakness, any drooping in the face, any change in his speech?
Caller -> No. None of that. His speech is the same. Maybe a tiny bit better. A little slow, but clear. His face is straight. No new weakness. I check every day. I'm always checking.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. What else is on your mind?
Caller -> The coughing. When he drinks. Water, juice, tea. He coughs right after he swallows. Not every time but a lot. It started when he came home from the hospital. They said at the hospital his swallowing was okay, but I don't think it is.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important, and I'm glad you told me. Does he cough with food too, or mostly with thin liquids?
Caller -> Mostly liquids. Soft foods are fine. Applesauce, mashed potatoes, he doesn't cough. But thin things, yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Does his voice sound wet or gurgly after he drinks?
Caller -> Sometimes. A little bit. Like he needs to clear his throat. He does that after the tea.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?
Caller -> No. No fever. He's been normal.
Nurse -> Good. Folasade, I'd like to go over his medicines with you, so I'm looking at the same list. The chart shows clopidogrel, seventy five milligrams once a day. Is he taking that?
Caller -> Yes. Every morning. Clopidogrel. I give it with the oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay. And atorvastatin, forty milligrams at night.
Caller -> Yes. At bedtime. Every night. The atorvastatin.
Nurse -> And the lisinopril, ten milligrams once a day, which is new since the hospital.
Caller -> Yes. Lisinopril. In the morning too. They told me it was for his pressure. I took his pressure this morning. One forty two over eighty four.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a little higher than I'd like, but it's only one reading. Keep checking it every day and write it down.
Caller -> I do. I have a notebook. Each morning and each evening.
Nurse -> Perfect. How are his spirits? Strokes can hit people hard emotionally.
Caller -> Down, a bit. He's quiet. He doesn't want to do his exercises some days. He says the physical therapy is killing him. Ha. That's his joke. He's not serious. He's still got his sense of humor. But I can tell he's tired.
Nurse -> That's a good sign that he's joking. Fatigue and low spirits are really common after a stroke. We'll keep an eye on it. Any thoughts of hurting himself, anything like that?
Caller -> No. Oh no. Nothing like that. He's tired and frustrated. He says it's killing him but he means his legs ache. He's fine. He goes to church on Sunday with my daughter. He sings.
Nurse -> Good. Thank you for telling me. Is he sleeping okay at night, and is he eating?
Caller -> He sleeps well, thank God. Eight hours. His appetite is good, he eats everything I put in front of him. That part is easy. It's the walking that he doesn't like. He is scared of falling.
Nurse -> That's very understandable. The physical therapist can work on that confidence too. Is there anything else?
Caller -> One more thing. He hasn't had a bowel movement in three days. It's making him uncomfortable. He's not eating a lot of fiber, he doesn't like the cereals.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Folasade, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message his provider about the coughing with liquids and the constipation.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'd also like a speech therapist to do a swallow evaluation. I'll schedule that for Friday.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. That would be great. Is that at the house?
Nurse -> Yes. The therapist comes to the house. And a nurse will come out Thursday to see him too.
Caller -> Thursday. And Friday. Okay. I'll write it down.
Nurse -> Until the swallow evaluation, here's what to do with drinks. Have him sit all the way up, take small sips, and tuck his chin down a little when he swallows. And avoid thin liquids through a straw for now.
Caller -> All the way up. Small sips. Chin down. No straw. Okay. He likes the straw. He'll be annoyed.
Nurse -> I know. It's only until the therapist sees him.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell him it's the nurse's orders.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. Now, for the constipation, try some prune juice, but have him take it in small sips like the others. Add fruit and fiber if he'll take it, and I'll ask the provider about a stool softener.
Caller -> Prune juice. Fruit. A stool softener, if they say. Okay. He actually likes prune juice, funnily enough.
Nurse -> That's lucky. Now, Folasade, I need to make sure you know the signs of another stroke. If his face droops, if his arm or leg gets weak, if he has trouble speaking, if he gets suddenly confused, or has a severe headache, call nine one one right away. Don't wait.
Caller -> Face, arm, speech, confusion, headache. Nine one one. Right away. I know. The nurse in the hospital went over it. I have a magnet on the fridge. F A S T.
Nurse -> That magnet is a great idea. And call us for a fever, a wet gurgly voice after he drinks, or coughing that doesn't settle.
Caller -> Fever, gurgly, coughing. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> Not about the medical. But I just want to say thank you. You have all been so kind. I was scared when we came home. I didn't know how I'd do it. And now I feel like I can.
Nurse -> You are doing it. You're doing a great job, Folasade.
Caller -> I pray every night. For him, and for the nurses. God bless you. And for the therapist who is four minutes late.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Thank you. That means a lot. We'll see you Thursday, and Friday for the therapist.
Caller -> Yes. Thursday and Friday. I'll have the notebook out so you can see the blood pressures. Thank you, Dennis. Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Rhonda, it's Doreen Pickett. My husband is Millard Pickett. He's sick. His stool is black. Black like tar. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Doreen, I'm here. Tell me his date of birth first.
Caller -> August thirteenth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> And two seven oh, five five five, zero one five two, is that the best number?
Caller -> Yes. The kitchen phone. I'm walking to the other room so he can't hear me.
Nurse -> Okay. Is Millard awake right now, can he talk to you?
Caller -> Yes. He's awake. He's grumpy. He keeps telling me not to call anyone. He says he's seen worse. He hasn't seen worse.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the black stools. How many, and when?
Caller -> Three. Since last night. The first one was about nine o'clock, then one in the middle of the night, and one this morning. All black. Sticky. It smells awful, a smell I've never smelled before.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, that must be frightening to see. Was there any bright red blood, or only black?
Caller -> Only black. No red. I looked in the toilet every time. I'm the one who flushes, I didn't want him to see it. I should have called last night, I thought it was something he ate. He had the blueberry pie.
Nurse -> Blueberries can darken stool, but it wouldn't look like tar. I'm glad you're calling now.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he vomited?
Caller -> Once. This morning. And it was dark. Brownish black, like coffee grounds. I thought it was coffee at first. But he hadn't had any coffee yet.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he dizzy or lightheaded?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, he is. He got up to go to the bathroom and halfway down the hall he grabbed the wall. His knees went. I caught him. He didn't pass out but he almost did.
Nurse -> Okay. What color is his skin?
Caller -> Pale. Really pale. Like paper. And he's sweaty. His forehead is cold and wet.
Nurse -> Okay. Where is he right now? Sitting, lying down?
Caller -> He's on the edge of the bed. He won't lie down, he says it makes him feel worse. He's got his hand on his stomach.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay with me, Doreen. I need a few more answers.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have pain anywhere?
Caller -> His belly. The top part, under the ribs. He says it's dull. Like a four. He keeps rubbing it.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. He says no chest pain. Millard, any chest pain? No. He says no.
Nurse -> Okay. Doreen, is he taking any medicines for pain, for his arthritis?
Caller -> Yes. The ibuprofen. Four hundred milligrams. Three times a day. He's been taking it for a week. His knees were bad. The doctor told him to only take it twice a day, but he takes three. He took one this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else? Aspirin?
Caller -> The baby aspirin. Eighty one. Every day. For his heart.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he ever had stomach problems, an ulcer?
Caller -> Yes. A long time ago. Fifteen years ago. He had an ulcer. They told him to stay off the ibuprofen then, and he forgot.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had any alcohol this week?
Caller -> A beer on Sunday. One. He's not a drinker. Not since the ulcer.
Nurse -> Okay. And has he been able to pass urine today?
Caller -> Yes. A little. This morning. It was dark yellow.
Nurse -> Okay. Doreen, do you have a blood pressure machine?
Caller -> Yes. I'll get it. Hold on. It's in the bedroom. Millard, give me your arm. I know. I know you're fine. Hold still. Okay. It says ninety eight over sixty.
Nurse -> Okay. And does it show a pulse?
Caller -> Yes. One twelve. One hundred and twelve.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Is he alert? Is he talking normally?
Caller -> Yes. He's talking. He's saying he's fine. He's saying I'm making a big fuss. He says he just needs to lie down. He says he doesn't want to go to the hospital.
Nurse -> Okay. Doreen, I need you to listen. I'm very concerned. Black stools and vomiting dark material, along with a low blood pressure and a fast pulse, mean he may be bleeding in his stomach. I want you to call nine one one right now.
Caller -> Nine one one? An ambulance? He's going to be angry. He hates the hospital. He was in for a week with the ulcer and he swore he'd never go back. He signed himself out early. My son will be furious with me if I don't, and Millard will be furious if I do.
Nurse -> I know. And I understand. But this can be life threatening, and he needs to be seen now. Please call. I'll stay on until you do.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hold on. Millard, I'm calling the ambulance. No, don't argue with me. I'm calling. Okay. I'll call from my cell. Can you hold on?
Nurse -> I'm here. While you do that, have him lie flat with his legs up on a pillow. Don't let him stand or walk by himself.
Caller -> Lie flat. Legs up. Okay. Millard, lie down. Lie down. Right now. I got a pillow. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Doreen, don't give him anything to eat or drink, and no more pills, not the ibuprofen, not the aspirin.
Caller -> Nothing to eat or drink. No pills. Okay.
Nurse -> And unlock the front door so the paramedics can walk right in. And get his medicine bottles together so you can hand them to the paramedics.
Caller -> Door. Bottles. Okay. I'm doing it. I put the bottles in a bag, the ibuprofen, the aspirin, the heart pills, the blood pressure ones. I'm dialing. It's ringing.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> They answered. Hello? Yes, I need an ambulance. My husband is bleeding in his stomach, the nurse said. Millard Pickett. Forty one Larch Street. Yes. Yes.
Nurse -> You're doing great, Doreen.
Caller -> They said ten minutes. They said stay with him. Millard, they're coming. Don't move.
Nurse -> Stay right by him. Keep him flat. I'm going to call the emergency room to let them know he's on his way.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Thank you. Is he going to be okay?
Nurse -> I can't promise that, but getting him there now is the right thing. They can treat this.
Caller -> He's gray. He looks gray, Rhonda. Millard. Millard, stay with me. Talk to me. Tell me what day it is. He says Saturday. It is Saturday. He knows.
Nurse -> That's good. That means he's thinking clearly. Keep asking him simple questions and keep him talking.
Caller -> What's our dog's name? Biscuit. He said Biscuit. Okay. He's with me. He's rolling his eyes at me, he's still got attitude.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. Keep him flat and don't let him sit up when they come in.
Nurse -> Is he talking?
Caller -> He's saying my name. He's saying he feels cold. He's shaking a little. I'll put the blanket on him.
Nurse -> Yes. Cover him with a blanket. Keep talking to him. The paramedics will be there soon.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I hear the siren. I hear it. They're on the street. I'll open the door.
Nurse -> Go ahead. Let them in. You did everything right.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Rhonda. I'm so scared. I've never called an ambulance for him in forty four years. He never lets me.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Tell the paramedics everything you told me, the black stools, the vomiting, the ibuprofen and the aspirin. And tell them about the ulcer.
Caller -> Black stools. Vomit. Ibuprofen. Aspirin. Ulcer. Okay. I have the bag of pills. I have my list. They're coming in. Hello. Back here. We're in the bedroom. Okay. I have to go.
Nurse -> Go. I'll call the ER now. Take care of him, Doreen.
Caller -> They're asking me questions. I'll call you from the hospital. Which hospital will they take him to, do you know?
Nurse -> They'll tell you. The closest emergency room. Just stay with him. You can call us any time from there.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Carla, it's Jelena Marinkovic. It's my husband, Zlatko. Zlatko Marinkovic. His back is killing him. It's so bad. It won't stop.
Nurse -> Okay, Jelena. I'm here. Let me get his date of birth.
Caller -> February eighth. Nineteen sixty.
Nurse -> And your number, five seven one, five five five, zero one two six?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm in the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the back pain. Where exactly is it?
Caller -> The low back. Here, across the bottom of his back. He says it feels like a knife. It started this morning when he woke up. He says it's an eight. An eight out of ten.
Nurse -> Okay. What has he taken?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Ten milligrams. He's supposed to take it every four hours. He took one at seven this morning, and then another one at eleven. It didn't help. It didn't touch it.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he on anything else for the pain? A steroid, maybe?
Caller -> Yes. The dexamethasone. Four milligrams every morning. He took it already. At seven with the first pill.
Nurse -> Okay. And Jelena, remind me of his diagnosis.
Caller -> The prostate cancer. It went to his bones. In his spine, his hip, a rib. That's why he's with you.
Nurse -> Okay. Now this is important. Has he had any new weakness in his legs, any numbness or tingling, or any trouble passing urine?
Caller -> No. His legs are the same. He can move them. He can feel when I touch his feet. And he went to the bathroom an hour ago. It was normal. I asked him all of those things already, because the nurse told us last time.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing. Okay. Jelena, how long has he been with us?
Caller -> Four months. Since June. He was in the hospital for the bone biopsy in March, and then they said there wasn't anything else to do, and they sent him home with you. He's been strong. He walks the dog every morning. Until this week.
Nurse -> I remember him telling me about the dog. What's the dog's name?
Caller -> Bruno. A big dumb lab. He's lying outside the bedroom door right now, he won't leave. He knows.
Nurse -> Dogs do know. Okay. Jelena, how are you doing? I can hear you're upset.
Caller -> I'm scared. I'm so scared. Is the cancer spreading? Is this it? He was fine yesterday. He ate dinner. He watched the football game. And today he's curled up on his side and he can't talk.
Nurse -> I understand. I can't tell you what's causing it over the phone, but I do know that pain this severe, with the oxycodone not helping, needs to be dealt with right now. I'm going to page our on-call nurse.
Caller -> Please. Can someone come out today? Please. I can't see him like this.
Nurse -> Yes. A nurse will come to the house, and she'll be there within two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Okay. That's, okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in twenty minutes with the plan for his pain.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until then, please don't give him any extra oxycodone until the on-call nurse tells you whether to give more and how much.
Caller -> Okay. No extra. I'll wait for the call. His next one isn't due until three anyway.
Nurse -> Right. Meanwhile, help him find the position that eases his back the most. Lying on his side with a pillow between his knees helps many people. And a warm pack on the low back, if he can stand the warmth.
Caller -> Side. Pillow between the knees. Warm pack. We have the heating pad with the cover. I'll put it on low.
Nurse -> Low and with the cover, and check his skin every few minutes. And Jelena, if his legs get weak or numb, or if he can't pass urine, call me right away. That's very important with this kind of pain.
Caller -> Weak legs, numb, can't pee. Right away. Okay. I know. I'll check.
Nurse -> Good. Has he had anything to eat or drink since this morning?
Caller -> A little water. He took a sip with the pill and that's all. He says he's not hungry. He doesn't want to talk much, it hurts too much to move his mouth, he says, which doesn't make sense, but that's how bad it is.
Nurse -> That's okay. When pain is severe, people go inward. Is anyone with you?
Caller -> My son is on his way. He lives twenty minutes away. He's coming now.
Nurse -> That's good. Let him help you. Is the door unlocked for the nurse?
Caller -> I'll unlock it now. Hold on. Done. The porch light is on. The house is the yellow one at the end of the street.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll talk to you in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Carla. Thank you so much. He says to tell you thank you too. He can hear me. He's nodding.
Nurse -> Tell him I said hang in there, we're on it.
Caller -> I'll tell him. Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Alicia Oseguera. I'm calling about my mother, Mirabel Oseguera. I'm worried about her. She's been saying some things.
Nurse -> Hi, Alicia. I'm glad you called. Let me get her date of birth.
Caller -> November eleventh. Nineteen thirty seven.
Nurse -> And is nine oh nine, five five five, zero one three one your number?
Caller -> Yes. The cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what she's been saying.
Caller -> Three times this week. Once on Tuesday, once on Thursday, and again tonight. She says, I wish I just wouldn't wake up tomorrow. Tonight she said it while I was putting her to bed. She said, I'm tired of being a burden. I wish I wouldn't wake up.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That must have been hard to hear.
Caller -> It was. I didn't know what to say. I told her she's not a burden. She just looked at me. And then she cried.
Nurse -> How is she right now? Is she with you?
Caller -> She's asleep, I think. She's in the bed. I just checked. She's breathing normally. But I'm worried to leave the room.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to ask you some direct questions, Alicia. It's what we do. Has she said anything about hurting herself, a plan, or taking extra pills?
Caller -> No. No plan. Nothing like that. She only says she wishes she wouldn't wake up. She's never said she'd do anything. And I count her pills. I do all of them myself. She doesn't touch them.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That helps. How is her pain?
Caller -> Fine. Her pain is fine. It's controlled. She says it's a one or a two. That's not it. She's just tired. And sad. She cries a lot. She says she's a burden to me. She isn't.
Nurse -> Okay. Alicia, tell me a little about her. What was she like before she got sick?
Caller -> Oh. She was the strong one. She raised us by herself. She cleaned houses for thirty years. She never missed a day. She was proud that she never asked anyone for anything. And now she has to ask me for everything, even to turn over in bed. I think that's what is killing her pride.
Nurse -> That makes sense. For someone like that, needing help can feel harder than the illness.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. That's exactly it.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating, sleeping?
Caller -> She sleeps most of the day. She eats a few bites. She's been like that for a few weeks. This is the first time she said the other thing.
Nurse -> Okay. Alicia, what's worrying you most right now?
Caller -> That I'll miss something. That I'll go to the bathroom and come back and something has happened. That I'm not doing enough. I don't want to leave her alone. But I have to sleep eventually.
Nurse -> That makes complete sense. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message her provider about what she's been saying.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also going to have our social worker come out tomorrow. She's very good with these conversations, and she'll talk with your mom and with you.
Caller -> Oh, that would be good. I think Mom might actually talk to her.
Nurse -> And a nurse will come out tomorrow too.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Both of them?
Nurse -> Yes. And I'll call you back tonight to see how she's doing.
Caller -> Tonight. Okay. Thank you. What time?
Nurse -> Before ten. If you don't hear from me by then, call me.
Caller -> Okay. Before ten. I will.
Nurse -> Alicia, if she ever says she has a plan, or if she tries to hurt herself, call nine one one. You can also call or text nine eight eight any time, for you or for her. And you can call us at any hour.
Caller -> Nine one one for a plan. Nine eight eight any time. And you. Okay. I'm writing it on my hand.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom. It's Esperanza Quintanilla. I'm calling about my father, Leopoldo Quintanilla. He won't take his pills. He's spitting them out. For three nights now.
Nurse -> Okay, Esperanza. Let's work through it. First his date of birth.
Caller -> March twenty fifth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And is eight three oh, five five five, zero one four seven the best number for you?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm at his house right now.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's been happening with the pills.
Caller -> In the mornings he's okay. I give him the pills with breakfast and he takes them. But at night, around seven, he gets agitated. He doesn't know who I am sometimes. He puts the pills in his mouth and he just holds them and then he spits them in the sink or on the floor. Three nights in a row.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds frustrating and frightening for both of you. Has he been eating and drinking okay otherwise?
Caller -> Eating, yes. Drinking, not as much as I'd like. I keep a cup by his chair and remind him. He eats the same three things. Eggs, rice, bananas. And a lot of pan dulce, which I'm trying to cut back on, but he gets so happy.
Nurse -> A little sweet bread is not the worst thing. Okay. Do you have the bottles in front of you?
Caller -> Yes. I have all of them lined up on the counter. There are eight. I made a little chart with the times, my brother helped me do it over video. Hold on. I'll go through them for you.
Nurse -> That's a great idea, the chart. Let's start with the morning ones.
Caller -> Okay. Sertraline. Fifty milligrams. Every morning. He takes that.
Nurse -> Okay. Sertraline fifty every morning, taking. Next.
Caller -> Pantoprazole. Forty milligrams. Every morning. He takes that one too. It's the one he takes before breakfast, with a glass of water.
Nurse -> Okay. Pantoprazole forty every morning, taking. Next.
Caller -> Metoprolol. It says metoprolol tartrate. Twenty five milligrams. Twice a day. He takes the morning one. The evening one, he spits it out.
Nurse -> Okay. Metoprolol tartrate twenty five twice a day, the morning dose taken and the evening dose missed. Next.
Caller -> Memantine. Ten milligrams. Twice a day. It's the same, he takes it in the morning and not at night.
Nurse -> Okay. Memantine ten milligrams twice a day, evening missed. Next.
Caller -> The tamsulosin. Point four milligrams. After dinner. He doesn't take that one at all lately. Three nights.
Nurse -> Okay. Tamsulosin point four after dinner, missed for three nights.
Caller -> And the donepezil. Ten milligrams. At bedtime. He spits that one out too. Three nights.
Nurse -> Okay. Donepezil ten at bedtime, missed three nights. I also see vitamin D on his list. Is he taking the vitamin D?
Caller -> Yes. In the morning. It's a little softgel. That one he takes.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all eight. Has anything changed in his routine, aside from the pills? Any new place, new people?
Caller -> Not really. Well. A few weeks ago my cousin's kids visited, and he got very upset by the noise. And we moved his chair. I moved his chair to the other window so he could see the birds. He didn't like that. He kept asking where his chair was. He was standing in the middle of the living room looking for his chair.
Nurse -> That can be unsettling. Little changes can matter a lot with dementia. Esperanza, have you checked his blood pressure?
Caller -> Yes. I took it this morning. One thirty four over eighty.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reasonable. Now, what are you thinking about doing with the pills?
Caller -> I was thinking of crushing them all up and putting them in applesauce. That's what I did with my mother's. So he won't know. Can I do that?
Nurse -> I'm glad you asked first, because there are two things. Esperanza, the pantoprazole, please do not crush it. It's a delayed release tablet, and crushing it makes it not work and can upset the stomach.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. I didn't know. I was going to crush all of them. I'm glad I asked.
Nurse -> Me too. And the others, some can be crushed and some can't, so I want the pharmacist and the provider to tell us which. I'm going to message his provider about the refusing and ask about other forms, like liquids.
Caller -> Okay. Is there a liquid memantine?
Nurse -> There is. That's the kind of thing I'll ask. I'm also going to ask his pharmacy about liquid forms, and about packaging the pills in a system that's easier for you.
Caller -> That would be great. Thank you.
Nurse -> And a nurse will come out Thursday to look at how the evenings are going and help you work out a routine.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'm here Thursday. I'm here every day.
Nurse -> In the meantime, here's what I'd try. Offer one pill at a time, with a spoonful of applesauce. Don't hide them in a drink, because if he tastes it, he may stop trusting you. And if he refuses, wait twenty minutes and try again.
Caller -> One at a time. Applesauce. Not in a drink. Twenty minutes. Okay. I did try to hide one in his juice last night and he made a face and refused all of them. That makes sense.
Nurse -> It often does. It's a hard thing, especially in the evening, when he's more confused.
Caller -> Yes. Sundowning. The doctor called it that. He's fine at ten in the morning and by seven he thinks I'm his sister.
Nurse -> That's very common. Try to keep the evenings calm. Dim the lights, turn off the TV, play some quiet music. Some people find a snack before the pills helps.
Caller -> He loves music. The old Mexican boleros. My mother used to dance with him in the kitchen to them. I'll put those on. Maybe he'll hold still. Maybe he'll even remember.
Nurse -> Music reaches people when words don't. It's one of the best tools you have.
Caller -> I've noticed. When I sing to him, even the old songs, he calms down. He knows every word. He can't tell me what he had for breakfast, but he knows every word of Sabor a Mí.
Nurse -> That's beautiful. Sing to him as much as you like.
Nurse -> That's a lovely idea. And Esperanza, call us if he has chest pain, if he faints, if his heart is racing, or if he gets so agitated that you're worried about his safety.
Caller -> Chest pain. Faints. Racing. Very agitated. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Good. Esperanza, how are you holding up? You sound tired.
Caller -> Tired. I moved in with him in July. My brother lives in Dallas and he calls on Sundays, but it's all me. I don't mind. He took care of us. But the evenings are hard.
Nurse -> I'm sure. You're doing a lot. Is there anyone who can give you a break?
Caller -> My cousin comes on Saturdays for a few hours. That's something. She takes him to the park. He sits on the bench and feeds the pigeons. I use the time to sleep, or grocery shop, or sometimes just sit in the car and listen to the radio. It's the only time I'm alone.
Nurse -> That sounds like exactly what you need. Please protect that time.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep that. And if you ever need more help, we can talk about it at the visit.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll bring it up. Thank you, Tom. Really. I feel like I have a plan now. Before I called, I was sitting on the kitchen floor with the bottles, just staring at them. I didn't know who to ask. My brother says to just put it in the applesauce, my cousin says to ask the doctor, my aunt says to give him tequila, I'm not kidding.
Nurse -> Ha. Please skip the tequila. You did the right thing by calling us.
Caller -> I know. I know. I'm not giving him tequila. I'm just telling you what it's like in this family.
Nurse -> I believe you. Families have a lot of opinions. The plan we made is a safe one.
Caller -> It is. Thank you, Tom.
Nurse -> You do. Call us any time if something changes.
Caller -> Okay. Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth. This is Saul Lowenstein. My mother is Harriet Lowenstein. She was admitted to your hospice last week. I have a bunch of questions, if you have a few minutes. I don't want to bother you.
Nurse -> It's no bother at all, Saul. Questions are what this call is for. Let me start with her date of birth.
Caller -> September third. Nineteen forty. She turned eighty six last month. We had a little party.
Nurse -> And your number, is it six four six, five five five, zero one three three?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm at her place.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead with your questions.
Caller -> Okay. So. She was admitted five days ago. It was Wednesday. They said her heart failure is, it's end stage, there isn't anything more the hospital can do. She's home now. And I'm still trying to figure out how this works.
Nurse -> That is a lot to take in. I'm sorry. Let's go step by step. What's she like today?
Caller -> Quiet. She sleeps a lot more than she used to. Maybe sixteen hours a day. She wakes up for a little while in the morning, and in the afternoon. Mostly she dozes in the bed.
Nurse -> Okay. And her eating?
Caller -> Much less. She used to love her breakfast. Now she takes two bites of toast and pushes it away. Dinner, three bites of anything. She drinks a little tea. I'm worried she's going to starve.
Nurse -> I understand that worry, Saul. It's one of the hardest parts for families. I'll talk about that in a minute. Does she have any pain?
Caller -> Some, in her hip. The left one. She said it's a three. Mostly when she shifts in bed.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you given her anything for it?
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid. I gave her five milligrams, the little syringe, twice since she came home. Once on Friday and once last night. It helped. She settled down and went to sleep.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's what it's for. Do you notice any swelling in her legs?
Caller -> A little. Her ankles. They look a bit puffy at the end of the day. They weren't like that last week.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the provider know. Saul, did the hospital bed get delivered?
Caller -> Yes. Monday. The men came and set it up in the living room. She likes it. She can see the garden from there.
Nurse -> Good. Now, tell me your other questions. I know you have a list.
Caller -> I do. I wrote it down. One. What does hospice actually do? Is it just you calling me back? Two. Does hospice mean we stop all her medicines? Because she's still on the water pill and the heart pill, and my aunt said that hospice takes everything away.
Nurse -> Those are great questions. Let me take them one at a time. Hospice is a team. A nurse, an aide, a social worker, a chaplain if you want one, and a provider who oversees her care. We focus on keeping her comfortable and supporting your family. And no, hospice does not take away all her medicines.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief. So she can keep the water pill?
Nurse -> Anything that helps her feel better can continue, like the pills for her heart and swelling, as long as they're comfortable for her. The provider will go over it with you at each visit. What we stop are the things that don't help her comfort anymore, like cholesterol pills and vitamins, and only with the provider's agreement.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. My aunt had it wrong, then. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> What was your third question?
Caller -> Three. Who do I call at night? If something happens at three in the morning. Do I call 911? Do I call you? I don't want to make the wrong decision.
Nurse -> This is the most important one. Call us first. The main number you called today answers any hour, day or night, and the on-call nurse will pick up. We can usually help over the phone, and if needed we'll send someone to the house.
Caller -> Any hour. The on-call nurse. Okay. Even for little things?
Nurse -> Even for little things. You never have to wonder whether it's important enough. Please call.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. That takes a load off. I'll put the number on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, about her eating. I want to tell you something, and I know it's hard. As the heart gets weaker, the body needs less food. Eating less is part of the illness. It isn't starvation, and she isn't suffering from it.
Caller -> Okay. But I feel like I should be doing more. Like I should make her eat.
Nurse -> Please don't force her. Offer small amounts, whenever she's awake. A few bites of something she loves, ice cream, applesauce, a little soup. Let her tell you when she's had enough. The offering is the love, not the amount.
Caller -> The offering is the love. Okay. I'll try to keep that in mind. She does like ice cream. Butter pecan.
Nurse -> Then butter pecan it is.
Caller -> Ha. Okay. I'll go get some. There's a store down the street.
Nurse -> Good. Saul, about the morphine. You're doing it right. Give it for pain or when she has trouble breathing. Write down each dose and the time in a notebook. If she needs it more often than every four hours, call us, because that means we need to adjust the plan.
Caller -> Every four hours at most. And write it down. I have a notebook. I wrote the two times already. Friday at nine and last night at ten.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Now, let me tell you what the team will do. A nurse will come out Wednesday.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. This Wednesday?
Nurse -> Yes, in two days. Our social worker will also call you Tuesday to talk about how you're doing, and about anything the family needs.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. That's tomorrow. That's nice. I could use someone to talk to.
Nurse -> That's what she's for. And a home health aide will come twice a week to help with bathing and personal care.
Caller -> Twice a week. That's great. My mother is very modest, so I want to make sure the aide is a woman.
Nurse -> I'll make a note of that preference. Saul, I'm also going to message her provider about the ankle swelling and her eating less.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Will they change anything?
Nurse -> It's possible. They may adjust her water pill or give you something for the appetite, though that often isn't needed. They'll tell the nurse on Wednesday, or I'll call you if it's sooner.
Caller -> Okay. Good. One more thing. The bed. It rolls. Yesterday I was changing her sheets and the whole bed moved a little. It scared me.
Nurse -> I'm glad you told me. Keep the wheels locked. There are foot levers on each wheel. Push them down, and the bed shouldn't move. And keep the side rails up when she's in the bed.
Caller -> Wheels locked. Rails up. Okay. I think I forgot to lock them. I'll go check right now.
Nurse -> Good idea. Go ahead, I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Mom, I'm just checking the bed. Okay. Two wheels were unlocked. Now they're locked. It doesn't move.
Nurse -> Great catch. Any other questions on your list?
Caller -> Just one. I'm not sure how to say it. Should I be telling my kids to come see her? Soon?
Nurse -> It's a good question, and a loving one. I can't give you a date, but she is declining, and I think now is a good time for the people who love her to visit, if they can. Many families are glad they did.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call them tonight. My daughter's in Boston and my son's in Seattle. I'll tell them this weekend.
Nurse -> That sounds right. And Saul, take care of yourself too. Eat something, sleep when you can.
Caller -> I'll try. Thank you, Beth. You've been so kind. I didn't know what to expect, and this helped so much.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Call me anytime.
Caller -> I will. Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Palliative Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Priya Raman. I'm a patient. The pharmacy gave me the wrong medicine. I took one.
Nurse -> Okay, Priya. I'm here. Let me get your date of birth.
Caller -> April twelfth. Nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> And is five one oh, five five five, zero one six eight your number?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> I picked up my refill yesterday. It's supposed to be Celexa. Twenty milligrams. For my mood. I took it this morning and then I looked at the bottle, and it says Celebrex. Two hundred milligrams. That's the arthritis one. I took a Celebrex.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for catching it. So you took one Celebrex two hundred this morning, instead of your Celexa.
Caller -> Yes. And I haven't had my Celexa. I've missed it today. I've never missed it.
Nurse -> Okay. How do you feel right now? Any stomach pain, nausea, anything unusual?
Caller -> No. Nothing. I feel the same as always. My stomach is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. I already called the pharmacy while you were telling me, and they're going to bring the right bottle.
Caller -> Oh. Good. They can bring it here? I'm not supposed to drive after the last treatment.
Nurse -> They'll arrange it. I'm also going to message your provider about the mix-up.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. What do I do until then?
Nurse -> Please don't take any more Celebrex, and keep that bottle so you can show the pharmacist. And hold off on the Celexa until the right bottle comes.
Caller -> Hold the Celexa until the new bottle. Keep the Celebrex bottle. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you back this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if you get stomach pain, black stools, vomiting, or if your mood dips because of the missed Celexa.
Caller -> Stomach pain, black stool, vomiting, mood. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Naomi. I was so upset when I saw the bottle. I thought I'd done something terrible.
Nurse -> You didn't. You caught it. That's what matters.

Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Hector.
Caller -> Hector, hi, it's Luciana Ibarra. It's my father, Gustavo Ibarra. He fell. I have my brother on speaker, he's here too.
Nurse -> Hi, Luciana. Hi to your brother. Let me get your dad's date of birth first.
Caller -> September nineteenth. Nineteen thirty six.
Nurse -> And your number, eight one eight, five five five, zero one four five?
Caller -> Yes. Mine.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> He fell in the bathroom. Tuesday night. He was getting up to pee and he slipped on the mat.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It wasn't Tuesday, Lucy. It was Wednesday. I was here Wednesday night. I helped him up.
Caller -> Matias, it was Tuesday. You weren't here Tuesday. You came Wednesday, after.
Caller -> I was here when he fell. I picked him up. It was Wednesday.
Nurse -> Okay, okay. You two, one at a time, please. So it was Tuesday or Wednesday. We'll sort it out. Was anyone with him when he fell?
Caller -> No. Nobody saw it. He told us in the morning. I found him on the bathroom floor, no, he got himself up, he told me he fell. I don't know which night. Matias, I don't know. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's okay. Luciana, did he hit his head?
Caller -> No. He says no. He landed on his side. His left side. His hip.
Caller -> He didn't hit his head. We checked. No bump, no bruise on the head.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Was he dizzy before he fell, or did he trip?
Caller -> He slipped. On the bath mat. The little one with the rubber backing that's coming off. I told him I'd replace it.
Caller -> I told you to replace it a month ago, Lucy. It's been peeling since the summer.
Caller -> I know, Matias. I know. I have it on my list. It's not like I don't have a hundred other things.
Nurse -> Let's take that mat out of the bathroom tonight. That's a simple fix. Okay. How is his hip? On a scale of zero to ten.
Caller -> I'd say a five. He winces when he stands up, but he can walk. A five.
Caller -> It's more than a five. It's a seven. You can see it on his face when he gets out of the chair.
Caller -> He says five. He told me five.
Caller -> He says five to you because he doesn't want you to worry. He told me seven.
Nurse -> Okay. I understand. We'll write that it's somewhere between five and seven. Can you see any bruising?
Caller -> Yes. A big purple bruise on the left hip. About the size of my hand. And it goes down the thigh a little.

Caller -> He ate breakfast and half his lunch. He's drinking. He slept in the chair last night because the bed hurts his hip. I think he'd rather sit up.
Caller -> He should be in the bed, the chair is worse for his back.
Nurse -> Sleeping in a chair is common after a fall. The nurse can look at that too. Okay. Is he walking?
Caller -> With the walker, yes. He's slow, and he leans. But he's walking. He walked to the kitchen for breakfast.
Nurse -> Okay. What has he taken for the pain?
Caller -> The acetaminophen. Five hundred milligrams. Every six hours. He's been taking it since Wednesday. Or Thursday.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he on anything else for pain? Like tramadol?
Caller -> Yes, the tramadol. He takes it at night. The little white pill.
Caller -> No, Lucy, he doesn't. They stopped the tramadol in the summer. He's not on it anymore. The bottle is still in the cabinet, but he doesn't take it.
Caller -> He took it last night. I gave it to him.
Caller -> You gave him the old bottle? Luciana! That's from June.
Nurse -> Hold on, let me look at the chart. I see tramadol discontinued in July. So he shouldn't be taking it. Luciana, do you remember giving him one last night?
Caller -> I, I think I did. One. Because he was in pain. I thought it was okay. I'm sorry. I didn't know it was stopped.
Nurse -> It's okay. Thank you for telling me. Please don't give him any more of the tramadol. We'll sort that out with the provider, and I'll take the old bottle to dispose of at the visit.
Caller -> Okay. No more. I'll put it in a bag.
Nurse -> Good. Now, does he have any other symptoms? Any numbness, tingling in the leg?
Caller -> No. His leg feels normal to him. He just says the hip hurts.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the leg turned out at all, or does it look shorter than the other one?
Caller -> No. Both legs look the same. He puts weight on it, it just hurts. Let me look. Same. They look the same.
Nurse -> Good. That's helpful. Is the bathroom on the same floor as his bedroom?
Caller -> Yes. Down the hall. Eleven steps from his bed, I counted once. There are no stairs. The house is all on one level.
Caller -> He has a grab bar by the toilet but not by the tub. I keep saying we need one by the tub.
Nurse -> A grab bar by the tub is a great idea, and it's something the nurse or the therapist can help you plan. Luciana, Matias, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message his provider about the hip pain after the fall, and ask whether he needs an X-ray.
Caller -> Okay. Good. That's what I wanted.
Caller -> I told you we should have taken him to urgent care on Thursday.
Caller -> You didn't say that. You said it would pass.
Nurse -> Please, you two. The important thing is we're taking care of it now. A nurse will come out tomorrow to examine him.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this evening after I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. Should I call you or you call me?
Nurse -> I'll call you. Make sure your phone is on.
Caller -> It will be. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, he should use the walker for every trip, even short ones. Keep a night light on in the hall and the bathroom, and have someone stand by when he uses the bathroom.
Caller -> Walker every time. Night light. Someone stands by. Okay. We'll take turns.
Caller -> I'm here all week. I took the week off from work.
Caller -> I can do the nights if you do the days. We'll set an alarm.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good system. Make sure each of you gets some sleep too.
Caller -> We will. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll sleep on the couch tonight. I'll hear him. The couch is right outside his door anyway, he can't get up without me knowing. I've lived in this house my whole life, I know every creak in the floor.
Nurse -> That's useful. Stay close, and wake him gently if he needs to get up.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. And call nine one one if he can't put weight on that leg, if the leg looks shorter or turned out, or if the pain gets severe.
Caller -> Can't put weight, leg looks different, severe pain. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> And one more thing. When you pick up the old tramadol bottle, put it somewhere he can't reach.
Caller -> I'll put it in my purse. Right now.
Caller -> Give me the bag, I'll write the date on it. June. Tramadol. Old. Do not use.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Thank you, Matias.
Caller -> He's a stickler for labels. He's an accountant.
Nurse -> Today it's a virtue.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I think that's everything. My dad is asking what we're talking about. He says he's fine. He says to tell you he's fine.
Nurse -> Tell him I said I'm glad to hear it, and we'll check on him tomorrow anyway.
Caller -> He says okay. He says you're the one with the deep voice on the phone.
Nurse -> Ha. That's me.
Caller -> Thank you, Hector. Sorry for the shouting.
Nurse -> No need to apologize. You both care a lot. That's what matters.
Caller -> Thank you, Hector. We'll be waiting for your call this evening. I'll keep my phone right by the sink while I make dinner.
Nurse -> Sounds good. Talk to you tonight.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Carla.
Caller -> Carla, it's Signe Eriksen. My husband, Torvald Eriksen. He's having a really hard time breathing.
Nurse -> Okay, Signe, I'm here. Let me get his date of birth.
Caller -> June third. Nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And is nine oh seven, five five five, zero one seven six the best number?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> He's sitting on the edge of the bed, bent over. He's breathing fast. He can say a few words. And there's a wheeze. A whistle when he breathes out. It started late this afternoon and it keeps getting worse.
Nurse -> Okay. Is his oxygen on?
Caller -> Yes. It's on two liters. That's his normal. I checked the tubing. It's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have the finger meter?
Caller -> Yes. Hold on. It says eighty eight. Eighty eight. He's usually ninety two, ninety three.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he used his nebulizer?
Caller -> Yes. Twice. The albuterol. Once about an hour ago and once about twenty minutes ago. It helped a tiny bit for a few minutes and then it came back.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have any chest pain?
Caller -> No. He said no. I asked him three times. Just can't breathe.
Nurse -> Okay. Signe, remind me, what is his diagnosis?
Caller -> The COPD. Very advanced. He's been on the oxygen two years. And he's told me, he told the doctor, he doesn't want to go back to the hospital. Not ever again. He had a bad time on the ventilator in March.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, Signe. That must have been frightening for both of you. How has he been this past week, before today?
Caller -> Up and down. He's been tired. He did laundry on Monday and then he had to lie down for two hours. But he wasn't like this. This is the worst since March. I keep thinking it's the same, it's starting all over.
Nurse -> I understand why you'd think that. Okay. Thank you for telling me. I'll honor that. We'll try to keep him home and comfortable. Signe, I'm going to page our on-call nurse right now.
Caller -> Please. Please send someone. Can someone come out? I'm scared he's going to stop breathing.
Nurse -> Yes. A nurse will come to the house, and she'll be there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until then, let's make him as comfortable as we can. Help him sit upright, leaning forward, with his arms resting on a table or a stack of pillows. And turn a fan on, pointing at his face.
Caller -> He's already bent over. Let me get the pillows. Okay. I'm putting the pillows on the tray table. Torvald, rest your arms. There. And the fan. I have one on the dresser. Okay. It's on.
Nurse -> Good. Now tell him to breathe in through his nose, and out slowly through pursed lips, like blowing out a candle.
Caller -> Like a candle. In the nose. Out slow. He's doing it. He's trying. I can see it helps a bit, his shoulders drop.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Keep coaching him. Signe, I want you to listen to this part. If his lips turn blue, if he can't speak at all, or if he becomes drowsy and hard to wake, call nine one one.
Caller -> Blue lips. Can't speak. Hard to wake. Nine one one. But he doesn't want the hospital.
Nurse -> I know. The ambulance can start treatment at home, and they'll know his wishes. It's a decision for you and him. But if that happens, please call.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I understand.
Nurse -> Signe, how are you doing? You sound steady, but I know this is hard.
Caller -> I'm shaking inside. But I've done this before, in March. I just don't want to do it again. He's my best friend. Thirty four years in October.
Nurse -> That's a long time. Stay close to him and keep talking. Your voice helps more than you know.
Caller -> I'll hold his hand. He likes when I hold his hand.
Nurse -> Is anyone with you?
Caller -> My sister is coming. She lives ten minutes away. She's on her way.
Nurse -> Good. Unlock the front door, and turn on the porch light for the nurse.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that now. Hold on. Done. Porch light on. Door's open.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call in ten.
Caller -> Thank you, Carla. Thank you so much. I hear the dog barking, I think my sister is here. She has a key. Yes. She's in. She's coming up the stairs. I'm going to let her sit with him while I talk to you.
Nurse -> That's good. Stay near him. I'll call you in ten minutes, no later.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right, Signe.

Nurse -> Meadowbrook Home Care, this is Samantha.
Caller -> Hi, Samantha. This is Pearl Gutierrez. I'm one of your patients. I started a new pill and I think it's making me dizzy.
Nurse -> Hi, Pearl. Let me get your date of birth.
Caller -> August eighth. Nineteen fifty three.
Nurse -> And is nine seven two, five five five, zero one four one your number?
Caller -> Yes. The cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the pill?
Caller -> Gabapentin. Three hundred milligrams. Three times a day. For the burning in my feet. I started it Friday, so four days.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you last take it?
Caller -> This morning. About nine. I'm due for the noon one but I haven't taken it yet. I wanted to call first.
Nurse -> That's a good instinct. Tell me about the dizziness.
Caller -> It's like the room tilts a little when I stand up. Or sometimes just sitting. It started the day after I started the pill. Not terrible. But it's every day.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you eating and drinking normally?
Caller -> Yes. I eat well. I might be drinking a bit less, I forget, because I'm so sleepy. I'll make an effort.
Nurse -> Good idea. Water helps with the dizziness too. And are you sleepy?
Caller -> Very. I fell asleep in my chair at ten in the morning. I never do that. And I fell asleep in the middle of my show last night, and I was awake all night after.
Nurse -> Okay. How about the foot pain? Is the gabapentin helping?
Caller -> It is. That's the thing. It was an eight, and now it's about a four. The burning isn't as bad. I'd hate to lose that. But I'm scared with the dizziness.
Nurse -> That makes sense. Have you fallen?
Caller -> No. But yesterday I stumbled in the kitchen. I grabbed the counter. I didn't fall. I didn't hit anything. Nothing hurts.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you didn't get hurt. Is there a rug or anything in the kitchen that you might have caught your foot on?
Caller -> A throw rug by the sink. It slides. My daughter said to take it up. I keep forgetting. I'll pull it up right now, after I hang up.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Pearl, I'm going to message your provider about the dizziness and sleepiness on the gabapentin.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Will they take me off it?
Nurse -> I can't say. It might be that the dose needs to change, or the timing. They'll decide. I'll call you back tomorrow to tell you what they say.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What should I do about the noon pill?
Nurse -> Don't stop the gabapentin on your own, and don't take extra. Stopping suddenly can cause problems. Take the noon dose as prescribed, with a little snack, and sit down for a while afterward.
Caller -> Take it with a snack. Sit down after. Okay. So I shouldn't skip the noon one. I was going to skip it.
Nurse -> Please don't skip it. If you're so dizzy you can't stand, call me instead of deciding on your own.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call you. I have a cracker and some peanut butter. That's a snack.
Nurse -> In the meantime, use your walker for everything, even short trips. Stand up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a moment first, and please don't drive.
Caller -> I don't drive anymore. My daughter takes me. But yes, walker, slow, sit first. I've been using the cane, I'll switch to the walker. It's steadier.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. And call us if you fall, faint, get confused, or are too sleepy to stay awake. If you fall and hit your head, call nine one one.
Caller -> Fall, faint, confused, too sleepy. Head, nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> Does anything else bother you with the pill, like an upset stomach, or swelling in your ankles?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. My ankles are the same. Just the dizzy and the sleepy. And maybe my mouth is a little dry.
Nurse -> A dry mouth can go with it. Sips of water or sugar free candy help. Anything else?
Caller -> My daughter wants to know if this is normal. Is it?
Nurse -> Dizziness and sleepiness are common with gabapentin, especially in the first week. It isn't unusual. It just needs to be managed.
Caller -> That's good to hear. I told her. She worries.
Nurse -> That's what daughters do. Does she live nearby?
Caller -> Ten minutes away. She comes every day after work. She brings me soup. She's a good girl. She's fifty one.
Nurse -> Ha. Still a girl. Please let her know I said hello, and that she's welcome to call me too.
Caller -> I will. She likes you. She says you have a nice voice. She says the other agency never called back and you always do.
Nurse -> Thank you. That's kind. I'll talk to you by two.
Caller -> Thank you, Samantha.

Nurse -> Meadowbrook Home Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Cornelia Whitby. That's C O R N E L I A, Whitby, W H I T B Y. I'm calling about my catheter supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Cornelia. Thanks for the spelling. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> November twenty seventh. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And is seven oh seven, five five five, zero one five six still your number?
Caller -> Yes. Same one for years.
Nurse -> Okay. What are you running low on?
Caller -> Let me look at my shelf. I keep everything on the shelf in the bathroom. The leg bags. I have one. Just one. And the big drainage bags for night, I have two.
Nurse -> Okay. And the securement devices, the strap that holds the tubing to your leg?
Caller -> Gone. I've been using tape and it's not working. I'm out. None.
Nurse -> Okay. And the adhesive wipes?
Caller -> Out too. I used the last one on Sunday.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you have help at home with the bags and the cleaning?
Caller -> My daughter comes on weekends. During the week it's me. I'm pretty good at it by now. It's been two years. I used to be embarrassed, but now it's just part of the routine, like brushing my teeth.
Nurse -> That's a great attitude. How have things been with the catheter? Any leaking, pain, anything odd about the urine?
Caller -> No. It's good. No leaking at all. No pain. The urine is clear, pale yellow. I drink a lot of water, my daughter nags me about it.
Nurse -> Good. When was your last catheter change?
Caller -> A month ago Friday. The nurse comes every four weeks. The next one is this Friday.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order the leg bags, the drainage bags, the securement devices, and the adhesive wipes.
Caller -> Thank you. How many leg bags will you send? I like to have a few so I can switch.
Nurse -> I'll ask for a box of leg bags so you have plenty.
Caller -> That would be wonderful.
Nurse -> They'll deliver Thursday, so you'll have everything before your change.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'll be home. And the nurse is still coming Friday?
Nurse -> Yes. A nurse will come Friday for the monthly catheter change.
Caller -> Friday. Good. I'll write it on the calendar. I have a calendar on the fridge with all my appointments.
Caller -> Thank you. Is there anything I should do with the old bags? I have a pile in the closet that I've washed.
Nurse -> Please don't reuse the single-use drainage bags. The leg bags can be cleaned and reused for a short time, but the nurse can show you how on Friday. For now, throw away any bag that smells or looks cloudy inside.
Caller -> Okay. I'll throw the old ones away. I felt wasteful, but I understand.
Nurse -> Perfect. While I have you, a few reminders. Empty the bag when it's half full, keep it below the level of your bladder, and keep the tubing free of kinks, especially when you're sitting or lying down.
Caller -> Half full. Below the bladder. No kinks. I do. I check the tubing every time I sit down. I learned that the hard way.
Nurse -> It's a good habit. And keep drinking, six to eight cups of fluid a day, unless the provider told you otherwise.
Caller -> Six to eight. I'm doing about that. Water and some tea. Not much coffee, my daughter says it irritates the bladder.
Nurse -> She's right. And call us if you have no urine in the bag for four hours, if the urine turns cloudy or bloody, if it starts leaking, or you get a fever or lower belly pain.
Caller -> No urine four hours. Cloudy. Bloody. Leaking. Fever. Belly pain. Okay. I have the list on the bathroom door.
Nurse -> That's smart. Anything else I can do?
Caller -> No. Just thank you. You girls are always so organized. The last agency I had, I called three times for the same box.
Nurse -> I'm sorry that happened. We try to get it right the first time.
Caller -> You do. You really do. I tell everyone at church.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you, Cornelia. That means a lot.
Caller -> I mean it. How is the weather by you? It's finally cooling off here. I opened the window this morning for the first time since May.
Nurse -> It's getting cooler here too. It's nice, isn't it? Fall is my favorite. The leaves are starting to turn on my street.
Caller -> Mine too. I'm going to bake apple bread this weekend. My neighbor brings me apples. She has a tree in her yard that is so heavy it bends. I'll make two loaves, one for her and one for me.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Enjoy it, Cornelia. We'll see you Friday.
Caller -> See you Friday. I'll have the kettle on. Do you like peppermint tea?
Nurse -> I do, thank you. See you then, Cornelia.
Caller -> Goodbye, dear.

Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Ana.
Caller -> Hello. Is this where I call about Delia Rousseau? I'm Hank. I'm a friend.
Nurse -> Hi, Hank. Yes, I can take your call. Do you know Delia's date of birth?
Caller -> No. No idea. I've known her ten years, I never asked. She's, I don't know, seventy something, eighty.
Nurse -> That's okay. What's going on?
Caller -> I'm at her place visiting. I come every Tuesday. And she's coughing a lot. Hacking. And when she breathes out there's a, a whistle. A kind of wheezy sound.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has she been coughing?
Caller -> I don't know. She wasn't coughing last Tuesday. But I don't know about the rest of the week. She doesn't like to complain. I'm sorry, I'm not much help.
Nurse -> You're helping a lot. Do you know if she has any illnesses, like a lung problem, or what medicines she takes?
Caller -> No. She has some pills in the kitchen. I never looked. I know she's had a hard year. Her husband passed in the spring. That's all I know.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she short of breath? Can she talk to you in full sentences?
Caller -> She's talking fine. She's been telling me about her granddaughter. She's not out of breath. She just keeps coughing in between.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a number I can reach you at?
Caller -> I'm using her phone. I'd rather not give out my number. Is that okay? I'll stay with her till you call.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'll call her number back this evening.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here. I'll stay until six.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to message her provider about the cough and the wheezing.
Caller -> Thank you. That's all I wanted. For someone to know.
Nurse -> Hank, if she starts to struggle to breathe, if her lips turn blue, or if she can't speak in full sentences, call nine one one.
Caller -> Struggle, blue, can't talk. Nine one one. Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you. I feel better having called.
