transcript:
Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Gwen, it's Harriet. Harriet Rutledge. My husband is Edmund Rutledge. He's okay. He's sleeping. I'm calling because of me.
Nurse -> Okay, Harriet, I'm here, and I'm glad you called. First, so I have it if we get cut off, what is Edmund's date of birth?
Caller -> January twelfth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number, four oh seven, five five five, zero one two six?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I have it in my hand.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> I can't do this anymore. I haven't slept in three days. I have been up and down with him, turning him, the pills, the bed. I'm so tired I'm seeing things.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a lot. Harriet, I want to ask you something directly. Are you having thoughts of hurting yourself?
Caller -> Tonight, yes. I sat on the edge of the bed with my sleeping pills in my hand. And I thought, I could take all of these, and I would finally sleep. And it would be over.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. Have you taken any of them?
Caller -> No. Not one. I put them back on the nightstand. They're right here. I'm looking at the bottle. I'm not going to, I don't think. But I wanted somebody to know.
Nurse -> I'm glad you told me. Harriet, is anyone with you in the house?
Caller -> Just Edmund. He's asleep. My son is coming. I called him an hour ago. He lives in Orlando, he's been driving. He should be here in about twenty minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. While we wait for him, I'd like you to do something. Can you take the bottle of pills and put it in another room, or somewhere you'd have to work to get to?
Caller -> I could put it in the kitchen. In the cabinet over the stove. I'd have to get a stool.
Nurse -> Perfect. Please do that now, and stay on the phone with me while you do.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm walking. Okay, kitchen. The cabinet. It's in. Stool out of the way. Okay. It's done.
Nurse -> Harriet, tell me about Edmund. How long have you two been together?
Caller -> Fifty three years in June. He was in the navy when I met him. He asked me to dance at a church picnic and stepped on my foot twice. I said yes anyway.
Nurse -> That's a wonderful story. And how is he tonight?
Caller -> Quiet. He sleeps most of the time now. He doesn't talk much. But sometimes he squeezes my hand. That's why I keep going, I guess, those little squeezes.
Nurse -> Those squeezes matter. And so do you. That's why I want you to get some rest too. Thank you, Harriet. That was hard, and you did it. When your son arrives, give him the bottle and ask him to keep it for now.
Caller -> I will. I'll give it to him. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm going to page our on-call provider right now so someone can talk with you tonight.
Caller -> I don't want to be a bother. Edmund is the patient, not me.
Nurse -> You matter too. You are not a bother. I'm also going to have our social worker call you in the morning. She can help with respite and with how you're feeling.
Caller -> Respite. Someone to give me a break. Yes. I think I need that. I didn't know I could ask.
Nurse -> You can. And I'll call you back in fifteen minutes, after I've reached the on-call provider.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> Harriet, if you ever feel you might act on these thoughts, or you take any pills, call nine one one right away. You can also call or text nine eight eight any time, and you can call us at any hour.
Caller -> Nine one one if I take any. Nine eight eight any time. And you. Okay. I'm writing it on the back of my hand.
Nurse -> Good. Is Edmund okay for the moment?
Caller -> He's sleeping. His breathing is calm. He's comfortable. It's just me that's falling apart.
Nurse -> You're not falling apart. You're exhausted, and you've been carrying too much. Let your son help when he gets there.
Caller -> I will. I'll go sit by the window and watch for his headlights. He drives a green truck, I'll know it from a mile away. He loves his father so much, he's been so worried about me too.
Nurse -> Then let him take care of you for a bit. That's a gift you can give him.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. I'll call you in fifteen minutes, and I'll stay on until you're ready to hang up.
Caller -> I'm okay to hang up. I'm okay. Thank you for talking to me. I feel less alone.
Nurse -> I'm so glad. Talk soon, Harriet. And I won't hang up on you, not tonight and not any night.
Caller -> Thank you for not putting me on hold. At the other agency they always did.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Dennis.
Caller -> Dennis, hi, it's Maxine Whitlow. I'm calling about my husband, Ambrose Whitlow. His catheter bag. There's nothing in it. Nothing for hours.
Nurse -> Okay, Maxine. Let's figure it out together. First, his date of birth?
Caller -> December seventeenth. Nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And your number, eight five oh, five five five, zero one three one?
Caller -> Yes. The house phone.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has it been since there was urine in the bag?
Caller -> About six hours. I emptied it at noon, there was a good amount then, and now it's six o'clock and the bag is dry. There's nothing at the bottom. Not a drop.
Nurse -> Okay. How is Ambrose feeling?
Caller -> Uncomfortable. He's pressing on his lower belly. He says there's a pressure. Like he has to go but can't.
Nurse -> Okay. Is any urine coming out around the catheter, around the tube itself?
Caller -> Yes. A little. His underwear was damp when I checked. It's been leaking a bit around where the tube goes in.
Nurse -> Okay. What did the urine look like earlier today?
Caller -> Cloudy. Yes. This morning it looked cloudy. Not red. Kind of like dishwater. I thought that was strange.
Nurse -> Okay. Any blood in the urine? Any red or pink?
Caller -> No blood. Not that I've seen. It was pale and cloudy, not red.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a thermometer? Could you take his temperature?
Caller -> I have one. Hold on. I'll go get it. Ambrose, open up. Okay. Ninety eight point nine.
Nurse -> Okay. No fever. That's good. When was the catheter put in?
Caller -> Three weeks ago on Friday. In the hospital. They said it was temporary, until he gets stronger.
Nurse -> Okay. Why did he need the catheter, do you remember what they told you at the hospital?
Caller -> He had trouble emptying his bladder after the surgery. They said his prostate is big and the anesthesia made it worse. They said the catheter would stay until he sees the urologist. That's in two weeks. I keep counting the days.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Okay. Maxine, let's try a few simple things. Where is the bag right now?
Caller -> It's hanging on the side of the bed. On the frame.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the bag lower than his bladder? Lower than his belly, I mean.
Caller -> Yes. It's hanging down below the mattress. It's lower.
Nurse -> Good. And has he been eating and drinking today?
Caller -> He ate breakfast and lunch. He drank about a cup of tea and a glass of juice. Not a lot of water. He says he doesn't like the taste, it tastes like metal to him since the surgery.
Nurse -> That can happen after anesthesia. We'll talk about it. Now, follow the tubing from the catheter down to the bag. Slowly. Is there any place where it's bent, kinked, or pinched?
Caller -> Okay. I'm following it. It goes from here, under the blanket, and down over the side. Hold on. Ambrose, lift your leg. Ambrose. Lift your leg. Oh. Oh my goodness. There. It's folded. The tube is folded under his leg. He's lying on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Gently straighten it out. Move his leg off of it, and make sure the tube runs straight downhill.
Caller -> Okay. I'm moving him. Okay, straight. There. It's straight. It's running down. Oh! There's urine coming through! It's filling the tube. It's going into the bag. Look at that. It's running. Ambrose, you're going to feel better.
Nurse -> That's great. Let it drain. Is it flowing steadily?
Caller -> Yes. It's coming fast. A lot. The bag is filling. I can see it going up. Maybe, I'd say three hundred milliliters already. It's about at the three hundred line.
Nurse -> Okay. How does he feel?
Caller -> He says the pressure is going away. He just said, oh, that's better. He's relaxing. His face is relaxed.
Nurse -> Good. That sounds like the kink was the problem. Maxine, I still want to look into the cloudy urine and the leaking. A kink would explain the no-urine, but not those.
Caller -> Okay. Will you message his doctor?
Nurse -> Yes. I'm going to message his provider about the cloudy urine and the leaking around the catheter. They may want a urine test.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And a nurse will come out tomorrow to check the catheter and the insertion site.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Thank you. I was going to ask, is it normal for the catheter to be a little uncomfortable? He says it pulls when he gets out of bed.
Nurse -> A little pulling is common, especially when he moves. There should be a strap on his thigh holding the tube in place, so it doesn't tug. Does he have one?
Caller -> I think so. A white strap with Velcro. It's a bit loose. I'll tighten it.
Nurse -> Good. Snug, not tight. The nurse will check it tomorrow too.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time, do you know?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call with a window. Is there a time that works better?
Caller -> Mornings. After nine. He takes his pills at eight and it takes him a while to get going.
Nurse -> I'll ask for after nine. I'll also call you back this evening to see how the drainage is going and what the provider says.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. I'll be here. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Now, Maxine, some things to remember for the tubing. Keep the bag below the level of his bladder, always. Keep the tube free of kinks, especially when he's sitting or lying down. And empty the bag when it's about half full.
Caller -> Below the bladder. No kinks. Empty at half. Okay. I should check under his leg every time I turn him. I'll put a reminder on the bed.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Also, encourage him to drink water through the day. About six to eight cups.
Caller -> Six to eight cups. He doesn't like water. He likes his tea. Can tea count?
Nurse -> Tea counts, but go easy on caffeine. Decaf is better. And water when he can.
Caller -> I'll make him some decaf and I'll add a little lemon.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call us if there's no urine for four hours even after you've checked the tubing, if you see blood in the urine, if he gets a fever or chills, or if his belly pain gets worse or he seems confused.
Caller -> No urine in four hours even after checking. Blood. Fever, chills. Belly pain, confusion. Okay. I'll write it on the whiteboard.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anything else you want to ask while I have you? Medicines, dressings, anything?
Caller -> Just one thing. He has a bit of constipation, he hasn't gone in two days. Is that related to the catheter?
Nurse -> It can be, since the bowel and bladder sit close together. More fluids and fiber help. If it goes beyond three days, tell the nurse tomorrow and we'll talk about a stool softener.
Caller -> Two days now. I'll watch it. Prunes. He likes prunes.
Nurse -> Prunes are perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> I feel so silly. A folded tube. And I got so worried. I was about to put him in the car and drive to the emergency room. I had my keys in my hand.
Nurse -> Please don't feel silly. A kinked tube is the number one reason a bag goes dry. You found it, and you fixed it.
Caller -> Thank you for talking me through it. I would have panicked and called an ambulance.
Nurse -> No need to be sorry. That's what we're here for. How are you doing, Maxine?
Caller -> I'm okay. Tired. We were up late last night. The neighbor's dog kept barking and Ambrose kept waking up. Then he was up early. I'll nap when he does.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> I will. You always make me feel calm, Dennis. My daughter says I get like this because I never learned to ask for help. My mother was the same. We just do everything ourselves until we can't.
Nurse -> It's a family trait, then. But you did ask for help today, and it worked out.
Caller -> It did. I'll call you sooner next time, I promise. Even if it turns out to be a kink.
Nurse -> Please do. Kinks are my favorite kind of call. They're easy to fix.
Caller -> Ha. Mine too, now. Okay. Thank you, Dennis.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll talk to you this evening.
Caller -> Okay. Goodbye.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Rhonda.
Caller -> Hi, Rhonda. It's Tamsin Brockman. I'm calling about my mother, Hazel Brockman. We just got her blood test results and I'm not sure what to do. It's the INR for her warfarin.
Nurse -> Okay, Tamsin, I'm glad you called. Let me get her date of birth.
Caller -> May nineteenth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number, two six two, five five five, zero one seven nine?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm at her house. I came over after work to do her pills for the week.
Nurse -> That's very good of you. How is your mom feeling today?
Caller -> Tired. She's been sleeping a lot since the infection started. But she's in good spirits. She's watching her cooking shows.
Nurse -> Okay. What was the INR?
Caller -> The lab called this afternoon and said four point one. Four point one. I wrote it on my hand. They said her goal is two to three. And I don't know what that means, other than it's higher than it should be.
Nurse -> Okay. It means her blood is thinner than we want it. Tamsin, tell me about the warfarin. What does she take?
Caller -> Five milligrams. Every evening at six. I give it to her myself. She took it last night.
Nurse -> Okay. Warfarin five every evening. And has anything changed with her medicines recently? Any new pills?
Caller -> Yes. The antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin. She had a urinary infection. She started it five days ago. Five hundred milligrams, twice a day. She took one this morning. She has two more days to go.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very important. Ciprofloxacin can make warfarin stronger, which could be why her INR is up. Did anyone tell you about that?
Caller -> No. Nobody said anything. The doctor at urgent care wrote the antibiotic. She didn't know about the warfarin, I guess.
Nurse -> It happens a lot. Okay. Tamsin, I'm looking at her chart now. I see warfarin five milligrams every evening. I see levothyroxine in the morning, we're not changing that. And I don't see the ciprofloxacin yet. Let me add that.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. That's all her pills, plus the antibiotic.
Nurse -> Now, is she bleeding anywhere? Any bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding gums?
Caller -> Her gums. This morning she was brushing her teeth and the sink had pink in it. She said they bled for a minute and stopped.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> A bruise. A new one. On her left forearm. About the size of a plum. She doesn't know what she bumped. It's dark purple.
Nurse -> Okay. Any black or bloody stools? Any nosebleeds, or a bad headache?
Caller -> No. Her stools have been normal brown, I checked. No nosebleeds. No headache. She's been telling me she feels fine. Just tired because of the infection.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fallen, or hit her head?
Caller -> No falls. She's been using her walker. She hasn't hit anything that I know of.
Nurse -> Did she eat and drink today?
Caller -> She had oatmeal and soup. She's drinking a lot of water because of the antibiotic. I keep a pitcher by her chair and I refill it all day.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Okay. Here's what I'd like you to do, Tamsin. Please hold tonight's warfarin. Don't give it.
Caller -> Hold it. Don't give tonight's warfarin. Okay. Even though it's almost six?
Nurse -> Yes. Even though it's almost six. The provider will tell us when to restart it, and at what dose. I'm going to message her provider right now about the INR and the antibiotic.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was afraid that I was supposed to give it and that I'd make it worse. I almost gave it at five thirty, I had the pill in my hand, and then I thought, wait, I should call first.
Nurse -> I'm so glad you waited. That small pause made the difference.
Caller -> I got a feeling from the lab call. The woman's voice changed when she said four point one.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing by calling first. I'd also like to recheck her INR. I'll schedule that for Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. Does the lab come to the house?
Nurse -> Yes. A nurse will draw it at the house. I'll make sure of that.
Caller -> That's great. She doesn't like going out when she's sick.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back tonight, once I hear from the provider, to tell you what to do about tomorrow's dose.
Caller -> Tonight. Okay. I'll stay until you call.
Nurse -> Tamsin, please also keep her away from aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen, like Advil or Aleve. And don't give any extra warfarin.
Caller -> No aspirin. No Advil. No Aleve. No extra warfarin. Okay. She has a bottle of Tylenol. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Tylenol in normal doses is generally okay, but I'd like the provider to confirm. Hold off tonight if she doesn't need it.
Caller -> Okay. She doesn't. I'll hold off.
Nurse -> And for her gums, use a soft toothbrush and be gentle. No hard flossing until we've checked the INR. If she shaves, use an electric razor.
Caller -> Soft toothbrush. No hard flossing. Electric razor. She doesn't shave, but I will remember. I'll swap her toothbrush right now, we have a soft one in the drawer.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, important. If she has black or bloody stools, if she vomits blood, a bad headache, if she falls, or if a nosebleed won't stop after ten minutes of pressure, call nine one one.
Caller -> Black or bloody stool. Vomiting blood. Bad headache. A fall. Nosebleed over ten minutes. Nine one one. Okay. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Good. Also, try to keep her diet steady this week. Don't suddenly add a lot of greens or change what she usually eats.
Caller -> She eats the same thing every day, practically. Oatmeal, toast, chicken soup. Her friend brings her a salad on Fridays, I'll tell her to skip it this week.
Nurse -> A salad now and then is fine, just keep it consistent. How long has she been on the blood thinner?
Caller -> Six years. Since her heart rhythm problem, the atrial fibrillation. She has been very good about it. She goes for her blood tests every month and she never missed one. This is the first time it was ever high.
Nurse -> That's a good record. Something small, like an antibiotic, can tip it, and that's why we check. How is she feeling otherwise?
Caller -> Tired. And she has a little burning when she pees still. The antibiotic is helping, I think. She's drinking a lot of water.
Nurse -> Good. Keep her drinking. And the nurse who comes Thursday will check on that too.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Rhonda. I'm so glad I called. My brother said I was overreacting, he said it was just a number.
Nurse -> It's a number that matters. You weren't overreacting.
Caller -> I'll tell him you said so. He lives in Phoenix, so he doesn't see her every day like I do. It's easy to say from far away.
Nurse -> It is. You're the one who's there. Thank you for being so careful.
Nurse -> I'm glad too. Do you have any other questions?
Caller -> No, I think I've got it. Hold the warfarin tonight. Wait for your call. Soft toothbrush. Watch for bleeding. Thursday blood draw.
Nurse -> You've got it exactly. I'll call you tonight.
Caller -> One more thing. Her friend's grandson is getting married next Saturday. She really wants to go. Will she be okay by then?
Nurse -> I can't promise, but once the INR is back in range and the infection is treated, there is no reason she can't. Let's get through this week first.
Caller -> Okay. I won't mention it to her yet. She'll want to buy a new hat.
Nurse -> Ha. Let her buy the hat. It will give her something to look forward to, and it will be good for her spirits while she finishes the antibiotic.
Caller -> Okay. Goodbye, Rhonda. Thank you again.

Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Bridget.
Caller -> Bridget, it's Zofia Kowalczuk. My mother is Berenice. Berenice Kowalczuk. I made a mistake with her patch.
Nurse -> Okay, Zofia, I'm here. Tell me what happened. First, her date of birth.
Caller -> February fifth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> And is nine one oh, five five five, zero one six two the best number?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. What did you do with the patch?
Caller -> This morning I put on a new patch. The fentanyl patch. The twenty five micrograms an hour. We change it every three days and today is the day. And just now, I was giving her a bath, and I saw another patch on her back. The old one. I forgot to take it off. She has two on.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me right away. When did you put the new one on?
Caller -> This morning. About eight. So nine hours. Maybe a bit less.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she right now?
Caller -> Very sleepy. She's been sleepy all afternoon, I thought it was just her usual. But now I know. When I say her name she opens her eyes and looks at me. And she goes back.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you count her breaths for a full minute?
Caller -> Hold on. One, two. Okay. I counted eleven. Eleven in a minute. It's slow but steady.
Nurse -> Okay. Zofia, take both patches off right now. Peel them off, fold them in half with the sticky sides together, and put them in a bag.
Caller -> Both off. Right now. Okay. Hold on, I'm doing it. Mom, I'm going to turn you. Okay. The old one is off. The new one is off. They're folded. In the bag. Done.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to page our on-call nurse right now.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Will she be okay?
Nurse -> We're going to watch her closely. I'll call you back in ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> Until then, stay beside her. Keep saying her name and see if she wakes up. Keep counting her breathing. And don't put another patch on.
Caller -> Stay. Name. Breathing. No patch. Okay.
Nurse -> And Zofia, if you can't wake her, if her breathing drops below eight a minute, or her lips turn blue, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't wake. Below eight. Blue. Nine one one. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call in ten.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm so careful with these. I just. I changed it on autopilot.
Nurse -> It happens to the most careful people. You caught it, and you told us. That's what counts.

Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Denise.
Caller -> Denise, hi, it's Genevieve Duplessis. I'm a patient. I had a little thing this morning. It's probably nothing.
Nurse -> Hi, Genevieve. Let me get your date of birth.
Caller -> July eighth. Nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> And is three three seven, five five five, zero one two four your number?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> What happened this morning?
Caller -> Tightness. In my chest. Around seven. Or maybe it was eight, after breakfast. I had eggs. I think it was heartburn, honestly. I get heartburn.
Nurse -> Okay. Did the tightness spread anywhere? Your arm, your jaw?
Caller -> My arm. A little. The left one. No. Not really. Maybe a little ache. I don't know. It might have been from sleeping on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Genevieve, did you feel sweaty, nauseous, or short of breath?
Caller -> A little sweaty. No, I was just warm because I was cooking. I wasn't short of breath. I don't think so.
Nurse -> Okay. How long did it last?
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Or maybe an hour. It came and went. Honestly I'm not sure. I took a Tums and it got better.
Nurse -> Okay. And how do you feel right now?
Caller -> Fine. Right now I feel fine. It's gone. No tightness at all. I feel silly calling.
Nurse -> You shouldn't feel silly. Chest symptoms are always worth a call. I'm going to message your provider about the tightness this morning.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Do you think it's my heart?
Nurse -> I can't tell from the phone, and that's why I want your provider and a nurse to look at you. A nurse will come see you today.
Caller -> Today. Okay. I'll be home.
Nurse -> Genevieve, if the tightness comes back, if it spreads to your arm or jaw, or if you get sweaty, nauseated, or short of breath, call nine one one right away. Don't wait, and don't drive yourself.
Caller -> Tightness back, arm, jaw, sweaty, sick, breath. Nine one one. Don't drive. Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Denise. I'll sit down and not do the dishes.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Rest until the nurse comes.

Nurse -> Meadowbrook Home Care, this is Samantha.
Caller -> Hi, Samantha. This is Esther Blumenthal. B L U M E N T H A L. I'm calling for a refill of my Klonopin.
Nurse -> Hi, Esther. Thanks for spelling that. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> December twenty second. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And is five one six, five five five, zero one four three your number?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at your medication list. Esther, I don't see Klonopin on your list. I see lorazepam, point five milligrams, at bedtime as needed. Could that be the one?
Caller -> Oh. Lorazepam. Yes. That's it. The little white one. I always call it my Klonopin. My old doctor called it that. I get them mixed up. It's the same family, isn't it?
Nurse -> It's a similar family, but they're different medicines. According to your chart, the lorazepam is what you're on. Is that the bottle you have in front of you?
Caller -> Let me look. Lorazepam, point five milligrams. Yes. That's it. That's the bottle. Not Klonopin. Silly me.
Nurse -> Okay. How many tablets do you have left?
Caller -> Three. I'm counting. Three.
Nurse -> Okay. How often are you using them?
Caller -> At bedtime when I can't sleep. Maybe four nights a week. Not every night.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll send the lorazepam refill request to your prescriber.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow to let you know where it stands.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay.
Nurse -> Esther, take the lorazepam only at bedtime and only when you need it, not with alcohol, and sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before you stand if you wake in the night.
Caller -> Only at bedtime. No wine. Sit first. Okay. I do have a glass of wine at dinner sometimes. Not at bedtime.
Nurse -> That's fine. Just not close to the lorazepam. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's all. Thank you, Samantha. And sorry about the Klonopin mix-up.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Palliative Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Roxanne Tavares. I'm a patient. My mouth is a mess.
Nurse -> Hi, Roxanne. I'm sorry to hear that. Let me get your date of birth.
Caller -> June thirtieth. Nineteen seventy one.
Nurse -> And is five oh seven, five five five, zero one three six your number?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about your mouth.
Caller -> I had chemo last Tuesday. And about two days after, I started getting sores. Inside my cheeks, and on my gums, and the sides of my tongue. It's been five days now. They hurt so much.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad is the pain, zero to ten?
Caller -> When I eat or drink, about a six. Even water stings sometimes. When I'm not eating, it's more like a three.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you eating?
Caller -> Less. I'm managing mashed potatoes and yogurt and ice cream. Anything with a texture, forget it. I had a piece of toast yesterday and I almost cried.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it the pain that's stopping you from eating, or is food tasting different too?
Caller -> Both. Everything tastes like metal. Even the ice cream. I know it's the chemo, they warned me. But it still makes me sad. I used to love to cook. My family jokes that I never left the kitchen.
Nurse -> That's very common, and it usually fades after treatment. Okay. And drinking?
Caller -> I'm drinking. Slowly. I use a straw. I'm getting about six cups a day, I think. I'm trying. Water mostly.
Nurse -> Good. Roxanne, look in a mirror with a good light. What do you see on your tongue?
Caller -> Okay, hold on. I'm getting my phone flashlight. There are white patches. On the top of my tongue, and on the side. Kind of like cottage cheese. They're not coming off when I scrape them with my toothbrush.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Are you using anything for it?
Caller -> Magic mouthwash. The prescription kind. Five milliliters, swish and spit, every four hours if I need it. It helps for about twenty minutes. Then it comes right back.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?
Caller -> No. I took it this morning. Ninety eight point two.
Nurse -> Good. Roxanne, those white patches might be thrush, which is a yeast infection that can happen after chemo. I'm going to message your provider about the sores and the white patches. They may want to give you something for it.
Caller -> Okay. That would be great. Can you do that today?
Nurse -> I'll send it right now. And a nurse will come see you Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. Is that when I get my next treatment? No, that's the following week. Okay.
Nurse -> No, Thursday is just a nurse visit. I'll also call you tomorrow with what the provider says.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, rinse your mouth several times a day with a mix of salt and baking soda in warm water, about a half teaspoon of each in a cup. And use a soft toothbrush.
Caller -> Salt and baking soda. Warm water. Soft toothbrush. Okay. I have a baby toothbrush, which is the softest one I could find.
Nurse -> That's perfect. And for food, stick to cold or room temperature soft foods. Avoid anything acidic, spicy, or crunchy, like orange juice, tomato, chips. And keep using a straw.
Caller -> No orange juice. I had some this morning and I regretted it. No tomatoes. Okay. Smoothies are good, I'll make those.
Nurse -> Smoothies are great. And call us if your temperature goes over one hundred point four, if you can't swallow even liquids, or if the sores bleed or spread.
Caller -> Over one hundred point four. Can't swallow. Bleeding or spreading. Okay.
Nurse -> Is there anything else going on, any trouble sleeping, or other questions about your treatment?
Caller -> I sleep okay, I wake up when my mouth gets dry. I keep a glass of water and a little lip balm on the nightstand. And I wanted to ask, should I still go to my appointment next Tuesday? The oncologist's office said they'd decide after bloodwork.
Nurse -> Yes, keep it for now. The oncology team will decide after the labs. I'll mention the mouth sores to the provider so they know before then.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. Thank you.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> My husband is making me broth. He's trying so hard. It's sweet. He burned the first batch. And the second one he put too much pepper. The third one was almost okay. My daughter is eleven and she gives him a score out of ten for every batch.
Nurse -> Ha. What was the third one's score?
Caller -> A seven. She's a tough judge. She says he's improving.
Nurse -> That's a good sign for broth number four.
Caller -> I'm having to give up coffee, which is the real tragedy. Even decaf burns. I look at my coffee maker like it's an old friend who moved away.
Nurse -> Ha. It will be there when your mouth heals. Maybe iced coffee in a week, through the straw.
Nurse -> Ha. That's love. Tell him thank you from us.
Caller -> I will. Thanks, Naomi. I just needed somebody to say it's normal.
Nurse -> It's common, and we'll get you comfortable. Talk to you tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi, Denise. It's Giselle Leclair. I'm calling about my husband, Bertrand Leclair. I'm doing the supply check and some things are low.
Nurse -> Hi, Giselle. You're so organized. Let me get his date of birth first.
Caller -> October second. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> And is three oh three, five five five, zero one three eight still your number?
Caller -> Yes. The house phone. I never leave the house much anyway.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead with your list.
Caller -> Okay. I have it on a clipboard. Suction catheters. The size fourteen. I have five. Five left. We use eight to ten a day lately.
Nurse -> Okay. Eight to ten a day is more than usual. We'll talk about that. Next.
Caller -> The inner cannulas. For his trach. I have two spares. Two. We change them daily.
Nurse -> Okay. Next.
Caller -> The trach ties, the Velcro ones. I have three. And the saline vials, the little ones for the suctioning, I have ten. I think that's enough for two or three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Next.
Caller -> The formula. For the feeding tube. Eight cartons. We use four a day, so that's two days. And the syringes, the big ones. Three.
Nurse -> Okay. Next.
Caller -> Distilled water. For the humidifier on the ventilator. I'm out. Totally out. I've been using boiled water that I let cool, because I didn't want to run it dry.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't use boiled tap water in the humidifier. We'll get you distilled right away. Next.
Caller -> The ventilator circuits. The tubing. I have one spare. One. I should change the one he has on in about a week.
Nurse -> Okay. How is the supply closet organized? Do you rotate the oldest supplies to the front?
Caller -> I do. I labeled the shelves with a marker. First in, first out. I used to work in a pharmacy, so it's second nature. The ventilator things are on the top shelf, the feeding things on the middle, and the suctioning at eye level because that's the one I reach for most.
Nurse -> That's a better system than most hospitals. Okay. That's everything on the list?
Caller -> That's the list. And then I have a couple of other things to tell you.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me.
Caller -> His secretions are thicker. This week. Yellowish. Sticky. And there's more of it. I'm suctioning him maybe every hour. Last month it was every three or four hours. That's why the catheters are going so fast.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I take it every morning. Ninety eight point one this morning. Normal.
Nurse -> Okay. Has anything else changed with his feeds, his skin, or his sleep?
Caller -> His feeds are fine. He's tolerating the four a day, no vomiting. His skin is good, I check under the trach ties every morning. He's sleeping okay, a bit more in the afternoon. Nothing unusual.
Nurse -> Good. Is the color changing, green, or bloody?
Caller -> Pale yellow. Not green. Not bloody. Just thick. Like mucus after a cold.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he seem more uncomfortable, or is his breathing different?
Caller -> No. He's calm. His numbers are the same on the monitor. I think he's just dry. I wondered about the water. Maybe that's why the secretions are thick, because of the humidifier.
Nurse -> That's a very good thought. Dry air can thicken secretions. Getting the distilled water in will help, and I'll ask the respiratory therapist too.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. He says, well, he blinks, that he's comfortable. We have a code. One blink for yes, two for no. He just blinked once at me. I asked if he was comfortable.
Nurse -> I love that. Tell him I said hello. And the other thing you mentioned was the battery.
Caller -> Yes. And the other thing is the battery. The backup battery for the ventilator. It's supposed to last four hours. Yesterday I tested it, I do it once a month, and it died after two hours. About two.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a serious one, Giselle. Thank you for testing it. I'll get the respiratory therapist on that today.
Caller -> Thank you. I got scared. We had a power outage last winter for six hours and I don't know what we would have done.
Nurse -> What did you do last winter?
Caller -> The battery lasted four hours then. And then the ambulance people brought a generator. The fire department. It was such a night. My son slept on the floor next to Bertrand's bed with a flashlight, and I counted his breaths on the monitor. The neighbors brought us hot coffee and a space heater at three in the morning.
Nurse -> I'm glad that worked out. We'll make sure you have a better plan this time. I'm going to order the suction catheters, the inner cannulas, the trach ties, the feeding syringes, the distilled water, and the ventilator circuits.
Caller -> What about the formula and the saline? Do I need to order those?
Nurse -> You have two days of formula, so I'll ask the pharmacy for a delivery too. I'll put it on the same order and make a note.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> It all comes Tuesday.
Caller -> Tuesday. That's four days. Is there any way sooner? I'm okay on most, but the distilled water and the catheters worry me.
Nurse -> I understand. Let me ask if the distilled water can come tomorrow. Meanwhile, if you can, buy a few jugs at the grocery store. Any store sells it.
Caller -> The grocery store. I can ask my son. He's coming by after work. He's twenty six, he works at the hospital in the billing office, so he understands about medical supplies more than most.
Nurse -> That's a big help. And does he help with Bertrand's care too?
Caller -> On weekends. He does the morning suctioning on Saturday so I can sleep till eight. It's the best gift. I also have a niece who comes on Wednesdays for the afternoon.
Nurse -> That's a good team. It matters to have people you trust.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a nurse will come Wednesday to check the equipment and look at him.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Giselle, a few reminders. Change the inner cannula once a day, and any time it's crusted. Use only distilled water in the humidifier. And keep the spare circuit in its package until you need it.
Caller -> Daily. Crusted. Distilled only. Spare sealed. Okay. I knew most of that. I just needed to hear it again.
Nurse -> It's a lot to keep straight. Also, here's the power outage plan. If the power goes out, switch to the backup battery, then call us and the power company. If the ventilator alarms and you can't fix it, or you can't ventilate him by hand with the bag, call nine one one.
Caller -> Power out, battery, call you and the power company. Alarm I can't fix or the bag doesn't work, nine one one. Okay. I have a laminated card with that. It's on the wall by the machine.
Nurse -> A laminated card is perfect. And call us any hour if the ventilator alarms or you have questions about the equipment.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. Thank you, Denise. You always remember everything about us.
Nurse -> It's easy to remember people like you. How is Bertrand doing otherwise?
Caller -> He's good. Mentally sharp as ever. He's using his eye-gaze computer. Yesterday he wrote me a poem. It was about the tomatoes in our garden.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Tell him I'd love to read it someday.
Caller -> I will. He'd be thrilled. He says the nurses are his favorite audience. He's working on a second poem right now, about the lake where we got married. It's taking him all afternoon, one letter at a time. But he insists.
Nurse -> It sounds worth the wait. Take care of both of you.
Nurse -> Ha. We're happy to be. Talk to you soon, Giselle.
Caller -> Thank you. Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hello? Hello? Is this the nurse? I can barely hear. Hold on. My hearing aid. It's dead. Can you talk louder?
Nurse -> Yes, this is Tom, the nurse at Lakeshore Home Health. Can you hear me better now?
Caller -> A little. Say it slow. It's Odell. Odell Whitmire. I'm calling because I did something silly.
Nurse -> Hi, Odell. I'm listening. First, what is your date of birth?
Caller -> What? Say again.
Nurse -> Your date of birth, Odell?
Caller -> January twenty eighth. Nineteen thirty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your phone number?
Caller -> Nine three one, five five five, zero one six five.
Nurse -> Nine three one, five five five, zero one six five. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to speak slowly. Odell, can you tell me what happened?
Caller -> What? Tell you what happened? Yes. Hold on. Let me turn the TV off. It's the game show. Hold on. Okay. It's off. I can hear you a little better.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> I took my pills this morning. And then I took them again. I forgot that I took them. Both times. The metro pro lol and the lay six. Both of them. Twice.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, I want to make sure I understand. Which pills did you take twice? Was it metoprolol, the heart pill?
Caller -> What? Metoprolol? Yes. Metoprolol. The twenty five. That's the one.
Nurse -> And the other one, was it Lasix, the water pill?
Caller -> Lasix. Yes, the water pill. The twenty. I took two. Twice. I mean I took the Lasix twice. And the metoprolol twice.
Nurse -> Okay. Metoprolol twenty five milligrams twice this morning, and Lasix twenty milligrams twice this morning. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's right. Twice. I'm ninety two years old and I forgot I took them. My daughter used to set them out for me but she moved to Arizona.
Nurse -> I understand. When did you take the second set?
Caller -> What? The second what?
Nurse -> The second time you took the pills. What time?
Caller -> About noon. Maybe a little after. I took the first at eight. I saw them on the table and I thought, oh, I forgot my pills.
Nurse -> Okay. How are you feeling right now?
Caller -> Dizzy. When I stand up. Lightheaded. And weak. My legs feel like noodles. And my heart is slow, I can feel it, thump, and then a wait, and then thump.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds uncomfortable. Let's check your blood pressure. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> What? A cuff? Yes. My daughter got me one with the big numbers. Hold on. Let me put it on. It takes a while. Okay. It says ninety eight over fifty six.
Nurse -> Ninety eight over fifty six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Ninety eight over fifty six. And the pulse says fifty too.
Nurse -> Fifty two? Did you say fifty two for the pulse?
Caller -> Yes. Fifty two. Not fifty too. Fifty two. That's what it says.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Odell, have you fallen, or fainted at all?
Caller -> What? Fallen? No. I almost did. I grabbed the counter. But no. I didn't fall. I'm sitting in my chair now.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Have you had anything to eat or drink today?
Caller -> What? Eat? Oatmeal at eight, with the pills. And coffee. Two cups. That's all. I wasn't hungry. And I don't drink much water, it makes me go to the bathroom.
Nurse -> Okay. Odell, I'd like you to drink a glass of water now, slowly, and eat a few crackers if you have them. The water pill can dry you out, and you took two.
Caller -> What? A glass of water and crackers. The water pill dries me out. Okay. I have crackers in the cupboard but I'll have to stand. I'll do it slow. Or I'll wait. I have a bottle of water here by my chair. I'll drink that.
Nurse -> Good, the bottle by your chair is perfect. Please stay seated, or better, lie down. I'm going to help you. Are you alone in the house?
Caller -> What? Alone. Yes. Just me and the cat. My wife passed ten years ago.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, Odell. Okay. First, I want you to hold your pills tonight. Don't take the evening metoprolol, and don't take any more Lasix, until the on-call nurse calls you.
Caller -> What? Hold the pills? Don't take them? Okay. Don't take the evening ones. Okay. Until she calls. I understand. I'll leave them in the box.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to page our on-call nurse right now.
Caller -> What? Page? Okay. I don't know what that is. But okay.
Nurse -> It means I'm sending a message to the nurse on call so she can help you tonight. A nurse will also come to your house within two hours.
Caller -> Within two hours. Okay. Someone is coming. Good. The door will be locked. I'll have to unlock it.
Nurse -> Yes. When you're able, please unlock the front door, but don't stand up fast. Go slowly.
Caller -> Slowly. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Twenty minutes? Okay. Will I hear the phone? My hearing aid is dead.
Nurse -> Odell, do you have a fresh battery for your hearing aid?
Caller -> What? Battery? I think there are some in the drawer. In the kitchen. I'd have to get up.
Nurse -> Wait until you feel steadier. When you can, replace the battery so you can hear the phone. If you can't find one, keep the phone right next to you, with the ringer turned up.
Caller -> Ringer up. Phone next to me. Okay. I'll try to find the battery after the nurse comes.
Nurse -> That works. Now, here are some safety things. Lie down, or sit with your feet up. Stand up slowly with a hand on the wall. And keep the phone beside you.
Caller -> Feet up. Hand on the wall. Phone beside me. Okay. I put a pillow under my feet. That's good. I feel a little better sitting.
Nurse -> Good. And Odell, call nine one one if you faint, if you have chest pain, if your pulse goes under forty, or if you can't get up.
Caller -> What? Nine one one if I faint. Chest pain. Pulse under forty. Can't get up. Okay. I understand that one.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, so this doesn't happen again, I'd like to help you with a pill organizer. The kind with the day and the time on each box, and a note where you write when you've taken them.

Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Sofia.
Caller -> Sofia, it's Gianna Pellegrino. It's my mom, Nadine. She's in so much pain. It's her hip. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Gianna, I'm here. We're going to get her some help. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> Uh, September second. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have three one three, five five five, zero one eight eight for you.
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. How bad is the pain right now, on a scale of zero to ten?
Caller -> She says nine. Nine out of ten. She's crying. She keeps saying it's a nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Where is it exactly?
Caller -> Her left hip. It goes down into the thigh. She had it this morning, too, but it was manageable. A five, maybe. It got worse around noon.
Nurse -> Okay. What kind of pain is it? Aching, burning, sharp?
Caller -> Aching all the time. But when she moves it's sharp. Like a knife, she says. She can't turn at all.
Nurse -> Okay. What has she taken for it?
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid. Ten milligrams. She had one at noon and another one at, um, I think two. The last one was about forty minutes ago, and it hasn't touched it.
Nurse -> Okay. So two doses today and the pain is still a nine.
Caller -> Yes. It's not helping. Not even a little.
Nurse -> And how often is she allowed to have it?
Caller -> Every four hours if she needs it. That's what the bottle says.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she fall, or twist it, or have any kind of injury today?
Caller -> No. Nothing. She was in her recliner and she got up to use the commode, and that's when it got really bad.
Nurse -> Okay. And is she sleepy at all? Any trouble breathing, any confusion?
Caller -> No. Breathing's fine. She's awake. She's the opposite of sleepy. She's wide awake and hurting.
Nurse -> Okay, Gianna. This isn't being controlled at home. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Please. Please. Is somebody coming to the house?
Nurse -> Yes. I'm also going to send a nurse out to you. I'm asking for it within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Sofia.
Nurse -> While you wait, please don't give any extra morphine on top of her schedule. The on-call clinician will tell you if she can have more and how much.
Caller -> No extra. Wait for the call. Okay. I don't want to make it worse. I just want it to stop for her.
Nurse -> I know. Let's help her get comfortable in the meantime. Can she lie on her right side, so the left hip is on top?
Caller -> She's in the recliner. Mom, can you, hold on. Mom, let me move your leg. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Okay. She says it's a little better if the leg is straight.
Nurse -> Okay. Put a pillow between her knees if she's on her side. And a warm blanket over her is fine, but no heating pad, nothing hot directly on the hip.
Caller -> Pillow between the knees. Blanket. No heating pad. Okay. I'm doing it. Okay, the pillow's in. She's, I think it's maybe a seven now. She says maybe a seven if she doesn't move.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to hear, but we still want the clinician to weigh in. I'll call you back in thirty minutes if you haven't heard from them.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. And they'll call from where? My phone doesn't pick up unknown numbers.
Nurse -> It may come up as unknown or blocked. Please answer anything for the next hour.
Caller -> I'll answer anything. I'll turn it all the way up.
Nurse -> Good. Is there someone there with you?
Caller -> My dad. He's in the kitchen. He can't watch her cry. He's been in there making tea nobody's drinking.
Nurse -> That's hard on all of you. Gianna, one more thing. If she becomes hard to wake up, or her breathing gets slow or shallow, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Hard to wake up. Slow breathing. Nine one one. Okay. But she's wide awake right now. Wide awake. Okay.
Nurse -> I know. It's just so you have it. You're doing a good job. You called at exactly the right time.
Caller -> Thank you. I just can't stand it. She's my mom.
Nurse -> I know. I'm here. Keep your phone near you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Gianna, while we wait, have you had anything to eat or drink tonight yourself?
Caller -> No. I had coffee at lunch. I haven't thought about it. I've just been sitting next to her since noon.
Nurse -> Please get a glass of water, and a cracker if you can. You need to be steady for her tonight.
Caller -> Okay. I'll have my dad bring me something. He needs a job anyway.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Give him that one.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Sofia. Really.
Nurse -> Anytime. Talk to you soon.

Caller -> A little sleepy. Kind of heavy. But I'm okay. I'm talking to you.
Nurse -> Okay. Is your breathing normal? Any trouble breathing, or slow breathing?
Caller -> No. My breathing's fine. I'm breathing normal, I think. My friend Lacey's here. She says I'm breathing fine.
Nurse -> Good. Lacey being there is very good. Tanya, tell me exactly what you took and when.
Caller -> I took one Percocet around eleven. Then my phone alarm went off, and I was confused, and I thought it was the alarm for my next one. And I took another one. That was maybe twenty minutes ago.
Nurse -> Okay. So two Percocet, about twenty minutes apart. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. One, then one. I know. I know. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> It's okay. You did the right thing by calling. Let me get your birth date, and the number you're on.
Caller -> January thirty first. Nineteen seventy nine.
Nurse -> And five oh three, five five five, zero one two two?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they can advise us.

Nurse -> No, not at all. We just want to make sure you're safe. Please don't take any more Percocet tonight, or anything else that makes you sleepy, until the on-call clinician says it's okay.

Nurse -> Meadowbrook Home Care, this is Samantha.
Caller -> Hi, Samantha. This is Odessa Pike. My husband Clifford feels warm. I took his temperature but I'm not sure about the number.
Nurse -> Okay, Odessa. Let me get his chart up. What's Clifford's date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty third. Nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> And I have nine one nine, five five five, zero one three one for you.
Caller -> That's right. That's the house phone.
Nurse -> Okay. What number did you get on the thermometer?
Caller -> It said one hundred point four. I think. The screen is cracked, it's got a line right through the last number. It might have been a hundred point eight. I couldn't tell. Hundred point four or eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Where did you take it? Under the arm, in the mouth?
Caller -> In the mouth. Under the tongue. I waited for the beep.
Nurse -> Okay. And how is he otherwise? Does he seem different?
Caller -> He's more tired than usual. Today. He's been lying on the couch since lunch, and he's never on the couch.
Nurse -> Okay. Any cough, runny nose, sore throat?
Caller -> No cough. Nothing like that. He says he just feels, you know, blah.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he drinking?
Caller -> Yes. He had a whole glass of juice and some tea. He's fine with the drinking. Not eating much, but drinking.
Nurse -> Okay. Odessa, because the screen is cracked, I don't want to go by that reading. Do you have another thermometer in the house?
Caller -> I think there's one in the bathroom drawer. The old ear one. Or the forehead one, I'm not sure which.
Nurse -> Either one is fine. Please take his temperature again with that one, and write down the number and the time.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth. It's Hannah Lindholm. My son is Ezra. I have a few things, but the big one is that he had a seizure last night.
Nurse -> Oh, Hannah. Okay. I'm glad you called. Let me pull up Ezra's chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> June twelfth, twenty nineteen.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I have four one five, five five five, zero one three eight for you. Is that still the best number?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. Caleb, put that down. Sorry. Sorry. Yes, that's the best one.
Nurse -> No worries. Okay, tell me about the seizure. What time did it happen?
Caller -> It was around two in the morning. I heard him from the monitor. A noise, a kind of a grunt. And I went in and he was stiff and shaking. His eyes were rolled up.
Nurse -> Okay. How long did it last, do you know?
Caller -> About three minutes. I looked at the clock on the wall. It felt like an hour. But I think three minutes. Maybe a little more than three.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you give him anything for it?
Caller -> I gave him the Diastat. The rectal one. I gave it at the two minute mark, like you taught us. And it stopped, I think, right after. Or maybe it would have stopped anyway.
Nurse -> Okay. You did exactly what the plan says. And then what happened?
Caller -> He was really sleepy. He slept the rest of the night. I stayed in the chair next to his bed. I didn't sleep.
Nurse -> Of course you didn't. How is he this morning?
Caller -> He's sleepy. Sleepier than normal. But he wakes up when I talk to him, and he knows me. He said "Mama" and he smiled. He's sort of floppy but I think that's the medicine.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that he's waking and responding. Did he hit his head, or bite his tongue, or get hurt in any way?
Caller -> No. He was in the bed with the rails up. No blood, I checked his mouth. Nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever? Have you taken his temperature?
Caller -> I did. At seven. It was normal. No fever. He felt cool, even.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Has he had his regular seizure medicine this morning?
Caller -> Yes, the Keppra. Five milliliters. I gave it through the tube at eight, like always. He tolerated it fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Twice a day, five milliliters?
Caller -> Twice a day. Eight and eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Hannah, how long has it been since his last seizure before this one?
Caller -> Oh, gosh. At least two months. It was the middle of August, I think. The last time. Mom, can you, hold on. Sorry. My mother just came in, she's asking about lunch. Mom, he's okay. We're talking to the nurse.
Nurse -> That's all right. Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry about that. It's been a morning. I'm back.
Nurse -> No problem. Two months seizure free is good, and now this one. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so they know about the seizure and the Diastat.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Do I need to take him to the hospital? I wasn't sure. He seems okay, but I didn't know.
Nurse -> It's a good question. The on-call clinician will make that call with us. Because he woke up and he's responding, and you gave the Diastat on time, I think it's okay to wait for them. But I'm also going to send a nurse out to see him this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. Thank you. Oh, that makes me feel better.
Nurse -> You mentioned a few things. What else is going on?
Caller -> Okay. The second thing is his tube. The G-tube. Around the button, it's red. And it's leaking a little. It started yesterday, I think. The formula is leaking out around the edge. And his shirt was wet this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. How red? Is it just around the opening, or is it spreading?
Caller -> Just around the opening. A ring. Like a pink ring. It doesn't look like it's spreading. It's not hot. There's no pus. I looked. Just wet and pink.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for describing it so well. The nurse will look at it when she's there. In the meantime, keep it clean and dry. Wash gently with soap and water, pat it dry, and don't put any creams or ointments on it.
Caller -> Soap and water. Pat dry. No creams. I did put some of the, what's it called, the barrier cream. On it. Last night. Should I not do that?
Nurse -> Let's hold off on that for now. The nurse will tell you whether it's okay. Just keep it clean and dry.
Caller -> Okay. No cream. Wash it, dry it. Okay.
Nurse -> What was the third thing?
Caller -> The formula. We're low. We have four cans of the Peptamen left. I thought the delivery was coming Monday, but I called and they said there was a mix-up with the order.
Nurse -> Okay. Four cans. How long does that last him?
Caller -> About two days. A little less, maybe. He takes about two cans a day. Or a little more with the water flushes. So, two days.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to put in a new order for the Peptamen now. It's done.
Caller -> Oh, thank you.
Nurse -> And I'm going to coordinate the delivery for tomorrow morning, so you don't run out.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. That would be wonderful. I'll be home. I'm always home.
Nurse -> Hannah, I'm also going to message Ezra's neurologist about last night's seizure, so they're aware.
Caller -> Please. His neurologist wanted us to tell them if he had another one. I was going to call but I wasn't sure if I should call them or you.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling us. I'll make sure they hear it. And I'll call you back within the hour, after I've reached the on-call clinician.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll keep my phone on me. Caleb. Caleb, no. Sorry. My other son, he's trying to feed the dog from the counter.
Nurse -> It sounds like you've got your hands full.
Caller -> I really do. My husband is at work until six. My mother is here, but she's, she's not much help with Ezra. She gets nervous around the tube.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing the heavy lifting. Let me go over a couple of things for today, in case there's another seizure. Keep Ezra on his side when he's sleeping. If he has another seizure, time it, stay with him, keep him on his side, and don't put anything in his mouth.
Caller -> On his side. Time it. Stay with him. Nothing in his mouth. Right. Okay. I know that. I always do that.
Nurse -> I know you do. And if a seizure lasts longer than five minutes, if he has another one right after, or if he turns blue, call nine one one.
Caller -> Longer than five minutes. Another one right after. Blue. Nine one one. Okay. I have the number by the phone.
Nurse -> Good. And call us if he gets a fever, if he vomits, if you can't wake him up like you do now, or if the leaking gets worse.
Caller -> Fever. Vomit. Can't wake him. Leaking more. Okay. I'm writing it on the whiteboard. We have a whiteboard in the kitchen for him.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Is there anything else going on, anything you've been wondering about?
Caller -> Well, there's one more thing, but it's not urgent. I wanted to ask about school. He's supposed to start part-time in November, and after last night I'm worried. Is that crazy?
Nurse -> It's not crazy at all. That's a good question for the neurologist and the team, and I'll add it to my message so they can talk with you about it.
Caller -> Okay. I'd like that. I don't want to panic. I just don't want to send him somewhere and then, you know.
Nurse -> I understand. Let's get through today first. How are you doing, Hannah? You were up all night.
Caller -> I'm tired. I'm really tired. But I'm okay. I had coffee. My mother made me eat toast.
Nurse -> Good. Please try to rest when the nurse is here this afternoon, even for a little bit.
Caller -> I'll try. I'll try. Thank you, Beth. You always make me feel like I'm not crazy.
Nurse -> You're not crazy. You're a great mom. I'll talk to you within the hour.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gail.
Caller -> Hello, Gail. This is Nadia Khoury. My husband is Elias Khoury, K H O U R Y. He has a rash.
Nurse -> Hi, Nadine. Thanks for spelling it. What's Elias's date of birth?
Caller -> March ninth, nineteen sixty three. No, I'm sorry. March eleventh. Eleventh. Nineteen sixty three.
Nurse -> Got it. March eleventh. And what number can I reach you at, Nadine?
Caller -> Seven one eight, five five five, zero one two six.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the rash. Where is it?
Caller -> On both his arms. The inside of the elbows mostly and down toward the wrists. It's red and bumpy and he's scratching it. He's had it two days.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he started any new medicine recently?
Caller -> Yes. The amoxicillin. The doctor started it on Friday for the chest. Five hundred milligrams, three times a day. He took one this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. That timing is helpful. Any swelling in his face, his lips, his tongue? Any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. No swelling. His face looks the same. He's breathing the same as always. It's just the arms and it itches.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to hear. I'm going to message the hospice provider today about the rash, since it started after the amoxicillin.
Caller -> Should I stop the amoxicillin?
Nurse -> I'd like the provider to answer that, so please wait for them. I'll let you know what they say. I'm also going to send a nurse to see him tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow. That's fine. I'll be here.
Nurse -> For the itching, cool compresses help. Keep his nails short, try not to let him scratch, and no hot showers for now.

Caller -> February twelfth, nineteen sixty.
Nurse -> And I have six one oh, five five five, zero one three eight for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the cough. What are you bringing up?
Caller -> Yellow-green phlegm. A lot more than usual. Thick. It started clear on Sunday and it turned yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a fever? Have you taken your temperature?

Nurse -> That's for the provider to decide. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow morning to listen to your lungs and check your oxygen.

Caller -> A hundred and one. Blood. Worse breathing. Nine one one for the chest. Okay. I have it.
Nurse -> Anything else, Lucille?
Caller -> No. Just thank you for calling me back so fast. Last time I waited all day.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Take care.

Caller -> Joel, it's Ruth Quillfeather. My husband Abner won't stop throwing up. Six times since this morning, and I gave him the Zofran twice and it isn't working.
Nurse -> Okay, Ruth. I'm sorry. I'm going to help. What's Abner's date of birth?
Caller -> December nineteenth, nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have four oh five, five five five, zero one one four?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Can he keep anything down, even a few sips?

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Alan.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Alan. Is this, is this the hospice? The nighttime number?
Nurse -> It is. This is the after-hours line. How can I help?
Caller -> Okay. Okay good. It's Gil Tessier. My dad is Harold Tessier. I'm sorry it's so late, I know it's, what is it, three?
Nurse -> It's a little after three. Don't worry about that, that's what we're here for. What's going on with your dad?
Caller -> Well, he's, he's agitated. He's been agitated at night, this is the second night now. He's up, he's calling for my mom, and she's, she passed in, uh, two thousand and nineteen.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm sorry, Gil. That sounds like a hard night. Let me pull up his chart. Can you give me your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> Yeah. It's July eighth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. Give me a second, I'm typing.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time. I'm just, I'm in the hallway outside his room. I didn't want him to hear me.
Nurse -> That's smart. Okay, I have him. And is eight oh one, five five five, zero one two nine the number you're on?
Caller -> Yes. Yeah. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. So tell me how it started. When did this begin?
Caller -> Um, so, Monday night. No wait. Tuesday. It was Tuesday, because the, the aide had come that day. Tuesday night and then last night. So two nights.
Nurse -> Okay, so Tuesday night and last night.
Caller -> Right. Right. And he's usually, he's fine in the day. A little foggy. He knows who I am. But then it gets dark and he gets, I don't know the word. Wound up. He's picking at the blanket. Pulling at it. Over and over.
Nurse -> Mm-hm. Picking at the blankets. Is he saying anything?
Caller -> He keeps saying, "Where's Ellen? Is Ellen coming?" That's my mom. Ellen. And I said Dad, Mom's not here, and that made it worse, he got really upset. So now I don't say anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Gil, that's helpful. And what, what's he doing right this minute?
Caller -> He's, hold on. Hold on, let me look. Dad? Dad, it's okay. It's Gil. Go back to sleep. Okay. He's lying down. He's mumbling. He's kind of, he's quieter now.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is he showing any signs of pain? Grimacing, moaning, guarding anywhere?
Caller -> No. No, I don't think so. I've been watching for that, because the nurse told us what to look for. His face is relaxed. He doesn't grimace. It's not that. It's, it's more like confused and scared.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had a fall? Or tried to get out of bed?
Caller -> No falls. He tried to sit up last night, I think, but I was right there. I just, I held his shoulder. No falls.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he on anything for agitation? What have you given him?
Caller -> Yes, the lorazepam. The point five milligram. The little white one. I gave him one last night. At nine. Around nine o'clock.
Nurse -> Okay. Did it help?
Caller -> It did. For a while. He was calm for about, I'd say two hours. Then he was up again, around eleven. But I didn't give him another because I wasn't sure if I was allowed.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that you checked. I'm looking at his list here. I see the lorazepam, I see the haloperidol, the furosemide, the atorvastatin.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, I don't give him the, the haloperidol. The nurse said that's only if the lorazepam doesn't work. And the other ones are, those are his regular ones. Morning ones.
Nurse -> Right. Okay. So you've only used the lorazepam, once, last night at nine.
Caller -> Yes. Just once. And tonight, nothing yet. I'm trying to wait.
Nurse -> Okay. How many tablets do you have left?
Caller -> Let me look. Hang on, I have the bottle in my, it's in my robe pocket. Okay. Six. There are six. Six left.
Nurse -> Okay. Six. Thank you.
Caller -> Is that enough? Should I be worried about running out?
Nurse -> For now it's okay. I'll mention it to the provider and we'll watch it.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Sorry. Sorry, I'm, can you hear me? I think I'm going to lose you, the signal in the hall is terrible.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine. If we drop, I'll call you right back at the number you gave me.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Sorry. It's just, it's hard to see him like this. He was a, he taught high school. History. Thirty-one years. And now he doesn't know what year it is.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's a lot to carry, watching that.
Caller -> It is. It really is. And my sister's in Phoenix, so it's mostly me.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job being there. Okay, here's what I'd like to do. I'm going to send a message to the hospice provider about the agitation, since it's happened two nights in a row.
Caller -> Okay. Will they change something? The medicine?
Nurse -> They might. That's their decision. They could adjust the dose or the timing, or add something. I don't want to promise. But they'll see it first thing in the morning.
Caller -> Okay. That's fair. That's fine.
Nurse -> And I'll have a nurse come out tomorrow to see him and look at the whole picture.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time, do you know?
Nurse -> I don't have a time yet. The scheduler will call you in the morning. I'll give them your number.
Caller -> Okay. Because I have to take my daughter to school at eight, but then I'm home.
Nurse -> I'll note that. And I'll call you tomorrow morning myself, once I've talked to the day team.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. You're, you're not even on in the morning though, are you?
Nurse -> I'm on until seven. I'll either call you before I go, or I'll hand it off, and one of the day nurses will call. Either way, you'll hear from us.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, for the rest of tonight. Keep a little light on in his room, a night light is perfect. Keep the room quiet, keep the TV off, and speak softly.
Caller -> Okay. A night light. We have one somewhere. I'll put the little one from the bathroom in there.
Nurse -> And Gil, when he asks for your mom, try not to correct him. You don't have to say she's gone, and you don't have to say she's coming. You can say something like, "You're safe, Dad, I'm here," and ask him about her.
Caller -> Ask him about her. Okay. That, that actually makes sense. I was trying to tell him the truth and it just upset him.
Nurse -> It's very common. You're not doing anything wrong.
Caller -> The Dodgers game was on earlier, I had it on for him, and I thought that would help. He used to love it. But he just stared.
Nurse -> That can be a lot of noise for him at night. The quieter the better, honestly.
Caller -> Yeah. I'll turn it off. I already did. I turned it off at midnight. I should've done it sooner.
Nurse -> You're learning as you go. Now, about the lorazepam. Please only give it the way the label says, and don't give it any sooner than the label allows. If you're not sure whether it's time, call me and ask.
Caller -> Okay. The label. Not sooner. And call if I'm not sure. Okay. It says every, I think every eight hours as needed. I'll look at it.
Nurse -> Good. Look at it and tell me what it says if you want to double-check.
Caller -> It says, one tablet by mouth every eight hours as needed for agitation. Okay. So it's been, it's been six hours, so not until nine or so.
Nurse -> Right. Okay. And Gil, one more thing. If he falls, if he tries to climb out of bed, if he starts striking out at you, or if he gets so upset that you can't calm him down at all, call us right away, any hour.
Caller -> Falls. Climbing out. Hitting. Can't calm him. Okay. I have the number. It's, it's on the fridge. I have it.
Nurse -> Good. Is there someone who can sit with you? Even a neighbor?
Caller -> Not at three in the morning. No, I'm good. I'll just sit in the chair. I do it every night.
Nurse -> All right. Try to rest if he settles. Even twenty minutes helps.
Caller -> I'll try. Okay. Thank you, Alan. Really. I didn't think anybody would pick up.
Nurse -> We always pick up. Anytime.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Bye now.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hello? Hello, is this the nurse? I need a nurse. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.
Nurse -> This is Tom, I'm a nurse. Take a breath. Who am I talking to, and what's happening?
Caller -> It's Beverly. I'm the night aide at Fernwood Commons. It's Mr. Chambers, Lyle Chambers, in room twelve. He can't breathe right. He's gasping.
Nurse -> Okay, Beverly. I'm here. Is he awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's sitting on the side of the bed. He's, he's trying to talk but he can't finish. He says, "I can't," and then he stops.
Nurse -> Okay. Look at his lips for me. What color are they?
Caller -> They're, oh. They're gray. Kind of blue. Gray-blue. I've never seen that. I've been here six years, I've never seen that.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a finger oxygen meter?
Caller -> Yes, we have, hold on. It's in the cart. Hold on. Hold on, don't go anywhere.
Nurse -> I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I got it. I put it on his finger. It's, it's going. It says, it keeps changing. Seventy eight. Seventy eight now.
Nurse -> Okay, Beverly. Seventy eight is very low. I need you to call nine one one right now. Not after this, right now.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Should I, do I, I have to call the director first. She said always call her before we call anybody.
Nurse -> No. Beverly, listen to me. Call nine one one first. You can call the director after. This is an emergency.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Nine one one first. Okay. Oh my God. Okay.
Nurse -> Is he on oxygen right now?
Caller -> Yes, he has the concentrator. He's got the nasal thing in. It's on two liters, I think. Two.
Nurse -> Okay. Leave it on. Don't take it off. Is he sitting up?
Caller -> Yes. On the edge of the bed. I'm holding him. I'm holding his back so he doesn't tip.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him sitting up straight. Don't lay him down. Do you have another staff member nearby who can make the call while you stay with him?
Caller -> Marisol is on, she's on the other hall. I can yell. Marisol! Marisol, come to twelve! Come now!
Nurse -> Good. Tell her to call nine one one.
Caller -> Marisol, call nine one one! Mr. Chambers, he can't breathe! Okay. Okay, she's going. She's calling. She ran.
Nurse -> Good. Stay with him. Talk to him. Tell him help is coming.
Caller -> Mr. Chambers, help is coming. I'm here. I'm not going anywhere. You're okay. Okay, he's looking at me. His eyes are huge.
Nurse -> That's good, he's looking at you. Beverly, does he have a DNR? Do you know if he has a do-not-resuscitate order?
Caller -> Oh. I, I don't know. I don't know. I think there's a paper. It's in the office, in his chart. I don't have the key to the office, the supervisor has the key. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all right. Don't worry about that right now. The paramedics will look for the paperwork, and the facility will get it to them. Send whatever he has with him, if someone can find it.
Caller -> Okay. His face sheet is here. I have a copy of his face sheet in the cart. It has his medicines on it. I'll give them that.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right. What's his date of birth, Beverly? I'll write it down in case they call us.
Caller -> Um. It's on the face sheet, hold on. Hold on. April third. Nineteen thirty five.
Nurse -> Got it. And what's the number there at the facility?
Caller -> Three three six, five five five, zero one one one. That's the station phone.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll stay on the line with you, but if the dispatcher calls back, answer that one first.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Marisol is here. She's, she's on the phone with them. She's saying the address.
Nurse -> Good. How's he doing right now?
Caller -> Same. He's still gasping. He's holding my arm. His hand is cold. His hand is really cold.
Nurse -> Okay. Try to keep him calm. Slow breaths, if he can do it with you. In through the nose, out slowly through the mouth.
Caller -> In, Mr. Chambers. In through your nose. And out. Out slow. There you go. There. He's doing it. Kind of.
Nurse -> Good. That's good. Keep doing that with him. Sit him up and keep his oxygen on, and stay right with him.
Caller -> Sit up. Oxygen on. Stay with him. Okay. I'm doing it. I'm doing it.
Caller -> Marisol says they're sending the ambulance. Four minutes. They said four minutes.
Nurse -> Four minutes. Okay. Tell Marisol to unlock the front door and turn on the lights, and have someone wait at the door to bring them to room twelve.
Caller -> Marisol, go to the front door! Open it! Wait for them! Okay. She went.
Nurse -> Good. Beverly, you're doing great. How are his lips now?
Caller -> They're, I think they're a little better? Not as blue. More gray. Or maybe I'm just, I don't know. Maybe it's the light.
Nurse -> It's hard to tell. Check the meter again if you can.
Caller -> Okay. It says, eighty one. Eighty one. Is that better?
Nurse -> It's a little better, but it's still low. We still want them to come. Keep him sitting up.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. He's, he's trying to say something. What, Mr. Chambers? What? He says, "Don't let them take me." Oh. He says don't let them take me.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something the paramedics and his family will need to talk about. Tell him you're staying with him and no one is going to rush him. They'll just help him breathe.
Caller -> I'm staying. I'm right here. They're just going to help you breathe, Mr. Chambers. Okay.
Nurse -> Does he have family you can call after the paramedics get there?
Caller -> Yes. His daughter. It's on the face sheet. I'll call her. I'll call the director too.
Nurse -> That's right. Do that once he's in good hands. For now, just him.
Nurse -> Good. While we wait, has he had any chest pain, or a fall tonight? Anything unusual today?
Caller -> I don't think so. He ate dinner. Not much. He had a cough, I think, the day shift said he was coughing a little. Nobody said anything about a fall.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics about the cough too.
Caller -> The cough. Okay. I'll tell them. Oh, Marisol's back. She says the dispatcher wants to know if the door is unlocked. It's unlocked. I told her it's unlocked.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Okay. I hear them. I hear the siren. They're here. They're here, Tom.
Nurse -> Good. Give them the face sheet and tell them what you told me. Gasping, gray-blue lips, oxygen seventy eight, on two liters.
Caller -> Seventy eight, two liters, gasping, gray lips. Okay. Okay, they're coming down the hall. Thank you. Thank you so much. I'm sorry I froze.
Nurse -> You didn't freeze. You did everything right. Go ahead and let them in.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Bye.

Caller -> The pick-up. The text said it was ready for pick-up today, and I just wanted to make sure before I drive over there.
Nurse -> Ma'am, this is Bluebell Home Care. We're a home care agency. We don't have pick-ups. Who were you trying to reach?
Caller -> The pharmacy. This is the pharmacy, isn't it? I called the number on the text.
Nurse -> No, it isn't. This is a home care agency, nurses and aides. I think the number might be a little different from the one you meant.
Caller -> Well, that's strange. It's the number from the text. Hold on, let me look. I have my glasses somewhere. Oh, here. It's, no, hold on, I have the wrong, I'm looking at the wrong one. That's my sister's text.
Nurse -> That's okay. Take your time.
Caller -> Oh, for heaven's sake. I'm sorry, dear. I've got two phones and I keep picking up the wrong one. Okay. Here's mine. It says, oh. I did dial it wrong. I dialed a seven where there should be a one.
Nurse -> It happens all the time. If you check the text again, the pharmacy's number should be right there to call back.
Caller -> I'll try again. Is it all right if I call back if this doesn't work?
Nurse -> Well, you'd want to call the pharmacy directly. We wouldn't be able to help with an order, I'm afraid. But if you're a client of ours and you need a nurse, you can always call.
