transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Priya. It's Rosa Ibarra. My husband, Fernando. I wanted to ask you about his sugar.
Nurse -> Okay, Rosa. Let me pull him up. Can you tell me his date of birth?
Caller -> September fourteenth. Nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> Okay, September fourth, nineteen fifty. Got it.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. That's him.
Nurse -> And a number for you? Is it nine five six, five five five, zero one four eight?
Caller -> Yes. Yeah, that's my cell. The house phone is broken. The dog chewed the cord. Ha.
Nurse -> Oh, no. Well, keep that cell charged, then, since it's the only line to you.
Caller -> It's plugged in right now. It's by the toaster. I learned that lesson last winter when it died in the middle of a storm.
Nurse -> Smart. Okay.
Nurse -> Oh no. Okay. So tell me about the sugar. What happened?
Caller -> So this morning, around, um, six thirty, I checked him because he was sweaty. I woke up and the sheets were wet. And he was, he was shaky. Shaking. And I took his sugar and it was fifty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Fifty eight. Was he awake? Was he making sense?
Caller -> He was awake. He was, he was a little slow. He was saying, "I'm fine, I'm fine," but his hands were shaking and I knew he wasn't. I know that look.
Nurse -> Has he had a low like this before?
Caller -> Once. In the summer, or maybe the spring. He got shaky at the church picnic and somebody gave him a cookie and he was fine. It wasn't this bad. It wasn't fifty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Caller -> I didn't tell the office that time. I didn't think it was a big deal. Is that bad?
Nurse -> No, no. It's good to tell us now. Let's keep going.
Nurse -> Okay. What did you do?
Caller -> I gave him juice. Orange juice. A whole glass. And I made him drink it, he didn't want it. Then I waited, I think fifteen minutes. I was watching the clock on the stove.
Nurse -> Good. That's what you do. Did you check again?
Caller -> Yes. After the fifteen minutes. Ninety two. It was ninety two. And then I made him eggs. And toast. And he ate all of it.
Nurse -> Okay, that's good. That's exactly the right thing. Rosa, did he take his insulin last night?
Caller -> Yes. The Lantus. Twenty units, at bedtime, like always. I drew it up myself because his hands, you know. I gave it at ten.
Nurse -> Okay. And the Lantus, it's the same dose he's been on? No change?
Caller -> Same. Same dose for, I don't know, a year? More. The doctor never changed it.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he eat a regular dinner last night?
Caller -> No. That's the thing. He didn't eat much yesterday. He said his stomach was off. He had some soup. A few crackers. That was all day, really. I should have told someone.
Nurse -> Okay. That could definitely explain a low in the morning, if he took the full dose and didn't eat much. Is he still shaky now?
Caller -> No. He's good. He's in the kitchen. He's, hold on. Fernando! Fernando, how do you feel? He says he feels fine, he says stop fussing. He's reading the paper.
Nurse -> Is he alert? Talking normally, reading?
Caller -> He's reading me the headlines right now. He's complaining about the price of gas. So yes. He's himself.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> He wants to know if he can go to the barber this afternoon. I said no. Not today. I want him home.
Nurse -> I'd agree with you on that. Let's see how his numbers look before lunch.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. I'd like to send a message to the provider about the low sugar, because it happened on his usual bedtime dose. They may want to adjust it.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. Should I skip the Lantus tonight?
Nurse -> Please don't skip it or change it on your own. Let the provider decide. I'll call you back with what they say.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait. I just didn't want it to happen again. It scared me.
Nurse -> I know it did. I'll call you back in two hours, and we'll talk about it.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. That's around, what, eleven.
Nurse -> Around eleven, yes. In the meantime, check his sugar again before lunch, and then again in the afternoon, and write each number down for me.
Caller -> Before lunch, again in the afternoon. Write it down. Okay. I have the little notebook.
Nurse -> And if it ever gets under seventy again, give juice or glucose tablets, recheck in fifteen minutes, and give him a snack once it's back up.
Caller -> Under seventy. Juice or the tablets. Fifteen minutes. A snack. I have the tablets, the ones that taste like chalk. He hates them.
Nurse -> Where do you keep them? Somewhere easy to grab if you need them in the night?
Caller -> In the nightstand drawer, on his side. And a box of juice boxes in the kitchen. My daughter bought a whole case. We have more juice than a school.
Nurse -> Good. Put a couple of the juice boxes by the bed too, so you don't have to leave him.
Caller -> That's a good idea. I'll do that today.
Nurse -> Juice is fine too. And Rosa, if he ever gets confused, can't swallow, or you can't wake him, call nine one one.
Caller -> Confused, can't swallow, can't wake. Nine one one. Yes. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else you're wondering about?
Caller -> No. Well. One thing. His appetite. It's been off for a few days. Is that something?
Nurse -> It might be. I'll include that in the message. If he's not eating, it matters for his insulin.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try to make him some of the soup again. The chicken one, the one his mother used to make. He'll eat that.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Small meals through the day are best.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Priya. You always make me feel better. My daughter says I worry too much.
Nurse -> You caught this early. That's the opposite of worrying too much.
Caller -> Ha. Okay. I'll tell her you said so. Bye, dear.
Nurse -> Take care, Rosa. I'll talk to you around eleven.
Caller -> Eleven. I'll keep the phone right next to me. Oh, and the dog says hello. He's staring at me because I'm on the phone and not feeding him.
Nurse -> Tell him hello back. And maybe feed him.
Caller -> I will. Ha. Okay. Bye now. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gail.
Caller -> Hello, Gail. Oh, I'm glad it's you. It's Philomena Boyle. I think I've got you before. I'm Ignatius Boyle's wife.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena. Yes, of course. How are you? How's Ignatius?
Caller -> Well, that's why I'm calling, honey. There's three things. Or four. I wrote them down on the back of an envelope and now I can't find the envelope.
Nurse -> That's all right. We'll go through them one at a time. First, let me confirm his date of birth.
Caller -> January twenty seventh. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I have two one five, five five five, zero one seven seven for you.
Caller -> That's the house. Yes. That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the first thing?
Caller -> His back. His back is bothering him. The low back. It's been, oh, it's been worse for a few days. He was up all night. I could hear him.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you ask him how bad it is, zero to ten? Is he near you?
Caller -> He's right here. He's on the couch. Ignatius. Iggy. Honey, what number is your back, zero to ten? Hm? He says a six. A six, honey? Okay. He says a six.
Nurse -> A six. Okay. And has he had anything for it today?
Caller -> The oxycodone. The five milligram. He had one two hours ago. I wrote it down. Hold on. Ten o'clock. He had it at ten.
Nurse -> Okay. And the label says what, how often?
Caller -> Every four hours if he needs it. So he can have the next one at two. It's what, a quarter after two now, no, it's, it's not quite. I'm looking at the stove clock. It's twenty past two, no, hm, the stove is five minutes fast.
Nurse -> It's fine. We can go by the label. So he's due at two, and it's just after two now. If he's in pain, he can have it.
Caller -> Oh. Oh good. Okay. I'll get it. Hold on a second, I'll, no, I'll do it after. Go on.
Nurse -> Okay. What else is going on?
Caller -> The second thing. He hasn't gone. The bathroom. Number two. Three days. It's been three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he taking anything for that?
Caller -> The senna. Twice a day. He takes it, I make sure. Morning and night.
Nurse -> Okay. Any belly pain? Is his stomach swollen? Any nausea or vomiting?
Caller -> No. No throwing up. No nausea, nothing like that. He's eating a little. He had half a sandwich. His stomach is, it's soft. I touched it. It's not hard.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. And what was the third thing?
Caller -> The bed! The bed. Oh, I almost forgot, thank you. The hospital bed. They were supposed to bring it yesterday. Wednesday. No, Tuesday. Hm. Yesterday was Thursday?
Nurse -> Today is Friday, so yesterday was Thursday.
Caller -> Then it was supposed to be yesterday, Thursday. They said between noon and four. I waited all day. Nobody came. And he's on the couch. He's been sleeping on the couch since Tuesday because he can't get up the stairs, and that's probably why the back is so bad.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. A couch is hard on a back. Did the company call you at all?
Caller -> No. Nobody called. I called twice and I got a recording.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call them for you. What's the company?
Caller -> I don't know. It's a name, it's on a sticker on the, hold on, wait. It's, it's on the paper from the social worker. I'll find it. I think it's, no. I don't remember. It's Peak something.
Nurse -> Is it Peak Medical Equipment, maybe?
Caller -> That's it! Peak Medical. Yes. Oh, you're a lifesaver. Is it in the computer?
Nurse -> It is. I'll have the number in front of me in a second.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll find it in his chart. I'll call them right after this and I'll push for delivery this afternoon.
Caller -> Oh, thank you, honey. This afternoon. By when? Because I want to make sure someone is here.
Nurse -> I'll ask for by three, but I'll call you as soon as I hear from them.
Caller -> Okay. By three. I'm not going anywhere. Where would I go.
Nurse -> Ha. Fair enough. Is there someone who can help get him to the bathroom in the meantime?
Caller -> My son comes after work. Around six. He's the one who lifts. I'm too small to lift him, I'm five foot one.
Nurse -> Philomena, for the back pain. A six, and he was up all night. I'm going to send a message to the hospice provider. I'd like them to know about the pain, and the three days without a bowel movement.
Caller -> Oh, please. Please do. Is there something stronger? Could the oxycodone be stronger?
Nurse -> That's the provider's decision. They might adjust it, or add something. I don't want to promise. But they'll see this today.
Caller -> Okay. That's all I'm asking. I just want him comfortable.
Nurse -> I know. We want that too. In the meantime, I'd go ahead and give him the oxycodone now, since it's been two hours, no, since it's due. Just the one, five milligrams.
Caller -> One. The five. Okay. I'll go do it. Hold on. Mrs. Kowalski, it's just the phone, sit down. Sorry, that's the neighbor. She comes by with soup.
Nurse -> That's very kind of her.
Caller -> She's very kind. She's very loud. Okay. Let me give him the pill. Hold on.
Nurse -> Does she need to be in the room while we talk? No hurry.
Caller -> No, no, she's in the kitchen with the soup. She's talking to the dog. We have a dog.
Nurse -> That's nice company for him, I bet.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'll be right here.
Caller -> Iggy, open up. Here's the pill. Water. There. Good boy, I mean, good, honey. Ha.
Caller -> Okay. Gave it. He swallowed it. He had water. Okay, I'm back.
Nurse -> Good. Write down the time. And keep giving the senna twice a day, don't skip it.
Caller -> Senna. Twice a day. I won't skip. I wrote the oxycodone time on the paper by the phone. It's, it's two twenty-five. No, two twenty. I'll write two twenty.
Nurse -> And you gave the last one at ten, so you're right on time.
Caller -> Oh good. I always worry I'm doing it wrong. I counted wrong once and gave it late and I felt terrible all day.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, for the constipation, offer him plenty of fluids, and prune juice is good. Even if he doesn't want much. And note if he has a bowel movement.
Caller -> Prune juice. We have prune juice. Mrs. Kowalski brought me a whole bottle. I think she thought, I don't know what she thought. Ha. Okay. Fluids. And write it down.
Nurse -> Right. Also, for his back, put a pillow behind his lower back when he's on the couch, and a warm blanket. No heating pad. And help him change position often.
Caller -> A pillow behind his back. Blanket. No heating pad. Move him around. Okay. I'm not strong enough to turn him by myself, though. Is that okay? Do I need to?
Nurse -> You don't have to turn him. Just encourage him to shift when he's awake, and I'll have the nurse show you some easy ways tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow? Is somebody coming tomorrow?
Nurse -> Yes. I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow to see him, check his back, and look at the bowel situation.
Caller -> Oh good. Oh, that's wonderful. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a time. I'll tell them you prefer after nine.
Caller -> Yes, after nine. I like to get him washed up first. He doesn't like visitors if he's not shaved. He's vain, you know. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. That's good, it keeps him going. And I'll call you back this afternoon about the bed and about what the provider says.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. Okay, honey. I'll have the phone in my pocket. I'll keep it on me, I'll walk around with it.
Nurse -> One more thing, Philomena. If he starts vomiting, if his belly gets hard and swollen, if the pain stays above a six even after a dose, or if he gets so sleepy you can't wake him easily, call us right away.
Caller -> Vomiting. Hard belly. Pain above a six. Hard to wake. Okay. I have a pen. Let me write it. Vomiting, hard belly, six, hard to wake. Got it. I'll put it on the envelope. If I can find it.
Nurse -> Ha. Put it on a new envelope. Is there anything else on your list?
Caller -> Oh. Hm. I don't think so. There was one more but I forgot it. It'll come to me.
Nurse -> If it does, call me back. Anytime.
Caller -> I will. I will. Thank you, Gail. Honestly. You don't know what it means. I was crying this morning. I wasn't going to call because I felt silly.
Nurse -> Is anyone checking on you, Philomena? You sound tired.
Caller -> My son, and my sister calls. And you do. I'm fine, I'm tougher than I look.
Nurse -> Never feel silly. These are real things, and you're handling a lot.
Caller -> I'm trying. Iggy says I'm doing a good job. He told me last night. He's sweet. When he's not grumpy. Ha.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Tell him I said hello.
Caller -> Iggy, Gail says hello. He waved. He can't talk, he's got the, he's chewing a cracker. Ha. He waved.
Nurse -> Take care, both of you. I'll call you this afternoon.
Caller -> Okay. Bye, honey. Bye bye.

Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Joel.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. Thank God somebody answered. I called the, I called three places already. I called the pharmacy, I called, the other number, it just rang. I'm sorry. Hi.
Nurse -> It's okay. You've got me now. I'm Joel, I'm a nurse. Who am I talking to, and what's going on?
Caller -> My name's Tiffany, Tiffany Okoro. I'm the caregiver. I'm the overnight caregiver for Wanda Fairchild. And her medicine ran out. The pain medicine.
Nurse -> Okay, Tiffany. Take a breath. Which pain medicine ran out?
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid morphine. The concentrate. I gave her the last of it three hours ago, and there's nothing in the bottle. I shook it. I held it up. It's empty.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she in pain right now?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, she's in a lot of pain. She's crying. She keeps saying her whole back is on fire. She can't get comfortable. I've turned her, I've put pillows.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you ask her to give me a number? Zero to ten. Is she able to answer?
Caller -> Wanda. Wanda, honey, what number is the pain? Zero to ten. She says seven. A seven. She's holding up, she held up seven fingers.
Nurse -> Okay. Seven. Thank you for asking her. Tiffany, what's Wanda's date of birth?
Caller -> Um. It's on the, hold on. I know this. It's November ninth. November ninth, nineteen seventy four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what number are you calling from?
Caller -> My cell. It's six seven eight, five five five, zero one two two.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Tiffany, I need to ask a couple of safety questions. Is she breathing normally? Is she awake and talking to you?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, she's awake. She's talking. She's just, she's hurting. She's breathing normal. Fast, a little, because she's crying. But normal.
Nurse -> Any fever, vomiting, anything else going on tonight?
Caller -> No fever. She threw up this afternoon, once, but not since.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Now, how did the family not know the bottle was low?
Caller -> I think they did. I think the family was going to pick it up, the daughter. But she works at the hospital and she had a double. And I don't know if anyone called the pharmacy. And the pharmacy by the house closes at eight on Fridays. And it's Saturday, I mean, technically. It's after midnight.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. I'm not blaming anyone. I'm trying to get her what she needs. Is there any other pain medicine in the house? Pills, anything in the cabinet?
Caller -> There's pills, there's a bunch. There's a basket. I don't know what's what. I didn't want to give her the wrong thing. I've been told not to give anything that's not on the sheet.
Nurse -> That's the right call. Please don't give anything from the basket. Not until the on-call clinician tells you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I won't. I won't touch the basket. I put it up on the shelf.
Nurse -> Good. Now, I'm going to do three things at the same time. First, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to call our twenty-four hour pharmacy and see if they have the morphine concentrate. And third, I'm going to see about getting it delivered. Stay on the line a second if you can, or I'll call you right back.
Caller -> I'll stay. I'll stay. Wanda, it's okay. It's the nurse. They're getting your medicine. Okay, baby. It's okay.
Nurse -> Tiffany, just keep talking to her. I'm going to put you on a short hold, a minute or two.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Wanda, the nurse is calling the pharmacy. Does it help if I rub your shoulder? There. Okay. Is that okay? Okay.
Nurse -> Tiffany, I'm back. I reached the pharmacy. They have the morphine concentrate and they're going to fill it right now.
Caller -> Oh. Oh, thank God. Thank you. How long?
Nurse -> I'm going to have their driver bring it to the house. They said it should be within the hour. I'll push for faster.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Within the hour. And what do I do until then?
Nurse -> For now, help her get as comfortable as you can. Use pillows to change her position. Keep the room dim and quiet. Hold her hand and keep your voice calm.
Caller -> Pillows, dim, quiet. Hand. Okay. She likes it when I sing. Is that okay? I sing to her.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Sing. Anything she likes.
Caller -> Okay. She likes the old gospel. I do some of that. Okay.
Nurse -> What's her favorite song?
Caller -> "I'll Fly Away." She asks for it every night.
Nurse -> That's a good one. Sing that one.
Caller -> Okay. I'll start in a minute.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes, whether or not the driver has gotten there yet, and by then I'll probably have heard from the on-call clinician too.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. I'll keep the phone right here.
Nurse -> And Tiffany, if she stops responding, or if her breathing becomes very slow, call nine one one.
Caller -> Stops responding. Slow breathing. Nine one one. Okay. She's not like that. She's awake. But okay. I'll remember.
Nurse -> Good. Is there someone else in the house? Anyone with you?
Caller -> Just her husband, he's asleep in the other room. He's been up for two days. I didn't want to wake him. Should I?
Nurse -> Let him sleep for now. If it goes past the hour, wake him up. It might help to have a second person.
Nurse -> Does Wanda have any allergies I should know about, or anything new she started this week?
Caller -> No allergies. Nothing new that I know of. The sheet says none.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's good. I don't want to, he's so tired.
Nurse -> I understand. You're doing great, Tiffany. You did everything right.
Caller -> I feel like I should have called earlier. When it got to half a bottle. I should have said something.
Nurse -> It's easy to look back and think that. Right now, you're doing exactly what she needs.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry I was so, I was crying earlier. I mean, I was upset.
Nurse -> No need to apologize. Anything else on your mind before I go?
Caller -> Just, will she be okay? Until it comes?
Nurse -> She's awake, she's talking, and you're with her. The medicine is on the way, and I'm going to keep checking.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I believe you.
Nurse -> One more thing. Write down the time we spoke and the time the driver arrives.
Caller -> I'll write both on the sheet.
Nurse -> Keep the phone close. I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Thank you. Thank you, Joel.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi, Marcus. Is this the nurse line? It's Lorna Marsh.
Nurse -> It is. Hi, Lorna. What can I do for you?
Caller -> It's about my husband's supplies. His bag supplies. We're getting low and it's Friday.
Nurse -> Okay. Who's the patient? Is it Delbert?
Caller -> Yes. Delbert Marsh. My husband.
Nurse -> Okay, let me pull up his chart. Can you give me his date of birth?
Caller -> June second. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I've got six oh five, five five five, zero one three six on file.
Caller -> That's the house. Yes.
Nurse -> Great. So how many pouches do you have?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me go look. I keep them in the hall closet.
Nurse -> No problem.
Caller -> Okay. I'm in the closet. There's, one, two. Two pouches. Two left.
Nurse -> Two pouches. And the wafers? The skin barrier?
Caller -> Those are the, the round flat ones with the hole?
Nurse -> Yes, that's the one that sticks to the skin.
Caller -> One. There's one box with, no, one wafer. There's one wafer in the box. The box is empty except for one.
Nurse -> Okay. One wafer. And how often do you change them?
Caller -> Every three days, usually. But the last two nights it's been leaking. So I've been changing it more.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the leaking.
Caller -> It leaks at night. Twice now. Wednesday night and last night. He woke up wet. All down his side, onto the sheets. It's awful. He's embarrassed.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's really hard on both of you. Do you know why it's leaking?
Caller -> I think the wafer isn't sticking. It's peeling up at the edge. I don't know if I'm cutting it wrong. I've been doing it the same way for two years.
Nurse -> It might be the skin. Can you describe the skin around the stoma?
Caller -> It's red. It's kind of angry looking. And he says it's sore. It burns when I take the old one off.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it open, or bleeding, or weeping at all?
Caller -> No. No bleeding. Just red. And a little shiny. Like it's raw, but not open.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like irritation from the leaking. Is the stoma itself, the actual stoma, pink and moist?
Caller -> Yes. It's pink. It looks the same as always. Red like a cherry. That's what the nurse said, it should look like a cherry.
Nurse -> That's right. That's good, that it looks like a cherry. Does he have any fever, any belly pain?
Caller -> No. No fever. He's eating. He's got output. It's just the leaking.
Nurse -> Good. Okay, Lorna. First, the supplies. I've put in the order for pouches and wafers just now. It's done.
Caller -> Oh. Oh good. Because I was worried about the weekend.
Nurse -> I know. The regular delivery won't come until Monday, so I'm going to coordinate that for Monday.
Caller -> Monday. Okay. But I only have two pouches. And one wafer. That's not going to do it.
Nurse -> You're right. Let me think. Do you have a neighbor or a friend who can pick up a few from the pharmacy? Some pharmacies carry them.
Caller -> The one in town doesn't. I called before. They have to order them.
Nurse -> Okay. In that case, I'm going to see about getting a weekend pack to you from our on-call supply. The on-call nurse can drop it by.
Caller -> Oh. They can do that? Oh, that would be wonderful.
Nurse -> I'll ask. I can't promise yet. I'll call you back and let you know.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be home. We're always home.
Nurse -> Now, I'd like a nurse to come see him Monday to look at the skin and check the fit.
Caller -> Monday. Okay. Is that morning?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time. I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Now, while we wait. When you change the pouch, make sure the skin is completely dry before the wafer goes on. That's the most common reason they peel.
Caller -> Completely dry. I pat it, but I think I'm in a hurry sometimes. Because he's squirming.
Nurse -> Take your time with it. And cut the hole to the size of the stoma, not bigger. Just a hair bigger. And change the pouch when it's about a third full, don't wait until it's heavy.
Caller -> A hair bigger. A third full. Okay. I wait too long sometimes, I think. I didn't want to bother him at night.
Nurse -> It's better to change it. The weight pulls on the wafer. Now, for the red skin. Clean it gently with just water, no soap, pat it dry, and put a little of the barrier powder on it.
Caller -> Water only. Pat dry. Powder. We have powder. It's in the bathroom. It's in a little puffer bottle.
Nurse -> That's it. Dust it lightly, wipe off the extra, then the wafer.
Caller -> Dust it. Wipe off. Wafer. Okay. I'll try that tonight.
Nurse -> And call us if the skin opens up or bleeds, if the stoma turns dark, if he has no output for a day, or if he gets a fever.
Caller -> Opens up, dark, no output, fever. Okay. I wrote it on the back of the, whatever this is. The electric bill.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. Anything else, Lorna?
Caller -> No, that's it. Oh, how is your day going? I never ask.
Nurse -> It's busy, but good. Yours sounds like a long one.
Caller -> It's been a week. But he's in good spirits. He's watching the baseball.
Nurse -> That's good. Is he rooting for anyone?
Caller -> The Cubs. Always the Cubs. For forty years. They break his heart every October.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, keep him comfortable. I'll call you back about the weekend pack.
Caller -> Thank you, Marcus. Have a good weekend.
Nurse -> You too, Lorna. Take care.
Caller -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Mina.
Caller -> Hello? Oh, I wasn't sure anyone would pick up on a Saturday. I'm so glad.
Nurse -> We're here all weekend. How can I help?
Caller -> My name is Dolores Whitt. I'm calling about a friend from church. I don't know if he's one of yours.
Nurse -> Okay. What's your friend's name?
Caller -> Abe. Abe Lieberman. Or is it Lieberson? Lieberman. I think Lieberman. I go to church with his wife, she passed, and I've only ever heard it said.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me try both. Do you know his address?
Caller -> It's on Fulton Street. Twelve oh four. Two doors down from the funeral home. Which is funny when you think about it, not that it's funny.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm looking. I do have an Abraham Lieberman on Fulton Street, and I don't see a Lieberson. I think that's him.
Caller -> Oh, thank goodness. Abraham. Yes. Abe is short for it. He's on hospice? I didn't know he was on hospice. He never said.
Nurse -> I can't share details about a patient, but I'm glad you called. Tell me what's worrying you. What's going on?
Caller -> I don't want to make a fuss. It's probably nothing. But I drive by on my way to the grocery, and his newspapers have been piling up on the porch. I think it's been three days.
Nurse -> Three days of newspapers. Okay.
Caller -> Yes. And the porch light has been on all day and all night. I noticed that too.
Nurse -> The light's been left on.
Caller -> Day and night. He's very careful about electricity, so that's not like him.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Caller -> And this morning I stopped. I knocked. He came to the door. He said, "Dolores, I'm fine, don't worry about me." But he didn't look fine.
Nurse -> What did you notice?
Caller -> He was pale. White as a sheet. And he was holding onto the door frame. Like he was holding himself up. And he was breathing kind of, I don't know, kind of heavy.
Nurse -> Okay. Was he steady on his feet? Did he seem confused?
Caller -> He knew me. He knew who I was. He made a joke about my hat. But he wouldn't let me in. He said the house was a mess.
Nurse -> Did you notice anything inside? The temperature, a smell, the TV?
Caller -> I couldn't see much. He kept the door open about this much. The TV was on. I could hear the weather lady.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It was warm in there. Very warm. He keeps it warm.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you see him fall, or see any bruises, or blood?
Caller -> No. No, nothing like that. I didn't see any bruises. He had his bathrobe on. It was, I'd say, ten o'clock.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have anyone else, family nearby, who checks in on him?
Caller -> A son in California. I don't have the number. And a neighbor on the other side, but she's away. So I'm kind of it.
Nurse -> Do you know the son's name?
Caller -> Daniel. Danny. I don't know his last name, it'd be Lieberman, wouldn't it? Ha.
Nurse -> Probably. We have a contact for him, I'll check.
Caller -> Oh good.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you're watching out for him.
Caller -> I'm a nosy old lady is what I am. Ha. But I couldn't sleep thinking about it.
Nurse -> You did the right thing to call. Dolores, do you know his date of birth? It helps me make sure I have the right chart.
Caller -> Oh, no. No, honey. I know his wife was born the same year as me, nineteen forty-six. But Abe, no. I couldn't tell you.
Nurse -> That's all right. I have the address and the name. And what number can I reach you at?
Caller -> Seven one eight, five five five, zero one six three. That's my home phone. I'm here all day. I'm making pies for the bake sale.
Nurse -> Pies. What kind?
Caller -> Apple and pecan. Pecan is the one that sells. Anyway. Ha. Sorry.
Nurse -> Dolores, I'm going to send a nurse out to see Abe today. They'll check on him.
Caller -> Today? Oh. That would be such a relief. Will he be upset? Will he know it was me?
Nurse -> The nurse will just say we were doing a routine check. You don't have to worry about that.
Caller -> Oh, good. He's very proud. He doesn't like anybody to know he's not well.
Nurse -> I understand. And I'll call you this evening, to let you know that someone saw him and that he's okay. I can't share details, but I can tell you that.
Caller -> That's all I need. That he's okay. Yes. This evening.
Nurse -> One more question. Has he mentioned any pain, or any falls in the past few weeks?
Caller -> No pain. A fall, hm. At church, in September. He tripped on the step. He said it was nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me that.
Caller -> I'd forgotten it until just now. Should I have said it before?
Nurse -> No, it's good to know now. I'll pass it on.
Nurse -> In the meantime, if you pass by again and you see him on the porch or in the window, on the floor, or if he can't be woken, or he's struggling to breathe, don't wait. Call nine one one.
Caller -> On the floor. Can't wake him. Struggling to breathe. Nine one one. Okay. I won't wait. I'll write it on my hand.
Nurse -> Ha. Write it on paper too. Is there anything else you remember? Anything he said?
Caller -> He said he was tired. Just tired. That's all he said.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll pass that along to the nurse.
Nurse -> And Dolores, I'll make sure the nurse has your number in case they need anything.
Caller -> That's fine. That's fine. Tell them to knock loud. His hearing is poor.
Nurse -> I'll tell them.
Caller -> And tell them I said hello. No, don't. He'll know it was me. Ha.
Nurse -> I'll just say it's a routine check.
Caller -> Okay. You're so kind. I feel better already.
Nurse -> Thank you for caring about him, Dolores. Go make your pies.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Goodbye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Hi, Tom, it's Gwen. Gwendolyn Raskin. I'm sorry, I think I'm confused about my pill.
Nurse -> No need to be sorry, Gwen. Which pill?
Caller -> The steroid. The dexamethasone. I have two papers and they don't agree.
Nurse -> Okay. Give me a second, I'll pull up your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> August twenty first. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> And is nine five two, five five five, zero one four seven still your number?
Caller -> Yes. That's the cell.
Nurse -> Great. And you're at home today? Anyone with you?
Caller -> My daughter was here this morning. She went to work. She's back at six. I'm alone right now.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. So tell me about the two papers.
Caller -> The pharmacy label says one tablet in the morning. Four milligrams. And the sheet from the hospital says something about, hold on, it says taper. Four, then two, then something. And I don't know when I'm supposed to switch.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you read me what the hospital sheet says?
Caller -> It's small. Hold on, let me get my glasses. They're on the, they're in the kitchen. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I got them. It says, four milligrams daily. Then, wait. Then it says, "decrease." And then there's a date. It's a Sunday. And I don't know if that Sunday is this one or last one.
Nurse -> Okay. I have the provider's note here in front of me. Let me read it to you, and tell me if it matches.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> It says four milligrams once a day through this Sunday. Then two milligrams once a day for three days. Then stop.
Caller -> Through this Sunday. This Sunday coming. Not the one that just passed.
Nurse -> Right. This coming Sunday. The twenty fifth.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. So I'm still on the four. Okay. That's good. That's what I thought. Then two for three days. Then done.
Nurse -> Then done. Exactly. Now, can you tell me what you've taken the last two days? Walk me through it.
Caller -> Okay. Yesterday. Yesterday I took one in the morning. Four. With my oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> And then, oh. And then last night I couldn't sleep, and I was looking at the sheet, and I thought maybe I was supposed to take two a day. Because it said "four daily" and I thought daily was like, four a day, or twice. And I took another dexamethasone. At about, maybe eight? Eight or nine.
Nurse -> Okay. So you may have taken a second four milligram tablet last night. Are you sure about that?
Caller -> I think so. I think. I have the bottle. Let me count. They gave me, hm, I don't remember how many they gave me. So I can't count it. Ugh.
Nurse -> That's okay. If you think you took it, we'll treat it as if you did. And this morning?
Caller -> This morning I didn't. I read the label again and it said one in the morning and I was like, well, I already had my extra. So I skipped it. Was that wrong?
Nurse -> Okay. That's not unreasonable, but the plan is to take it once a day. Have you taken any today?
Caller -> No. Not today. It's three o'clock. Should I take it now?
Nurse -> Let me ask something first. Did you eat today? Anything at all?
Caller -> A piece of toast. And coffee. Which is probably why I'm jittery. Ha. I'm drinking coffee on top of it.
Nurse -> That'll do it. Maybe switch to decaf for the rest of the day.
Caller -> I will. I will switch. Okay.
Nurse -> Let me check one thing first. I'd like to message the provider before you take today's dose, because of the extra last night. Can you hold off for now?
Caller -> I can hold off. Okay. But what if it makes it, I'm worried I'll get sick if I skip.
Nurse -> One missed morning on a taper isn't dangerous, but I'd like the provider to tell us what to do. I'm going to send them a message right now.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I feel so stupid.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. Two papers that say different things would confuse anyone.
Caller -> I just want to do it right.
Nurse -> I know. And Gwen, how are you feeling? You mentioned you couldn't sleep.
Caller -> I'm jittery. I feel shaky. I feel like I had five coffees. And I didn't sleep, I was up till four.
Nurse -> Okay. That's common with steroids, especially with an extra dose. Any stomach pain? Any black stools? Any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. No stomach pain. My stomach's fine. No. I mean, a little acid, but I always get that. No black stools.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Caller -> My daughter says I should write everything on a calendar.
Nurse -> Your daughter's right. That's what I'd do too. Write each dose on a calendar, and make it a habit. Take the dexamethasone once a day, in the morning with food, and don't stop it early.
Caller -> Once a day. Morning. With food. Calendar. Don't stop early. Okay. I'll get a calendar. I think I have one from the vet. It has cats on it.
Nurse -> A calendar with cats works.
Caller -> Ha. It's the one the vet gave out. Okay.
Nurse -> What kind of cats?
Caller -> Orange ones. All orange. Twelve orange cats. One for each month. I have two orange cats at home so it's fitting.
Nurse -> Also, with steroids it's a good idea to watch for high sugar, stomach pain, black stools, or any strong mood changes, and let us know.
Caller -> High sugar. Stomach pain. Black stools. Moods. Okay. I get weepy sometimes. I thought that was just me.
Nurse -> It can be the medicine. I'm glad you mentioned it. I'll add it to the message.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm so sorry for calling.
Nurse -> Please don't be. You did the right thing asking. I'll call you this evening after I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. What time?

Caller -> Hi. Hi, I need, I need to talk to someone. It's my dad. It's my dad, he's a patient.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm here. I'm a nurse. What's your name?
Caller -> Marisa. Marisa Delacroix. My dad is Gaston Delacroix.
Nurse -> Okay, Marisa. Take a breath. I'm listening. What's happening with your dad?
Caller -> He said something. About an hour ago. He said, "I'm done. I'm going to take all of them tonight."
Nurse -> All of them. His pills?
Caller -> His pills. Yes. I think so. He didn't say pills but I know what he meant. The basket on the counter. He looked at the basket.
Nurse -> Okay. Marisa, I'm really glad you called me. Where is your dad right now?
Caller -> He's in the living room. He's watching TV. He's on the recliner. I can hear it from here. I'm in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he taken anything? Any pills at all, since he said it?
Caller -> No. No. I don't think so. I've been in here, I've been, I haven't gone back in. I couldn't. I came in here and I stood at the sink.
Nurse -> Okay. That's okay. Is the basket where you are? In the kitchen?
Caller -> Yes. It's right here on the counter. By the toaster. It's the basket with all of his bottles.
Nurse -> Okay. Marisa, I'd like you to pick up the basket, and take it somewhere he can't reach. Do you have a closet or a box that locks, or a drawer?
Caller -> I have a lockbox. A little one. For papers. It's in my bedroom. It's got a key.
Nurse -> That's good. Can you go get it, and put the bottles in it? Stay where you can hear the TV.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hold on. Hold on, I'll put the phone, I'll take the phone with me.
Nurse -> Yes. Take me with you.
Caller -> I'm walking. I'm in the hall. Okay. I'm in my room. I have the box. It's open. Okay. I'm putting the basket in, it's too big. I'll take out the bottles. One. Two. Three. There's seven. There's seven bottles.
Nurse -> Take your time. Put all seven in, and close it. Is there anything else? Any liquid in the fridge, any patches, anything like that?
Caller -> The morphine is in the fridge. The liquid. Oh. I forgot. I'll get it. Hold on.
Nurse -> Okay. Go get it. I'll stay here.
Caller -> Okay. I'm in the kitchen. I have it. It's the little brown bottle. I'll put it in the box too. Okay. Done. I'm locking it. It's locked. I have the key. It's on a string. I'm putting it around my neck.
Nurse -> Good. That's very good, Marisa. That was a hard thing to do and you did it quickly.
Caller -> I'm shaking. Look at my hand.
Nurse -> I can hear it. That's okay. You're doing everything right. Now I want to ask you something. Has your dad said anything like this before?
Caller -> No. Not like that. He's been quiet this week. He stopped eating at the table. He just wants to be in his chair. He doesn't want the aide to come.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's been low and withdrawn this week.
Caller -> Yes. Since his friend died. Last Sunday. His friend Leon, they played cards for fifty years. He didn't go to the funeral. He said he didn't want to.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. That's a big loss for him, and for you. Okay. Marisa, I'd like to page the on-call clinician right now so that someone who can help is looking at this tonight.
Caller -> Please. Yes. Please. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> I'm also going to ask our social worker to reach out to your dad, and to you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. He might not want to talk to her.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll go at his pace. Right now the most important thing is that someone stays with him tonight. Can you do that?
Caller -> Yes. I'm not going anywhere. I'll sit in the living room with him. I'll sleep on the couch.
Nurse -> Good. Stay within sight of him, and you give him his medicines yourself, from the box, when it's time. Nobody else.
Caller -> I give him his medicine. From the box. Okay. I have the key. Okay.
Nurse -> Is there anyone who can come be with you tonight? A sibling, a neighbor?
Caller -> My brother lives in Baton Rouge. I could call him. He'd come but it's three hours. My neighbor Pat has a key.
Nurse -> Maybe call Pat. Even just to sit with you for a bit.
Caller -> Okay. I'll text her. She's up late. She does crosswords.
Nurse -> Marisa, I'd like you to go back and sit with him now. Keep the phone with you. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Okay. I'm walking. Hold on. I'm in the hall. I can see him. He's in the chair. He's got the blanket. He's awake. He's looking at the TV.
Nurse -> Good. Don't confront him. Just sit near him. If he talks, listen. You don't have to fix anything.
Caller -> Okay. I'm sitting. I'm on the couch. He looked at me. He said, "What are you doing?" I said, "Nothing, Dad. I'm just sitting with you." He said okay.
Nurse -> That's perfect. That's exactly what to say.
Caller -> He's looking at the screen again. It's a game show. It's something with a wheel.
Nurse -> Does he seem drowsy at all? Or confused? Any slurring?
Caller -> No. He's sharp. He answered a question on the show before the contestant did.
Nurse -> That's a good sign that he's clear. Okay.
Caller -> He always does that. He used to say he should be on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Marisa, can I get your dad's date of birth, and your phone number? In case we get cut off.
Caller -> February eighteenth. Nineteen fifty one. And my number is five oh four, five five five, zero one three nine.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm going to hang up and page the on-call right now, and I'll call you back in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. Don't, you won't, you'll call me?
Nurse -> I'll call you. And if you need me before then, call right back. This number, any hour.
Caller -> Okay. Any hour. Okay.
Nurse -> And Marisa, if he does take any pills, or tries to hurt himself, don't wait for me. Call nine one one. You can also call or text nine eight eight, the crisis line, any time, for him or for you.
Caller -> Nine one one if he takes anything. Nine eight eight. Okay. I have my phone. I wrote it on my hand.
Nurse -> Good. You're not alone in this. I'm going to page the on-call now.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much. I'm so scared.
Nurse -> It makes sense that you are. You're also being very brave.
Nurse -> I know. I'll call you in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Okay.

Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gail.
Caller -> Hi, hello. I'm calling about the volunteer. The lady who comes on Tuesdays to sit with my mother.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there something you need changed?
Caller -> Well, yes. Tuesday won't work this week. I have to take Mom to, no, I have to go to the dentist. I mean, I'm going, not Mom. And I need someone here to stay with her.
Nurse -> I see. So you'd like the volunteer to come on a different day?
Caller -> Thursday would be good. If she can do Thursday. Same time. Two o'clock.
Nurse -> I can't schedule the volunteers from this line, I'm afraid. The volunteer coordinator handles that. Her office is open until four-thirty today.
Caller -> Oh. Is that a different number?
Nurse -> It's the same main number. Press two when the menu comes up, or ask for volunteer services.
Caller -> Press two. Okay. I'm writing it down. Two for volunteers.
Nurse -> That's it. If you get the voicemail, leave your name and a good number, and she'll call you back, usually the same day.
Caller -> Okay. Same day. Good. Oh, and, could you ask her something? Or I can ask her. Could she bring that book again? The one about the lighthouses. Mom loved it.
Nurse -> I'd mention that when you talk to the coordinator. She'll pass it on.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Lighthouses. It's a big blue book.
Nurse -> Ha. That should be easy to find.
Caller -> She reads it to Mom every week. She does the voices. It's lovely.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful. We're lucky to have our volunteers.
Caller -> You really are. It's the only hour I get to myself. I go sit in the car and eat a sandwich. Don't tell anyone.
Nurse -> Your secret's safe. Everybody needs that hour.
Caller -> Thank you. It's raining here, isn't it? Is it raining where you are?
Nurse -> It is. It started this morning and hasn't stopped.
Caller -> Terrible. My knees always know. Well, I'll let you go. Thank you, dear.
Nurse -> Anytime. Call the volunteer office and they'll get you sorted out.
Caller -> Will do. Goodbye now.

Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Renee.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, um, hello. Is this the nurse? I'm calling from Brightwater Manor. I'm the, I'm the med tech tonight. I'm kind of new.
Nurse -> Okay. Hi. What's your name?
Caller -> Omar. I'm Omar. I've been here three weeks.
Nurse -> Welcome to the team, Omar. Three weeks is plenty of time to get a feel for the place.
Caller -> It's a lot. The med cart still confuses me some nights. But the residents are sweet.
Nurse -> Hi, Omar. Thanks for calling. What do you need?
Caller -> I have a resident. She's one of yours. Her name is Wilhelmina. Wilhelmina Hrabowski. H R A B O W S K I. It's a hard one.
Nurse -> Thanks for spelling it. Let me find her. I have a Wilhelmina Hrabowski. What's going on?
Caller -> Okay. Okay so she's, um, she's sleeping a lot. More than usual. And she's not eating.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has this been going on?
Caller -> I think since Saturday? I'm looking at the, at the charting. The day shift wrote, "poor intake," on Saturday. And Sunday. So two days.
Nurse -> Okay. How much has she been eating?
Caller -> A few bites. That's what the sheet says. A few bites of oatmeal. A few bites of, I don't know, applesauce. And she drinks a little. Juice.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she swallowing okay? Any coughing or choking when she eats or drinks?
Caller -> No coughing. She swallows slow. She holds it in her cheek a little. But no choking.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me.
Nurse -> Okay. And is she hard to wake?
Caller -> No. No, she wakes up. If I say her name she opens her eyes. She's just really sleepy. And then she goes back to sleep.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she talking? Does she know where she is?
Caller -> She said, "Hello." She said "Hello, dear." That was it. I don't know what she knew.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Omar, can I get her date of birth from the face sheet?
Caller -> Sure. Hold on. It's, it's March fourteenth. Nineteen thirty three.
Nurse -> Thank you. And the number I have for the facility is seven one six, five five five, zero one eight five.
Caller -> That's the nurses' station. Yes. I'm here until seven.
Nurse -> Perfect. And is there someone on tonight who's a nurse, a charge nurse, I can talk to?
Caller -> There's Denise, but she's on the other wing tonight. She's got a resident who's, there's a thing going on. I didn't want to bother her.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tell her we spoke when she has a minute.
Caller -> I will. I'll write it in the log too.
Nurse -> Okay. You mentioned something else?
Caller -> Yes. Oh. She has a bruise. A new bruise. On her arm. Her forearm. It's purple. I saw it when I was changing her.
Nurse -> Okay. Which arm? How big?
Caller -> Her left. The left forearm. It's, it's like the size of a, a half-dollar? Maybe bigger. Purple. And a little yellow on the edge.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it a new one, or has it been there?
Caller -> I don't know. I didn't see it before. The day shift didn't write it down. I looked. I looked in the book.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she fall? Did anyone see her bump it?
Caller -> No. Nobody saw anything. No falls in the book. I asked the other aide, Dee, and she said she didn't see anything either.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a fever? Have you taken her temperature?
Caller -> I did. Ninety eight point four. So no fever. I think that's normal.
Nurse -> That's normal. Okay. Is she on any blood thinner?
Caller -> I don't know. I'd have to look at the MAR. Hold on. I'm scrolling. I don't see it. No. No blood thinners on the list.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Is she in pain, do you think? Has she had anything for pain?
Caller -> She got the acetaminophen. The five hundred. At six last night. The order says as needed, and she was grimacing, so I gave it.
Nurse -> Okay. Did it help?
Caller -> I think so. She relaxed. She was quiet.
Nurse -> Okay. Omar, I'm going to send a message to the provider about the sleepiness, the poor eating, and the bruise.
Caller -> Okay. Is that, is that enough? Should I be doing something else?
Nurse -> It's the right thing. I'm also going to send a nurse to see her tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow morning. I'll tell the day shift. I'm going to write it in the book. Big letters.
Nurse -> Good. And I'll call back in the morning, before you go, or I'll hand it to the day team and someone will call.
Caller -> In the morning. Okay. I'm here until seven. I'll write that too.
Nurse -> For the rest of tonight, check on her every two hours. Note how easily she wakes, offer her sips of fluid, and chart what she takes.
Caller -> Every two hours. Wake. Sips. Chart. Okay. I do rounds anyway. I'll make sure to stop at her room.
Nurse -> And protect that arm. Keep the bed low, pad the rail, and use two people to turn her, gently. Don't pull on the arm.
Caller -> Pad the rail. Low bed. Two people. Okay. There's a pad in the closet. I'll find it.
Nurse -> Perfect. If she gets a fever, has any trouble breathing, if you can't wake her up, or if you find another bruise, call us right away.
Caller -> Fever, breathing, can't wake her, new bruise. Okay. I'm writing it. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else you want to ask me?
Caller -> No. I mean, one thing. Is this normal? The sleeping a lot? She's ninety three.
Nurse -> It can be part of the changes at her age and with her illness. That's why I want the provider and the nurse to look at her. I don't want you to worry that you did something wrong.
Caller -> Okay. I thought maybe I missed something. I'm still learning.
Nurse -> You didn't. You noticed, you checked, and you called. That's exactly right.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. I'll check on her now.
Nurse -> Good. Take care, Omar.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth, it's Jasmine Sandoval. I'm Mateo Sandoval's mom. I need supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Jasmine. Okay, let me find him. What's Mateo's date of birth?
Caller -> April ninth. Twenty twenty three.
Nurse -> Thanks. I have two one four, five five five, zero one one six on file.
Caller -> That's me. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Is Mateo asleep right now?
Caller -> He is. Finally. He had a long day. He had his bath and his meds and he went right down.
Nurse -> Good. Then we can talk.
Nurse -> Great. What do you need?
Caller -> The suction catheters. And the saline, the little vials. We're running low. I should have called last week. Diego! Diego, give it back! Sorry. Sorry.
Nurse -> No problem.
Caller -> Sorry, my boys. Okay. Where was I. The catheters.
Nurse -> How many catheters do you have?
Caller -> Let me look. Hold on. They're on the shelf. Five. There's five.
Nurse -> Five. And the saline vials?
Caller -> Three. Three vials. I think three. There might be another in the bag. Hold on. Let me, no. Three.
Nurse -> Okay. How many times a day are you suctioning him?
Caller -> A lot. More than usual. That's why I'm running low. He's been, his secretions are thicker. Since yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about that.
Caller -> It's thicker. Like glue. Like it's stringy. I have to put the saline in and then suction. Before it was thin and easy. Now it's, Marcus! Stop it! Put that down! I'm on the phone!
Nurse -> It sounds like you've got a full house.
Caller -> I have three. He's the middle one. The older two are, ugh. Sorry. They're fighting over the tablet.
Nurse -> It's okay. Let's keep going. What color is it?
Caller -> Clear. White-ish. Kind of white and clear. Not yellow. Not green. No blood.
Nurse -> Okay. Any smell to it?
Caller -> No smell. Nothing. It just looks like thick white goo.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I checked at dinner. It was ninety eight something. Normal.
Nurse -> Okay. And his breathing? Is he working harder than usual?
Caller -> No. Same as always. His color's good. His sats are normal. He's actually asleep. I'm in the hall.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And the trach ties? Are they secure? Any redness?
Caller -> Ties are fine. I changed them yesterday. Skin's fine. No redness.
Nurse -> And the site? Any redness, drainage, or bleeding around the stoma?
Caller -> No. It's clean. I did the cleaning this morning and it looked pink and dry. The same as always.
Nurse -> Okay. Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay, Jasmine. I've put in the order for the suction catheters and the saline vials. It's done.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. I was so worried. We only have five, and with the thick stuff, I'm using, I don't know, eight a day?
Nurse -> That's why I want to move fast. I'm going to coordinate the delivery for tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I'll be home. Diego, go to your room! Sorry.
Nurse -> It's fine. Jasmine, the secretions being thicker is something I want a nurse to see. I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow too? Okay. That's good. Is it a cold, do you think?
Nurse -> It could be early cold, or it could be dry air. The nurse will check him. In the meantime, make sure the humidifier is on in his room at night.
Caller -> It's on. I filled it today. I'll keep it on.
Nurse -> Good. Use a fresh catheter each time, and use saline only if the secretions are thick. Suction for no more than five seconds at a time.
Caller -> Fresh each time. Saline when thick. Five seconds. Okay. I do that. I count out loud.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. Does Mateo tolerate it okay?
Caller -> He hates it. He gets mad. But he calms down quick, and his color stays good.
Nurse -> Good. That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Good. And call us right away if he gets a fever, if the secretions turn yellow or green or have blood, if he's working harder to breathe, or if the trach comes out.
Caller -> Fever, yellow or green, blood, working hard, trach out. Okay.
Nurse -> And if he turns blue, or you can't get a breath into him, call nine one one.
Caller -> I know. I know. I have the emergency bag by the door. And the number is on the fridge.
Nurse -> And is the spare trach in the bag? The same size?
Caller -> It's in there, and one a size smaller. I checked it last week. And the suction machine is charged.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're way ahead of me.
Nurse -> I know you do. You're a pro.
Caller -> I'm not a pro. I'm tired. Ha. But thank you.
Nurse -> Is anyone helping you at night?
Caller -> My husband does Wednesday and Sunday nights. The nurse does Monday and Friday. The other nights it's me.
Nurse -> That's a lot. Let's talk about it with the nurse tomorrow. There might be more night hours available.
Caller -> Really? Oh, that would be amazing. Nobody told me that.
Nurse -> You're doing a wonderful job, Jasmine.
Caller -> Thanks, Beth. Okay. Marcus! No! I have to go. Bye!
Nurse -> Bye, Jasmine.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Kim.
Caller -> Hi, Kim. It's Estelle Ferrante. I need a refill for my blood pressure pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Estelle. Let me pull up your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> May thirtieth. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have four one five, five five five, zero one four eight for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house. I'm always here.
Nurse -> Good. And how have you been feeling lately? Any dizziness, headaches?
Caller -> No. I'm good. My head's been fine. A little tired in the afternoons, but I'm seventy, nearly.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. That's all right then.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pill is it? Do you have the bottle in front of you?
Caller -> I do. Hold on. It's the, the hydroxyzine. No. Hydralazine. Hydro, hydralazine. It's the one I take three times a day.
Nurse -> Okay. So hydralazine. Let me look at your list. I see two that start with H.
Caller -> I know. I know. I always get them mixed up. That's why I said it wrong. There's two H ones. They're both little yellow pills, almost the same yellow.
Nurse -> It happens a lot with those two. The names are close.
Caller -> My daughter bought me a magnifying glass for the labels. It's in the drawer. I never use it.
Nurse -> Maybe start using it. Ha.
Nurse -> I see hydralazine, twenty five milligrams, three times a day. That's the blood pressure one. And I see hydroxyzine, for itching, as needed.
Caller -> Yes. That's right. The hydroxyzine is for when my skin itches at night. I only take it when I need it.
Nurse -> Okay. So the refill you're asking about is the hydralazine.
Caller -> Yes. The hydralazine. Twenty five milligrams. Three times a day.
Nurse -> How many tablets do you have left?
Caller -> Let me count. I put them in my pill organizer on Sundays. I did it this past Sunday, so, I put in, hold on. The bottle. There's four. Four in the bottle. And whatever's in the organizer, which is today and tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. So four in the bottle plus what's in the organizer. That's enough for how long, do you think?
Caller -> Maybe, two days? Two and a half. Because it's three times a day. Four tablets is a day and a third. Then the organizer is two days. I don't know. I'm not good at the math.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let me do it for you. It's tight, so I don't want to wait.
Caller -> Oh, I appreciate that. I'd hate to run out on a Saturday.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll get it going today so you don't run out.
Caller -> Oh, good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And how is the hydroxyzine? Do you have plenty left?
Caller -> Oh, plenty. I have a whole bottle. I don't use it much. A few nights a week. I don't need a refill on that.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. I'll leave that one alone. I'm sending the hydralazine refill request to your prescriber now. It's done.
Caller -> Oh, wonderful. Thank you, dear. How long does it take?
Nurse -> Usually a day or two. I'll call you tomorrow to let you know where it stands.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. I'll be here. Well, I have the beauty shop at ten, but I'll have my phone.
Nurse -> That's fine. Leave the phone on loud.
Caller -> I will. Though in the dryer chair I can't hear a thing. Ha. I'll check it after.
Nurse -> That's fine. Leave a message if I miss you.
Caller -> I will. I will. Oh, you know what I did the other day? I put the wrong pill bottle in the wrong bag. In my purse. I had my, what do you call it, my pocketbook, and I put the one bottle in with the other.
Nurse -> Okay. That's what I was going to ask you about. How do you keep them straight?
Caller -> I don't. That's the problem. They're both in the cabinet next to each other. And they look the same. And they start with the same letter. I read the label every time but I'm squinting.
Nurse -> Let's fix that. Can you put the hydralazine in one bag and the hydroxyzine in another, each with a big label? Write on a piece of tape in marker, in big letters.
Caller -> Two bags. Big labels. Marker. I can do that. I have a marker. I have a bag from the pharmacy.
Nurse -> And put them in different places. The hydralazine where you keep your daily pills, and the hydroxyzine on your nightstand, since it's the one for night itching.
Caller -> Different places. Hydralazine in the kitchen, hydroxyzine by the bed. Oh, that's smart. That's very smart.
Nurse -> And if you ever see a pill and aren't sure what it is, don't take it. Call me or call the pharmacy.
Caller -> Don't guess. Okay. I never guess. Well. Once. Ha. It was one of those vitamins.
Nurse -> Let's not guess.
Caller -> I know, I know.
Caller -> No. Agreed.
Nurse -> That way you'll never grab the wrong one in the night.
Caller -> Right. I won't. Because I won't be in the kitchen at night. I'm not a late-night snacker. Ha. Well, sometimes. A cookie.
Nurse -> Ha. A cookie is allowed.
Caller -> Okay. Is there anything else I should do?
Nurse -> Keep taking the hydralazine three times a day, and use the hydroxyzine only for itching.
Caller -> Three times a day. Only for itching. Okay. And if I forget, what do I do? Do I take two?
Nurse -> No. Don't double up. If you miss one, take it when you remember, and skip it if it's close to the next one.
Caller -> Don't double up. Okay. That's what I thought. My sister takes two when she misses. She says it's fine. I told her to ask.
Nurse -> It's a good thing you told her to ask.
Caller -> She never listens. She's older. Seventy-four. She thinks she knows everything.
Nurse -> Ha. We all have one of those.
Caller -> We do. Well, I'm glad I called.
Nurse -> Tell her to ask her nurse or her pharmacist. It's different for every medicine.
Caller -> I will. I will tell her. Okay. That's it, dear. Thank you.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Estelle. I'll call you tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Bye now. Have a good one.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Joel.
Caller -> Hi, Joel. It's Tamsin. I'm calling about my mom, Cornelia Mbeki.
Nurse -> Hi, Tammy. Thanks for calling. Let me pull up your mom's chart. What's her birth date?
Caller -> September twenty third. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Got it. And is three one two, five five five, zero one two one the best number for you?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm at her house.
Nurse -> Great. What's going on with your mom?
Caller -> Her mouth. Her mouth is sore. She's got white stuff on her tongue. And inside her cheeks. It's been four days.
Nurse -> White patches. Can you wipe them off with a cloth, or do they stay?
Caller -> I tried yesterday. With a washcloth. They didn't really come off. Some of it did, and it was red underneath. She flinched.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds uncomfortable for her.
Caller -> It is. She keeps touching her mouth. She says it burns.
Nurse -> Does she seem otherwise like herself? Alert, talking?
Caller -> She's herself. Sharp. She told me my sweater was ugly this morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, that's a good sign.
Caller -> It is. She's always honest.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she able to eat?
Caller -> Barely. She says it hurts to chew. I made her some oatmeal and she took, I don't know, two spoonfuls. And she pushed it away.
Nurse -> And what about swallowing? Does it hurt to swallow?
Caller -> Yes. She says it's like swallowing glass. Well, she didn't say glass. She said, "It's sharp."
Nurse -> Okay. And her pills? How is she managing those?
Caller -> She's not. She's spitting them out. I put them in her mouth and she makes a face and then I find them in the napkin.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pills is she taking in the morning?
Caller -> The, oh, I don't have the list. I'd have to look. It's her heart one and the water pill and the stool softener. I think three. Or four.
Nurse -> That's okay. I can see her list. Don't worry about naming them.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Because I'm bad with the names.
Nurse -> Has she had any fever?
Caller -> No. I took it this morning. It was ninety eight. Ninety eight point two. She's not hot. She feels normal.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. How is she drinking?
Caller -> A little. Small sips. She likes the ginger ale. With a straw. She drinks that.
Nurse -> That's fine. Ginger ale's a little acidic, though. Maybe try water or apple juice that's been watered down.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't know that. I'll switch. She'll complain. She loves her ginger ale.
Nurse -> I know. Ha. It's a small thing, but it might sting a little.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Tammy, I'd like to send a message to the hospice provider about the mouth. This sounds like it could be thrush, which is a yeast infection, and they can treat it.
Caller -> Oh. Thrush. My mother had that once before. A long time ago. She was on antibiotics. She got it then.
Nurse -> That's very common. I don't want to diagnose over the phone, but the provider will want to know. I'll send it now.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Will they send something to the pharmacy?
Nurse -> They might. I'll let you know once I hear. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to look inside her mouth.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. Is that in the morning?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time. What works best for you?
Caller -> Mornings are better. She's more awake. After ten, if possible. She has her bath at nine.
Nurse -> I'll pass that on.
Caller -> Thank you. Oh, I forgot. My brother's coming this weekend. He's flying in from Seattle. Should I tell the nurse about that?
Nurse -> It might be good for the nurse to know, so she can plan a longer visit. It's good to have family there.
Caller -> He's very excited. And nervous. He hasn't seen her in six months.
Nurse -> It'll mean a lot to her.
Caller -> I hope so. She asks about him every day. She calls him by the dog's name sometimes. Ha.
Nurse -> That happens. It's the love that counts.
Nurse -> That's a big visit. Okay. In the meantime, for her mouth, rinse it gently with plain water after meals, or use a soft swab. Cool, soft foods are best. Stay away from anything acidic or spicy.
Caller -> Plain water after meals. Soft swab. Cool, soft. No acid, no spice. Okay. I have the little sponge sticks from the hospital.
Nurse -> Those are perfect. And offer small sips often. A straw or a spoon. Popsicles and ice chips can feel good on a sore mouth too.
Caller -> Popsicles. She'll like that. I'll get the orange ones. Those are her favorite.
Nurse -> Orange is acidic. Maybe a banana one, or a vanilla one.
Caller -> Oh. Right. Okay. Banana. I'll find one.
Nurse -> And call us if she gets a fever, if her mouth bleeds, if she's drooling, or if she can't swallow even liquids.
Caller -> Fever, bleeding, drooling, can't swallow liquids. Okay. I'm writing it down. On the back of this receipt.
Nurse -> Perfect. What about the pills? What should she do about those?
Caller -> I was going to ask you. Should I keep trying?
Nurse -> Don't force them. I'll ask the provider about which ones are essential right now and which can wait. Hold off on forcing any of them.
Caller -> Okay. I won't force. I'll just offer. If she says no, I'll put them back.
Nurse -> Exactly. And write down which ones she took and which she didn't, so the nurse can see.
Caller -> I'll write it on the sheet by the pill box. Taken. Not taken.
Nurse -> That's right. Pressure won't help. We'll sort it out tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. You're so helpful.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care, Tammy.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Carla. I think we made a mistake. A medication mistake. It's Beatriz Quintanilla. My mother is Rosalie Quintanilla.
Nurse -> Okay, Beatriz. I'm glad you called. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hold on, let me sit down. I'm in the hall. My mother's room is right there.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm here.
Caller -> I'm shaking a little. I haven't slept.
Nurse -> That's okay. Go ahead when you're ready.
Caller -> So it was time for her lorazepam. The point five. The bedtime one. And I gave it to her. At about, um, twelve forty.
Nurse -> Okay. Twelve forty.
Caller -> And then my brother, he came in, and he didn't know I had given it. And he gave it to her too. About twenty minutes later.
Nurse -> I see. So she's had two doses of the lorazepam, about twenty minutes apart.
Caller -> Yes. Two. A half milligram each. I mean, I think. I can check the bottle.
Nurse -> Can you check the bottle for me, please? Just to confirm the strength.
Caller -> Sure. Hold on. I have it in my hand, actually. I took it out of the room. It says, point five milligram, take one tablet at bedtime. That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Caller -> And it says "as needed for anxiety or sleep." So I thought, you know, she was restless, so.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let's keep going.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she right now?
Caller -> She's sleepy. She's really sleepy. But she's awake. If I talk to her she opens her eyes. She said, "What?" She said "What, honey?"
Nurse -> Okay. And her breathing? Is it regular? Is it slow?
Caller -> It's normal. I think. I'm watching her. Her chest is going up and down, it's regular. It's not slow. It's like how she breathes when she's sleeping.
Caller -> Daniel, I'm on the phone. Yes, it's the hospice. Because of you. Because you didn't tell me.
Nurse -> Beatriz, is your brother there with you?
Caller -> He's right here. He's standing here. He's saying it's my fault because I didn't write it down.
Caller -> Daniel, stop. Not now. Go sit with Mom.
Caller -> Sorry. He's going in to sit with her. He's more upset than he's showing.
Nurse -> Of course he is. It's frightening.
Nurse -> It doesn't matter whose fault it is right now. What matters is that your mother is safe. Let's focus on her.
Caller -> Okay. You're right. I'm sorry. It's one in the morning. We're both exhausted.
Nurse -> I understand. It's an easy mistake when two people are giving medicine. Beatriz, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> January nineteenth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And is your number seven one three, five five five, zero one one nine?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. Is that the best number tonight?
Caller -> Yes. Daniel's phone is dead. He lost his charger. Don't ask.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. I'll call you.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so we know what to watch for.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Is she going to be okay?
Nurse -> She's awake, she's breathing normally, and she's responding to you. That's reassuring. But I want the on-call clinician to weigh in.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. What do I do until then?
Nurse -> No more lorazepam tonight. Not from either of you.
Caller -> No more. I told Daniel. He knows. He said he'd throw the bottle away. I said no, don't throw it away.
Nurse -> No, don't throw it away. Just put it up where neither of you will grab it by accident. Then write down both doses, with the times, on one sheet.
Caller -> Both doses. The times. Twelve forty and, one o'clock? I'll write twelve fifty-five. No, it was closer to one. I'll write one.
Nurse -> Write what you think. It's okay if it's approximate.
Caller -> Okay. I have the sheet. It's on the refrigerator. I'm writing.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> There's already a sheet. I never used it. It has columns. Date, time, medicine, who.
Nurse -> That's the one. Use that.
Caller -> Okay. Done. Date. Time. Lorazepam. Beatriz. And then Daniel. Two lines.
Nurse -> From now on, pick one person who gives the medicines, and that person writes it down. That way this can't happen again.
Caller -> Yes. I'll do it. Daniel can do the mornings. I'll do nights. And we'll both write it down.
Nurse -> Good. And if you're ever not sure whether a dose was given, call us. Don't give it just in case.
Caller -> Right. Don't guess. I understand that now.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Now, for tonight. Keep her on her side, and check on her every hour. Make sure she wakes up easily and that her breathing is normal.
Caller -> Every hour. On her side. Wakes easily. Breathing normal. Okay. We'll take turns. I'll set an alarm on my phone.
Nurse -> Good. And Beatriz, if she can't be woken up, or if her breathing slows down or gets shallow, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Can't wake her. Slow breathing. Nine one one. Okay. I've got it. Daniel, you hear that? Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in an hour to check on her.
Caller -> In an hour. Okay. It'll be two. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Yes. I'll be up. And Beatriz, call me before then if you're worried about anything at all.
Caller -> I will. I will. Thank you, Carla. I'm sorry for the, you know, the yelling.
Nurse -> No need. You're both doing a hard thing.
Caller -> We are. We really are. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Talk to you in an hour.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Alan.
Caller -> Hi. I hope I'm calling the right place. My dad was with you folks. He passed in August.
Nurse -> I'm very sorry for your loss. How can I help you today?
Caller -> Thank you. It's about the bills. I got some paperwork in the mail, and it says there's a balance, and I thought hospice was covered. I don't understand it.
Nurse -> I understand. That can be confusing. This is the clinical line, so I can't see billing or insurance. The billing office handles that.
Caller -> Is that a different number?
Nurse -> It's the same main number. Press three for billing when the menu comes up. They're open weekdays until five.
Caller -> Three for billing. Okay. I'm writing that down.
Nurse -> They can go through each line with you and tell you what insurance covered.
Caller -> I just want to know if the supplemental covers it. He had Medicare and a supplement. I don't know how they work together.
Nurse -> That's exactly what the billing office can explain. They'll need the account number from the statement.
Caller -> It's on the top right. I see it. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> And there's another thing. My sister wants a copy of the care notes. From the last few weeks. She lives in Oregon and she wasn't here. She wants to read what happened.
Nurse -> I understand. Records requests go through our medical records department. They'll need a signed authorization from the family member listed on the account.
Caller -> I'm the executor. I have the papers.
Nurse -> Good. Then you can start the request with them. That's option four on the menu, medical records.
Caller -> Four. Medical records. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Is there anything else I can help with?
Caller -> Not really. I just, I wanted to say thank you. For what you all did. The night nurse, a woman named Sofia, she was so good to him. And to us.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along. She'll be glad to hear it.
Caller -> Please do. He really liked her. She used to sing to him.
Nurse -> That sounds like her. I'm so glad she was there.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you again.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself. And again, I'm sorry for your loss.
Caller -> Thank you. Goodbye.
