transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Priya, it's Hyacinth Blackwood. Something is wrong with my husband Everton. Something is really wrong.
Nurse -> Okay, Hyacinth. I'm here. Tell me what's happening.
Caller -> His face. The side of his face is drooping. The right side. And he can't talk right. He's slurring.
Nurse -> Okay. When did this start?
Caller -> Just now. Ten minutes. Maybe ten minutes ago. We were watching TV and I looked at him and his mouth was crooked.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he awake? Is he answering you?
Caller -> He's awake. He's trying. He says things but they come out wrong. Like his mouth is full of, I don't know, marbles.
Nurse -> Okay. Can he lift both arms for me, for you? Can you ask him to lift them?
Caller -> Everton. Everton, lift your arms. Both arms. Up. The left one goes up. The right one comes up a little and then it drops. It just falls.
Nurse -> Okay. Hyacinth, I need you to call nine one one right now. I think he may be having a stroke.
Caller -> A stroke. Oh, God. Oh my God. Okay. Okay. Nine one one. Do I hang up?
Nurse -> Yes. Hang up and call. Tell them his face is drooping, his speech is slurred, and his right arm is weak. And note the time this started.
Caller -> Ten minutes ago. It's, hold on. It's ten twenty five now. So it started at ten fifteen. About ten fifteen.
Nurse -> Ten fifteen. Good. Tell the dispatcher that.
Caller -> Ten fifteen. Okay. Wait. Is he confused? He keeps looking at me. He asked me what day it was and then he asked me again.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's confused too. Tell them that.
Caller -> He's confused. Yes. Everton, honey, look at me. It's okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Hyacinth, don't give him anything to eat or drink, not even water, and not his pills. Keep him sitting or lying with his head just a little raised.
Caller -> Nothing to eat or drink. No pills. Head up. Okay. He's sitting. He's on the couch. I'll leave him there.
Nurse -> Good. Stay with him. I need you to call now. Quickly, his birthday and your number, in case they ask.
Caller -> May twelfth, nineteen sixty. And nine five four, five five five, zero one zero seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Call right now. Unlock the door and turn on a light.
Caller -> Unlock the door. Light. Okay. I'm calling. Oh, God. Thank you, Priya.
Nurse -> Go. Go ahead.
Caller -> He's trying to say something. What, honey? What? I can't understand. Everton, it's okay. Don't try to talk. Don't try.
Nurse -> That's right. Let him rest. Is anyone else in the house with you?
Caller -> No. Just us. Our son is on his way home from work. I'll call him after.
Nurse -> Okay. Call nine one one first. Then your son. Go.
Caller -> Okay. I'm dialing. It's ringing. It's ringing.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. My husband, I think he's having a stroke. The address is four oh two Larkspur Lane.
Nurse -> Good. Stay on with them. I'm still here.
Caller -> They're asking me questions. Is he breathing. Yes. Is he awake. Yes. They're sending someone. They said stay on the line.
Nurse -> That's right. Do what they say. I'll stay quiet unless you need me.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Everton, they're coming. Honey, they're coming.
Caller -> He's trying to say my name. He said "Hy." Just Hy.
Nurse -> That's a good sign that he's trying. Keep talking to him calmly.
Caller -> Everton, you're okay. You're okay. They're coming. Don't try to talk.
Caller -> The dispatcher wants to know what medicines he takes.
Nurse -> Do you have his list?
Caller -> It's on the fridge. Hold on. Hold on. I'm getting it. He takes a blood pressure pill and a, oh, I can't read it, my hands are shaking.
Nurse -> Don't worry about reading it. Hand it to the paramedics when they get there. Just tell them he's on blood pressure medicine.
Caller -> Blood pressure medicine. And the list goes to the paramedics. Okay. I'll put it by the door.
Nurse -> Does he take a blood thinner? Do you know?
Caller -> I don't think so. No. The doctor didn't want him on one because of his stomach. I think no.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that too: no blood thinner, as far as you know.
Caller -> No blood thinner. As far as I know. Okay.
Caller -> They said eight minutes. The ambulance is eight minutes away.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he any different? Better, worse?
Caller -> Same. His mouth is the same. He's holding his right arm in his lap with his left hand.
Nurse -> Is he breathing okay?
Caller -> Yes. Normal. He's just looking at me.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't move him unless he needs to. Keep him comfortable.
Caller -> I put a pillow behind his head. He seems to like it.
Nurse -> Good. How about you? Are you doing okay?
Caller -> I'm shaking. I'm trying to be strong. He'd want me to be strong.
Nurse -> You are. You're doing everything right, Hyacinth.
Caller -> Thank you. Oh, I see lights. I see the lights through the window. Is that them? I think that's them.
Nurse -> Go let them in. Leave the phone on the table.
Caller -> Okay. I'm going. They're at the door. Yes, he's in here. In the living room. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> Hyacinth, I'll let you go. I'll call the office so they know.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Priya. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Take care of him.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi, Carla. Esperanza Pruitt. I'm one of the caregivers for Marguerite Sutherland.
Nurse -> Hi, Esperanza. How can I help?
Caller -> I need to order supplies for her wound. We're running low. And it's Thursday, and I don't want to wait until Monday.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull her up. Do you have her date of birth?
Caller -> March seventh. Nineteen eighty two.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have eight three two, five five five, zero one one three.
Caller -> That's the house. I'm on the house phone. It's in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Are you the only one there with her right now?
Caller -> Yes. Her husband is at work. He's back at six. She's in the living room on the couch.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you have left.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Let me go to the supply closet. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I won't.
Caller -> Marguerite? Marguerite, honey, I'm just counting supplies. Go back to your show. Okay.
Nurse -> No rush.
Caller -> Okay. I'm in the closet. Gauze pads. The four by fours. One, two. There's eight. Eight left.
Nurse -> Eight gauze pads. And the abdominal pads, the thicker ones?
Caller -> The big ones. The ABD pads. There's two. Two left.
Nurse -> Okay. And saline?
Caller -> The wound wash? The bottle? One. There's one bottle, and it's about half. Half full. Maybe less.
Nurse -> One bottle, half full. Okay. Esperanza, how often are you changing the dressing?
Caller -> It's supposed to be once a day. But today I did it twice. It soaked through. This morning at nine and again at two.
Nurse -> Soaked through. Okay. Tell me about the drainage.
Caller -> It's more than yesterday. A lot more than yesterday. The pad was wet all the way through. It was heavy. And the color is yellowish. Kind of a light yellow. Not bloody.
Nurse -> Okay. Any smell?
Caller -> No. No smell. I checked. I'd know. I've worked with wounds before. It smells like nothing. Just a little like the saline.
Nurse -> Okay. And the skin around it? Is the redness spreading, any heat?
Caller -> No. It's the same red ring it's had. It's not bigger. I took a picture on Monday and I compared. It's the same. And it's not hot.
Nurse -> That's very good that you tracked it. Is she in pain? Any fever?
Caller -> She says it's sore. Not worse than before. A three, she said. And no fever. I took it at lunch. Ninety eight six.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating and drinking normally?
Caller -> She ate half a sandwich at lunch. She's drinking her tea. Her appetite is okay.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> She's tired, though. But she's always tired after the dressing change. It takes it out of her.
Nurse -> That's understandable.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. That's helpful.
Caller -> Is the heavy drainage normal? Should I be worried?
Nurse -> It's something I want the nurse to look at. It's not an emergency with no odor and no fever. But the increase is worth looking at. I'm going to send a nurse tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. That's good. I'll tell Marguerite.
Nurse -> Now, supplies. I've put in the order for gauze, abdominal pads, and saline just now. It's done.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you. When will they come?
Nurse -> The regular delivery is Monday. That's too long. I'm going to try for a courier tonight.
Caller -> Tonight? Oh, that'd be amazing. Because eight pads at twice a day is four days if I use one at a time. But I use more than one per change.
Nurse -> Right. That's why I don't want to wait. I'll call you back as soon as I know the courier time.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here until ten. And then the night person comes. Her name is Wanda. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Good. Please leave her a note.
Caller -> I will. In the notebook.
Nurse -> Esperanza, for the dressing in the meantime. When it soaks through, change it. Don't wait. Clean it with saline from the center outward, keep the skin around it dry, and use one abdominal pad on top.
Caller -> Change when soaked. Saline, center out. Skin dry. One ABD on top. Okay. That's what I've been doing.
Nurse -> Good. If you start to run out before the courier comes, call me. Don't stretch the supplies.
Caller -> Okay. I won't stretch them. I've heard that's bad.
Nurse -> It is. A wet dressing sits on the skin and breaks it down.
Caller -> Right. Right. Okay.
Nurse -> And wash your hands before and after, and use clean gloves each time.
Caller -> Gloves. We have plenty of gloves. Those didn't run out.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> And call us if you notice a bad smell, if the redness spreads, if she runs a fever, if the drainage turns green or bloody, or if it suddenly gets much heavier.
Caller -> Smell. Redness spreading. Fever. Green or bloody. Heavier. Okay. I'll write that in the notebook for Wanda too.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you, Carla. I was a little nervous about asking for more.
Nurse -> Never be nervous. You did the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you. Have a good evening.
Nurse -> You too. I'll call you back about the courier.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gail.
Caller -> Hi, hello. Um, this is Rafael Vasquez. I'm calling about my mother. She's one of your patients.
Nurse -> Okay, Rafael. What's your mom's name?
Caller -> Imelda. Imelda Vasquez. She lives with my sister in Austin. I live in Denver.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull her up. Can you give me her date of birth?
Caller -> Yeah. October second. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks. And what's a good number for you?
Caller -> Five one two, five five five, zero one zero four. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's going on with your mom?
Caller -> I don't know. I don't know exactly how to say it. I flew in this weekend, I just got in last night, and she's not herself.
Nurse -> Not herself. Can you tell me what you mean?
Caller -> She's quiet. She's slower. She used to be the one who talked all through dinner. Now she just sits there.
Nurse -> Okay. And when did you last see her?
Caller -> September. The middle of September. I was here for a long weekend. She was fine then. She was walking around. She cooked. She was herself.
Nurse -> So it's changed since the middle of September.
Caller -> I think so. But I don't know when. My sister says it's been like this about two weeks. But then yesterday she said maybe longer. And I said, how long? And she said she didn't know. So I don't know.
Nurse -> That's okay. It's hard to pinpoint, especially when you see her every few weeks. What else have you noticed?
Caller -> She forgets words. She was trying to say "napkin" and she said "the thing for your mouth." And she laughed about it. But she looked embarrassed.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> She's not eating. Well, not nothing. She picks at it. She'll take three bites and push the plate away. My sister says she's been doing that.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fallen? Any bumps, bruises?
Caller -> No. No falls. My sister would have said. She told me no falls. I asked twice.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she sleeping more?
Caller -> Maybe. She naps in the afternoon. But she always napped. I don't know if it's more.
Nurse -> Does she wake up easily from the naps?
Caller -> Yes. When I say her name. She wakes up and says "Hi, mijo." And then she's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Nurse -> Okay. And has anything changed with her medicines? Anything new?
Caller -> I don't know. I don't handle the medicines. My sister does. I could ask her, but she's at work till six.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. Could your sister call me when she gets home? Or could you ask her to write down the medicine list?
Caller -> I can ask her. I'll text her now. Hold on. I'm texting. She's not answering. She probably can't look at her phone at work.
Nurse -> That's okay. Rafael, I'd like a nurse to see your mom in the next two days.
Caller -> Two days. Okay. That's quick. I'm only here till Tuesday. Could it be before then?
Nurse -> I'll ask for the soonest. I'll put a note that you're in town through Tuesday.
Caller -> Thank you. I really want to be there when they come. Because my sister, she doesn't always tell me everything. She doesn't want me to worry.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm also going to message the hospice team about the changes you've noticed.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Do you think it's, is it the, is she dying? Is that what this is?
Nurse -> I can't say that over the phone. Changes like this can mean a few different things, and the nurse and the provider need to look at her. That's why I want her seen.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's fair. I just, I wanted to know. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. It's a fair question. It's a hard thing to see.
Caller -> It is. She used to run the church bake sale. Now she can't find the word for napkin.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's hard for a son to see.
Caller -> Thank you. Yeah. Okay.
Nurse -> After the nurse sees her, I'll call you and let you know what they found.
Caller -> I'd appreciate that. My sister can call too. Should I give her number?
Nurse -> We have her on file as the contact. I'll call both of you.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> In the meantime, could you ask your sister to start writing down when your mom is most alert, what she eats and drinks, and anything new? And to have the medicine list ready for the nurse.
Caller -> Most alert. What she eats. Anything new. Medicine list. Okay. I'll tell her tonight. Or I'll do it. I'll write it down myself while I'm here.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Thank you.
Caller -> Anything else?
Nurse -> Yes. If she falls, if she gets suddenly confused, like she doesn't know where she is or who you are, if she runs a fever, or if you can't wake her up, call us right away.
Caller -> Falls. Sudden confusion. Fever. Can't wake her. Okay. She's in the living room right now, watching her telenovela.
Nurse -> That's good that she's engaged.
Caller -> She laughed at it earlier. She laughed at a joke. So she's in there.
Nurse -> She's in there. Yes.
Caller -> I think that's all. Thank you for listening, Gail. I'm sorry I'm such a mess.
Nurse -> You're not a mess. You're a worried son.
Caller -> Ha. Yeah. Okay.
Nurse -> One more thing. Does she seem to be in any pain? Any grimacing?
Caller -> No. Not that I've seen. She holds her side sometimes. But she's always done that.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll tell the nurse to ask her.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> I'll talk to you soon. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Hi, Beth, it's Odette Fontaine. I'm calling about Etienne.
Nurse -> Hi, Odette. Hang on, let me pull him up. Birthday?
Caller -> July nineteenth. Twenty eighteen.
Nurse -> And I have five oh four, five five five, zero one eight six.
Caller -> Yes, that's right. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. Is Etienne with you right now?
Caller -> He's in his chair next to me. He's watching his show. The one with the trucks.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. A truck show.
Caller -> He loves them. Every episode. He knows the theme song. He hums.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on with Etienne?
Caller -> He's stiff. He's been stiffer. His legs especially. And his arms, he's holding them tight against his chest. And the spasms are worse.
Nurse -> How long has it been worse?
Caller -> Three days. I think three. Since Sunday night. Yes, Sunday. So three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it all day, or at certain times?
Caller -> Mostly mornings. And when I change him. When I move his legs he cries out. He doesn't usually do that.
Nurse -> Okay. Does anything seem to trigger it?
Caller -> I don't know. I thought maybe it was the cold weather. It got cold on Sunday. But it could be something else.
Nurse -> Has anything else changed? New foods, new medicines, a new sleeping position?
Caller -> Not that I can think of. We got a new mattress pad. Last week. It's the foam kind. But he sleeps fine on it.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll mention it.
Nurse -> It could be. Cold can make it worse. Is he on a muscle relaxant?
Caller -> Yes. The Baclofin. I give it three times a day. Five milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. The Baclofin. And when did he have it last?
Caller -> At noon. I gave it at noon. And the one before at, um, eight this morning. And the one at, at four yesterday afternoon. Wait. That's not right. It's eight, noon, and then evening. About eight at night.
Nurse -> Okay. So he gets it at eight in the morning, at noon, and at eight at night. Five milligrams each. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Eight, noon, eight. Five milligrams. The Baclofin.
Nurse -> Perfect. Thank you for being so careful with that.
Caller -> I write it all down. It's on the fridge. Date, time, who gave it.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you missed any doses?
Caller -> No. Not that I know of. I've been careful. My husband does the night one and he's good about it. He writes it down.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Is he sleepy after he takes it?
Caller -> A little. He gets sleepy after the noon one especially. He naps for an hour. He's been sleepier since the stiffness started, I think.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever? Any cold symptoms?
Caller -> No fever. I took it this morning. Ninety eight four. No cold. His nose is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. And he's eating and drinking?
Caller -> He's eating fine. He had a whole waffle this morning. And a cup of milk. His stomach's fine. He's pooping. Everything's regular.
Nurse -> That's good. Okay, Odette. I'd like to send a message to Etienne's neurologist about the stiffness getting worse. They might want to adjust the Baclofin.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Because I don't want to change it myself. I'd be afraid to.
Nurse -> No, don't change it on your own. Please don't skip a dose either. Keep giving the Baclofin the way it's prescribed until you hear from them.
Caller -> Okay. No changes. I'll keep giving it. The Baclofin. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to see him.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. Is that the physical therapist or a nurse?
Nurse -> It's the nurse. She can check his muscle tone and talk to the therapist about whether he needs a visit.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds good. He loves the nurse. He calls her "the lady with the cold hands."
Nurse -> Ha. Warm them up, I'll tell her.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Does he tolerate the bath well, or does the water stiffen him up?
Caller -> He likes the water. It helps. He relaxes in it. It's the one time he's loose.
Nurse -> That's great. Then the bath is a good plan.
Nurse -> In the meantime, a warm bath can help loosen his muscles. And do some gentle stretching afterward, just like the therapist showed you. Position him with pillows, and keep him warm.
Caller -> Warm bath. Gentle stretching. Pillows. Warm. Okay. I'll do the bath tonight. He likes the bath. He kicks the water.
Nurse -> And call us if he runs a fever, if the spasms won't stop, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he starts vomiting.
Caller -> Fever. Constant spasms. Breathing. Vomiting. Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Anything else, Odette?
Caller -> No. I just worry. When he's stiff like this, it breaks my heart. He can't tell me what hurts.
Nurse -> I know. That's the hardest part. You read him very well, though.
Caller -> I try. Thank you, Beth.
Nurse -> How are you holding up? Are you getting any sleep?
Caller -> Some. My husband takes the nights. I take the days. We trade off.
Nurse -> That's a good system. Make sure you rest when he naps.
Caller -> I try. The laundry doesn't fold itself though. Ha.
Nurse -> Anytime. I'll call you after I talk to the neurologist.
Nurse -> Say hi to Etienne for me.
Caller -> I will. He's waving at the phone. Okay. Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Mina.
Caller -> Hello. Hi. Is this the, is this the right place? The hospice?
Nurse -> Yes, it is. This is Mina, I'm a nurse. How can I help?
Caller -> My name is Theodore Castellane. My wife is Winona. She's your patient. I wanted to ask, I have a question. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Please don't be sorry. Ask me anything.
Nurse -> First, so I have the right chart. What's Winona's date of birth?
Caller -> April twenty sixth. Nineteen fifty three.
Nurse -> Thank you. And is six one five, five five five, zero one six seven the best number for you?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. It's in my pocket.
Nurse -> Good. And you're at home with her now?
Caller -> I'm in the kitchen. I came in to make a call where she wouldn't hear. Is that silly? She's asleep.
Nurse -> It's not silly at all.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I wanted to ask what to expect. I guess. In the next few days. Because she's, she's changing.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> She's sleeping. Most of the day. She's been doing it three days. Maybe three. I lose track. She used to get up for a few hours, and now she just sleeps.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she waking up at all?
Caller -> A little. If I talk to her she opens her eyes. She'll squeeze my hand. But she doesn't say much. She said "Teddy" this morning. That was it.
Nurse -> That's a nice thing to hear. Okay. And is she eating or drinking?
Caller -> No food. She won't take food. And she barely drinks. I put a straw to her lips and she takes a tiny sip and turns away.
Nurse -> Okay. Any other changes you've noticed? Her skin, her hands?
Caller -> Her hands are cool. And her feet. They feel cold. Even with the socks. I put a blanket on her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she showing any sign of pain? Frowning, moaning, tense?
Caller -> No. She looks peaceful. She looks calm. I check. I check all the time. She doesn't look like she's hurting.
Nurse -> That's good. Theodore, thank you for telling me. What you're describing is common when a person is getting closer to the end of life.
Caller -> Is she, is it days? Is it hours? I'm sorry. I don't know how to ask.
Nurse -> It's a fair question. I can't give you an exact time. But the changes you've described, sleeping most of the time, not eating or drinking, cool hands and feet, these usually mean that her body is slowing down, and it could be days.
Caller -> Days. Okay. Okay. Thank you for being honest. I wanted someone to be honest with me.
Nurse -> I know. Is there anything you're afraid of?
Caller -> That I won't be there. That she'll go when I step out. I've been afraid to leave the room.
Nurse -> A lot of people feel that. Some people go when family steps out, and some when they're there. It isn't anything you do or don't do.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief. Thank you for saying it.
Nurse -> I'll always be honest with you. I'd like to send a nurse out today to see her and to be with you.
Caller -> Today? Oh. Yes. Please. I'd like that.
Nurse -> I'm also going to message the hospice team, so everyone knows what's changing.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> And I'd like our chaplain and social worker to reach out. They help families through this part.
Caller -> I'd like that. We're not very religious. But Winona liked the chaplain who came last month. Reverend Alvarez. She said he was kind.
Nurse -> I'll ask for him if he's available.
Caller -> Thank you. That would mean a lot.
Nurse -> Theodore, can I give you a few things you can do for her right now?
Caller -> Yes. Please. I want to do something. I feel useless.
Nurse -> You're not useless. Keep her mouth moist with the little swabs, and a bit of lip balm. Keep the lights low and a soft blanket on her. And keep talking to her. Hearing is often the last sense to go.
Caller -> Swabs. Lip balm. Low lights. Blanket. Talk to her. I've been talking. I tell her about the garden. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's perfect. Tell her anything.
Caller -> I tell her the tomatoes finally came in. She'd be so happy. She's been waiting for those.
Nurse -> She'll hear that. And don't worry about food or drink. Offer sips or ice chips only if she wants them. Don't force her.
Caller -> Don't force. Okay. I've been feeling bad that she's not eating. Like I'm not doing enough.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. This is part of the process. Her body doesn't need food the way it used to.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. That helps a lot.
Nurse -> Should we talk about your family? Are your children nearby?
Caller -> Two of them are. Our daughter is in town. Our son is in Chicago. I should call him, shouldn't I?
Nurse -> I'd call him today. If he wants to come, this would be a good time. I don't want to frighten you, but I'd rather he have the chance.
Caller -> I understand. I'll call him right after this. I'll call Dana first. Then Michael.
Nurse -> Take your time with those calls. You can tell them what you told me.
Caller -> I will. I'll just read them what I wrote on the envelope. I wrote down everything the other nurse said.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. And Theodore, you can call us any hour. If she seems uncomfortable, if her breathing gets noisy, or if you want someone here with you. Anytime.
Caller -> Any hour. Uncomfortable. Noisy breathing. Or just me. Okay. I have the number on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. The nurse will be there this afternoon. Is there anything you need before then?
Caller -> No. I don't think so. I've got coffee. Ha. I've been drinking a lot of coffee.
Nurse -> Try to eat something too. And if you can, sit with her. She knows you're there.
Caller -> I will. I'm sitting right here. Thank you. Thank you so much, Mina.
Nurse -> Of course. I'll see you this afternoon, or the nurse will. Take care.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll keep the porch light on for the nurse.
Nurse -> That's thoughtful.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Palliative Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Mei Liang. My husband Oswald is your patient. I have a question about his patch.
Nurse -> Hi, Mei. Of course. Let me find him. What's Oswald's date of birth?
Caller -> December thirtieth. Nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And a good number? I have four two five, five five five, zero one seven one.
Caller -> That's it. That's the cell. I'm in the garage, so if it cuts out, call back.
Nurse -> Okay. Why the garage?
Caller -> I didn't want him to hear me worry. He's in the den. He gets upset when I make phone calls about him.
Nurse -> I understand. Okay. Tell me about the patch.
Caller -> The new pain patch. The fentanyl. The doctor started it two days ago. The nurse put it on his shoulder. Twenty five micrograms per hour.
Nurse -> Okay. That's every three days, correct?
Caller -> Yes. Every three days. So it's due on Tuesday.
Nurse -> Right. And which shoulder is it on?
Caller -> The left. Upper back, kind of toward the shoulder blade. The nurse said to rotate it.
Nurse -> That's correct. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's your question?
Caller -> Since he got it, he's been nauseous. Like, queasy. He says it's about a four. And the skin where the patch is, it itches. He keeps scratching around it.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's take those one at a time. The nausea. Has he thrown up?
Caller -> No. Not thrown up. Just queasy. He doesn't want to eat much. He had a cracker. And ginger tea.
Nurse -> Okay. And when you say a four, is that what he said?
Caller -> Yes. He said, "About a four." He's always good with numbers.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. That helps me.
Caller -> He used to be an accountant. Everything gets a number.
Nurse -> Okay. And the itching. Is the skin red? Any rash, any blisters?
Caller -> A little red. Right around the edge of the patch. Like the shape of it. And it's itchy. Not terrible. Mild. He just keeps rubbing.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the redness spreading beyond the patch, or is it just under and around it?
Caller -> Just around it. It follows the edge. It's not spreading.
Nurse -> Any blisters, oozing, or heat?
Caller -> No. It's dry. It just looks pink. I put my hand on it and it wasn't hot.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. That can happen with the adhesive. Now, a really important question. Is he sleepy? Is he harder to wake than usual?
Caller -> No. He's awake. He's in the den doing his crossword. He's alert. He asked me about the weather.
Nurse -> Okay. And his breathing? Any slowness, any shortness of breath?
Caller -> No. His breathing's normal. I'd notice. I listen all the time.
Nurse -> That's good. Okay. Mei, should the patch come off? That's what you're asking.
Caller -> Yes. That's what I'm asking. Should I take it off? Because he's so queasy, and I don't want to make him sick. But I also don't want him in pain.
Nurse -> Please don't take it off on your own. The patch is releasing medicine slowly, and it's his pain control. Taking it off could leave him in pain, and another patch isn't something to change without the provider.
Caller -> Okay. Don't take it off. I thought that might be the answer. Okay.
Nurse -> I know it's hard to watch him feel queasy.
Caller -> It is. He's been through so much already. I just want one thing to be easy.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll work on it.
Nurse -> Nausea is common for the first few days when a patch starts. It often settles. I'm going to message the provider to let them know, and about the itching, too.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. What can I do for the nausea in the meantime?
Nurse -> Small, bland meals. Crackers, toast, rice. Sips of clear fluids. Ginger tea is fine.
Caller -> Crackers, toast, rice. Sips. Ginger tea. Okay. He likes ginger.
Nurse -> Also, keep the patch away from heat. No heating pad, no hot water bottle, no electric blanket over it, and avoid really hot baths or showers directly on it.
Caller -> Oh. Oh no. He has an electric blanket. He's been using it. He's had it on in the den.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's turn that off for now, or keep it off that shoulder. Heat can make the patch release too much medicine.
Caller -> I'll turn it off right now. I'll go in and unplug it. Hold on. No, I'll do it after. I'll do it after I'm off the phone.
Nurse -> And if he gets chilly, use a regular blanket, a cotton one, instead.
Caller -> A cotton one. We have a quilt his mother made. That's what I'll use.
Nurse -> Please do. That's important.
Caller -> I will. I'm so glad I called. I had no idea about the blanket.
Nurse -> It's a common thing to miss. Now, call us if he starts vomiting and can't stop, if he's hard to wake, if his breathing slows down, or if the rash spreads past the patch.
Caller -> Vomiting. Hard to wake. Slow breathing. Rash spreading. Okay. I'll keep an eye.
Nurse -> I'll call you back tonight after I've heard from the provider.
Caller -> Tonight. What time, about?
Nurse -> Probably between seven and nine.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine. I'll have my phone.
Nurse -> And Mei, you can tell Oswald that I said it's okay to say when he doesn't feel right. We'd rather hear it.
Caller -> I'll tell him. He's stubborn. He says he doesn't want to be a complainer.
Nurse -> Ha. We hear that a lot. Tell him it's helpful, not complaining.
Caller -> I'll tell him. Thank you, Naomi.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Tom.
Caller -> Tom, it's Walter Penhaligon. My wife has a nosebleed and it won't stop. It's been forty minutes.
Nurse -> Okay, Walter. I'm here. What's her name?
Caller -> Doris. Doris Penhaligon.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake? Talking to you?
Caller -> She's awake. She's talking. She's mad because it's on her good blouse.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. That's a good sign that she's alert.
Nurse -> Okay. Walter, tell me exactly. Where is the blood coming from, and how much?
Caller -> Her nose. Both sides now. It started on the left. We pinched it. We pinched it for ten minutes, I counted. And it kept going. It's soaking the towel. I've gone through three towels.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she swallowing blood? Is it going down the back of her throat?
Caller -> Yes. She keeps spitting. She says it tastes like pennies. It's dripping down. She coughed some up.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she on a blood thinner?
Caller -> Yes. The warfarin. She takes it every night. She took it last night.
Nurse -> Has she had any injury to her nose? A bump, a fall, a sneeze?
Caller -> No. She sneezed hard, I think. That's all. Then it started to drip. And then it just poured.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything like this before?
Caller -> A small one in the summer. It stopped in a few minutes. Not like this.
Nurse -> Okay. How does she look? Is she pale? Dizzy?
Caller -> She's pale. She's really pale. She said she feels dizzy. Her hands are shaking. She's sitting at the kitchen table.
Nurse -> Okay. Walter, I need you to call nine one one right now. A nosebleed this long on a blood thinner needs the hospital.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Right now? Okay. Should I hang up?
Nurse -> Yes. Hang up and call. But first, have her sit up and lean forward. Not back. Forward. And pinch the soft part of her nose, right below the bone, firmly, and hold it.
Caller -> Lean forward. Pinch the soft part. Okay. Doris, lean forward. Honey, lean. Pinch right here. Hard. Hold it.
Nurse -> Good. Don't tip her head back. Have her spit the blood out, not swallow it. Tell the dispatcher it's been forty minutes and she's on warfarin.
Caller -> Forty minutes. Warfarin. Okay. Dispatcher. Okay. I'm hanging up. I'm calling.
Nurse -> Walter, quickly, before you go. Her birthday?
Caller -> June eighth. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight six oh, five five five, zero one three eight.
Nurse -> Go. Call now.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Calling.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. My wife has a bad nosebleed. Forty minutes. She's on a blood thinner. The address is, it's nineteen Birch Hollow Road. Yes.
Nurse -> Walter, I'm still on the line.
Caller -> They said an ambulance is coming. They said keep pinching. They said don't let her lie down.
Nurse -> That's right. Do exactly what they say.
Caller -> Doris, they're coming. Keep pinching. You're doing great. Look at me. Look at me, honey.
Nurse -> Walter, is she holding the pinch the whole time, without letting go to check?
Caller -> I keep telling her not to check. She keeps wanting to check. Doris, don't peek!
Nurse -> That's right. Keep it pinched until they get there.
Nurse -> How is the bleeding now?
Caller -> It's slower. It's maybe slower? I can't tell. There's still blood on the towel. She's still pinching.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake and answering you?
Caller -> Yes. She says, "I'm okay." But she's so pale, Tom. She's the color of the wall.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep her sitting. If she feels faint, help her lean forward onto the table or lower her head toward her knees, but don't lay her flat.
Caller -> Lean forward. Don't lay her flat. Okay. She's leaning on the table. She's got a pillow.
Nurse -> Good. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> No. I'll go. Hold on. Doris, hold your nose. I'll be right back. I'm going to the door. Okay. It's unlocked. The porch light is on.
Nurse -> Perfect. Go back and stay with her.
Caller -> I'm back. She's okay. She's pinching. She says her head is spinning.
Nurse -> Does she have anything in her stomach? Did she eat this morning?
Caller -> Toast. And coffee. Around seven.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that too. And bring her pill bottles, including the warfarin, in a bag.
Caller -> The pill bottles. In a bag. I'll get them. Hold on. I'll get them after they come. No, now. Hold on.
Caller -> Okay. I have the bag. It's on the table. All the bottles. The warfarin is in there.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> That's from the blood loss. It's why we want the hospital. They'll take good care of her.
Caller -> I hope so. We just celebrated our fifty-second anniversary. Last Sunday.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. She's going to be okay, Walter. Keep talking to her.
Caller -> Doris, remember the trip to Niagara? Remember the boat? We got soaked. You laughed so hard. Remember?
Caller -> She's smiling. She's smiling a little.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Keep going. Tell her about it.
Caller -> I hear a siren. I hear it. They're coming.
Nurse -> Good. Go let them in. They'll take over. Walter, let me know how she's doing later.
Caller -> I will. I'll call you. Thank you. Thank you, Tom. They're here. They're at the door.
Nurse -> Go. Take care of her.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Eleanor.
Caller -> Hi, Eleanor. This is Annika Reinholt. My father is Gunther Reinholt. That's R E I N H O L T. I have a bunch of questions about his medicines.
Nurse -> Thank you for spelling it. Okay, Annika. Let me pull up his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> February sixth. Nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Great. And I have six one two, five five five, zero one nine two for you.
Caller -> That's right. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Is your dad able to hear you right now? Are you somewhere private?
Caller -> I'm in the laundry room. The dryer's running, so he can't hear. I'm sorry about the noise.
Nurse -> No problem. I can hear you fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead. What are your questions?
Caller -> Okay. So I wrote them down. But I wrote them on a grocery list, so there's also eggs on here. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll skip the eggs.
Caller -> Okay. First. His hip. His right hip is hurting. He says it's about a five. It's been like that for two days.
Nurse -> A five. Is it worse than usual, or is that his normal?
Caller -> It's worse. His normal is a two or a three. Now it's a five, and he's wincing when I move him. I think I'm not giving the right things at the right times.
Nurse -> Okay. Where exactly in the hip? The side, the groin, the back of it?
Caller -> The side. Where the bone sticks out. He puts his hand right there. It's an ache. And when he stands it's sharp.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had any falls or bumps?
Caller -> No. None. He's very careful. He uses the walker for the five steps to the bathroom.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through what he's taking. Start with the long-acting morphine.
Caller -> The morphine extended-release. Fifteen milligrams. Twice a day. I gave it at eight this morning. And the next one is at eight tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. That matches what I have. And the liquid morphine?
Caller -> The liquid. The morphine liquid. The little bottle. It says twenty milligrams per milliliter. And the dose is a quarter of a milliliter. Every two hours if he needs it.
Nurse -> That's right. And when was the last time you gave the liquid?
Caller -> Three hours ago. About three. At noon. I gave it at noon and it didn't really help.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's been three hours since his last liquid dose. And he's at a five. Is he able to have another one?
Caller -> That's my question. Can I give another? It says every two hours. It's been three. So I can. Right?
Nurse -> Yes. It's been more than two hours, so you can give another quarter milliliter.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. But then I worry about giving too much. Because he's also on the extended-release.
Nurse -> That's what the liquid is for. It's for the pain that breaks through. The extended-release works in the background. They're meant to work together.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's what the other nurse said, too. I just get nervous.
Nurse -> That's normal. Do you have the syringe?
Caller -> I do. The oral syringe. It's got the lines. The quarter is, which line?
Nurse -> The quarter milliliter is the smallest line near the tip. Draw it up to that line and no further.
Caller -> Smallest line near the tip. Okay. I'll do it after we hang up. I don't want to do it while I'm on the phone.
Nurse -> That sounds wise. Okay. What's your next question?
Caller -> Okay. The pills. I have a worry. I think I mixed up his Zyprexa. Or I was going to mix it up. The Zyprexa. The allergy one. No. The, wait.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I mean the Zyrtec. The allergy one. Zyrtec. The one for his allergies is Zyrtec. And the Zyprexa is the one for the, for the evenings. When he gets restless.
Nurse -> Okay. So let me make sure I have it right. Zyrtec for allergies, once a day, ten milligrams. And Zyprexa at bedtime, two and a half milligrams.
Caller -> Yes. That's it. That's right. They look so alike on the list. Z-Y-R and Z-Y-P. I can't tell them apart.
Nurse -> It's a very common mix-up, and the names are close. Which one did you give him today?
Caller -> The Zyrtec. This morning. With breakfast. And that's all. I haven't given the Zyprexa. That's tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. That's exactly right. Zyrtec in the morning, Zyprexa at bedtime.
Caller -> Okay. Good. So I didn't mess up. I thought I'd given the wrong one yesterday, but I think I had it right.
Nurse -> It sounds like you did. Let me suggest something to make it easier. Keep the Zyrtec and the Zyprexa in two different bags, each with a big label. And keep them in different places.
Caller -> Two bags. Big labels. Different places. I'll do that today. The Zyrtec in the kitchen and the Zyprexa by his bed.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Next question.
Caller -> Okay. Number three on the list. His bowels. He hasn't gone in two days.
Nurse -> Two days. What's he been eating and drinking?
Caller -> Not much. He drinks his tea and a little juice. He picks at his food. I think the morphine is making him constipated.
Nurse -> It can. Is he on something for it?
Caller -> He's on, there's a stool softener. The little pink one. But it ran out. I think we're out. I didn't want to say.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order more. I've put in the order for the stool softener just now. It's done.
Caller -> Oh. Oh good. Thank you. How soon?
Nurse -> It'll come with the regular delivery tomorrow. In the meantime, offer him fluids and prune juice, and note any bowel movement on the sheet.
Caller -> Prune juice. We have that. Fluids. And write it on the sheet. Okay.
Nurse -> And does he get any exercise, even walking to the kitchen?
Caller -> A little. Bathroom and back. And the chair by the window. He doesn't walk much.
Nurse -> That's okay. Just keep him moving a little as he's able.
Nurse -> Is his belly soft, or hard? Any belly pain?
Caller -> It's soft. He doesn't say it hurts. It's just that he hasn't gone.
Nurse -> Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?
Caller -> No. No nausea. He's fine that way. Eating less, but no nausea.
Nurse -> How's his appetite compared to last week?
Caller -> Less. Maybe half of what he ate last week. He used to eat two eggs. Now it's one. Or half.
Nurse -> Okay. That's useful for the nurse to know.
Caller -> He says everything tastes like paper.
Nurse -> Good. Annika, how is his breathing? Any shortness of breath, any chest pain?
Caller -> No. He's not short of breath. No chest pain. Nothing like that. He breathes fine. He's just got the hip.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring.
Caller -> Okay. Next question. This one's a little embarrassing. He said something yesterday and I didn't know how to take it.
Nurse -> Okay. What did he say?
Caller -> He said, "I'm ready to go." And I froze. I thought, oh no. Is he saying he's ready to die?
Nurse -> Okay. What was the context?
Caller -> I asked him a few minutes later what he meant, and he said, "Ready to go to church. Sunday." He wants to go to church on Sunday. In his wheelchair. He's been asking for two weeks.
Nurse -> Oh. Okay. So he meant he's ready to go to church.
Caller -> Yes. He was getting his coat. He had his coat on the chair. I felt so silly.
Nurse -> It's okay. I'm glad you asked. And actually, it sounds wonderful. Let's see if the nurse can help plan that.
Caller -> Could they? Could he go? He misses it so much.
Nurse -> It depends on his pain and his energy that day. But if his pain is better controlled, it might be possible. We can talk with the team about it.
Caller -> Oh. That would make him so happy. Thank you.
Nurse -> Does he have his own wheelchair, or would you need one for the trip?
Caller -> We have one. A folding one. It's from the loan closet. We'd need help with the ramp at church, though.
Nurse -> I'll make a note. The social worker might be able to help with that, too.
Caller -> Oh, that would be wonderful. The church has a ramp but the door sticks.
Nurse -> Let's get his pain better first. For the hip, when he's on his side, put a pillow between his knees. And help him change position every couple of hours.
Caller -> Pillow between the knees. Change position every couple of hours. Okay. He does like the pillow. Sometimes he kicks it out.
Nurse -> Ha. Put it back. Annika, I'm going to message the hospice provider about the hip pain and the constipation.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Will they change the medicine?
Nurse -> They might adjust the doses or the timing. It's their decision. I'll make sure they know the pain is a five and that it's been two days.
Caller -> Okay. That's all I want. For him to be comfortable.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse tomorrow. To see him, look at the hip, and go through the medicines with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow? Oh good. I'd like someone to go through all the pills. I'm a mess with them.
Nurse -> The nurse can set up a chart for you with times and colors. It can make it much simpler.
Caller -> That'd be wonderful. I'll have all the bottles on the table.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow morning, before the nurse comes, to see how the night went.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I'll be up. I'm always up at six.
Nurse -> Perfect. One more thing. Call us if his pain stays above a six after a dose, if he starts vomiting, if his belly gets hard and swollen, if he's hard to wake, or if his breathing slows down.
Caller -> Above a six. Vomiting. Hard belly. Hard to wake. Slow breathing. Okay. I wrote it on the list. Next to the eggs.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect.
Caller -> Okay. Is that everything? I think I've asked everything.
Nurse -> I think so. Is there anything else on your mind?
Caller -> No. Well. Maybe. Is it normal that he's sleeping more in the afternoon? He sleeps two, three hours after lunch.
Nurse -> It can be. As people get weaker they sleep more. I'll mention it to the nurse. As long as he wakes up and is himself when he's awake, that's okay.
Caller -> He does. He's himself. He told me my hair looked messy this morning.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a very good sign.
Caller -> Ha. Yes. He's still got his opinions.
Nurse -> Does he have any questions he'd like to ask us himself? Is he able to talk?
Caller -> He's napping right now. But I'll ask him when he wakes. He likes to be asked.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Please do.
Nurse -> Well, I'll let you go give him that dose. Do it now, before the pain climbs.
Caller -> I will. I'll do it right now. Thank you, Eleanor. You've been so patient.
Nurse -> And Annika, how are you holding up? You sound tired.
Caller -> I am. I have a brother who lives in Tucson who says he'll come, but he hasn't. So it's me. But I'm okay.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. I'm going to ask the social worker to check in with you, too.
Caller -> That would be nice. Nobody asks me anything.
Nurse -> We will. I'll put it in the note.
Nurse -> Of course. Take care, Annika.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi, Marcus. It's Bohdan. Bohdan Przybylski. P R Z Y B Y L S K I.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks, Bohdan. I always want to say that wrong. Prizzy, Prizzy-bill-ski?
Caller -> It's Pshih-BILL-skee. Close enough. Everybody says it wrong. I don't mind.
Nurse -> Pshih-BILL-skee. I'll get it. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> July twenty eighth. Nineteen seventy one.
Nurse -> And is seven seven three, five five five, zero one four five still good?
Caller -> That's it. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. What can I do for you today?
Caller -> Just an update, really. On my leg. You said to call if it was better or worse.
Nurse -> Right. I appreciate that. Are you still staying off the leg mostly?
Caller -> Mostly. I get up for the bathroom and to heat soup. That's it.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> I did. Tell me.
Caller -> It's better. It's definitely better. The red patch on my shin is smaller. Monday it was about the size of my hand. Now it's like a, a couple of fingers wide.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good news. And the warmth?
Caller -> Still a little warm. But not like Monday. Monday it was hot. Now it's just warm. Like warm compared to the other leg.
Nurse -> Okay. And did you mark the edge with a pen, like the nurse showed you?
Caller -> I did. I drew the line. The redness is inside the line now. It's about a half inch inside, all the way around.
Nurse -> That's excellent. That's exactly what we want to see.
Caller -> Yeah. I'm pleased. I was nervous it'd spread.
Nurse -> What about your temperature? Have you taken it today?
Caller -> I did. Ninety eight point nine. This morning. And again at lunch, ninety eight nine.
Nurse -> Okay. No fever. Any chills, any sweats?
Caller -> No. No chills. No fever. Nothing. I feel normal. Better than normal. I'm just bored.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. And any chest pain, shortness of breath? Anything like that?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. No chest pain. My breathing's totally fine.
Nurse -> Good. How's the antibiotic going? Are you taking it every time?
Caller -> Every time. The cephalexin. Five hundred milligrams. Four times a day. I set an alarm on my phone. I took the last one at noon.
Nurse -> Perfect. And you're on day four, is that right?
Caller -> Day four. Of seven. I counted. I've got three more days. And I'm dying to get out of the house, honestly. I've been stuck on the couch since Saturday.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, hold on a bit longer. Keep the leg up.
Caller -> I know, I know. Elevated. I've got it on a pillow right now. I'm elevated as we speak.
Nurse -> Good. Above the level of your heart if you can.
Caller -> I'll try. I'm on the couch with three pillows. It's a whole arrangement.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> My neighbor brought soup. It's been the highlight.
Nurse -> What kind?
Caller -> Chicken and dumplings. She puts way too much pepper. I love it.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds good.
Nurse -> Soup is a good highlight. Okay, Bohdan. I'm going to send a message to the provider with your update, just so they know it's improving.
Caller -> Okay. Do they need to change anything?
Nurse -> Probably not. But I like them to hear when it's going well. And I'm going to have a nurse come out Thursday to look at it and do a recheck.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. Is that morning?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time. Do you have a preference?
Caller -> Morning is better. I'm more awake. Before noon.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along. And I'll call you tomorrow to check in.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Great.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep taking every dose of the cephalexin until it's finished, even if the leg looks completely better.
Caller -> Every dose. Until it's done. Even if it looks great. I won't stop early. I know people do that.
Nurse -> It's important. And keep the leg raised when you're sitting, and try not to scratch it or pick at anything.
Caller -> Raised. Don't scratch. Don't pick. I want to scratch it, though. It itches sometimes.
Nurse -> That's normal as it heals. A cool cloth over it can help instead of scratching.
Caller -> A cool cloth. Okay. I'll try that.
Nurse -> And call us if you get a fever of a hundred and one or higher, if the redness spreads past your pen line, if you see pus, or if you get chills.
Caller -> A hundred and one. Past the line. Pus. Chills. Okay. I have it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Anything else you want to ask?
Caller -> Just, when can I shower? I haven't had a real shower.
Nurse -> Short showers are fine. Just pat the leg dry, don't scrub it, and avoid soaking in a tub.
Caller -> Short shower. Pat dry. No tub. Great. Thank you. That's going to feel amazing.
Nurse -> And if you have to wrap the leg, use a bag, not a tight bandage.
Caller -> A bag. Not tight. I've got a bag. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Ha. Enjoy. Take care, Bohdan.
Caller -> You too, Marcus. Bye.

Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Carla.
Caller -> Hi. Is this, uh, the hospice? I'm calling for my aunt. She's one of yours.
Nurse -> Yes, this is hospice. What's your aunt's name?
Caller -> Simone Dubois. D U B O I S. Like the French.
Nurse -> Dubois. Okay. And your name?
Caller -> I'm Cyrus. Cyrus Dubois. I'm her nephew. My dad is her brother.
Nurse -> Okay, Cyrus. Can you give me Simone's date of birth?
Caller -> Um. August fifteenth? Nineteen forty four. I think. I had to ask my cousin earlier.
Nurse -> Okay. And a number for you?
Caller -> Five oh four, five five five, zero one zero two.
Nurse -> Got it. Cyrus, what's going on?
Caller -> She's restless. She's been, since this morning I think, since before I got here. The caregiver said that. She keeps pulling at the tube. The oxygen tube. In her nose.
Nurse -> Okay. Pulling at the oxygen tubing. How long have you been with her?
Caller -> I got here around, I don't know. Two? The regular lady left at three. So I've been here since the afternoon. Since two or three.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're there alone with her.
Caller -> Yes. It's just me. I'm the only one here. My cousin's on the way, but she's an hour away.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the front door locked or unlocked? In case the nurse arrives before your cousin.
Caller -> I'll unlock it. It's the blue door with the wreath. There's a ramp on the side.
Nurse -> Perfect. Leave the porch light on.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake? Is she talking?
Caller -> She's sort of awake. Her eyes are open. She's mumbling. I can't really tell what she's saying. She keeps reaching up and tugging. Then I put it back, and then she does it again.
Nurse -> Okay. Cyrus, I'm sorry, you faded out for a second. Can you say that again?
Caller -> I said she keeps tugging at it. And I keep putting it back.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she breathing okay? Does she look short of breath?
Caller -> I don't know. She, I'm not really sure. It looks fast to me. Faster than before? But I'm not good at this. I don't know what normal is.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you count her breaths for thirty seconds? Watch her chest.
Caller -> Hold on. Hold on. I'm, ugh, I lost count. She moved. I'll try again. Hold on.
Caller -> I got, it's, I think twelve? In the thirty seconds? Or fourteen? I'm sorry, it's hard.
Nurse -> That's okay. That's helpful. That could be a little fast. How are her lips?
Caller -> Her lips are, they're pink. Not blue. Well, I think pink. The lamp is yellow so it's hard to tell. They don't look blue.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fallen, or is she sitting up in the bed?
Caller -> She's in the hospital bed. It's raised. She's propped up. No fall. She's just in the bed.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you turn on a brighter light and look at her lips again?
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm turning on the overhead. Okay. They're pink. Normal pink. Not blue.
Caller -> Sorry, my phone is dying. I'm plugging it in. Hold on.
Nurse -> Cyrus? Hello? Cyrus?
Nurse -> Hello? If you can hear me, please call back.
Caller -> Sorry. Hi. Sorry. It cut out. I had to plug in the phone. Are you there?
Nurse -> I'm here. Okay. Cyrus, I want to get a nurse out to see her tonight. I'm going to page the on-call clinician now.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you. Will you call me?
Nurse -> Yes. I'll call you back in an hour.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. And somebody's coming? Tonight?
Nurse -> I'm sending a nurse out this evening.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Because I'm kind of scared. I've never done this alone.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing fine. Let's go through a couple of things you can do right now.
Caller -> Okay. Yes. Please.
Nurse -> Keep the oxygen on. Make sure the machine is running and the tubing isn't kinked or bent. And if she pulls at it, gently move her hand away and put it back.
Caller -> Machine's on. It's humming. The tube isn't kinked, I checked. I'll hold her hand when she reaches. Okay.
Nurse -> Does she seem to be in any pain? Is she grimacing or moaning?
Caller -> No. She's not moaning. She's more like, agitated. Like she's looking for something.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the on-call clinician know that.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Talk to her calmly. Tell her who you are.
Caller -> I told her. She looked at me and said, "Cyrus." So she knows. She knows me.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. That's a good sign.
Caller -> Okay. Yeah.
Nurse -> One more thing. If her lips turn blue, if she's struggling to breathe, or if you can't wake her, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Blue lips. Struggling. Can't wake her. Nine one one. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> Okay. And Cyrus, who is the regular caregiver? Do you have her number?
Caller -> Her name is Joyce. I have her number on my phone. I could call her.
Nurse -> It might help to call her and let her know. Maybe she can come back, or tell you what's normal.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call her. Right after this.
Nurse -> And if the phone dies again, call this number back. We're here all night.
Caller -> I plugged it into the wall. It's at five percent. It's coming up.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. I'll let you go so you can do that. And I'll call you in an hour.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Carla.
Nurse -> You're welcome. You're not alone in this.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Alan.
Caller -> Hi, Alan. Dolly Greer. I'm calling about Alphonse. My husband. He's, ugh. I need help with his pills.
Nurse -> Hi, Dolly. Let me get his chart. What's Alphonse's date of birth?
Caller -> April eleventh. Nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> And I have six seven eight, five five five, zero one four three on file.
Caller -> Yes. That's the house. I'm sitting at the kitchen table. I've been sitting here for twenty minutes.
Nurse -> Is Alphonse nearby?
Caller -> He's in the living room. He's got the game on. The volume is up. He can't hear me, ha.
Nurse -> Good. Then we can talk freely.
Nurse -> Take a breath. Tell me what's going on with the pills.
Caller -> Okay. So he has this potassium. It's a big pill. It's like a horse pill. It's this big, it's the size of my thumbnail. And every morning I give it to him and he spits it out. Or he coughs. Or he just holds it in his cheek until I turn around.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he been taking it at all?
Caller -> Not for three days. Three days I haven't gotten it into him. I've tried applesauce. I've tried pudding. I tried cutting it, but then it's powder and it tastes awful. He makes a face like I'm poisoning him.
Nurse -> Okay. What is the potassium for, do you know?
Caller -> It's because of the water pill. The doctor said he loses potassium. I don't remember all of it.
Nurse -> That's right. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't cut it or crush it. I'll come back to that. What about his other pills?
Caller -> The little ones go down fine. The levothyroxine. The tiny one. He takes it every morning with water. No problem.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's just the big one.
Caller -> Just the big one. He chokes on it. He coughs and says it's stuck. He can eat soft food and drink, no problem. But the big pill, no.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Does he cough or choke with meals, or only with the big pill?
Caller -> Just the pill. Meals are fine. He ate a whole bowl of oatmeal this morning.
Nurse -> Does he drink liquids without coughing?
Caller -> Yes. Tea, juice, water, no problem. He had two cups of coffee this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm just, I'm at the end of my rope. He's driving me up the wall. Every morning it's a fight and I'm about to jump out of my skin.
Nurse -> It sounds like it's wearing you down. Are you doing this all by yourself?
Caller -> By myself. Yes. It's just me. Our daughter lives in Phoenix. I haven't slept past five in two weeks. I'm going to lose my mind, I swear.
Nurse -> That's a long stretch. Do you get any breaks? Does anyone come in?
Caller -> The aide comes on Tuesdays and Fridays for two hours. I go to the grocery store. That's my break. It's a nice break. Ha.
Nurse -> I hope you get a coffee too.
Caller -> I sit in the car. In the parking lot. Five minutes. Don't tell.
Nurse -> Your secret's safe.
Nurse -> I hear you. Dolly, I want to make sure I understand. When you say you're going to lose your mind, you mean you're overwhelmed and exhausted. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. I'm not, I'd never do anything. I'm just tired. I'm so tired. I'm seventy-two.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's what I thought. You're doing a very hard job.
Caller -> Thank you. It's nice to hear.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's fix the pill problem. First, please don't crush or cut the potassium. Some potassium is made to release slowly, and crushing it can cause stomach irritation or too much at once.
Caller -> Oh. Oh. I didn't know that. I cut it once. Last week. Only once.
Nurse -> It's okay. Let's not do it again. I'm going to message the hospice provider and ask for a liquid form, or a smaller tablet.
Caller -> They make a liquid? Oh, that would be wonderful. He'll drink anything. He'd drink the pickle juice if I put it in a cup.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll see what the provider says. I can't promise, but it's a very common request.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I'd be so grateful.
Nurse -> Can I ask the name of your pharmacy, in case they have to change the order?
Caller -> It's the one on Dawson Street. The big chain one. I can get the name. It's on the bag.
Nurse -> That's okay. We have it on file.
Caller -> Oh good.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep giving the levothyroxine as usual. And for any pill, sit him fully upright, give small sips with each pill, and stop if he coughs or chokes.
Caller -> Upright. Small sips. Stop if he coughs. Okay. He's usually on the couch. I'll put him in the dining chair.
Nurse -> The dining chair is better. And it's okay to skip the potassium for another day or two until the provider answers. I'll make sure they see this today.
Caller -> Okay. A day or two. Not dangerous?
Nurse -> I'd like the provider to weigh in on that, but it's not an emergency. I'll call you tomorrow with what they say.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Dolly, I'd also like our social worker to call you. She helps caregivers. You deserve some help too.
Caller -> Oh. That would be nice. I haven't talked to anybody in a long time. Not really.
Nurse -> I'm sorry it's been so lonely.
Caller -> It's okay. I talk to the TV. Alphonse says I talk to the TV too much.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet the TV doesn't mind.
Nurse -> I'll put in the referral. And you can call us any hour, even if it's just that you're having a hard night.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. Thank you, Alan. You're very kind.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself. Maybe have a cup of tea and sit for a minute.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hello, Priya. It's Folasade Oyelowo. I'm a patient. F O L A S A D E. O Y E L O W O.
Nurse -> Hi, Mrs. Oyelowo. Thank you for spelling that. How can I help?
Caller -> I've been dizzy. For three days. Whenever I stand up. It's frightening.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm sorry to hear that. Let me pull up your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> April third. Nineteen forty seven. No, no, no. I'm sorry. April thirteenth. I always say third. I was born on the thirteenth.
Nurse -> Okay. April thirteenth, nineteen forty seven. Got it.
Caller -> Yes. Yes, that's it.
Nurse -> And is there a good number to reach you?
Caller -> My son gave me a new cell phone and I don't know the number. I never memorize it. I'm sorry. He wrote it on a piece of paper but I can't find the paper.
Nurse -> That's all right. We have a number on file. I'll use that one.
Caller -> Yes, please. The old one is the house phone. It's the same, I think. I'll be here.
Nurse -> Okay. And are you at home right now?
Caller -> Yes. I'm in my chair by the window. I haven't gotten up since I called. I'm afraid to.
Nurse -> That's wise. Stay put for now.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the dizziness. When does it happen?
Caller -> When I get up. From the chair, from the bed. Everything spins, and I have to hold on to the wall. It lasts a few seconds. Then it goes away.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it a spinning feeling, or more like lightheaded, like you might faint?
Caller -> Lightheaded. Like the blood has gone out of my head. And my vision goes dark, a little, around the edges.
Nurse -> Does that happen every time you stand, or only sometimes?
Caller -> Most times. Not every time. It's worst in the morning, when I first get out of bed.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. My son got me one. I took it this morning. It said ninety eight over fifty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety eight over fifty eight. Is that lower than your usual?
Caller -> Much lower. I'm usually around one thirty over eighty. So that's very low. I don't like it.
Nurse -> Did you take the reading sitting down, with your arm resting?
Caller -> Sitting. At the kitchen table. With my arm on the table. Like the paper says.
Nurse -> That's right. Good job.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for checking. Did anything change recently with your medicines?
Caller -> Yes. On Monday the doctor added a water pill. A new one. Hydrochlorothiazide. Twelve and a half milligrams. Once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. And are you still taking the lisinopril?
Caller -> Yes, the lisinopril. Twenty milligrams. Once a day. In the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So you started the water pill on Monday, and the dizziness started within a day or two.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. Wednesday I think. Wednesday I felt it. Then yesterday, and today.
Nurse -> Have you been eating and drinking normally these last few days?
Caller -> Eating okay. Drinking less, maybe. I don't like to drink a lot when I'm dizzy because I have to go to the bathroom.
Nurse -> That makes sense. We'll talk about that in a minute.
Nurse -> Okay. That helps. Have you fallen? Anything like that?
Caller -> No. Thank God. I've been very careful. I hold on to things. I haven't fallen.
Nurse -> And any chest pain, or palpitations?
Caller -> No. Nothing in my chest. My heart feels normal. It's just the dizzy.
Nurse -> Okay. Mrs. Oyelowo, I'm going to send a message to your provider right now about the dizziness and the low pressure, since it started after the water pill.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Should I stop it? Should I stop the new pill?
Nurse -> Please don't stop it or change either one on your own. Let the provider decide. I'll tell them exactly what you told me.
Caller -> Okay. I won't stop. I'll wait. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to see you.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's good.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this afternoon after I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This afternoon. Good. I'll stay near the phone.
Nurse -> In the meantime, be careful when you stand. Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a minute first. Then stand up slowly, holding on to something steady.
Caller -> Sit for a minute. Stand up slowly. Hold on. Okay. I do hold on to the wall. But I'll sit first.
Nurse -> Good. And have someone nearby when you walk, if you can. Do you have someone who could stay with you?
Caller -> My neighbor, Bernice. She comes by in the afternoon. And my son calls every day. But he lives in Dallas.
Nurse -> Bernice sounds like a good person to have close by. Maybe ask her to stay a while today.
Caller -> I'll ask her. She'll bring her knitting. She loves to sit.
Nurse -> What is she knitting?
Caller -> A blanket. For her great-grandchild. It's yellow. They don't know if it's a boy or a girl.
Nurse -> Ha. A safe color.
Nurse -> Perfect. And drink plenty of fluids through the day, unless a doctor has told you to limit them.
Caller -> Fluids. Yes. I drink a lot of tea. I'll add water.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anything else you want to tell me?
Caller -> No, I think that's all. I'm just glad I called. I was going to wait until my appointment on Friday.
Nurse -> I'm glad you didn't wait. Thank you for calling.
Caller -> Thank you, Priya. God bless you.
Nurse -> And you, Mrs. Oyelowo. Take care.
Caller -> Goodbye, dear.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bluebell Home Care, this is Kim.
Caller -> Hi, Kim. This is Shanice Boateng, I'm the aide for Terrence Kowalski. His oxygen machine is beeping.
Nurse -> Okay, Shanice. Let me pull him up. What's Mr. Kowalski's date of birth?
Caller -> December ninth. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have three one seven, five five five, zero one six eight for you.
Caller -> That's my cell. Yes.
Nurse -> Great. And are you at his house right now?
Caller -> Yes. I'm in the living room with him. I do twelve to ten, usually.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has the machine been beeping?
Caller -> Since about two. Two or three. It's a steady beep. Every few seconds. And there's a red light.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a message on the screen?
Caller -> Hold on, I'll read it. It says, "Low, flow." L-O-W. Flow. And then, "Check, tubing."
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Is he having any trouble? How's he doing?
Caller -> He's fine. He's sitting in his chair watching TV. He's not struggling. He says he's comfortable. I asked him three times.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have his oxygen level? Does he have a finger meter?
Caller -> Yes. I put it on. It says ninety three. It was ninety four a minute ago. Ninety three.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine for him. Is it going up and down much?
Caller -> Ninety two. Ninety three. Ninety four. It goes around a little. But it's in the nineties.
Nurse -> That's what I'd expect. Is his color okay?
Caller -> His color is good. Pink. His lips are pink. His nails are pink.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Good. What is the flow set to?
Caller -> It's, let me look. It says three. Three liters. That's the number on the dial.
Nurse -> Okay. Shanice, did anything change today? Was the machine moved?
Caller -> Yes. This morning. The cleaning lady moved it. To vacuum. She moved it to the other wall. The other outlet. I don't know why I didn't think of that.
Nurse -> Okay. That might be it. Is the machine plugged straight into the wall, or into a power strip?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me look. There's a, it's plugged into one of those multi-plug things. A strip. On the floor.
Nurse -> Okay. That can cause the low-flow alarm. Can you plug it directly into the wall?
Caller -> Directly into the wall. Okay. Hold on. I have to move the chair. Mr. Kowalski, I'm just moving the machine, hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. It's plugged into the wall. It's making a different sound. Hold on. Hold on. It's still beeping.
Nurse -> Okay. Check the tubing next. Follow the tubing from the machine to his nose. Is anything kinked, pinched, or caught under the chair leg?
Caller -> Let me follow it. Okay. It goes under the chair. Under the leg of the recliner. It's squished. It's flat there. Oh my goodness.
Nurse -> Okay. Move the chair off the tubing and straighten it out.
Caller -> Moving it. Okay. I lifted the chair. The tube is straight now. Hold on. The beeping stopped. It stopped. It's quiet.
Nurse -> Great. That was it. The tubing was pinched and the strip was making it unhappy.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I feel silly. I should have checked that first.
Nurse -> It's easy to miss. You did the right thing to call when you weren't sure.
Caller -> Thank you. He's looking at me. He says, "Is the dragon quiet?" He calls it the dragon.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him the dragon's asleep.
Caller -> Ha. I did. He's laughing.
Nurse -> Now, you mentioned the portable tank is low?
Caller -> Yes. That's the other thing. The little tank, the backup. The gauge is at a quarter. I used it this morning when we went to the doctor.
Nurse -> Okay. A quarter tank. Do you have a spare?
Caller -> No. That's the only one. The last delivery brought one. I think we're supposed to have two.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order a tank now. It's done. I've put in the order for the portable tank.
Caller -> Oh, good. Thank you. When will it come?
Nurse -> I'm going to coordinate the delivery for this evening. Will you be there until eight?
Caller -> I'm here till ten. Then the night aide comes.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll try for before eight. And I'm also going to message the equipment technician about the low-flow alarm, so they can check the machine on their next visit.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Because I'm not sure if the machine is okay. It's been a bit loud.
Nurse -> They'll look at it. In the meantime, check that the tubing isn't kinked, the filter is clean, and the machine is plugged directly into a wall outlet. If it alarms again, switch to the portable tank.
Caller -> Tubing, filter, wall outlet. If it beeps again, the tank. Okay. I have a note.
Nurse -> When did you last clean the filter, do you know?
Caller -> I don't know. The nurse does it, I think. I've never done it. Where is it?
Nurse -> It's a small foam piece on the side or back of the machine. The nurse can show you tomorrow. Don't worry about it tonight.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask her to show me.
Nurse -> And keep the tank upright and secured, and no flames or smoking near the oxygen.
Caller -> Upright. Secured. No smoking. He doesn't smoke. I don't either. The cleaning lady lit a candle once. I told her.
Nurse -> Good. No candles either.
Caller -> No candles. Right.
Nurse -> And Shanice, if his lips turn blue, if he's struggling to breathe, or if his reading stays below eighty eight, call nine one one.
Caller -> Blue lips, struggling, below eighty eight. Nine one one. Okay. I wrote it on the fridge. I mean on the notepad.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I think we're good. Thanks, Kim.
Nurse -> Anytime. I'll call you if the delivery driver is delayed.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gail.
Caller -> Hi, Gail. This is Lars Strand. My father is Everett Strand. He's got a problem with his bowels.
Nurse -> Hi, Lars. Let me pull your dad up. What's Everard's date of birth?
Caller -> November twenty first. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> Got it. And I have six one two, five five five, zero one seven five for you.
Caller -> Yes. That's me. That's the cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Where are you right now?
Caller -> I'm at his place. I'm staying over. I'm on the couch. He's in the bedroom.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's moaning a little. Hold on. Dad? Dad, it's okay. I'm on with the nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's going on with Everard.
Caller -> Well, he hasn't gone to the bathroom in five days. Five days.
Nurse -> Five days. Okay. And what has he been taking for it?
Caller -> The senna. And the other one, the powder you mix in water. I gave him both. Yesterday and today. And nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. When was the last dose of the powder?
Caller -> This morning. At nine. And the senna at nine and again at, around eight tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. And he drank the full cup of the powder?
Caller -> He drank most of it. He said it was awful. He left a little.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. And how is he feeling?
Caller -> Terrible. He's crampy. His belly hurts, it comes in waves. And it's big. It's swollen. It's hard to the touch.
Nurse -> Okay. Hard like firm, or hard like a board?
Caller -> Firm. Not like a board. Like a, like a full balloon. Tight.
Nurse -> Does it hurt when you press on it, or when you let go?
Caller -> I haven't pressed. I don't want to hurt him. I touched it and he said ow.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't press on it. That's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Any vomiting?
Caller -> Yes. Once. About an hour ago. He threw up some, uh, it was clear, a little bit yellow. Once.
Nurse -> Any blood in it, or does it smell like stool?
Caller -> No. No blood. No smell. It was just kind of watery with some yellow.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he passing any gas?
Caller -> A little. He passes a little. Not a lot. He did one a few minutes ago.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that he's passing some. Does he have any pain medicine that he's been taking?
Caller -> The morphine. He's been on it a couple weeks. I'm sure that's it. That's what the nurse said last time.
Nurse -> Okay. When was his last bowel movement exactly, do you remember?
Caller -> Sunday morning. It's Thursday now, in the middle of the night. So Sunday. Four days. No wait, five, it's after midnight.
Nurse -> Okay. Five days. Thank you.
Caller -> I counted wrong before. I'm tired.
Nurse -> Okay. Lars, with five days without a bowel movement and now the belly pain, the firmness and the vomiting, I'd like the on-call clinician to look at this right away. I'm going to page them now.
Caller -> Okay. Yes. Please. Is it serious?
Nurse -> It could be. I don't want to wait on it. I'm also going to send a nurse out within two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. I'll be here. He's in bed.
Nurse -> Is the front door unlocked, or should the nurse call when she arrives?
Caller -> I'll unlock it. Or no, have her call, I'll go to the door. The dog barks.
Nurse -> Okay. She'll call first.
Nurse -> In the meantime, don't give him any more laxatives tonight, and no enemas, until the on-call clinician tells you.
Caller -> No more laxatives. No enemas. Okay. I almost gave him another one. I'm glad you said.
Nurse -> Good. And hold off on solid food. Give him only small sips of clear fluid, and keep his head raised.
Caller -> Sips only. Head up. Okay. I'll put another pillow.
Nurse -> And if he asks for water, just a few sips at a time. Not a whole glass.
Caller -> A few sips. He's thirsty. He keeps asking.
Nurse -> A sponge swab wet with water can help his mouth too.
Caller -> We have those. Pink sponges. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> And Lars, call us right away if he vomits again, if the pain gets severe, or if his belly gets hard like a board.
Caller -> Vomits again. Severe pain. Board. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> Anything else I should know?
Caller -> No. Just that I feel terrible. I should have called yesterday.
Nurse -> You called now. That's what matters.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Gail. I'll keep the phone right here on the arm of the couch.
Nurse -> Good. Try to stay calm. He'll feel it if you're calm.
Caller -> I'll try. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Talk to you soon, Lars.
