Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Renee.
Caller -> Hi, hi, yes. This is Latoya Simmons. I'm a, I'm the substitute aide, I'm filling in today. I'm with a client and she's on the floor.
Nurse -> Okay, Latoya. Is she hurt? Is she awake?
Caller -> She's awake. She's talking. She's not hurt, she says. She slid out of her chair. Right onto the rug. I was in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Okay. How long ago?
Caller -> Ten minutes? Maybe. I tried to get her up and I can't. I'm not strong enough. She's a big lady.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing the right thing by calling. Are you safe, are you okay yourself?
Caller -> I'm fine. I pulled my shoulder a little, trying. It's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't try again.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't try to lift her. Who is the client? What's her name?
Caller -> Miss Bernice. That's what she told me. Bernice. I don't have her last name. I just got the assignment this morning. They gave me the address.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the address?
Caller -> It's, hold on, the paper. It's four fourteen Willow Run Court. Apartment B.
Nurse -> Okay. Give me a second. Let me look that up.
Caller -> Sure. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I have a client at that address. I see Bernice. I'll have her last name in front of me in a second. Latoya, do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> No, ma'am. I don't know anything about her. I don't know her medicines or her history. They only gave me the schedule. Sorry.
Nurse -> That's okay. I have her chart. I can see it. I just need to make sure I have the right person. Is she in an apartment on the first floor?
Caller -> Yes. Ground floor. With a green door. And a little wreath.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the door unlocked? Will the nurse be able to get in?
Caller -> It's unlocked. I'll leave it. I'll stay with her.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> That's her. Okay. Latoya, tell me about the fall. Did she hit her head?
Caller -> I don't think so. I asked. She said no. She slid down, she said. She didn't fall hard.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she complaining of any pain, in her hip, her back, her neck?
Caller -> No. She keeps saying she's fine. She's laughing a little. She says it's happened before.
Nurse -> Okay. What's she doing now?
Caller -> She's sitting on the floor with her back against the chair. She's got her legs out in front. She's looking at me. She says, "Honey, don't worry about me."
Nurse -> What color is her face? Pale, flushed, normal?
Caller -> Normal. She's got nice color. She had a little bit of lipstick on.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Can you check if she can move her arms and legs normally?
Caller -> Miss Bernice, can you wiggle your toes? Okay. She wiggles. Move your arms? Yes. She can do all of it.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is she short of breath, or confused?
Caller -> No. She's talking fine. She knows who I am. She told me what year it was. She's sharp. She's telling me where the tea is.
Nurse -> Does she take any blood thinners that you know of? Anything on the counter?
Caller -> I don't know. There's a lot of pill bottles on the counter. I haven't looked. I don't want to touch them.
Nurse -> That's fine. The nurse will check. Don't give her anything.
Caller -> No. I won't give her anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Latoya, here's what I'd like you to do. Don't try to lift her. Put a pillow under her head, if she's lying back, and put a blanket over her so she doesn't get cold. And stay with her.
Caller -> No lifting. Pillow. Blanket. Stay with her. Okay. I'll grab the pillow from the couch.
Nurse -> I'm going to send a nurse out within the hour. The nurse will help get her up safely.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Thank you. I was panicking a little.
Nurse -> You did the right thing by not lifting her. And by calling.
Caller -> I almost called 911. I wasn't sure.
Nurse -> If she has any pain, hits her head, has trouble breathing, or gets confused, call nine one one right away. Otherwise, I'd like the nurse to come.
Caller -> Pain, head, breathing, confused. Then 911. Otherwise wait. Okay.
Nurse -> Exactly. I'll call you back in twenty minutes to check on her.

Nurse -> Perfect. Latoya, can you do me a favor and write down the time she slid, and what she's said about pain?

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care, this is Denise.
Caller -> Hi. Sorry. I know it's late. It's Rebekah. Rebekah Alderman. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi, Rebekah. It's okay. I'm glad you called. What's going on tonight?
Nurse -> Rebekah, before we go on, so we have it in case we get cut off. Can I confirm your date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty fourth. Nineteen seventy seven.
Nurse -> And three oh three, five five five, zero one eight four is your cell?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Now, tell me what's going on tonight.
Caller -> I don't know. I couldn't sleep. I thought, I'll just call. I don't know why. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> It's the right thing to do. What time did you wake up?
Caller -> I didn't go to sleep. I've been lying here since ten. I watched the ceiling for a while. Then I got up and made tea. I didn't drink it.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like a long night.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. I'm here. Tell me what's been going on.
Caller -> I'm just tired. I'm so tired. Of all of it. I want it to be over.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. When you say you want it to be over, what do you mean?
Caller -> I mean all of it. The treatments. The pain. Being a burden. I'm not going to be a burden much longer.
Nurse -> Who tells you you're a burden?
Caller -> No one. No one says it. I just feel it. My sister drives forty minutes every weekend. My neighbor brings me soup. I feel like I'm taking and taking.
Nurse -> It sounds like they love you. And that you feel guilty for needing help.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. That's it. I feel so guilty.
Nurse -> Okay. Rebekah, I want to ask you directly. Are you thinking about ending your life?
Caller -> I don't know. Not exactly. I don't have a, a plan. I haven't thought about how. I just, I want it to stop.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being honest with me. Have you been thinking about it a lot?
Caller -> More this week. I've been doing a lot of thinking. I gave my sister my jewelry. On Sunday. And I gave my neighbor my books. All of them. She came and took them in a box.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you tell them why?
Caller -> I said I was cleaning out. I said I was simplifying. I told my sister she should have the necklace. I said, "I won't need them where I'm going." And she gave me a look. I said, I meant the hospice. Eventually.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you mean hospice? Or did you mean something else?
Caller -> I don't know. I meant both. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's honest. Rebekah, are you taking your medicines?
Caller -> No. I stopped. Three days ago. The pain pills. All of them. I just stopped. I didn't see the point.
Nurse -> Okay. You've been in pain without them for three days?
Caller -> Yes. It's bad. It's a six. A seven at night. But I figured, I don't know, I deserve it, or something. That's silly.
Nurse -> A six to seven out of ten. That's a lot of pain to carry alone. I'm glad you told me.
Caller -> I didn't want to tell anyone. I thought you'd all think I was crazy.
Nurse -> No one thinks that. Pain this strong can change how a person thinks and feels.
Nurse -> It's not silly. I hear that you're hurting, in more than one way. Rebekah, are you alone right now?
Caller -> Yes. I live alone. My sister is in Boulder. She's forty minutes away.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have the medicines in the house? The pain pills?
Caller -> Yes. They're in the bathroom. In the cabinet. I haven't touched them. I promise. I'm not going to take them all. I'm not.
Nurse -> Okay. I believe you. And I'd like to help you keep it that way. Can I ask you to do something?
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Can you put the bottles somewhere that's hard to reach? Maybe in the trunk of your car, or a high shelf? Or give them to a neighbor tonight?
Caller -> I could put them in a bag. And put it in the garage. In the freezer chest. I never go in there.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Can you do that right now, while we're on the phone?
Caller -> Hold on. I'll take the phone. I'm walking to the bathroom. Okay. I have them. There's, one, two, three. Three bottles. Okay. I'm putting them in a bag. Okay.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'm right here.
Caller -> I'm going to the garage. Okay. It's cold in here. Okay. I put it in the freezer chest. Under the frozen peas. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Thank you, Rebekah. That was hard and you did it. How are you feeling now?
Caller -> A little better. I don't know. Calmer. My hands are shaking.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so that someone who can adjust your pain medicines and talk with you tonight is looking at this.
Caller -> Okay. Is somebody going to come? Is somebody going to take me away?
Nurse -> No one is going to take you anywhere you don't want to go. I want to get you help with the pain and the way you've been feeling. I'm also going to ask our social worker to call you.
Caller -> Okay. I'd like that. I think I need to talk to someone. I haven't told anyone how bad it's been.
Nurse -> I'm glad you told me. And I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. You'll really call?
Nurse -> I'll really call. And Rebekah, if the thoughts get stronger, or you feel like you might act on them, call nine one one. You can also call or text nine eight eight any time, and you can call us any hour.
Caller -> Nine one one. Nine eight eight. You. Okay. I wrote it on my hand.
Nurse -> Good. Is there someone who can come and stay with you tonight? Your sister?
Caller -> I could call her. She'd come. She's a night owl. She's probably awake. But I didn't want to scare her.
Nurse -> I think she'd want to be called. Would you be willing to call her after we hang up?
Caller -> Yeah. Okay. I'll call her. I'll tell her I want her to come.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good plan. I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Denise. I'm sorry for calling so late.
Nurse -> Never be sorry. Call anytime.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Beth.
Caller -> Beth, it's Fiona Wetherell. It's Callum. It's his sugar. And the pump. I don't know what's going on.
Nurse -> Okay, Fiona. I'm here. Let's take it one step at a time. Callum is spelled C A L L U M?
Caller -> Yes. C A L L U M. And Wetherell is W E T H E R E L L. Double L.
Nurse -> Got it. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> March eighteenth. Twenty twenty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number is nine one eight, five five five, zero one three three?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Is anyone there with you? Another adult?
Caller -> My husband is on night shift. He's at the plant until six. It's just me and the kids. His sister is asleep in the other room.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. Let's go.
Nurse -> Okay. Fiona. Is Callum awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's on the couch with his stuffed dog. He's quiet. He's not himself. He's a little sleepy.
Nurse -> Okay. What's his sugar?
Caller -> It's three twelve. Three hundred and twelve. I checked it ten minutes ago. It was two forty at supper, and I gave a correction on the pump, and it's gone up.
Nurse -> Okay. And you said the pump?
Caller -> The pump has been beeping. It says "occlusion." It started at supper. I changed the site. I put a new set in his belly, the other side. And it beeped again.
Nurse -> Okay. You changed the set once already, and it alarmed again.
Caller -> Yes. I'm so tired. I'm sorry. I did the whole thing. I filled the reservoir. I primed it. And after I put it in, it started again. Occlusion, occlusion.
Nurse -> No apologies. You did it right. What's the infusion set you're using? Is it the same brand as always?
Caller -> Same. The ones with the little tube. The nurse says they sometimes kink. I used one from a new box.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's frustrating. Did you check for ketones?
Caller -> I did. I have the urine strips. It's moderate. It's the dark pink. Almost purple. It's moderate.
Nurse -> Okay. Moderate ketones. Thank you for checking. How is his tummy? Is he nauseated?
Caller -> A little. He said his tummy hurts. He said he feels like throwing up. But he hasn't. He hasn't thrown up.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he drinking?
Caller -> He drank some water. He had half a cup. I'm trying to get him to drink more.
Nurse -> Good. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I took it. Ninety eight. Normal. He feels cool.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Is he breathing normally? Or is it fast and deep?
Caller -> Normal. I think. I'm counting. It's normal. He's not breathing hard. He's just tired. And he's awake. He answered me. I asked him what his dog's name was and he said "Biscuit."
Nurse -> Okay. That's very reassuring. Fiona, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, because his sugar's over three hundred with moderate ketones, and the pump isn't delivering.
Caller -> Please. Please. I don't know whether to go to the hospital. Do I take him in?
Nurse -> The on-call clinician will help decide. He's awake, he's drinking, and he's not vomiting, so we have a little time. But I want you to do a few things right now.
Caller -> Okay. Yes. Tell me.
Nurse -> Change the set one more time, with a brand new set, not the one you already opened. Use a different spot, and prime it. And if the pump still won't deliver, give a correction dose with a pen, by injection. Do you have a pen?
Caller -> I have a pen. The rapid acting one. In the fridge. The nurse showed us.
Nurse -> Good. Do you remember the correction amount? Is it on his sheet?
Caller -> It's on the sheet. On the fridge. For three hundred it's, hold on. Let me look. It says, one unit for every fifty over a hundred and fifty. Hmm. Three twelve. Let me do the math.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'll stay right here. Or wait. Actually, let's wait for the on-call clinician before you give a dose. They'll tell you the exact number.
Caller -> Wait for them. Okay. But change the site.
Nurse -> Right. Don't worry about the math right now.
Caller -> Okay. I'm terrible at math when I'm scared.
Nurse -> Yes. Change the set, new spot, prime. That's the first step.
Caller -> Okay. I have a new set. Hold on. Let me do it. I have to put the phone down. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I won't. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. Callum, honey, Mama has to do your tummy again. Just one more. One more, I promise. Okay. Okay. It's in. I primed it. I'm connecting it. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Does the pump show an alarm now?
Caller -> No. It says, "delivering." No alarm. It's working. Oh. Oh, thank God. It's not beeping.
Nurse -> Okay. That was likely a bad set. Keep a close eye on it. Offer him water in small sips, often. No sugary drinks.
Caller -> Water. Small sips. No juice. Okay. I'll get him water. Callum, drink, baby.
Nurse -> And Fiona, call nine one one if he vomits more than once, if he gets hard to wake, if he's breathing fast and deep, or if he seems confused.
Caller -> Vomiting, hard to wake, breathing fast and deep, confused. Okay. I'll watch him. I'm not leaving him.
Nurse -> Does he have any other symptoms I should know about? Thirsty, going to the bathroom a lot?
Caller -> He's been peeing a lot since dinner. And he's thirsty. He keeps asking for water.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits with the high sugar. I'll tell the on-call clinician.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call you back in thirty minutes with what the on-call clinician says.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. And I'll recheck his sugar in thirty. And the ketones.
Nurse -> Perfect. Write it down.
Caller -> I will. I'll write the time. Thank you, Beth. I was about to lose it.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right.
Caller -> I'm so tired. I've been up since five.
Nurse -> I know. Hang in there. I'm paging now.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Alan.
Caller -> Hi, Alan. This is Julian Montenegro. I'm calling about my mother, Odalys Montenegro. I have a question about her morphine.
Nurse -> Hi, Julian. Let me pull up her chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> December first. Nineteen thirty five.
Nurse -> And I have seven eight six, five five five, zero one four one for you.
Caller -> That's right. That's my cell. I'm in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Is your mom in the room with you, or somewhere else?
Caller -> She's in her bedroom. I have the baby monitor on the counter. I can hear her breathing. It's calm.
Nurse -> Good. Then we can take a minute.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> So the pharmacy delivered a new bottle today. The liquid morphine. And it looks different.
Nurse -> Different how?
Caller -> The old one was brown. Amber. This one is clear. And the label is a different kind. Different pharmacy name. It used to say Oak Street Pharmacy and now it says something else.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you read the strength on the new label?
Caller -> Yes. That's the problem. The old one said twenty milligrams per milliliter. This one says ten. Ten milligrams per milliliter.
Nurse -> Okay. You're right to notice that. That is a different strength. Good catch.
Caller -> I almost gave it. I had the syringe ready. I was going to draw up a quarter, like I always do. And then I looked at the bottle.
Nurse -> What made you look at the bottle?
Caller -> The color. It looked weird. Clear. I thought, huh, is this water? So I picked it up and read the label.
Nurse -> That's a great instinct.
Nurse -> And you stopped. That was exactly right. Tell me, how is your mother right now?
Caller -> She's comfortable. She's asleep, I think. She's in the bedroom. She said her pain was a three earlier.
Nurse -> Okay. A three. And when was her last dose?
Caller -> Four hours ago. About one o'clock. A quarter milliliter from the old bottle. That's five milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. And what does her order say? Every four hours as needed?
Caller -> Yes. Every four hours if she needs it. The label on the old one says that. The new one has the same instructions, but it says, "one half milliliter." Is that right?
Nurse -> Let me check what I have in her chart. Give me a moment.
Caller -> Sure. Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay. I see her order. It's for five milligrams every four hours as needed. With the old twenty milligram per milliliter bottle, that's a quarter of a milliliter. With the new ten milligram per milliliter bottle, five milligrams is half a milliliter.
Caller -> Half a milliliter. Okay. So it's twice as much liquid, because it's half as strong.
Nurse -> That's right.
Caller -> I'm an electrician. I understand ratios. I don't understand why the pharmacy changed it without telling anybody.
Nurse -> It's a fair question. I'll make sure our office follows up with them.
Nurse -> Exactly. The dose in milligrams is the same. The volume is twice as much, because the new bottle is half as concentrated.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. But I'm still a little scared. Because if I'd given a quarter from the new bottle, she'd get less. But if I'd used the half from the old bottle, she'd get way too much.
Nurse -> That's exactly why this is risky, and why I want to make sure we get it right. Julian, I'm going to call the pharmacy right now to confirm the strength change.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Yes. I'd feel better.
Nurse -> Can you hold on a moment? Or I'll call you right back.
Caller -> I'll hold. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Okay. Julian, I'm back. I reached the pharmacy about the morphine. They confirmed it. They're switching to the ten milligram per milliliter bottle for all their hospice patients. They should have called you.
Caller -> Nobody called. There was just a bag on the porch.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about that. I'll let our office know. So the plan is the same, five milligrams, which is half a milliliter from the new bottle.
Caller -> Half a milliliter from the new bottle. Okay. And what about the old bottle? There's still some left.
Nurse -> Please put the old bottle away, somewhere separate, so you don't use it by mistake. The nurse can collect it tomorrow.
Caller -> I'll put it in a bag. And mark it. In the cabinet above the fridge. Okay.
Nurse -> And write the strength and dose on the new bottle, big letters. Ten milligrams per milliliter. Half a milliliter.
Caller -> Ten per milliliter. Half a mil. In marker. I have one here. Okay. I'm writing. Done.
Nurse -> Take a picture of the label with your phone too, if you can.
Caller -> Good idea. Okay. I took one. Front and back.
Nurse -> Perfect. And use the oral syringe. Draw up to the half milliliter line.
Caller -> The half line. It's the middle of the first section. Okay. I see it.
Nurse -> That's it. You'll have the nurse come tomorrow to double-check. I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. I'd like that. I want somebody to watch me do it the first time.
Nurse -> That's a smart plan. Julian, what time is she due for her next dose?
Caller -> Five o'clock. In about fifty minutes. If she needs it.
Nurse -> And how many doses has she needed the last few days? Is it about the same?
Caller -> About two a day. Sometimes three. Never more than three.
Nurse -> Okay. That's useful for the nurse tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. If she's in pain by then, you can give the half milliliter from the new bottle. If she's comfortable, you don't have to.
Caller -> Okay. If pain, half milliliter, new bottle. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if her pain stays above a five after a dose, if she's hard to wake, or if her breathing gets slow.
Caller -> Above a five. Hard to wake. Slow breathing. Okay. She's resting easy right now.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have my number if you want to double-check before you give it?
Caller -> I have the hospice number on the fridge. I'll call if I'm unsure. Thanks, Alan. I'm glad I called.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. You did everything right.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Alan.
Caller -> Hello? Hi, can you hear us? We're on the speaker.
Nurse -> I can hear you. This is Alan, I'm a nurse. Who's calling?
Caller -> It's Winnie. Winnie Ormsby. And my brother Percy's here. We're calling about our dad. Thaddeus Ormsby.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Alan. This is Percy. I wanted to ask something. I think we need to take him to the hospital.
Nurse -> Okay, Percy. Let's slow down a little. First, so I have the right chart. What's your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> March seventeenth. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thanks. And what's the best number for you two?
Caller -> Mine. Two one two, five five five, zero one five nine. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Tell me what's going on with your dad.
Caller -> He's not eating. He's hardly eating anything. For about a week now. A few bites of toast, that's all.
Caller -> And he's sleeping all the time. He sleeps twenty hours, practically.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he waking up when you talk to him?
Nurse -> Yes. He wakes up. He's with it. He knows us. He's just really tired.
Nurse -> Does he talk with you when he's awake?
Caller -> A little. Short sentences. He asked about the dog yesterday. He asked if we fed the dog.
Nurse -> That sounds like him.
Caller -> It does. He's still in there.
Caller -> He said he's hurting. His back. He said it's a four. A four out of ten.
Nurse -> Okay. A four. Is he taking anything for it?
Caller -> The Tylenol. And the little pills from the nurse. I'd have to check the names.
Nurse -> No worries. Is he able to swallow them okay?
Caller -> Mostly. Sometimes he holds one in his mouth for a while. We give them with a spoonful of applesauce.
Nurse -> That's a good trick. Keep doing that.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll look at the list. What I'd like to know is, is the pain controlled or is it getting worse?
Caller -> About the same. It's a four. It was a four yesterday. He says it's bearable.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. No trouble breathing. He's fine with his breathing. He's pretty quiet.
Nurse -> And falls? Has he fallen at all?
Caller -> No. He's mostly in bed. He gets up with us to go to the bathroom. No falls.
Caller -> Alan, can I say something? I think he's dehydrated. I think he needs an IV. I think we should take him to the ER. They can give him fluids.
Caller -> Percy, we talked about this.
Caller -> I know, but he's not drinking. He's going to dry up.
Caller -> Percy. He said he doesn't want to go to the hospital. He told us. He told the nurse. It's in the papers.
Nurse -> Can I jump in for a second? I hear that you're both worried. And you both love your dad. That's clear.
Caller -> Yes. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. This is a really hard time. Winnie, what has your dad said about where he wants to be?
Caller -> He wants to stay home. He's said it a hundred times. He said, "Don't let them take me back to the hospital." That's what he said.
Caller -> I know he said it. But I can't just watch him not eat.
Nurse -> Percy, I understand. It feels like doing nothing. But when a person is at this stage, not eating and drinking much is part of how the body slows down. IV fluids at the hospital often don't make a person feel better, and the trip can be hard on him.
Caller -> Even the fluids? They don't help?
Nurse -> They may not. And sometimes they cause discomfort, like swelling or more fluid in the lungs. That's why we usually focus on comfort. But I hear you, and I'd like the team to talk with you about it.
Caller -> Okay. I guess I didn't know that.
Nurse -> It's not something people think about until they're in it. Nobody expects to have to learn this.
Caller -> No. We didn't. We thought he'd get better for a while. He did get better for a while.
Nurse -> He did. And now he's changing again. That's the nature of it.
Caller -> I told you, Percy. The nurse told us before. You weren't there.
Nurse -> It's a lot of information. It's easy to miss. Let me ask, has your dad talked about this himself, in the last few days? Is he able to tell you what he wants?
Caller -> Yesterday he was awake for a while. He said he's tired but he's okay. He said, "I'm where I want to be." Right here. In the den.
Caller -> He said that? I didn't hear that.
Caller -> You were at the store.
Nurse -> That's what I'd go by, then. He's told you he wants to stay home and he's comfortable. Our job is to keep him comfortable there.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That's what I want too. I just don't want him to suffer.
Nurse -> Of course. And he doesn't have to. Let me tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow to see him, and to talk with both of you.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call in the morning. I'll ask for after ten.
Caller -> After ten works. We'll both be here.
Nurse -> Good. I'm also going to message the hospice provider about the eating, the sleeping, and the back pain.
Caller -> Okay. Will they change his pain medicine?
Nurse -> They might. They'll look at the pain and at what would keep him most comfortable.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'd like our chaplain and social worker to reach out to you both. This is a hard time for the family.
Caller -> I'd like that. Percy, would you like that?
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, I think so. I think I need it.
Nurse -> Good. I'll put in the request. I'll also call you back tomorrow after the nurse has been out, to see how things went.
Caller -> Tomorrow after the visit. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, don't push food or fluids. Offer sips and his favorite foods, but only what he wants. Don't force.
Caller -> Don't force. Okay. He likes ice cream. He had a spoonful this morning.
Nurse -> Perfect. Ice cream is great. Anything he enjoys.
Caller -> Okay. We'll give him ice cream.
Nurse -> What flavor does he like?
Caller -> Butter pecan. It's the only kind he eats. The only kind he's ever eaten.
Nurse -> Then butter pecan it is.
Nurse -> For his back, use pillows to support him, change his position every few hours, and keep the room quiet and calm.
Caller -> Pillows. Change position. Quiet. Okay. We've been doing the pillows.
Caller -> I'll turn off the TV in the den. Dad likes the game on, but it's loud.
Nurse -> Maybe keep it low. If he likes the sound, it can be comforting.
Caller -> Low. Okay.
Nurse -> Do you have everything you need in the house? Mouth swabs, lip balm, the comfort kit?
Caller -> We have the swabs. The lip balm we're almost out of. And I think the comfort kit is in the fridge, in the door.
Nurse -> Good. I'll make sure the nurse brings more lip balm.
Caller -> That'd be great. His lips are dry.
Caller -> Um, and the, the aide who comes on Thursdays, does she know about all this? Because she keeps trying to get him to sit up for lunch.
Nurse -> Good question. I'll note it so the team lets her know to follow his lead and not push him to sit up.
Caller -> Okay, thank you. She means well. She just, she likes him to eat.
Nurse -> And call us any hour. If he seems uncomfortable, if his breathing changes, or if you two want to talk. Day or night.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. Thank you, Alan. I'm sorry we were arguing.
Nurse -> Please don't apologize. You're both trying to do right by him.
Caller -> We are. Thank you.
Caller -> Thank you, Alan. I'm sorry, Winnie. You're right.
Caller -> It's okay. I'm scared too.
Nurse -> It's okay to be scared. Is there anything else you want to ask me?
Caller -> I don't think so. Percy, you?
Caller -> No. I feel better. I think I just needed someone to say it.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Take care of each other tonight.
Caller -> We will. Bye, Alan. Thank you.
Nurse -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sunrise Home Care, this is Dana.
Caller -> Oh. Hi. Hi, Dana. Um, I'm not sure I've got the right number. I'm calling about my neighbor, he gets, you all send somebody to him?
Nurse -> What's your neighbor's name? I can look him up.
Caller -> It's Walter. Walter Pruitt. P R U I T T. I'm Gloria. Gloria Fennimore. I live next door.
Nurse -> Okay, Gloria. Hold on, let me pull him up. Walter Pruitt. Yes, I see him. What's going on?
Caller -> Well. I don't know if it's anything. I'm probably being a worry wart.
Nurse -> No, that's what we're here for. Tell me.
Caller -> So I brought him some soup. Chicken and rice, I make too much, always. And I went over around noon, and he was in the recliner. And I was putting the soup in the kitchen and I saw his pill thing. The box with the days on it.
Nurse -> The pillbox. Okay.
Caller -> Yes. And it's full. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, all the little doors have pills in them still. And today's Wednesday, so. That's three days. I think he hasn't been taking them.
Nurse -> Okay. And you're sure it's Monday through Wednesday that are full?
Caller -> Um, Monday, Tuesday, and today. Wednesday. Yes. Sunday's empty. So the last one he took was Sunday, I'd guess.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you ask him about it?
Caller -> I did. I said Walter, you didn't take your pills. And he said he knows, he's just not hungry, and he doesn't like taking them on an empty stomach.
Nurse -> That makes sense. Some of them can upset the stomach.
Caller -> That's what he said. I said well, you could eat some soup, and he said maybe later.
Nurse -> Gloria, do you know which pills he's supposed to take?
Caller -> Well, I looked at the bottles. I hope that's okay. I didn't open anything. They were on the counter. There's the, hold on, I wrote it down. The metformin. Five hundred milligrams, twice a day. And the lisinopril, ten milligrams, once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Metformin and lisinopril. Thank you for writing that down. That's very helpful.
Caller -> I figured you'd want it. I used to be a school secretary, so. I write everything down.
Nurse -> It shows. Okay. And you said the last day those were taken was Sunday?
Caller -> Sunday, yes, I think. I'm guessing from the box.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, can I get Walter's date of birth? Just so I have the right record.
Caller -> I don't know it by heart. Oh. He wears one of those, the medical alert thing around his neck. Hold on. Walter! Walter, what's your birthday? No, I mean, can I read your thing? Okay. It says, it's on the back, June ninth. Nineteen fifty four.
Nurse -> June ninth, nineteen fifty four. Good, that matches.
Caller -> Oh good.
Nurse -> And what's a good number to reach you, in case we need to call you back?
Caller -> I'm in the book, but you can use my cell. Six one five, five five five, zero one seven seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Thanks. Now, how has Walter been otherwise? You said he's tired?
Caller -> He's tired. He's been tired. I'd say, since the weekend maybe? A few days. He's just sitting. He's not himself. He usually walks around the block and waves at everybody. And he hasn't been eating much. Just crackers.
Nurse -> Okay. And is he talking with you normally? Does he make sense?
Caller -> Oh yes. Oh, he makes sense. He told me all about the football game. He's sharp as a tack. Just tired.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have any chest pain? Or is he confused at all?
Caller -> No. No, no chest pain. I asked him. He said no. And he's not confused. I'd know. He corrected my grammar.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. That's a good sign.
Caller -> He does that. Anyway.
Nurse -> Does Walter have diabetes? Is that what the metformin's for?
Caller -> He does, yes, he has the sugar. He has the little meter. And I said let's check it, and he said fine. So I did it for him. I don't love doing the finger, but I did.
Nurse -> Thank you. What did the meter say?
Caller -> Two forty eight. It said two, four, eight. That's high, isn't it?
Nurse -> It's higher than we want, especially in the morning. But it's not an emergency number. When was that?
Caller -> That was just now, like twenty minutes ago. He hadn't eaten anything but the crackers.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. That helps us know what's going on.
Caller -> I didn't know if I should call you or, who do I call? I don't have the daughter's number. She's in Oregon.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling us. Gloria, what I'm going to do is have a nurse come out tomorrow morning to see Walter, check his sugar and his pressure, and go over his pills with him.
Caller -> Oh good. Tomorrow morning. Should I be there?
Nurse -> You don't have to be. But if you're around, it might help. He might like the company.
Caller -> I'll be around. I'm always around. I'll bring muffins.
Nurse -> That's very kind. Now, I'll also send a message to our supervising nurse today about the missed pills and the sugar, so they know before the visit.
Caller -> Okay. Okay good.
Nurse -> And I'm going to call Walter myself this afternoon, just to check on him and see how he's feeling.
Caller -> He'll like that. He likes you girls. He talks about you.
Nurse -> That's nice to hear.
Caller -> Is he in trouble? For not taking the pills?
Nurse -> No, not at all. We just want to understand what's going on and help.
Caller -> Okay. Because he's proud. He doesn't like being fussed over.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll be gentle.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Now, here's what's important, Gloria. Please don't give him the missed pills all at once to catch up. He should just take the next one on schedule, with a little food, until the nurse checks the plan.
Caller -> Oh. No, I wouldn't, I wouldn't do that. Okay. Just the next one. With some food. Like some of that soup.
Nurse -> The soup would be perfect.
Caller -> I'll heat it up for him before I go. I'll make him eat a bowl. Or half a bowl.
Nurse -> And if anything changes, if he has chest pain, or gets confused, or he's very hard to wake up, or he's throwing up and can't keep fluids down, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for us.
Caller -> Chest pain, confused, hard to wake up, throwing up. Okay. Nine one one. I've got it. I'm going to write that on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> Can I ask something silly? Is it okay if I pop in a couple times today? Just to look.
Nurse -> That's not silly at all. It would help a lot.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I'm only next door. I can see his porch light from my kitchen.
Nurse -> That's a good neighbor.
Caller -> Well, he's a good neighbor too. He shovels my walk every winter. Or he did. I guess I'll shovel his this year.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully he'll be back to it by then.
Caller -> I hope so. Okay. So tomorrow morning, the nurse. And you'll call Walter this afternoon.
Nurse -> Yes. Is there anything else you want me to know?
Caller -> I don't think so. Oh, one thing. He has a little dog. Pepper. Somebody's been walking her, I think, but I'm not sure it's every day. I'll take her out too.
Nurse -> That would be wonderful. Thank you, Gloria.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Dana. Sorry to bother you.
Nurse -> It's no bother at all. Take care.
Caller -> Bye bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Heron Valley Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Yeah, hi, Priya, this is Marcus Tillery over at Maple Court. Assisted living. We have one of your clients. Hold on. Hold on one sec. Sorry. Okay.
Nurse -> No problem. Take your time. Which client?
Caller -> It's Mrs. Valdivia. Irene Valdivia. We're running out of the dressings for her, her bottom, the sacral. And the wash stuff too.
Nurse -> Okay. Irene Valdivia. Can I get her date of birth?
Caller -> Um, I have it right here on the sheet. February twenty sixth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Perfect. And what's a good number to call you back at?
Caller -> The med room line. It's two one two. Five five five. One two four. Wait, zero one two four.
Nurse -> Two one two, five five five, zero one two four. Okay. Is that a direct line?
Caller -> It's, uh, it rings at the med cart station, so somebody picks up, but it might not be me.
Nurse -> Got it. So if I call I should ask for Marcus.
Caller -> Yeah, ask for Marcus. Or whoever. They'll find me.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the dressings. How many does she have left?
Caller -> Let me look. Let me go count. Hold on. Hang on. Don't hang up. Okay, I'm in her room, she's sleeping. I'm trying to be quiet. Okay. The foam ones. There's two. Two left in the box. And the box says change every three days.
Nurse -> And these are the foam dressings, the four by four ones?
Caller -> Four by four, yes. The square ones with the, the sticky border.
Nurse -> Okay. And you mentioned the wound wash?
Caller -> The saline. The bottle, it's, it's almost empty. There's like a splash in the bottom. I don't think it'll do one more change.
Nurse -> Okay. Got it. So two dressings and a nearly empty bottle of saline.
Caller -> Yes. That's all we've got for her.
Nurse -> When was her dressing last changed?
Caller -> The nurse did it Monday. And it's due again Thursday, I think. That's what the sheet says.
Nurse -> And it's what day today?
Caller -> Wednesday. It's Wednesday. So tomorrow. No wait. Thursday's tomorrow. Yeah.
Nurse -> Right. So she's due tomorrow. How does the dressing look right now?
Caller -> It's, so, that's the other thing. Yesterday I noticed it was kind of wet. Like it soaked through. The drainage went through the edge of the dressing and got on her gown. So I changed the gown. And I put a little gauze over it. I hope that's okay.
Nurse -> That's fine. It sounds like she's draining more than usual.
Caller -> A little bit more. It was wet yesterday and it's wet again today a little bit.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have a fever? Is she warm at all?
Caller -> No. She's not warm. They took her temperature this morning. It was normal. I think ninety eight something.
Nurse -> And any bad smell from the wound? When the dressing is off, or on?
Caller -> No. No smell. I would notice. Her room smells like lavender. Her daughter brings the, the spray.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's reassuring.
Caller -> Oh, hold on. Hold on. Her light's going off next door. I have to, I'll be right back. Sorry. Sorry.
Nurse -> No problem. I'll be here.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry. It was Mr. Delgado. He wanted the TV remote. Every time.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the job, right?
Caller -> That's the job. Okay. So, do you guys send the stuff, or do we get it ourselves? Because the last time the lady said it takes three days from the, the supplier.
Nurse -> I can place the order for you. I'll put in a box of the foam dressings and two bottles of the saline wash, and I'll mark it urgent since she's almost out.
Caller -> Oh, that'd be great. Yes. Please.
Nurse -> Okay. Give me a second. I'm entering it now.
Caller -> Sure. Sure. Take your time.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for the dressings and the saline wash.
Caller -> Oh, great. Great. Thank you.
Nurse -> Where should they deliver it? To your front desk?
Caller -> The front desk. Yes. Ask for Carla. She signs for everything. Don't leave it with the door guy, he sets it on the floor and forgets.
Nurse -> Got it. Front desk, Carla. I'll ask them to deliver it tomorrow morning before noon. I'll note on the order that it needs to go to Carla at the front desk.
Caller -> Perfect. That works. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, you've got two dressings. If the dressing soaks through before her next change, put a clean foam dressing on, wash your hands first, and write the time on her chart. Don't reuse a wet one.
Caller -> Okay. Wash hands. Clean dressing. Write the time. Not reuse the wet one. Got it. I'm writing it on my hand. Hold on, I need a pen.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I have it.
Nurse -> And with the saline, if you run out before the delivery, use a clean sterile saline vial from the med room if you have any. Otherwise just wait and don't use tap water.
Caller -> Okay. We have the little vials in the med cart. I'll check.
Nurse -> Good. Now, I'll also have a nurse come out to see her in two days, so I can look at the wound and the drainage.
Caller -> Two days. So Friday. Is it going to be you?
Nurse -> Probably me, or one of the other nurses. I'll write on the schedule.
Caller -> Okay. Because Mrs. Valdivia likes you. She said you're gentle.
Nurse -> Aw. That's nice to hear.
Caller -> She said the other one pulls too hard.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll make a note.
Caller -> Please do. She's very particular.
Nurse -> Now, call us back right away if she gets a fever, if the wound smells bad, if the redness is spreading, or if the drainage suddenly gets a lot heavier.
Caller -> Fever, smell, redness spreading, a lot more drainage. Okay. Got it. I'll tell the next shift too. They don't always read the notes.
Nurse -> That would be great. Let them know to call us.
Caller -> I will. I'll put it on the board in the med room.
Nurse -> Is there anything else she needs? Any other supplies?

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Palliative Care, this is Gus.
Caller -> Yes, hello. This is Leonard Szymanski. I'm calling about my wife. Her feet are all swollen up. Her legs. More than they were.
Nurse -> Okay, Mr. Szymanski. Sorry to hear that. What's your wife's name?
Caller -> Marguerite. Marguerite Szymanski. M A R G U E R I T E. And Szymanski is S Z Y M A N S K I. People always get it wrong.
Nurse -> Okay. Margaret Shimanski. Let me pull up her chart. Hold on.
Caller -> Marguerite. With the, the U E.
Nurse -> Got it. I see her. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> November fourth. Nineteen forty eight. No. Wait. Forty seven. Nineteen forty seven. I'm sorry. I'm eighty, my brain. She's older than me. She's forty seven.
Nurse -> November fourth, nineteen forty seven. Okay. And a good number for you?
Caller -> The house phone is dead half the time. Use my cell. Four one four. Five five five. Zero one two eight.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, zero one two eight. Great.
Caller -> That's it.
Nurse -> Alright, tell me about the swelling. When did you notice it?
Caller -> Well, she's had a little. A little puffiness. Always. Ever since the heart thing. But last week it was just the ankles, like the sock line. And now it's up past the ankle. It's up the shin. It's, I pressed on it and my finger left a dent.
Nurse -> A dent that stays for a bit?
Caller -> Stays. Stays a while. I counted. I counted to ten and it was still there.
Nurse -> Okay. Both legs?
Caller -> Both. The left is worse. A little.
Nurse -> And how's she doing otherwise? How's she feeling?
Caller -> Tired. She's always tired. She's sitting in the chair. She won't go out to the porch. Her friend Dolores came by and she said she didn't feel like talking.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she been weighing herself?
Caller -> I weigh her. I do the weighing. We have the scale in the bathroom. Every morning. And she was, the number I wrote down, she was one forty one on Sunday. And this morning she was one forty five. That's four pounds. In three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Four pounds in three days. Thank you for keeping track.
Caller -> Well I'm not stupid. The nurse told us to. I just don't always understand what the number means.
Nurse -> No, you're doing it right. That weight gain is likely fluid, and that's what the provider needs to look at.
Caller -> Fluid. That's what I thought.
Nurse -> Now. Is her breathing different? Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. She says no. And the breathing is the same as it always is. She's a little short on the stairs but she doesn't do the stairs anymore. She sleeps with two pillows. Same as always.
Nurse -> Okay. Same as usual. That's good to hear.
Caller -> It's good.
Nurse -> Mr. Szymanski, let me ask about her medicines. Can you read me what she's taking, from the bottles?
Caller -> Sure. Sure. Hold on. I have them in the, the little basket. Let me get my glasses. Okay. These two look alike. They give me a headache. One is hydroxyzine. H Y D R O X Y Z I N E. Twenty five milligrams. At bedtime, if needed, for the itching.
Nurse -> Okay. Hydroxyzine, twenty five milligrams, bedtime as needed for itching.
Caller -> Yes. She hardly uses it. And the other one. Hydralazine. H Y D R A L A Z I N E. Twenty five milligrams. Three times a day. That's her blood pressure one.
Nurse -> Okay. Hydralazine twenty five, three times a day. Did she get her dose this morning?
Caller -> This morning, yes. At eight. And she'll get one at two and one at bedtime. I do the pillbox. I'm very careful because the names are alike.
Nurse -> That's smart. Those two get mixed up a lot.
Caller -> I put a sticker on the hydroxyzine. A blue dot. For the itch.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Caller -> Dolores gave me the stickers. She's a retired teacher.
Nurse -> Ha. That's lovely.
Caller -> Is she okay? The swelling. Should I be worried?
Nurse -> I don't think it's an emergency right now, because she's breathing the same and has no chest pain. But I do want the provider to know about it today. I'll send a message to the palliative provider about the ankle swelling and the four pound weight gain.
Caller -> Will they change the water pill?
Nurse -> They might. That's the sort of thing they'd decide. I don't want to promise.
Caller -> No, no. I know.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse to see her tomorrow, to listen to her heart and lungs, check her legs, and weigh her.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I'm home. I'm always home.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this evening to let you know what the provider says.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. After supper?
Nurse -> Probably around six or seven. I'll try.
Caller -> That's fine. We eat at five.
Nurse -> Okay. In the meantime, Mr. Szymanski, keep weighing her every morning. Right after she uses the bathroom and before breakfast, same scale, same clothes. Write it down. If she goes up two pounds in a day, call us.
Caller -> Every morning after the bathroom. Write it down. Two pounds in a day. Okay. Two pounds. I'll put it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. And when she's sitting or lying down, put her legs up on pillows. That helps the swelling.
Caller -> Up on pillows. She has the footstool but it's too low. I'll use the couch pillows.
Nurse -> The couch pillows are perfect.
Caller -> She'll complain. But she'll do it.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her it's doctor's orders.
Caller -> I will. I'll say Gus said.
Nurse -> There you go. And one more thing. Call nine one one if she has chest pain, if she has trouble breathing sitting still or lying down, or if she gets confused.
Caller -> Chest pain, can't breathe lying down, confused. Nine one one. I've got it.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have any questions for me?
Caller -> Just, will the swelling go down?
Nurse -> It often does when the provider adjusts the water pill. We'll see what they say.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you. I feel better. I was worried I was missing something.
Nurse -> You're not missing anything. You're paying attention. That's what she needs.
Caller -> Thank you, Gus. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> Talk to you this evening, Mr. Szymanski.
Caller -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Home Health, this is Tess.
Caller -> Oh my gosh. Hi. Hi, I need, I don't know who to call, my uncle fell, he fell in the bathroom and he hit his head and there's blood.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm here. What's your name and what's your uncle's name?
Caller -> I'm Cassandra. Cassandra Brandt. He's, my uncle is Osmond Lindqvist. L I N D Q V I S T.
Nurse -> Okay, Cassandra. Is he awake right now?
Caller -> He's awake. He's sitting on the bath mat. He's sitting, I told him not to get up, he's trying to get up.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell him to stay down. Where is he bleeding from?
Caller -> The back of his head. There's a lot, I mean there's, it's on the mat and on the towel. I put a towel but it's soaking. It happened like five minutes ago. Maybe less.
Nurse -> Okay. You're doing fine. How did he fall?
Caller -> He was getting out of the tub. I came over to bring him groceries and I heard a bang. And he, he slipped, I think. His foot slipped and he went back and hit the edge. The edge of the tub. The back of his head.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he pass out? Did he lose consciousness at all?
Caller -> No. No. He was awake. He said ow. He said a bad word. I was right there. He didn't pass out.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he take a blood thinner?
Caller -> Yes. Yes he does. Oh no. He takes the, hold on. It's on the fridge. It's the Xarelto. He takes it with supper. Twenty milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. Xarelto, twenty, once a day. Thank you. Cassandra, how is he acting? Is he making sense?
Caller -> He's, kind of. He keeps asking me what happened. I told him. And he asked me again. And he's a little sleepy. He's groggy. He's not himself. He's usually very sharp.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to ask you to do something right now. I want you to call nine one one. Right now. Hang up with me, call nine one one, and tell them he fell, hit his head, he's bleeding, he's on a blood thinner, and he's groggy.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Right now? I'm on the phone with you.
Nurse -> Yes, right now. I can stay on while you call on another phone, or you can put me on speaker. Do you have a second phone?
Caller -> I have my husband's. No wait, he's not here. Hold on. I can use the house phone. It's in the kitchen. Hold on.
Nurse -> Okay. Before you go, what's the address? I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> I'm putting you on speaker. Okay. I'm going to go in the kitchen. The address is, oh my gosh, I know this, it's forty one Alder Way. Forty one Alder.
Nurse -> Forty one Alder Way. Good. Go ahead and call them. I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hold on. Uncle Oz, stay there. Don't move.
Nurse -> I'm here.
Caller -> Okay, it's ringing. It's ringing. It, hi, hello. Yes. My uncle fell and he hit his head. Forty one Alder Way. Yes. He's on a blood thinner. Yes. Yes. They said stay on the line but I can't. I'm with him. I'm going back to him. They said they're sending someone.
Nurse -> Good. That's exactly right. Now, go back to your uncle. Press a clean towel firmly on the bleeding spot. Firm pressure, and don't peek. Keep it there until the paramedics come.
Caller -> Firm pressure. Don't peek. Okay. I have a clean towel from the closet. I'm pressing. Uncle Oz, I'm pressing. It's okay.
Nurse -> Is he still sitting up?
Caller -> He's sitting. He's leaning on the tub.
Nurse -> Okay. I'd like him to lie down flat if he can, on the mat, with a pillow or a folded towel under his head. But don't pull him or lift him. If he can lie back slowly by himself, okay. If not, keep him still where he is.
Caller -> He says he wants to sit. He says he's fine.
Nurse -> I know. Tell him I said please stay still until the paramedics look at him. Just stay as he is. And keep talking to him. Keep him awake.
Caller -> Okay. Uncle Oz, talk to me. Who's the president? No. Tell me about your boat. He's telling me about the boat.
Nurse -> That's good. That's good. Keep him talking.
Caller -> He's talking about the boat. He's got it on the lake. He's doing the whole thing about the engine.
Nurse -> That's a good sign that he can tell you a story. Now, Cassandra, while you hold the towel, is there someone who can unlock the front door for the paramedics?
Caller -> I'm the only one here. The front door's locked. I came through the garage.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you leave him for ten seconds? Make sure he's lying still, and go unlock the front door. Then come right back and hold the towel.
Caller -> Okay. Ten seconds. Uncle Oz, I'm coming right back. Okay. Hold on. Door. Okay, the door's open. I'm back. I'm pressing.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, it would help the paramedics if you had his medicine list. Is it on the fridge with the Xarelto?
Caller -> It's on the fridge. There's a sheet. His pills and his doctors. A magnet holds it.
Nurse -> Good. After the paramedics come, hand them that sheet. Tell them the name of his blood thinner, Xarelto, and what time he last took it.
Caller -> He takes it with supper. So last night. He hasn't had today's yet.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell them that.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> How's the towel? Is it soaking through?
Caller -> It's, there's some. It's, I think it's slowing down? It's not dripping. I put a second towel over the first one.
Nurse -> Good. Keep the pressure on. Don't lift the towel to look.
Caller -> I won't. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I'm shaking.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now so they know what's happening, and I'll let the agency know.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> Can I get the best number to reach you, in case the line drops?
Caller -> It's my cell. Two one two. Five five five. Zero one three two.
Nurse -> Two one two, five five five, zero one three two. Got it. And I have Mr. Lindqvist's date of birth on file but let me confirm. Is it December thirtieth, nineteen forty six?
Caller -> I think so. Yeah. December thirtieth. Nineteen forty six. He's seventy nine. Eighty in December.
Nurse -> Okay, good. Cassandra, can you hear sirens yet?
Caller -> Not yet. Oh. Maybe. I think I hear something. Is that them?
Nurse -> It might be. Keep pressing. Keep talking to your uncle.
Caller -> Uncle Oz, they're coming. They're almost here. He says he's cold.
Nurse -> Okay. Put a blanket or a coat over him if you have one. Don't move him.
Caller -> There's a robe on the hook. I'll put it over his legs. Okay. I put it on him.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to call you back in fifteen minutes to see how he is, and where they're taking him.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay. I'll answer. I might be in the ambulance. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll call that cell number. Pick up if you can.
Caller -> Okay. Oh. They're here. I see the lights. They're here. They're pulling in.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let them in. Tell them everything we talked about. Go ahead and hang up and be with your uncle.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much. Bye.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Bye, Cassandra.

Nurse -> Quiet Waters Hospice, this is Carol.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. I got a, I got a statement in the mail and I don't understand one of the charges. Is this the right place?
Nurse -> Billing has a separate line, but I can help you get to the right person. Is this about a current patient or someone who has passed?
Caller -> My mother. She passed in August. But the bill came this week and there's a line on it, it says equipment recovery fee, two hundred something dollars. I don't know what that is.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm so sorry about your mother. Equipment recovery fee. I can't see billing from here, but the billing office can explain it.
Caller -> Thank you. That's nice of you.
Nurse -> Do you have the number for billing? It's on the statement, usually near the top.
Caller -> Let me look. I've got it somewhere. It's, hold on. I put it in a folder. Okay. There's a number. It says questions call. Eight hundred. Five five five. Oh, it's a long one.
Nurse -> That's the billing line. Their hours are Monday to Friday, eight to four thirty.
Caller -> It's Saturday.
Nurse -> It is. They'll be back Monday morning. If you'd like, I can leave them a message with your name and number and they can call you.
Caller -> That'd be better. I'm not good with the phone menus.
Nurse -> Sure. What's your name and number?
Caller -> It's Dennis. Dennis Hartwell. My mother was Phyllis Hartwell. She was with you the last couple of months. It's account something. It's on the statement. I can read it.
Nurse -> That's okay. Billing can look her up by name. I'll put a note that you have a question about an equipment recovery fee on the statement.
Caller -> Yes. That's it. The number is five five five, oh one four three. The area code is, oh. Three one two.
Nurse -> Three one two, five five five, zero one four three. I'll pass that along.
Caller -> Thank you. And, can I ask you something not about the bill?
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> The flowers. For the service, you all sent flowers. The big white ones. I wanted to say thank you. My sister said it was your group.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Your mom was well loved by the team. I'll tell them you said so.
Caller -> Please do. The nurse who came on Tuesdays, Lena, she was wonderful. My mom talked about her all the time.
Nurse -> I'll let Lena know. She'll be touched.
Caller -> Okay. Well. That's all. I'll wait for the billing call.
Nurse -> Monday morning. Again, I'm so sorry for your loss, Mr. Hartwell.
Caller -> Thank you, Carol. Bye now.
Nurse -> Take care.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pinecrest Home Health, this is Lucy.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Lucy. It's Naomi. Naomi Fairweather. I'm, sorry, I'm on my break so I have like fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> No problem. We'll be quick. How are you doing, Naomi?
Caller -> Okay. Mostly okay. A couple of things. My left hand is acting weird. And I need a refill.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's start with that. Can you spell your last name for me so I get the right chart?
Caller -> Yeah. F A I R W E A T H E R. Fairweather. Like the weather is fair. People always put a space in the middle.
Nurse -> Got it. Fairweather. And your date of birth?
Caller -> August nineteenth. Nineteen eighty four.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a good callback number?
Caller -> Oh gosh. I just switched phones. Ugh. My number changed and I can't remember it. I'm at work so it's the front desk line but that's not good. Hang on, let me, I don't have it. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's fine. You have a cell number on file with us. I'll use that one and you can tell me if it's wrong.
Caller -> Yeah. Please. I'll check it when I get home. It'll be fine.
Nurse -> Okay. So, your hand. Which hand, and what's it doing?
Caller -> The left one. It's tingly. Like pins and needles. And parts of it are numb. Like my thumb and my first two fingers. It started Thursday morning. So, two days. I thought I slept on it. But it didn't go away.
Nurse -> Okay. Does it come and go, or is it constant?
Caller -> Mostly constant. It's worse when I type. I type all day. I'm in billing. Not your billing, a different one. A dentist's office.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Is it affecting your grip? Are you dropping things?
Caller -> Sort of. I dropped my coffee. Twice. Not on purpose. It just slips.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you had this before? Is this like your MS flares?
Caller -> I think so? My last flare was in the spring, and it was my leg. It wasn't a hand. But the nurse said it could do anything. So I thought I should call before it got worse.
Nurse -> That was the right call. Any other changes? Vision, balance, speech?
Caller -> No. My vision's fine. I would know, the last time I had the blurry eye. That scared me. This is not that. And walking is okay. I'm not wobbly or anything.
Nurse -> Good. How about energy? How are you feeling overall?
Caller -> Tired. More tired than usual. Like I'm dragging. I come home and I just lie on the couch. My roommate is making dinner every night. I feel bad.
Nurse -> That's a lot. How long has the tiredness been going on?
Caller -> Maybe the same time? Since Thursday? Maybe a little before. I don't know. Everyone's tired, you know? It's October.
Nurse -> Ha. True. Any falls?
Caller -> No. No falls. Well, so Friday I tripped on the rug in the hall. The one that curls up. I caught myself on the wall. I didn't fall down. My roommate said I should throw the rug out.
Nurse -> Your roommate is right. That rug is a hazard. Maybe tape it down or get rid of it for now.
Caller -> I took it up last night. It's in the closet.
Nurse -> Good. So the rug is gone. And you said you needed a refill?
Caller -> The baclofen. The ten milligrams. I take it three times a day for the stiffness. And I'm down to, let me count, I have three days left. I looked this morning. Three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Three days. That's not much time, so we'll get that moving today. Do you know which pharmacy you use?
Caller -> The same one. The one on Delaney Street. It's all in my file.
Nurse -> Okay. I see it. Delaney Street. Good.
Caller -> Thanks. I always forget to do this until it's almost out.
Nurse -> Everyone does. Naomi, I'm going to message your neurology provider today about the numbness and tingling in your left hand and how long it's been going on. They'll want to know since it's a new symptom.
Caller -> Do you think it's a flare?
Nurse -> It could be. I can't say for sure, and I don't want to guess. That's why the provider needs to hear about it.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense.
Nurse -> I'll also send the refill request for the baclofen to your provider, since you only have three days left.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll have our scheduling person call you to set up an appointment for this week. Is there a day that works better?
Caller -> I work Monday to Friday, nine to five. Afternoons are hard. But I can do a lunch. Or I can leave early on Thursday.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll tell scheduling you prefer a lunch time or Thursday late afternoon. They'll call to set it up.
Caller -> Okay. That works.
Nurse -> Now, a couple of important things. If the numbness spreads, like to your face or your leg, or you lose vision, or you get new weakness, or you have trouble speaking, go to the emergency room. Don't wait for a call back.
Caller -> Spreads, vision, weakness, speaking. Okay. I'll go to the ER. Yeah. I know. I did that in the spring.
Nurse -> Good. And try to write down when the tingling comes and goes, and what makes it worse. Also, avoid hot showers and getting overheated. Heat can make MS symptoms worse.
Caller -> Oh. I took a really hot shower last night. Because my hand was cold. That might be it.
Nurse -> It could make it feel worse for a while. Keep the water warm, not hot, for now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Meadowlark Hospice, this is Ingrid.
Caller -> Hi. Hi. Okay. I don't know if I'm supposed to call this number on a Saturday but my mom's in a lot of pain and we ran out of the morphine.
Nurse -> You called the right number. I'm here. Who am I speaking with?
Caller -> It's Tobias. Tobias Okafor. I'm the son. My mom is Rosalind Okafor.
Nurse -> Okay, Tobias. Thanks. What's your mom's date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty second. Nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> Got it. And a number I can call you back on?
Caller -> This one. The one I'm on. It's three zero three. Five five five. Zero one one four.
Nurse -> Three zero three, five five five, zero one one four. Great. Okay. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> So, she, her pain is bad. Her stomach. Her belly. She's been moaning for like an hour and I can't make it stop. I asked her what the number is and she said eight. Eight out of ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Eight. Is she awake and able to talk?
Caller -> She's awake. She's in bed. She's kind of moaning and moving around. She can't get comfortable. She's restless. She keeps pulling at the blanket.
Nurse -> Okay. And you said you ran out of the morphine. Which one? The liquid?
Caller -> The morphine liquid. The little bottle with the syringe. It's the, it's the twenty milligrams per mL. She gets a quarter of a mL. Every two hours if she needs it. And I gave the last one at nine last night. And then the bottle was empty. I thought I had more.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's been about, that's twenty-some hours without a dose?
Caller -> I think so. Yes. I'm so sorry. I should have called yesterday. I thought the pharmacy was bringing more. They said Friday. Friday afternoon. And nobody came.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't worry about that right now. We'll sort it out. Did you call the pharmacy today?
Caller -> I called. It's closed. It says open Monday. Monday at eight. And I didn't know who else to call.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tobias, is she having any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. No. Her breathing's fine. It's regular. She's not gasping or anything. It's just the pain. It's just the moaning.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's important. And when did the pain start getting worse?
Caller -> This morning. It was a four this morning. And it got worse all day. And now it's, by dinner it was a six, and now it's an eight. I tried the heating pad. I tried Tylenol. It did nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Let me do two things right away. First, I'm going to page the on-call clinician. Second, I need you to find something for me. Do you have a comfort kit in the house? A little box or a bag the hospice nurse brought? It might be in the refrigerator.
Caller -> The fridge. Oh. Yes. There was a box. The nurse put it in the door of the fridge. She said not to touch it. It's the emergency thing. I forgot about it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's exactly what I need. Can you go get it? Take your phone with you. I'll stay here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hold on. I'm walking. Mom, I'm getting something. I'll be right back. Okay. It's in the kitchen. Okay. The fridge. I see it. It's a white box. It says comfort kit.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is the seal still on it?
Caller -> There's a sticker. It's not broken. Yes.
Caller -> Wait, should I wash my hands? I was doing dishes. They're wet.
Nurse -> Dry them off, that's fine. Quick rinse is plenty.
Caller -> Okay. Drying. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Open it. What do you see inside?
Caller -> Okay. Let me. Hold on, the tape is stuck. There are bottles. Three. One says morphine. One says lorazepam. One says something with an H. Haloperidol. And there's syringes. And a paper.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's work with the morphine one. Read me what the label says.
Caller -> It says morphine concentrate. Twenty milligrams per mL. Give point two five mL under the tongue every two hours as needed for pain.
Nurse -> That's the same strength and dose as your mom's bottle. So I'm going to have you give her a dose from the kit. Draw up a quarter of a mL, which is the first little line on the syringe, and give it under her tongue, in the cheek pocket. Slowly. Then write down the time. Don't give another for two hours.
Caller -> Quarter mL. Under the tongue. Write the time. Two hours. Okay. Hold on. I'm drawing it up. The first line. Is that right? It's the line closest to the tip.
Nurse -> Yes. That's the quarter. Go to her now. Give it slowly into the cheek.
Caller -> Okay. Mom, I'm giving you the medicine. Open your mouth a little. Okay. There. Good. She took it. She swallowed a little. I put it in the cheek. It's done.
Nurse -> Good job, Tobias. What time is it right now?
Caller -> It's eleven fifteen. Oh. Eleven sixteen. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, and I'll also call the after-hours line at the pharmacy to see about getting a refill out to you tonight.
Caller -> Tonight? They said Monday.
Nurse -> They have an after-hours number for hospice. It doesn't always work, but I'll try, and if I can't, the on-call clinician will find another way.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much. I feel so stupid.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. Delivery mix-ups happen. You did the right thing calling. I'll call you back in twenty minutes to check on your mom and tell you what I've found out.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. I'll stay with her.
Nurse -> Good. And if she's still in a lot of pain after the dose, or she's hard to wake up, or her breathing gets slow or noisy, call me right back. Don't wait for twenty minutes.
Caller -> Hard to wake, slow breathing, noisy breathing. Still in pain. I'll call.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she doing right now?
Caller -> She's still moaning a little. But she's not, she squeezed my hand. She's looking at me.
Nurse -> That's good. It takes about fifteen to twenty minutes to work. Talk to her. Hold her hand.
Caller -> I'm holding it. Mom, it's okay. The nurse is going to help.
Nurse -> Is there anyone else there with you?
Caller -> My wife is at her sister's tonight with the kids. It's just me. I'm okay. I'm okay.
Nurse -> You sound like you're doing a great job. Would it help to have your wife come home?
Caller -> Maybe. I'll text her. Yeah. She'd want to be here.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> She's going to be mad I didn't call her earlier. She's been saying we should get a night nurse.
Nurse -> That's something we can talk about on Monday. I'll note it.
Caller -> I'll text her now. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay, sent. Thank you, Ingrid. I'm sorry I'm kind of a mess.
Nurse -> It's perfectly fine. I'll talk to you in twenty minutes. Sit with your mom.
Caller -> I will. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Tobias.
