transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Palliative Care, this is Mina.
Caller -> Hi. Um. Hi. Sorry. Is this too early? I didn't know if somebody would answer.
Nurse -> No, someone is always here. I'm glad you called. Who am I talking to?
Caller -> It's Desmond. Desmond Achterberg.
Nurse -> Hi, Desmond. I'm Mina, I'm a nurse. How can I help?
Caller -> I, uh. I can't sleep. That's the main thing. I'm sorry to bother you.
Nurse -> It's no bother. That's what this line is for. Can I get your date of birth so I can pull up your chart?
Caller -> Sure. It's May thirteenth. Nineteen sixty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what's the best number to reach you at?
Caller -> This is my cell. Three zero three. Five five five. Zero one seven eight.
Nurse -> Got it. Desmond, you're talking quietly. Is somebody else there?
Caller -> My wife is upstairs. Annette. She's asleep. I'm in the kitchen. I don't want to wake her. She doesn't sleep much either. She's finally out.
Nurse -> Okay. That's kind of you. So, you can't sleep. How long has this been going on?
Caller -> A while. I mean, I haven't slept. Not really. Three nights now. I lie there and I watch the clock. I might get an hour. Then I'm up.
Nurse -> That sounds exhausting. What's keeping you up? Is it pain, or your mind going?
Caller -> Both. It's a bit of both. The pain is there. It's in my belly. It's a five, I'd say. It's not terrible. It's a dull one. It's always there.
Nurse -> Okay. A five. And you're taking something for it?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Five milligrams. Every four hours if I need it. I took one at ten last night. I try not to take it too often. I don't like how foggy it makes me.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. And are there any other medicines you take at night?
Caller -> The mirtazapine. Fifteen milligrams. At bedtime. They said it would help me sleep and my appetite. I took it at nine. It's not doing much.
Nurse -> Okay. Mirtazapine, fifteen, at bedtime, and it's not helping with sleep.
Caller -> No. I think I'm too wound up. My brain doesn't turn off.
Nurse -> What's your brain doing when it's going?
Caller -> Just, you know. Going around. The same things.
Nurse -> What kind of things?
Caller -> Oh. Just. Everything. My daughter's wedding is in June. I won't be there. That's what I think about. I think, I won't be there to walk her down. And then I think about the garden. I never planted the bulbs this year. That's silly. It's a silly thing to be upset about.
Nurse -> It's not silly at all. It sounds like those things matter a lot to you.
Caller -> They do. They do. I put the tulips in every fall. Every year since we bought the house. And this year I just didn't. I looked at the bag in the garage. It's still sitting there. Annette keeps saying I'll do it next week.
Nurse -> It sounds like you've been carrying a lot.
Caller -> I guess.
Nurse -> How have you been feeling in yourself, emotionally, the last week or so?
Caller -> Tired. I'm just tired. Of all of it. The pills and the appointments and the, everyone being so careful with me. The looks. I don't know. I'm tired of all of it.
Nurse -> That makes sense. That's a lot to be tired of.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Desmond, can I ask you more about that? When you say you're tired of all of it?
Caller -> I don't know. It's just that, sometimes I think it would be easier if I just didn't wake up. You know? I just wish I wouldn't wake up. Not in a bad way.
Nurse -> Thank you for telling me that. I know that's not easy to say. I want to ask you about it directly, if that's okay.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> When you say you wish you wouldn't wake up, are you having thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?
Caller -> No. No. I'm not saying that. I wouldn't do anything. I'd never do that to Annette. Or Josie. That's my daughter. I'd never. I'm just saying I wish it was over. It's not me wanting to do something.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you. Have you thought about how you might do something, even if you wouldn't?
Caller -> No. No plan. No. I'm not planning anything. I just, I get low at night. It's the nights. It's not like that during the day. During the day I'm okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I believe you. And I'm really glad you told me. Has there been any time in the past few weeks you thought about acting on those thoughts?
Caller -> No. Honestly. No. It's just a wish. It's like, a heavy wish. I don't know how to say it.
Nurse -> You're saying it fine. It's a heavy feeling at night, and you wish it would just end, but you're not thinking about hurting yourself.
Caller -> Right. Right. That's exactly it.
Nurse -> Okay. Desmond, I want to make sure you're not alone with this. Have you told Annette or anyone how you've been feeling?
Caller -> I haven't. I don't want to scare her. She's got enough. She's doing everything. I don't want to put this on her.
Nurse -> I understand. She loves you. She'd probably want to know. But we can come back to that. Is there anyone else you talk to? Josie? A friend?
Caller -> Josie, I call her on Sundays. I don't tell her the bad stuff. I tell her about the football. My buddy Walt comes by on Thursdays. We watch the game.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Do you talk about how you're feeling with Walt?
Caller -> No. No, we talk about the Broncos. It's fine. It's what I like about Walt. He doesn't ask.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Some people are good like that.
Caller -> He's good like that.
Nurse -> Desmond, do you have a lot of medicines in the house? The oxycodone, the others?
Caller -> Some. The bottles are in the drawer in the bathroom. Upstairs. And a few down here in the cabinet.
Nurse -> Okay. And Annette knows where they are?
Caller -> She does the pill sorting for the week. She puts them in the little box. But the bottles are around.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to ask you something, and it's not because I think you'd do anything. It's just a way of keeping things safe on a hard night. Would you be okay with Annette keeping the bottles, and handing out your doses for now?
Caller -> She already does most of them. I'd have to tell her why.
Nurse -> You don't have to tell her everything tonight. You could say the team suggested it. And tomorrow, the social worker can help you talk to her if you want.
Caller -> I could do that. I'd say the nurse said to. Okay.
Nurse -> I'd like you to do that. Maybe tonight, or first thing in the morning. Wake her if you need to.
Caller -> I'll talk to her in the morning. She's up at six.
Nurse -> That's soon. Okay. How's your pain right now? Still at a five?
Caller -> About that. It's a five. It's a steady five.
Nurse -> Would a dose of your oxycodone help? It's been more than four hours since ten.
Caller -> Maybe. Yeah. I could take one. I was holding off.
Nurse -> I think that would be a good idea. It might help you rest. And let me page the on-call clinician right now. They might have something to suggest for the nights too.
Caller -> Okay. Is that a big deal? Calling the doctor?
Nurse -> It's not a big deal. It's what we do. I just want them to know what you told me, about being worn out and the nights being hard. You deserve to have this looked at.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine.
Nurse -> I'd also like our social worker and our chaplain to come see you tomorrow. They're really good at this part of things. The worry, the heavy nights, the wedding.
Caller -> The chaplain. I'm not really a church guy.
Nurse -> That's fine. Ours are not preachy. Some people just like to talk to someone who isn't family. You can say no.
Caller -> Okay. I'll see them. I'll see the social worker. Maybe the chaplain. Let me see.
Nurse -> That works. And I'm going to send a nurse out in the morning to see you, too. To check your pain and your sleep, and just sit with you.
Caller -> What time?
Nurse -> Morning. The scheduler will call you with a window. I'll ask for early.
Caller -> That's fine. We're home. We're always home.
Nurse -> Good. Desmond, I also want to give you a number. If these thoughts ever get stronger, or you ever feel unsafe, you can call or text nine eight eight, any time, day or night. It's the crisis line. Anyone can use it.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay.
Nurse -> Do you want to write it down?
Caller -> I can remember. Nine eight eight. Like a, like a phone number. It's easy.
Nurse -> That's right. And you can also call us here, any hour tonight, and if the thoughts change, wake Annette. She would want you to.
Caller -> I'd rather not wake her. But I'll call you.
Nurse -> That's fine. Call me. I'll be here. And I'm going to call you back in about thirty minutes, after I talk to the on-call clinician, to see how you're doing and tell you what they said.
Caller -> You'll call me? On this phone?
Nurse -> On the cell, yes. Three oh three, five five five, zero one seven eight.
Caller -> That's right. Okay.
Nurse -> Is the phone going to be on?
Caller -> I'll keep it in my pocket. I'll put it on vibrate so it doesn't wake her.
Nurse -> Good idea. Take your medicine now, if you're going to. And try to have some water.
Caller -> I'll go get the pill. It's in the kitchen cabinet. Hold on. I'll be a minute.
Nurse -> I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. Got it. I'm taking it. Water. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Good. Thank you. Desmond, I want to say something. I'm really glad you called. It took courage to say what you said.
Caller -> I don't feel brave. I feel foolish.
Nurse -> There's nothing foolish about it. A lot of people in your situation feel this way, especially at night. It's very human.
Caller -> Yeah. I suppose.
Nurse -> And we're going to help. Okay? You're not on your own.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Tell me about the tulips. What color do you plant?
Caller -> Red and yellow. A mix. Annette likes the red. I like the yellow ones, they look like little suns. I get them from a place on Federal Boulevard. They have the best ones.
Nurse -> That sounds beautiful. Maybe someone could help you plant them, even if you just sit and tell them where.
Caller -> Josie could. She said she'd come in a couple weeks. We could do it together. If the ground's not frozen.
Nurse -> That would be a lovely thing to do together. Hold on to that.
Caller -> Okay. I like that idea.
Caller -> She sends me pictures of the dress fabric. Little squares. I don't know the difference between any of them. They all look white to me.
Nurse -> Ha. That's every father of the bride.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to go page the on-call clinician now. I'll call you in about thirty minutes. Is there anything else you want to tell me before I go?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you for not making it weird.
Nurse -> Of course. Talk soon, Desmond.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Cedarbrook Home Care, this is Hector.
Caller -> Hi, Hector. I'm, um, I'm one of the aides, but I'm not her regular aide. I'm covering today. My name's Yolanda. Yolanda Prewitt.
Nurse -> Okay, Yolanda. Welcome. Which client are you with?
Caller -> That's the thing. I'm so embarrassed. I have it written down but my sheet is in the car. Her name is, it's something like Quintana. Or Quintanilla. Mrs. Aurelia Quintana. Maybe.
Nurse -> Okay. No worries. Do you have the address?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. It's four twelve Larch Street. Apartment two. The daughter let me in this morning. Her name's Rosa. Rosa something.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look. Larch Street, apartment two, daughter Rosa. Give me a second. I see an Aurelia Quintanilla at four twelve Larch. Is that her?
Caller -> Yes. Yes, Quintanilla. That's it. That's her. Okay. Oh good.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And do you have her date of birth?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'm sorry. It's not on my sheet. It's just the name and the schedule. Can you get it from the file?
Nurse -> Yes, I have it here. Don't worry. What's a good number to call you back on, Yolanda?
Caller -> My cell. Two zero six, five five five, zero one nine six.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Tell me what's going on with Mrs. Quintanilla.
Caller -> So she's coughing. A lot. A wet cough. Like there's something in her chest. And her daughter said it started yesterday. And this morning she was warm. And she's not eating. She had like three bites of oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the cough bringing up anything? Phlegm?
Caller -> I think so. I saw her spit into the tissue. It was kind of yellow. I'm not sure. I didn't look close.
Nurse -> Okay. And did you take her temperature?
Caller -> I did. We have a forehead one. It's the kind where you wave it. It said a hundred point four. I did it twice. Hundred point four, and then hundred point three.
Nurse -> Okay. Hundred point four. Thank you for doing it twice. Does she feel warm to you?
Caller -> Yes. Her forehead is hot. She's wrapped up in a blanket and she says she's cold. But she's hot. You know what I mean.
Nurse -> Chills. Okay. Has she had anything for the fever?
Caller -> The daughter gave her a Tylenol before she left. At noon. Five hundred milligrams. She wrote it on the fridge. I checked.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol five hundred at noon. What time is it right now?
Caller -> It's, hold on, it's one fifty. Almost two. So a couple hours.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she having any trouble breathing? Any shortness of breath?
Caller -> No. No. She's breathing okay. She's not panting. She's just coughing. She's sitting in the chair. I'd say she's okay. She's talking. She told me about her garden.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. Is she alert? Does she know where she is?
Caller -> Oh yes. She knows. She told me I put the kettle on the wrong burner. She's sharp.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Hold on, she's calling me. Mrs. Quintanilla? Yes, ma'am. I'm on the phone with the office. No, not about you. Well, about you. Okay. She wants her sweater.
Nurse -> Go ahead, get her the sweater. I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. She says the house is cold. It's not cold. It's the fever.
Nurse -> It's probably the chills from the fever. A light blanket is fine, just not too many layers.
Caller -> Okay. I'll take one off after.
Caller -> A little. I gave her water. She had half a glass. She doesn't like water. She likes the, the hibiscus tea. I made her some.
Nurse -> That's fine. Tea counts. Okay, Yolanda. Here's my plan. I'm going to send a nurse out to see her this afternoon. I'll try for three or four o'clock.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. Good. I'm here until six.
Nurse -> Good. So you'll be there. I'm also going to notify her physician about the cough and the temperature. They'll want to know about the fever.
Caller -> Okay. Should I do anything else?
Nurse -> Yes. Offer her water, broth or juice in small sips, about every half hour. And let her eat whatever she wants, small amounts. Don't push.
Caller -> Small sips. Every half hour. Whatever she wants. Okay. She'll like the broth. The daughter left some in the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Warm it up. Not too hot.
Caller -> Okay. The microwave's a little weird, it does the thing where the middle is hot and the edges are cold. I'll stir it.
Nurse -> Good plan.
Nurse -> And Yolanda, this is important. If she has trouble breathing, if her lips look blue, if she gets confused, or if you can't wake her up, call nine one one right away.
Caller -> Trouble breathing, blue lips, confused, can't wake her. Nine one one. Okay. Okay. I've got it. I'll write it down. Wait, I need a pen. I have a pen. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call you back within the hour to check on her.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. On this number. I'll keep it on me.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have anything else you want me to pass along?
Caller -> Just that I'm sorry I didn't know her name. I only got the call this morning. They said just go.
Nurse -> It's okay. It happens. Next time, take a picture of the sheet before you leave. Ha.
Caller -> I will. I'll do that. I'll take a picture.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have any allergies you know about?
Caller -> I don't. It's not on my sheet. I can ask the daughter if she calls.
Nurse -> That's okay. I have it in the chart. I'll tell the nurse.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Is the daughter reachable if we need her?
Caller -> She said she's at work till five. Her phone's on. She said call anytime. I have the number on the sheet in the car.
Nurse -> I have it too. I'll try her if we need to.
Caller -> Does she need to stay in the chair? Or should I put her in bed?
Nurse -> Whichever is more comfortable. If she sleeps, prop her up on a couple of pillows so the cough isn't as bad lying flat.
Caller -> Pillows. Okay. She has the big ones.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Hector. I feel better having talked to you.
Nurse -> You did great, Yolanda. Thanks for calling.
Caller -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverside Home Health, this is Dante.
Caller -> Hi, Dante. This is Beverly Hale. I'm calling about my mother, Corinne Ostrowski. She's been dizzy.
Nurse -> Okay, Beverly. Sorry to hear that. Is she with you right now?
Caller -> She's right here at the kitchen table. I'm at her house. I come over on Thursdays. She's fine right now, she's sitting. It's when she stands up.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull up her chart. Can you give me her birth date?
Caller -> April second. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Perfect. And your number?
Caller -> Three zero three, five five five, zero one one eight.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Tell me about the dizziness. When does it happen?
Caller -> It's when she stands. She gets up from the chair or from the bed and she says the room tilts. And she holds the wall. It's been, I think two days. Since Tuesday. She didn't tell me till today. She never tells me anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Does it last long? Once she's up?
Caller -> A few seconds. She stands and waits and then it passes. It's not the room spinning, it's more like she's going to black out. But she hasn't.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fainted or fallen? Any falls?
Caller -> No. No falls. She's careful. And she hasn't passed out. She just says she gets lightheaded. She hangs on to the counter.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have a blood pressure cuff there?
Caller -> I do. I brought the one from my house. It's the wrist one. I took it this morning when I got here. Ninety two over fifty eight. And that's sitting. I took it twice. Same both times.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety two over fifty eight. And what's her pulse? Did the cuff give a pulse?
Caller -> Fifty four. It said fifty four. That's low, isn't it? She's usually in the sixties or seventies.
Nurse -> It's lower than what she normally runs. Thank you for checking. What's her pressure usually?
Caller -> A hundred thirty something over seventy something. She's always been a little high. That's why she's on the pills.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pills? What does she take for the pressure and the heart?
Caller -> Let me look, it's in the pillbox, no, the bottles are on the windowsill. She takes the, I can't pronounce it. Metaprolol. Twenty five milligrams. Twice a day. Eight and eight. She took this morning's at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. The Metaprolol, twenty five, twice a day, and she took this morning's at eight. Is there anything else for her heart or pressure?
Caller -> There's one for her cholesterol. And her aspirin, the baby one. That's all. I think. Mom, is that all? She says yes. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. And has she been eating and drinking okay?
Caller -> Hold on. Mom, stop. Don't stand up. Stay there. Sorry. She tried to get up for the kettle.
Nurse -> That's exactly what we're talking about. Let her stay put and you do the kettle.
Caller -> I'm doing the kettle. Okay. Sorry. What did you ask?
Nurse -> Eating and drinking. How has she been?
Caller -> She's been eating. She's drinking, maybe not enough. She doesn't like to drink. I tell her. She says it makes her go to the bathroom too much.
Nurse -> That's common. Okay. Beverly, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to send a message to her provider right now about the dizziness, the pressure of ninety two over fifty eight, and the pulse of fifty four.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Will they call?
Nurse -> Yes. They'll call back, or I will. Until then, I'd like you to hold her evening Metaprolol. Don't give the eight o'clock one tonight until the provider calls.
Caller -> Hold it. Don't give it. Okay. Is that safe? To skip?
Nurse -> For one dose, while we wait to hear from the provider, yes. Her pressure and pulse are low and we don't want to push them lower. But please don't stop it on your own after that. Let the provider decide.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll wait for the call. I'll tell my brother too, he stays with her at night.
Nurse -> Good. Please do. What time will the evening dose be?
Caller -> Eight. Eight o'clock.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call you back this evening, before eight, so you know what to do.
Caller -> Before eight. Okay. I'll be at my house. I'll answer. I have my phone on me.
Nurse -> Perfect. In the meantime, a few safety things. When she gets up, have her sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a full minute first. Then stand slowly and hold on to something solid, like the counter.
Caller -> Sit for a minute. Stand slow. Hold on. Okay. She does the opposite. She jumps up. She says she's not an invalid.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people say that. Tell her it's temporary.
Caller -> I'll tell her. Mom, you have to wait. Wait a minute. She's rolling her eyes.
Nurse -> That means she heard you. Also, can you check her pressure and pulse again before the callback? Once sitting, then again a minute after she stands. And write the numbers down so you can read them to me.
Caller -> Sitting and standing. Okay. And write it down. I have the paper from the cuff, it has a place for notes.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> What if it's lower?
Nurse -> If it drops a lot, or she gets worse, call me right away. And call nine one one if she faints, has chest pain, trouble breathing, or if her pulse gets under forty.
Caller -> Faints, chest pain, can't breathe, pulse under forty. Okay. Nine one one. Got it.
Nurse -> Good. Does she have anyone here overnight?
Caller -> My brother. Joe. He's there nights. He's a heavy sleeper. I'll make sure he knows.
Nurse -> Please do. Anything else you want me to pass along to the provider?
Caller -> I don't think so. Oh, she had some diarrhea last week. For a day. I forgot. It went away.
Nurse -> Okay. That could play a part if she was dry. I'll add that.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And did she eat lunch today?
Caller -> She had a sandwich. Half. And a banana. And some tea.
Nurse -> Good. Keep offering fluids. Water, tea, broth. Whatever she'll take.
Caller -> I'll make her a big glass and sit with her till she finishes it.
Nurse -> Ha. That works.
Caller -> Should I be worried about leaving her at night? With my brother? He's not a nurse or anything.
Nurse -> He doesn't need to be. As long as she stands slowly and he knows the warning signs, she'll be okay. Tell him to keep a light on in the hallway.
Caller -> A nightlight. We have one. I'll plug it in.
Caller -> Thank you, Dante. I was so worried when I saw that number.
Nurse -> You did the right thing checking. I'll call you before eight.
Caller -> Okay. Bye now.
Nurse -> Bye, Beverly.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Home Nursing, this is Marisol.
Caller -> Hi, Marisol. It's Gilbert. Gilbert Brubaker. I'm calling about my wife Hattie. Hattie Brubaker. Her feeding supplies. They haven't come.
Nurse -> Hi, Gilbert. Okay. I'll look into it. What's Hattie's date of birth?
Caller -> December fifth. Nineteen fifty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I think I've got a number on file. Is it nine zero one, five five five, zero one six zero?
Nurse -> Is that still good?
Caller -> That's the house phone. That's fine. Yes. We never got rid of it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay. How much formula do you have left?
Caller -> Let me go count. I keep them in the hall closet. Hold on. Don't go anywhere. Okay. I count four. Four cans. Four of the big ones. The ones with the green label.
Nurse -> Okay. Four cans. And how much does she use in a day?
Caller -> Well, three cans a day, roughly. She gets it five times. Eight, noon, three, six and ten. A little over two cans a day, really. So that's, I guess, a day and a half. Maybe a little more.
Nurse -> Okay. That's tight. Good call checking. And the syringes?
Caller -> The syringes, I think there's ten. Maybe eleven. I wash them and reuse them like they said. But they get cloudy. The numbers wear off.
Nurse -> Okay. About ten left. We'll replace those too.
Caller -> I'd appreciate it. I can't read the lines on a couple of them.
Nurse -> That's definitely time for new ones. Gilbert, when does the delivery usually come?
Caller -> The first of the month. Always the first. The truck comes in the morning, the guy leaves it on the porch. Today's the thirtieth. It's been, hold on, it was supposed to be Saturday the first, no. It's October thirtieth. So the first is this Saturday. Oh. Oh no. I'm confused. The last one came September first. So it should have come in October, on the first. And it didn't.
Nurse -> Okay. So the October delivery never came.
Caller -> Right. Right. I thought it was late, and then I forgot to call. I'm sorry. I should have called weeks ago.
Nurse -> No, no. It's fine. Sometimes these get lost. Let's fix it now. How is Hattie doing otherwise?
Caller -> She's the same. She's doing okay. She's in the chair. She's watching her show. She can't talk much anymore but she gives me a look when I'm doing it wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that. Any problems with the tube site? Redness, leaking?
Caller -> Hang on, the dog's at the door. Biscuit, no. Sorry. He wants out every ten minutes. Where was I.
Nurse -> The tube site. Redness or leaking.
Caller -> No. It's clean. I do the cleaning every morning like they showed me. There's no redness. It's dry. It doesn't leak. The nurse looked at it last week and said it looked great.
Nurse -> Good. That's really good to hear. Okay. Let me put in the order. Give me a second.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm just standing here.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm putting in a case of the formula, the green label ones, and a box of syringes, and I'm marking it rush because you're low.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company, formula and syringes, marked rush.
Caller -> Oh, good. Good. That's a relief.
Nurse -> I'm going to call the supply company's dispatch and ask them to deliver it tomorrow morning. Is anyone home?
Caller -> I'm always home. We're here. I'll be here.
Nurse -> I'll ask them to bring it to the door and call you when they get there. Tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Okay. That'd be great. They never call. They just drop it.
Nurse -> I'll put a note on it. I can't promise they'll read it, but I'll put it.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm going to let the dietitian know about the delay, so they're aware. In case she needs to adjust anything.
Caller -> Okay. The dietitian. The young lady. She's very nice.
Nurse -> She is. Gilbert, until the delivery comes, keep doing everything exactly the same. Flush the tube with water before and after every feeding, same schedule. Don't stretch the formula or skip feedings to save it.
Caller -> No. I wasn't going to. I'd never. I was going to maybe give her a little less at night. Because of the cans. But no. I'll keep it the same.
Nurse -> Please don't cut back. You have enough for today and tomorrow morning. That's what we need.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I'll do.
Nurse -> And if the delivery hasn't come by ten tomorrow morning, call the office line right away. Don't wait. And tonight, if the tube leaks or gets clogged, call right away too.
Caller -> Ten o'clock. Or the tube leaks. Okay. What's the number? I have it on the fridge but I want to be sure.
Nurse -> It's the same number you called. And after hours it forwards to me or the on-call nurse.
Caller -> Good. That's the one on the fridge. Good.
Nurse -> Do you have enough water for the flushes?
Caller -> We have a pitcher. I boil it, like they said. Let it cool. I do a big batch in the morning.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right.
Caller -> The nurse said not to use the tap straight. But the pitcher's fine, right? I leave it on the counter with a cloth over it.
Nurse -> That's fine for the day. Make a fresh batch each morning.
Caller -> It's just the supplies. It's always the supplies. Everything else I can manage. But I get so nervous about running out.
Nurse -> That's understandable. We'll try to make sure it doesn't happen again. I'll ask them to put you on a reminder.
Caller -> That'd be good. A reminder.
Nurse -> Do you need anything else? Gauze for the site? Tape?
Caller -> Gauze. We have plenty of gauze. The little pads. I'm fine on those.
Nurse -> Good. Okay. Is there anyone helping you at home? Do you get a break?
Caller -> My daughter comes on Sundays. She takes her to the barber, I mean, she does her hair. Hattie likes to look nice.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. It's important for you to have a break too.
Caller -> I know. I know. I take a nap when she's here. Don't tell anyone.
Nurse -> I won't. Ha.
Caller -> Okay. Well. Thank you, Marisol. You've been very kind.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Gilbert. Hopefully the delivery comes tomorrow. If not, call me.
Caller -> I will. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Hollow Hospice, this is Renata.
Caller -> Hi, Renata. It's Tamika over at Willowbrook Memory Care. Tamika Dunbar. I'm one of the aides on the second floor.
Nurse -> Hi, Tamika. Good to hear from you. What can I do for you?
Caller -> Oh, nothing's wrong. I just wanted to give you all an update on Mr. Fuentes. The nurse here said to call if anything changed and I think it's a good change, so I thought I'd call.
Nurse -> I love good news. Which Mr. Fuentes? Abelardo?
Caller -> Yes. Abelardo Fuentes. Room two eleven. The one by the window.
Nurse -> Got it. I have him. What's his birth date, just so I'm sure I've got the right one?
Caller -> I have it on the board. It's September twelfth. Nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a number for you?
Caller -> The second floor desk. Two zero six, five five five, zero one eight three. If I'm not there, whoever answers will find me.
Nurse -> Great. So tell me the good news.
Caller -> So, he ate. This morning at breakfast he ate about half of his oatmeal and a whole banana and he drank all his juice. Last week he wasn't eating anything. We had to feed him and he'd just clamp up. But today he picked up the spoon himself. Well, he held it. I helped. But he did a lot of it.
Nurse -> That's really nice. Half a bowl is good.
Caller -> It is for him. He's tiny now. He's not like he was. Used to be such a big man. Worked on the railroad. Now he's like a little bird.
Nurse -> Aw. How's he doing otherwise? How's his mood?
Caller -> He's pleasant. He's calm most of the day. He's sleeping a lot. He naps after lunch for like three hours. But when he's up, he smiles at people. He says hi to everyone who walks by.
Nurse -> That's sweet. Any restlessness? Sometimes in the evenings, they get stirred up.
Caller -> A little. Around sundown. Around four, five. He gets kind of fidgety. He pulls at his sleeves. He says he has to go to work. He asks where his lunch pail is. I tell him it's in the car and that seems to settle him.
Nurse -> That's a good approach. Meeting him where he is.
Caller -> Yes. The training said that. Don't argue. Go with it.
Nurse -> Exactly. Is it bad? Or just a little?
Caller -> Just a little. It's mild. It lasts maybe twenty minutes. Then he's fine. And the music helps. We put on the old hymns. The Sunday morning stuff. He knows the words. He hums.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Okay. And at night? Is he sleeping okay?
Caller -> He sleeps pretty good. He gets his lorazepam at bedtime. The half a milligram. The night nurse gives it at eight. He got it last night and he slept through.
Nurse -> Okay. The lorazepam, half a milligram at bedtime. And he slept through. That's good.
Caller -> He did. No wandering. No getting up.
Nurse -> Does he seem to be in any pain? Grimacing, moaning, guarding anywhere?
Caller -> No. No. I watch for that. They taught us the signs. His face is relaxed. No moaning. When we turn him he doesn't flinch. He seems comfortable.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> Me too. Oh. And his daughter is coming Saturday. She lives in Tucson. She comes about every two months. She's driving up. She's going to stay at the Hampton down the road.
Nurse -> That'll be a treat for him.
Caller -> He won't know it's her, maybe. He sometimes calls her by her mother's name. But he lights up when she walks in. He knows something.
Nurse -> That's what matters. They feel it, even if the name isn't there.
Caller -> That's what I told her on the phone. I said, it's not about the name.
Nurse -> You said exactly the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you. Oh, and one other thing I wanted to ask. His daughter said he used to sing in the choir at his church. For like thirty years. Do you all have a chaplain who could come? Maybe sing with him? Or just sit with him?
Nurse -> We do. We have a chaplain who does visits. I'd be happy to request that. Would Saturday work, with the daughter? Or earlier in the week?
Caller -> Earlier would be better. Maybe before the daughter comes. Then he'd be warmed up. Ha. I mean, you know, he'd have had company.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll request a chaplain visit for this week, early if I can. And I'll make a note about the choir, so the chaplain can bring some songs.
Caller -> Oh, that'd be wonderful. He loves "Amazing Grace." He goes right into it.
Nurse -> I'll put that in the request.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. You all are so good to us.
Caller -> Oh, and sorry, one more tiny thing. His roommate's wife keeps bringing him cookies. Mr. Fuentes sneaks one. Is that okay? He doesn't have any restrictions?
Nurse -> A cookie is perfectly fine. At this point, whatever he enjoys and can swallow safely.
Caller -> That's what I figured. I just didn't want to get in trouble. He has such a sweet tooth.
Nurse -> Let him have the cookie. Just sit him upright and keep an eye on him while he eats.
Nurse -> You're the ones doing the work. You're with him every day.
Caller -> It's nothing. It's the job. But I love it. I love him. He's one of my favorites. Don't tell the others.
Nurse -> Ha. Our secret.
Caller -> Ha. Okay.
Caller -> Sorry, the call light. I have to, hold on. Okay it's the next room. Someone else is getting it.
Nurse -> No problem.
Nurse -> I'll also pass this update to the hospice team so they have it in his notes. The better appetite, the sundown restlessness, and that he's comfortable.
Caller -> Okay. That's great.
Nurse -> A couple of things for the evenings. Keep doing the hymns. Play them softly, in the late afternoon, before he starts to get fidgety. Keep the lights low and the room calm, and keep the evening routine the same every day. He'll do better if it's predictable.

transcript:
Nurse -> Mountain View Hospice, this is Cal.
Caller -> Cal, it's Wanda Prentiss. It's Lowell. He can't breathe. He can't catch his breath. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Wanda. I'm here. Take a breath. Is Lowell awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's in his chair. He's sitting up. He's gasping. He's working so hard. His shoulders are going up and down.
Nurse -> Okay. What's his date of birth, Wanda?
Caller -> June twenty seventh. Nineteen forty two. Please, Cal.
Nurse -> Got it. And your number?
Caller -> It's three one four, five five five, zero one four six. It's the house.
Nurse -> Okay. Is anyone else there with you right now?
Caller -> No. It's just us. Our son is in Kansas City. My neighbor's at her daughter's. It's just me. It's always just me at night.
Nurse -> Okay. You're not alone, I'm right here. Is he on his oxygen?
Caller -> He is. He's on the two liters. It's been on all day. The machine is running, I can hear it. But it's not helping. He started getting worse about three, around the middle of the afternoon, and now it's like he's drowning.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have the finger oximeter?
Caller -> I do. It's on him. I put it on. It says eighty four. Eighty four. Is that bad? It was ninety one this morning.
Nurse -> It's lower than we want. Wanda, look at his lips. What color are they?
Caller -> They look kind of blue. Purple. Bluish. Oh God. I didn't notice. They're blue around the edges.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician and send a nurse. But first, did he have a breathing treatment?
Caller -> He had the nebulizer. The albuterol. About an hour ago. It helped for like ten minutes and then he got worse again. I did it again at the same time, that's the second time, no, it's just the one. I did one. One time an hour ago.
Nurse -> Okay. One treatment an hour ago. Does he have any chest pain?
Caller -> No. He hasn't said chest pain. He's pointing at his throat. Not his chest. He says it's his breathing, not his heart.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is he able to talk at all, even a word or two?
Caller -> A word. A word at a time. He said my name. He said hurts to breathe. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. Wanda, I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, and I'm sending a nurse out to you. I want her there within the hour.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. Should I call nine one one? Should I call an ambulance? I don't want to. He doesn't want to go. He has the paper. The DNR. He said no hospital.
Nurse -> I know. And I'm not going to send an ambulance unless you and he want that. Our job is to keep him comfortable at home. That's what we're doing. Does Lowell still want to stay home?
Caller -> Yes. He told me. He told me this afternoon, between breaths. He said, "Don't let them take me." I won't. I promised him.
Nurse -> Okay. Then we'll do everything here at home. Let's do some things right now while we wait. Can you sit him up straighter? Put pillows behind his back, so he's upright, leaning a little forward.
Caller -> He's sitting up. He's in the recliner. I'll put the pillows. Okay. I'm putting them. He's leaning on the pillow.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have a fan? A small one?
Caller -> I have the box fan. In the bedroom. Hold on. I can get it. It's heavy. I'll get the little one off the dresser.
Nurse -> The little one is perfect. Put it on a table, pointing at his face, on low. Moving air on the face helps a lot with the feeling of not getting enough air.
Caller -> Okay. A fan on his face. Okay. I'm plugging it in. It's on his face. He's closing his eyes. He likes it.
Nurse -> Good. Now, Wanda, check the oxygen tubing. Follow it from the machine to his nose. Is it connected everywhere? Any kinks? Is it under the chair leg?
Caller -> It's, hold on. Let me follow. It goes from the machine across the floor, around the corner, through the door. Oh. The wheel of the chair is on it. The wheel of the recliner. It's pinched. Oh my God.
Nurse -> Okay. Lift the chair a little or move the tubing. Free it up.
Caller -> Okay. I'm moving it. I got it out. Okay. It's free. I straightened it. It was flat.
Nurse -> Good. That might have been part of it. Check that the machine is running and set to two liters.
Caller -> It's on. It's humming. The ball is at the two. The little ball on the tube. It's at two.
Nurse -> Okay. Now look at the oximeter again. Give it a minute.
Caller -> It's, it's changing. Eighty six. Now eighty seven. It's going up. Eighty eight.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep the fan on him. Stay calm, and keep your voice soft. He'll breathe easier if you're calm.
Nurse -> Is there a comfort kit in the house? The little box from the hospice?
Caller -> In the fridge. It's in the fridge door. I haven't touched it. Should I?
Nurse -> Not yet. Let's see what the nurse and the on-call clinician say. I just want you to know where it is.
Caller -> Okay. In the fridge. I won't touch it.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm trying. I'm shaking. Lowell, honey, the nurse is helping. You're doing so good. Cal, he's nodding. He's looking at me.
Nurse -> That's what I want to see. I'll stay on. The on-call clinician is being paged and the nurse is on the way. I'll call you back in ten minutes with an update, but I'm here.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay. But I can stay on? I'm scared to hang up.
Nurse -> I'll stay on the line until the other phone is ready. Or if you hang up, I'll call right back in ten minutes. Which would you like?
Caller -> Call me back. I want to sit with him. I'll keep the phone next to me.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call you back in ten minutes. Keep the fan on, keep him upright, and watch the number on the finger monitor.
Caller -> Okay. And if it goes down again?
Nurse -> Call me right back, any time. Call if he gets worse, if he gets very sleepy and you can't wake him, or if the number drops again.
Caller -> Worse, can't wake him, number drops. Okay. Okay. Thank you, Cal. I was going crazy.
Nurse -> You're doing great. You noticed the tubing. That was the key.
Caller -> I can't believe the wheel was on it. I've been so careful. I check it every morning.
Caller -> He moved the chair himself this afternoon. He wanted to see the window. I should have looked.
Nurse -> It happens all the time. Don't blame yourself. Is the front door unlocked for the nurse?
Caller -> Oh. No. Let me. I'll unlock it. I'll leave the porch light on too. Hold on, stay with him for a second, Lowell, I'm just going to the door. Okay. It's open.
Nurse -> Good. Back to him. Nothing else to do but sit with him.
Caller -> Okay. I'm back. He's looking at me.
Nurse -> Don't blame yourself.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I just want him comfortable.
Nurse -> We'll make sure. Ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Seaside Palliative Care, this is Owen.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Owen. I did something. I think I did something bad. I'm Priscilla. Priscilla Ferreira. I'm the daughter-in-law. My husband's mother, Odalys. I gave her too much of her medicine.
Nurse -> Okay, Priscilla. Thank you for calling right away. Let's figure this out. Is Odalys awake?
Caller -> She's sleepy. She's in the bed. She's been asleep, but she wakes up when I talk to her. I just checked. She said my name.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Is anyone else in the house with you?
Caller -> No. It's just me and the baby monitor. My little one is asleep. I've been going back and forth. I hope I'm not too loud.
Nurse -> You're fine. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> Um. It's March thirtieth. Nineteen fifty nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Number to reach you?
Caller -> This one. Four one four, five five five, zero one seven four.
Nurse -> Got it. Priscilla, tell me exactly what happened. What did you give her?
Caller -> The oxycodone liquid. The bottle with the syringe. It's the five milligrams per five mL. She gets five mL, the nurse told us, every four hours if she has pain. And I gave her, it was ten. I gave her ten mL. Because I read the syringe wrong.
Nurse -> Okay. So she got ten mL instead of five. When did you give it?
Caller -> About forty minutes ago. Maybe a little less. It was 1:30. It's almost two now. Almost.
Nurse -> Okay. Forty minutes. Thank you. How did it happen? Can you tell me?
Caller -> My husband's brother usually does it. He's the one. He's got the, he knows. He went home. He's at his place tonight. And my husband's at work. I'm just covering. I never did it before. I looked at the syringe. It has two sets of numbers. One side says mL, the other says something else. And I counted up to the wrong set. And then I thought, wait, it looks like a lot. But I'd already given it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a really easy mistake. The syringes can be confusing. You called right away. That's the right thing.
Caller -> I feel awful. I'm so sorry. I should have asked.
Nurse -> I'm not going to let you beat yourself up. We're going to take care of her. First, how is she right now? You said she's sleepy. Sleepier than usual?
Caller -> Yes. She's more sleepy. She was awake and talking at ten, and now she's, she's out. But when I say her name loud she opens her eyes. She says what. She answers. And then she goes back.
Nurse -> Okay. That's what I'd expect with a double dose. Priscilla, I need you to do something for me. Look at her chest and count her breaths. One in and out is one breath. Count for a whole minute. Can you do that?
Caller -> Okay. A minute. Okay. I'm going to go in. The light is off. I'll use the flashlight on my phone, no, that'll wake her. I'll use the hall light. I'll use my phone timer. Hold on. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'm right here.
Caller -> Sorry, the floorboard creaks. Okay. I'm by the bed. I'm counting. One. Two. I'll count in my head. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Done. It's, I counted fourteen. Fourteen in the minute.
Nurse -> Okay. Fourteen. That's a good number. That's normal. Is her breathing noisy? Gurgly? Any snoring?
Caller -> No. No, it's quiet. It's regular. She's just breathing. Her lips look normal. They're pink. Not blue. She's not struggling. I'm not saying she's fine, I'm saying it looks okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. That's reassuring. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, so they know about the double dose.
Caller -> Okay. Is she going to be okay?
Nurse -> Her breathing is good and she's waking up to your voice. Those are good signs. But I want to be careful, so I'm also sending a nurse out to see her. I want someone there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. It's two in the morning.
Nurse -> I know. We have someone on nights. I'll call you back in thirty minutes with an update from the on-call clinician.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. Okay. What do I do until then?
Nurse -> Several things. First, do not give her any more oxycodone until the clinician says it's safe. Even if she wakes up in pain. Hold it.
Caller -> Hold it. No more. Okay. Is it okay if she has water? She was thirsty earlier.
Nurse -> A few sips if she's awake enough to swallow. Don't wake her just for that.
Caller -> Okay. Just if she wakes up. Okay. She said her stomach hurt earlier. Before. If she wakes up and she's hurting, what do I do?
Nurse -> Call me. Don't give anything. We'll sort out the pain. Okay?
Caller -> Okay. Call you.
Nurse -> Second, stay with her. Check on her every fifteen minutes. Count her breaths for a full minute each time, and make sure she wakes up when you say her name. If she's hard to wake, call me.
Caller -> Every fifteen minutes. Count breaths. Say her name. Okay. I'll set the timer on my phone. I'll sit in the chair.
Nurse -> That's perfect. And call nine one one if you can't wake her at all, if her breathing drops below eight breaths a minute, or if her lips turn blue.
Caller -> Can't wake her, below eight, blue lips. Okay. Nine one one. I'll put the phone right here. I'm so scared.
Nurse -> I know. But she's doing okay right now. You're doing everything right.
Caller -> Should I put her on her side? I saw that somewhere.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Roll her gently onto her side with a pillow behind her back, so if anything comes up it can drain. Keep her head a little raised.
Caller -> Okay. Side. Pillow behind. I'll do it after we hang up so I'm not holding the phone.
Nurse -> Do it now if you can, I can wait.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Odalys, I'm going to turn you a little. Okay. There. She mumbled something. She's on her side.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Owen.
Nurse -> One more thing. For the future. Do you have a tape or a marker? When the nurse comes tonight, she'll help you mark the syringe. But for now, I want you to put a little piece of tape at the five mL line on the syringe. Then you can't go past it.
Caller -> I have masking tape. In the kitchen drawer. I can do that. I'll do it now, while I wait.
Nurse -> Good. And write down every dose and the time, on the sheet. So everyone can see.
Caller -> I have the sheet right here on the nightstand. It's the one with the little boxes. Everyone's been initialing. I'll write this one down. The ten. And the time. And that I did it wrong. Is that okay to write?
Nurse -> Yes. Write exactly what happened. That's helpful to the clinician.
Caller -> Okay. I'm writing it. I feel terrible.
Nurse -> Priscilla, you did the right thing by calling. People make this mistake all the time. It's not your fault that the syringe is confusing.
Caller -> My husband's going to be so mad. I don't want to tell him.
Nurse -> He won't be mad. He'll be glad you called and that she's okay. And I'll talk to him if you want.
Caller -> Thank you. Okay. I'll tell him when he gets home.
Nurse -> Good. Go sit with her now. I'll call you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Priscilla.

Nurse -> Pine Ridge Hospice, this is Faye.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Faye. It's Marcus. Marcus Rothgeb. I'm at my dad's. I'm calling about my dad. Anselm. Anselm Rothgeb.
Nurse -> Hi, Marcus. What's going on tonight?
Caller -> He's hurting. It's his hip. His left hip. And I don't know if I gave him the medicine or, I did give it. I'm just, I'm not sure what time.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's slow down and we'll figure it out together. First, what's your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> November twenty first. Nineteen thirty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> It's nine one eight, five five five, zero one four one. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. How bad is the pain? If you were to ask him a zero to ten.
Caller -> I asked him. He said a six. Then he said, no, a seven. No, a six. He keeps going back and forth. I'd say six. Six is what he said first and last.
Nurse -> Okay. A six. Is it the same hip as always, or somewhere new?
Caller -> It's the same one. Where the cancer is. It's always the left hip. It gets bad at night. And it's worse when he moves. When I turn him.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, you said you gave him medicine. What did you give?
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid one. The bottle with the little syringe. It's half a mL. It's the twenty milligrams per mL. He gets half a mL, every four hours, if he needs it.
Nurse -> Okay. Half a mL of the morphine liquid, every four hours as needed. And when did you give the last one?
Caller -> I gave it at six. At six o'clock. Because we had dinner at five thirty and I gave it after. So six.
Nurse -> Okay. Six o'clock. And what time is it now?
Caller -> It's, hold on. It's three twenty. In the morning. Three twenty.
Nurse -> Okay. So that's over nine hours since six. That's a long time.
Caller -> Is it? No. Wait. It wasn't six. I mean, I think it was nine. Because my sister called at nine, and I remember I was holding the syringe when she called. So I must've given it at nine. Not six. Nine.
Nurse -> Okay. So maybe six, maybe nine. Is there a way to check? Do you write the doses down?
Caller -> There's a sheet. On the fridge. I haven't written it down. I always forget. My brother's the one who writes it. I was going to write the time and then the phone rang.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all right. So the last dose was either six or nine. If it was nine, it's been six and a half hours. If it was six, it's been over nine. Either way, it's been more than four hours.
Caller -> Yeah. Yes. So I can give him one.
Nurse -> Let me ask a few more things first, and then I'll tell you. How's he eating?
Caller -> He ate dinner. He ate everything. He had the chicken and the mashed potatoes. He cleaned his plate.
Nurse -> Oh, good. That's great.
Caller -> Well, no. I mean he had a few bites. He pushed it around. My sister said he barely touched it. She was here. He ate like, three bites of potato. And then I made him a milkshake and he drank half. I don't know. I'd say he ate a little. Not a lot. He's not hungry.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's eating very little. The milkshake is great, though.
Caller -> He loves the milkshakes. The vanilla ones. I make them with the ice cream and a banana. He doesn't know about the banana.
Nurse -> Ha. Sneaky. Is he drinking other things besides the milkshake? Water, juice?
Caller -> A little water. He takes sips when I hold the cup. Sometimes he says no and turns his head. He had a few sips of ginger ale around supper. I don't know, a quarter of a can.
Nurse -> Okay. Small sips are fine. Okay. Marcus, has he had a bowel movement lately?
Nurse -> Not since Tuesday. That's four days, I think. It's Saturday. Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. Four. And he's straining. He tried this afternoon and nothing.
Nurse -> Does he take anything for constipation?
Caller -> The senna. The little pills. Eight point six milligrams. He takes it at bedtime. He took it last night. It hasn't done anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Senna, eight point six, at bedtime, taken last night. Okay. Is he nauseated? Is he throwing up?
Caller -> No. No nausea. He's not throwing up. He says his stomach's fine. It's just full. He says it feels like a rock.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like the constipation. And how's he sleeping? Is he restless?
Caller -> He's kind of restless. He moves around. He can't get comfortable. I think it's the hip. And the, you know, the stomach. He wakes up every hour and mumbles. It's mild. He's not agitated. Just can't settle.
Nurse -> Okay. That all makes sense together. Marcus, I'm going to message the hospice provider tonight about the hip pain, the four days without a bowel movement, and that he's eating very little. They'll look at his bowel regimen and his pain plan.
Caller -> Will they call me?
Nurse -> Someone will call you in the morning, or I will. I'll make sure.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> I'm also going to have a nurse visit your dad tomorrow, to examine him and see what's needed for the constipation.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's Sunday.
Nurse -> It is. We have nurses on weekends.
Caller -> Oh good. I didn't know that.
Caller -> Marcus, here's what I would do about tonight's pain. If his pain is still at a six and it's been more than four hours since the last dose, whether it was six or nine, you can give a half mL of the morphine liquid now. Then write the time right away.
Caller -> Okay. A half. Now. Write the time. And it's okay? Even if it was nine?
Nurse -> Yes. Six and a half hours is more than four. It's okay.
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting the syringe. I'm going to draw it up. The half is, it's the second line. Right? The first line is quarter.
Nurse -> The half mL is the line at the five tenths. Let me read what yours says. Is it marked?
Caller -> It says point five. There's a line at point five. And the tape. My brother put a piece of tape there.
Nurse -> Perfect. Draw it to the tape.
Caller -> Okay. I did. It's at the tape. Okay. Dad? Dad, I'm going to give you your medicine. For your hip. Okay. Open. There. Under your tongue. Good. He took it. He said thank you.
Nurse -> Good job. What time is it?
Caller -> Three thirty five. I'm writing it on the sheet. Three thirty five. Done.
Nurse -> Perfect. From now on, write the time right when you give it, every time, so nobody has to guess. Even at three in the morning.
Caller -> Yeah. I should've. I know. I felt so dumb not knowing.
Caller -> The sheet has all these little boxes and my brother's handwriting is so small. I can't even read his writing half the time. He writes in pencil.
Nurse -> A pen is better. Maybe leave a pen on a string next to the sheet so it's always there.
Caller -> A pen on a string. Ha. My mother used to do that with the grocery list.
Nurse -> You're not dumb. It's the middle of the night, you're tired, you've been taking care of him. It happens to everybody.
Caller -> I've been here three nights. My sister did the first two. I'm not good at nights. I fall asleep in the chair.
Nurse -> It's a lot. How are you holding up?
Caller -> Okay. Tired. My wife keeps calling. She wants me to come home. But my sister's got the kids this weekend. So it's me.
Nurse -> You're doing a good job. Marcus, for the constipation, I'd like you to offer him some prune juice, or warm water, in small sips. Whatever he'll take. Let him eat or drink only what he wants. Don't push.
Caller -> Prune juice. Do we have any? I think there's a bottle in the pantry. Dad hates it. He calls it purple medicine.
Nurse -> Ha. A few sips with a little water might go down easier.
Caller -> I'll try. Or the warm water with lemon. He likes that.
Caller -> He used to drink prune juice every morning when he was younger, my mom said. Then he decided he hated it. Same with oatmeal. He went on strike one day and never ate it again.
Nurse -> Ha. People are funny about food.
Nurse -> That's fine too.
Caller -> What if he doesn't go? By tomorrow?
Nurse -> That's what the nurse will look at tomorrow. There may be something stronger the provider orders, or a suppository. But we don't want you giving anything extra tonight without checking.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll wait for the nurse.
Nurse -> Good. And I'll call you tomorrow morning, after I talk to the provider, to tell you the plan.
Caller -> Morning. What time?
Nurse -> By nine, I'd think. Probably earlier.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine. I'll be up. I'm always up.
Nurse -> And if tonight the pain isn't eased in an hour, or he starts throwing up, or he's very restless, call me back, any hour.
Caller -> An hour, throwing up, restless. Okay. I'll call.
Nurse -> Good. How is he now? Does he look more comfortable?
Caller -> He's, I don't know yet. It's only been a minute. He's got his eyes closed. He's breathing slow. Normal slow.
Nurse -> Okay. Give it twenty minutes or so. The medicine takes time.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. I'll sit here. I'll watch him.
Nurse -> Good. Marcus, do you have everything you need? Mouth swabs, lotion, pillows?
Caller -> We have the swabs. His lips get dry. And the lotion for his feet. My sister does his feet every night. He likes that.
Nurse -> That's a lovely thing.
Caller -> I think so. We have the pillows. The sheepskin thing under his hip. That helps a little.
Nurse -> The sheepskin is good. Keep him turned every couple of hours if you can.
Caller -> I was supposed to turn him at two. I fell asleep. Oh no.
Nurse -> It's okay. Can you turn him now? Gently, onto his right side, so he's off the left hip. With a pillow between his knees.
Caller -> Okay. Yes. I'll do it. Let me put you on speaker. I'll turn him slowly. Dad? Dad, I'm going to turn you. Okay. Here we go. He's grunting. He's saying ow. Sorry, Dad. Sorry. Okay. He's on his right side. I put the pillow between his knees.
Nurse -> Good. Is he more comfortable?
Caller -> I think so. He sighed. He's relaxing.
Nurse -> Good. That's what I want to hear.
Caller -> This is a hard thing. I never thought it'd be like this.
Nurse -> I know. It's a lot. You're doing it though. He's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I don't know about that. I wasn't around much when I was younger. We didn't get along. Then this happened and I just came.
Nurse -> That counts. He knows you're here.
Caller -> I hope so. He called me by name tonight. He said Marcus. That was the first time in days.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Hold on to that.
Caller -> He also asked for the radio. The ballgame. At three in the morning. I told him it's not on. He said put on the replay. I said Dad there's no replay. He laughed. A little.
Caller -> I will. Okay. I'll call if I need you. Thank you, Faye. Sorry I was all over the place.
Nurse -> You were fine. Take care, Marcus.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeside Home Health, this is Naveen.
Caller -> Oh good, a person. Hi. Hi. I've been on hold on the other number for twenty minutes. I'm Harriet. Harriet Voss. I'm calling for my friend Imogene Castellanos. She's the one who had the hip.
Nurse -> Hi, Harriet. Sorry about the hold. Let me pull up Imogene. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> August eighth. Nineteen forty four. She's going to kill me for telling you that. She says she's thirty nine.
Nurse -> Ha. Our secret. And I think I have a number on file for you. Is it six four six, five five five, zero one two zero?
Caller -> That's right. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect. So tell me what you need.
Caller -> Sorry, the kettle. Hold on. Okay. No, it's not boiling yet. Where was I.
Nurse -> You said you had a list.
Caller -> I do, I do. It's on an envelope from the electric company. Ha. Don't tell them.
Caller -> So, there are a few things. I wrote a list because I knew I would forget. Hold on, it's on the back of an envelope. First one. The walker. The rubber foot came off. The bottom of the leg. Like the, the cap. She was walking to the kitchen this morning and it came off and rolled under the sofa. I found it but it's cracked. It won't stay on.
Nurse -> Oh no. Okay. So one of the rubber feet is cracked and won't stay on.
Caller -> Right. And the other three are fine. They're a little worn but they're okay. I mean, I don't know what's okay. I'm not a walker expert.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine. I'll send a replacement. We'll replace all four if we can.
Caller -> Oh good. That'd be better. I don't want her falling.
Nurse -> No one does. Has she fallen at all since she came home?
Caller -> No. No falls. She had one near miss, on Sunday. She grabbed the counter. She was fine. She yelled at me for hovering.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Good she caught herself.
Nurse -> Exactly. Is she using it right now?
Caller -> No. I made her sit. I took it away. It's in the hall. She's in the recliner with a blanket, watching her stories.
Nurse -> Good. Keep it that way for now. We'll come back to that. What's number two on your list?
Caller -> Two. The toilet seat. The raised one. The hospital said it'd be delivered Monday. And it's Thursday. And nothing came. And she's, you know, she's been using the regular one, and it's low, and it's hard for her to get up. I help her. I get her under the arms. But I'm sixty eight myself.
Nurse -> Okay. So the raised toilet seat was supposed to be delivered Monday and never came. That's definitely something we need to fix today.
Caller -> Yes please. My back is killing me.
Nurse -> Do you have a way to rest it? Have you been able to sit down at all?
Caller -> I sit in the kitchen chair. I have my heating pad. My daughter says I should stop doing it all myself. But who else.
Nurse -> It's okay to ask for help. Maybe your grandson can come in for lifts.
Caller -> He's sixteen. He eats everything in the house. But he's strong. I'll ask him.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll get it moving. What's number three?
Caller -> Three. The stockings. The white ones. The compression ones. She's supposed to wear them all day. And there's, there was a package of three pairs. And she washes them at night and they dry on the towel rack. But I think there's only one pair left. One pair that's clean. The others are, one's got a run in it, and I can't find the third.
Nurse -> Okay. One pair left that's usable. We'll send more.
Caller -> And the gloves. For the incision. The little blue ones. We're out of those.
Nurse -> Oh. The disposable gloves. You're doing the dressing?
Caller -> No, no. I just put them on when I help her wash it. The nurse said to. When I'm near it. We have none. I used the last one yesterday. I mean the last pair.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll add a box of gloves too.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Thank you so much. See, I knew I'd forget something.
Nurse -> It's what the list is for. Okay, let me ask about Imogene.
Caller -> Please.
Nurse -> You're doing great. Harriet, how's Imogene herself? Let's make sure she's okay. Is she in pain?
Caller -> She says it's a three. I asked her this morning. She says a three. It's more of an ache. She has the pills, she takes them. I don't keep track of that part. Her daughter does that on the phone.
Nurse -> That's fine. Is she icing it? Doing her exercises?
Caller -> She's doing the little exercises, the ankle pumps. She does them during the commercials. She's very good about it. And she ices it after lunch. The ice pack in the dishtowel.
Nurse -> That's great. How does the incision look? Any drainage, redness, any fever?
Caller -> It looks fine. It's dry. It's got the, the strips. There's no goo. There's no redness. I looked this morning when I helped her get dressed. It's a little pink at the edges but the nurse said that's normal. No fever. We took her temperature last night, it was ninety eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That all sounds right.
Caller -> I'm glad. I was worried. I didn't know what to look for.
Nurse -> You'd be surprised how many people say that. Is she eating okay?
Caller -> Oh yes. She's eating better than I am. She wants soup. I make a big pot of chicken noodle and she eats it for three days.
Nurse -> Perfect. Protein helps healing.
Nurse -> You know exactly what to look for. Okay. Let me place the order. Give me a minute to enter it. Are you still there?
Caller -> I'm here. I'm making tea. I'll be quiet.
Nurse -> Take your time. Typing. Hold on.
Caller -> I hear you typing. You're fast.
Nurse -> Ha. Years of practice.
Nurse -> Take your time. Okay. I'm ordering the raised toilet seat, four rubber feet for the walker, two more pairs of compression stockings, and a box of gloves. I'm marking it urgent.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's done. I just placed the order with the equipment company for the toilet seat, the walker feet, the stockings and the gloves.
Caller -> Oh, wonderful. When will they come?
Nurse -> I'm going to call and ask them to deliver tomorrow, in the morning if they can. I'll ask them to call you when they're on the way.
Caller -> I'll be there. I'll be at her house. I'm there every day, practically. I'm retired.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll also have a nurse come out Friday, to check on Imogene and the incision. That's the day after tomorrow, so the walker should be fixed by then.
Caller -> Friday. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call to give a window. Is mornings okay?
Caller -> Morning is best. She's more awake. After lunch she nods off.
Nurse -> I'll ask for morning. In the meantime, Harriet, please don't let her use the walker with the cracked foot. Use the wheelchair if you have one, or just stay close and steady her. And I'd rather she not go into the bathroom alone until the new seat comes.
Caller -> We have the wheelchair. In the garage. From her husband. Oh, he passed a few years ago. It's still there. I can get it out. I'll have my grandson bring it in.
Nurse -> That would be good. And for the bathroom, you can help her. But go slowly, and don't pull on her arm or her bad hip. Hold under the arm on the good side.
Caller -> The good side. Okay. The right. The surgery was on the left. I mean the left was the surgery.
Nurse -> Right. So you stand on her right.
Caller -> Got it. I'll do that. Right side.
Caller -> And the shower? She hasn't had a real shower. I give her a sponge bath. She hates it.
Nurse -> Sponge baths are fine for now. The nurse will tell you when she can shower and what chair to use.
Caller -> A chair in the shower. Okay. I'll ask Friday.
Nurse -> Also, keep the incision clean and dry, and wash your hands before you touch the dressing, even when you use the gloves.
Caller -> Wash hands, then gloves. I do that. I'm very clean. I was a dental hygienist for thirty years.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you know. Last thing. Call us if she gets a fever, if the incision gets red or starts draining, if her calf gets swollen or painful, or if she falls at all. Even if she seems okay.
Caller -> Fever, red, draining, calf, fall. Even if she seems okay. I'll tell her daughter too. She'll want to know all that.
Nurse -> Please do. Anything else on your list?
Caller -> Let me look. Nope. That was it. Four things. Walker, seat, stockings, gloves. I did it. I got through the list.
Nurse -> You did great.
Caller -> I'm proud of myself. Ha. Oh, one more thing, not on the list. The therapist, the physical therapist. When's she coming back?
Nurse -> Let me check the schedule. I see the therapist is scheduled for next Tuesday.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. Imogene was asking. She likes her.
Nurse -> That's good. She'll check the walker then too.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you so much, Naveen. You've been a lifesaver.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Harriet. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bright Steps Pediatric Home Care, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Joanna Lindgren. Theo's mom. I'm calling with an update on Theodore, and a couple of little things.
Nurse -> Hi, Joanna. Good to hear from you. How's Theo?
Caller -> He's good. He's, he's a wild man today. He's running laps around the living room with a pot on his head.
Nurse -> Ha. A pot?
Caller -> A big metal one from the kitchen. With a wooden spoon for a sword. I'm afraid to look at the cabinets.
Nurse -> Ha. Sounds like a great day.
Caller -> A pot. It's a helmet. Apparently he's a knight.
Nurse -> Love it. Can you confirm his date of birth for me?
Caller -> May seventeenth. Twenty twenty three.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number, in case I need to call back?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one five four.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's the update?
Caller -> So we went to the neurologist on Tuesday. The appointment. And she changed his dose. The seizure medicine. The levetiracetam. She went up on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know. What's the new dose?
Caller -> It used to be two and a half mL of the levetiracetam, twice a day. Now it's three mL. Twice a day. The same bottle. The liquid. A hundred milligrams per mL. She said the pharmacy would have the same concentration so I wouldn't have to do math.
Nurse -> Okay. Three mL, twice a day, of the hundred milligrams per mL. Perfect. Did you start the new dose already?
Caller -> Yes. We started yesterday. Wednesday morning. He got the three mL this morning. And I'm going to give it again tonight, at eight. I think I did the morning one right. I put the thing at the three. The syringe.
Nurse -> Good. I'll go over the syringe in a minute. Why did she increase it? Was he having seizures?
Caller -> No, not really. He had one, a week and a half ago. A short one. Like a minute. And she said better to go up now, he's growing.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. And has he had any since the increase?
Caller -> No. None. None this week. Not a single one. He's been great. He's been sleeping fine. He's been eating. Eating like a horse.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Did they weigh him at the clinic?
Caller -> They did. Twenty eight pounds. He's gained. He was twenty six in the summer. So that's good. The doctor was happy.
Nurse -> That's great. Twenty eight pounds.
Caller -> I know. He's a big boy now. He won't let me carry him anymore.
Nurse -> They grow so fast.
Caller -> Too fast. He's got his father's feet already.
Nurse -> Aw. How's he feeling otherwise? Any cough, fever, anything?
Caller -> He's got a runny nose. A little. It started over the weekend. Clear. Not green. He's not coughing. No fever. He's not bothered by it. I wipe it every five minutes. We're going through the tissues.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like a regular cold. Keep an eye on it. Let me know if he gets a fever or it changes.
Caller -> I will. I will.
Nurse -> Anything else about the visit? Did they change anything else besides the dose?
Caller -> No. Just that. And she wants to see him in three months. And she said keep the log. I write down his seizures and the med times. I'm doing that.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep doing that. Okay, Joanna. I'm going to update the dose in his chart right now so everyone has the right one.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Give me a second. I'm in his record. Levetiracetam, hundred milligrams per mL. Three mL, twice a day. Okay. I just updated the medication list in his chart with the new dose. It's saved.
Caller -> Wonderful. Will the other nurses see it?
Nurse -> Yes. Everyone who sees his chart. I'll flag it so they notice it's new.
Caller -> Thank you. I always worry that they won't know.
Nurse -> It's a good thing to worry about. That's why you called. What was the other thing?
Caller -> Oh. Thursday. Our visit tomorrow. Can we move it to the afternoon? The morning is bad because Theo has speech therapy from ten to eleven. I forgot to tell you.
Nurse -> Sure. What time in the afternoon works?
Caller -> After one. One thirty, two. He naps from noon to one, so after that.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll ask scheduling to move the visit to Thursday afternoon, after one thirty. I'll let you know if they can do it.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> Joanna, let me go over the syringe with you, just to be sure. When you give the three mL, you pull the plunger until the top of the black rubber ring lines up with the three on the side. Not the tip. The top edge of the ring.
Caller -> The top of the ring. Hmm. I think I was using the bottom. Or the middle. Hold on. Let me get the syringe. I'll show you.
Nurse -> I can't see it on the phone. But describe it.
Caller -> Okay. It's the oral syringe. It's got a clear barrel and a black rubber thing at the end of the plunger. The ring. Okay. The top edge. At the three. Yes. I think I've been putting the top. Mostly. Sometimes the middle.
Nurse -> The top edge. Always the top edge. It's a small difference but it adds up. Give three mL twice a day starting tonight, and flush the tube with water after.
Caller -> Top edge. Three mL. Twice a day. Flush after. Okay. I'll do that tonight. At eight.
Nurse -> Good. And I know you know this, but if he has a seizure that lasts longer than five minutes, or he has trouble breathing after, call nine one one.
Caller -> Five minutes. Or trouble breathing. I have the rescue medicine too. The nasal one. And I'd call anyway.
Nurse -> Good. You're on top of it.
Caller -> I try. I'm exhausted but I'm on top of it. Ha.
Nurse -> How are you doing? Are you getting any rest?
Caller -> A little. He sleeps through, mostly. My husband takes the early mornings. It's okay. We're okay.
Nurse -> That's good. You have a lot on your plate. Make sure you take time for yourself.
Caller -> I'm trying. I went to a yoga class on Sunday. For the first time in a year.
Nurse -> Oh, I love that. How was it?
Caller -> I fell asleep during the relaxation part. Ha. The teacher had to wake me up.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best compliment. You needed it.
Caller -> I did. Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Gwen.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Joanna. I'll call you about Thursday.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.
