transcript:
Nurse -> Oak Hollow Home Health, this is Brenda.
Caller -> Hello? Hello, can you hear me? I'm in the kitchen. The reception is bad here. It's Delphine Whitlock. I'm calling about my husband Terrence. Terrence Whitlock.
Nurse -> I can hear you, Delphine, but you're breaking up a little. Let me know if I lose you. What's Terrence's date of birth?
Caller -> February fourteenth. Nineteen fifty eight. A Valentine's baby.
Nurse -> Ha. That's easy to remember. Are you still there? The line cut out for a second.
Caller -> I'm here. I'm here. I walked to the window. Better? Can you hear me better?
Nurse -> Much better. And your number?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one six two.
Nurse -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one six two. Is that right?
Caller -> That's right. That's right.
Nurse -> Great. What's going on with Terrence today?
Caller -> His sugar was high this morning. It was too thirty ate. Too thirty ate. And that's high for him. He's usually a hundred and something.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, Delphine, you cut out on the number. Did you say two thirty eight?
Caller -> Two thirty eight. Yes. Yes. Two, three, eight. It was the fasting one. Before breakfast.
Nurse -> Okay. Two thirty eight before breakfast. And has it been high other days?
Caller -> Yesterday it was, it was one ninety. Two days ago a hundred and eighty something. It's been climbing. And he's so thirsty. He's drinking and drinking. He had like eight glasses of water yesterday. And he's going to the bathroom every hour. All night.
Nurse -> Okay. Thirsty and going to the bathroom a lot. How long has that been going on?
Caller -> Two days. Since Sunday night. He said I'm drinking the whole lake. Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you check his pressure?
Caller -> I did. I did this morning too. It was won fifty for over ninety. Won fifty for. That's high, right?
Nurse -> Sorry, the line's fuzzy. Won fifty for? You mean one fifty four over ninety?
Caller -> One fifty four over ninety. Yes. That's what I said. That's what the cuff said.
Nurse -> Okay. One fifty four over ninety. It's higher than his usual?
Caller -> He's usually one thirty something. One thirty over eighty something. So yes, it's up.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, his insulin. He takes the Lantus?
Caller -> He takes the Lantus. At bedtime. Twenty units. He took it last night. I watched him do it. Twenty. I always watch. After the stroke I don't trust him to count.
Nurse -> Okay. Lantus twenty units at bedtime, and he took it last night. Did he eat dinner? And did he eat more than usual yesterday?
Caller -> He ate dinner. The usual. Chicken and rice. And he had a piece of cake. It was his sister's birthday. One piece. A big piece.
Nurse -> Ha. A big piece. That could do it. Birthday cake does that.
Caller -> I know. I should have said no. But it was his sister.
Nurse -> No judgment. Is he vomiting? Or nauseated?
Caller -> No. No, no. His stomach's fine. He's eating. He had eggs this morning. And he's not confused. He's himself. He's bossing me around. He told me my coffee was too weak.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. Is he sleepy? Hard to wake?
Caller -> No. He's wide awake. He's watching the news. He's yelling at the television.
Nurse -> Ha. Politics?
Caller -> Everything. The weather. He yells at the weather lady.
Nurse -> Sounds like normal Terrence.
Caller -> That's exactly it. Normal Terrence.
Nurse -> Okay. Delphine, here's the plan. I'm going to send a message to his provider about the sugar and the pressure and the thirst. I'll mention the cake.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Do you think he needs more insulin?
Nurse -> That's for the provider to decide. Please don't change his dose yourself.
Caller -> Oh, I wouldn't. I'd never. I just wondered.
Nurse -> I'll call you back this afternoon with what the provider says.
Caller -> This afternoon. About what time?
Nurse -> Between two and four. I'll call this number.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be home. The reception is better in the living room. I'll go sit there.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to check him, review his insulin, and look at his pressure.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Morning or afternoon?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time.
Caller -> Okay. Fine. We'll be here.
Nurse -> In the meantime, can you recheck his sugar in about two hours, and again at bedtime? Write down each number with the time.
Caller -> Two hours and at bedtime. Write them down. With the time. I have a notebook. Okay.
Nurse -> And keep offering him water through the afternoon. But no sugary drinks. No juice or regular soda.
Caller -> Water. No juice. He likes the orange juice. He's going to complain.
Nurse -> Ha. A little complaining is okay. Tell him it's temporary.
Caller -> I'll tell him. He'll say it's my fault for buying the cake. It wasn't me. It was his sister.
Nurse -> Ha. Blame the sister.
Caller -> I do. Brenda, what number should worry me? What's the too high number?
Nurse -> If it's over three hundred twice in a row, or if he's vomiting, call us right away. And if he gets confused or very hard to wake up, call nine one one.
Caller -> Over three hundred twice. Vomiting. Confused. Hard to wake. Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> You got it. Any other questions?
Caller -> Is the cake going to hurt him? Long term?
Nurse -> One piece of cake won't hurt him long term. It's just a bump. We'll get him back on track.
Caller -> Thank you. I feel better. I was so worried when I saw the number.
Nurse -> You did the right thing checking and calling. Go sit where you get good reception, and I'll call this afternoon.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Brenda. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Delphine.

transcript:
Nurse -> Heartland Hospice, this is Lorraine.
Caller -> Hi, Lorraine. I'm hoping you can help me. I'm with Grace Lutheran, the church on Pine Street. We have a group of about eight people who want to volunteer with you all. Do you do trainings?
Nurse -> We do. That would be our volunteer coordinator. I can take down the information and she'll call you back, or I can tell you what I know.
Caller -> What do you know? I'm just trying to figure out how it works.
Nurse -> Our volunteer training is usually two Saturdays, nine to one. It's at our main office. There's a background check and a short health screening before.
Caller -> Okay. Two Saturdays. That's doable. Can they do it in a group, together?
Nurse -> Sometimes, yes. We can schedule a group if there's enough interest. Eight is a nice number.
Caller -> Wonderful. And where's the main office? I have the address but I want to know about parking.
Nurse -> It's off Highway Nine. There's a lot behind the building. It's free. On Saturdays it's usually empty.
Caller -> Good. Some of our people are older. They like to be close.
Nurse -> There are a few spots right by the back door.
Caller -> Perfect. Is there any age limit? A couple of the group are in their eighties.
Nurse -> No upper limit. As long as they can do the training and are comfortable with the work.
Caller -> I'll tell them. They're fit as fiddles. One of them still bowls.
Nurse -> Ha. That's great.
Caller -> So what do I do next? Do I give you names?
Nurse -> The coordinator will collect that. Her name is Pamela. I can have her call you this week. What's your name and best number?
Caller -> It's Reverend Joyce. Joyce Hallstrom. I'm at the church office. It's five five five, oh one one two, I think. No, zero one one five. Let me check. Zero one one five.
Nurse -> Zero one one five. And what's the area code?
Caller -> Oh. Three one four. Silly me.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, zero one one five. I'll pass it to Pamela.
Caller -> Thank you. Is there anything I should tell the volunteers beforehand?
Nurse -> Just that it's rewarding work, and that no medical background is needed. We teach everything.
Caller -> I'll say that. Several of them lost someone in hospice and want to give back.
Nurse -> That's often how people come to us. Thank you for organizing it.
Caller -> My pleasure. Bless you all. Goodbye.
Nurse -> Goodbye, Reverend.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oak Hollow Home Health, this is Brenda.
Caller -> Brenda, this is Lucille Pacheco. It's Wendell. His face. His whole face is, it's drooping, on one side. And he can't talk right.
Nurse -> Okay, Lucille. I'm listening. Which side of his face?
Caller -> The right. The right side. His mouth is hanging down. And his words are all mushy. He's trying to say something and it's, it doesn't come out.
Nurse -> Okay. When did this start?
Caller -> I don't know. Twenty minutes ago? Maybe. He was reading the paper at the kitchen table. At twelve fifteen. I looked in and he was fine. He said something about the crossword. Then I went to the bathroom. And when I came out, he dropped his coffee cup. It broke. And I looked at him and his face was like that.
Nurse -> Okay. Twelve fifteen was the last time he was normal. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Twelve fifteen. It's twelve forty now, so about twenty five minutes. Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Lucille, I need you to hang up and call nine one one right now. This sounds like it could be a stroke and he needs an ambulance.
Caller -> A stroke? Oh my God. Oh no. Okay. Wait. Can't you send someone? Can't a nurse come?
Nurse -> A nurse can't get there fast enough. The ambulance can. Time matters with a stroke. Call nine one one right now. Do you have another phone, so I can stay on with you?
Caller -> There's the house phone. The kitchen one, on the wall. It has the long cord. I'm on my cell. Hold on. I'll put this one on the counter.
Nurse -> Perfect. Put me on speaker on the counter, and call from the wall phone. I'll stay right here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. It's on speaker. Wendell, honey, stay in the chair. I'm calling. I'm calling the ambulance.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I can hear you.
Caller -> It's ringing. Hello? Yes. I need an ambulance. My husband. I think he's having a stroke. Forty one Birch Lane. Yes. Yes. It's Pacheco. Wendell Pacheco. His face is drooping and he can't talk right.
Nurse -> Tell them it started around twelve fifteen to twelve twenty, and that he takes a blood thinner.
Caller -> Around twelve fifteen. He's on a blood thinner. Yes. The Eliquis. Yes. Yes. Okay. She says they're sending someone. She says about eight minutes. She says stay on the line but I can't, I have two phones.
Nurse -> Stay on with the dispatcher. I'm right here too. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> It's not. Hold on. I'll go. The cord won't reach. I'll put the wall phone down. Hold on. Okay. It's unlocked. I turned on the porch light.
Nurse -> Good. Now go back to Wendell. Is he still sitting up?
Caller -> He's in the kitchen chair. He's looking at me. He's trying to talk. He said something. I couldn't understand. He's frustrated. He hit the table.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tell him you know, and help is coming. Keep your voice calm.
Caller -> Wendell, honey, the ambulance is coming. It's okay. They're coming. Oh, he's crying. Brenda, he's crying.
Nurse -> That's understandable. Hold his hand. What about his other hand? Can he squeeze?
Caller -> His left one he can. His right hand. It's limp. It won't squeeze at all. It's like a dead thing.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that. Is he taking anything for his heart? A blood thinner?
Caller -> The Eliquis. Five milligrams. Twice a day. He took the morning one at eight. The list is on the fridge. I'll give it to them.
Nurse -> Good. Give the paramedics the list. Don't give him anything to eat or drink, not even water or pills. And keep him sitting or lying down. Don't let him walk around.
Caller -> Nothing to eat or drink. Sit or lie. Okay. He wants to get up. He's trying to stand up. No, honey. Sit. Sit down. Okay. He sat.
Nurse -> Good. Is he in a safe spot? Not near the edge of the chair?
Caller -> I put a pillow on each side. He's fine. He's leaning on me.
Nurse -> That's good. Lucille, can you tell me his date of birth? For the chart. In case the line drops.
Caller -> January ninth. Nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> Thanks. And the number you're on?
Caller -> This one is my cell. Four one four, five five five, zero one seven six.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now. They'll want to know.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you. How long did they say? Eight minutes. That's forever.
Nurse -> It feels long. Let's use the time. Has Wendell had any falls today? Or hit his head?
Caller -> No. No falls. He got up fine this morning. He had his oatmeal. He did the stairs. He was fine. He was joking about the crossword.
Nurse -> Okay. And did he complain of a headache, or his vision, before this?
Caller -> He said his eye was a little blurry at breakfast. But he wipes his glasses all the time. I didn't think anything of it. Oh God. Should I have?
Nurse -> No. You couldn't have known. Tell the paramedics about the eye too.
Caller -> The blurry eye. Okay. I'll tell them.
Caller -> Should I call my daughter? She's at work. She's twenty minutes away.
Nurse -> After the paramedics are with him. Right now, stay with Wendell. I can have the agency call her if you give me her number.
Caller -> No, I'll do it. I'll call her from the ambulance. Oh. Hold on. The dog. The dog is barking. Shh. Biscuit, quiet.
Nurse -> It's okay. Let him bark.
Caller -> He knows something's wrong. He's pressing against Wendell's leg.
Nurse -> Dogs do know. Is Wendell's breathing okay?
Caller -> Yes. He's breathing fine. He's just, one side. His mouth is crooked. He's drooling a little. I wiped it with a towel.
Nurse -> Good. That's all right.
Caller -> Is it going to be okay? Can they fix this?
Nurse -> The sooner he gets to the hospital, the better the chance. You did the right thing calling right away. They have treatments for strokes, but they have to start early.
Caller -> That's why you said time. I understand. Okay. I'll stay calm.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you. I can hear something. Is that a siren?
Nurse -> It might be. Listen.
Caller -> I hear it. I hear it. It's getting louder. It's the fire truck. They said the fire truck comes first.
Nurse -> That's normal. Go to the door and wave them in. Tell them everything we went over.
Caller -> I'll go. I'll go. Wendell, I'll be right back. Don't get up. The nurse is on the phone. I'll be right back.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll stay on until you tell me.
Caller -> Okay. They're here. They're in the driveway. Two men. They have a bag. I'm waving. Here, he's in the kitchen. Right here. He's in the chair.
Nurse -> Lucille, I'm going to let you go so you can talk to them. I'll call you back in fifteen minutes. Pick up if you can, even from the ambulance.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll answer. Thank you. Thank you so much, Brenda.
Nurse -> You did everything right. Go be with him.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Meridian Home Health, this is Quentin.
Caller -> Hi. Quentin? Hi. I need to tell somebody something and I'm afraid. I made a mistake with my dad's pills. A bad one.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called. Let's go through it. Who am I speaking with?
Caller -> It's Noelle. Noelle Abernathy. My dad is Ignatius Doyle. Everybody calls him Iggy.
Nurse -> Okay, Noelle. Hi. Can I get Mr. Doyle's date of birth?
Caller -> October second. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> It's four one four, five five five, zero one eight one.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay, Noelle. Tell me what happened. Take your time.
Caller -> So, I do his pillbox on Sundays. The big one, the seven day one with the morning and bedtime. And I do it at the kitchen table after church. And I take out all the bottles. And I did it on Sunday, like always. And this morning I was, I was cleaning out the cabinet. And I looked at the bottles and I looked at the pillbox. And the pills in the morning slots don't match the bottle I thought they came from.
Nurse -> Okay. So what did you find?
Caller -> I put the wrong one. There are two bottles that look the same. Clonidine and clonazepam. They both start with C L O N. They're both small white pills. I got them mixed. The clonidine is for his blood pressure, in the morning and at night. And the clonazepam is for his nerves. Just at bedtime.
Nurse -> Okay. So which pill did you put in the morning slots?
Caller -> The clonazepam. I put the clonazepam in the mornings. In every morning slot. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, all of them. And the clonidine, I put in the bedtime ones. Oh God. He's been taking the nerve pill in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's gotten the clonazepam in the morning on Monday, and today, Tuesday. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Monday and today. Two mornings. And then the clonidine at night. Which he was supposed to have in the morning and at night. So he's getting one clonidine instead of two. Wait, no. I put one in the evening slot. So one, not two. I think. I'm confusing myself.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let's go slowly. His normal plan is clonidine, point one, twice a day, morning and night. And clonazepam, point five, at bedtime. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's right. The clonidine point one milligrams. Twice a day. And the clonazepam point five. At bedtime.
Nurse -> Okay. So over the last two mornings, he's gotten an extra point five of clonazepam in the morning, and he missed his morning clonidine both days. What about last night? What did he get at bedtime?
Caller -> He got the clonidine. From the bedtime slot. Because I put the clonidine there. And he didn't get his clonazepam at bedtime, because there wasn't any in that slot. So he had the nerve pill in the morning instead of at night.
Nurse -> Okay. So the pills got swapped. Did he get his clonidine on Sunday night?
Caller -> Sunday night was from the old box. Saturday night I mean. I did the new box Sunday afternoon. He took the last of the old box Sunday morning. So the last real clonidine in the morning was Saturday night, or Sunday morning. Let me think. I think the last correct dose was Saturday night.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's say the last full correct pair was around Saturday night. That's fine. Now how is he doing? How does he seem?
Caller -> He's sleepy. He's been sleepy since yesterday. He's kind of out of it. He's sitting in the recliner and he keeps dozing off. And when he stands up he's wobbly. He grabbed the wall this morning. He said he feels like he's on a boat.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he fallen?
Caller -> No. He hasn't fallen. He grabbed the wall and he didn't fall. I was right there. I haven't let him go alone. No falls.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he confused? Does he know where he is, who you are?
Caller -> He knows me. He knows where he is. He told me the Packers lost. He's not confused. Just sleepy. Slow. Slow to answer.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. I took it twenty minutes ago because I was scared. It was one sixty four over ninety six. That's high for him. He's usually one thirty.
Nurse -> Okay. That's higher because he missed the clonidine. And what's his pulse?
Caller -> Eighty eight. I think. It said eighty eight. That's okay, right?
Nurse -> That's okay. Thank you for taking it. Noelle, did you give him anything else this morning besides what was in the pillbox?
Caller -> No. Just the pillbox. And his breakfast. He didn't eat much. He had toast.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he breathing normally? Any slow breathing or snoring that worries you?
Caller -> He breathes normal. He snores a little in the chair. He always does. I checked on him just now. He's breathing. I counted. It's like sixteen.
Nurse -> Good. That's normal. Thank you for checking. Noelle, I want you to know you did the right thing calling. This is a mistake that happens, and we can fix it.
Caller -> I'm so ashamed. I'm a pharmacist's assistant. I work at a drugstore. Of all people. I should know better.
Nurse -> Does your pharmacy do the pillboxes for him? Some do blister packs.
Caller -> They offered. Last year. I said no. I said I'd do it. I wanted to be the one. I didn't want to pay the fee. Now I feel like an idiot.
Nurse -> You're not an idiot. When the nurse comes, we can talk about blister packs. It might be a good idea.
Caller -> I think it is. I'll call them tomorrow. I'll ask them to start it.
Nurse -> It can happen to anyone. Especially with look-alike names. Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now to tell them what happened, and ask what they want for today's doses.
Caller -> Okay. Please.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse out to see him today. To check his pressure, look him over, and sort out the pillbox with you.
Caller -> Today. Okay. What time? I'm off today. I'm here all day.
Nurse -> I'll ask for this afternoon. The scheduler will call you with a time.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> And until the on-call clinician calls back, please don't give him anything else from the pillbox. No clonidine, no clonazepam. Hold everything until we tell you what to do.
Caller -> Nothing from the pillbox. Okay. But his blood pressure, he needs the clonidine, doesn't he? Isn't that dangerous, to stop it?
Nurse -> It can be, if it's stopped for a long time. That's why I'm paging right away. The clinician may tell you to give the clonidine from the bottle, today. I don't want to guess. We'll know within the half hour.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait. I'll wait.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes with their answer.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. I can do that.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep him in the recliner or in bed. Don't let him walk alone. Someone should be with him any time he stands, even to go to the bathroom. Use his walker.
Caller -> Walker. Someone with him. Okay. He hates the walker. He says it makes him feel old. But I'll make him.
Caller -> He's eighty two. He says eighty two is not old. He says his father lived to ninety six.
Nurse -> Ha. Then he's got a long way to go. Tell him the walker is just for today.
Caller -> Okay. I'll pass that along. He'll grumble.
Nurse -> Tell him it's just for today.
Caller -> I will. I'll bribe him with ice cream.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. Also, call nine one one if he's very hard to wake, if his breathing gets slow, if he gets confused, or if he has chest pain or a really bad headache.
Caller -> Hard to wake, slow breathing, confused, chest pain, bad headache. Nine one one. Okay. I wrote it on my hand.
Nurse -> Good. How is he right now? Can you check on him?
Caller -> Hold on. I'll go. Dad? Dad. Dad, it's Noelle. Open your eyes. Okay. He opened them. He said what. He's okay. He's looking at me. He said why are you yelling.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. He's responding.
Caller -> He is. He's grumpy. That's him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Noelle, while we wait, can you do something? Can you get the two bottles and put them in front of you? Read me the labels, so I can make sure we've got the doses right.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Okay. The first one. Clonidine. C L O N I D I N E. Point one milligram. Take one tablet by mouth twice a day. And the other one. Clonazepam. C L O N A Z E P A M. Point five milligram. Take one tablet by mouth at bedtime.
Nurse -> That matches what I have. Now, for the future, what I'd suggest is keep those two bottles in separate places. Different shelves, or put a colored sticker on one. And read the label twice before you fill.
Caller -> Wait, I need a pen. And a sticker. Do I have stickers? I have the dots from my kid's garage sale.
Nurse -> Those will work.
Caller -> Red dots. Perfect. Okay, I have them.
Caller -> Different shelves. A sticker. Yes. I'll put a red sticker on the clonazepam. Red for the nerves. And the nurse can help me redo the pillbox. I'd like that. I don't trust myself.
Nurse -> You can trust yourself. You just need a double check. The nurse will do it with you.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I feel a little less sick. I felt like I poisoned him.
Nurse -> You didn't poison him. He got a dose of a medicine he's already prescribed, at the wrong time. That's a medication error, and we take it seriously, but it's not a disaster. We'll monitor him.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I needed to hear that.
Nurse -> How's your dad's mood? Is he eating, drinking?
Caller -> He had some juice. He's drinking. He asked for a sandwich. I'll make him one. Turkey.
Nurse -> Good. Small amounts. Is he able to swallow okay, sitting upright?
Caller -> Yes. He eats fine. He just falls asleep in the middle of chewing sometimes. Ha. Don't laugh. It's not funny.
Nurse -> It's a little funny. Make sure he's awake and sitting up for the sandwich.
Caller -> I will. I'll hold the plate.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anyone else who can help you today? Someone to sit with him while you rest?
Caller -> I haven't slept. I was up at four. When I realized. I just lay there. I thought, what have I done.
Nurse -> That's a long morning. Try to eat something. Have some coffee, if that helps.
Caller -> I had two cups. My hands are shaking from the coffee and the fear.
Caller -> My husband comes home at five. And my brother. He's on his way. He lives twenty minutes away. I called him when I found the mistake. He said stay calm and call the nurse.
Nurse -> Your brother was right.
Caller -> He usually is. Don't tell him.
Nurse -> Ha. I won't.
Caller -> He's going to tease me about it forever. Mistake Noelle. That's what he'll call me.
Nurse -> Maybe. But he'll also be glad you caught it. A lot of people wouldn't have noticed.
Caller -> I only noticed because I was cleaning. I almost didn't.
Nurse -> Then it was lucky. That's what counts.
Caller -> I guess so. I keep thinking, what if I hadn't. What if it was a whole week.
Nurse -> You caught it on day two. That's early.
Caller -> That's true. Day two. Okay.
Nurse -> Exactly.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go and get the page done. I'm going to sit with Dad.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call you in thirty minutes. Pick up even if the number's unfamiliar. It'll be me or the clinician.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you, Quentin. You've been so kind.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Noelle. Sit with your dad.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Granite State Home Health, this is Dev.
Caller -> What? Say that again, son. I can't hear you good. I've got the phone turned up all the way.
Nurse -> This is Granite State Home Health. This is Dev, the nurse.
Caller -> Oh. Dev. Okay. This is Ira. Ira Gleason. It's my wife. Sylvie. Her tube. The catheter. It's not, it's not doing what it's supposed to.
Nurse -> Okay, Ira. Sorry to hear that. I'm going to speak up. Can you tell me Sylvie's date of birth?
Caller -> What's that? Her birthday? July twenty third. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what's your phone number, Ira?
Caller -> It's, uh, four one four, five five five, zero one seven three.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me what's happening with the catheter.
Caller -> The bag is empty. Her bag. The leg bag. It's been empty since, since, I looked at four. And now it's almost eight. Four hours. Nothing in it. She hasn't, it hasn't, I looked at the, at the, I checked the. Nothing's coming.
Nurse -> Okay. Nothing in the bag for about four hours. Is she drinking?
Caller -> What? Oh. She's drinking. She had tea. She had, she's had a few glasses of water. And a juice. So it should be coming. It should.
Nurse -> You're right. It should be draining. Is she having any pain? Any belly pain?
Caller -> She's hurting. Down low. Down here. She says it hurts. She says it's a six. A six out of ten. I asked her. She's holding her stomach and she's grimacing.
Nurse -> Okay. Lower belly pain, six out of ten. Is there any leaking?
Caller -> Leaking. Yes. Yes there is. That's the other thing. It's coming out around the tube. Around where it goes in. Her nightgown is wet. I changed her once already. And her bed pad. It's wet again.
Nurse -> Okay. That can happen when the catheter is blocked. The urine backs up and leaks around it. Ira, did you check the tubing? Is it kinked anywhere?
Caller -> I did. I looked at all of it. I looked at the tube from where it comes out, down her leg, to the bag. There's no kink. I even, I straightened it. And I made sure she's not lying on it. It's, I did it twice. It's not kinked. Not that I can see.
Nurse -> Good. That was the right thing to check. When was the catheter last changed?
Caller -> The nurse did it. The girl with the red hair. Three weeks ago. Maybe three and a half. She said it should last about a month.
Nurse -> Okay. Was that the first change since it was placed, or has she had it a while?
Caller -> The second one. She had it put in at the hospital in September. Then the nurse changed it. Then this one.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's due soon anyway. Is Sylvie warm? Does she have a fever? Chills?
Caller -> What? A fever? Hold on. Let me, no. No fever. I put the thermometer in her ear. It said ninety eight. Ninety eight and something. No shaking. No chills. She's cold, actually. She wants her sweater.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's reassuring. Is the urine, what little there is, is it a normal color? Any blood?
Caller -> What blood? There's no blood. It's just, hmm. The little bit on the pad looks dark. Dark yellow. Like tea. I don't see red.
Nurse -> Okay. Dark yellow. Okay. Ira, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, because her bag is empty and she has pain.
Caller -> Okay. Will you send somebody?
Nurse -> Yes. I'm sending a nurse out to see Sylvie, and I want her there within two hours. They'll check the catheter, flush it or change it.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. It's late. It's nearly eight.
Nurse -> I know. We have a night nurse. I'll call you back in twenty minutes to let you know who's coming and when.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. I'll sit by the phone.
Nurse -> Is the phone near you? Can you hear it ring?
Caller -> It's right here on the kitchen table. I'll hear it. Unless I'm in the bedroom. I'll bring it in. It has a long cord. No, it's a cordless. It's the old cordless. I'll bring it.
Nurse -> Bring it with you.
Nurse -> Until then, a few things you can do. First, make sure the bag is below the level of her bladder. Even when she's lying in bed. Hang it on the bed frame, low. And check the tubing one more time, the whole length, for any kinks or places she's lying on it. And don't pull on the catheter.
Caller -> Below the bladder. Low. Check the tube. Don't pull. Okay. I'll look again. Hold on. Let me put you down. I'll go look. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. I looked. The bag is on the bed rail. It's about even with her hip. It's not that low. I'll move it down. Okay. It's hanging off the bottom of the frame now. Down by her knee. Is that better?
Nurse -> Yes. That's much better. That might help it drain.
Caller -> I'm looking at the tube. Nothing. Wait. There's a little bit. A drip. In the tube. I see a drop. Is that good?
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Something's moving. Let's see if it keeps going.
Caller -> I'm watching. Oh. There's another. It's slow. It's real slow. But it's moving.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Still, I want the nurse to come. A slow drip isn't enough after four hours.
Caller -> I understand. Yes.
Nurse -> Can she drink some water now? Small sips? Water or juice.
Caller -> I'll get her some juice. The apple. She likes it. Hold on. I'll bring it. Sylvie, honey, the nurse says drink. Here. Small sips.
Nurse -> That's right. Don't rush.
Caller -> She's drinking. She says thank you to the nurse. She says you have a nice voice.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her thank you. How is she sitting? Is she propped up?
Caller -> She's in the hospital bed. The head is up. She's comfortable. Well, as much as. The pillow is under her knees.
Nurse -> Good. That's fine.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her thank you. Ira, I know this is stressful. Keep offering sips of water or juice while we wait.
Caller -> Sips. Water or juice. Okay.
Nurse -> And call me right away if she gets a fever, chills, blood in the tube, worse pain, and call nine one one if she gets confused or can't catch her breath.
Caller -> What? Say that again. Fever. Chills. Blood. Worse pain. And the other, confused or breathing. Nine one one. Okay. I wrote it down.
Nurse -> Perfect. Are you okay on your own tonight? Is anyone else there?
Caller -> My son is two hours away. I'll call him. He'll want to know. He worries.
Nurse -> Does he know the plan for the night? Who he should call?
Caller -> He has the number. He's on the fridge. He calls every night at nine. He's going to hear about this and want to drive over.
Nurse -> It's okay if he does. But there's no need to drive at night. The nurse is coming.
Caller -> I'll tell him that. He listens to the nurses more than he listens to me.
Nurse -> Call him. I'll talk to you in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Dev. Thank you. You're a good man.
Nurse -> Take care, Ira.
Caller -> Bye. Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Prairie Wind Hospice, this is Tomás.
Caller -> Hey. Hi. Yeah. I'm calling about my uncle. Barnaby Whitcomb. I'm Corbin, his nephew. Corbin Whitcomb.
Nurse -> Hi, Corbin. Thanks for calling. What's going on with your uncle?
Caller -> Well, so, he stopped taking his pills. His water pill. He told me last weekend he's done. He said "I'm done with the pills, Corbin." And I didn't think much of it. And then I came by tonight and his legs are like balloons.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called. Let me pull up his chart. What's Mr. Whitcomb's date of birth?
Caller -> Uh, May thirtieth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Got it. And a number I can reach you at?
Caller -> Yeah. Three zero three, five five five, zero one four five.
Nurse -> Great. Which pill did he stop? Do you know the name?
Caller -> The Lasix. It's the little white one. He took it every morning. The forty. Forty milligrams. I know because I set up his pill organizer sometimes. He stopped it a week ago. Last Tuesday. Wait. It's Thursday. So a week ago Tuesday. Two days ago? No. Nine days. Hmm. A week and a couple days.
Nurse -> About a week and a half, then. Let me make sure I have it right. He took the Lasix, forty milligrams, once a day, and the last dose was around a week ago Tuesday.
Caller -> Yeah. Yes. That's it. A week ago Tuesday.
Nurse -> And did he stop any of the other pills too, or just the Lasix?
Caller -> I think just that one. I looked at the organizer. The rest are gone, like he's still taking them. It's just the one with the white ones.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. Why did he stop? Did he tell you?
Caller -> He said he's tired. He's tired of the pills. He takes like eleven of them. And the Lasix makes him run to the bathroom all day. He said he'd rather swell up than live in the bathroom.
Nurse -> That's a common complaint. Okay. Tell me what you saw tonight.
Caller -> His legs. Both legs. They're puffy all the way up. Up to the knees. Last week it was just the ankles, and now it's the whole shin. And his feet are shiny. And it's, I pushed with my thumb and it left a dent.
Nurse -> Okay. Both legs swollen up to the knees, with pitting. Is he short of breath at all?
Caller -> A little. Well, more than a little. He came out on the porch to see me, three steps, and he sat down and he was huffing. Like he'd run a mile. He couldn't talk for a minute.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he short of breath right now, sitting?
Caller -> No, not now. He's in the chair. He's okay sitting. He's breathing normal. He's watching the game.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he sleep flat, or does he use pillows?
Caller -> Two pillows. And he said last night he slept in the chair. He said he couldn't lie down. I don't know if that's a thing.
Nurse -> It can be. Does he cough at night, or wake up gasping?
Caller -> He coughed some. Dry. He didn't say gasping. He did say he sat up a couple times.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll add that for the provider.
Nurse -> That can be a sign. We'll make sure the provider knows. Does he weigh himself?
Caller -> He does. There's a scale in the bathroom. I made him step on it tonight. He was one ninety four. And I looked at the sheet that the nurse left, the log. A week ago he was one eighty eight. So that's six pounds.
Nurse -> Okay. Six pounds up in about a week. That's a lot. Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. I asked him. He said no. He said if he had chest pain I'd know because he'd be on the floor. Ha. That's how he talks.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. It's good he doesn't have it.
Caller -> Yeah.
Nurse -> Corbin, I'm glad you noticed. Is Mr. Whitcomb able to talk with me? I'd like to hear from him.
Caller -> He's, um, he's kind of cranky. He doesn't like when I call you guys. But I'll see. Uncle B? Uncle B, it's the hospice. The nurse wants to talk to you. He says tell him I'm fine.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. I understand. Tell him I hear you and I'm not going to nag. I just want to make sure he's comfortable.
Caller -> I told him. He's making a face. He says he's comfortable. He says he's fine and I'm a worry wart.
Caller -> He says the last nurse was nice but she talked too much. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll make a note. Short and sweet.
Caller -> He'd like that.
Nurse -> Okay. I get it. Corbin, a lot of people in his situation get tired of the pills. It's okay to talk about it. What's important is that the team knows, so we can adjust things in a way that works for him. Maybe fewer pills, maybe a different schedule.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah, he said that too. Like, he's not against all of it. He just wants fewer.
Nurse -> That's very reasonable. I'm going to send a message to the hospice provider tonight about the stopped Lasix, the swelling, the six pound weight gain, and that he wants fewer pills.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds good.
Nurse -> I'm also going to have a nurse visit him tomorrow. She can check his legs, listen to his lungs, and talk with him about what he wants.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. He's usually up by nine. He doesn't like early.
Nurse -> Afternoons are better for him?
Caller -> After lunch. He naps around one. So before one or after three.
Nurse -> I'll note before one or after three.
Nurse -> I'll tell them afternoon. And I'll call you back this evening to let you know what the provider says.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. I'll be around. I'll stay till nine. I'm gonna eat dinner here.
Nurse -> Great. In the meantime, can you do some things? Weigh him every morning, same time, after the bathroom, before breakfast. And write it down. If he gains two pounds in a day, call us.
Caller -> Every morning. Two pounds. Okay. He'll hate it. But I'll tell my cousin to do it. She stops by.
Nurse -> And when he's sitting or lying down, put his legs up on pillows. Let him rest between things. Don't push him to do stairs.
Caller -> Legs up. Okay. He has a footstool. I'll find a pillow too.
Nurse -> Good. And please call nine one one if he has chest pain or trouble breathing even when he's sitting still. And call us back if he can't lie flat.
Caller -> Chest pain, can't breathe sitting, can't lie flat. Okay. I got it. I'll tell my cousin.
Nurse -> Does he have anyone who stays with him at night?
Caller -> My cousin, Lena, sleeps on the couch most nights. She's there tonight.
Nurse -> Good. Please tell her too.
Caller -> I will. I'll text her right now. Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> Oh, one question. Is it okay if he has salty stuff? He's been eating canned soup every day. He says it's the only thing that tastes like anything.
Nurse -> I'd cut back on the salty things for now, since the swelling. Maybe half a can instead of a whole one. But let him have what he enjoys. The nurse will go over it.
Caller -> Half a can. Okay. I'll tell Lena.
Nurse -> Don't scold him about the pills. Okay? Let the nurse and the provider talk with him.
Caller -> I won't. I'll bring him a milkshake. That's what he likes. Chocolate.
Nurse -> That sounds like a plan.
Caller -> Thanks, Tomás. I thought I was overreacting.
Nurse -> You weren't. You were right to call.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Corbin.

Nurse -> Cascade Palliative Care, this is Imani.
Caller -> Imani. Hi. It's Philippa. Philippa Santoro. I'm having, my back, it's a nine. I took my pill at four and it did nothing. Nothing. This pain is killing me.
Nurse -> Okay, Philippa. I'm here. I'm so sorry you're hurting. Let's get you help. Can you tell me your date of birth?
Caller -> February twentieth. Nineteen sixty three.
Nurse -> Thanks. And what number are you on?
Caller -> It's my cell. Eight one six, five five five, zero one seven three.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about the pain. Where is it?
Caller -> My back. The middle of my back. Between the shoulder blades. And it goes around, like a belt. It's been getting worse since yesterday. And tonight, it's like someone's twisting a knife. I could scream. I've been crying for an hour.
Nurse -> I hear you. On a scale of zero to ten, where is it right now?
Caller -> A nine. It's a nine. It was an eight at dinner. It's a nine now. I thought a ten was the worst you could imagine. This is the worst I can imagine.
Nurse -> Okay. A nine. And what did you take?
Caller -> The oxycodone. The ten milligram. I took one at four. That's the usual. Every four hours if I need it. I took it at four. It's, what, almost midnight? No. It's eleven twenty. So it's been seven hours. I should have taken another at eight. But I didn't, because I felt okay at eight. Then it got bad at nine. And I was afraid to take more.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me make sure I have it right. You took a ten milligram oxycodone at four this afternoon, and nothing since. Is that right?
Caller -> Nothing since. I should have. I was being stubborn. I didn't want to use too much. My daughter said, take it, take it. But I didn't.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something we can work on. Are you taking anything else for the pain?
Caller -> The gabapentin. The three hundred. Three times a day. I took the last one at eight. That's it. Oh, and I used the heating pad. For ten minutes. It made it worse. Or it didn't make it better.
Nurse -> Okay. Gabapentin three hundred, three times a day, last at eight. Thank you. Philippa, I want to ask you something, because I care about how you're doing. When you say the pain is killing you, are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself?
Caller -> What? No. No, no. God, no. That's just a thing you say. I'm not going to hurt myself. I just want the pain to stop. I want it to stop. That's all.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. I believe you. I just needed to ask.
Caller -> I understand. I'm sorry. I sound crazy. I'm exhausted and I'm in pain.
Nurse -> You don't sound crazy. You sound like someone in a lot of pain. Okay. Is there any new weakness in your legs, or numbness? Any trouble walking?
Caller -> No. No numbness. My legs are fine. They feel normal. I walked to the bathroom ten minutes ago, and it was fine. It's just the back pain.
Nurse -> Okay. And is your bladder or bowel working normally? Any trouble holding it, or trouble going?
Caller -> Normal. I went to the bathroom. It was normal.
Nurse -> Good. Have you had a bowel movement in the last couple of days?
Caller -> Yesterday. It was fine. I take the stool softener every night. So that's not it.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know.
Nurse -> Good. Any nausea, vomiting?
Caller -> A little nausea. From the pain. I think. I feel queasy. I haven't thrown up. I had some crackers earlier. They stayed down.
Nurse -> Okay. Philippa, here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, so they can decide on the next step for your pain medicine.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Can I take another pill?
Nurse -> I want the clinician to tell us the right dose, since the pain is so high and the last one didn't hold. Please wait for the callback before taking more. I know it's hard. I'll call you in ten minutes.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Okay. I can do ten minutes. I think.
Nurse -> I'm also sending a nurse to your home. I want her there within the hour. She can check you and bring medicine if the clinician orders it.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. It's nearly midnight. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Absolutely. We have a night nurse for exactly this.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> While you wait, let's try to make you a little more comfortable. Can you lie on your side, with a pillow between your knees? And a small pillow behind your back. Heating pad on low, over a thin shirt, not on bare skin. Keep the room dark and quiet.
Caller -> On my side. Pillow between my knees. Okay. I'm doing it. It's a little better. A little. Hold on. Okay. The heating pad. It's on low. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Breathe slowly. In through your nose, out through your mouth. Slow.

Nurse -> I know. Even a little helps. Do you have the TV on or any noise?
Caller -> The TV's on. A cooking show. It's on mute. I can't concentrate.
Nurse -> Maybe turn it off for now. Keep it dark and quiet.
Caller -> Okay. Off. Hold on. Okay.
Nurse -> I know. Just try.

Nurse -> That's it. Is anyone with you tonight?

Nurse -> Would you be okay with waking her, so she can be with you while we wait? She might want to know.

Nurse -> Good. Philippa, please don't take any extra oxycodone until the clinician calls. And write down every dose and time on your sheet.
Caller -> Write it down. Okay. The sheet's on the table. I'll write that I took the four o'clock one. And the gabapentin at eight.

Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Imani. I'm sorry I was dramatic.
Nurse -> You were not dramatic. You were in pain. We take it seriously.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Philippa.

transcript:
Nurse -> Redwood Home Health, this is Alicia.
Caller -> Hello? Alicia? It's Bao. Bao Nguyen. We're on the speaker, my daughter and me. About Linh. My wife. She fell this morning.
Caller -> Dad, she didn't fall. She slid. Hi, I'm Mai, I'm the daughter.
Nurse -> Hi, Bao. Hi, Mai. I can hear you both. Let me get Linh's chart open. What's her full name and date of birth?
Caller -> Linh Nguyen. L I N H. N G U Y E N. November ninth, nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> Got it. And a number I can call you at?
Caller -> It's my cell. It's eight one six, five five five, zero one six two.
Nurse -> Thanks. And is Linh near the phone? I'd like to hear from her too, if she's comfortable talking.
Caller -> She's on the couch. Mai, hold the phone closer to your mom. Linh, say hello.
Caller -> Hello, nurse. I'm fine. Everybody's fussing.
Nurse -> Great. So tell me what happened this morning. One at a time, if you can.
Caller -> So she was sitting on the edge of the bed. At six. I was in the bathroom. And I heard a bang.
Caller -> It wasn't a bang. It was a thump. Dad, you weren't there. I was in the room.
Caller -> I was in the bathroom, I heard it. A bang. And I came out and she was on the floor and her head was by the nightstand.
Caller -> Her head was not by the nightstand. Her legs were by the nightstand. Her head was on the rug.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me see if I've got this. Linh was sitting on the edge of the bed, and she ended up on the floor. Mai, you were in the room?
Caller -> I was in the hallway. I came in when I heard it. I was maybe five seconds behind Dad. I saw her slide down. Like her legs gave out. She slid off the side and sat down on the floor, and then she lay back.
Nurse -> Okay. And Bao, you said you heard a bang. Do you think she hit her head?
Caller -> I think she hit her head on the nightstand. I heard it. There's a little mark on the nightstand, a scuff.
Caller -> That scuff has been there for a year.
Caller -> Mai, you don't even live here. How would you know about the scuff?
Caller -> I'm here every weekend, Dad. I see it. It's been there since the Christmas you moved the dresser.
Caller -> Nobody moved the dresser at Christmas. That was Easter.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's leave the scuff for now. The important thing is what we do next.
Caller -> No, it's new.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you both. Linh, are you there? Can you hear me?
Nurse -> I can hear you. I don't think I hit my head. I don't remember hitting it. My hip hurts a little.
Nurse -> Thank you, Linh. Okay. So Linh doesn't think she hit her head, Mai didn't see her hit it, and Bao heard a bang. Is that fair?
Caller -> That's fair. I just heard a bang.
Caller -> Yes. That's fair.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what we'll do. We'll treat it as possible, just to be safe. Was there any bleeding? Any bump you could feel on her head?
Caller -> No blood. I looked. I looked through her hair. I didn't feel a bump. Her hair is thick.
Caller -> I checked too. Nothing. No lump.
Nurse -> Good. Is she having a headache? Any nausea, vomiting? Is she acting like herself?
Caller -> No headache. She says no. No vomiting. She had her tea this morning. She's talking normally. She was complaining about my driving.
Caller -> She's herself. She's bossing everybody.
Caller -> I'm right here, you two.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. Okay. Linh, how's the hip?
Nurse -> It's sore. On the left. It's a two. Mostly when I move. I can bear weight. I can walk with the walker.
Nurse -> Okay. A two. Thank you. Has she tried to walk since?
Caller -> She walked to the bathroom with the walker. With me next to her. She did okay.
Caller -> She held the grab bar. I was behind her with my hands out. In case.
Caller -> I did the same on the other side. We looked like a parade.
Nurse -> A parade is good. Better too many hands than too few.
Caller -> She was slow. But okay.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have a blood pressure cuff? Could you check her pressure?
Caller -> We have one. Mai, get the cuff. It's in the drawer. Okay. We did it twice. It was one twenty six over seventy eight. Second time one twenty four over seventy something.
Nurse -> That's a normal reading. Thank you. Does Linh take any blood thinners? Aspirin, anything like that?
Caller -> No. No blood thinners. Not since the doctor stopped the aspirin last year. Nothing like that. Right, Linh? No blood thinner.
Nurse -> I'm here. No. No blood thinners.
Nurse -> Okay. And her MS medicines. What does she take, and did she take it this morning?
Caller -> She takes the tizanidine. Four milligrams. Three times a day. For the stiffness. She took the morning one at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Tizanidine, four, three times a day, last at eight. Does that make her sleepy?
Caller -> A little. It makes her tired. But she's been taking it for a year. She's used to it.
Caller -> She slides down sometimes. Her legs get weak in the morning. That's why she needs help getting up. We were all just trying to help her stand and it went wrong.
Caller -> This morning she said she was dizzy a second, when she sat up. Just a second. That's why her legs went.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Linh, did you feel dizzy when you sat up?
Nurse -> A little. For a second. The room tipped. Then my knees went.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll make sure the provider hears that, too.
Nurse -> Okay. Is that something that's been happening? The legs giving out in the mornings?
Caller -> Sometimes. Not every day. Maybe twice a week. It's worse when she's tired.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the provider know about that, too.
Caller -> Can I ask? Is it safe to leave her alone? I have to go to work at two.
Nurse -> I'd rather someone stay with her today. Can your daughter stay?
Caller -> I can stay. I have class online. I can do it from here.
Caller -> What are you studying again?
Caller -> Dad. Nursing. I've told you four times.
Caller -> Right. Nursing. Good. You'll be good at it.
Caller -> Good. Thank you, Mai. That settles it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay. Here's the plan. Bao, I'm sending a nurse to examine Linh today. I want someone there within two hours. They'll check her head, her hip, and her neurologic status.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. That's good. That makes me feel better.
Nurse -> I'm also going to message her provider about the fall, the possible bump, and the morning weakness.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this evening to see how she's doing.
Caller -> This evening. What time?
Nurse -> Around six or seven. I'll call this number.
Caller -> Okay. We'll be home.
Nurse -> Now, because we're not sure about the head, I'd like you to keep a close eye on her for the next day. Check on her every hour. Look for a headache that gets worse, vomiting, being sleepy or hard to wake, confusion, or any new weakness. And wake her once tonight to make sure she's easy to wake.
Caller -> Every hour. Headache, vomiting, sleepy, confused, weak. And wake her once tonight. Okay. I'll set an alarm.
Caller -> I'll write it on a sticky note and put it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Also, keep her in the recliner or in bed with someone nearby. If you have a hospital bed or the bed adjusts, lower it. And help her any time she stands. Don't let her stand alone today.
Caller -> The bed does go lower. I'll put it down. And she can stay on the recliner. She likes it anyway.
Nurse -> And Linh, please let them help you today. I know you like to do things yourself.
Nurse -> I'll try. They fuss too much.
Nurse -> Ha. Just for today.
Caller -> She's rolling her eyes. I can hear it.
Nurse -> One more thing. Call nine one one if she vomits, if her headache gets worse, if she's hard to wake up or confused, if she gets new weakness or has a seizure. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Vomit, worse headache, hard to wake, confused, weak, seizure. Nine one one. Okay. Mai, did you get that?
Caller -> I wrote it down.
Nurse -> Great. Do you have any questions for me?
Caller -> Just, will she be okay? Is this something to worry about?
Nurse -> I think she's likely okay. She's alert, she's talking, no bleeding, and her pressure is normal. But we want to be careful and have a nurse look at her. That's why I'm sending someone.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I appreciate it. I panicked this morning. I thought, oh no.
Caller -> He did panic. He called me three times. I was in the next room.
Caller -> Mai! I called you once. Then I came out.
Nurse -> Ha. It's okay. It's scary when someone falls.
Caller -> Mai said I should have called her first. Before I called you. I said you're the nurse.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Calling us was exactly right.
Caller -> It was. It was very scary.
Nurse -> How are you doing, Bao? Are you holding up?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. I haven't slept well since the weekend. Linh's been having bad nights.
Nurse -> That's a lot. I'll mention it to the nurse. Maybe we can talk about getting you some help.
Caller -> That would be good. I'm not complaining.
Nurse -> You're not complaining. You're telling me the truth.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. The nurse will be there within two hours. I'll call this evening. In the meantime, call me if anything changes.
Caller -> We will. Thank you, Alicia.
Caller -> Thank you.
Caller -> Alicia, sorry, one more thing. The neighbor wants to bring a casserole. Is that okay? She's been asking all morning. She heard the ambulance. I mean, there wasn't an ambulance, but she heard Dad yelling.
Nurse -> A casserole is lovely. Just keep the visit short today so Linh can rest.
Caller -> I'll tell her to leave it on the porch. She'll be offended. She likes to see the inside of the house.
Caller -> Dad. Be nice. Mrs. Okafor means well.
Caller -> She means to find out everything. Okay. Porch. I'll tell her tomorrow.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. Anything else on your mind?
Caller -> Linh wants to know if she can still do her stretches. The physical therapy ones.
Nurse -> Gentle ones, lying down, are fine. Nothing standing today. The nurse can show her what's okay.
Caller -> Okay. I'll just do the arm ones. And my ankles.
Caller -> That sounds right.
Nurse -> And Mai, since you're studying nursing, you already know the hourly checks. But if you ever feel unsure, call us. Don't second guess yourself.
Caller -> I won't. Honestly, I'm glad it's not just me deciding.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for. You and your dad did well today. You called early and you kept her still.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot. I was so nervous when you picked up.
Nurse -> Take care, all of you.
Caller -> Bye bye.

Nurse -> Birchwood Hospice, this is Raul.
Caller -> Hi, Raul. This is Keisha. Keisha Montrose. I'm the overnight aide at Silver Maple. I've got one of your people.
Nurse -> Hi, Keisha. Which resident?
Caller -> Mr. Brandvold. Oswaldo Brandvold. B R A N D V O L D. Room fourteen.
Nurse -> Got him. Can you give me his date of birth to confirm?
Caller -> It's on the whiteboard. August fourteenth. Nineteen thirty five. He's ninety one. He's going to be ninety one in August, no wait, he turned ninety one in August.
Nurse -> Perfect. And a number I can call you at?
Caller -> The nurses' station. It's six one zero, five five five, zero one nine eight. Somebody will grab it.
Nurse -> Great. What can I do for Mr. Brandvold tonight?
Caller -> So I'm doing my four o'clock rounds, no, my five thirty. And I noticed we're about out of his things. His briefs. The large ones. There's about six left in the closet. And the day shift said the order didn't come.
Nurse -> Okay. About six large briefs. How many does he use in a day?
Caller -> Maybe five or six. He's changed every two or three hours. So that's one day. If that. I wanted to say something before the day aide ran out and had to go borrow from another resident.
Nurse -> That was smart. Anything else running low?
Caller -> The cream. The barrier cream. The white one. In the tube. It's almost empty. I squeezed it and it was a little bit. Not enough for tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. Almost empty. Got it.
Caller -> And then there's the thing with the bed. The mattress. The air one. It's been beeping on and off since last night. The alarm. I looked at the screen and it says low pressure. It stops after a minute and then it starts again.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. Is he lying on it right now?
Caller -> He is. He's asleep. He's fine. I checked the mattress. It feels firm. But it beeps. And it wakes up the guy next door.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you checked the hose and the plug?
Caller -> I did. The hose is on tight. I checked where it goes in the pump and in the mattress. I wiggled it. The plug is in the wall. It's green on the pump. It says power on. But it still beeps.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. How's his skin? Any new red spots, open areas?
Caller -> I looked when I changed him at three. No new red. No open spots. His tailbone is a little pink but it's the same as the day shift charted. It goes away when I turn him. I didn't see anything new.
Nurse -> Good. That's what I want to hear. Is he turned every two hours?
Caller -> Every two. We do it on the clock. He's bedbound. He can't turn himself. Me and the other aide do it. We take turns. I did him at three and then at five.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay, Keisha. Let me place the order. Give me a minute.
Caller -> Take your time. I'll be right here. Oh. Hold on. A light's on. Room eleven. I'll be quick. Don't hang up.
Nurse -> I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. That was Mrs. Aguilar. She wanted her water. She wants her water every ten minutes. She has a cup. She knows she has a cup.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Back to Mr. Brandvold. I'm ordering a case of the large briefs and two tubes of the barrier cream. I'm marking it urgent so it comes this morning.
Caller -> Do they come in a case? The last time they came in a bag of twenty.
Nurse -> The standard is a case of eighty. That should last him a while.
Caller -> Eighty. Wow. Where am I going to put them? The closet is full of Mrs. Aguilar's.
Nurse -> The day shift can sort that out. Ha.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's done. I just placed the order with the supply company for the briefs and the cream.
Caller -> Oh, wonderful. Where will they deliver?
Nurse -> To the nurses' station, I'd think. Is that where the day shift receives?
Caller -> Yes. The front desk, or the nurses' station. Tell them nurses' station, second floor. The front desk guy gets confused.
Nurse -> Got it. I'll ask them to deliver it to the nurses' station this morning. I'll write second floor.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll leave a note for the day nurse.
Nurse -> Good. Now, about the pump. I'm going to message the equipment company about the alarm, so they can send a tech or swap the pump.
Caller -> That'd be great. It's been going all night. I'm tired of hearing it.
Nurse -> I bet. In the meantime, can you check a few more things? Make sure the air hose is firmly connected, not kinked, the plug is in, and the mattress isn't leaking. If the alarm keeps sounding, call us back.
Caller -> Hose, kink, plug, leak. I did most of that. I'll do the leak. I can listen for a hiss. Okay. I'll walk over. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I'm by the bed. I'm listening. I don't hear a hiss. The mattress is pretty firm. I'm pushing on it. It's firm. The hose is not kinked. I think it's the pump. It sounds weird. It has a click.
Nurse -> Okay. That's useful. I'll tell the equipment company it's clicking.
Caller -> Yes. Tell them it clicks. And it says low pressure.
Nurse -> I will.
Caller -> Is it okay if he stays on it?
Nurse -> As long as the mattress is firm and he's not bottoming out. If it feels soft or he feels the bed frame under him, we'll need to move him. Keep turning him every two hours and keep checking his skin.
Caller -> Every two hours. I will. And the cream. I'll use what's left. And I'll check his skin at every change.
Nurse -> That's right. Keep him clean and dry after each change. And put the barrier cream on the buttocks and the tailbone.
Caller -> Clean, dry, cream. Okay. I have that. I do it every time.
Nurse -> Perfect. How's he doing otherwise? Eating, drinking? Comfortable?
Caller -> He sleeps a lot. He ate some oatmeal yesterday. He doesn't complain. He's very quiet. He had a visitor yesterday, his granddaughter. She read to him.
Nurse -> That's nice. Any pain?
Caller -> No grimacing. No moaning. He seems comfortable.
Nurse -> And is he due for any medicine soon? Anything the night nurse gives?
Caller -> The nurse does his meds. I don't touch them. She'll be around at six for the morning ones.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'll leave a note on the chart for the day team.
Caller -> Thank you. They love when you leave notes.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> I don't think so. I just wanted to get ahead of it. Thank you, Raul.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling early. Have a good rest of your shift.
Caller -> Two more hours. Ha. Thank you.
Nurse -> Take care.

Nurse -> Brightwater Home Health, this is Colin.
Caller -> Hi, Colin. It's Yesenia. Yesenia Valderrama. I just had my knee replaced and you guys come to the house. I have a question about my pills.
Nurse -> Hi, Yesenia. Of course. Let me find you. Can you spell your last name for me?
Caller -> V A L D E R R A M A. Valderrama. Two R's. People always leave one out.
Nurse -> Two R's. Got it. Sorry, one more time, is it Yesenia with a Y?
Caller -> Y E S E N I A. Yes. Like the flower, almost. Nobody gets that one either.
Nurse -> Y E S E N I A. Okay. I have you now.
Nurse -> Got it. Date of birth?
Caller -> June eleventh. Nineteen eighty two.
Nurse -> Perfect. And your number?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one eight four.
Nurse -> Great. So, your question. What's going on with the pills?
Caller -> Sorry, my dog is barking. Hold on. Luna! Luna, no. She's barking at the mailman. He comes at the same time every day and every day it's a surprise.
Nurse -> Ha. Dogs. Take your time.
Caller -> So I'm on two medicines that sound the same and I'm worried. One is Celexa. And one is Celebrex. And I think I might be mixing them up. The pharmacist said they were different but they have the same letters at the start.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a really common thing. They do sound alike. Let's go through each one. Which one do you take every day?
Caller -> The Celexa. It's for my mood. It's twenty milligrams. I take it every morning with breakfast. I've been on it for like two years. I took it this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Celexa, twenty milligrams, every morning, and you took it this morning. Good. And Celebrex?
Caller -> The Celebrex is new. The surgeon gave it to me for the knee. It's two hundred milligrams. And I'm supposed to take it only if I need it. Once a day at the most. I took one yesterday. That's it. I took it with lunch.
Nurse -> Okay. Celebrex, two hundred, once a day as needed, and you took one yesterday. So you've had one so far?
Caller -> One. Just one. I didn't take it today. I was scared to. Because I thought maybe I should check first. Because of the, because of the mood pill. Is it okay to take both?
Nurse -> That's a smart thing to check.
Caller -> I figured. I didn't want to mess up my head. I've been doing really well for a year.
Nurse -> That's great to hear.
Nurse -> It's different medicines for different things. Celexa is for mood. Celebrex is an anti-inflammatory for pain. They're not the same, and as far as I can see in your chart, you're prescribed both. I'm going to double check with the provider just to be sure about taking them together.
Caller -> Okay. That would make me feel better. I looked it up on my phone and one site said they're fine and one site said be careful.
Nurse -> Websites can say lots of things. That's why checking is smart. How's your stomach? You said you were worried. Any stomach upset?
Caller -> A little. For three days. Since I started the Celebrex, I think. No wait. I started it Tuesday and I took the first one Wednesday. It's Friday. So three days. It's a mild queasy. Like a pit. Not terrible.
Nurse -> Okay. Mild queasiness for about three days. Have you been throwing up?
Caller -> No. Not throwing up. Just queasy. I ate toast this morning. It was okay.
Nurse -> What else did you eat today?
Caller -> Toast and a banana at breakfast. A yogurt at lunch. I wasn't very hungry. The queasy thing.
Nurse -> Okay. Are you drinking water?
Caller -> Lots. I'm trying. My sister says I drink like a camel.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you noticed black stools? Or any blood in your vomit or stool?
Caller -> No. No black. No blood. I looked. I was nervous so I looked. Everything's normal.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. How's the knee? On a scale of zero to ten?
Caller -> It's a five. It's about a five. It hurts when I bend. And at night. Ice helps. The Celebrex helped yesterday. It went down to a three for a few hours. And now it's back to a five.
Nurse -> Okay. That's pretty typical after a knee replacement. Are you doing your exercises?
Caller -> Yes. The therapist comes Tuesdays and Fridays. She was here this morning. I did my bends and the straight leg lifts. She said I'm ahead of schedule.
Nurse -> That's great. How far can you bend it?
Caller -> She measured. It was ninety degrees. I think. She said the goal is a hundred and ten by next week.
Nurse -> That's wonderful progress.
Nurse -> That's great. Okay, Yesenia. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message the provider to confirm that the Celexa and the Celebrex are okay together, and to tell them about the queasy stomach.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Will they call me?
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow morning with their answer.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What do I do tonight? If the knee hurts? Can I take the Celebrex?
Nurse -> I'd say if the knee is really bothering you, you can take the Celebrex tonight, with food. Something real. Not just toast. A sandwich or yogurt. And not more than one a day. If your stomach feels worse, hold off and wait for the call.
Caller -> With real food. Not more than one. Okay. I have yogurt. And leftover pasta.
Nurse -> Pasta is fine. And keep taking the Celexa every morning. Don't skip it.
Caller -> Celexa every morning. Okay. I won't skip. I never do. I'm good about that one.
Nurse -> Do you use a pill organizer?
Caller -> Yes. A weekly one. The Celexa goes in the morning slot. The Celebrex stays in the bottle because it's as needed.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep the Celebrex bottle in a different spot so they don't get mixed up.
Caller -> I'll put it by the bed. Celexa is in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Good. I'm also updating your medication list right now so both are listed clearly with the doses. I'll put a note about the look-alike names.
Caller -> Oh, that's smart. A note. Can you add the reason? Celexa for mood. Celebrex for the knee.
Nurse -> Yes. I'll write the reason next to each. It's done. I've updated your list with the reason beside each one.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. I'm going to put a sticker on the bottle. Celebrex, knee. Celexa, mood.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Also, please call us right away if you notice black or bloody stools, if you vomit blood, or if you get severe stomach pain. And nine one one for chest pain or trouble breathing.
Caller -> Black stool. Blood. Bad stomach pain. Chest pain. Breathing. Okay. I wrote it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Any other questions, Yesenia?
Caller -> No. I feel better. I was spinning about it. I have anxiety. That's part of why I'm on the Celexa. And when it's a new medicine I spiral.
Nurse -> That's understandable. It's good you called. We'd rather you ask.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Colin. You're very patient.
Nurse -> My pleasure. Talk to you tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Marcy.
Caller -> Marcy, hi, it's Calvin Vanterpool. It's my mother. Eudora. She's got chest tightness and she can't catch her breath. It's been like half an hour.
Nurse -> Okay, Calvin. I'm here. Is your mother awake and talking?
Caller -> She's awake. She's in her chair. She's talking but she's out of breath. She's sweaty. Her forehead is wet.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have any pain anywhere else? Her arm, her jaw?
Caller -> Her left arm. She says it aches. Down the arm. And she's sweating. She's clammy. I touched her hand and it's cold and wet.
Caller -> Should I take off her sweater? She's sweating but she says she's cold.
Nurse -> Put a light blanket over her shoulders. Don't bundle her up.
Caller -> A light one. There's the afghan on the couch. I'll get it. Hold on. Okay. It's over her shoulders.
Nurse -> Okay. Calvin, I need you to call nine one one right now. This sounds like it could be her heart.
Caller -> Her heart. Okay. Okay. Should I call you back? Or call them first?
Nurse -> Call them first. Do you have a second phone so I can stay on with you?
Caller -> There's a landline. In the hall. With the cord. I'm on my cell. Hold on. I'll put you on speaker.
Nurse -> Perfect. Put the cell on speaker where you can hear me, and call from the landline.
Caller -> Okay. It's on the chair arm. Mom, I'm calling the ambulance. Don't get up. Don't move. It's okay.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My mother is having chest pain. Chest tightness. Yes. Eighty one. Forty four Marigold Court. Marigold. M A R. Yes. She had a heart attack before. Yes. They're sending someone. She says six minutes.
Nurse -> Good. Stay on with them if they ask. Let me ask you a few things for the paramedics. Did she take anything for it?
Caller -> The nitroglycerin. The little tablet. Under the tongue. She has a bottle. She put one under her tongue about ten minutes ago. It didn't help.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she keep it with her? Is it a new bottle?
Caller -> It's in her pocket. She carries it always. It's a few months old. The pharmacist said they lose strength over time, so she gets a new one.
Nurse -> Good. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. One tablet, ten minutes ago, no relief. Is she allergic to aspirin? Does she have stomach bleeding or ulcers?
Caller -> No allergy that I know of. She takes a baby aspirin every day. No ulcers. She's never had bleeding. Mom, are you allergic to aspirin? She shakes her head. No.
Caller -> She also says she had her baby aspirin this morning. With her tea.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that. They'll want to know she already had one baby aspirin today.
Caller -> Baby aspirin this morning. Plus the big one now. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. If she's not allergic, have her chew one regular aspirin, the full strength, three twenty five, while you wait. Chew it, don't swallow it whole. Do you have one?
Caller -> I have the bottle in the cabinet. Hold on. Hold on. I'll go. Okay. I have the Bayer. Regular strength. Mom, chew this. Chew it. Okay. She's chewing. She made a face. She says it's bitter.
Nurse -> That's normal. Good. Now keep her sitting upright. Don't let her lie down flat, don't let her walk. Keep her still.
Caller -> Sitting up. Still. Okay. She wants to get up, she says she has to go to the bathroom.
Caller -> She says she feels like she might be sick to her stomach.
Nurse -> Okay. If she's nauseated, keep a bowl nearby. Stay with her.
Caller -> I'll grab the mixing bowl. It's right here on the counter.
Nurse -> No bathroom. Have her stay put. Tell her I said so.
Caller -> Mom, the nurse says stay. Okay. She's staying. She's holding my hand.
Nurse -> Good. While we wait, Calvin, I need your mother's date of birth for my notes. Do you know it?
Caller -> March twenty fifth. Nineteen forty five. I know it because it's the day before my parents' anniversary.
Nurse -> Thank you. And the number you're calling from?
Caller -> It's my cell. Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one zero.
Nurse -> Got it. Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one zero. Thank you.
Nurse -> Good. Calvin, can you take her pulse? Do you have a watch?
Caller -> I have my smart watch. I'll put two fingers. Okay. Let me count. It's fast. I'm counting for fifteen seconds. Twenty eight. Times four. A hundred and twelve.
Nurse -> Okay. A hundred and twelve. That's useful for the paramedics. Is she having any trouble speaking? Is she confused?
Caller -> No. She knows me. She knows where she is. She's scared. She keeps saying it feels like an elephant on her chest.
Caller -> She's looking at me. She's scared. Her eyes are big.
Nurse -> Hold her hand. Tell her she's doing everything right. Keep your voice low and slow.
Caller -> Mom, you're doing great. They're coming. Look at me. Breathe slow.
Nurse -> That's it. Slow breaths in through the nose.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell her I'm here and help is coming. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> No. I'll go. Hold on. I have to let go of her hand. Mom, I'll be one second. Okay. It's unlocked. I turned on the light on the porch.
Nurse -> Good. Now, is her medicine list nearby?
Caller -> It's on the fridge. A sheet. And her pill bottles are in the cabinet. I'll grab the sheet.
Nurse -> Get the sheet and the nitroglycerin bottle. When the paramedics come, hand them the sheet and tell them what time she took the nitroglycerin.
Caller -> The sheet and the bottle. And tell them the time. I wrote it on my hand. It was nine oh five. Nine oh five. Okay.
Caller -> Is there something I'm forgetting? I always forget something.
Nurse -> You're doing great. Is her purse nearby, or her insurance card?
Caller -> Her purse is by the door. I'll grab it when they come. And her glasses. She'll want her glasses.
Nurse -> Good thinking.
Nurse -> Great. Do you remember when this started?
Caller -> About eight forty five. She was making her tea. She sat down and she said she didn't feel right. And it got worse. So thirty minutes. A little over.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics eight forty five. Anything else you want me to know? Any history besides the heart attack?
Caller -> The heart attack was in two thousand nineteen. She has high blood pressure. She takes a blood pressure pill. A cholesterol pill. And the baby aspirin. That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Did anything unusual happen this morning? Any stress, any exertion?
Caller -> She was making tea. That's it. She was a bit upset about my sister's call yesterday. They had a fight. Maybe that.
Caller -> I shouldn't have said that. It's not the sister's fault.
Nurse -> Nobody is blaming anyone. Stress can sometimes bring things on, but it isn't anyone's fault.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I just feel so guilty.
Nurse -> Is there anyone who can meet you at the hospital? Another family member?
Caller -> My sister. She'll go crazy. I'll call her once Mom's in the ambulance. She lives fifteen minutes from the hospital.
Nurse -> That sounds right. Call her once they're on the way.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right.
Nurse -> Okay. Not important now. I'm going to page the on-call clinician so they know she's going to the hospital.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Marcy. Thank you.
Nurse -> Calvin, do you hear the sirens?
Caller -> Not yet. Wait. Maybe. A far one. I think I hear it.
Nurse -> What's her breathing like now?
Caller -> Same. Fast. She's trying to talk and I tell her not to. She keeps trying to tell me where her will is.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her to save her energy. There's time for that later.
Caller -> She says it's in the blue folder. I told her I know.
Nurse -> Good. Go stand at the door and wave them in. Mom will be okay for a few seconds. Tell her you're coming right back.
Caller -> Mom, I'm going to the door. I'm coming right back. Okay. I'm at the door. I see them. They turned onto the street. The lights. They're here.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let them in. Tell them everything. I'll let you go. I'll call you back in about twenty minutes. Answer if you can, even from the hospital.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you so much. Thank you.
Nurse -> You did everything right. Go be with your mom.
Caller -> Bye.
