Nurse -> Evergreen Valley Hospice, this is Hannah.
Caller -> Hi, Hannah. It's Siobhan Kearney. S I O B H A N. I'm calling about my dad. Desmond.
Nurse -> Hi, Shivon. Good to hear from you. Is everything okay?
Caller -> Oh yes. Yes. It's an update, mostly. And a question. It's nothing urgent.
Nurse -> Good. Sorry, I'm just finishing a note. Give me one second. Okay. I'm with you.
Caller -> No rush. I'm in the car, in the driveway. I didn't want him to hear.
Nurse -> Good. Let me pull up your dad's chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> January thirty first. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Perfect. And your number, Shivon?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one seven one.
Nurse -> Great. So tell me how he's been.
Caller -> He's been better. This week especially. He's eating. Last week he was barely eating, remember I called? And now he's asking for seconds. He had a whole bowl of the soup yesterday, and half a sandwich. And pudding.
Nurse -> What kind of soup?
Caller -> Chicken and rice. My neighbor brought it. Then I made vegetable. He prefers the neighbor's.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course he does.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Do you have any idea why?
Caller -> I think it's the weather. It got cooler. He likes soup season. Ha. Or it's the new spoon. I got him a bigger spoon with a fat handle. It's easier to hold.
Nurse -> Ha. A fat handle. That's a good tip. And how's he sleeping?
Caller -> Much better. He's sleeping through. Four nights in a row. He used to be up at two, three, wandering to the kitchen. Now he sleeps till six. I think the walks are helping. We do a little walk after dinner, around the yard.
Nurse -> How far does he walk?
Caller -> Around the garden. Maybe a hundred steps. He stops by the tomato plants and tells them they did a bad job this year.
Nurse -> Ha. A critic.
Caller -> Always.
Nurse -> That's great. And pain?
Caller -> Just the knees. The usual. He says they ache when it rains. It's a mild one. I'd say a two. A two or a three. He takes a Tylenol if it's bad. Five hundred milligrams. Maybe twice a day at the most. He took one last night.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol five hundred, twice a day if needed, and last night he took one. Good. Any falls?
Caller -> No falls. Not since the summer. He's careful. I hover. He doesn't love it. But no falls.
Nurse -> Hovering is good. He'll forgive you.
Caller -> He says I'm like a mother hen. I say I am his hen.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. So what's the question, Shivon?
Caller -> It's about the bath. He's having trouble getting in and out of the tub. He's unsteady. He holds on to the towel bar. And I'm afraid the towel bar is going to come off the wall. I don't have a shower chair. I'd like one. Can you get us one?
Nurse -> Absolutely. A shower chair is a good idea. Do you want a regular one, or one with a back?
Caller -> With a back. And arms if they have them. He likes to push up with his arms.
Nurse -> Okay. A chair with a back and arms. Let me put in the order. One second. Okay. I'm entering it. It's a shower chair with back and arms.
Caller -> Thank you. Is it free? I mean, covered?
Nurse -> Yes, it's covered under hospice. No cost to you.
Caller -> Oh good. I was going to buy one at the drugstore. They're sixty dollars.
Nurse -> No need. Okay. It's in. I just placed the order with the equipment company for a shower chair with back and arms.
Caller -> Oh that's quick. When will it come?
Nurse -> I'll ask them to deliver it Friday. Is somebody home Friday?
Caller -> Yes. I work from home on Fridays. I'll be here. Friday works.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll also have a nurse come see him Thursday. That's his regular visit, I think. I'll make sure it's on the schedule.
Caller -> Thursday. That's tomorrow. Yes. Marjorie comes Thursdays. She's the nurse with the red glasses.
Nurse -> Yes, that's Marjorie. She'll see him. Okay. Until the chair comes, Shivon, I'd suggest sponge baths. And if he does get into the tub, put a non-slip mat in the bottom. And stay with him whenever he stands up. Don't leave him alone in the bathroom.
Caller -> Sponge baths. Non-slip mat. Stay with him. Okay. I have a mat in the closet. It's old. I'll put it in. He won't like it. He hates sponge baths. He says I'm treating him like a baby.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him it's temporary. Just till the chair comes.
Caller -> I will. I'll bribe him with pie.
Nurse -> What kind of pie?
Caller -> Apple. From the bakery on Pine. He says it's the only thing worth leaving the house for.
Nurse -> Ha. Good motivator.
Nurse -> Pie always works.
Caller -> It does. Is there anything else I should be doing? He's doing well. I feel like I should be doing more.
Nurse -> You're doing a lot. The walks, the spoon, the mat, the call. That's a lot.
Caller -> Thanks. I'm a worrier. I read too many websites.
Nurse -> Ha. Don't read the websites. Call me instead.
Caller -> I will. I do.
Nurse -> And please call any time if he has a fall, new pain, or stops eating. Even in the middle of the night.
Caller -> Fall, new pain, stops eating. Any time. Okay. I have the number on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else, Shivon?
Caller -> Oh, one more tiny thing. Is it okay if he has a little glass of wine? With dinner? He asked. He used to have a glass of red every night.
Nurse -> A small glass is fine, if he wants it and it doesn't make him sleepy or dizzy. At this point, enjoy what you enjoy.
Caller -> Okay. I'll give him a small one. With dinner. He'll be so happy.
Nurse -> Make sure he's sitting when he drinks it.
Caller -> Of course. Thank you so much, Hannah.
Caller -> Oh wait. I forgot, my brother says hi. He's flying in on Saturday. He wants to see Dad.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Tell him we said hello.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Shivon. Have a good evening.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Summit Home Health, this is Deepa.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Deepa. I'm so glad someone's there on a Sunday. It's Gwen Ostrander. Gwendolyn. I'm calling about my husband Millard. We ran out of his Parkinson's pill. The Sinemet.

Caller -> Sorry. Hold on. I'm in the kitchen and the kettle is whistling. Let me take it off. Okay.
Nurse -> No problem.
Caller -> I make tea when I'm nervous. I've had four cups.
Caller -> So, he takes the Sinemet. The twenty five slash one hundred. One tablet, four times a day. At eight, noon, four and eight. And he took his last one yesterday at noon. And then we didn't have any.
Nurse -> Okay. So the last tablet was yesterday at noon. Twenty-some hours ago. Did you run out yesterday afternoon?
Caller -> I opened the bottle for the four o'clock one and it was empty. I thought there was more. I counted wrong. I thought I had a week left. I only had the one day. I feel so stupid.
Nurse -> Did you count the pills before this weekend?
Caller -> I did on Wednesday. I counted twelve. Then I realized the bottle had a different number on it. I think I was reading the fill count, not what was left. It's my eyes.
Nurse -> That's an easy mistake. The labels are small.
Caller -> They are so small. I use the magnifying glass now.
Nurse -> It happens. Don't beat yourself up. Did you call the pharmacy?
Caller -> I called. Yesterday. It was Saturday. They close at two on Saturdays. I called at three. They were closed. And today they're closed. Sundays. They open tomorrow at eight.
Nurse -> Is there a particular pharmacist you usually speak to?
Caller -> Oh yes. Mr. Patel. He's lovely. He knows Millard by name. But he's off on weekends. A young man was on yesterday and he wasn't much help.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Well, we'll make some calls.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you request the refill earlier this week?
Caller -> I did. On Thursday. I called it in. And they said they'd get it ready. And I went in yesterday morning, no, I called yesterday morning, and they said it needed an authorization from the neurologist. The prior auth, whatever. And they said they'd sent the request and hadn't heard back. So it wasn't ready.
Nurse -> Okay. So the refill got stuck waiting for the neurologist's office. That's frustrating.
Caller -> It is. I'm so frustrated. I've been up since five. He's so stiff.
Nurse -> Tell me about him. How is he doing right now?
Caller -> He's, I can't, he can barely move. He's in bed. He tried to get up this morning and he froze at the doorway. His feet were stuck. He couldn't move them. I had to pull him back. He was just standing there. Like a statue. And his whole body is stiff. It's like moving a plank.
Nurse -> Does that happen sometimes even with the medicine?
Caller -> Sometimes in the mornings, before the first pill kicks in. But it passes within half an hour. This is the worst I've ever seen it. It's been going on since last night.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he fall?
Caller -> No. No falls. I caught him. I'm small but I caught him. He leaned on me. We got him back to bed.
Nurse -> Good. That was the right thing. And the tremor?
Caller -> It's worse. His hand is shaking so much. He can't hold the cup. I'm holding the cup for him. His whole arm. His right arm. It's shaking like crazy.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he able to swallow okay? Any trouble with food or water?
Caller -> He's swallowing. I gave him some juice with a straw. He drank it. He said it's harder than usual. But he got it down. No choking.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is he alert? Is he making sense?
Caller -> He's alert. He's frustrated. He knows what he wants to do and his body won't. He keeps saying, I can't make my legs go. He gets angry. He cried a little.
Caller -> He hates this. He was a carpenter for forty years. He built this house with his hands. And now he can't hold a cup.
Nurse -> That's a lot to lose. I'm sorry.
Caller -> I know you are. Everyone is. It's okay. It just gets me sometimes.
Nurse -> That's very hard for him. And for you. Okay, Gwen. Here's what I'm going to do. First, I'm paging the on-call clinician right now so they know about the missed doses.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Second, I'm going to try the 24-hour pharmacy. There's one on Mill Street that has the full hours. Do you know if Millard's prescription can be filled there?
Caller -> It's on the same chain. It might be. I never used the one on Mill Street.
Nurse -> I'll call and find out. They can usually see the prescription on file. If they can fill it, can you or someone pick it up tonight?
Caller -> My son can. My son lives in town. He can drive over. He's at his place. I'll call him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me do the calls. Don't hang up your phone, I'll call you back. Actually, hold on. I can put you on hold and call from the other line. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. Yes please. I'll wait. I'll listen to the music.
Caller -> It's the jazz station. Millard's favorite. I'll put it on for him while I wait.
Nurse -> Okay. Just a minute.
Caller -> Okay. Hi, honey. No, it's just me. I'm on hold with the nurse. She's calling the pharmacy.
Caller -> Hi again. Sorry. I was talking to Millard. He says hi. He says he's sorry for the trouble.
Nurse -> Tell him it's no trouble. Okay, Gwen. I'm back. I spoke with the pharmacist at the 24-hour pharmacy on Mill Street. They have the prescription and they have the Sinemet in stock. They can fill it tonight, but they need the neurologist to approve the authorization, because the insurance won't pay without it.
Caller -> He says thank you, nurse. He says you have a kind voice.
Nurse -> That's very sweet. Tell him it's what we're here for.
Caller -> Oh. So it's still the authorization.
Nurse -> Yes. But the pharmacist told me they can give a short emergency supply, three days, without the authorization, if the prescriber verbally okays it. So I'm going to send an urgent request to the neurologist's office for the authorization, and I'm also going to ask the on-call clinician to call in that emergency supply.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds like a plan. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> I'm sending the urgent authorization request to the neurologist's office now. I've marked it urgent because he's out of the medicine.
Caller -> What if they don't answer? It's Sunday.
Nurse -> The on-call clinician can authorize the short supply. That's why I paged them. I should hear back within twenty or thirty minutes. I'll call you back as soon as I do.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. And then my son goes to the pharmacy.
Nurse -> Yes. Have him ready. Tell him to bring Millard's insurance card and his ID, in case.
Caller -> Insurance card. Where is it? In the drawer. By the phone. With the blue folder. I'll find it.
Nurse -> Good. Put it by the door so he can grab it.
Caller -> I will. Let me call him now. Can I hang up and call him?
Nurse -> Yes. Go ahead. I'll call you back. Make sure your phone is on.
Caller -> It's on. It's always on. Okay. Wait. One more thing. What do I do for Millard tonight? Until the pill comes?
Nurse -> A few things. He needs to be assisted any time he moves. Don't let him walk alone. If he needs the bathroom, use the bedside commode if you have one, instead of walking to the bathroom. Do you have one?
Caller -> We have a commode. The nurse gave us one last year. It's in the closet.
Nurse -> Good. Please get it out and put it next to the bed. It's safer than the bathroom while he's like this.
Caller -> Commode next to the bed. Don't leave him alone. Help whenever he moves. Okay. Hold on, I'll get it.
Nurse -> I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. It's out. It's by the bed. It's a little dusty. I'll wipe it off.
Caller -> Do I need a plastic bag for it? The liner? We have the liners.
Nurse -> If you have them, yes. Put one in so cleanup's easy.
Caller -> I have a whole box. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Good. And when the medicine comes, give him one tablet right away, with a little food. A cracker or some applesauce. Write down the time. Then go back to the usual schedule. Don't give him extra to make up for the missed ones.
Caller -> One tablet, with food, write the time. Not extra. Okay. Not double. I won't. I know not to.
Nurse -> It may take an hour or two to work. He might not be better right away. That's normal.
Caller -> Okay. An hour or two. I'll be patient.
Caller -> Do you think he'll be back to normal after the pill?
Nurse -> It should help a lot. He might be a little off for a day while his levels come back up. That's why we'll check on him tomorrow.
Caller -> A day. Okay. That's not so bad.
Nurse -> I'm also going to have a nurse come see him tomorrow morning, to check how he's doing and make sure there's a plan so this doesn't happen again.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Yes. I'd like that. I want to set up some kind of reminder for the refills.
Nurse -> Good idea. The nurse can help you set up auto refills.
Caller -> Good. I think my daughter said her mother-in-law has that. She never runs out of anything. Ha.
Nurse -> It really helps. We can put the reminders on your calendar too.
Caller -> Auto refills. I didn't know you could do that.
Nurse -> It's a good option. Okay. And call us right away if he falls, can't swallow, has a fever, or gets confused. And nine one one if he chokes or has trouble breathing.
Caller -> Falls, can't swallow, fever, confused. Choking or breathing, nine one one. Okay. I wrote it down on the envelope.
Nurse -> Good. Gwen, how are you? Are you getting any help?
Caller -> My son. And my daughter in Phoenix, on the phone. And a neighbor who brings dinner on Tuesdays. I'm okay. I'm tired.
Caller -> Mrs. Ruiz from next door. She makes the most wonderful tamales. She sends enough for the week.
Nurse -> That's a blessing.
Caller -> Oh, it is. I think the Lord sends her.
Nurse -> Make sure you eat something, too. And sit down for a minute.
Caller -> I had a banana. And tea. I'll have a cracker.
Nurse -> Good. I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Deepa. I'm so grateful. I was almost crying when you picked up.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for. Go call your son.
Caller -> Oh, and Deepa, thank you for not making me feel foolish about the count.
Caller -> I will. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Gwen.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harvest Home Care, this is Ellis.
Caller -> Hi, Ellis. It's Cecilia. Cecilia Marrero. I'm the night aide with Mrs. Pennington. Gladys Pennington. I'm just leaving but I wanted to call before I went home.
Nurse -> Hi, Cecilia. Thanks for calling. What's going on?
Caller -> I'm in the parking lot. I'm sitting in my car with the heater on. It's freezing out. Sorry if you hear the engine.
Caller -> It's about the nights. She's been, I don't want to say she's confused. She's not confused. She's just, she doesn't know where she is sometimes. At night.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me more about that. What happens?
Caller -> She gets up. Around two. Three. And she walks around the house. And she goes to the front door and tries the handle. And she says she's looking for Walter. That's her husband. He passed away in two thousand eleven.
Nurse -> Okay. And when you tell her he's passed, what does she do?
Caller -> She says oh. Oh right. And she cries. And then she's fine. And then she goes back to bed. And then twenty minutes later she does it again. But I don't think she's confused. I think she misses him.
Nurse -> What was he like, Walter?
Caller -> She says he was a tall man who whistled. She keeps humming a tune in the night. I don't know what it is. It sounds old.
Nurse -> That's sweet. Okay.
Nurse -> That could be part of it. Okay. How long has this been going on?
Caller -> Two nights. No wait. Three? Monday night was fine. Tuesday she did it once. Wednesday she did it three times. And last night, twice. So two nights of the bad. Or three, if you count Tuesday.
Nurse -> Okay. So it started Tuesday night or Wednesday night, and it's been getting worse.
Caller -> I guess. Yes. A little worse each night.
Nurse -> Cecilia, has anything changed in her routine, or her medicines, this week?
Caller -> Well. They started her on a sleeping pill. On Monday. For the sleep. The Ambien. Five milligrams. She takes it at nine. But I don't think it's the pill. She was having trouble sleeping, and the pill helps her fall asleep. She falls asleep fine. It's after that.
Nurse -> Okay. Ambien, five milligrams, at bedtime, started Monday. And she took it last night at nine?
Caller -> Yes. I gave it to her at nine. I wrote it on the sheet.
Nurse -> Okay. And the wandering started after she started the pill, right? Tuesday?
Caller -> I guess. But I think she just misses her husband. She's been talking about Walter all week. It's the anniversary. It's the anniversary of when he passed. It's in November.
Nurse -> That might be part of it. It might also be the pill. Sometimes a sleeping pill can make an older person more confused or wander at night. I'm not saying that's what it is, but it's something the provider should know.
Caller -> Oh. Really? I didn't know that. I thought sleeping pills were just sleeping pills.
Nurse -> A lot of people think so. They can have side effects, especially in older adults. It's good you called.
Caller -> Oh no. I hope I didn't make it worse. I gave it to her every night.
Nurse -> You gave it as prescribed. That's what you're supposed to do. Don't worry.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And how is she when she goes back to sleep? Does she settle?
Caller -> She settles. She holds my hand and she goes right off. Then she wakes up an hour later and it starts over.
Nurse -> Has she fallen? Or hurt herself? Anything like bumping into things?
Caller -> No. No falls. No injuries. I follow her around. I'm right there. She's steady. She just walks. She had a little bruise on her arm but it's from the thing with the rail, a week ago. Not from this.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Does she recognize you? Does she know you when she's up?
Caller -> Yes. She calls me Cecilia. She knows me. She says, oh Cecilia, what are you doing here. And I say, I'm keeping you company. And she says, how nice.
Caller -> Sometimes she calls me Rosa. That was her sister. But mostly Cecilia.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good for me to know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good sign. During the day, is she herself?
Caller -> During the day she's fine. She's sharp. She does the crossword. She tells me stories about her garden.
Caller -> She has roses. She says they're ready for winter. We cut them back together last week.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Nurse -> Okay. Cecilia, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to send a message to her provider this morning about the night wandering, and that it started after the Ambien.
Caller -> Okay. Good. They might change it?
Nurse -> They might. That's their decision. In the meantime, please don't give tonight's Ambien until the provider calls back. Hold it.
Caller -> Hold the pill. Okay. But she won't sleep. She'll be up all night.
Nurse -> It's possible. But I'd rather she be a little awake than more confused. And I'll make sure we call you before nine.
Caller -> Before nine. I start at eight. So I'll be there. Okay. I'll wait for the call.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse to see her tomorrow, to look at her and talk with the family.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Her daughter will want to know.
Nurse -> I'll call the daughter too. And I'll call you back this afternoon, Cecilia, with an update from the provider.
Caller -> This afternoon. I sleep in the day. But I'll keep the phone on. Call me. I'll answer.
Nurse -> Good. Now, for tonight. A few safety things. Can you put a night light in the hall and the bathroom? And is there a chime or an alarm on the front door? So you know if she opens it.
Caller -> There's a night light in the bathroom. Not the hall. I can bring one from my house. The front door, no alarm. But there's a bell. I can hang a bell on the knob. Like a Christmas bell.
Nurse -> A bell is great. And stay close to her at night. Don't sleep deep. Just doze in the chair in the hall.
Caller -> I always do. I'm a light sleeper. I'm used to it.
Nurse -> Are you getting enough rest yourself? You're up all night.
Caller -> I sleep six hours when I get home. I'm okay. I raised four kids. This is nothing.
Nurse -> Ha. Good point.
Nurse -> Good. And call us right away if she falls, gets hurt, can't be calmed down, or leaves the house.
Caller -> Falls, hurt, can't calm, leaves the house. Okay. I'll call. I have the number.
Nurse -> Perfect. Cecilia, can I get her date of birth, and your number, for my notes?
Caller -> Her birthday is May sixth. Nineteen forty two. And my cell is three one two, five five five, zero one zero three.
Nurse -> Got it. Thank you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for listening. I didn't want to get anyone in trouble.
Nurse -> No one's in trouble. You did right by Mrs. Pennington. Get some rest.
Caller -> I will. Bye, Ellis.
Nurse -> Bye, Cecilia.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sunflower Pediatric Nursing, this is Rosa.
Caller -> Hi, Rosa. It's Annika Hargrove. I'm calling about my son, Tobias Hargrove. I have two things. His cough, and the vials.
Nurse -> Hi, Annika. Let me pull up Tobias. Date of birth?
Caller -> February eighth. Twenty seventeen.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, zero one nine two.
Nurse -> Got it. Let's start with the cough. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm putting him to work. Tobias, honey, go get your inhaler. The blue one. Yes, that one. Okay.
Nurse -> No problem. Is that for later or now?
Caller -> For after dinner. He likes to line things up.
Caller -> It's worse. It's been worse for three days. It's wetter. And the stuff he coughs up is thick and yellow. Yesterday it was clear. Today it's yellow. And he coughs more at night.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he bringing it up easily?
Caller -> Sort of. He does his vest and it comes up. But it takes longer. He coughs and coughs and then it comes.
Nurse -> Does he complain of any chest pain with the coughing?
Caller -> No. He says his ribs are tired. That's how he puts it. His ribs are tired.
Nurse -> That's a good way to say it.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. His temperature this morning was ninety eight point four. And he feels fine. He's eating. He's running around. He's not breathless. He did soccer practice on Saturday.
Nurse -> That's wonderful that he can still play. Is he getting short of breath on the field?
Caller -> He gets winded a little. The coach lets him sit out for a minute. He doesn't mind.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. What about his breathing treatments? How often is he doing them?
Caller -> Four times a day. The albuterol first, then the saline, then the vest. He does it at seven, noon, four and bedtime. He did the seven this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Four albuterol treatments, and he did the morning one. Are you doing any extras for the cough?
Caller -> I did an extra saline last night, because he was coughing. And I'm almost out of the vials. That's the other thing.
Nurse -> Okay. How many saline vials do you have left?
Nurse -> Four. Four vials left in the box. And there's no more in the closet. I looked. I thought I had a second box.
Nurse -> Okay. Four vials. That's about a day and a half.
Caller -> Right. So I wanted to get ahead of it. I don't want to run out on Thursday.
Nurse -> Smart. Okay. I'm going to place the order right now. Give me a moment. I'll enter it.
Caller -> I'm placing the order for the saline vials now. A box of sixty, marked urgent, so it comes tomorrow. It's in.
Caller -> Thank you. That's great. When will it come?
Nurse -> I'll ask them to deliver it tomorrow afternoon. Is somebody home?
Caller -> Yes. Me, in the afternoon. After two. My husband gets home at five.
Nurse -> Perfect. They should call when they get there.
Nurse -> Good. Annika, now about the cough. I'm going to message his pulmonologist today about the worse cough and the thick yellow mucus. They'll probably want to see him or change something.
Caller -> Okay. Should I do something different tonight?
Nurse -> Keep doing the treatments on schedule. The vest, the saline, all of it. The extra saline you did last night is fine. Keep him drinking water.
Caller -> He drinks a lot of water. He has a big bottle.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to have a nurse come see him Thursday. That's the day after tomorrow, right?
Caller -> Thursday. Yes. That's our regular day. Is it going to be you?
Nurse -> Probably. I'll listen to his lungs and check his oxygen.
Caller -> Okay. He likes you. He says you have funny shoes.
Nurse -> Ha. They're the sparkly ones.
Caller -> Do you want me to tell the school about the cough? He has a gym class on Friday.
Nurse -> Let him do what he feels up to. If he coughs a lot, he can sit out. The school nurse can help.
Caller -> I'll let her know. She's good about it.
Caller -> He loves the sparkly ones.
Nurse -> Annika, one thing about the vials and the nebulizer. After every treatment, wash the cup and the mouthpiece with warm soapy water, rinse well and let them air dry. And use a fresh vial each time. Don't reuse the leftover.
Caller -> Wash the cup, mouthpiece, air dry. Fresh vial each time. I do. Mostly. I sometimes put the leftover in the fridge for later.
Nurse -> Please don't. Throw the leftover away. Bacteria can grow in it.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. I thought that was okay. The one nurse said it was okay for a few hours.
Nurse -> It's safest to use a fresh one. We have plenty coming.
Caller -> Got it. Fresh every time.
Caller -> Thanks for telling me. I'm going to put a note on the fridge. Fresh vial, every time.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Nurse -> And please call us if he gets a fever, if you see blood in the mucus, if his breathing gets fast, or his lips look blue. And call nine one one if he can't speak a full sentence.
Caller -> Fever, blood, fast breathing, blue lips. Nine one one if he can't talk in a whole sentence. Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing? Are you getting enough rest?
Caller -> I'm okay. His dad helps in the evenings. It's a lot but we're used to it.
Nurse -> And Tobias, how is he handling it? Is he in good spirits?
Caller -> He's great. He's always been. He says his lungs are just extra loud. He calls the vest his robot suit.
Nurse -> I love that. A robot suit.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job.
Caller -> Thanks, Rosa. I appreciate it. I'll wait for the delivery.
Nurse -> And I'll message the pulmonologist right away. Bye, Annika.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Maple Creek Home Health, this is Josephine.
Caller -> Hey. Hi. Yeah. Is this the nurse line? I'm Dario. Dario Whitfield. I'm one of your guys, the, I have the colostomy.
Nurse -> Hi, Dario. Yes, this is the nurse line. I'm glad you called. Let me pull up your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> April twenty second. Nineteen seventy four.
Nurse -> Perfect. I think I have a number on file for you. Is it nine zero one, five five five, zero one two seven?
Caller -> That's my cell. Yep. Don't call it between one and one thirty, I'm on the floor. I mean, I'm on lunch right now. I'm in the break room.
Nurse -> Noted. I'll try to reach you outside your shift if I need to.
Caller -> Evenings are best. After six. I'm usually home eating something out of a box.
Nurse -> Got it. Not during the shift. What can I do for you?
Caller -> I'm running low. On my stuff. The pouches. I only have like three left. And the wafers. I think five. And I'm out of the wipes. The remover wipes. I've been using a washcloth and it's not great.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me write those down. Three pouches?
Caller -> Three. Let me count again. I'm looking in my bag. I keep a spare kit in my locker. One, two, three. Three pouches. Yeah. And I have more at home. Hold on. No, that's the same three. I took them from home.
Nurse -> So three pouches total. Okay. And the wafers?
Caller -> Five wafers. I changed the wafer this morning so that's one used. I have five new ones. Yeah. Five.
Nurse -> Okay. And the adhesive remover wipes?
Caller -> None. Zero. I used the last one Sunday. I've been peeling the wafer off. I know I'm not supposed to. It hurts.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll fix that. So three pouches, five wafers and no wipes.
Caller -> Correct. And before you ask, yeah, I know. I should've called last week. I just didn't want to deal with it.
Nurse -> Does anyone at work know about the colostomy?
Caller -> My boss. That's it. I don't tell the guys. It's none of their business. I carry a bag with my stuff and say it's my lunch.
Nurse -> That's your choice. You're doing fine.
Nurse -> It's okay. It happens. What happened with your regular order? Usually it comes monthly, right?
Caller -> It does. It came on the fifth. Always the fifth. This month it didn't come. I called the company, and they said they changed suppliers. And that the new supplier has my info but it'll take a few weeks. And I said I don't have a few weeks.
Caller -> They put me on hold for forty minutes. The music was terrible. I almost hung up twice.
Nurse -> Ugh. I'm sorry. We'll sort it out from here.
Nurse -> Okay. That's frustrating. We'll get you what you need today.
Caller -> That'd be great. I'd really appreciate it.
Nurse -> Now, you mentioned peeling the wafer. How's the skin around your stoma?
Caller -> It's not great. It's red. Kind of sore. Around the edge where the wafer sits. Like a ring. It stings when I take the wafer off. It's not bleeding. It's not open. But it's red and angry.
Nurse -> Have you used anything on it? A cream, powder?
Caller -> My sister gave me a diaper rash cream. I put a thin layer. I don't know if I should have.
Nurse -> A lot of creams stop the wafer from sticking. The nurse will look. Don't put anything else on it for now.
Caller -> Okay. No more cream. Noted.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it itchy, burning?
Caller -> A little burning. Right when I peel. And then it calms down. It's mostly just red.
Nurse -> Okay. Any leaking? Does the wafer stay on?
Caller -> It stays on. I get about three, four days. No leaks. Well, one leak last Saturday. A little. But that's because I got sweaty. I was moving furniture.
Nurse -> What were you moving?
Caller -> A couch. My nephew's. Up four flights. My back is still mad at me.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a lot of stairs. Try not to lift heavy things, with the stoma.
Caller -> I know, I know. The doctor said no more than twenty pounds. I may have ignored that.
Nurse -> That can happen. Any blood from the stoma, or around it?
Caller -> No blood. Just a tiny bit of pink on the wafer when I peel it. Not blood really. Just the skin.
Nurse -> And your output? Is that normal for you?
Caller -> Normal. Same as always. Regular. I eat the same stuff. I'm not having diarrhea or anything. It's fine. It's been fine.
Nurse -> Good. Okay, Dario. Let me place the order. Give me a minute. Stay on, okay?
Caller -> Yep. I'm just sitting here. Oh, sorry, hold on. Hey! Hey, I'm on the phone. Yeah. Five minutes. Sorry. That's my supervisor. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Do you need to go?
Caller -> No, no. He says five minutes. I told him I'm on a medical call. He's cool about it.
Nurse -> No problem. Okay. I'm ordering a box of thirty pouches, a box of the wafers, and two boxes of the adhesive remover wipes. I'm marking it urgent.
Caller -> Thirty pouches. That's like a month. Good.
Nurse -> And I'm adding a barrier ring and some skin barrier powder, since your skin is irritated. If you don't mind.
Caller -> I don't mind. I've never used the powder. What is it?
Nurse -> It helps protect the skin. We'll go over it. It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for the pouches, wafers, and the wipes, marked urgent.
Caller -> Oh man. Thank you. That's a load off. When will it get here?
Nurse -> I'm going to arrange for delivery to your house tomorrow evening. Will somebody be home?
Caller -> I'm home after five. Anytime after five thirty. I live in an apartment, though. Third floor. No elevator. The delivery guy hates it.
Nurse -> Is there somewhere safe to leave a package downstairs if you're not there?
Caller -> There's a mailroom with a lockbox. But I'd rather be there. It's medical stuff.
Nurse -> I'll note the third floor. I'll ask them to deliver tomorrow evening, after five thirty, and to call you when they're on the way.
Caller -> That's great. Seriously. I was getting kind of stressed about it.
Nurse -> I understand. Dario, I'd also like a nurse to look at the skin. I'll send someone Friday. Is there a good time?
Caller -> Friday. I'm off Friday. Anytime. Morning's best. I sleep in, so after nine.
Nurse -> After nine on Friday. I'll put that in. She'll check the skin, the stoma, and show you a few tips.
Caller -> Okay. Cool. I'll make coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. She won't need coffee, but she'll take it.
Caller -> Everybody takes coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. Between now and then, here's what I'd do for the skin. When you change the wafer, use a remover wipe, which you'll have tomorrow. Until then, use warm water and a soft cloth to loosen the edge. Then push the skin away from the wafer. Don't peel the wafer off the skin.
Caller -> Push the skin away. Not peel the wafer. Okay. So like hold the skin down and the wafer comes up.
Nurse -> Exactly. Slowly. Then clean around the stoma with plain water only, no soap with lotion, and pat it dry. Let it air dry for a minute before putting on a new wafer.
Caller -> Plain water. Pat dry. Air dry. Got it. I use the baby wipes. Is that bad?
Nurse -> Skip those for now. They can have oils that stop the wafer from sticking.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. That might be my problem. I've been using them for weeks.
Nurse -> That might be part of it. Plain water and a soft cloth is best.
Caller -> I'll go with that. Oh, and I'll stop peeling. I'm an idiot.
Nurse -> You're not an idiot. You were without the right supplies.
Caller -> Ha. True. Thanks.
Nurse -> Also, call us if the skin gets broken, bleeding, or really painful, if there's a bad smell, if the leaking won't stop, or if you have no output for a day with belly pain or vomiting.
Caller -> Broken skin, bleeding, pain, smell, leaking, no output with pain or throwing up. Okay. That's a list. I'll remember the throwing up one.
Nurse -> Good. Any other questions?
Caller -> Not really. Oh. Can I still go swimming? My buddy invited me to a lake thing this weekend.
Nurse -> With the skin like that, I'd wait until the nurse looks at it on Friday. Then she can tell you if the wafer will hold up in the water.
Caller -> Yeah, that's what I figured. Bummer. Okay. I'll wait.
Nurse -> A lake in October. Brave.
Caller -> It's heated. It's a hot tub situation. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Even more reason to wait.
Caller -> Yeah, yeah. Okay. Thanks, Josephine. You made my day easier.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Dario. Go finish your lunch.
Caller -> Will do. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Gentle Hands Hospice, this is Walter.
Caller -> What? Hello? Is this Gentle Hands? Speak up, dear, I can't hear you very well.
Nurse -> Yes, this is Gentle Hands Hospice. This is Walter, the nurse. Can you hear me better now?
Caller -> Oh, that's better. Hello, Walter. This is Agnes. Agnes Thibodeaux. T H I B O D E A U X. It's a French name. From Louisiana.
Nurse -> Hi, Agnes. Nice to hear from you. Is everything all right?
Caller -> Oh yes. Everything is fine. I just wanted to call and tell you how I am. Nobody called me so I called you. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best kind of call. I'm glad you did.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. Let me pull up your chart. Can you tell me your birthday?
Caller -> My birthday? July seventeenth. Nineteen thirty three. I'm ninety three. Can you believe it?
Nurse -> Ninety three. That's wonderful. And your phone number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Six oh two. Five five five. Zero one seven two. It's the house phone. I have a cell but I don't know how to work it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Six oh two, five five five, zero one seven two. Okay, Agnes. Tell me how you've been feeling.
Caller -> Better. I feel better. Stronger. Last week I was so weak. I couldn't get up from the chair. And this week, I made my own toast. I stood at the counter. And I ate a whole egg. And a piece of pie.
Nurse -> That's great news. A whole egg and pie.
Caller -> Lemon meringue. My neighbor Dolores made it. She knows it's my favorite. My husband, Rene, God rest him, he was a baker. Had a bakery on Magazine Street for thirty one years. He made the best lemon meringue. Oh, I miss that pie.
Nurse -> What was in his meringue?
Caller -> Oh, it was a secret. He never told anyone. Not even me. Maybe a little vinegar. I never found out.
Nurse -> A baker's secret.
Caller -> The best kind.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful. A bakery for thirty one years.
Caller -> Thirty one. He got up at three every morning. Three in the morning. I don't know how he did it. I'd hear the alarm and roll over.
Caller -> I'd say, Rene, five more minutes. And he'd say, Agnes, the bread doesn't wait.
Nurse -> Ha. He sounds like a character.
Nurse -> Ha. Sounds like a hard worker.
Caller -> Oh, he was. He was a good man. Now, what was I saying?
Nurse -> You were telling me you feel stronger.
Caller -> Stronger. Yes. And my appetite. It's good. And my sleep. I sleep okay. I wake up once. For the bathroom. And I go right back.
Nurse -> Do you use the walker at night when you go to the bathroom?
Caller -> I do. I keep it right by the bed. And the little light. Dolores plugged it in for me.
Nurse -> Good. That's safe.
Nurse -> That's good. What about your ankles? Any swelling?
Caller -> My ankles? Oh, they're the same. A little puffy. Not worse. Not better. About the same. They swell more in the afternoon and go down at night.
Nurse -> Okay. Same as last week. Are you taking your water pill?
Caller -> My water pill. Yes. The furosemide. Twenty milligrams. Every morning with my coffee. I took it this morning. Before the toast.
Nurse -> Perfect. Agnes, how many tablets do you have left?
Caller -> Let me look. Hold on. I'll get the bottle. It's on the kitchen table. Hold on. Don't go anywhere. I'm walking. I'm using the walker. It takes me a minute.
Caller -> Dolores says I should get one of those scooters. I said I'm not that old.
Nurse -> Ha. You're doing great with the walker.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'll be here.
Caller -> Okay. I'm at the table. Where are my glasses? Oh, they're on my head. Ha. Okay. It says. It says. Furosemide. Twenty milligrams. Take one tablet by mouth every morning. And I count. One, two, three, four, five. Five tablets.
Nurse -> Five tablets. Okay. So that's five days. I'll ask the provider for a refill today.
Caller -> Oh good. That's what I was hoping you'd say. I didn't want to run out. Last time I ran out my ankles were like melons.
Nurse -> Ha. We don't want that. I'll send the refill request right now.
Caller -> Thank you, dear. And what else? Oh. Tired. I'm a little tired in the afternoon. I get tired around two. I take a nap in the chair. And then I'm fine. It's not bad tired. It's just old tired.
Nurse -> What do you do in the afternoons when you're tired?
Caller -> I watch my stories. Two of them. Then I doze. Then I wake up and I don't know what happened.
Nurse -> Ha. That happens to me too.
Nurse -> That's pretty normal. Are you having any chest pain? Shortness of breath?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. I don't get short of breath unless I do the stairs. And I don't do the stairs. The bedroom is downstairs. They moved it.
Caller -> My son and his boy moved the bed. Two summers ago. I said I'd never sleep in the dining room. Now I love it. I can see the garden from the bed.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Nurse -> Good. That's a good setup. Agnes, you mentioned a visit. Thursday?
Caller -> Thursday. Yes. The nurse comes on Thursdays. The tall one. With the nice shoes. Is she still coming at ten?
Nurse -> Let me check the schedule. Yes. I see it here. Thursday at ten. That's still the plan.
Caller -> Ten o'clock. Good. I'll be up. I'll put on a dress. She likes it when I put on a dress.
Nurse -> Ha. She'll love it.
Caller -> I'll wear the blue one. And I'll put my hair up.
Caller -> I haven't had it done in a month. Dolores does the curlers. She's very good. A little heavy on the spray.
Nurse -> Ha. A little spray is fine.
Nurse -> Perfect. Agnes, a couple of tips. If you can, weigh yourself each morning on your scale and write it down. If you notice you've gained a couple of pounds in a day or two, tell the nurse.
Caller -> Weigh myself. I have a scale. It's in the bathroom. I'll try. It's hard to get on it. I have to hold the sink.
Nurse -> Only if it's safe. Hold on tight. Or have Dolores help.
Caller -> Dolores could help. She comes by every day. She brings me the paper.
Nurse -> That's nice. And in the afternoon, when your ankles are puffy, put your feet up on the footstool and rest when you're tired.
Caller -> Feet up. I do that. In the chair with the footstool. Rene made that footstool. Out of cypress. It's sturdy.
Nurse -> That's lovely. A good keepsake.
Caller -> Oh, it is. I won't give it up.
Nurse -> Anything else you wanted to tell me?
Caller -> No, dear. That's all. I just wanted somebody to know I was okay. I get lonely sometimes. You know. In the afternoon.
Nurse -> Do you get to see anyone besides Dolores?
Caller -> My son comes Sundays. He brings the grandkids. They climb all over me. It's wonderful.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful. Sundays are good.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm glad you called. You can call any time.
Caller -> Thank you. You have a nice voice. You sound like my grandson.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a compliment. Take care, Agnes. See you Thursday, well, Marcy will see you Thursday.
Caller -> Marcy. That's her name. Thank you. Goodbye, Walter.
Nurse -> Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Joel.
Caller -> Hi. Hi there. I'm not sure who I need to talk to. My mother passed away a few weeks ago, with you. And the insurance company is asking for a copy of her records.
Nurse -> I'm sorry for your loss. For records, you'll want our medical records office. It's a separate department.
Caller -> Okay. Do you have their number?
Nurse -> I can give it to you. It's the main number and then option four. Do you have a pen?
Caller -> I do. Go ahead.
Nurse -> It's eight hundred, five five five, zero one nine zero. Then press four.
Caller -> Eight hundred, five five five, zero one nine zero. Four. Okay.
Nurse -> They're open Monday to Friday, nine to four. They'll ask for her name and date of birth and your relationship to her.
Caller -> Do I need to bring anything? Do I have to come in?
Nurse -> Usually you'll need to fill out a request form, and show an ID and proof you're the executor or next of kin. They can often email or mail the records.
Caller -> Proof. I have the letter from the court. The probate letter. Will that work?
Nurse -> That should be the right document. They'll tell you for sure.
Caller -> Good. I was worried it'd be a whole thing.
Nurse -> It can be a little paperwork. But they're helpful.
Caller -> How long does it take?
Nurse -> I think five to ten business days. They can tell you.
Caller -> That's fine. The insurance company said thirty days. So we have time.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anything else I can help you with?
Caller -> No. I just wanted to say, you all were wonderful to her. The nurses. The aide, Brenda. They were so kind. I wanted to thank somebody.
Nurse -> That means a lot. I'll pass it along to the team. I'm sorry again for your loss.
Caller -> Thank you. She was ninety one. She had a good life. Thank you, dear.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself.
Caller -> I will. Goodbye.
Nurse -> Goodbye.

not_applicable.reason: Administrative request for copies of medical records with no clinical content.

transcript:
Nurse -> Compass Hospice, this is Nadia.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Nadia. This is Imelda Achebe. I'm calling about my dad. Leopold Achebe. I'm not sure if this is the right thing to call about.
Nurse -> Hi, Imelda. Thanks for calling. You can call about anything. What's on your mind?
Caller -> Last night my dad said something. And I can't stop thinking about it. He said he's thinking about taking all his pills. To end it.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called. Take a breath. I'm going to ask some questions, and we'll go through this together. First, can I get your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> December third. Nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one eight two.
Nurse -> Got it. Is your dad home right now? Where is he?
Caller -> He's here. He's in the den. He's watching the TV. I'm in the kitchen. I came in here so he wouldn't hear me.
Nurse -> That was thoughtful. Is the TV loud enough that he won't hear you?
Caller -> It's a game show. It's loud. He has the hearing aids out. I'm fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me exactly what he said last night, as best you remember.
Caller -> We were sitting at the table after dinner. He wasn't eating. And he said, I've been thinking about taking all my pills. And ending it. Just like that. And then I looked at him and he laughed. He said, I'm kidding. Don't look at me like that. But he didn't sound like he was kidding.
Nurse -> What did you say to him?
Caller -> Nothing. I froze. I got up and I cleared the dishes. I didn't know what to say.
Nurse -> That's very normal. Most people freeze.
Nurse -> Okay. That must have been scary. You're right to take it seriously.
Caller -> I didn't sleep. I kept thinking about it. I kept getting up to check on him.
Caller -> I stood at his door at two. And at four. I could hear him breathing. It was okay. I just stood there.
Nurse -> That must have been exhausting.
Nurse -> That makes sense. Has he said anything like that before?
Caller -> Not like that. He's said he's tired. He's said he's ready to go. He said that a lot in the spring after Mom died. But not about the pills. Not about doing it himself.
Nurse -> Okay. How has he been this past week? Tell me about his mood.
Caller -> He's quiet. He's withdrawn. He doesn't want to talk. He stays in the den. He doesn't want his friend to visit. The friend from church, Mr. Okoro. He told me to tell him not to come. And he's not eating much. He's not himself.
Nurse -> Okay. About a week of that?
Caller -> About a week. It started after the anniversary. It was a month since Mom died on the twenty fourth. And then it was Halloween week and she loved Halloween. She decorated the whole porch. Every year. And this year I didn't. I couldn't. I think that hit him.
Nurse -> That makes sense. The holidays and the anniversaries can be hard.
Caller -> She would have decorated the whole house by now. Spider webs. The inflatable ghost.
Nurse -> It sounds like she brought a lot of joy.
Caller -> She did. She really did.
Nurse -> That's a lot of grief. For you both. Imelda, I'm sorry about your mom.
Caller -> Thank you. It's been hard. She died in April. April eleventh.
Nurse -> Okay. Your dad lives with you?
Caller -> He moved in with me when she got sick. In February. It's me and him and my teenager. My husband works nights.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me ask something directly, because it's important. Do you know if he's done anything to hurt himself? Has he taken extra pills? Any pills missing?
Caller -> No. No. I checked. I counted. I counted the morphine and the others this morning while he was in the shower. Everything's there. Nothing's missing. He hasn't done anything. I would know. I do his pills.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Where does he keep his medicines?
Caller -> In the nightstand. In his bedroom. The drawer. There's the pill bottles, all of them, and the liquid morphine. The whole bottle. It's on the top. I do his doses but the bottles stay in the drawer.
Nurse -> Okay. And does he know where they are, obviously. And he could get to them.
Caller -> Yes. He could. They're right there. I never thought about it.
Nurse -> Have you ever had guns or anything else in the house that he could reach?
Caller -> No. My husband never wanted guns. Just the kitchen knives. And the garage tools.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me.
Nurse -> That's okay. You didn't have a reason to before. We'll fix that. Imelda, I'm going to ask a few more things, and then I'll tell you what we're going to do. Is your dad having any pain right now?
Caller -> He says no. He says his breathing is the same. He's got the oxygen on. He hasn't complained about pain.
Nurse -> Okay. And has he said anything else about wanting to die, or about being a burden?
Caller -> He said he's a burden. He says I shouldn't have to take care of him. He says I should be with my kids. I told him he's not a burden. He just shakes his head.
Nurse -> Has he said what he wants for the days ahead?
Caller -> He wants to stay home. He said that. He said he doesn't want to go to a hospital or a home. He wants to be here, with the kids.
Nurse -> That's what we're here to help with.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. What I'm going to do now is page the on-call clinician right away, so they know what he said and so they can talk with him.
Caller -> Okay. Will they take him away?
Nurse -> No. They won't take him anywhere. Our job is to keep him comfortable at home. But we want to understand what he's feeling and support him. The clinician might want to talk with him by phone.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine. I don't want him to be sent anywhere. He'd hate that.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm also going to send a nurse to see him, within two hours. She'll talk with him and with you.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'd like our social worker and our chaplain to come visit today. They're very good at this. They can talk with your dad about grief and about how he's feeling. And they can talk with you, too.
Caller -> Mr. Okoro is his friend. The chaplain would be like a stranger. Will he talk to them?
Nurse -> Some people do and some don't. Sometimes it's easier to talk to a stranger. We can ask him. He can say no.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask him. I'll tell him it's okay to say no.
Nurse -> And Imelda, if he does want to talk to someone, the chaplain doesn't have to talk about religion. Some just listen.
Caller -> That would suit him. He's not a talker. But he listens.
Nurse -> That's a good approach. Now, Imelda, a few things for today. First, can you put his pill bottles and the morphine somewhere safe? A lockbox if you have one. Or put them in your room, in a drawer or a closet that he can't easily get to. And you give him his doses yourself.
Caller -> I have a lockbox. For my husband's tools. I can empty it. I'll put the pills in there. And the key goes on my keychain.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Do it today. Right after this call, if you can. And try not to leave him alone for long stretches today.
Caller -> Okay. My teenager is home. She's in her room. I can ask her to sit with him. She loves her grandpa.
Nurse -> That would be great. Just having someone around helps. Not to watch him, just to be there.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask her to bring her homework to the den.
Caller -> She'll complain. But she'll do it. She has a physics test. She can study in there.
Nurse -> Perfect. A quiet study partner.
Nurse -> Good. I also want you to have a phone number. If you ever feel overwhelmed, or he does, you can call or text nine eight eight, any hour. It's the crisis line. It's for him, and for you.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay. I didn't know it was for family.
Nurse -> It is. It's for anyone who is struggling or worried about someone.
Caller -> I'll write it down. I'm putting it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. And if he takes extra pills, or tries to hurt himself, or says he's about to, call nine one one right away. Don't wait for us.
Caller -> Nine one one. If he takes extra, tries to hurt himself, says he's about to. Okay. I don't think he will. But I'll remember.
Nurse -> I hope he won't. But we plan for the worst. How are you doing, Imelda?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm shaking. I haven't slept. I'm so tired.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. You noticed, you counted the pills, you called. That's exactly what to do.
Caller -> Thank you. I just feel so guilty. I should have seen how bad it was.
Nurse -> You saw it. That's why you called. Grief is hard to see inside of. You can't blame yourself.
Caller -> I'll try not to. My husband says the same thing.
Nurse -> He's right. I'm going to call you back in twenty minutes, after I talk to the clinician.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. I'll go get the lockbox now.
Nurse -> Do that. I'll talk to you soon.
Caller -> Thank you, Nadia. Thank you for taking me seriously.
Nurse -> Of course. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Pediatric Home Care, this is Candace.
Caller -> Candace, hi. I need to tell somebody something. I gave Jasper the wrong insulin.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm here. Let's slow down. Who is this?
Caller -> It's Dahlia. Dahlia Montague. D A H L I A. Jasper's mom. Jasper Montague. He's fourteen.
Nurse -> Dahlia, D A H L I A. Got it. And Jasper, J A S P E R, right?
Caller -> Yes. Like the park. Like Jasper National Park. My husband picked it.
Nurse -> Okay, Dahlia. Thank you. What's Jasper's date of birth?
Caller -> August thirtieth. Two thousand twelve.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one zero one.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me exactly what happened.
Caller -> So at dinner I drew up his insulin. He gets the Humalog with meals. Five units. And I drew it up and I gave it. And then I went to put the vial back in the fridge and it said Humulin. Humulin R. The regular one. The one from his grandfather's. I had grabbed the wrong vial. They're in the same drawer.
Nurse -> Okay. So you gave five units of Humulin R instead of five units of Humalog.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Five units. Of the wrong one. I'm so upset.
Nurse -> Take a breath. You're doing the right thing by calling right away.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm breathing. In. Out.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me right away. What time was the shot?
Caller -> It was six thirty. It's seven thirty now. About an hour ago. Maybe a little more.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a pump or injections?
Caller -> Injections. Pens for the long acting at night, and vials and syringes for the mealtime ones. He's on the vials because the pens kept breaking.
Nurse -> Okay. About an hour ago. And his usual Humalog is how many units with dinner?
Caller -> It's five tonight. Five units, because he ate a normal dinner. Sometimes it's six. His plan is on the fridge.
Caller -> The plan has a table. For the carbs. Sixty grams, five units. Seventy five, six units. I follow the chart. I'm very careful. This is the first time in two years.
Nurse -> Okay. So the dose was the right number, just a different insulin. Humulin R acts slower than Humalog and lasts longer. That's why we want to watch him tonight. How was his sugar?
Caller -> Before dinner it was one sixty eight. And I just checked it. It's one fifty. It went down a little.
Nurse -> Okay. One fifty. Thank you for checking. How's he feeling? Is he shaky, sweaty, confused, hungry?
Caller -> No. No. He's fine. He's playing video games. He's laughing. He's yelling at his friend through the headset. He's not shaky. No sweat. He's himself.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. What did he have for dinner?
Caller -> Pasta. Chicken. Garlic bread. A salad. And some ice cream. He had a normal dinner. I counted the carbs. Sixty grams.
Nurse -> Did he do any exercise after dinner?
Caller -> No. He's been on the couch. He did soccer this afternoon, a practice. Before dinner. That's probably why his sugar was a little lower.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Exercise can lower sugar later too. I'll tell the clinician.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. So he has some food on board. Dahlia, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so they can give us instructions for tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Do I need to go to the hospital?
Nurse -> Not right now. He's feeling fine and his sugar is okay. But I want the clinician to weigh in. Meanwhile, please do not give any more Humalog tonight, even for a snack, until the clinician says.
Caller -> No more Humalog. Okay. He usually has a snack at nine. Do I still give the snack?
Nurse -> If he's hungry, he can have a snack, but no insulin for it. Let's wait for the clinician.
Caller -> No insulin for the snack. Okay.
Caller -> What if he says he's low? Before the call? Should I call you back?
Nurse -> Yes, call right away. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in an hour.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. And until then?
Nurse -> I want you to check his sugar every hour until I call, and then every two hours through the night. Write down each number with the time. Can you set an alarm on your phone?
Caller -> Every hour. Then every two. Write it down. I'll set an alarm. Yes. I'm setting it. For eight thirty. Nine thirty.
Nurse -> Good. And if the sugar is under seventy, give him fifteen grams of fast sugar. Juice, glucose tablets. Then recheck in fifteen minutes. And call nine one one if he's unresponsive or has a seizure.
Caller -> Under seventy. Fifteen grams. Juice. Recheck in fifteen minutes. Nine one one if he's out or seizing. Okay. We have glucose tabs. In the drawer. I'll put them next to his bed.
Nurse -> Good. And keep the juice in the fridge, in case.
Caller -> We have apple juice boxes. Four of them.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I've never done this. In two years.
Nurse -> It happens to everybody. The vials are easy to mix up. After this, I'd suggest putting the Humulin in a different spot. Or taking it out of the house if it's not being used.
Caller -> I'll take it to my dad. Or throw it away. Yeah. I'll put it in a bag and get it out of the fridge tonight.
Nurse -> Good idea. Just don't do it now. Stay with Jasper.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do it later.
Nurse -> How's his mood about it? Does he know?
Caller -> I told him. He said it's okay, Mom. He said it's the same number of units. He's very calm. He's more calm than me.
Nurse -> That's a great kid. How long has he been managing his own sugar?
Caller -> He checks it himself since twelve. I still do the shots, mostly. He's learning.
Nurse -> Good. He'll be fine tonight with your help.
Nurse -> Good. Let him help keep an eye on himself. He can tell you if he feels funny.
Caller -> I told him to tell me if he feels shaky or weird. He said okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll talk to you in an hour.
Caller -> Thank you, Candace. Thank you.
Nurse -> Bye, Dahlia.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Orchard Park Home Health, this is Felix.
Caller -> Hi, Felix. It's Cassidy. Cassidy Oyelaran. I'm calling about my grandma. Bernadette. She's one of your patients.
Nurse -> Of course. How old is she now?
Caller -> Eighty five. She'll say eighty five and a half. She's very particular.
Nurse -> Hi, Cassidy. Let me find Bernadine. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> It's Bernadette. B E R N A D E T T E. March eighth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> Sorry about that. Bernadine, Bernadette. Okay, I have her. And a number to reach you at?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one nine four. It's my cell.
Nurse -> And is Cassidy your first name or a nickname?
Caller -> It's my first name. C A S S I D Y. Like the singer's last name. Almost.
Nurse -> Got it. Cassidy.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's going on with your grandma?
Caller -> So, the clinic called. The coagulation clinic. The one that checks her blood. They called the house this morning and I answered because I live with her. And they said her number was too high. And that I should call somebody. They said talk to her nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. Did they say what the number was?
Caller -> They said her INR was for point to. For point to. That's what it sounded like. And I was like, what?
Nurse -> Was it a nurse or a pharmacist who called?
Caller -> A nurse. Her name was Lindy, I think. Or Mindy. She had a very fast voice. She talked really fast and I was writing and my pen died.
Caller -> I asked her to repeat it twice. She sighed. I felt like I was being a pest.
Nurse -> You weren't. You were being careful.
Nurse -> Ha. The pen. Okay.
Nurse -> Sorry, I'm not sure I caught that. Did you say four point two?
Caller -> Four point two. Yes. Four point two. I wrote it on the back of an envelope. Four point two.
Nurse -> Okay. Four point two. That's higher than her target. What is her target, do you know?
Caller -> Two to three, they said. So it's high. They said she was in the range last time. Two point six.
Caller -> It's weird. She's been so stable. For two years. The same dose. And now suddenly.
Nurse -> It happens. Little things can change it. Food, medicines, how she's eating.
Caller -> She hasn't been eating much. This week. She said her stomach was off because of the antibiotic.
Nurse -> That can also affect the number. I'll let the clinic know.
Nurse -> Okay. So she's gone up quite a bit. Cassidy, what blood thinner does she take?
Caller -> The Cumadin. She takes the Cumadin. It's the little pill. The five milligram one. It's peach colored. At five o'clock every evening. She took it last night at five.
Nurse -> Okay. Cumadin, five milligrams, every evening at five. And she took last night's. Did she miss any doses, or take extra, that you know of?
Caller -> No. I give it to her myself. No missed. No extra. Well, one time last week she asked for another one because she forgot she took it. But I said no. So no extra.
Caller -> She gets confused about the pills sometimes. That's why I do them. She used to do the pillbox herself. We took that over after Easter.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good decision.
Nurse -> Okay. That was the right call. Has anything changed with her diet, or other medicines? Any antibiotics?
Caller -> Antibiotics. Hmm. She had that cough last week. Her doctor gave her something. A Z pack. Azithromycin. She finished it Tuesday.
Nurse -> Anything else new? Over-the-counter things, like aspirin, or herbal teas, or vitamins?
Caller -> She takes a vitamin. The senior kind. And a fish oil. For her joints. She started the fish oil a month ago.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll mention the fish oil too.
Caller -> Should I stop it?
Nurse -> Let the clinic decide. Don't change anything on your own.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> Okay. That could play a part. Antibiotics can raise the number. I'll mention it to the clinic.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't think of that. I didn't know that.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. A lot of people don't. Now, Cassidy, let's talk about how she's doing. The clinic mentioned a number but did she have any bleeding?
Caller -> Yes. A nosebleed. This morning. It started when she was brushing her teeth. Out of her left side. And it bled for about ten minutes. I held a tissue. I pinched her nose. It stopped. It was a medium one. A lot of tissues.
Nurse -> Did she feel dizzy or weak afterwards?
Caller -> A little tired. She sat down for a bit. She had some tea. She's been okay since. Not dizzy.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know.
Nurse -> Okay. Has it started again?
Caller -> No. It stopped. It's been maybe five hours. No more. Her nose is dry. She was sniffing earlier but no blood.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know.
Caller -> She hates the dry air. She keeps a glass of water by the bed and drinks it all night.
Nurse -> Good. Staying hydrated helps.
Nurse -> Okay. Any other bleeding? Gums, urine, stool?
Caller -> Her gums. A little bit of pink on the toothbrush. That's all. And she has bruises. On her arms. The forearms. New ones. Big purple ones. I noticed them when I was helping her dress. They weren't there on Sunday.
Nurse -> Okay. Both arms?
Caller -> Both. The right is bigger. Like the size of a plum. And the left has two small ones.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she bump them? Did she fall?
Caller -> No fall. She didn't fall. She bumped her arm on the counter maybe. Last week. She doesn't remember.
Caller -> She doesn't remember most of what happens. Her memory's getting worse. It's all right. She's happy.
Nurse -> That sounds like a peaceful place to be.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she hit her head? Any fall at all?
Caller -> No head bump. No fall. I would know. I'm with her all day. And her stool. It's normal. Brown. I checked. I know that's weird. But the clinic said to check. No black. No blood.
Nurse -> That's not weird. That's exactly right. Okay. Cassidy, here's the plan. First, I'm going to message the anticoagulation clinic right away and mark it urgent. I'll tell them about the nosebleed and the bruising, and the antibiotic.
Caller -> Okay. Will they change her dose?
Nurse -> They probably will. That's their decision. But until they call you, I want you to hold tonight's Cumadin. Don't give the five o'clock pill until the clinic calls and tells you what to do.
Caller -> Hold the Cumadin. Don't give it. Okay. But isn't she supposed to take it every day? Won't she clot?
Nurse -> She might need to skip a dose or two, to bring the number down. That's actually very common. Her number is high, so she's thinner than she should be. Holding one dose is safe while we wait. The clinic will tell you what to do after.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. I'll hold it. I'll write on the pillbox. Do not give. Hold. Until clinic.
Nurse -> Perfect. Also, I'll have a nurse come out tomorrow to recheck her, and maybe draw another INR if the clinic wants one.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. That's good. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning. I'll ask for early.
Caller -> Okay. Early works. I'm home.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this afternoon, after I hear from the clinic.
Caller -> This afternoon. Before five?
Nurse -> Definitely before five. That's the point.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'll keep my phone on me.
Nurse -> Now, let's talk about keeping her safe in the meantime. Use a soft toothbrush. Try an electric razor, not a blade. Avoid anything that could cause a bump or a fall. Have her wear shoes or slippers in the house.
Caller -> Soft toothbrush. She has one. An electric razor. She doesn't shave. I mean her legs. She does. With a razor. I'll switch her to the electric. Shoes or slippers. She likes her socks. I'll get the slippers with the grips.
Nurse -> The grips are perfect.
Caller -> I'll get them out of the closet.
Nurse -> Also, if she bleeds anywhere, press firmly on it for ten full minutes. Don't peek. And call nine one one if the bleeding won't stop, if she hits her head, if she has black or bloody stools, or if she vomits blood.
Caller -> Ten minutes. Don't peek. Nine one one for bleeding that won't stop, head bump, black stools, or blood vomit. Okay. I got it. I wrote it on the envelope under the four point two.
Caller -> I'm going to tape the envelope to the fridge. So anyone who comes sees it.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Nurse -> Perfect. And each day, look at her skin and her gums for new bruises or bleeding, and let the nurse know.
Caller -> Every day. Skin and gums. I'll look in the morning when I help her dress.
Nurse -> And do you have anyone to help you during the day?
Caller -> My uncle comes on Fridays. And a neighbor, Mr. Adeyemi, sits with her sometimes. I work from home. I can do most of it.
Caller -> He plays checkers with her. She always wins. He lets her.
Nurse -> Ha. Good neighbor.
Nurse -> It sounds like you've set it up well.
Nurse -> That's a good time.
Caller -> Felix, is she in danger? Right now?
Nurse -> A number of four point two isn't an emergency by itself, especially since she has no major bleeding. But it needs attention today. That's why we're acting. I think she'll be okay.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was so scared when the lady said too high.
Caller -> I called my mom. She said call the nurse. Then she said call the clinic. Then she said call the nurse again.
Nurse -> Ha. Mothers.
Caller -> I'm glad I called you.
Nurse -> I understand. It sounds scary. But you did everything right. You checked her, you called.
Caller -> She's right here. She says hello. She says tell the young man thank you.
Nurse -> Tell her thank you. And that I said to take it easy.
Caller -> She says she's been taking it easy for ninety years. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Eighty five. But okay.
Caller -> She's laughing. She likes you. She says you sound like her late husband's brother.
Nurse -> That's a compliment, I hope.
Caller -> It is. He was her favorite.
Caller -> She says she's eighty five and a half. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her that's even better.
Caller -> She just asked me what day it is. I said Wednesday. She said, the day for the doctor? I said no, Grandma, the nurse. She said oh, the nice boy.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll take it.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk to you this afternoon, Cassidy.
Caller -> One more tiny thing. Can she still have her evening tea? With the Cumadin held? She has it every night at five. It's part of the routine.
Nurse -> Tea is fine. Just not the pill. Give her the tea and a biscuit, and keep her routine the same.
Caller -> Okay. Tea and a biscuit. Good. She'll like that.
Caller -> Thanks again, Felix. Truly.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Quiet Pines Hospice, this is Tamsin.
Caller -> Hello, Tamsin. This is Everardo Ibarra. E V E R A R D O. Ibarra. I'm calling about my wife. Roslyn.
Nurse -> Hi, Mr. Ibarra. Nice to hear from you. How is Roslyn?
Caller -> Sorry, one second. The phone is on the kitchen counter and the kettle is on. Let me move to the chair. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> She's about the same. A little better and a little worse. You know how it is. I have a few things to tell you. I wrote them down. Are you ready?
Nurse -> I've got a pen. Go ahead whenever you are.
Caller -> I wrote six things. I like lists. I was a bookkeeper for forty years.
Nurse -> Then you're the right person to keep her chart.
Caller -> Ha. I do keep a binder.
Nurse -> I'm ready. Let me pull up her chart first. Can you tell me her date of birth?
Caller -> June fourteenth. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Thanks. And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one zero four. That's the house. I'm always here.
Nurse -> Perfect. Go ahead with your list.
Caller -> Number one. The coughing. She coughs when she drinks. Water, juice, coffee. Every time. She takes a sip and she coughs. It's been going on for two weeks, I'd say. At first I thought it was a cold. But there's no cold.
Nurse -> Is the cough wet or dry?
Caller -> Dry. Just a little throat clearing cough. And then she looks at me like what did I do.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she cough with food too, or just liquids?
Caller -> Mostly the liquids. The food seems okay. Applesauce is fine. Pudding is fine. Toast is harder. But drinks, yes. She coughs with the drinks.
Nurse -> What kind of cup does she use? A regular cup, a straw?
Caller -> I use a spoon, sometimes. A small spoon. And a cup with a spout. She doesn't like the spout. She says it makes her feel like a baby.
Nurse -> That's very common. We'll work on making it comfortable.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she choke? Does she turn red, or gasp?
Caller -> No choking. Not really. She coughs and clears her throat and then she's fine. She doesn't turn colors. And no fever. I took her temperature this morning. Ninety eight point two.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Number two?
Caller -> Number two. Her hip. It's the right hip. It's bothering her a little. It's a two. A two out of ten. It's been there for months, since she fell in March. It's the same. It's not worse.
Nurse -> Does she take anything for it?
Caller -> The Tylenol, now and then. Not every day. Her sister, no wait, her friend Marge, brings her a heating pad. Marge says it works. I don't know.
Nurse -> Ha. A heating pad is fine on low with a cloth between.
Nurse -> Okay. A two, same as before. Good. Number three?
Caller -> Number three. Her sleep. She's sleeping better. She sleeps through the night now. Since you all started the lorazepam. The half a milligram. At bedtime. She took it last night at nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Lorazepam half a milligram at bedtime, and she's sleeping through. Good.
Caller -> She doesn't wake up as much. She used to get up and call for her sister. Her sister has been gone for ten years. It was breaking my heart. Now she sleeps. So that's good.
Nurse -> And how are you sleeping, Mr. Ibarra?
Caller -> Oh, me? I sleep in the chair next to her. I'm not too bad. My back is not too happy. But I'm okay.
Nurse -> I'd like you to get some rest too. Which is why I'm glad about the volunteer.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Number four?
Caller -> Number four. The thickener. The powder. The packets. We're almost out. We have two packets. They're the little ones. The nurse said to use one in every drink. We go through four, five a day. So two is, what, half a day.
Nurse -> Where do you keep them? In the kitchen?
Caller -> In a drawer. Next to the spoons. With the sugar packets. Once I almost put one in my coffee. I'd have been choking.
Nurse -> Ha. Please don't.
Caller -> I won't. I labeled the drawer.
Nurse -> Okay. Two packets left. We definitely need to order more.
Caller -> Please. I didn't want to wait till we ran out. I used to run out of everything. My wife did all the ordering. Now I'm learning.
Nurse -> You're doing well. Let me place the order right now. How many do you want?
Caller -> Whatever you think. A lot. A hundred?
Nurse -> I'll order a box of a hundred packets. Hold on. I'm entering it. It'll take a minute.
Caller -> Take your time. Don't rush on my account. I have all day.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for a box of the thickener packets.
Caller -> Oh good. When do they deliver?
Nurse -> Usually within two days. I marked it urgent, so maybe tomorrow. I'll ask them to call you.
Caller -> They never call. They just leave it on the porch. But okay. As long as it comes.
Caller -> Last month the guy left it in the rain. The box was soaked. The packets were okay, but the box fell apart.
Nurse -> I'll ask them to leave it inside the door if they can. Or under the awning.
Caller -> The awning is good. I'll put a chair there to keep it dry.
Nurse -> It'll come. Mr. Ibarra, since she's coughing with thin drinks, I'd like our speech therapist to look at her swallowing. I'm going to message the therapist today about the coughing.
Caller -> A speech therapist. For her swallowing. I didn't know you had that.
Nurse -> We do. She'll watch Roslyn drink and eat and tell us what's safest.
Caller -> That sounds good. She doesn't talk much anymore. But she'll cooperate.
Nurse -> She doesn't need to talk. I'll also send a nurse to see Roslyn on Monday. That's regular visit day. She can check her swallowing and her hip.
Caller -> Monday. Okay. That's fine. I'll be here.
Nurse -> Was there a number five?
Caller -> Yes. Number five. This is the hard one. I need to go to the pharmacy. And to the bank. I haven't left the house in two weeks. And I don't want to leave her alone. And my daughter lives in Texas. And I thought, you all have volunteers. Right? Someone who could sit with her for a couple of hours?
Nurse -> That's a long time. How are you holding up?
Caller -> I'm tired. I'm okay. It's the little things. I can't get to the pharmacy, I can't get my own prescriptions. My blood pressure pills ran out last Friday.
Nurse -> Oh. That's something to take care of. Did you call your doctor?
Caller -> I called. They said come in. I can't come in. That's why I want the sitter.
Nurse -> Let's get that arranged first. Then you can go pick them up.
Nurse -> We do. We have volunteers who sit with patients so caregivers can have a break. I'd be happy to ask the volunteer coordinator to call you.
Caller -> Oh, that would be wonderful. Is it free?
Nurse -> It's part of hospice. No cost.
Caller -> No cost. God bless you. I didn't want to ask. I felt silly.
Nurse -> It's not silly. It's one of the things we're here for. You deserve a break.
Caller -> I haven't had a haircut since August. I look like a mountain man.
Nurse -> Ha. You'll be a new man.
Caller -> I'll get a shave too. Maybe. The barber, Sal, is ninety. He's still cutting.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for Sal.
Caller -> Ha. I hope so. My wife would be mad if she saw me.
Nurse -> Okay. Before we hang up, let's go over the drinks. Until the new thickener comes, use one packet in each drink, and mix it well. It should be as thick as honey. Give small sips, with her sitting all the way up. And keep her upright for thirty minutes after she eats.
Caller -> Thick like honey. Small sips. All the way up. Thirty minutes after. Okay. I do prop her up. With the pillows. But sometimes she slides down. I'll watch.
Nurse -> If she slides, sit her back up. And call us if she gets a fever, if her voice sounds wet or gurgly after drinking, if she chokes and it doesn't clear, or if she has a new cough with trouble breathing.
Caller -> Fever, wet voice, choking, trouble breathing. Okay. I'll watch. I wrote it on my list under number five.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else on your list?
Caller -> No, that was it. Oh. Number six. Thank you. That's on the list too. I wrote it at the bottom. Thank you for all your help. You and the other girls. You've been wonderful.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Mr. Ibarra. It's our pleasure.
Caller -> Tell the nurse on Monday to bring her knitting. Roslyn likes to watch her knit.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll pass that along. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye now.
Nurse -> Bye.
