transcript:
Nurse -> Meadowlight Hospice, this is Bridget.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Bridget. This is Priyanka Sethi. I'm an aide at Cedar Grove Memory Care. I'm kind of new. This is my second week.
Nurse -> Hi, Priyanka. Welcome. What can I do for you?
Caller -> Is this okay to call at this time? It's evening. I wasn't sure about the hours.
Nurse -> Absolutely. We're here all night. You can call any time.
Caller -> Oh good. They didn't tell us that at orientation. They gave us a binder but it's like three hundred pages.
Nurse -> Ha. Nobody reads the binder.
Caller -> I'm calling about one of our residents. He's one of yours. A hospice patient. He's got a skin tear. On his arm. From the bed rail.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's find him. What's the resident's name?
Caller -> That's the thing. I'm so embarrassed. I only know him as Mr. Ray. Ray. Raymond, maybe. His last name starts with a W. Something Polish. Wizniak? I don't have it. It's in the chart and the nurse took the chart with her to the other hall.
Nurse -> That's okay. Which room is he in?
Caller -> Room six. By the nurses' desk. The one with the Packers blanket.
Nurse -> A Packers blanket. Okay. That helps.
Caller -> He loves the Packers. He yells at the TV on Sundays. Mostly Cheesehead stuff. His daughter brought him the blanket.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look at our patients at Cedar Grove. Room six. I see a Raymond Wozniak. W O Z N I A K. Is that him?
Caller -> Wozniak. Yes. Wozniak. That sounds right. I think that's him. Raymond Wozniak. I think so. I'm like ninety percent.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I should know his name. I just can't pronounce half the names here. Everyone is Mr. or Mrs. something.
Nurse -> Don't worry. It takes time. You'll learn.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he around eighty eight, small man, white hair?
Caller -> Yes. White hair. He's tiny. And he has a hearing aid. The left ear.
Nurse -> That matches. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like the right gentleman. Do you happen to have his birth date?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'm sorry. It's not on the board. It's in the chart. And the chart is with the nurse. She's on break. She'll be back in twenty minutes.
Caller -> She's the one who knows everything. Her name is Gloria. She's been here twenty years. She's amazing. But she goes on break at seven and I don't want to interrupt.
Nurse -> It's fine. Just have her call us when she's back.
Nurse -> No problem. We can pull that from our end. Priyanka, what's a good number for us to reach you at?
Caller -> The second floor desk. Three one two, five five five, zero one three zero.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about the skin tear.
Caller -> So I was turning him. We turn him every two hours. And he moved. He's confused. He tried to roll himself. And his arm caught on the rail. The metal part. And it scraped. And it tore. A piece of skin came up. Like a flap.
Nurse -> What color is the area around it? Is it red, or just the tear?
Caller -> It's red right around the edge. A little. And there's a little bruise coming. Purple around it. Like a half inch.
Nurse -> Okay. That's normal with a skin tear.
Nurse -> Okay. Where on the arm?
Caller -> The right forearm. About here. Between the wrist and the elbow. On the outside. It's about two inches long. I measured with my finger. Two finger widths, no. Two inches. A long one.
Nurse -> Okay. Two inches. Is the flap still attached?
Caller -> It's attached. On one side. I put it back down. Like a flap of paper. Is that okay? I wasn't sure.
Nurse -> That's exactly right. You did it right. Did it bleed?
Caller -> It bled. A lot at first. It was dripping. I pressed it with a gauze. For like five minutes. And it stopped. It's not bleeding now.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is the flap pink or dark?
Caller -> Pink. It's pink. I think. Maybe a little pale. I'm not sure. It's pink-white.
Caller -> Should I take a picture? We have the facility tablet. We take pictures for the chart.
Nurse -> If your facility allows it, that's fine. The nurse will see it in person too.
Caller -> I'll ask Gloria. I don't want to do it wrong.
Nurse -> That's okay. The nurse will look. Now, did he fall? Did he hit his head?
Caller -> No. No fall. He was in bed. He didn't fall out. He didn't hit his head. It was just the arm.
Nurse -> Good. Does he seem to be in pain? Grimacing, moaning?
Caller -> No. He doesn't seem to be. He's calm. He's watching the TV. He didn't make a sound when it happened. I felt bad. I think he didn't feel it. He's face is relaxed.
Nurse -> Is he talking? Does he know where he is?
Caller -> He's talking. He told me his wife is picking him up at five. She passed a long time ago. I said okay. I said she called and she's running late.
Nurse -> That's a kind way to handle it.
Caller -> They taught us that. Go with it. Don't argue.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Is he on any blood thinners? Do you know?
Caller -> I don't know. That would be in the chart. I'm sorry. I can find out when the nurse gets back.
Nurse -> That's fine. Have her call us. Okay, Priyanka. Here's what I'm going to do. I'll send a nurse out to see Mr. Wozniak today.
Caller -> Today. Okay. Thank you. When?
Nurse -> I'd say within a couple of hours. I'll call the facility desk to let them know she's coming.
Caller -> The desk is staffed. Marcus is at the desk tonight. He's the security guy. He'll let her in.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll ask her to check in with Marcus.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell the nurse when she's back.
Nurse -> I'm also going to message our team and the facility nurse about the skin tear, so everyone knows what happened.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until the nurse gets there, here's what I'd like you to do. Leave the skin flap where it is. Cover it with a non-stick pad, the kind that doesn't have a sticky side on the part that touches the wound. Then wrap it loosely with gauze. Don't put tape on his skin. Use paper tape on the gauze, or the wrap. And leave it alone until the nurse comes.
Caller -> Wait, the paper tape is that the white one that looks like a bandage? Or the cloth?
Nurse -> The paper one. It's usually white or tan. It peels easily.
Caller -> I think I know the one. It's in the drawer under the medication cart.
Caller -> Non-stick pad. Loose gauze. No tape on the skin. Don't touch it. Okay. We have the non-stick pads. The pink ones? In the supply room.
Nurse -> Those are probably the ones. They're Telfa. Okay.
Caller -> Now I remember. The nurse showed me. She said never use the regular band-aids on the old skin.
Nurse -> Exactly. Regular adhesive can tear the skin more.
Caller -> Telfa. Yes. I'll get them. And the gauze. And the paper tape.
Nurse -> Great. Also, can you pad the rail? Fold a blanket and tie or tuck it around the metal part. Or use a rail pad if you have one.
Caller -> We have rail pads. Somewhere. I'll find them. In the linen closet maybe.
Caller -> I'm going to go get it now. Can I put the phone down?
Nurse -> Sure. Take your time. I'll hold.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm going to the supply room. Hello? Okay. I'm in. I found the pads. And the gauze. And the tape. Wait, there are three kinds of tape.
Nurse -> The paper one. The one that looks like a plain roll.
Caller -> Got it. And the rail pad is here too. It's under the pillows. Oh good.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> And check on him every two hours, like you do. Look at the dressing for bleeding. And call us if it bleeds through.
Caller -> Every two hours. Look for blood. Call if it bleeds through. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Thank you, Priyanka. You did a good job. You called right away and you took care of him.
Caller -> Thank you. I was so nervous. I thought I'd done something wrong.
Nurse -> You didn't do anything wrong. Skin tears happen. Older skin is thin.
Caller -> Does it hurt them? I mean, does it hurt him?
Nurse -> It can. But sometimes people with dementia don't show it. We watch their faces and their body. That's what you're doing.
Caller -> I'll keep watching.
Caller -> That's what the other aide said. She said skin tears are the worst. They look worse than they are.
Nurse -> They do. Okay. Have the nurse call me when she's back, and we'll confirm his info.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Bridget.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bayview Home Health, this is Anselm.
Caller -> Anselm, it's Marlene Brandt. Hollis is throwing up blood. Bright red blood. A lot of it.
Nurse -> Okay, Marlene. I'm here. Where is Hollis right now?
Caller -> He's in the bathroom. On the floor. I mean, he's sitting on the edge of the tub. He's holding the toilet. He threw up twice. Just now. Twice in fifteen minutes. It's all over the floor.
Nurse -> Marlene, are you in the room with him?
Caller -> I'm in the doorway. I came in when I heard him retching. I called his name and he couldn't answer. He just waved his hand.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay with him.
Nurse -> Okay. How much blood? Can you tell?
Caller -> A lot. A cup. Maybe more. Each time. It's bright red. Not dark. It's like a bright red. It's terrible. I've never seen that.
Caller -> I'm a retired school nurse, and I've never seen this much. I don't know what to do with my hands.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'm going to tell you exactly what to do. First thing is the call.
Nurse -> Okay. Marlene, I need you to call nine one one right now. This is an emergency. He needs an ambulance.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Should I? Yes. Yes. Okay. But I'm scared to leave him.
Nurse -> You don't have to leave him. You can call from the next room or the hall. Just stay within sight.
Caller -> Okay. I can see him from the hallway. I'll stand where I can see his feet.
Nurse -> I know. Do you have another phone besides this one? So I can stay on with you?
Caller -> I have the cordless in the bedroom. It's charging. I'll get it. Hold on. Let me put you on speaker.
Caller -> It's ringing. Is it supposed to take this long?
Nurse -> It may take a few rings. Hang on.
Nurse -> Perfect. Go.
Caller -> Okay. Got the cordless. I'm dialing. Hello? Yes. My husband is vomiting blood. Bright red blood. Yes. He has liver disease. Forty four Seabright Road. Brandt. Hollis Brandt. They said they're coming. Seven minutes.
Caller -> They want me to stay on with them until the paramedics are there, so I'll put this one down on the counter right here.
Caller -> They said stay on the line but I can't hear them well with two phones. They said they'll stay on until the crew gets here.
Nurse -> Stay on with them. I'll be right here too.
Nurse -> Good. Stay on with them if they ask. Is Hollis awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's pale. His face is gray. He's sweaty. He says he's dizzy. He says the room is moving.
Nurse -> Is he able to answer you when you speak to him?
Caller -> Yes. He says yes and no. He's slow. He's mumbling. He knows my name. He called me Marley, which is what he calls me when he's, when he's soft.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Keep talking to him.
Nurse -> Okay. Marlene, here's what I want you to do. Get him to lie down on his left side, with his head turned a little, so if he vomits again he doesn't choke. Can you do that?
Caller -> On the floor? On the bath mat? I'll put towels. He's so heavy.
Nurse -> Don't lift him. Slide a towel or a blanket under his head and let him lie where he is.
Caller -> Okay. A towel. I have the thick one. There. Okay.
Nurse -> Don't try to lift him. If he can lie down where he is, have him do that. If he can't, he can stay sitting leaning against the tub. But no standing. Put a bowl or a bucket next to him. And nothing by mouth. No water, no pills.
Caller -> No water. No pills. A bowl. I have the big pot. I'll put it beside him. Hollis, honey, lie down. On your side. Slow. There. He's on his side. He's on the mat. I put a towel under his head.
Nurse -> Good. That's right. Is he breathing okay?
Caller -> He's breathing. He's breathing fast. He's pale. He says he's cold.
Nurse -> Is his breathing noisy? Gurgly?
Caller -> No gurgling. It's quick and shallow. Short breaths. He looks scared.
Nurse -> Tell him you're right there.
Nurse -> Cover him with a blanket. Don't overheat him. Just a light one.
Caller -> There's a towel. And the bathrobe. I'll put the robe on him. Okay. Done.
Nurse -> Good. Marlene, has he had any black stools? Today or yesterday?
Caller -> Yes. This morning. He said it was black. Like tar. He didn't tell me till after. I should have called then.
Nurse -> It's okay. A lot of people don't realize how serious it is. You called now.
Caller -> I just thought it was his stomach. He's had a stomach thing all week.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. We'll get him help.
Nurse -> It's okay. You called now. That's what matters. Does he have a history of this? You said liver disease.
Caller -> He has cirrhosis. And the varices. The veins in his throat. They banded them in the spring. The doctor said if they bleed he needs to go right away.
Nurse -> Exactly. And that's what we're doing.
Caller -> I just wish I'd called sooner.
Nurse -> Don't blame yourself.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Tell the paramedics that. Tell them it's varices that were banded in the spring. Is he on any blood thinners?
Caller -> No. No blood thinners. He takes the propranolol. Twenty milligrams. Twice a day. For the varices. He took the morning one at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Propranolol, twenty, twice a day, last at eight. Good. Marlene, can you go unlock the front door while he's lying there? He should be okay for a few seconds.
Caller -> Okay. Hollis, I'll be right back. One second. I'm unlocking the door. Okay. It's open. I'm back. I turned the porch light on.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have his medicine list?
Caller -> On the fridge. I'll grab it. Hold on. Okay. I have it. The list. And his bottles are in the cabinet. I'll bring the propranolol.
Nurse -> Good. Bring the bottle with the list.
Nurse -> Perfect. When they arrive, hand them the list and tell them the varices, the blood, and that it started fifteen minutes ago.
Caller -> Varices. Blood. Fifteen minutes. Okay. It's more like twenty now. I'll say twenty.
Caller -> It was on a Tuesday, the last time, a few years back. The ambulance came. It was different. This one is worse.
Nurse -> I know. They'll take good care of him.
Nurse -> Say twenty. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so they know.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, in case the paramedics ask?
Caller -> February nineteenth. Nineteen fifty five. He's seventy one.
Nurse -> And the number you're on?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one zero nine. It's the cordless.
Nurse -> Great. Is he still awake?
Caller -> He is. He's looking at me. He says he feels weak. He says he's so tired.
Nurse -> Is he trying to sit up? Please keep him down.
Caller -> He's trying. He wants to go to the bed. I told him no. He's frustrated.
Nurse -> Tell him the nurse says stay put. Doctor's orders.
Caller -> Hollis, the nurse says stay put. He says okay. He's closing his eyes.
Nurse -> Keep him talking. Don't let him fall asleep.
Caller -> Hollis. Hollis, look at me. Tell me about the boat. He's saying the boat. The boat in Florida.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep him telling you about the boat.
Nurse -> Keep talking to him. Tell him help is coming.
Caller -> Hollis, they're coming. You're going to be okay. I'm here. I'm right here.
Nurse -> Do you hear anything?
Caller -> Sirens. I hear the siren. It's close.
Caller -> The dog is going crazy. Duke! Duke, quiet. I'll put him in the garage. No, I can't. I'll leave him.
Nurse -> Don't worry about the dog. The paramedics are used to it.
Nurse -> Good. Go to the door and bring them in. I'll let you go. I'll call you back in twenty minutes. Answer if you can.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Anselm. Oh God, they're here.
Nurse -> Go. Be with him.

transcript:
Nurse -> Prairie Home Health, this is Layla.
Caller -> Hi, Layla. This is Odessa Mullins. I'm calling about my brother. Clifford Mullins. He's on the oxygen.
Nurse -> How long has he been on it?
Caller -> About two years. Since the hospital in the spring before last. He says it's his leash. I say it's his lifeline.
Nurse -> Hi, Odessa. Thanks for calling. Let me find Clifford. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> September sixteenth. Nineteen sixty eight. He's fifty eight. He hates when I say it.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. And a number to reach you? I have one on file but I want to confirm.
Caller -> It's my cell. Six one oh, five five five, zero one six three. I'm staying at his house this week.
Nurse -> And where are you from, Odessa?
Caller -> Atlanta. I flew in Monday. I'm a school bus driver there. I took the week.
Nurse -> That's wonderful of you.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's going on with his oxygen?
Caller -> So this morning I was refilling the little water bottle. The humidifier. And I dropped it. It cracked. On the bottom. It's leaking. It's done. And I thought, okay, we'll use the spare. But there's no spare. We had one and it's the one that cracked.
Nurse -> How did you drop it? Was it on the floor?
Caller -> It slipped out of my hand when I was washing it. It hit the edge of the sink. I'm so clumsy.
Nurse -> It happens all the time. The plastic is brittle.
Nurse -> Okay. So the humidifier bottle is cracked and there's no spare. Is the concentrator still running?
Caller -> It's running. We're using it without the water bottle. The tubing goes straight from the machine to him. He said that's fine. But he says his nose is dry.
Nurse -> Is the machine making any unusual noise, or is any light on?
Caller -> It sounds the same. A hum. A green light. No alarm. I looked.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fair. We'll get you a new bottle. What about the tubing? The cannula?
Caller -> That's the other thing. He has the one he's wearing. And one spare. And the spare has a split. Near the, where it connects. A little tear. I can hear the air hiss when I hold it. So the spare is no good. He's wearing the other one, but it's been on for a while. Like three weeks.
Nurse -> Okay. Three weeks is about right to change it, actually. So the one he's wearing is okay for now?
Caller -> It seems fine. It's a little stiff. It's yellowed. But no holes.
Nurse -> Does he wear it all day?
Caller -> Mostly. He takes it off for meals. And in the bathroom. He puts it back on after. He's good about it.
Nurse -> Okay. And how's his nose? Dry? Sore?
Caller -> Dry. Sore on the inside. He says it feels like it's cracked. There's a little crust. No blood. He keeps picking at it, I tell him not to.
Caller -> He gets cranky about his nose. He says it's the one part of him that worked fine and now even that's complaining.
Nurse -> Ha. He has a sense of humor.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he using any saline spray or gel?
Caller -> No. He doesn't have anything. I could pick up the saline spray at the store. Is that okay with oxygen?
Nurse -> A water based gel or saline is fine. Not Vaseline or oil. Don't use anything oily around the oxygen.
Caller -> No Vaseline. Okay. I'll get a saline gel. The water kind.
Nurse -> Good. Odessa, how is his breathing? And does he have the finger monitor?
Caller -> He does. He has the little clip. It's reading ninety two. It's usually ninety two or ninety three on the two liters. So it's normal for him.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety two on two liters is his usual. Any extra shortness of breath?
Caller -> No. He's the same. He's sitting in his chair doing a crossword. He's not winded. He walked to the kitchen and back and was okay.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Okay, let me place the order. A new humidifier bottle, how many? Two?
Caller -> Two. In case I drop another one. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Two bottles. And a few cannulas. I'll order a box so you have plenty. Hold on. Entering it.
Caller -> No rush. I'm just standing here. Oh, the cat is staring at me. Shoo. He wants his dinner.
Nurse -> What's the cat's name?
Caller -> Mister Biscuit. He's thirteen. He sleeps on Clifford's feet. Every night.
Nurse -> Aww. A good companion.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the oxygen supplier for two humidifier bottles and a box of nasal cannula tubing.
Caller -> Wonderful. Thank you. When will they come?
Nurse -> I'm going to arrange for delivery tomorrow morning. Will somebody be home?
Caller -> Yes. I'm here. We're both here. We don't go anywhere.
Nurse -> Does he get out at all? Any appointments?
Caller -> The doctor, once a month. My niece takes him. Otherwise he stays home. He doesn't like the portable tank. It's heavy.
Nurse -> We have lighter ones. I'll ask the nurse to talk to him about it at the next visit.
Nurse -> Great. I'll ask them to deliver tomorrow morning and call when they're close.
Caller -> Perfect. Should I do anything in the meantime?
Nurse -> Yes. Until the bottle comes, keep the oxygen on at two liters, without the humidifier. That's safe for a day. Use the saline gel for his nose. Don't use the split tubing, unless you can tape it and there's no hiss. If it hisses, don't use it. And when the new bottle comes, fill it with distilled water only. Not tap water.
Caller -> No humidifier for now. Saline gel. Don't use the split tubing. Distilled water later. Okay. We have a gallon of distilled water. In the garage. From the last time.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's what you want.
Caller -> Good. I'll write that on the fridge. I write everything on the fridge. My brother says it looks like a ransom note.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Nurse -> And call us if his oxygen reading falls under ninety, if he gets more short of breath, if his lips look blue, or if the concentrator alarms.
Caller -> Under ninety. Short of breath. Blue lips. Alarm. Okay. I'll watch. The alarm hasn't gone off. It's been quiet.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing, Odessa? Is it a lot, staying there?
Caller -> It's okay. He's easy. He just needs someone around. I flew in from Atlanta. I'm here till Sunday and then my niece takes over.
Nurse -> That's wonderful that you're helping.
Caller -> He's my baby brother. Even though he's fifty eight. I'd do anything.
Nurse -> Do you have other family nearby?
Caller -> Our mother is in the nursing home across town. Ninety four. She doesn't know him anymore. But she knows me.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's a lot to carry.
Caller -> It is. But we manage. Family is family.
Nurse -> I can tell. Anything else?
Caller -> I don't think so. Thank you, Layla.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Mesa Verde Home Health, this is Pilar.
Caller -> Pilar. Hi. It's Everett. Everett Lowry. I did something dumb. I took my sugar pill twice. And I'm feeling kind of, kind of off.
Nurse -> Okay, Everett. I'm here. Let's figure it out. Are you sitting down?
Caller -> I'm in the kitchen. I'm sitting on the stool. I'm shaking a little. My hands are shaking.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm holding the phone with both hands. It keeps slipping.
Nurse -> No problem. Put me on speaker on the counter if that's easier.
Caller -> Okay. Speaker. Can you hear me better?
Nurse -> Loud and clear.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay sitting. Which pill did you take twice?
Caller -> The glipizide. The ten milligram one. I take one in the morning. And this morning I took one at eight. And then I stood there and I thought, did I take it? I couldn't remember. So I took another one.
Nurse -> Okay. So you took two ten milligram tablets of glipizide, about eight o'clock?
Caller -> Yes. At eight. Right on top of each other. Like two minutes apart. I saw the empty slot afterwards. Both slots. I put two in my hand and saw that.
Nurse -> Okay. It's good you caught it. What time is it now?
Caller -> Ten. It's ten. I'm looking at the clock. It's ten oh five.
Nurse -> Okay. Two hours. Did you eat breakfast?
Caller -> No. I didn't. I was going to. And then I didn't. I'm not hungry in the morning. I usually have coffee. I had coffee. That's it.
Nurse -> Do you usually eat with that pill?
Caller -> I'm supposed to. With breakfast. I know. I keep forgetting. The pharmacist wrote it on the bottle in red.
Nurse -> We'll go over that with the nurse too.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Everett, did you check your sugar?
Caller -> I did. Just now. Sixty eight. I have a meter. It says sixty eight. That's low, right?
Nurse -> Yes, sixty eight is low. Thank you for checking. How are you feeling? Tell me everything.
Caller -> Shaky. And sweaty. My shirt is wet. My forehead is wet. And kind of, I'm hungry now. Really hungry. And a little dizzy, not bad.
Nurse -> Okay. Right now I want you to do something. Do you have juice in the house? Or regular soda? Or glucose tablets?
Caller -> I have orange juice. In the fridge. And I have the glucose tablets in the cabinet. For emergencies.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let's do the juice. Get up slowly, hold on to the counter, and pour a small glass of orange juice. About four ounces. Half a cup. Drink it all now.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm getting up. I'm holding the counter. It's okay. Walking to the fridge. It's six steps. Okay. Opening it. Orange juice. I'm pouring. It's spilling. My hands. Okay. I'm drinking it. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Drink it all. Take your time.
Caller -> I drank it. All of it. Ugh. That's sweet.
Nurse -> Sorry about the taste. How's your vision? Can you see okay?
Caller -> No, I can see fine. Just the shaking.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> That's what we want. Now, in fifteen minutes, check your sugar again. If it's still under seventy, drink another half cup, or take four glucose tablets. And check again fifteen minutes after that.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Check. Under seventy, more juice or four tablets. Check again. Okay. I got it. I'll set the timer on the stove.
Nurse -> Good. I'm also going to page the on-call clinician right now, so they know about the double dose. With that medicine, the sugar can keep dropping for many hours.
Caller -> Many hours? Oh no. Okay.
Nurse -> That's why we're being careful. I'm going to call you back in fifteen minutes. Right when you've done your recheck.
Caller -> Okay. Fifteen minutes. I'll have the number.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse to see you within two hours, so you're not alone with this.
Caller -> Within two hours. That's good. That makes me feel better. I live alone. My wife died last year.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. It's good you called. Is there anyone who can come over? A neighbor?
Caller -> My neighbor, Tom. He's next door. He's retired. I could call him. He wouldn't mind.
Nurse -> I'd call him. Just so someone's with you.
Caller -> I'll call him after we hang up. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Call him now, if you want, and I'll wait.
Caller -> No, no. I can do it. After. I'm okay. I just feel weird.
Nurse -> Are you confused at all? Do you know where you are, what day it is?
Caller -> Oh no. I'm not confused. It's Tuesday. I'm in my kitchen. It's two thousand twenty six. I know my name. I'm Everett. I'm sixty one. I didn't pass out. I'm just slow. And shaky.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very reassuring. It's good that you're talking clearly.
Caller -> Thanks. Is this going to be bad? Am I going to die? I mean, no. I'm not saying that. I mean, is this serious.
Nurse -> It can be, if the sugar drops a lot. But you're doing the right things, you caught it early. It's not a joke, but we've got it. I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. That helps.
Nurse -> Everett, can I get your birth date, and a number? In case we get cut off?
Caller -> May twenty fifth. Nineteen sixty five. And my cell is two oh six, five five five, zero one one six.
Nurse -> Got it. Thank you. How are you feeling now?
Caller -> A little better. Not so shaky. I think the juice is working. Or I'm calming down. My heart is going fast.
Nurse -> That's the sugar coming up. Good. When your sugar is back above one hundred, eat something with protein. A real snack. Like peanut butter on toast. And keep eating regular meals today, don't skip any.
Caller -> Peanut butter toast. I have that. And a banana. Okay. And not skip meals. I'll do lunch at noon.
Nurse -> Good. And if you get confused, can't swallow, pass out, or the sugar won't come up, call nine one one. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Confused, can't swallow, pass out, won't come up. Nine one one. Okay. I won't hesitate.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have a pillbox that has the days on it?
Caller -> I do. It's the seven day one. The morning slot for today is empty. I took both. That's how I knew. I think I put two in by mistake yesterday.
Nurse -> We'll go over that with the nurse. There might be a better way to set it up.
Caller -> I'd like that. I don't want this to happen again. I'm embarrassed.
Caller -> My daughter is going to kill me. She set up the pillbox. I told her I could handle it.
Nurse -> She'll be glad you called. We'll let her know if you'd like.
Caller -> Maybe tomorrow. I don't want to scare her today.
Nurse -> It's easy to do. Don't be embarrassed. Okay. The timer's about to go. How are you feeling?
Caller -> Better. Pretty good. I think I could eat the toast.
Nurse -> Wait for the recheck first. Then eat.
Caller -> Okay. Ten more minutes. Ten more minutes. I'm sitting here.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call you at ten twenty. Stay put.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Thanks, Pilar.
Nurse -> Bye, Everett.

Nurse -> Riverside Home Health, this is Dante.
Caller -> Hey. I'm a driver with Tri-County Freight. I got a delivery for you. A pallet. Office supplies. I'm outside and I can't find the dock.
Nurse -> Okay. Where are you right now? On Mill Street?
Caller -> I'm on Mill. In front of a brick building. There's a sign that says Riverside Medical Center.

transcript:
Nurse -> Seaport Hospice, this is Marco.
Caller -> Hello? Marco? Can you hear me? It's Odette Quill. About my husband. Bartholomew Quill.
Nurse -> I can hear you. Barely. Hold on, let me turn up my headset. Okay. Go ahead, Mrs. Quill.
Caller -> Is that better? I'm standing by the washing machine. It's noisy. The washer is on.
Nurse -> A little better. Maybe move away from the washer.
Caller -> Okay. Moving. I'm by the door now. The garage door. It's open a crack. Better?
Nurse -> Much better.
Nurse -> Hi, Mrs. Quill. I can hear you, a little crackly. Let me pull up Mr. Quinn. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> It's Quill. Q U I L L. Not Quinn. And his birthday is June twelfth. Nineteen forty. No. Forty one. Nineteen forty one. He's eighty five. Forty, forty one.
Nurse -> Sorry about that. Quill. June twelfth, nineteen forty one. And your number?
Nurse -> Is Mr. Quinn awake? Can he come to the phone?
Caller -> Quill. It's Quill. He's asleep in the recliner. I don't want to wake him. He had a bad night.
Nurse -> Okay. Let him sleep.
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one eight five. Can you hear me? I'm in the garage. The signal is bad inside.
Nurse -> I got it. Five oh three, five five five, zero one eight five. Yes, I can hear you. What's going on?
Nurse -> Is that a cell or a landline?
Caller -> Cell. I carry it everywhere. The house phone is broken. The kids bought me this one for Christmas.
Caller -> He's constipated. He hasn't gone in five days. Five days. And he's bloated. And he's cranky.
Nurse -> What's he doing that tells you he's cranky?
Caller -> He's snapping at me. He doesn't snap. He told me my coffee tastes like dishwater. After fifty seven years of coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a bad sign for the coffee.
Caller -> Ha. It's a bad sign for me.
Nurse -> Okay. Five days. Is that right? You said five?
Caller -> Five. Last Wednesday. It's Monday. So Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Five days. Maybe six.
Nurse -> Okay. Five or six days. What does he take for it?
Caller -> The senna at night. The eight point six. He took it last night. And the Miralax in the morning. The powder. In his juice. Seventeen grams. A capful. He took it this morning. It's not working.
Nurse -> Okay. Senna eight point six at bedtime, Miralax seventeen grams in the morning. Both taken. Is he drinking enough?
Caller -> He drinks. He drinks juice and water. Maybe five glasses. Not much solid food. He eats a little. Toast. Soup.
Nurse -> Does he eat any fruits or vegetables?
Caller -> Some applesauce. He eats pears sometimes. Not the skins. He never liked the skins.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Is his belly swollen?
Caller -> A little. It's tight. Round. He says it's gassy. It's not hard like a rock. Soft but big. Bloated. Mild.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he nauseated? Throwing up?
Caller -> No. No nausea. No vomiting. He's eating, a little. His stomach isn't upset. It's just full.
Nurse -> Good. Any pain in the belly?
Caller -> A little cramping. When he tries. But he can't go. He sits there for twenty minutes and nothing.
Nurse -> Does he strain a lot?
Caller -> A little. I tell him not to push so hard. The doctor said it can hurt his heart.
Nurse -> That's good advice. Don't strain.
Nurse -> Okay. Mrs. Quill, I'm going to message the hospice provider about this today. Five days without a bowel movement with the senna and the Miralax. They'll probably want to add something.
Caller -> Add what? A suppository?
Nurse -> Possibly. I don't want to guess. I'll ask them.
Caller -> Please. I'd hate to give him something that I shouldn't.
Nurse -> Right. Don't give anything extra without checking. Okay?
Caller -> I won't. Not even a glass of that fiber stuff.
Caller -> Okay. Can you speak up? You cut out a bit.
Nurse -> I said I'll ask the provider. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to examine him.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. And you'll call me?
Nurse -> Yes, I'll call you back this evening to tell you what the provider says.
Caller -> This evening. Good. I'll go into the living room so I can hear.
Nurse -> Good idea. In the meantime, offer him fluids through the day. Water, warm prune juice, or broth. Small amounts, often.
Caller -> Warm prune juice. He hates cold. Warm prune. Okay. I have prune juice. I'll warm it on the stove.
Caller -> He likes it with a little cinnamon. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's fine. A little cinnamon is nice.
Nurse -> Also, a warm compress on his belly can help. And gently rub his belly in a clockwise circle. And if he can, help him walk a little, to the bathroom after meals.
Caller -> Warm compress. Clockwise. Walk after meals. Okay. I have a heating pad. I'll wrap it in a towel. He walks with the walker.
Caller -> He gets up slowly. And I stand behind him. In case.
Nurse -> Good. Always stay close.
Caller -> I do. I'm like a shadow.
Nurse -> Great. And call us if he starts vomiting, if his belly gets hard and swollen, if the pain gets bad, or if liquid stool starts leaking out.
Caller -> Vomiting, hard belly, bad pain, leaking. Okay. I'll watch. I wrote it on the notepad.
Nurse -> Mrs. Quill, how are you doing? Are you getting any rest?
Caller -> I'm okay. My daughter is coming Thursday. She'll help. She lives in Spokane.
Nurse -> That's good. Let her help.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Marco. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> Bye, Mrs. Quill.
Caller -> Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sunrise Valley Home Care, this is Wren.
Caller -> Hi, Wren! It's Carmela Pellegrino. I'm calling about my son, Jonah Pellegrino. I'm calling with a few little things. Nothing big.
Nurse -> Hi, Carmela. Good to hear your voice. How's Jonah?
Caller -> He's good. He's happy. He's in his chair watching the football highlights. He's got his Eagles shirt on. He says hi.
Nurse -> What are the Eagles doing this season?
Caller -> Don't ask. He's been grumpy since Sunday. They lost. He pouted all day. Ha.
Nurse -> Hi, Jonah. I can't hear him but I bet he's smiling.
Caller -> He's smiling. He's making the sound. The happy sound. You know.
Nurse -> I do. Okay, let me pull up his chart so I have everything in front of me. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> July eighth. Two thousand three.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one nine five. Same as always.
Nurse -> Perfect. So what are the little things?
Caller -> Okay. Number one. He has a cold. A mild one. A little cough and a runny nose. Started Saturday. So two days. He's sneezing. He's not coughing a lot. It's a little dry cough.
Nurse -> Was anyone else in the house sick?
Caller -> My husband had the sniffles last week. And Jonah's cousin was here. She's four. She's a germ factory.
Nurse -> Ha. Kids are. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Two days of a mild cough and a runny nose. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> I took it this morning. Ninety nine point one. In the ear. So just a little warm. Not a fever.
Nurse -> Okay. And tonight?
Caller -> I haven't done it again. I'll do it before bed. I just wanted to check in.
Nurse -> What kind of thermometer do you use?
Caller -> The ear one. The one the nurse gave us. It beeps. He hates the beep. He covers his ear with his hand.
Nurse -> Ha. That works.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Ninety nine point one this morning.
Caller -> Yes. Which is nothing. He's normally ninety seven something. So it's up a bit.
Nurse -> Right. That's a little warm. Is he eating and drinking okay?
Caller -> He's eating great. He had pancakes this morning. Two. He had a whole pancake with the syrup. And he's drinking. I use the cup with the straw. He drinks a lot of water.
Caller -> I also put a little apple juice in it. For taste. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's fine.
Nurse -> Good. Any trouble breathing? Wheezing? Noisy breathing?
Caller -> No. His breathing's quiet. He's a little stuffy at night. I put the humidifier on. But it's not noisy. He's breathing normal. He has the same color. His lips are pink.
Nurse -> Where do you keep the humidifier?
Caller -> On the dresser across from the bed. The cool mist one. I wash it every day. The nurse showed me how.
Nurse -> Good. That's the right way.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very reassuring. How about the cough? Is it wet, dry?
Caller -> Dry mostly. A little tickle. He clears his throat. It's not bothering him much. It's more bothering me.
Nurse -> Does it keep him awake?
Caller -> No. He sleeps through. I wake up and check on him four times, though. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Moms. Okay. What about his medicine? Is he taking the baclofen as usual?
Caller -> Yes. The baclofen. Ten milligrams. Three times a day. He took the morning one at eight. The next one's at two. And one at bedtime. Same as always. I haven't changed anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Baclofen ten, three times a day, and he took this morning's. Good. Any extra stiffness or spasms with the cold?
Caller -> A little more stiffness in the mornings. But that's the same as when he gets any cold. It goes away after the stretches.
Nurse -> Does he seem uncomfortable during the stretches?
Caller -> Not really. He grunts. He likes the one where Marisol rolls his ankles. He closes his eyes.
Nurse -> Okay. That's pretty normal. Do you do the stretches in the morning?
Caller -> Yes. Every morning. Fifteen minutes. The aide helps. Marisol. She's wonderful.
Caller -> She brought him a birthday card in July. And a balloon. She's the only one he lets do his hair.
Nurse -> Aw. That's special.
Nurse -> Marisol is great. Okay, what's number two?
Caller -> Number two. Thursday. I have a dental appointment. Thursday morning at ten. And Marisol comes at nine. And I'd like to move it. To the afternoon. Is that possible? I tried to call scheduling but nobody answered.
Caller -> The voicemail was full. I felt bad. I didn't want to be annoying.
Nurse -> You're not annoying. The voicemail is full because it's Monday.
Caller -> Ha. Mondays.
Nurse -> I can help with that. Let me message the scheduling coordinator now. What time in the afternoon would work?
Caller -> After one. One thirty, two. My appointment's at ten and I'll be back by noon. Jonah naps from noon to one. So after one.
Nurse -> Do you need me to arrange anything for the dentist trip? A ride?
Caller -> No, my husband is taking me. He works from home. He'll stay with Jonah until I'm back.
Nurse -> Perfect. Then the aide isn't even necessary in the morning.
Caller -> Right. But Thursday is the day I do the laundry. I need her for the afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll message the coordinator to move Thursday's shift to after one in the afternoon.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That would be wonderful.
Nurse -> I'll also move the nurse visit to Thursday afternoon. That way both can overlap if that's easier.
Caller -> Oh, that works. The nurse comes Thursdays too? I forgot.
Nurse -> She does. At ten, I see here. I'll move it to the afternoon too.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you. You're an angel.
Nurse -> No problem. I'll call you tomorrow morning to confirm the new times.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. Good. Number three. Can the nurse check his weight on Thursday? He's been looking thin. And I want to check his weight to see if the feeding is enough.
Nurse -> Sure. I'll note that on the visit. We'll weigh him in his chair and subtract the chair. Do you remember what he weighed last time?
Caller -> A hundred and ten. A hundred and ten pounds. That was in August. He's six foot. He's long.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll make a note.
Caller -> Thank you. I just worry. He's twenty three and he's still my baby. He can't tell me what's wrong.
Nurse -> I understand. You know him better than anyone. If you think something's off, trust that.
Caller -> I do. That's why I called about the cold. A mom knows.
Nurse -> Absolutely. What does your dentist say about the tooth?
Caller -> It's a crown. I'm getting a crown. I'm terrified. My mouth is the one thing I don't let anyone near.
Nurse -> Ha. You'll be fine. They numb it.
Nurse -> You were right to call. Okay, Carmela. For the cold, a few things. Check his temperature morning and evening and write it down. And watch his breathing and how much he's drinking.
Caller -> Morning and evening. Write it down. Breathing. Drinking. I have a notebook.
Nurse -> And keep offering fluids. Water, watered down juice, warm broth. Small amounts, often. Keep him sitting up for meals.
Caller -> Water, juice, broth. Small and often. Sitting up. Yes. I always sit him up straight.
Nurse -> And please call us if his temperature gets to one hundred one or higher, if his breathing gets fast or noisy, if his mucus turns thick and green, or if he refuses to drink. And nine one one for blue lips or if he's struggling to breathe.
Caller -> One hundred one. Fast or noisy breathing. Green mucus. Won't drink. Nine one one for blue lips or struggling. Okay. I have it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else?
Caller -> No. That's all. Thank you for listening. It helps to talk to someone who knows him.
Nurse -> Of course. Tell Jonah I said go Eagles.
Caller -> Oh, he'll love that. He's laughing. He heard you. He likes you.
Nurse -> Aw. I like him too. Talk to you tomorrow, Carmela.
Caller -> Bye, Wren. Thanks again.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tidewater Pediatric Home Care, this is Paloma.
Caller -> Paloma, it's Lucinda Ibanez. It's Mateo. He can't breathe right. He's wheezing and his chest is going in and out. The treatments aren't working.
Nurse -> Okay, Lucinda. I'm here. How old is Mateo? Is he awake?
Caller -> He's seven. He's awake. He's sitting on the couch. He's leaning forward. He's gasping. His ribs are sucking in. Every time he breathes, the skin between his ribs goes in.
Nurse -> Is he making a whistling sound when he breathes out?
Caller -> Yes. It's loud. I can hear it from across the room. A high whistle. And a cough in between.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the wheeze.
Nurse -> Okay. What treatments have you done?
Caller -> The albuterol. The two point five milligram vial in the nebulizer. I did one at four. It helped a little for a few minutes. Then he got worse. I did another at four thirty. Nothing. He's worse. The machine is still going. I mean the second one finished.
Nurse -> Did he use his rescue inhaler at all, the one with the spacer?
Caller -> Before the machine. Four puffs. At three forty. It did a little. Then nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics that too.
Nurse -> Okay. Two treatments. At four and four thirty. What time is it now?
Caller -> Five. Five oh five. Almost. It's almost five oh five.
Nurse -> Okay. Lucinda, I need you to hang up and call nine one one right now. He needs an ambulance.
Caller -> Nine one one. Okay. Okay. Okay. Wait. Is he going to be okay?
Nurse -> We're getting him help right now. The best thing is the call.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm dialing. I'm dialing.
Nurse -> Call them right now. I'll stay with you. Do you have another phone? A landline?
Caller -> My husband's phone is on the counter. He's at work. It's here. I'll use his. Put you on speaker. Hold on.
Nurse -> Good. Go.
Caller -> Mateo, honey, stay sitting. Mama's calling the ambulance. Okay. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My son can't breathe. He has asthma. He's seven. He's wheezing. His chest is pulling in. Forty nine Cypress Lane. Ibanez. Yes. Yes. They're coming. Six minutes.
Nurse -> Great. Stay on with them as long as they want. I'm right here on the other phone. Lucinda, does Mateo have a pulse oximeter?
Caller -> They want me to stay on. But I can't hold two. I'll put you on speaker and them on the other. They're both on the counter.
Nurse -> That works.
Caller -> They said unlock the door and put away the dog. We don't have a dog.
Nurse -> Ha. Standard instruction.
Caller -> Yes. The little clip. On his finger. I put it on when he got worse. It says ninety. Ninety. It was ninety six this morning.
Nurse -> Good that you have the clip. Is he cooperating with it?
Caller -> He's holding his hand still. He's being so brave. He's my brave boy.
Nurse -> He is. Tell him I said so.
Caller -> Mateo, the nurse says you're brave. He's nodding.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety. That's low for him. Tell the paramedics ninety. Look at his lips. What color are they?
Caller -> A little blue. Bluish. Around the edge. Not a lot. But yes. Oh God.
Nurse -> Take a breath, Lucinda. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm breathing.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay calm for him. Can he talk to you?
Caller -> He says short things. One word. Two words. He said help. He said Mama. He can't say a full sentence. He tried and he ran out of air.
Nurse -> Is he using his belly to breathe? Does his stomach move a lot?
Caller -> Yes. His belly goes in and out. Fast. And his nostrils. They flare. Like a horse.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the effort. The paramedics will see it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Tell the paramedics he can only speak in short phrases. Lucinda, you can give him another treatment while we wait. Another albuterol. Is the nebulizer set up?
Caller -> It's on the table. The cup is there. I have vials. I can do it. Yes.
Nurse -> I want you to give a third albuterol treatment now. Put the vial in, turn it on, and have him breathe through the mouthpiece. Sitting up, leaning forward a little.
Caller -> Okay. Third treatment. Now. I'm doing it. I'm twisting the vial. It's in. I'm turning on the machine. It's going. Mateo, here, breathe this. Breathe in. Slow. Good boy. It's misting. He's holding it.
Nurse -> Good. Keep it on his mouth. Sit him on your lap if you can, leaning forward on a pillow or against your chest. Keep your voice calm. He feeds off your fear.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm trying. He's on my lap. He's leaning on me. I'm holding him. Shh, shh. I've got you. It's okay.
Caller -> He's tapping my arm. He wants me to rub his back. I'm rubbing. It's helping a little. He's closing his eyes.
Nurse -> Don't let him fall asleep. Keep him talking, even short things.
Caller -> Mateo, tell me your favorite color. Blue. He said blue. Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep him telling you things.
Nurse -> That's perfect. You're doing so well, Lucinda. What's been going on today? How did this start?
Caller -> We were at my sister's. In the afternoon. Her house. They have a cat. A new cat. A fluffy one. Mateo was playing with it. He was on the floor. And he started coughing. And then wheezing. We left. I brought him home and did the neb.
Nurse -> How long were you at your sister's?
Caller -> Two hours. He was playing with the cat the whole time. I didn't think. He's never reacted that bad.
Nurse -> It doesn't matter now. We'll focus on the next few minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I took his temperature at four. Ninety eight point six. No fever. He's not sick. It's the cat. I know it's the cat. He's allergic. He's always been. I should have known.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. Keep him on the neb. Is the front door unlocked for the paramedics?
Caller -> My husband is going to be so upset I didn't call him first. He's driving a truck on the interstate, he doesn't answer.
Nurse -> You can call him once the ambulance is with you. Right now it's about Mateo.
Caller -> I know. I'll call him from the ambulance. He'll meet us at the hospital.
Nurse -> Which hospital do they usually take you to?
Caller -> Children's. The one by the river. It's twelve minutes. He's been there before. For the asthma, two winters ago.
Nurse -> Then they know him. That helps.
Caller -> They have all his records. They know his weight, his allergies. The doctor there, Dr. Rahman, he's the one who set up the neb for us. He's very kind.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. I'm sure he'll be in good hands.
Caller -> I hope they have a bed. Last time we waited in the hall for three hours.
Nurse -> With oxygen of ninety and chest pulling, they'll take him right back. Don't worry about the wait.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel a little better. A little.
Nurse -> Keep breathing yourself. In and out.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm doing the breathing with him. We're both breathing together.
Nurse -> That's beautiful. He's following your breathing. Keep it slow and steady.
Caller -> In and out. In and out. He's matching me. His shoulders are coming down a little.
Caller -> No. I'll have to get up. The door is locked. Can I?
Nurse -> Put the neb on the table and carry him. Or is there someone else in the house?
Caller -> My daughter. Isabel. She's twelve. She's upstairs. Isabel! Isabel, come down! Open the front door! Right now! The ambulance is coming!
Nurse -> Good. She can unlock the door and wait for them.
Caller -> She's coming. She's running. Isabel, unlock the door. And turn on the porch light. And wait outside. Okay. She did. She's on the porch.
Caller -> She's crying. She's scared. She's twelve.
Nurse -> Tell her she's doing a great job. She's helping her brother.
Caller -> Isabel, the nurse says you're doing great. She's nodding. She's wiping her eyes.
Nurse -> Good. Now, grab his inhaler, the nebulizer, the vials, and his medicine list. Is the list on the fridge?
Caller -> On the fridge. Isabel! Bring me the list from the fridge! And Mateo's backpack. The blue one. It has the inhaler. Yes. She's bringing.
Caller -> She's here. She has the blue backpack. And the list. And his stuffed bear. I didn't ask for the bear. But he wants it.
Nurse -> Bring the bear. He'll feel better with it.
Nurse -> Perfect. When the paramedics arrive, hand them the inhaler, the nebulizer and the list. Tell them the oxygen was ninety, the treatments were at four and four thirty, and the third one is going now.
Caller -> Ninety. Four, four thirty. Third one now. Okay.
Caller -> Should I take off his shirt? He's sweaty.
Nurse -> If he's hot, loosen it. Don't take it all off.
Caller -> I loosened the collar. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm paging the on-call clinician right now so they're aware.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Lucinda, can I get Mateo's date of birth for my notes? And your number?
Caller -> April seventeenth. Two thousand nineteen. And my cell is five oh three, five five five, zero one three six.
Nurse -> Got it. How is he breathing now?
Caller -> The same. A little slower? He's still pulling. Maybe a little less. The color is the same. The neb is almost done. It's sputtering.
Nurse -> Check the oximeter again.
Caller -> Ninety one. Ninety one. It went up one. It's ninety one.
Nurse -> Good. Slow improvement. That's what we want.
Caller -> It was ninety. Now ninety one. Maybe ninety two. It's jumping. It's hard to tell. He's moving.
Nurse -> Don't worry about the exact number. Tell the paramedics what you see.
Nurse -> Good. That's a little better. Keep him upright. Don't lay him down.
Caller -> I won't. He's on my lap.
Nurse -> Is he able to cough? Is anything coming up?
Caller -> He's coughing. A little. Dry. It's tight. He says his chest is tight. He says it's a rock.
Caller -> He says he's scared. He said, Mama, I'm scared. Oh. My heart.
Nurse -> It's okay to be scared. Tell him you're right here and the ambulance is coming. You're not leaving him.
Caller -> I'm not leaving you. I'm right here. Mama's here.
Nurse -> A rock. That's how it feels. The paramedics will have stronger medicine. They'll help him.
Caller -> I hear the siren. I hear it. It's close.
Nurse -> Is Isabel at the door?
Caller -> She's at the curb waving her arms. She's good at it. She's so serious.
Nurse -> She's doing a great job.
Nurse -> Good. Isabel's outside. Good job, Isabel. Lucinda, I'm going to let you go. They're here. I'll call you in fifteen minutes. If you're at the hospital, pick up.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you so much, Paloma. Thank you.
Nurse -> You did everything right. Go.
Caller -> Bye. They're here. They're coming in.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Hearthstone Home Health, this is Imogen.
Caller -> Hello. Hello, I'm calling about my neighbor. I think he's one of your people. I have a key. I let myself in.
Nurse -> Okay. Take a breath. We'll sort it out.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm a little shaky. My heart is going. I'm seventy four. I don't do well with surprises.
Nurse -> That's okay. You're doing great.
Nurse -> Okay. What's your name, and your neighbor's name?
Caller -> I'm Wilhelmina Strand. Wilhelmina. W I L H E L M I N A. Strand. I live next door at forty two. And he's Mr. Pryce. Cornelius Pryce.
Nurse -> Could you spell his last name for me?
Caller -> P R Y C E. Pryce. Like the price of something but with a Y.
Nurse -> Got it.
Nurse -> Okay, Wilhelmina. Is Mr. Pryce okay right now?
Caller -> I don't know. That's why I'm calling. I don't know what to think.
Nurse -> Take your time. Tell me what you saw.
Caller -> So his newspaper was still on the porch. At ten. He's up at six, every day. He gets the paper and he reads it on the porch with his coffee. And I looked out my window and it was still there. So I went over. And I knocked. And nobody came. And I have a key. He gave me a key in case.
Caller -> He gave it to me after his fall in the winter. I've never used it. Not once. Not until today.
Nurse -> It sounds like a good arrangement.
Caller -> It is. He does the same for me. He has a key to my house. We take care of each other.
Nurse -> Okay. That was the right thing to do. What happened when you went in?
Caller -> He was on the couch. In the front room. Lying there. With his shoes on. And I said Cornelius. And nothing. And I said it louder. And nothing. And I thought, oh no. And I stood there and I didn't know if he was breathing. And then I heard it. A snore. A big snore.
Nurse -> Was he breathing normally in between? Any long pauses?
Caller -> It was regular. In and out. A big snore, then a breath, then another. Like a lawn mower. He always snored. His wife used to say she slept in the garage.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. So he was snoring. That's reassuring. Then what?
Caller -> Then I shook his shoulder. Gently. And he woke up. Sort of. He said what. He said what, what is it. He was cranky. Like I woke him up. And he sat up. But slow. He's slow. His eyes are heavy. He's like, not all there yet.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he talking now? Does he make sense?
Caller -> He's talking. He asked me what I was doing in his house. I said I was checking on you. He said I'm fine. Go away. He's grumpy. That's him. He's always grumpy. But he's slow. He's not himself. Usually he's quick.
Nurse -> Did he say what day it is? Does he know where he is?
Caller -> I asked him. He said it's Tuesday. It's Tuesday. He said and why are you asking. He knows where he is. He's in his own house, in his own couch, with his own shoes on.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me ask a few questions. Is his speech slurred? Is it hard to understand him?
Caller -> No. I can understand him. He sounds like he sounds. A little sleepy. But not slurred. Not like a stroke. I checked. I looked it up on my phone.
Nurse -> Good. Is one side of his face drooping? Smile for me. Can you ask him to smile?
Caller -> Hold on. Cornelius. Cornelius, smile for me. Oh, he's making a face. He's smiling. It's even. Both sides. And his arms. I asked him to lift his arms. He did. Both. They're the same.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very helpful. How's his breathing now? Is it normal?
Caller -> It's normal. He was snoring before. Now he's awake so he's not. He's breathing normal. He's not gasping. He's not breathing fast. He's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Wilhelmina, do you know his date of birth, or what medicines he takes?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'm his neighbor. I don't know his birthday. I know he takes a lot of pills. I see the bottles on the kitchen counter. But I don't know what. I didn't look.
Nurse -> Is there a pillbox or a list out on the counter?
Caller -> There's a plastic box with the days. It's the big one. I don't want to open it. It's his.
Nurse -> That's fine. The nurse will look.
Nurse -> That's okay. We have his chart. What number can I reach you at?
Caller -> I'm on my cell. Five oh three, five five five, zero one eight seven.
Nurse -> Got it. Does he live alone?
Caller -> He does. His wife passed. Years ago. His son is in Portland. I have the son's number but not in my pocket.
Nurse -> Do you know if the son knows he's not well?
Caller -> I don't think so. Cornelius doesn't like to bother him. He says Peter has his own life.
Nurse -> We'll find the son's number in our records. Don't worry about it now.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. I'll find it. Here's what I'm going to do. I'll send a nurse to see Mr. Pryce today.
Caller -> Today. Oh good. That's what I hoped. What time?
Nurse -> I'll ask for within the next two or three hours. I'm also going to message his provider about him being hard to wake this morning, and slow.
Caller -> Good. Because I don't think he's right. I don't think he's sick sick. But something's off.
Nurse -> I agree. It's good that you noticed. Can you stay with him until the nurse comes?
Caller -> I can stay. I have nothing. I was going to do my crossword. I can do it here.
Caller -> I'll just sit in his chair. The green chair. It's very comfortable. He'll be annoyed.
Nurse -> Ha. He'll get over it.
Nurse -> That would be great. Stay close to him. Keep him sitting up, or lying on his side if he wants to lie down, so he doesn't choke if he gets sleepy. And every fifteen minutes, ask him a question and make sure he answers and wakes up.
Caller -> Sitting or on his side. Every fifteen minutes, ask him something. Okay. I'll ask him what he had for breakfast.
Nurse -> That works. And call nine one one right away if you can't wake him, if his speech gets slurred, if his face droops, if he gets weak on one side, or if his breathing changes.
Caller -> Can't wake. Slurred. Droop. Weak. Breathing. Nine one one. Okay. I've got it. I'll write it on the newspaper.
Nurse -> Is the front door locked? I want the nurse to be able to get in.
Caller -> I'll leave it unlocked. I'll sit by it. I'll watch for her. What's her name?
Nurse -> It might be Carolyn or one of the other nurses. They'll have an agency badge.
Caller -> Okay. I'll look for the badge.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call you back after the nurse has been out.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'll tell him you called. He'll hate it.
Nurse -> That's okay. He doesn't have to like it.
Caller -> Ha. He won't. Thank you, dear.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling. Stay with him.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Foxglove Hospice, this is Callum.
Caller -> Hi, Callum. It's Dwight Larkin. L A R K I N. I'm calling about my wife, Winnifred. She's got a rash. And I have a question about a pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Mr. Larkin. How are the two of you doing today?
Caller -> We're managing. We've had better days. We had a good morning and then this rash.
Nurse -> Hi, Mr. Larkin. Let me bring up Winnifred's chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> August twenty third. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one two seven. That's the house.
Nurse -> And is that the best number for the afternoon?
Caller -> It is. I'll be here. I don't go out much. I can get the groceries delivered now. My daughter set it up on the computer.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about the rash.
Caller -> It started Saturday. Two days. It's little red blotches. Like hives, maybe. On her arms. Both arms. And on her chest. And she's scratching. She's scratching and scratching. She's scratched till she's red. And she's miserable.
Nurse -> Is she scratching in her sleep too?
Caller -> At night, yes. I wake up and she's scratching in her sleep. I put socks on her hands. Ha. Like a baby.
Nurse -> That's smart. It helps protect the skin.
Nurse -> Okay. Are the blotches raised, flat?
Caller -> Raised. A bit. Like bumps. Not blisters. Some are like a welt. Some are flat and red. The size of a quarter, some of them. Some are smaller.
Nurse -> Any burning or stinging, or is it only itch?
Caller -> Just the itch. She says it's crawling. Like ants under the skin.
Nurse -> Okay. And do they come and go, or are they staying?
Caller -> They come and go. They move. This morning they were on her left arm. Now they're on her right arm too. And her chest. They fade after an hour and come back.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like hives. Is there any swelling of her lips, face, tongue?
Caller -> No. No. I looked. Her lips are normal. Her face is normal. Her tongue's fine. I asked her to stick it out. She did. She said you're being silly.
Caller -> She's always been the stubborn one. She told the nurse last week that she's not an invalid.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll bet she is a fighter.
Caller -> Forty four years of marriage. I know it.
Nurse -> Good. Any trouble breathing, wheezing, a tight throat?
Caller -> No. Her breathing's the same as always. She's comfortable. No tightness. No cough. She's just itching.
Nurse -> Any fever, chills? Has she felt warm?
Caller -> I took it at lunch. Ninety eight and a half. No fever.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Has anything changed recently? A new soap, a new laundry detergent, a new food? A new medicine?
Caller -> I thought about that. I did. I haven't changed the soap. Same soap. Same detergent. Same food. She eats the same. Toast, eggs, soup. I can't think of anything new. She's on the same pills.
Caller -> The only new thing is the dog. My daughter brought her dog over. A little poodle. He sat on Winnie's lap Friday. She loves him. Do you think it's the dog?
Nurse -> It could be an allergy, or it could be something else. We'll note it. Keep him off her lap for now, until we know.
Caller -> Oh no. She'll cry. But okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pills is she taking right now?
Caller -> The oxycodone. For the pain. Five milligrams. Every four hours if she needs it. She's been taking it about three or four times a day. She took one at noon. And a few others for her stomach and her sleep. But I'd have to look.
Nurse -> That's fine. The oxycodone five, every four hours as needed, last at noon. Anything new in the last week?
Caller -> No. I don't think so. Hmm. The nurse added a stool softener, last Monday. A new one. But that's not it, is it?
Nurse -> It could be. Rashes can come from medicines. I'll check what that one is. Do you remember the name?
Caller -> No. It's a white pill. Starts with D. Doc something. I'd have to find it. It's in the cabinet.
Nurse -> Could you do me a favor and read me the name off the bottle? While I'm on the line?
Caller -> Sure. Hold on. Let me get my glasses. They're on the TV. Okay. I'm in the kitchen. The cabinet is stuck. There. It says docusate. D O C U S A T E. Hundred milligrams. Once a day.
Nurse -> Docusate. Thank you. That's a very common stool softener. I'll include it for the provider.
Caller -> Is that the one?
Nurse -> It might be. It's rare. We'll let the provider decide.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll find it in her chart. Dwight, you mentioned a question about a pill.
Caller -> Yes. I wanted to give her a Benadryl. I have some in the cabinet. The twenty five milligram. It's what my mother always used for hives. But I didn't know if it's okay with the oxycodone. Because the box says it makes you drowsy. And I don't want to make her too sleepy. Or worse.
Nurse -> Your mother was onto something. It is a common medicine for hives. We just need to check it with the other pills.
Caller -> My mother raised six kids. She knew everything.
Nurse -> Ha. I believe it.
Nurse -> That's a really good question to ask before giving it. Both can make her drowsy. I'd like you to hold off on the Benadryl until I check with the provider. Don't give it yet.
Caller -> Okay. I won't give it. She's itching so bad though. Can't I give a half?
Nurse -> I know it's hard to wait. Even a half can make her sleepy with the oxycodone. And I want the provider to say.
Caller -> I understand. I trust you. I just hate to see her like this.
Nurse -> I know.
Nurse -> I understand. Please wait for the provider. It shouldn't take long. In the meantime there are things we can do.
Caller -> Okay. What?
Nurse -> First, I'm going to message the hospice provider right now about the rash and the Benadryl question. I'll include the new stool softener.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this afternoon with their answer.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> Within a couple hours. Probably by three or four.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'll keep the phone close.
Nurse -> Now, for the itch. Cool damp cloths on the itchy spots help a lot. Loose cotton clothes. Keep her nails short, so if she scratches she doesn't break her skin. And a fragrance free lotion, if she likes lotion.
Caller -> Cool cloths. Cotton. Short nails. Lotion with no smell. Okay. We have the cotton nightgowns. And I'll cut her nails. I do that anyway. She trusts me with the clippers.
Nurse -> Good. Don't use anything with a lot of perfume.
Caller -> She likes the lavender. I'll skip it for now.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Just for now.
Caller -> Okay. Is it contagious? The rash?
Nurse -> Hives aren't contagious. They're a reaction. We just need to find the cause.
Caller -> Good. I was worried about me. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. You're fine.
Caller -> Callum, what should worry me? What would be an emergency?
Nurse -> If her lips, tongue or face swell, or she has trouble breathing or wheezing, call nine one one right away. And call us back if the rash spreads a lot, or blisters.
Caller -> Swelling, trouble breathing. Nine one one. Spreads or blisters, call you. Okay. I wrote it on the notepad.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is she doing otherwise? Is her pain okay?
Caller -> Her pain is okay. It's about the same. A three. She's comfortable when she's not scratching.
Nurse -> Good. Is she eating and drinking?
Caller -> Yes. Soup for lunch. She had half a sandwich. She's drinking tea.
Nurse -> What kind of tea? Is it herbal?
Caller -> Just regular. Black tea. With honey. She doesn't like the herbal.
Nurse -> That's fine. Nothing new.
Caller -> Nothing new. Same tea since nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> Great. Okay, Mr. Larkin. I'll call you this afternoon.
Caller -> Thank you, Callum. I appreciate it.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> One more thing. The chaplain was going to come by Thursday. Is that still on?
Nurse -> Let me look. Yes. Thursday at two. It's on the schedule.
Caller -> Good. She likes him. They talk about birds.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Maplewood Home Care, this is Giorgio.
Caller -> Hi, Giorgio. This is Rhoda Pettibone. P E T T I B O N E. I'm one of the aides. I'm with Mrs. Echeverria today. Juanita Echeverria.
Nurse -> Hi, Rhoda. What can I do for you?
Caller -> First, is this a good time? I know you're probably in the middle of a hundred things.
Nurse -> This is a good time. I'm all yours.
Caller -> Okay good. Because I wrote this down so I wouldn't forget.
Caller -> I'm checking her supplies and we're low. On the diabetes things. Her testing stuff. I wanted to tell you before she runs out.
Nurse -> Where are you right now? In her kitchen?
Caller -> In her bedroom. She's in the recliner. I'm standing by the dresser where she keeps the kit. She keeps it in a zipper bag. A blue one.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Let me pull up her chart. Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> December twelfth. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> And I think I have a number for you on file. Is it six one oh, five five five, zero one one five?
Caller -> That's the agency cell. Yes. That's me when I'm out.
Nurse -> Perfect. Which supplies are low?
Caller -> The strips. The test strips. I counted. There's five left. In the box. And she checks three times a day. So that's less than two days.
Nurse -> What times does she usually check?
Caller -> Before breakfast, before supper and at bedtime. She's very regular. She writes it all down in a little book. With a gold pen.
Nurse -> Ha. Good habit.
Nurse -> Okay. Five test strips. What about the lancets?
Caller -> That's the thing. There's none. We ran out of the little needles for the finger. Lancets. The nurse said they're called lancets. There are none. I've been using the same one over and over. For a couple days.
Nurse -> Did you tell her the lancet was reused?
Caller -> She knows. She said it's okay. But I could tell she didn't like it.
Nurse -> It's not okay. But you're fixing it, so don't feel bad.
Nurse -> Oh. Okay. We don't want to reuse them. That's no good. Does it hurt her?
Caller -> It does. A little. She says her fingers are sore. They're tender. The tips. She winces. She has little red spots on her fingers. But no infection. They look okay.
Nurse -> No pus, swelling, warmth?
Caller -> No. Just a little pink. Like a pinprick, only a lot of them. She says it's like having tiny paper cuts.
Nurse -> Okay. They should heal fast with new lancets.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll fix that. And what about the insulin pen needles?
Caller -> The pen needles. The ones for the pen. There's about ten left in the box. She uses two a day. So five days. Maybe more. I didn't count exactly.
Nurse -> Okay. About ten left. Good. Rhoda, what was her sugar this morning?
Caller -> I did it before breakfast. A hundred and thirty one. That's a good one for her. She was proud.
Nurse -> Good for her. Is she eating well, taking her medicines on time?
Caller -> She eats like a bird, but regularly. She does her own pen. I just watch. She doesn't let me touch it.
Nurse -> That's wonderful that she's independent.
Nurse -> That's a great number. Okay. Let me place the order. Do you know who her supplier is?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'm sorry. The box says something. Hold on. Let me look. It says, hmm, it's a long name. Midland Diabetic. I think. Midland something.
Nurse -> That's okay. I have it in her chart. Midland Diabetic Supply. I'll use that.
Caller -> Oh good. That's it. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm going to order a box of test strips, a box of lancets, a box of pen needles, and I'll mark it urgent. Give me a minute.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm sitting with her. She's watching her shows.
Nurse -> What does she like to watch?
Caller -> Her stories. Day time. And the cooking shows. She doesn't cook anymore but she watches everyone else.
Nurse -> Ha. A fellow connoisseur.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for the strips, lancets and pen needles.
Caller -> Oh wonderful. How fast?
Nurse -> I'm going to arrange delivery for Thursday. Is somebody going to be there?
Caller -> Thursday. Yes. I work Thursdays. Eight to four. I'll be here.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll ask them to deliver Thursday, and I'll make a note about calling the agency if they can't find the house.
Caller -> Good. Because last time they went to the wrong house. Two doors down. The lady had to walk it over. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll note the address. Rhoda, until Thursday, you have five strips and no lancets. Is there a spare lancet somewhere? A different brand?
Nurse -> Is the house number clearly visible from the street?
Caller -> It's on the mailbox. In big silver stickers. And on the porch light. It's number eleven.
Nurse -> Good. I'll note it.
Caller -> I don't know. Let me check her kit. In the drawer. Hold on. Let me look. There's a few lancets. In the bottom of the bag. They're a different kind. Little ones with a cap. Twelve of them. Oh good. Twelve.
Caller -> They're from the old kit. From the hospital. I forgot she had them.
Nurse -> That's lucky. They'll tide her over until Thursday.
Nurse -> Perfect. Use a new one every time. Never reuse. Prick the side of her fingertip, not the pad. And rotate fingers, so she's not hitting the same one.
Caller -> New one each time. Side of the fingertip. Rotate. Okay. I'll show her. She's been using the pad. Right on the middle.
Nurse -> The side hurts less and heals faster.
Caller -> Good. She'll be thrilled. She hates this.
Caller -> She tells me every time she'd rather have her teeth pulled. But she does it. She never skips.
Nurse -> She sounds tough.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course. Okay. And call us if the supplies haven't come by Thursday afternoon, or if her sugar is ever over three hundred or under seventy.
Caller -> Over three hundred. Under seventy. Or no supplies by Thursday afternoon. Okay. I got it.
Nurse -> Great. Anything else, Rhoda?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Giorgio. You're always so helpful.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care of Juanita.
Caller -> I will. Bye.
