transcript:
Nurse -> Oak Hollow Home Health, this is Brenda.
Caller -> Hi, Brenda. It's Maribel Aldridge. I'm calling about my mother, Fenella Aldridge. I think I messed up her pills. I'm not sure. I'm not sure if I messed up.
Nurse -> Okay. Take a breath. Mix-ups with pills are very common, and it sounds like you caught it. Let's go through it.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry, I'm a little rattled. I've been looking at these bottles for an hour.
Nurse -> Okay, Maribel. Let's go through it. What's your mother's date of birth?
Caller -> June thirtieth. Nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> Got it. And a good number to reach you?
Caller -> You have it. It's the same as last time. It's in her chart. I'm at her house but I don't remember the landline number. Can you use the one in the file?
Nurse -> Yes. I can see one on file. I'll use that. Thank you.
Caller -> Great. Thanks.
Nurse -> Is your mom there with you right now?
Caller -> She's in the living room. In her chair. She has her yarn. She's making a scarf for my son.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
Nurse -> Tell me what happened with the pills.
Caller -> So I came over this morning and I was organizing her kitchen. And I noticed two bottles on the shelf. Side by side. The same size. Orange. White caps. And one says Prilosec and one says Prozac. And they both say twenty milligrams. And I thought, wait. These look the same. And what if she mixed them up.
Nurse -> Are the labels from the same pharmacy?
Caller -> Yes. Same pharmacy. Same label design. Same font. The only difference is the name. P R I L O S E C and P R O Z A C. They look so alike on the label.
Nurse -> They do. That's why they're often mixed up.
Nurse -> Okay. So you found Prilosec and Prozac, twenty milligrams each, next to each other. What does she take them for?
Caller -> The Prilosec is for her stomach. Her heartburn. One a day, in the morning. And the Prozac is for her mood. Her depression. One a day in the morning. So she takes both, every morning. With breakfast.
Nurse -> And who sets up her pills? You?
Caller -> Usually me, on weekends. During the week, she does it herself. I started checking more often.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. We'll talk about that with the nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. So she should take one of each every morning, twenty milligrams each.
Caller -> Yes. That's right. But yesterday, I was here, and I put her pills out in the little cup. And I was in a rush. And I think I might have put two of the same one. Two Prilosec. And no Prozac. I'm not sure. I was on the phone with my husband.
Nurse -> Okay. What makes you think that?
Caller -> Because this morning I counted. The Prozac bottle has more pills than it should. And the Prilosec bottle is lower. Like by one. If I put two Prilosec in the cup yesterday, then the count would be off. By one. One less Prilosec. One more Prozac.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good detective work. So it might be that she took two Prilosec and missed her Prozac yesterday. Or it might be that the count is just off.
Caller -> Right. I don't know. I can't be sure. My mother can't remember. I asked her. She said she took her pills. She doesn't know which ones.
Nurse -> How many pills should be in each bottle by now?
Caller -> I filled the bottles on the first. They're thirty pills each. It's the twenty sixth. So it should be four left. And one has five, and one has three. So it's off by one.
Nurse -> That fits a swap by one pill. Okay.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let me read you the list from her chart. Tell me if it matches. Lisinopril ten milligrams once a day. Prilosec twenty milligrams once a day. Prozac twenty milligrams once a day. And Tylenol as needed. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's all of them. Lisinopril, Prilosec, Prozac. And the Tylenol for her knees. I didn't mix up the lisinopril. That one's a different color. It's pink. And it's a different bottle. It's the other two.
Caller -> The lisinopril is pink. Little pink. I always do that one first so I don't mix it.
Nurse -> Good system.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. The lisinopril is fine. How is your mother feeling today?
Caller -> She has a little heartburn. Mild. She said her stomach burns a bit. It's the same as usual. And she says she feels a little down. A little blue. But she says it's the weather. It's gray out. She's not, you know, I'm not saying anything bad. She's just a little down.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she talking about hurting herself, or not wanting to go on? Any thoughts like that?
Caller -> No. No, no. Nothing like that. She's not saying that. She said she's tired of the rain. That's all. She's not, I don't think so. She's fine. She was knitting this morning.
Nurse -> What's she knitting?
Caller -> A scarf for my son. In red and gold. His school colors. She's on her third scarf this year.
Nurse -> Aw. She's keeping busy. That's good.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. Any black stools, or vomiting, or severe stomach pain?
Caller -> No. No black. No vomiting. No pain. Just the heartburn. A little. Nothing else.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Maribel, here's what I think. If she did take two Prilosec yesterday, that's a double dose of a stomach medicine, which is generally not dangerous. And if she missed one day of Prozac, that's usually not a big problem either, but I want the provider to know. I'm going to message the provider today about the possible mix-up.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you. Should I give her the Prozac now? To catch up?
Nurse -> No. Please don't double up. Just give her the usual dose tomorrow morning with breakfast. Wait for the provider's call if you're worried.
Caller -> What if it's a big deal? What if she needs to go to the hospital?
Nurse -> It doesn't sound like it. The medicines are not dangerous in these amounts. But the provider will make sure.
Caller -> Okay. That helps.
Caller -> Okay. No double. Tomorrow morning. One of each.
Nurse -> Perfect. And let's make this safer. Put the Prilosec and Prozac on different shelves. Not side by side. And read the label twice before you pour the pills. One more time when you put them in the cup.
Caller -> Different shelves. Read it twice. Okay. I have a Sharpie. I could mark the Prozac with a purple dot. For mood. Purple for the blues.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. I'm also going to add a note on her medication list about the two look-alike names, so everyone on the team sees it.
Caller -> Oh, that'd be wonderful. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's done. I added it to her list just now. And I'll call the number on file this evening to let you know what the provider says.
Caller -> This evening. Good. I'll be at her house. I'll stay for dinner.
Nurse -> One more thing. Call us if she gets black or bloody stools, vomiting, or really bad stomach pain, or if her mood gets worse. Like if she seems hopeless, or says she wants to hurt herself.
Caller -> Black stools, vomiting, bad pain. Hopeless or hurting herself. Okay. I don't think so. But I'll watch. I'll call.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing, Maribel?
Caller -> I'm okay. I just feel guilty. I should have been more careful.
Nurse -> You caught it quickly. That's what matters.
Caller -> Thank you. I appreciate it.
Nurse -> Talk to you this evening.
Caller -> Bye, Brenda.

transcript:
Nurse -> Silverleaf Hospice, this is Eliza.
Caller -> Eliza, hi. It's Rowena. Rowena Tillman. It's my dad. Barnabas Tillman. He's not settling. He's thrashing and moaning. I gave him the lorazepam twice and it's not working. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Rowena. I'm here. I'm glad you called. You're not alone. Are you with your dad right now?
Caller -> I'm in the room. I'm sitting next to the bed. I have the phone on the bed. I'm holding his hand. He keeps pulling it away.
Nurse -> That's fine. Don't worry if he pulls away. Just stay close.
Caller -> I will. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. Let me get his chart up. Can you tell me his date of birth?
Caller -> March fifteenth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one zero four. It's my cell. I'm here with it.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me what you're seeing.
Caller -> He's moving all over. His arms, his legs. He's pulling at the sheet. He's pulling at his gown. He's trying to get up. He can't. He's too weak. But he's trying. And he's making a sound. A moaning sound. Over and over. Like a groan.
Nurse -> Okay. When did this start?
Caller -> This afternoon. Around one. He was sleeping and then he woke up and he was like this. And it's getting worse. It's been, what, ten hours? It's eleven now. Ten hours.
Nurse -> And before the afternoon, how had he been? Was he sleeping, eating?
Caller -> Sleeping mostly. He's been sleeping more all week. He stopped eating Friday. He took sips until yesterday. He hasn't opened his eyes much.
Nurse -> Okay. That helps me understand.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm so sorry. That's a long time to watch. What have you given him?
Caller -> The lorazepam. The point five. The little tablet under the tongue. Or the liquid. I used the liquid. I gave him one at two. And another at six. It's every four hours if needed. I gave the six one at six. It's not working. He's still like this.
Nurse -> Okay. Lorazepam half a milligram at two and again at six. Nothing since six?
Caller -> Nothing since. It's five hours. It's past the four. Can I give another? I wanted to ask first. I didn't want to give too much.
Nurse -> It's always okay to ask. You did exactly the right thing.
Caller -> I was so afraid of hurting him. That's why I called.
Nurse -> That was the right thing to ask. I'm going to get the on-call clinician right now. But first, tell me a bit more. Does he seem to be in pain?
Caller -> I don't know. He's grimacing. His face is all scrunched. His forehead. And he's moaning. I can't tell if it's pain or he's scared. Or confused. He doesn't know me. Not really. He looked at me at six and said who are you. And that's the first time.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very hard. Thank you for staying with him. Has he had anything to drink? Any urine today?
Caller -> He hasn't had anything to drink since yesterday. I tried a swab. He turns his head. And he hasn't peed. Not since this morning. The diaper is dry. I checked at ten. It was dry.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for checking. And his breathing? Can you describe it?
Caller -> It's weird. It goes fast. Then it stops. Like a long pause. Ten seconds. Maybe more. Then he takes a big breath. And then fast again. It's scary. I keep thinking he's stopped.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a pattern we see sometimes near the end of life. It can look frightening but it doesn't hurt him. Rowena, I want you to know I'm going to help you through this. First I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'm sending a nurse to your house. I want her there within the hour. She'll sit with you and your dad.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. It's eleven at night.
Nurse -> I know. We have a night nurse. She's on her way as soon as we hang up.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, I want you to give him something from the comfort kit. Do you know where it is?
Caller -> It's in the fridge. In the door. The white box. I haven't opened it. The nurse said not to unless we call.
Nurse -> Right. This is a good time. Can you get it? Take the phone with you.
Caller -> Okay. Dad, I'm going to the kitchen. I'll be right back. Mama's coming. No, I'm Rowena. I'm Ro. Okay. I'm in the kitchen. The fridge. I have it. It's cold. I'm opening it. There's three bottles.
Nurse -> Perfect. Read me the labels.
Caller -> One says lorazepam. One says morphine. One says haloperidol. H A L O P E R I D O L. Two milligrams per mL. There's a syringe in a bag.
Nurse -> Okay. The haloperidol is the one we want. Two milligrams per mL. I want you to give a quarter mL. That's point two five mL. That's half a milligram. The syringe has lines. Do you see the line that says point two five?
Caller -> Let me look. The syringe is in a bag. It's a little one. Oh. It's an oral syringe. It has numbers. Point two five. Yes. I see it. The first long line.
Nurse -> That's the one. Draw up to that line. Take the cap off the bottle, push the syringe in, pull the plunger back slowly to the point two five line. Tell me when it's there.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. I'm doing it. I'm pulling. Slowly. Okay. Oh. It's too much. I went past. It's at the point five. Let me push it back. Okay. Back. Point two five. Okay. It's at the line.
Nurse -> Good. Now let the air bubbles go. Tap the syringe and push the plunger just until the first drop. Then pull back to point two five again.
Caller -> Tapping. A little drop came out. Back to point two five. There. Right at the line.
Nurse -> Great. Check again. The top of the black plunger tip should be exactly on point two five.
Caller -> It is. The top of the black. It's at the line. Point two five.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now go back to your dad. Carry it carefully. Give it slowly into his cheek, in the pocket between the cheek and the gum. Not straight down his throat. Squeeze very slowly, a little at a time.
Caller -> In the cheek pocket. Slowly. Okay. I'm walking. Dad, I'm back. I have the medicine. Open your mouth a little. Daddy, open. Come on. There. I'm putting it in the cheek. Slowly. He's moving his head. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Okay. It's almost all in. Okay. Done. All of it.
Nurse -> You did that perfectly. What time is it right now?
Caller -> It's eleven fifteen. Eleven sixteen.
Nurse -> Write that down. Eleven sixteen. Haloperidol, point two five mL.
Caller -> I'm writing. On my hand. Eleven sixteen. I'll write it on the sheet too.
Nurse -> Good. It can take twenty or thirty minutes to work. It won't be instant. In the meantime, let's make him a little more comfortable. Can you turn him gently onto his side? Put a pillow behind his back, and one between his knees. Keep the room dim and quiet. Put a cool damp cloth on his forehead. And talk to him softly. Or put on quiet music.
Caller -> Okay. On his side. Pillow. Okay. I'm turning him. He's so thin. Okay. He's on his right side. I put the pillow. I'll get the cloth. I have a washcloth. Cool water. Okay. On his forehead. I'm turning off the big light. The lamp is on. It's low.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there music he likes?
Caller -> Frank Sinatra. He loved Sinatra. I have it on my phone. Hold on. I'll find it. Okay. I'm playing it. Soft. "Fly Me to the Moon."
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Hearing is the last sense to go. He can hear you.
Caller -> Really? I didn't know that. Oh. Daddy. I love you. I love you, Daddy.
Nurse -> He knows.
Nurse -> Beautiful. Hold his hand. Let him hear your voice. Tell him you're here.
Caller -> Daddy, I'm here. It's Ro. I'm right here. You're okay. You're safe. We love you. Oh. He's quieter. He's still moving a little. But he's quieter. His arm isn't thrashing so much.
Nurse -> That's good. That's what we want. Keep talking to him.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep talking. He used to sing this. He used to sing it in the car. Badly. Ha.
Nurse -> That's a lovely memory. Keep telling him.
Caller -> Daddy, you used to sing this in the car. You sang it so loud. Mama used to say, Barney, stop. And you'd sing louder.
Caller -> Oh. He's squeezing my hand. He's squeezing. Eliza, he squeezed.
Nurse -> That's beautiful. He's with you.
Nurse -> Rowena, has he had a fall or hurt himself today? Anything like that?
Caller -> No. No falls. He's been in bed. He hasn't moved off the bed. He can't. He's not hurt. No bruises. Nothing. He's just agitated.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Rowena, is anyone else with you tonight?
Caller -> My brother. Danny. He's at the airport. He's flying in. He gets in at midnight. I'm alone right now. My husband is home with the kids.
Nurse -> Okay. Would you like me to call your husband? Or a friend?
Caller -> No. I'm okay. I'll call my husband after. He's sleeping.
Nurse -> Alright. I'm here with you for as long as you need. You're not alone.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. I've been alone with this all day. The aide left at five.
Nurse -> Did the aide say anything about how he was this afternoon?
Caller -> She said he'd been restless since lunch. She wanted to stay but her shift ended. She hugged me when she left. She's so sweet.
Nurse -> That's kind.
Nurse -> That's a lot. You've been doing something very hard and very loving.
Caller -> I don't know if I'm doing it right.
Nurse -> You're doing it right. You called, you gave the medicine, you're holding him, playing his music. That's exactly right.
Caller -> Is he dying? Is that what this is?
Nurse -> I think his body is getting very tired. The pauses in the breathing, the not drinking, the little urine, they're signs that he is near the end of his life. I can't tell you exactly when. It could be hours, or a day or two. The nurse who comes tonight will know more.
Caller -> Should I call the rest of the family? My sisters? They're in Ohio and Texas.
Nurse -> If you'd like them to say goodbye, you can call them. Phone calls count. You can hold the phone to his ear.
Caller -> I'll call them after. After you call me. Maybe now. I'll text them to call me.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I thought so. I just needed someone to say it.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. I know that's hard to hear. Do you want to tell me about him?
Caller -> He was a mailman. For thirty five years. He knew everyone on his route. He used to carry dog biscuits in his pocket. The dogs loved him. He'd come home with a bite on his ankle at least once a year.
Nurse -> Ha. A dog biscuit man. That sounds like a good man.
Caller -> He was the best. He taught me how to ride a bike on the street in front of the house. He ran behind me. I thought he was holding on. He wasn't.
Nurse -> What did he say when you got it?
Caller -> He said, there she goes. He said it like I was a rocket. I still hear it.
Nurse -> That's a wonderful memory.
Nurse -> That's a beautiful story.
Caller -> He's calmer. I think the medicine is working. He's not moaning. His face is relaxing.
Nurse -> Good. That's what we want to see. How's his breathing now?
Caller -> Still the pauses. But he's not fighting. He's breathing with it. Like he's resting.
Nurse -> Good. Stay close. Keep the music on. I'll call you back in thirty minutes to check, and the nurse will be there before that.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. And you'll call my cell.
Nurse -> Yes. Three one four, five five five, zero one zero four.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> And Rowena, call any hour tonight. If he gets more restless, if you have a question, or if you just want someone on the phone with you. Day or night. I'm here.
Caller -> Any hour. Okay. I won't hesitate. I might call just to hear a voice.
Nurse -> Please do.
Caller -> I'll let you go so you can page the doctor. Thank you, Eliza. I don't know how to thank you.
Nurse -> You just did. Stay with your dad. I'll talk to you soon.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Rowena.

Nurse -> Heartland Hospice, this is Lorraine.
Caller -> Hi, Lorraine. This is Maxine Oduya. I'm the volunteer coordinator. I'm not calling about my own patient. I'm calling because one of my volunteers told me something about one of your patients, and I thought you should know.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called. Do you want to start from the beginning?
Caller -> Yes. Let me find the note. I have it on my desk. Hold on. It's under my coffee.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Nurse -> Okay, Maxine. Thanks. Which patient?
Caller -> His name is Alvin. Alvin Tuckerman. Tuckerman. I'm looking at the note. The volunteer is Dolores Ng. She sat with him this afternoon. She writes everything down.
Caller -> She's been with us eight years. She does the Tuesday and Thursday afternoons at three homes. She's wonderful. Her notes are beautiful. She writes with a fountain pen.
Nurse -> Ha. A fountain pen.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me pull up Alvin Tuckerman. I see him. What did Dolores write?
Caller -> Okay. I'm going to read it. She wrote, and I quote, "Mr. Tuckerman tried to stand up by himself from the recliner. He got halfway up and said he was dizzy. He grabbed the table and held on. I helped him sit back. He said his legs turn to jelly when he stands. He said it's been happening a few days." Then she wrote, "Daughter was at the store."
Nurse -> Okay. That's very helpful. So he was dizzy when he stood, grabbed the table, and didn't fall.
Caller -> That's what it says. He didn't fall. She caught his elbow. It says, "I held his arm. He sat down slowly. No fall."
Nurse -> Did she say how long he was dizzy for? A few seconds or longer?
Caller -> It doesn't say. Hold on, let me read it again. Nope. It just says he said he was dizzy. And that he sat back down. And that he felt better after a few minutes. Oh, here it is, she wrote he felt better after sitting.
Nurse -> Okay. That helps.
Nurse -> Okay. And the legs turning to jelly?
Caller -> That's his words. She put it in quotes. It says he said it's been happening for a few days. A few days. Hmm. It doesn't say more. I don't want to guess.
Nurse -> No, that's fine. It's helpful to have his exact words. Is Dolores still there? Can I talk to her?
Caller -> No. She left at four. She's gone home. I can give you her number. Or I can ask her to call you tomorrow.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll work with what I have. Maxine, does Dolores say whether he was alone? Whether anyone else was in the house?
Caller -> Just the daughter. Who was out. At the store. It's the daughter who lives with him. Her name is, hold on, I think it says Gabrielle. Gabby.
Nurse -> Okay. Gabrielle. Got it. I have her in the chart as the contact.
Caller -> I met her once. Gabby. She's very nice. She brought us muffins at the volunteer luncheon.
Nurse -> That sounds like her.
Caller -> Good. So that's the whole note. I thought it was important. He almost fell.
Nurse -> Did Dolores say whether she'd seen him do this before? Or if the daughter had mentioned it?
Caller -> No, nothing like that. She says in the note it was the first time she saw it. But he said it's been happening.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> It is important. You did the right thing. Do you happen to know his date of birth? Or what medicines he takes?
Caller -> No. I don't. I don't have access to that. I just have the volunteer notes. I don't know the clinical stuff. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's fine. We have it in the chart. What's the best number for you, Maxine, if I need to follow up?
Caller -> My desk is six four six, five five five, zero one one one.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll send a nurse to see Mr. Tuckerman tomorrow morning, to check his blood pressure, his medicines and his balance.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Good. Should I tell Dolores?
Nurse -> You can if you like. It might make her feel good that it was acted on.
Caller -> She'll be pleased. She was worried. She almost called 911.
Caller -> She told me on the phone. She was so shaken. She said, Maxine, I almost dialed. She said he turned white for a second.
Nurse -> Turned white. Okay. Did he turn pale, or was he gray?
Caller -> She said pale. She didn't say gray. I don't want to put words in her mouth.
Nurse -> No, that's good. Pale for a second when he stood. I'll note it.
Nurse -> I'm glad she didn't need to. I'm also going to message the hospice provider this evening about the dizziness on standing and the near fall.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call his daughter this evening, since she lives with him. I'll tell her what Dolores saw, and ask her to help him get up.
Caller -> Oh good. That'd be great. She was out when this happened. She might not even know.
Nurse -> I'll fill her in. Tell me, Maxine, did Dolores say whether he had a walker nearby?
Caller -> She didn't write that. I'll ask her. I'll call her tonight and text you. I don't have your direct number. Just the office line.
Nurse -> The main line is fine. They can reach me.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that.
Nurse -> For the daughter, I'll tell her to have him sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a minute before standing, to help him whenever he stands, and to use his walker.
Caller -> Okay. I'll note that. Dolores can mention it to the daughter next time too.
Caller -> She's very good with the families. They love her.
Nurse -> I can tell.
Nurse -> Yes. And if he falls, faints, has chest pain, or the dizziness gets worse, she should call us right away.
Caller -> Falls, faints, chest pain, worse dizziness. Call right away. Okay. I'll make sure Dolores knows.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else in Dolores's note I should know?
Caller -> Hmm. Let me read. She wrote that they played cards. Gin rummy. He won. She said he was sharp and funny. And that he had a small lunch. A sandwich, half. And a glass of juice.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. He's got some fight left.
Nurse -> What does he like to do? Cards?
Caller -> Gin rummy, cribbage. Dolores says he cheats. She calls him Fast Hands.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect.
Caller -> That's what she said. She says he's a character.
Nurse -> It sounds like it. Thank you, Maxine. Thank your volunteer for me.
Caller -> I will. She'll love hearing it. Have a good night, Lorraine.
Nurse -> You too.

transcript:
Nurse -> Great Plains Hospice, this is Dmitri.
Caller -> Hi. Hi. Is this a real person? I've been talking to machines all week. I'm Carolyn Salazar. I'm calling about my father. Hubert Salazar.
Nurse -> It's a real person. I'm Dmitri. I'm a nurse. How can I help, Carolyn?
Caller -> Sorry. I'm not usually like this. I'm a middle school teacher. I'm good at being calm. I'm good at kids who throw things. This I can't do.
Nurse -> That's okay. This is a different kind of hard.
Caller -> It is. It really is.
Caller -> I don't even know where to start. I'm so tired. I'm so tired I can't think. I haven't slept in two weeks.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. Tell me about it. But first, so I have the right chart, what's your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> April fourth. Nineteen thirty nine. He's eighty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one four six. That's my cell. It's on the charger. I sleep with it by my head. In case.
Nurse -> Where are you right now? At home with your dad?
Caller -> In the kitchen. He's asleep in the den. He's finally asleep. It's seven in the morning and he's finally asleep. I came in here to call.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Take a minute for yourself.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay, Carolyn. Tell me what's going on at night.
Caller -> He wakes up every hour. Every single hour. Dad, I need water. Carolyn, I need the bathroom. Carolyn, I'm cold. Carolyn, I'm hot. Carolyn, where's my wife. Every hour. All night. I get up. I help him. I get him water. I put him back. And I lie down and he calls again.
Nurse -> Does he know what's happening? Is he confused at night?
Caller -> Sometimes. Sometimes he thinks it's morning and he wants to get up and make breakfast. Sometimes he thinks he's at work. He worked at the post office. He thinks he's late.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. I'll tell the team.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds exhausting. How long has it been like this?
Caller -> Two weeks. Two weeks today. I counted. I've slept maybe three hours a night. In bits. Twenty minutes. Forty minutes. I'm going to kill myself if he asks for water one more time. I'm not, I'm not saying that. That's just, you know, an expression. I could scream.
Nurse -> It sounds like you've been carrying a lot.
Caller -> I have. I really have.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you. I'm going to ask something directly, because I care. Are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself, or of hurting your dad?
Caller -> No. No. God, no. I would never. I would never hurt myself. I would never hurt him. I love him. I'm just, I'm at the end of my rope. I'm saying it badly. I'm so tired I'm saying the wrong things.
Nurse -> It's okay. People say that when they're desperate for rest. I want to make sure you're safe, and I believe you.
Caller -> I'm safe. I'm safe. I just want to sleep.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. I believe you. You're not saying the wrong thing. You're saying you're worn out. That's a real thing, and we take it seriously.
Caller -> Thank you. I just. I haven't talked to anyone. I'm the only one. My brother's in Denver. My sister doesn't talk to us. I live here with Dad. It's just me.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's you alone at night, with no relief?
Caller -> No relief. I sleep in the chair in his room. Because if I go to my room I won't hear him. And I'm afraid of him falling. So I'm in the chair. My neck is a mess.
Nurse -> Do you have any pain from sleeping in the chair?
Caller -> My neck and my back. I take ibuprofen. It helps a bit.
Nurse -> That's okay. Try a pillow behind your lower back if you can.
Caller -> I have one. It's flat now. I'll get a better one.
Nurse -> Okay. Carolyn, let me tell you what I'm going to do. First, I'm going to ask our social worker to call you today. She can talk through what help is available, and look into respite care, which is where someone else takes over for a few days or nights so you can rest.
Caller -> Respite. Is that real? Can I get that?
Nurse -> It's real. Hospice can often cover up to five days of respite care in a facility. There are also volunteers and aides who can help at night. I'm going to message our hospice team about your situation so they can plan.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. I didn't know. Nobody told me. I thought I just had to do it. I thought that was the deal.
Caller -> My friend said hospice has something like it. But I thought it was for rich people.
Nurse -> No. It's part of the benefit. The social worker will explain.
Nurse -> A lot of people think that. You don't. That's what we're here for.
Caller -> I'm going to cry. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. Cry. It's okay.
Caller -> I haven't cried in a month. I haven't had time.
Nurse -> Take a minute. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm better. Thank you.
Nurse -> What do you do for yourself, Carolyn? When you have a minute?
Caller -> I used to run. I haven't run since March. I used to do the sunrise run by the lake. I miss it. I miss the quiet.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Let's work toward getting you back on that run.
Caller -> I'd cry again if I thought too hard about it.
Nurse -> I'll call you back tomorrow morning to see how the night went and to hear from the social worker.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. What time? I'm up. I'm always up.
Nurse -> Around nine. If you're asleep, I'll leave a message.
Caller -> If I'm asleep, wake me up. Please. I need to hear this.
Nurse -> Ha. I will.
Caller -> What do I do tonight? Can I do anything differently?
Nurse -> A couple of small things. Leave a small cup of water with a straw within his reach, so he doesn't have to call for it every hour. And a urinal or the bedside commode close to the bed. And when he sleeps in the day, try to nap too. Even twenty minutes.
Caller -> A cup of water. A urinal. I have the urinal. It's in the closet. He refuses to use it. He says it's undignified.
Nurse -> Ha. Maybe make it part of the routine. Hand it to him before you lie down, as a standard step. Let him decide.
Caller -> I'll try. I'll say it's the hospice rules.
Nurse -> Tell him the nurse insisted.
Caller -> Ha. He'll believe that. He loves bossing the nurses.
Caller -> He's been a hospice patient for two months. He's trained half of you.
Nurse -> Ha. Then I have a lot to live up to.
Nurse -> Carolyn, I want to give you a number. If the tiredness ever turns into something heavier, like thoughts of hurting yourself, or you feel unsafe with him, call or text nine eight eight, any hour. It's the crisis line. It's for caregivers too.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. Okay. I don't think I'll need it. But I'll write it down. I'm putting it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. And put the hospice number right next to it.
Caller -> Already there. In red marker. Next to the pizza coupons.
Nurse -> Ha. Good placement.
Nurse -> Good. And you can also call us any hour if you feel unsafe or at the end of your rope. Day or night.
Caller -> Any hour. Thank you. That means a lot. I thought I was the only one who felt this way.
Nurse -> You're not. Almost every family caregiver feels this. It's a sign of how much you care.
Caller -> My friends say I should put him in a home. I can't. I promised my mother I wouldn't.
Nurse -> That's a big promise. You don't have to decide anything today. Let's get you some rest first.
Caller -> Yes. Rest first. Then decide.
Caller -> I guess so.
Nurse -> How's your dad doing otherwise? Is he comfortable?
Caller -> He's comfortable. He's not in pain. He's sweet, actually. Just needy. He holds my hand and says thank you. Every hour. Thank you for the water. Thank you for the blanket. It breaks my heart. And it drives me crazy.
Nurse -> Is he eating?
Caller -> A little. Applesauce. Toast. Some Ensure. He drinks the chocolate one. Not the vanilla.
Nurse -> Chocolate it is.
Nurse -> Both can be true.
Caller -> Both. Yes. Both.
Nurse -> I'll talk to you tomorrow morning, Carolyn. You did the right thing calling.
Caller -> Thank you, Dmitri. I feel lighter. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Highland Hospice, this is Isidro.
Caller -> Isidro, hi. It's Delores Quigley. I did something wrong with my husband's medicine. Marshall Quigley. I gave him the wrong one. I think I gave him the wrong one.
Nurse -> Okay, Delores. Let's slow down. I'm here. Tell me your husband's date of birth first.
Caller -> July eighteenth. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I have a phone number on file. Is it two one two, five five five, zero one six seven?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house. That's the one. I'm in the kitchen. He's in the bedroom.
Nurse -> Is he able to hear you from there?
Caller -> No. The door is half closed. I took the cordless to the kitchen so he wouldn't hear me upset.
Nurse -> That's thoughtful. You're doing fine.
Caller -> I don't feel fine. I feel like I poisoned my husband.
Nurse -> You didn't poison him. We'll go through it step by step.
Nurse -> Good. Now, what happened?
Caller -> So. Marshall's belly hurts. It's been hurting all day. And I was supposed to give him the Dilaudid. The pain one. And I went to the pill basket, and I picked up the bottle that I thought was Dilaudid. And I gave him one. And then I looked at the bottle again after, and it says Dilantin. D I L A N T I N. It was the wrong bottle.
Nurse -> Where was the bottle when you gave it? In the basket?
Caller -> In the basket. I picked it up and tapped one out. I didn't read it. I always read it, I always do, but I was in a hurry because he was groaning and I wanted to help.
Nurse -> That's understandable.
Nurse -> Okay. So you gave him a Dilantin tablet instead of the Dilaudid. Do you know what time?
Caller -> At three. It's nine thirty now. That's six and a half hours ago. And it's not his regular time. His regular time for the Dilantin is eight, two and eight. Three times a day. So I gave him an extra. Plus the two o'clock one. An hour later.
Nurse -> Okay. So he got his regular two o'clock Dilantin and then an extra one at three. How many milligrams is the tablet?
Caller -> Hundred. Hundred milligrams. Each one. So he got two hundred in one hour. Oh God.
Nurse -> Take a deep breath, Delores.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm breathing. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the amount. Thank you for being so clear. And the Dilaudid, what is the dose?
Caller -> Two milligrams. Every four hours if he needs it. For the pain. But I haven't given him any today. Not one. He's been in pain all day and I didn't give him any Dilaudid because I gave him the wrong thing. So his pain is bad. And I made it worse.
Nurse -> Okay. Delores, you didn't make his pain worse. You made a mistake, and we'll fix it. But I want to ask about the pain. What would he say it is, zero to ten?
Caller -> He says seven. A seven. He's been a seven since lunch. He was a five this morning. Now a seven. He says it's the low belly. Like a squeezing. He's curled up.
Nurse -> Does he say where exactly it hurts? Low on one side, or all across?
Caller -> Low, across. Like a belt. He's holding his stomach. He's got his knees pulled up.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the usual place for him?
Caller -> Yes. The cancer is in his bowel. It's always there. But today it's worse.
Nurse -> Okay. A seven. That's significant and we need to take care of it. How is he otherwise? Since the extra Dilantin, is he different?
Caller -> He's sleepy. Very sleepy. He's been dozing since four. And when he wakes he's slow. And he tried to go to the bathroom at six and he was wobbly. He bumped into the door frame. He wasn't like that before.
Caller -> His speech is a little slower. Not slurred. Just slow, like he's thinking before each word.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something to tell the clinician.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he still sleepy right now?
Caller -> He's asleep. He's snoring. I just checked. I woke him a few minutes ago, to ask if he wanted a drink, and he said no. And then he went right back to sleep.
Nurse -> Are his lips pink? Is he breathing at a normal pace?
Caller -> Pink. Normal. In and out. Slow, like sleeping. About, I counted, fourteen in a minute.
Nurse -> That's normal. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Can he be woken easily? If you say his name loudly or touch his shoulder?
Caller -> Yes. He wakes up. He opens his eyes and says what. And then he closes them. He's not unconscious. He just goes right back.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Any seizure activity? Jerking, staring, anything like that?
Caller -> No. No seizure. Nothing. He's had seizures before, in the spring. So I'm watching. But no. Nothing like that.
Nurse -> Good. Nausea? Vomiting?
Caller -> A little queasy. He said he felt sick to his stomach. Around seven. He didn't throw up. He had a couple of crackers and a little ginger ale and kept it down.
Nurse -> Has he had anything else to eat or drink today?
Caller -> Toast this morning. Some broth at noon. A little pudding. He doesn't eat much anymore.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. Delores, I want to explain something. Dilantin in a higher amount can cause sleepiness, unsteadiness and nausea. That's what you're seeing. It's usually not dangerous with one extra tablet, but I want the on-call clinician to decide what to do. I'm going to page them right now.
Caller -> Okay. Please. What do I do about the pain?
Nurse -> Here's what I want. Please don't give the Dilantin or the Dilaudid until the clinician calls back. Not the next Dilantin, not the Dilaudid. Hold both until we hear.
Caller -> But he's in pain. A seven. Can't I give him anything?
Nurse -> I understand. The Dilaudid is a strong pain medicine and it can make him even sleepier. Because he's already sleepy from the Dilantin, I need the clinician to say what's safe. It should only be a short wait. I'll call you back in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. And I just wait. And he hurts.
Nurse -> I know. It's hard. In the meantime, there are non-medicine things we can do. A warm heating pad on low, over a thin cloth, on his belly. A pillow under his knees. Quiet. And talk to him gently.
Caller -> A heating pad. We have one. I'll get it. Okay.
Caller -> It's on the shelf in the hall closet. I'll plug it in by the bed. I'll put a towel under it so it's not directly on him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Only on low.
Nurse -> Also, I'm sending a nurse out within the hour. She'll bring supplies and examine him.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. Good. That's good.
Nurse -> Delores, tell me about the bottles. You said they're side by side?
Caller -> Yes. In a basket on the kitchen counter. All his bottles. There are eight. They look the same. Same orange bottle. Same white cap. The labels have the same layout. And they both start with D I L A. Dilantin and Dilaudid. I picked up the one on the left. I thought the Dilaudid was on the left.
Nurse -> Do all of his bottles have child caps?
Caller -> Most do. Two don't. I asked for easy ones because of my arthritis. So some are the easy kind and some are the kind you push and twist.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. We'll talk about organizing.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a classic mix-up. They look alike and sound alike. Have you been giving his medicines for long?
Caller -> Just since last week. His sister was doing it. She went back to Phoenix. So it's me now. I'm not good with this. I'm a bookkeeper. I'm good with numbers. But not with this.
Caller -> I do the books for a bakery. Twenty two years. I'm fine with ledgers. Medicines are different. The numbers are all in the little print.
Nurse -> Ha. I'd rather read a ledger.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. You noticed the mistake and you called. That's what counts.
Caller -> I'm so scared. I'm scared he's going to have a seizure. Or not wake up.
Caller -> His last seizure was in April. It was awful. His whole body. For two minutes. Then he was out for an hour.
Nurse -> That sounds frightening. I'm glad you're watching for it.
Nurse -> I understand. Let's talk about what to watch for. Call nine one one if he has a seizure that lasts more than five minutes, if you can't wake him up, or if his breathing is slow or noisy.
Caller -> Seizure over five minutes. Can't wake him. Slow or noisy breathing. Nine one one. Okay. I'm writing it down. I have a pen.
Nurse -> Good. Also, keep him in bed or in his recliner. Help him every time he gets up, even to the bathroom. Keep the rail up and a light on. I don't want him falling.
Caller -> Rail up. Light on. Help him up. Okay. I'll sit by the bed. I'll bring the chair.
Caller -> I have the rocking chair. It was my mother's. It's the most comfortable one.
Nurse -> Bring it in. You'll be there a while.
Nurse -> Perfect. And after this is sorted, let's make the bottles safer. Put the Dilantin and the Dilaudid on different shelves. Read each label twice before you give anything. And write down every dose and time.
Caller -> Different shelves. Two times. Write it down. I'll put a sticker on the Dilaudid. A big red one. For pain.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> His sister calls every night at nine. She's going to ask. Do I tell her?
Nurse -> That's up to you. If you'd like me to talk to her, I can, with your permission.
Caller -> No. I'll tell her. She'll yell. But I'll tell her.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.
Nurse -> Don't apologize. Mistakes happen, especially for someone new to this. You did the right thing by calling right away.
Caller -> Thank you for not yelling at me. My sister yells at me.
Caller -> She thinks I'm incompetent. She's been saying it for thirty years. Since I was nineteen.
Nurse -> That sounds hard. You're doing a hard job right now.
Caller -> I'm trying. Marshall says I'm doing fine.
Nurse -> Then trust Marshall.
Nurse -> No yelling here. We just fix it.
Caller -> Can I ask something? Is he going to be okay after this? Is there any lasting harm?
Nurse -> One extra tablet like this is very unlikely to cause lasting harm. The clinician will tell us whether to adjust his doses. I don't want to promise, but this is fixable.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I needed to hear. Fixable.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll go sit with him. I'll get the heating pad.
Caller -> Should I wake him to check on him? Or let him sleep?
Nurse -> Let him sleep, but peek at him every ten or fifteen minutes. If he stirs, check that he answers you.
Caller -> Every fifteen. I'll set a timer on the stove.
Nurse -> Perfect. And keep your phone close.
Caller -> It's in my apron pocket. I haven't put it down since three.
Nurse -> Good. We'll talk soon.
Nurse -> Do that. I'm paging now. I'll call you in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Thank you, Isidro.
Nurse -> Bye, Delores.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Lights Pediatric Nursing, this is Sunita.
Caller -> Hi, Sunita. It's Noor Whitaker. I'm the mother of Ezra Whitaker. I'm calling about the supply delivery. It didn't come.
Nurse -> Hi, Noor. Let's look into it. What's Ezra's date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty sixth. Two thousand twenty one.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have a number for you on file, seven one three, five five five, zero one seven two?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. Same one. Don't call the house, it's disconnected.
Nurse -> Got it. Cell only.
Caller -> Cell only. We got rid of the landline when we moved. It's all cell. Is that a problem?
Nurse -> Not at all.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay. Tell me what's going on with the supplies.
Caller -> So we get a delivery on the twentieth. Every month. I get an email. And this month, the email said it was delivered. Delivered to the front door. But there was nothing. I looked. I called the company. They said it went to the old address. We moved in August. I updated my address in the portal. And they sent it to the old place anyway.
Nurse -> Did you speak to a person or a machine?
Caller -> A person, finally. After forty minutes. She was very nice but she didn't have the authority to do anything. She said she'd put in a ticket.
Nurse -> Ugh. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Oh no. That's frustrating. Where's the old address?
Caller -> Maple Court. The apartment. It's across town. They said they'd try to retrieve it. But it'll take a week. And I don't have a week. I'm low.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's see what you have. Let's start with the suction catheters.
Caller -> Three. I counted. Three. Ezra needs suctioning four, five times a day. More when he's congested. So that's less than a day. That's tonight and tomorrow morning.
Nurse -> When does he need it most? Mornings, nights?
Caller -> Mornings, definitely. When he wakes up he's gurgling. And after naps. And when he's been lying down a long time.
Nurse -> That's pretty typical.
Nurse -> Okay. Three. That's tight. HME filters?
Caller -> Five. The little filters that go on the end of the trach. I change them once a day. And when they get wet. So five is maybe three days. Four.
Nurse -> Okay. And the trach ties?
Caller -> None. Zero. I used the last one this morning. I have the one on him and nothing else. If it gets dirty or wet, I don't have a clean one. I made one out of a shoelace once. In an emergency. I don't want to do that again.
Nurse -> Was that an emergency?
Caller -> At two in the morning, the tie got soaked from a spit up. And I had no spare. I used a shoelace from my running shoe. It held for the night. The nurse next morning nearly fainted.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet. Please, let's not do that again.
Nurse -> Oh my goodness. No shoelaces. We'll fix that today. Noor, how's Ezra doing? You mentioned congestion?
Caller -> A little. He's got thicker secretions this week. It's been about a week. They're thicker. Yellowish. Not green. He needs more suctioning. And it takes more passes to clear. But it clears. He's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Thick yellow secretions for about a week. Do you use the humidifier? And saline?
Caller -> Humidifier all the time. And saline drops before suctioning. I do the saline when it's thick. I've been doing that. It helps.
Nurse -> Good. How many drops?
Caller -> Two to three. Per the sheet. Never more. Too much makes him cough forever.
Nurse -> Exactly right.
Nurse -> Good. Is he running a fever?
Caller -> No. Ninety eight point five. This morning. And his color is good. Pink. Lips pink. Fingernails pink. No blue. No gray.
Nurse -> Good. And his oxygen reading?
Caller -> Ninety seven. It's been ninety seven or ninety eight all day. He's on room air. He's doing fine. He's playing with his trains.
Nurse -> How many trains does he have?
Caller -> Too many. They take up the whole living room. My husband steps on the track every morning and curses.
Nurse -> Ha. A hazard.
Nurse -> That's very reassuring. Is he eating, drinking, active?
Caller -> Eating great. He had pancakes. He wants chocolate milk. He's loud. He's running up and down the hall. With his trach. He doesn't let it slow him down. Ha.
Caller -> We bought a little tracheostomy shield for the bath. And a sprinkler outfit for the summer. He's not scared of anything.
Nurse -> What a brave kid.
Nurse -> I love that. Okay. Noor, I'm going to order your supplies right now. Let me enter it. Suction catheters, what size does Ezra use?
Caller -> The ten French. Ten Fr. I think. The green ones. In the sleeve.
Nurse -> Ten French. Got it. And the HME filters, the pediatric ones. And trach ties. Velcro or cotton?
Caller -> Velcro. The soft ones. The foam-lined ones. The cotton ones scratch him.
Nurse -> Velcro foam. Okay. I'm ordering a case of ten French suction catheters, two boxes of the pediatric HME filters, and a box of foam Velcro trach ties. I'm marking it urgent and using your current address.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much. The new address is, do you have it? Cedar Hollow Lane. Forty seven.
Nurse -> Is there an apartment number?
Caller -> No. It's a house. It's the yellow house with the blue door. There's a ramp.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll add the description.
Nurse -> Yes. Forty seven Cedar Hollow. Good. It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for the suction catheters, the filters and the trach ties, marked urgent, to your new address.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. When?
Nurse -> I'm going to arrange for a delivery tomorrow morning. I'll ask them to call you when they're on the way. Will someone be home?
Caller -> I'm home. I'm always home. I have a delivery man who knows our dog. Ha. He has treats.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. I'll arrange tomorrow morning for the delivery.
Caller -> Perfect. Sunita, what about tonight? I have three catheters. What if I run out?
Nurse -> I'd like you to use them only when he needs it. Suction when you hear gurgling, see a drop in oxygen, or he looks distressed. Not on a schedule. One catheter per pass, and don't rinse and reuse a catheter. Use a fresh one each time, as you've been trained. If you're down to your last one tonight, call me and I'll figure out something.
Caller -> Okay. Only when he needs it. A fresh one each time. I won't reuse. I know. One of the nurses told me you can rinse them out and use them again, but I said no.
Nurse -> Right. We don't do that at home for the lower airway.
Caller -> Okay. And call you if I'm down to one.
Nurse -> Yes. Day or night. I'll bring one myself if I have to.
Caller -> You'd do that? Wow. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a nurse to see Ezra tomorrow. She can look at him, listen to his lungs, and check the thicker secretions.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. Ten o'clock? Eleven?
Nurse -> Either. The scheduler will call.
Caller -> Okay. Ezra likes the nurse with the braids. She does voices. She does a pirate voice.
Nurse -> Ha. That's Tabitha. I'll ask for her.
Caller -> She taught him to say trach. He says it like a pirate. Trarrrch.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect.
Caller -> He'll be so happy.
Nurse -> Noor, one more thing, since the secretions are thicker. Make sure the humidifier is running at night too. And call nine one one if the trach comes out and can't go back in, if he turns blue or gray, or if suction doesn't clear him.
Caller -> Trach out and can't replace. Blue or gray. Suction doesn't work. I know the plan. It's on the fridge. We have a go-bag. A spare trach, one size smaller. Everything.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Keep the go-bag by the door.
Caller -> It's by the door. Always.
Nurse -> You're a very prepared mom.
Caller -> I laminated the emergency plan. Twice. Because he colored on the first one.
Caller -> I have to be. Thank you, Sunita. I appreciate you.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Noor. Hang in there. Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye. Say hi to the pirate nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. Bye.

Caller -> Yeah. It's eight hundred, five five five, oh one three three. Extension four one.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Henrik.
Caller -> Hi, Henrik. It's Francesca Brannigan. I'm calling about my daughter. Ottilie. O T T I L I E. Brannigan. She had her tonsils out on Tuesday.
Nurse -> And how old is she again? Four?
Caller -> She turned four in March. She's tiny for her age. She's been on the small side. The anesthesia scared me. I was a wreck.
Nurse -> It's a lot for a parent. Everyone gets through it.
Nurse -> Hi, Francesca. Yes, I remember. How's she doing?
Caller -> She's doing okay. I think. I'm calling because I have a question and I want to check in. It's been four days.
Nurse -> Good. Let me bring up her chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> March twenty ninth. Twenty twenty two.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one four eight.
Nurse -> Perfect. Tell me how her throat is.
Caller -> It hurts but not terribly. She says it's a three. We use the faces chart. The faces. She points to the little frowny one. Not the crying one. A three.
Nurse -> Which faces chart? The one with the numbers?
Caller -> The Wong-Baker. The one from the surgeon's office. I taped it to the fridge. She points to the one she is.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the right one.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it getting better or worse than yesterday?
Caller -> Better. Yesterday she was a four. The day before a five. So it's going down.
Nurse -> That's a good trend. What is she taking for the pain?
Caller -> The Children's Tylenol. The liquid. It says one sixty milligrams in five mL. I give her seven and a half mL. Every six hours if she needs it. I gave her one at noon. So it's been six hours. She's due. She says she's okay. She's due but she doesn't want it.
Nurse -> What flavor is the Tylenol? Does she take it okay?
Caller -> Grape. She hates grape. I mix it with a little applesauce. She takes it that way. It's a battle.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Nurse -> Okay. Seven and a half mL of the one sixty per five. At noon, and she's due now. Does she seem like she needs it?
Caller -> She's playing. She's coloring. She doesn't seem to need it. But the doctor said stay ahead of the pain. So I'm thinking I should give it. Before bed.
Nurse -> That's reasonable. If she's okay now, you can give it at bedtime so she sleeps comfortably. Just don't go over every six hours.
Caller -> Okay. At bedtime. Eight thirty.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is she having ear pain?
Caller -> A little. Her ears hurt. She grabs her ear and says ow. It's mild. The doctor said that's normal. Referred pain.
Nurse -> That's right. It's very common. Is she eating and drinking?
Caller -> She's drinking. She had apple juice and water and a popsicle. She's eating ice cream. And mashed potatoes. And scrambled eggs. And she's eaten half a banana. She's not eating the toast. It scratches.
Nurse -> Does she complain of the food getting stuck, or pain when swallowing?
Caller -> Only for dry things. Cold and soft goes down fine. She likes the ice cream the best. We went through two cartons.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the recovery diet.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Eating and drinking are the main things. Any bleeding? Spitting up blood?
Caller -> No. No blood. I checked her mouth. I used a flashlight. The back of her throat is white. That's normal, the nurse said. It's the scabs. No red blood. And no blood on the pillow. And no fever. Ninety nine point one this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. The white patches are normal. Ninety nine one is fine. Francesca, what's your question?
Caller -> Can I alternate the Tylenol with ibuprofen? I read that you can. Every three hours. And the nurse at the surgeon's office said no ibuprofen, but then my mother in law said it's fine. And I'm confused.
Nurse -> Good question to ask. After a tonsillectomy, a lot of surgeons say no ibuprofen for the first two weeks because of bleeding risk. I wouldn't add anything until the surgeon says. I'll message the surgeon's office to confirm and I'll tell them you asked.
Caller -> Oh good. The surgeon is Dr. Pavlov. P A V L O V.
Nurse -> Does Dr. Pavlov's office usually call back quickly?
Caller -> Usually by the next morning. They have a nurse named Gina. She's good. She always calls.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll also reach out to Gina.
Nurse -> Got it. Dr. Pavlov. And I'll call you tomorrow with their answer.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. In the meantime, just the Tylenol.
Nurse -> Just the Tylenol, as directed. Don't give any ibuprofen or aspirin or anything with those in it.
Caller -> Okay. No ibuprofen. No aspirin. I read the labels. I have a cold medicine that has something. I'll check.
Caller -> It's the children's one. The purple one. I haven't given it. She doesn't have a cold, I just keep it.
Nurse -> Good. Don't give it unless the surgeon says.
Nurse -> Good. Check anything you give her.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> A few other things. Keep offering cool fluids. Popsicles, ice cream, cold water. Soft foods. And avoid anything sharp, crunchy, hot or acidic. No chips, no toast crusts, no orange juice.
Caller -> No chips. No toast. No OJ. Got it. She's been wanting toast. I keep saying not yet.
Nurse -> Right. Another week or so. Call nine one one if she has bright red blood coming from her mouth, or if she keeps spitting up blood. And call us for a fever over one hundred one, if she refuses all fluids, or if she hasn't peed in eight hours.
Caller -> Bright red blood, nine one one. Fever over a hundred one, no fluids, no pee, call. Okay. I'll watch. I wrote it on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is she sleeping okay?
Caller -> She wakes up at night. She cries a little and then goes back. She sleeps with me. In my bed. I know. I know I shouldn't.
Caller -> My husband sleeps on the couch. He says he doesn't mind. He's a champ.
Nurse -> Ha. Give him credit.
Nurse -> It's okay. She's recovering. Do what comforts her.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I felt guilty.
Nurse -> No guilt needed.
Caller -> Thank you, Henrik. Is it okay if I call again if I think of something?
Nurse -> Anytime. Talk to you tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Northgate Hospice, this is Lorenzo.
Caller -> Lorenzo, it's Marguerite Delgado. I think I gave my husband, Everhart Delgado, too much morphine. I think something's wrong. He's hard to wake.
Nurse -> Okay, Marguerite. I'm here. Tell me exactly what you gave and when.
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid. From the new bottle. The pharmacy delivered a new bottle yesterday. I gave him five mL. Like always. Twenty minutes ago.
Nurse -> Okay. The new bottle. Do you know what strength it says?
Caller -> Hold on. I have it here. It says twenty milligrams per mL. And the old one said five milligrams per five mL. Oh. Oh no. It's different. It's concentrated. I gave him five mL of the strong one. That's a hundred milligrams. That's twenty times what he usually gets.
Nurse -> Marguerite, listen to me. We're going to get help right now. You did the right thing calling.
Caller -> I'm so stupid. I'm so stupid.
Nurse -> You're not. Let's focus on Ev.
Nurse -> Okay. Marguerite, I need you to hang up and call nine one one right now. This is an emergency. Is Ev breathing?
Caller -> He's breathing. It's slow. It's very slow. He's hard to wake up. I called his name. I shook him. He opened his eyes for a second and closed them.
Nurse -> Is he making any sound? Snoring, gurgling?
Caller -> A little snore. And a groan. It's a low sound.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. Call nine one one. Do you have another phone so I can stay on with you?
Caller -> I have my cell and the house phone. I'm on the house phone. I'll use the cell. Hold on.
Nurse -> Put me on speaker and call from the other phone. Go.
Caller -> Okay. I'm dialing. Hello? My husband took too much morphine. He's seventy four. He's hard to wake and his breathing is slow. Yes. Hospice patient. Yes. Twenty two Larkspur Drive. Yes. Yes. They're coming. They said six minutes.
Caller -> They said stay on the line but I need to be with him. They said they're sending the engine and the ambulance.
Nurse -> That's right. They send both. Stay with Ev.
Nurse -> Good. Stay on with them if they ask. Marguerite, count his breaths for me. For a full minute if you can. Watch his chest.
Caller -> The dispatcher is on the other phone. She says unlock the door and clear a path. I did the door. I'll move the coffee table.
Nurse -> Good. Do that. I'll wait.
Caller -> The table is moved. The dog is in the bedroom. I closed the door.
Caller -> Okay. I'm looking at his chest. I'm counting. One. Two. Hold on. Long pause. Three. Pause. Four. This is so slow. I counted eight. In the minute. Eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Eight breaths a minute. That's too slow. Keep rousing him. Call his name loudly. Rub his chest firmly with your knuckles. Don't let him fall asleep.
Caller -> Ev! Ev, wake up! Look at me! Ev! I'm rubbing his chest. He's moaning. He opened his eyes a little. He said what. He's falling back.
Caller -> Ev! Ev, I'm sorry! Wake up! He squeezed my hand. He squeezed.
Nurse -> Good. That's a response. Keep going.
Nurse -> Keep doing it. Keep rousing him. Is his color okay? His lips?
Caller -> His lips are a little blue. Gray, maybe. And his eyes. His pupils. They're tiny. Like pinpoints. I've never seen that.
Nurse -> Marguerite, how long has he been on this morphine?
Caller -> Three weeks. The old bottle was fine. I gave him five mL. It was the same every time. I don't know how I missed it.
Nurse -> It's an easy mistake. The packaging was probably similar.
Caller -> It was. The same box. The same label color.
Nurse -> Okay. That's what we see with too much morphine. The paramedics will have a medicine to reverse it. Keep him awake. Marguerite, is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> Will he wake up? Will they bring him back?
Nurse -> They will do everything they can. The medicine they carry works quickly. Stay with him and keep talking.
Caller -> I'm talking. I'm telling him about the lake house.
Caller -> No. It's locked. I'll go. Ev, I'm just going to the door. Stay awake. Ev! Okay. Oh my God. Okay. The door's unlocked. I put on the light.
Nurse -> Good. Now, get both morphine bottles. The new one and the old one. And his medicine list. When the paramedics come, hand them everything and tell them exactly how much and when.
Caller -> Both bottles. Okay. I have them. The old one and the new one. On the counter. And the list from the fridge. I have it. A hundred milligrams. Twenty minutes ago. Ten oh five. No. It was nine forty five. Nine forty five.
Nurse -> And Marguerite, don't put anything else in his mouth. No water, no pills.
Caller -> No. Nothing. I won't. I put the cups away.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Does he usually take other medicines at the same time? Any pills this morning?
Caller -> His morning pills. At eight. He took those. A heart pill and a stool softener. And the morphine at nine forty five. That was the extra.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics all of it.
Caller -> I will. I've got the list.
Nurse -> Marguerite, you're doing everything right. Breathe.
Caller -> I'm breathing. I'm crying.
Nurse -> That's okay. Keep going.
Caller -> The old one is almost empty. The new one is full. I'm putting them both in a bag. I'm holding the bag.
Nurse -> Good. Keep them together.
Nurse -> Nine forty five. Tell them that. Is Ev still breathing?
Caller -> It was nine forty five. I looked at the clock when I gave it. I always do. I write the time. I wrote nine forty five.
Nurse -> Good. Show them the sheet.
Caller -> He's breathing. It's slow. Seven. Maybe seven. Ev! Ev!
Nurse -> Is he still on his side?
Caller -> Yes. I have my hand on his back. I'm patting him. I'm talking to him. His skin is cool.
Nurse -> Okay. Cover him with a light blanket. Don't overheat him.
Caller -> There's the quilt. I'll get it. Hold on. Okay. It's over him.
Nurse -> Keep rousing him. Turn him on his side if you can, so if he vomits he doesn't choke. Can you roll him?
Caller -> I'll try. He's heavy. Ev, roll over. Help me. Okay. I got his shoulder. There. He's on his side. His left side. I have a pillow behind him.
Caller -> Okay. His face is toward me. His mouth is open a little. He's still breathing.
Nurse -> Count again for me.
Caller -> One. Two. A long gap. Three. It's slow. Maybe six or seven.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep rousing him. The siren is close.
Nurse -> Good. Keep talking to him. Don't stop rubbing his chest. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Ev, you're going to be okay. Remember our trip to Maine? The lobster? You ate three. You said you'd never eat again.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep him hearing your voice.
Caller -> He's moaning again. He's trying to say something.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I hear the siren.
Caller -> The dog is barking. It's the siren. Biscuit, hush. He thinks they're here for him.
Nurse -> Ha. Let him bark. They're used to it.
Caller -> I'll get the door as soon as they pull in.
Nurse -> Is there anyone else at home?
Caller -> No. Just us. Our son lives in Tucson. I'll call him after.
Nurse -> Okay. After the paramedics arrive.
Nurse -> Good. Go to the door and let them in. Tell them about the concentration, twenty milligrams per mL, and that he got five mL. I'll call you in fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Twenty per mL. Five mL. Nine forty five. Okay. Okay. They're here. They're coming in. Oh thank God.
Nurse -> Marguerite, one more thing. What's Ev's date of birth, and your number?
Caller -> August twenty first. Nineteen fifty two. And three oh three, five five five, zero one one five.
Nurse -> Got it. Go be with Ev. I'll call you in fifteen.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Lorenzo. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Quiet Pines Hospice, this is Tamsin.
Caller -> Hello? Hello, Tamsin? It's Obinna. O B I N N A. Obinna Okeke. I'm calling about my wife. Philomena Okeke.
Nurse -> Okay. And can you spell Okeke for me, just to be sure?
Caller -> O K E K E. Okeke. It's a Nigerian name. Igbo. People often say Okee-key.
Nurse -> Okeke. Got it.
Nurse -> Hi, Mr. Okeke. I can hear you, but it's a little choppy. Let me get Philomena's chart. What's her birth date?
Caller -> March fifth. Nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> Got it. And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one six zero. Can you hear me? It keeps cutting out.
Nurse -> I got most of it. Six oh two, five five five, zero one six zero?
Caller -> Yes. That's it. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. You said you had her numbers for the day?
Caller -> I do. I wrote them down like the nurse said. Her weight this morning is to eleven. To eleven.
Nurse -> Sorry, the line cut out. Did you say two eleven?
Caller -> Two eleven. Yes. Two hundred eleven. And on Sunday she was two oh seven. So that's up four.
Nurse -> Okay. Two eleven, up from two oh seven. Thank you. What about her blood pressure?
Nurse -> Does she weigh herself, or do you help?
Caller -> She stands on the scale and I read it. She can't see the numbers without her glasses. She holds the sink. I hold her elbow.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's safe.
Caller -> It was won thirty ate over eighty too. Won thirty ate.
Nurse -> One thirty eight over eighty two?
Caller -> One thirty eight over eighty two. Right. That's what it said on the machine. I took it twice. It was the same.
Nurse -> What kind of cuff do you use? Wrist or arm?
Caller -> The arm. With the Velcro. It goes on the left. Her right arm has the old fistula.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Use the left arm.
Nurse -> Okay. And the pulse?
Caller -> Ninety for. Ninety for. That's a little fast for her. She's usually in the seventies.
Nurse -> Ninety four? Is that right?
Caller -> Ninety four. Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for the numbers. Now tell me how she's feeling. Any swelling?
Caller -> Her ankles. They're more swollen than Sunday. A little more. I pushed on them and it leaves a dent. It was less before. It's up to the middle of her shin now.
Nurse -> Is the swelling in both legs or one?
Caller -> Both. The left is a bit more. Same as always.
Nurse -> Okay. Any redness, warmth, or pain in the legs?
Caller -> No pain. No red. They're tight. Shiny. She says they feel heavy.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits fluid.
Nurse -> Okay. And her breathing?
Caller -> She's a bit more short of breath. When she goes up the stairs. She stops halfway. She gets winded. It's the stairs to the bedroom. She stops and holds the rail. She didn't do that last week.
Nurse -> Does she need to rest for long?
Caller -> A minute. A minute and she goes on. She says she's fine. I can see her chest going up and down.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the nurse know that.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she short of breath sitting still?
Caller -> No. No. Sitting she's fine. She's in the chair watching television. She's breathing normal. Just the stairs.
Nurse -> And chest pain? Any?
Caller -> No chest pain. She would tell me. She tells me everything. She'd complain about it.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Can she lie flat at night?
Caller -> She has two pillows. Same as usual. She sleeps okay.
Nurse -> And how's her appetite? Her salt intake?
Caller -> She eats okay. I'm trying to cut the salt. She loves her fried plantains and the soup. I've been making the soup without salt. She says it tastes like water.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep trying. Spices help.
Nurse -> Good. Mr. Okeke, I'm going to message the hospice provider this afternoon about the weight gain, the swelling and the stairs. They may want to adjust her water pill.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds right. The nurse said call if the weight goes up two pounds. It's up four.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing. I'm also sending a nurse out tomorrow to examine her.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you this evening with the provider's answer.
Caller -> This evening. I'll be home. Where does the signal work? I'll stand by the window.
Caller -> I put the phone on the windowsill. I'll watch it like a hawk.
Nurse -> Good idea. Keep weighing her every morning, same time, and write it down for the nurse.
Caller -> Every morning. I write on the calendar. It's on the refrigerator.
Nurse -> Perfect. Also, have her put her feet up on a stool or pillows when she's sitting. And try to limit the stairs to what she really needs.
Caller -> Feet up. Fewer stairs. Okay. She sleeps downstairs. I'll make her a bed in the den. She wants her own bed. She's stubborn.
Nurse -> Ha. A little stubbornness is healthy.
Caller -> After fifty three years I know it well.
Nurse -> It's worth it for a few days. And call nine one one for chest pain or trouble breathing even when she's sitting still. Call us back if she can't lie flat or the weight keeps going up.
Caller -> Chest pain. Breathing at rest. Nine one one. Can't lie flat or weight up, call. Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you. I'm sorry about the connection. I'm on my daughter's old phone.
Nurse -> You did great. Talk soon.
Caller -> Goodbye.
