transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Palliative Partners, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Joanne, hello. It's Lucius Hargreave. L U C I U S. Hargreave. H A R G R E A V E. I hope this isn't a bad time.
Nurse -> Not at all. I'm at my desk. I just finished a visit. I'm all yours.
Caller -> Good. Because I'm going to ramble. I always do when I'm nervous.
Nurse -> Ramble away.
Nurse -> Not at all, Mr. Hargreave. It's always good to hear from you. How are you today?
Caller -> I'm well. I'm very well, actually. I had a good day. I sat on the porch for two hours. The sun was out. A cardinal came to the feeder. I don't think I've felt this good in a month.
Nurse -> What kind of cardinal? A male, the red one?
Caller -> The red one. And his wife. She's a dull brown with a little red on the wings. They come every morning at seven. I put out sunflower seeds. I've named them. Duke and Duchess.
Nurse -> Ha. Duke and Duchess. That's lovely.
Caller -> I watch them over my coffee. It's the best part of the day.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. I'm so glad. What can I do for you?
Caller -> Well. I'll tell you. I've been thinking. And I want to do something while I feel clear. I want to get some things in writing. About what I want. At the end.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm glad you called about that. Let me bring up your chart so I have everything. May I confirm your date of birth?
Caller -> May twenty seventh. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number where I can reach you?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one seven zero. This is the house phone. I keep the cell on the charger. I never remember to carry it. My daughter scolds me.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Mr. Hargreave, tell me what you've been thinking.
Caller -> I've been thinking about the machines. The breathing machine. And the compressions. The pounding on the chest. I saw it done to my brother. In nineteen ninety eight. They cracked his ribs. They shocked him. And he died anyway. And I thought, I don't want that. I don't want any of that.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. So you don't want CPR, and you don't want to be on a breathing machine.
Caller -> No. No machine. No pounding. And no hospital, if I can help it. I want to be here. In this house. With my chair and my cardinal. My daughter, Marcia. She'll be here. I don't want to be in a hospital with the lights and the beeping.
Nurse -> Okay. You want to stay home. That's something we can absolutely support. Have you talked to Marcia about this?
Caller -> Not in so many words. She knows I'm tired. She knows I'm not fighting it. But I haven't said the words. I'm afraid she'll cry. She's a crier. She cries at commercials.
Caller -> She gets it from her mother. My late wife. Norma. She cried at everything. Weddings, funerals, dog food ads.
Nurse -> It sounds like a family trait. A loving one.
Caller -> It is. I miss her crying. Can you imagine?
Nurse -> I can.
Nurse -> Ha. Some people are. It might be good for her to hear it from you, in a gentle way. We can help with that.
Caller -> I was hoping you'd say that. That's the other reason I called. Can someone help me talk to her? Maybe the social worker?
Nurse -> Would you like me to be there too? Or the chaplain?
Caller -> Just the social worker for now. And Marcia. I don't want a crowd. Maybe the chaplain another day. He's the one with the harmonica.
Nurse -> Ha. Father Dominic?
Caller -> That's the one. He plays "Danny Boy" and I always get misty.
Nurse -> Danny Boy would get anyone.
Caller -> My mother used to sing it. In the kitchen. In Gaelic when she thought nobody was listening.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good memory to carry.
Caller -> It is. I carry a lot of good ones.
Nurse -> Absolutely. That's what our social worker does. She can sit with you and Marcia, together, and help with the conversation and the paperwork.
Caller -> What paperwork?
Nurse -> There's a form called a POLST. It stands for Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. It's a bright pink form. It says in writing that you don't want CPR, and what other treatments you do or don't want. Your provider signs it, and then paramedics and doctors follow it.
Caller -> A pink form. That sounds right. Like a ticket. I want it. How do I get it?
Nurse -> I'll arrange for it. First, may I write down what you've told me, in your chart? The no CPR, no breathing machine, and wanting to stay home?
Caller -> Please. Write it down. Write it big.
Nurse -> Anything else you want me to put?
Caller -> Put that I'm of sound mind. I want that in there. I did the crossword this morning, all of it. In pen.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll note that you're sharp as a tack.
Nurse -> I will. I've recorded your wishes in your chart. No CPR, no breathing machine, and you want to stay at home. It's saved.
Caller -> Thank you. That's a load off. I feel lighter.
Caller -> I've been carrying that around for weeks. Saying it out loud was the hard part.
Nurse -> It often is. You did it beautifully.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Next, I'd like to ask our social worker to come on Thursday. She'll bring the POLST form. She'll go over it with you, and with Marcia, if you'd like her there.
Caller -> Thursday. Yes. Marcia is off on Thursdays. She works at the school. She's a cafeteria manager. She'll be home.
Caller -> She makes a good lasagna on Thursdays. She'll have the house smelling like garlic. The social worker will have to stay for dinner.
Nurse -> Ha. She'd probably accept.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll ask for early afternoon. And once you've filled it out, I'll message the provider to sign it.
Caller -> Good. Good. And then it's official.
Nurse -> Then it's official. Mr. Hargreave, can I ask how you're feeling otherwise? Physically?
Caller -> I'm fine. I'm good. A little tired. I get tired in the afternoon, I nap. But I feel at peace. That's the word. At peace. I haven't felt that in a long time.
Nurse -> What changed? Do you know?
Caller -> I stopped fighting it. Really. I stopped arguing with the doctors in my head. I decided. And then it all got quiet.
Nurse -> That sounds like a real kind of peace.
Caller -> It is. It really is.
Nurse -> That's a gift. Do you have any pain?
Caller -> My hip, a little. The left one. A two. A two or a three. I take a Tylenol if I need it. Five hundred. I took one last night.
Nurse -> Does the pain ever keep you up?
Caller -> No. I sleep fine. I wake at five for the bathroom. Then I sit up and watch the dark turn blue. Then the cardinals come.
Nurse -> What a nice routine.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol five hundred as needed, and one last night. Good. Are you eating?
Caller -> I'm eating less. I eat smaller meals. A little at a time. Half a sandwich. A bowl of oatmeal. I don't have the appetite I used to. But I'm not hungry. I'm fine with it.
Caller -> Marcia keeps trying to make me eat. She brings me milkshakes. I drink half. I don't want to hurt her feelings.
Nurse -> You can tell her what you need. Half is enough.
Nurse -> That's pretty typical. As long as you're comfortable. Any shortness of breath? Chest pain?
Caller -> No. None. My breathing is fine. I use the pillows at night. Same as always. No chest pain. I'm quite comfortable.
Caller -> Do you want to know the truth? I'm not afraid. I thought I would be. I'm not.
Nurse -> That's a gift.
Caller -> It is. And I wanted someone to know before I forget how I feel.
Nurse -> Good. That's what I like to hear. Mr. Hargreave, after the form is signed, I want you to keep it somewhere easy to find. The refrigerator is the best place. The paramedics look there. And please tell Marcia where it is.
Caller -> On the refrigerator. With a magnet. I have a magnet shaped like a fish. It'll hold it. And I'll tell her. I'll show her. I'll say, Marcia, this is the pink paper.
Nurse -> That's perfect. The pink paper on the fridge.
Caller -> I like that. Pink paper. It doesn't sound so scary.
Nurse -> It's a good way to say it.
Caller -> Joanne, can I ask you something? Is it okay to change my mind? If I change my mind later?
Nurse -> Always. You can change your mind at any time. You can ask us to update the form, or tear it up. It's yours.
Caller -> It's mine. That's a good way to say it. It's my paper.
Nurse -> Exactly. It's your choice, always.
Caller -> Good. I don't think I will. But it's good to know.
Nurse -> And please call any time if you change your mind, have questions, or just want to talk before Thursday. I'm happy to talk.
Caller -> I will. I appreciate that. You've been very patient with an old man.
Nurse -> You're not old to me. You're my favorite cardinal watcher.
Caller -> I have a bird book. A Peterson. It's older than you. I mark them with a pencil when I see a new one.
Nurse -> How many have you marked this year?
Caller -> Forty six. A pileated woodpecker last week. Norma would have loved it.
Nurse -> A pileated! That's a big one.
Caller -> Ha. Is that on my chart?
Nurse -> It will be.
Caller -> Ha. Good.
Nurse -> Is there anything else on your mind?
Caller -> I think about whether I did enough. As a father. I was gone a lot. I drove a truck. Thirty years on the road. I missed her recitals.
Nurse -> It sounds like you're proud of her and you love her. That comes through.
Caller -> I do. I tell her. Not enough.
Nurse -> You can tell her on Thursday.
Caller -> I will. In front of the social worker. So she can't cry alone.
Caller -> Just that I'd like a hymn at the end. When it comes. "Abide With Me." Is that something you can write down?
Nurse -> Absolutely. I can pass that to the social worker and the chaplain. We'll make a note of your music.
Caller -> I'd also like a short service. At home. With the neighbors. And the cardinals, if they'll come.
Nurse -> The chaplain can help plan all that when you're ready. There's no rush.
Caller -> No rush. Good. I'm not rushing anything. I want to enjoy the seeds.
Caller -> That's wonderful. I think that's all. I'm done. For today. Thank you.
Caller -> Actually, hold on. Do you think the weather will hold until Thursday? I'd like to sit out on the porch with the social worker. The porch is where I do my best thinking.
Nurse -> I'll check the forecast for you. It's looking clear at the moment.
Caller -> Wonderful. Then we'll do it on the porch. With the seeds out. If the cardinals cooperate.
Nurse -> Thank you for trusting me with this, Mr. Hargreave. It's an honor.
Caller -> One more thing. Marcia likes the coffee cake from the corner bakery. Maybe you could tell the social worker to let her pick it up on Thursday. It'll keep her busy. She likes to feel useful.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along. That's thoughtful.
Caller -> She's a good girl. A worker. Like her mother.
Caller -> The honor's mine. Goodbye, Joanne.
Nurse -> Goodbye. Enjoy the cardinal.

Nurse -> Millbrook Home Health, this is Anjali.
Caller -> Hi, Anjali. It's Barrett Moxley. B A R R E T T. I'm calling about my mother. Henrietta Moxley. The wound vac. I'm not saying it's an emergency. I'm just calling about supplies.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. Supplies matter, and so does the drainage. Let me open her chart.
Nurse -> Hi, Mr. Moxley. I'm glad you called. Let me get your mom's chart open. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> April tenth. Nineteen sixty.
Nurse -> And I have a number on file. Is it seven zero four, five five five, zero one nine three?
Caller -> That's mine. Yes. That's me.
Nurse -> And is your mom home with you now?
Caller -> She's in the recliner with her leg up on the pillow. The machine is on the end table next to her. She carries it in a little bag when she walks.
Nurse -> Does she walk much?
Caller -> To the bathroom, to the kitchen. With the walker. She's careful.
Nurse -> Great. So what supplies are you low on?
Caller -> The canisters. The little canisters that collect the, you know, the fluid. We have two. Two spare. And the one on the machine, which is about half full.
Nurse -> What size canister is it? Three hundred, five hundred?
Caller -> The little one. Three hundred. It says three hundred mL on the side. It's marked.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. Two spares. How often do they change it?
Caller -> The nurse changes the canister and the dressing three times a week. Monday, Wednesday, Friday. But if the canister gets full, we can change the canister ourselves. They showed me. I know how.
Nurse -> Have you ever changed one yourself?
Caller -> Once. At two in the morning. The nurse walked me through it on the phone. Clamp, pull, twist, new one. I did it in four minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're a pro.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. And the dressing kits?
Caller -> One. One kit. In the box. With the foam and the drape. The nurse brings her own on visit days, but there's supposed to be a spare kit here. For emergencies. I'm not saying we need it. But there's one.
Nurse -> Okay. One spare kit. That's low. Let's fix that. How is the drainage?
Caller -> That's the other thing. It's a little heavier. Since yesterday. The canister fills faster. Yesterday it was maybe a quarter full after a day. Today it's half. It's still yellow, clear yellow. It's not red. It's not cloudy.
Nurse -> Has the color changed at all since last week?
Caller -> A little darker yellow. Honey. Not brown. It looks like iced tea with milk. No, that's wrong. It looks like straw. Light.
Nurse -> Okay. Straw colored. That's normal.
Nurse -> Okay. Heavier drainage since yesterday. Any fever?
Caller -> No fever. Her temperature was ninety eight point two. No chills. She's not sick. She's eating. She's in good spirits.
Nurse -> What's she eating? Is she getting enough protein?
Caller -> I make her eggs every morning. Chicken at dinner. She drinks the protein shakes. The vanilla ones. She hates them but she drinks them.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Protein helps healing.
Nurse -> Any bad smell from the wound or the dressing?
Caller -> No smell. I smelled the canister. I smelled around the dressing. Nothing. Just the plastic smell.
Nurse -> Okay. Any bright red blood in the tube or the canister?
Caller -> No blood. No red. It's yellow. I wouldn't be calling for supplies if there was blood. I'd be calling nine one one. We don't need an ambulance. It's not like that.
Nurse -> Right. I appreciate that. And the machine? Is it running okay?
Caller -> It's running. No alarms. The screen says therapy active. It's humming. The seal is good. It's tight. It's holding. The next change is Friday. The nurse is coming Friday.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Barrett, I'm going to order the supplies. I'll put in a box of canisters and a few dressing kits. Let me place it. One second.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm just standing here. My mom's watching her shows.
Nurse -> What's she watching?
Caller -> The cooking competition. She yells at the screen when someone burns the risotto. She's a retired caterer. She knows food.
Nurse -> Ha. A critic.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the supply company for canisters and dressing kits.
Caller -> Wonderful. When will they come?
Nurse -> I'll arrange delivery for tomorrow. Is someone home during the day?
Caller -> I'm here. I work from the spare room. I'll be here all day.
Caller -> I do insurance claims. On the computer. I've got three monitors. She says it looks like a spaceship.
Nurse -> Ha. A spaceship command center.
Nurse -> Great. I'll ask them to deliver tomorrow, and call before they arrive.
Caller -> Perfect. They never call. But okay.
Nurse -> I'll try. Now, since the drainage is heavier, I'm going to message the wound care nurse about it so she knows before Friday's visit.
Caller -> Oh good. Yes. Please. I didn't want to worry her, but it's a change.
Nurse -> It's good you noticed. You did right. Barrett, if the machine alarms, there are a few things to check. Look at the tubing for kinks. Check that the clamps are open. Make sure the canister is seated all the way. If you can't get it running again within two hours, call us right away. The dressing has to be changed.
Caller -> Kinks. Clamps open. Canister seated. Two hours. Call. Okay. I know the drill. We had an alarm in September and the nurse walked me through it. It was the clamp.
Nurse -> It often is. Also, call us for a fever, a bad smell, bright red blood in the tubing or canister, or if the canister fills up in a day.
Caller -> Fever. Smell. Red blood. Full in a day. Okay. It's not close. It's about half a day.
Caller -> If I get nervous can I call anytime? Even at night?
Nurse -> Yes. Anytime. The same number. Night calls forward to the on-call nurse.
Caller -> Good. That helps.
Nurse -> Right. Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Anjali.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk to you soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Palliative Care, this is Mina.
Caller -> Hi, Mina. It's Rosalind. Rosalind Fairbanks. I'm sorry for the hour. I couldn't sleep. And I wanted to talk to someone who isn't family.
Nurse -> There's no wrong hour. I'm glad you called.
Nurse -> It's okay, Rosalind. I'm glad you called. That's what I'm here for. How are you doing?
Caller -> I'm, I don't know. I'm okay. I'm calm. That's the weird thing. I'm very calm. I've been taking care of business. I gave my sister the jewelry. I wrote letters. I gave away my books. I'm kind of done.
Nurse -> Tell me what you mean by done.
Caller -> I mean, I did everything I wanted to do. I'm ready. I'm just ready.
Nurse -> Okay. I want to hear all of it.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like a lot of preparing. Rosalind, can I get your date of birth so I can pull your chart?
Caller -> September second. Nineteen seventy seven. I'm forty nine. I know. Young. Everyone says that.
Nurse -> Forty nine. And you've been through so much already.
Caller -> I have. I was diagnosed at forty five. I got four years. Four good years and then three bad ones. Hm. Something like that.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what number are you calling from?
Caller -> My cell. Two oh six, five five five, zero one eight two.
Nurse -> Got it. Rosalind, I want to ask about what you said. You said you're done, and you've been giving things away. Can you tell me what you mean?
Caller -> I mean. I'm done fighting. I've had three rounds. The chemo, the radiation, the new trial. Nothing worked. I'm tired. I'm so tired. And I've been thinking about ending it. Not in a dramatic way. In a practical way.
Nurse -> That sounds so heavy. I'm sorry you're carrying this.
Caller -> Thanks. It's nice to hear someone say it out loud.
Nurse -> Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. When you say ending it, do you mean ending your life?
Caller -> Yes. I mean that. I've been thinking about it every night this week. At night, mostly. When it's quiet.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm really glad you told me. I want to ask you some direct questions, because I want to understand. Have you thought about how?
Caller -> I have. I've been saving my pills. I have a bottle in the closet. Forty, maybe forty five. Mostly my pain pills. And some sleeping pills. I've been putting a few aside every week since August. In case.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being honest. Do you have a plan for when you would do it?
Caller -> No. No date. I just feel better knowing they're there. Like a way out. I don't know if I would. Honestly. I'm not saying I will. I'm saying the thought is there. Every night. And it gets louder.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you. And have you told anyone?
Caller -> No. No one. Just you. Not my sister. She'd come and take over. She'd cry. I can't deal with the crying. And not my oncologist. He'd send me to the hospital. I don't want the hospital.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense. So you're calling me because you needed to say it out loud.
Caller -> Yes. Exactly. I needed someone to hear it.
Nurse -> I'm glad it was me.
Caller -> Me too.
Nurse -> I'm hearing it. Rosalind, I'm going to stay on the phone with you, and I'm going to ask you some more things. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes. I'd like that.
Nurse -> Where are you right now?
Caller -> I'm in my kitchen. At the table. I made tea. I'm alone. I live alone. My sister is in Tacoma. It's an hour and a half.
Nurse -> Okay. Are the pills near you right now?
Caller -> In the bedroom closet. On the shelf. I'm not touching them. I'm in the kitchen. I don't want to say I'm not tempted. But I'm sitting here talking to you.
Nurse -> Does it feel like it would be easy to go and get them?
Caller -> It would be easy. They're fifteen steps away. But I'm choosing to sit here. I like being here.
Nurse -> I'm glad you're choosing that.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. You're talking to me. Rosalind, how's your pain tonight?
Caller -> A four. It's manageable. It's the bone pain in my back. I took my pill at ten. I'm okay. It's not the pain. It's not really about the pain.
Nurse -> What is it about, if you don't mind me asking?
Caller -> It's about the end of the road. Seeing it. I'd like to control how it ends. I don't want to be in a bed, unable to move. I don't want to be helpless.
Nurse -> That's an important wish. We can talk about it. There are ways to keep you comfortable and keep control.
Caller -> Maybe. I haven't believed that. But I'm listening.
Nurse -> Okay. And sleep?
Caller -> Terrible. I sleep two, three hours. I wake up at three. And then it's the thoughts.
Nurse -> Okay. Rosalind, I want you to know this is something we take very seriously, and I'm glad you didn't wait. I'm going to do a couple of things. First, I'm going to page our on-call clinician right now to talk with you.
Caller -> Will they send someone? The police? Please don't send the police.
Nurse -> I'm not sending the police. I'm asking a nurse to come visit you, and the clinician to call you. I want to get you support, not punish you. Is that okay?
Caller -> A nurse. Okay. As long as it's not an ambulance with sirens.
Nurse -> No sirens. A nurse, in a regular car. Within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. It's five in the morning.
Caller -> Do I need to get dressed? Straighten up the place?
Nurse -> No. Just stay as you are. Put on a sweater if you're cold. The nurse doesn't care about the house.
Caller -> Okay. It's a mess. I haven't cleaned in a week.
Nurse -> It's a house. It's allowed to be lived in.
Nurse -> I know. We have a night nurse and she's ready. And this morning I'd like our social worker to call you and visit, to talk about how you're feeling and what support we can add.
Caller -> A social worker. I've met her. Tanya. She's nice. I liked her. Okay.
Caller -> She brought me a scarf once. Knitted it herself. I still have it. It's on the chair.
Nurse -> What a lovely gift.
Nurse -> Good. Now Rosalind, I need to ask for something. The pills in the closet. Would you be willing to put them in a bag, and give them to your neighbor, or leave them outside your door for the nurse to take when she comes?
Caller -> My neighbor is asleep. Mr. Almeida. He's old. I don't want to wake him. But I could leave them outside the door. In a bag. On the mat.
Nurse -> That would be wonderful. Would you do that now, while I'm on the phone? I'll wait.
Caller -> Now? Okay. Okay. Let me think. Okay. I can do that. Hold on. I'm going to the bedroom. Mina, you're still there?
Nurse -> I'm right here. I'm not going anywhere. Take your time.
Caller -> I'm in the bedroom. I have the closet open. I see the bottle. It's an old vitamin bottle. I put a label on it. I wrote vitamins. Ha. Okay. I have it in my hand. It's heavy. It's more than I thought.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a bag? A paper bag or a plastic bag?
Caller -> Plastic. A grocery bag. Hold on. Okay. I put it in. I tied it. Okay. I'm going to the front door. I'm opening it. It's cold. I'm putting it on the mat. There. I closed the door. It's outside.
Nurse -> Thank you, Rosalind. That took strength. How do you feel?
Caller -> Relieved. And sad. And a little scared. But relieved.
Nurse -> That's very honest. I'm proud of you for doing that.
Caller -> I'm proud too. Weirdly.
Nurse -> It's not weird. It was hard.
Nurse -> That makes sense. All of that is okay. Is there anything else in the house you're worried about? Other pills, other things?
Caller -> I have my regular pain pills. The ones I take. The nurse gives me a week at a time. That's all. I don't have more.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a way the nurse can hold onto the rest of your pills for a few days?
Caller -> Yes. That's fine. She can take them. I'll take what I need when she comes.
Nurse -> Good. Rosalind, I want to give you a number. If the thoughts get louder, or you feel like you might act, you can call or text nine eight eight at any hour. It's the crisis line. And call nine one one right away if you take any of the pills or feel like you might.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. And nine one one. Okay. I won't. I won't take them. I think I'm okay for now. I feel calmer. Thank you.
Nurse -> That's good to hear. I want to keep checking in, though. That's why I'm calling back.
Caller -> I appreciate it. I do.
Nurse -> I'm glad. I'd still like you to not be alone tonight, if possible. Could you call your sister? Even just to talk?
Caller -> I don't want to wake her. I don't want to scare her.
Nurse -> She'd want to know. If you're not ready to tell her everything, you could just ask her to come and stay with you for a few days. You don't have to explain it all right now.
Caller -> I could do that. I could say, I'm not doing great, can you come? She'd come. She'd drive right now.
Nurse -> She sounds like someone who loves you.
Caller -> She does. She's the only one left. My parents are gone. My ex is gone. It's me and her and Pickle.
Nurse -> That would be a good thing. I'd also like you to stay on the phone with me until the nurse comes, or call me back any hour. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stay on. For a bit. I want to tell you about my cat. Is that okay? She's been my best friend. Her name is Pickle.
Nurse -> Tell me about Pickle.
Caller -> She's seven. She's a gray tabby. She sleeps on my feet. She has this thing where she kneads my stomach. Right on the incision. It hurts but I let her. She's been my person.
Nurse -> A gray tabby. Does she talk to you?
Caller -> All the time. She yells at me for food. She has a whole vocabulary. I swear she says hello.
Caller -> She sleeps in my bed. On my pillow, actually. I wake up with a paw on my face.
Nurse -> That's a lovely image.
Nurse -> Aw. It sounds like she's very loved. Who would take care of Pickle if you weren't around?
Caller -> My sister. Nobody else. She knows. She always said she would.
Nurse -> It sounds like she loves you both. Rosalind, I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, and I'll call you back in fifteen minutes. I'd like you to put the kettle on and call your sister while you wait. Can you do that?
Caller -> I'll call her. I'll text first. I'll say I'm up and I'd like company. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. And I'll call you back in fifteen minutes. If you'd rather stay on, say so.
Caller -> No, you go. Page them. I'll be okay. I have Pickle. And I'll text my sister. And the pills are outside.
Nurse -> Okay. You're doing great. I'll call in fifteen.
Caller -> Thank you, Mina. Truly. I'm so glad I called. I almost didn't.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Rosalind.

Nurse -> Quiet Waters Hospice, this is Carol.
Caller -> Hm.
Nurse -> Hello? This is Quiet Waters Hospice. Is anyone there?
Caller -> Mm. Mm.
Nurse -> Hello? Can you hear me?
Caller -> The, the.
Nurse -> I can hear something in the background. Is someone there who needs help?
Caller -> Hi.
Nurse -> Hi there. Hello. Who is this?
Caller -> Hi. I'm four.
Nurse -> Hi, four year old. Is a grown up there?
Caller -> Mommy's sleeping.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you tell me your name?
Caller -> Lucy.
Nurse -> Hi, Lucy. Can you wake up Mommy for me, gently?
Caller -> She's sleeping on the couch. She has a blanket.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you tap her shoulder?
Caller -> Mommy! Mommy! The phone!
Nurse -> That's right. Say it a little louder.
Caller -> Mommy! The phone is talking!
Caller -> Oh. Oh no. Hello? Who is this? Oh my goodness. I'm so sorry. Lucy, give me that. Hello? I'm sorry. This is, I think she called. Did she call someone?
Nurse -> Hi. This is Quiet Waters Hospice. A call came in to us and your daughter answered, I think. Is everything okay?
Caller -> Oh gosh. Yes. Everything's fine. It must have been a pocket dial. Or she got my phone. She loves to press the buttons. I'm so sorry. I fell asleep on the couch. We're fine.
Nurse -> No problem at all. I just wanted to make sure nobody needed help.
Caller -> No, no. We're fine. She called the wrong place. Sorry to bother you.
Nurse -> It's no bother. Have a good night.
Caller -> You too. Come on, Lucy. Say bye.
Caller -> Bye bye!

transcript:
Nurse -> Pine Ridge Hospice, this is Faye.
Caller -> Hi, Faye. It's Lydia Whitlow. I'm calling about my mother, Cordelia Whitlow. She was up all night.
Nurse -> Hi, Lydia. I can hear you're tired. Take a breath. Tell me when you're ready.
Caller -> I'm ready. I just needed to hear a person.
Nurse -> Hi, Lydia. I'm sorry to hear that. Let me bring up her chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> December nineteenth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> Got it. And your number?
Caller -> Three one two, five five five, zero one nine two.
Nurse -> Is that a cell or the house?
Caller -> My cell. The house phone is in the kitchen. I'm in the hall. I can see her through the door. She's asleep in the chair now.
Nurse -> Good. I'll try the cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened last night.
Caller -> Where do I start? She went to bed at nine. I thought we were good. I gave her the pill, I turned on the night light, I sat with her till she was asleep.
Nurse -> That sounds like a good routine.
Caller -> It was. Until midnight.
Caller -> She wandered. She was up from about midnight. She went from room to room. She was shouting. She was calling for her mother. Her mother passed in nineteen eighty. She was going door to door. She opened the front door. I had to bring her back.
Nurse -> Was she dressed? Was it cold outside?
Caller -> In her nightgown and her slippers. It was cold. Forty degrees. I put a coat on her. She didn't even feel it.
Nurse -> That's frightening. I'm glad you were there.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds scary. Did she fall?
Nurse -> No. No fall. I was right behind her. I had my hand on her back the whole time. And no injuries. And she doesn't have pain. I asked her, does anything hurt? She said no.
Nurse -> Good. Is she on anything for sleep or agitation?
Caller -> She takes the Seer oh quell. Twenty five milligrams. At bedtime. I gave it to her at nine. Like always.
Nurse -> Okay. The Seer oh quell, twenty five at bedtime, given at nine. And it didn't settle her?
Caller -> It didn't. She was up at midnight and didn't sleep till five. And I'm exhausted. And I don't know if I should give her more. Or call someone.
Caller -> I'm so afraid of drugging her. I don't want her to be a zombie.
Nurse -> That's a real concern. We want her calm but still herself. The provider can help find the balance.
Caller -> Lydia, you did the right thing calling. Don't give more yet. I'll message the provider about the night agitation despite the Seer oh quell.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I didn't want to give her extra.
Nurse -> Was she frightened or angry when she was wandering?
Caller -> Frightened. She was crying. She kept saying, Where is Mama. Where's my mama. She wanted to go home.
Nurse -> That sounds very sad.
Nurse -> How is she in the daytime?
Caller -> Calm. She's calm all day. She eats. She smiles. She watches her shows. It's only at night. After dark. Around five or six it starts. She gets restless. And then midnight is the worst.
Caller -> I draw the curtains at four. I turn on all the lights. I thought it would help. It doesn't seem to.
Nurse -> That's a thoughtful idea. Sometimes bright lights make it worse in the evening. We can talk about adjusting.
Nurse -> That's called sundowning. It's very common with dementia. Lydia, I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow to see her.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call. And I'll call you this evening after I hear from the provider.
Caller -> This evening. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> For tonight, a few things. Keep the same calm routine every evening. Dim the lights after dinner. No caffeine, and try to avoid naps late in the afternoon. Use a night light and some soft music.
Caller -> Dim lights. No caffeine. Short naps only. Night light. Music. Okay. She likes Patsy Cline. I can play that.
Nurse -> Patsy Cline is perfect. Soft and familiar.
Caller -> "Crazy." She sings along even now. She forgets the words but gets the tune.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Music reaches people in a special way.
Caller -> She has her tea at four. Decaf. Is decaf okay?
Nurse -> Decaf is fine. A weak herbal tea is even better.
Caller -> Chamomile. She loves chamomile.
Nurse -> That sounds perfect. And for safety, put a chime or a bell on her door, clear the path to the bathroom, and stay close to her at night.
Caller -> A bell on the door. I'll use the jingle bells from Christmas. Ha. Clear the path. Stay close. I sleep in the chair.
Nurse -> Do you have gates or locks on the front door?
Caller -> A deadbolt. She can't turn it. But she was working on it last night. Pulling and pulling. I heard the rattle.
Nurse -> A slide lock up high can help. Something she can't reach.
Caller -> My husband can put one up this weekend.
Nurse -> How are you holding up? Are you getting any sleep?
Caller -> A couple of hours. In the chair. My husband helps on weekends. He's a good man. He doesn't complain.
Nurse -> I'm glad you have him. Please let us know if you need more help.
Caller -> I may. Thank you. I might.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else, Lydia?
Caller -> One thing. Should I be worried that she's going to die soon? She's been so confused. And she lost weight.
Nurse -> It's a fair question. She has a serious illness, and the confusion and weight loss are part of that. The nurse tomorrow can talk with you about what to expect. I don't want to guess over the phone.
Caller -> That's fair. I'll ask her.
Caller -> No. Thank you. You were really helpful.
Nurse -> Talk to you this evening.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Golden Meadow Hospice, this is Rafael.
Caller -> Rafael, hi, it's Alma Duarte. My mom is throwing up. She's been throwing up since the morning. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Take a breath. I'm here. We'll figure it out step by step.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm in the kitchen. Dad's in the bedroom. Mom's in the den. I'm running back and forth.
Nurse -> Okay, Alma. Sorry to hear that. I want to make sure I have the right person. Which patient is it? Your mom?
Caller -> Yes. My mom. Imelda. She's been, no wait. Hold on. Hold on. No. It's him. He threw up again. Sorry. It's my dad. It's Dad.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's your dad who's throwing up. Both your parents are patients with us, right?
Caller -> Yes. Both. I keep mixing them up. I'm so sorry. It's Dad. It's Hector. Hector Duarte. Mom's fine. She's asleep. She's fine. It's my father.
Nurse -> Good. Is your mom comfortable?
Caller -> She's fine. She had lunch. She's on her oxygen. She's asleep in the recliner. Her breathing is normal.
Nurse -> How long has she been with us?
Caller -> Three months. Dad came on in August. They were both on within a month of each other. It was awful. We got the news twice.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. That's a lot for a family.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's get back to Hector.
Nurse -> No need to be sorry. It's been a long day. So Hector Duarte. I'll pull up his chart. Can you give me his date of birth?
Caller -> May eighteenth. Nineteen forty seven. He's seventy nine. Mom's the one who's eighty one. Imelda. Ugh.
Caller -> I swear I know who is who. It's just the long day. I have their charts open on the kitchen table, one on top of the other.
Nurse -> It happens. With two patients in one house, it happens all the time.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one eight eight.
Nurse -> Is that the cell, or the house?
Caller -> Both. It's a landline that forwards to my cell. When I'm out. I'm home now.
Nurse -> Perfect. Okay, Alma. Tell me about your dad. When did the vomiting start?
Caller -> This morning. Around eight. He threw up his breakfast. Then again at noon. And again at, I think three. Three times. He can't keep anything down. Not even water. He sips water and it comes up.
Nurse -> Is he able to take the Zofran under the tongue, or is it coming back up too?
Caller -> It melts. It dissolves. I put it on his tongue. It's gone before he can throw up. But the vomiting still came.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful.
Nurse -> What was breakfast?
Caller -> Oatmeal. And half a banana. And his tea. It all came up. Like it was never in him.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Three times since the morning, and he can't keep fluids down. Is it bile? Green, yellow? Any blood?
Caller -> Yellowish. Greenish yellow. A bit brown at the end. No blood. I don't think. I looked. No red.
Nurse -> Does it smell bad? Like stool?
Caller -> A little. A sour smell. Not exactly like stool. I don't know. It's sour.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he taken anything for the nausea?
Caller -> The Zofran. The little tablet that melts. Four milligrams. He took one at ten. It didn't help. He took another at two. Still nothing. He threw up at three.
Nurse -> Okay. Zofran four, at ten and again at two, no relief. What does his belly look like?
Caller -> Big. Swollen. Hard. Tight like a drum. It's bigger than yesterday. He says it hurts. He's holding it. A six, he said. A six. He keeps rubbing it.
Nurse -> Okay. A six. Is it constant or does it come and go?
Caller -> Comes and goes. Cramps. Then it's steady. He groans. He curls up.
Nurse -> Is he able to find a comfortable position?
Caller -> On his side with his knees up. He's been like that all afternoon. He gets up to try the bathroom and nothing happens.
Nurse -> Okay. That fits what I'm worried about.
Nurse -> Okay. And when was his last bowel movement?
Caller -> Oh. Oh no. It's been days. Six days. I think. I don't know. It's been about six days. I've been telling him to take the stool softener but he forgets. He says he's not constipated.
Nurse -> What's he taking for his bowels?
Caller -> The softener. One at night. And the senna. They gave it to him when they started the morphine. But he hasn't been taking it. Not since last Wednesday.
Nurse -> Okay. That could be part of it. We'll sort that out.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Six days. Does he pass gas?
Caller -> No. I asked. He says no. He says nothing's moving.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. His temperature was ninety eight two. At noon. No fever. He's cool. He's not hot.
Nurse -> Okay. Alma, what you're describing is something I want the on-call clinician to look at right away. The vomiting that isn't stopping, the swollen hard belly, and no bowel movement or gas. I'm paging them now.
Caller -> Is it serious? Is he dying? Is this the end?
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm scared. It's a lot.
Nurse -> It's okay to be scared. That's normal.
Nurse -> I understand the fear. Let's not jump ahead. I'm going to get him help now. That's the plan.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. You're right.
Nurse -> I can't say that. What I can say is it needs attention today. It could be a blockage, which is something we can treat to make him comfortable. I'm also sending a nurse to your house. I want her there within two hours.
Caller -> Within two hours. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until she arrives, please hold off on any pills by mouth. He won't keep them down anyway. Give him only small sips of water, or ice chips. Nothing to eat. Keep him upright or lying on his side, with a bowl next to him.
Caller -> No pills. Sips. Ice chips. Bowl. Upright or on his side. Okay. I'll get the bowl. I have a basin.
Caller -> I have a salad bowl too. A big one. Should I use that?
Nurse -> Any bowl or basin works. Put a towel under it for spills.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call you back in thirty minutes with what the on-call clinician says.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. Rafael, what about my mom? She's fine. She's asleep. Should I be worried about her?
Nurse -> It sounds like she's fine. If anything changes for her, call us. Right now, let's focus on Hector.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And please call back right away if he vomits again, if the pain gets worse, or if he stops responding normally.
Caller -> Vomits again, pain worse, not responding right. Okay. I'll call. I'll write it down.
Nurse -> Alma, tell me about the pain medicines. Is he on something for the belly pain, other than the Zofran?
Caller -> He has the morphine liquid. He took it yesterday. He hasn't taken any today. He forgot. Or he didn't want it.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't give anything by mouth for now. We'll ask the clinician about another way.
Nurse -> You're doing great, Alma. I know it's overwhelming with both parents.
Nurse -> And Alma, one more thing. Please don't give him anything else by mouth, not even a cracker. Let the clinician decide.
Caller -> Nothing. Not a cracker. I'll tell Mom too. She likes to bring him soup.
Nurse -> Good idea. No soup tonight.
Caller -> It's a lot. My brother lives in Denver. It's mostly me. But I'm okay. I'll be okay.
Caller -> My mom doesn't really know what's happening. She thinks he's just tired. I don't want to tell her till I know.
Nurse -> That's your decision. We can help you tell her when the time comes.
Nurse -> Is there someone who can stay with you tonight?
Caller -> My husband gets home at seven. He'll help.
Nurse -> Good. I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thank you, Rafael. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Alma.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hi, Ruth. It's Leland Ashworth. I'm calling about the pills. I messed up last night. I took the wrong one. I took the tramadol instead of the sleeping pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Take your time. Are you somewhere safe right now?
Caller -> I'm at my sister's, sitting on her couch. She's making tea. She's fine. She says I'm being dramatic.
Nurse -> Hi, Leland. I'm glad you called. Let me find your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> March twenty fourth. Nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> Got it. And a number to reach you?
Caller -> Oh, I'm on my sister's phone. I don't have mine. It's dead and the charger is at my house. I don't know my own number by heart. Can you use the one in the file?
Nurse -> Sure. I have one on file. I'll use that.
Caller -> Great. Thanks.
Nurse -> What's the name of the surgery you had? Just so I know the context.
Caller -> A hernia repair. Six weeks ago. I'm doing well. I only needed the tramadol for the first couple weeks.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Healing well.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened last night.
Caller -> I took the pill in the dark. I didn't turn on the light because I didn't want to wake my sister. She's staying with me. I reached into the drawer and I grabbed a bottle. And I thought it was the trazodone. And it was the tramadol. I looked at it this morning and it was the wrong bottle. The tramadol is left over from my surgery. I'm not supposed to take it anymore.
Nurse -> Okay. And you took one fifty-milligram tablet?
Caller -> One. Fifty milligrams. At about ten. I just took one. I'd like to say that. Just one. I'm not trying to hurt myself. I want to be clear. It was a mistake. I didn't know.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm glad you said it. Thank you for being clear.
Caller -> I just didn't want you to think that. It's not that.
Nurse -> I don't. I believe you.
Nurse -> I appreciate you telling me. I believe you. And your usual bedtime pill is the trazodone, fifty milligrams?
Caller -> Yes. Trazodone. Fifty. At bedtime. For sleep. I didn't take it. So I missed my sleeping pill.
Nurse -> Okay. How did you sleep?
Caller -> Terrible. I tossed and turned. I woke up four, five times. I was hot. I couldn't get comfortable. I'm wiped out today.
Nurse -> Did you take anything else for sleep, like an over-the-counter sleep aid?
Caller -> No. Nothing else. I just lay there.
Nurse -> Okay. That helps me know.
Nurse -> Okay. How are you feeling right now?
Caller -> Dizzy. When I stand up. And a little queasy. Not throwing up. Just a mild nausea. It started this morning when I got up. I had some toast and it stayed down.
Nurse -> Okay. Dizzy on standing and mild nausea. Are you confused at all? Any shaking, jerking, anything like a seizure?
Caller -> No. No. Nothing like that. I'm clear. I know where I am. I know what day it is. No shakes. No jerking. I don't have a history of seizures. I'm just tired and dizzy.
Nurse -> Do you have anyone with you today?
Caller -> My sister. She took the week off. She's been great. She makes me eat vegetables.
Nurse -> Ha. Good sister.
Nurse -> Have you eaten and had fluids today?
Caller -> Toast and coffee. Some water. I've been drinking. I'll eat more at lunch.
Nurse -> Good. Keep drinking water.
Nurse -> Good. Is your heart racing? Are you sweating, agitated?
Caller -> No. My heart's normal. I took my pulse. Seventy something. I'm not sweaty. I'm just tired.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all reassuring. Leland, I'm going to message your provider today about the mix-up. They'll decide if there's anything to do.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Should I take the trazodone tonight?
Nurse -> Yes, unless the provider says otherwise. Take your usual trazodone fifty at bedtime. And do not take any more tramadol. Not tonight, not any other night, until the provider tells you.
Caller -> No tramadol. Trazodone tonight. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll call you this afternoon, on the number on file, to let you know what the provider says.
Caller -> This afternoon. I'll be at my sister's. I'll have her phone. I'll charge mine too.
Nurse -> If you miss my call, I'll leave a message and try again.
Caller -> Okay. Her ringer is loud. I'll hear it.
Nurse -> Good idea. Now let's make it safer. Put the old tramadol in a bag and get it away from your bedside pills. Keep the trazodone right by the bed with a light on. And read each label before you take anything at night.
Caller -> Away from the bed. Light on. Read the label. I'll take the tramadol to the pharmacy to throw away. I don't need it.
Nurse -> Good. Many pharmacies take back unused medicines.
Caller -> Yes. The one on Elm has a box. I'll drop it this afternoon.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. Also, call nine one one for a seizure, a fast heartbeat with agitation, severe confusion or trouble breathing. And call us if the dizziness gets worse or you start vomiting.
Caller -> Seizure, fast heartbeat, confused, breathing, nine one one. Dizzy worse or vomiting, call you. Okay. I don't think so. But okay.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> Nope. Just that. Well, tell the nurse who's coming Friday I said thank you for the dressing change last week.
Nurse -> I'll pass it along.
Caller -> Actually, one more. What if I can't sleep tonight, even with the trazodone? Can I take something else?
Nurse -> Please don't add anything on your own. If you have trouble, call us and we'll sort it out.
Caller -> Okay. I'll call.
Caller -> No. Thanks, Ruth. I feel dumb.
Nurse -> Don't feel dumb. It's easy in the dark. You called, and that's right.
Caller -> I'm going to keep a little flashlight on the nightstand. A reading light. Nothing fancy.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Caller -> My sister already ordered me one that clips on.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bluebird Home Health, this is Kamal.
Caller -> Kamal, hi. It's Clyde Penhallow. P E N H A L L O W. I'm calling about my wife. Opal Penhallow. Her breathing machine broke.
Nurse -> Hi, Clyde. Let me get Opal's chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> Is this a bad time? I can call back if you're busy.
Nurse -> Not at all. I'm right here.
Caller -> October twenty seventh. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> And a number to reach you at?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one two one. That's the house phone. We keep it on the wall in the kitchen. It's the only one that works inside. The cell is no good.
Nurse -> Is the signal bad at your house?
Caller -> Terrible. We're in a hollow. You have to go out to the mailbox to get a bar. We kept the old landline for that reason.
Nurse -> That makes sense.
Nurse -> Got it. Okay. Tell me about the machine.
Caller -> It's the nebulizer. The little box. The compressor. This morning I plugged it in and nothing. No light. No sound. It's dead. I tried a different outlet. I tried a different cord. Nothing. I think the motor's gone. It's seven years old.
Nurse -> Who supplied it originally?
Caller -> The same company as the oxygen. Lakeside Medical. The one with the green truck.
Nurse -> Good. I know them.
Nurse -> Okay. The nebulizer machine won't turn on at all. Did it make any noise before it died?
Caller -> Yesterday it was louder. A rattly sound. And hot. It smelled like burning plastic. I should have called then.
Nurse -> You did the right thing to unplug it. Please don't plug it back in.
Caller -> I haven't. It's sitting on the counter. I put a note on it. Do not use.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good information. When was the last time Opal used it?
Caller -> This morning at six. I plugged it in and nothing came out. So she hasn't had a treatment since last night at midnight. Wait. No. She had one at midnight. At six I tried and it was dead. So the last real treatment was at midnight. Six hours ago. Now it's noon. Twelve hours ago? No. I'm confusing myself.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's say the last treatment was around midnight, and she's due. How is she breathing right now?
Caller -> She's wheezy. A little. Not bad. I can hear it when she breathes out. A whistle. She's sitting in her chair. She's not struggling. She's talking in full sentences.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have her finger oxygen monitor handy?
Caller -> I do. It's on her finger. Ninety three. It's usually ninety four, ninety five. So a little lower.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety three. Is she short of breath at all? Is she gasping, or using her neck muscles?
Caller -> No. No gasping. She's comfortable. She's a bit winded if she gets up. But sitting she's fine. She's just wheezy. She's doing a crossword.
Nurse -> What are the words today?
Caller -> I don't know. She just asked me what a seven letter word for sorrow is. I said I don't do the crossword.
Nurse -> Ha. Sadness. Maybe melancholy?
Caller -> I'll tell her. She'll say that's eight letters.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. Does she have a rescue inhaler?
Caller -> She does. The blue one. Albuterol. It's in her purse. It's almost empty. The counter says forty. Forty puffs.
Nurse -> Okay. Forty puffs left. Does she have a spacer? A tube that attaches to it?
Caller -> I don't know what that is. A tube? Hm. No. I don't think so. Just the inhaler. She uses it straight.
Nurse -> How often does she use the rescue inhaler?
Caller -> A few times a week. Mostly when she walks to the mailbox. Or the stairs. She didn't use it yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine for today. Clyde, here's what I'm going to do. I'm ordering a new nebulizer machine right now. Hold on. I'll put it in as urgent.
Caller -> Oh good. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's in. I just placed the order with the equipment company for a replacement nebulizer machine, marked urgent, same day.
Caller -> Same day? Really? That's great.
Nurse -> I'm going to call and ask them to deliver this evening. Will someone be home?
Caller -> I'm home. I don't go anywhere. I take care of her. She can't be alone for long.
Nurse -> How long have you been her main caregiver?
Caller -> Four years. Since the diagnosis. I used to work at the lumber yard. I retired to take care of her. It's the best job I've had.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll ask for this evening, and I'll ask them to call when they're close.
Caller -> Perfect. Is it going to be the same kind? The same machine?
Nurse -> A similar one. A small compressor. It comes with the tubing and the mask and the cups. Do you have extra albuterol vials for the neb?
Caller -> I have a box. About twenty. We're good on those.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. In the meantime, let's use the inhaler. I'd like you to have her use the rescue inhaler. Shake it first. Two puffs, one minute apart. Breathe in slowly, hold for ten seconds, then breathe out.
Caller -> Shake. Two puffs. A minute apart. Slow breath. Hold ten. Okay. Hold on. I'll get it from her purse. Opal, honey, here's your inhaler. Okay. She's doing it. Puff one. Hold. Okay. She's holding. I'm counting. Seven, eight, nine, ten. Out. Okay. A minute. I'll wait. I'm looking at the clock.
Caller -> She's rolling her eyes at me. She says she can do it herself. She can. I'm hovering.
Nurse -> Ha. A little hovering is allowed.
Nurse -> Good. Wait a full minute. Then the second puff.
Caller -> Okay. A minute. Okay. Second puff. Hold. Counting. Okay. Done. Whew. She says it tastes like chalk.
Nurse -> Ha. It does. How is she feeling?
Caller -> A little better. Her wheeze is softer. She says it's easier. She's smiling. She's at ninety four.
Nurse -> Does she feel any jitteriness or fast heartbeat from it?
Caller -> A little. She says her heart is going a bit. She always gets that. It passes in ten minutes.
Nurse -> That's normal with albuterol.
Nurse -> Good. That's what we want. She can use it again in four to six hours if she needs it. You've got forty puffs, so there's plenty for today.
Caller -> She's put the crossword down. She's telling me about the neighbors now. She's feeling more herself.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Keep her sitting up and relaxed.
Caller -> I will. I'll make her some tea. Does tea hurt?
Nurse -> A warm drink is fine. It can even loosen the chest a bit.
Caller -> Okay. Four to six hours. If she needs. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Does she keep a log of when she uses it?
Caller -> I do. On the calendar. I write an X. It's right next to the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. The nurse will like that.
Nurse -> I'm also sending a nurse out tomorrow to check on Opal and set up the new machine, if it arrives.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Good. Morning or afternoon?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you with a time.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Clyde, please call nine one one if she gets severely short of breath, her lips turn blue, or the inhaler doesn't help. And call us back if the new machine hasn't arrived by nine tonight.
Caller -> Severe, blue lips, inhaler doesn't help. Nine one one. Machine not here by nine, call you. Okay. I wrote it on the back of an envelope.
Caller -> I have a lot of envelopes. I never throw them out.
Nurse -> Ha. A habit I respect.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Kamal. You've been a big help.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care of Opal.
Caller -> I will. She says thank you. She says you sound like a doctor.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her I'm just a nurse.
Caller -> She says the best kind.
Nurse -> Aw. Thank you. Bye, Clyde.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Wildflower Hospice, this is Abigail.
Caller -> Hi, Abigail. It's Rupert Strickland. You wanted to go over my mom's medicines. Evangeline Strickland.
Nurse -> Hi, Rupert. Yes. Thanks for calling back. It's a routine check. I have her list here and I'd like to read it to you and have you tell me if it matches what she's actually taking. Is that okay?
Caller -> Sure. I have the bottles in front of me. I put them all on the table.
Nurse -> Great. How many bottles do you have out?
Caller -> Seven. There's five prescriptions and two vitamins. Her calcium and a fish oil. I didn't know if the vitamins count.
Nurse -> We'll get to those. Let's do the prescriptions first.
Caller -> Okay. I have a pen.
Nurse -> Perfect. First, her date of birth, just to confirm?
Caller -> September fourth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> And the best number for you?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one one eight.
Nurse -> Great. Okay, number one on the list. Levothyroxine, seventy five micrograms, every morning. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. The thyroid pill. Levothyroxine. Seventy five. One every morning. On an empty stomach. She took it today at seven.
Nurse -> Does she take the levothyroxine with her coffee, or water?
Caller -> Water. Then a half hour later coffee and toast. The pharmacist told us to wait. I set a timer on my phone.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect. Number two. Metoprolol succinate, fifty milligrams, every morning.
Caller -> I have that one as Toprol XL. The bottle says Toprol XL. Fifty milligrams. Is that the same?
Nurse -> Yes. Toprol XL is the brand name for metoprolol succinate. Same medicine. Did she take it this morning?
Caller -> She did. At seven, with the thyroid pill. Together. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's fine for those two. I'd prefer she take them with a little food, though. Number three. Lorazepam, half a milligram, as needed for anxiety or restlessness.
Caller -> Yes. I have that. Half a milligram. I use it at night if she's anxious. The last time was two nights ago. It helped.
Nurse -> Okay. Two nights ago. Number four. Oxycodone, five milligrams, as needed for pain.
Caller -> Yes. Five milligrams. I gave her one last night. She says her hip hurts when she lies down. One pill. She went right to sleep.
Nurse -> Any problems with sleepiness during the day after she takes it?
Caller -> No. She wakes up fine. She's alert. She watched her game shows and answered most of the questions. She beat me, actually.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for her.
Nurse -> Good. Number five. Docusate, a hundred milligrams, once a day. A stool softener.
Caller -> That one. She's not taking it. She stopped about two weeks ago. It upset her stomach. She said it gave her cramps. So I stopped giving it. I should have told you.
Nurse -> Don't worry. It's good you're telling me now. Who told you to stop it? Did you decide, or did she?
Caller -> She did. She said it hurt. I didn't want to push. I figured I'd tell you at the visit. Then I forgot.
Nurse -> That makes sense.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's helpful. So docusate is stopped. Is she having regular bowel movements without it?
Caller -> Pretty regular. Every other day. A little hard, but she goes. She drinks a lot of prune juice. She loves it.
Nurse -> How much prune juice does she drink?
Caller -> A small glass in the morning. A half glass at night. She says it's the only thing that works.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep it up.
Nurse -> Good. That sounds like it's working. How's her pain overall?
Caller -> Pretty good. A two. A two out of ten. Just the hip, when she's in bed. It's controlled.
Nurse -> Okay. And her appetite, her breathing?
Caller -> Good. She's eating. Her breathing's fine. She's comfortable.
Nurse -> And mood? Is she in good spirits?
Caller -> She's a little weepy some days. But mostly fine. She was telling stories about her sister yesterday.
Nurse -> That's good. Stories are good.
Nurse -> Wonderful. Rupert, I'm going to update her medication list right now to show the docusate as stopped.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> It's done. I've updated her medication list. And I'll message the hospice provider about the stopped docusate and the stomach upset, in case they want to try something different.
Caller -> Okay. That sounds right. If it's not needed, fine. She does okay with the prune juice.
Nurse -> Right. A couple of reminders. Give the morning pills with a little food. A piece of toast is enough. And keep the as-needed ones, the lorazepam and the oxycodone, in a separate box from the daily pills. Write down each as-needed dose and the time.
Caller -> Toast with the morning pills. Separate box for the as-needed. Write it down. I have a notebook. I do write them. Mostly. I'll be better.
Caller -> I have a lined notebook from the dollar store. Does that count?
Nurse -> It counts perfectly.
Nurse -> That's all I ask. And call us if she goes three days without a bowel movement, or if her pain goes up.
Caller -> Three days. Or pain up. Okay.
Nurse -> Anything else you'd like to ask about her medicines?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you for checking.
Nurse -> Thanks for going through it with me.
Caller -> Do you want me to read the vitamin labels?
Nurse -> Sure, if you don't mind. Just the names and the amounts.
Caller -> Calcium with D, six hundred milligrams. And a fish oil, one thousand milligrams. She takes one of each with lunch.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks for reading them out.
Caller -> Sure. Anything else you need from me?
Nurse -> No, that covers it.
Caller -> Great. I'll let you go.
Caller -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Prairie Rose Home Health, this is Nolan.
Caller -> Nolan, hi. It's Winston Ellsworth. W I N S T O N. Ellsworth. I'm calling about my wife, Marjorie. She's been thirsty and tired.
Caller -> I'm not tired, I'm just resting my eyes.
Nurse -> Hi, Marjorie. Good to hear you. How are you feeling?
Caller -> Fine. I'm fine. He worries.
Nurse -> Hi, Winston. Hi, Marjorie. Is that you in the background?
Caller -> That's her. She's in the chair. She's got opinions. Don't mind her.
Nurse -> I like opinions. Let me pull up her chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> March second. Nineteen fifty one. No. Fifty two. Nineteen fifty two. I'm sorry. She'll correct me.
Caller -> Fifty two. You always get it wrong. Fifty two.
Nurse -> Nineteen fifty two. Thanks, both. And your number, Winston?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one seven five.
Nurse -> Great. Okay. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> Two days she's been drinking and drinking. Water, tea, juice. Always a glass in her hand. And she's tired. She's napping all day. That's not like her.
Nurse -> About how many glasses a day, would you say?
Caller -> Twelve, fifteen. The big blue cup. I fill it at the sink and by the time I'm back it's gone.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a lot.
Caller -> I'm tired because I was up all night peeing. That's the sugar. That's what the lady said.
Nurse -> Marjorie, you've been up at night going to the bathroom?
Caller -> Four times. Five. I counted. It's the sugar.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you check her sugar, Winston?
Caller -> This morning. Two twelve. It was two twelve before breakfast. That's high for her. She's usually one forty, one fifty.
Nurse -> Okay. Two twelve before breakfast. And has she had a sugar check since?
Caller -> No. I haven't done it since. I'll do it after we talk.
Nurse -> Do you have a meter that gives you the number right away?
Caller -> The one with the strips. It takes five seconds. She doesn't like the poke so I do her finger.
Caller -> He pokes too hard.
Nurse -> A new lancet each time helps. We'll show you tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, her pills. Is she taking the metformin?
Caller -> She takes it. Five hundred milligrams, twice a day. Morning and night. She took it this morning. I put it in her hand.
Caller -> I did not. I forgot this morning. And I forgot last night too. I think. I fell asleep in the chair.
Caller -> She did take it. I watched her.
Caller -> You did not watch me. You were making eggs.
Nurse -> Okay, okay. It sounds like we're not sure if she took this morning's, or last night's. Is that right?
Caller -> I think she took it. But she says she didn't. I don't know. I put it in her hand but I didn't see her swallow.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. We'll say it's unclear. Marjorie, do you remember if you swallowed it?
Caller -> I remember the pill in my hand. I remember putting it on the table. I don't remember swallowing. The pill might still be on the table. Winston, look on the table.
Caller -> There's nothing on the table. There's a napkin. A plate. No pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Maybe the dog got it. Ha. No, I'm kidding. Let's not worry about that. Marjorie, how's your vision?
Caller -> A little blurry. Mostly when I read. The newspaper is fuzzy. It was fine last week.
Nurse -> Okay. That can happen when the sugar is high. Any nausea or vomiting?
Caller -> No. None. My stomach's fine. I ate a big breakfast. Eggs and toast. I'm hungry all the time.
Nurse -> Any weight change that you've noticed?
Caller -> She's lost a bit. Her clothes are loose. But she's eaten more lately.
Caller -> I lost five pounds. I'm happy about it.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the provider know about that too.
Nurse -> Okay. Winston and Marjorie, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to message the provider about the high sugar, the thirst, and the question about the metformin.
Caller -> Okay. Will they change her pills?
Nurse -> They might. That's their decision. Don't give extra metformin tonight to make up for the possible missed dose. Just the regular dose. Okay?
Caller -> Just the regular. Okay. I'll do the evening one. And I'll watch her swallow.
Caller -> I'll swallow it. I always swallow it. I just forget I did.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm also sending a nurse out tomorrow to check her sugar and look at her medicines.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back this evening with the provider's answer.
Caller -> This evening. We'll be here. We're always here. Where would we go?
Nurse -> Ha. Right. Winston, check her sugar before dinner and again at bedtime. Write down each number and the time. And from now on, write down when each pill is given, so you both know.
Caller -> Write the pill time. Yes. I'll make a chart. On the fridge. With a pen on a string.
Caller -> I told him to do that last year.
Nurse -> Ha. A good idea. Also, keep offering her water through the evening. Avoid juice and regular soda.
Caller -> No juice. I love my orange juice.
Nurse -> I know. It's just for tonight, until we see the number tomorrow.
Caller -> Fine. Then I'll have water with a lemon.
Caller -> Water. Just for tonight.
Nurse -> Right. And call nine one one if she gets confused, can't stop vomiting, has fruity smelling breath, or is hard to keep awake. And call us back if the sugar is over three hundred.
Caller -> Confused, vomiting, fruity breath, can't stay awake. Nine one one. Over three hundred, call. I'm writing it down.
Nurse -> Perfect. Thanks, both.
Caller -> Thank you, Nolan.
Nurse -> Anything else I can help with?
Caller -> No. It was nice to talk to somebody.
Caller -> We don't get many calls.
Nurse -> You can call anytime.
Caller -> Bye, Nolan. Don't let him write anything wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Harbor Pediatric Palliative Care, this is Gwendolyn.
Caller -> Gwen, hi. It's Saoirse Abernethy. It's Kieran. He's in so much pain. The medicine isn't working. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay, Saoirse. I'm here. Take a breath. Is Kieran with you right now?
Caller -> He's on the couch. In the living room. He's crying. He's holding his leg. He can't get comfortable.
Nurse -> Is anyone else at home with you?
Caller -> His little sister, Maeve. She's six. She's in her room. She's scared. She keeps coming out and asking if Kieran is okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's hard for her too.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me his date of birth, and I'll pull up his chart.
Caller -> June twelfth. Two thousand fourteen.
Nurse -> Thanks. And a number for you?
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, zero one six four.
Nurse -> Okay. Where's the pain?
Caller -> His right leg. Above the knee. Where the tumor is. He says it's burning and stabbing. He says it's an eight. He's twelve. He doesn't say numbers like that. He says eight.
Nurse -> Does he usually say numbers? When he's hurting?
Caller -> Usually he says four or five. He's tough. He never says eight. This is the first eight.
Nurse -> Okay. That tells me this is a real flare.
Nurse -> An eight. Okay. When did the pain start getting worse?
Caller -> Around five. After dinner. He was okay in the afternoon. Then it got bad. He cried out when he moved. I've never seen him cry like this.
Nurse -> Is he able to move the leg? Is there any swelling or change in color?
Caller -> It looks the same. A bit swollen at the top. The skin is warm. It's always a bit warm. Same as the last visit.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. What have you given him?
Caller -> The breakthrough. The morphine. The liquid. Two milligrams per mL. One point five mL. A mL and a half. I gave it at four. It took the edge off for an hour. And then it came back. And it's worse.
Nurse -> Okay. So a mL and a half of the two milligram per mL morphine at four, and it helped for about an hour. Anything since?
Caller -> Nothing. I wasn't sure if I could give more. The sheet says every three hours. It's been, let me look. It's seven. It's been three hours.
Nurse -> It's always okay to ask. You did the right thing waiting until you called.
Caller -> I didn't want to give too much. Last time I gave it too early and the nurse scolded me. Not scolded. Gently told me.
Nurse -> It's three hours now. That's the right time.
Nurse -> Right. It's been three hours, so you can give the next dose now. I want you to give it right away. I'll walk you through it.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Please. I have the bottle. I have the syringe. I'm in the kitchen. Hold on. Let me get it.
Nurse -> Take your time. Do you have the dosing sheet?
Caller -> It's taped to the cabinet. It says one point five mL. Every three hours as needed for breakthrough pain. I'm reading it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Draw up one and a half mL. Tell me when you've got it.
Caller -> Okay. I'm drawing. Slowly. One. One point five. There. It's at the one point five line.
Nurse -> Great. Check that the plunger is exactly on the line.
Caller -> It is. The top of the black. It's on the line.
Nurse -> Good. Go to Kieran. Give it slowly into his cheek, a little at a time. Not straight down the throat. Then write the time on the sheet.
Caller -> Okay. I'm walking. Kieran, honey, I have your medicine. Open up a little. Good boy. Slow. There. There. He took it all. He swallowed. Good job, sweetheart.
Caller -> He says it tastes like cherry. It's not cherry. It's morphine. But he says cherry.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sign he's talking.
Nurse -> Perfect. What time is it?
Caller -> Seven oh six. I'll write seven oh six. It's on the sheet. I wrote it.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're so organized. Saoirse, do you have a long acting medicine too?
Caller -> The patch. The fentanyl patch. It's on his shoulder. We changed it Sunday. It's due Wednesday.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. I'll tell the clinician.
Nurse -> Good. It'll take about twenty or thirty minutes to work. While we wait, let's make him as comfortable as possible. Saoirse, I'm also going to page the on-call clinician now, because the pain is high and the last dose didn't last.
Caller -> Will they change his medicine? Make it stronger?
Nurse -> They might. That's their decision. They'll look at the whole plan. I'm also sending a nurse out to see him. I want her there within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Thank you. Thank you.
Caller -> Should I get a bag ready? In case they want to take him to the hospital?
Nurse -> Not yet. We'll plan for home. If the clinician wants him seen, we'll arrange it.
Caller -> Okay. I'd like to keep him home if possible.
Nurse -> That's our goal too.
Nurse -> Now, can you help him get into a position of comfort? Support the leg on pillows. One under the knee, one under the foot. Don't squeeze the leg or press on it. Cover him with a warm blanket. Keep the room quiet. And if he likes, put on a show or music. A distraction can help.
Caller -> Pillows. Yes. I'll put them. Kieran, I'm going to lift your leg a tiny bit. Okay? Here comes a pillow. Okay. And another. There. He says that's better. A little. He says it still hurts but it's not so sharp.
Nurse -> That's good news. Is he using his pain faces chart?
Caller -> No. He doesn't like the chart. He says it's for babies. I ask him a number. Eight, he said earlier. Now I'll ask. Kieran, what number now? He says six. He says six.
Nurse -> A six. That's progress. It's only been a few minutes.
Nurse -> Good. What does he like to watch?
Caller -> Minecraft videos. A guy who builds castles. He loves it. I'll put it on. Hold on. I'm setting up the tablet. Okay. It's on. He's watching. He's still crying a little. But he's looking.
Nurse -> Does he play Minecraft too?
Caller -> All the time. On the tablet. He builds with his friends online. They have a world. They call it the kingdom.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. It sounds like a great escape.
Caller -> It is. It's his happy place.
Caller -> He's built a whole castle with a moat. It's his masterpiece. He wants to show it to you someday.
Nurse -> I'd love to see it.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Keep talking to him. Tell him the medicine is working.
Caller -> He asked if he's going to be able to go to school Friday. His friends are making him a card. They're having a pizza party for him.
Nurse -> That's so sweet. We'll see how he does. He can decide on Friday morning.
Caller -> I told him no pressure. He said he wants to go if the leg lets him. He's stubborn like his father.
Nurse -> Ha. I'd say determination is a good trait.
Caller -> He's been so strong through all of it. The surgery, the chemo. He's twelve and he's been braver than me.
Nurse -> Sounds like he gets it from somewhere.
Caller -> Maybe. I just cry in the car.
Nurse -> Crying in the car is a classic. You're allowed.
Caller -> Kieran, the medicine's going to work. It takes a little while. Gwen says. He says okay. He's holding my hand.
Nurse -> What a brave boy. Tell him I said so.
Caller -> Kieran, Gwen says you're brave. He says tell her I'm not brave. I'm just in pain. Ha. He's such a smart aleck.
Nurse -> I love it.
Nurse -> Saoirse, is he sleepy at all? Does he seem too sleepy, or is he alert?
Caller -> He's alert. Wide awake. He's looking at the screen. He's not drowsy. His breathing is normal. He's breathing fast because he's crying. But normal. And he's moving both legs. The left one fine. The right one's just in pain. No new weakness.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a fever? Has he been hot?
Caller -> No. No fever. I took it at five. Ninety eight point four. He's cool.
Nurse -> Good. Okay. I want to go over a few things. If he becomes very sleepy, hard to wake up, or his breathing slows down, call me right away. And call nine one one if you can't wake him. That's unlikely at this dose, but I always mention it.
Caller -> Very sleepy, hard to wake, slow breathing, call you. Can't wake, nine one one. Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> Good. How are you holding up?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm crying a little. I hate this. I hate seeing him hurt. I'd take it all for him.
Nurse -> That's what every parent says. It's the hardest part of this.
Caller -> It is. It's just the hardest. I'm sorry. I'm crying again.
Nurse -> Don't apologize. Cry. It's okay.
Nurse -> I know you would. You're doing everything right. You gave the dose on time, you called, you're comforting him.
Caller -> Thank you. Is my husband supposed to be here? He's working late. He doesn't know yet. Should I call him?
Nurse -> If you'd like him here, call him. It's okay to ask him to come home.
Caller -> I'll text. He'll come. He'd want to. He's at the plant.
Nurse -> Does Kieran ask for his dad when he's hurting?
Caller -> Always. They have a thing. His dad sings to him. A silly song about a goat. It always makes him laugh.
Nurse -> A song about a goat. That's wonderful. Tell him to sing it when he gets home.
Caller -> He's going to feel awful that he wasn't here. He works nights for the overtime. For the bills.
Nurse -> He's doing what he can. It will be okay.
Nurse -> That's fine. Do that after we hang up. I'll call you back in twenty minutes to see how Kieran is doing and what the clinician says.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. Seven twenty six.
Caller -> I set a timer on my phone for twenty minutes. Just so I'm not watching the clock.
Nurse -> That's smart. Let the timer do the watching.
Nurse -> Right. If he's worse before then, call me. Any time.
Caller -> I will. I'm watching him. He's a little calmer now. His face is softer. He's looking at the video. The castle is huge.
Nurse -> Does he want a drink of water or juice?
Caller -> He says apple juice. I'll bring him some. Through a straw.
Nurse -> Good. Small sips.
Caller -> He's pointing at the screen. He says that's the dragon room. Oh, Gwen, he's smiling.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Keep that going.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Let him watch. Keep the leg up.
Caller -> I'm trying to remember everything. The pillows, the show, the warm blanket, the time on the sheet.
Nurse -> You're doing it all. You're not forgetting anything.
Caller -> It feels like I'm forgetting something.
Nurse -> Then call me. That's what I'm here for.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Gwen. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk soon.
Caller -> Gwen, one small thing. Thank you for answering at this hour. I know it's late.
Nurse -> It's what I do. I'm happy to be here for you and Kieran.
Caller -> Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Saoirse.
