Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hey. Is Dolores there?
Nurse -> I'm sorry, there's no Dolores here. This is Cottonwood Home Health.
Caller -> Home health? Is this Dolores's Plumbing?
Nurse -> No, sir. We're a nursing agency. I think you have the wrong number.
Caller -> Oh. Hm. She gave me this number for the estimate. For the water heater. Let me look at my paper.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I wrote it down. Five five five, oh one one four. Is that right?
Nurse -> This number ends in zero one one one. Yours ends in one four.
Caller -> I'm reading it wrong. It's a four. I think the one is a four. I have bad handwriting.
Nurse -> Ha. It happens. Dolores's Plumbing is probably the one ending in four.
Caller -> Probably. I'll try that. Sorry about that.
Nurse -> No problem at all. Good luck with the water heater.
Caller -> Thanks. It's been leaking for a week. My wife is losing her mind.
Nurse -> Ha. I hope it gets fixed soon.
Caller -> Me too. Have a good one.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

not_applicable.reason: Wrong number; the caller was trying to reach a plumber.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Henrik.
Caller -> Hi, Henrik. It's Annelise Orloff. I'm calling about my son. Dashiell Orloff. D A S H I E L L. We spoke Tuesday about his cold.
Nurse -> Hi, Annelise. Good to hear from you. Dashiell, D A S H I E L L, right? Like the detective?
Caller -> Like Dashiell Hammett. My husband's a mystery nut. Everyone thinks it's a typo.
Nurse -> Ha. It's a great name.
Nurse -> Hi, Annelise. Yes, I remember. How is he doing?
Caller -> So much better. I wanted to give you an update. And ask about day care.
Nurse -> I'm so glad. Tuesday you were pretty worried.
Caller -> I was a wreck. He was coughing so hard he threw up. I thought it was pneumonia. It turned out to be just a bad cold.
Nurse -> That's a relief.
Nurse -> Good. Let me pull up his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> August ninth. Two thousand twenty four. He's two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one seven five.
Nurse -> Perfect. Tell me about the cough.
Caller -> It's mostly gone. It's dry now. Just a little tickle in the morning. It was wet and rattly on Tuesday. Now it's just a cough here and there. Maybe five times a day.
Nurse -> Does it wake him at night?
Caller -> No. Not since Thursday. He sleeps through. He wakes up at six and yells for waffles.
Nurse -> Ha. Waffles are a good sign.
Nurse -> Okay. That's improving. Any fever?
Caller -> No fever. I took it this morning. Ninety eight point two. And last night ninety eight point five. He's been normal since Wednesday.
Nurse -> What kind of thermometer?
Caller -> The forehead one. The kind you swipe. It beeps. He tries to eat it.
Nurse -> Ha. A toddler.
Nurse -> Good. And his appetite?
Caller -> Back to normal. He ate me out of house and home. Pancakes, an egg, a banana, half my toast. He's sleeping through the night too. Since Thursday. He's back to waking at six like a rooster.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is he breathing comfortably? No fast breathing or wheezing?
Caller -> No. Totally normal. He's running around. He's climbing on the couch. He's a monkey. He's totally himself.
Nurse -> Is he using a lot of tissues, runny nose?
Caller -> A little runny. Clear. I wipe it about ten times a day. We've gone through three boxes.
Nurse -> That's normal for a cold.
Nurse -> Great. Are you still using the humidifier?
Caller -> Yes. The cool mist. At night. I clean it every day. Like you said.
Nurse -> Do you use plain water in it?
Caller -> Distilled. The gallon jugs. It's in the garage. I'm rinsing it with vinegar like the nurse showed me.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect. So what's your day care question?
Caller -> Can he go back Monday? He's missed a week. And I have to go back to work. I'm a dental assistant. I took four days off. I'm out of time. Do I have to keep him home longer?
Nurse -> Does the day care have a policy sheet?
Caller -> They do. Twenty four hours fever free. I don't know if it's with or without medicine.
Nurse -> Without. That's the standard.
Nurse -> It sounds like he's doing great. The usual rule is he can return when he's been fever free for twenty four hours without any fever medicine, and he's eating and drinking normally. Does that sound like him?
Caller -> Yes. No fever since Wednesday. No Tylenol since Tuesday. So that's well over twenty four hours. He's eating and drinking. So he should be okay.
Nurse -> It sounds like he qualifies. If he's still fever free Monday morning, he can go. Check his temperature before you leave. And keep an ear on that cough.
Caller -> Okay. Check the temperature Monday. And listen to the cough. Okay. Thank you. That's a relief.
Nurse -> Remind the day care about the cough, so they don't worry. And wash hands often, his and yours. Offer lots of fluids.
Caller -> I will. Handwashing. Fluids. I'm a dental assistant. I wash my hands about two hundred times a day.
Nurse -> Ha. You're the right person for this.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Caller -> I do worry about him going back. He picks everything up there. Last winter he got four colds.
Nurse -> That's very typical for a kid in day care. The first year is rough.
Caller -> I know. It's a sneeze factory.
Nurse -> And call us if his temperature goes to one hundred one or higher, if his breathing gets fast or noisy, or if he stops drinking.
Caller -> One hundred one. Fast or noisy breathing. Not drinking. Okay. I wrote it on a sticky note.
Caller -> I put it on the fridge. Right next to the magnet of the moon.
Nurse -> Ha. A lunar fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll check in with you Monday morning, to see how the first day goes.
Caller -> Oh, that's nice. Thank you. Monday morning. I'll be at work by then. Call my cell. It's the same number.
Nurse -> Will do. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I just wanted to say thanks. You helped me not panic on Tuesday.
Nurse -> Anytime. Glad he's better.
Caller -> Henrik, one more thing. He's been chewing on a pacifier again. He's two. Is that a problem?
Nurse -> It's not an emergency. Many kids go back to old habits when they're sick. It will pass.
Caller -> That's what I thought. Okay.
Caller -> Me too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Silver Lake Home Health, this is Zane.
Caller -> Zane, hi. It's Beatrice Kettleman. It's my husband Ambrose. He's been home from the hospital three days and he's not right. He's dizzy and he's gray.
Nurse -> Gray how? His face, his lips?
Caller -> His face. Kind of ashy. His lips are pink. He looks like he's lost his color.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay, Beatrice. Thanks for calling. Let me bring up Ambrose's chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> February twelfth. Nineteen fifty four.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one six three.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me how he's been feeling since he got home.
Caller -> Tired. Washed out. He can barely get out of the chair. And when he stands, he's dizzy. Really dizzy. He grabs the wall. It's been since we got home. Getting worse today.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a blood pressure cuff and pulse?
Caller -> Yes. I just did it. His pulse is fifty two. Fifty two. And his pressure is ninety eight over sixty. That's low, right?
Nurse -> It's lower than I'd like, especially with the dizziness. Has he fainted or had chest pain?
Caller -> No. No fainting. No chest pain. He just feels like he's going to pass out when he stands. But he hasn't. I make him sit.
Nurse -> Is he sitting or lying down right now?
Caller -> He's in the recliner. With his feet up. He's watching the news with the sound off.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him there.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Beatrice, I want to go over his medicines with you. Do you have all the bottles and the discharge paper in front of you?
Caller -> They're all on the kitchen table. I put them out. There's like ten bottles. And the discharge sheet from the hospital.
Nurse -> Is the discharge sheet a printed list, with sections?
Caller -> Yes. There's a part that says continue, a part that says new, and a part that says stop. I didn't look at the stop part carefully.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll go through it together.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let's go through them one at a time. I'll ask you to read the name and the directions on the bottle, and tell me whether he's taking it. Start with the first one.
Caller -> Okay. The first one. It says furosemide. Twenty milligrams. Take two tablets once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Furosemide, twenty milligram tablets, two tablets a day, that's forty milligrams. Is that what the discharge sheet says?
Caller -> Forty milligrams, once a day. Yes. It matches. And he took it this morning. Two tablets. At eight.
Nurse -> Does the bottle say what it's for?
Caller -> For the swelling. The water pill. For his heart.
Nurse -> Right. Good.
Nurse -> Good. Next bottle.
Caller -> The next one. Metoprolol tartrate. T A R T R A T E. Twenty five milligrams. Take one tablet twice a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Metoprolol tartrate, twenty five, twice a day. Is it on the discharge sheet?
Caller -> Yes. It's new. They changed it. The sheet says metoprolol tartrate twenty five twice a day. Start. And it says stop the old one. But I couldn't find the old one. I mean, I found it, but I wasn't sure.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's slow down. What's the old one?
Caller -> The old one is, here it is. Metoprolol succinate. S U C C I N A T E. Fifty milligrams. Once a day. It's in the other bottle. A bigger bottle. From before.
Nurse -> Is the label from the same pharmacy?
Caller -> The old pharmacy. The one near the old house. The new ones are from the hospital pharmacy. I should have thrown the old ones out.
Nurse -> It's common to keep them. We'll sort it.
Caller -> I keep everything. My mother was like that. Every pill bottle since nineteen ninety, in a shoebox. I get it from her.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of us do.
Caller -> The shoebox is still in the hall closet. I should deal with that someday, but not today.
Nurse -> Today we just need the kitchen table.
Caller -> Right. The kitchen table. Okay. I'm focusing.
Caller -> Sorry, the dog is barking. Hold on. Biscuit, quiet. Okay. He wants his walk and I can't take him with Ambrose like this.
Nurse -> The dog will survive. Is someone else around who could walk him later?
Caller -> My neighbor Phil usually does. I'll text him after this call. He's a good guy. Retired, bored, loves the dog more than we do.
Nurse -> Ha. That works out for everyone.
Caller -> It does. Okay. Sorry. Where were we? The bottles. Right. The next one.
Nurse -> Take your time. Whenever you're ready.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. Take your time with each label.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the extended release metoprolol he used to take. The discharge sheet says to stop that one. Beatrice, has he been taking the succinate too?
Caller -> Oh no. Oh no. Yes. I've been giving him both. I thought the new one was an extra. I gave him the old one in the morning like always. And the new one morning and night. So he gets the succinate in the morning with the tartrate. Both.
Nurse -> Okay. So he's been getting both forms of metoprolol. When was the last of each?
Caller -> This morning. At eight. Both. The tartrate and the succinate. Together. And the tartrate again last night. I think last night just the tartrate.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That helps explain the slow pulse and low pressure. Let's keep going. What's the next bottle?
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. I didn't know. I should have read it.
Nurse -> It's okay. This happens all the time after a hospital stay. The lists change and the old bottles are still in the cabinet. You're doing the right thing by going through them now. Next bottle.
Caller -> Okay. Lisinopril. L I S I N O P R I L. Ten milligrams. Once a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Is lisinopril on the discharge sheet?
Caller -> Hmm. Let me look. It says, under stop taking, lisinopril. Hmm. Yes. It's on the stop list. Oh. Oh no. I gave him that too. This morning. At eight.
Nurse -> Okay. So he took the lisinopril this morning too, and it was supposed to be stopped. Beatrice, that's another blood pressure medicine, and it can lower his pressure further.
Caller -> Oh my God. I've been giving him that for three days. I gave him that every morning. I thought it was the same as before.
Nurse -> It's easy to think so. The hospital changes lists all the time.
Caller -> I'm just so tired. Three nights in a row I've barely slept.
Nurse -> I understand. Let's get this sorted so you can rest.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. The list is confusing. Let's finish the bottles. What else?
Caller -> Okay. There's an aspirin, eighty one. And a potassium pill. And a stool softener. And his cholesterol pill. And the water pill. I did the water pill.
Nurse -> And the potassium, is that in a pill form?
Caller -> A big pill. He hates it. I cut it in half. Is that okay?
Nurse -> We'll look at that with the nurse. Don't cut any more pills until she's here.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll go over those with the nurse tomorrow. Right now I'm most concerned about the metoprolol, the lisinopril and the water pill, because they all lower his blood pressure and heart rate. Beatrice, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Do I need to call an ambulance? Is he in danger?
Nurse -> He's awake, talking, no chest pain, and no fainting, so I don't think we need an ambulance right now. But I want a clinician to look at this today. I'm also sending a nurse to your home. I want her there within two hours.
Caller -> Within two hours. Okay. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until the clinician calls back, please don't give him the metoprolol, either kind, or the lisinopril or the water pill. Hold all three.
Caller -> Hold all three. Metoprolol, both. The lisinopril. The furosemide. Okay. I won't give them. What about the others?
Nurse -> The aspirin, the potassium, the cholesterol pill and the stool softener, those can wait too until the clinician calls. Just hold everything for now except water and food.
Caller -> Hold everything. Okay. Water and food. I have it.
Caller -> Can he have his coffee? He gets a headache without it.
Nurse -> A small cup is fine. Not too strong.
Caller -> Half a cup. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. What do I do until then?
Nurse -> Have Ambrose sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a minute before he stands. Stand slowly. And have you next to him whenever he walks. Don't let him walk alone.
Caller -> Sit first. Stand slow. Me next to him. Okay. He wants to go to the bathroom. I'll walk him.
Nurse -> Good. Also, please take the old metoprolol and the lisinopril bottles and put them in a bag, away from his current pills. And have every bottle ready for the nurse to review when she comes.
Caller -> A bag for the old ones. All the bottles on the table. Okay. I'll do that now. I'll get a grocery bag.
Nurse -> And call nine one one if he faints, has chest pain, trouble breathing, or his pulse drops under forty.
Caller -> Faints, chest pain, breathing, pulse under forty. Nine one one. Okay. I'll check his pulse every fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Write down the numbers.
Caller -> I will. Zane, I feel awful. I almost hurt my husband.
Caller -> If something happens, I'd never forgive myself.
Nurse -> Nothing is going to happen that we can't handle. We're on it.
Nurse -> You didn't hurt him. You caught it. Many people never notice. And he's awake and talking. We'll fix it.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for not scolding me.
Nurse -> No scolding. You're doing what you can. Is anyone with you tonight?
Caller -> He keeps asking me if he's going to be okay. I don't know what to tell him.
Nurse -> Tell him the nurse is on it and the doctor will call soon. Tell him to rest.
Caller -> Ambrose, the nurse says rest. He says he's resting. He's grumpy.
Nurse -> Grumpy is fine.
Caller -> He's grumpy because I took away his coffee. I gave him half a cup.
Nurse -> A half cup is plenty.
Caller -> My son comes at six. He's on his way.
Nurse -> Good. Let him help with the walking.
Caller -> He's a big man. Six two. When he leans on me I feel it.
Caller -> His pants are baggy now. He's lost twenty pounds since the summer. The doctor said it's the fluid, then it's not the fluid.
Nurse -> The team will go over that. It's a lot to follow.
Caller -> It is. I wrote it all in a notebook. Fourteen pages.
Nurse -> Bring the notebook to the visit.
Nurse -> Let your son take the heavy part.
Caller -> I will. He used to be a linebacker.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Zane. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> Talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Dana.
Caller -> Hi Dana. It's Marisol Quintero. M A R I S O L, Q U I N T E R O. I'm the knee replacement. I'm calling for my check in.
Nurse -> Hi Marisol. Yes. I have you. M A R I S O L. I got it.
Caller -> Everybody spells it with a Z. It's an S.
Nurse -> Ha. S. Got it.
Caller -> Thanks.
Nurse -> And you're calling about yourself, right? So you're the patient?
Caller -> Yes. Me. I'm the one with the new knee. Day six.
Nurse -> Day six. Great. Let me pull up the chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> May twenty first. Nineteen seventy two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a good number to reach you?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one one zero.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one one zero. Is that right?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. So how are things going? I'm hoping it's a good update.
Caller -> It's pretty good. I think. Um. I'm calling because I wanted to make sure I'm on track. I wanted to give you an update.
Nurse -> That's what I'm here for. Start with the pain.
Caller -> The pain is, I'd say a four. With the pill. Without the pill it's like a six, but I take it. A four right now. It's mostly when I stand up from the couch.
Nurse -> A four, okay. Is it getting better or staying about the same?
Caller -> Better. It was an eight the first night. A six by Sunday. Now a four.
Nurse -> That's a good trend.
Caller -> Yeah. I'm happy about that.
Nurse -> And the swelling?
Caller -> Some. It's, um, mild I guess. The knee is puffy. Like a grapefruit instead of a melon.
Nurse -> Ha. A grapefruit is better than a melon.
Caller -> It's much better than Monday. It's puffy at the end of the day. In the morning it's less.
Nurse -> That's normal. Is it warm or red?
Caller -> Warm a little. Not hot. Not red. I checked the incision with my phone flashlight. It's dry. No drainage on the bandage. Nothing is red. It looks like a long zipper.
Nurse -> Good. Did you take your temperature?
Caller -> This morning. Ninety nine point one. That's normal for me. I run low.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety nine point one is fine. Are you getting chills?
Caller -> No chills. Just tired.
Nurse -> Tired is expected.
Caller -> I'm sleeping, like, ten hours. My husband says I'm a teenager.
Nurse -> Ha. Your body is healing. Sleep is good.
Caller -> That's what I told him.
Nurse -> How's the walking?
Caller -> With the walker, I'm doing the hallway. Four laps. I do the exercises too, the leg lifts and the bending. The therapist gave me a sheet. I'm up to a ninety degree bend.
Nurse -> That's right on schedule.
Caller -> Really? I thought I was slow.
Nurse -> No. You're doing well.
Caller -> Okay good.
Nurse -> Are you icing?
Caller -> Um. Sometimes. I forget. I have the ice machine, the one with the pad. It's loud.
Nurse -> Try to ice after your exercises and in the evening. Twenty minutes at a time, and keep the leg up above your heart when you can.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Up above the heart. Okay. I've been keeping it on a pillow, but flat. I'll prop it higher.
Nurse -> Higher is better for the swelling.
Caller -> Got it. I'll do that tonight.
Nurse -> I also want you to call if you get a fever over one hundred and one, any drainage from the incision, redness that spreads, or pain and swelling in your calf.
Caller -> Over one oh one. Drainage. Spreading redness. Calf pain and swelling. Okay. I'm writing it on the whiteboard.
Nurse -> Good. The calf one is important, so don't wait on that.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> I'll see you Thursday for the visit. We'll look at the incision and check how you're bending.
Caller -> Thursday. What time?
Nurse -> Sometime in the afternoon. I'll call before I head over.
Caller -> That's fine. My husband will be at work, but I'll be here. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet.
Caller -> I can't even drive. I'm stuck with Netflix.
Nurse -> How is your husband handling being the chauffeur and the cook?
Caller -> He's good. He makes eggs. Only eggs. Every meal is eggs. I told him there are other foods.
Nurse -> Ha. At least it's protein.
Caller -> That's his argument.
Nurse -> What are you watching?
Caller -> A baking show. I can't bake. It's a problem.
Nurse -> Ha. It's good motivation.
Caller -> I want a cake. I want a whole cake.
Nurse -> Eat the cake. After you do your laps.
Caller -> Ha. Deal.
Nurse -> Anything else you wanted to ask?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thanks, Dana.
Nurse -> You're welcome. See you Thursday.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi, yes, this is Karin Brandvold. I'm calling about my dad, Walter Brandvold. I think the pharmacy made a mistake.
Nurse -> Hi Karin. Okay. Let's look at it together. Can I get Walter's date of birth first?
Caller -> August fourth, nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> Thank you. And the best number for you?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one five three.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, zero one five three. Did I get that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> So, um. Dad takes a blood pressure pill. He's supposed to. And I was, I was setting up his pill box last night and I looked at the new bottle. And it says hydroxyzine. But his list from the doctor says hydralazine. They look the same, almost.
Nurse -> Okay. They do look alike. Read me the whole label, if you can. Slowly.
Caller -> H Y D R O X Y Z I N E. Twenty five milligrams. One tablet three times a day. It says, take with food. The pharmacy sticker is, it's from the new place. The one by the grocery store.
Nurse -> Okay. Hydroxyzine twenty five milligrams, three times a day. And what does his list say?
Caller -> The list says hydralazine. H Y D R A L A Z I N E. Twenty five milligrams. Three times a day. So same dose, same schedule, different word.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. That's what the doctor ordered, hydralazine. For the pressure. Hydroxyzine is a different medicine, an antihistamine, for itching or anxiety.
Caller -> Oh no. Oh no. That's what I was afraid of.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay with me. How long has he been taking the new bottle?
Caller -> Since Saturday. So, three days. I picked it up Friday. Before that he had the old bottle, the right one, but it ran out. So three days of the new one.
Nurse -> And when did he last take one?
Caller -> This morning. At eight. With his oatmeal. Eight o'clock.
Nurse -> Okay. Has anything seemed different with him these three days?
Caller -> He's been sleepy. A lot. He sleeps in the chair all afternoon. And his mouth is dry. He keeps asking for water. I thought it was the weather.
Nurse -> That fits with hydroxyzine. Did you take his blood pressure?
Caller -> I did this morning. One sixty eight over ninety two. That's higher than usual. Usually it's one thirty something.
Nurse -> Okay. That makes sense too, since he hasn't had the right medicine. Any chest pain, any falls?
Caller -> No chest pain. No falls. He's been steady, just slow. He's not complaining of anything.
Nurse -> Good. Is he awake now?
Caller -> He's right here. He's watching the game show. He's awake. He just yelled an answer at the TV.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Good. I'd like to tell you what to do now.
Caller -> Okay. Please.
Nurse -> Don't give him any more of the hydroxyzine. Not the afternoon dose, not tonight. And keep the bottle, don't throw it out. We'll need the label.
Caller -> Don't give any more. Keep the bottle. Okay. I'll put it in a bag.
Nurse -> Good. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, because he's been on the wrong medicine and his pressure is up. The clinician will tell us what to do about the blood pressure medicine.
Caller -> Okay. Should I give him the old one? The hydralazine? I don't have any left.
Nurse -> No. Don't give him anything else for now. Wait for the clinician. I'll also be calling the pharmacy to straighten this out and get the right bottle.
Caller -> Thank you. I was so upset last night. I almost called at ten.
Nurse -> Ten last night? You could have called the after hours line. It's always open.
Caller -> I didn't want to bother anyone. I figured I'd wait until morning.
Nurse -> It's never a bother. Next time, call.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> I'm glad you caught it. It's a very common mix up. They look so similar on paper.
Caller -> I only caught it because Dad's list is taped to the fridge. I read it every time.
Nurse -> That's a good habit.
Caller -> My mom started it. She made the list ten years ago.
Nurse -> It's saving you now.
Caller -> I know.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send someone out this afternoon, to check his pressure and see how sleepy he is.
Caller -> This afternoon. Okay. I'll be here. I work from home on Tuesdays.
Nurse -> Great. Until then, keep him seated or lying down, help him up slowly, and stay with him when he walks. He may be unsteady because of the sleepiness.
Caller -> Slowly. Stay with him. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us right away, or 911, if he has chest pain, trouble breathing, a really bad headache, confusion, or if he gets hard to wake up.
Caller -> Chest pain, breathing, headache, confusion, hard to wake. Okay. Okay. I'm writing it on my hand. I don't have paper.
Caller -> I have a pen. Hold on. I'm writing on my hand. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. That works.
Caller -> My handwriting on my hand is terrible.
Nurse -> As long as you can read it.
Caller -> Can he eat lunch?
Nurse -> Yes. Lunch is fine. Plenty of water too, since his mouth is dry.
Caller -> Okay. I'll make him a sandwich.
Nurse -> Is he eating okay, other than the dry mouth?
Caller -> He ate his oatmeal. Half of it. He's a slow eater these days.
Nurse -> And Karin, you did the right thing calling.
Caller -> Thank you. I feel better. I was kicking myself.
Nurse -> Don't. The pharmacy is the one who should feel bad.
Caller -> Ha. I'm going to have words with them.
Nurse -> I'll have words first. I'll keep you posted.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Bye now.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi Marcus. This is Roland Paddock. I'm calling about my wife. She's on your service. Her name is Eilidh. E I L I D H. It's Scottish.
Nurse -> Okay Roland. Ally, A L L Y. Let me pull up Ally Paddock.
Caller -> Eilidh. E I L I D H. But she answers to Ally. Everybody says Ally.
Nurse -> Okay. Got it. Ally Paddock. And what's her date of birth?
Caller -> December ninth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a good number to reach you?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one four four.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one four four. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house phone.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on with Ally today?
Caller -> It's her bowels. She hasn't gone in four days. I'm worried. She's uncomfortable.
Nurse -> Four days. I'm sorry. When was the last time she went?
Caller -> Saturday. In the morning. It was small and hard. Like pebbles. Since then, nothing. It's Wednesday now. So four days.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she having any belly pain or bloating?
Caller -> Her belly feels full. She says it's tight. She keeps rubbing it. And she's a little queasy. Not throwing up. Just says she feels yucky. Mild.
Nurse -> Okay. Mild nausea and a full belly. Is she passing any gas?
Caller -> Yes. She is. A little. She's, um, she passed gas this morning. And no vomiting. She's keeping her tea down.
Nurse -> That's good to hear. What is she taking for her bowels right now?
Caller -> Senna. The little brown pills. Eight point six. Twice a day. And the Miralax. The powder. One scoop in juice. Every morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Senna twice a day, and Miralax once a day. Is she taking all of that?
Caller -> She's been taking the senna. The Miralax she skipped yesterday. She said she was sick of drinking it. It tastes like nothing but she says it's slimy.
Nurse -> Okay. Today?
Caller -> I got her to take it today. In apple juice. She drank half of it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a start. Let me ask a few more things. Is she eating?
Caller -> A little. Toast. Soup. Not much. She's not that hungry. I think the, I think it's because she's backed up.
Nurse -> That's very possible. And she's getting fluids?
Caller -> I'm pushing them. Tea. Juice. Water. She sips. She doesn't like to drink a lot at once.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she moving around, or mostly in bed?
Caller -> She's in the recliner. She does a little walk to the bathroom. Then back.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you, Roland. I'm going to send a nurse to see Ally tomorrow, and we'll check her belly.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> I'll have the scheduler call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Good. That's good. I was afraid you'd say Friday.
Nurse -> Not Friday. I'm also going to leave a message for the team, to ask about a stronger bowel regimen for Ally. Something more than the senna and the powder.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. I was hoping you'd say that. Because what she's taking isn't doing it.
Nurse -> I agree. The doctor may add something. I can't promise, but I'll ask.
Caller -> That's all I ask.
Nurse -> Does she have anyone else who helps during the day?
Caller -> My sister in law comes Tuesdays. She does the laundry and talks Ally's ear off. Ally loves it.
Nurse -> That's a good thing to have.
Nurse -> In the meantime, offer her small sips of fluids all day, prune juice if she likes it, and small frequent meals instead of big ones.
Caller -> Small sips. Prune juice. Small meals. She hates prune juice. But I'll try. Maybe I'll warm it up. Like tea.
Nurse -> Warm prune juice. Some people swear by it.
Caller -> I'll try anything.
Nurse -> And call us back if she starts vomiting, if her belly gets hard or very painful, or if she can't keep fluids down.
Caller -> Vomiting. Hard belly. Pain. Can't keep fluids down. Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> If it's after hours, you can call this same number. Someone is always here.
Caller -> Okay. I didn't know that. I thought it was just during the day.
Nurse -> No. Twenty four hours, seven days.
Caller -> That's a relief. I'm up at three in the morning half the time.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you can call at three in the morning.
Caller -> Ha. I just might.
Nurse -> How are you holding up, Roland?
Caller -> Tired. But okay. My daughter comes on weekends. She gives me a break. I go to the hardware store and walk around.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like a good break.
Caller -> It's the only place I can be alone. Nobody talks to me in the plumbing aisle.
Nurse -> What are you working on at the store?
Caller -> Nothing. I look at faucets. I bought a faucet in August. We don't need a faucet.
Caller -> I look at the washers and the little rubber rings. Very calming.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Nurse -> Take the break. You've earned it.
Caller -> Thanks, Marcus.
Nurse -> Anything else for Ally today?
Caller -> No. I think that's everything. Please tell the nurse to come early if she can.
Nurse -> I'll put that in the note. Take care, Roland.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Colette.
Caller -> Hi Colette. It's Tavian Okafor. T A V I A N. Okafor, O K A F O R. I'm one of your patients. I use a catheter.
Nurse -> Hi Tavian. Yes, I know you. I've got you in the chart. Can I confirm your date of birth?
Caller -> September seventeenth. Nineteen eighty four.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one one two.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one one two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yep.
Nurse -> What can I do for you today?
Caller -> I'm running low on supplies. The catheter stuff. I wanted to catch it before I run out. Last time I waited until I was out and it was a mess.
Nurse -> Smart. Okay, let's count. How many leg bags do you have?
Caller -> Two. Two left. One is the one I'm wearing, I think. So one in the box and one on. Two total.
Nurse -> Okay. Two leg bags. And the night bags, the big ones?
Caller -> One. I have one left. I rinse them. But they get gross after a while, I want a fresh one.
Nurse -> Okay. And the catheter kits? The ones for the changes?
Caller -> None. Zero. The last one was used on the, uh, on the third. The nurse used it. I didn't realize.
Nurse -> Okay. So no kits at all. I'll make sure we get those. When is your next scheduled change?
Caller -> Um. I think it's next week. Monday? Tuesday? I wrote it on the calendar. It's in the kitchen. I'm in the bedroom.
Nurse -> No worries. I can see it in the chart. It's due next Tuesday. So we need the kit before then.
Caller -> Okay. That works.
Nurse -> Does the supply company still have your address as the apartment?
Caller -> Yes. Building C. The buzzer doesn't work, so they call me from the lot.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll make a note to have the driver call your cell.
Caller -> Please. Last time he left a box in the wrong building.
Nurse -> Is there anything else going on? With the catheter, I mean. How's the output?
Caller -> Okay, so. The urine looks a little cloudy. Like, since Sunday. And it smells stronger than usual. Strong. Kind of sharp.
Nurse -> Okay. Two days of cloudy urine with a stronger smell. Any fever, chills?
Caller -> No fever. I took it. It was ninety eight something. No chills. I feel fine. I just noticed the bag.
Nurse -> Any blood in the urine? Pink, red?
Caller -> No blood. It's yellow. Just cloudy.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. I'm going to ask the team about getting a urine sample from you. Sometimes cloudy urine with a smell is just not enough water, and sometimes it's an infection. They'll want to decide.
Caller -> I figured. I had a UTI in March. It started like this. But I didn't feel it. I never feel anything. That's the thing.
Nurse -> Right. With your injury, you can't rely on pain. That's why we watch for the signs.
Caller -> Yeah. I look at the bag. It's my only dashboard.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good way to put it.
Caller -> I'm drinking more. A lot more. Like two liters since yesterday.
Nurse -> Keep that up. Extra water through the day, spread out.
Caller -> I'm carrying a big water bottle. It has the little time marks on it. It says, drink by ten, drink by noon. It's kind of motivational. It's kind of annoying.
Nurse -> What flavor are you putting in it?
Caller -> Nothing. Plain. Okay, sometimes a lemon. A lemon slice. It feels fancy.
Nurse -> Ha. It works though.
Caller -> It does. I hate it.
Nurse -> I'll place the order for the supplies today. Leg bags, night bags, and the catheter kits. Then I'll arrange the delivery, and I'm aiming for Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'm home all day Thursday. Nobody's coming over. Just leave it at the door if I don't answer. I take a while to get to the door.
Nurse -> I'll note that. Leave at the door.
Caller -> Perfect.
Nurse -> And I'd like to send a nurse out Friday. To look at everything, check the catheter, and see what the team said about the sample.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Can they come in the afternoon? I have a physical therapy thing in the morning.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the afternoon.
Caller -> What's therapy going to think if I miss it?
Nurse -> You won't miss it. The nurse comes after.
Caller -> Right. Sorry. I'm overthinking. It's been a long week.
Nurse -> No problem. That's what the chatter is for.
Caller -> Thanks.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep the bag below the level of your bladder, and empty it when it's about half full. Wipe the spout with alcohol before and after. And rinse the leg bag with vinegar and water once a day.
Caller -> Below the bladder. Half full. Wipe the spout. Vinegar and water. Okay. I do all that. I do the vinegar on Sundays. I'll do it daily now.
Nurse -> Good. And call us if you get a fever or chills, blood in the urine, or no urine coming into the bag. Also, if you get a pounding headache and start sweating, that's an emergency. Call 911 if it's severe.
Caller -> Yeah. Yes. The autonomic thing. The pounding headache. I know that one. I had it once. It was scary.
Nurse -> You know the signs. That's good.
Caller -> Yes. I know. Fever, blood, no urine, headache. I got it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else, Tavian?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thanks for catching the count. I know it's a pain to keep track.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for. Call anytime.
Caller -> I will. Have a good one.
Nurse -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice, this is Raymond.
Caller -> Hello, hello. I'm, uh, I'm Odalys. I work with a client. She's your patient. She is in pain. A lot of pain. I need help.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm here. Take a breath. Tell me your name again, and the patient's name.
Caller -> Odalys. O D A L Y S. Reyes. And she is Mrs. Whitcombe. Lorraine Whitcombe.
Nurse -> Okay Odalys. Are you with Lorraine right now?
Caller -> Yes. I am in the room. I'm with her. She is on the bed. I am the, the home aide. The agency sends me, five days a week.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Let me get a few things quick. Do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> It's on the sheet. Hold on. It's on the paper on the refrigerator. No, I'm in the room. Um. I have my phone, I have the photo of the sheet. March twenty sixth, nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what's a number I can call you back on?
Caller -> My cell. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one zero four.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one zero four. Is that correct?
Caller -> Yes, yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Now. Tell me about the pain. Where is it?
Caller -> Her back. The lower. She holds it. She says, oh, oh. And she moans. She was fine this morning, she ate her oatmeal. Now since two o'clock, she is moaning.
Nurse -> Can she tell you a number? Zero is no pain, ten is the worst.
Caller -> I asked her. She said eight. She said it in Spanish first, ocho, and then in English. Eight.
Nurse -> An eight. Okay. Is she awake and talking to you?
Caller -> Awake. Yes. She talks. She is grabbing the rail. The bed rail. She holds it very hard. Her knuckles are white.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she on any pain medicine? Anything for breakthrough pain?
Caller -> Yes. The bottle. The morphine. It says morphine concentrate. Twenty milligrams per mL. And it says, point two five mL, every four hours if needed.
Nurse -> Okay. Morphine concentrate, twenty milligrams per mL, point two five mL, every four hours as needed. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That is what the label says. The family wrote on the sheet when she takes it. I look at the sheet.
Nurse -> When was the last dose?
Caller -> On the sheet it says twelve thirty. The daughter gave it before she left for work. Twelve thirty.
Nurse -> Okay. Twelve thirty. And did it help at all?
Caller -> A little. For maybe one hour. Then it comes back. And now it is worse. Much worse than before.
Nurse -> Okay. And it's about ten after five now. So it's been more than four hours. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. More than four. Almost five hours. I did not want to give it myself, because I did not know if I can.
Nurse -> Good question. I'll tell you what to do in a minute. First, is the daughter there?
Caller -> No. She is at work. She is a nurse at the hospital. She works until seven. I called her three times. She does not answer. It goes to voicemail.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all right. I can help from here. Has Lorraine fallen, or hit anything, today?
Caller -> No. No fall. She did not fall. She did not hit. She was in bed and the chair. Only that.
Nurse -> Okay. Any trouble breathing? Is she breathing normally?
Caller -> Normal. Not fast. Just the moaning.
Nurse -> Alright. Here's what we're going to do. Because it's been more than four hours, she's due for the next dose of the morphine. You can give it right now. I'll walk you through it.
Caller -> I can give it? Me? Because the agency told me I cannot touch the medicines.
Nurse -> This is an emergency situation, and I'm a hospice nurse telling you to do it, on the phone. I'm giving you permission. I'll stay on the line while you do it.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Tell me.
Nurse -> Find the little syringe that came with the bottle. The one with the marks.
Caller -> I have it. It is in the bag. The plastic bag with the bottle.
Nurse -> Draw up point two five of an mL. That's a quarter of an mL. It's the very small line. Tell me what you see on the syringe.
Caller -> I see lines. It says point two. Point four. Point six. There is a line between. A small line. Is that the point two five?
Nurse -> Yes. Halfway between point two and point three, or the line between the two marks. Put the tip in the bottle, pull back slowly until the top of the black part lines up with that.
Caller -> I'm doing. Slowly. Okay. It is there. At the line.
Nurse -> Check again. Is the black part exactly at the little line?
Caller -> Yes. I checked. I'm sure. I'm very careful.
Nurse -> Good. Now give it slowly into her cheek, between her gum and her cheek, a little at a time. Let her swallow in between.
Caller -> Mrs. Whitcombe. Lorraine. Open, please. A little. Okay. I'm doing. Slowly. It goes. She swallows. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. Has she taken it all?
Caller -> All. All is in. She made a face. It tastes bad, she says.
Nurse -> Yes, it does. You did well. Write the time on the sheet. What time is it?
Caller -> Five fifteen. I write it. Five fifteen. Done.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, I'm also going to page the on-call clinician right now, because this pain is an eight and the first dose didn't hold her. They may adjust the medicine.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Please. She is suffering.
Nurse -> I know. And I'm sending a nurse out to see her. Within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I will be here. I do not leave until the daughter comes.
Nurse -> Good. Now let's make her more comfortable. Can you ease her onto her side? With a pillow behind her back, and one between her knees.
Caller -> Onto her side. Okay. She does not want to move. It hurts when I move her.
Nurse -> I understand. Go slowly, and let her help. You say, one, two, three, and roll together. Support her hip and shoulder.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Mrs. Lorraine, we turn a little. One, two, three. She says ow. Ow, ow. Okay. She is on the side. The pillow is behind. And one between the knees. I put it.
Nurse -> Good. Is she more comfortable like that?
Caller -> A little. She stopped holding the rail. She holds my hand now.
Nurse -> Then hold her hand. Keep the room quiet, and keep the lights low. Talk to her softly.
Caller -> I'm doing. I sing a little. She likes the old songs. Boleros.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Sing.
Caller -> I am singing. Quiet. Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in twenty minutes to see how she's doing. Keep your phone near you.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. I keep the phone. It is in my pocket. I do not move.
Nurse -> And Odalys, watch her closely. If she gets very sleepy, hard to wake up, or her breathing slows down or gets noisy, call me right away.
Caller -> Very sleepy. Hard to wake. Breathing slow or noisy. Call right away. Okay.
Nurse -> It's the same number you called. Don't hang up on me until I say.
Caller -> I stay. I am here.
Nurse -> Is she saying anything?
Caller -> She says, the pain is a little less. She says, six. She said six. Is that good?
Nurse -> That's a start. The medicine takes time to work. Keep holding her hand. You're doing everything right.
Caller -> Thank you. I was so scared. I never had a client in so much pain.
Nurse -> You did the right thing calling. How long have you been with her?
Caller -> Seven months. She is like my abuela. She calls me mija.
Nurse -> That's a beautiful thing. She's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I am lucky to have her. She tells me stories about her husband. He was a pilot.
Nurse -> I'd love to hear those sometime.
Caller -> I will tell you. Next time.
Nurse -> Alright. I'm going to page now. Stay right there with her, and I'll call you in twenty.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you so much, Raymond.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Ines.
Caller -> Oh, hi. Hello. I, um, I don't know if I'm calling the right place. I have the card on his fridge. For Hubert Dunmore. It says Pinecrest.
Nurse -> Yes, that's us. Hubert Dunmore is one of our patients. And who am I speaking with?
Caller -> I'm Leona. Leona Fitch. I'm a friend. From church. I take him to lunch on Fridays.
Nurse -> Okay Leona. Thank you for calling. What's going on?
Caller -> Well. I came to pick him up. And he's, I don't know. He's different. He's foggy. He kept asking me where we were going. I told him lunch. And then he asked again.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he with you now?
Caller -> I'm in his kitchen. He's in his chair. He's watching the TV. He's got it on, but I don't think he's watching it.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he more confused than he usually is?
Caller -> I don't know. That's the thing. I don't know. He's always been a little forgetful, he'll say the same story twice. But this is different, I think. He didn't know me for a second. He said Leona who? And then he laughed and said of course.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. When did you last see him?
Caller -> Last Friday. We had lunch. He was sharp. He was telling a joke about a mule. He was fine. So it's been a week.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he eating?
Caller -> That's the other thing. There's a plate on the counter from yesterday. A sandwich, with maybe two bites gone. I asked him what he had today and he said coffee. Just coffee.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he drinking anything?
Caller -> Coffee. And I gave him a glass of water just now and he drank about half.
Nurse -> Good. Has he fallen, hit his head, any chest pain, any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. I would have seen. He's not out of breath. He walked to the chair on his own. He's steady. He didn't fall, as far as I know. I think.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you know his date of birth, by any chance?
Caller -> No. I don't. He's older than me. I'm seventy four. He's eighty something. I never asked a man his birthday.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll find it in the chart. What about his medicines? Do you know what he takes?
Caller -> No. I don't know any of that. There's a lot of bottles on the counter. A basket. I didn't touch them. His daughter handles that, she lives in Arizona. She calls every Sunday.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. I'd like to get a nurse out to see him today. Will you be around for a while?
Caller -> I can stay. I canceled the lunch. I told the restaurant, it's fine. I'll sit with him. I brought my knitting.
Nurse -> What are you knitting?
Caller -> A scarf. For my grandson. It's blue. It's been blue for two years. I knit a row a month.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a patient scarf.
Nurse -> That's very kind. I'm going to send a nurse out today. Probably this afternoon. I'll call you when I know the time.
Caller -> Okay. That's good. I was hoping you'd say that. I didn't know if I should call 911.
Nurse -> From what you're telling me, he doesn't need 911 right now. He's awake, he's talking, he's breathing normally. But I'm glad you called us.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'm relieved.
Nurse -> What's a good number for you, Leona?
Caller -> My cell. Six one oh, five five five, zero one one six.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one one six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. And I'm going to leave a message for the team to reach his daughter in Arizona, so she knows what's going on.
Caller -> Oh, good. I have her number but I didn't want to scare her. She worries.
Nurse -> The team will take care of it. They know how to talk to families.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, Leona, stay with him until the nurse gets there. And please don't let him drive or use the stove.
Caller -> He doesn't drive anymore. His daughter took the keys in the spring. The stove, I'll watch. I'll turn the knob off at the wall.
Caller -> He has one of those old stoves. With the dials. I'll pull the dials off and put them in my purse.
Nurse -> That works too.
Nurse -> That's smart. Is there a way to turn off the gas?
Caller -> I'll do the little valve. Behind the stove. I know where it is.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> And what about food? Should I make him something?
Nurse -> Offer small sips of water or juice, and a few bites of something soft, like applesauce or pudding, if he wants. Don't push.
Caller -> There's applesauce. I saw it in the fridge. The little cups. I'll try.
Nurse -> And if he can't be woken, if his face droops on one side, if his speech slurs, or he has trouble breathing, call 911 right away.
Caller -> Can't wake him. Face droops. Slurred. Trouble breathing. Call 911. Okay. I have it. I'll watch him.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in an hour to check in.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll be here. Do I stay on the line or hang up?
Caller -> Should I write down your name? Ines? How do you spell that?
Nurse -> I N E S. And the number is the one you called. It's on his fridge card.
Caller -> Oh, the card. Right. I'll get it. I put on my glasses.
Nurse -> You can hang up. I'll call.
Caller -> Okay. I'm sorry, I'm a little nervous. I've never done this before.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. You noticed something was off, and you called.
Caller -> He's a good man. He always brings me tomatoes.
Nurse -> It sounds like you two look after each other.
Caller -> We do. He fixed my gate last spring. Seventy nine years old, up on a ladder. I yelled at him.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet.
Caller -> I'll let you go. Thank you, Ines.
Nurse -> Thank you, Leona. Talk to you in an hour.
Caller -> Bye bye.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Joan.
Caller -> Hi. Um. I'm not sure I'm calling the right place. I need to get some paperwork. Records. For an insurance claim.
Nurse -> Okay. What kind of records are you looking for?
Caller -> Well, the life insurance company says they need something from the hospice. A letter. Or a form. About the dates of service.
Nurse -> I see. That would go through our medical records department. They're the ones who handle requests like that.
Caller -> Okay. Is that a different number?
Nurse -> It's a different line. I can give it to you. Do you have a pen?
Caller -> I do. Go ahead.
Nurse -> The records line is eight eight eight, five five five, zero one seven two. They're open Monday through Friday, nine to four.
Caller -> Eight eight eight, five five five, zero one seven two. Monday through Friday, nine to four. Got it.
Nurse -> They'll ask you to fill out a release form. If the patient has passed, they may need a copy of the paperwork that shows you're the representative of the estate.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. The executor paper. I have that. The lawyer gave me a stack.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's what they'll want. Bring it, or send a copy.
Caller -> Can I send it by email?
Nurse -> They'll tell you how when you call. Some forms need a signature on paper.
Caller -> Okay. How long does it usually take?
Nurse -> I don't know the exact time. I'd ask them. It's usually a couple of weeks.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine. The insurance company said there's no rush. Sixty days.
Nurse -> Then you have time.
Caller -> Good. Thank you. I'm sorry, I don't know what I'm doing. This is my first time doing any of this.
Nurse -> It's a lot. You're doing fine. Take it one form at a time.
Caller -> That's what everyone says. One form at a time.
Nurse -> Ha. It's true.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for your help.
Nurse -> You're welcome. I'm sorry for your loss, whoever it was.
Caller -> Thank you. It was my brother.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sunflower Pediatric Nursing, this is Beatriz.
Caller -> Hi, Beatriz. It's Ximena. Ximena Villanueva. Mateo's mom.
Nurse -> Hi, Ximena. How are you? How's Mateo?
Caller -> We're good. I think. I have a few questions, and a few updates. Is now a good time? I know it's the end of your day.
Nurse -> It's a fine time. I'm at my desk. Go ahead.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Let me get my notes. I wrote everything down because I forget when I call.
Nurse -> Smart. Take your time.
Caller -> Mateo Villanueva, he's five. M A T E O. You have him as Mateo with the one T, right?
Nurse -> Yes. M A T E O. One T. I've got him.
Caller -> Okay good. Sometimes the pharmacy puts two Ts. It drives me crazy.
Nurse -> Does the pharmacy ever get his birthday wrong too?
Caller -> Once. They had him as a girl, even. Mateo, F. I had to call twice.
Nurse -> Ugh. Those little errors add up.
Caller -> I check every label now. Every bottle. I'm the label police.
Caller -> And his sticker chart. We have a sticker chart for the whole week. Gold stars for every feed with no fussing.
Nurse -> Does it work?
Caller -> Mostly. He negotiates. Two stars for the morning feed. Three if it's a Monday.
Nurse -> Ha. A tough negotiator.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll watch for it. Can I confirm his date of birth?
Caller -> April thirteenth, two thousand twenty one.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one four nine.
Nurse -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one four nine. Is that right?
Caller -> That's it.
Nurse -> Great. So, what's going on?
Caller -> Mostly good news. I wanted to give you an update on the feeds and ask about changing the schedule. And we're running low on stuff.
Nurse -> Okay. Start with the update. How are the feeds going?
Caller -> They're going great. He's tolerating the pump. All night, and then the bolus in the morning that he, no, wait. Not bolus. The pump. We're still on the pump. The pump runs at night and a little in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Pump feeds. And is he tolerating them? Any belly pain, bloating, gagging?
Caller -> No gagging. No bloating. He sleeps right through. The pump beeps sometimes if the tubing is kinked, and I hear it from my room, and I go in. But it's usually the dog.
Nurse -> The dog?
Caller -> The dog lies on the tubing. I swear. He loves the warm formula bag. We have a dog who is a pillow thief.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a new one.
Caller -> I know. He's a golden retriever. He thinks he's helping.
Nurse -> Does Mateo mind?
Caller -> Mateo thinks it's hilarious. He says the dog is his night nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. That's sweet.
Caller -> It is. Okay. Weight. I weighed him Sunday. Thirty eight pounds. He was thirty six last month.
Nurse -> Thirty eight pounds. That's two pounds in a month. That's great.
Caller -> I couldn't believe it. I weighed him twice. On the bathroom scale, and then I did me holding him and subtracted. Same.
Nurse -> That's a good method. We'll confirm at the next visit on the clinic scale.
Caller -> Okay. He's so proud of himself. He says he's a big kid now. He tells everybody he's thirty eight.
Nurse -> Ha. He should. And his stools? Any diarrhea, constipation?
Caller -> Normal. Every day. Soft. Not watery. No vomiting. Not once this week. He did gag on a cough Tuesday. He had a little cough. But it was nothing. No vomiting.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever?
Caller -> No fever. I don't think. I took it Wednesday, when he coughed. It was normal. I don't remember the number. Ninety eight something.
Nurse -> That's fine. How's the g-tube site? The skin around it?
Caller -> I look every morning. It's clean. It's dry. No redness. No drainage. No crusty stuff. I clean it with the soap and the warm water like you showed me. It looks great. Like a little belly button.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is he complaining at all about it? Pulling on it?
Caller -> He pulls on it sometimes. He thinks it's a toy. I put a little onesie under his shirt so he can't reach. Like a belt.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> My sister told me. She's a nurse. She works with adults though.
Nurse -> Ha. She gave you good advice.
Caller -> She does. She does. Okay. Next. School. He started kindergarten. Half days. And the school nurse is great. But the feeds are the problem. The pump is, it's slow. It takes him two hours for a feed, and the school day is only four hours. So he's hooked up to the pump half of the day. He can't play. He can't do circle time.
Nurse -> Oh. I see. That's hard on him.
Caller -> It is. He's sitting there with a backpack with a pump in it. He looks like a little astronaut. The other kids are fine with it. But he wants to run. And the backpack beeps.
Caller -> The teacher made him a name tag for the backpack. It says Captain Mateo. He wears it like a medal.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. She sounds kind.
Caller -> She is. She asked me to come in and show the class how the pump works. I might do that. Do you think that's okay?
Nurse -> Ask the school nurse first, but kids usually love that.
Caller -> I'll bring the dog. No, I won't bring the dog.
Nurse -> Ha. Probably not.
Nurse -> That's a real concern. What were you hoping for?
Caller -> I was thinking. Could we do the bolus feeds? In the day? Like, a syringe, five or ten minutes, and then he's done and he can go play. And keep the pump for the night. I read about it in a parent group. Some kids do it.
Nurse -> Some do. It's something the team has to decide. It depends on how his stomach handles a faster feed. I can't change the schedule myself. But I can ask them.
Caller -> Would you? That would be so great. I don't want to do anything without asking. I just want him to be able to run.
Nurse -> Of course. I'm going to leave a message for the team to ask about moving him to daytime bolus feeds. And I'll let you know what they say.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much. I was nervous to ask. I thought you'd say no.
Nurse -> It's a good question. Not a no. It's an ask.
Caller -> An ask. Okay. I like that.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep him on the schedule you have. Don't change anything until they say.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll keep it the same.
Nurse -> What was the other thing? Supplies?
Caller -> Yes. The extension sets. The little tubes that connect to the button. We have three left. They're supposed to last a week each, but I replaced one early because it got gross. And the school wants their own, one for the nurse's office. So I need a few more.
Nurse -> Okay. Three left. I'll place an order with the supply company for more extension sets. Do you know how many you need?
Caller -> I'd say, um, a box? Do they come in a box? The box of ten?
Nurse -> I'll order a box. Ten. That'll cover you and the school for a while. I'll put the order in today.
Caller -> Perfect. Thank you. And the school one, can they deliver to the school? Or I'll pick it up?
Nurse -> It comes to your house. You can bring one to the school.
Caller -> Okay. That's easy.
Nurse -> While we're talking about the tube. How are you flushing?
Caller -> Water. Before and after. Ten mL. With the syringe. I do it with every feed. And after the medicines. He doesn't have a lot of medicines now. Just the vitamin.
Nurse -> Perfect. Ten mL of water before and after each feed and after any medicine. Keep doing that. It keeps the tube from clogging.
Caller -> I know. I got a clog once. In July. That was a nightmare. I never want that again.
Nurse -> That's why the flushes matter.
Caller -> I know. I'm religious about it now.
Nurse -> And keep cleaning the site once a day, with warm water and a mild soap. Rinse it well and pat it dry.
Caller -> Warm water, mild soap, rinse, pat dry. That's what I do. Yes. I use the baby soap.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> I do it after his bath. He loves the bath. It's, like, an hour of splashing. I get more water on the floor than in the tub.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a five year old.
Caller -> It's an ocean.
Caller -> And he sings in the tub. The same song. About a bus. Forty minutes of the bus song.
Nurse -> The wheels on the bus?
Caller -> A different bus. He made up the verses. There's a verse about a dinosaur who drives.
Nurse -> Ha. I'd like to hear that one.
Nurse -> Ximena, I also want to go over when to call. Call us if he's vomiting with feeds, if he has a fever, if you see redness or drainage at the site, or if the tube comes out. If the tube comes out, cover the site with a clean gauze and get to us right away, because the opening can start to close within hours.
Caller -> Vomiting with feeds. Fever. Redness or drainage. Tube comes out. Cover it and come in right away. I know. I have the spare button in the kit. And the phone number is on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. You're prepared.
Caller -> I'm paranoid. But I'm prepared.
Nurse -> Paranoid is good with a g-tube.
Caller -> Ha. That's what the surgeon said.
Nurse -> Smart surgeon. Okay. I'll call you back Friday. By then I should know what the team says about the bolus feeds.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. Call my cell. I'm at work but I'll see it. I'm a dental hygienist, I can step out between patients.
Nurse -> A hygienist. That's a good job for a mom who has to keep things clean.
Caller -> Ha. It helps. I'm the one in the house with the sterile technique.
Nurse -> I bet. How's your husband handling the night feeds?
Caller -> He's great. He does the Tuesday and Thursday nights. He sets up the pump, he reads the story, he tucks in the dog. He says he's the best night nurse.
Nurse -> A second night nurse. Mateo's lucky.
Caller -> He thinks so. We all take turns.
Nurse -> That's a lot of help. How are you holding up?
Caller -> Tired. But good. Not as tired as when we first started. I used to set an alarm every two hours. Now I sleep through. Unless the dog sits on the tubing.
Nurse -> Ha. The dog.
Caller -> I'm going to buy him a bed. A separate bed. With heat.
Nurse -> That might work.
Caller -> It might. If not I'm going to buy a bigger dog.
Nurse -> What's the dog's name?
Caller -> Biscuit. Biscuit, get off the couch. Sorry. He's looking at me.
Nurse -> Ha. He knows you're talking about him.
Caller -> He always knows.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Anything else on your list?
Caller -> No. That's all. I checked. I crossed it all off. I feel so organized.
Nurse -> Do you keep the notes in a notebook?
Caller -> On my phone. Plus a paper one on the fridge, in case my phone dies.
Nurse -> You are organized. You're doing a great job with him.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed to hear that. Some days I feel like I'm just guessing.
Nurse -> Everyone is guessing a little. You're doing it well.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you again, Beatriz.
Nurse -> Anytime. Talk to you Friday.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Palliative Care after hours line, this is Imani.
Caller -> Hi. Hi. I'm sorry to call so late. I didn't know who else. It's Dolores. Dolores Teague. T E A G U E. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Hi Dolores. I'm glad you called. It's okay that it's late. We're here all night. What's going on?
Caller -> I can't sleep. I'm just. I'm sitting on the edge of the bed. I'm crying. I don't, I don't know how to do this anymore.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. I'm right here with you. Take your time.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I don't want to wake my husband. He's so tired. He's been up with me every night.
Nurse -> It's okay. You're not bothering anyone. Is he in the house with you?
Caller -> He's upstairs. He's asleep. We sleep in separate rooms now. Because of the, because I'm up and down. I'm on the first floor. We have the hospital bed in the den.
Nurse -> Okay. So you're alone down there right now.
Caller -> Yes. Alone. With the TV off. It's very quiet.
Nurse -> Okay. Dolores, can I get your date of birth so I can pull up your chart?
Caller -> February eighth. Nineteen seventy four. I'm fifty two. I know. Young for this.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what number are you calling from, in case we get disconnected?
Caller -> It's the house line. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one three two.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one three two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Now tell me what's been going on tonight.
Caller -> I had a bad day. The pain is bad. And I got the call from the oncologist. The scan. It's, it's grown. They said there's nothing else to try. So that's it. That's the end of the line.
Nurse -> Oh, Dolores. I'm so sorry. That's a lot to take in. When did you hear that?
Caller -> This afternoon. Four o'clock. I was in the kitchen. I told my husband. We cried. And then we ate dinner like nothing happened. And then I came down here.
Nurse -> That's a very hard day. Tell me about the pain tonight. How bad is it?
Caller -> It's, I'd say a six. In my belly and my back. It goes around. It's okay with the medicine but it's never gone. A six right now.
Nurse -> A six. What have you taken for it?
Caller -> The oxycodone. Ten milligrams. I took one at nine. That's it. I know the rules. Every four hours, as needed. I only took the one.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Thank you for telling me. And how are you feeling in yourself? Besides the pain.
Caller -> I feel hopeless. Just, completely hopeless. I'm crying all the time. I don't want to talk to anyone. I don't want to eat.
Nurse -> That sounds incredibly heavy. I want to ask you something, and I want you to be honest with me. Is that okay?
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or ending your life?
Caller -> Um. Yes. Sort of. I keep, I keep thinking about the pills. About taking all of them. So it stops. So I don't have to, so it doesn't get worse. I keep thinking about it.
Nurse -> Thank you for telling me. That took courage. I'm really glad you told me. Dolores, I want to ask a few more questions so I understand. Have you taken any extra pills tonight?
Caller -> No. No. I haven't. Just the one at nine. I swear. I just think about it. I haven't done anything.
Nurse -> I believe you. Do you have a plan? Have you decided when or how?
Caller -> Not, not tonight. I don't think. I just, they're right here. In the drawer next to my bed. I look at the drawer. I keep looking at the drawer.
Nurse -> Okay. So the pill bottles are in the drawer right next to you.
Caller -> Yes. All of them. The oxycodone. The other ones. I've got maybe, I don't know, five or six bottles.
Nurse -> Okay. And do you intend to take them tonight? Are you planning to act on these thoughts?
Caller -> I don't think so. I don't want to. Part of me doesn't want to. I think about my husband. And my daughter. She's in college. I don't want her to find, I don't want to hurt them.
Nurse -> That's the part of you I want to hear from. The part that thinks about your husband and your daughter. Can you tell me more about her?
Caller -> Marnie. She's a sophomore. She's coming home on Friday. For the weekend. She doesn't know about the scan.
Nurse -> She's coming Friday. That's something to hold on to.
Caller -> Yeah. Friday.
Nurse -> Dolores, I want to make sure you're safe tonight. And I want to make a plan with you. Can we do that together?
Caller -> Yeah. Okay.
Nurse -> First thing. I want you to wake up your husband. Right now. Can you do that? Go upstairs, or call him. And I want you to hand him the pill bottles, all of them, so he can keep them somewhere you can't reach, and give you your doses.
Caller -> Oh. I don't want to wake him. He's so tired. He has work.
Nurse -> I know. I understand. But this is important, and he'd want to know. He would be so upset if he found out tomorrow that you went through this alone.
Caller -> He would. He would. He'd cry. He'd be so mad that I didn't wake him.
Nurse -> He wants to help you. Let him.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll call him. Can I use the intercom? We have a baby monitor. From when Marnie was little. We use it now. For me.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Use the intercom. I'll stay on the phone with you.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Hold on. I'm pressing the button. Gary? Gary. It's me. I need you. Can you come down? Please. Yes. I'm okay. I just need you.
Nurse -> Good job. I'm right here.
Caller -> He's coming. I hear him on the stairs. He's, he's fast. He's running.
Nurse -> That's love, Dolores.
Caller -> Yeah. Okay. He's here. He's in the doorway. He looks scared.
Nurse -> Can you tell him what's going on? Or I can talk to him if you want.
Caller -> I'll tell him. Gary, I've been, I was thinking about the pills. I didn't take any. I just thought about it. I called the nurse. Come sit.
Caller -> He's sitting. He's holding my hand. He's crying. I'm crying. Okay. He says he'll take the pills.
Nurse -> Perfect. Ask him to take the whole drawer. All the bottles. Put them somewhere safe, upstairs, in a locked cabinet or in his car, whatever he has. And he'll bring you your doses on schedule.
Caller -> He says he has a lockbox. For his gun. No. Not the gun. Wait. He has a lockbox, for his papers. He says he'll put them in there.
Nurse -> Okay. And I'm glad you mentioned a gun. Is there a firearm in the house?
Caller -> Yes. In the garage. In a safe. He keeps it locked. I don't know the code. I don't. I've never known it.
Nurse -> Good. Gary, if you're listening, please keep that locked, and don't tell her the code.
Caller -> He says he won't. He says okay. He says he understands.
Nurse -> Thank you, Gary. Dolores, how are you feeling now? With him there?
Caller -> A little better. A little. He took the bottles. He's carrying them. He's going up. He said he'd be right back.
Nurse -> Okay. While he does that, I want to tell you a few things. If these thoughts get stronger, or if you ever feel you might act on them, I want you to call 911 right away. Or tell Gary to.
Caller -> Call 911. Okay.
Nurse -> And there's another number that's available any time, day or night. Nine eight eight. You can call or text. It's the suicide and crisis lifeline. They talk to people who feel the way you feel tonight.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. I've heard of that. I never thought I'd need it.
Nurse -> Lots of people never think they will. It's a good number to have.
Caller -> I'll write it. Gary will write it. He's back. He's got a pen.
Nurse -> Good. I'm also going to page the on-call clinician right now. They'll want to know about tonight, and they can talk about your medicines and how you're feeling.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I didn't think anyone would. I thought I'd be a bother.
Nurse -> You're not a bother. This is what we're here for. Also, I'm going to ask our social worker to reach out to you. She helps with exactly this, with the feelings and the fear.
Caller -> A social worker. Okay. I think I'd like that. I don't really have anybody to talk to. Besides Gary. And I don't want to put all of it on him.
Nurse -> She'll be someone just for you. I'll put the request in tonight so she sees it first thing.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I want to send a nurse out to see you tomorrow morning. To check on you, check on the pain, and talk.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. Gary's staying home. He's going to call in.
Nurse -> Good. I'm glad. Dolores, I'm going to call you back in thirty minutes to check in on you. Is this phone okay?
Caller -> Yes. The house phone. Thirty minutes. I'll be here. Gary says he's not going anywhere. He's getting a blanket.
Caller -> He's back. He has the blanket. The yellow one, from the couch. He put it around me.
Nurse -> That sounds nice. Is it warm in there?
Caller -> It's okay. The heat's on. He's making tea. He went to the kitchen. I can hear the kettle.
Nurse -> Tea sounds good. I'll stay on the line while he makes it.
Caller -> The kettle is so loud. It's the old one. He won't replace it. It whistles like a train.
Nurse -> Ha. A train at three in the morning.
Caller -> It's the sound of home. I don't mind.
Caller -> He's coming with two cups. He put honey in mine. I don't like honey, but I'll drink it.
Nurse -> Take a few sips if you can.
Caller -> Okay. It's hot. It's good. He sat down on the bed. He's close.
Nurse -> What's he saying?
Caller -> He's not saying anything. He's just here. He's patting my hand.
Nurse -> Sometimes that's all there is to say.
Caller -> I know. He's not a talker. Thirty years. I'd have to say he talks to the dog more than me.
Nurse -> Ha. Is there a dog?
Caller -> Yes. Pickles. He's asleep on the rug. He sleeps through everything.
Nurse -> A good dog for a hard night.
Caller -> He snores. I can hear him from here. It's a funny little whistle. Like the kettle.
Nurse -> Ha. The two of them could start a band.
Caller -> Gary would be the drummer. He taps on everything.
Nurse -> Does Marnie play anything?
Caller -> The cello. She was in the orchestra. I never miss a concert. Or I didn't.
Nurse -> Good. Stay with him. Sit together. You don't have to do anything right now except get through the next half hour. Can you do that?
Caller -> I can do that.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anything else you want to tell me before we hang up?
Caller -> I just, I wanted to say thank you. For answering. At three in the morning.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. It was the right thing. You're not alone, okay? Gary's there, and we're here.
Caller -> Okay. I know. I feel it a little. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Dolores.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Frances.
Caller -> Hello. This is Vernon Fairbairn. I'm calling about my wife, Edna Fairbairn. I have a question about her pills.
Nurse -> Hi Mr. Fairbairn. I can help. What's your wife's date of birth?
Caller -> November twenty second, nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And a number I can reach you at?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one eight six.
Nurse -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one eight six. Is that right?
Caller -> That's right. That's the kitchen phone.
Nurse -> Is that a cordless one? In case we need you to move around the house.
Caller -> It's a cord. A long cord. Twenty feet. My son in law put it in. I can reach the stove.
Nurse -> Ha. That's convenient.
Nurse -> Okay. What's your question?
Caller -> It's the pain pills. Her knee. She has two. I get them mixed up. One is, it says take three times a day. The other says take as needed. And I don't know what that means. As needed.
Nurse -> That's a good question. Let's go through them. What are they called?
Caller -> One's Tylenol. Five hundred milligrams. Three times a day. The other is, hold on, I have my glasses. It's tramadol. Fifty milligrams. Every six hours as needed.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol five hundred, three times a day. Tramadol fifty, every six hours as needed. Is that what's on the bottles?
Caller -> Yes. Those are the labels.
Nurse -> Good. So here's the difference. The Tylenol is a scheduled one. That's the three times a day. You give it every day at the same times, whether she hurts or not. Like breakfast, lunch, and supper.
Caller -> No matter what? Even if she says she's fine?
Nurse -> Even if she says she's fine. It works best when it's steady in her system.
Caller -> Okay. And the tramadol?
Nurse -> That one is as needed. That means you only give it if she's hurting, and the Tylenol isn't enough. Not on a schedule. And not sooner than six hours after the last one.
Caller -> So I don't give it with the Tylenol. Or do I give it with the Tylenol?
Nurse -> You can give it at the same time as a Tylenol, if she needs it. They don't cancel each other out. Think of the Tylenol as the floor, and the tramadol as the extra.
Caller -> The floor and the extra. Okay. I like that. That I can remember.
Caller -> I used to be a carpenter. Floor and extra. I can picture it. A floor, and then a shelf on top.
Nurse -> A shelf. Even better.
Caller -> Forty years of floors and shelves.
Nurse -> How is she doing right now? What's her pain?
Caller -> She says it's a five. Her left knee. She's sitting with it propped up. She had her lunch, and the Tylenol with lunch. At noon.
Nurse -> When was her last tramadol?
Caller -> Yesterday evening. About seven. I gave her one for bedtime. She didn't need one this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's been more than six hours. Is she sleepy, or confused, or dizzy today?
Caller -> No. She's sharp. She did the crossword. She's mad at me for giving her the wrong word for seven across.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Then I'd say, if her pain is staying above a four, and it's been at least six hours, it's okay to give her a tramadol now. And keep giving the Tylenol at breakfast, lunch, and supper no matter what.
Caller -> Above a four. Six hours since the last one. Tylenol every meal. Okay. And if she's a three, I don't give it.
Nurse -> Right. If it's a three or less, she can probably go without.
Caller -> I wrote that down. Four. Six hours. Meals. I have it on the pad.
Caller -> The pad is by the phone. The one from the pharmacy with the little green cross on it. I use it for everything.
Nurse -> Great. Keep it near the pill box.
Caller -> It's right next to it. I'm very careful about the pill box. I fill it every Sunday.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm going to leave a message for the team to make a little chart for your fridge. Times for the Tylenol, and a box for the as needed one. So you don't have to remember.
Caller -> A chart. Oh, that would be wonderful. I'd put it right on the front. With the magnet.
Nurse -> Great. And call us if she gets very sleepy or confused, or if the pain stays above a seven even after the tramadol.
Caller -> Very sleepy. Confused. Above a seven. Okay. I'll watch. She hasn't been above a six, I don't think.
Nurse -> That's good. I'll call you tomorrow to see how it's going with the new routine.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's fine. I'm home. I'm always home. I don't go anywhere.
Nurse -> Ha. That's easy then.
Caller -> I do the crossword with her. We do it in pen. She finishes it by ten.
Nurse -> In pen? That's brave.
Caller -> She never makes mistakes. I make all of them.
Nurse -> Ha. Seven across?
Caller -> Five letters. Starts with a T. I said tempo. She said tangy. It was tangy.
Nurse -> Ha. Edna wins.
Caller -> She always wins.
Nurse -> Anything else, Mr. Fairbairn?
Caller -> No. That's what I wanted. Thank you. I felt silly asking.
Nurse -> It wasn't silly. It's a very common question.
Caller -> My son says I should have a smart phone and look it up. I said I'd rather call a person.
Nurse -> A person is better. We're happy to help.
Caller -> That's what I told him.
Caller -> Thank you, Frances.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.
