transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gloria.
Caller -> Hi, Gloria. This is Tamika Osei. I'm the med tech at Maplewood Assisted Living. I'm calling about Mr. Alfred Brisbane. He's in room twelve.
Nurse -> Hi Tamika. Good to hear from you. Is everything okay with Mr. Brisbane?
Caller -> Everything's fine. I'm just doing my weekly update. The director asked me to call on the ones who've been on service a month.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Can I confirm his date of birth?
Caller -> I have it right here on the face sheet. June thirtieth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> The med cart phone. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one three three.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one three three. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes, that's it. It rings at the nurses' station if I'm not there.
Nurse -> Good to know. Who's on with you today?
Caller -> Just me and one aide. The other med tech called out.
Nurse -> Short staffed. Sorry.
Caller -> It happens. We manage.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead with your update.
Caller -> So. I'm looking at my notes. Okay. He's had a good week. His appetite is good. He's eating about seventy five percent of every meal. He had the pot roast on Sunday and asked for seconds.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is he gaining or losing weight?
Caller -> We weigh him on Mondays. He's a hundred and fifty one. Same as last week. Same as the week before. He's very stable.
Nurse -> Good. How's his breathing?
Caller -> Fine. No shortness of breath. No chest pain. He walks to the dining room with his walker, and he's not winded. I asked him if he's okay and he told me to mind my own business.
Nurse -> Ha. He sounds like himself.
Caller -> Oh, very much. He's feisty.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. And his blood pressure?
Caller -> I took it this morning. One twenty eight over seventy four. That's his normal.
Nurse -> Perfect. Any new swelling, pain, skin problems?
Caller -> Yes, the swelling. His ankles. Both of them. They're a little puffy. Mild. I noticed it on Friday. The aide who does his shower noticed it too. Not red. Not hot. Just puffy, like when you press and it leaves a little dent.
Nurse -> Okay. Mild swelling in both ankles since Friday. Is it above the ankle, up the calf?
Caller -> No. Just the ankles. And the tops of his feet. Not the legs. His socks leave a line.
Nurse -> Okay. Is one worse than the other?
Caller -> About the same. I'd say the right a tiny bit more. But that could be me.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Let me ask. Is he getting his regular medicines on time?
Caller -> Yes. Let me read you the MAR so you can see. At eight o'clock, he gets his furosemide, twenty milligrams. His metoprolol, twenty five. And his apixaban, five. All given. Initialed. Nothing missed this week. The evening ones are given at eight too.
Nurse -> Thank you for reading that. Nothing's been missed. That's good to know.
Caller -> I'm very careful about the MAR. Our director audits us.
Nurse -> That's good practice.
Caller -> She audits us on Fridays. With a clipboard. She wears the reading glasses on a chain. Everyone straightens up.
Nurse -> Ha. I know the type.
Nurse -> I'm sure. Okay. I'd like to send a nurse out Thursday to look at his legs and listen to his lungs.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'll write it on the board. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Good. I'll put it on the whiteboard in the med room. I'll let the day shift know.
Nurse -> Great. I'm also going to leave a message for the team about the swelling, to see if they want to change anything.
Caller -> Okay. That would be good. I'm not sure if it's the salt. Our cook put a lot of ham in the bean soup.
Nurse -> Ha. That could do it. In the meantime, can you raise his legs on pillows or a footstool when he sits? And at night, if he'll let you.
Caller -> He has a recliner. I'll put the footrest up. At night I can put a pillow under his legs. He hates pillows but I'll bribe him with a cookie.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Caller -> Chocolate chip. He loves them.
Nurse -> And please call us if the swelling goes up past the ankles, if he gets short of breath, if he gains weight quickly, or any chest pain.
Caller -> Past the ankles. Short of breath. Weight gain. Chest pain. Okay. I'll write that on his board. I'll tell the night shift.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is the weekend nurse going to be able to weigh him again before Thursday?
Caller -> We do it Mondays. I'll do it Wednesday too. Extra.
Nurse -> Thank you. That would help.
Caller -> No problem. Anything else you need from me?
Nurse -> No. That's all. How are things at Maplewood?
Caller -> Busy. We got a new resident. A retired band director. He conducts at dinner. With a breadstick.
Nurse -> Ha. That's wonderful.
Caller -> The whole dining room hums along. It's the best part of my day.
Nurse -> What does he conduct?
Caller -> Anything. The radio. The vacuum cleaner. Sunday it was the dishwasher.
Caller -> He gives the dishwasher a downbeat and everyone cheers. It's a whole thing.
Nurse -> Ha. A tough crowd.
Nurse -> It sounds like it.
Caller -> It is. Okay, I have to go. The lunch cart is here.
Nurse -> Go. Thank you, Tamika.
Caller -> Thanks, Gloria. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Hospice, this is Patrick.
Caller -> Hello. Yes. Hello. This is Ngozi Adeyemi. N G O Z I. It's a Nigerian name. I'm calling for my father. Chinedu Adeyemi. C H I N E D U.
Nurse -> Hi, Ngo Zee. Okay. And your father is Chinedu. Let me find him.
Caller -> Ngozi. It's N G O Z I. It sounds like Ngo-zee. Close enough.
Nurse -> Okay. Ngo Zee. Got it. Let me pull up Chinedu Adeyemi. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> September fourteenth, nineteen thirty five.
Nurse -> Thank you. And what's your number?
Caller -> Three one two, five five five, zero one eight eight.
Nurse -> Three one two, five five five, zero one eight eight. Did I get that right?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> And is your father's number the same, or just yours?
Caller -> Just mine. He doesn't have a phone anymore. He lost his hearing aids in the spring, so phones don't help.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll use yours.
Nurse -> Okay Ngo Zee. What's going on with your father?
Caller -> He's coughing. When he drinks. He chokes. It started on Wednesday. It's gotten worse. Today it's every time. Every time he drinks anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Three days, getting worse. Does it happen with water? Tea? Everything?
Caller -> Thin things. Water. Tea. Juice. Not the oatmeal. Not the pudding. The thin things.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a helpful detail. What happens when he coughs? Does he turn red? Blue?
Caller -> He gets red. His eyes water. He coughs, coughs, coughs. Then he clears. Then he's okay. But it scares me.
Nurse -> I understand. That's scary to watch. Does his voice sound different after he drinks?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. It sounds wet. Gurgly. Like he has water in his throat. And he clears his throat a lot.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he having any fever?
Caller -> I took it before I called. Ninety nine point four. That's a little warm for him. He's usually ninety seven something.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety nine point four. Any chills? Shaking?
Caller -> No chills. No shaking. He's wrapped up in his blanket, but he's always cold.
Nurse -> What about breathing? When he's sitting quietly, resting. Is he breathing normally?
Caller -> Yes. Normal. Not fast. No noise. He sleeps fine. It's only when he drinks.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is he eating?
Caller -> Yes. The soft stuff. Eggs. Oatmeal. Mashed potatoes. Pudding. Yogurt. He eats it fine. No cough with those.
Nurse -> That's good. That's an important detail. Ngo Zee, what drinks is he getting?
Caller -> Mostly water and tea. With a cup. He holds the cup himself. He insists. He's very stubborn. A proud man.
Nurse -> Is he able to hear you well?
Caller -> If I'm close. Face to face. I write things on the whiteboard sometimes.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. We can make sure the nurse knows.
Nurse -> Okay. How is he sitting when he drinks?
Caller -> In his chair. Leaning back a little. The recliner. He likes it reclined.
Nurse -> Okay. Understood. I'd like to send a nurse out tomorrow to see him and listen to his chest.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Yes. That's good. What time?
Nurse -> I'll have the scheduler call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I'm here all day. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Is there someone who can help you if you need to step out? A relative, a neighbor?
Caller -> My brother lives forty minutes away. He comes on Saturdays. And my husband is here in the evenings. He cooks.
Nurse -> That's good. You're not alone in this.
Caller -> No. We have a lot of people. But the days are mine. I took a leave from work. I teach fourth grade.
Nurse -> That's a big thing to set aside.
Caller -> It is. But I couldn't leave him. He raised me alone after my mother passed. It's my turn.
Nurse -> Great. I'm also going to leave a message for the team, to ask about a swallow evaluation for your father. That's where a specialist checks how he swallows and tells us what's safest.
Caller -> A swallow evaluation. Oh. Yes. I heard about that from my neighbor. Her mother had one. They gave her a different cup. Is that something that will happen?
Nurse -> It might. I can't promise. The team will decide. But I'll ask.
Caller -> Please. I would like that. I don't want him to choke.
Nurse -> I know. In the meantime, there are a few things that will help. When he eats or drinks, sit him all the way up. As upright as you can get him. Not reclined. And keep him upright for thirty minutes after.
Caller -> All the way up. Thirty minutes after. Okay. But he doesn't like to sit up. He says it hurts his back.
Nurse -> Can you prop him with pillows? Behind his back, so he's straight, but supported?
Caller -> Yes. I have two big pillows. I can do that.
Nurse -> Good. And give him small sips, with a spoon if you can, instead of the cup. Let him swallow before the next one. If he starts coughing, stop and let him clear it.
Caller -> A spoon. Small sips. Stop if he coughs. Okay. He's going to complain. He says spoons are for babies.
Nurse -> I know. Maybe a teaspoon at first, and tell him it's temporary, just until the nurse sees him.
Caller -> Temporary. That might work.
Nurse -> And until the team decides, offer soft foods and thicker drinks, like a smoothie or a nectar style drink, instead of thin things like water and tea.
Caller -> A smoothie. Okay. He likes bananas. I can do a banana one. With yogurt. A thick one.
Nurse -> Perfect. That counts.
Caller -> And tea? He loves his tea. He's going to be upset.
Nurse -> Maybe a spoonful at a time, sitting upright. Not a big cup.
Caller -> A spoonful. He'll hate it. But okay.
Nurse -> And Ngo Zee, call us if he gets a fever, if his breathing gets fast or noisy, or if the cough doesn't stop. And call 911 if he can't breathe.
Caller -> Fever. Fast or noisy breathing. Cough that doesn't stop. 911 if he can't breathe. Okay. I have it. I wrote it on the back of an envelope.
Nurse -> Good. Do you know what to do if he chokes on something and can't cough or talk?
Caller -> I took a class, years ago. For my babies. The Heimlich. I hope I remember.
Nurse -> The 911 operator will walk you through it. Call right away.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> I know that's a lot to take in.
Caller -> It is. But I feel better having a plan.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Do you have our after hours number handy?
Caller -> It's on the refrigerator. On the magnet from the hospice. I looked at it ten times today.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's what it's there for.
Nurse -> That's what I want. A plan.
Caller -> My father is a retired engineer. He believes in plans. I'll show him the list.
Nurse -> Ha. He'll approve.
Caller -> He'll correct the spelling.
Caller -> He built bridges, you know. Thirty years in Lagos and then Chicago. The man has opinions about every overpass.
Nurse -> Ha. A bridge builder. That's a good career.
Caller -> He drives me crazy on the highway. Every bridge is a lecture.
Nurse -> I bet he's got stories.
Nurse -> Ha. Is he awake? Can I say hello?
Caller -> He's napping. I don't want to wake him.
Nurse -> No, let him rest.
Caller -> I'll tell him you called. He'll want to know who Patrick is.
Nurse -> Tell him I'm the one who asked for the smoothie.
Caller -> Ha. He'll like that.
Caller -> He still sketches. On napkins. He draws little beams and arrows. I have a drawer of napkins.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Keep them.
Caller -> I will. I'm going to frame one.
Nurse -> Anything else, Ngo Zee?
Caller -> No. That's everything. Thank you for listening. And thank you for saying my name. Almost. Most people can't.
Nurse -> I'm trying my best.
Caller -> You're doing fine. Thank you, Patrick.
Nurse -> Take care. We'll see you tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Ruben.
Caller -> Oh, thank God. This is Odessa Hargis. It's my husband. Leroy. He can't breathe. Please. He can't breathe.
Nurse -> Odessa, I'm here. Is Leroy awake and talking to you?
Caller -> He's awake. He's in his chair. He can't talk. He can't finish a sentence. He says a word and he has to stop.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has he been like this?
Caller -> Since this morning. It's been getting worse. He was okay at breakfast. And now it's bad. It's very bad.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he on his oxygen?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. The machine. It's on two. He's had it on all day. It's the tube in his nose.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a little finger clip, the oxygen meter?
Caller -> I do. I put it on. It says eighty four. It was eighty eight an hour ago. It keeps going down.
Nurse -> Okay. Odessa, look at his lips for me. What color are they?
Caller -> They're, they look blue. A little blue. Purple. And his fingers. I don't like it.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he use his rescue medicine?
Caller -> The albuterol. The nebulizer. I did it at three o'clock. It didn't help. Not at all.
Nurse -> Okay. Any chest pain? Is he holding his chest?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. He says it's just air. He can't get air.
Nurse -> Okay. I need you to call 911 right now. Odessa, this is an emergency. Hang up with me and dial 911. Tell them your husband has COPD and can't breathe.
Caller -> Should I? Yes. Okay. Should I hang up on you?
Nurse -> No, no. Put me on speaker, or call 911 from another phone. Do you have a cell?
Caller -> I have my cell. It's in my pocket. Okay. Okay. Let me. I'll put you on the house phone, on the speaker.
Nurse -> Good. Do it now. I'm staying on the line.
Caller -> I'm dialing. Nine one one. It's ringing. It's ringing.
Nurse -> I'm here, Odessa. Tell them the address.
Caller -> Yes. Hello? Hello. Yes. My husband can't breathe. Four oh two Maple Court. Yes. Yes. He has COPD. He's on oxygen. They're sending someone.
Nurse -> Good job. How far away are they?
Caller -> They said four minutes. Four minutes. They said to unlock the door.
Nurse -> Is the door unlocked? And the porch light on?
Caller -> The light's on. It's daytime but I turned it on anyway. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Good thinking.
Nurse -> Yes. Go unlock the front door. Right now. Then come right back to him.
Caller -> I'm going. I'm going. The door's open. I'm back. He's okay. He's still in the chair.
Nurse -> Good. Now, keep him sitting up straight. Keep the oxygen on. Do not lay him down.
Caller -> Sitting up. Oxygen on. Okay.
Nurse -> Can you get a pillow and put it on the table in front of him? Have him lean forward, with his arms on the pillow. That helps him breathe.
Caller -> A pillow. On the table. Leroy. Lean forward. Honey, lean. Here. Lean on this. Okay. He's leaning.
Nurse -> Good. Tell him to breathe slowly. In through the nose, out through the lips, like he's blowing out a candle.
Caller -> Honey, slow. Like a candle. In. Out. In. Out.
Nurse -> Is it helping at all?
Caller -> He's gripping the table. He's holding on very tight.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let him hold on. Keep your hand on his back.
Caller -> I'm rubbing his back. Slow circles.
Caller -> A little. I think. He's less panicky. His shoulders went down.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing that. Odessa, while we wait, can you gather his medicine list and his oxygen settings? The paramedics will want them.
Caller -> The list is on the fridge. I'll get it. Hold on. I'm taking it. I have it.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to let the on-call team know, and tell the hospital he's on the way.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. Please.
Nurse -> What's his date of birth, Odessa? I'll give it to the hospital.
Caller -> December second, nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your cell number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one seven seven.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one seven seven. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's it. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I've got it. Is Leroy still awake?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. His eyes are open. He's looking at me.
Nurse -> Good. Keep talking to him. Tell him help is coming.
Caller -> Leroy, help is coming. They're almost here. You're doing so good. Hold on.
Nurse -> What's his color now?
Caller -> Still blue. Maybe a little less. I can't tell. It's the light.
Nurse -> That's okay. They'll be there soon.
Caller -> I hear the siren. I hear it. It's close.
Nurse -> Good. Go to the door. Let them in. Leave the phone on the table.
Caller -> I'm going. Here they are. They're coming up the walk. Okay.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll stay on until they're in the room.
Caller -> In here! He's in here! In the chair! He's in the living room. They're here.
Nurse -> Odessa, you did everything right. I'll let the hospital know. They'll take good care of him.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Ruben. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Go with him. Call us when you can.
Caller -> I will. Bye. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverside Home Health, this is Lucille.
Caller -> Hi. I hope I'm not interrupting your Sunday. It's Marcel Pelletier. I'm calling about my dad. Gustavo Pelletier. His oxygen machine is acting up.
Nurse -> Hi Marcel. You're not interrupting. That's what the line is for. What's going on with the machine?
Caller -> It's beeping. A high beep. Every few minutes. And it shuts off. Then it turns back on. Then it beeps again. It started about an hour ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a light on it? A red light, or a code?
Caller -> There's a red light. It says, hold on. It says low flow. And then a little wrench symbol.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it plugged in, firmly? The outlet?
Caller -> I checked. Twice. I unplugged and plugged it. I moved it to a different outlet. Same thing.
Nurse -> Okay. And you've called the oxygen company?
Caller -> I called their after hours number. Twice. I left messages. Nobody called back. It's been an hour and a half.
Nurse -> Okay. That's frustrating. How's your dad doing right now?
Caller -> He's okay. He's breathing okay. He's watching the football game. He's cranky about the beeping but he's fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a finger oxygen meter?
Caller -> Yes. We have one. Hold on. I'll put it on. Dad, give me your finger. It says ninety three. Ninety three.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Ninety three is okay for him. Is that his usual?
Caller -> I think so. It's usually ninety two to ninety four.
Nurse -> Perfect. Do you have the backup tanks?
Caller -> The little portable ones. The green tanks. We have two. One is a quarter full, I think, and one's full.
Nurse -> Okay. Two tanks. Marcel, what's your dad's date of birth, so I can pull him up?
Caller -> April seventeenth, nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five zero.
Nurse -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five zero. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to call the oxygen company myself, on the priority line, and ask for an emergency visit and a replacement concentrator. And I'll arrange the delivery for tonight.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Would they come tonight? Really?
Nurse -> They have an on call tech for equipment failures. I'll push it. I'm aiming for tonight.
Caller -> Thank you. That would be a relief. I was about to drive down and pick something up myself.
Nurse -> No, don't do that. Let me call. In the meantime, I want you to switch your dad to a tank. Set it at two liters, the same as the machine. Is that how he's set?
Caller -> Two liters. Yes. It's set to two. I can switch him. How do I do it?
Nurse -> Take the tube off the concentrator, connect it to the tank. Open the valve on top. Set the dial to two. You should hear a hiss and see the gauge.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. The valve. It's like a little silver knob?
Nurse -> Yes. Turn it a quarter turn to open. Look at the gauge. Is it in the green?
Caller -> The full one is in the green. The other one is in the yellow.
Nurse -> Use the full one first. Only one at a time. And check that the tubing isn't kinked or pinched. Follow it down with your hand.
Caller -> Okay. I'm doing it. Dad, I'm switching you. It's okay. Okay. The tank's on. Two liters. The tubing's straight. I followed it.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is he comfortable?
Caller -> He says he's fine. He says the football game is the only thing bothering him. The refs.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. How long does a full tank last at two liters?
Caller -> The tag says about four hours. I don't know if it's four. I'll watch the gauge.
Nurse -> Good. Keep an eye on it. Also, Marcel, keep the oxygen away from any flames. No candles, no stove, and no one smoking nearby.
Caller -> No flames. No stove. He doesn't smoke. My wife burns a candle in the kitchen. I'll blow it out. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Thank you. Better to be safe.
Caller -> Yes, ma'am. Of course.
Nurse -> And call us right away, or 911, if he gets short of breath, if his lips turn blue, or if he gets confused or very sleepy.
Caller -> Short of breath. Blue lips. Confused or sleepy. Call. Okay. I'll watch him.
Nurse -> Good. I'll call the oxygen company now. And then I'll call you back in thirty minutes with an update.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. I'll be right here. I'm on the couch next to him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Thank you for staying calm.
Caller -> I'm not calm. I'm just quiet.
Nurse -> Ha. That works.
Caller -> My dad's been on oxygen for two years. This never happened before.
Nurse -> It does happen. These machines are good, but they're machines.
Caller -> I know. He's called it Betsy since the day they delivered it.
Nurse -> Betsy the concentrator.
Caller -> He's offended. He says she's never let him down.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll get Betsy fixed.
Caller -> Please. He'll sulk.
Nurse -> Does Betsy have a warranty or a service sticker on the side?
Caller -> There's a sticker. It says serviced in March. And a phone number.
Nurse -> Good. The company will have it on file.
Caller -> Okay. Should I read the serial number?
Nurse -> They'll have that too. Don't worry about it.
Nurse -> Anything else, Marcel?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Maple Lane Home Care, this is Hortense.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Hortense. It's Brittany Szymanski. I'm Bernadette's granddaughter. Bernadette Szymanski. We live together. I need to ask about her pills.
Nurse -> Hi Brittany. Sure. What's the question?
Caller -> Okay. So. I give her the morning pills. I put them in her little cup. I gave them to her at eight. Including the water pill.
Caller -> No you didn't, Brittany. I didn't get the water pill.
Nurse -> Is that Bernadette in the background?
Caller -> Yes, that's Grandma. She's right next to me. She's saying she didn't get it.
Caller -> I got the pink one. I didn't get the water one. It's the white one.
Nurse -> Hi Bernadette. I can hear you. Let's figure this out.
Caller -> She's wrong. She took it. I watched her. I handed her the cup, she swallowed all of them with the juice.
Caller -> I took the pink one and a yellow one. There was no white one.
Nurse -> Okay. Brittany, let me ask. Which pills are in the cup, usually? What does the morning cup have?
Caller -> There are four. Her heart pill, her thyroid, her vitamin, and the water pill. The furosemide. A white round one. Forty milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. Furosemide forty milligrams, every morning. And you're sure you put it in the cup?
Caller -> I think so. I always do. I fill the box on Sundays. I filled it Sunday. I'm pretty sure. I mean, I always put it in.
Caller -> I didn't see a white one, Brittany. I counted them. There were three.
Nurse -> Okay. Bernadette, you counted three pills?
Caller -> Three. I counted. I always count. I'm ninety. I count everything.
Nurse -> That's a good habit. Brittany, can you check the pill box for me? Look at Thursday's slot, or whatever day it is today. Is it empty?
Caller -> It's, hold on. It's Sunday today. The Sunday morning slot. It's empty. It's empty, but that doesn't tell us, because empty means she took what was in it. Either way it's empty.
Nurse -> Right. Is there a white pill on the floor, in the sink, anywhere?
Caller -> I'll look. Hold on. Grandma, don't move. I'll look under the table. Nothing. I don't see it. I can't tell.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me ask another way. Bernadette, do you feel like you took the water pill today?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'd remember. It makes me go to the bathroom a lot. I haven't gone much this morning. I've gone once.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Brittany, has she gone to the bathroom a lot this morning?
Caller -> No. Once. Maybe twice. She went when she got up, and then I think once after breakfast. I wasn't counting.
Nurse -> Okay. So we really can't tell. And that's okay. Is she short of breath?
Caller -> No. She's fine. She's sitting here. She's breathing fine. She did the dishes.
Nurse -> Okay. Any swelling in her legs or ankles?
Caller -> A little. Her ankles are a little puffy. Mild. They're about the same as yesterday.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Here's what I want you to do. Don't give her another water pill today. If she did take it, a second one could make her dizzy or dehydrated. And leave the pill box just as it is. Don't refill it.
Caller -> Okay. Don't give another. Leave the box. Should I just wait until tomorrow, then?
Nurse -> I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow to check her ankles, her pressure, and go over the pill box with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'll leave a message for the team, to ask whether she should get the water pill again today or just wait until tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Good. Yes. I don't want to guess. I was afraid I'd either double it or miss it.
Nurse -> I understand. That's the right instinct.
Caller -> It's really hard sometimes. She says one thing and I remember another.
Nurse -> It happens a lot. For the future, it helps to write down the time every time a pill is given. A little chart by the pill box. A check mark and the time.
Caller -> A check mark. I can do that. We have a notepad. I'll tape it to the box.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call us if the swelling gets worse, if she gets short of breath, or if she gets dizzy.
Caller -> Swelling. Short of breath. Dizzy. Okay. I'll watch. Grandma, you tell me if you feel dizzy.
Caller -> I will. Don't fuss.
Nurse -> Ha. She sounds feisty.
Caller -> She is. She's the boss. I work full time and she still tells me what to do.
Nurse -> How long has Bernadette lived with you?
Caller -> Three years. Since Grandpa passed. I moved in to help. Now I think she's helping me.
Nurse -> Ha. It goes both ways.
Nurse -> Where do you work?
Caller -> The hospital. In billing. I'm home on Sundays, thank goodness.
Caller -> Sundays we do the crossword and the soap opera reruns. It's our thing.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Caller -> She likes the one with the evil twin. Every episode has an evil twin.
Caller -> Every one.
Nurse -> Good. Can I get a number for you? In case the team calls back today.
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one nine four.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, zero one nine four. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. And Grandma's birthday is May ninth, nineteen thirty six. In case you need it.
Nurse -> Thank you. That helps. Okay, Brittany. We'll get this sorted out.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much. And thank you for not making me feel stupid.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. You're careful.
Caller -> Ha. I don't feel careful.
Nurse -> Honestly, calling to ask is the careful thing.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed that today.
Nurse -> Take care, you two.
Caller -> Bye, Hortense.
Caller -> Bye, dear.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Colette.
Caller -> Hey. Colette? It's Jerome. Jerome Castellano. I'm the guy with the shoulder surgery. Yeah. I have a question. Kind of a confession.
Nurse -> How's the shoulder doing, by the way?
Caller -> Sore. I'm doing the exercises. Mostly.
Nurse -> Mostly. Ha. We'll talk about that.
Nurse -> Hi Jerome. I remember. A confession, huh? Go ahead.
Caller -> Okay. So. Don't be mad. I stopped taking my Keppra.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm not mad. I'm glad you told me. When did you stop?
Caller -> Five days ago. Last Tuesday. I took the morning one and then I just didn't take the night one. And I haven't since.
Nurse -> Okay. Five days. What made you stop?
Caller -> It makes me mean. I swear. I snap at my wife. I yelled at the guy at the pharmacy over nothing. I felt like a different person. My wife said, you're a jerk on that stuff. So I stopped.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a real side effect. It's good to say. Did you talk to your neurologist before you stopped?
Caller -> No. I thought, I'll just skip it for a week and see. I feel fine. I haven't had a seizure in, like, three years.
Nurse -> Okay. And you've had no seizure at all since you stopped?
Caller -> No. None. Nothing. I feel great actually. I'm calm.
Nurse -> Calm is nice. I'd still like to keep you safe.
Caller -> I know. I know. I figured you'd say that.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. What's the dose you were on?
Caller -> Five hundred milligrams. Twice a day. The generic. I call it Keppra.
Nurse -> Okay. Jerome, I need to ask a few more questions. Have you had anything odd? Any twitching, any strange feeling, any blank moments?
Caller -> Um. Not really. Wait. Yesterday I had a funny feeling in my right hand. A tingling. Like it fell asleep. For a minute. Maybe two. Then it went away. I figured I slept on it. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. That's important. Did it spread up your arm, or did you feel strange anywhere else?
Caller -> No. Just the hand. I don't think. I wasn't really paying attention.
Nurse -> Okay. Jerome, I'm going to be honest with you. Stopping seizure medicine suddenly, without a plan, can be risky, even if you've been seizure free for a long time. It can bring on a seizure. The tingling may be nothing. But I don't want to take a chance.
Caller -> Oh. Man. I didn't think. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm paging the on-call clinician now. They'll call you to talk about whether to restart it and how. In the meantime, don't stay off the Keppra on your own, and don't restart the Keppra on your own either. Wait for their instructions.
Caller -> Wait for the call. Okay. Don't restart and don't stay off. Okay. That's confusing but okay.
Nurse -> It is confusing. What I mean is, the clinician may tell you to start it at a lower dose, or a different medicine. They need to decide.
Caller -> Oh. Right. A different one. That would be great. That's what I wanted.
Nurse -> That's a good thing to ask them. Now, I need your date of birth.
Caller -> July eleventh, nineteen eighty two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one three six.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, zero one three six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yep.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes to let you know what they said. If the clinician calls you first, take that call.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Got it. I'll keep the phone on me.
Nurse -> Now, until you hear from them, Jerome, I need you to be careful. Don't drive. Don't take a bath alone, and don't use the stove or climb a ladder alone. And is someone with you today?
Caller -> My wife's home. She's in the kitchen. She's making a casserole. I'm in the garage, on the couch. No ladders. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> Tuna noodle. The one with the potato chips on top. She makes it every time somebody's sick.
Nurse -> Comfort food. Ha.
Caller -> I'm not even sick. I'm just a jerk. But I get the casserole anyway.
Nurse -> Good. Have her stay close. And tell her about the medicine, so she knows.
Caller -> I will. She's going to say I told you so. She's going to say it for a week.
Nurse -> Ha. Let her. She's probably right.
Caller -> She's always right. It's annoying.
Nurse -> Jerome, you also need to know what to do if you do have a seizure. Call 911 if it lasts more than five minutes, if you have a second one, if you have trouble breathing afterward, or if you get hurt.
Caller -> More than five minutes. A second one. Trouble breathing. Hurt. 911. Okay. I'll tell my wife that too. She knows. She's seen one. Years ago.
Nurse -> Good. She'll know what to do.
Caller -> She'll time it. She's a timer person. She has a stopwatch app for everything.
Caller -> She timed my kid's tantrums. She timed the oven. She timed the dog's walks.
Nurse -> Sounds useful.
Caller -> Mostly it's just loud. The thing beeps. Our house is a chorus of beeps.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else going on?
Caller -> No. Just the shoulder. It's okay. It's sore.
Nurse -> We'll cover that on the visit. Right now, the medicine is the priority.
Caller -> Should I tell the doctor about the hand when they call?
Nurse -> Yes, tell them everything you told me. The hand, the mood, the days.
Caller -> Okay. I wrote it on my phone. Hand. Mood. Five days.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's what they need.
Caller -> Okay. I'm sorry. I should've called before I stopped.
Nurse -> You called now. That's what counts.
Caller -> Thanks, Colette.
Nurse -> Talk to you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Quiet Pines Hospice, this is Delphine.
Caller -> Hi. Delphine. It's Cordelia Vanterpool. Mom's daughter. Rosalind Vanterpool. I'm sorry it's so late. I just, I needed to talk to somebody.
Nurse -> Hi Cordelia. It's okay. I'm glad you called. Is your mom okay?
Caller -> She's okay. She's fine. I'm the one who's not. This is killing me. I'm sorry. That's a terrible thing to say.
Nurse -> It's not a terrible thing. Tell me what's happening.
Caller -> I haven't slept in, I don't know. Days. It's me up all night. I'm on the couch next to her bed. And every time she moves, I wake up. And that oxygen thing, the concentrator, it beeps sometimes. And I swear, if that beeps one more time I'm going to die. I'm going to scream.
Nurse -> That sounds exhausting. Cordelia, I want to ask you something. When you say it's killing you, and you'll die, I understand you mean you're worn out. But I ask everyone. Are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself?
Caller -> No. God, no. No. I'm sorry, I didn't mean it like that. It's just an expression. I'm just so tired. I'm not going to do anything. I would never. I just want to sleep for a week.
Nurse -> Okay. I appreciate you saying that so clearly.
Caller -> I say it all the time. Dying to sit down. Killing time. My husband says I talk like a crime novel.
Nurse -> Ha. It's a funny way we talk.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. I'm glad you said it plainly. And has your mom said anything like that? Anything about wanting to die, or hurting herself?
Caller -> No. Never. She has never said anything like that. She's at peace. She's been at peace for a while. She says she's ready, but she's not sad about it. It's me who's not ready.
Nurse -> That's a very honest thing to say.
Caller -> I keep rehearsing. What I'll say. Who I'll call. It doesn't help.
Nurse -> It never quite does. But you're clearly loving her well.
Caller -> I'm trying.
Nurse -> That makes sense. That's very common. Let's talk about how she's doing. What's she like today?
Caller -> She sleeps a lot. More than last week. Twenty hours, it feels like. She wakes up for a few minutes, says a couple of words, goes back.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating or drinking?
Caller -> A few bites. Yogurt, applesauce. A spoonful at a time. Today she had maybe four spoonfuls of applesauce and some sips of tea. That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. That's expected at this stage. Is she in any pain? Does she grimace, moan, seem restless?
Caller -> No. Nothing. She's very comfortable. She's calm. Her face is relaxed. I check every hour.
Nurse -> Every hour. Cordelia, that's a lot of checking. Does she wake when you check?
Caller -> Sometimes she opens her eyes and smiles. Then she's out again.
Nurse -> That smile is a good sign. She knows you're there.
Nurse -> Good. That's what we want. Cordelia, what's your date of birth? No. I mean your mom's. For the chart.
Caller -> Ha. Mine is nineteen seventy five. Mom is October third, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one nine.
Nurse -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one nine. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Now. You're doing the nights by yourself. Is anybody helping?
Caller -> My brother lives in Seattle. He calls. My husband takes the day. But the nights are mine. I don't want to wake him, he has to work.
Nurse -> I hear you. Cordelia, I think you need more help. I'm going to ask our social worker to call you tomorrow, to talk about respite care and about getting you some support.
Caller -> Respite. They do that? Like, someone comes at night?
Nurse -> There are options. Volunteers who sit with her, short stays at our inpatient unit, some aides. She'll go over what you qualify for.
Caller -> I didn't know. I thought I had to do it all myself.
Caller -> My mother raised four of us alone. I think I got it from her. You don't ask for help. You just do it.
Nurse -> It runs in families. But you've already done a great deal.
Nurse -> Many people think that. You don't have to.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Yes. I would like that. I would really like that.
Nurse -> I'll put the request in tonight. And I'm also sending a nurse out Wednesday, to check on your mom and on you.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. That's good.
Nurse -> In the meantime, for your mom, keep her mouth moist with the little swabs. Offer sips or ice chips only if she wants them. Don't push food. She doesn't need it.
Caller -> I keep thinking I should push food. I feel like I'm starving her.
Caller -> Every time I walk past the kitchen I feel guilty. There's a whole pot of soup in there from the neighbors.
Nurse -> The soup is for you. Eat some.
Caller -> Ha. I haven't. Maybe I will.
Nurse -> You're not. Her body doesn't need much now. Not eating is part of the process. The swabs and your company are what she needs.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. That actually helps.
Nurse -> Cordelia, I want you to remember that you can call us any time. Day or night. Even if it's just to talk, even if nothing's wrong. The nurse on at night will answer.
Caller -> Even at three in the morning?
Nurse -> Especially at three in the morning.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I didn't think I could.
Nurse -> You can. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Just, thank you. I feel a little lighter.
Caller -> Can I ask you something silly? Is it normal that I keep listening to her breathing, to count it?
Nurse -> Very normal. Everyone does it.
Caller -> Okay. I thought I was losing my mind.
Nurse -> You're not. You're paying attention.
Nurse -> Good. Try to lie down next to her and close your eyes. The concentrator will beep. You'll hear it. It's okay.
Caller -> I'll try. Maybe I'll put the pillow over my ear.
Nurse -> Ha. That's allowed.
Caller -> Okay. Goodnight, Delphine.
Nurse -> Goodnight, Cordelia. Rest.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice after hours, this is Calvin.
Caller -> Calvin, hi, this is Dwayne Ferreira. D W A Y N E. I'm the night aide at Cedar Court Assisted Living. I got a resident who fell. She's bleeding from the head. I need a nurse.
Nurse -> Okay Dwayne. I'm a nurse. I'm here. Tell me the resident's name.
Caller -> Lucinda Farragut. F A R R A G U T. Room fourteen. She's one of yours. She's on hospice.
Nurse -> Okay. Lucinda Farragut. Is she awake?
Caller -> She's awake. She's sitting on the bathroom floor. I'm with her. I've got a towel on her head.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> She got up to go to the bathroom. About, I don't know, ten minutes ago. I heard a crash. I came running. She'd slipped. There was water on the floor, from the sink. She hit her head on the sink. The edge. And then she was on the floor.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she pass out, as far as you know?
Caller -> No. She says no. She was awake when I got there. She was talking. She said, oh my, I fell. She never passed out.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Now, the cut. Where is it? How big?
Caller -> On her forehead. The right side, up by the hairline. It's about two inches, I'd say. It's open. It's bleeding a lot. I've had pressure on it with a towel for ten minutes and it's soaked through.
Nurse -> Okay. Ten minutes of pressure and it's still bleeding. Dwayne, is she on any blood thinners?
Caller -> Let me look at the MAR. Hold on. Yes. Apixaban. Five milligrams. Twice a day. Eliquis, it says in parentheses.
Nurse -> Okay. When was her last dose?
Caller -> Last night at eight. The evening one. And she gets one in the morning at eight. So not yet this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. Dwayne, because of the blood thinner and the head injury, I need you to call 911 right now. This is an emergency. Do you have another phone?
Caller -> I have the facility phone and my cell. I can use my cell. Should I hang up with you?
Nurse -> No. Put me on speaker. Use your cell to call 911, and keep me on the facility phone, right next to you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm putting you on speaker. Dialing. Hold on.
Nurse -> I'm right here. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> It's ringing. Hello? Yes. I need an ambulance. At Cedar Court Assisted Living. It's twenty one oh three Pine Street. A resident fell and hit her head. She's bleeding and she's on a blood thinner. Yes. She's awake. Room fourteen. Yes. Okay. They're sending a crew.
Nurse -> Good job. Did they give you a time?
Caller -> They said six to eight minutes. The firehouse is on the next block.
Caller -> The dispatcher is a woman. She stayed on at first, then said the crew had my location and I could go back to my resident.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'm here with you.
Nurse -> Good. Now, Dwayne. Keep your hand on that towel. Press firmly. Do not lift it to look. If it soaks through, put another one on top. Don't take the first one off.
Caller -> Press firmly. Don't lift. Add on top. Okay. I'm doing that. She's saying ow. I'm sorry, Mrs. Farragut. I know it's tight.
Nurse -> It has to be tight. Keep it steady.
Caller -> She's holding my arm. Her hand is cold.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she on the floor, lying down, or sitting?
Caller -> Sitting against the wall. Next to the toilet.
Nurse -> I'd like her lying flat, if you can do it without moving her head and neck much. Is there a pillow or a folded blanket you can put under her head? Don't move her if she says her neck hurts.
Caller -> Mrs. Farragut, does your neck hurt? She says no. Just my head. Okay. I'm going to have her lie back. I have a bath mat, folded. And a towel.
Nurse -> Slowly. Let her go down slowly. Keep the pressure on the cut the whole time.
Caller -> Slowly. Okay. She's down. She's lying on the mat. Her head's on a folded towel. I still have my hand on it.
Nurse -> Good. Is she cold? Does she have a blanket?
Caller -> She's got her robe. I'll get a blanket from the closet. I can reach it. Hold on.
Nurse -> What's the resident like, usually? Chatty? Quiet?
Caller -> Chatty. She plays the piano in the lobby on Thursdays. Show tunes. She's got the whole floor singing.
Nurse -> What a lovely thing.
Caller -> She taught music for forty years. She corrects the off key ones.
Nurse -> Don't let go of the cut. Can someone else help?
Caller -> There's one other aide on the floor. Marguerite. I'll holler. Marguerite! Bring a blanket! Room fourteen! Hurry!
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> She's coming. Okay. She's here. She's putting the blanket on. She's got the face sheet. She's going to get the medicine list.
Nurse -> Perfect. Have her put those by the door so the paramedics get them. And Dwayne, tell the paramedics she's on apixaban and tell them the time she last took it. Last night at eight.
Caller -> Apixaban. Eight last night. Okay. I wrote it on my hand. I always do that.
Nurse -> Good. Now, how is she acting? Is she making sense?
Caller -> She's a little, she's asking me the same thing. She keeps asking, did I fall? Did I fall? And I say yes. And then she asks again. And she says her head hurts.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important. Tell the paramedics that too. The repeating and the headache.
Caller -> I will. Is that bad?
Nurse -> It can be after a head injury, so we want her checked. That's why we called. You're doing the right thing.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. She's looking at me. She says, who are you? Oh no.
Nurse -> Stay calm. Tell her your name. Gently.
Caller -> Mrs. Farragut, it's Dwayne. Your night aide. I bring you your tea. She says, oh, Dwayne. Okay. She knows me. Whew.
Nurse -> Good. Keep talking to her. Tell her where she is. Tell her help is coming.
Caller -> She's looking around the bathroom. She says, this isn't my house. I say, it's your room at Cedar Court.
Nurse -> That's right. Keep orienting her.
Caller -> She says, where's my husband? He passed in March. I don't know whether to tell her.
Nurse -> Don't argue. Just say he's not here right now, and that you're here.
Caller -> Okay. Mrs. Farragut, he's not here right now. I'm here. She says, okay.
Caller -> You're at Cedar Court, Mrs. Farragut. You fell in the bathroom. The ambulance is coming. You're going to be okay.
Nurse -> Good. Dwayne, I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, so they know what's happening. I'll still be on the line with you through the speaker.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm shaking a little.
Caller -> My hands are cold. I took a first aid class in June. I'm glad I did.
Nurse -> It shows. You're calm and clear.
Caller -> Inside I'm a mess. My heart's going like a drum.
Nurse -> Breathe. Slowly. You're doing fine.
Nurse -> That's normal. You're doing great.
Caller -> I've never had one bleed this much.
Caller -> I've been here four years. Mostly it's falls where nobody's hurt. Maybe a bruise.
Nurse -> This is a different level. Which is why you call.
Caller -> Yeah. Yeah. I know.
Nurse -> Head cuts bleed a lot. It looks worse than it is, usually. But because of the blood thinner, she needs to be seen.
Caller -> Is it going to leave a scar?
Nurse -> I can't say. The doctors at the hospital will decide how to close it.
Caller -> She's vain about her hair. She'll be upset about the shaved spot.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll worry about that later.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. I understand.
Nurse -> What's Lucinda's date of birth? I'll give it to the hospital.
Caller -> January twenty eighth, nineteen forty one. It's on the face sheet.
Caller -> The sheet is right here. I'm holding it in my other hand. I can read you anything. Her doctor, her room, her emergency contact.
Nurse -> Good. Keep it by the door for them.
Caller -> Okay. I'll put it on top of the pile.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a good number to reach you?
Caller -> My cell. Three oh three, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one five two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> Marguerite is going to the front. She'll bring them back. The code's on the keypad. She knows it.
Nurse -> Good. Check the towel. Is it still soaking through?
Nurse -> How's she feeling? Is she cold?
Caller -> She says she's cold. Marguerite put a second blanket. And I put the sweater over her feet.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Her feet are tiny. Like a little girl. I don't know why I noticed.
Caller -> It's, hold on. I put the second one on. It's slowing down, I think. It's not dripping.
Nurse -> Good. Keep it on.
Caller -> Okay. She's breathing fine. Her color is okay. Maybe a little pale.
Caller -> Marguerite is at the front door. She's flashing the porch light. So they find us.
Nurse -> Smart.
Caller -> It's raining a little. The ground's wet. I hope they don't slip.
Nurse -> They're used to it.
Nurse -> That's okay.
Caller -> I hear them. I hear the sirens. It's the fire truck first.
Nurse -> Is the hallway clear for them? Any walkers, carts, wheelchairs?
Caller -> Marguerite moved the med cart. There's a walker by room twelve. I'll have her push it aside.
Nurse -> Good. Clear a path.
Caller -> She's doing it. It's tight in the hall. We have the old carpet runner and it bunches up.
Nurse -> Make sure nobody trips on it.
Caller -> I'll write that up too. I keep telling the director about that runner.
Nurse -> Good. Tell Marguerite to bring them straight in.
Caller -> Marguerite is bringing them. They're in the hall. Here they are. Back here! Room fourteen! In the bathroom!
Nurse -> Dwayne, give the paramedics a quick report. Fall, head, bleeding, apixaban, last dose last night at eight, repeating herself, headache.
Caller -> Yes. I will. Hi. Yes. She slipped. She hit her head on the sink. She's on apixaban. Last dose eight last night. Yes. She's been repeating herself.
Nurse -> I'll stay on until you tell me they've got her.
Caller -> They're taking over. They're looking at her head. They're asking her questions. Okay. They're going to put her on a stretcher.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead and let go. They've got her. Which hospital are they taking her to?
Caller -> They said Saint Anne's. The emergency room.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll let the hospital know she's coming and that she's on hospice. I'll call you after she gets there.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much, Calvin. I didn't know what to do.
Nurse -> You knew exactly what to do. You did everything right.
Caller -> I feel like it's my fault. The water on the floor.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. Accidents happen. Write it up when things calm down.
Caller -> I will. Okay. They're rolling her out. I have to go.
Nurse -> Go. Thank you, Dwayne.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oak Hollow Home Health, this is Bernard.
Caller -> Hello? Hello? Can you hear me? I'm in the, the kitchen, the signal is bad. This is Rosario. Rosario Delgado. I'm the aide for Mr. Lindqvist. Clifford Lindqvist.
Nurse -> Rosario? You cut out. Can you move closer to a window?
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm walking. Is that better? I'm by the back door.
Caller -> Hello? Are you there?
Nurse -> I'm here. Say it once more. Slowly.
Nurse -> A little. Keep going.
Nurse -> I can hear you, Rosario. A little choppy. Let me know if I cut out. What's going on with Mr. Lindqvist?
Caller -> He's dizzy. When he stands up. He says the room goes round. It's, it's been since this morning.
Nurse -> Does the spinning last long?
Caller -> A few seconds. Then it settles. If he stays standing it comes back a little.
Nurse -> Okay. Dizzy when he stands. Is he dizzy sitting down, or only when he stands?
Caller -> Only when he stands. When he's sitting he's okay. I checked his pressure. I have the machine.
Caller -> It's the arm one. From the drugstore. The cuff is old but it's okay. I tried it on myself last week and it matched mine.
Nurse -> Good check.
Nurse -> Good. What did it say?
Caller -> It said won fifty too over ate tea. Won fifty too.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, Rosario, it broke up. Can you say that again?
Caller -> One fifty two over eighty. One fifty two. Eighty. Is that better?
Nurse -> Much better. One fifty two over eighty. Okay. Is that higher than his usual?
Caller -> A little, I think. His chart on the fridge says one thirty something.
Nurse -> Okay. Any headache, blurry vision, chest pain?
Caller -> A mild headache. He says it's behind the eyes. A little one. No chest pain. No blurry vision. He read the paper this morning with no glasses trouble.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he fallen, or almost fallen, or passed out?
Caller -> No. No fall. I was with him every time. I hold his arm. He hasn't passed out.
Nurse -> Good. Did he take his morning pills?
Caller -> Yes. At eight. I give them. The amlodipine. Five milligrams. Once a day. He took it with his oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay. Amlodipine five, this morning. Rosario, I need his date of birth to pull up the chart. Do you have it?
Caller -> It's, hold on. His birthday is February fourteenth. Nineteen thirty nine. No, no. Thirty eight. Nineteen thirty eight. He's eighty eight. Not eighty seven. Thirty eight.
Nurse -> February fourteenth, nineteen thirty eight. Got it. Valentine's Day.
Caller -> He says his wife was never impressed.
Nurse -> Ha. And a number for you?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one two two.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one two two. Is that correct?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Thanks. Okay. Here's what I'd like to do. I'm going to send a nurse out tomorrow to check his pressure sitting and standing and to look at his medicines.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. I'm here until five. Tomorrow too.
Nurse -> Does he have family nearby?
Caller -> A daughter in Tempe. She calls every night at seven. She likes to hear the blood pressure numbers.
Nurse -> Okay. Please let her know about today.
Nurse -> And I'll leave a message for the team now, about the dizziness and the pressure numbers. They may have something to say before tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Because I'm worried. He's a big man and if he goes down I can't catch him.
Nurse -> That's what I want to talk about. Until we hear back, have him sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before he stands. Then stand slowly. And stay right beside him when he walks.
Caller -> Sit a minute. Stand slow. Stay beside him. Okay. I do that mostly. I'll do it every time.
Nurse -> And offer him water through the day. And a small snack with the morning pills, so they sit better.
Caller -> Water. A snack with the pills. He likes toast. I'll do toast.
Nurse -> Perfect. Call us for a fall, fainting, chest pain, a bad headache, or blurred vision. Call 911 for chest pain or fainting.
Caller -> Fall. Faint. Chest pain. Headache. Blurry. And 911 for the chest and the faint. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Is he with you now?
Caller -> He's in his recliner. Watching the cooking show. He's saying the chef is doing it wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. Then he's feeling like himself.
Caller -> Oh, yes. He's a critic.
Caller -> Right now he's saying the chef used too much butter.
Nurse -> Ha. A strong opinion.
Caller -> He doesn't even cook. He microwaves soup.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Keep him in the recliner for now. Stay near.
Caller -> Hold on. He's calling me. Mr. Lindqvist, I'm on the phone. I'll be right there. Sorry. He wants the remote.
Nurse -> Go ahead and give him the remote.
Caller -> Okay. Done. He's happy.
Caller -> I will. I'll make the toast and bring it to him.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else, Rosario?
Caller -> No. Just that. The connection was terrible, sorry.
Nurse -> It's no problem. We got there.
Caller -> Thank you, Bernard. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gloria.
Caller -> Hi there! Good afternoon! How are you today?
Nurse -> I'm fine, thanks. How can I help you?
Caller -> Wonderful. I'm calling on behalf of a company that works with hospices and home health agencies on supply savings. Am I speaking with the person who handles purchasing?
Nurse -> No, I'm one of the nurses. I don't handle purchasing.
Caller -> No problem at all. Could you tell me who does? A name, an extension?
Nurse -> I'm not able to give out names. If you want to send information, there's a general office email.
Caller -> Perfect. That would be great. What's the email?
Nurse -> It's on our website, under contact. I don't have it memorized.
Caller -> Oh, sure. I can find it. We have a program where agencies save up to thirty percent on gloves, wipes, briefs, and wound care supplies. Is that something you might be interested in?
Nurse -> I really can't speak to that. The office manager would be the one to look at it.
Caller -> Totally understand. Would it be okay if I call back tomorrow and ask for her?
Nurse -> You're welcome to try, but I can't promise she'll take the call. This line is mostly for patients and families.
Caller -> Oh. I'm so sorry. I didn't realize. I'll use the email then. I'm sorry to take your time.
Nurse -> No problem. Thank you for understanding.
Caller -> Have a great afternoon.
Nurse -> You too. Goodbye.

not_applicable.reason: Vendor sales call asking for the purchasing contact; no patient or clinical content.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Anneliese.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Anneliese. This is Tomasz Wierzbicki. It's a mouthful. T O M A S Z. Wierzbicki is W I E R Z B I C K I. I'm one of your patients.
Nurse -> Hi Tomasz. I have you. Thank you for spelling it. What can I do for you?
Caller -> I think there's a mistake with my medicine. My refill. I think the pharmacy gave me the wrong pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's look at it together. Do you have the bottle in front of you?
Caller -> I do. I'm holding it. I got it five days ago. The label says metoprolol. M E T O P R O L O L. Twenty five milligrams. One tablet twice a day.
Nurse -> Okay. Metoprolol twenty five, twice a day. And what do you think it should be?
Caller -> Metformin. M E T F O R M I N. For the sugar. I'm diabetic. My list from the doctor says metformin five hundred milligrams twice a day. It looks almost the same on paper. Metformin, metoprolol. I mean, I didn't even notice at first.
Nurse -> It does look similar. Those two get mixed up a lot. When did you start the new bottle?
Caller -> Five days ago. No. I think I took it four days. I took the first one the next morning. So four days. Twice a day. Eight, eight pills. Seven. I don't know. It's been about four days.
Nurse -> Do you remember anything that was different with the pills themselves? The color, the size?
Caller -> Now that you say it, they're smaller than the old ones. And white. The old ones were white too but bigger, and a little oval. I thought they changed the manufacturer. They do that.
Nurse -> They do. It's a common reason people don't notice.
Caller -> That's what I told myself. Different maker, same medicine. Wrong.
Nurse -> Okay. Four days is fine. When did you last take one?
Caller -> This morning. Around eight. I took it with breakfast. I haven't taken the night one. I just noticed the label an hour ago. I was getting my pills out.
Nurse -> What was breakfast?
Caller -> Oatmeal. And the donuts. Two donuts. I'm not proud.
Nurse -> No judgment. I just like to know.
Nurse -> Okay. Good that you noticed. Tomasz, how have you been feeling?
Caller -> Not great. I'm tired. And dizzy, a little, when I stand up. I thought it was the flu. I thought, I'm coming down with something.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you checked your sugar?
Caller -> Yes. I check in the morning. This morning it was three twelve. Three hundred and twelve. That's high for me. I'm usually one forty, one fifty.
Nurse -> That's quite high. Okay. And have you checked your pulse, or your blood pressure?
Caller -> I have the wrist machine. It does both. It said fifty four for the pulse. Fifty four. I was surprised. I'm usually seventy something.
Nurse -> Okay. That's slow. That makes sense with the dizziness. Do you have chest pain? Have you fainted, or nearly?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. No fainting. I held the counter once yesterday. When I got up too fast. But I didn't pass out.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being so clear. Now. Are you taking any other medicines? Can you read me the other bottles on your counter?
Caller -> Sure. I have them all out. It's like a pharmacy in here. Okay. Here's the first. Lisinopril. Ten milligrams. Once a day. That's the blood pressure one. I took it this morning.
Nurse -> Ha. Take your time with each one.
Caller -> Okay. I'm putting on my reading glasses. They're on top of my head. I always do that. My wife says I look for them for ten minutes and they're sitting there like a hat.
Nurse -> Everyone does that. Don't feel bad.
Nurse -> Okay. Lisinopril ten, once a day. That matches your list?
Caller -> Yes. Lisinopril, ten. It matches. Next. Atorvastatin. Forty milligrams. Once a day at night. I haven't taken it yet today.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the cholesterol one. Does that match?
Caller -> It does. And the aspirin. Eighty one milligrams. Every morning. Took it. And then there's the metformin I'm supposed to have, which I don't have. It's the one that's missing.
Nurse -> Okay. So the lisinopril, atorvastatin, and aspirin all match your list, and the metformin is the one that was switched for metoprolol.
Caller -> Right. That's it. Exactly.
Nurse -> Okay. Tomasz, here's what I want. Don't take any more of the metoprolol. Not tonight, not tomorrow. Not until a clinician calls you. Keep the bottle.
Caller -> Okay. Don't take the metoprolol. Keep the bottle. And what about the sugar? I haven't had my metformin in four days.
Nurse -> That's what the clinician will decide. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. Your sugar is high, your pulse is slow, and you've been on the wrong medicine. They'll call you back.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm a little scared. My brother has had heart trouble.
Nurse -> I'm sorry to hear about your brother. Is he doing okay?
Caller -> He's okay now. He had a stent two years ago. He's in Pittsburgh. We talk on Sundays.
Nurse -> It's good you have each other.
Caller -> He's going to tell me I told you so about the diabetes. He's been after me for years.
Nurse -> I understand. You did the right thing by calling. Your pulse of fifty four is slow, but you're not having chest pain, and you're awake and talking. We just want to be careful.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll be careful.
Nurse -> I'm also going to call your pharmacy to find out what happened and to get the right medicine.
Caller -> Good. Because I'll tell you, I called them yesterday about something else and the guy on the phone was rude. He said they don't make mistakes.
Nurse -> Well. We'll see about that. I'll talk to the pharmacist.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I need some information for the chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> October twenty ninth. Nineteen sixty nine.
Nurse -> And a number I can call you back on?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one nine two.
Nurse -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one nine two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. It's my cell. I'm home all day. I work from home.
Nurse -> What do you do?
Caller -> I'm an accountant. Taxes. This is the slow season, thankfully. Or it will be.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm sure.
Caller -> Wait till April. I'll be a zombie.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to send a nurse out tomorrow morning, to check your sugar and your pulse and go through all your bottles with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. That's good. I'll be here.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in an hour, after I talk to the clinician. If they call you first, take that call.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll keep the phone close.
Nurse -> In the meantime, I'd like you to check your sugar every four hours while you're awake. Write down each number with the time. And check your pulse each time too.
Caller -> Every four hours. Sugar and pulse. Write it down. I have a notebook. I'll start now. Should I check it right now again?
Caller -> And the meter is acting strange. It says error sometimes. I need to put in a new strip. Hold on. I'm opening the vial. There. It's in.
Nurse -> That's fine. Take your time.
Nurse -> You checked this morning. Let's check again now, to see where it is. Go ahead.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Let me get the meter. Okay, I'm pricking. Hold on. It's, three oh one. Three oh one.
Nurse -> Okay. Three oh one. Slightly lower than the morning. Write it down.
Caller -> Writing it. Three oh one. And the time is, it's six fifty five.
Nurse -> Good. And drink plenty of water. Keep your meals like usual, but skip the extra sweets until the clinician talks to you.
Caller -> Water. No sweets. I had a donut this morning. Two. Oops.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll start fresh.
Caller -> Starting fresh. Yes.
Nurse -> And Tomasz, I want you to call us if your sugar goes over four hundred, if you start vomiting, feel confused or very thirsty, or if your pulse drops below fifty. And call 911 right away for fainting or chest pain.
Caller -> Over four hundred. Vomiting. Confused. Thirsty. Pulse under fifty. 911 for fainting or chest pain. I wrote it down.
Nurse -> Good. Is there someone with you at home?
Caller -> My wife is at work. She gets home at six thirty. Oh, it's nearly seven. She should be here any minute.
Nurse -> Good. Tell her what happened. Have her stay close.
Caller -> I will. She's going to be furious at the pharmacy. She's a lawyer.
Nurse -> Ha. That might help.
Caller -> She'll be on the phone with them all night.
Nurse -> I'll try to get there first.
Caller -> Ha. Good luck. She's fast.
Nurse -> What does your wife do, as a lawyer?
Caller -> Contracts. She reads fine print for a living. She would have caught the label in two seconds. I handle the pills because I'm home. I'm the one who messed up.
Nurse -> It's not on you. The label is where the mistake began.
Caller -> That's what she'll say too. Right before she calls them.
Nurse -> Tomasz, how's the dizziness right now? Sitting down?
Caller -> I'm sitting at the kitchen table. It's okay. It's not bad when I sit. I just feel kind of floaty.
Caller -> The cat is on my lap. She doesn't like it when I'm up and down. She keeps digging in.
Nurse -> Ha. A built in seat belt.
Nurse -> Okay. Stay seated. When you need to stand, go slow.
Caller -> I will. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> Honestly the worst part is I feel stupid. I read labels for a living, sort of. Numbers, fine print. And I missed it.
Nurse -> The names are very close. Even pharmacists mix them up on the shelf sometimes.
Caller -> That's kind of you to say.
Nurse -> Do you need anything to eat? Have you had dinner?
Caller -> Not yet. I was going to make some pasta. Maybe that's not good.
Nurse -> A small portion is fine. Maybe add some vegetables and a protein. Keep it simple.
Caller -> Chicken and broccoli. I have leftover chicken.
Nurse -> Good. Do you cook most nights?
Caller -> Mostly my wife does. Tonight's my night, since she's late. She makes me do Mondays.
Nurse -> Ha. A fair deal.
Caller -> She leaves a recipe on the counter. It's like a test.
Nurse -> That sounds good.
Caller -> Okay. I'll heat that up.
Caller -> I'll set my phone timer for the hour. So I don't miss your call.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> I have like five timers going already. A chorus of beeps.
Nurse -> Ha. Another one won't hurt.
Nurse -> Is there anything else you want to ask me?
Caller -> Just, will I be okay? Four days on the wrong one.
Nurse -> The clinician will go over that. What I can say is, you caught it, you've told us everything, and you have no chest pain or fainting. That's good.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. Thank you, Anneliese.
Nurse -> You're welcome. I'll call you in an hour.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Larkspur Hospice, this is Yolanda.
Caller -> Hi, Yolanda. It's Annika Dahlberg. A N N I K A. Dahlberg, D A H L B E R G. I'm calling about my mother. Philomena Greer. She's on your service.
Nurse -> Hi Annika. Different last name than your mom. Okay. I have Philomena Greer here. How can I help on a Saturday?
Caller -> I know, it's the weekend, I'm sorry. I just realized we're running out of her supplies. The briefs, the pads. I didn't want to wait until Monday.
Nurse -> Is your mom comfortable right now?
Caller -> Yes. She's asleep. She's been sleeping most of the morning.
Nurse -> No problem. That's what the weekend line is for. Let's count. How many briefs do you have left?
Caller -> Four. I counted this morning. Four briefs. I think that's two days.
Nurse -> Okay. Four briefs. And the underpads, the blue ones for the bed?
Caller -> Six. I have six left. They last a little longer.
Nurse -> Okay. And the barrier cream? The tube for her bottom?
Caller -> None. Empty. I squeezed the last of it out on Thursday. I've been using the diaper cream from the drugstore. I hope that's okay.
Caller -> It has a lavender smell. My husband picked it. I didn't think about it.
Nurse -> Plain is better. We'll fix that.
Nurse -> It's okay for a few days. We'll get her the right one. How's her skin looking?
Caller -> That's the other thing. There's some redness. On her tailbone. Right at the bottom of her back. It's pink. Mild. Like a sunburn. It's not open. It's not broken. I looked with a flashlight.
Nurse -> Okay. Pink, not open. Is it warm to the touch? Does it hurt her when you touch it?
Caller -> It's a little warm. She doesn't say it hurts. She moans a little when I turn her, but she moans when I turn her anyway.
Nurse -> Okay. Does the skin look blistered, or dark, or have any drainage?
Caller -> No. No blister. No dark spot. No drainage. Just pink. Just the one patch. About, I don't know, the size of a half dollar.
Nurse -> Does she wear anything tight at the hip, or has she been lying in one spot?
Caller -> She lies on her back mostly. We try to turn her but she likes her back. She's stubborn.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people are.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that it's caught early. What's your mom's date of birth, Annika?
Caller -> December seventeenth, nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a good number for you?
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one four six.
Nurse -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one four six. Is that right?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to place an order with the supply company for briefs, underpads, and barrier cream. I'll ask them to deliver Monday.
Caller -> Monday? Can they do earlier? I'm worried about running out Sunday night.
Nurse -> Monday is the earliest the company delivers.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> What size does she use?
Caller -> Large. Medium doesn't fit. She's tall. She was five nine.
Nurse -> Large. Got it.
Caller -> And the cream. The one in the white tube. With the zinc.
Nurse -> I'll put that on the order.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Also, I'd like to send a nurse out Tuesday to look at that patch of skin.
Caller -> Tuesday. Okay. I'll be here. I work from home on Tuesdays.
Nurse -> In the meantime, change her right away when she's wet. Clean with warm water and a soft cloth, pat dry, don't rub. And put the barrier cream on after every change.
Caller -> Right away. Warm water. Soft cloth. Pat dry. Cream after every change. Okay. I'm using wipes sometimes. Should I stop?
Nurse -> If the wipes have alcohol or perfume, yes. Use plain water for now.
Caller -> Plain water. Okay.
Nurse -> And turn her to a different side at least every two hours, and keep the sheets smooth, no wrinkles under her.
Caller -> Every two hours. I set an alarm. I've been doing it overnight too. My husband helps. We take turns.
Nurse -> That's great. You're doing it right.
Caller -> I try. I feel like I'm always behind.
Caller -> There's laundry, there's meals, there's her. And then my own kids. I'm always chasing something.
Nurse -> That's what caregiving feels like. You're keeping all the plates in the air.
Caller -> Mostly. A couple have dropped.
Nurse -> That's okay. Plates break.
Nurse -> You're not. You caught this early.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Call us if the redness turns dark red or purple, if the skin opens, or if she gets a fever or seems to be in new pain.
Caller -> Dark red. Purple. Opens. Fever. New pain. Okay. I'll check twice a day.
Nurse -> Good. How's your mom otherwise today?
Caller -> Sleepy. Comfortable. She had a few sips of juice. She's peaceful.
Nurse -> Does she still recognize you?
Caller -> Sometimes. Yesterday she called me by my sister's name. Then she smiled and said, you're the other one.
Nurse -> That's sweet.
Caller -> It is. I'm taking it.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you for calling back so fast.
Nurse -> Of course. Call anytime.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Yolanda.
Nurse -> Take care.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pine Ridge Hospice, this is Walter.
Caller -> Hello. Yes. Hello. This is Hildegard Pfeiffer. H I L D E G A R D. Pfeiffer is P F E I F F E R. The P is silent. Well, no, it isn't silent, you say it. Never mind. I'm a patient.
Nurse -> Ha. It's a tricky one. I'll practice.
Caller -> Nobody ever gets it. Fine, fine. Just say Hilda.
Nurse -> Hi Hildegard. I've got you. Thank you for spelling it. What's going on today?
Caller -> I have a bruise. A big one. On my hip. The left. I found it this morning when I was getting dressed. It's purple and yellow. And I don't know where it came from.
Nurse -> Okay. A big bruise on your left hip. Do you remember hitting it, or falling?
Caller -> That's the thing. I don't know. I might have fallen last night. Or I might have dreamed it. I had a dream where I was on the floor. And I woke up in bed. So I don't know if I did or I didn't.
Nurse -> Okay. That's honest. Let me ask. When you woke up, were you in your bed, or on the floor?
Caller -> In my bed. Under the covers. But I got up in the night to use the bathroom. So I don't know. Maybe I fell on the way, and got up, and went back to bed. I don't remember.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you remember anything about the bathroom trip?
Caller -> Not really. It was dark. I used the walker, I think. It was parked by the bed. This morning it was by the dresser. So I moved it, I suppose.
Nurse -> Okay. How does your hip feel? Is it painful?
Caller -> It aches. A three, I'd say. When I walk, it's a little more. Sitting, it's fine. A three.
Nurse -> A three. Okay. Can you walk on it?
Caller -> Yes. I walked to the kitchen. With the walker. I made my tea. I'm slow, but I walked. I don't have trouble putting weight on it. Just aching.
Nurse -> Okay, that's good. Did you hit your head? Any headache, dizziness, or feeling confused?
Caller -> No. My head's fine. No headache. No dizzy. I'm clear. I did the crossword. I got twelve down.
Nurse -> Twelve down. What was the clue?
Caller -> A bird. Five letters. Heron. Easy. I've been doing these for sixty years.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for you.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Hildegard, I need your date of birth for the chart.
Caller -> June second. Nineteen forty six. No. Forty five. Nineteen forty five. I'm eighty one. Forty five.
Nurse -> June second, nineteen forty five. Thank you. And what's a good number for you?
Caller -> Oh, goodness. My number. I never call myself. It's on the thing. The sticker, on the phone. Hold on. I can't see it. I don't have my glasses.
Nurse -> No problem. I have a number on file in your chart. Can I use that one?
Caller -> Yes. Please use that one. That's right. That's the right one. It's the same.
Caller -> Is that all right? It's the landline? I only have the landline. I don't do the cell phone.
Nurse -> The landline is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll use the number we have on file. Now, I'd like to send a nurse out this afternoon to look at your hip and check you over.
Caller -> This afternoon. Oh good. I'll be here. I'm always here.
Nurse -> Are you eating okay today?
Caller -> Toast and tea. A banana. I'm a small eater.
Nurse -> That sounds fine.
Nurse -> I'll also leave a message for the team, to let them know about the bruise and the possible fall.
Caller -> Do they need to know? I don't want to be a bother.
Nurse -> They do. A fall, even a possible one, is something we always want to know about.
Caller -> Okay. If you say so.
Nurse -> Until the nurse gets there, please use your walker every time you get up. Keep a light on at night. And wear your slippers, the ones with the grips.
Caller -> The walker. A light. The grippy slippers. I have a night light in the hall. It's a little duck. I'll put one in the bedroom too.
Nurse -> A duck night light. I like it.
Caller -> My granddaughter gave it to me. It quacks if you clap.
Nurse -> Ha. Please don't clap.
Caller -> I won't clap at three in the morning.
Nurse -> And Hildegard, call us if the pain gets worse, if you can't put weight on the leg, or if you get a headache or feel confused. If you fall and can't get up, call 911.
Caller -> Worse pain. Can't stand. Headache. Confused. 911 if I can't get up. Okay. I have the button. The necklace. Should I wear it?
Nurse -> Yes, wear it. Always.
Caller -> I took it off in the shower and I think I left it on the sink. That might be why I don't remember. I didn't have it on last night. Oh dear.
Nurse -> Put it on right now, please. Go get it.
Caller -> Hold on. I'm going. With the walker. Slowly. I'm in the bathroom. There it is. On the sink. Okay. I'm putting it around my neck. Done.
Nurse -> Good. Press it to test it, if you like. It will call the center.
Caller -> Not now. I'll leave it. I'm fine.
Caller -> It's a heavy thing on my neck. I forget it. Like glasses on my head.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of people do. It's worth wearing.
Caller -> Yes, Walter.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anyone who checks on you daily?
Caller -> My neighbor, Dolores. She brings the paper. And my granddaughter calls at night.
Nurse -> Good. I'll let the nurse know when she comes.

Nurse -> Ha. I'm a nurse. But thank you.
Caller -> Well, thank you. Goodbye now.
Nurse -> Goodbye, Hildegard. See you this afternoon.
