transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Grove Palliative Care, this is Hassan.
Caller -> Hi, hi, this is Tess Aldridge. I'm the niece of Beulah Marchetti. I'm staying with her. Her sugar's low. It's really low. She's confused. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Okay Tess. I'm here. Is Beulah awake?
Caller -> She's awake. She's in the kitchen chair. She's sweating. Her hands are shaking. She's saying funny things. She said the stove was a cat.
Nurse -> Okay. What does her sugar read?
Caller -> Forty eight. Forty eight. I checked it twice. The first time it said forty nine. Then forty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Forty eight. That's low. Did she pass out? Is she having a seizure?
Caller -> No. No passing out. No seizure. She's sitting up. She's looking at me. She's just, off. She's not making sense.
Nurse -> Okay. Can she swallow? Can she hold a cup?
Caller -> She can drink. She sipped water a minute ago. Her hands shake but she can hold it.
Nurse -> Okay. Tess, I need you to give her four ounces of juice, right now. Orange juice or apple juice. A half cup. Do you have some?
Caller -> I have orange. In the fridge. Hold on. Can you hear me? I'm walking. I'm getting it. Okay. Pouring. Half a cup. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. Have her drink it slowly. All of it. Don't force her.
Caller -> Aunt Beulah, drink this. It's orange juice. Drink it. Come on. There you go. She's drinking. Little sips. She's making a face.
Caller -> It's too sour. I want the coffee.
Nurse -> Is that Beulah?
Caller -> Yes, that was her. She wants her coffee. She's talking. That's good, right?
Nurse -> That's good. No coffee yet. Juice first. When did she take her insulin?
Caller -> This morning. At eight. The Lantus. I gave it to her. Twenty units. I did it the way the nurse showed me.
Nurse -> Okay. Twenty units of Lantus this morning. And what did she eat for breakfast?
Caller -> Almost nothing. A few bites. She had two bites of toast and some tea. She wasn't hungry. I should have said something.
Nurse -> Okay. That's probably what happened. The insulin worked but she didn't eat. It's not your fault. Is she still sweating?
Caller -> Yes. Her face is wet. She's pale. But she's drinking the juice. The glass is half gone.
Nurse -> Good. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, while you stay with her. They'll want to talk about her insulin.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Thank you. Hold on, she's saying something.
Caller -> Where's Gerald? Where's my husband?
Caller -> Aunt Beulah, he's not here right now. It's me. Tess. Oh dear. Her husband passed years ago. She gets mixed up.
Nurse -> That's the low sugar. It should clear as her sugar comes up. Just stay calm and keep her talking.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm holding her hand. She finished the juice.
Nurse -> Good. We'll recheck in fifteen minutes. Set a timer on your phone. Right now. Fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Setting it. Okay. It's set. Fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> In the meantime, Tess, what's Beulah's date of birth?
Caller -> March eighth. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And what's your cell number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one four zero.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one four zero. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll stay on the phone with you till we recheck. If she becomes unresponsive, has a seizure, can't swallow, or if the sugar doesn't come up after the juice, call 911 right away.
Caller -> Unresponsive. Seizure. Can't swallow. Sugar doesn't come up. 911. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> Is she still talking?
Caller -> She's talking. She's asking for her glasses. She says the room is too bright. I think she's coming around.
Nurse -> Good sign. Keep her sitting. Let her rest.
Caller -> Okay. She's leaning back. She's closing her eyes. Is that okay? Should she sleep?
Nurse -> Don't let her fall asleep yet. Keep her talking. Ask her something simple.
Caller -> Aunt Beulah, what did you do this morning? She says, I made the bed. I didn't. I did.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep chatting.
Caller -> What's your favorite song, Aunt Beulah? She says, Moon River. Moon River. She's humming.
Nurse -> That's good. She's more alert.
Caller -> Yes. She's humming. She looks better. Her color is coming back.
Nurse -> Good. Check the timer. How long?
Caller -> Ten more minutes. I'll keep singing.
Nurse -> You do that.
Caller -> Wait. The timer. It's the alarm. It went off. Fifteen minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. Check her sugar again.
Caller -> Checking. Hold on. Okay, it says eighty four. Eighty four. Oh, thank God.
Nurse -> Eighty four. That's much better. Tess, good job.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I was terrified.
Nurse -> Now, give her something to eat. Crackers with peanut butter, or half a sandwich. And no more insulin today until the clinician talks to you.
Caller -> Crackers and peanut butter. No more insulin. Okay. She wants her coffee now. Can she have it?
Nurse -> After she eats a little, yes.
Caller -> Okay. I'm making the sandwich.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in fifteen minutes to see how she is, and with the clinician's instructions.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay. Thank you, Hassan. You saved us.
Nurse -> You did all the work. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Home Health, this is Mario.
Caller -> Hello, Mario. This is Anselm Boudreaux. A N S E L M. Boudreaux. B O U D R E A U X. It's French. People say Boo-dreaux.
Nurse -> Hi Mr. Boudreaux. Boo-dro. Am I close?
Caller -> Boo-dro. You got it. The Louisiana way. Most people from up here say it wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll try to say it right. How can I help?
Caller -> It's about my wife. Lenora. L E N O R A. Lenora Boudreaux. You've been coming to see her since she got out of the hospital.
Nurse -> I've got her. Heart failure, two weeks out. How's she doing?
Caller -> She's doing good. That's why I'm calling. I'm calling to give you an update, because the nurse Friday said call if there's anything, and there isn't, but I wanted to anyway.
Nurse -> I like that. Go ahead. Let me have her date of birth, first.
Caller -> August twenty third, nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one one four.
Nurse -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one one four. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the home number. It's a landline. Lenora refuses to give it up.
Nurse -> Ha. A lot of folks feel that way.
Caller -> She says a cell phone can't be used to hit a burglar over the head.
Nurse -> Does she keep a bat by the phone?
Caller -> A rolling pin. By the bed. She's been threatening burglars with it since nineteen eighty four. We've never had one.
Nurse -> Ha. They stay away because of the rumor.
Nurse -> Ha. She makes a point.
Caller -> She does.
Nurse -> Okay. So tell me about the weights. Are you doing them every day?
Caller -> Every morning. I wrote it on the calendar. Today was a hundred sixty four. Yesterday a hundred sixty four. The day before, one sixty four and a half. It's been steady. She came home from the hospital at one seventy two, so she's lost eight pounds.
Nurse -> That's excellent. One sixty four. And how's her blood pressure?
Caller -> I took it this morning. One twenty two over seventy. That's good, right?
Nurse -> That's a good number. And the swelling in her ankles?
Caller -> Much better. They're still a little puffy in the evening. Mild. But in the morning they're almost normal. You can see her bones again. She's pleased.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is she short of breath? Chest pain?
Caller -> No. None. She walks to the mailbox and back. She doesn't stop. No chest pain, no pressure. She says she feels better than she has in a year.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. How's she sleeping? Is she having to prop up with pillows?
Caller -> One pillow. Same as always. She sleeps through. No waking up gasping. The hospital told us to watch for that.
Nurse -> Good. And her medicine? Is she taking the water pill?
Caller -> Every morning. The furosemide. Forty milligrams. She took it at eight. And the rest of them, I fill her box on Sunday.
Nurse -> Good. How's her appetite?
Caller -> Good. Too good, she says. She wants to eat everything. Grits, gumbo. That's my question, actually. Salt. I don't know what to do about it.
Nurse -> Okay. What's going on with the salt?
Caller -> Well. My sister. She comes Wednesdays and brings soup. A big pot. Chicken and sausage. And it's delicious, but I know it's loaded with salt. The sausage alone. I don't want to hurt my sister's feelings. But I don't want to hurt Lenora either.
Nurse -> That's a hard spot. It's lovely that she brings food. Let me tell you what I'd suggest.
Caller -> Please.
Nurse -> The key is keeping salt low. Canned soup and deli meats and sausage are the biggest sources. Check labels for sodium. And season with herbs, garlic, lemon, pepper, instead of salt.
Caller -> Herbs. Lemon. Garlic. Okay. We have garlic. We have a whole braid of garlic.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect. Maybe you could ask your sister to make a low salt version. You could give her a recipe.
Caller -> She's seventy eight. She doesn't take recipes. She takes opinions.
Nurse -> Ha. Then maybe let her bring the soup, and Lenora has a small cup. Not the whole bowl.
Caller -> A small cup. That might work. And the rest I eat.
Nurse -> Ha. Mr. Boudreaux, your heart.
Caller -> I know. I know. I'm no better.
Caller -> My cardiologist tells me the same thing. I tell him, doc, I'm eighty one, let me have my sausage.
Nurse -> Ha. What does he say?
Caller -> He says he'd like me to reach eighty two.
Nurse -> Smart man.
Nurse -> I'm going to leave a message for the team to have a dietitian call you, to go over this. They're very good at it. They even have tips for Cajun cooking.
Caller -> A dietitian. That would be wonderful. Maybe they can talk to my sister.
Nurse -> Ha. Maybe they can.
Caller -> I'll hand her the phone and run.
Nurse -> Ha. Smart. Also, keep up the daily weights. Weigh her every morning, after she uses the bathroom and before she eats, in the same kind of clothes, and write it down.
Caller -> After the bathroom, before breakfast. Same nightgown. Write it down. We do. I use the calendar.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call us if she gains three pounds in a day, or five pounds in a week. Or if the swelling gets worse, if she gets short of breath, or needs more pillows to sleep. And call 911 for chest pain.
Caller -> Three in a day. Five in a week. More swelling. Short of breath. More pillows. 911 for chest pain. I wrote that on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. I'm sending a nurse out Friday for a visit.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. That's the regular day. Will it be the same lady?
Nurse -> It might be. The scheduler will confirm. I'm not sure who's on.
Caller -> Lenora likes her. The one with the red hair.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along.
Caller -> She calls her the sunshine nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good one.
Caller -> She says she's bright and she's not too chatty.
Nurse -> The perfect combination.
Caller -> Last time she ran the visit in thirty minutes flat. Pressure, weight, listen to the chest, done.
Nurse -> Efficient. Good.
Caller -> Ha. I'm the chatty one.
Nurse -> I can tell. Mr. Boudreaux, how are you doing?
Caller -> Me? I'm fine. I'm tired. I'm up at six. I'm doing the cooking and the laundry. I never did that before. Fifty three years and I never did laundry.
Nurse -> Fifty three years. Congratulations.
Caller -> Thank you. She keeps the score. She says I owe her thirty years of laundry.
Nurse -> Ha. It's a long ledger.
Caller -> I'm paying it off. Slowly.
Nurse -> Anything else you wanted to ask?
Caller -> No, that's everything. I feel better knowing I said it all. It's easy to forget.
Nurse -> One more thing. Is she able to get around the house on her own?
Caller -> Mostly. With her cane. She's slow but she's steady. She does the stairs one at a time. I stand behind her. Like a spotter.
Nurse -> Good. A spotter is helpful.
Caller -> I've been practicing. I'm a good spotter. I used to spot bowlers.
Nurse -> Bowlers?
Caller -> Ha. Never mind. A bad joke.
Nurse -> That's why you write it down.
Caller -> I do. On the calendar. I have a calendar for everything. Weights, pills, the dog's pills.
Nurse -> You have a dog?
Caller -> A beagle. Gus. He's fourteen. He has a heart pill too. We're a matched set.
Nurse -> Ha. A whole heart failure household.
Caller -> Ha. Yes. Three of us.
Caller -> Gus gets his pill in a piece of cheese. Lenora gets hers with applesauce. I take mine with coffee.
Nurse -> Everyone has a system.
Caller -> The cheese is the best system.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll ask the vet for a cheese approved version.
Nurse -> Take care, Mr. Boudreaux. Tell Lenora I said hello.
Caller -> I will. You have a good evening.
Nurse -> You too.
Caller -> Au revoir.
Nurse -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Seaport Hospice, this is Tobias.
Caller -> Yes, hello. This is Philippa Sandoval. I'm calling about my husband, Everett Sandoval. He's on your service.
Nurse -> Sorry, the line is a little fuzzy. Is it Sandoval, S A N D O V A L?
Caller -> Yes. Sandoval. Like the, it's Spanish. My husband's family is from Laredo.
Caller -> We had a bakery in town for thirty years. Everett did the bread. Four in the morning every day.
Nurse -> What a life. I bet the town misses it.
Nurse -> Got it. Thank you.
Nurse -> Hi Philippa. Good to hear from you. What's happening with Everett?
Caller -> He's sleepy. Very sleepy. And wobbly. He's been like this since Monday. It's Wednesday. I think it's the new dose of his pill.
Nurse -> Sorry, which pill? You broke up.
Caller -> I'll say it again, slowly. It is his nerve pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Which pill are you thinking of?
Caller -> The nerve one. The Gabba pen tin. For his feet. They went up on it Monday. From two hundred to three hundred. Three times a day.
Nurse -> Okay. The gabapentin. Three hundred milligrams, three times a day. Was that your understanding of the new dose?
Caller -> Yes. Gabba pen tin. Three hundred. Three times. That's what the nurse wrote on the sheet.
Nurse -> Okay. And when did he last take one?
Caller -> This morning. At eight. He'll take the next at two. And the last at bedtime.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the sleepiness. Is he hard to wake up?
Caller -> Not hard. But he dozes all the time. In his chair. At the table. He fell asleep with his fork in his hand. Yesterday at supper. His head went down. I'd say he's asleep half the day. Before, he'd be up reading.
Nurse -> Does he sleep through his meals?
Caller -> Only some. Supper mostly.
Nurse -> Okay. When you wake him, is he okay? Does he know where he is?
Caller -> Yes. He knows. He's a little slow. He says, what? And then he's back. He's not confused. Just slow and sleepy.
Nurse -> Okay. And you said wobbly. What do you mean?
Caller -> When he walks. He sways. Like he's had a drink, but he hasn't. He holds the wall. He uses the walker but he sways even with it.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he fallen?
Caller -> No. No fall. Not once. I stand next to him when he goes to the bathroom. He didn't pass out, either. He hasn't fainted.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Any trouble breathing?
Caller -> No. His breathing is regular. I checked a few times. At night too. It's slow and steady. I check at night.
Nurse -> What time was that?
Caller -> About two. Three. I get up and put my hand on his chest. Like with a baby.
Nurse -> That's what a lot of spouses do.
Nurse -> Okay. And his nerve pain? Is the new dose helping?
Caller -> Oh, yes. His feet are much better. He said last night, for the first time in months, I can feel my socks without it burning. That's why I don't know what to do. The sleepiness is bad but the pain is so much better.
Nurse -> That's a real trade off. Okay. Philippa, I need Everett's date of birth.
Caller -> January nineteenth. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one zero five.
Nurse -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one zero five. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Do you have a cell too?
Caller -> Yes, but I never carry it. It's in a drawer. The house phone is the one that rings.
Nurse -> The house phone is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'm going to leave a message for the team, to ask whether the dose of the Gabba pen tin should come down a little. Maybe a different schedule. They'll decide.
Caller -> Would they lower it? I don't want him to lose the pain relief.
Nurse -> They may find a middle dose. That's what I'll ask. I can't say for sure.
Caller -> Okay. I'd like that. A middle.
Nurse -> Until we hear back, don't change or skip the dose yourself. Give it as written. The team will call you with any change.
Caller -> Don't change it. Okay. I almost skipped the two o'clock one today. I'm glad I called.
Caller -> My daughter said call. I said wait. She was right.
Nurse -> Daughters often are.
Nurse -> Yes, wait for the team. I'll call you back tomorrow with their answer.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. I'll be here.
Nurse -> Meanwhile, because he's wobbly, have him use the walker every time, and stay beside him when he walks. Clear the floor of rugs and cords, and keep a night light on.
Caller -> Walker. Stay beside. Clear the floor. Night light. We have the little duck. No. That's my neighbor's. We have a lamp. I'll leave the lamp on.
Nurse -> A lamp works.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if he gets very hard to wake, becomes confused, or his breathing slows down. If you can't wake him at all, call 911.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Confused. Breathing slows. And 911 if I can't wake him. Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> Good. How are you holding up?
Caller -> Tired. I'm checking on him at night. I'm not sleeping.
Caller -> I keep hearing the old house settle and thinking it's him. I've been like that for a week.
Nurse -> It's the hypervigilance. It happens.
Nurse -> That's understandable. Try to rest when he rests.
Caller -> I try. The chair is comfortable.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's all. Thank you, Tobias. You're very patient.
Nurse -> My pleasure. Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Redwood Home Health, this is Ingrid.
Caller -> Hi. Ingrid. This is Anton Vandermeer. My wife is Rochelle Vandermeer. She has the PICC line. For the antibiotics.
Nurse -> Right. Sorry, Anton, what was that last name again, with the V?
Caller -> Vandermeer. V A N D E R M E E R. Dutch. It means from the lake. Or something. My grandfather said.
Nurse -> Got it. Thank you.
Nurse -> Hi Anton. Yes, I know the name. What's going on?
Caller -> We're running low on supplies. And the dressing is peeling. I wanted to call before the weekend.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Let's start with the supplies. How many saline flushes?
Caller -> I'm looking at the box. Two. Two saline.
Nurse -> Okay. And the heparin flushes?
Caller -> One. Just one.
Nurse -> Okay. Dressing change kits?
Caller -> None. The nurse used the last one on Monday. There's none in the box.
Nurse -> Okay. None. So two saline, one heparin, and no kits.
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> How often is she flushing?
Caller -> Do you want me to read the lot numbers off the box?
Nurse -> No, the pharmacy has them. I just want the counts.
Caller -> Okay. I'm an engineer. I like numbers.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you're perfect for this.
Caller -> After each infusion. Twice a day. So we have about a day. Maybe a day and a half.
Nurse -> Okay. That is low. I'll get an order in today.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Tell me about the dressing. What's it doing?
Caller -> The corner. The top corner. The edge is lifting. It's about, I'd say, a half inch. The clear part. She says it itches.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the skin under it red? Any drainage, or swelling in the arm?
Caller -> I looked. No redness. No drainage. Her arm is normal. No swelling. It's just the edge that's lifting. She showered and I think the steam did it.
Nurse -> Does she complain about the arm? Any ache?
Caller -> No. She says it feels like nothing. She forgets it's there. Except the itching.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever or chills?
Caller -> No. We take her temperature twice a day. It's been normal. Ninety eight something.
Nurse -> Good. Anton, what's Rochelle's date of birth?
Caller -> May thirtieth. Nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one four nine.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one four nine. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to call the infusion pharmacy and order saline flushes, heparin flushes, and dressing change kits.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. How soon can they come?
Nurse -> I'll ask for delivery Thursday. I'll push for earlier.
Caller -> Thursday is cutting it close. We'll run out Wednesday night.
Nurse -> I know. That's why I want a nurse to come out tomorrow. She can bring flushes from our stock and change the dressing.
Caller -> Oh. Good. Tomorrow. That works. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here. I work from home.
Nurse -> And she's comfortable with the schedule? The morning and evening infusions?
Caller -> She's fine. I do the hookup. I set the timer. She reads a book for the thirty minutes.
Nurse -> Sounds like a good routine.
Caller -> It is. We're pros now. Three weeks in.
Nurse -> Perfect. In the meantime, don't pull at the peeling corner. Cover the dressing with the plastic shower cover when she showers. And wash your hands before touching the line.
Caller -> Don't pull. Shower cover. Wash hands. We have the cover. It's a sleeve. It didn't fit well. The steam got under.
Nurse -> Okay. The nurse will check the fit tomorrow.
Caller -> We got the cover from the pharmacy. It's blue. It came with the supplies. Maybe it's the wrong size.
Nurse -> Possibly. The nurse can bring another.
Caller -> Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And call us if she gets a fever or chills, redness or drainage at the site, swelling or pain in the arm, or if the line leaks or comes out. If it bleeds a lot, press on it and call 911.
Caller -> Fever. Chills. Red. Drainage. Swelling. Leaking. Out. Bleeding, press and 911. Okay. I'll write that down.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. How long does she have left on the antibiotics?
Nurse -> I don't have the date in front of me. The nurse can tell you tomorrow.
Caller -> Okay. I think it's two more weeks.
Nurse -> The nurse will confirm.
Caller -> She's ready to be done. She says she's tired of the bag and the pole.
Nurse -> That's understandable. It's a long course.
Caller -> She's named the pole. Gerald. She says Gerald is the only man who follows her everywhere.
Nurse -> Ha. Gerald the pole.
Caller -> Thanks, Ingrid. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Quiet Waters Hospice, this is Rafael.
Caller -> Hi. Hi. This is Maren Hesselgrave. I'm calling about my mother. Ottilie Hesselgrave. I found something. She has two patches on. Two. I don't think she's supposed to.
Nurse -> Okay Maren. Take a breath. Tell me about the patches. Are these her pain patches?
Caller -> Yes. The fentanyl. I was giving her a bath. A sponge bath. I turned her and there's one on her back, the left shoulder blade. And another one, lower, on the right. Two.
Nurse -> Okay. Two patches on. Do you know when each was put on?
Caller -> The new one, my brother put it on this morning. At nine. It was changing day. He didn't take the old one off. I asked him just now. He said, I thought the old one fell off. The old one is from Friday. Friday night.
Nurse -> Okay. So one from Friday night, and one from this morning. How strong is each one?
Caller -> They both say fentanyl twenty five. Micrograms. Twenty five. It's printed on them. Twenty five.
Nurse -> Okay. Twenty five micrograms each. So she's had fifty for about the last twelve hours. How is she acting? Is she sleepy?
Caller -> She's sleepier. Yes. She's been asleep all afternoon. More than usual. But she wakes up when I say her name. She opened her eyes and said, Maren, you're hurting my back.
Nurse -> Okay. She wakes to her name. That's a good sign. Is she talking normally?
Caller -> A little slow. She's mumbling a little. But she makes sense. She asked for her tea.
Nurse -> Okay. Maren, I want you to look at her breathing. Count how many breaths she takes in one minute. Can you do that?
Caller -> Yes. Hold on. I have my phone timer. Okay. I'm looking at her chest. One, two, three. I'll count to sixty. Okay. Fourteen. Fourteen breaths.
Nurse -> Fourteen is okay. Is her breathing regular, not shallow?
Caller -> Regular. A little deep. No pauses. It's like she's sleeping.
Caller -> She's snoring a little. A soft snore. She does that when she's really out.
Nurse -> Okay. Soft snoring is fine, as long as she wakes up.
Nurse -> Okay. Look at her lips and fingertips. What color?
Caller -> Pink. Normal. No blue. And she wakes up. She's not hard to wake. She's grumpy when I wake her.
Nurse -> Good. Okay. Now I'd like you to do something. I want you to peel off the older fentanyl patch now. The one from Friday. Keep the new one on. Is that clear?
Caller -> Take off the old one. The one from Friday. Which is the lower one, I think. The brother said he put the new one on the left. So the right is the old one.
Nurse -> Check the date. People write the date and time on the patch. Does either one have writing on it?
Caller -> Yes. The right one says Friday, ten p.m. The left one says today, nine a.m. So take off the right. The Friday one.
Nurse -> Correct. Peel it off slowly. Hold the skin down with your other hand.
Caller -> Okay. Peeling. It's sticky. It's coming. Okay. It's off. I have it. It's in my hand.
Nurse -> Good. Now fold it in half, sticky sides together. Then put it in a bag, a sealed bag, and then another bag. Keep it away from kids and pets until the nurse takes it.
Caller -> Fold. Sticky sides together. Double bag. I have a freezer bag. And another. I'm doing it. There. Done. I put it in the cupboard above the sink. The high one.
Nurse -> Perfect. Wash your hands. And wipe her skin where it was, with plain water.
Caller -> Washing my hands. I'll wipe her back. Okay. There's a mark. A little red square. It looks like a sunburn.
Caller -> The water's warm. She says thank you. She's awake enough to say thank you.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Nurse -> That's normal where a patch has been. Okay. I'm paging the on-call clinician now. They'll want to know about the two patches and how sleepy she is.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I'm scared. Is she going to be okay?
Caller -> I keep thinking, what if I'd waited until tomorrow to bathe her. I almost did.
Nurse -> You didn't wait. That's what matters.
Nurse -> I know it's frightening. Let's take it one step at a time.
Caller -> Okay. One step.
Nurse -> She's awake, she's talking, she's breathing at a good rate. Those are all good. But we need to watch her closely. That's why I'm sending a nurse out within the next two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. I'll keep my phone with me.
Nurse -> In the meantime, I need you to check her every ten minutes. Look at her breathing, and say her name to see if she wakes up.
Caller -> Every ten minutes. Breathing. Say her name. I'll set a timer. Ten minutes.
Nurse -> Good. And if she's hard to wake, if her breathing slows or gets shallow, or if her lips turn blue, call 911 right away. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Slow breathing. Blue lips. 911. Okay. I'll do it.
Nurse -> Is there someone else with you?
Caller -> My brother is here. He's in the kitchen. He feels terrible. He's crying.
Caller -> He drove in from Tucson on Sunday. He's been doing the nights so I can sleep. He's exhausted.
Nurse -> It's easy to make a mistake when you're that tired.
Nurse -> Tell him it's okay. Mistakes like this happen. He did the right thing by telling you.
Caller -> I'll tell him. He's a mess. He keeps saying, I killed her. I told him she's fine.
Nurse -> Reassure him. She's fine right now, and we're watching.
Caller -> He's in the doorway now. He's asking if he can come sit with her.
Nurse -> Yes. Let him sit with her. That might help him too.
Caller -> Okay. Come in, Dev. Sit. He's sitting. He took her hand.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> What's your mother's date of birth, Maren? For the on-call.
Caller -> February third. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one five five.
Nurse -> Five oh five, five five five, zero one five five. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll talk to you in twenty minutes.
Caller -> Thank you, Rafael.
Nurse -> You did well.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Tidewater Pediatric Home Care, this is Noelle.
Caller -> Hi, Noelle. It's Ibrahim Nasser. I'm Zainab's dad. Zainab, Z A I N A B. Nasser, N A S S E R. We talked on Monday.
Nurse -> And how do you say her name, so I get it right? Zay-nab?
Caller -> Zay-nab. Yes. It means a fragrant flower. My grandmother's name.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> Hi Ibrahim. Yes. Zainab. I remember. How is she?
Caller -> She's good. She's really good. I'm just calling with an update. My wife said call, since she has the appointment tomorrow, and I wanted to say before that.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me grab her chart. Do you have her date of birth?
Caller -> March fourteenth, twenty twenty six. She's seven months. Almost.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one five seven.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one five seven. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's mine.
Nurse -> Great. So how is the feeding?
Caller -> Great. She eats four ounces every three hours. Takes all of it. Burps. Sometimes she spits up a little, but that's normal, right? A tiny bit. Not a lot.
Nurse -> Is she on formula or breast milk?
Caller -> Formula. The preemie kind, the higher calorie one. My wife pumps some but not enough.
Nurse -> Do you burp her in the middle of the feed, or only after?
Caller -> Both. Halfway, and after. My wife showed me the pat on the back. I'm still learning the rhythm.
Nurse -> A little spit up is normal. Is it forceful? Projectile?
Caller -> No. It dribbles. Just a little on the burp cloth.
Nurse -> Good. And her weight?
Caller -> We weighed her at the pediatrician on Tuesday. Fourteen pounds. She was thirteen and a half three weeks ago. Fourteen pounds, one ounce, actually.
Nurse -> That's a great gain. And her oxygen?
Caller -> The monitor says ninety six. Ninety six most of the time. It goes to ninety five when she's fussing. It's on a quarter liter. A quarter. The little dial on the concentrator.
Nurse -> Good. Any fever, cough, fast breathing?
Caller -> No fever. We take her temperature every morning. No cough. And her breathing's regular. No fast breathing, no pulling in at the ribs. I know what to look for. You showed me.
Nurse -> Good memory. And her color? Pink?
Caller -> Pink. Pink cheeks. A little round. She looks like a peach.
Nurse -> Ha. A healthy peach.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Is she sleeping okay?
Caller -> She sleeps five hours. In a row. At night. From ten to three. And then she eats. And she goes back down till seven. My wife thinks we should name her Rip Van Winkle.
Nurse -> Ha. Rip Van Winkle. That's a good sleeper.
Caller -> She gets it from my wife.
Nurse -> Ha. What are her wake windows like during the day?
Caller -> She's awake about an hour and a half. Then she naps. She likes to look at the ceiling fan.
Nurse -> Ha. A ceiling fan fan.
Caller -> She loves it. She watches it go round. Like it's the best show.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Ibrahim, how are you and your wife doing?
Caller -> Better. Much better. At first it was hard. The oxygen, the monitor, all the alarms. But now it's routine. We don't jump every time.
Nurse -> That's good. It's a lot at first.
Caller -> It was. I had a spreadsheet. Of every feed, every diaper. I printed it out and put it on the fridge.
Nurse -> A spreadsheet. I love it.
Caller -> I'm an accountant. It's how I cope.
Caller -> My wife calls it my security blanket. I say it's my data.
Nurse -> Data is a fine blanket.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Caller -> Anyway. She's good. That's the update.
Nurse -> It's a great update. I'll send a nurse out Thursday to see her and to look at the equipment.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. My wife will be home. I'll be at work.
Nurse -> That's fine. In the meantime, keep checking the little tubing, the nasal cannula, for kinks. And wipe the prongs and her cheeks with a damp cloth every day. Keep the tank upright, away from any flames.
Caller -> Check the tube. Wipe the prongs and cheeks. Tank upright, away from flames. Yes. We don't light candles anymore. My mother in law is upset. She had a candle thing.
Nurse -> Ha. Safety first.
Caller -> I told her, Mama, I love you, but no candles.
Nurse -> And call us if she has fast or hard breathing, blue lips, a fever of one hundred point four or higher, if she's feeding poorly, or if she has fewer wet diapers. Call 911 for blue color or if she stops breathing for a few seconds.
Caller -> Fast breathing. Blue lips. Fever, one hundred point four. Poor feeding. Fewer wet diapers. 911 for blue or pauses. Okay. I have it on the spreadsheet.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course you do.
Caller -> It has its own tab.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you, Noelle. You've been great.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Give Zainab a kiss from me.
Caller -> She smiles when she hears a woman's voice on the phone. I think she thinks you're her.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her it's me, the voice from the phone.
Caller -> She's looking at the phone right now. Wide eyes.
Nurse -> Say hi for me.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

Nurse -> Redwood Home Health, this is Valerie.
Caller -> Val. Valerie. It's Graham. Graham Pettibone. P E T T I B O N E. I'm, I'm having a bad. Bad day.
Nurse -> Graham, I can barely hear you. Can you speak up a little, or hold the phone closer?
Caller -> Is this. Better? I'm. Using. The speaker.
Nurse -> A little better. Keep it close.
Nurse -> Hi Graham. I'm sorry. Take your time. I'm listening.
Caller -> I ran out. Of my. My Sinemet. The pharmacy. Didn't have it.
Nurse -> You ran out of your Sinemet. The pharmacy didn't have it. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. They said. Back order. They said. Wednesday. Tomorrow.
Nurse -> Which pharmacy is it?
Caller -> The. One. On Fifth. By the. Bank.
Nurse -> The one on Fifth by the bank. Okay. I have it.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you take your last dose?
Caller -> Last night. Eight. Eight o'clock. Nothing since. Four doses. I missed. Four.
Nurse -> Okay. Last night at eight, and nothing since. So you've missed four doses. How's your body feeling?
Caller -> Stiff. So stiff. Like a board. I can't. I can hardly move. And slow. Everything's slow.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry. Is your tremor different?
Caller -> Worse. Much worse. My hand. Shaking. Can't hold the cup.
Nurse -> Okay. Graham, have you fallen?
Caller -> No fall. No. But this morning. I froze. At the bathroom door. My feet. Stuck. Like glue. Couldn't move. Five minutes.
Nurse -> Five minutes. That's a long time to be stuck.
Caller -> Felt like. An hour. My son. Calls me. A statue.
Nurse -> Ha. A statue with a sense of humor.
Nurse -> That sounds scary. Did you stay on your feet?
Caller -> I held the door. Frame. I held it. Then it. Let go. And I went in. No fall.
Nurse -> Did you hurt anything?
Caller -> No. Just. My pride.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Is anyone with you?
Caller -> My son. He's. At work. He's coming at five. I'm alone. Now.
Nurse -> What does your son do?
Caller -> He's a mechanic. At the. Dealership. He comes. Home. For lunch. But not. Today.
Nurse -> Okay. Graham, I'm going to do a few things. First, I'm going to call your pharmacy right now. I'll see if they can find the Sinemet anywhere, another store, and get it to you today.
Caller -> That would. Be great. They said. Wednesday. But I need. Today.
Nurse -> I understand. I'll push. And I'm going to page the on-call clinician too, to ask what to do for you until the pills arrive. Sometimes they can bridge it.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Thank you.
Nurse -> Graham, your voice is very soft. I'm having trouble with some words. I'm going to repeat what I hear, and you tell me if I got it wrong.
Caller -> Okay. Yes. That's. Fine.
Nurse -> You ran out of Sinemet, last dose was last night at eight. You're stiff, your tremor is worse, and you froze this morning but didn't fall. Right?
Caller -> Right. Yes. All right.
Nurse -> And your son's coming at five. Is that right?
Caller -> Five. Yes. Five.
Nurse -> Okay. And you take the Sinemet how often?
Caller -> Sinemet. One. Tablet. Five times. A day. Twenty five. A hundred. The strength.
Nurse -> One tablet, five times a day. Thank you. Now, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> September. Twelfth. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> September twelfth, nineteen sixty four. And your number, Graham?
Caller -> Six four six. Five five five. Zero one nine eight.
Nurse -> Six four six, five five five, zero one nine eight. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm also going to send a nurse to see you this afternoon. I'll try for the next couple of hours.
Caller -> Pardon? Say. Again.
Nurse -> I'm going to send a nurse out to see you.
Caller -> This afternoon. Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Until then, stay seated unless someone's with you. If you have to get up, use your walker. If your feet freeze, stop. Shift your weight side to side, like rocking. Then try to step over a line on the floor, or count out loud, one, two, three, and step on three.
Caller -> Rock. Side to side. Step over. A line. Count. One. Two. Three. Yes. I know. The trick. It helps. Sometimes.
Nurse -> Good. And call us right away if you fall, if you have trouble swallowing or breathing, if you get a high fever, or if your muscles get very rigid and you feel confused. Call 911 if you fall and can't get up.
Caller -> Fall. Swallow. Breathe. Fever. Rigid. Confused. 911. If I can't. Get up. I have. The button.
Nurse -> Good. Wear the button. Is it on?
Nurse -> Is there water within reach? A drink?
Caller -> Yes. A cup. With a. Straw. Lid. My son. Set it.
Nurse -> Good. Sip when you can.
Caller -> Yes. Around. My neck.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call the pharmacy now and call you back as soon as I know.
Caller -> Thank you. Val. You are. Very. Kind.
Nurse -> Hang in there, Graham. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Ines.
Caller -> Hi, Ines. This is Cheryl Alderete. I'm calling about my mother, Winona Alderete. I might be overreacting. I just. I don't know.
Nurse -> Overreacting is not a thing here. Tell me what you're noticing, and I'll tell you what I think.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I wrote some notes on the back of an envelope. In case I forgot.
Caller -> Last time I called I forgot half the questions. The nurse said write it down.
Nurse -> Yes. I'm glad you did.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's a good habit.
Nurse -> Hi Cheryl. You're not bothering me. Tell me what's on your mind.
Caller -> It's just. I don't know if she's getting worse or if it's a bad week. That's what I can't tell.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you're seeing and we'll sort through it together. First, can I get her date of birth?
Caller -> November sixth. Nineteen forty.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one four five.
Nurse -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one four five. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. So what's been different?
Caller -> She's tired. More tired. I think. She sleeps late, she naps after lunch. But then she was up at four in the afternoon doing her puzzle. So I don't know if she's more tired or just tired.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she more tired than last week?
Caller -> Maybe. Yes. A little. I think. Last week she was up by eight. This week it's nine, ten. But it's cold. It's raining. Everybody's tired when it rains.
Nurse -> Is there anything else different about the house this week? Visitors, changes in routine?
Caller -> My nephew was here Sunday with the kids. They were loud. She loved it, but she was wiped out Monday.
Caller -> She told the little one a story about when she was a girl in Hawaii. She hasn't told that story in years. I sat and listened.
Nurse -> What a gift. Those stories matter.
Caller -> I recorded some on my phone. I didn't tell her. Is that bad?
Nurse -> I think it's lovely. Keep them.
Nurse -> That can do it. Visitors take a lot of energy.
Caller -> I know. She did the whole thing. She made them cocoa. And then paid for it.
Nurse -> That's possible. What about eating?
Caller -> She's eating less. About half. Half of what she usually eats. Yesterday she had half a scrambled egg and some toast, and half a bowl of soup at lunch. She says she's not hungry.
Nurse -> Does she mention the taste of food? Does anything taste off?
Caller -> She says everything tastes like paper. Except the pastries. And tea with honey.
Nurse -> That's common. Tastes change.
Caller -> I noticed. I put honey in everything now.
Nurse -> Okay. Half of her usual. Is that a change from last week?
Caller -> Yes. Last week she had a whole plate. I'd say last week was a full plate.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Tea. A lot of tea. Water when I bring it. She sips.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything with her thinking? Is she more confused?
Caller -> Well. Once. She called me Darlene. That's my sister. Darlene, she said, bring me my glasses. And I said, Mom, it's Cheryl. And she said, oh, I know. I know. Don't fuss. So I don't know. Was that confusion or was that a slip?
Nurse -> It could be either. When was that?
Caller -> Tuesday. And it hasn't happened again. Today she knew me perfectly. She told me my slip was showing.
Caller -> She was in a mood. She told me my hair looks like a haystack. Then she asked for lipstick.
Nurse -> Lipstick. That sounds like someone who feels like herself.
Caller -> That's what I thought! I almost cried. She hadn't asked for lipstick in a month.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like her.
Caller -> My slip wasn't showing.
Caller -> It was a little.
Nurse -> Is that your mom in the background?
Caller -> Yes. She's in the next room. She's watching her show. She can hear me. Mom, I'm talking to the nurse!
Caller -> What? I can't hear you, Cheryl!
Caller -> I'm on the phone with the hospice! Never mind!
Nurse -> Does she use a hearing aid?
Caller -> She has two. She keeps them in the drawer. She says they whistle. I put them in for her in the morning and she takes them out by ten.
Nurse -> That explains the shouting.
Caller -> It explains everything. The whole house shouts.
Nurse -> Ha. She sounds sharp.
Caller -> She is. That's what makes it so confusing. One minute she's sharp, the next she's quiet. I can't tell what's the disease and what's just her.
Nurse -> That's really common, Cheryl. It doesn't move in a straight line. Is she in any pain?
Caller -> No. She says no. She says she's fine. She grimaces when I move her but she says that's her hip.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have any other pain, or trouble breathing, nausea?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. Her breathing is fine. No nausea. She's comfortable.
Nurse -> Is she having regular bowel movements and passing urine?
Caller -> Yes. Same as always. I keep track on a chart. Don't ask me why I keep track. It's a thing I do.
Nurse -> It's a good thing to do.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fallen?
Caller -> No. She uses her walker. She's been careful.
Nurse -> Okay. Cheryl, I think what I'm hearing is a few small changes, more tired, less eating, one mix up, but she's comfortable, she's alert, and she's doing her puzzle. That could be a gradual change or a rough patch, and I can't tell from the phone either.
Caller -> That's what I thought. It's so hard to know.
Caller -> My brother says I worry too much. He lives in Denver. He calls and says, Mom sounds great! She always sounds great on the phone.
Nurse -> A lot of patients rally for the phone. Family who live close see the whole picture.
Caller -> Exactly. That's what I told him. He doesn't see the afternoons.
Nurse -> Maybe he could come for a visit and see for himself.
Caller -> I'll mention it. He might say he's too busy. He's always too busy.
Nurse -> I'd like a nurse to see her. I'm going to send someone tomorrow to check her and compare with her last visit. That's the best way to tell the trend.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Yes. That would help. I'd feel better if someone looked.
Nurse -> And I'll leave a message for the team about the tiredness and the eating, so they have it.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, offer her small portions of her favorite foods, and sips of fluids through the day. Don't push. It's normal for appetite to come and go.
Caller -> Small portions. Favorites. Don't push. Okay. She loves the little pastries from the bakery. The ones with the cinnamon.
Nurse -> Then give her a cinnamon pastry. Honestly.
Caller -> I'll go tomorrow. I'll go first thing.
Nurse -> What bakery is it?
Caller -> Sullivan's. On Maple. They've been there fifty years. My mother knows the owner's mother.
Nurse -> A good bakery is a public service.
Caller -> That's what my mother says. She says it's the only reason she's still alive.
Nurse -> Ha. Then she should get one every day.
Nurse -> And Cheryl, call us any time. Day or night. Even for small changes. You don't have to wait until it's an emergency.
Caller -> I never know what counts as small. I felt silly calling.
Nurse -> It's never silly. This is exactly the kind of call we want.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps.
Caller -> Cheryl! Is that the hospice? Tell them I want the pastry!
Caller -> Mom! Yes. I'll tell them.
Nurse -> Ha. Message received.
Caller -> She heard everything.
Nurse -> She's in good form.
Caller -> Better than mine. Okay. I'll let you go.
Nurse -> You can call back any time.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Ines.
Nurse -> Take care, Cheryl.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Heartland Hospice, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hello. Hello? It's two in the morning, I'm sorry. This is Lucia Benedetti. It's my husband. Aurelio Benedetti. He is up. He is not sleeping.
Nurse -> Hi Lucia. No apology. I'm here. What's he doing?
Caller -> He is restless. Since midnight. He pulls the sheet. He picks. Like this, I'm showing you, but you can't see. He picks and picks at the blanket. And he mumbles.
Nurse -> Okay. Picking at the sheets since midnight. Is he awake with his eyes open?
Caller -> Open. Yes. He looks at me but he's not, he's not here. I say Aurelio and he says what, what. And then picks again.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he seem to be in pain? Is he grimacing, groaning, holding anywhere?
Caller -> No pain. I don't think. No face. No groans. His face is calm. Only the hands. Only the hands are busy.
Nurse -> Does he know where he is, usually? At night?
Caller -> Sometimes he thinks it's the old house. The one on Garfield. He asks for his mother.
Nurse -> That can happen. It's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever? Does he feel hot?
Caller -> No. He is cool. I touched his head. Not hot. I don't have the thermometer here. Downstairs. He is not hot.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he had anything for the restlessness?
Nurse -> He had the Ativan at nine last night. The little one. And nothing since.
Caller -> Yes. Right. The Ativan. At nine. Point five. That's what the label says. One small tablet. Point five milligrams.
Nurse -> Okay. Ativan, point five milligrams, every four hours as needed. Is that what the bottle says?
Caller -> Yes. Every four hours if needed. As needed. I gave it at nine.
Nurse -> Okay. Lucia, it's been about five hours since nine. So he's due. You can give him another one now.
Caller -> Now? I can give it now? I was afraid it was too soon.
Nurse -> It's not too soon. It's been more than four hours.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I will get it. Hold on, I go to the cabinet. I am walking. The bottle is in the kitchen. I have it. Point five. I give him one. Under the tongue? Or swallow?
Nurse -> Whichever the label says. Either way, with a little water or under the tongue.
Caller -> It says under the tongue. Okay. Aurelio, open. Open, please. Under the tongue. Good. He took it. It melts.
Nurse -> Perfect. What time is it now?
Caller -> Two ten. Two ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Write down the time on the sheet. Two ten.
Caller -> I write. Two ten. Done.
Nurse -> Now let's help him settle. Keep the room dim and quiet. Speak softly. Sit with him and put your hand on his arm. If you have pillows or blankets padding the bed rails, that helps him not bump.
Caller -> The room is dim. I have the little lamp. I sit. I put my hand. He is looking at my hand. He is quiet. A little.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep talking to him in a low voice. Tell him you're here.
Caller -> Aurelio, I'm here. Lucia. I'm here. It's okay. It's okay. He is touching my hand now. He is not picking.
Nurse -> Good. That's the calming. Lucia, what's his date of birth for the chart?
Caller -> July twenty sixth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one nine one.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, zero one nine one. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call you back in thirty minutes to see how he's doing.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay.
Nurse -> And I'm sending a nurse out this morning to see him.
Caller -> This morning. Yes. Thank you. What time, do you know?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you at seven with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I am awake. I will be awake.
Caller -> Priya, one more thing. Is it normal, this? The picking?
Nurse -> Yes. It's common at this stage. It looks distressing but often it isn't painful for them.
Caller -> That helps. I thought maybe he was cold.
Nurse -> You can add a light blanket if he feels cool.
Nurse -> Call us back if he's not settling thirty minutes after the dose, if he tries to climb out of bed, or if he has any new pain or a fever.
Caller -> Not settling. Climb out. Pain. Fever. Okay. I understand.
Nurse -> Do you have someone with you? A family member, a neighbor?
Caller -> My son is asleep upstairs. I don't want to wake him. He works at the, at the plant. The early shift.
Nurse -> That's okay. But if you need him, wake him.
Caller -> I will. If it's worse. Not now.
Nurse -> Is the front door locked?
Caller -> Yes. And the porch light is on. I always leave it on for the nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. How are you doing? Are you tired?
Caller -> I am always tired now. But it's okay. He did everything for me for fifty years. Now it is my turn.
Nurse -> That's beautiful, Lucia.
Caller -> He is looking at me. Now he is looking like himself. A little.
Nurse -> The medicine's starting to work, maybe.
Caller -> I think. Yes. His hands are still. He is closing his eyes.
Nurse -> Good. Stay with him. I'll call you in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Thank you, Priya. Thank you.
Nurse -> Goodnight, Lucia.
Caller -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hello, Priscilla. This is Rutherford Kaminski. R U T H E R F O R D. Kaminski. I had my cataract done on Monday.
Nurse -> Which eye was it?
Caller -> The left. They'll do the right in six weeks. I'm told it's even easier the second time.
Nurse -> That's what people say.
Nurse -> Hi Mr. Kaminski. Yes. I have you. How's the eye?
Caller -> It's fine. It's good. It's a little scratchy. But I'm calling about the drops. I got confused. I want to make sure I'm using the right ones.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through them. Do you have the bottles in front of you?
Caller -> I do. I have the little white bag from the eye doctor. There are two bottles. One is prednisolone. P R E D N I S O L O N E. It says one drop in the left eye, four times a day.
Caller -> The cap is white. The tears have a blue cap. I put a rubber band on the blue one so I can feel the difference.
Nurse -> Clever. That helps a lot.
Nurse -> Okay. Prednisolone, one drop, four times a day. And the other?
Caller -> Artificial tears. As needed. It says use as needed for dryness.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. So what's confusing you?
Caller -> The pill bottle. In my kitchen. For my arthritis. It says prednisone. P R E D N I S O N E. They look the same! Almost the same word. And I thought, am I using the pill in my eye? Or am I swallowing the eye drops? I thought, what a dumb question. But I didn't want to guess.
Nurse -> That's not a dumb question at all. Those two names look very alike. The drops in the white bag are prednisolone, for the eye only. The pill bottle in your kitchen is prednisone, for your arthritis, to swallow. They're different medicines.
Caller -> Okay. So the drops are only for the eye. And the pill is only to swallow.
Nurse -> Exactly. Don't mix them up.
Caller -> Good. Good. I wasn't sure. I put the bottles in different places now. The drops are by the bed. The pills are by the coffee maker.
Caller -> I tried the dog's food shelf but my wife said no.
Nurse -> Ha. Probably wise.
Nurse -> That's a good system.
Caller -> My wife's idea.
Nurse -> Smart. When was your last drop of prednisolone?
Caller -> This morning. Ten o'clock. I do eight, twelve, four, and eight. Four times. With a drop each time. I use the little alarm on my watch.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the artificial tears?
Caller -> Only when it feels dry. I used it once this morning and once yesterday.
Nurse -> Good. How's the eye feeling? Pain?
Caller -> No pain. Scratchy. Like a little sand. It's not bad. I'd say mild. The doctor said that was normal.
Nurse -> It is normal for a few days. How about your vision?
Caller -> Better every day. It's brighter. The colors are different. The sky is bluer. I didn't know it was supposed to be this blue.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what people say. No sudden loss of vision, no floaters, no flashes?
Caller -> None. No pain, no loss. It's just getting better.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. Mr. Kaminski, let me ask about technique. How are you putting the drops in?
Caller -> I tilt my head back, and pull the lid down, and drop it in. Sometimes I miss. Some goes on my cheek.
Nurse -> That's very common. Wash your hands first, every time. Pull the lower lid down gently, put one drop in the pocket, and don't let the tip touch your eye or lashes. Then close your eye for a minute. And wait five minutes between different drops, like the tears and the prednisolone. Use the tears only if it feels dry.
Caller -> Wash hands. Pull the lid. One drop. Don't touch. Close the eye. Wait five minutes. Tears only if dry. Okay. I'll write that down.
Nurse -> And at night, wear the eye shield. Don't rub or press on the eye. And avoid bending over or lifting anything heavy for now.
Caller -> The shield. Yes. The plastic one with the holes. I wear it. I don't rub. My wife slaps my hand when I try.
Caller -> Gently. Like a mother. Fifty one years, she knows where to slap.
Nurse -> Ha. Experience.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for her.
Caller -> She's been terrific.
Nurse -> What's your date of birth, Mr. Kaminski? For the chart.
Caller -> April eighth, nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one six nine.
Nurse -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one six nine. Is that right?
Caller -> That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll have a nurse come out Friday to look at the eye and watch you put the drops in.
Caller -> Friday. Oh, that would be nice. Can I ask her to show my wife too? She's going to do it when I travel.
Nurse -> Absolutely.
Caller -> I'm going to Maui in two weeks. For my daughter's wedding. After the doctor says I can fly.
Nurse -> What a nice reason to get your eyes fixed.
Caller -> That's what I told the surgeon. I want to see her walk down the aisle.
Nurse -> What's her name?
Caller -> Kailani. She's marrying a surfer. I told her, please don't get married in the water.
Nurse -> Ha. Did she listen?
Caller -> She said we'll see.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Call us if your eye pain gets worse, if you suddenly lose vision, if you see new floaters or flashes of light, or if the eye gets redder or starts to drain.
Caller -> Pain worse. Vision loss. Floaters. Flashes. Redder. Drain. Okay. I'll watch for all of that.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you. You cleared up my confusion.
Nurse -> Anytime. See you Friday.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Joan.
Caller -> Hi Joan. It's Claudette Rousseau. I'm calling about my mother, Mathilde Rousseau. The bed is broken. The hospital bed. It won't go up.
Nurse -> Sorry, let me make sure I have the spelling. Rousseau, R O U S S E A U?
Caller -> Yes. Like the philosopher. Or the painter. Take your pick.
Nurse -> And is it the first floor bedroom? Easy for the delivery person to get to?
Caller -> First floor. Front door, then left. There's a ramp. They've been here before.
Nurse -> Ha. Got it.
Nurse -> Hi Claudette. Okay. Let's see what we can do. Is your mom comfortable right now?
Caller -> She's propped on pillows. I stacked every pillow in the house. She's okay for now. But the bed is flat. The head won't raise.
Nurse -> Okay. What happened? Did it stop suddenly?
Caller -> I pushed the button on the remote and it did a click. Just a click. And then nothing. The foot goes up and down a little, but the head won't move. It's stuck flat.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it plugged in? Is the cord in the wall?
Caller -> Yes. I checked. I unplugged and plugged back in. I tried the other outlet. I tried the backup button on the side. Nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. You've done all the checks. Claudette, when she lies flat, what happens?
Caller -> My brother in law says to pull the plug out and wait ten minutes. Like a computer.
Nurse -> Did you try that?
Caller -> Yes. Ten minutes. Then plugged it in. Nothing.
Nurse -> It's likely the motor. They'll need to swap it.
Caller -> She coughs. And she gets short of breath. She says she can't get air. So I have to prop her up with pillows and she slides down. I keep pulling her up.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she short of breath right now, with the pillows?
Caller -> No. Right now she's okay. She's propped at an angle. She's breathing fine. Her lips are pink. She's chatting with the cat.
Nurse -> What's the cat's name?
Caller -> Pepin. He sits on her chest. She says he's her oxygen.
Nurse -> Ha. A very important cat. Just make sure he isn't pressing on her when she's flat.
Caller -> I'll put him on the chair. He'll sulk.
Nurse -> Good. That's a good sign. Have you called the equipment company?
Caller -> I did. Twice. Their after hours line. I left a message. They said someone would call me within four hours. It's been two. I'm worried they won't come until tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll call them myself, on our priority line. Claudette, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> January fourteenth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And a good number for you?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one nine six.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one nine six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's mine.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to call the equipment company and ask for an urgent repair or a replacement bed. I'll tell them she can't breathe lying flat, so it can't wait.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. They didn't seem to hear the urgency when I called.
Nurse -> I'll make sure. And I'll ask for it to be delivered or fixed today.
Caller -> Today. Oh, thank God. I was dreading the night.
Nurse -> Let me see what they say. I'll call you back in an hour with an update.
Caller -> If they say tomorrow, can you tell them no?
Nurse -> I'll tell them it has to be today. I'll do my best.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll be here. Where else would I be.
Caller -> Sorry. That sounded rude. I'm just tired.
Nurse -> Not rude at all. You're doing a lot.
Nurse -> In the meantime, let's make her more comfortable. Do you have a wedge pillow, or can you firm up the pillows with a folded blanket behind her back so she doesn't slide?
Caller -> I have a foam wedge. From when I had back surgery. It's in the closet. I forgot about it. I'll get it.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Put it behind her back and head. Keep her knees slightly bent, a pillow under them. And open a window or run a fan so she feels air moving. That can help with breathing.
Caller -> Wedge behind. Knees bent. Fan. Okay. We have a fan. I'll set it on low.
Nurse -> Good. And call us if she's struggling to breathe, if her lips turn blue, or if she can't stay propped. If she has severe trouble breathing, call 911.
Caller -> Struggling. Blue. Can't stay propped. 911 for severe. Okay.
Nurse -> What did she eat today? Is she eating?
Caller -> Soup. A little. And applesauce. She likes it when I warm it.
Nurse -> Good. Small amounts are fine.
Caller -> She says it's better than the hospital.
Nurse -> Is there anyone who can help you lift her if you need to adjust her?
Caller -> My husband's here. He's in the garage. He can help. He's not strong, but he's tall.
Nurse -> Ha. That counts.
Caller -> Tall counts.
Caller -> Honestly he's useless with the bed. He keeps pressing the same button and saying hm.
Nurse -> Ha. Let him help lift, not diagnose.
Caller -> That's his job description.
Nurse -> Anything else, Claudette?
Caller -> No. Just, please call me. I know you will. But please.
Nurse -> I will. One hour. Talk soon.
Caller -> Thank you, Joan.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Summit Home Health, this is Emmett.
Caller -> Hi. Good afternoon. My name is Linh Tran. L I N H. Tran. T R A N. I'm calling for my father. Hoang Tran. H O A N G.
Nurse -> Hi Lynn. Okay. Lynn Chan. And your father is, sorry, Wong Tran?
Caller -> Hoang. Hoang Tran. H O A N G. It's pronounced like Hwong. And I'm Linh, it's like Lin.
Nurse -> Got it, Lynn. Thank you. Hoang Tran. Let me pull him up.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> And how long have you been helping with his care?
Caller -> Since the fall. Three weeks. I moved into the spare room. My mother passed two years ago, so it's just us.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about your mother. It's good he has you.
Nurse -> Can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> March fifth. Nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> And a number for you, Lynn?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one one three.
Nurse -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one one three. Did I get that right, Lynn?
Caller -> Yes. That's right.
Nurse -> Great. What can I help you with today?
Caller -> It's mostly an update. And a question. He's doing so well, and I wanted to make sure I'm doing everything right.
Nurse -> Go ahead.
Caller -> So it's three weeks since the surgery. His hip. He had the fracture. He walks to the kitchen now. With the walker. By himself. I walk behind him but he doesn't need me. He makes his own tea.
Nurse -> Does he carry the cup himself? That can be tricky with a walker.
Caller -> He has a walker bag. A little pouch. He puts the cup in the bag and slides it. Clever, right?
Nurse -> Very. I'll tell the therapist.
Nurse -> That's wonderful progress. How's his pain?
Caller -> He says a three. A three out of ten. In the hip. Mostly in the morning when he stands. He takes the Tylenol twice a day, morning and night. This morning at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Pain is a three, with Tylenol twice a day. Is it getting better, same, worse?
Caller -> Better. It was a seven in the first week. Then a five. Now a three.
Nurse -> That's a good trend. How's the incision?
Caller -> It's good. It's closed. It's dry. No redness. No drainage. No bad smell. It's a long line on the side of his hip. It's turning from pink to white.
Nurse -> Good. And his appetite?
Caller -> Good. He eats everything. Rice, fish soup. He had two bowls of pho on Sunday. I was worried he'd lost his appetite, but no. He's back.
Nurse -> Is he drinking enough? Water, tea?
Caller -> Lots of tea. Jasmine. And water with every meal.
Nurse -> That is great news. So what's the question, Lynn?
Caller -> Showering. Can he shower yet? He's been sponge bathing. He hates it. He keeps asking when he can take a real shower. He says he smells like a hospital.
Caller -> He told the dog to stay away because he smells like a hospital. The dog doesn't care.
Nurse -> Ha. Dogs are forgiving.
Caller -> He's a corgi. He forgives everything for a piece of chicken.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a common complaint. The answer depends on his incision and how steady he is. Is the incision fully closed, no scab?
Caller -> Closed. No scab. No stitches. The surgeon took the staples out two weeks ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Then I think he can shower, with precautions. I'd want a nurse or the therapist to look at the setup first. Do you have a shower chair?
Caller -> We have one. From the rental. And the handheld shower. We installed it Friday.
Nurse -> Great. Here's what I'd say. Use the shower chair, the handheld shower, have someone with him, and keep the walker right next to the tub. And no bending the hip past ninety degrees, so no leaning forward to wash his feet.
Caller -> Chair. Handheld. Someone with him. Walker next to the tub. Don't bend past ninety. I'll wash his feet. Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll send a nurse out Wednesday to look at the incision and check the bathroom.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I take Wednesday off. I'm a pharmacist. I can change my schedule.
Nurse -> Does he take any other medicines you want to ask about?
Caller -> No, I handle them. I'm a pharmacist. I set up the pill box. I have the list.
Nurse -> That helps a lot.
Nurse -> A pharmacist. That helps. I'm also going to leave a message for the team about a physical therapy visit, since he's walking so well. They may want to progress him.
Caller -> Yes! That's great. He's been doing his exercises from the paper. But he'd like someone to watch him.
Nurse -> I'll ask.
Caller -> Thank you, Emmett.
Nurse -> And, Lynn, call us if he falls, if he has new pain in the hip, if the leg looks shorter or turned out, if he gets a fever, or if the incision gets red or starts to drain.
Caller -> Fall. New pain. Leg looks different. Fever. Red, drain. Okay. I wrote it on a sticky note.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else, Lynn?
Caller -> No. That's it. Thank you. And it's Linh. But it's okay. Lynn is fine.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. Linh. I'll get it right next time.
Caller -> It's okay. Everybody does that.
Caller -> It's okay. At the pharmacy it's the same. Lynn, Lin, Leen. I answer to all of them.
Nurse -> Ha. A good attitude.
Caller -> Practice.
Nurse -> Take care, Lynn. Linh. Sorry.
Caller -> Ha. Bye.

Nurse -> Oak Hollow Home Health, this is Bernard.
Caller -> Hi. Bernard? Yes. Hi. It's Teodor Raskin. T E O D O R. Raskin. R A S K I N. I'm calling about my mother. Verna Raskin. I think she's been given the wrong medicine.
Nurse -> Sorry, Teodor, I want to get the name right. Is it Verna with a V?
Caller -> V E R N A. Verna. After my grandmother.
Nurse -> Beautiful name. Okay.
Nurse -> Okay Teodor. Let's look at it. What makes you think so?
Caller -> Her pill bottle. It came in the mail. From the mail order pharmacy. It says Celexa. C E L E X A. Twenty milligrams. But her list says Celebrex. C E L E B R E X. Two hundred milligrams. For her knee.
Nurse -> Okay. Celexa twenty on the bottle, and Celebrex two hundred on the list. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Those are very close. They look the same when you glance. I almost didn't see it. I only caught it because I was putting the bottle in the pill box and the name looked different from the old bottle.
Nurse -> Do you set up her pill box every week?
Caller -> Sundays. After church. Nine years now. I was doing it in the kitchen and I just looked at the label and went, hm.
Nurse -> Good instincts.
Nurse -> That's a good catch. Has she taken any from this bottle?
Caller -> Yes. Three mornings. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and today. No. Four. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. This morning too. At eight. With her oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay. About four mornings. Teodor, how is your mother feeling?
Caller -> Not great. She's nauseated. She's jittery. Her hands shake a little. She says she feels wired. And she isn't sleeping. She was up all night Tuesday and Wednesday. I thought it was her knee.
Nurse -> Okay. Nausea, jittery, and not sleeping. Has she been vomiting?
Caller -> No vomiting. She feels like she's going to. She had crackers.
Nurse -> Okay. And her knee? The Celebrex was for her knee. How's the pain?
Caller -> Bad. A six. A six out of ten. It's worse without the right medicine, I guess. She's limping again.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have chest pain, a racing heart, trouble breathing, confusion?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. Her heart's okay, I think. I checked her pulse. Eighty something. She's clear in the head. She's complaining about me, so she's clear.
Nurse -> What's her pulse like, if you can tell?
Caller -> I counted for a minute. Eighty something. Regular.
Caller -> She told me I'm hovering. She said, Teodor, go find something to do. That's how I know she's herself.
Nurse -> Ha. Hovering is what we're here for.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Teodor, here's what I want you to do. Don't give her any more of the Celexa. None tonight, none tomorrow. And keep the bottle, because the pharmacy will need to see it.
Caller -> Stop the Celexa. Keep the bottle. Okay. What do I give her for the knee?
Nurse -> Don't give anything else for pain until a clinician calls you. I'm paging the on-call clinician now. They'll tell you what's safe.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Her knee is really bothering her. I hate to just let her hurt.
Nurse -> I know. It's going to be quick. They'll call you back soon. And I'm going to call the mail order pharmacy to find out how this happened and get the right medicine out fast.
Caller -> Please. They've been awful. I called last month about a late delivery and the guy hung up on me.
Caller -> They have a recording that says your call is important. It's not.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll make it important.
Nurse -> I'll take it from here.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> What's your mom's date of birth?
Caller -> August nineteenth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one three seven.
Nurse -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one three seven. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to see her tomorrow morning, to check her over and look at all her bottles with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Good. I'll be here.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back in forty minutes, with what the clinician says.
Caller -> Forty minutes. Okay. I'll keep the phone on me.
Caller -> Do you want me to take a picture of the bottle and the list?
Nurse -> That would help the nurse tomorrow. Keep both together.
Caller -> I'll put them in a bag. Zip bag. And write a note on it. Do not use.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> In the meantime, stay with her. Keep her sitting if she's jittery. Offer sips of water or ginger ale for the nausea.
Caller -> Sitting. Water. Ginger ale. We have ginger ale. She loves it. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if she starts vomiting and can't stop, if her heart starts racing, if the shaking gets worse, if she gets confused or faints. Call 911 for chest pain or trouble breathing.
Caller -> Vomiting. Racing heart. Worse shaking. Confused. Faint. 911 for chest or breathing. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> Only that she wants to know if she can still watch her game show.
Nurse -> Of course. Rest and fluids and her show.
Caller -> No. Thank you. I feel awful I didn't catch it sooner.
Nurse -> You caught it. That's what counts.
Caller -> Thanks, Bernard.
Caller -> Is it okay if I stay a minute? I'm still shaking.
Nurse -> Take a breath. I'm not rushing you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Better. Thank you.
Nurse -> Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Heartland Hospice, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. I don't know if this is the right person. I'm not calling about anything urgent. I just wanted to say thank you.
Nurse -> Oh. Thank you for calling. Who am I speaking with?
Caller -> My father was a patient. He passed away last month. On the fourth. I just. I wanted to call and thank the nurses. I didn't get to do it then. Everything was a blur.
Nurse -> I'm so sorry for your loss. It means a lot that you called.
Caller -> Thank you. Your nurse Marcus, and the aide, I think her name was Denise. They were incredible. They were so gentle with him. He was a difficult man. He gave them a hard time and they were so patient.
Nurse -> I'll pass that along to them. They'll be glad to hear it.
Caller -> Please do. And the social worker, she sat with me for two hours the night before. I'll never forget that.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for. I'm glad she could be there.
Caller -> Yes. Anyway. I also had a question. I got a letter about a bereavement group. On Thursdays? Do they still meet?
Nurse -> Yes. The group meets every Thursday evening at six thirty. It's at the community room, next to our office.
Caller -> Six thirty. Thursdays. Can I just show up? Or do I have to sign up?
Nurse -> You can just come, but it's nice if you call the office ahead, so they have chairs and coffee. The office number is on the letter.
Caller -> I have the letter. It's on the fridge. I'll call them tomorrow.
Nurse -> That would be great. Mondays through Fridays they're in from nine to four.
Caller -> Okay. Nine to four. I'm a little nervous about going. I've never done anything like that.
Nurse -> Most people feel that way. It's a small group. Everyone is kind, and nobody has to talk.
Caller -> That's a relief. I might just sit and listen the first time.
Nurse -> That's perfectly fine.
Caller -> My sister says I should go. She says I'm bottling it up.
Nurse -> Your sister sounds like she cares about you.
Caller -> She does. She's bossy but she cares.
Nurse -> Ha. That's often the best kind.
Caller -> It is. Okay. Thank you. I won't keep you.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling. Take care of yourself.
