transcript:
Nurse -> Riverside Home Health, this is Lucille.
Caller -> Lucille, thank God. This is Constance Thackeray. It's my husband. Raymond Thackeray. He's got chest pain. Bad chest pain. He had the stent two weeks ago.
Nurse -> Okay Constance. I'm here. Is Raymond awake and with you?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. He's awake. I'm so sorry, I'm shaking. I can't think.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. Just answer my questions one at a time.
Caller -> He's right here. He's on the couch. He's gray. He's sweating. He's holding his chest.
Nurse -> Okay. How long has he had the pain?
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Maybe twenty. It started when he was sitting watching the news. Just sitting. It got worse.
Nurse -> Was he doing anything strenuous? Walking, lifting, shoveling?
Caller -> No. He did his walk this morning. Around the block. Slow. The cardiac rehab lady said that's fine. This evening he just sat.
Nurse -> Okay. Ask him to describe it. Where is the pain?
Nurse -> I know that's a lot of questions. I'm asking so I can tell the hospital.
Caller -> I understand. Go ahead.
Caller -> Raymond, where? He says in the middle of his chest. Like an elephant. A heavy pressure, an eight, and it goes to his left arm. Down the arm. And his jaw a little.
Nurse -> Okay. On a scale of zero to ten, with ten the worst, how bad is it?
Caller -> He says eight. An eight. He can hardly talk.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he having nausea? Is he sweating?
Caller -> Yes, both. He's drenched. His shirt is wet. And he says he feels like he's going to throw up.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he take the nitroglycerin?
Caller -> Yes. I gave it to him. One tablet. Under the tongue. About ten minutes ago. It didn't help. The pain is the same.
Nurse -> Okay. Constance, this is an emergency. I need you to call 911 right now. Hang up with me and dial 911. Or put me on speaker and dial from your cell. Do you have a cell phone?
Caller -> Yes. I have my cell. In my hand. Should I put you on the speaker? I'm so scared.
Nurse -> Put me on speaker, set the phone down, and use your cell to call 911. Do it now.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Dialing. Nine one one. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My husband is having chest pain. Heart attack. He has a stent. Four fifteen Elm Street. Yes. Two weeks ago. They're sending an ambulance.
Nurse -> Good job. How long did they say?
Nurse -> Did the dispatcher stay on the line with you?
Caller -> She said to stay with him and she'd send them right away. She said they know the address.
Nurse -> Good. Do exactly what she says as well.
Caller -> Six minutes. They said unlock the door.
Nurse -> Unlock the door now. Then come right back.
Caller -> Going. I'm going. It's open. I'm back. He's the same.
Nurse -> Good. Constance, do you have aspirin in the house? Regular aspirin, not the coated kind?
Caller -> Yes. In the kitchen. The bottle. Three hundred twenty five. The regular. Do I get it?
Nurse -> Yes. Get one regular aspirin. Have him chew it, not swallow it whole. Is he allergic to aspirin?
Caller -> No. He takes it every day. He takes the baby one. I'm getting it. I have the bottle. Okay. One tablet.
Nurse -> Have him chew it and swallow it. Do it now.
Caller -> Raymond, chew this. Chew. All the way. Good. He's chewing. He made a face. It's bitter. He swallowed.
Nurse -> Good. Now, keep him sitting. Don't let him stand or walk. Loosen anything tight around his neck or waist.
Caller -> He's trying to talk. He says tell the nurse thank you. He says it's a six now. The pain. Maybe a six.
Nurse -> That's okay. Tell him to rest and not to talk much. The paramedics will check him.
Caller -> Raymond, rest. She says rest. He's nodding. He's very pale.
Caller -> He's sitting on the couch. Leaning back. I unbuttoned his collar. His belt's loose. Okay.
Caller -> The dog is going crazy. He's barking at the door. Should I put him out?
Caller -> The cat is under the table. Everyone's scared. Even the fish tank is bubbling louder.
Nurse -> Ha. Animals feel it.
Nurse -> Put him in another room, so the paramedics can get through. Close the door.
Caller -> Okay. Biscuit! Come! Come here, baby. I'm putting him in the bathroom. There. Quiet. Good boy. I'm back.
Nurse -> Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is his color?
Caller -> Should I call my son? He's at college. He'd want to know.
Nurse -> Not yet. Stay with Raymond. Call him from the hospital, when you know more.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait. He's going to be so upset. They're very close. They watch the games together.
Nurse -> Then Raymond has a lot to come home to.
Caller -> He does. He does.
Caller -> Gray. Pale. Sweaty. He's closing his eyes.
Nurse -> Talk to him. Keep him awake. Is he responding?
Caller -> Raymond! Raymond, look at me. He opened them. He said I'm here. He says I'm here, Connie. He called me Connie. He only does that when he's scared.
Nurse -> Does he have any history of heart trouble besides the stent?
Caller -> He had a heart attack in March. That's why the stent. They did the procedure two weeks ago. He's been doing so well. He walked the block this morning.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll tell the hospital.
Nurse -> Good. He's responding. Keep talking to him.
Caller -> Raymond, can you hear me? Squeeze my hand. He squeezed. He's squeezing very hard.
Nurse -> That's good. He's with you.
Caller -> I'm counting. One, two. I don't know why. I'm just counting.
Nurse -> That's okay. Count if it helps.
Caller -> Raymond, the ambulance is coming. They're almost here. Stay with me. Okay.
Caller -> I keep looking at the clock. It's been two minutes since she said six. It feels like an hour. Why does it feel like an hour?
Nurse -> Because you're scared, and every second counts for you. They're on their way. I can hear nothing but your voice, and you sound clear and strong.
Caller -> I don't feel strong. I feel like I'm made of paper.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. You called, you gave the aspirin, you unlocked the door. That's all anyone can do.
Caller -> Thank you. Raymond keeps saying he's sorry. Sorry for scaring me. Isn't that just like him.
Nurse -> It is the sweetest thing. Tell him not to apologize.
Caller -> Raymond, don't apologize. Hush. Hush. Okay.
Nurse -> Has he fainted or passed out at all?
Caller -> No. He hasn't passed out. He's awake. He's holding my hand. Hard.
Nurse -> Good. Constance, I'm going to page the on-call team and let the hospital know he's coming. I'll stay on with you.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> What's Raymond's date of birth? I'll give it to the hospital.
Caller -> February eleventh, nineteen sixty five.
Nurse -> And your cell number?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one two five.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, zero one two five. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's right.
Nurse -> Do you have his medicine list and the stent card? The paramedics will want them.
Caller -> The list is on the fridge. And the card is in his wallet. It's in his back pocket. Hold on. I'll get the list. I'm getting the list. Okay. I have it. The card, I'll get it from the wallet. It's in the bedroom. On the dresser. I'll go get it.
Nurse -> Quickly. Then come back to him.
Caller -> I'm going. I have it. I have the wallet. Okay. Back.
Nurse -> Good. Put them by the front door. And Constance, when the paramedics come, tell them about the nitroglycerin and what time he took it. Ten minutes ago, right?
Caller -> About ten minutes ago. Yes. Around nine ten. I'll tell them.
Nurse -> Don't let him walk to the ambulance. Let them bring a stretcher.
Caller -> Okay. He won't walk. He wants to walk. He's trying to stand.
Nurse -> Tell him to stay seated. Stay still.
Caller -> He wants water. His mouth is dry. Can I give him water?
Nurse -> Not now. No food or drink. Just a little ice chip if his mouth is dry. Only if the paramedics say.
Caller -> Okay. No water. I'll wet his lips with a cloth. A wet cloth.
Nurse -> That's fine. Just wet his lips.
Caller -> Raymond, stay. Sit. No. They'll come to you. Sit down. He's sitting. He's frustrated.
Nurse -> That's okay. He's stubborn. You're doing fine.
Caller -> He says it's a little better. The pain. Maybe a seven.
Caller -> My neighbor is here! She heard the dog. She's at the door. Marla! Come in! It's Raymond! Chest pain!
Nurse -> Is a neighbor with you now?
Caller -> Yes, Marla from next door. She's a retired nurse. She's holding his other hand. She's talking to him.
Nurse -> That's very good. Let her stay with him.
Caller -> She says his pulse is fast. Marla, what is it? She says one twenty.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell the paramedics.
Nurse -> That's okay. We still want him checked. Keep him still.
Caller -> I hear the siren. I think it's them.
Caller -> They're getting closer. I can hear the siren. It's loud now. It's turning onto our street.
Nurse -> Good. Go ahead and check the porch light is on.
Caller -> Marla turned it on. The porch light's on. The front door is wide open.
Nurse -> Marla, are you there? Can you hear me?
Caller -> She says yes. She says hello. She says she'll stay until they take him.
Nurse -> Good. Go to the door. Wave them in.
Caller -> They're pulling up. The lights. Okay. I'm going. I'm leaving the phone here. They're coming up the steps.
Nurse -> Go. I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> In here! He's on the couch! Chest pain! Two weeks since a stent! He took one nitro at nine ten, and an aspirin! He's sweating! Over here!
Nurse -> Constance, you're doing great. Let them work.
Caller -> They're hooking him up. They have the machine. They're putting stickers on his chest.
Caller -> They're hooking him up. They have the machine. They're putting stickers on his chest.
Caller -> They're asking me what time the pain started. I said about eight fifty five. Is that right? I think so.
Nurse -> Tell them what you know. They'll sort it out.
Caller -> They're asking if he has allergies. Raymond, are you allergic to anything? He says penicillin. Penicillin.
Nurse -> Tell the paramedics that.
Caller -> I told them. They wrote it down. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them everything you know. I'll let the hospital know.
Caller -> They're asking questions. Okay. They say to go. They're taking him now. I'm going with him. I have to go.
Nurse -> Go. Call us when you can. I'm thinking of you both.
Nurse -> Do you have your keys and your phone and a purse?
Caller -> Marla is getting them. She's putting my purse by the door. She's going to lock up and bring Biscuit to her house.
Nurse -> Good. That's one less thing to worry about.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Lucille. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Constance.

transcript:
Nurse -> Quiet Pines Hospice, this is Delphine.
Caller -> Hello. Hello. I'm not sure I got the right number. I'm calling for my sister in law. She has a card on her refrigerator that says Quiet Pines. I'm her brother in law. Walter. Walter Brenneman.
Nurse -> Hi. Can you hear me okay? The line is a little crackly.
Caller -> I can hear you. I'm on the old kitchen phone. It's the cord one. The reception is fine, it's just my ears.
Nurse -> Hi Walter. You've got the right place. Who is your sister in law?
Caller -> Ginny. Ginny H. Something with an H. Hollis. Holland. I never remember. My wife calls her Ginny. We all call her Ginny.
Nurse -> Does Ginny have a last name on the refrigerator card, or the nurse's number?
Caller -> The card just says the hospice. And a phone number. I dialed it.
Nurse -> Okay. That works. I'll find her.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look for a Ginny. What's the address?
Caller -> Forty one twelve Linden. Linden Court. It's a little blue house with a ramp.
Nurse -> Forty one twelve Linden Court. I do have a patient there. Virginia Hollis. H O L L I S. Is that her?
Caller -> Virginia. Yes. Virginia Hollis. That's Ginny. Hollis. I think. I'm pretty sure. Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Walter, what's happening with her?
Caller -> She's breathing funny. It's a rattle. Wet. Like a, like a straw in the bottom of a milkshake. It started this afternoon. It's loud. I can hear it from the kitchen.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake?
Caller -> No. She's been asleep all day. Since the morning. I came at noon. My wife left at one to go to the store and the pharmacy. I'm just watching her. She hasn't woken. I said Ginny a few times, and she kind of moved her head, and that was it.
Caller -> I do this every Sunday afternoon. We take turns. My wife does mornings, I do afternoons. Today she had to run out.
Nurse -> That's a good system.
Caller -> It was working until today.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she moaning, or frowning, or does she look uncomfortable?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. Her face is smooth. She looks peaceful. She looks like she's sleeping. The breathing is loud but she doesn't look upset.
Caller -> She's wearing the blue nightgown with the roses. My wife picked it. She loves that nightgown.
Nurse -> That's a nice detail. She's cared for.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. That's important. Walter, is anyone else there with you?
Caller -> No. Just me. And the cat. My wife is out. She'll be back in an hour. Maybe an hour and a half.
Nurse -> Is the front door unlocked, so the nurse can get in?
Caller -> Yes. I unlocked it when I came. I'll leave it.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a number for her, in case I need to reach her?
Caller -> She has her cell but I don't have it memorized. It's in my phone. I'm on the house phone. I'm in the kitchen. Hold on, let me look. I can't find it. The kitchen phone has no contacts.
Nurse -> That's okay. What's a good number to reach you?
Caller -> My cell. Four one four, five five five, zero one eight six.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, zero one eight six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I have it in my pocket.
Nurse -> Walter, do you know Virginia's date of birth?
Caller -> No. I don't. I'm sorry. I've known her forty years and I couldn't tell you her birthday. My wife knows. She has it written down.
Nurse -> That's fine. We have it in the chart. Do you know what medicines she takes?
Caller -> No. There's a basket on the counter. A lot of bottles. I didn't touch them. I don't want to give her anything wrong. Do I need to?
Nurse -> No. Please don't give her anything. Just let her be. I'm going to get a nurse to you quickly. I'll send someone within the next two hours.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. Good. I'll tell my wife when she gets back. She'll be so relieved. She's been so tired.
Nurse -> Walter, I'm also going to page our on-call clinician right now, because of the breathing. They may be able to suggest something sooner.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm not sure what's happening. Is she dying?
Nurse -> I can't say for certain over the phone. What you're describing, the sleeping, the rattling breath, can happen when someone is getting close to the end of life. The nurse will tell you more when she sees her.
Caller -> Oh. Oh my. I thought maybe. I wasn't sure. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. I know that's hard to hear, especially when you're alone with her.
Caller -> It is. It is. I'll just sit with her. I'm not afraid. I just wasn't expecting.
Caller -> Is it okay if I talk to her? Is that silly?
Nurse -> It's not silly. Hearing is thought to be one of the last senses to go. Talk to her.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Nurse -> That's okay. Is the rattle bothering her, do you think?
Caller -> I don't think so. She seems far away. But it bothers me. It sounds terrible.
Nurse -> It often bothers the people listening more than the person. That's what we see. Here's something that can help. Can you gently turn her onto her side? Put a pillow behind her back, and one between her knees.
Caller -> Onto her side. She's in a hospital bed. In the living room. I can do that. Gently. Okay. Let me put the phone down. I'm going. Hold on. I have the pillows. Ginny, I'm going to turn you a bit. Sorry, sweetheart. There. She's on her left side.
Nurse -> Good. Can you raise the head of the bed a little, or add a pillow under her head?
Caller -> There's a button. I'll push the head up. A little. Okay. It's going up. Is that enough? About, I don't know, thirty degrees.
Nurse -> That's good. Is the sound any different?
Caller -> A little. It's a little quieter. Maybe. I can't tell. It's still there. But maybe less.
Nurse -> Okay. That's fine. Now there are little pink sponge swabs by her bed. Do you see them? On a stick?
Caller -> Yes. A pack of them. On the table. With a cup of water.
Nurse -> Dip one in the water and gently wipe the inside of her mouth and lips. Not deep. Just the lips and cheeks.
Caller -> I'm doing it. Her lips are dry. They're cracked. I'm wiping. Gently. She made a little sound. A small one. Not a groan. Like a sigh.
Nurse -> That's fine. That's a sigh. You're doing it well.
Caller -> Thank you. I've never done anything like this.
Nurse -> You're doing it right. I'm going to stay on with you a minute. Then I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I'll sit by her. I'm holding her hand. It's warm.
Nurse -> That's good. Walter, I'd like you to watch for a few things. If she starts to frown or moan or look restless, if you see long pauses in her breathing, or if you or your wife want someone to come sooner, call us right away.
Caller -> Frown. Moan. Restless. Pauses. Call. Okay. I'll watch her face.
Nurse -> And remember, the noise itself isn't a sign she's suffering. It's often the secretions that can't be cleared when someone is very sleepy.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. I was imagining she was drowning.
Nurse -> She's not. She's resting. Her body is slowing down.
Caller -> That's a better way to think about it.
Nurse -> It is. Does your wife have a key to the house? So the nurse can get in if you step out?
Caller -> The front door's unlocked. I'm here. I'm not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Good. I'll let the nurse know you're there.
Caller -> Thank you, Delphine. You've been very kind.
Nurse -> You're doing something very kind too. Sitting with her.
Caller -> It's an honor. She raised my wife. She was her second mother. I owe her.
Caller -> Her husband died when they were young. She took in my wife and her brother when their mother got sick. Eight years she raised them.
Nurse -> A remarkable woman.
Caller -> She is. She'd be annoyed that we're fussing.
Nurse -> Ha. Sounds like she's earned a little fuss.
Nurse -> That's lovely. I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Bye now.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Ruth, hello. It's Imogene Pruett. I'm calling about Alvin. Alvin Pruett. My husband. I need to ask about his heart pill.
Nurse -> Sorry, let me pull him up. Pruett, P R U E T T?
Caller -> Two Ts. P R U E T T. People always drop one.
Nurse -> Hi Imogene. Sure. What's the question?
Caller -> I took his pulse like you taught me, and it's low. It's forty eight. And the sheet says if it's under fifty don't give the digoxin. So I'm not sure if I give it or not.
Nurse -> Okay. You did the right thing to check. Let me ask a few things. How long did you count?
Caller -> A full minute. I used the kitchen clock. The second hand. I counted forty eight. I did it twice. Forty eight, forty eight.
Nurse -> Which fingers did you use? Not your thumb?
Caller -> Two fingers. On the inside of his wrist, like you showed me. I never use the thumb.
Nurse -> That's right. Good technique.
Nurse -> Good. Was he resting when you took it?
Caller -> He was sitting at the table. Having his coffee. He'd been sitting a while. Maybe twenty minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. How does he feel? Any dizziness, light headedness, chest pain?
Caller -> No. He feels fine. He says he feels the same as always. No dizzy. No chest pain. He's reading the paper and telling me about the weather.
Nurse -> What's the weather?
Caller -> Cold. He says it's going to snow. It's not going to snow. It's fifty degrees.
Nurse -> Ha. A man of opinions.
Nurse -> Good. What's the dose of digoxin on the bottle?
Caller -> Point one two five. Milligrams. One tablet once a day in the morning. He took yesterday's at eight. Yesterday morning. Today's is the one I'm holding.
Nurse -> Okay. Digoxin point one two five, once a day. Imogene, can you read me the hold instructions on the sheet?
Caller -> It says, check pulse before giving. If the pulse is less than fifty, hold the digoxin and call the nurse. That's what it says. I'm looking at it. The sheet is on the fridge.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly what we want. Since his pulse is forty eight, please hold the digoxin this morning. Don't give it.
Caller -> Hold it. Don't give it. Okay. I wasn't sure if I was being silly.
Nurse -> Not silly. You followed the sheet exactly.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'm putting the pill back in the bottle. Wait. I'll put it on the saucer. So I don't lose it.
Nurse -> Put it back in the bottle. Don't leave loose pills around.
Caller -> Back in the bottle. Okay.
Nurse -> What are his other medicines this morning? Did he take those?
Caller -> Let me read the list. Metoprolol, twenty five, in the morning. He took it. Furosemide, twenty, in the morning. He took it. And the warfarin. At night. That's later. Those he took already. I only held the digoxin because I hadn't given it yet.
Nurse -> Which pill box do you use? The weekly kind?
Caller -> A big one. With the little doors. Morning, noon, evening, bedtime. I fill it on Sundays at the kitchen table with a cup of tea.
Nurse -> Good system. It's easy to check.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. I'm going to leave a message for the team about the slow pulse and the held digoxin. They may want to look at his other heart pills too.
Caller -> Okay. That would be good. I wasn't going to say, but the metoprolol also lowers the pulse. I read that on the paper.
Nurse -> It can. That's something the clinician will look at. Don't change anything else yourself.
Caller -> I won't.
Caller -> Is it bad that I'm nervous? My hands are a little shaky.
Nurse -> It's not bad. You're being careful with someone you love.
Caller -> That's the thing. Fifty one years. I don't want to mess it up.
Nurse -> You're not messing anything up. You did exactly right.
Nurse -> I'd like a nurse to visit today, to check his pulse and his pressure.
Caller -> Today. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the next hour with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I'm here. I'm always here.
Caller -> We have the grandkids coming at four. Do I tell them to cancel?
Nurse -> No need. The nurse will come before or after. They'll work around you.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back within the hour with what the team says.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay.
Nurse -> In the meantime, let him rest. In about fifteen minutes, take his pulse again for a full minute, and write it down with the time.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Pulse again. A full minute. Write it. I have a notebook. I'll do it.
Nurse -> And call us if he gets dizzy, faints, has chest pain or nausea, sees yellow halos around lights, or if his pulse drops below forty. Call 911 for fainting or chest pain.
Caller -> Dizzy. Faint. Chest. Nauseous. Yellow halos. Under forty. 911 for faint or chest. Yes. I wrote it on the notepad.
Nurse -> Perfect. What's his date of birth, for the chart?
Caller -> December thirtieth. Nineteen forty five.
Nurse -> And a number?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one nine six.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one nine six. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. It's the house.
Nurse -> Great. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you for letting me ask. I always feel like I'm bothering you.
Nurse -> You're never bothering us.
Caller -> Alvin says hello. He says you're a good nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him thank you.
Caller -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Seaside Palliative Care, this is Dahlia.
Caller -> Hi Dahlia. It's Tabitha Lindemann. T A B I T H A. Lindemann, L I N D E M A N N. My husband Corbin is your patient. C O R B I N. The ALS.
Nurse -> Sorry, I'm pulling up the chart. Is it Lindemann with two Ns at the end?
Caller -> Two Ns. Yes. German. Like the town.
Nurse -> Got it.
Nurse -> Hi Tabitha. Yes, I know Corbin. How can I help?
Caller -> It's his BiPAP mask. The cushion is shot. It's worn out and leaking. And we don't have a spare. I should've called last week.
Nurse -> No worries. How long has he been on the BiPAP?
Caller -> Eleven months. Since last December. At first just at night, now sometimes in the afternoon too.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a long time on one cushion.
Caller -> I keep stretching them. They're supposed to last a month. I got seven.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's count what you have. How many mask cushions?
Caller -> None. Zero. The one on the mask is the last one. I opened the drawer and it's empty.
Nurse -> Okay. And the tubing?
Caller -> One. One extra set. The one on the machine is about two months old. The extra is in the bag.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the leak. What are you noticing?
Caller -> It hisses. Around the nose. The air blows out. Corbin says it hits his eyes. He tightens the straps to stop it, and then it digs in. He's got a red mark now. On the bridge of his nose.
Nurse -> Okay. A red mark. Is the skin broken, open, bleeding?
Caller -> No. It's red. Just red. Mild. Like where your glasses sit. But it's deeper. I put some cream on it. I looked this morning. No sores. No open spots.
Nurse -> What cream did you use?
Caller -> The barrier cream we have for his chin and the drool. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's fine for now.
Nurse -> Good. That's important. Is he breathing okay on the machine, aside from the leak?
Caller -> Yes. He's fine on it. He sleeps. He doesn't wake up gasping. His oxygen's fine. The machine's working. It's just the mask.
Caller -> We check it every night with the little clip. Ninety five, ninety six, most of the time.
Nurse -> That's good to hear.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. Tabitha, what's Corbin's date of birth?
Caller -> March twenty first. Nineteen seventy seven. He's forty nine.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one one one.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one one one. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to place an order with the respiratory supply company for mask cushions and tubing.
Caller -> Thank you. How many cushions? I hate running out. I think we should get a few.
Nurse -> I'll ask for a box of four. And two sets of tubing. And I'll ask for delivery Wednesday.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. That's fine. We'll make it. I can do a pillow fort until then.
Nurse -> And the supply company still has your address as the one on Birch?
Caller -> Yes. The same. Ring the bell twice, he can't get to the door.
Nurse -> I'll make a note.
Caller -> Honestly we've been pretending the leak is a ghost. Corbin says the ghost has asthma.
Nurse -> Ha. A ghost with asthma. I love that.
Caller -> He types a lot of ghost jokes.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully not a fort. Let me tell you how to make tonight easier. First, loosen the headgear a little. Put the mask on, adjust it, and then turn the air on. Don't over tighten. The cushion should seal with the air pressure, not with the straps.
Caller -> Loosen. Put it on, adjust, then turn the air on. Don't over tighten. Okay. I've been doing it backwards. I put on the air and then tighten.
Nurse -> Lots of people do. It's a common mistake.
Caller -> I feel like a rookie.
Nurse -> You're not. Also wipe the cushion with a damp cloth every morning. It helps it last.
Caller -> I only rinse it on Sundays. I'll do it every day.
Nurse -> Perfect. For the skin, put a thin foam or gel pad over the bridge of his nose. Under the mask. Clean and dry the skin first. And give his nose a break during the day, if he can.
Caller -> Foam pad. Clean and dry. Break during the day. I have gel pads from the first mask. They're in the drawer with the old stuff. I'll find them.
Nurse -> Great. I'd like a nurse to see Corbin Thursday, to check his skin and the mask fit.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'm home all day. I work from the dining room.
Nurse -> And call us if the skin breaks open, if he wakes short of breath, if the machine alarms and won't stop, or if the mask won't seal. Call 911 for severe trouble breathing.
Caller -> Skin breaks. Short of breath. Alarm won't stop. Won't seal. 911 if severe. I have it. It's on the machine already. A sticker. You put it there.
Nurse -> Good memory. Anything else, Tabitha?
Caller -> There is one thing. I wanted to say thank you for the nurse last week. She taught me how to move him in the bed without hurting my back.
Nurse -> I'm glad that helped. Your back is part of the care team.
Caller -> I told her she saved my spine.
Nurse -> Ha. Spines matter.
Caller -> No. How are you?
Nurse -> Doing well, thank you. How's Corbin's mood?
Caller -> He's good. He's funny. His voice is going but he still jokes. He types on the tablet with his eyes. He typed, tell the nurse thank you. And a smiley face.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him I got it, and I sent one back.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Harbor Pediatric Palliative Care, this is Camille.
Caller -> Camille, it's Brigitte. Brigitte Halvorsen. Lucas is seizing. He's having a seizure right now. It's been four minutes.
Nurse -> Okay Brigitte. I'm here. Stay with me. Where is Lucas?
Caller -> I'm sorry, I'm shaking so hard. I don't know what to do with my hands.
Nurse -> Put one hand near his head to protect it. That's all.
Caller -> On the living room floor. On the rug. He was on the couch and he slid down. He's stiff and jerking. His arms and legs. His eyes are rolled up.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he on his side? Turn him on his side if he isn't.
Caller -> I turned him. He's on his right side. There's a cushion under his head. I moved the coffee table.
Nurse -> Good. Is there anything sharp or hard near him? A toy, the TV stand?
Caller -> I pushed the toys away. There's a Lego tower. I knocked it over. It's across the floor. It's far from him.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Good. That's exactly right. Is there anything in his mouth?
Caller -> No. Nothing. I haven't put anything. Just his teeth together. Foam, a little foam. He's drooling.
Nurse -> That's normal. Don't put anything in. Brigitte, what time did it start?
Caller -> I looked at the clock. It was six forty one. It's six forty five now. Four minutes. Almost five.
Nurse -> Okay. You've done everything right. Do you have the rescue medicine? The nasal spray?
Caller -> Yes. It's in the bag. In the bag by the door. Midazolam. The nasal one. It says give for a seizure longer than five minutes.
Nurse -> Is the bag where it usually is?
Caller -> Yes, by the door. With the seizure plan, the extra clothes, the little oxygen sensor.
Nurse -> Great. You were ready.
Caller -> We practice every month. I never thought I'd be doing it for real.
Nurse -> Okay. Get it now. Open the package. We're about to hit five.
Caller -> I have it. I'm opening it. It's the little blue thing. One spray in each nostril? Or one?
Nurse -> Read me the dose on the box. Or the card in the bag. The seizure plan.
Caller -> The plan says one spray, one nostril. Five milligrams. He's thirty five pounds. Yes. One spray in one nostril.
Nurse -> Okay. It's five minutes now. Give the midazolam. Tilt his head slightly back, put the tip in one nostril, and push the plunger firmly.
Caller -> Okay. I'm doing it. Tilting. In. Pushing. It went in. I pushed it all the way. Okay. I did it.
Nurse -> Good. You gave it at about five minutes. Write that down, six forty six. Also, I need you to call 911 now. Seizure over five minutes. Put me on speaker and dial from another phone.
Caller -> Another phone. My cell is on the counter. Let me. I'm getting it. Dialing. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My son is having a seizure. He has epilepsy. It's been five minutes. We gave the nasal medicine. Eleven nineteen Pine Ridge Road. Yes. Yes. They're coming.
Nurse -> Good. Did they give a time?
Caller -> They said seven minutes. I told them he's nine. He's thirty five pounds. He's on hospice. Palliative care. They said okay.
Caller -> The dispatcher said she wants me to stay on with her too. But I have you. I'm on both. Is that okay?
Nurse -> It's okay. Do whatever she says. I'll be quiet if she's talking.
Nurse -> Good. Brigitte, how are his lips? Look at his color.
Caller -> A little blue. Dusky. Around the mouth. I think. It's hard to tell. The light is dim.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he breathing?
Caller -> Yes. I see his chest. He's breathing. Fast. And noisy. With the jerking he isn't breathing deep.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep him on his side. Don't hold him down. Just keep him safe from hitting anything.
Caller -> Okay. I'm just keeping my hand near his head. It's still going. It's still jerking. How long? Six minutes?
Nurse -> It's about to be six. The medicine takes a few minutes. Hang on.
Caller -> My husband's at work. He's twenty minutes away. I called him on the way and he's driving. He said he's coming.
Nurse -> Good. He'll meet you at the hospital or here.
Caller -> Oh God. Oh Lucas. It's okay, baby. Mommy's here. Mommy's here.
Nurse -> Keep talking to him. It helps you, and he may hear you.
Caller -> Lucas, it's Mom. You're okay. You're okay. The medicine's going to work. The ambulance is coming.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call team and let the hospital know. I'll stay on with you.
Caller -> Thank you.
Caller -> It's slowing. I think it's slowing. The jerking. It's getting less. His arm stopped. His legs are still, a little. Now they're stopped. It stopped!
Nurse -> Okay. What time is it?
Caller -> Six forty seven. No. Six forty eight. It stopped at six forty eight. That's seven minutes.
Nurse -> Okay. Seven minutes total. Good job timing. Is he breathing?
Caller -> Yes. He's breathing. Slower. Deep now. He's snoring a little.
Nurse -> That's normal after a seizure. He'll be very sleepy. Keep him on his side. Check his lips again.
Caller -> They're pinker. Much pinker. Oh, thank you. Thank God. He's so limp. He's sleeping.
Nurse -> That's what we expect. He's sleepy, he's breathing, and his color is coming back. The paramedics will still check him.
Caller -> Yes. I want them to. Should I wake him?
Caller -> His eyelids are fluttering. He's stirring. Lucas? Lucas? He's not awake. He moved his hand.
Nurse -> That's okay. He may drift in and out. Let him.
Nurse -> No. Let him sleep. Just keep watching his breathing.
Caller -> Okay. I'm watching. His chest is going up and down. In, out. In, out.
Caller -> He's so little. He's so limp. His hair is wet with sweat.
Nurse -> That's normal. He worked hard. His body is wiped out.
Caller -> He looks like a baby. He was a baby ten minutes ago. He was singing at dinner.
Nurse -> What was he singing?
Caller -> The theme to his cartoon. He sings it every night. I'm going to hear it for the rest of my life.
Nurse -> And you'll hear it again tomorrow.
Caller -> Please.
Nurse -> Brigitte, what's Lucas's date of birth? For the hospital.
Caller -> June twenty sixth. Twenty seventeen.
Nurse -> And your cell?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one four.
Nurse -> Nine one eight, five five five, zero one one four. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I called from the house phone. The cell is the one with the 911.
Nurse -> Okay. When the paramedics arrive, tell them when the seizure started, six forty one, and when you gave the spray, six forty six. And loosen anything tight on him.
Caller -> Started six forty one. Spray six forty six. It stopped six forty eight. I wrote it on my hand. I always do that.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is the door unlocked?
Caller -> My husband is going to the door. He just got home. He's here. He heard me yelling. He's at the front.
Nurse -> Good. Let him bring them in.
Caller -> They're here. I hear them. The siren. They're at the door. Okay. In here! He's on the rug!
Nurse -> Go. I'll stay on until they're with you.
Caller -> They're asking me about his medicines. I'm reading from the list on the fridge. They're writing it down.
Nurse -> Good. Take your time.
Caller -> They said he did well. They said I did well. I don't feel like I did anything.
Nurse -> You timed it, you gave the spray, you called. That's everything.
Caller -> They're kneeling. They're checking him. They're asking me what happened. I'm telling them. Okay. They have a mask. They have the oxygen on him.
Nurse -> Good. That's all right. You did great, Brigitte.
Caller -> They want to take him to Children's. I'm riding with him. My husband's following.
Nurse -> Go. I'll let the hospital know. Call us when you can.
Caller -> Thank you, Camille. Thank you so much. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Brigitte.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Dana.
Caller -> Hi, Dana. It's Rosalind Aguilar. I'm calling about my husband, Dominic Aguilar. Five weeks out from the stroke.
Nurse -> And Aguilar, A G U I L A R. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Like the eagle, in Spanish. Dominic's grandfather came from Jalisco.
Nurse -> Hi Rosalind. I remember Dominic. How is he doing?
Caller -> Honestly, better than I expected. I'm calling to give an update, and I have one question.
Nurse -> Perfect. Can I get his date of birth first?
Caller -> January ninth. Nineteen sixty eight.
Nurse -> And the best number for you?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one six eight.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one six eight. Is that right?
Caller -> That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. Go ahead.
Caller -> So his speech is so much clearer. At first it was slow and slurred. Now you can understand every word. Yesterday he told a whole joke. A long one. He didn't lose a word.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. And his right hand?
Caller -> Better. He can grip. He squeezed my hand and it hurt. That was the first time. He's been doing the putty exercises. The therapy putty. He can button his shirt now, slowly.
Nurse -> That's great progress. How about walking?
Caller -> With the cane. He walks around the block with me. Slowly. He drags the right foot a little. But he doesn't stop.
Nurse -> Is the cane on his right or left?
Caller -> The left. The therapist adjusted it. She showed us how.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. And his blood pressure?
Caller -> I took it this morning. One twenty eight over seventy eight. It's been about that all week.
Nurse -> That's excellent. Any new problems? Any new weakness, headache, vision changes, confusion?
Caller -> No. None of that. No new weakness. No headaches. His vision is fine. He's reading the sports page. He's sharp. He argued with me about the score.
Caller -> He watches the games with the sound off and reads the closed captions aloud. To practice his speech. The speech therapist suggested it.
Nurse -> That's a clever exercise.
Caller -> He does the announcers' voices. He's terrible.
Nurse -> Ha. But clear.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. Is he taking his medicines?
Caller -> Every one. I set them out. The Plavix. Seventy five. Once a day in the morning. He took it at eight. And the others. Atorvastatin and the lisinopril. All in the pill box.
Nurse -> And the pill box is filled weekly?
Caller -> By me. Sunday night. With the news on. It's become a ritual.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, your question?
Caller -> Driving. He's itching to drive. He says he feels fine. He wants to take the car to the hardware store. I said absolutely not. But he asked me to ask you. He thinks you'll say yes.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm afraid I'll say the same as you. It's a question for his doctor. After a stroke, they check vision, reflexes and thinking before clearing driving.
Caller -> I knew it. He's going to be so mad.
Caller -> He's going to sulk. He's going to say he's thirty years a safe driver.
Nurse -> He was. And he will be again.
Caller -> I'll tell him you said that.
Nurse -> I'll leave a message for the team to ask the doctor about driving. And I'll ask about occupational therapy, to work on his hand.
Caller -> Oh good. Yes. The occupational therapy would be great. He wants to get his hand back.
Nurse -> I'll ask. I'd also like to send a nurse out Wednesday, to see how he's moving and check his pressure.
Caller -> Wednesday. Okay. I'll tell Dominic. He likes the nurse. The one who tells him jokes.
Nurse -> Ha. That's probably Dana. I mean me. I'm Dana.
Caller -> Oh! You're the one! He says you tell the worst jokes.
Nurse -> Ha. I have a reputation.
Caller -> He tells them to the mailman. The mailman groans every time.
Nurse -> A tough crowd. In the meantime, no driving until the doctor clears him. Use the cane on stairs and uneven ground. Keep up his walks, with someone beside him.
Caller -> No driving. Cane on the stairs. Walks with me. Okay. I walk with him every evening.
Nurse -> How are you doing, Rosalind?
Caller -> Tired, but good. I'm sleeping better since he's more independent. I used to hear him in the night and jump. Now I only jump half the time.
Nurse -> Ha. Progress.
Nurse -> And, Rosalind, you know the warning signs. If his face droops, his arm gets weak, his speech slurs, he suddenly can't see, he has a severe headache or gets confused, call 911 right away. Note the time it started.
Caller -> Face. Arm. Speech. Time. Call 911. We learned FAST in the hospital. I have it on the fridge. A magnet.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Just, thank you. I wanted to tell someone. We don't see many people.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. Tell Dominic hi.
Caller -> He's yelling hi from the living room. He says tell Dana a joke.
Nurse -> Ha. What do you call a fake noodle?
Caller -> What?
Nurse -> An impasta.
Caller -> Dominic! She said impasta! He's groaning. He loves it.
Nurse -> Ha. See you Wednesday.
Caller -> Bye, Dana.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hello? Yes, hello. My name is Harriet Pickett. I'm the neighbor of Mr. Marchand. Leopold Marchand. He's one of yours. He's in pain and he's out of his medicine.
Nurse -> Hi Harriet. Thank you for calling. I'm here. Are you with Mr. Marchand right now?
Caller -> I'm in his bedroom. On the chair by the bed. He's looking at me. He says hello.
Nurse -> Hello, Mr. Marchand. Okay.
Caller -> I'm at his house. I have a key. I come every evening at six with his supper. I came and he was lying in bed, wincing. He told me the medicine was gone.
Nurse -> Okay. Which medicine?
Caller -> The morphine. The little pills. I have the bottle. It's empty. I shook it. Nothing. It says morphine, fifteen milligrams, every four hours as needed.
Nurse -> Okay. Morphine fifteen, every four hours as needed. When did he last take one?
Caller -> He says three o'clock. He took the last one at three. And that was the last pill. He didn't tell anyone. He didn't want to bother me.
Nurse -> That's very considerate of him. Does he often hide when he's hurting?
Caller -> All the time. He's from a generation that doesn't complain. He said his back was fine, and I could see it wasn't.
Nurse -> Okay. So it's been about eight and a half hours. How is he now? How's his pain?
Caller -> He says it's a five. A five out of ten. He's grimacing. He keeps his teeth shut. He says, oh, when he moves. He's trying to be tough.
Caller -> I told him tough guys take their pills. He told me tough guys wait for Monday.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll fix that.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he awake and talking to you?
Caller -> Yes. He's talking. He's cranky. He said, don't call, it's Sunday, they'll be closed. I said, hospice is never closed, Leopold.
Nurse -> Ha. You're right. We're never closed. Harriet, thank you for calling. Can I get his date of birth?
Caller -> September third. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one nine nine.
Nurse -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one nine nine. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now. They need to approve an emergency supply.
Caller -> Okay. His regular pharmacy closes at six on Sundays. It's closed. It opens at nine tomorrow.
Nurse -> I understand. We have an on-call pharmacy that works with us. I'll contact them to get an emergency supply of the morphine delivered tonight.
Caller -> Delivered? Oh, that would be wonderful. To his house? I'll be here.
Nurse -> To his house. It may take a couple of hours. I'll let you know the time.
Caller -> I'll wait. I don't have anywhere else to be. My husband's at the lodge meeting.
Caller -> I made extra pot roast. I'll bring it over for his lunch tomorrow.
Nurse -> That's very kind. Thank you.
Nurse -> What lodge?
Caller -> The Elks. They meet the first Sunday. He'll be home late. They have a raffle.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully he wins.
Caller -> He never does. Forty years.
Nurse -> Thank you, Harriet. In the meantime, let's make him more comfortable. Can you help him find the position that hurts the least? Pillows under his knees, or behind his back?
Caller -> He's on his side. With a pillow between his knees. I can add one behind his back. Hold on. Leopold, can you lean? There. He says that's a little better. A four.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Is there a warm blanket, or a heating pad?
Caller -> A heating pad. In the closet. I'll find it.
Nurse -> Put it on low, and over a cloth, not against his skin. And play some quiet music if he likes. And sit with him.
Caller -> He likes the old country songs. I'll find the radio. Hold on. I have it. Okay. It's on low.
Nurse -> Good. How's he doing?
Caller -> He says, that's Patsy Cline. He's humming.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Caller -> He knows every word. Every Patsy Cline song ever recorded.
Caller -> He sings along when he thinks I'm not listening. Terrible voice. Really loud.
Nurse -> Music is great medicine.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in thirty minutes with the pharmacy plan.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. I'll keep the phone near.
Nurse -> And call if his pain gets worse than a seven, if he can't get comfortable, or if he gets confused or short of breath.
Caller -> Worse than seven. Can't get comfortable. Confused. Short of breath. Okay. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Is he able to take sips of water? Is he eating?
Caller -> He ate half his supper. The pot roast. And he drank his tea.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring.
Nurse -> Does he have anyone else, Harriet? Family?
Caller -> A son in Oregon. He calls on Sundays. He called this morning. I didn't tell him about the pills. I didn't know.
Caller -> I wrote the son's number on a card on the refrigerator. I can call him if you want me to.
Nurse -> Not yet. Let's get the medicine sorted first.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll tell him as needed. Thank you for being there.
Caller -> He'd do the same for me. He did, when my husband was sick. He brought casseroles for a month.
Nurse -> Good neighbors are rare.
Caller -> We take care of each other. Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Marcus.
Nurse -> Talk soon, Harriet.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Seaport Hospice, this is Tobias.
Caller -> Hi, Tobias. It's Noreen Castellanos. C A S T E L L A N O S. I'm calling about my mother, Estelle Castellanos. I have a question about her morphine. I don't want to mess it up.
Nurse -> Hi Noreen. I'm glad you called before giving anything. Let's go through it slowly. Do you have all the bottles in front of you?
Caller -> I'm so sorry to call on a Monday night. I was going to wait until morning but my mother woke up and said her back hurt and I panicked.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. The line is for exactly this.
Caller -> I feel like I've called you ten times this month.
Nurse -> You've called three times. And I'm glad each time.
Caller -> I do. I laid them out on the table. Like a pharmacy. There's three. Well, four if you count the one in the cabinet.
Nurse -> A whole shelf. Okay. Is there a good light where you are? The labels can be tiny.
Caller -> I'm at the dining table with the lamp. I have my reading glasses on. Plus the magnifying glass from my husband's stamp collection.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect.
Nurse -> Okay. Start with whichever you want. Let's go one at a time. What's the first?
Caller -> The first is the MS Contin. The pills. Fifteen milligrams. It says every twelve hours. I give it at eight in the morning and eight at night. I gave this morning's at eight.
Nurse -> Okay. MS Contin fifteen, every twelve hours. That's her scheduled one. Good. And the next?
Caller -> The second is the new bottle. The morphine liquid. The pharmacy sent it Friday. It says morphine oral solution, twenty milligrams per mL. And the directions say, point two five mL every two hours as needed for pain.
Nurse -> Okay. Twenty milligrams per mL, point two five mL, every two hours as needed. That's her as needed one. And it came Friday?
Caller -> Friday. The old bottle was different. The old one is also on the table. It says morphine, ten milligrams per five mL. And the old directions said two mL. Two mL, every two hours. And I've been measuring two mL for a month. With the old syringe. The one with the pink plunger.
Caller -> It was easy. The syringe had big numbers. Two was a big line, right in the middle. This one has tiny numbers. Point two. Point four. I can barely see them.
Nurse -> That's why I'm walking you through it.
Nurse -> Okay. Noreen, stop right there. That's the important part. The old bottle was a weaker concentration. Ten milligrams in five mL. The new one is much stronger, twenty milligrams in one mL. So the amount you give has to be smaller with the new one.
Caller -> That's what I was afraid of. I thought, wait, why does it say point two five? That's tiny. I thought maybe it was a typo. I thought the pharmacy made a mistake.
Nurse -> It's not a typo. It's correct. Point two five mL of the new one equals about the same as the two mL of the old one. If you gave two mL of the new one, that would be about eight times too much.
Caller -> Oh my God. I haven't. I haven't given the new one. I didn't dare. I haven't given any since Friday. Wait. I gave one. Today at one. I gave one today. Did I give it right?
Nurse -> Tell me what you did. Which bottle did you use today at one?
Caller -> The new one. But I measured it with the new syringe, the little one that came with it. I drew it up to the first line. The tiny line. And I gave it. I wasn't sure what the first line meant. It said point two five on the box. I looked at the syringe and I thought, that's the first line, that must be it.
Nurse -> Okay. That was exactly right. The first small line on the new syringe is point two five. You gave the right dose.
Caller -> I did? Oh, thank goodness. I was so nervous. I almost didn't do it.
Nurse -> You did it correctly. Good for you for being careful.
Caller -> Thank you. I was shaking.
Caller -> I stood in the kitchen for ten minutes before I did it. My husband said, you don't have to do it alone, call somebody. I said who. He said the hospice nurse.
Nurse -> He's right. You can always call.
Caller -> I know. I just hate to bother.
Nurse -> Noreen, let me make sure I have this right. Today at one o'clock, you gave point two five mL of the new morphine liquid with the new syringe. That's it?
Caller -> That's it. At one o'clock. Point two five.
Nurse -> Okay. And how is her pain now?
Nurse -> Where is your mother right now? Is she awake?
Caller -> She's in the recliner in the den. With her blanket. She's awake. She's watching the weather channel with the sound off.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> She says a five. In the back and the hip. It's worst in the afternoons. She says the pill wears off by two. That's why I wanted to give the liquid.
Nurse -> Okay. A five now. Let me finish the bottles, and then we'll talk about whether she's due. What's the third bottle?
Caller -> The third is hydromorphone. H Y D R O M O R P H O N E. Two milligrams. It says every four hours as needed. It's tablets. From the older prescription. They look so similar, the names. Hydromorphone, morphine. I can't tell which to give.
Caller -> The pharmacist told me once, the one with the long name is the strong one. But they both have long names.
Nurse -> Ha. That would confuse anyone.
Nurse -> That's a very good concern. Those are two different strong pain medicines, and the names are close. Let me check her current orders. Hold on. Okay. Hydromorphone was discontinued last week, when the new morphine liquid was started. It's not on her list anymore.
Caller -> It's not? Nobody told me. I've been keeping it just in case.
Nurse -> It's okay. It's not your fault. Please set the hydromorphone tablets aside and don't give them. We'll have the team arrange to take them.
Caller -> Set aside. Don't give. Okay. I'll put them in a bag. Away from the others. Should I write on it?
Caller -> I'm putting them in a freezer bag. The zipper kind. Away from the other stuff. In the top cabinet where my mother can't reach.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Yes. Write do not use on the bag, with a marker. And the same for the old morphine bottle, the weaker one.
Caller -> Do not use. The old morphine too. Okay. I'm writing. Wait. I need a marker. I have a Sharpie. There. Done. Two bags. Do not use.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tape the bags to the cabinet door. So I can't forget. And my husband can see them too.
Nurse -> Smart. Tell him what the bags are.
Caller -> I will. He thinks everything is vitamins.
Nurse -> Ha. He'll learn.
Nurse -> Perfect. And the old syringe, the one with the pink plunger, throw it out. Don't use it with the new bottle.
Caller -> The pink one. Out. It's in the trash. Okay. The fourth bottle is the one in the cabinet. It's lorazepam. And a senna. I know those. Those are fine. The lorazepam is for anxiety. The senna is for her bowels. They aren't confused with anything.
Nurse -> Right. Those are fine. Now, the new morphine. Because it's strong, I want you to only use the new syringe. Draw up exactly point two five mL, the very first small line. Give it slowly, into the cheek, between the gum and the cheek. Write down the time. Wait at least two hours before another dose.
Caller -> First small line. Slowly into the cheek. Write the time. Wait two hours. Okay. I'm writing on the sheet. The time today is one o'clock. Last given at one.
Caller -> I keep the sheet on a clipboard. I got it from the dollar store. With a pen on a string.
Nurse -> Great system.
Nurse -> Right. It's coming up on five hours since the last dose. So she can have another now if she needs it. Her pain is a five. Do you want to give her one?
Caller -> Yes. I think so. She's wincing. She said, it's coming back.
Nurse -> Okay. Do it now, with the new syringe. I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> Okay. Getting the syringe. The little one. In the bottle. Pulling back. First line. Is this the line? It's at the line. The black part is at the first line.
Nurse -> Look from the side. Is the top edge of the black rubber exactly on the first line?
Caller -> I'm holding it up to the lamp. I put it at eye level. Hold on. It's right on the line. It's a hair above, maybe? No. On it.
Nurse -> If it's a hair above, push the plunger in slightly until it's exactly on it.
Caller -> Okay. I pushed a tiny bit. It's right on the line now.
Caller -> Yes. Right on it. Okay. Mom, open. Into the cheek. Slowly. There. She swallowed. It's done.
Nurse -> Perfect. What time is it?
Caller -> Six fifteen. Six fifteen. I'm writing. Done.
Nurse -> Good. That was perfect, Noreen.
Caller -> Thank you. I felt so stupid.
Nurse -> You weren't stupid. It's a confusing situation. The pharmacy should have told you.
Caller -> My mother raised six kids and never made a mistake with a pill. I feel like I'm letting her down.
Nurse -> You aren't. You've been caring for her carefully for a month.
Caller -> It's been five weeks. It feels like five years.
Nurse -> I know. It's a lot.
Caller -> They did. They said something at pickup. But the counter was loud, and I was in a rush. I didn't hear.
Nurse -> It happens. I'm going to leave a message for the team, to confirm the pain plan and to arrange for the old bottles and the hydromorphone to be picked up.
Caller -> Thank you. I'd love to get them out of the house. They make me nervous.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to visit tomorrow, to go over everything with you in person.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Yes. Please. That would help. I'm here all day.
Nurse -> Is there anyone helping you, Noreen? Your husband? Siblings?
Caller -> My husband in the evenings. My brother Saturdays. The others are far.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something.
Caller -> It's enough. We manage. My mother says she's in good hands.
Nurse -> She is.
Nurse -> Noreen, what's your mother's date of birth? For the chart.
Caller -> April twenty ninth. Nineteen forty two. No. Forty three. Nineteen forty three. She's eighty three. Forty three.
Nurse -> April twenty ninth, nineteen forty three. And a number for you?
Caller -> My number. Oh, I never remember it. It's a new phone. I just got it. I can't. It's saved as Me. Do you have a number for me already?
Nurse -> I have a number on file in your mother's chart. I'll use that one. Is that still good?
Caller -> I think so. Yes. I think it's the same. Use that one.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll use the number on file. Now, call us if she gets very sleepy, hard to wake, if her breathing slows, or if the pain stays above a seven after a dose.
Caller -> Very sleepy. Hard to wake. Breathing slows. Pain above seven after a dose. Okay. I wrote it on the sheet.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's it. You've been so patient.
Nurse -> Anytime, Noreen. Call if you have any questions at all.
Caller -> One more thing. Do I need to wake her at night for the dose?
Nurse -> No. Let her sleep. Give the as needed dose only when she's hurting.
Caller -> Okay. Only when she hurts. Thank you.
Caller -> Thank you, Tobias. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye now.

transcript:
Nurse -> Oakhaven Home Health, this is Priscilla.
Caller -> Hi, Priscilla. It's Xiomara. X I O M A R A. Villasenor, V I L L A S E N O R. I'm on the chemo. I've been sick all day.
Nurse -> Villasenor, V I L L A S E N O R. Okay. Thank you for spelling it.
Nurse -> Sorry you're having such a hard time. Let's get a few details so I can help.
Caller -> Okay. Go ahead. I'm lying on the couch with a bucket.
Nurse -> Hi Zeomara. Okay. Zeomara Villasenor. I'm sorry you're feeling bad. What's going on?
Caller -> Xiomara. It's like See-oh-mara. Like the, never mind. I've been throwing up. Three times today. And I'm nauseated all the time.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm sorry, Zeomara. Three times today. When did it start?
Caller -> This morning. Around nine. After my breakfast. I had toast. It came right back up. And then again at noon. And again at two. Just now. Before I called.
Nurse -> Was there any pain in your belly with it, or cramping?
Caller -> Just a little cramping when it comes. Not constant. It goes away after.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you take your anti-nausea medicine?
Caller -> The Zofran. Yes. At ten. Four milligrams. It's every eight hours if I need it. It helped for an hour and then it came back. And I can't take another until six.
Nurse -> Okay. Zofran four, every eight hours as needed, last at ten. And your other medicine? The steroid?
Caller -> Dexamethasone. Four milligrams. Twice a day. I took the morning one with the toast, before I threw up. I don't know if it stayed down.
Nurse -> Do you take it with food?
Caller -> With breakfast and with lunch. It keeps me awake if I take it late.
Nurse -> Good. That's the right way.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good detail. Is there any blood in the vomit?
Caller -> No. No blood. It's just food and then clear. Yellowish. No blood. And no fever. I took my temperature at one. Ninety eight point four.
Nurse -> Do you have the thermometer you use for chemo days?
Caller -> The digital one. It beeps. I use it under the tongue. Morning and evening and when I feel off.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Caller -> My oncologist said never skip a check. Even if I feel fine.
Nurse -> She's right.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Are you able to keep any fluids down?
Caller -> Little sips. Water. If I sip slowly I can keep it. If I gulp, it comes back. I've been sipping since the last time. Half an hour. It's staying.
Nurse -> Sip slowly. Not gulping.
Caller -> Yes. I learned that the hard way last cycle.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a good sign. Zeomara, can I get your date of birth?
Caller -> December sixth. Nineteen eighty. No. Eighty one. Nineteen eighty one. I'm forty five. I always do that. I think I'm a year younger.
Nurse -> December sixth, nineteen eighty one. And your number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one eight two.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one eight two. Is that right, Zeomara?
Caller -> Yes. That's it. My cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to leave a message for the team, to ask about a stronger anti-nausea medicine. Sometimes they can add another one that works differently.
Caller -> Oh, please. I'd love that. The Zofran isn't enough. I had a different one last cycle, a patch, I think. It worked better.
Caller -> Or a pill that dissolves on the tongue. I don't remember the name. I wrote it in my journal. I keep a chemo journal.
Nurse -> That's helpful for the team. Read it to them tomorrow.
Nurse -> I'll mention that. They'll see your chart too.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to see you tomorrow, to check your fluids and your weight and see how you are.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. I'll be home. I'm on the couch. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> My sister's coming at five with soup. I don't want soup. But I can't tell her.
Nurse -> Ha. Take a spoonful for her sake, only if it sits well.
Nurse -> In the meantime, take small sips of clear fluids, a sip every fifteen minutes. Try crackers or dry toast when you feel up to it. Avoid greasy or strong smelling food. And stay sitting up after you eat.
Caller -> Sips every fifteen. Crackers. No grease. Sit up after. Okay. I have ginger ale and saltines. My sister stocked me up.
Nurse -> Is she staying with you?
Caller -> On the weekends. During the week she comes after work. She brings groceries and teases me about my hair.
Nurse -> Ha. How's the hair?
Caller -> Gone. She says I'm very aerodynamic.
Nurse -> That's perfect. And call us if your temperature goes to one hundred point four or higher, if the vomiting won't stop, if you see blood, if you can't keep fluids down for eight hours, or if you're dizzy when you stand.
Caller -> One hundred point four. Won't stop. Blood. Eight hours. Dizzy. Okay. I know the fever one. They drilled it into me.
Nurse -> Good. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Just, thank you. I hate this part.
Caller -> Two more cycles. Then scans. I keep counting down.
Nurse -> One cycle at a time. You're doing it.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps.
Nurse -> I know. It's hard. Hang in there, Zeomara.
Caller -> It's Xiomara. But thank you. It's fine.
Caller -> Honestly with chemo brain I can't remember my own name half the time. Zeomara is fine. It sounds exotic.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm sorry. Xiomara.
Caller -> Ha. Yes. Close.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. Xiomara. I'll get it.
Caller -> No worries. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Little Oaks Pediatric Home Care, this is Naomi.
Caller -> Hi, Naomi. It's Alina Thibodeaux. T H I B O D E A U X. I'm calling about Wesley. He's fourteen months. He has a fever. I have my husband on speaker.
Nurse -> Hi Alina. Hi to your husband. Wesley Thibodeaux. Let me pull him up. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> He's been a little off since breakfast. I thought it was teething. He has two molars coming in.
Nurse -> That can cause a low fever. Let's see what else.
Caller -> He's hot. He's fussy. Since this afternoon. I took his temperature just now. A hundred and one point eight.
Nurse -> Okay. A hundred and one point eight. How did you take it?
Caller -> Under the arm. And then the forehead one. Both said about the same. One oh one eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he drinking? Wet diapers?
Caller -> He's drinking. Not as much as usual. But he took his bottle. Two diapers since noon. Both wet.
Nurse -> What color is the urine? Pale, or dark?
Caller -> Pale. Like lemonade. Greg checked the second one.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. Has he had anything for the fever?
Caller -> Yes. Tylenol. The drops. The liquid. It's, the concentration is on the box, hold on. It says one sixty milligrams per five mL. And he got three point seven five mL. That's the dose on the card from the doctor. Once. This afternoon.
Nurse -> Okay. Three point seven five of the one sixty per five. That's right for his weight. What time did he get it?
Caller -> Two o'clock. I gave it at two.
Caller -> No you didn't. I gave it. It was after nap. It was four.
Nurse -> Is that your husband?
Caller -> Yes, that's Greg. He says four. I say two. I was at the pharmacy at two. Wait, maybe I was at the pharmacy at four. I don't know. We're not sure.
Caller -> I gave it at four. I remember because the Daniel Tiger had just started.
Caller -> Daniel Tiger is at three. Greg, it's at three.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear two different times. That's fine. We can work with that. Neither of you is sure, right?
Caller -> No. We're not sure. Two or four.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what we'll do. We'll count from the later time. Treat it as four. That way we don't give the next dose too early. The next Tylenol wouldn't be until ten tonight. Is that okay?
Caller -> Ten tonight. Okay. Yes. Count from four. Greg, you heard. Ten.
Caller -> We have the card from the doctor on the fridge. Weight and dose. It says nine kilograms.
Nurse -> Good. That matches what I have.
Caller -> Ten. Got it.
Nurse -> Good. How's he acting right now? Besides fussy.
Caller -> He's fussy, he's clingy. But he's playful for a minute, and then he's whiny. He took a few sips of juice. He's in my lap. He's not lethargic. He looks at me.
Caller -> He grabbed my glasses and tried to eat them. So he's himself.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Okay. Any rash? Any stiff neck, vomiting, trouble breathing, pulling at the ears?
Caller -> No rash. No stiff neck, he turns his head. No vomiting. His breathing is normal. He's pulling at his left ear a little, maybe. No. He's pulling at his hair. I can't tell.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Alina, what's Wesley's date of birth?
Caller -> August thirtieth. Twenty twenty five.
Nurse -> And your cell?
Caller -> Three one two, five five five, zero one seven nine.
Nurse -> Three one two, five five five, zero one seven nine. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to leave a message for the team about the fever and the dose timing. They may want to look at his ear.
Caller -> Okay. Good. Would they send someone?
Nurse -> That depends on what they say. I'll call you back in two hours with an update, or sooner.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. We'll be here.
Nurse -> In the meantime, use only the syringe that came with that bottle. And write each dose and the time on a piece of paper next to the bottle. That way you both see it.
Caller -> Paper by the bottle. Write the time. I'm doing it now. Greg, get a pen. Four o'clock. Tylenol. Three point seven five.
Caller -> I'm writing it. Four. I put a star next to it because we aren't sure.
Nurse -> That works. And offer small, frequent drinks. Keep him lightly dressed, not bundled.
Caller -> Small drinks. Lightly dressed. He's in a onesie. Okay.
Nurse -> And call us if his temperature goes to one hundred four or higher, if the fever goes past three days, if he gets very sleepy or hard to wake, has fewer wet diapers, a rash, or a stiff neck. Call 911 for a seizure or trouble breathing.
Caller -> A hundred four. Three days. Sleepy. Fewer diapers. Rash. Stiff neck. 911 for seizure or breathing. Okay. I have a magnet on the fridge with all that.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Naomi. I'm sorry about the arguing.
Caller -> We argue about everything. The thermostat. The dishwasher. The cartoon.
Nurse -> Ha. Welcome to parenting.
Caller -> It never ends.
Nurse -> It's very common. Parents remember times differently. That's why we write it down.
Caller -> Greg says he'll write it from now on.
Nurse -> Does Wesley go to day care?
Caller -> No, he stays home with Greg. Greg works from the garage. He's a woodworker. Wesley bangs on a drum next to him.
Nurse -> Ha. A busy shop.
Caller -> I will. I promise.
Nurse -> Good. Talk to you in two hours.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Frances.
Caller -> Frances, hello. It's Maeve Fitzgerald. M A E V E. I'm calling about my husband, Boyd Fitzgerald. I think I did something wrong with his pain pill.
Nurse -> Hi Maeve. Okay. Tell me what happened. Take your time.
Caller -> I'm sorry, I'm talking fast. I can't catch my breath.
Nurse -> Take a slow breath with me. In, and out. Better?
Caller -> A little. Okay.
Caller -> He has trouble swallowing pills. They get stuck. So I crush them. I put them in applesauce. I do it with all his pills. And this morning I did it with the OxyContin. And he's very sleepy now. Very slow.
Caller -> The nurse who came last month showed me the pill crusher. The little plastic one. She said it's fine for his heart pills. I assumed it was fine for all of them.
Nurse -> It's fine for some. Not for all.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. I'm going to ask a few questions, and then I'll tell you what to do. Which pill did you crush?
Caller -> The OxyContin. O X Y C O N T I N. Twenty milligrams. Every twelve hours. I gave it at eight this morning. I crushed it between two spoons. And I mixed it in applesauce.
Nurse -> Okay. And he ate all of it?
Caller -> All of it. He ate the whole cup. He said it tasted bitter. I said it's the medicine.
Caller -> I gave him a spoonful of pudding after. To get the taste out. He liked the pudding.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Maeve, I need to tell you something important. OxyContin is a long acting tablet. It's meant to release slowly over twelve hours. When it's crushed, the whole dose goes into the body at once. That's why he's so sleepy.
Caller -> Oh no. Oh no. Oh God. I didn't know. Nobody told me. The label doesn't say.
Caller -> My mother always crushed pills for my father. I just copied her.
Nurse -> It's a very natural thing to do. Plenty of people do it.
Nurse -> It may say swallow whole, in small print. It's very common to miss. Please don't blame yourself. We're going to take care of him.
Caller -> What do I do? Is he going to die?
Nurse -> Let's check on him together. First, is he awake?
Caller -> He's in his chair. He's awake. His eyes are half open. He answers when I say Boyd. But he's slow. He says what? And then he answers.
Caller -> It's the recliner by the window. He likes to watch the birds. The feeder's right there. He's been watching the cardinals.
Nurse -> A lovely spot.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good that he wakes up. Can you count his breaths for me for a full minute? Watch his chest.
Caller -> Yes. I'll use the clock on the stove. Hold on. One, two, three. I'm counting. I'm up to, it's about twelve. Twelve breaths in the minute.
Nurse -> Twelve is on the low side but acceptable. Is his breathing even and regular?
Caller -> Yes. Slow but even. No gasping. He sounds like he's sleeping. A little snore.
Nurse -> Okay. Look at his lips and his fingers. What color?
Caller -> Pink. A little pale. No blue. I looked. And he wakes up. I can wake him. He just keeps drifting.
Caller -> His hands are warm. His fingernails are pink. I pressed on one and it went white and then pink again. Like the nurse showed me.
Nurse -> Good. That means good blood flow.
Nurse -> Good. How is he otherwise? Is he in pain?
Caller -> No pain. He's comfortable. He's too comfortable. That's what scared me. He's never this sleepy.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he take any other pain medicine?
Caller -> The oxycodone. The little one. Five milligrams. Every four hours if he needs it. He had one yesterday evening. Not today. He hasn't needed it.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. Don't give him any more pain pills. None. Not the oxycodone, not another OxyContin. Not until the clinician calls you.
Caller -> No more pills. None. Okay. The next OxyContin is due at eight tonight. Do I skip it?
Nurse -> Don't give it. Wait for the clinician's instructions. They'll tell you what to do.
Caller -> Okay. I won't give anything. I'll write a note. Do not give. On the pill box.
Caller -> He has a lot of medicines. Metformin. His heart pills. His water pill. Should I hold those too?
Nurse -> Just the pain pills for now. Give the rest as usual. The clinician will tell you if they want anything else changed.
Caller -> Okay. Just the pain pills.
Nurse -> Good. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now. And I'm sending a nurse to your house within the hour to check on him.
Caller -> Within the hour. Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> Maeve, I want you to keep him sitting up with his head raised. And every ten minutes, check his breathing and say his name to see if he wakes.
Caller -> Every ten minutes. Breathing. Say his name. Sitting up. I'll set a timer on my phone. Ten minutes. There. It's set.
Nurse -> Perfect. And I'll call you back in fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Fifteen. Okay. I'll be right here. I'm not leaving his side.
Nurse -> If he becomes hard to wake, if his breathing slows to less than ten or gets shallow, or if his lips turn blue, call 911 right away. Don't wait for me to call.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Under ten breaths. Shallow. Blue lips. 911. Okay. I understand. I have the phone right here.
Nurse -> Good. Maeve, what's Boyd's date of birth?
Caller -> October fourteenth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house line.
Nurse -> Is there anyone else at home? A neighbor, a relative?
Caller -> My son, Brett, is coming at three. He works nights. He sleeps in the morning. I don't want to wake him.
Nurse -> Wake him if you need help. It's okay.
Caller -> He's a heavy sleeper. I'd have to shake him.
Nurse -> Ha. Then shake him.
Nurse -> Okay. Going forward, don't crush OxyContin, ever. We'll ask the team about a liquid or another form that's safe for him to swallow.
Caller -> A liquid. That would be wonderful. His throat is getting worse. The pills get stuck. I just didn't know what to do. I'm so sorry.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. You were trying to help him.
Caller -> I was. I always crush his metformin. It's fine?
Nurse -> Some pills are okay to crush and some aren't. Ask before crushing anything. I'll have the pharmacist review the list.
Caller -> I'll ask. I'll never crush another thing without asking.
Nurse -> That's the right plan. How is he now?
Caller -> The same. He's looking at me. He said, Maeve, I'm fine. He's slurring a little.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep checking him. I'm going to stay on until you've done your first check.
Caller -> Okay. The timer isn't up yet. Seven minutes.
Nurse -> Talk to him. Keep him engaged. Ask him something simple.
Caller -> Boyd, what's your favorite fish to catch? He says, walleye. Walleye. Okay. He's with it.
Nurse -> That's a good answer. He's awake enough to know his fish.
Caller -> He's very serious about walleye.
Caller -> He has a boat in the garage that hasn't been in the water in three years. He still polishes it on Saturdays.
Nurse -> That's love.
Nurse -> Ha. I believe it.
Caller -> Frances, thank you for not yelling at me.
Nurse -> I'd never yell. You called. That's what matters.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll call you if anything changes.
Caller -> Should I tell my son when he comes? Brett?
Nurse -> Yes, tell him what happened and what to watch for. The nurse will go over it again too.
Caller -> Okay. He'll tell me I should have asked first. He's right.
Nurse -> Next time, call first. Even for small questions.
Caller -> I will. I promise.
Nurse -> And I'll call you in fifteen minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
