transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hi, Ruth. It's Marisol Fuentes. I'm the personal care aide for Mr. Okamoto. Terrence Okamoto. I work the evening shift. I have a supply question and a wound question.
Nurse -> How long have you been with Mr. Okamoto?
Caller -> Eight months. Since March. He's my favorite. He teaches me chess. I lose every game.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good client to have.
Nurse -> Hi Marisol. Go ahead. Supplies first?
Caller -> The foam dressings. For the sore on his tailbone. There's only three left in the box. We change them every other day. So that's six days. Maybe less.
Nurse -> Okay. Three foam dressings. How about the saline and gauze?
Caller -> Plenty of those. A whole case of saline. The gauze, we have like twenty packs. It's the foam that's low.
Nurse -> Who usually orders the supplies? The nurse?
Caller -> The nurse does. But she's been out sick. So nobody noticed.
Nurse -> I'll take care of it.
Nurse -> Good. I'll order the foam. Marisol, tell me about the wound.
Caller -> I changed the dressing tonight. There was more drainage than usual. It was soaked through. And it had a smell. A mild smell. Not terrible. But I noticed it. It's different from last week.
Nurse -> Did you take a picture of it, by chance?
Caller -> I did. On my phone. But I can't send it. The agency said no pictures on personal phones.
Nurse -> That's fine. The nurse will see it tomorrow.
Nurse -> Okay. Was the drainage clear, yellow, green, bloody?
Caller -> Yellowish. Like pale yellow. Not green. Not bloody. A lot more than last week.
Nurse -> Okay. What about the skin around it? Redness, warmth, swelling?
Caller -> The redness is the same. About the size of a, like a silver dollar around the open part. I measured it with the paper ruler. Same as Monday. Not bigger. Not hot. No fever, he feels normal. I checked his temperature before I called. Ninety eight point eight.
Caller -> I took it under his arm. I don't have the oral one. The oral one is at the other apartment.
Nurse -> The underarm is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for measuring. That's very helpful. How is he feeling in general?
Caller -> He's fine. In a good mood. Complaining about the football game. He doesn't feel the sore, you know, with his injury. He can't tell.
Caller -> I tell him every shift. I say, Terrence, how's your back? He says, what back? He jokes.
Nurse -> Humor helps. But we keep checking.
Nurse -> Right. That's why we watch it. Marisol, I need his date of birth.
Caller -> June eighteenth. Nineteen seventy four.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one three three.
Nurse -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one three three. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. It's my cell.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll place an order with the supply company for foam dressings. And I'll arrange delivery tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's great. I'm here till eleven tonight. Tomorrow I'm back at three.
Nurse -> I'll ask them to deliver to the front desk of the building. Is that okay?
Caller -> Yes, there's a doorman. He signs for packages. His name is Elias.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm also going to leave a message for the team about the increased drainage and the smell. I'd like them to take a look.
Caller -> Good. I wasn't sure if I was overreacting.
Nurse -> You weren't. And I'd like a nurse to see him tomorrow. To look at the wound and change the dressing with you.
Caller -> Okay. Tomorrow. I'll be there at three. Is that okay?
Nurse -> I'll ask for an afternoon visit.
Caller -> Great.
Nurse -> What's the unit number, so the delivery goes to the right place?
Caller -> Four fourteen. Fourth floor. The doorman is Elias. He knows everybody.
Nurse -> Got it.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep him off his back as much as you can. Change his position at least every two hours. Only change the dressing if it's soiled or leaking, and clean around the sore with saline.
Caller -> Off his back. Every two hours. Only if soiled or leaking. Saline around. He has the air mattress. And the turning schedule is on the wall.
Nurse -> Good. And call us if he has a fever or chills, if the redness spreads, if the smell gets strong, if you see pus. Also, if he gets a pounding headache or his face is flushed and sweaty, call right away. That can be a sign of a problem for people with his injury.
Caller -> Fever. Chills. Spreading. Smell. Pus. Pounding headache, flushed, sweaty. Yes. I know that one. It's the dysreflexia. Autonomic. They trained us.
Nurse -> Good. You know what to look for.
Caller -> Yes, ma'am.
Caller -> He's got a big day Thursday. His niece is getting married and he wants to go. In the wheelchair. We've been practicing the transfer.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. We'll make sure the wound is protected.
Caller -> He bought a new suit. He wears it around the apartment to break it in.
Nurse -> Ha. A man with priorities.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> No, just that. Wait, actually, can you tell the nurse tomorrow to bring the good tape? The paper one. The cheap tape pulls his skin.
Nurse -> I'll put that in the note.
Caller -> No. That's all. Thank you for answering so fast.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> Oh, wait. One more thing. His mother wants to visit Sunday. She's flying in.
Nurse -> That's nice. Just keep the same routine while she's there.
Caller -> I will. She's going to try to cook for him. I'll watch.
Nurse -> Ha. Please do.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Creek Hospice after hours, this is Raymond.
Caller -> Raymond, hi. It's Halina. Halina Dabrowski. I'm calling about my dad. Casimir Dabrowski. I'm in the driveway. The reception in the house is awful.
Nurse -> Hi Halina. I can hear you. A little choppy. Tell me what's going on with your dad.
Caller -> Sorry about the connection. It's always like this out here.
Caller -> He's been up since. He won't. I can't get him to. It's the third night in a row.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, you cut out. He's been up since when? Can you say that again?
Caller -> Since ten. He's been up since ten. He won't go to bed. He gets so agitated. Every evening. For a week.
Nurse -> Okay. Agitated every evening for a week. What does the agitation look like?
Caller -> He paces. He gets angry. He says we're not letting him go home. He says he has to go to work. He, the door. He keeps going to the front.
Nurse -> Okay. I missed part of that. He keeps going to the front door?
Caller -> The front door. Yes. He tries the knob. He says, I have to go. Tonight he got the, the door open. I caught him. He was on the porch. In his socks.
Nurse -> Okay. He got the door open and was on the porch. That's important. Is he safe now?
Caller -> Yes. He's inside. I locked it. I moved the chair against it. He's in the kitchen with my husband. They're having tea.
Caller -> My husband puts a little honey in his. Dad says it's the only good thing in the house.
Nurse -> A hot cup of tea is a good wind down.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. What is he taking at bedtime?
Caller -> My husband just waved at me through the window. He's making a face. He wants to know if I'm okay.
Nurse -> Tell him thank you for staying with your dad.
Caller -> I will. He's a good man. He's been patient.
Caller -> The Seroquel. Twenty five. Milligrams. At nine. He took it. It didn't. It never.
Nurse -> Sorry, Halina, I'm losing some words. He takes Seroquel twenty five milligrams at bedtime, and he took it at nine tonight. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. At nine. And it's not helping. He's still. Still up.
Caller -> Sorry, the wind is loud. Did you hear me?
Nurse -> I heard most of it. You said it's not helping and he's still up. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Right. That's it.
Nurse -> Okay. How much does he sleep?
Nurse -> And during the day, is he agitated, or only in the evening?
Caller -> Only from about four on. In the morning he's sweet. He asks about the dog. He eats breakfast. He's himself.
Nurse -> That fits with what's called sundowning.
Caller -> That's the word my neighbor used. Sundowning.
Caller -> Three hours. Maybe. Then he's up again. Then he sleeps in the chair in the afternoon. Hours.
Nurse -> Does he nap during the day?
Caller -> A lot. In his recliner. After lunch until four, five. He says he's just resting his eyes.
Nurse -> Ha. That's common.
Nurse -> Okay. About three hours at night, naps in the afternoon. Has he fallen?
Caller -> No. No falls. He's steady. He's ninety two but he's steady. And he doesn't hit. He's never hit anyone. He yells. But he's never hurt me. Or my husband.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. And sleep, did you say three hours?
Caller -> Pardon? You said sleep?
Nurse -> I said, did you say about three hours?
Caller -> Yes. About three, four at most. It's usually three.
Caller -> Three hours. Yes. About three.
Nurse -> Okay. Halina, what's your dad's date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty third. Nineteen thirty four.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Five oh three. Five five five. Zero one nine four.
Nurse -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one nine four. Did I get that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the cell.
Nurse -> Is there another number, in case we lose the connection?
Caller -> My husband's. Don't have it. I'll text it to you. No, you can't text. Forget it. Just call this one.
Nurse -> I'll call this one.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to leave a message for the team, about his night agitation despite the bedtime Seroquel. They may want to adjust something.
Caller -> Please. I'm so tired. We're all so tired. My husband works. I haven't slept.
Nurse -> It sounds like it's been a long week.
Caller -> A long month. A long year. Since the stroke. Two years.
Nurse -> Two years of caregiving is a lot.
Nurse -> I understand. I'd like to send a nurse out tomorrow to see him and talk with you about the nights.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Yes. What time?
Nurse -> The scheduler will call you in the morning with a window.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here. I'm here every day.
Nurse -> And I'll call you tomorrow too, to check in.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> In the meantime, there are some things that can help the evenings. Keep a calm routine, dim the lights as it gets dark, and play soft music. Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and long naps. And if he gets agitated, redirect him gently instead of arguing.
Caller -> Calm. Dim lights. Soft music. No caffeine. Short naps. Don't argue. He loves to argue. I argue back. I shouldn't.
Caller -> We have a record player in the den. His old Polish polkas. Could that work?
Nurse -> Soft polkas could be lovely, if they calm him. Not too lively.
Caller -> The slow waltzes then. He used to dance with my mother.
Nurse -> Ha. It's natural. Try agreeing, and then changing the subject.
Caller -> Agree and change the subject. Okay. Like, yes, Dad, we'll go to work. After breakfast.
Nurse -> Exactly.
Caller -> I can do that.
Nurse -> For the door, can you put a chime or alarm on it? And a night light in the hall. And put the keys out of sight.
Caller -> We have an alarm somewhere. A little chime. I'll find it tomorrow. Tonight I'll put the chair and a bell. The Christmas bell. Hang it on the knob.
Nurse -> A bell on the knob works. And call us if he becomes violent, falls, can't settle for a full night, or leaves the house. If he's missing, call 911 right away.
Caller -> Violent. Fall. Can't settle. Leaves. 911 if missing. Okay.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job, Halina. How are you holding up?
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. I'm just. It's hard to see him like this. He was a machinist. He ran the whole plant. Now he doesn't know what a fork is half the time.
Caller -> Forty one years at the same company. They gave him a clock when he retired. It's still on the mantel. It's always ten minutes fast. He set it that way.
Nurse -> Ha. A man who liked being early.
Caller -> He was never late a day in his life. That's why the door thing, the work thing. It makes sense now.
Nurse -> It does. He thinks he's late for his shift.
Nurse -> Is there anyone who can give you a break, even for an hour?
Caller -> My brother says he'll come Saturday. He lives in Gary. He's not great with Dad. They fight.
Nurse -> Even an hour helps.
Caller -> I'll take what I can get.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's really hard.
Caller -> It is. Thank you for listening.
Nurse -> Tell me a little about him. What was it like growing up with a machinist for a father?
Caller -> Oh, he'd take me to the plant on Saturdays. I'd sit on a stool and watch the lathes. The smell of the oil. I thought it was magic.
Nurse -> That's a beautiful memory.
Caller -> He made me a little brass ring once. Out of a scrap. It still fits my pinky.
Nurse -> You'll have that always.
Caller -> I wear it every day.
Nurse -> Anytime. Get some rest.
Caller -> Thanks. My dad's in the kitchen, he just yelled something about the weather.
Nurse -> What did he say?
Caller -> He said it's going to rain in Gdansk. He's never been to Gdansk.
Nurse -> Ha. Maybe in his dreams.
Caller -> I will. Goodnight, Raymond.
Nurse -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Evergreen Hospice, this is Gloria.
Caller -> Hello, dear. This is Ludmila Petrakova. L U D M I L A. Petrakova, P E T R A K O V A. I am one of your patients. I am calling for no reason. I am fine. I want to report.
Nurse -> Hi Lou Mila. Good to hear from you. Lou Mila Petra Cova. That's a lot of syllables. Say it for me one more time?
Caller -> And you, dear. I always say, the nurse with the nice voice. That is you?
Nurse -> I hope so.
Caller -> It is you. I am sure.
Caller -> Lyud-mee-la. Pet-ra-ko-va. Russian. Everyone makes a mess of it. It's all right.
Nurse -> What do your friends call you?
Caller -> Mila. Or Lusya. My husband called me Lyuda. Nobody calls me anything now. Only you.
Nurse -> I could call you Mila if you like.
Caller -> No, no. Lyudmila. It is a beautiful name. You say it right, you win a prize.
Nurse -> Lyudmila. I'll work on it. Thank you.
Caller -> You are doing good. Better than the last one.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you. So tell me, how are you feeling?
Caller -> I am good. A little pain in my back. Not much. I would say a two. Like a small ache. Like a cat is sitting on my back. A light cat.
Nurse -> Does it get worse when you move?
Caller -> A little when I get out of bed. Then it is gone. I walk in the kitchen, it is gone.
Nurse -> A two. Okay. Do you take anything regularly for it?
Caller -> The Tylenol. Six hundred fifty. Three times a day. In the morning, at lunch, at night. I took this morning's at eight. It works.
Nurse -> Good. And the as needed one? The Ativan for nerves?
Caller -> The Ativan. I took one Tuesday night. Only one. This week. I could not sleep because the neighbor was playing the television. Half milligram. I took the little one and I slept.
Nurse -> Did you feel groggy the next morning?
Caller -> No, no. I got up and cleaned the stove. Like a young girl.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Once this week, Tuesday night. Good. How is your sleep otherwise?
Caller -> Good. I sleep nine, ten hours. Like a baby. I wake up, I drink tea, I sleep again.
Caller -> The neighbor's television is gone now. He went to his daughter. Quiet. I like quiet.
Nurse -> Peace is a nice thing.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. And your appetite?
Caller -> I eat little. A piece of bread with butter. Some soup. A boiled egg. Tea with jam. Little, little. I am not hungry like before. But I do not feel sick.
Nurse -> That's okay. Eating small amounts is common. Lyudmila, I need your date of birth.
Caller -> July fourth. Nineteen thirty eight. I am an American citizen since nineteen seventy six. I was born on Independence Day, in a different country, you see the joke.
Nurse -> Ha. A good joke. And a number for you?
Caller -> My number? Oh, my. I do not know my number. I never call myself. It is on a paper by the telephone but I cannot find my glasses. Do you have it?
Nurse -> I have a number on file. Is it okay if I use that?
Caller -> Yes, yes. Use that. It is the same. I have the same number for thirty years.
Caller -> The telephone is the black one. With the cord. My daughter bought me a new one with buttons for the numbers. I do not use it.
Nurse -> The old phone works.
Caller -> It always works.
Nurse -> Perfect. Thank you. So what did you want to report?
Caller -> I want to ask. For a person. A priest. No, not a priest. I am Orthodox, but the chaplain is fine. A man or a woman, it does not matter. I would like to talk to someone about, you know. About things. Before.
Nurse -> Of course. I'm going to leave a message for the team to request a chaplain visit. They'll find someone who is right for you.
Caller -> Thank you. That is what I want. I have been thinking. I am not afraid. But I would like to talk.
Nurse -> That's very natural. It's good that you asked.
Caller -> My late husband used to say, you must say what is in your heart. Before it is too late. I think he was right.
Nurse -> He sounds wise.
Caller -> He was a stubborn man. But wise. Yes.
Nurse -> I'd also like to send a nurse out Friday, to see you and check how you're doing.
Caller -> Friday. Good. I will make tea. Do you like tea? The nurse will like my tea.
Nurse -> Ha. I'm sure.
Caller -> I make it with a spoon of jam. Like at home. In the glass with the metal holder.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Lyudmila, remember, you can call us any time, day or night. Even if it's just to talk. An after hours nurse always answers.
Caller -> Even at night? I do not want to bother.
Nurse -> Even at night. You are never a bother.
Caller -> That is a kindness. Thank you.
Nurse -> And keep eating small portions of whatever you like, whenever you feel hungry. And sip fluids through the day.
Caller -> Little portions. Tea with jam. Yes. This I can do very well.
Nurse -> Ha. You're an expert.
Caller -> Fifty years of practice.
Nurse -> Do you have a visitor today?
Caller -> My daughter at six. She brings the groceries. She scolds me about the stairs. She is right.
Caller -> I drink five or six glasses a day. My daughter says that is too many. I say no.
Nurse -> Tea counts as fluid. That's good for you.
Nurse -> Anything else you wanted to tell me?
Caller -> No. Only that I am fine. And thank you. Goodbye, dear.
Nurse -> Goodbye, Lyudmila. See you Friday.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Light Home Health, this is Colette.
Caller -> Hi, Colette. It's Beverly Pennington. I'm calling about my husband, Millard. Millard Pennington. I'm not sure if I'm worried or if I'm just a worrier.
Nurse -> Beverly, let me just get the last name right. Pennington, P E N N I N G T O N?
Caller -> That's right. Like the English town. His grandfather was from Kent.
Nurse -> Got it. I'll find his chart.
Caller -> Take your time. We're not going anywhere.
Caller -> Because I'm not allowed to drive. Doctor's orders. So I'm stuck with her.
Caller -> The doctor took my license, actually. After the second fall. I'm not mad about it. I'm a little mad about it.
Caller -> He's very mad about it.
Caller -> I got a bus pass.
Nurse -> A bus pass. That's a good plan.
Caller -> The bus driver and I are on a first name basis. Marty. He saves me a seat.
Nurse -> Hi Beverly. Tell me what you're noticing.
Caller -> He's been wheezing. At night. I can hear it. A whistling. When he lies down. I think it's new. Or maybe it's not new. I don't know.
Caller -> I'm not wheezing. I'm snoring.
Nurse -> Is that Millard in the background?
Caller -> Yes, that's him. He's in the recliner next to me. He's been listening. He says he's fine.
Caller -> I'm fine. She's making a fuss.
Caller -> He is not fine. He coughs all night. He was up three times.
Caller -> I got up to go to the bathroom.
Caller -> You got up three times to go to the bathroom, and you coughed twice each time.
Caller -> Are you counting my coughs now?
Caller -> I'm a counter. Forty years as a bookkeeper.
Nurse -> Ha. Bookkeeper's data is useful.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. It sounds like you two see it differently. That's all right. Let me ask a few questions. Beverly, how long has the wheeze been going on?
Caller -> A week. Maybe two. I said a week. He says never. I'd say a week. It's worse the last three nights.
Nurse -> Does he sleep in the bed or in the recliner at night?
Caller -> The recliner. He hasn't slept in the bed since the hospital in March. He says it's easier to breathe.
Caller -> I sleep better in the chair. It's got a hum.
Caller -> The hum is the oxygen concentrator.
Caller -> I know what the hum is.
Caller -> It's the same as it's always been.
Caller -> It is not the same, Millard. It whistles.
Nurse -> Millard, I'm going to ask Beverly to hold the phone closer, and then I'll ask you a couple of things, okay?
Caller -> Go ahead. I'm listening. I'm fine though.
Nurse -> I'm sure. Do you have your oxygen meter handy, Beverly? The finger one?
Caller -> Yes. Millard, put your finger. There. It says ninety two. Ninety two.
Nurse -> Ninety two. What's his usual?
Caller -> Ninety three, ninety four. It's been ninety two since yesterday. He says that's normal.
Caller -> It's normal for me.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he coughing?
Nurse -> And the oxygen meter. Does it jump around, or is it steady?
Caller -> It was steady at ninety two. It went to ninety one when he coughed, and back up.
Nurse -> That's normal with coughing.
Caller -> I watch it like a hawk.
Caller -> She watches it more than she watches the TV.
Caller -> Yes. A dry cough. Not much phlegm. Mild. It's more at night. I'd say mild.
Nurse -> Is the cough bringing anything up? Color?
Caller -> A little white. Clear. Not yellow, not green. A tablespoon in a day. Maybe less.
Caller -> He says it's the dust. From the furnace. They put in a new furnace and the whole house smelled like toast for a week.
Nurse -> A new furnace can stir things up. I'll have the nurse ask about it.
Caller -> We changed the filter. I changed it. He supervised.
Caller -> He says it's the dust. From the furnace. They put in a new furnace and the whole house smelled like toast for a week.
Nurse -> A new furnace can stir things up. I'll have the nurse ask.
Caller -> We changed the filter. I changed it. He supervised.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Nurse -> Okay. Any fever, chest pain, chills?
Caller -> No fever. No chest pain. No chills. He feels warm sometimes but that's the blanket. He says no chest pain. And I ask him every day.
Caller -> No chest pain. My chest is fine. My lungs are old.
Nurse -> Ha. They're allowed to be. Has he used his inhaler?
Caller -> Yes. The albuterol. The rescue one. He used it at noon today. And at seven this morning. Twice today.
Nurse -> Okay. And his daily medicines? The Spiriva?
Nurse -> Beverly, is he using oxygen at night, or just the inhalers?
Caller -> Oxygen at night. Two liters. The concentrator by the chair. He takes it off sometimes. I put it back on him.
Caller -> I take it off when it makes my nose dry.
Nurse -> Millard, a humidifier bottle on the concentrator helps with that. The nurse can show you.
Caller -> Okay. Good to know.
Caller -> Every morning. He took it at eight. The Spiriva. One capsule in the little inhaler. And the others. The water pill, the blood pressure pill. All in the pill box.
Nurse -> Okay. Beverly, what's Millard's date of birth?
Caller -> November nineteenth. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one two two.
Nurse -> Nine oh one, five five five, zero one two two. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house.
Nurse -> Does anyone else live with you, or is it just the two of you?
Caller -> Just us. Our son is in Dallas. He calls every Sunday. He wants us to move there.
Caller -> We are not moving to Dallas.
Caller -> Dallas is too hot.
Nurse -> It does get warm.
Caller -> We keep the cell in the car. He forgets to charge it.
Caller -> I charge it every Sunday.
Caller -> You do not.
Nurse -> The house line is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I think. Millard, I know you feel fine. But a wheeze that's gotten worse the last three nights, and an oxygen reading that's a point or two lower, deserves a look. I'd like to send a nurse this afternoon.
Caller -> I don't need a nurse.
Caller -> Millard, yes you do.
Nurse -> It's a short visit. They'll listen to your lungs, check your inhaler technique. If everything's fine, you can say I told you so.
Caller -> Ha. I like that. Okay. Send her.
Nurse -> Thank you. Beverly, I'll also leave a message for the team about the wheezing and the oxygen number, so they have it.
Caller -> Thank you. That makes me feel better.
Caller -> I'm so glad I called. I almost didn't. I thought, they'll think I'm a nag.
Nurse -> We never think that. Please call when you're unsure.
Caller -> She's a nag, but she's my nag.
Caller -> Careful, Millard. I'm holding the phone.
Nurse -> In the meantime, if he's wheezy, have him sit upright and lean forward, with his arms on a table or a pillow. Breathe in through the nose and out slowly through pursed lips, like blowing out a candle. And keep a fan on low nearby.
Caller -> Lean forward. Pursed lips. Candle. Fan. He does that already. He knows.
Caller -> I do it when I need it. It's called the pursed lip. The therapist taught me.
Caller -> That's the respiratory therapist who came in September. She was a tough one. She made me practice for twenty minutes.
Caller -> He still talks about her.
Caller -> She had a ponytail like a horse.
Nurse -> Does he do the breathing exercises on his own?
Caller -> When I remind him. I put a sticky note on the remote. Breathe, you stubborn man.
Caller -> It says breathe, please.
Caller -> It says stubborn man. I know what I wrote.
Nurse -> Ha. A sticky note with attitude.
Nurse -> Perfect. And with the albuterol, use the spacer if you have one. One puff, wait a minute, then a second puff if needed. And rinse his mouth after the Spiriva.
Caller -> Spacer. One puff. Wait a minute. Rinse. We have the spacer. It's in the drawer. He hates it.
Caller -> It's a big tube. I look like a trumpet player.
Nurse -> Ha. A trumpet player with healthy lungs. It helps more of the medicine reach them.
Caller -> Fine. I'll use the trumpet.
Caller -> He did a concert last Christmas. For the grandkids. With the spacer.
Caller -> I got a standing ovation.
Nurse -> Ha. I believe it.
Nurse -> And call us if the oxygen reading drops below ninety, if he can't finish a sentence, if his lips turn blue, or if he needs the inhaler more often than every four hours. Call 911 for severe trouble breathing.
Caller -> Below ninety. Can't finish a sentence. Blue lips. Inhaler more than every four hours. 911 for severe. Okay. I wrote it on the pad.
Caller -> She wrote it in capital letters.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Anything else?
Caller -> One more thing. He wants to know if he can have his coffee. He's had three cups already.
Caller -> Two cups. And a half.
Nurse -> A little coffee is fine. Just don't skip the water.
Caller -> What time will the nurse come, do you think? Millard has a card game at four. At the senior center.
Caller -> I'm not missing it. It's a tournament.
Nurse -> Millard, if you feel okay, you can go, after the nurse sees you. I'll ask for an early afternoon time.
Caller -> Early. Before three. Okay. I'll tell the card players.
Caller -> There are sixteen people at the tournament. They need a fourth at his table. He can't be late.
Nurse -> We'll aim for early. Beverly, will you be home to let the nurse in?
Caller -> I will. I'm always home. I'll put the porch light on.
Nurse -> It's daytime. You don't need the light.
Caller -> I put it on anyway. It's a ritual.
Caller -> There are sixteen people at the tournament. They need a fourth at his table. He can't be late.
Nurse -> We'll aim for early. Beverly, will you be home to let the nurse in?
Caller -> I will. I'm always home. I'll put the porch light on.
Nurse -> It's daytime. You don't need the light.
Caller -> I put it on anyway. It's a ritual.
Nurse -> What card game is it?
Caller -> Pinochle. He's the champion. Four years running.
Nurse -> Are you good at bluffing, Millard?
Caller -> Pinochle isn't a bluffing game. It's a game of memory.
Caller -> His memory is selective.
Caller -> Ha. Selective.
Caller -> Five years.
Caller -> Five. He's right. I forget. Five years.
Nurse -> Ha. A champion. We'd better make sure he's at the table.
Caller -> His friends call him the Professor. For the pinochle. He keeps a little notebook of every hand since nineteen eighty one.
Nurse -> Every hand? That's dedication.
Caller -> Thirty one boxes of notebooks in the basement. I tell him they'll go to the library.
Caller -> They are not going to the library.
Caller -> They're going to a museum.
Nurse -> Ha. The Museum of Pinochle.
Caller -> I'd pay to visit.
Caller -> Thank you, Colette. You've been very good.
Caller -> Can I tell you something? My husband is the sweetest man alive. He just doesn't like to admit when he's not well.
Nurse -> A lot of people are like that.
Caller -> I said, the nurse is on the phone. And he said, tell her I'm busy.
Nurse -> Ha. Busy with pinochle.
Caller -> Always.
Caller -> Can I tell you something? My husband is the sweetest man alive. He just doesn't like to admit when he's not well.
Nurse -> A lot of people are like that.
Caller -> I said, Millard, the nurse is on the phone. And he said, tell her I'm busy.
Nurse -> Ha. Busy with pinochle.
Caller -> Always.
Nurse -> Anytime. Both of you take care.
Caller -> Bye, nurse.
Caller -> Goodbye.

Nurse -> Aspen Bridge Palliative Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Joanne. It's Rochelle Tuttle. T U T T L E. I'm a patient. I have a, um, a question about my pills.
Nurse -> No rush. Take a breath. I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry. I'm a little shaky. It's the coffee too.
Nurse -> Hi, Rochelle. Of course. What's going on?
Caller -> I think I might have mixed up two of my bottles. They look the same. They have almost the same name. I picked one this morning and I'm not sure I picked the right one.
Nurse -> Okay, let's slow down and sort it out together. Can I confirm your date of birth first?
Caller -> March twelfth, nineteen seventy one.
Nurse -> Thank you. And a number where I can reach you?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one four five. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect. Do you have both bottles in front of you?
Caller -> I'm holding them. One in each hand. Like I'm weighing them.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Read me the first label.
Caller -> It says clonidine. C L O N I D I N E. Point one milligram. Take one tablet by mouth twice a day.
Nurse -> Good. That's the one for your blood pressure. And the second?
Caller -> The second one says clonazepam. C L O N A Z E P A M. Point five milligram. Take one tablet as needed for anxiety.
Nurse -> Right. Clonazepam is the as needed one. You don't take it on a schedule.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I thought, but the names are so close. And the pills are both little white ones. I can't tell them apart without the bottle.
Caller -> My eyes are not what they used to be. I'm fifty four, not ninety four.
Nurse -> Ha. I hear you. Lots of folks have trouble with those two.
Caller -> I reached for the bottle in the cabinet and then I wasn't sure it was the right one. The cabinet is a mess.
Nurse -> Which one did you take this morning, as best you can tell?
Caller -> I took the clonidine. I'm pretty sure. I checked the bottle after. It was the one that said clonidine. And I have taken it in the morning and at night for a month.
Nurse -> And did you take any clonazepam today?
Caller -> No. No, I haven't needed it. I felt okay this morning. No anxiety. Just a normal day. And I didn't take two of anything. I only took the one.
Nurse -> Good. So you took the clonidine, the right one, once this morning, and you have not taken any extra. That sounds correct.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. That's a relief. I was freaking out a little.
Nurse -> Totally understandable. Taking the wrong pill is scary.
Caller -> I've never had a mix-up before. Not once in three years.
Nurse -> Then you're doing great. This is just a quirk of the bottles.
Caller -> I keep a notebook where I write down each pill. I forgot to write today. That's why I panicked.
Nurse -> A notebook is a smart habit. Write down the clonidine now so it's there.
Caller -> Okay. Writing. Clonidine, morning. Done. I'm using the purple pen.
Caller -> My sister told me to just call. She said, you're allowed to call.
Nurse -> She's right. You are.
Caller -> She lives in Tucson. She calls me every morning at seven. She's the reason I'm even up.
Nurse -> Ha. Good to have a sister like that.
Caller -> I know. She's bossy. But she's right a lot.
Caller -> She sent me a casserole dish by mail. Who mails a casserole dish?
Nurse -> Ha. A very determined sister.
Caller -> It arrived with a note. It said, eat. That's it. One word.
Nurse -> That's love, Tucson style.
Nurse -> So here's how I'd like to make it easier. I'll message our team and your pharmacy and ask whether they can put separate labels on those two, or give you a pill organizer.
Caller -> Oh, that would help. A big sticker on the clonazepam. Something that says anxiety only.
Nurse -> Good idea. I'll pass that along.
Caller -> Because my pharmacy gives me the same kind of bag for everything.
Nurse -> They do that with every customer. We'll ask for a different one.
Nurse -> In the meantime, remember, the clonidine is your scheduled blood pressure pill. The clonazepam is only for anxiety, only when you need it. Read the label every time, and keep the two in different spots, or in a pill organizer.
Caller -> Different spots. Okay. I'll put the clonazepam on the top shelf in the kitchen. And the clonidine by the toaster.
Caller -> Maybe I should also tell my neighbor. She waters my plants. She might touch the cabinet.
Nurse -> It's a good idea to let her know the bottles stay put.
Caller -> She's very nosy. In a good way. She reads everything.
Nurse -> The toaster is a good reminder.
Caller -> I use the toaster every morning. I'll see it.
Nurse -> And if you're ever unsure which pill is which, call us before you take one. We're happy to help.
Caller -> I will. I don't want to feel silly.
Nurse -> It's never silly.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I feel better.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow to see how the sticker plan is going.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Sure. I'll be home. I'm doing a puzzle. It's a thousand pieces. A lighthouse.
Caller -> Is the afternoon better? The mornings I have the lab appointments.
Nurse -> Afternoon is fine. I'll try for after one.
Nurse -> Ha. A thousand pieces. How far along are you?
Caller -> The border. The sky is all blue. It's a nightmare.
Nurse -> The sky is the worst part.
Caller -> I know. Honestly, I would rather take the wrong pill than finish the sky.
Nurse -> Ha. Please do not do that.
Caller -> I'm kidding. I'm kidding.
Nurse -> I know. Take care, Rochelle.
Caller -> You too, Joanne. Bye bye.

Nurse -> Larkspur Home Health, this is Dana.
Caller -> Hi, Dana. It's Anselm Delacroix. I'm calling about my wife, Marguerite. D E L A C R O I X. She's on the IV antibiotics.
Nurse -> Hi, Anselm. Good to hear from you. How are things going?
Caller -> Pretty good, actually. I wanted to give you an update. Nothing urgent. Just checking in.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear.
Caller -> I figured I'd call before the weekend rather than on a Sunday night.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Let me pull up her chart. Can I confirm her date of birth?
Caller -> February twenty seventh. Nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> And the best number for you?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, zero one three one.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, zero one three one. Got it.
Nurse -> Thank you. So how's the incision looking?
Caller -> Better. I think. The redness at the edge is smaller than last week. It used to be about the size of a quarter and now it's a dime. And there's a tiny bit of clear drainage on the gauze in the morning. Not a lot.
Nurse -> Is the drainage clear or yellow?
Caller -> Clear. Maybe a little pink. Not yellow. No smell.
Caller -> I change the gauze every morning like you showed me. I wash my hands for a full song. The happy birthday one.
Nurse -> Ha. Twice through.
Caller -> Twice. Marguerite counts it out loud to make sure.
Nurse -> Good. Has she had any fever?
Caller -> I took it this morning. Ninety eight point nine. And last night ninety eight point six.
Nurse -> That's great. Any chills, or sweats at night?
Caller -> No chills. She said she was warm one night but that was the electric blanket. I told her to turn it down.
Nurse -> Ha. Blanket fever. Okay. And how is she breathing? Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. No chest pain. She's breathing fine. She walked up the stairs yesterday and didn't get winded. She's not having any trouble breathing at all.
Nurse -> Good. And her appetite?
Caller -> Better. She ate a whole sandwich yesterday. Turkey and cheese. First time in a week. And some soup.
Nurse -> That's a really good sign.
Caller -> I know. I almost cried. I'm just so relieved.
Caller -> She even asked for ice cream. Butter pecan. I drove to the store at nine at night.
Nurse -> That's devotion.
Caller -> The cashier said, long day? I said, you have no idea.
Nurse -> It's been a rough couple of weeks for you both.
Caller -> It has. And I'm honestly worn out. My feet are killing me. I've been on them since six.
Nurse -> Ha. You've been running the whole house.
Caller -> And the neighbors keep bringing casseroles. Tuna casserole. Chicken casserole. Another tuna casserole. If I eat one more casserole I'm going to shoot myself.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Tell them she likes salad.
Caller -> I'll tell them. They mean well. I'm joking, I'm not, you know, I'm fine. I'm just tired of beige food.
Caller -> The lady two doors down brought one with potato chips on top. I did not know that was legal.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a classic.
Nurse -> I understand. It was a joke, and I'm glad you're able to laugh. If you ever do feel low, you can tell me.
Caller -> I know. I'm fine. I'm just tired.
Nurse -> Good. How's she doing with the IV line? Any pain or swelling at the site?
Caller -> It looks fine. No swelling. She says it itches a little under the tape. But it's fine.
Caller -> I flush it with the saline like the nurse showed me. It goes in smooth. No resistance.
Nurse -> Good. You're doing a great job.
Nurse -> Okay. The itching can be the tape. Keep the dressing clean and dry, wash your hands before you touch it, and don't pull at the little strips on the incision.
Caller -> I won't touch it. She won't let me touch it anyway. She's very protective.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for her.
Caller -> She tells me, don't touch, don't touch. Like I'm going to eat it.
Nurse -> Ha. Spouses.
Nurse -> I'll plan to come out Thursday for the usual visit and to change the dressing.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. What time, roughly?
Nurse -> Probably after lunch. I'll call that morning.
Caller -> Okay. I'll put it on the calendar. We have the calendar with the cats on it. Marguerite loves cats.
Nurse -> How many cats do you have?
Caller -> Two. Pickle and Waffles. Waffles is a menace. He sat on her incision pillow yesterday.
Nurse -> Ha. He's helping.
Nurse -> And remember, call us if the redness spreads, if there's more drainage, if her temperature gets to one hundred point four or higher, if she has chills, or if the IV site gets painful.
Caller -> Spreading. More drainage. A hundred point four. Chills. Pain at the site. Okay. I've got a magnet on the fridge with the number.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> One more thing. She asked if she can take a shower yet.
Nurse -> Not until I see her Thursday. Keep it covered for a sponge bath until then.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her. She'll be sad.
Caller -> She's already planning what shampoo to use. She's got a list.
Nurse -> Ha. A shampoo list.
Nurse -> Ha. One more day. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I think that's all. Thanks for listening, Dana.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care of your feet.
Caller -> Ha. I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Hospice, this is Tobias.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. This is Imogen Strand. It's about my father. Cornelius Strand. He's a patient with you.
Nurse -> Of course. Mr. Strand. I know the name.
Caller -> Thank you. Sorry. I'm a bit frazzled. We've had a long day.
Nurse -> Hi, Imogen. How can I help tonight?
Caller -> He's hurting. A little. More than a little. And I wanted to ask about his medicine. I think I can give him more but I don't want to give too much.
Nurse -> Good that you called first. Let me get his chart open. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> July eighth, nineteen forty eight. No. Forty nine. Nineteen forty nine. He's seventy seven. He'd correct me.
Nurse -> Forty nine. Got it. Tell me about the pain. Where is it, and how bad on a scale of zero to ten?
Caller -> His hip. And his back. He says six. A six. He's grimacing when I move the pillow.
Caller -> Dad, you said a six, right? He nods. A six.
Nurse -> Thank you for asking him directly.
Caller -> I always ask him. Even when he doesn't answer. He gets annoyed if I don't.
Nurse -> Okay. And what is he taking for pain?
Caller -> There's a patch. A fentanyl patch. Fifty micrograms per hour. It's on his shoulder. It's changed every three days. We put it on Sunday.
Nurse -> So the next change is Wednesday?
Caller -> Wednesday morning. And then there's the liquid. The oxycodone liquid. It's the bottle with the syringe. Five milligrams in five milliliters. The label says give five milliliters every four hours as needed.
Nurse -> Okay. Five milliliters is five milligrams. When did he last get a dose?
Caller -> Two hours ago. About. At six. I gave him five mils at six. And it's now eight. And he's still hurting. So can I give another one now?
Caller -> My brother says give him more. My brother says give him the whole bottle. I said no. I said call the nurse.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Is your brother there with you?
Caller -> He's in the kitchen. He's yelling from the kitchen. He says it's just a little liquid.
Caller -> He's also making grilled cheese. At eight at night. I don't know why.
Nurse -> Ha. Comfort food.
Nurse -> Imogen, I'll explain it to both of you. Please don't give a second dose yet. The oxycodone is every four hours. That means waiting until ten o'clock.
Caller -> Ten. Two more hours. That's a long time when he's hurting.
Caller -> Dennis, the nurse says ten. Ten o'clock. Stop banging the pan. Sorry, the pans.
Nurse -> Ha. I can hear it.
Caller -> What? Yes, Dennis, I'm on the phone. Dennis, he says wait. He says wait until ten.
Nurse -> The medicine is still working. It can take thirty to sixty minutes to reach its full effect, and the patch is also working all the time in the background.
Caller -> Okay. But what if he's still at a six at ten?
Nurse -> Then you can give the next dose at ten, five milliliters, using the oral syringe. Measure at the number five. If it's still bad, call me.
Caller -> Five milliliters. At ten. The syringe. Okay.
Caller -> Should I write it down? I have a chart on the fridge. It has the times.
Nurse -> Yes, write the time you gave each dose. That helps us a lot.
Caller -> Okay. I'm writing. Six o'clock. Five mils. Next ten o'clock. I'm using the green marker.
Nurse -> And please don't change the patch early, or cut it, or add a second patch. The next one is Wednesday.
Caller -> I wasn't going to. Dennis wanted to. I said no.
Caller -> He read online that you can put two on. He reads everything online.
Nurse -> The internet is not always right about that. Two patches can be dangerous.
Caller -> That's what I told him. He didn't believe me.
Nurse -> Good. Let's try some other things in the meantime. Can you help him shift position? Maybe a pillow under his hip, or between his knees?
Caller -> He's on his back. Hold on. Dad, can you roll a little? Okay. He's on his left side now with a pillow. He says that's easier. A five, he says.
Nurse -> A warm blanket over his back, and some quiet music, can help too.
Caller -> He loves the blues. B. B. King. Dennis, find the blues station. It's on the speaker. Okay. It's on.
Nurse -> Good. How's he breathing? Is he sleepy, or hard to wake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's tapping his foot to the music. He's totally himself.
Caller -> He just told Dennis to turn it down. So he's definitely awake.
Nurse -> Ha. Good sign.
Nurse -> That's good. I'd like to send a nurse out this afternoon to look at the pain plan with you, and maybe adjust the doses.
Caller -> This afternoon? I thought you only came on Mondays. Oh, that would be wonderful.
Nurse -> It's no problem. I'll also call you back in an hour to see how the pain is.
Caller -> In an hour. Okay. At the number you have.
Nurse -> I'll use the number on file. Is it still the same one?
Caller -> It is. It's the same. It's my cell. I'm not giving it again, I'm tired, I just said it twenty times to the pharmacy.
Nurse -> Ha. No problem. I have it.
Caller -> Dennis wants to know if he can sit with Dad. I said fine.
Caller -> By the way, we had a nurse named Gloria last week. Is she coming again?
Nurse -> I'll ask who is covering. I'll make sure you know who to expect.
Nurse -> That's great. He can hold his hand and talk to him. That's good medicine too.
Caller -> He's actually crying a little, Dennis. He doesn't cry. I think he just needed to be asked.
Nurse -> It's a hard night for everyone. Thank you for calling.
Caller -> Thank you, Tobias. I really appreciate you picking up.
Nurse -> Anytime. We're here. Bye for now.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Willowmere Home Care, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. This is Marisol Reyes. I'm one of the caregivers. I work with Mr. Thaddeus Okafor in the mornings. T H A D D E U S. Okafor.
Nurse -> Hi, Marisol. Thanks for calling. Is everything okay?
Caller -> Yes, yes. Nothing wrong. It's just supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Marisol. And you're calling about Tadeus?
Caller -> Yes. He's, um, almost out of supplies. The briefs. And the pads. And I'm here alone until his daughter comes at four.
Caller -> She works at the bakery. She's there till three thirty. She brings pastries sometimes.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a nice perk.
Nurse -> Okay. Not a problem. Let's get you sorted. What's his date of birth, Marisol?
Caller -> December fourteenth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> Thanks. And a number where I can call you back?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one one six. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect. So tell me what he has left.
Caller -> I counted. There are three briefs in the closet. Three. Large. And I used one this morning. So that's two after the one he's wearing. I need to tell you the number. It's three, plus the one on him.
Nurse -> Okay. So three left. How many does he use in a day?
Caller -> About five or six. He's on a lot of water pills. And the underpads, the blue ones, there are maybe four. I put one on the chair and one on the bed.
Nurse -> So he'll run out before the end of the day tomorrow.
Caller -> That's what I figured. I wanted to call before it became a crisis.
Caller -> Last month we ran out on a Sunday and I had to go to three stores. I'm not doing that again.
Nurse -> I hear you. We'll keep a closer eye.
Nurse -> Smart. Are the pull-ups an option? Does he have any?
Caller -> I'd rather be early than late. My last client ran out and the agency said it was my fault.
Nurse -> It's never your fault. Supplies are our job to track.
Caller -> No pull-ups. He won't wear them. He says they're for babies. He wants the tape kind.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine. Large briefs with tabs it is.
Caller -> He told me last week he's not a baby and he'll wear what he wants. I said, yes sir.
Nurse -> Ha. You handle him well.
Caller -> Large. Yes.
Nurse -> And do you use any wipes or only the washcloths?
Caller -> The wipes. The fragrance free ones. The scented ones make him itch.
Nurse -> And how is his skin? When you change him, is there any redness?
Caller -> A little. On the tailbone. Just a pink patch. About the size of a half dollar. It's not open. It doesn't look sore. He says it doesn't hurt.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to catch it now.
Caller -> I put the cream on. The white one. The zinc one. Twice a day.
Nurse -> Good. Keep using it. Here's what I'll do. I'll place an order for a case of large briefs and a case of underpads.
Caller -> A case? Oh, good. That'll last.
Nurse -> It should last about three weeks. I'll coordinate the delivery for Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. I'm here Thursday morning. I can sign for it. I'm here from eight to noon.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll ask them to come in that window. I'll note that you'll sign.
Caller -> I'll leave the porch light on in case it's early. The gate sticks. You have to lift it.
Nurse -> I'll add a note about the gate.
Caller -> Okay. And in the meantime? Three briefs and he's using five.
Nurse -> Is there a pharmacy near you that sells them? Just to bridge until Thursday?
Caller -> There's a drugstore two blocks away. I can run over on my break. I'll buy a small pack. Just for tonight.
Nurse -> Good idea. Keep the receipt. We can look into a reimbursement.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep it. Thank you.
Caller -> It's raining here, I hope the delivery trucks aren't stuck. The street floods by the school.
Nurse -> I'll ask them to call before they arrive.
Caller -> That's good. The street name is Mill Road. They always go to Mill Street. It's confusing.
Nurse -> I'll note Mill Road in the delivery notes.
Nurse -> For his skin, change him as soon as he's wet. Clean gently with the wipes. Don't scrub. Put on the barrier cream. And try to reposition him every two hours, so he's not sitting on his tailbone the whole time.
Caller -> Every two hours. Okay. I set a timer on my phone. It plays a chicken sound.
Caller -> He mostly sits in his recliner. I put a cushion with a hole in it. The donut.
Nurse -> The donut cushion can actually hold pressure in one place. A regular foam cushion is better. I'll ask the team.
Nurse -> Ha. A chicken?
Caller -> I have a rooster alarm. It wakes up the whole house. Mr. Okafor loves it. He crows back.
Nurse -> Ha. That's wonderful.
Caller -> He does the whole rooster thing. It's a tough crowd at four in the afternoon.
Nurse -> And call us again if the redness gets darker, if it opens up, or if the briefs run out before Thursday.
Caller -> Darker. Opens. Run out before Thursday. Okay. Got it.
Caller -> I should tell the daughter. She'll want to know about the tailbone.
Nurse -> Yes, please let her know. It's a good thing to share.
Nurse -> Anything else, Marisol?
Caller -> No. Oh, wait. Is it okay if I write down the order number?
Nurse -> I'll text you a confirmation. I'll send it to the cell you gave me.
Caller -> Thank you. That's helpful. I'm terrible with paper.
Nurse -> Ha. We all are. Have a good rest of your shift.
Caller -> You too. Bye, Gwen.

transcript:
Nurse -> Brightwater Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Priya, please, it's Odalys Abernathy. It's my husband, Wendell Abernathy. His face is falling. His whole face on one side. And he can't talk right.
Nurse -> Odalys, I'm here. Stay with me. Is he awake?
Caller -> I don't know what to do. I don't know what to do. He was fine. He was fine ten minutes ago.
Nurse -> I know. You called the right place. I'm going to walk you through it.
Caller -> He's awake. He's sitting at the table. He's looking at me. He's trying to say something and it comes out wrong. It's mush. It sounds like mush.
Caller -> He keeps saying the same word. It sounds like, I don't know, like a name. I can't tell.
Nurse -> That's okay. Don't try to figure it out. Just stay calm.
Nurse -> Which side of his face is drooping?
Caller -> The right. The right side. His mouth is pulled down. And his eye is, it's sagging. He looks like a different person.
Nurse -> Okay. Listen to me. Can he lift both arms for me, can you ask him?
Caller -> Wendell, lift your arms. Lift them up. Like this. He's lifting the left one. The right one is, it just drops. It's like it's made of sand. He can't hold it up.
Nurse -> Okay. Odalys, what you're describing sounds like a stroke. This is an emergency. I need you to hang up and call 911 right now. Do you understand?
Caller -> A stroke? Oh my God. Oh no. Oh my God.
Nurse -> I know. It's scary. But you can help him by acting fast. Hang up with me and call 911. Or put me on speaker, and dial from your cell. Which is easier?
Caller -> My cell. Hold on. I'm putting you on speaker. It's on the table. I'm dialing. Wendell, stay with me. It's ringing.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them your address, and that you think your husband is having a stroke.
Caller -> It's ringing. It's still ringing. Why is it still ringing?
Nurse -> It will pick up. Take a breath.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. Hello. My husband is having a stroke. It's, um, the address is, forty one forty Larch Avenue. In Tulsa. Larch Avenue. Yes. Yes, I'll stay on. Okay.
Caller -> They're sending someone. They said stay on the line with them. Priya, they want me to stay on with them.
Nurse -> Then do what they ask. I'm here too. You can listen to both of us.
Caller -> Okay. They're asking me questions. Is he breathing? Yes. Is he awake? Yes. Okay.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'll stay right here. Put them on speaker too if you can. Odalys, when did this start? What time?
Caller -> I don't know. Twenty minutes ago? We were having breakfast. He was reading the paper out loud. Like he does. And he stopped in the middle of a word. Then his face went. That's when it started. About twenty minutes ago. It was eight forty.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very important. He was normal at eight forty. Tell the paramedics that exact time. They'll ask.
Caller -> Eight forty. He was normal at eight forty. Okay.
Caller -> Eight forty. I looked at the clock when it happened. I always look at the clock. It's a habit from nursing.
Nurse -> That's very helpful, Odalys. You were a nurse?
Caller -> Forty years. Labor and delivery. And I can't think straight right now. Isn't that something?
Nurse -> It's different when it's your own husband. You're doing great.
Nurse -> Did he fall? Did he hit his head on anything?
Caller -> No. No. He didn't fall. He didn't hit anything. He was in his chair the whole time. He just, slumped a little to the side. I caught him.
Nurse -> Good. Odalys, I need you to not give him anything. No food, no water, no pills. Not even aspirin. Okay?
Caller -> No aspirin. Nothing. Okay. I was going to give him water. His mouth is dry.
Caller -> Why not aspirin? I always hear aspirin.
Nurse -> With a stroke we don't know yet if it's a clot or bleeding. The hospital has to find out first. Aspirin could make a bleed worse.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. I understand. No aspirin.
Nurse -> No water. Not right now. He could choke, because the muscles in his throat may be weak. Wet his lips with a damp cloth if you want, but nothing to swallow.
Caller -> A damp cloth. Okay. I have a paper towel. I'm wetting it. Wendell, here. Honey. There.
Caller -> He's drinking from the paper towel. Sucking on it a little. He seems better with his mouth wet.
Nurse -> Good. Just keep it to the lips. Nothing to swallow.
Nurse -> Keep him sitting up, or lying down with his head raised. Don't let him stand or walk. If he tries to stand, gently keep him seated.
Caller -> He's sitting. He's slumping to the right. Should I prop him up with a cushion?
Nurse -> Yes, a cushion on the right side to support him. Gently. Don't pull on the weak arm.
Caller -> I'm putting the couch pillow there. There. He's straighter now.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right. Keep him comfortable and keep talking to him.
Caller -> He's trying to stand up. Wendell, no, sit. Sit down. You have to sit. He's mad at me. He's trying to say something. I can't understand him.
Nurse -> It's okay. He's frustrated. Just keep your voice calm and keep him seated. Odalys, is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> Wendell, honey, I know. I know. They're coming. I'm right here.
Caller -> He pushed my hand away. He's never done that.
Nurse -> It's the stroke. He's scared and frustrated. It's not you.
Caller -> It's locked. The deadbolt. I'll go. Wendell, I'm going to the door, stay in the chair. I'm going. Priya, are you still there?
Nurse -> I'm still here. Go unlock it, and turn on the porch light. Then come right back to him.
Caller -> Okay. It's unlocked. Back. I'm back. He's still in the chair. He's holding on to the table with the good hand.
Nurse -> Good job. You're doing everything right.
Caller -> I'm so scared. He's my whole life. We've been married fifty one years.
Nurse -> I know. And you're helping him right now. This is exactly what he needs you to do.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> Odalys, I'm going to page our on-call team, and let the hospital know a possible stroke is on the way. I'll stay with you the whole time.
Caller -> Please. Thank you. I'm going to keep talking to him. Wendell, you're okay. The ambulance is coming.
Nurse -> Can you tell me his date of birth while we wait? So I can give it to the hospital?
Caller -> April twenty first. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> Thank you. Does he take any blood thinners, or any other medicines you can think of?
Caller -> He takes a few things. For blood pressure. And cholesterol. I'll have the list. It's on the refrigerator. I'll grab it in a second. I don't think blood thinners. I don't think so. I'll check the list.
Nurse -> Good. Get the list and put it by the door. And his insurance card, if it's handy.
Caller -> The wallet. His wallet is on the dresser. I'll get it. Hold on. Wendell, I'm going to the bedroom, I'll be one second. Don't move. Okay. I have the wallet. And the list. Both.
Nurse -> Perfect. Put them by the front door.
Caller -> Done. They're on the bench. Priya, I can hear sirens. Is that them?
Caller -> Should I put on a coat on him? He's only in his shirt. It's cold out.
Nurse -> Put a blanket over his shoulders. Keep him seated.
Caller -> The afghan. The one from the couch. I'll get it. Wendell, here, I'm putting this on you. There. Warm.
Nurse -> It might be. Let's keep the line open. Is the porch light on?
Caller -> It's on. I turned it on. I don't see them yet. I'm looking out the window.
Nurse -> How is he doing right now? Any change in his face or his arm?
Caller -> Same. The same. His face is still drooping. He's still holding on with the left hand. He's looking at me. He's crying a little. I think he knows something's wrong.
Nurse -> That's okay. Hold his good hand. Tell him help is coming.
Caller -> Wendell, honey, help is coming. I'm right here. I have you.
Nurse -> Odalys, you're doing everything right. When the paramedics arrive, tell them what happened, and tell them eight forty was the last time he was normal.
Caller -> Eight forty. Okay. Eight forty. I'll tell them. I've said it so many times I'll never forget it.
Caller -> I see a truck. A red truck. The fire truck. They're pulling in. They're getting out. Priya, they're here.
Caller -> The neighbors are coming out. They're on the lawn. Mr. Delgado is waving.
Nurse -> That's okay. The paramedics can handle it.
Nurse -> Good. Open the door and let them in. Leave the phone on the table. I'll stay on until you tell me to go.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Coming. In here! He's in the kitchen! Right here! It's a stroke! His face and his arm! Since eight forty! Over here!
Nurse -> I can hear them. Odalys, answer their questions. I'll be right here.
Caller -> He's in the chair. Eight forty. No, he didn't fall. The list is by the door. Yes. Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> Odalys, are they with him now?
Caller -> Yes. They have him. They're talking to him. They're checking his hand. They're asking him to squeeze.
Nurse -> Good. Which hospital are they taking him to?
Caller -> They said Saint Gabriel's. The one on Peoria. The stroke center.
Nurse -> That's a good one. I'll call them now and let them know he's coming. I'll also tell our on-call clinician.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much. I'm going to go with him in the ambulance. They said I can.
Nurse -> Go with him. Take the list and your phone. Do you have your keys?
Caller -> Should I bring his slippers? He'll want his slippers. He hates cold floors.
Nurse -> Bring them if they're near, but don't delay. The paramedics can wait a moment.
Caller -> The slippers are by the bed. Got them. I'm taking his glasses too. He can't read without them.
Caller -> Yes. In my purse. I have my purse. I'm putting on my shoes. Wait. Can you lock the door? No, I can't ask you that.
Nurse -> I can't, but the paramedics usually wait while you lock up. Take your time. Lock it behind you.
Caller -> Okay. I'm going. They're lifting him. They have a stretcher. Wendell, I'm coming. I'm right behind you.
Nurse -> Odalys, before you go. Is your cell still nine one eight, five five five, zero one three seven?
Caller -> Yes. Nine one eight, five five five, zero one three seven. That's it. I'll have it on.
Nurse -> Good. Go. Take care of him. We'll follow up tomorrow.
Caller -> Thank you, Priya. Thank you for staying on. I couldn't have done it.
Caller -> I'm in the ambulance now. I'm sitting by his head. He's looking at me. He squeezed my hand. With the good hand.
Nurse -> That's a great sign that he knows you. Keep talking to him.
Caller -> Wendell, I love you. I'm right here.
Nurse -> You did it. You called fast. Go be with him. Bye for now.
Caller -> Bye. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Marlowe Home Health, this is Fatima.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Fatima. My name is Mackenzie Dunleavy. I'm the granddaughter of Philomena Vandersloot. V A N D E R S L O O T. She's one of your patients.
Nurse -> Thanks for calling, Mackenzie. Take a breath. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. Breathing. In and out.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm just nervous. I've never done this before.
Nurse -> Hi, Mackenzie. Yes, I know Mrs. Vandersloot. What's going on?
Caller -> I think I forgot to give her one of her pills. At noon. I'm visiting. I'm staying for the week. And I just noticed on the chart it's one thirty.
Caller -> My mom normally does it, but she's at a conference in Denver. So it's me.
Caller -> She left a list on the fridge. A long one. With dates and little hearts.
Nurse -> Ha. Your mom sounds organized.
Nurse -> That's a lot of responsibility. You're doing well to call.
Nurse -> Okay. Not a problem. Let's work through it. Can you tell me her date of birth?
Caller -> October thirtieth, nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Nurse -> And are you with her right now?
Caller -> I'm in the kitchen. She's in the living room. I can see her through the door.
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one seven six.
Nurse -> Perfect. Which pill did you miss?
Caller -> It's the, um, hydrolazine. Hydro lazine? I'm not sure how to say it. It's the blood pressure one. Twenty five milligrams. Three times a day. She had the eight o'clock this morning. I forgot the noon.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like hydralazine. Twenty five milligrams, three times a day, for her blood pressure.
Caller -> Yes. That one. Hydralazine. Sorry. I'm bad with these names.
Caller -> I'm a graphic designer. I'm good with colors. I'm terrible with chemistry.
Caller -> I color code everything. My closet. My calendar. My sock drawer.
Nurse -> Ha. Then color is a great tool. Use stickers.
Caller -> I have a pack of dots in my bag. Green and white. Perfect.
Nurse -> It's a tough name. Did she take anything else for pain or itching today?
Caller -> Yes. The itch pill. Hydroxyzine. Ten milligrams. It's for her itchy skin, only when she needs it. I gave her one at nine this morning. She's been scratching her arms all day.
Nurse -> Okay. So hydroxyzine ten milligrams, as needed, last given at nine. Those two names are very close, but they're different medicines. Hydralazine is for blood pressure and hydroxyzine is only for itching.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't realize they were so close. I got them mixed up on the chart. I wrote the wrong time next to the wrong one.
Nurse -> That's an easy mistake. How is she feeling now? Any dizziness, or headache, or feeling faint?
Caller -> No. She's in the chair. She's watching her game show. She seems fine. She just ate a sandwich.
Caller -> She's got her afghan and her tea. She likes tea at one thirty. Chamomile.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
Caller -> It is. She's watching The Price Is Right and yelling at the contestants.
Nurse -> Ha. She has opinions.
Caller -> She's always right, too. She guessed a blender within three dollars.
Nurse -> Good. Here's what I'd do. Give the missed hydralazine now. Since it's one thirty, and the next one is at six, give it now and keep the six o'clock dose as usual. Don't double up.
Caller -> Give it now. And still give the six o'clock. Okay. And not two at once.
Caller -> What about at ten? Is there a ten o'clock one?
Nurse -> No. It's three times a day. Eight, noon, six in her usual schedule. So today it'll be eight, one thirty, and six.
Nurse -> Right. Just the one now, one at six.
Caller -> Got it. One now, one at six. I'm setting a phone alarm for six. It plays a harp.
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting it. The hydralazine. I see it. The bottle with the green cap. And the itch one has the white cap. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. A pill organizer would help a lot here. I'll message our team and the pharmacy and ask about setting one up.
Caller -> That would be great. I'm only here till Sunday. Her son is coming after.
Nurse -> Then we'll make sure he gets the same instructions.
Caller -> His name is Barnaby. I'll text him a photo of the chart. He's very organized. He has a spreadsheet.
Caller -> His kids' soccer schedule is color coded too. We get it from my dad's side.
Nurse -> Perfect. A spreadsheet will help.
Caller -> Okay. She's taking it now. With a glass of water. She says, what are you giving me? I said, your pressure pill, Grandma.
Caller -> She says it tastes like chalk. I told her it's just the pill. Her face is making a chalk face.
Caller -> Now she wants a cookie. To get the taste out.
Nurse -> A small one is fine.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully she's not too upset.
Nurse -> Ha. A good explanation.
Caller -> She says she's been taking them since nineteen eighty. She knows what she's doing.
Nurse -> Ha. She's right.
Nurse -> If she gets dizzy or faint, or if anyone's unsure which pill is which, please call us.
Caller -> Dizzy. Faint. Which pill. Okay. I'll write it on the chart. In red.
Caller -> I also wrote on the chart that hydralazine is for pressure and hydroxyzine is for itch. In big letters.
Nurse -> That's excellent. It'll help the next person too.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else, Mackenzie?
Caller -> No. Thank you. I feel better. I was kind of freaking out.
Nurse -> You did the right thing by calling. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sycamore Row Hospice, this is Beatrice.
Caller -> Hi. I'm not sure I'm calling the right place. I'm looking for information. For my mother. She's not a patient yet. I just want to understand what hospice is.
Nurse -> Of course. I'm happy to talk about that. Is she at home right now, or in the hospital?
Caller -> She's at home. Her doctor mentioned it last week. I didn't know what to say. I said I'd call and ask.
Nurse -> That's very common. Hospice is care focused on comfort and quality of life, for someone with a serious illness. It is provided at home, and the team includes a nurse, a social worker, an aide, and a chaplain if you want one.
Caller -> Okay. And does it cost a lot? She has Medicare. And a small supplemental.
Nurse -> If she qualifies, Medicare covers the hospice benefit, including the nurse visits, equipment, and medicines related to her illness. Most families pay very little.
Caller -> Oh, that's a relief. I was so worried. I thought we'd have to sell the house.
Nurse -> No, nothing like that. The first step is a conversation, called an evaluation. A nurse comes out, talks with her and with you, and reviews her records.
Caller -> Does that mean she has to sign up that day?
Nurse -> No. It's only information. You can say no at any point.
Caller -> Okay. Good. I'd like to think about it. I want to talk to my brother first. He's in Phoenix.
Nurse -> Of course. Take your time. I can send you a packet in the mail, or you can look us up online. Would you like a call back later this week?
Caller -> Not yet. I'll call when we're ready. Thank you for being so kind. I was nervous to call.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Calling is the hardest part. We're here whenever you want to talk.
Caller -> Thanks. Bye.
Nurse -> Take care. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tern Harbor Hospice, this is Raul.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Raul. This is Sunniva Brandvold. S U N N I V A. I'm calling about my husband, Lucian. Lucian Brandvold. He's with you, and I'm not sure if this is a real emergency.
Nurse -> Hi, Sunniva. I'm glad you called. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> I almost didn't. I thought, he's fine, I'm overreacting. And then I thought, no, call.
Nurse -> You did the right thing.
Caller -> Well. He didn't fall. I want to say that first. He didn't fall. But he sort of ended up on the floor.
Nurse -> Okay. Take me through it. What time was this?
Caller -> About an hour ago? Maybe a little more. I was in the kitchen. I heard a thump. Not a loud thump. A soft one.
Nurse -> And where was Lucian when you heard it?
Caller -> In his chair. The recliner. The big one by the window. And when I came in, he was on the floor next to it. Sitting. Sort of slumped.
Nurse -> So he went from the chair to the floor.
Caller -> Yes. But he slid. He slid down. It wasn't a fall. A fall is when you trip. He was in the chair and he slid down.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you see it happen?
Caller -> No. I was in the kitchen. So I don't know exactly. I think he slid. Or maybe he leaned and went over. I really don't know.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll call it what it is when I see him. For now, let's check how he is. Did he hit his head?
Caller -> No. He says no. He says he didn't hit anything. And I looked. There's no mark. Nothing on his head.
Nurse -> Does anything hurt? His hip, his back, his wrist?
Caller -> He says nothing hurts. I asked him three times. Is anything sore, Lucian? He shakes his head. No. No pain. He's very stubborn. He'd say that anyway.
Caller -> Forty years of marriage. He once drove to the hospital with a broken toe and told the nurse it was a stubbed toe.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds familiar.
Caller -> Actually, he winced when I helped him sit up. A little. Around his hip. But then he said it was nothing. So I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something I want to look at. Let me ask more. Is it his left or his right hip?
Caller -> I think the left. The left side. I'm not sure. He was pointing at it and then he stopped.
Nurse -> All right. How did you get him up?
Caller -> I couldn't do it alone. He's too heavy. I called my neighbor. Mr. Tolliver. He came over in his slippers. Together we lifted him back into the chair. He's in the chair now.
Caller -> He's eighty one. He shouldn't be lifting anything. I felt terrible. But he insisted.
Nurse -> It was kind of him. Next time we'll try to have a better plan.
Nurse -> Good. Did he help at all, or was he limp?
Caller -> He helped a little. He pushed with his legs. He wasn't limp. He's awake. He's talking. He asked for the TV remote.
Caller -> It's his favorite thing. He holds it all day even when it's not on.
Nurse -> Ha. The remote is a lifeline.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. Is he confused at all? Talking normally?
Caller -> He's talking like he does. Slow, soft. His voice is always soft now. But he's making sense. He told Mr. Tolliver his shoe was untied.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. And is there any bruising, or swelling, or any bleeding that you can see?
Caller -> No bruises. I looked at his arms and his legs. Nothing. No blood. No cuts. His skin is okay. I didn't look at his hip because he had his pants on. I didn't want to pull them down.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'll look when I see him. Sunniva, what's Lucian's date of birth?
Caller -> September fourteenth. Nineteen sixty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your callback number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one seven four.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one seven four. Good.
Caller -> Do I need to call 911? I wasn't sure. I almost called them, but he said don't. He said it's embarrassing. He doesn't want the ambulance and the neighbors.
Nurse -> From what you're telling me, he's awake, talking normally, no head strike, no obvious injury. That doesn't sound like an emergency right now. But I'd feel better if a nurse saw him. Let me ask a few more things.
Caller -> Okay. Please.
Nurse -> Is he short of breath? Any chest pain?
Caller -> No. None of that. He's breathing normal. He's not in pain. He's not dizzy, he says. He's just, tired. He's always tired.
Nurse -> Does he take anything that makes him drowsy? Any new medicines this week?
Caller -> No. Same as always. We didn't change anything. The nurse last week said to keep going.
Nurse -> Good. I'd like to send a nurse out tomorrow to check him over, including his hip. If anything changes tonight, you call.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> The morning, probably. The nurse will call you with a time.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be here. I'm always here.
Nurse -> I'm also going to message our team about getting a mechanical lift and a physical therapy evaluation. If he's sliding out of the chair, we may need a different seat or a belt.
Caller -> A lift? Like the hospital kind? Oh, that would be wonderful. My back is killing me.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand. We'll look into it.
Caller -> He's getting heavier because he's not moving. And I'm getting older.
Nurse -> You're doing an amazing job. That's a lot to carry.
Caller -> Thank you. I try. I didn't sleep well last night.
Nurse -> Sunniva, please don't try to lift him alone, even if he insists. Use two people, or call for help. And keep the path clear around the chair. Maybe push the chair against the wall so he can't slide that way.
Caller -> Against the wall. Okay. The chair is by the window. I can turn it. There's a bookcase on the other side. I'll move the small table.
Nurse -> That sounds good. And please call us right away if he hits his head, if he has new pain, if he vomits, if he gets drowsy or confused, or if he falls again.
Caller -> Hits his head. New pain. Vomits. Drowsy. Confused. Falls again. I'll write it on the back of an envelope. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Is he eating and drinking okay?
Caller -> He ate dinner. Chicken and rice. Not a lot. Half. He had water with a straw.
Nurse -> That's fine. Is he comfortable right now?
Caller -> He's watching a cooking show. Which is funny because he hasn't cooked since two thousand eleven.
Nurse -> Ha. What's he watching?
Caller -> Some baking thing. With tents. They make cakes in tents.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that show.
Caller -> Everyone loves it. Lucian says the British guy is too nice.
Nurse -> Ha. He has opinions.
Caller -> He does. He's quite grumpy. He's the grumpiest man I've ever met. I adore him.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Okay, I'll pass this along to the team tonight. If you need anything before the nurse arrives, call.
Caller -> I will. Is it okay if I check on him through the night?
Nurse -> Absolutely. Look in on him every couple of hours, and make sure he's easy to wake up.
Caller -> Should I wake him at night to check? He sleeps so lightly.
Nurse -> Just a peek, a glance. If he's breathing normally, let him sleep.
Caller -> Easy to wake. I'll set an alarm. Every two hours. I have the one with the rooster.
Caller -> I keep a small flashlight by the bed. The kind with the red light. It doesn't wake him up as much.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Nurse -> Ha. That's popular. Alright.
Caller -> Do you think I should have called 911? I keep going back and forth.
Nurse -> You made a reasonable choice. He's awake, he's alert, no injury. If it were different, I'd tell you. Trust your instincts and keep calling.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. I've been second guessing.
Nurse -> Everybody does. Is there anyone who can stay with you tonight?
Caller -> My sister says I should have called her. She lives in Duluth. What would she do?
Nurse -> She'd probably be the second voice on the phone. It helps to have one.
Caller -> My daughter is coming at nine. She's driving from Allentown. She'll sleep on the couch.
Nurse -> That's good. Two people is better.
Caller -> I'll tell her about the lift. And the envelope.
Nurse -> Perfect. Talk to you soon, Sunniva.
Caller -> One more thing. The tents on that show are the best part. Sorry. I'm rambling.
Nurse -> Ha. Not at all. Take care.
Caller -> Thank you, Raul. Bye.
