transcript:
Nurse -> Orchard Lane Home Health, this is Samir.
Caller -> Samir, hi. It's Gretchen Halvorsen. H A L V O R S E N. I'm a patient. My blood sugar is low. It's forty eight. And I'm shaky.
Nurse -> Gretchen, thank you for calling. Forty eight is low. Are you awake and able to drink something?
Caller -> Yes. I'm awake. I'm sitting at the table. I'm sweating. My hands are trembling. I can hold the phone but it's shaking.
Nurse -> Before we go on, what's your date of birth, so I have the right chart?
Caller -> June second. Nineteen seventy three.
Nurse -> Okay. I need you to drink something sweet right now. Do you have orange juice, or regular soda, anything with sugar?
Caller -> I have orange juice. In the fridge. Hold on. I have to stand up. I'm a little dizzy.
Nurse -> Take your time. Hold on to the counter. Don't rush.
Caller -> I'm at the fridge. I have the juice. I'm pouring a glass. My hand is shaking so much, it's going on the counter.
Nurse -> That's fine. Spill it. Just get some in a glass.
Caller -> Okay. I have about, um, half a glass. Is that enough?
Nurse -> About four ounces is what we want. Half a cup. Drink it now.
Caller -> Drinking. Okay. It's cold. It's good. I'm drinking it.
Nurse -> Good. Drink it slowly but steadily.
Caller -> It's the kind with pulp. I hate pulp. But today I love pulp.
Nurse -> Ha. Pulp is your friend.
Nurse -> Sit back down. I'm going to stay right here with you. While you sit, tell me what happened. How did you get low?
Caller -> I took my insulin before lunch. The Humalog. Ten units. And then the phone rang and I got distracted and I never ate. It was my sister. She talks. Three hours later I felt this.
Nurse -> Okay. So ten units of Humalog before lunch, and no lunch. That will do it. Is that your usual dose?
Caller -> It's my usual dose with a meal. I've been doing it for years. I never skip a meal. I don't know how I did it.
Nurse -> It happens to everyone. When did you last check before this?
Caller -> My sister was telling me about her cruise. Forty five minutes about a buffet. I should have said I have to go eat.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the ironic part.
Caller -> This morning. It was one forty. A hundred forty. I mean, one hundred forty. Sorry. I'm foggy.
Nurse -> No problem. Now, have you passed out, or felt like you were going to? Any trouble swallowing?
Caller -> No. No passing out. I haven't passed out. I can swallow fine. I just drank it. I'm shaky and sweaty and my head feels light.
Nurse -> Good. That's very good. Gretchen, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, so they know. Stay on with me.
Caller -> I'm paging the on-call clinician now. Give me one moment. I'll get a call back to them.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm still here. I feel a little better already.
Nurse -> That's the juice working. It takes about ten or fifteen minutes. Let's talk while we wait. How is your head?
Caller -> I'm checking the clock on the stove. It's four oh five. So fifteen minutes is four twenty.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're thinking clearly already.
Caller -> It's okay. The dizzy is getting less. I'm warm. My shirt is wet.
Nurse -> That's the sweating. It will pass.
Caller -> I feel silly. I've done this for thirty years.
Nurse -> You're not silly. A phone call can derail anyone. Would you like me to stay on the line the whole fifteen minutes?
Caller -> I'd like that. It's nice to have someone. I live alone. My cat is staring at me.
Nurse -> Ha. What's his name?
Caller -> Pickles. He's a gray one. He knows something is wrong. He sat on my feet.
Nurse -> Ha. A good nurse.
Caller -> He's a better listener than my ex-husband.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a high bar.
Caller -> He's the best one. He's also a thief. He stole my sandwich last week.
Nurse -> Ha. Well, we'll make you a better one soon.
Caller -> I do have crackers. And peanut butter. I could have those after.
Nurse -> Yes, that's exactly right. In fifteen minutes, recheck your sugar. If it's above seventy, eat a snack with some protein, like the crackers and peanut butter. Then check again in an hour.
Caller -> I have a granola bar too. The chewy kind. The chocolate chip.
Nurse -> Crackers and peanut butter is better for staying steady, the granola bar is fine for a quick fix.
Caller -> Above seventy. Crackers and peanut butter. And check in an hour. Okay.
Nurse -> And if you ever feel like you're going to pass out, or you can't swallow, you hang up and call 911. Don't wait.
Caller -> Call 911. Okay. I have my phone. I'm not going to pass out. I think.
Caller -> Do I have a glucose gel somewhere? I think I have one in the bathroom drawer. Expired maybe.
Nurse -> Check the date later and replace it. For now, juice is fine.
Nurse -> Good. Tell me when you've got your meter in front of you.
Caller -> It's here. On the table. It's been fifteen minutes. Or twelve. I'll check now.
Nurse -> A couple more minutes would be better. Let's wait. I'll call you back in fifteen minutes either way.
Caller -> Okay. You call me back in fifteen. I'll check my sugar when you call. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's perfect. I'll call you in fifteen minutes.
Caller -> What's your name again?
Nurse -> Samir.
Caller -> Samir. I'm writing it on the napkin. With the juice. Thank you.
Caller -> I'm going to take a picture of the napkin. I never remember names. My doctor says it's the stress.
Nurse -> Ha. A napkin is as good as any chart.
Nurse -> Anytime. I'll call at the number on file. It's still the one ending in oh one seven four?
Caller -> Yes. Three one two, five five five, zero one seven four.
Nurse -> Great. Sit tight. Sip some water too, if you want.
Caller -> I will. Bye for now.
Nurse -> Talk to you soon, Gretchen.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harborview Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Hello, Lena. This is Ottoline Brennan. I'm the neighbor of Mr. Pellegrino. P E L L E G R I N O. Ignatius. I sit with him in the afternoons.
Nurse -> Hi, Ottoline. I know you. You're the one with the lemon cake.
Caller -> That's me. I'll bring you one next time.
Nurse -> Hi, Ottoline. Thanks for calling. What's going on today?
Caller -> It's the mattress. The air one. The alarm has been beeping since I got here. I think since this morning. It beeps and beeps and I can't make it stop.
Nurse -> Okay. Is Mr. Pellegrino resting comfortably right now?
Caller -> He's asleep. He's fine. He's not bothered. But I'm bothered. It's like a smoke alarm.
Caller -> He had a good morning. He ate half an egg. His daughter fed him.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Nurse -> Ha. That's annoying. What does the pump look like? Is there a light on it?
Caller -> I've tried pressing every button. I pressed the mute one and it beeped louder.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the test button, probably.
Caller -> There's a red light. It's blinking. And a little picture of a battery. No, a little picture of a, what do you call it, a hose.
Nurse -> Okay. That sounds like a low pressure alarm. That usually means air is leaking, or the hose is kinked. Can you look behind the bed? Where the hose goes from the pump to the mattress?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me get on my knees. These knees. I'm eighty one. Hold on. I see it. The hose goes from the pump on the floor to the mattress. And it's, oh. It's bent. It's folded over, behind the leg of the bed.
Nurse -> That's very likely it. Can you gently straighten it?
Caller -> I'm straightening it. Okay. It's straight. Oh. The beeping stopped. It stopped. Wonderful. Thank goodness. I can hear myself think.
Nurse -> Ha. Good job. The light should turn green in a minute.
Caller -> I feel like a plumber. My late husband would be proud. He was a plumber.
Nurse -> Ha. He taught you well.
Caller -> It's green now. It's solid green. Oh, you're a miracle worker.
Nurse -> You're the one who found it. Now, you said the mattress felt soft. Is it filling up?
Caller -> It's coming up. I can hear the air. It's making a whoosh. But one side is still soft. The left side, where his legs are. It was flat before. Like a deflated tire. It's coming back slowly.
Nurse -> It can take twenty to thirty minutes to fill again. Is the pump making any unusual noise?
Caller -> It's rattling. A little. Like a marble in a can. It does it every few seconds. It's not loud but it's not right.
Nurse -> That's worth having a technician look at. I'm going to call the equipment vendor and ask them to come service the pump.
Caller -> Oh, good. They have my number? They called me last month when the delivery came.
Caller -> They called last month about the walker. A very young man. He said ma'am a lot.
Nurse -> Ha. They train them well.
Nurse -> I'll give them yours too. What's the best number for you?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one nine three. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one nine three. Got it. And what's his date of birth, Ottoline? For the order.
Caller -> I don't know it by heart. Let me think. It's in his chart. It's on the folder. August seventeenth. Nineteen thirty three. He's ninety two.
Nurse -> Great. I'll ask them to come out tomorrow. I'll coordinate the timing with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow. I'm here in the afternoons. His daughter is here in the mornings, but she's at work. I can let them in.
Caller -> I have my bridge group at noon, but I'll be back by one thirty. I'll tell them to wait.
Nurse -> I'll ask for after two, to be safe.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll note that. And I'd also like a nurse to see him tomorrow, to check his skin and the mattress.
Caller -> That would be good. I worry about his skin. He's so thin.
Caller -> I put lotion on his hands every day. The lavender one. He likes the smell.
Nurse -> That's a lovely touch.
Nurse -> Let's check it together. Ottoline, have you noticed any redness, or open areas, on his heels, hips or back?
Caller -> I haven't looked. I didn't want to roll him on my own. He's very sensitive.
Nurse -> That's fine. Don't roll him by yourself. When his daughter comes, ask her to look. Anything red that doesn't go away is worth telling us.
Caller -> I did see his heels yesterday. They looked fine. Pink but normal. No sores. No redness that I could tell.
Caller -> His socks have the grippy bottoms. I bought them at the dollar store. They are pink.
Nurse -> Ha. Pink is fine.
Nurse -> Good. Until the technician comes, keep the hose straight and don't unplug the pump, even if it's noisy. The mattress needs to keep running.
Caller -> Straight hose. Keep it plugged in. Even if it rattles. Okay.
Nurse -> And if he's awake, and with help, he should be turned about every two hours. Look at his heels, hips and tailbone when you do.
Caller -> Every two hours. His daughter does that in the morning. I'll do it with the aide, if the aide comes. I can't do it alone.
Caller -> His daughter is a bank teller. She leaves early and tells me everything on a sticky note.
Nurse -> That's fine. Never lift him alone.
Caller -> I know. I know.
Caller -> He's waking up. Hello, Ignatius. How's my favorite neighbor? He's smiling. He says the beeping is gone. That's the first thing he said.
Nurse -> Ha. That's wonderful. Tell him hello for me.
Caller -> Lena says hello. He says tell her I want a cheeseburger.
Caller -> His eyes are twinkling. He's got a lot of life in him for a man of ninety two.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll see what I can do.
Caller -> He's been asking for that for three days. I made him soup.
Nurse -> Maybe a small bite of a cheeseburger would be a nice treat, if he feels like it.
Caller -> I'll tell his daughter. She might sneak one. From the diner on Maple.
Caller -> She'll say she doesn't know anything about it. But I know.
Nurse -> Ha. A diner burger.
Caller -> The best in the county. I'll bring him a pickle, at least.
Nurse -> A pickle is a great start.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Lena. You saved my afternoon.
Nurse -> Anytime. Call if the alarm comes back, or if the pump stops.
Caller -> I will. Goodbye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harborview Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Lena, hi. I need help. It's Folasade Hayes. My mother is Beatrix Oyelaran. She's one of yours. I think I gave her too much morphine.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called right away. Tell me your name again, slowly?
Caller -> Folasade. F O L A S A D E. Hayes. My mother is Oyelaran. O Y E L A R A N.
Nurse -> Okay, Folasade. I'm here. We'll work through this together. Is she awake right now?
Caller -> She's sleepy. She's in the bed. But she woke up when I said her name. She opened her eyes. She said, what.
Caller -> She's in her hospital bed in the living room. The lamp is on. I turned it low.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep the light low.
Nurse -> Good. That's a good sign. Tell me exactly what you gave her, and when.
Caller -> The morphine. The liquid. The little brown bottle. The concentrate. I gave her one milliliter. It was forty minutes ago. About.
Nurse -> One milliliter. Of the concentrate. What does the label say for her dose?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me get the bottle. I'm looking. It says morphine, twenty milligrams per milliliter. Give point two five milliliter every four hours as needed.
Nurse -> Point two five. That's a quarter of a milliliter. And you gave a full milliliter.
Caller -> Yes. A whole one. I filled the syringe to the one. I thought the one was the right one. I thought, one milliliter, twenty, no, five milligrams. I mixed up the numbers. Oh God.
Nurse -> Folasade, stay with me. It's a mistake, and it's fixable. A full milliliter is twenty milligrams. Her dose was five. So she got four times her dose.
Caller -> Four times. Oh no. Oh no, oh no.
Caller -> I can't believe I did that. I've done it a hundred times.
Nurse -> The numbers are small and the bottle is strong. It's easy to slip.
Nurse -> I know. Take a breath. I need you to do a few things. Is she breathing right now?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. She's breathing. She's breathing slowly.
Nurse -> Let's count. Look at her chest. Count each breath for a full minute. I'll wait.
Caller -> Okay. One. Two. Three. Hold on. I'm counting out loud. Four. Five. This is so long. Six. Seven.
Nurse -> Take your time. You're doing fine.
Caller -> Eight. Nine. Ten. That's ten. In a minute. Is ten bad?
Nurse -> Ten is on the low side. Normal is twelve to twenty. But she's breathing, and she woke up to her name. That's reassuring.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Ten.
Caller -> Her chest goes up. Down. It's slow, but it's even. It's not jerky.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Thank you for describing it.
Nurse -> Look at her lips and her fingertips. What color are they?
Caller -> Pink. They're pink. Her lips are pink. Her fingers are okay. Not blue. No blue.
Nurse -> Good. Now say her name again, and gently shake her shoulder. Does she wake up?
Caller -> I'm going to do that. I'm pulling the blanket back a little so I can see her better.
Caller -> Mama. Mama, can you hear me? She's opening her eyes. She's looking at me. She's saying, I'm tired. She's slurring a bit. She's sleepy but she knows me.
Nurse -> That's what I wanted to hear. Okay. Here's what happens now. No more morphine. Nothing else tonight until a nurse says so. Do you understand?
Caller -> No more. Not until the nurse says. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. And I'm sending a nurse to your house immediately.
Caller -> Now? Thank God. How long will it take?
Caller -> Will they bring anything? Medicine? I don't know what they do for this.
Nurse -> The nurse will assess her first. Let's wait and see what she says.
Nurse -> I'll get you an exact time. It's usually thirty minutes at this hour. I'll stay on the phone with you until we confirm.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. I'm always so careful.
Nurse -> I know you are. It happens, even to careful people, especially at night. You called right away. That's the most important thing.
Caller -> I was so tired. I'd been up since five. She was moaning, and I rushed.
Nurse -> That makes sense. We'll talk about making this safer. First, her. Can you turn her onto her side?
Caller -> I keep a notebook with the times. I wrote nothing down yet. I was going to write after.
Nurse -> Write it down now, so the nurse can see the time and the amount.
Caller -> I'm writing. It's two oh five. One milliliter. The blue pen.
Caller -> I'll try. Mama, I'm going to turn you. There. She's on her left side. Her face is toward me.
Nurse -> Good. Put a pillow behind her back so she stays there. And raise her head a bit if you can.
Caller -> She smells like her lotion. The cocoa butter one. She loves that smell.
Caller -> I put two pillows. Her head is up. She's comfortable. She's blinking.
Nurse -> Perfect. Folasade, I need her date of birth for the on-call page.
Caller -> May twenty sixth. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your callback number?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one seven nine.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, zero one seven nine. I have it. Now here is the most important part. If at any time she can't be woken up, if her breathing drops below eight a minute, or if her lips turn blue, hang up and call 911 right away.
Caller -> 911 if she can't wake. Below eight. Blue lips. Okay. Okay. I've got it.
Nurse -> Count her breaths for a full minute every ten minutes, and talk to her. Keep her on her side. Stay in the room.
Caller -> Every ten minutes. I'll set a timer. I'm setting it. Okay. Ten minutes. I'll count.
Nurse -> Good. I'm paging on-call now. Don't hang up. I'll put you on hold for just a moment. Can you wait?
Caller -> Yes. I'll wait. I'm here. Mama, I'm right here.
Nurse -> Folasade, I'm back. I've paged the on-call clinician, and the nurse is on the way. She's about twenty five minutes out. Her name is Denise.
Caller -> Denise. Twenty five minutes. Okay. I know Denise. She came last week. She's lovely.
Caller -> I'll turn on the porch light. And the hall light. So she can see the number.
Nurse -> That will help.
Nurse -> She is. She'll check her breathing, her oxygen, and decide on next steps. She may want to give something to reverse the effect if needed. But your mom is doing okay right now.
Caller -> She's very kind. She always asks about my mother's garden, even in winter.
Nurse -> She likes to talk to the family. She'll take her time.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief. I'm going to stay right here. My brother is asleep upstairs. Should I wake him?
Nurse -> It might help to have a second person in the room. Yes, wake him.
Caller -> Okay. Hold on. Dayo! Dayo, come down! Mom needs us! Sorry. He's coming. I can hear him on the stairs.
Nurse -> That's fine. Take your time.
Caller -> He's here. He's rubbing his eyes. He says what happened. I'm telling him. He's looking at the syringe.
Nurse -> Please don't use the syringe again until the nurse is here. We'll go over it.
Caller -> I put it in the sink. I'm not touching it. He's sitting by her now. He's holding her hand.
Caller -> It's strange. Ten minutes ago I was asleep. Now it's like the whole house is awake.
Nurse -> That's adrenaline. It will settle once the nurse is here.
Caller -> I know. My heart is pounding. Dayo is making tea. He puts three sugars in everything.
Nurse -> Good. Let's talk about how to measure it right, so it doesn't happen again. Do you have the syringe nearby?
Caller -> Dayo says he can set up a little station in the kitchen. With a lamp, so we can read the numbers.
Nurse -> A bright light and a magnifier are a great idea for reading the syringe.
Caller -> I have a reading magnifier from my mother's sewing box. It's the one with the handle.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep it with the bottle.
Caller -> It's in the sink. I'll get it. Okay. I have it. It's the little one. Marked in tenths.
Nurse -> For a quarter of a milliliter, you draw up to the line between point two and point three. A better way is to have the nurse put a piece of colored tape right at the dose line.
Caller -> Tape. Yes. That would be so helpful. I have blue tape in the garage. Or the nurse can bring it.
Nurse -> She'll bring it. We'll also ask the pharmacy for a syringe with only the dose marked. No more math at two in the morning.
Caller -> Please. I would so appreciate that. I never want to do this again.
Nurse -> And one more thing. Don't blame yourself. Caregivers do the best they can with very complicated medicines.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm trying not to cry.
Nurse -> It's okay to cry. Let it out. I'm here.
Caller -> She taught me how to cook. She taught me everything. I can't lose her yet.
Nurse -> I know. I know. One thing at a time.
Caller -> I love her so much. I just want her to be comfortable.
Nurse -> And she is. She's being cared for by someone who loves her. That's what matters.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm better. Let me check her breathing again. It's been a few minutes.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll wait.
Caller -> One, two, three, four, five. Eleven. I counted eleven. Over a minute.
Nurse -> Good. Eleven is a bit better. Is she waking when you speak?
Caller -> Yes. She said, stop fussing. Dayo told her he loves her and she said, I know. That's her. That's my mother.
Nurse -> Ha. That sounds like a good sign. Her spirit is intact.
Caller -> She told me last week she's going to outlive all of us. She's been saying it since she was sixty.
Nurse -> Ha. A strong will is a wonderful thing.
Caller -> Dayo says she's too stubborn to leave. I hope he's right.
Caller -> She's got an attitude even on morphine.
Nurse -> Ha. We love it. Okay, Folasade, I'm going to call you back in fifteen minutes to check on her, even before Denise arrives.
Caller -> She used to run a seamstress shop. She's bossy about hems.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course she is.
Caller -> Fifteen minutes. Okay. I'll have the phone in my hand.
Nurse -> And if anything changes before then, don't wait. Call 911 first, then call me.
Caller -> 911 first. Then you. Okay.
Nurse -> Are you holding up okay?
Caller -> I think so. I'm shaking. But I'm okay. Dayo is here. That helps.
Nurse -> Drink some water. Sit down. You don't have to stand.
Caller -> I haven't eaten since lunch. Dayo is going to make toast.
Nurse -> Good. Eat something small. You'll need your strength.
Caller -> I'm sitting. I'm on the edge of the bed. Next to her feet.
Nurse -> Good. I'll talk to you soon.
Caller -> Should I keep the lamp on or turn it off?
Nurse -> Keep it low so you can see her face and her breathing.
Caller -> Thank you, Lena. Thank you for not hanging up. I would have lost my mind.
Nurse -> You didn't. You did exactly the right things. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Odile.
Caller -> Hi, Odile. This is Declan Fennessy. I'm calling about my son. Colm. C O L M. Colm Fennessy. It's an Irish name.
Nurse -> It's a lovely name. I've never heard it spelled that way.
Caller -> Most people read it as Colm like column. It's said Collum. Everyone gets it wrong.
Nurse -> Hi, Declan. Good to hear from you. And how is Callum today?
Caller -> He's good. Really good. I just wanted to check in. Nothing urgent.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear on a Sunday.
Caller -> I'm doing laundry. I figured I'd call while it's tumbling.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Let me open his chart. Can I confirm his date of birth?
Caller -> December fifth. Two thousand sixteen.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number, Declan?
Caller -> Sure. It's the cell. It's the one on his forms.
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one one five.
Nurse -> Perfect. So tell me how his chest is.
Caller -> He's coughing in the mornings. After the vest. He brings up some mucus. It's clear, mostly. Sometimes a little light yellow. Not green.
Nurse -> How much, would you say?
Caller -> A couple of spoonfuls. After the morning vest. Less in the evening.
Nurse -> And does he cough at night at all?
Caller -> A little at the start, then he settles. He sleeps with the humidifier on.
Nurse -> That sounds about the same as last week.
Caller -> Maybe a bit less. He's doing the vest twice a day, thirty minutes each. He doesn't complain too much.
Nurse -> That's great. And his medicines?
Caller -> The Pulmozyme. The nebulizer. Two point five milligrams, once a day. We did it this morning before the vest.
Nurse -> Good. Any trouble getting him to do it?
Caller -> He likes the steam. He pretends he's a dragon.
Caller -> He has a dragon puppet that he brings to the vest. It sits on the couch and watches.
Nurse -> Ha. A cheering section.
Nurse -> Ha. A dragon. I love that.
Caller -> He named it Sparky. Sparky is not allowed to skip the vest either.
Caller -> He roars between breaths. The neighbors must think we have a zoo.
Nurse -> Ha. And how is his appetite?
Caller -> Great. He eats like a teenager. He had two breakfasts yesterday. We weighed him on Sunday. Same as last week. Sixty one pounds.
Nurse -> That's good. Steady weight is what we want.
Caller -> My wife keeps a chart on the fridge. It has stickers.
Nurse -> Ha. Stickers make everything better.
Caller -> She buys them in bulk. Dinosaurs for him, unicorns for his sister.
Nurse -> Any fever, or trouble breathing?
Caller -> No fever. I check when he's flushed. And he's not short of breath. He plays soccer at recess. He was out of breath after, but only like the other kids.
Nurse -> Good. That sounds normal.
Caller -> I worry anyway. It's a dad thing. My wife says I read too much online.
Nurse -> Ha. A little worry is part of the job.
Caller -> His teacher says he's the fastest in the class.
Nurse -> Ha. A dragon and a sprinter.
Caller -> I was going to ask. The cold weather is coming. Should I do anything different?
Nurse -> Make sure he drinks lots of fluids. Keep up the high calorie snacks. And on hot or sweaty days, he needs extra salt.
Caller -> Extra salt. Right. In summer. The soccer. He gets salty on his face.
Nurse -> That's very common with cystic fibrosis. Keep a bag of salty snacks in his backpack.
Caller -> Pretzels. He likes the big ones.
Caller -> The soft ones from the mall. With the cheese. He would eat them for every meal.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> And remember, call us if he gets a fever of one hundred point four or higher, if his mucus gets green or bloody or there's a lot more of it, if he's breathing fast, or if his appetite drops.
Caller -> Fever. Mucus green. Fast breathing. Appetite. Okay. I'll tell my wife. She'll put it on the chart.
Nurse -> Great. I'll plan to call you Friday to see how things are going.
Caller -> Friday is good. After five. I'm at work till then.
Caller -> If I don't answer, leave a message. The warehouse is loud.
Nurse -> I'll leave a message with a good time to try again.
Nurse -> I'll try after five.
Caller -> Perfect. Oh, one more thing. His sister has a cold. Should I keep her away from him?
Nurse -> A mild cold is usually okay with good handwashing, but try to keep their sleeping spaces apart. Let us know if he starts coughing more.
Caller -> Okay. She's seven. She doesn't wash her hands. She says they're clean.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll bet.
Caller -> She told me yesterday that germs are a myth. She's seven.
Nurse -> Ha. Bold claim.
Caller -> I'll make it a game. Soap bubbles.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Odile. I feel better. We're lucky to have you.
Nurse -> It's my pleasure. Say hello to Callum for me.
Caller -> I will. He's right here. He says hello. He's roaring.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him I heard it.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Linden Park Home Health, this is Mei.
Caller -> Mei, hello. This is Hector Castellanos. My wife is Winifred. Winifred Castellanos. She's not right. She had black stools today. Black like tar.
Nurse -> Hector, thank you for calling. I'm here. When did she have the black stools?
Caller -> I didn't know who else to call. Our doctor's office is closed on Mondays.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. I'm glad you called us.
Caller -> Twice today. Once this morning, and once about an hour ago. It smells terrible. It's sticky. She was embarrassed to tell me.
Caller -> I've never seen anything like it. I thought maybe it was something she ate. She had blackberries yesterday.
Nurse -> Blackberries can darken a stool, but not like tar, and not with dizziness. Let's take it seriously.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she with you? Can she talk to me?
Caller -> She's on the couch. She's pale. She's lying down. Winifred, the nurse wants to know how you feel. She says tired. And dizzy.
Caller -> She's got that look. Gray. Like paper. I've been married to her for forty four years and I know her face.
Nurse -> Dizzy how? All the time, or when she stands?
Caller -> When she stands. She tried to go to the bathroom and she had to hold the wall. She said the room spun. She sat right back down.
Caller -> She's never dizzy. She's the one who runs up the stairs and tells me to hurry.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you checked her blood pressure or pulse?
Caller -> Yes. I have the cuff. It says ninety eight over sixty. And the pulse is one hundred eight. It's usually a hundred thirty over eighty.
Caller -> I bought it at the drugstore. It's a good one. Automatic. I check it every Sunday.
Nurse -> That's very helpful today.
Nurse -> That's lower than her usual, and her heart rate is fast. Did she vomit? Any blood in the vomit, or anything that looks like coffee grounds?
Caller -> No. No vomiting. Her stomach hurts a bit. A burning. She said it's been going on for a week. But no throwing up. No blood.
Caller -> She's been saying heartburn. She takes the pink chewable ones. They don't help anymore.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll note that. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. What medicines does she take? Anything for pain, arthritis?
Caller -> The ibuprofen. Six hundred milligrams. Three times a day. For her knees. She's been taking it for months. The doctor said to take with food. She takes it with toast.
Caller -> The pharmacist told her once to stop. Or to take less. She said she can't. Her knees are bad.
Nurse -> And when was the last dose?
Caller -> This morning. About eight. With breakfast.
Nurse -> Does she take a blood thinner, or aspirin?
Caller -> No blood thinner. A baby aspirin, I think. Yes. Eighty one. Every day.
Nurse -> Okay. Hector, I'm worried this may be bleeding in her stomach. Black, tarry stools, dizziness and a low blood pressure are warning signs. She needs to be seen in the hospital now. I want you to hang up and call 911 right now.
Caller -> Nine one one? Oh. Is it that serious?
Nurse -> It can be. Bleeding can get worse fast. Please don't drive her. If she faints in the car, you can't help her. Paramedics can start treatment right away.
Caller -> I'm trying to stay calm. My hands are shaking. I'm going to dial now.
Nurse -> Take a breath, then dial. I'm right here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm dialing. Wait. Should I stay on with you?
Nurse -> Put me on speaker, if you can, and dial from your cell. I'll stay on. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> It's on the table. It's on speaker. I'm pressing the numbers. Nine, one, one.
Caller -> It's unlocked. We don't lock it in the daytime. I'm dialing. It's ringing.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them your wife has black, tarry stools and is dizzy and pale.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. My wife, she's having bleeding I think. Black stools. She's dizzy. Yes, forty one thirty Elm Court. Yes. They're sending someone, Mei.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep her lying down with her feet up. Put a pillow under her ankles. Give her nothing to eat or drink.
Caller -> Feet up. No food or water. Okay. I'm putting the pillow. Winifred, lift your feet. There.
Caller -> She wants a glass of water. She's thirsty. Is it okay to wet her lips?
Nurse -> A damp cloth on her lips is fine. Nothing to swallow.
Caller -> Okay. I'm using a washcloth. She says thank you.
Nurse -> And please gather all her medicine bottles, including the ibuprofen and aspirin, and put them in a bag to go with her. And stop the ibuprofen. Do not give her any more.
Caller -> No more ibuprofen. Bag of bottles. Hold on. I'm getting them from the kitchen. They're all on the windowsill. I'm putting them in a grocery bag.
Caller -> There's the arthritis cream too. The tube. Should I bring that?
Nurse -> Sure, bring everything. The more they see, the better.
Nurse -> Good. And grab her insurance card and a list of her medical conditions, if you can.
Caller -> The card is in her purse. The purse is on the chair. I have it. I'll put it all by the door.
Nurse -> Hector, I'm paging our on-call clinician now so they know she's headed to the hospital.
Caller -> Thank you. Winifred, you're doing fine. The ambulance is coming.
Caller -> It's a long street. They have to come from the fire station on Third. Maybe six minutes.
Nurse -> That's fine. They're on the way.
Nurse -> What's her date of birth? I'll give it to the hospital.
Caller -> December twenty eighth. Nineteen fifty three.
Nurse -> And is your cell the one on file, ending in oh one two oh?
Caller -> Yes, eight one six, five five five, zero one two zero.
Nurse -> Good. How is she now?
Caller -> Same. She's pale. She's cold. Her hands are cold. She says she's okay. She keeps saying she's okay.
Caller -> She's shivering a little. I'm warming her feet in my hands.
Nurse -> Put a blanket over her. Stay close. Talk to her.
Caller -> I have the afghan. I'm putting it on. Winifred, look at me. She's looking at me. She's awake.
Nurse -> Good. Is she answering you clearly?
Caller -> Yes. She said, I'm fine, Hector. She said call the cat sitter. Ha. She's worried about the cat.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a sign she's thinking clearly. We'll handle the cat.
Caller -> I'll text the neighbor. After. She has a key.
Nurse -> Good. Let's keep focused on her for now.
Caller -> You're right. I'm sorry. I'm a little scattered.
Nurse -> You're doing great. Just keep talking to her.
Caller -> I hear a siren. Is that them? It's close.
Nurse -> It might be. Go to the front door and wave them in. Leave me on the phone on the table.
Caller -> Okay. Going. Here! Over here! In the living room! She's on the couch! Black stools! Dizzy! Pressure ninety eight over sixty!
Nurse -> Hector, answer them. I'll be here.
Caller -> They're with her. They're asking questions. They're putting something on her finger. They're saying her heart rate is fast.
Nurse -> That's what they do. Tell them about the ibuprofen and the baby aspirin.
Caller -> Ibuprofen six hundred, three times a day. And aspirin eighty one. They're writing it down.
Nurse -> Which hospital?
Caller -> Mercy General. On Chambers. They said she'll get blood tests and a scope probably.
Nurse -> That's a good hospital. I'll call ahead. I'll also let the team know.
Caller -> They did her knee there two years ago. The staff was nice. Dr. Ibarra. I hope he's on.
Nurse -> I'll mention it to the team. The nurse will follow up tomorrow.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm going in the ambulance. They said I can.
Nurse -> Go with her. Take the bag of bottles and your phone. We'll check in tomorrow.
Caller -> Thank you, Mei. Thank you for being there. I didn't know what to do.
Nurse -> You did exactly the right thing. Go. Bye for now.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Linden Park Home Health, this is Mei.
Caller -> Hi, Mei. This is Rupert Penhaligon. I'm calling for my dad. Alistair Penhaligon. P E N H A L I G O N. He's on the steroid taper.
Nurse -> Hi, Rupert. How's your dad doing today?
Caller -> He's resting. He's in the recliner with the blanket I got him. He's fine. Just the pill question.
Nurse -> Hi, Rupert. Thanks for calling. What's the question?
Caller -> It's probably nothing. I just don't like uncertainty.
Caller -> I think there's a mix up. The sheet from the hospital says prednisone. But the bottle I picked up says prednisolone. Are those the same?
Nurse -> Good catch. They look alike, but they're different drugs. Let me pull up his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> I read both names three times. They are practically one letter apart. I got a headache.
Nurse -> Ha. That's exactly how they get people.
Caller -> March fourteenth. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And your number, Rupert?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one oh six.
Nurse -> Thanks. Read me the label on the bottle.
Caller -> Let me find my glasses. They're on my head. Hold on. Okay.
Caller -> It says prednisolone. P R E D N I S O L O N E. Oral solution. Fifteen milligrams per five milliliters. Take twenty milligrams, that's, uh, six point seven milliliters, by mouth once a day in the morning.
Nurse -> Hold on. Say that last part again. How many milliliters does it say?
Caller -> Six point seven. Six point seven milliliters. I can't see how I'd measure six point seven. The syringe has lines every half.
Nurse -> Okay. I see his discharge order says prednisone twenty milligrams a day, tapering. The pharmacy may have switched to the liquid because he has trouble swallowing pills. Prednisolone is a close cousin. It does the same job in the body.
Caller -> So it's okay to give the liquid? It's a different drug but it's okay?
Nurse -> It's often used when someone can't swallow tablets. But I don't want to guess. I'll call the pharmacy and confirm they meant to substitute it, and that the dose is right.
Caller -> He did say the pills were hard. They get stuck. He coughs.
Nurse -> That's a good reason for the liquid, then. I'll mention it when I call.
Caller -> Please. I'd feel better. I don't want to get it wrong.
Caller -> The pharmacy was packed when I went. There was a line out the door. The tech seemed rushed.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll make sure everything is double checked.
Nurse -> Is he taking the dose this morning already?
Caller -> Yes. I gave him the liquid at eight. I measured six and a half. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's close enough for one dose. We'll get the exact amount sorted tomorrow. For now, no change tonight.
Caller -> I used the little cup first, then switched to the syringe. The syringe is much easier.
Nurse -> Always use the syringe. The cup is not accurate.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> How is his breathing today?
Caller -> Better. Much better. He's not wheezing. He walked to the kitchen and back without stopping. Two days ago he couldn't do that.
Caller -> He even hummed this afternoon. He hasn't hummed in weeks.
Nurse -> That's great. Does he have a fever?
Caller -> No. I took it at noon. Ninety eight point four. No fever.
Nurse -> Good. Is he using the rescue inhaler?
Caller -> The albuterol. Yes. Two puffs, every four hours if he needs it. He used it this morning. Just once. Not since.
Nurse -> That's an improvement. The rescue inhaler is only as needed. The steroid is scheduled every day until the taper is done.
Caller -> He tells me he doesn't want to be a bother, so he waits too long before he uses it.
Nurse -> Please encourage him to use it when he needs it. It's not a bother.
Caller -> I get confused. One's every day and the other's only when he needs it.
Nurse -> It's easy to mix up. Give the steroid with breakfast. Use the oral syringe, not a kitchen spoon. And finish the taper as written. Don't stop it early, even if he feels fine.
Caller -> Finish the taper. Syringe. With breakfast. Okay. I'll tape a note on the bottle.
Caller -> The taper chart is on the fridge. It has a calendar with days crossed out. He crosses them off himself.
Nurse -> That's great. It keeps him involved.
Nurse -> A good idea. Write the dose in milliliters, once the pharmacy confirms.
Caller -> I have a sharpie. And a roll of blue painter's tape.
Nurse -> Perfect. The painter's tape works great.
Caller -> My wife says I'm over organized.
Nurse -> Ha. In this case, it helps.
Caller -> She calls me the label maker.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep it up.
Nurse -> And call us if his breathing gets harder, if he gets a fever, or if he needs the albuterol more often than every four hours.
Caller -> Harder breathing. Fever. Inhaler more than every four hours. Okay. I'll write it on the tape too.
Caller -> His dog, Biscuit, sits right by the chair. Biscuit has been very needy since he got sick.
Nurse -> Ha. Dogs know.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow to let you know what the pharmacy says.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. I'm home after three.
Caller -> I work from home, but I teach online classes in the morning. I can't pick up during those.
Nurse -> After three then. I'll leave a message if I miss you.
Nurse -> I'll aim for after three.
Caller -> Is it normal to feel like I'm failing him? I keep thinking I'll do something wrong.
Nurse -> It's very normal. You're asking the right questions. That's what a good caregiver does.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. He's a tough one. He fought in a war. He doesn't ask for anything.
Nurse -> Then he's lucky you're there.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Mei.
Nurse -> Anytime. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Linden Park Home Health, this is Mei.
Caller -> Hi, Mei. Can you hear me? It's Genevieve Thibodeaux. I'm calling about my husband. Maurice Thibodeaux. T H I B O D E A U X.
Nurse -> Barely. Is there a better spot in the house?
Caller -> I'll try. I'm walking toward the kitchen. Still bad. I'll stay here.
Nurse -> I can hear you, but you're breaking up a bit. Hi, Genevieve. What's going on with Maurice?
Caller -> It's his sugar. I wanted to ask about his sugar. I'm in the garage. The reception is terrible.
Nurse -> Okay. It's not urgent, is it? He's not unwell right now?
Caller -> No, no. He's fine. I just want to be sure.
Nurse -> Okay. Take your time. Let me get his chart. Can I have his date of birth?
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry to bother you on a Tuesday.
Caller -> August third. Nineteen fifty nine.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> It might drop again. If it does, I'll call back from the landline.
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one four eight.
Nurse -> Got it. So what's his sugar this morning?
Caller -> It was won ate too. This morning. Won ate too.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, I didn't catch that. Can you say it again, slowly?
Caller -> Sorry. The phone cuts out. It was one. Eight. Two. One hundred eighty two.
Caller -> There's a metal shelf in here, I think it blocks the signal. My husband says the garage is a Faraday cage.
Nurse -> Ha. He sounds like a handy guy.
Nurse -> One eighty two. Okay. Is that before breakfast?
Caller -> Yes. Fasting. He hadn't eaten. He checked it at six thirty.
Caller -> He uses the meter with the big screen. I can read it without my glasses.
Nurse -> And how does that compare to his usual?
Caller -> I have the log here. Let me read. Yesterday morning was two ten. The day before, a hundred ninety. Last week was a hundred sixty five. It goes up and down.
Nurse -> So one eighty two this morning is within his recent range. Okay. How is he feeling?
Caller -> Fine. A little thirsty, maybe. He's drinking a lot of water. He keeps refilling his big jug.
Caller -> He says it's the dry heat from the furnace. We keep it warm. He gets cold easily.
Nurse -> Is he urinating more than usual?
Caller -> A bit more. Maybe. He's up once at night. That's not new.
Caller -> I keep telling him to drink the water before dinner, not at bedtime. He doesn't listen.
Nurse -> Ha. A common story.
Nurse -> Okay. Any vomiting, or confusion, or feeling very tired?
Caller -> No. None of that. He's normal. He went for a walk this morning. He's out in the yard now, raking leaves.
Nurse -> Good. What insulin does he take?
Nurse -> And can you tell me, does he ever skip a dose?
Caller -> Never. He's like clockwork. Nine o'clock, every night. He's got an alarm.
Caller -> The Lantus. Thirty units. At night. He took it last night at nine. As always.
Nurse -> Okay. Lantus thirty units at night. Any changes in what he's eating? Any holiday food?
Caller -> It's early for that. But yes, he had a slice of pie on Sunday. Pumpkin. And bread at dinner.
Caller -> I'm already planning the Thanksgiving menu. He wants the sweet potatoes with the marshmallows.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll talk about those too.
Nurse -> That may explain the higher numbers. I'm going to message our team about the trend and ask them to look at his insulin dose.
Caller -> He said the pie was worth it. I said, tell that to your meter.
Nurse -> Ha. Good line.
Caller -> Please. I don't want to change anything myself.
Caller -> My sister says to cut the dose when it goes up. That doesn't sound right to me.
Nurse -> Right. Please don't change it on your own. We'll look at it together.
Nurse -> Good. Don't change anything. We'll decide together.
Caller -> I won't touch it. He wouldn't let me anyway.
Nurse -> Ha. In the meantime, keep checking before breakfast and before supper. And write down each number and the time.
Caller -> Before breakfast and before supper. Write the time. Okay. I use the notebook with the green cover.
Caller -> He sometimes forgets to write. I write it for him when I see the meter.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Teamwork.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call us if his sugar goes above three hundred, or below seventy, if he vomits, gets confused, or has really heavy thirst and urination.
Caller -> Three hundred. Seventy. Vomit. Confused. Very thirsty. Okay. I'll tell him.
Caller -> I'm writing that on a sticky note for the garage. It's cold and my hand is shaking.
Nurse -> I'll call you Thursday to go over the new numbers.
Caller -> Thursday. Okay. I'm home on Thursday. He has a podiatry appointment in the morning.
Caller -> He's very proud of his feet. The podiatrist says they look better than mine.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good report.
Nurse -> I'll try after lunch.
Caller -> That works. Thank you, Mei. Sorry about the bad line.
Caller -> You're always so patient with me. I appreciate that.
Nurse -> It's what I'm here for.
Nurse -> No problem at all. Go back inside where it's warmer.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

Nurse -> Tern Harbor Hospice, this is Raul.
Caller -> Hello. Hello, is this the hospice? Yes? My name is Ludmila Kowalczyk. I'm calling about my neighbor. She's a patient. Philippa.
Nurse -> Yes, this is Tern Harbor Hospice. I'm Raul. How can I help?
Caller -> Oh, good. I wasn't sure I dialed right. My hands are cold. I'm in her kitchen.
Nurse -> Hi, Ludmila. Thank you for calling. What's her last name, Philippa?
Caller -> Dunmoor. Or Dunmore. I think it's Dunmore, with an E. I've always said Dunmoor. She's never corrected me.
Nurse -> No problem. A lot of names have two spellings.
Caller -> It's on the mailbox. I'm looking out the window. It's too dark.
Nurse -> Okay. Philippa Dunmore. I see a Philippa Dunmore in our system. Is she around eighty?
Caller -> Eighty four, I think. Eighty three? She's older than me. I'm seventy nine. I don't know her birthday. I'm sorry.
Caller -> She told me once she was born the year of some big flood. I can't remember which.
Nurse -> That's all right. We'll find it in the chart.
Nurse -> That's okay. We can sort it out. What's happening today?
Caller -> She's not herself. She's been restless all day. I came at nine, and again at noon, and now I'm back. She won't settle. She keeps picking at her sheets.
Nurse -> Picking at the sheets. Is she pulling at the covers, plucking at them?
Caller -> Yes. Like she's folding something. Over and over. Her hands never stop. She's pulling at her nightgown too.
Caller -> She was a seamstress for forty years. I think she's sewing. Her fingers move like she's threading a needle.
Nurse -> That's a lovely way to see it. Those movements can be very familiar to her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake? Talking?
Caller -> She's awake. Her eyes are open. She talks, but it doesn't make sense. She said Walter was here.
Nurse -> Who's Walter?
Caller -> Her husband. He died eleven years ago. She said, Walter's in the chair. I looked. Nobody was there. I don't know if she was dreaming, or what.
Nurse -> Was she upset by it, or peaceful?
Caller -> Peaceful, mostly. She smiled. But then she got agitated again. She wanted to get up and go somewhere. I don't know where. I said it's night, Philippa, and she said no, it's morning.
Caller -> She said, he looks so young. That's what she said. He looks so young.
Nurse -> That sounds comforting.
Caller -> It was. I almost cried. I cried a little in the hallway.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had any medicine for the restlessness?
Caller -> The lorazepam. The little pill. The label says point five milligram, as needed for restlessness. I gave her one at noon. It helped. She slept for two hours. But now she's up again.
Nurse -> Okay. So lorazepam point five at noon. Has she had another since?
Caller -> No. I didn't know if I'm allowed. It says every four hours, I think. It's been, what, five hours. But I was scared to give her another.
Nurse -> That's a reasonable worry. I'll get you an answer in a moment. A few more questions first. Has she eaten or had anything to drink?
Caller -> My own husband had pills and I never knew what was safe. Nobody told me anything.
Nurse -> You're doing a great job asking before giving. That's the right instinct.
Caller -> Not since yesterday. I made her tea this morning. She took two sips. She says she's not hungry. She pushes the spoon away.
Caller -> I tried applesauce. She turned her head. I tried pudding. Same thing.
Nurse -> That's okay. At this stage, a few sips or tastes are enough.
Nurse -> Okay. And has she had a bowel movement?
Caller -> I think not for four days. I look at the chart the aide keeps. The last mark was Friday. Four days ago. She hasn't said.
Caller -> I'm sorry I don't know more. I'm only her neighbor. The aide comes on weekdays, and the aide's gone by three.
Nurse -> You're doing more than most. Thank you.
Nurse -> And her bowel medicine? Does she take senna, or something at night?
Caller -> The senna. One tablet every night. But she didn't take it last night. Or the night before. She refused. She said it tastes like dirt.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Does she seem to have any pain? Grimacing, holding her stomach?
Caller -> She touched her belly once. I don't know. She didn't say. She doesn't complain.
Caller -> She groaned, once, when I helped her turn. It was a small groan. But it could mean something.
Nurse -> I'll make a note of that for the nurse.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she passing urine? Any strong smell, or dark color?
Caller -> I don't know. The pad was wet. I changed it at noon. It smelled a bit strong. But she hasn't had much to drink. So, I don't know.
Nurse -> That's okay. Ludmila, you've given me a lot to work with. There are a few possible reasons she's restless. It could be a change from her illness, it could be constipation, it could be a bladder infection. We need a nurse to look at her.
Caller -> A nurse? Today? It's already getting dark.
Nurse -> Yes, today. I'm going to page the on-call clinician for orders, and send a nurse as soon as possible.
Caller -> Oh. Thank God. I was afraid you would say wait until morning.
Caller -> I was ready to wait all night. I thought, they don't come at night. That's what I thought.
Nurse -> We do. Hospice is available any time.
Nurse -> No. If she's restless now, we don't wait. What's the best number to reach you?
Caller -> The street is slippery. It rained. Tell the nurse to be careful on the driveway.
Nurse -> I'll pass that on. Thank you.
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one two five. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one two five. And do you have a house key, or will someone be there to let the nurse in?
Caller -> I have a key. I'm here. I'm sitting by her bed. I'll let the nurse in.
Nurse -> Perfect. While we wait, let's make her more comfortable. Is the room bright?
Caller -> I've been rubbing her hand. Is that okay?
Nurse -> It's more than okay. Touch is very calming.
Caller -> The overhead light is on. And the TV is on. She had the news.
Nurse -> Turn off the TV, and put on a small lamp instead. Keep the room quiet. Low light. Speak softly.
Caller -> The remote is under the afghan. Hold on. I can't find it. I'll just press the button on the set.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> TV off. Lamp on. Okay. Hold on. There. It's much quieter. She's looking at me.
Nurse -> Good. You can play soft music, if she likes it. And offer sips of water, or touch a moist swab to her lips.
Caller -> She hums along to some of them. Not the words, just the tune. She used to sing in the choir.
Caller -> She likes the radio. The classical station. I'll find it. I think it's on the nightstand. There. It's low.
Caller -> Oh. She's relaxing a little. Her hands are slowing down.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Ludmila, please stay with her. Don't leave her alone right now.
Caller -> I won't. I'm not going anywhere. I have my knitting.
Caller -> I made a sandwich earlier. It's still on the counter. I'll eat it in a minute.
Nurse -> Eat it. You have to look after yourself too.
Nurse -> Ha. What are you knitting?
Caller -> A scarf. For my grandson. It's blue. It's too long. I keep forgetting to stop.
Nurse -> Ha. A very long scarf is fine.
Caller -> I started it in September. Every time I finish a row I think, he's going to be taller.
Caller -> He's six. It reaches his knees.
Nurse -> He'll love it.
Nurse -> And if she says she sees Walter, or someone else, don't argue. Just say, I'm here, you're safe. It's okay.
Caller -> Okay. I did say it wasn't real. Is that wrong?
Nurse -> It's natural. But next time, just be gentle, and stay calm. She may be in a peaceful place in her mind.
Caller -> It's hard not to correct someone. I'm a retired teacher. I correct everything.
Nurse -> Ha. This is one time to let it go.
Caller -> I understand. I'll say Walter's welcome. I'll say that.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Is the bed low? Does it have rails?
Caller -> I touch the quilt on her bed. It's one of hers. The squares are all different colors. She made it for her wedding.
Caller -> It's a hospital bed. The rails are up on one side. The other side is against the wall.
Nurse -> Good. Put a pillow along the open side, so she doesn't roll off, and keep the bed low.
Caller -> I'll lower it. I know how. The button is on the side. Hold on. It's lower.
Nurse -> Great. Now, about the lorazepam. I'm going to ask the on-call clinician if she can have another dose now. I'd like you to hold off until I call back.
Caller -> I understand. I'm sorry about asking so many questions.
Nurse -> Never apologize. Ask as many as you want.
Caller -> Okay. I'll hold off. Please call soon.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in an hour at the latest, sooner if I have an answer.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll watch the clock.
Nurse -> And call right away if she can't be calmed, if she falls, if she seems to be in pain, or if her breathing changes.
Caller -> If she can't be calmed. Falls. Pain. Breathing. Okay.
Nurse -> Is she breathing normally now?
Caller -> Yes. She's breathing slow and easy. She's closing her eyes.
Caller -> I can hear the clock. It's loud. She's got a big old grandfather clock in the hall.
Nurse -> That sounds good.
Caller -> Do you think she's dying? I want to know. I've been with her for fourteen years. I'm the only one.
Nurse -> I don't know yet. The nurse will help us understand. Restlessness can be part of the final weeks, but it can also be something treatable. We'll find out.
Caller -> Thank you for being honest. I don't want anyone to lie to me.
Caller -> My sister was like that. Everyone told me she'd be fine. She wasn't. I never forgave them.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. I won't do that to you.
Nurse -> I'll always be honest with you.
Caller -> She has a niece in Ohio. I don't have her number. It's in the book on the kitchen counter.
Nurse -> Let's check the book when the nurse is there. She can call the niece if you'd like.
Caller -> I'd like that. She should know.
Nurse -> We'll take care of it.
Caller -> She'll want to know about the quilt. It goes to the niece. I'll tell her.
Caller -> She baked me a pie for my seventieth. Pecan. She was a wonderful baker. Nobody made a crust like her.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. She sounds special.
Caller -> She is. She's the bravest woman I know.
Nurse -> It's good she has you.
Caller -> I'll let you go. I'll sit with her. I'll keep the phone close.
Caller -> If she wakes up and asks for me, is there anything I should say?
Nurse -> Just tell her you're here and that she's safe. That's all she needs to hear.
Nurse -> I'll talk to you soon, Ludmila. Thank you for calling.
Caller -> Thank you, Raul. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Linden Park Home Health, this is Mei.
Caller -> Hi, Mei. This is Terrence Boateng. B O A T E N G. I'm the med tech at Maplewood Assisted Living. I'm calling about one of our residents. Mrs. Hortense Abernethy.
Nurse -> Hi, Terrence. Good to hear from you. What do you need for Mrs. Abernethy?
Caller -> You too. It's been busy here. We have a flu shot clinic today. The hallway smells like rubbing alcohol.
Caller -> Oxygen supplies. We're running low. I'm doing inventory and it looks bad.
Nurse -> Is anything urgent? Is she in distress?
Caller -> No, no. She's fine. It's just a count.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through it. Can you confirm her date of birth first?
Caller -> May ninth. Nineteen thirty four. She'll be ninety two in the spring.
Nurse -> Thanks. And I have your number on file. Is it still the front desk line, ending in oh one two two?
Caller -> I hope I'm not interrupting your lunch.
Nurse -> Not at all. I eat at my desk anyway.
Caller -> Yes, that's it. Two oh six, five five five, zero one two two.
Nurse -> Great. So tell me what you have.
Caller -> The cannulas. The nasal ones. I count two in the drawer. One on her face, one spare. And the tubing, there's one spare, but it has a kink in it.
Nurse -> So two cannulas, and tubing in questionable condition.
Caller -> The tubing is the green kind. The long kind. Twenty five feet. She likes to move around.
Caller -> Yes. I'd feel better with a new box. They're supposed to change every two weeks. The last order was in October. I'm looking at the date sheet. October third.
Nurse -> Okay. What about the humidifier bottle?
Caller -> None. Zero. The last one ran dry yesterday. I topped it up with distilled but the bottle itself is cloudy. I'd like a new one.
Nurse -> Yes, that's right. Cloudy means it needs replacing. And her tank?
Caller -> I found a gallon of distilled water in the supply closet. Expired in August though. I won't use it.
Nurse -> Good call. Use fresh.
Caller -> The portable one. For when she goes to dinner. The gauge is in the yellow. It says about a quarter full. The concentrator in the room is fine. It's just the portable.
Nurse -> Got it. Is Mrs. Abernethy comfortable on the oxygen?
Caller -> She's the only one in the building who still has her own typewriter. She uses it for her letters.
Caller -> She's very comfortable. She's at two liters. Her saturation is ninety four. She's not short of breath. She's watching a movie in the common room with a blanket.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's what I like to hear. Let me place the order. I'll order a box of cannulas, tubing, and humidifier bottles from the oxygen supply company.
Caller -> She's wrapped up like a burrito. Three blankets. She says the common room is freezing.
Nurse -> Ha. It's November.
Caller -> Wonderful. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll write it on the whiteboard in the med room so the next shift knows the order is in.
Nurse -> And I'll coordinate a swap for the portable tank, along with the delivery. They usually come Fridays in your area.
Caller -> Friday works. Our receiving door is around the back. There's a buzzer. Tell them to ask for me, or Dolores at the front desk.
Nurse -> I'll add that to the delivery notes. Terrence, how long can the portable last until Friday?
Caller -> I think about a day. If she only uses it for dinner. It's about fifteen minutes each way. I'll keep her on the concentrator in her room otherwise.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Please check the gauge before every trip. If it drops into the red, don't use it for a trip.
Caller -> Check the gauge. Red means stay put. Okay.
Caller -> I printed the little chart. Green, yellow, red. It's taped to the cart.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly the kind of thing that helps.
Nurse -> A few reminders while I have you. Change the cannula and tubing about every two weeks. Only use distilled water in the humidifier. And check the tank gauge each shift.
Caller -> Distilled only. Every two weeks. Gauge each shift. We have a sheet for that. I'll make sure the night crew sees it.
Caller -> I do the walk-through at six every morning and six at night. I check all the oxygen residents.
Nurse -> Perfect. And keep the oxygen safe. No smoking or open flames nearby. Keep the tubing out of walkways so no one trips. And please don't use petroleum jelly on her nose. Use a water based gel.
Caller -> Water based. Yes. We have the little tubes. No petroleum. Okay.
Caller -> We had a resident last year who tripped on the tubing. Since then, I'm a fanatic.
Caller -> It was Mr. Delgado. He's fine now. He broke his wrist. But it was a scare.
Nurse -> That's smart. A good habit.
Caller -> I tape it along the wall. It looks silly but it works.
Nurse -> It doesn't look silly. It looks safe.
Caller -> The new aide thought it was a mistake. I explained it was on purpose.
Caller -> Mrs. Abernethy tells me every day I'm too cautious. She says, Terrence, I've been on oxygen for six years, I know what I'm doing.
Nurse -> Ha. She does.
Caller -> She taught me how to play gin rummy. She wins every time.
Nurse -> Ha. You're in good company.
Caller -> I bet her a dollar. I owe her eleven dollars.
Caller -> I think she lets me win the first hand just to hook me.
Nurse -> Ha. A card shark.
Nurse -> Ha. That adds up.
Caller -> It does. She has a ledger.
Nurse -> Of course she does.
Caller -> Okay. Anything else you need from me?
Nurse -> No. I'll send you a confirmation when the order is in. Call us if the concentrator alarms, or if her breathing changes.
Caller -> Will do. Thanks, Mei. Have a good one.
Nurse -> You too, Terrence. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Orchard Lane Home Health, this is Samir.
Caller -> Hi, Samir. This is Leonard Vasquez. V A S Q U E Z. I'm a patient. And, um, I have a confession. I stopped my Eliquis. The five milligram pill, twice a day.
Nurse -> Thanks for telling me, Leonard. I'm glad you called. When did you stop?
Caller -> I almost didn't. I wanted to see if the bruises would fade first.
Nurse -> I'm glad you didn't wait any longer.
Caller -> Three days ago. Saturday. I took the morning one and then I didn't take the night one. And I haven't taken any since.
Caller -> I was out of town. At a wedding. I had too much cake, and then I felt bad about everything.
Nurse -> Okay. Can I ask why?
Caller -> It's silly, when I say it out loud.
Caller -> The bruises. They're huge. On both forearms. Purple, like grapes. I bumped the cabinet door and it turned black. I got scared. I thought I'd bleed to death over a cabinet.
Caller -> I keep my sleeves down. My cousin asked if I got in a fight. I said, with a cabinet.
Nurse -> Ha. A cabinet is a tough opponent.
Nurse -> That's a scary thing to see. How big are the bruises?
Caller -> One is the size of my hand. The other, a bit smaller. And a few small ones. They don't hurt too much. They're just ugly.
Caller -> I took a picture. Do you want me to send it? I can send it to the team.
Nurse -> The nurse will look at them tomorrow. A photo can't hurt, if you want.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me ask a few things. Is there any bleeding right now? Nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in your urine or stool?
Caller -> No. None. Nothing like that. I checked. I even looked in the toilet. Which is gross, but I looked.
Caller -> I haven't cut myself shaving either. I used the electric one, just in case.
Nurse -> Good. Any chest pain, or trouble breathing?
Caller -> My heart has been quiet. I keep checking the watch like a nervous kid.
Caller -> No. I feel fine. My heart feels normal. No fluttering. No pain.
Nurse -> And any signs of a stroke? Face drooping, weakness in an arm, trouble speaking?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. I'm talking fine. I did the smile thing in the mirror. It's even.
Nurse -> Good. Leonard, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> I feel like such an idiot. I'm sorry for wasting your time.
Nurse -> You're not wasting my time at all.
Caller -> February eighteenth. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. And the number to reach you? I want to be sure I have it right.
Caller -> It's the same one as always. You have it. I don't want to say it again, I've said it to three people this week.
Nurse -> No problem. I'll use the number on file. Leonard, I want to explain something. The Eliquis is what protects you from forming clots in your heart, which can travel to your brain and cause a stroke. When you stop it suddenly, the risk goes up, especially in the first days.
Nurse -> Is there another way to reach you, like a text?
Caller -> The cell is best. I keep it on the loud setting. I even took the ring off silent.
Caller -> I know. I know. I looked it up after. I felt guilty. But the bruises scared me more.
Caller -> I read it on three different websites. They all said the same thing. I should've called sooner.
Nurse -> Bruising is a very common side effect of blood thinners. It's usually not dangerous. But it's something we should talk about with the clinician. They might adjust things.
Caller -> Can I just restart it tonight? Is that okay?
Nurse -> I'd like you to wait for the clinician to call you before you restart or stop anything. I'm going to page them right now. It shouldn't be long.
Caller -> Okay. I'll wait. I just don't want to have a stroke.
Caller -> I'm just sitting in the kitchen. I made coffee but I can't drink it. My stomach is in knots.
Nurse -> I understand. That's why you did the right thing by calling. Please don't restart on your own, and please don't stop anything else. Let the clinician decide.
Caller -> Okay. Not on my own. Got it.
Caller -> I'll put the bottle in the cupboard so I'm not tempted to take one by habit.
Nurse -> Actually, leave it where you can see it. We want to make it easy to restart once the clinician says to.
Caller -> Oh. Right. I'll leave it on the counter.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to come see you tomorrow, look at the bruises, and go over your medicines.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's good. I'm home. I'm off on Fridays.
Caller -> I'll have my pill bottles out on the table. All of them. And my list.
Nurse -> That's great. It helps a lot.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I feel embarrassed. I'm sixty two. I should know better.
Nurse -> Don't be. Lots of people stop a medicine out of fear. Calling is what counts.
Caller -> My wife is going to kill me. She told me not to stop.
Nurse -> Ha. She'll be glad you called.
Caller -> She's at her sister's. She'll be back tonight. I'll tell her. She'll roll her eyes.
Nurse -> Ha. Let her.
Caller -> She's the one who counts my pills every Sunday. She'll know right away.
Nurse -> In the meantime, call 911 right away if your face droops, if an arm gets weak, if your speech slurs, if you have chest pain, or if you get suddenly short of breath.
Caller -> Face. Arm. Speech. Chest pain. Short of breath. Nine one one. Okay. I know the signs. My dad had a stroke.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's a good reason to be careful.
Caller -> He was seventy. He survived. But it changed everything.
Nurse -> Then you know how serious it is. Thank you for calling instead of waiting.
Caller -> I'll wait by the phone. Thank you, Samir.
Nurse -> The clinician will call you. Take care, Leonard.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willowmere Home Care, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Marta Hrabovsky. H R A B O V S K Y. I'm calling about my mother. Zdenka. Z D E N K A. Zdenka Hrabovsky.
Nurse -> Hi, Marta. How have you been?
Caller -> Tired. But good. Getting ready for the holidays.
Nurse -> Hi, Marta. Yes, I know your mother. How is she?
Caller -> She talks about you all the time. She says you're the one with the nice handwriting.
Nurse -> Ha. That's flattering.
Caller -> She's good. I just wanted to give an update. Nothing wrong.
Nurse -> I like those calls. Let me get her chart. Can I have her date of birth?
Caller -> I figured I'd call before Thanksgiving gets crazy. We have twenty two people coming.
Nurse -> Twenty two! Where do they all sit?
Caller -> At folding tables in the living room. My mother insists on a real tablecloth. Three of them, end to end.
Caller -> March twenty second. Nineteen thirty three. No. Thirty two. Nineteen thirty two. She'd be offended.
Nurse -> Thirty two. Got it. And your number, Marta?
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, zero one three two.
Nurse -> Perfect. So how's her week been?
Caller -> We went for her annual eye appointment on Tuesday. The doctor said she has the eyes of a sixty year old.
Caller -> Good. Really steady. She walks with the walker all around the house. She doesn't need me hovering. She's faster than me.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Any falls, or near falls?
Caller -> I keep her appointment calendar on the fridge. It has a picture of lighthouses on it.
Nurse -> Lovely. A calendar is a good way to keep track.
Caller -> She told me she wants to go back to church on Sunday. It's three blocks. I said we'd drive.
Nurse -> That sounds like a nice goal.
Caller -> None. And no pain. She says her knees don't hurt. Which is a miracle at ninety three.
Nurse -> Great. And her ankles? Is the swelling the same?
Caller -> The same. A little puffy at the end of the day. Both sides. Not worse. If I press, it leaves a little dent that goes away fast.
Nurse -> Okay. That's what we saw last time. Is she keeping her feet up?
Caller -> Sometimes. When she watches her shows. She puts them on the ottoman.
Nurse -> Good. And her appetite?
Nurse -> And fluids? Is she drinking enough water, besides the tea?
Caller -> I think so. She has a pitcher on the table. It's about half empty by dinner.
Caller -> She mostly likes plain foods, but the stuffed cabbage is her favorite. I make it with rice, not barley.
Caller -> Great. She eats everything. She asked for seconds on the stuffed cabbage. And she sleeps well. Eight hours, then she gets up and has her tea.
Caller -> Dessert too. She says calories don't count after ninety.
Nurse -> Ha. She has a point.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Caller -> She made me wash the teapot twice. She says it has to be clean to taste right.
Nurse -> Ha. Spoken like a perfectionist.
Caller -> The cups too. They have to hang on hooks, handles all facing the same way.
Caller -> She's a retired bookkeeper. Everything has to balance.
Nurse -> Ha. I love it.
Caller -> She still does her checkbook by hand. Every month. She catches my mistakes.
Nurse -> A few reminders. Keep her feet up when she's sitting. And tell us if the swelling goes above the ankle, or if one leg swells more than the other.
Caller -> Feet up. Above the ankle. One leg more. Okay. I'll look every evening.
Caller -> I'll write it on the whiteboard in the kitchen. We have one with a little magnet pen.
Nurse -> And for safety, keep the walker within reach, clear away any rugs and cords, and use night lights.
Caller -> I put night lights in the hall. She says they're too bright. I said, Mama, you'll thank me.
Nurse -> Ha. She will.
Caller -> She turned them off once and walked in the dark. I found her in the hall with a flashlight.
Nurse -> Ha. Then she needs the lights.
Nurse -> I'll come by Thursday for the regular visit.
Caller -> Thursday. Good. She likes when you come. She makes cookies.
Caller -> She tells everyone at church about the nice nurse. They all want to meet you.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll be hungry.
Caller -> She's already planning. She asked what flavor you like. I said, she likes everything, Mama.
Caller -> They're poppyseed. They're dangerous. They get stuck in your teeth.
Nurse -> I'll bring floss.
Caller -> Ha. Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> And thank you for always picking up. It means a lot.
Nurse -> It's my pleasure.
Caller -> Oh, one thing. Is it okay if she skips her nap sometimes? She says she doesn't need one.
Nurse -> That's fine if she's not tired. Let her follow her energy.
Nurse -> No. Thanks for the update, Marta. Tell your mother hello.
Caller -> I will. She's calling from the other room. She wants to know who I'm talking to. I'll tell her. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Orchard Lane Home Health, this is Samir.
Caller -> Samir, it's Adaeze Okonjo. My husband is Desmond Okonjo. He has the PICC line. He has a high fever and he's shaking.
Nurse -> Adaeze, I'm glad you called. Tell me what's going on.
Nurse -> Adaeze, I'm here. How high is the fever?
Caller -> I don't know what to do. He was fine this morning. He ate eggs. He watched his show.
Nurse -> I know. Let's take it step by step.
Caller -> One hundred two point eight. I just took it under his tongue. It was a hundred and one an hour ago. It's going up.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the shaking.
Caller -> I put the heating pad on him. It didn't help. He says he's cold in his bones.
Caller -> He's shaking all over. Like he's freezing. He has three blankets on and his teeth are chattering. It started right after the noon flush. I flushed the line like the nurse showed me.
Nurse -> Okay. Does the area around the line look red or swollen?
Caller -> Yes. It's red. All around where it goes in. About the size of a half dollar. Maybe bigger. And it's warm.
Caller -> It wasn't red this morning. I look at it every day when I change the dressing.
Nurse -> Okay. That's important information.
Nurse -> Is he awake and talking to you?
Nurse -> And is he able to answer in full sentences?
Caller -> He's awake. He's talking, but, he's a little off. He just asked me what day it is. He knows what day it is. He's never confused. And his heart is going fast. I can feel it when I hold his wrist.
Nurse -> Adaeze, this sounds like a serious infection, possibly in the bloodstream, from the line. This is an emergency. I need you to hang up and call 911 right now.
Caller -> Nine one one? Now? Not the clinic?
Caller -> It's Friday night. The clinic is closed. I thought maybe in the morning.
Nurse -> No. Not in the morning. Now.
Nurse -> Yes. Right now. Put me on speaker and dial from your cell, or hang up and dial. He needs to be in the hospital within the hour.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm dialing. Oh my God. Desmond, stay with me. I'm calling the ambulance.
Caller -> My hands won't work. I keep hitting the wrong number. Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them he has a PICC line, a fever of one oh two point eight, shaking chills, and confusion.
Caller -> It's ringing. Why is it ringing? Come on.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. My husband has a fever, a hundred and two point eight, and he's shaking. He has a PICC line. He's confused. Yes. They're coming, Samir.
Nurse -> Perfect. Don't use the line. Don't flush it. And unlock the front door. Is he lying down?
Caller -> I haven't touched the line since the flush. I have the cap on it. The little blue cap.
Nurse -> Good. Leave it exactly as it is.
Caller -> He's on the couch, on his side. With the blankets. I'm unlocking the door. Hold on. It's open. I'm back.
Caller -> The cat is on him. She won't leave. I'm moving her. Shoo.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him lying down with a blanket. Don't give him anything to eat or drink. Not even water.
Caller -> His forehead is so hot. I can feel it from here. He's sweating now through the shirt.
Caller -> Nothing to drink. Okay. He wants water. He says he's thirsty.
Nurse -> Wet his lips with a damp cloth. Nothing to swallow, in case they need to put him to sleep for treatment.
Caller -> A cloth. Okay. I'm doing it. Honey, here. Just your lips.
Caller -> He's trying to say something. He says, I'm sorry. He says, I'm sorry, Adaeze.
Nurse -> He doesn't need to be sorry. Tell him that.
Caller -> Desmond, you don't need to be sorry. I love you. It's okay.
Nurse -> Adaeze, I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, so they know. And I'll tell the hospital he's coming.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I'm so scared.
Caller -> He's my best friend. We've been together twenty six years.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm right here with you.
Nurse -> I know. You're doing everything right. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> The clock says eight twenty. I should write the time. For the paramedics. Do they ask?
Nurse -> They'll ask when the chills started. Yes, write it down.
Caller -> October eleventh. Nineteen sixty seven.
Nurse -> And your cell is the one ending in oh one three three?
Caller -> Yes. Six oh two, five five five, zero one three three.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have the list of his medicines and antibiotics?
Caller -> On the fridge. The yellow sheet. I'll grab it. And the box with the line supplies. Should I bring that?
Nurse -> Yes. Bring the sheet and the box. And your phone charger.
Caller -> Okay. Getting it. Hold on. I have the sheet. I'm putting it in my bag. Sorry. I'm shaking too.
Caller -> Where did I put my keys? They were on the hook. I'm looking. I found them in my pocket. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> That's okay. Take a breath. They're on their way.
Caller -> I hear the siren. I think that's them. The porch light is on. Let me go to the door.
Caller -> The dog is barking. I'll shut her in the bedroom. Sorry.
Nurse -> Go. Leave the phone on the table. I'll stay on until they're with him.
Caller -> The porch light, I turned it on. Their lights are blue in the window.
Caller -> They're here. Come in. In here! He's on the couch! He has a PICC line, fever, a hundred and two point eight, chills! He's confused! They're taking his temperature again.
Nurse -> Tell them the antibiotics and the time of the last dose.
Caller -> The antibiotic is vancomycin, I think. Last dose was at eight this morning. It's on the yellow sheet. They have the sheet.
Nurse -> Good. Adaeze, they have what they need. Go with him. We'll follow up tomorrow.
Caller -> I'm going. Thank you, Samir. Thank you for staying on.
Nurse -> Go. Take care of him. Bye.
