transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hi, Ruth. It's Anders Rasmussen. I'm calling about my mother, Ottilie. Ottilie Rasmussen. I have a question about her heart pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Anders. What's the question?
Caller -> It's probably not a big deal. But I'd rather ask than guess.
Caller -> I don't know if she took it. The digoxin. This morning. The little one.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's figure it out. What does she say?
Caller -> She's in the kitchen. I can hear the toaster. She's very busy this morning.
Caller -> Mama! Mama, did you take your heart pill? She says yes. She says she took it. She says she always takes it.
Caller -> Mama, stop. Let me talk. Mama. Okay. Sorry, Ruth.
Caller -> But the box, the weekly box, Thursday's compartment is empty. And Wednesday's is also empty. Wednesday was yesterday. So, did she take Wednesday's today and Thursday's today? Or did she take one and forget one? I don't know.
Nurse -> Hmm. So both are empty. That is confusing.
Caller -> She says Wednesday she took hers at breakfast. She says it clearly. But she also says that about everything.
Caller -> She says, I took it, Anders. I took it. She's yelling from the kitchen.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she able to come to the phone?
Caller -> She's coming. No, she's not. She's walking away with the toast.
Caller -> She says no. She says she's making toast. She says leave her alone.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine. What's her date of birth, so I can open her chart?
Caller -> February thirteenth, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, zero one three five.
Nurse -> Thanks. And the dose on the digoxin?
Nurse -> No rush. I'm in no hurry.
Caller -> I'm reading the bottle now. It's got a yellow label. Hold on. I'm putting on my glasses.
Caller -> Point one two five milligram. Once a day. In the morning. That's what the label says.
Nurse -> Okay. Anders, how is she feeling? Any nausea, or vomiting, or blurry vision?
Caller -> No. She says no. She's fine. She's eating toast. She's cranky. That's her normal.
Caller -> She even did the crossword already. In pen. She was done by eight.
Nurse -> Anything about her vision, like seeing yellow or halos around lights?
Caller -> Mama, are you seeing yellow? She says what? She says no. She says she sees a very annoying son.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. That's reassuring. And her heartbeat? Does it feel regular?
Caller -> She is feisty. She'd argue with the president. She did, once. At a rally.
Nurse -> Ha. A strong woman.
Caller -> I took her pulse. I'm no nurse. I counted for a minute. Seventy something. Regular. Not skipping.
Nurse -> Good. Now, what you're describing, with both compartments empty, could mean a few things. She might have taken Wednesday's by accident today, or she may have taken Thursday's twice, or she skipped Wednesday and took only one. We can't tell from here.
Caller -> Right. That's what I can't figure out. She's adamant she took one. And I believe her. But I don't know about yesterday.
Caller -> I live forty minutes away. I come on Sundays and Thursdays. This isn't my day, I just stopped by.
Nurse -> Then it's good you were there to notice.
Nurse -> What I'd like to do is play it safe. Don't give her any more digoxin today, even if you're unsure. Just take the next one at the usual time tomorrow morning.
Caller -> No more today. Tomorrow's the next one. Okay. And that's safe? What if she missed?
Nurse -> One missed dose is generally safer than doubling up, especially with this medicine. I'm going to message our team about it, and have them check her pill box.
Caller -> Thank you. That makes me feel better.
Caller -> I was about to give her another one just in case. I'm glad I called.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did too.
Nurse -> I'll also send a nurse tomorrow to look at the pill box and her pulse.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. In the morning? She takes it in the morning.
Nurse -> Probably late morning, after she's taken it. The nurse will see what's left in the box.
Caller -> Good. That'll tell us for sure.
Caller -> She has a second pill box at her sister's. I'll bring it home and check that too.
Caller -> Mama, the nurse is coming tomorrow. Don't touch the box. She says she won't. She says I never trust her.
Nurse -> Ha. It's not about trust. It's just a good check.
Caller -> She hears everything. She just heard that. She says the nurse is a smart girl.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank her for me.
Nurse -> And call us if she has nausea, vomiting, blurry or yellow vision, a very slow or irregular pulse, or any new confusion.
Caller -> Nausea. Vision. Pulse. Confusion. Okay. I'll write it on the box.
Caller -> Do you want me to take a photo of the empty box and send it to you?
Nurse -> Yes, you can send it to the team. It might help the nurse.
Caller -> I'll text it to the number on the card. Okay. Done in a second.
Caller -> I have the roll of masking tape and a marker. I'll put it on the lid.
Nurse -> Perfect. Anything else?
Caller -> No. I'm sorry. This is silly.
Caller -> My wife says I worry too much. She says I'm like my father.
Nurse -> Ha. Some worry is useful.
Nurse -> It's not silly. It's the right call.
Caller -> Okay. Thanks, Ruth. Mama says thank you. She says bye. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Anders.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Bridge Palliative Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Hi, Joanne. This is Jerome Ellsworth. It's about my mom, Marguerite. Marguerite Ellsworth. She's still queasy.
Nurse -> Hi, Jerome. I'm sorry to hear that. How long has she been feeling queasy?
Caller -> Thank you. I wasn't sure whether to call on a Saturday. I figured you'd have someone.
Nurse -> We're always here. You did the right thing.
Caller -> Since Tuesday. Since the treatment. It comes in waves. It's better in the morning, worse at night.
Caller -> She was supposed to feel better by Friday. That's what the paper said. It's Saturday and she's not.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me open her chart. Can I confirm her date of birth?
Caller -> Take your time. I'm just standing in the hallway. She's napping in the bedroom.
Caller -> December ninth. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, zero one nine four.
Nurse -> Got it. What is she taking for the nausea?
Caller -> The little tablet. It's called Zo fran. Z O, then F R A N. Four milligrams. It melts on her tongue. The label says every eight hours as needed.
Nurse -> That's Zofran, the brand name for ondansetron. Zo fran, yes. When did she last have one?
Caller -> Okay. So the label might have the generic name on the bottom. Yes, it does. I see it now. Small print.
Nurse -> That's the same medicine.
Caller -> This morning. Around eight. She took one and said it helped a little. For a couple of hours.
Caller -> I wrote it on the chart. Eight oh five. With the green pen. My sister gave me a chart.
Nurse -> And how is the nausea now?
Caller -> Moderate, I'd say. She's holding her stomach. She says it's a six. A six out of ten. She's pale. She keeps swallowing.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she vomiting?
Caller -> Not today. Yesterday she threw up once. But not today. She's afraid to try. She's scared she'll throw up if she eats.
Caller -> It was after she tried the oatmeal. It's probably the oatmeal. I won't make that again.
Nurse -> What has she been able to eat or drink?
Caller -> Crackers. Saltines. About six of them. And ginger ale, flat. A few sips. That's it. She's not hungry.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something. It's important to keep sipping. Is she urinating regularly?
Caller -> Yes. Three times today. Normal color. Pale yellow.
Caller -> I'm watching, believe me. I pay attention to the bathroom more than I ever thought I would.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what caregivers do.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring.
Caller -> I don't know what else to do. I made her toast. I made chicken soup. She looks at it and turns green.
Caller -> My neighbor brought a casserole. A tuna one. My mom smelled it from the porch and had to lie down.
Nurse -> Ha. Tuna is definitely off the list.
Nurse -> The smell can set it off. A lot of people do better with cold or room temperature food, because there's less smell.
Caller -> Oh. That makes sense. Cold chicken? I could do a cold chicken sandwich.
Nurse -> Maybe a very small one. Or plain yogurt, or applesauce.
Caller -> She likes applesauce. I'll try that. With cinnamon?
Nurse -> Skip the cinnamon. Keep it plain.
Caller -> Plain. Okay.
Caller -> I'm writing it all down. Small meals. Cold food. Plain. No cinnamon.
Nurse -> Here's my plan. I'll message the team and ask whether they want to add a second anti-nausea medicine, since the Zofran only helps for a little while.
Caller -> Oh, please. That would be great. She hates feeling this way.
Nurse -> In the meantime, the tablet can only be taken every eight hours. That means the next one is at four tomorrow morning, or whenever eight hours have passed. Please don't give extra doses.
Caller -> No extras. I won't. It's one of those you don't want to double.
Caller -> I'll set an alarm for four in the morning. Or I'll just stay up. I'm not sleeping much anyway.
Nurse -> Right. And let it dissolve on her tongue, don't swallow it.
Caller -> On the tongue. That's how she does it. She makes a face.
Nurse -> Ha. It's fine.
Nurse -> For food, offer small bland meals every two hours, even a few bites. Sip clear fluids or suck on ice chips. And avoid greasy or strong smelling foods.
Caller -> Small meals every two hours. Clear fluids. Ice chips. No greasy. I'll set a timer.
Nurse -> That's a good plan. I'll call you tomorrow to see how she's doing, and tell you what the team says.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time, roughly?
Caller -> I have to run to the pharmacy for her mouth rinse. It'll take thirty minutes. I'll be back by one.
Nurse -> In the afternoon, after lunch.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll be here. I'm taking the week off. I'm sleeping on her couch.
Caller -> My boss was great about it. He said take whatever you need. I almost cried at my desk.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. She's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I'm lucky to have her. She raised me alone. I owe her everything.
Nurse -> It shows. You're doing a lot.
Caller -> She keeps saying she's a burden. I tell her, you carried me nine months, I can carry a bowl.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good answer.
Caller -> I made it up on the spot. I'm proud of it.
Nurse -> You should be.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Joanne.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Brightwater Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Hi, Priya. It's Magnus Sorensen. I'm calling about my mother, Evangeline Sorensen. I have a question before I give her pills.
Nurse -> Hi, Magnus. Happy Sunday. I'm glad you called before giving anything.
Caller -> Thanks. It's been a quiet morning. The sun is out. The birds are at the feeder.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
Caller -> Me too. I almost didn't. I was standing there with the pills in my hand.
Nurse -> That's exactly the right moment to call.
Nurse -> Hi, Magnus. Of course. What's going on this morning?
Caller -> I took her blood pressure and it's low. It's lower than usual. I'm not sure what to do with the pills.
Caller -> It's an automatic cuff. The kind with the arm band. I bought it last spring at the pharmacy.
Nurse -> Those are good. Was she sitting when you took it?
Caller -> Yes. Sitting, feet flat, arm on the table. Like they showed me.
Caller -> I waited five minutes before I took it. I read that online. Then I did it twice.
Nurse -> Perfect technique. You could teach a class.
Nurse -> Okay. What did the cuff say?
Caller -> Ninety four over fifty eight. Ninety four. Fifty eight. I did it twice. The second time was ninety six over sixty.
Nurse -> And what's her usual?
Caller -> About one thirty over eighty. She's almost never under a hundred.
Nurse -> And does she have a headache, or any chest pain?
Caller -> No headache. No chest pain. She would have said something loudly.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she feeling okay?
Caller -> She's sitting at the kitchen table. She says she's fine. But when she stood up to get the juice she said she felt woozy. She held the counter. It passed after a few seconds.
Caller -> She's doing her word search. She does one every morning. She's on the fifth one this week.
Nurse -> Ha. A busy mind.
Caller -> It's all animals this week. She found a wolverine.
Caller -> She taught me what a wolverine is. I thought it was a mascot.
Nurse -> Ha. A fierce one.
Nurse -> That's lightheadedness when she stands. Okay. Let me get her chart open. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> September seventh. Nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number? The one on file is the cell?
Caller -> Sure thing. I always forget which number is on the form.
Caller -> Yes, the cell. Six oh two, five five five, zero one five two.
Nurse -> Good. Now, tell me what pills she takes in the morning.
Caller -> I fill the box on Saturdays. I use the big one with the days and times. Morning, noon, evening, bedtime.
Nurse -> That's a great setup. It makes this much easier.
Caller -> There's a bunch. I'm looking at the box. Let me read. The lisinopril, ten milligrams. And the furosemide, twenty milligrams. And a thyroid pill. And a vitamin. And the baby aspirin.
Nurse -> Okay. The lisinopril and the furosemide are the ones I'm looking at. Both can lower her blood pressure. Did she take them yesterday?
Caller -> I know the lisinopril is for pressure. The water pill is for her ankles. The thyroid one is for the tired.
Caller -> Yes. Yesterday morning. Both. Like always.
Nurse -> Let me check her orders. I see a note here. Hold the lisinopril if the top number is under one hundred. Does that match what you have?
Caller -> I have a sheet on the fridge. Hold on. Let me go look. Okay. It says hold lisinopril if systolic is under one hundred. Systolic is the top number, right?
Nurse -> Right. The top number. Ninety four is under one hundred, so by that order, we hold the lisinopril this morning.
Caller -> I have it highlighted in yellow. Hold if under one hundred. The nurse who came last month did that for me.
Nurse -> Good. Highlighting is smart.
Caller -> Okay. So I don't give it. But what about the water pill? The furosemide?
Nurse -> That one has no hold parameter written, but it can lower her pressure even more by making her lose fluid. I want the clinician to look at this. I'd rather you hold both until they call you back.
Caller -> Hold both. Okay. Is that safe? I don't want her swelling up. She had that last year.
Caller -> She had swollen ankles last year. They were like balloons. I don't want to go back there.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll watch her weight and her ankles too.
Nurse -> It's safe for a few hours. Her pressure is the bigger concern right now. We'll decide about the furosemide when the clinician calls.
Caller -> Okay. I trust you. I just don't want to make a mistake.
Nurse -> It's not a mistake to ask. That's what we're here for.
Caller -> Okay. So no lisinopril. No furosemide. The rest is okay? The thyroid? The aspirin?
Nurse -> The thyroid pill and the vitamin are fine. The aspirin, give it with food.
Caller -> With food. Okay. I'll make her a piece of toast.
Caller -> Wheat toast or white? She likes the wheat with butter.
Nurse -> Wheat is fine. A little butter is okay.
Nurse -> Good. Offer a glass of water or some broth, too. A light breakfast helps.
Caller -> She doesn't like to drink much. She says it makes her go to the bathroom too much.
Nurse -> That's a common worry. Small sips through the morning are better than big glasses.
Caller -> Broth. We have chicken broth. In the cupboard. The carton.
Caller -> It's the low sodium kind. She's supposed to watch the salt.
Nurse -> Perfect. Low sodium is the right choice.
Nurse -> Perfect. How much has she had to drink this morning?
Caller -> One cup of coffee. And the juice, half a glass. That's all so far.
Nurse -> Then a little extra fluid will help.
Caller -> I'll fill her water bottle too. The one with the straw. She keeps it by her chair.
Caller -> I'll warm the broth. She likes it in her teacup.
Nurse -> Ha. A fancy tea cup.
Caller -> It's the one with the roses. She's very particular.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to message our team and the clinician about the low reading, and the two medicines. They'll tell us whether to restart them or change the dose.
Caller -> Thank you. How long will that take?
Caller -> I know the doctors don't always call back quickly on weekends.
Nurse -> The on-call clinician is quick for medicine questions. I'll push for it.
Nurse -> I'll call you back within two hours. Sooner if I hear.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. I'll keep my phone on.
Caller -> I'll put it on loud. I have it on vibrate usually and my dog steps on it.
Nurse -> Ha. A dog mishap. Loud is better.
Nurse -> And I'd like to send a nurse out today to check her pressure, her heart rate, and her fluid status.
Caller -> Today? On a Sunday? That's wonderful.
Nurse -> We have weekend coverage. A nurse will call before arriving.
Caller -> That's a relief. I was going to take her to urgent care but she hates that place.
Nurse -> There's no need to go. A nurse will come to you.
Caller -> I'll be here. I'm not going anywhere. I took the day off.
Nurse -> Good. Now, let's talk about keeping her safe until then. When she gets up, have her sit up slowly first. Dangle her legs for a minute. Then stand with the walker, and stay close.
Caller -> She was a nurse's aide herself, thirty years. She knows all this. She just doesn't like being told.
Nurse -> Ha. The best patients are the hardest.
Caller -> Sit. Wait. Walker. Stay close. Okay. She usually pops right up. She hates waiting.
Caller -> I moved the rug out of the way. The one by the sink. It always bunches up.
Nurse -> Good. Fewer trip hazards the better.
Nurse -> I know. That's when falls happen. A slow start is the safest.
Caller -> She tried to carry the laundry basket yesterday. I took it from her. She was mad.
Nurse -> Good for you. Less carrying for now.
Caller -> I'll hover. She'll hate it.
Nurse -> Ha. Hover anyway.
Caller -> She says I'm like a helicopter. I say, Mama, I'm a Black Hawk. Because they're more serious.
Nurse -> Ha. A Black Hawk is a good call.
Caller -> I can't believe I said that. I think I'm a little nervous.
Nurse -> It's okay. Humor helps.
Nurse -> And call us right away if she faints, if she has chest pain, if she gets confused, or if the top number drops below ninety.
Caller -> Faints. Chest pain. Confused. Below ninety. I'll write it down. I have a pen. Okay. Did you say ninety?
Caller -> I have a roll of blue tape. I put the paper on the cuff box. There. It's not going anywhere.
Nurse -> Yes. Ninety. If it goes below, call immediately.
Caller -> Okay. Ninety. It's written. I'll tape it by the blood pressure cuff.
Nurse -> Great idea.
Caller -> I feel better having a plan. I was frozen. I almost gave her everything.
Caller -> I told her we're checking in with the doctor and she said, the doctor is younger than my shoes.
Nurse -> Ha. She has a way with words.
Caller -> It's my first time handling this alone. My sister usually does the medicine talks.
Nurse -> You're doing great. Truly.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. You checked first. Many people don't.
Caller -> My sister told me to check. She's a nurse in Denver. She calls every morning.
Nurse -> Smart sister.
Caller -> She thinks I work too hard. I'm an accountant. It's tax prep season soon. I'll be buried.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you'll appreciate the help we can send.
Caller -> She's bossy. But she knows her stuff.
Nurse -> Ha. I think we'd get along.
Caller -> She'd talk your ear off. You'd have to hang up on her.
Nurse -> Ha. I've been known to talk back.
Caller -> Everyone does. She's got a very big personality.
Nurse -> Okay, Magnus. Anything else before I let you go?
Caller -> Just one. Is it okay if she has her coffee? She had one cup. She wants another.
Nurse -> Coffee is fine in moderation. It might even nudge her pressure up a little. But pair it with water.
Caller -> She drinks it black. Very strong. Her father drank it like tar.
Caller -> One more cup and a glass of water. I'll tell her.
Caller -> Oh, and she's asking if she can take a shower. It's her routine. Before lunch.
Nurse -> Not until the nurse sees her. Let's wait on the shower. A sponge bath is fine.
Caller -> She'll complain. But okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. Talk soon.
Caller -> Actually, hold on. She's saying something. She wants to know if you're the nurse with the red hair.
Nurse -> Ha. No, that must be someone else on the team.
Caller -> She says that nurse was nice. She says you sound nice too.
Nurse -> Tell her thank you. I'll look forward to meeting her.
Caller -> Thank you, Priya. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Magnus.
Caller -> Wait, one last thing. Will the nurse bring a new cuff? Mine squeezes a little loud.
Nurse -> She'll bring her own and compare it to yours. That's a good check.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll leave mine on the table.

transcript:
Nurse -> Orchard Lane Home Health, this is Samir.
Caller -> Hi. Is this a bad time? I can call back.
Nurse -> Not at all. You have my full attention.
Caller -> Hi, Samir. It's Ingrid Valdivia. I-N-G-R-I-D. Valdivia, V A L D I V I A. I'm a patient. I need a refill.
Nurse -> Hi, Ingrid. Sure. Let me pull up your chart. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> Thank you. I hate to bug you for this. It feels like such a small thing.
Nurse -> It's not small. Running out of a medicine is a real problem.
Caller -> April thirtieth. Nineteen eighty five.
Nurse -> Thanks. And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> It's my cell. The landline is disconnected. I only keep it for my alarm system.
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one eight eight.
Nurse -> Got it. Which medicine is it?
Caller -> The muscle relaxer. The baclofen. I'll tell you the dose. I'm just going to read it off the bottle so I don't mess it up.
Caller -> The baclofen. Ten milligrams. Three times a day. I have, let me count, I have twelve tablets. That's four days.
Nurse -> Okay. Four days left. When did you ask for the refill?
Caller -> I'm very careful about my counts. I keep a spreadsheet. Of course I do. I work in billing.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course.
Caller -> Last Monday. I called the pharmacy and they said they sent a request to the doctor. But nothing has come back. And I called again yesterday and they said still waiting.
Nurse -> Okay. That happens. Let me see if I can push it through from here. How have the spasms been?
Caller -> The pharmacist said the doctor's office has a new portal. Nobody knows how to use it.
Nurse -> I've heard that about a few offices. We'll try a call instead.
Caller -> Better. Honestly, better. On this dose I've been doing well. The legs used to lock up at night. Now they just twitch. It's been a month since I had a bad one.
Caller -> The new physical therapist showed me stretches. I do them after my morning shower. They help.
Nurse -> That's a great combination with the medicine.
Nurse -> Good. That's what we want. Any new weakness, or falls?
Caller -> No falls. No new weakness. Same as always. I use the cane when I go out. I haven't needed the chair.
Nurse -> Great. When did you last take a dose?
Caller -> I'm careful about the times too. I take it with food. Otherwise I get a stomachache.
Caller -> This morning at eight. And I'll take one at two and one at eight tonight.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll send a refill request to your prescriber and your pharmacy right now. Is it still the same pharmacy on Capitol?
Nurse -> It might take a day for the prescriber to approve. I'll mark it urgent.
Caller -> Urgent is good. I like urgent.
Caller -> Yes. The same one. Capitol Drugs. They're nice. They know me.
Caller -> The pharmacist there, Mr. Nakamura, always asks about my cat. He's a good man.
Nurse -> Perfect. Ingrid, it's important that you don't stop the baclofen suddenly. If you run out, it can cause withdrawal, with seizures and bad spasms. Keep taking it at your usual times until the refill is in your hand.
Caller -> I know. I would never. I'd rather take half than run out. Is that okay? To stretch it?
Caller -> I read the leaflet front to back. It says very specifically not to stop. I take it seriously.
Nurse -> Please don't cut the dose on your own. Let me get the refill moving. If it's not here soon, we'll find another way.
Caller -> You're right. I read that you can get rebound spasms. I don't want that.
Caller -> Okay. Not half. I won't. I just panicked a little.
Caller -> Thank you for not making me feel silly.
Nurse -> You're not silly at all. Asking early is smart.
Nurse -> I understand. It's a scary thought. I'll call you tomorrow to let you know where it stands.
Caller -> Tomorrow. I'm home. I work from home. I do medical billing.
Nurse -> Ha. Then you know how these things get stuck.
Caller -> I once spent three weeks tracking a single claim. It had a typo in the zip code.
Nurse -> Ha. A small thing, big trouble.
Caller -> I know exactly. Somewhere there's a fax machine that is jammed.
Nurse -> Ha. A fax machine in twenty twenty six. Unbelievable.
Caller -> I had an insurer that still mailed paper. I get a letter every Tuesday.
Nurse -> And if the refill hasn't come by Thursday, or if you get down to one day of tablets, call us again.
Caller -> Thursday, or one day left. Okay. I'll mark it on my calendar.
Caller -> I'll also put a note on my phone. It reminds me at nine in the morning. I never miss a reminder.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I have a cat who sits on my calendar. So it's mostly cat hair, but I'll find it.
Nurse -> Ha. What's the cat's name?
Caller -> She's seven. She came from a shelter. She was a stray in the parking lot of a grocery store.
Caller -> Mochi. She's a tuxedo cat. She thinks she's a supervisor.
Nurse -> Ha. A good coworker.
Caller -> She's the best. She doesn't answer emails.
Nurse -> Ha. Even better.
Caller -> She sits on my keyboard during meetings. My coworkers love her more than they love me.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Samir. I feel much better.
Nurse -> Anytime. Take care, Ingrid.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Odile.
Caller -> Hi. Hi there. I hope this isn't a bad time.
Nurse -> No, I'm here. What can I do?
Caller -> Hi, Odile. It's Priscilla Wickersham. I'm calling about my son, Tobias Wickersham. T O B I A S. We need supplies.
Nurse -> Hi, Priscilla. Of course. I'll get his chart. Can you tell me his date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry for calling this late in the day. I was on a work call until just now.
Nurse -> No problem. I'm glad you called.
Caller -> July twenty first. Two thousand thirteen. He's thirteen.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Nurse -> And are you the best contact for medical questions, or is his dad?
Caller -> I am. His dad travels. He's a pilot. He's in Singapore until Friday.
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, zero one nine one.
Nurse -> Perfect. What do you need?
Caller -> I should have checked sooner. I always say I'll check on the first of the month, then it slips.
Caller -> Pen needles. We have six left. Six. And test strips, there's about half a vial, maybe fifteen strips. He checks about six times a day. So it's two or three days.
Nurse -> Okay. That's tight. When did you last order?
Caller -> I keep a bag of spare things in the car. Glucose tablets, juice boxes. But not supplies.
Caller -> I put a sticky note on the fridge. It fell behind the fridge. I found it last night with a dust bunny.
Nurse -> Ha. Dust bunnies keep good records.
Caller -> Three weeks ago. I thought it was a month's supply. But he's growing, he's testing more. And he's doing a lot more injections with his school lunch.
Nurse -> Makes sense. How have his sugars been?
Caller -> He wears a continuous monitor too, but the strips are for the backup. When the monitor is off.
Caller -> Pretty steady. In the one hundreds, mostly. No lows. Nothing under seventy in two weeks. Which is good for us.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. I'll place the order now for pen needles and test strips.
Caller -> His doctor said the numbers look great. She wants to see him in January.
Caller -> Thank you. And can they come by Monday? He has a field trip Wednesday and I want everything packed.
Nurse -> Where's the field trip?
Caller -> They're going to sleep next to the dinosaur skeletons. In sleeping bags.
Nurse -> Ha. How fun.
Caller -> The science museum. An overnight. Two days. It's his first overnight since the diagnosis.
Nurse -> That's a big step. I'll coordinate delivery for Monday.
Caller -> Monday. I'm home. I work remotely.
Caller -> If I'm on a call, the front desk, I mean my husband's, no. If I'm on a call, my neighbor can sign.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll note that a neighbor can sign.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'd also like to see Tobias on Tuesday to go over the trip plan.
Caller -> Oh, that would be great. The teacher is nervous. I'm nervous.
Caller -> She emailed me a list of twelve questions. I answered nine. I don't know the rest.
Nurse -> We'll cover the rest on Tuesday.
Caller -> She's a new teacher. Very sweet. She asked me three times what to do if he faints.
Nurse -> We'll make the plan very clear for her.
Nurse -> That's very normal. We'll write a plan together.
Caller -> He says he doesn't need a plan. He says he's thirteen, he's fine.
Caller -> He told me, Mom, I've had this since I was nine. I know my body.
Nurse -> He's right. And the plan is a backup for the adults.
Nurse -> Ha. I bet he does.
Caller -> He has been giving himself shots since he was nine. He once did one in a movie theater.
Caller -> He's a very independent kid. He changes his own needle. He's really good.
Nurse -> That's great. Remind him to use a new needle every injection, rotate the injection sites, and put used needles in the sharps container.
Caller -> New needle, rotate, sharps. Yes. He knows. I'll remind him anyway.
Caller -> He has a little travel sharps container shaped like a yellow submarine. He picked it himself.
Nurse -> For the trip, pack extra strips, extra needles, glucose tablets, and the log. And tell the teacher the signs of a low.
Caller -> I made a list. Shaky, sweaty, pale, cranky. My son gets cranky and says everything is stupid.
Caller -> It's got the words in big letters. And a picture of a juice box, so she can't miss it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a classic low.
Caller -> His father is the same. When he's low he says the whole world is wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. It runs in families.
Caller -> I told the teacher, if he says everything is stupid, give him juice.
Nurse -> Ha. That's perfect.
Caller -> I'm putting a tiny laminated card in his backpack too. With the numbers.
Nurse -> A great idea.
Caller -> He's rolling his eyes right now. I can feel it.
Nurse -> Ha. It's your job to embarrass him.
Caller -> He's wearing his hoodie up. That's his armor. When it comes down I know I've said too much.
Caller -> I do it well. I'm the best.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else for now?
Caller -> No. Thank you, Odile. You're a lifesaver.
Nurse -> My pleasure. See you Tuesday. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Home Health, this is Dana.
Caller -> Dana, it's Florence Appiah. I'm the caregiver for Dmitri Yaroshenko. He just had a seizure. A bad one. He's on the floor.
Nurse -> Florence, slow down for me. I'm here. I've got you.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Sorry. I'm shaking.
Nurse -> No need to apologize. This is scary, and you're doing well. Keep your eyes on him and tell me what you see.
Nurse -> Florence, I'm here. Is he breathing?
Caller -> Yes. He's breathing. But it's loud. Like snoring. Like gurgling. And he won't wake up.
Caller -> I've seen him have a small one before, but never this long. Never this scary.
Nurse -> I understand. Stay with him.
Nurse -> Okay. How long did the shaking last?
Caller -> I think three minutes. Maybe a little more. I looked at the clock when it started. It was seven forty five. And it stopped at seven forty eight.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he still shaking?
Caller -> No. It stopped. He's still. He's limp. His eyes are closed. I said his name and nothing. I shook his shoulder and nothing.
Caller -> His arms stopped jerking. His legs stopped. He's just lying there like a doll.
Nurse -> Okay. That can happen after the shaking ends.
Nurse -> Florence, he needs an ambulance. I need you to hang up and call 911 right now.
Caller -> Nine one one. Yes. Okay. Should I put you on hold?
Caller -> I don't want to hang up on you. I feel better with you here.
Nurse -> Put me on speaker and dial from your cell, or hang up and dial. Whichever is fastest.
Caller -> I'll dial. I'm putting you on the counter. Hold on. It's ringing.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them your client had a seizure that lasted about three minutes and is not waking up.
Caller -> It's ringing. Pick up, pick up. Okay, it picked up.
Caller -> Hello? Yes. My client had a seizure. He's not waking up. He's breathing, but loud. The address is three seventy two Birch Hollow Road. Yes. Apartment B. Yes, I'll stay on.
Caller -> They're sending an ambulance. They want me to stay on with them. Dana, they want me on.
Nurse -> Tell them his name, Dmitri, and his age, thirty four. They'll ask.
Caller -> Dmitri. Thirty four. Okay. They wrote it down.
Nurse -> That's fine. Put them on speaker. I'll be right here. Florence, is he on his back?
Caller -> Yes. He's flat on the living room floor. On the rug. On his back.
Caller -> The rug is thick. That helped. I put a cushion under his head when it started.
Nurse -> Okay. I need you to roll him onto his side. Gently. Face turned toward the floor a bit, so anything in his mouth can drain.
Caller -> I'm turning him. He's heavy. I got his shoulder. There. He's on his left side. His mouth is open. There's some, there's foam. And a little blood.
Nurse -> That's from biting his tongue, probably. That's common. Don't put anything in his mouth.
Caller -> I've never touched his mouth. His mother told me never to. She said it's a myth about swallowing the tongue.
Nurse -> She's right. It's a myth. You did the right thing.
Caller -> I won't. I won't touch his mouth. The blood is small. It's a little on his lip.
Nurse -> Good. Is there furniture near him that he could hit?
Caller -> The room is small. I keep the corners clear because of this. His mother made me promise to always keep a clear space around him.
Nurse -> That was smart planning. It helped him today.
Caller -> The coffee table is right there. I pushed it back already when he started. The chair too. I moved the lamp.
Nurse -> You did the right things. Florence, did he hit his head when he went down? Did he fall?
Caller -> I took a first aid class last spring. I never thought I'd use it.
Nurse -> It shows. You were prepared.
Caller -> No. He was sitting on the couch. He was watching a game. He just stiffened and slid down onto the rug. I caught his head. I put a cushion under. He didn't hit anything.
Nurse -> That's very good. Okay. Now, has he had seizures before?
Caller -> Yes. He has epilepsy. He hasn't had one in a year. A year and two months. He's been so good.
Caller -> His mother is going to be devastated. She's at her sister's in Charlotte. I should call her.
Nurse -> Call her after the paramedics arrive. Focus on him first.
Nurse -> Is he on medicine for it?
Caller -> The Keppra. Five hundred milligrams. Twice a day. He takes it morning and night.
Nurse -> Did he take it today?
Caller -> The morning, yes. But last night, no. He fell asleep early. And I wasn't on until this morning. His mother was supposed to remind him. I think he missed it. I just checked the pill box and last night's slot is full.
Nurse -> Okay. That could be why. That helps the paramedics. Tell them he missed one dose.
Caller -> Missed last night. Okay. I'll tell them.
Caller -> I feel awful. I should've checked the box when I came in this morning.
Nurse -> This isn't your fault. Let's keep going.
Caller -> He's moving a little. His hand just moved. Dmitri? Dmitri, can you hear me?
Nurse -> Don't try to get him to sit up. Just talk to him. Keep him on his side. Does he open his eyes?
Caller -> No. Not yet. He's groaning. He made a sound. It's a little better, the breathing. Not as loud.
Nurse -> That's normal after a seizure. He can be groggy for a while.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm staying with him. I'm holding his hand. Dmitri, it's Florence. You had a seizure. You're okay. Help is coming.
Caller -> Dmitri, if you can hear me, squeeze my hand. He did it. Just barely. A tiny squeeze.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. He's coming back.
Nurse -> That's perfect. Keep your voice calm and low.
Caller -> He has this stuffed bear, a little brown one, on the shelf. Should I put it by him? He sleeps with it when he's sick.
Nurse -> If it's close, yes. But don't leave him for it. Stay by his side.
Caller -> It's right here on the arm of the couch. I'm grabbing it. There. I tucked it by his hand.
Caller -> I'm trying. My heart is going so fast.
Nurse -> It's okay. Take a breath. You're doing great. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> I'm counting my breaths. In for four. Out for four. It's what I do when I'm nervous.
Caller -> It's locked. The deadbolt. Let me go. Dmitri, I'm going to the door, I'll be right back. I'm going. Dana, are you still there?
Nurse -> I'm here. Go unlock it, and turn on the porch light.
Caller -> It's unlocked. The light is on. I'm back at his side. He's still on his left.
Nurse -> Good. Can I ask his date of birth, for the hospital?
Caller -> I can hear the dog next door barking at the siren. It's a husky. It sounds like it's singing.
Nurse -> Ha. Dogs always join in.
Caller -> November eighteenth. Nineteen ninety one.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number? Is it the cell ending in oh one six five?
Caller -> I have my phone in my hand. If it dies, I'll use the landline.
Caller -> Yes. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one six five.
Caller -> If I don't answer, it's because I'm in the ambulance. I'll call you back as soon as I'm at the hospital and know what room.
Nurse -> That sounds good. We'll keep trying until we reach you.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician and let the hospital know he's on the way.
Caller -> Thank you. Please. He's, he's such a good guy. He's thirty four. He shouldn't have to deal with this.
Caller -> He plays the guitar. He plays every afternoon. He's teaching me chords. I'm terrible.
Nurse -> It sounds like you two have a good bond.
Nurse -> I know. You're taking good care of him. How is he now?
Caller -> He's opening his eyes a little. He's looking around. He doesn't know me. He's looking at me and he doesn't know me.
Nurse -> That's very common. He'll be confused. Just tell him where he is and that you're here.
Caller -> He said something. It sounded like a name. Mama. He said mama.
Nurse -> That's all right. He's still coming out of it.
Caller -> Dmitri, you're at home. It's Florence. You're safe. Okay. He closed his eyes again. He's breathing better.
Nurse -> Good. Is his color okay? Lips and face?
Caller -> Pink. Not blue. He was a little gray before. It's better now. It's coming back.
Caller -> His cheeks have color. His hands are warm. That's good, right?
Nurse -> Yes, that's good.
Nurse -> That's what I wanted to hear.
Caller -> His chest is going up and down nice and even now. I'm watching it like a hawk. I've never watched anything so hard in my life.
Nurse -> That's exactly what you should be doing. You're his eyes right now.
Caller -> I hear the sirens. They're close. They're really close.
Caller -> The neighbor is outside on his porch. He's waving them in. Thank goodness.
Nurse -> Good. Open the door and stay with him until they come in. Leave me on the speaker.
Caller -> They're here. In here! He's on the floor! He had a seizure, three minutes! He's on his side! He's breathing! Seven forty five to seven forty eight! He missed his Keppra last night! Over here!
Nurse -> Florence, I can hear them. Answer their questions. I'll be right here.
Caller -> He's been on Keppra five hundred twice a day. A year and two months seizure free. No head injury. He bit his tongue. Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> Which hospital are they taking him to?
Caller -> They said Presbyterian. The one on Hawthorne. I'm going to follow in my car. They said it's okay.
Caller -> Should I bring a bag? Clothes for him? A phone charger?
Nurse -> Quickly grab his charger and a sweater. Don't delay.
Nurse -> Okay. Take his medicine list and the pill box. Bring his insurance card if you can find it.
Caller -> I'll take the whole box. The weekly one. And the bottle too, the Keppra bottle with the label. They'll want to see it.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Bring everything he takes.
Caller -> It's in the kitchen drawer. I have it. And the list from the fridge. Okay. They're lifting him. Wait. Dana, they're asking if I'm family.
Nurse -> Tell them you're the caregiver, and that you have the authority to give information. I'll make a note.
Caller -> I told them. They said okay. Thank you. Thank you so much for staying on.
Caller -> I'm going to lock the door behind us. The keys are in my pocket. I have my purse and his sweater. The stove is off. The lights are on.
Nurse -> Good. You've thought of everything.
Nurse -> You did everything right, Florence. Go. We'll check in later.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Caller -> Sorry, one more thing before I go. His mother may call the agency line. He's on the way to Presbyterian and I'm with him, if anyone asks, and I will call her myself.
Nurse -> That sounds right. Go ahead now. Take care, and drive carefully behind them.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Ruth, hi. It's Barnaby Lindqvist. L I N D Q V I S T. I'm a patient. I ran out of my heart pill, the metoprolol, two days ago. And now my heart is acting up.
Nurse -> Barnaby, thanks for calling. Let's sort this out. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> I hope I'm not interrupting anything. I know it's a weekday.
Nurse -> You're not. I'm glad you called.
Caller -> January twenty sixth. Nineteen fifty six.
Nurse -> And a number I can reach you at?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one eight one.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about the pill. What's the dose?
Caller -> I have the empty bottle in my hand. It's got my name on it. I keep looking at it as if it will refill itself.
Nurse -> Ha. If only.
Caller -> Fifty milligrams of the metoprolol. Twice a day. I take it morning and night. My last one was Sunday night.
Nurse -> And why did you run out?
Caller -> The mail order. The pharmacy that ships. They said it went out last Tuesday and it never came. I called them yesterday and they said wait another day. I should have called you then.
Caller -> I switched to mail order in the summer. It was supposed to be cheaper. It's been nothing but trouble.
Nurse -> Okay. It happens. How is your heart feeling?
Caller -> Honestly, I'm a bit embarrassed. I'm seventy years old. I should know to reorder before I run out.
Nurse -> It's the shipping company's fault. Not yours.
Caller -> It's fluttering. Racing. Since this morning. Like a bird in my chest. It comes and goes, but it's mostly there.
Nurse -> Can you check your pulse?
Caller -> I have the watch. It says one hundred ten. A minute ago it said one oh eight.
Nurse -> Okay. And what's it usually?
Caller -> I got the watch for my birthday. It tells me everything. My heart rate, my sleep, my steps. Too much information.
Nurse -> Ha. But it's useful today.
Caller -> Sixty something. Sixty eight. On the pill.
Nurse -> Any chest pain? Pressure, tightness?
Caller -> My wife had a heart attack two years ago. So I know what that feels like when it's described to me. This isn't that.
Nurse -> Thank you for telling me. I'll keep that in mind.
Caller -> No. No pain. No pressure. Just the fluttering.
Nurse -> Have you fainted, or felt like you might?
Caller -> No fainting. A little lightheaded when I stand up. But I sit back down and it passes.
Nurse -> Any shortness of breath?
Caller -> No. I'm breathing fine. I'm sitting at the kitchen table. I can talk without trouble.
Caller -> I took my blood pressure too, but the machine is in the other room. I can go get it.
Nurse -> Don't get up quickly. The nurse will check it later.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Barnaby, stopping metoprolol suddenly can make the heart race. I want to get you your medicine today. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now.
Caller -> Today? Oh good. I was afraid you'd say to wait.
Caller -> I almost drove myself to the urgent care. My daughter took my keys.
Nurse -> She did the right thing.
Nurse -> No waiting. I'll also contact a local pharmacy and ask them to fill an urgent supply today.
Caller -> There's a Walgreens on Elm. Five minutes from here. I can pick it up if my daughter drives.
Nurse -> Is your daughter nearby?
Caller -> She's in the other room. She's visiting for the week. She came for the holidays early.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me confirm with the clinician. I'm also going to send a nurse out this afternoon to check your heart rate and blood pressure.
Caller -> She's good. She makes me eat vegetables. I don't know where she gets it.
Caller -> This afternoon. That's wonderful. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll have the front door unlocked. And the dog put away. He barks at nurses.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you for the warning.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in an hour with the pharmacy plan.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll be right here.
Nurse -> In the meantime, if you feel lightheaded, sit or lie down. Rise slowly. And skip the coffee until the medicine is back.
Caller -> No coffee. Ugh. I've had two cups already. That might be part of it.
Caller -> I'll make decaf. My daughter has some in the back of the pantry.
Nurse -> It could be. No more today.
Caller -> Okay. I'll switch to water. And I'll rest on the couch.
Nurse -> And I want you to call 911 right away if you get chest pain, if you faint, if you have trouble breathing, or if your pulse goes over one hundred thirty.
Caller -> Chest pain. Faint. Breathing. One thirty. Okay. I'll watch the watch.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm sorry for the trouble. I feel like I'm always calling about something.
Nurse -> You call when you need to. That's what we're here for.
Caller -> My daughter says I'm a worrier. She says I should relax.
Nurse -> Ha. Easier said than done.
Caller -> She's making soup. Smells like heaven. Chicken noodle. She puts dill in it.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely. Have a little, if you feel up to it.
Caller -> I will. Thank you, Ruth.
Nurse -> Talk soon, Barnaby. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tern Harbor Hospice, this is Raul.
Caller -> Raul, hi. I'm so sorry to call right at suppertime.
Nurse -> No problem. Take your time, Dorothea.
Nurse -> It's no trouble. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hello? Raul? It's Dorothea Kettleborough. Can you hear me? I'm calling about my husband, Lawrence Kettleborough. K E T T L E B O R O U G H.
Nurse -> Yes, Dorothea. You're a little choppy. I can hear you. What's going on with Lawrence?
Caller -> I'm in the hallway. The signal is bad in the house. The walls are thick. They're old plaster walls.
Caller -> It's his bowels. He hasn't had. In three days. And he's, I think he's uncomfortable.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, I lost part of that. He hasn't had what in three days?
Caller -> A bowel movement. He hasn't had a bowel movement in three days. Three days.
Nurse -> Okay. Three days. Thanks for repeating that. Let me get his chart open. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry. I'm not good with these phones. My granddaughter set it up and I don't know half the buttons.
Caller -> June nineteenth. Nineteen forty five.
Nurse -> Thank you. Is he awake right now?
Caller -> He's in his chair with the crossword. He's doing it in pencil. He's very proud of his pencil.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we lose you?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one six eight.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me about his belly. Is it swollen? Does it hurt?
Caller -> Sorry, one second, the line dropped again. I'm back. Can you still hear me?
Nurse -> I can. You're clear now.
Caller -> A little bloated. It's tight. He says it's uncomfortable but not a pain. Not sharp. He keeps rubbing it.
Nurse -> Is he nauseated? Has he vomited?
Caller -> No vomiting. No throwing up. He ate a little toast this morning and kept it down.
Nurse -> Good. What is he taking for pain?
Caller -> He's been on it since September. The pain has been much better. He's sleeping again.
Caller -> The oxycodone. Every four hours. It's the one that stops him up, I know. The nurse told us.
Nurse -> Right. Is he taking anything for his bowels? Do you have MiraLAX, or senna?
Caller -> We have MiraLAX. The powder. Seventeen grams in water, once a day as needed. But he won't drink it. He says it tastes like a swimming pool.
Nurse -> Ha. Some people say that. Have you tried mixing it in juice?
Caller -> I told him it's like medicine in a pool. He said, I don't swim in medicine.
Nurse -> Ha. He has a point.
Caller -> I tried apple juice. He said no. He said I was trying to trick him. Which I was.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the right approach. Okay. Dorothea, I'd like to ask the team about a stronger bowel regimen. I'll message them.
Caller -> Thank you. You're always so kind. I don't know what we'd do without hospice.
Caller -> Yes, please. I don't want him to be uncomfortable. He's been so good. He never complains.
Caller -> He did go every day before the pain pills. Like a clock. It's strange to see him like this.
Nurse -> It's a common side effect. We have a lot of ways to help.
Nurse -> And I'll have a nurse visit tomorrow to examine him and see what's needed.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. Could they come in the morning? He's better in the morning.
Caller -> I'll put the kettle on and make sure the porch is clear. It snowed a little. A dusting.
Nurse -> I'll ask for morning.
Caller -> Thank you. Oh, are you still there? The line is cutting out.
Nurse -> I'm here. I can hear you.
Caller -> Okay. I'm standing by the window. It gets better by the window.
Nurse -> Smart. Stay there. For now, try prune juice. Warm if he'll take it. Small bits of fruit and fiber. And get him moving a little, if he's up to it.
Caller -> Prune juice. He likes prune juice. Warm. Okay. And fruit. And walking? He can walk to the kitchen.
Nurse -> Ha. That's good. It's an old remedy but it works for many people.
Caller -> We have a carton in the pantry. I bought it for him last month. I'll put it in a mug and warm it up.
Nurse -> Short walks are great. Don't push him.
Caller -> I won't. He has his walker. He'll take it slow.
Caller -> He thinks the walker is a nuisance. He calls it the chariot.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good name.
Nurse -> And call us if he vomits, if the pain gets severe, if his belly gets hard and swollen, or if he still hasn't had a bowel movement after the nurse comes tomorrow.
Caller -> Vomiting. Severe pain. Hard swollen belly. Still nothing after tomorrow. Okay. I wrote it.
Caller -> Do I need to worry tonight? Should I call if he's up in the night?
Nurse -> Call if any of those warning signs show up, any time of day or night.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> He's calling me from the other room. He says, who are you talking to? I'll tell him.
Nurse -> Tell him hello from Raul.
Caller -> I will. He likes it when people remember him.
Caller -> Lawrence! It's Raul from hospice! He says hello. He says tell him to bring cake.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll see what I can do.
Caller -> He's a charmer. Okay. Thank you. Goodbye.
Caller -> He says the cake should be chocolate. With the fudge on top. He's very specific.
Nurse -> Bye, Dorothea.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sycamore Row Hospice, this is Beatrice.
Caller -> Hi, Beatrice. It's Ramona Pierce. I'm the daughter of Cornelia Whitlock. I'm calling for the weekly update.
Nurse -> Hi, Ramona. I was hoping it was you. How is your mom this week?
Caller -> You're sweet. I always hope it's you who answers. The other nurse rushes me.
Nurse -> I'll never rush you. I've got all the time you need today.
Caller -> Thank you. I made a list this time. I wrote everything on the back of an envelope so I wouldn't forget.
Caller -> She's okay. Mostly okay. I have a few things. Do you have time for a few things?
Caller -> It's been a quiet week. Not as scary as the last one. We got through Tuesday and Wednesday without any big moments.
Nurse -> Absolutely. Take your time. Let me open her chart. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> I won't take long. I know you have other families to talk to today.
Nurse -> Don't worry about that. You're my priority right now.
Caller -> February twenty fifth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your cell is still the one ending in oh one five oh?
Caller -> I got a new phone, but the number's the same. I'm still figuring out how the screen works.
Nurse -> It takes time. They're so complicated now.
Caller -> Yes. Four oh four, five five five, zero one five oh.
Nurse -> Great. Where would you like to start?
Caller -> The hip. Her hip pain. It's better. She says it's a two. Mostly in the mornings when she gets up. By lunch it's gone.
Nurse -> That's an improvement. Is she taking the acetaminophen on schedule?
Caller -> Yes. The acetaminophen. Six fifty milligrams. Every six hours. I give it at six, noon, six, and midnight. She took the morning one at six today.
Caller -> I have a pill organizer for her, the big kind with four slots a day. It's color coded. My neighbor helped me set it up.
Nurse -> That sounds like a great system.
Nurse -> Perfect. Any nighttime pain?
Caller -> Not really. Sometimes she shifts and says ow. But she goes right back to sleep.
Caller -> I sleep on the recliner in her room so I can hear her. I wake up every time she moves. That's partly why I'm so tired.
Nurse -> Good. How is she eating?
Caller -> About half of everything. Half the oatmeal. Half the sandwich. She used to clean her plate. Now she looks at it and says, that's enough.
Caller -> I made her favorite, chicken and dumplings, on Sunday. She ate three dumplings and said it was too much. Three. She used to eat ten.
Nurse -> That's a lot of love in that bowl, even if she only ate a bit.
Nurse -> That's a common change. Is she drinking?
Caller -> Tea mostly. And water with a straw. About five or six cups a day, I think. I count.
Caller -> I keep a small cup by her bed with a lid. She sips between naps. It's one of those ones with the bendy straw from the dentist.
Nurse -> That's reasonable. What about sleep?
Caller -> She's sleeping a lot more in the daytime. She naps after breakfast and after lunch. Two or three hours each. Then she's up at night, not always, but some nights.
Nurse -> Is she confused when she wakes up?
Caller -> No. She knows me. She knows where she is. She's just sleepy. She wakes up and asks what day it is.
Caller -> This morning she woke up and said, Ramona, you look tired. I said, I am, Mama. She said, go to bed.
Nurse -> Ha. A mother's instinct.
Nurse -> That sounds normal for this stage.
Caller -> I figured. I just wanted to tell you.
Caller -> My sister says it's normal too, but she lives in Florida and she's not here. It's different when you see it every day.
Nurse -> It is. Seeing it up close makes it more real.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. How is her mood?
Caller -> I almost didn't mention it. I didn't want to make it sound worse than it is.
Nurse -> It's important. These details help us take better care of her.
Caller -> She cries sometimes. Not a lot. A few times this week. She looked at a picture of my father and teared up. And last Saturday she cried at a commercial.
Nurse -> That's very understandable. Does she say what she's feeling?
Caller -> She says she's just thinking. She says don't worry about me. She says she's had a good life.
Caller -> She told me last night she's not afraid. She said she's ready whenever it happens. I didn't know what to say. I just squeezed her hand.
Nurse -> That's exactly the right thing. You don't have to say anything.
Nurse -> She sounds peaceful in her own way. Sitting with her when she's tearful can help. Let her talk if she wants to, or just sit quietly.
Caller -> Sometimes I cry with her. Is that okay? I don't want to upset her.
Nurse -> It's more than okay. It tells her she isn't alone. Crying together is a form of closeness.
Caller -> I do that. I hold her hand. I don't know what else to do.
Nurse -> That's exactly what to do. Play her favorite music, and keep visits short and quiet, so she doesn't get tired.
Caller -> I also read to her sometimes. She likes the old poems. Robert Frost. Her voice moves along with the words.
Caller -> She loves Sinatra. I'll put on the CD.
Nurse -> That's lovely. Now, how are you doing, Ramona?
Caller -> I put it on in the evenings with a cup of tea. We both fall asleep to it. It's the best part of my day.
Caller -> Honestly? I'm exhausted. I'm up two or three times a night with her. My brother lives in Seattle and my husband works nights. I'm doing most of it.
Nurse -> That sounds like a lot. Do you have any help at all?
Caller -> My husband tries. He works nights at the bakery and sleeps all day. I can't ask him for more. He's worn out too.
Caller -> A neighbor comes on Tuesdays for two hours. That's all. I haven't left the house for more than two hours in a month.
Caller -> She's a retired schoolteacher, Mrs. Abbott. She brings her knitting and sits right next to my mother. They talk about nothing for two hours.
Nurse -> Ramona, I'm so glad you told me. I'd like our social worker to call you. She can talk about respite care and other support.
Caller -> Respite? Like someone to stay with her so I can sleep?
Nurse -> Yes. There are options, including volunteers, and short stays at a facility if you need a few days.
Caller -> A volunteer. Like someone who sits and reads or talks to her? That would be wonderful. She'd love the company.
Nurse -> Yes, exactly that. The social worker can arrange it.
Caller -> I didn't know that. I thought I had to do it all.
Nurse -> You don't. You shouldn't. Hospice is for the whole family.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed to hear that. I was afraid to ask.
Nurse -> Never be afraid. What else do you need?
Caller -> I'm the type who brings a casserole to everyone else. I'm not used to being on the other side of the table.
Caller -> I'm so used to doing everything myself. Asking feels strange. Like I'm failing.
Nurse -> You're not failing. You're doing one of the hardest jobs there is.
Caller -> The shower. She wants to take a real shower. We've been doing sponge baths. She hates them. We don't have a shower chair. She can't stand for long.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll order a shower chair for you.
Caller -> We tried the kitchen chair once in the bathroom, and it was slippery and wobbly. I almost dropped her. I won't do that again.
Caller -> She used to take such long, hot showers. It was her favorite part of the day. I miss seeing her enjoy something.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That would make a huge difference. And a handheld shower, can that be arranged?
Nurse -> We'll ask the equipment company. Some chairs come with a handheld. If not, hardware stores sell them cheap.
Caller -> We have a handheld in the garage from the old house. I'll put it on.
Caller -> My husband can mount it on the wall bracket. He's good with tools. It'll take him ten minutes.
Nurse -> Perfect. When you use the chair, keep the water warm, not hot, and stay with her the whole time. Don't leave her alone, even for a second.
Caller -> I won't. I'll sit on the toilet lid with a towel. I'll keep my hand on her shoulder.
Caller -> I also have a nonslip mat. A blue one with suction cups. I'll put it in the tub.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's a good safety step.
Nurse -> That's right. Ramona, I'd also like to send a nurse out on Wednesday for a visit.
Caller -> Wednesday. Good. Morning or afternoon?
Caller -> I'll write it on the calendar. We have a big kitchen calendar. My mother's appointments are in red. Mine are in blue.
Nurse -> The nurse will call to set a time. Probably late morning.
Caller -> Late morning works. She's up and alert then.
Nurse -> For her eating, offer small frequent meals and her favorite foods. Don't push if she says no.
Caller -> Small meals. Favorite foods. She likes pudding. And applesauce. And those little cheese crackers.
Caller -> She asked for ice cream yesterday. Butter pecan. I almost cried. It was the first thing she's asked for in days.
Nurse -> Then butter pecan it is. Enjoy every spoonful.
Nurse -> Perfect. Any of those are fine.
Caller -> I tried the protein shakes once. She wrinkled her nose and said it tasted like chalk. I won't try those again.
Nurse -> No need. Her favorite foods are better than any shake.
Caller -> I feel better already. It's good to just say it out loud.
Caller -> I've been carrying this all by myself. I didn't realize how heavy it was until I said it all out loud.
Nurse -> Anytime you need to say it, call. Day or night. You don't have to wait for the weekly check-in if something changes.
Caller -> Day or night. Okay. I'll remember that. I wasn't sure about the night.
Nurse -> The line is open all night. A nurse will answer.
Caller -> That's a comfort. Honestly, it is.
Caller -> Sometimes at three in the morning I just want to hear a human voice. Now I know I can call.
Nurse -> You can. Anytime. I mean that.
Caller -> Oh, one more thing. Is it normal for her to want the TV on all day, even when she's asleep?
Nurse -> It's very common. Familiar sounds are comforting. Just keep the volume low.
Caller -> It's on one of those home makeover shows. She loves the before and after.
Nurse -> Ha. A good choice. Lots of nice endings.
Caller -> She keeps a little notebook by her bed and writes down the ideas she likes. A tile pattern. A paint color. It makes her happy.
Caller -> That's what she says. She says she likes the endings.
Nurse -> I like that.
Caller -> Me too. Okay, I'll let you go. Thank you, Beatrice. Really.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself, Ramona. Talk soon.
Caller -> Wait, I forgot. She asked me to tell you thank you. She said the hospice nurses are the nicest people she's met in her life.
Nurse -> That means a lot to me. Please tell her thank you back.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willowmere Home Care, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi. Is this a good time? I know it's Friday.
Nurse -> It's a fine time. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. This is Ximena Calderon. X I M E N A. I'm calling about my father, Octavio Calderon. I need to order some equipment.
Nurse -> Sure. Tell me what's going on at home.
Nurse -> Hi, Himena. Of course. Let me open your father's chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Thanks. Sorry to call in the middle of the afternoon. I just woke up. I work the night shift at the hospital laundry.
Caller -> March eighth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks, Himena. And a number to reach you?
Nurse -> Is that a cell?
Caller -> It's my cell. I don't have a landline. Nobody does anymore.
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, zero one zero zero.
Nurse -> Great. What do you need?
Caller -> I should have called a week ago. I kept thinking we'd manage. And then he nearly fell on Tuesday.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called now.
Caller -> A commode. A bedside commode. The loaner we had went back to the hospital last week. Now he's using a urinal, and for the other, he has to walk to the bathroom. It's too far at night.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a fall risk. Let's fix that. And what else?
Caller -> It was a close call. He grabbed the doorframe. His knuckles were white. I heard it from the other room.
Caller -> The wheelchair cushion. It's flat. It's worn through on one side. It's been three years. He sits on it most of the day. I think it's not doing anything anymore.
Nurse -> A flat cushion can cause skin trouble. Have you checked his skin?
Caller -> It's the gel kind, but the gel has all moved to one side. It feels like a bag of sand. I pressed on it and it was empty in the middle.
Caller -> I look every evening. No redness. No sores. His tailbone is fine. His heels are fine. I put lotion on. I'm careful.
Caller -> I learned that from the first nurse. She showed me how to look for the red spots that don't go away.
Nurse -> That's great. You're doing a good job, Himena. I'll order a bedside commode and a new pressure-relieving cushion.
Caller -> Thank you. I don't hear that very often. It's a lonely job sometimes.
Nurse -> It's a big job. I hope you know how much it matters.
Caller -> Thank you. How fast can it come? It's already been a week.
Caller -> My father is not the kind of man who asks for help. If he's asking for a commode, he must really need it.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll get it to you quickly.
Nurse -> I'll coordinate the delivery for Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. I'm home. I work nights, so I'm here during the day.
Caller -> I sleep from nine to three. If I don't answer, the aide will. Her name is Pilar.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> The doorbell doesn't work. I'll tell them to knock. Or call. They can call my cell.
Caller -> What if he needs to use it tonight? I don't want him to walk to the bathroom alone.
Nurse -> Until Thursday, keep the urinal at the bed, and go with him if he walks. Use a night light and a gait belt, if you have one.
Caller -> He hates the urinal. He says it's undignified. I keep telling him it's temporary.
Caller -> I don't have a belt. I have a bathrobe tie. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A robe tie isn't safe, it can slip. Hold him at the waist and walk slowly beside him.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that.
Nurse -> When the commode comes, lock the wheelchair brakes and put the commode on a flat floor before every transfer. And please have two people help, until a nurse or therapist shows you the safest way.
Caller -> Two people. Brakes. Flat floor. My brother can come on weekends. During the week, it's me and the aide.
Caller -> My brother lifts weights. He'll be good for this. He likes to say he's the muscle of the family.
Nurse -> Ha. Good to have a muscle.
Caller -> He also makes the best coffee. So everyone forgives him.
Nurse -> That's fine. And check his skin every day, his tailbone, hips and heels. Have him shift his weight every hour when he's sitting.
Caller -> Shift weight every hour. I'll set a timer. He'll complain.
Nurse -> Ha. He probably will.
Caller -> He says he's going to buy a timer that plays mariachi music. So he can enjoy his shifts.
Caller -> He says, I'm not a baby. I say, you're my favorite baby.
Caller -> He's an easy patient mostly. He only complains about the food. He says nobody makes tamales like my mother.
Nurse -> Ha. That's sweet.
Caller -> He was a mechanic for forty years. He's all about working parts. I tell him his hips are his parts.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good way to put it.
Caller -> My mother used to say a good mechanic listens to the engine. I listen to my father the same way.
Caller -> He says they're rusted. I say, then we oil them.
Nurse -> Ha. A little WD forty.
Caller -> He has a whole garage of tools he can't use anymore. He sits and looks at them through the window.
Nurse -> That's a bittersweet picture.
Caller -> He'd love that. Okay. Anything else I need to do?
Caller -> I just want to say thank you for not rushing me. The last agency made me feel like a number.
Nurse -> You're not a number here.
Nurse -> No. That covers it for now.
Caller -> Thank you, Gwen. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Himena.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkspur Home Health, this is Dana.
Caller -> Dana, it's Georgiana Halloran. My husband, Everett Halloran. He just took the new antibiotic and he's broken out in hives. He can't breathe right.
Nurse -> Georgiana, take a breath. I'm Dana. I'm right here with you.
Nurse -> Georgiana, I'm here. Tell me what you see.
Caller -> I don't know where to start. His face is red. He's scratching his arms. He keeps saying something's wrong.
Nurse -> Slow down, I need you with me. Describe what you see, one thing at a time.
Caller -> Hives. All over his chest. They're spreading up his neck. And his lips are puffy. His tongue feels thick. He says his throat is tight.
Nurse -> Is there swelling anywhere else, like his eyes or his hands?
Caller -> His eyelids look a little puffy. His hands, I don't know. I'm not looking at his hands.
Caller -> They're big. Raised, like welts. Some of them are joining together. They weren't there ten minutes ago.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep looking at him while we talk.
Nurse -> Is he wheezing? Can he talk?
Caller -> He's wheezing. I can hear it. He can only say a few words at a time. Hold on. Everett, say something. He said, can't swallow. He said it in pieces.
Caller -> His voice sounds different. Hoarse. It's like he's talking through a straw.
Nurse -> That's important. Thank you for telling me.
Nurse -> Georgiana, this sounds like a severe allergic reaction. What medicine did he take, and when?
Caller -> It's an allergic reaction? From the pill? But the doctor prescribed it. The doctor wouldn't prescribe something he's allergic to.
Nurse -> We'll sort out how it happened later. Right now, let's help him breathe.
Caller -> The Augmentin. It was the first dose. Eight seventy five milligrams. About ten minutes ago. He took it with dinner.
Nurse -> Does he have any allergies?
Caller -> Penicillin! He's allergic to penicillin! It's in the chart! It's on his bracelet! I forgot. The pharmacy gave us this and nobody checked. Oh my God. I should have looked.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll deal with that. Right now, we focus on his breathing.
Caller -> I feel sick. I am so angry at the pharmacy, and at myself. I am angry at everyone.
Nurse -> That's understandable. Stay with Everett right now.
Nurse -> Georgiana, listen to me. This is an emergency. Do you have an epinephrine auto-injector in the house? An EpiPen?
Caller -> Yes! Yes, we have one. For his bee stings. In the kitchen drawer. By the stove. I'll get it.
Caller -> It's in the drawer with the batteries and the tape. I keep it there because the kids can't reach it. No, wait, we don't have kids at home anymore. It's just habit.
Nurse -> Go get it now. Stay on the phone. Take me with you.
Caller -> I'm running. My slippers are slipping. I almost fell. Okay. I'm at the stove.
Caller -> Running. I'm in the kitchen. It's in the drawer. I have it. It's in the orange case. It's expired? No. It says March next year. It's good.
Nurse -> Good. Use it now. Take off the cap, and push the tip into his outer thigh, through his clothes if you need to. Hold it for three seconds.
Caller -> I've never used one. I watched the video in the doctor's office. I'm scared. What if I do it wrong?
Nurse -> You can't do it wrong. Just push it firmly into the thigh. You'll hear a click.
Caller -> Outer thigh. I'm going. Everett, I'm coming. I'm kneeling. Okay. Cap off. Pushing. I hear a click. One, two, three. It's in. It's done.
Caller -> It's done. It's in. The needle came out and there's a little orange cover now. Is that normal?
Nurse -> Yes, that's normal. Hold on to the pen so you can show the paramedics.
Caller -> He flinched. He said, ow. But he's still breathing. Is that good?
Nurse -> Yes. Feeling it means it went in.
Nurse -> Good. Now call 911 right now. Put me on speaker, if you can, and dial from your cell.
Caller -> Wait. Should I call 911 first or give him more? I'm confused. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> You've already given the first one. Now call 911. You're doing it in the right order.
Caller -> I'm dialing. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My husband is having an allergic reaction. He took penicillin by accident. He can't breathe. I gave him the epinephrine. The address is eleven twelve Cranberry Lane. Yes. Yes. They're coming, Dana.
Nurse -> Perfect. Tell them it's anaphylaxis, and when you used the epinephrine. What time was it?
Caller -> The operator asked me a hundred questions. I couldn't answer half of them. He's still looking at me.
Nurse -> That's okay. They're sending help. That's what matters.
Caller -> It's nine forty eight. I just gave it. Nine forty eight.
Nurse -> Write that down, or say it to the paramedics. Georgiana, how is he now?
Caller -> I'm writing it on my hand. With the pen from the junk drawer. Nine forty eight.
Caller -> He's, his chest is going up and down fast. He's pale. The hives are still there. He's holding his throat.
Nurse -> Lay him down with his legs raised, unless it's easier for him to breathe sitting up. Which is easier for him?
Caller -> Sitting. He says sitting. He's on the kitchen floor with his back against the cabinet.
Nurse -> Then keep him sitting. Don't give him anything by mouth. Not water, not pills. Is the front door unlocked?
Caller -> Everett, you can sit up against the cabinet. I'll put a cushion behind you. There. He's leaning back. He's blinking at me.
Caller -> No. It's locked. I'll go. Everett, stay. I'll be right back. Don't move. I'm going to the door. Okay. It's open. The porch light's on.
Caller -> The lock sticks sometimes. Come on. Come on. There. It's open.
Nurse -> Good. Go back to him. Georgiana, I'm paging the on-call clinician now, and I'll tell the hospital he's coming.
Caller -> Everett, I'm here. I'm here. Don't talk. Just breathe. I've got you. You're going to be okay.
Caller -> Please. Please. He's turning red. His face is flushed. Is that the medicine or the reaction?
Caller -> His neck is red and blotchy. The hives are on his arms now. I'm afraid to touch him.
Nurse -> You can touch him. Hold his hand. It will help him feel safe.
Nurse -> It's from the reaction, and the epinephrine can make the heart race, too. That's expected. Is his breathing any better?
Caller -> A little. Maybe. The wheezing is softer. He's still tight. He's saying it's a little better.
Caller -> His color is a little better. Not so gray. He's gripping my hand really hard.
Nurse -> Good. That means the epinephrine is working. But he still needs the hospital. Don't skip it, even if he feels better.
Caller -> I thought it would fix everything right away. Like in the movies.
Nurse -> It buys time. The hospital will take it from here.
Caller -> I won't. I won't skip it. Everett, you hear that? Don't argue. He's shaking his head. He's stubborn.
Caller -> He's so stubborn. He once drove himself to the ER with a broken finger and then argued about the bill.
Nurse -> Ha. This time he's going in the ambulance.
Nurse -> He needs to be seen. If the symptoms come back before the ambulance gets there, there's a second dose he can have in five to fifteen minutes. Do you have a second injector?
Caller -> It came as a two pack. The second one is in the case. I have it in my hand.
Caller -> The second pen is yellow, the first was too. I mean, they're the same. I'm shaking so much I can barely hold it.
Nurse -> Keep it in your hand. If the breathing gets worse again, use it the same way, on the other thigh.
Caller -> I'm holding it like it's made of glass. My hand is cramping from gripping it.
Nurse -> That's fine. Just keep it handy until the paramedics arrive.
Caller -> Other thigh. Okay. I'm holding it. Hold on. Everett, are you okay? He's looking at me.
Nurse -> Keep talking to him. What's his date of birth, so I can tell the hospital?
Nurse -> You're doing so well. Keep your voice low and steady. He can hear you.
Caller -> Everett, you're doing great. They're almost here. Just breathe slowly for me.
Caller -> Everett, stay with me. Look at me. Look at me, honey. He's looking.
Caller -> April ninth. Nineteen seventy one.
Nurse -> And your cell is the one ending in oh one seven three?
Caller -> Yes. Six one oh, five five five, zero one seven three.
Nurse -> Good. Now, can you hear the sirens?
Caller -> He's holding my hand so tight. His fingers are cold. But his lips look less puffy. A little.
Nurse -> That's encouraging. Let the paramedics take a look as soon as they arrive.
Caller -> Yes. I think so. Yes! They're close. The dog is going crazy. The porch light's on.
Caller -> The neighbor is on his porch. He sees the lights. He's waving his arms to get them to turn. Come on.
Nurse -> Go to the front door and wave them in. Leave the phone on the counter. I'll stay on.
Caller -> The dog is going to bark at them. I'll put her in the laundry room. Hold on. Here, Bella. In. Good girl.
Caller -> I'm going. Over here! In the kitchen! He's having anaphylaxis! Penicillin! I gave him the EpiPen at nine forty eight! He's wheezing! Hives! Over here!
Caller -> They're asking me to move. I'm backing up. I'm out of the way. Dana, I have to put the phone down.
Nurse -> Georgiana, I can hear them. Answer their questions. I'll be right here.
Caller -> He took Augmentin. First dose, ten minutes before the EpiPen. He's allergic to penicillin. He has a bracelet. Yes. Yes, a second pen, here, I didn't use it. Yes.
Caller -> He's on oxygen now. They put a mask on his face. They're giving him something in his arm.
Nurse -> That's what they do. Let them work.
Nurse -> Which hospital?
Caller -> It's about fifteen minutes. I used to take my mother there. They know me at the front desk.
Caller -> They said Methodist. The emergency room. I'm going with him. They're putting him on a stretcher.
Nurse -> Bring the bottle of Augmentin and his medicine list. And his bracelet is on him?
Caller -> The list is on the fridge. Under the magnet. I'm grabbing it. Is there anything else?
Nurse -> Your phone and your keys. Lock up behind you.
Caller -> The bracelet is on his wrist. I have the bottle in my hand. And the used pen. They said to bring it.
Nurse -> Good. Go with him. Tell the ER about the pharmacy mix up. We'll follow up tomorrow.
Caller -> Thank you, Dana. Thank you for staying on. I'm going.
Caller -> I would have panicked if you weren't on the line. I really would have. I was frozen.
Nurse -> You weren't frozen. You acted fast. That's what saved him.
Nurse -> Go. Take care of him. Bye.
Caller -> I'll call you from the hospital when I know more. And I'll call the pharmacy tomorrow. They need to know.
Nurse -> Yes, please. They'll want to hear it.
