transcript:
Nurse -> Marlowe Home Health, this is Fatima.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Fatima. My name is Cedric Alvarado. I'm calling about my neighbor. I don't know if she's one of your patients. She has a nurse who comes. Mrs. Bellingham. Or Bellinger. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> Hi, Cedric. Thanks for calling. What's the address?
Caller -> I hope I'm not wasting your time. I just didn't know who else to call. I looked up the number on her refrigerator.
Nurse -> You're not wasting my time at all.
Caller -> Forty one Orchard Lane. The yellow house with the blue shutters. She lives alone.
Caller -> There's a big maple in the front yard. It's bare now. Her rake is leaning on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me look. I have a Winona Bellingham on Orchard Lane. Is that her?
Caller -> Winona. Yes. Winona. That sounds right. Bellingham, with the G. I always said Bellinger. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Don't worry about it. We hear all kinds of versions of names.
Nurse -> No problem. What's going on?
Caller -> I went over at noon because her newspapers were piling up. Three days. And her porch light has been on all night. I knocked and knocked. It took her a long time to come.
Caller -> I usually see her on her porch with her coffee in the morning. She waves. I didn't see her wave for two days.
Nurse -> And when she came to the door?
Caller -> She was in her robe. At noon. Her hair was a mess. She was holding the wall. She said hello, and she called me Harold. I'm not Harold.
Caller -> She's always dressed by eight. Even in a storm. Lipstick and earrings. Today none of that.
Nurse -> Does she usually know you?
Caller -> Always. We've been neighbors for eleven years. She brings me tomatoes.
Caller -> Last Christmas she knitted me a scarf with my initials. She never forgets anything. That's why this is so strange.
Nurse -> Okay. Did she say anything else that didn't make sense?
Caller -> I asked how she was. She said it's Tuesday. It's Sunday. And she said she had to go to work. She retired in nineteen ninety eight.
Caller -> I said, Winona, it's Sunday. She looked at me like I was joking. Then she laughed. Then she stopped laughing.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake and talking now?
Caller -> I'm standing in her kitchen. She's at the table. She's sipping tea. She's, I don't know. She's slow. She answers, but late. And she's sleepy. I can see her eyelids dropping.
Caller -> She's wearing one slipper. I don't know where the other is. It's not on the floor. I looked.
Nurse -> Did she fall? Any bruises, or blood?
Caller -> I didn't see her fall. I don't see any blood. No bruises on her arms. I didn't look at her legs. I didn't want to be rude.
Caller -> Her walker is by the back door, folded up. She hasn't been using it in the house, apparently.
Nurse -> That's okay. Thank you for being careful. Cedric, do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> No. No idea. I'm sorry. She's in her eighties. Eighty five? Eighty six?
Caller -> I know her cat's birthday. It's in March. But hers, no. Ha. That's embarrassing.
Nurse -> Ha. That's all right. Cats are easier to remember.
Nurse -> That's okay. I have her chart. And your number, in case I need to reach you?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, zero one two three.
Nurse -> Got it. What else do you see in the kitchen?
Caller -> Dirty dishes. A plate with a half sandwich from, I think, yesterday. The stove is off. The refrigerator door was open a little. I closed it. And the mail is everywhere. It looks like she hasn't been out in days.
Caller -> It's not like her. She washes the dishes right after she eats. There's no mold or anything. It's just messy.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a lot of useful information. I'm going to send a nurse out this afternoon to check on her.
Caller -> This afternoon? Oh, thank you. I was afraid you wouldn't be able to come until tomorrow.
Caller -> I'll watch for the car. I'll stand on the porch. I'll wave them in.
Nurse -> We'll get someone there. I'll also message the rest of the team about what you found.
Caller -> Thank you. I didn't know whether to call you or 911. She wasn't in an emergency, I didn't think. She was just off.
Nurse -> You made a good call. If she's alert and sipping tea, calling us first is right. If anything changes, call 911.
Caller -> I almost called her son, but I don't have his number. It's in her address book.
Caller -> What would be a change?
Nurse -> If she's hard to wake, if she falls, if she can't speak clearly, or if she has trouble breathing. Then 911 right away.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Falls. Can't speak. Breathing. Okay. I'm writing it on her notepad.
Nurse -> Can you stay with her until the nurse arrives?
Caller -> I can. I'm retired. I have nothing but time. I'll stay. I'll make her some toast.
Nurse -> That's very kind. Offer her a glass of water, and keep her sitting. And make sure the stove stays off.
Caller -> Water, sitting, stove off. Yes. I'll turn off the burner knob anyway.
Caller -> She's looking at me. She's saying, Cedric, why are you in my house? So she knows me again.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Stay calm and answer gently.
Nurse -> Good. Cedric, thank you so much for looking out for her.
Caller -> It's what neighbors do. When my wife passed, she brought me a casserole every day for a month.
Nurse -> That sounds like a real friendship.
Caller -> She'd do the same for me. Last winter she shoveled my walk. She's eighty five. I told her to stop.
Nurse -> Ha. She sounds like a character.
Caller -> She's the best neighbor. I just worry. She has a son in Arizona. He calls on Sundays. He called this morning, I think. She didn't answer. I heard the phone ring.
Caller -> I feel bad I didn't check sooner. I should have noticed the papers on the first day.
Nurse -> You noticed. That's what counts.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks for telling me that.
Caller -> You're welcome. Okay. I'll let you go. I'll stay right here.
Nurse -> Thank you again, Cedric. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Marlowe Home Health, this is Fatima.
Caller -> Hi, Fatima. This is Nadine Okwuosa. O K W U O S A. I'm the nurse at Sunnyfield Assisted Living. I'm calling about Mr. Lyle Stroheim. S T R O H E I M. The pharmacy delivered the wrong pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Nadine. Thanks for calling. Tell me what you found.
Caller -> Thanks for picking up. I have been on hold with three different offices this morning.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about that. Let's get you answers.
Caller -> His order says glipizide. Five milligrams. Twice a day before meals. The new bottle that came this morning says glyburide. G L Y B U R I D E. Five milligrams. Similar name. Similar pill.
Nurse -> Okay. Glipizide on the order, glyburide in the bottle. Did anyone give him any?
Caller -> I took a photo of both labels with my phone. I can send it if you want it for the record.
Nurse -> Keep it for now. You can show the clinician later.
Caller -> No. I caught it. I always compare the label to the order before I pour. Nobody gave him any. It's on my cart, set aside.
Caller -> It's a habit from nursing school. My instructor drilled it into us. Three checks before you pour. Right drug, right dose, right patient.
Nurse -> Ha. She'd be proud.
Nurse -> Good catch. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> It could have been bad. He lives on his own schedule, and his appetite is not always reliable.
Caller -> December third. Nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> Thanks. And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one five seven.
Nurse -> And his sugar today?
Caller -> I use the facility's meter. It's calibrated every week. I have the log right here.
Caller -> I checked it before breakfast. One forty. That's a good number for him.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he eat breakfast without the pill?
Caller -> Eggs and toast and a little fruit. He ate it all. He eats well at breakfast.
Caller -> Yes. He ate a normal breakfast. I held the pill because I didn't want to give the wrong one. His lunch is in about forty minutes.
Caller -> No dizziness, no shakiness. He's fine. I checked on him twice.
Nurse -> That was the right decision. Now, Nadine, glyburide is stronger and can drop sugar more than glipizide, especially in older adults. We don't want him to have it.
Caller -> That's what I was worried about. I almost gave it. The pills are the same white color. Same shape.
Caller -> The other nurses on the floor said they've seen that mix up before. At another facility.
Nurse -> It's one of the most common look-alike errors.
Nurse -> It's a common mix up. Let me page the on-call clinician so we can decide what to do about his dose at lunch.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Do I give nothing until you call?
Caller -> I don't want to withhold anything for too long. But I don't want to guess either.
Nurse -> Right. Hold his diabetes pill until the clinician calls back. Set the glyburide bottle aside, label it do not use, and keep it away from the cart.
Caller -> Do not use. I have a red sticker. I'll put it on now.
Caller -> I stuck one on the lid and one on the side. Now it looks like a hazard. Good.
Nurse -> Ha. That's exactly the point.
Nurse -> Good. I'll also contact the pharmacy and ask them to correct the order and send the right medicine.
Caller -> Please. I called them but they put me on hold for twenty minutes and I gave up.
Caller -> The pharmacist on the phone was nice, but she had to go find a manager. I think the manager was on lunch.
Nurse -> Phone lines are slow today. Thank you for your patience.
Caller -> Thank you. I've already filled out our incident report. The administrator knows.
Caller -> They have to track these things. State rules. I have to give them a copy of the labels too.
Nurse -> That's good. I'll call you back in an hour with the clinician's answer.
Caller -> Do you want me to call the family? His daughter is his contact. She might worry.
Nurse -> That's up to your facility's policy. It's fine to wait until we have the plan.
Caller -> An hour. Okay. I'll hold the lunch tray for a few minutes if I need to.
Caller -> I also held the dessert. Because he had pudding at breakfast. Don't tell him.
Nurse -> Ha. A secret.
Nurse -> And in the meantime, check his sugar before each meal and at bedtime, and write the numbers down. Call us if it goes under seventy or over three hundred.
Caller -> Before each meal, bedtime. Under seventy or over three hundred. I will. I have his log.
Caller -> He keeps a little notebook too. He writes the numbers in blue ink and draws a smiley face if it's under one fifty.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is he feeling?
Caller -> He's good. He's playing cards in the lounge. He doesn't know there's a fuss.
Caller -> He says if he loses a hand, it's the pharmacist's fault. He blames everyone.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sport.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. Let's keep it that way.
Caller -> He's a retired postal worker. He calls me Postmaster. I don't know why.
Nurse -> Ha. You're in charge of the mail of the facility.
Caller -> He says he's going to promote me to Postmaster General if the pills show up on time.
Caller -> I told him I only handle pills. He said, close enough.
Nurse -> Ha. He sounds fun.
Caller -> He tells the same joke every morning. About a mailbox. It's actually pretty good.
Nurse -> Ha. A morning ritual.
Caller -> He is. Okay. I'll wait for your call. Thanks, Fatima.
Nurse -> Anytime, Nadine. Bye.
Caller -> I'm glad I called. I almost wasn't going to bother you.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willowmere Home Care, this is Gwen.
Caller -> Hi, Gwen. It's Yolanda Mbeki. M B E K I. I'm one of the caregivers for Mr. Bertrand Lockhart. I'm calling with a quick update on his catheter.
Nurse -> Hi, Yolanda. Thanks for calling. Let me bring up his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Sure. Sorry for calling at the end of my shift. I wanted to make sure I told you before I forgot.
Nurse -> No need to apologize. I'm glad you did.
Caller -> June twenty first. Nineteen fifty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one five three.
Nurse -> Great. How's the catheter doing?
Caller -> I'm so glad he's doing well. The last client I had with a catheter had a lot of trouble.
Caller -> Good. It's draining well. The urine is clear. Light yellow. Like lemonade. No sediment, no blood. I check the bag every time I empty it.
Nurse -> And no smell?
Caller -> No smell. Just normal. I'm careful about cleaning the area every morning.
Nurse -> And how often are you emptying it?
Caller -> Every three or four hours. I record it on the sheet. Today we're at about eleven hundred milliliters since morning. That's about right for him, from the sheet.
Nurse -> That's good record keeping.
Caller -> I have a clipboard on the bedside table. I write the time and the amount in pencil.
Nurse -> Good. Any fever?
Caller -> No. I took his temperature at noon. Normal. No burning that he says. And no leaking around the catheter. The skin around it is clean and dry.
Caller -> He's also been walking more with the walker. His legs are stronger than last month.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Nurse -> That's great. Is he drinking enough?
Caller -> I think so. He has water, juice, and he loves his tea. About eight cups a day. I keep a glass by him.
Caller -> His favorite is peppermint tea. He drinks it from a mug that says World's Okayest Grandpa.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that.
Nurse -> Good. And is the bag staying below his bladder when he's up in the chair?
Caller -> Yes. I hook it to the side of the chair, low. It never touches the floor. I put it in the cloth cover.
Caller -> It has a little clip. I found it in the supplies box. It's handy.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right.
Caller -> Thanks. I was nervous about doing it right when I started. Now it's second nature.
Nurse -> It shows in how well you describe things.
Caller -> I also wanted to confirm. The catheter change. Is it still Thursday?
Nurse -> Let me check. Yes, I have it down for Thursday. I'll come by myself.
Caller -> Thursday. What time? He gets nervous. He likes to know.
Caller -> He's fine once it's over. It's just the waiting. He's a bit of a worrier.
Nurse -> Probably around ten in the morning.
Caller -> Ten. Okay. I'll tell him the night before, so he can mentally prepare.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. A few reminders. Keep the bag below the level of the bladder, never on the floor. And make sure the tubing isn't kinked.
Caller -> Below the bladder. Never on the floor. No kinks. Yes. I check the tubing every time I turn him.
Caller -> I'm teaching the weekend caregiver all of this too. She's new. She's nervous.
Caller -> I also clean the bag with vinegar water once a week, like the sheet says.
Nurse -> Good. Keep following the sheet.
Nurse -> Good. Everyone should follow the same routine.
Nurse -> And keep offering fluids, and wash your hands before and after you empty the bag.
Caller -> I wash for twenty seconds. Happy birthday, twice. Like they taught us.
Nurse -> Ha. The classic.
Caller -> It works. Twenty seconds feels long until you start singing.
Caller -> I sing it quietly. Mr. Lockhart tells me I'm off key.
Caller -> His granddaughter calls on Sundays. She wants him to teach her to play the piano over video.
Nurse -> Ha. He's a critic.
Caller -> He also corrects my grammar. Gently. He's a retired English teacher.
Caller -> He sings in a church choir. He's a bass. He says I should try alto.
Nurse -> Ha. A music coach for free.
Caller -> He says the choir needs a soprano. I told him I would be a disaster.
Caller -> Exactly. He also gives me crossword hints. He's better at them than me.
Nurse -> Sounds like a good match.
Caller -> His wife passed three years ago. He has her picture on the piano. He says good morning to her every day.
Nurse -> That's a sweet detail.
Caller -> He's the nicest client I've had. He says thank you for everything.
Caller -> This week he gave me a card with a ten dollar bill. I told him I can't take it, so I put it in the donation jar at the agency.
Nurse -> That's a lovely gesture, and the right thing to do.
Nurse -> That makes a difference. Okay, Yolanda. Anything else?
Caller -> No. That's all. Thanks, Gwen.
Caller -> Thank you for always being so patient with my questions. I've learned so much from you.
Nurse -> Thanks for the update. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harborview Hospice, this is Lena.
Caller -> Lena, hi. It's Gideon Dragomir. I'm calling about my mother, Seraphina Dragomir. D R A G O M I R. I'm sorry for the hour. I just need to make sure I didn't mess something up.
Nurse -> Hi, Gideon. Don't apologize. We're here at night too. Tell me what you're worried about.
Caller -> It's just that it's one thirty in the morning. I feel bad. You probably have other calls.
Nurse -> I have time for you. Take a breath.
Caller -> The bottles. She has three that look the same. I've been giving her pills all day and now I'm not sure I got them right.
Nurse -> It sounds like you want to double check everything. That's smart.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through them together. First, her date of birth.
Caller -> October twenty fourth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Perfect. She's eighty three, then.
Caller -> She'll be eighty four next month. She keeps saying she's going to be eighty four forever.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your cell, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, zero one three oh.
Nurse -> And that's your cell?
Caller -> Yes, I never leave it. It's glued to my hand tonight.
Nurse -> Got it. Now, read me the first bottle.
Caller -> The first one says MS Contin. Thirty milligrams. One tablet every twelve hours. It's the one for the steady pain.
Caller -> It's the big white bottle with the orange cap. At least I think so. The caps are all kind of orange.
Nurse -> Okay. MS Contin. That's the long acting morphine, the scheduled one. When did you give it today?
Caller -> I know. The nurse told us. She said it's like the background. And the other one is the extra.
Caller -> This morning at eight. I'm sure of that one. I wrote it down. The next one is eight tonight. I haven't given the eight tonight yet because it's only, what time is it? One thirty in the morning?
Nurse -> It's after midnight, so the eight tonight means the evening, which was a few hours ago. Did she get a dose at eight in the evening?
Caller -> I'm trying to remember. I don't think I didn't give it. I mean, I'm pretty sure I gave it. I wouldn't say I didn't. Wait.
Nurse -> That's a lot of negatives. Let's make it simple. Do you have the log?
Caller -> Ha. Yes, let me look. I'm sorry. My brain is mush.
Nurse -> Take your time. Is it written on your log?
Caller -> Let me find the log. It's under the pill organizer. Okay. It says eight PM. MS Contin. One tablet. There's a check mark. So yes, I gave it. I gave the MS Contin at eight tonight.
Caller -> It's in a spiral notebook. The cover has a cat on it. My daughter's old notebook. I use it for all of this.
Nurse -> Perfect. So she got the MS Contin at eight this morning and eight this evening. That is exactly right.
Caller -> I'm so relieved. For a second I thought I had skipped it. Or given it twice.
Nurse -> It happens to the best caregivers. The log is the answer.
Caller -> Okay. Good. That's the first one. A relief.
Nurse -> And the second bottle?
Caller -> The second one is hydromorphone. H Y D R O M O R P H O N E. The liquid. It says one milligram per milliliter. Take two milliliters, that's two milligrams, every four hours as needed for pain.
Caller -> This one is the brown bottle with the oral syringe in the box. It's the one I measure. I have a little cup too.
Nurse -> Always use the syringe. The cup is not accurate for small amounts.
Nurse -> Okay. That's the as needed one. When did she last get it?
Caller -> I gave her some two hours ago. I didn't not give it. I think I did. About eleven thirty, a little before midnight. Because she was moaning a bit. I measured two milliliters in the syringe.
Caller -> I stood in the kitchen and looked at the line on the syringe three times. I didn't want to get it wrong.
Nurse -> Okay. So you gave the hydromorphone liquid, two milliliters, about two hours ago, for pain.
Caller -> Yes. That's what I'm saying. I gave it. Sorry, I'm confusing myself with the doubles.
Nurse -> Perfect. No need to apologize.
Nurse -> It's late, you're tired. It's okay. The next dose of that one wouldn't be until about three thirty.
Caller -> Three thirty. Four hours. Got it. I won't give it before then.
Caller -> I'll set an alarm on my phone. I'll call it a drug alarm. No, a medicine alarm. Sounds better.
Nurse -> Ha. Medicine alarm it is.
Nurse -> And the third bottle?
Caller -> Hydroxyzine. H Y D R O X Y Z I N E. Twenty five milligrams. One tablet at bedtime as needed for itching.
Caller -> This is the little white bottle. The tiniest one. It's almost full. We hardly ever use it.
Nurse -> Right. That's the itching one, a completely different medicine from the hydromorphone. Did you give her any hydroxyzine tonight?
Caller -> No. I didn't give her the itch pill. She wasn't itchy. She hasn't been scratching tonight. So I did not give that one. I'm sure.
Caller -> She was itchy last week, after the new lotion. We stopped the lotion and it got better. So we only needed two pills the whole week.
Nurse -> Good. So the hydroxyzine wasn't given, and nothing is mixed up. The three are hydromorphone for pain as needed, MS Contin for steady pain on a schedule, and hydroxyzine for itching only.
Caller -> Okay. So none of them are wrong. I got them right.
Caller -> You can't imagine what that means. I've been so scared of getting this wrong.
Nurse -> I understand. You've been doing it carefully.
Nurse -> From what you've told me, yes. Everything you gave tonight was the right medicine at the right time.
Caller -> Thank God. I was sitting here at the kitchen table doubting myself. The names are so close. Hydromorphone. Hydroxyzine. They start with the same letters. It makes my head spin.
Caller -> I feel like a jigsaw puzzle with half the pieces missing. A tired puzzle.
Nurse -> They really do. Many people mix them up. That's why I want to help make it harder to mistake them.
Caller -> Please. What can I do?
Nurse -> A few things. Keep the three bottles in different places, not all together. Read the name on the label out loud before each dose. And write the dose and the time on the log right after you give it.
Caller -> Out loud. I like that. I'll do it. I'll feel silly but I'll do it.
Caller -> My mother used to read labels out loud at the grocery store. She would hold up each can and announce what was in it.
Nurse -> Ha. A family tradition.
Caller -> She also reads the ingredients of everything. She once refused a cake because of the margarine.
Nurse -> It's not silly. It works.
Caller -> And the log. I do write it. I just didn't check it as often as I should.
Nurse -> The log saved you tonight.
Caller -> It did. I'll put it right on the table in front of me.
Caller -> I'll also put a pen on a string, so it doesn't walk off like the last one did.
Nurse -> Gideon, how is her pain right now?
Caller -> She says it's a four. Four out of ten. She's resting. Her face is relaxed. She's not wincing right now.
Nurse -> Is she awake? Is she drowsy, or confused?
Caller -> She's awake. She just asked for water. She's not confused. She knows me. She's not drowsy, if anything. She's not not awake, if that makes sense. I mean she's very awake.
Caller -> I gave her a few sips with the straw. She said thank you, and then she said, you're a good boy.
Nurse -> Ha. That's sweet.
Nurse -> It makes sense. Good. And her breathing is normal?
Caller -> Normal. Regular. I'm sitting right next to her. I'd notice.
Caller -> I've been watching her chest on and off tonight, out of habit. It has been steady all evening.
Nurse -> That's what I want to hear. Gideon, I'm going to message our team and the pharmacy and ask for separate bags for each medicine, large print labels, and a medication schedule sheet that shows each one with its time.
Caller -> A schedule sheet would be fantastic. Right now I'm working from a handwritten list. I made it myself.
Caller -> My handwriting is terrible. I drew little suns and moons for morning and night, to help my wife read it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's creative.
Nurse -> A printed one will be easier. I'd like a nurse to visit tomorrow to go through the whole setup with you.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's great. In the morning would be best. My wife can sit with my mother.
Caller -> My wife teaches school, so she leaves at seven. But my daughter's grandmother comes at ten, so there's always someone.
Nurse -> Morning should work. I'll also call you back tonight, in an hour or so, to check on her pain and see if you have questions.
Caller -> Oh, that would be wonderful. I'm not going to sleep anyway. I'll be up with her.
Caller -> I'll make coffee. Decaf. I'm a bit wired already.
Nurse -> One more thing about the doses. The MS Contin is only at eight and eight. Never crush it or cut it. The hydromorphone liquid is only when she has pain above a three, and at least four hours apart. And the hydroxyzine is only at bedtime.
Caller -> MS Contin eight and eight, never crush. Hydromorphone for pain over a three, four hours apart. Hydroxyzine bedtime only. I'm writing all of it. The pen is dying. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I have it. I'm also going to write the three names on three different colored sticky notes. Blue, yellow, pink. Blue is the MS Contin.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Color coding helps.
Caller -> I have a pack of sticky notes in the drawer. My daughter uses them for school.
Nurse -> How old is your daughter?
Caller -> Eleven. She's fifth grade. She's asleep. She loves her grandma. She draws her pictures every day.
Nurse -> That's sweet.
Caller -> She taped one to the wall by the bed. It's a drawing of a garden. With a purple dragon. For some reason.
Nurse -> Ha. A purple dragon sounds like good company.
Caller -> She says the dragon protects the garden. And my mother. She's very serious about it.
Nurse -> I love that.
Caller -> Me too. It's the little things.
Nurse -> And Gideon, call us any time, day or night, before you give a dose, if you're ever unsure which bottle is which. We'd rather you ask than guess.
Caller -> Any time. Before giving a dose. Okay. I will. That makes me feel so much better.
Nurse -> You did a great job tonight, checking and calling.
Caller -> Thank you. I really appreciate it, Lena. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> Talk soon, Gideon. Get some rest if you can.
Caller -> One last thing. If my mother wakes up and asks for her pills, what should I tell her?
Nurse -> Tell her you've given her everything she needs, and that she can rest. She's comfortable.
Caller -> That's good. She worries about being a bother.
Caller -> I'll try. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sycamore Row Hospice, this is Beatrice.
Caller -> Beatrice, it's Leontyne Waldrop. My father, Augustus Waldrop. He can't breathe. He's panicking. His lips look blue. Please.
Nurse -> Leontyne, take a breath. I'm Beatrice and I'm with you.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Leontyne, I'm here. We'll get him help. Is he awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's gasping. He's sitting on the edge of the bed. He keeps saying, I can't, I can't. His eyes are huge.
Nurse -> Is he able to talk in sentences, or just single words?
Caller -> Just words. One or two at a time. He can't finish a sentence.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the oxygen set to?
Caller -> Three liters. It's on. The tubing is in his nose. I checked. It's not kinked. But he's pulling at it. He says it's not enough.
Nurse -> Is the concentrator humming and the tubing connected to it?
Caller -> Yes. I can hear it. The machine is on. I feel air at the end of the tube.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he have a do-not-resuscitate order? A DNR?
Caller -> Yes. We have it on the refrigerator. He doesn't want to go to the hospital. He said it clearly. Never again. He doesn't want 911.
Caller -> He signed it two years ago. He told the whole family. He said no tubes, no machines, no ICU. Just home.
Nurse -> Then we'll honor that. Let's keep him as comfortable as we can.
Nurse -> Okay. Then we'll treat this at home, and I'm going to help you. Leontyne, I need you to do a few things quickly. First, is he sitting up straight?
Caller -> He's leaning over. His elbows on his knees.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him upright. Put a pillow in front of him to lean on, if you want. Is there a fan in the house?
Caller -> He's still leaning forward. I put the pillow on his knees. Now he's resting his arms on it.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the position that helps him breathe.
Caller -> A box fan. In the bedroom. Hold on. I'll turn it on. It's on the dresser. I'm pointing it at him. His hair is blowing.
Caller -> It's an old one. It's loud. It rattles. He's had it since before I was born.
Nurse -> Then it's lucky. Turn it to the lowest setting.
Nurse -> Perfect. A fan on his face helps. Loosen his shirt at the neck. Keep the oxygen on.
Caller -> I'm unbuttoning his collar. I'm talking to him. Dad, I'm here. The nurse is here. Breathe slow with me.
Caller -> His chest is wet with sweat. He's burning up. Should I take his shirt off?
Nurse -> You can, if he's too warm. Keep a blanket handy for later.
Nurse -> That's good. Speak calmly. He'll feed off your calm. Now, do you have the comfort kit? The box from the refrigerator, with the vials and bottles?
Caller -> The comfort kit. Yes. It's in the refrigerator door. I'll get it. Running. I have it. The box with the blue label.
Caller -> The nurse put it in the refrigerator last month and told us exactly where. I never opened it until tonight.
Nurse -> Open it. Find the bottle of morphine. It's a small brown bottle with a dropper or an oral syringe.
Caller -> Morphine. M O R P H I N E. I have it. It says twenty milligrams per milliliter. Concentrate. And a little oral syringe.
Caller -> My hands are shaking. I'm afraid of dropping the bottle. I'm holding it with both hands.
Nurse -> Take your time. Set it on the nightstand if you need to.
Nurse -> That's the one. Is there a dose written on the label for breathlessness?
Caller -> It says point two five milliliter, that's five milligrams, every hour as needed for shortness of breath.
Nurse -> Good. Read me the line on the syringe so we know it's the right one.
Caller -> The syringe has little lines. Point one, point two, point three. Point two five is between two and three.
Nurse -> Right. Leontyne, I want you to give him point two five milliliter. Five milligrams. Draw it up in the oral syringe to the point two five line. Put it in his cheek, between the cheek and gum. Not down his throat.
Caller -> Point two five. I'm drawing. The line is so small. I see it. I'm on the line. Okay. Dad, open. Cheek. There. It's in. I gave it. I gave it.
Caller -> I got it. I checked it three times. The liquid is right at the line.
Nurse -> Good job. What time is it?
Caller -> Three twelve. It's three twelve in the morning.
Caller -> I hear a siren somewhere. No, wait. That's a car. Sorry.
Nurse -> Write that down. Don't give any more for at least fifteen minutes. It takes some time to work. In the meantime, keep him upright, with the fan, and stay with him.
Caller -> Okay. I'm writing. Three twelve on the back of my hand. I'm staying. I'm holding his hand.
Caller -> I'm also texting my brother. He's coming. He's twenty minutes away. He'll be here soon.
Nurse -> Good. It's good to have family nearby tonight.
Nurse -> I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, and sending a nurse to your house right away.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. How long?
Caller -> The doctor said this might happen. I thought I was ready. I'm not ready.
Nurse -> No one ever feels ready. You're doing exactly what he needs.
Nurse -> About thirty minutes. I'll stay on the phone until I hear the page confirmed. Are you okay?
Caller -> I'm scared. He's looking at me. He's terrified. His chest is going so fast.
Caller -> He grabbed my hand. His fingers are so cold. He's squeezing so hard.
Nurse -> I know. The medicine will help the feeling of panic and the air hunger. Keep talking to him. Tell him he's safe.
Caller -> Dad, you're safe. I'm right here. You're not alone. We're not going anywhere. I love you.
Caller -> He's nodding. He understands me. He's trying to say something. He says, thank you.
Nurse -> That's beautiful. He knows you're there.
Nurse -> Leontyne, what's his date of birth?
Caller -> September twelfth. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And your number is the one ending in one five nine?
Caller -> Yes. Four one four, five five five, zero one five nine.
Nurse -> Good. How are his lips now?
Caller -> Still a little blue. Dusky. Not as blue as before. I think.
Caller -> His nail beds are pink, I think. It's hard to tell in this light. The lamp is orange.
Nurse -> And his breathing?
Caller -> Still fast. But he's a bit calmer. He's not gasping as much. His shoulders are relaxing. The fan is helping.
Caller -> His eyes are closing a little. Not all the way. He's blinking slowly. That's better than the wide eyes.
Nurse -> Good. That's the morphine and the fan working. Give it a few more minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I'm counting. It's been five minutes. Six.
Caller -> The fan makes the curtains flutter. It's like the room is breathing too.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right. I'll call you back in fifteen minutes, whether or not the nurse is there yet.
Caller -> Fifteen. Okay. I'll keep the phone near. I'll keep him sitting up.
Caller -> Should I give him anything to drink? Water? He's very thirsty.
Nurse -> Little sips only, if he can swallow safely. Or a damp sponge on his lips.
Caller -> A sponge. I have the little pink ones from the kit. I'll use those.
Nurse -> If he gets worse, or if he stops breathing, or if you need me sooner, call right away. I'll pick up.
Caller -> Okay. I will. I have the number. I'll keep it on speed dial.
Caller -> My brother says there's a flashlight on the front step. He's trying to find the porch light switch. It's the one that sticks.
Nurse -> You are not alone. We're coming.
Caller -> I'm going to unlock the front door now, for the nurse. I'll be one second. Dad, I'm going to the door.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll wait here.
Caller -> It's unlocked. I'm back. I put the porch light on.
Caller -> Thank you, Beatrice. I don't know what I'd do without you.
Nurse -> You're doing it. Take care of him. We'll talk in a few minutes.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Odile.
Caller -> Hi, hello. Is this a good time? I can hear a baby crying. Oh, that's mine, I'm sorry.
Nurse -> It's a fine time. That's no problem.
Caller -> Hi, Odile. It's Katarzyna Branch. K A T A R Z Y N A. I'm calling about my son Theodore. Theodore Branch. The ear infection. I wanted to check in.
Nurse -> Hi, Katarzyna. How was your Thanksgiving?
Caller -> Chaotic. Twenty people. My mother in law made four pies and my father in law made zero. He says he supervised.
Nurse -> Hi, Katarzyna. Of course. How is Theodore? Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> He's right next to me, building a tower. He says hi. Say hi, Teddy. He's shy.
Caller -> June fourteenth. Twenty twenty three. He's three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, zero one nine five.
Nurse -> Perfect. Got it.
Nurse -> Great. So how's his ear?
Caller -> I took him to the pediatrician on Sunday night. The urgent clinic. They looked in both ears. Only the right one was red.
Caller -> Much better. He's not pulling at it. He was crying so much on Sunday. Now he's playing with his trucks. It's much better.
Caller -> He sleeps through the night now. Sunday and Monday he woke up every hour. I was a zombie.
Nurse -> That sounds exhausting. I'm glad he's sleeping.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Any fever?
Caller -> He still feels a little warm after his nap, but it goes away. I think it's the heated blanket.
Caller -> Ninety nine point four. This morning. It was a hundred and one on Sunday.
Caller -> I use the forehead thermometer. It beeps twice. He hates the beep.
Nurse -> Good. And the amoxicillin? How is that going?
Caller -> I wrote the times on a calendar. I put a star each time he takes it. He likes the stars.
Nurse -> I gave him five milliliters this morning at eight. The bottle says four hundred milligrams per five milliliters, twice a day. He takes it fine. He likes the pink one.
Caller -> That's good. Is he spitting it up?
Nurse -> No, he swallows it all. No spitting up.
Caller -> Finish all ten days, even if he seems well. Shake the bottle each time. And use the oral syringe, not a spoon.
Nurse -> Okay. Finish all ten days. Shake. Syringe. I will. We shake it like a maraca. He helps.
Nurse -> Good. That's the right routine.
Caller -> Ha. A maraca.
Nurse -> A good trick. Kids love to help.
Caller -> His grandma bought him a real maraca for Christmas. We have been hiding it.
Nurse -> Any vomiting, diarrhea, or a rash?
Caller -> I checked his tummy and back this morning. Not a single spot. I'm watching because he had a rash once from a different medicine.
Caller -> No vomiting. No rash. A little loose stool yesterday, but just once. Nothing since.
Nurse -> That can happen with antibiotics. Keep an eye on it. Is he drinking?
Caller -> I give him yogurt with his breakfast. The pediatrician said it helps. He thinks it's dessert.
Caller -> Lots. Milk, water, juice. He asked for apple juice about ten times today.
Nurse -> That's great. Fluids are important with an ear infection.
Nurse -> Ha. Good appetite?
Caller -> He drank a whole cup of milk in one go. He wiped his mouth with his sleeve like a cowboy.
Caller -> He's been eating like a little horse. Maybe it was holding him back all week.
Caller -> He ate two waffles for breakfast. And a banana. He's back to normal.
Nurse -> I'm so glad. Katarzyna, call us if his fever goes to one hundred two or higher, if he gets a rash or hives, if he throws up the doses, or if you see drainage from his ear.
Caller -> One hundred two. Rash. Throwing up. Ear drainage. I'm writing it down. I have the fridge pad.
Caller -> It has a magnet shaped like a banana. Teddy picked it. It's a good fridge pad.
Nurse -> Ha. A banana magnet is the best.
Caller -> Do I call you or the pediatrician if it happens at night?
Nurse -> Call us any time. We'll tell you what to do.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call you tomorrow to see how he's doing.
Caller -> His preschool wants a note. When can he go back? I know it's early.
Nurse -> He can go back once he's been fever free for a full day and feels well. We'll go over it tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. I'll be home. We're just playing trains.
Caller -> I'll have the phone near. It's usually in the kitchen under the dishtowel. I'll put it on the table.
Nurse -> Ha. Choo choo.
Caller -> Choo choo is also his word for bedtime now. Choo choo time.
Caller -> He says choo choo about forty times a day.
Caller -> His father bought him a wooden train set. It takes up the whole living room. We walk around it like a minefield.
Nurse -> Ha. He's three.
Nurse -> Ha. A train conductor at heart.
Caller -> He told his teacher he's a train engineer and he drives all the way to Chicago.
Caller -> I know. He's my little conductor. Okay. Thank you, Odile.
Nurse -> Anytime. Bye.
Caller -> Thank you for always calling back so fast. It really helps with the worry.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Hi, Marcus. It's Mabel Brannigan. B R A N N I G A N. I'm calling about my husband, Hollis. I just want to give you the weekly report.
Nurse -> Hi, Mabel. Good to hear from you. Let me open his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> You too. I'm sorry I'm calling the day after Thanksgiving. I figured you'd be home.
Nurse -> We're always here. How was the holiday?
Caller -> Quiet. Just the two of us. And the dog. We had turkey breast and one slice of pie each.
Caller -> February nineteenth. Nineteen forty. No, no. Nineteen forty one. He's eighty five. He was born the year after his brother. I always mix that up.
Nurse -> Forty one. Got it. And your number?
Caller -> Sure. It's still the same cell. I haven't changed it since two thousand ten.
Caller -> Seven one three, five five five, zero one nine seven.
Nurse -> Perfect. Tell me how he's doing.
Caller -> I got a new pen for the log. It writes smoothly. I've been using a bad pen for weeks and my handwriting was awful.
Caller -> Better. His back is better. I have the log here. Let me read it to you. Monday was a six. Tuesday was a five. Wednesday was a three. And today, Thursday, he said a two.
Nurse -> Okay. So today is a two. That's a nice downward trend.
Caller -> Sorry, I tend to read everything on the page. My daughter says I should skip the old days.
Nurse -> No, it's helpful to see the trend. Thank you.
Caller -> It is. I don't want you to think Monday is today. Monday was bad. Today is good.
Nurse -> Got it. Today is a two.
Caller -> Yes. The Tylenol schedule you changed on Tuesday. Five hundred milligrams every six hours. It's helping. I give it at six, noon, six and midnight. He took the noon one today.
Nurse -> Good. Any other pain medicine?
Caller -> The doctor mentioned a patch once. I told him no. Hollis doesn't like being stuck with things.
Caller -> No. Just the Tylenol. He doesn't want the strong stuff. He says he's not in that kind of pain. And I agree. He's not wincing. He's not holding his back. It's mostly in the morning when he gets up.
Nurse -> That's good. How is he sleeping?
Caller -> Wonderful. He went to bed at nine and slept until six. No waking up. I didn't hear a peep. I slept too. First time in a week.
Caller -> I put on the white noise machine. The one that sounds like rain. It helps him.
Nurse -> That's great news for both of you.
Caller -> He snored like a freight train. I never thought I would be happy about snoring.
Caller -> I know. I woke up and I felt human.
Nurse -> Any falls, or near falls?
Caller -> No falls. None. He's using the walker. He hasn't tried to stand without it. He wouldn't dare. I'd yell at him.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. And his appetite?
Caller -> I've been making him soups. He likes the barley soup. He asks for the barley soup by name.
Caller -> Fine. He ate a whole pork chop on Sunday. I almost cried.
Nurse -> Ha. A big pork chop.
Caller -> It was a thin one. But he ate all of it. And mashed potatoes.
Nurse -> That sounds wonderful.
Nurse -> Mabel, for his back in the mornings, you could try a warm pack on his lower back for about twenty minutes. Wrap it in a towel, so it's not too hot. And have him change position often.
Caller -> A warm pack. We have the rice sock. I heat it in the microwave. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A rice sock is perfect. Just test it on your wrist first.
Caller -> My mother taught me that. She knitted the sock. It has stripes. Hollis calls it the sausage.
Nurse -> Ha. A hot sausage.
Caller -> I do. I've burned myself before. Once. Not again.
Nurse -> Ha. Learned the hard way.
Caller -> Anyway. My point is the rice sock works. It's the best invention since the toaster.
Caller -> I learned very hard. Anyway. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll come out Friday for the regular visit.
Caller -> Friday. In the afternoon? He's best after lunch.
Caller -> I'll make coffee. He likes it when the nurse stays for a cup. It's his only social outing.
Nurse -> I'll try for after one.
Caller -> Wonderful. Oh, and Marcus, the dog is in the yard. He'll bark. He's friendly.
Nurse -> Sounds good. I'll see you then.
Nurse -> Ha. I remember him. A big golden.
Nurse -> What a sweetheart.
Caller -> He sits by Hollis's chair all day. He thinks he's a lap dog. He weighs eighty pounds.
Caller -> That's Duke. He loves everyone. He loves you in particular, you smell like a cheeseburger.
Nurse -> Ha. I did eat a burger yesterday.
Caller -> He sniffed your shoes last time and made a little noise of approval.
Caller -> He knows. They always know.
Nurse -> Call us if his pain goes above a four, or if the Tylenol stops working for him.
Caller -> Above a four. Tylenol stops working. Okay. I'll write it on the log.
Caller -> I'll also tell my daughter. She calls every night at seven. She'll want to know.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll let you go. Happy Thanksgiving weekend.
Nurse -> You too, Mabel. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Point Hospice, this is Marcus.
Caller -> Marcus, hi. This is Lucius Ostrowski. My mother is Clementine Ostrowski. She came home from the hospital today on hospice. And none of the equipment is here.
Nurse -> Hi, Lucius. I'm glad you called. Take a breath and tell me what's going on.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm frazzled. It's been a very long day. We were at the hospital until noon.
Nurse -> Hi, Lucius. I'm sorry about that. Let's fix it right now. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> It's not your fault. I know it's the vendor. I just don't know who to yell at.
Nurse -> You can yell at me. I can take it.
Caller -> Ha. I'm not going to yell at you. You're the first person who picked up.
Caller -> March thirtieth. Nineteen thirty three. She's ninety three.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number? I have a cell on file. Is it still the one ending in oh one one one?
Caller -> I switched phones last week. The number is the same. The screen is cracked.
Caller -> Yes. Seven oh four, five five five, zero one one one.
Nurse -> Great. So tell me what you're missing.
Caller -> The hospital bed. The oxygen machine, the concentrator. And the commode. They said it would all be here by two o'clock. It's four. Nobody has called.
Nurse -> And did anyone from the vendor call you today?
Caller -> One call this morning. A voicemail. Saying they would deliver between noon and two. And then nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Where is she right now?
Caller -> She's been asking for her own pillow all afternoon. It's the one with the blue case. We forgot it at the hospital, I think, or it's in the car. I have to check.
Caller -> On the sofa in the living room. We put pillows behind her. It's the only place she can sit. Her own bed is upstairs and she can't climb the stairs.
Caller -> We have a leather sofa. She's slipping down. We keep pushing her up. She hates it.
Nurse -> Keep adding pillows behind her. I'll tell you more in a moment.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she comfortable? Is she breathing okay?
Caller -> The hospital sent her home with a bag of papers an inch thick. Medication lists, instructions, phone numbers. It's all on the kitchen table in a pile. I haven't read half of it.
Nurse -> That's normal. We'll go through it together when the nurse comes.
Caller -> She's fine. She's comfortable. She's watching her program. She's breathing easily. She's on the portable tank, two liters, the one they sent from the hospital.
Caller -> She's watching a game show, the one with the spinning wheel. She's shouting at the TV. That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Ha. A very good sign.
Caller -> She's also correcting the contestants out loud. She knows the answers better than they do. She was a librarian for thirty years.
Nurse -> Good. How much is left in the tank?
Caller -> I asked the hospital nurse how to read the gauge. She said green is full, yellow is half, red is almost empty. It's between yellow and red. That's what has me nervous.
Caller -> The gauge is down near the red. The nurse at the hospital said it would last about four hours. We left at one. So I figure we have two hours left. Maybe less.
Caller -> It has a little needle. It's in the yellow, and the yellow is shrinking. I stare at it.
Nurse -> Do you have a second tank?
Caller -> No. Just the one. That's why I'm worried.
Caller -> The hospital gave us the tank and a small cart with wheels. They said the home company would bring the rest. Everyone said everything would be ready.
Nurse -> Okay. Lucius, I'm going to call the equipment company right now. I'll order the bed, the concentrator, the commode, and an extra portable tank.
Caller -> Thank you. Please. I've been on hold with them for twenty minutes, and then it hung up.
Caller -> The automatic voice kept saying my call is important. It's not important to them, apparently.
Nurse -> I'll call from here. Is there someone at the house to let them in?
Caller -> The doorbell sticks, so they should knock hard. Or call my cell. I'll be right here either way, I'm not going to leave my mother alone.
Caller -> Me and my wife. We're both here. My wife is in the kitchen making soup.
Nurse -> Good. Is there room for a hospital bed? Where would you like it?
Caller -> We measured it. Seven feet by four. My wife used a tape measure and a ball of string. She's very thorough.
Caller -> We cleared the dining room. It's on the first floor. There's a door to the bathroom. We moved the table out. It's ready.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me make the call. It may take a few minutes. Can you hold, or should I call you back?
Caller -> While you're calling, I'll find her medication list. It's in the hospital folder somewhere. There was a page that says current medications, and one that says stopped medications. I get them mixed up.
Caller -> I'll hold. I'll just walk around the house in circles. I'm too tense to sit.
Caller -> I'll hold. I don't mind. I'm standing here in the dining room staring at the empty space.
Nurse -> Okay. Give me about five minutes.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> I'll fold some towels. For the commode, so we have something ready.
Caller -> And I'll put clean sheets on the bed frame when it comes. My wife washed a whole set this morning and ironed them. She irons when she's anxious.
Nurse -> Lucius, I'm back. I spoke to the dispatcher. They had a delay with the truck this afternoon. They can bring the bed, the concentrator, a second tank, and the commode tonight. They're targeting between seven and nine.
Caller -> Tonight. Between seven and nine. Okay. Can they bring the tank first? The tank is the thing I'm worried about.
Caller -> My mother is going to need to use the bathroom before then. We have the little walker. We'll manage.
Nurse -> Walk with her and hold her waist. Two people if you can.
Nurse -> I asked for that. They said a driver can drop off the tank within the hour, and the rest comes later.
Caller -> If the tank doesn't come, my wife says she'll drive to the hospital and ask for one. I told her to wait for your call. She doesn't like waiting.
Caller -> That would be a huge relief.
Nurse -> In the meantime, check the gauge every thirty minutes. Keep her on two liters. And when it goes into the red, we'll switch to the second tank as soon as it arrives.
Caller -> Every thirty minutes. Two liters. Okay. I'll set the timer on my phone.
Caller -> I printed a sheet with the times. Four thirty, five, five thirty, six. I taped it to the sofa.
Nurse -> And I'd like to send a nurse out this evening, to see her and make sure everything is set up.
Caller -> This evening. Oh, that's great. Thank you. What time?
Caller -> My wife keeps asking if she needs to clean. I told her the nurse won't judge. She says I'm wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. Please tell her not to worry about the house.
Nurse -> Probably around six. She'll call from the car.
Caller -> I'll turn on the porch light. And the hall light. And I'll shovel the walk. It's only an inch but it's slippery.
Caller -> Six. Good. My wife will be happy. She's been worried.
Caller -> She's been calling every pharmacy in the county to find a spare oxygen tank. She found nothing.
Nurse -> Lucius, keep her sitting upright on the sofa with the pillows. No smoking or open flames near the oxygen, including candles. And keep the tubing out of the walkway so nobody trips.
Caller -> No candles. My wife was going to light one. She likes the vanilla one. I'll tell her.
Caller -> She lights a candle every night in memory of my father. It's a tradition. She'll use a battery one tonight.
Nurse -> A battery candle is a lovely idea.
Nurse -> Ha. Not near the oxygen.
Caller -> Right. And the tubing is across the rug. I'll move it. I'll tape it to the wall.
Nurse -> Great. Is she eating or drinking?
Nurse -> Small sips are fine for now. Don't push food. The nurse will go over everything tonight.
Caller -> We bought some of the nutrition shakes at the pharmacy. She doesn't like the chocolate one. She says it tastes like glue.
Caller -> She had a few spoonfuls of broth when we got home. And some water. She was tired from the trip. She was in the hospital for nine days.
Nurse -> That's a long stay. I'm glad she's home.
Caller -> She kept asking when she could go home. The nurses said soon, soon, and then the paperwork took all day.
Caller -> Me too. She was so happy to see the house. She cried a little in the driveway.
Nurse -> That must have been beautiful.
Caller -> It was. She looked at the maple tree and said, I'm home.
Caller -> It was a big red maple, and half the leaves were still on it. She said it was waiting for her.
Nurse -> I'm glad you could bring her.
Caller -> My brother wanted to come, but he's flying in from Seattle tomorrow. He can't get here until the evening. I'll tell him everything.
Caller -> Marcus, one question. When the bed comes, who sets it up?
Caller -> It's a strange feeling, setting up a hospital bed in your dining room. The table was my grandmother's.
Nurse -> It's hard to move familiar things. It's a sign of how much you care.
Nurse -> The delivery team will set it up, and show you how to use the controls.
Caller -> Good. I'm not a handyman. My wife says I can't hang a picture.
Caller -> I once put a shelf up backwards. My wife still brings it up at parties.
Nurse -> Ha. Don't worry, they do it every day.
Caller -> When the delivery men come, should I help or stay out of the way? I never know which one is polite.
Nurse -> Stay nearby but let them work. Ask questions if you're unsure.
Caller -> What if I have a question after they leave?
Caller -> Our old neighbor used hospice for her husband. She said the nights were the scariest.
Nurse -> Call us anytime. The nurse on call will walk you through it.
Caller -> That's a comfort. Honestly, this is the first time I felt like someone was in charge.
Caller -> The hospital discharge was like being handed a baby and told good luck. At least you pick up the phone.
Nurse -> We're here. You don't have to figure it out alone.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you, Marcus. I mean it.
Caller -> I'm sorry for rambling. When I'm worried, I talk. My wife says I narrate my own life.
Nurse -> Ha. It's fine. I like hearing the details.
Caller -> I'm going to go tell my wife the plan. She's going to cry. In a good way.
Nurse -> You're welcome. We'll see you tonight.
Caller -> Marcus, one more thing and I'll let you go. If the bed comes late, say nine thirty, is it too late for the nurse to come after? I don't want to burden anyone.
Nurse -> The nurse will adjust. It's never a burden. We work evenings for exactly this reason.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Lucius.

transcript:
Nurse -> Ash Grove Hospice, this is Beatrice.
Caller -> Hi. Is this the right number? I'm calling about a resident. I'm sorry for the hour.
Nurse -> This is the right number. It's no trouble. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. My name is Priscila Montoya. I'm an aide at Rosewood Memory Care. I'm calling about one of our residents. Mr. Osvaldo Treadwell. T R E A D W E L L. He's one of yours.
Nurse -> Hi, Priscila. Thank you for calling. What's going on with Mr. Treadwell?
Caller -> I've never called hospice at night before. I'm nervous. The night nurse said I should.
Caller -> He didn't eat dinner. He pushed the tray away. Twice. And he's been calling out since six. He keeps saying, I want to go home. I want to go home.
Nurse -> How long has he been calling out?
Caller -> Since six, about. It's two in the morning. Eight hours? No, no, it's two in the morning now. It started at six last night. Eight hours.
Caller -> I got off from my other job and came here at eleven. I heard him as soon as I walked in the door.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he in bed?
Caller -> He's in the day room. He's in the recliner. He doesn't want to go to his room. I tried. He said no.
Caller -> The TV is on with the sound off. There are three other residents asleep in their chairs. It's very quiet except for him.
Nurse -> Is he awake and talking to you?
Caller -> He's awake. He's sort of mumbling. He says, take me home. He says, where's Rita. Rita was his wife. She passed.
Caller -> His hands keep patting the arms of the chair like he's looking for something. His car keys, maybe.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. Does he know where he is?
Caller -> No. I don't think so. He thinks it's his old house. The one in Milwaukee.
Caller -> He told me yesterday I was his sister. Which I'm not. But I said yes. It seemed to calm him.
Nurse -> That's often kind. Go with it.
Nurse -> Does he seem to be in pain? Grimacing, holding any part of his body?
Caller -> No. I don't see that. I looked. He's not grimacing. He's not holding anything. I asked him if anything hurts, and he said no. But he says no to everything.
Caller -> His forehead is smooth. His jaw is relaxed. His hands aren't clenched. He just looks lost.
Nurse -> Has he had a fever? Any cough, or trouble breathing?
Caller -> I took his temperature at ten. It was normal. I don't know the number. I wrote it on his sheet. He's not coughing. His breathing seems okay. Slow, but okay.
Caller -> It's one of those forehead ones. It was in the green. Nothing flashing. That's what the sheet says.
Nurse -> Has he been aggressive, or hit anyone?
Caller -> No. He's not hitting anyone. He's not throwing anything. He's sad. He's just sad and loud. He cries, a little.
Nurse -> Has he been sleeping today?
Caller -> Most of the day. The day shift said he barely woke up for lunch. He ate three bites. And he dozed through the afternoon.
Caller -> They said he was up earlier in the week, walking around, singing a little. This is different for him.
Nurse -> Okay. Priscila, what's his date of birth?
Caller -> I don't know it. I'm sorry. I'm new. I've only been here two weeks. It's in the chart, but the chart is locked in the nurse's office and she left at eleven.
Caller -> I can ask the night nurse to look at the chart. She's on a break but she should be back soon.
Nurse -> That's okay. I can find him with the name and facility.
Nurse -> That's okay. I can find him by name and facility. What's the best number to reach you?
Caller -> The unit phone. Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one nine eight.
Nurse -> Good. Priscila, I'm going to plan a nurse visit tomorrow morning to see him.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning? Not tonight?
Caller -> I wasn't sure what hospice does at night. I thought maybe you come right away for everything.
Nurse -> From what you're describing, he isn't in distress, he isn't in pain, and he isn't hurting anyone. It can wait until morning. If that changes, call me back.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I just wasn't sure. He's so sad. I wanted to do something.
Caller -> I feel awful that I can't fix it. I'm just an aide. I want to do more.
Nurse -> You're doing a lot. You noticed, you called, you stayed with him.
Nurse -> I understand. I'll also message the team about his mood and his appetite, and whether he needs anything to help him settle.
Caller -> Thank you. That would help. The night nurse said she can't give anything without an order.
Nurse -> That's right. We'll look at it in the morning.
Caller -> Is there anything I can do tonight?
Nurse -> Yes. Speak softly. Tell him you hear him. Say, you want to go home, I understand. Offer him a warm drink, maybe warm milk or decaf tea, and a familiar blanket. Try some music or a short walk with him.
Caller -> A walk. He likes to walk. I'll go around the hallway with him. And I'll put on some music. What kind?
Caller -> He walks the hall every afternoon, back and forth, with his hands behind his back like a general.
Nurse -> Something from when he was young. Old songs. Ask what his favorites were.
Caller -> The Polka station. I saw him tap his foot to polka once.
Nurse -> Perfect. Polka it is.
Caller -> Ha. The other residents will be thrilled at two in the morning.
Caller -> I'll close the door to the day room if we go down the hall. Mrs. Pellegrini sleeps like a log anyway.
Nurse -> Ha. Use headphones, if you can.
Caller -> We don't have any. I'll turn it way down.
Nurse -> And call us back if he gets combative, if he falls, if he seems to be in pain, if he runs a fever, or if he stops drinking.
Caller -> Combative. Falls. Pain. Fever. Stops drinking. Okay. I'll tell the next shift.
Caller -> I'll write it on the whiteboard in the nurses' station, right next to his name, in red.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling, Priscila. You did the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you. I feel better. Goodnight.
Caller -> I'll go find the polka station now. Wish me luck.
Nurse -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Bridge Palliative Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Joanne, it's Thaddeus Delacourt. My wife is Rosemary Delacourt. Her pain is out of control. Nothing is working. She's been in agony for three hours.
Nurse -> Thaddeus, take a breath. I'm right here. We'll get her help.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm sorry, I'm shaking. It's four in the morning and I woke up to her crying.
Nurse -> Thaddeus, I'm here. Let's get her help. Where is the pain?
Caller -> Her belly. The upper part, and it goes through to her back. She says it feels like a knife.
Caller -> It's under her ribs on the right side and in the middle, and then it wraps around. She keeps pressing her hand there.
Caller -> She's had this pain before but never like this. It's different. It's sharper. It's constant.
Nurse -> I understand. That's important.
Nurse -> And on a scale of zero to ten, how bad?
Caller -> Hold on. Let me ask her again. Rosie, a number. She says nine. Same as before.
Caller -> She says nine. A nine. She's curled up like a ball. She's crying. She never cries.
Caller -> I asked her three times. Is it a nine? She said, ten, if I could. I said, let's say nine. She nodded.
Nurse -> Okay. What has she taken for it?
Caller -> I'm looking at the kitchen counter while I talk. There's the pill box, the patch box, a cup of ice water, her pill crusher. It all looks like a pharmacy.
Nurse -> Don't worry about the counter. Just stay with her.
Caller -> She has the fentanyl patch. Seventy five micrograms an hour. We changed it two days ago. And the oxycodone tablets. Ten milligrams. Every four hours if she needs it. She took one an hour ago.
Caller -> The patch is on her left shoulder. I checked it, it's still stuck. I thought maybe it had peeled off. It hasn't.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Thank you for checking.
Nurse -> Okay. And the one an hour ago didn't help?
Caller -> It took the edge off for maybe twenty minutes. Then it came right back. It's worse now. She asked if she could take another one but I said wait, because you said four hours.
Caller -> I wrote the times on the log. Midnight, one fifteen, three. I gave her one at three fifteen. It's all there on paper.
Nurse -> You did the right thing. Thaddeus, I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now for an order.
Caller -> Please. Thank you. How fast? She's suffering.
Caller -> I called the number on the refrigerator magnet. The after-hours line. A recording picked up first. I almost cried.
Nurse -> Very fast. I'll also send a nurse to your home right now.
Caller -> Tonight? Right now? Oh, thank God.
Caller -> I'll turn on the porch light. And the hall. Is there anything I should move out of the way?
Nurse -> Just keep the path to her room clear. The nurse knows the way.
Nurse -> Yes. While we wait, can you tell me, is she vomiting?
Caller -> No. She felt a little sick earlier but she hasn't thrown up. She hasn't eaten since dinner.
Caller -> She keeps asking for ice chips. I gave her a few. She says the cold feels good in her mouth.
Nurse -> Is she alert? Does she know where she is?
Caller -> She's totally alert. She's talking. She's just, she's in pain. She keeps saying, I can't. She's very clear. She's not confused.
Caller -> She even told me which medicine to look for. She's still the boss. She's bossing me from the bed.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Good. Thaddeus, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> I'm sorry if I'm answering slowly. My head isn't working right. It's like wading through water.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. There's no rush.
Caller -> August twenty third. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll pass that to the clinician.
Nurse -> And your cell is the one ending in oh one six seven?
Caller -> Yes. Two oh six, five five five, zero one six seven.
Nurse -> Thank you. Now, let's try to ease her until the clinician calls. Can she curl up on her side?
Caller -> She is. She's on her left side with her knees up.
Caller -> She's wearing my old flannel shirt. She says it smells like me and it helps.
Nurse -> Put a pillow against her belly, and one between her knees. Do you have a heating pad, or a warm pack?
Caller -> We have a heating pad. In the hall closet. I'll get it. Running. Okay. I have it. It's plugged in.
Caller -> I haven't used it in years. It's got a funny cord. Let me make sure the cord isn't frayed. It looks okay.
Nurse -> Put it on low, wrapped in a towel. Not directly on her skin. On her belly, where it hurts.
Caller -> Okay. A towel. It's on. Rosemary, is that okay? She says a little better. A tiny bit.
Caller -> She's breathing a little slower. Her hands are less tight. It's only a tiny bit, but I'll take it.
Nurse -> Good. Keep the room quiet and dim. Breathe slowly with her. In through the nose, out through the mouth.
Caller -> The cat jumped on the bed. Should I move her? She's purring right next to Rosemary's shoulder.
Nurse -> If it's soothing, leave her. If the cat bothers her, move her gently.
Caller -> Dim. Slow. I'm turning off the overhead. I'm breathing with her. In. Out. She's following me.
Caller -> I put the lamp on the floor so it throws a soft light on the wall. She likes it that way.
Nurse -> That's great. Now, Thaddeus, please don't give her an extra dose until the clinician calls back. We need to decide what's safe.
Caller -> I won't. I'm waiting. I'm holding the bottle and I won't open it.
Caller -> The bottle has a child cap, and my hands are too shaky to open it anyway. So I won't be tempted.
Nurse -> Ha. Good point. Keep it closed.
Nurse -> Good. And if she gets very sleepy and hard to wake up, or her breathing slows down, call 911 right away.
Caller -> 911 if she's hard to wake. Or if her breathing slows. Okay. Got it.
Caller -> I have my phone ready. The number is on the screen. My thumb is over the button.
Nurse -> I'll call you back in twenty minutes, even if the nurse isn't there yet.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. Okay. I'll keep the phone right here.
Caller -> I'm putting the phone on the pillow next to her so she can hear you if she wants.
Nurse -> How is she right now?
Caller -> Still crying. But quieter. She's holding my hand. She's squeezing hard.
Caller -> She said, tell the nurse thank you. Even now she's polite.
Nurse -> That's okay. Let her squeeze. Keep talking to her.
Caller -> Rosie, I'm here. The nurse is coming. We'll fix this. I'm not leaving you.
Caller -> I have a song she likes, a waltz. I'm humming it very softly. She used to teach it.
Nurse -> You're doing everything right.
Caller -> I'm trying not to panic. I'm trying to be the calm one. She needs me calm.
Caller -> I feel so helpless. I can't take the pain away.
Caller -> I keep thinking about what I could have done differently this week. Maybe the patch should have been stronger.
Nurse -> That's for the clinician to decide. Right now we're doing everything right.
Nurse -> I know. But being there with her is a big part of it.
Caller -> I've never seen her like this. She was a ballet teacher. She never complained about anything.
Caller -> Thirty one years of marriage. I've never heard her raise her voice, and tonight she screamed. It scared me.
Nurse -> She sounds strong. And she's allowed to be in pain and to cry.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps. I keep telling her it's okay.
Caller -> Is it normal to feel angry at the cancer? I want to punch a wall.
Nurse -> It's very normal. We can talk about that with the nurse tomorrow, too.
Nurse -> It is okay. I'll talk to you soon, Thaddeus. Stay with her.
Caller -> Please hurry. I know you are. Sorry. I'm just saying it out loud.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Brightwater Home Health, this is Priya.
Caller -> Oh good, you answered. I was afraid I'd get the machine. Hello? Can you hear me now?
Nurse -> I can hear you. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Priya. It's Lavinia Anstruther. Can you hear me? I'm calling about my husband, Percival. P E R C I V A L. Anstruther. A N S T R U T H E R.
Nurse -> Take your time. Which numbers are you worried about?
Nurse -> I can hear you, Lavinia, but the line is fuzzy. What's going on with Percival?
Caller -> His numbers are off. His blood pressure, and his weight. I wanted to tell someone.
Caller -> I don't want to be a pest. I know you have sick people. But I don't like when his numbers change.
Nurse -> You're not a pest. This is what we're here for.
Nurse -> Okay. Let me open his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> May fifth. Nineteen fifty.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, zero one seven six.
Nurse -> Thanks. So tell me the numbers.
Caller -> I wrote them on the pad. My handwriting. I'll read them. One second. I'm putting on my glasses.
Caller -> The blood pressure this morning was won fordy ate over nigh tea too.
Nurse -> I'm sorry, Lavinia, I couldn't make that out. Can you say it again slowly, number by number?
Caller -> It sounds like I'm in a tunnel. I'm going to move closer to the window. Maybe that helps.
Caller -> Sorry. The line. One. Four. Eight. Over nine. Two. One forty eight over ninety two.
Nurse -> One forty eight over ninety two. Okay. What's his usual?
Caller -> About one twenty eight over seventy eight. This is higher.
Nurse -> It is. What about his weight?
Caller -> We have the digital scale. The kind that talks. It says the number out loud. Percival hates it. He says it judges him.
Nurse -> Ha. A talking scale. Wow.
Caller -> He weighs himself every morning. Monday he was one eighty one. Today one eighty four. That's up three pounds in two days. And his ankles are puffy. More than usual.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he taking his water pill?
Caller -> I put the pills in the organizer on Sundays. Morning, noon, evening, bedtime. I watch him swallow.
Caller -> The furosemide. Forty milligrams, every morning. He took it today at eight. He has never missed.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he short of breath?
Caller -> No. Not walking. And not at night. I asked him. He sleeps on two pillows like always. He's not waking up gasping. He's fine lying flat.
Nurse -> Good. What has he eaten? Anything salty?
Caller -> I keep telling him no salt. And then he shakes it over his eggs. I take away the shaker. He finds another.
Caller -> We had a ham at the church supper on Sunday. And then leftovers. And he had canned soup yesterday. Chicken noodle. I know. I should know better.
Nurse -> That can do it. Don't be hard on yourself. Lavinia, I'll message the team and the clinician to review his water pill.
Caller -> I'm a worrier. My mother was a worrier. We're a long line of women who count other people's pills.
Caller -> Thank you. Should I give him an extra one?
Caller -> My neighbor said her husband takes two when he swells. She said the doctor told her.
Nurse -> Every person is different. Please wait for the clinician.
Nurse -> Please don't change it. Let the clinician decide.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. I'll wait.
Nurse -> I'd also like to send a nurse out tomorrow to check him over.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's good. In the morning?
Caller -> He has a haircut at eleven. I told him to cancel it. He says nobody cancels a haircut. It's the barber's birthday.
Nurse -> I'll ask for morning.
Caller -> Perfect. He's more alert in the morning.
Nurse -> Keep weighing him every morning, after he uses the bathroom and before breakfast. Write down the weight and the blood pressure.
Caller -> Every morning. After the bathroom. Before breakfast. Write both. I do. I have the chart on the fridge.
Caller -> He stands on the scale in his socks. I told him to take them off. He says socks don't weigh anything.
Nurse -> Ha. A small difference. Same socks or no socks, as long as it's the same each day.
Nurse -> And keep the salt low. No canned soups or deli meats. And put his feet up when he's sitting.
Caller -> No canned soup. I'll make my own. Feet up on the ottoman.
Caller -> I make a good chicken soup. No salt. I use lemon and garlic and pepper. It tastes fine. He says it tastes like water with ideas.
Nurse -> Call us if he has trouble breathing, if he needs more pillows to sleep, if he has chest pain, if his weight goes up five pounds, or if the swelling gets much worse.
Caller -> Trouble breathing. More pillows. Chest pain. Five pounds. More swelling. I wrote it down.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Sorry about the bad line. I'm in the basement. The washer is going. I'm folding towels.
Nurse -> Ha. You're multitasking.
Caller -> The basement is the only place I get quiet. The cat keeps coming down to supervise.
Caller -> Always. Percival says I never sit still. He says I'll fold the whole house one day.
Nurse -> Ha. A useful hobby.
Caller -> It beats worrying. When I fold, I can't think about anything else.
Caller -> And it's warm down here, by the dryer. My feet are cold in the winter.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
