transcript:
Nurse -> Marlowe Home Health, this is Fatima.
Caller -> Fatima, hi. It's Danielle Fontaine. I'm calling about my mother, Marguerite Fontaine. I think I made a mistake with her pills this morning. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> Hi, Danielle. I'm glad you called. Tell me, is she safe right now?
Caller -> She's fine. She's right here at the table. She doesn't look sick at all. I'm just panicking.
Nurse -> Okay, Danielle. Take a breath. Tell me what you think happened.
Caller -> I've been up since five. I made her breakfast, I did the laundry, I packed her lunch. It was a normal morning and then this.
Caller -> I set out her morning pills. She takes two things in the morning that sound almost the same. Celebrex and Celexa. I think I might have given her the Celexa twice and not given the Celebrex.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's go through it slowly. First, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> I wrote down the name of every pill last week on a chart. But I didn't look at the chart this morning. I just went on autopilot.
Caller -> July twenty eighth. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> And your cell is the one ending in oh one two nine?
Caller -> Yes. Eight oh eight, five five five, zero one two nine.
Nurse -> Thank you. Now, what exactly did you do this morning?
Caller -> I'm so sorry for the long explanation. I tend to over explain when I'm anxious.
Nurse -> No, I need details. They help.
Caller -> I was in a rush. I had the two bottles, one in each hand. They're both in white bottles with the same blue cap. And I put the pills in her little cup. One from each bottle. At least I thought one from each.
Nurse -> So you thought one from each, but you're not certain.
Caller -> Right. I can't say I didn't give the Celexa twice. I mean, I don't think I didn't. I wouldn't swear I gave one of each. And the Celebrex slot in her organizer, I checked, and it's empty. But the Celexa slot is also empty. So I can't tell.
Caller -> It's one of those things where the more I think about it, the less I remember. Like when you can't remember if you locked the door.
Nurse -> I know that feeling. It's very human.
Nurse -> Okay. So both of her slots are empty, but you only handed her two pills.
Caller -> Yes. Two pills. And the cup is in the sink. Gone. I don't know which two.
Caller -> I washed the cup. I washed it before I even thought. I'm so stupid. I should have looked in it first.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. You couldn't have known.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's read the labels. What does the Celexa bottle say?
Caller -> It says Celexa. C E L E X A. Twenty milligrams. One tablet every morning. For depression.
Nurse -> And the Celebrex?
Caller -> Celebrex. C E L E B R E X. Two hundred milligrams. One capsule every morning. For arthritis. It's a capsule, not a tablet.
Nurse -> A capsule. Is the Celexa a tablet?
Caller -> A tablet. A small white one. A round one.
Caller -> The capsule is bigger. White and blue, I think. Or white and green. I don't remember. They sort of blur together in my mind.
Nurse -> Did you give her a capsule or only tablets?
Caller -> I'm trying to remember. She swallowed them fast. With applesauce. I didn't look. I really can't say. I wish I could.
Caller -> She likes to take everything at once. She takes a big gulp and it's gone. She's a champ at taking pills.
Nurse -> That's okay. Honesty is the most helpful thing. How is she feeling right now?
Caller -> I would give anything to go back and do it slowly. I always tell myself to slow down. And I never do.
Caller -> She's fine. She says she feels fine. She's sitting at the table. She's doing her sudoku. She says her hands feel a bit jittery. But she's had coffee. Two cups.
Caller -> She even asked me if I wanted a cup of tea. She's serving me. She thinks I'm the one who needs help.
Nurse -> Ha. She's looking after you. That's a good sign for her.
Nurse -> Okay. A little jittery, from coffee or from the medicine.
Caller -> I don't know which. She says it's the coffee.
Caller -> She's right, probably. She has two cups every morning at the same time. She had them today. It could just be the coffee.
Nurse -> Does she have a fast heartbeat? Can you check her pulse for a full minute?
Caller -> I'll do it. I'm walking to the kitchen. Mom, give me your wrist. She says leave me alone. Okay. I'm counting. One, two. This is hard to do on the phone.
Nurse -> Take your time. I'll wait.
Caller -> Seventy something. I got seventy two. Regular. Not fast.
Caller -> I feel silly counting out loud. She's laughing at me. She says I look like I'm timing a marathon.
Nurse -> Good. Is she confused, dizzy, or having any trouble walking?
Caller -> No. No confusion. She's sharp. She knows the date. She knows I'm late for work. She's not dizzy. She walked to the bathroom on her own. She didn't faint, or nothing like that.
Nurse -> Okay. That's reassuring. Does she have any stomach upset, or sweating, or a fever?
Caller -> No. Nothing like that. She had her toast. She's not sweaty. I haven't taken her temperature but she feels normal.
Nurse -> Thank you. Danielle, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician now, because Celexa is a medicine where a double dose matters.
Caller -> Are you going to send an ambulance? Should I be scared?
Nurse -> No ambulance right now. She's stable, and you're being careful. This is the safest next step.
Caller -> Is it dangerous? Did I hurt her?
Nurse -> I don't think she's in danger right now. She has no fast heartbeat, no confusion, no fainting. But we need the clinician to tell us what to watch for, and whether to hold her other medicines.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm so sorry. I feel sick.
Caller -> I'm shaking. I'm sitting down. I'm putting my head between my knees.
Nurse -> That's fine. Take a minute. I'll wait.
Nurse -> Don't be hard on yourself. This is one of the most common mix ups. The names are too close. Is she taking anything else?
Caller -> Yes. The tramadol. Fifty milligrams. Every six hours if she needs it for the pain. She took one at midnight. She hasn't asked for another.
Caller -> She hasn't asked for it today. She says her knees feel okay. She said the weather is warm.
Nurse -> Okay. Please don't give her any tramadol until the clinician calls. That medicine can interact with Celexa. And give nothing more of either of the other two today.
Caller -> No tramadol. No Celexa. No Celebrex. Okay. Not until the clinician calls. Got it.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to come this afternoon to see her, count the pills in both bottles and the organizer, and figure out exactly what she took.
Caller -> Counting the pills. Oh. That's smart. That will tell us. I'll leave the bottles on the table. Both of them.
Caller -> I can also take pictures of everything on the table, if that helps. The bottles, the labels, the organizer. I have a good camera on this phone.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. Take the pictures and keep them.
Nurse -> Good. Don't touch them. And don't refill the organizer until the nurse sees it.
Caller -> I won't. Is there a time?
Nurse -> After lunch, probably between one and three. She'll call when she's close.
Caller -> I'm leaving work early. I'll be home by one. I'll be here.
Caller -> My boss said go. He said family comes first. He's lovely about this stuff.
Nurse -> Perfect. In the meantime, if your mother has a racing heartbeat, shaking, fever, confusion, a lot of stomach upset, or if she faints, call me right away.
Caller -> Racing heart. Shaking. Fever. Confusion. Stomach upset. Faints. I'll watch all of it. I'm putting it on a sticky note.
Caller -> I have a small notebook. It's the one I keep in my purse. I'll put the symptoms on the first page.
Nurse -> And Danielle, call 911 if she faints or has a seizure. Don't wait for me.
Caller -> Faints. Seizure. 911. Okay. Gosh. This is scary.
Caller -> I have my phone. It's charged. The ringer is on loud. I'll keep it in my pocket.
Nurse -> I know. But right now she is fine, and you're acting quickly. That's what matters.
Caller -> She's looking at me funny. She says what are you so worried about. I said, I might have given you too much of your pill. She said, I don't remember taking too much.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her it's under control.
Caller -> She's a rock. She was raising four kids on her own when she was my age. She doesn't flinch.
Caller -> Mom, the nurse says it's under control. She says good. She says now let me finish my sudoku.
Caller -> She just offered me a cookie. She says I need sugar. She's right, I haven't eaten.
Nurse -> Ha. She sounds calm. That helps.
Caller -> She told the neighbor yesterday she's going to live to a hundred and ten, just to annoy her.
Caller -> She's always calm. She was a school bus driver for thirty years. Nothing rattles her.
Nurse -> Then she'll be fine today. Danielle, I'll also message our team and the pharmacy about the look-alike bottles. Separate bags, bigger labels, maybe a pill pack with the times on it.
Caller -> Please. That would be amazing. I should have asked for that long ago.
Caller -> I told the pharmacist last month the bottles look alike and she said, I know, everyone says that. Nothing changed.
Nurse -> We'll push harder on this one.
Nurse -> It's not your fault. The system should help you more. Until then, keep the two bottles in different places, read the name on the label out loud before each dose, and fill the organizer one medicine at a time.
Caller -> Different places. Read it out loud. One at a time. I'll do all of that.
Caller -> I'll put the one in the kitchen cupboard and the other on her bedside table. That should keep them apart.
Caller -> I'm also going to write Celexa on a bright yellow sticker and put it on one bottle. And Celebrex on a pink one.
Nurse -> That's an excellent idea.
Caller -> I have a whole pack of stickers from my daughter's classroom. She's a teacher's pet. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Use them.
Caller -> My daughter will be thrilled. She loves it when her stickers get used for real life.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you, Fatima. I feel a bit better. I was panicking.
Caller -> Before I go, if the nurse finds that it was only one of each, will you still need the clinician?
Nurse -> We'll let the clinician decide. Either way, you did the right thing.
Nurse -> You did the right thing to call. I'll be in touch as soon as I hear from the clinician.
Caller -> I'll keep the phone on me. Bye.
Caller -> One more thing, sorry. If the clinician wants to speak to me directly, should I call the agency line or will they call my cell?
Nurse -> They'll use the number you gave me, so keep your cell with you.
Nurse -> Bye.

Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hi. I'm sorry to call. I hope this is the right line for this. I wasn't sure who to ask.
Nurse -> You've reached the right place. Go ahead.
Caller -> Ruth, hi. This is Rhonda Eastman. R H O N D A. I'm a staff member at Maple Court Residence. One of our residents got the wrong pill this morning. His name is Thurgood Beauchamp.
Nurse -> Okay, Rhonda. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> It was a busy morning. We had four residents needing meds at once and one of the aides called out sick.
Caller -> I gave him Zyprexa instead of Zyrtec. Ten milligrams of Zyprexa. The Zyrtec is for his allergies, ten milligrams. I picked up the wrong bottle. They were next to each other.
Nurse -> Okay. When did you give it?
Caller -> About an hour ago. Eight thirty. I realized when I put the bottles back and saw the label.
Caller -> I noticed because the pharmacy label has a different color border. Green for the allergy one and blue for the other. I just looked at the wrong color.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he awake?
Caller -> He's awake. He's a little sleepy. He's in the day room, in the armchair. I asked him how he feels and he said tired. He answered me. He walked from the table to the chair without trouble.
Caller -> He told me he'd like to nap. He never says that in the morning. He's usually up and in the kitchen helping with the dishes.
Nurse -> Is he breathing normally? Any trouble waking him?
Caller -> He's breathing normally. He wakes up when I say his name. He's not unconscious. I checked. He hasn't fainted, nothing like that.
Caller -> His color looks good. His lips are pink. I looked at his chest while I talked to him.
Nurse -> Good. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> I have his chart open. It's right here in front of me. I'm looking at his picture on the cover. He's smiling.
Caller -> March twenty sixth. Nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, zero one three oh.
Nurse -> Thanks. Does he take Zyprexa regularly?
Caller -> The doctor prescribed it a few years ago. It helps him sleep and keeps his mood steady. He's done really well on it.
Caller -> Yes. At bedtime. Ten milligrams. Every night. So he took his morning dose of a medicine he usually takes at night. He's used to it. But in the morning it hits him differently.
Nurse -> Okay. He's also on the Zyrtec as needed for allergies?
Caller -> As needed. Once a day. Ten milligrams. His allergies are bad this week. That's why I was giving it to him.
Caller -> It's been a rough pollen season. He sneezes a lot. His eyes water. He walks around with a tissue box.
Nurse -> Rhonda, I'll page the on-call clinician right now and let them know what happened.
Caller -> Thank you. Should I call his family? His sister is his contact.
Caller -> His sister is very involved. She calls every Sunday. I don't want her to hear it from someone else first.
Nurse -> Follow your facility's policy. I'd tell her after the clinician weighs in.
Caller -> Okay. I've already told my supervisor. She's coming in.
Caller -> She was calm about it. She said we'd file an incident report and review our process. I think we need a second check on the cart.
Nurse -> Good. I'd also like a nurse to see him this afternoon.
Caller -> This afternoon. Perfect. I'll be here until four.
Caller -> The front door sticks, so the nurse should push it hard. And there's a ramp around the side.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep him seated or lying down, with someone nearby. Offer him fluids. And check him every fifteen minutes, to be sure he wakes easily and is breathing normally.
Caller -> Every fifteen minutes. Wake easily. Breathing normal. I'll set a timer and I'll check.
Caller -> I've never had to do this before. Do I write down what I see?
Nurse -> Yes. Note the time and how he looks each time you check.
Nurse -> And don't give tonight's Zyprexa until the clinician decides. Also, put the two bottles in separate places, and have a second staff person double check every cup.
Caller -> Not tonight until you call. Separate bottles. Second person. Yes. We've already moved them. The Zyrtec is on the top shelf now and the Zyprexa is in the locked cabinet.
Caller -> We do have a second pair of eyes at night, but I think we should have it in the morning too.
Nurse -> Great. That will help.
Caller -> I'll make a big sign and tape it to the cabinet. Check the name, check the name, check the name.
Caller -> I feel terrible. I've been doing this job for six years. I've never made a mistake.
Caller -> I tell all the new staff to check the label three times. And then I go and do this.
Nurse -> It happens to everyone. The names are very close. You called right away. That's what matters.
Caller -> That makes me feel a little better. It doesn't make it right, but it helps.
Caller -> Thank you. I just want him to be okay.
Caller -> He's a favorite of everybody in the house. He brings the mail to the staff every day like a little postman.
Nurse -> He seems stable. We'll keep a close eye. Is there anything else going on with him?
Caller -> No. He's usually cheerful. He loves to watch the cooking channel. He's going to love this, I'll tell him he gets to nap in the chair.
Nurse -> Ha. A free nap.
Caller -> I'll lower the blinds in the day room and dim the lights. It's quiet in there at this time of day.
Caller -> He'll wake up and ask what's for lunch.
Nurse -> Ha. Probably. Keep him hydrated, and make sure lunch is light.
Caller -> He always says the cooking show chefs are cheating, that nobody can chop that fast. He's a hard judge.
Caller -> Light lunch. Soup and crackers. Okay.
Caller -> He likes the tomato soup from the can. With the little oyster crackers on top. I'll warm it slowly.
Nurse -> Thank you for calling it in right away.
Caller -> Thank you, Ruth. I appreciate it.
Nurse -> Anytime, Rhonda. Bye.
Caller -> Take care, Ruth. I'll call if anything changes before the nurse gets here.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cottonwood Home Health, this is Ruth.
Caller -> Hello, hello. Can you hear me? I'm in the greenhouse and there's a funny echo.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Ruth. It's Annelise Hartwell. A N N E L I S E. I'm calling about my husband, Siegfried. S I E G F R I E D. Hartwell. H A R T W E L L. His leg.
Nurse -> Hi, Annelise. How's Sigfrid doing?
Caller -> He's right inside, in the kitchen window. I can see him from here. He's waving. Hi, honey.
Caller -> He's doing well. The wound is better. I wanted to give you an update.
Nurse -> Great. Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Nurse -> Take your time with the date. No pressure.
Caller -> October ninth. Nineteen forty eight. No. Forty seven. Nineteen forty seven. He's seventy nine. I always add a year.
Nurse -> Forty seven. Thanks. And the best number to reach you?
Caller -> It's the same one as always. You have it. I won't read it out, it's a long number on my phone and I'm in the garden. Please use the one you have.
Nurse -> No problem. I'll use the number on file.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> So how does the wound look?
Caller -> Smaller. It was the size of a half dollar. Now it's the size of a dime. Pink. Dry around the edges. No more drainage on the gauze.
Caller -> I measure it with a quarter. It's smaller than the quarter now, and it was bigger than the quarter last week.
Nurse -> That's real progress. How often are you changing the dressing?
Caller -> Every other day. Monday, Wednesday, Friday. Today is Friday, so I did it this morning.
Caller -> I keep the supplies in a basket by the bed. Gauze, tape, saline, gloves. It's a whole production.
Nurse -> Any pus, or bad smell?
Caller -> No pus. No smell. And no fever. I took his temperature at noon. And he says it hurts less. Not more. He says he can barely feel it now.
Caller -> I'm very careful about smells. My nose is excellent. I'd know.
Nurse -> That's what I like to hear. Any redness spreading up his leg?
Caller -> No. The skin around it is a normal color. A little pink right at the edge. That's it.
Caller -> I look at it with the big lamp, the one with the magnifier, so I can see every detail.
Nurse -> Good. How are you doing the dressing? Walk me through it.
Caller -> I'm very particular. I like it neat. He teases me. He says it looks like a gift.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a lovely compliment, really.
Caller -> I wash my hands. I peel off the old one slowly. I rinse the wound with the saline from the bottle. I pat it dry around the edges. Then I put on the new one. Flat, no wrinkles. And I tape it.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's exactly right. Remind him to keep his leg up when he's sitting.
Caller -> The nurse who taught me, Margit, made me practice on an orange. I peeled the whole thing.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good way to practice.
Caller -> On the ottoman. He's there now. With the crossword. He doesn't like it, but he does it.
Nurse -> Ha. A good patient.
Caller -> He grumbles but he does it. I bribe him with chocolate.
Caller -> He says the ottoman is for people with bad knees. I said, you have bad knees.
Nurse -> Ha. He does.
Caller -> He has a cane too, but he leaves it at the front door. He claims it's decorative.
Nurse -> I'll come by on Wednesday for the regular visit and to see the wound myself.
Caller -> Wednesday. Good. What time?
Caller -> I have the schedule on the fridge. In red. Wednesday is a red day.
Nurse -> Mid morning.
Caller -> I'll make cinnamon rolls. They'll be coming out of the oven right when you arrive.
Caller -> I'll be home. I'm going to the garden club in the afternoon.
Nurse -> And call us if you see redness spreading, yellow or green drainage, a bad smell, a fever, or if the pain gets worse.
Caller -> Redness. Yellow or green. Smell. Fever. More pain. I'll tell him.
Caller -> I tell him about the signs each time, but he says he'll know. I say, you can't see the back of your own leg.
Caller -> I'll put it on the fridge with the other lists. The fridge is a bulletin board at this point.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm in the greenhouse right now, by the way. We have a little heated one. The tomatoes are still going.
Nurse -> A heated greenhouse. That sounds lovely.
Caller -> It's my favorite place. I read in there. I hum to the plants.
Nurse -> Ha. Do they respond?
Caller -> The tomatoes do. They grow better when I sing.
Nurse -> A heated greenhouse. Lucky you.
Caller -> My husband built it. Before the leg. He was proud of it.
Nurse -> It sounds wonderful.
Caller -> He designed the whole thing on graph paper. He was an engineer. Every pane is measured to the millimeter.
Nurse -> That's impressive.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Ruth.
Caller -> The nurse before you said I'm one of the best caregivers she's seen. I almost cried.
Nurse -> She was right.
Nurse -> Bye, Annelise.
Caller -> Oh, and thank you for always being so gentle with him. He talks about you.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pebble Creek Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Odile.
Caller -> Hi, Odile. This is Briony Calloway. I'm calling about my daughter, Wren. W R E N. Calloway. I have the weekly update.
Nurse -> Hi, Briony. I was hoping you'd call. How's our little Wren?
Caller -> I almost didn't. I thought, what if I'm bothering you with small stuff. But my husband said, call. He's the sensible one.
Nurse -> Never small stuff. Small stuff is exactly what keeps babies healthy.
Caller -> She's doing great. I think. I have a few questions too, but let me start with the numbers.
Caller -> I second guess everything. Is she eating enough? Is she sleeping too much? Is she too warm? I Google at three in the morning.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll try to cut down the late-night Googling.
Nurse -> Sure. First, her date of birth, so I have the chart.
Caller -> I have a list on my phone of all the things I want to say. I forget everything the moment someone picks up.
Caller -> October second. Two thousand twenty six. She's two months. Eight weeks and two days. She was born five weeks early.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your cell?
Caller -> I hope I'm not calling at a bad time. I know it's the weekend.
Caller -> Same as always. It's my husband's too. We share a plan. His is one digit different.
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, zero one five four.
Nurse -> Perfect. What's her weight?
Caller -> Our scale isn't the exact medical kind. It's the one from the registry. But the numbers have been steady.
Caller -> We weighed her on the kitchen scale this morning, the baby one. Nine pounds, four ounces. Last week it was eight pounds, ten ounces. So that's six ounces.
Nurse -> That's a lovely gain. Six ounces in a week. How is her feeding?
Caller -> The lactation consultant said four to seven ounces is great. So six is in the middle. I felt like I got an A.
Nurse -> Ha. A solid A.
Caller -> Good. She's taking three ounces every three hours. Sometimes a little more at night. She wakes up on her own. She doesn't need me to wake her.
Nurse -> Is she breastfeeding or taking formula?
Caller -> Both. Bottle in the daytime with the pumped milk and a little formula for the night feeds. She doesn't mind either.
Caller -> I pump at five, noon and nine. It's a lot of work. But I like seeing the milk in the bottles. It feels like I'm doing something.
Nurse -> And how is she finishing the bottles?
Caller -> She finishes them. She gets this milk drunk look. And she burps pretty easily. Three or four burps per feed.
Caller -> Her eyes roll back and her mouth falls open. My husband takes a picture every time. We have hundreds.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Any spit-up?
Caller -> A little. A teaspoon, maybe, after most feeds. It doesn't shoot out. It just kind of dribbles. It's on the burp cloth. She's not bothered by it. She doesn't cry.
Caller -> Sometimes more on the sleeper. I just wash it. We do a lot of laundry. I have a tiny load every night.
Nurse -> That sounds like normal reflux. Is she happy afterward?
Caller -> Very. She coos. She smiles at me. Her first real smile was on Tuesday. I cried.
Caller -> She smiled at the ceiling fan too. I think the fan is jealous.
Nurse -> I'm so glad. What about her sleep?
Caller -> Three hours at a stretch. Once, last night, four. I stared at the clock and didn't sleep for fear. But then I did.
Caller -> The monitor lights up when she makes a noise. It's a baby sleep monitor, the camera kind. I watch her on the little screen at night.
Nurse -> That's normal for this age. Briony, how are you sleeping?
Caller -> Better than you'd think. My husband does the midnight feed. He loves it. He sings to her. Terrible singing.
Caller -> I nap when she naps. I don't clean. I don't cook. Take-out is a food group.
Nurse -> Ha. Bonding time.
Caller -> He does a rock star voice. He changed the words to a song. It's about diapers.
Caller -> She loves it. She goes right to sleep. She hates my singing. I'm better, but she prefers him.
Nurse -> Ha. What medicines is she on?
Caller -> Just the vitamin D drops. One milliliter every day. It's four hundred international units per milliliter. I give it with the first bottle in the morning. I gave it today.
Caller -> I set a phone reminder. It says Wren drops with a heart. I don't dare skip them.
Nurse -> Good. Measure with the dropper, right?
Caller -> The little dropper that comes with it. I fill to the line. I squeeze it in the cheek. She makes a face.
Caller -> I keep the bottle in the refrigerator door, no, the cupboard. The label says room temperature. I always get that wrong.
Nurse -> Ha. A little face is normal. Any fever? Any trouble breathing, or noisy breathing?
Caller -> No fever. I take her temperature if she feels warm. It's ninety eight something. And her breathing is quiet. Sometimes she makes little sighs, and she snorts a bit when she's sleeping. It's cute.
Caller -> I know I don't have to take it every day. But it comforts me. I wipe the thermometer with alcohol every time.
Nurse -> Those little sounds are normal. Is her color good? Pink?
Caller -> Pink all over. Her lips are pink. Her hands are pink. She's very pink. She looks like a tiny pink bun.
Caller -> Her fingernails are tiny. Like grains of rice. I trimmed them with the baby clippers and cried when I was done. Not because I hurt her. Just because.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a very normal new mom moment.
Nurse -> Ha. A bun. Briony, what questions do you have?
Caller -> A few. First, burping. How long should I hold her up after a feed?
Nurse -> Go right ahead. I'm listening.
Nurse -> About twenty minutes. Burp her halfway through the bottle and again at the end. Keep her upright, on your shoulder or sitting on your lap, until the twenty minutes is up.
Caller -> Twenty minutes. I do about ten. I'll try for twenty.
Caller -> She likes the shoulder position the best. She puts her face in my neck and snuggles. It's the best part of my day.
Nurse -> And feed her on cue, about every three hours. Don't force it, but don't let her go more than four hours without a feed at this age.
Caller -> Every three hours. Four at most. Okay. I wrote it down.
Caller -> I have a feeding tracker app. It reminds me. It also lets my husband see what I've done so we don't double feed.
Nurse -> Smart. Teamwork.
Caller -> Second question. Safe sleep. My mother in law keeps telling me to put a blanket on her. She says babies get cold.
Caller -> My mother in law brought a quilt. A beautiful hand-sewn one with ducks. I love it. But it can't go in the crib, right?
Nurse -> Always put Wren on her back to sleep, alone, in a bare crib with a firm, flat mattress. No blankets, no bumpers, no stuffed animals. A sleep sack is the safest way to keep her warm.
Caller -> A sleep sack. We have two. The wearable blanket ones. I told my mother in law, and she rolled her eyes.
Caller -> One has little stars and the other has foxes. She looks like a burrito with a head.
Nurse -> Ha. A safe burrito.
Nurse -> It's okay. Tell her it's what the pediatrician and the nurse recommend.
Caller -> I will. She'll complain, but she'll listen. She loves Wren more than anything.
Caller -> She raised four kids on blankets and bumpers. She says nobody died. I said, times have changed.
Nurse -> Ha. Of course. Grandmas love to help.
Caller -> Third question. When should I worry? What's an emergency?
Caller -> I read that preemies can be more fragile. I don't want to be paranoid, but I don't want to miss something.
Nurse -> Call us right away for a temperature of one hundred point four or higher, fewer than four wet diapers in a day, forceful vomiting that shoots out, fast or labored breathing, or if she looks bluish.
Caller -> One hundred point four. Under four wet diapers. Forceful vomiting. Fast or hard breathing. Blue. I'm writing it on the fridge. In red marker.
Caller -> I'll count the diapers each day. We use the ones with the line that changes color. That helps.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call any time, day or night. Don't wait if you're worried about feeding or breathing.
Caller -> Any time. That's reassuring. Sometimes I feel like I'm bothering you.
Caller -> You and the other nurses have been such a lifeline. I told my sister, if I had to do this alone I'd fall apart.
Nurse -> You're not. That's why we're here. Especially with a baby who was born early.
Caller -> Thank you, Odile. I mean it.
Caller -> I'm sorry I'm getting emotional. The hormones are still running things.
Nurse -> It's okay. Let it out. You're allowed.
Nurse -> You're doing a beautiful job. I'd like to come by Thursday for a weight check and to look at her.
Caller -> Thursday. Wonderful. She'll be so happy. She loves your hands.
Caller -> I'll have the changing table ready and the scale clear. She'll be freshly fed. Is it better before or after?
Nurse -> Right after a diaper change and before a feed is best.
Nurse -> Ha. Warm hands.
Caller -> You warm them on your cup of coffee before you touch her. I noticed. She appreciates it. So do I.
Caller -> What time? I'd like her to have just eaten, but not too full.
Nurse -> Mid morning is perfect. And I'll call you Monday, to see how the weekend went.
Caller -> Monday. Great. I'll be home. We don't go out much in December. It's too cold for her.
Caller -> My sister is coming Sunday to help. She'll stay till Tuesday. She's good with babies. She's a kindergarten teacher.
Nurse -> That's okay. Fresh air in a stroller is fine on mild days, with a hat.
Caller -> We took her to the porch yesterday. She loved it. She stared at the bare tree.
Caller -> She wore her little knit hat with the bear ears. It's too big. It covers her eyes. I kept lifting it.
Nurse -> Ha. Birds and branches are fascinating.
Caller -> My husband built a mobile with paper birds. She follows them with her eyes now.
Caller -> He cut them out of old maps. They're all different places. A bird from Ohio, a bird from Spain.
Nurse -> Ha. A geography lesson.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Caller -> It's wonky. One bird is bigger than the rest. But she doesn't mind.
Caller -> She stares at the big one the most. I think she's a leader. She's going to be a bossy little girl.
Nurse -> Ha. It's perfect.
Caller -> He says the little one from Spain is the best flyer. He's very serious about his birds.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let you go. Thank you, Odile.
Caller -> If I think of anything else, can I call back this afternoon? I always remember a question the second I hang up.
Nurse -> Of course. Call any time. We'll answer.
Nurse -> Take care, Briony. Kiss Wren for me.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Bridge Palliative Care, this is Joanne.
Caller -> Hi. It's Odessa Whitcombe. I'm a patient. I'm sorry to call this late. I just. I can't do this anymore. I've been sitting here looking at my pills and I thought about taking all of them.
Nurse -> Odessa, I'm so glad you called. Thank you for telling me. I'm right here with you. Are you safe right now?
Caller -> I almost hung up three times before I dialed. I had the phone in my hand for twenty minutes.
Nurse -> I'm glad you stayed with it. I'm here now.
Caller -> I think so. I'm at the kitchen table. I haven't taken anything. I haven't. They're all here in front of me. The bottles. I just looked at them for a long time.
Caller -> It's dark in here except for the light over the stove. It's so quiet I can hear the refrigerator humming.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm really glad you haven't. Can I ask, have you taken any of them tonight, any more than you're supposed to?
Nurse -> Take a slow breath with me. In through the nose. Out slowly.
Caller -> Okay. In. Out. I'm doing it.
Caller -> No. None. Only my regular bedtime ones, at nine. That was seven hours ago. Nothing since. I couldn't sleep, so I came downstairs.
Caller -> I counted them. I even counted the ones in the organizer. Everything is where it should be.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. And is anyone else in the house with you?
Caller -> My husband. He's asleep upstairs. He doesn't know I'm down here. I didn't want to wake him. He's so tired. He's been taking care of me for months.
Caller -> Leo works in construction. He gets up at five. I hate that he has to carry all of this and work too.
Nurse -> Odessa, I want to ask you something directly, because I care about you. Are you thinking about ending your life tonight?
Caller -> I don't know. I don't think so. Not tonight. I mean I thought about it. I thought, maybe I'd just be done. No more pain. No more being a burden. But I called you instead. I don't think I want to do it. I just didn't want to be alone with the thought.
Caller -> I know it sounds strange. I want to be here, and I want the pain to stop, and I don't know how both can be true.
Nurse -> It isn't strange. A lot of people feel exactly that way.
Nurse -> That makes sense. And I'm glad you didn't stay alone with it. That took courage. Do you have a plan? Is the plan the pills?
Caller -> It's the pills. It's the first thing I thought of. They're right here. But I haven't. I won't. I think I won't. I just needed to say it out loud to someone.
Caller -> I think about it in a quiet way. It's not like a movie. It's just a little voice that says, you could stop. And I tell it to be quiet.
Nurse -> Thank you for saying it out loud. I want to help you stay safe. Can you do something for me right now? Can you push the pill bottles away from you, to the other end of the table, or even put them in a drawer?
Caller -> Nobody else knows. Not even my sister. I didn't want to worry her.
Caller -> Okay. I'm moving them. I'm putting them in the cabinet over the fridge. It's high. I can't reach it without the step stool. There. They're gone.
Nurse -> Thank you. That is a very good step. How do you feel now?
Caller -> Shaky. Tired. Crying a little. I feel like I've been holding my breath for weeks.
Caller -> My hands are so cold. I'm wrapping them in the sleeves of my robe.
Nurse -> It's okay to cry. You're not a burden to us, and I doubt you're a burden to your husband. Can you tell me what's been making things so hard?
Nurse -> It sounds like you have been holding a lot by yourself. I'm glad you let some of it out.
Caller -> The pain. It's been worse this week. It wakes me up at three. Every night. And I can't sleep after. And I keep thinking about the scan results. And Leo. And how he'll manage. And I feel like everything is a countdown.
Caller -> The new medicine was supposed to help. I thought it would be better by now. I feel like everything is failing, my body, the treatment, all of it.
Nurse -> That's a heavy load to carry at four in the morning. Thank you for sharing it. Odessa, would you be willing to wake your husband, so you're not alone?
Caller -> I see the clock turn to three, and it's like a bell rings in my head. Every night. I lie there with my eyes open.
Caller -> I think so. I don't want to scare him.
Nurse -> He would want to know. He would want to be with you. And I can stay on the phone while you do it. Will you wake him?
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'll go. Don't hang up. Leo? Leo, I need you. Come down. Please. I'm going to call him. Hold on.
Caller -> My legs feel like jelly. I'm holding the counter to stand up. I'm going to the stairs.
Caller -> He's coming. I hear him on the stairs. He's in his robe. He looks scared.
Caller -> His hair is sticking up. He's squinting at me in the light. He looks so young without his glasses.
Nurse -> Odessa, tell him. Tell him you called the nurse, because you were having dark thoughts.
Caller -> Leo, I called the nurse. I was having dark thoughts. I was thinking about the pills. I'm okay. I'm okay. He's hugging me. He's crying.
Caller -> He didn't say anything at first. He just opened his arms. I'm still in them. I can hear his heart beating.
Nurse -> That's a good moment. Can you put him on the phone for a moment?
Caller -> He's here. He says hello.
Caller -> He's holding the phone like it might break. He's saying hello, hello. Hello, Joanne.
Nurse -> Hello, Leo. This is Joanne, the palliative nurse. Odessa did exactly the right thing by calling. I'd like you to stay with her tonight. I'm going to send a nurse in the morning, and I'm paging our on-call clinician now.
Caller -> Okay. I'm here. I'm not going anywhere. She said she had the pills out. They're in the cabinet over the fridge. I'll put the whole box in the car.
Caller -> She's been so strong for so long, I forget she's allowed to fall apart sometimes. I should have seen it.
Nurse -> It's not your fault, Leo. You didn't miss anything. She chose to reach out, and that's what matters.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Lock them up, or put them somewhere out of her reach, just for now.
Caller -> I will. Thank you. Thank you for talking to her.
Nurse -> Odessa, I'm back with you. Is that okay?
Caller -> I'm here. He's sitting next to me. I have my hand in his.
Caller -> It's strange. I feel lighter. Like I put down a very heavy bag and I can finally stretch my arms.
Nurse -> Good. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm paging the on-call clinician right now, to review her pain and her sleep.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> I'm also going to ask our social worker to call you and Leo. She can talk with you about how you're feeling, and about support for both of you.
Caller -> I'd like that. I think I need that. I've been pretending I'm fine.
Caller -> I've never talked to a counselor. I always thought it wasn't for me. I think I'd like to try.
Nurse -> There's no wrong time to start.
Nurse -> You don't have to pretend with us. And I'd like to send a nurse to see you tomorrow morning.
Caller -> Tomorrow morning. Okay. I'll be here.
Caller -> Leo is calling his boss to say he won't be in. He's sending a text. He says he's staying home with me.
Nurse -> That's good. Having him there will help.
Nurse -> Odessa, what's your date of birth? Let me make sure I have your chart.
Caller -> June eighth. Nineteen seventy four.
Nurse -> And you're using the cell ending in oh one two three?
Caller -> Yes. Six one five, five five five, zero one two three.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll call you back in thirty minutes to see how you're doing, and to tell you what the clinician says.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. We'll be right here.
Nurse -> There's also a crisis line you can call or text any time, day or night. It's nine eight eight. If the thoughts get stronger, call or text it, or call us, or call nine one one.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. I've heard of that. I'll put it in my phone. Leo, can you do that? He's putting it in. Nine eight eight.
Caller -> It has a little heart on the sticker in the pharmacy window. I saw it once and thought, that's for other people.
Nurse -> It's for anyone, anytime. Including you.
Nurse -> Thank you. And I'm here too. You called, you talked, you moved the pills, and you woke your husband. You did everything right.
Caller -> I don't feel like I did. I feel like I failed.
Caller -> I told myself I'd be strong. I told Leo I'd never be a burden. And here I am, waking him up at four in the morning.
Nurse -> Reaching out is the opposite of failing. It's the strongest thing you could have done.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I believe you. A little.
Caller -> It helps to hear it from someone who isn't related to me. People who love you say things because they have to.
Nurse -> I'm not saying it because I have to. I'm saying it because it's true.
Nurse -> That's enough for now. Is there something that would help you feel calmer while we wait? Tea? A blanket?
Caller -> Leo is making tea. Chamomile. I can hear the kettle.
Caller -> The kettle just whistled. It always sounds so cheerful. It's strange to hear something cheerful right now.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Stay with him. Stay in the kitchen where you can both be together.
Caller -> We will. He's getting the blanket from the couch. The green one. My mother made it.
Caller -> It has little squares in orange and green. She made it from old curtains, I think. It's heavy and scratchy and perfect.
Nurse -> That sounds comforting.
Caller -> It is. It smells like her house. Even though she's been gone for ten years.
Nurse -> What was her name?
Caller -> Clarice. She used to hum when she cooked. I hum when I cook.
Nurse -> It sounds like she's still with you in a lot of ways.
Caller -> She is. I think she'd be disappointed that I was down here with the pills.
Caller -> She was a nurse's aide for thirty years. She cared for strangers in the night. She'd probably say, call somebody, Odessa. So I did.
Nurse -> I think she'd be relieved that you called. And proud of you for waking your husband.
Caller -> Maybe. Maybe so.
Nurse -> Odessa, I'm going to let you go for thirty minutes, but I want you to promise me one thing. If the thoughts come back, stronger, before I call, you tell Leo and you call me or nine eight eight right away.
Caller -> I promise. I promise. I'll tell him.
Caller -> He's holding my hand so tightly I can feel my pulse in my fingers. It feels good. It feels real.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll talk to you soon.
Caller -> Thank you, Joanne. Thank you for picking up.
Caller -> I wasn't sure anyone would answer at this hour. I thought it might ring and ring.
Nurse -> Always. Talk soon. Bye.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Orchard Lane Home Health, this is Samir.
Caller -> Hi, Samir. It's Imelda Rossiter. R O S S I T E R. I'm a patient. The pharmacy gave me the wrong pill and I've been without my seizure medicine for two days.
Nurse -> Thanks for calling, Imelda. Let's sort it out. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm shaking a little. I've been waiting on hold for the pharmacy for almost an hour and I'm about to lose it.
Nurse -> No need to apologize. You're in the right place.
Caller -> February fourteenth. Nineteen ninety.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, zero one six nine.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Got it. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> I'll try to be clear. I'm usually good at this. I work in insurance claims. I read fine print all day.
Caller -> I take lamotrigine. L A M O T R I G I N E. A hundred milligrams, twice a day. My refill was due Monday. I ran out Sunday night. I took my last one Sunday evening. Two days ago.
Nurse -> And the refill didn't come?
Caller -> It did, in a way. I picked it up this morning. I got home and the bottle says Lamisil. L A M I S I L. Two hundred fifty milligrams. That's a nail fungus pill. That's not mine.
Caller -> I stood in the parking lot reading the bag. The tech was gone by then. I went back in and the pharmacist was on break. I waited fifteen minutes, and no one came.
Nurse -> Okay. You didn't take any, did you?
Caller -> No. I didn't. I read the label first. I always read the label. But I couldn't swear I didn't almost. I mean, I had the cap open. Then I saw the name. I put it back.
Caller -> I'm kind of shaken by how close it was. It's the same color pill. I'd have taken it with my coffee and never known.
Nurse -> Good. That's very good. Have you had any seizures, or any warning signs?
Caller -> No. No seizure. No aura. I didn't have the funny smell or the deja vu feeling. I'm not lightheaded. I'm not saying I don't feel anxious. I do. But no, nothing physical.
Nurse -> That's reassuring. Imelda, it's important not to go without your seizure medicine. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now to get an urgent supply.
Caller -> I know. I know it is. I told the girl at the counter. She just said, sorry, we'll fix it tomorrow.
Caller -> Thank you. I've been terrified. The last time I missed two days, I had a seizure on the bus.
Caller -> It was on the number nine bus. A stranger held my head. I woke up in the ambulance with the paramedic asking me what day it was.
Nurse -> That sounds frightening. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll move fast. I'll also contact the pharmacy to correct the fill and send the right medicine today.
Caller -> I called them. They said it would be tomorrow. They said the system flagged it.
Caller -> Tomorrow is too far. I'm only just keeping myself calm. The thought of another night without it makes me want to cry.
Nurse -> I'll push for today. In the meantime, please don't take the Lamisil. Set the bottle aside for the pharmacy. And don't restart the lamotrigine on your own until the clinician tells you how.
Caller -> Okay. I won't touch it. It's in a plastic bag on the counter. I wrote DO NOT TAKE on a sticky note.
Caller -> I put it next to the sink where I can see it. I didn't want to throw it away in case you need it as proof.
Nurse -> Good thinking. Keep it for the pharmacy.
Nurse -> Perfect. And I'd like a nurse to come see you tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. That's good. I work from home on Wednesdays. I'll be here.
Caller -> My boss is very understanding. I'm going to let her know I might need to be offline for a bit tomorrow.
Nurse -> Until the medicine is back, please be careful. Don't drive, don't take a bath alone, don't climb on a ladder. Keep someone with you if you can. If you have a seizure that lasts over five minutes, call 911.
Caller -> No driving. No bath. No ladders. Someone nearby. Five minutes, 911. Okay. My roommate is here. She works nights, so she's home during the day. I'll tell her.
Caller -> My roommate Priya is a nurse. She'll keep an eye on me. She's already looked at my pupils twice.
Nurse -> Good. How are you feeling about all this?
Caller -> I told my mother and she wanted to drive over. I said stay home, I'm fine. She said she's coming anyway. She's an hour away.
Caller -> Scared and angry. I don't want to be a person who has a seizure at work. It feels so unfair. I did everything right.
Nurse -> Tell me more about the fear.
Caller -> I've been seizure free for fourteen months. Fourteen months. I keep a tally on my calendar. I don't want to start over at zero.
Nurse -> You did. You read the label, you caught the error, you called. That's exactly right.
Caller -> I know. But it's scary anyway.
Nurse -> It is. We'll get you the right medicine as quickly as we can.
Caller -> I'm trying to think positive. Fourteen months is something. I'm going to keep saying that.
Nurse -> It is something big. Remember that.
Caller -> Thank you. Is there anything else I should do?
Nurse -> Drink water, eat regular meals, and try to sleep tonight. Stress and poor sleep can make a seizure more likely.
Caller -> I haven't eaten much today. Too nervous. I'll make some eggs.
Nurse -> Eggs sound perfect.
Caller -> I'll try. I'll make some tea. And I'll go to bed at nine. Not that I'll sleep.
Nurse -> Ha. Do your best.
Caller -> I'll try. I have a book I haven't finished. A mystery. It might work better than a pill.
Caller -> I have a weighted blanket. It helps. It's like a hug.
Caller -> I got it for my birthday. It's twelve pounds of beads, and it's navy blue. I fall asleep under it in five minutes usually.
Nurse -> That sounds good. Use it.
Caller -> I'm also going to listen to the rain sounds on my phone. They calm me down.
Nurse -> Ha. Rain is soothing for many people.
Caller -> Okay. Thanks, Samir.
Caller -> You were so calm. I needed someone calm. I'm a bit of a wreck today.
Nurse -> You're handling it well.
Nurse -> Anytime, Imelda. Bye.
Caller -> I'll keep my phone close. I'm going to leave the ringer on high.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Harbor Bend Hospice, this is Daniela.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, Daniela. This is Matthias Brandvold. I'm calling about my father, Leopold Brandvold. It's about his oxygen stuff. We're running low on a couple of things.
Nurse -> Hi, Matthias. Okay. Let's take a look. Is he comfortable right now?
Caller -> He is. He's napping in the recliner. The game's on and he's not even watching it.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good nap.
Caller -> Yeah, it's the one thing he's good at lately. Sorry. That was a joke. He'd say it too.
Nurse -> It's okay. What's running low?
Caller -> The nasal cannulas. The little ones with the prongs. There's two left in the bag. And he changes one every week. So that's two weeks. Maybe.
Nurse -> Okay. Two cannulas left. What about the tubing?
Caller -> Um, there's one spare set. One. But the one on the machine now, well, I looked at it today, and there's a crack. Near the connector. The part where it plugs in. It hisses a little.
Nurse -> The spare set. Is the spare in good shape?
Caller -> I think so. It's still in the plastic. I haven't opened it. So one spare set, and the cracked one.
Nurse -> Okay. Thanks for checking that.
Caller -> I'm sorry, I should have called sooner. I noticed it Sunday.
Nurse -> No, you did the right thing calling now. Is the oxygen still getting to him? Is he comfortable?
Caller -> I think so. He's fine. No trouble breathing. His color is good. He was telling the same story about the boat at lunch. For the tenth time.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign.
Nurse -> Any other problems? How does his nose look?
Caller -> A little dry. He says it tickles. Like when you have a cold. It's not bleeding. Just dry.
Nurse -> Okay. That's common with oxygen. We'll talk about it.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> September twenty seventh. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> Perfect. And your best number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, oh one nine seven.
Nurse -> Eight oh eight, five five five, oh one nine seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. How old is the concentrator?
Caller -> I don't know. The company brought it in the spring. It's the white one. It makes a noise like a fish tank.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Do you know when you last cleaned the filter?
Caller -> Hm. Um. Honestly, I don't think we have. Is that bad? I know there's a filter. It's on the side. I just never thought about it.
Nurse -> It's very common. We'll go over it in a minute.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> First, here's what I'll do. I'll put in an order with the equipment company for new nasal cannulas and a new oxygen tubing set.
Caller -> Good. Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'll arrange delivery tomorrow. Will somebody be home?
Caller -> Yes. I'm here all day. I work from the kitchen table.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is the address the same, on Alder Street?
Caller -> Same. The blue house. Dad calls it the blue whale.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a message to the equipment team and ask them to check the concentrator when they come.
Caller -> That'd be great. Because of the noise. It's been a little louder, maybe. I don't know.
Nurse -> I'll include that in the note.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Now, for the filter. It's in the back or on the side, a little gray foam piece. Take it out and rinse it with warm water. Let it dry completely, and then put it back. Until the new tubing arrives, don't use the cracked tubing. Switch to the spare.
Caller -> Okay. Gray foam. Warm water. Dry it all the way. Put it back. Switch to the spare tubing. Got it. I'll do the spare right after we hang up.
Nurse -> Good. Do you need the number on the cylinder, or the setting?
Caller -> It's on two. Two liters. It's taped. Dad tapes everything.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> Also, keep the area clear. No smoking, no candles, no open flame near the oxygen. Even a gas stove.
Caller -> Nobody smokes here. But my aunt lights candles. For the mood. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> Please do. Thanks.
Caller -> I'm putting a sticky note on the machine now. No flame.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> And for the dry nose, a little water-based gel is fine. Not petroleum jelly.
Caller -> Okay. The water based kind. We have some. In the bathroom.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> My dad also asked if we can get a longer tube. So he can go to the porch.
Nurse -> I'll mention that to the equipment team. They can tell you what's available.
Caller -> Okay. He loves the porch. He waves at the neighbor's dog.
Nurse -> Ha. A porch wave.
Caller -> Every day. The dog doesn't wave back.
Nurse -> Anything else you need right now?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Thank you, Daniela.
Nurse -> You're welcome. You can call any time.
Caller -> Oh, wait. Is the filter dry in an hour? Or should I wait longer?
Nurse -> Give it a good while, until it's dry to the touch. You can use the spare filter if you have one.
Caller -> We don't. I'll wait.
Nurse -> The delivery tomorrow should include one.
Caller -> Okay. Great. Thanks.
Nurse -> Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Willow Fork Home Health, this is Teodoro.
Caller -> Hi, Teodoro. This is Perpetua Aldana. I'm calling about my father, Cosmo Aldana. I give him his medicines through the tube and I think I've been doing something wrong.
Nurse -> Hi, Perpetua. Thanks for calling. Tell me what you've been doing.
Caller -> So every morning I crush up his metoprolol. The fifty milligram one. It's the long acting kind, the succinate. I stir it in water and push it down the tube.
Nurse -> Okay. And when did you find out it might be a problem?
Caller -> Today. I called the pharmacy for a refill and the pharmacist asked how he takes it. I told her and she got quiet. Then she said you're not supposed to crush that one.
Nurse -> Okay. You did the right thing calling.
Caller -> I feel awful. I've been crushing it for three weeks. Three weeks.
Nurse -> You were trying to get his medicine in. You didn't know. Let's focus on how he is.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Sorry.
Nurse -> How is he feeling today?
Caller -> He's a little off. He's been dizzy this week. He says his head feels light when he sits up. Not bad. But he told me twice.
Nurse -> Dizzy when he sits up. Okay. Have you checked his pulse or blood pressure?
Caller -> I did the pulse this morning with the machine. It said fifty four. I thought it was a mistake so I did it again, and it said fifty four again.
Nurse -> Fifty four. Okay. Has he fainted, or passed out at all?
Caller -> No. No fainting. And no chest pain. He would tell me. He's not shy about complaining.
Nurse -> Ha. That's useful.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he breathing comfortably?
Caller -> Yes. He's watching his cooking shows. Right now there's a man making a big pot of rice.
Caller -> He says he could make it better.
Nurse -> I bet he could.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Good.
Nurse -> Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> March eleventh. Nineteen fifty one.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one six eight.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one six eight. Correct?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. When did he get his dose today?
Caller -> Around eight. This morning. I did the same thing. Crushed it, water, down the tube.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Here's what I want you to understand. That pill is made to release slowly through the day. When it's crushed, it can all come out at once. That can drop the pulse and the blood pressure. It may be why he's dizzy.
Caller -> Oh no. Oh, no. That's what I was afraid of.
Nurse -> He's not in danger right this minute from what you tell me. But I want to be careful. Please don't crush that tablet again. Don't give tomorrow's dose until the clinician calls you back.
Caller -> Don't crush it. Don't give tomorrow's dose. Wait for the call. Okay. I'm writing that down.
Nurse -> I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, about the crushed pill, the low pulse and the dizziness.
Caller -> Okay. How long will that take?
Nurse -> Usually within thirty minutes. Keep your phone near you.
Caller -> It's on. It's right here in my hand.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'm holding it like it's going to run away.
Nurse -> I'll also call the pharmacy and ask for a form that's safe to go down a tube. There is a short acting one that can be split or a liquid. The clinician will decide.
Caller -> That would be good. The pharmacist seemed to want that too.
Nurse -> Good. And I'd like a nurse to come see him tomorrow. To check his pulse and pressure and look at the tube site.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning. They'll call you before.
Caller -> Perfect. I'm home all day.
Nurse -> In the meantime, let him rest. Have him get up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed for a minute first.
Caller -> Sit on the edge. Slowly. Okay. He hates that, he wants to jump up. He's stubborn.
Nurse -> Ha. Most men are.
Caller -> He cooks, you know. He did all the cooking for years.
Nurse -> That must be hard to watch.
Caller -> It is. But he still bosses me from the couch.
Caller -> Ha. Yes.
Nurse -> Call 911 if he faints, has chest pain, has trouble breathing, or if his pulse is under forty.
Caller -> Faint. Chest pain. Trouble breathing. Under forty. Okay. I'll check his pulse again at lunch.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. And write the numbers down so the nurse can see them.
Caller -> I have a notebook. The green one.
Caller -> It has the feeding schedule in it too. And the water flushes.
Nurse -> Good. Bring it to the visit.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I feel so bad. Three weeks.
Nurse -> Perpetua, you caught it. Not everyone asks. That matters.
Caller -> Thank you. That helps.
Caller -> I needed to hear that.
Nurse -> Of course.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> I do the rest of his pills the same way. The other ones. Are those okay?
Nurse -> Good question. Read me the names from the bottles when the clinician calls. We'll go through every one.
Caller -> Okay. I'll put them all on the table.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> Thank you, Teodoro. Really.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Cedar Mill Home Care, this is Bettina.
Caller -> Hi. Hi. My name is Rosalind Tuohy. I'm the neighbor of Wilhelmina Strand. She's one of your clients. She fell. She's on the bathroom floor and she says her hip is killing her.
Nurse -> Okay. Take a breath. I'm here.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm just a little shaky. I've never found anybody on a floor before.
Nurse -> Okay, Rosalind. Are you with her right now?
Caller -> Yes. I'm on my cell. I'm kneeling next to her. I have a key. She gave me a key for emergencies. I heard her calling out through the wall.
Nurse -> Good thing you heard her.
Caller -> The walls here are thin. Thank goodness.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she awake? Is she talking to you?
Caller -> She's awake. She's talking. She's scared, but she's talking.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep talking to her.
Caller -> I am. I'm telling her about my sister's wedding. To keep her calm.
Nurse -> When did she fall?
Caller -> About twenty minutes ago. She says. She was getting up from the toilet. I think. She isn't sure.
Nurse -> That's okay. We don't need an exact time.
Caller -> She keeps saying she's sorry for the trouble.
Nurse -> Did she hit her head? Did she black out?
Caller -> She hit her forehead on the edge of the sink. There's a cut. A small one. It bled and it's stopped now. She didn't pass out. She knows me. She knows what day it is. She's mad at herself.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> She also asked me whether I fed her cat. I said the cat is fine.
Nurse -> Okay. Where does it hurt?
Caller -> She's looking at me. She keeps squeezing my hand.
Caller -> Her hip. The right one. She says it's a sharp pain whenever she tries to move. She tried to sit up and she screamed. I told her not to.
Nurse -> Okay. Please have her stay flat.
Caller -> Wilhelmina, honey, stay flat. Don't try again.
Nurse -> How bad is the pain, on a scale of zero to ten?
Caller -> Wilhelmina, how bad is it? Zero to ten? She says eight. Eight out of ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Can she move her leg or stand?
Caller -> No. She can't stand. She tried and she says she can't put weight on it. The leg looks a little turned. The foot is pointing out. I don't know if that's normal for her.
Nurse -> Okay. That is helpful to know.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm not a nurse.
Nurse -> You're doing fine.
Nurse -> Okay, Rosalind. I need you to call 911 right now. She needs to be seen in the emergency room.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Right now?
Caller -> I thought you would send somebody.
Nurse -> I understand. This one needs an ambulance faster than we can get there.
Nurse -> Yes. Right now. Put me on speaker, if you can, and call from another phone. Or hang up and call, and call us back.
Caller -> I'll hang up and call. I'm doing it.
Nurse -> Before you go. Don't move her. Keep her warm with a blanket. Press gently on the cut with a clean cloth. And stay with her until they arrive.
Caller -> Don't move her. Blanket. Clean cloth on the cut. Stay. Okay. I'm getting the blanket from her bed.
Caller -> It's a quilt. It's heavy. Is that okay?
Nurse -> A quilt is fine. Just keep it light on her.
Nurse -> Good. Tell the crew she lives alone and where the key is. Unlock the front door for them.
Caller -> I'll unlock it. I'll tell them.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> The door is the green one. They can't miss it.
Nurse -> I'm going to let the team know about the fall and the 911 call right now.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I didn't know who to call.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I keep saying thank you.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for.
Caller -> Her son lives in Denver. I'll call him after.
Nurse -> You did the right thing.
Caller -> I'm calling now. Hold on.
Caller -> Oh, my phone is dying. I have eleven percent.
Nurse -> Then let's keep this short. Go ahead and call.
Nurse -> Go ahead. Call 911 and I will stay on the other line.
Caller -> No, I'll call you back. I need both hands.
Nurse -> Okay. Before you hang up, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> I don't know off the top of my head. She's seventy nine. Hang on, she's telling me. December third, nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we get disconnected?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one four seven.
Nurse -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one four seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Yes. I'm calling them.
Caller -> Okay. I have the keypad open.
Caller -> It's ringing. It's ringing.
Nurse -> Go. I'll be here.
Caller -> Okay. Dialing.
Caller -> Wilhelmina, you stay still. Help is coming. I'm right here.
Nurse -> Good. Talk to her until they get there.
Nurse -> Rosalind, you're doing great.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm calling. Bye.

Nurse -> Lantern Hill Hospice, this is Gretchen.
Caller -> Hi, Gretchen. It's Adaeze Oyelaran. My father is Ferdinand Oyelaran. I have a question about the morphine. The liquid one. I don't want to get it wrong.
Nurse -> Hi, Adaeze. I'm glad you called instead of guessing. What's your question?
Caller -> The bottle says twenty milligrams per milliliter. And the nurse said his dose is five milligrams. And I don't know how much that is. On the syringe. There are little lines and they're very small. I'm squinting.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I took my glasses off and put them on again. It didn't help.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the syringe the clear one with the purple tip?
Caller -> Hang on. Let me get it. It's in the little basket with the log.
Caller -> Yes. Purple. And it says one milliliter on it. And then lines. Lots of lines.
Nurse -> Okay. And when did you last give a dose?
Caller -> About two hours ago. I gave him the morphine at eleven forty. Five milligrams. And I think I gave the right amount. But I'm not sure. I want to be sure for the next one.
Nurse -> What did you give him at eleven forty? How much did you draw up?
Caller -> I filled it up to the line that said point two five. Because the nurse wrote that on the box. Is that right?
Nurse -> Yes. A quarter of a milliliter of that concentrate is five milligrams. So you gave the right dose.
Caller -> Oh. Oh, thank you. Thank goodness. I've been worried for two hours.
Nurse -> That's a long time to worry.
Caller -> I kept checking on him every ten minutes. He's probably sick of me.
Nurse -> I understand. It's a strength that confuses a lot of people. The bottle number is per milliliter, and the dose is a small part of a milliliter.
Caller -> Exactly. The numbers look huge. Twenty. And I'm giving him five.
Nurse -> They do.
Nurse -> Right. Twenty milligrams of morphine in a whole milliliter, and a quarter of that is five. Draw up to the line marked point two five. Have someone else read it before you give it. Write the time down on the log.
Caller -> Draw to point two five. Have someone read it. Write the time. Okay. My husband can read it. He has better eyes than me.
Nurse -> Good. Two sets of eyes.
Caller -> He says he'll use his magnifying glass.
Nurse -> Perfect. How is your father's pain now?
Caller -> About a four, I think. He said four an hour ago. Before he fell asleep. He's sleeping now. He looks comfortable.
Nurse -> Good. Rest is the best thing.
Caller -> He snores. It's the best sound I've heard all week.
Nurse -> Okay. A four. And how long can he go between doses?
Caller -> Every four hours if he needs it. The nurse said that. I wrote it on the log. As needed.
Nurse -> Good, you're keeping it organized.
Caller -> The log is on a clipboard. It's by the bed.
Nurse -> Good. That's right. Now, anything else bothering him? How is he eating? His bowels?
Caller -> That's the other thing. He hasn't had a bowel movement in three days. Three. And he's uncomfortable. He's straining and nothing happens.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That is uncomfortable.
Nurse -> Okay. Is his belly hard or swollen?
Caller -> A little tight, I think. But he didn't say it hurts. And he's not throwing up.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Constipation is very common with this medicine. I'd like the team to look at a bowel regimen for him. I'm going to send them a message tonight.
Caller -> Tonight? Thank you. I'm so glad. He's so uncomfortable. And he won't ask.
Nurse -> In the meantime, offer small sips of water or prune juice. A warm drink in the morning can help. And help him sit up for meals if he can.
Caller -> Prune juice. Warm drink. Sit up. Okay. He hates prune juice. He says it tastes like sadness.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Try a little. Or a warm tea.
Caller -> I'll try the tea. He likes the ginger one.
Nurse -> That's fine. Let me get his chart. What is his date of birth?
Caller -> May twenty second. Nineteen thirty nine.
Nurse -> And a good number for tomorrow?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, oh one one three.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, oh one one three. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Thank you.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Sorry, I'm writing this all down.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow to see how his bowels are and how his pain is.
Caller -> What time?
Nurse -> Morning, around ten.
Caller -> Ten. Okay. I'll put it on the fridge.
Caller -> I'll be here. I'm staying with him all week. I took off work.
Nurse -> That's wonderful for him. And for you.
Caller -> It's hard but I wouldn't want to be anywhere else.
Nurse -> I know.
Caller -> My brother is coming Friday. He's driving from Memphis.
Nurse -> It'll be good to have help.
Caller -> Yes. We take turns. I do nights, he'll do afternoons.
Nurse -> Make sure you sleep too.
Caller -> I try. I nap when he naps.
Nurse -> That's the best way.
Caller -> Is there anything else I should know about the dose?
Nurse -> Only that you can call me any time. Day or night. If you're unsure, call, don't guess.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you, Gretchen.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Good night.
Caller -> Good night. Bye.

Nurse -> Sable Creek Home Health, this is Odalys.
Caller -> Hi, Odalys. This is Marguerite Lindqvist. I'm calling about my husband, Hollis Lindqvist. His weight is up and his ankles look puffy. We have a question.
Nurse -> Hi. Is Mr. Lindqvist there too?
Caller -> He's here. He's in his chair. He's got the other phone. Can you hear him?
Nurse -> I can hear a little echo.
Caller -> It's the speaker. Let me turn it down.
Nurse -> Hi, Marguerite. Okay. Tell me about the weight.
Caller -> He weighed this morning. It was, what was it, Hollis? One hundred seventy eight?
Caller -> One hundred seventy eight. That's what the scale said. I said one seventy eight.
Nurse -> Sorry, you both talked at once. Can you say that again?
Caller -> Sorry. You go. No, you go. Okay, I'll say it.
Nurse -> And what was it before?
Caller -> Yes, one hundred seventy eight today. Two days ago it was one hundred seventy five. So up three pounds. In two days. I wrote it on the chart. Hollis, give me the— no, let me say it.
Caller -> Where did I put that chart? It's right here.
Nurse -> No rush.
Nurse -> One seventy eight, up three pounds in two days. Okay.
Caller -> Yes. And he says it's nothing, because he had a big dinner.
Caller -> I said it's not the dinner. Three pounds is three pounds.
Nurse -> You're right to call. How are his ankles?
Caller -> Puffy. Both of them. A little. Not terrible. If I press, it leaves a small dent. Not deep. He has the socks marks too.
Nurse -> Is it worse than it was last week?
Caller -> A little bit. Last week they were fine. Hollis, were they fine? He says yes.
Nurse -> How is his breathing? Any shortness of breath, climbing stairs, lying flat?
Caller -> No. He's fine with the stairs. He did the stairs this morning to get the paper. Slowly. But he didn't get winded. And he sleeps on his usual pillows.
Nurse -> Good. Any chest pain, dizziness?
Caller -> No, no. He's grumbling, that's all. He's right here. He says hello.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> He's been grumbling since nineteen eighty.
Nurse -> Hello, Mr. Lindqvist.
Caller -> Hello. I'm fine. She worries.
Nurse -> Ha. That's her job.
Caller -> That's what I say.
Nurse -> I'd like to know his medicines. Is he taking his water pill?
Caller -> Yes. The furosemide. Forty milligrams. Every morning. He took it this morning with his coffee. I set it out.
Nurse -> Okay. Furosemide, forty, once a day, and he took it this morning. Has he missed any this week?
Caller -> No. I check. I put them in the box. Monday through Sunday. All taken.
Nurse -> And is he watching his salt?
Caller -> We try. His brother brought soup on Saturday. It was the canned kind. I think that might be it.
Nurse -> Canned soup can have a lot of salt. That could be part of it.
Caller -> Hollis, I told you.
Caller -> What? I did tell you.
Caller -> Marguerite, let the nurse talk.
Nurse -> It's all right. I can hear both of you.
Caller -> It was good soup.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand. What's his date of birth, for the chart?
Caller -> August fourteenth. Nineteen fifty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one oh, five five five, oh one one three.
Nurse -> Six one oh, five five five, oh one one three. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'd like a nurse to come see him tomorrow. To check his weight, his lungs, and the swelling.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. We're home. We're always home. Hollis doesn't go anywhere.
Nurse -> That's fine. We'll come to you.
Caller -> I go to the store. He stays.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll also send the team a message about the weight gain and the swelling.
Caller -> I'll send a message to the team about the weight gain and the swelling. Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Marguerite, can you write this down? Weigh him every morning after he uses the bathroom and before breakfast. Same scale. Write it down. And keep his feet up when he sits.
Caller -> Every morning. After the bathroom. Before breakfast. Write it. Feet up. Okay. We have a notebook.
Caller -> I'll put the chair by the window. He can put his feet on the stool.
Nurse -> Perfect. Call us if he gains another two pounds or more, if he gets short of breath, or if he needs more pillows to sleep. And call 911 if he has severe trouble breathing or chest pain.
Caller -> Two pounds. Short of breath. More pillows. And 911 for bad breathing or chest pain. I got it.
Caller -> Hollis, did you hear that? He heard. He's nodding.
Caller -> He heard. Okay, I'll stop talking for him.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> One more thing. Can he have the soup if it's low salt?
Nurse -> The nurse can talk about that tomorrow. For now, I'd skip the canned kind.
Caller -> Okay. I'll hide the soup.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Thank you, Odalys.
Caller -> Thank you. Yes. Goodbye.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care both of you.
Caller -> You too.

transcript:
Nurse -> Redbud Home Health, this is Colette.
Caller -> Hi, Colette. It's Thaddeus Wojciechowski. I'm one of your patients. I'm calling with a check in about my hip.
Nurse -> Hi, Thaddeus. Could you spell the last name for me? I want it right in the chart.
Caller -> Sure. Everyone struggles. W O J C I E C H O W S K I.
Nurse -> Got it. W O J C I E C H O W S K I. Wojciechowski. Did I say it right?
Caller -> Close enough. Vo-chay-HOF-ski. But nobody gets it. The pharmacy calls me Mr. W.
Nurse -> I'll get it. Eventually.
Caller -> Don't worry. My own mother couldn't say it until she married into it.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll practice. How are you feeling today?
Caller -> Pretty good. Better every day. I'm on day nine since the surgery.
Nurse -> Good to hear. Are you at home today?
Caller -> In the recliner. I'm not allowed to do much else.
Nurse -> That's great. Let's go through everything. Where's the pain?
Caller -> At the incision. Down the side of the hip. It's about a two. A two out of ten. Mostly when I get up from the chair. Then it goes away.
Nurse -> Okay. What do you take for it?
Caller -> Tylenol. Five hundred milligrams. I take it when I need it. Every six hours at the most. I took one this morning around eight. Just one.
Caller -> I have a pill organizer. It's the kind with the days on it.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol, five hundred, as needed. Not more than every six hours.
Caller -> Right. I don't take it much. Two a day, maybe. Some days none.
Nurse -> That's very good. Any swelling in the leg?
Caller -> A little. The leg on that side is a little puffy by the evening. My ankle. Not as much in the morning. I prop it up.
Nurse -> Okay. Mild swelling by evening. Is it painful when you touch the calf?
Caller -> No. The calf is fine. No pain there.
Nurse -> Any fever, chills?
Caller -> No fever. I haven't taken my temperature though. I feel normal. No chills.
Nurse -> And the incision? Redness, drainage, any opening?
Caller -> I looked this morning. In the mirror. Using my phone. It's clean. No redness. No drainage. The staples came out Monday so there's just those little strips. They're curling up at the ends.
Nurse -> Let them fall off on their own. Don't pull them.
Caller -> I won't. My wife keeps trying to peel them. I say leave it.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Every time she walks by she looks at them.
Nurse -> Ha. Good for you.
Caller -> She's a nurse. Retired. She can't help herself.
Nurse -> I bet. Okay, Thaddeus. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> March fourteenth, nineteen fifty eight. Sorry. May. May fourteenth. Nineteen fifty eight. I get the months mixed up. My daughter is March.
Nurse -> May fourteenth, nineteen fifty eight. Okay.
Caller -> Yes. Sorry.
Nurse -> It happens all the time.
Nurse -> No problem. And your number?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, oh one five oh.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, oh one five oh. Correct?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> How are you getting around? Walker or cane?
Caller -> The walker. I'm trying the cane in the house. Just a little. My therapist said Thursday I can try without the walker. With her next to me.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good progress.
Nurse -> I'd keep the walker for now. Use it every time you're up. Clear the rugs and the cords. And remember your hip precautions. Don't bend past ninety degrees.
Caller -> Walker every time. Clear rugs. Cords. Ninety degrees. Okay. My wife already took all the rugs. She rolled them up and put them in the garage.
Nurse -> Perfect. She sounds like a good helper.
Caller -> She is. A little bossy.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the job.
Caller -> She makes me do the exercises three times a day. I have a chart. She puts a star.
Nurse -> Good. Keep it up.
Nurse -> Stars are good.
Caller -> I have eleven stars so far this week.
Nurse -> I'd like a nurse to come see you Thursday to check the incision and the leg.
Caller -> Thursday. What time?
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning. They'll call you before.
Caller -> Okay. My therapist comes at one. So the morning is good.
Nurse -> Perfect. Call us if you get a fever, if the redness spreads or anything drains, if your calf becomes painful and swollen, or if you get sudden shortness of breath.
Caller -> Fever. Redness. Drainage. Calf. Short of breath. Okay. I wrote it on the back of an envelope.
Nurse -> Put it on the fridge.
Caller -> My wife already did. She has a magnet for everything.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Can I ask something? When can I drive?
Nurse -> The surgeon decides that. Ask at your follow up.
Caller -> Okay. I figured. I miss my truck.
Caller -> It's just sitting in the driveway. The neighbor's kid keeps asking to start it.
Nurse -> Ha. Please say no.
Nurse -> Soon enough.
Caller -> I'm going to go sit on the porch. It's sunny. Thanks, Colette.
Nurse -> Enjoy it. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.
