Nurse -> Foxglove Home Care, this is Anselm.
Caller -> Hi. Hello. My name is Gideon Pruitt. I'm calling about a neighbor. Miriam Halvorsen. She's one of yours. I think. I'm worried about her.
Nurse -> Hi there. Take your time.
Caller -> I wasn't sure if I should call. My wife said call. So I'm calling.
Nurse -> Hi, Gideon. Thanks for calling. Marian Halvorsen. Can you spell that?
Caller -> It's Miriam. M I R I A M. Halvorsen. H A L V O R S E N. I think. She's Norwegian. Or her husband was. He passed.
Nurse -> Okay. Marian Halvorsen. I'm looking now. Give me a moment.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> Miriam. With an I.
Nurse -> Got it, thank you.
Caller -> Sorry. Everybody gets it wrong. Even the mailman.
Nurse -> I have a Marian Halvorsen. Is she in her eighties, lives on the corner of Pike?
Caller -> That's her. Yes. The yellow house. I'm next door. I'm in the gray one.
Caller -> She has the wind chimes on the porch. You can hear them from my yard.
Nurse -> Okay. I see the address.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what's got you worried.
Caller -> She hasn't been coming to the door. I've been bringing her the paper for years. Every morning. She opens the door and takes it. Today she didn't. I knocked. She came after a long time.
Nurse -> Okay. How did she look when she came?
Caller -> Tired. Sleepy. Slow. She was in her robe. She said she was fine. But she didn't look fine. She seemed sleepier than usual. I think. I'm not a doctor.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> She held on to the door frame. I don't know if that means anything.
Nurse -> Okay. Was she confused? Did she know who you were?
Caller -> She knew me. She said my name. She said the paper was late. It wasn't late.
Nurse -> That's good.
Caller -> She asked after my wife. She always does.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she eating?
Caller -> I don't know. I don't think she eats much. Her daughter said last week she hardly eats. I don't know. I'm just a neighbor. I see her bring in the groceries and they just sit on the counter.
Nurse -> That's helpful anyway.
Caller -> I wish I knew more.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you see her fall, or any bruises?
Caller -> No. I didn't see a fall. I don't think she fell. She didn't say. She was walking. Slow, but walking.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she have family close by?
Caller -> A daughter. In Tucson. She calls on Sundays. I don't have her number. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Her name is Karin, I think. K A R I N. Or with a C.
Nurse -> That's all right. We have her on file.
Caller -> Good. I figured you would.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I don't want to cause trouble.
Nurse -> You're not. Thank you for calling. Gideon, do you know her date of birth?
Caller -> No. No, no. I have no idea. She's old. Eighty something.
Nurse -> That's fine. And a number for you?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one seven three.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one seven three. Right?
Caller -> Right. It's my cell. I'm home.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep it handy.
Caller -> It's on the counter. I'm at the kitchen table. I can see her house.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you seen her any other times this week?
Caller -> Tuesday. She was in her garden. Out front. Doing something with the pots.
Nurse -> So Tuesday she was out and about.
Caller -> She waved. She waved at me.
Caller -> Yes. That's why this is strange.
Nurse -> Okay. I'd like a nurse to go out and see her today. Check on her.
Caller -> Today? Oh, good. Good. Will she mind? She's very private.
Nurse -> We'll call before we come. And I'll send a message to the team about your concern.
Caller -> Please tell them it's not an emergency. I don't want her to think I called the police.
Nurse -> I'll let them know.
Nurse -> I'll tell them. They'll be gentle.
Caller -> Thank you. She's a sweet lady. She bakes. She gave me a pie at Thanksgiving.
Nurse -> Ha. Those are the best neighbors.
Caller -> Cherry. Best I ever had.
Nurse -> I'm jealous.
Caller -> Ha. She might share the recipe. She won't.
Nurse -> Gideon, if you go back over and she's hard to wake, confused, or on the floor, please call 911 right away. And please don't go into her house unless she lets you in.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Confused. On the floor. Call 911. Don't go in. Okay. I will. Should I check on her tonight? Knock?
Nurse -> A knock is fine. If she answers, that's good. Just be kind about it.
Caller -> I'll bring a bag of rolls. I have extra.
Nurse -> Wonderful.
Nurse -> That's nice of you.
Caller -> It's no trouble.
Nurse -> Thanks for calling, Gideon. You did the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you. I feel better. I hope she's okay.
Nurse -> We'll find out soon.
Caller -> Okay. Bye.

Nurse -> Pinecrest Hospice, this is Valentina.
Caller -> Hi, Valentina. It's Loretta Achterberg. My husband is Wendell Achterberg. We ran out of the morphine yesterday afternoon and he's in terrible pain.
Nurse -> Loretta, I'm so sorry. Let's fix this. First, is he awake, is he breathing okay?
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you for picking up.
Nurse -> I'm right here.
Caller -> He's awake. Breathing's okay. But he's moaning. He keeps trying to get up and he can't. I don't know what to do. I've been calling since six. Nobody called back.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about that.
Nurse -> I'm sorry you had to wait. I'm here now. How bad is the pain? Zero is none, ten is the worst.
Caller -> He said nine. I asked him a minute ago. He said nine. He can hardly talk. He's grimacing.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> He keeps squeezing my hand.
Nurse -> Where is the pain?
Caller -> All over. His back, mostly. And his hip. It started last night, when the last dose wore off. Then it kept going up.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm writing it all down.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me about the morphine. How much did he take, and when was the last dose?
Caller -> The ten milligrams. Every four hours when he needs it. The last one was yesterday afternoon, about three. Then the bottle was empty. I scraped what I could.
Nurse -> That's okay. You did what you could.
Caller -> I felt so helpless.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you call the pharmacy about a refill?
Caller -> Tuesday. I called Tuesday. They said it would come Thursday. It didn't come Thursday. I called Friday and got the machine. And then it was too late. The office closed.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That should not have happened. I'm so sorry. We'll make it right tonight.
Caller -> I just want him to stop hurting.
Nurse -> I know. That is exactly what we are going to work on.
Caller -> I know you will.
Nurse -> I know. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. I'll tell them he's out of morphine and in severe pain.
Caller -> Please. Please hurry.
Nurse -> I will.
Nurse -> I will. I'll also call the pharmacy tonight, and get an emergency supply sent to your house.
Caller -> Tonight? Can they do that?
Nurse -> Yes. We have an after hours line. I'll stay on it until it's arranged.
Caller -> I didn't know that. Nobody told us.
Nurse -> It's on the refrigerator magnet we left. Do you see it?
Caller -> Oh. Yes. It's right in front of me. I never looked.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you so much.
Nurse -> And I'd like a nurse to come out tonight to see him and bring a dose with them if the clinician approves it.
Caller -> Tonight. Oh, thank God.
Caller -> What do I do when the nurse arrives? Do I unlock the door?
Nurse -> Yes. Leave the porch light on.
Caller -> I will. I'll leave it on.
Nurse -> What time do you think he last slept?
Caller -> He hasn't. Not really. He dozes a few minutes and wakes up moaning. It's been almost a whole day.
Nurse -> Okay. Loretta, let me get a few details so I can get things moving. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> February ninth. Nineteen forty eight.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Three one four, five five five, oh one three seven.
Nurse -> Three one four, five five five, oh one three seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. It's in my hand.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep it near you. Is there anything that seems to help even a little?
Caller -> When I hold his hand he calms down a little. But then it comes back.
Nurse -> That helps more than you know.
Nurse -> Okay. Until the medicine comes, keep the room dim and quiet. Gently move him with pillows, one under his knees and one at his back. And a warm blanket can help.
Caller -> Dim. Quiet. Pillows. Warm blanket. Okay. I have a heated one. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Warm is good. Not hot. Check it on your own arm first.
Caller -> The dog keeps pacing too. She knows something is wrong.
Nurse -> Dogs notice.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that.
Caller -> I'll go put it on him now.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Keep your phone near you.
Caller -> Please. I'll be right here.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep my phone right here. Valentina?
Nurse -> Yes?
Caller -> I'm sorry I'm crying.
Caller -> Thirty eight years. I don't want him to hurt.
Nurse -> Don't be sorry. You're doing everything right. You called.
Caller -> I've been so scared since last night. I thought he would have to go to the hospital. He doesn't want to.
Nurse -> We're going to do our best to keep him at home.
Caller -> That's all he wants. To be in his own bed.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm paging now. Stay by your phone.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Lark Meadow Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Ignacio.
Caller -> Hi, Ignacio. It's Phuong Ng. I'm calling about my son Calloway Ng. He's six. He has asthma and I think his cough is back. And I want to make sure I'm doing his inhaler right.
Nurse -> Hi, Phuong. Good to hear from you. Tell me about the cough.
Caller -> Sorry it's late. We just got the kids in bed.
Nurse -> Don't apologize. That's what the evening line is for.
Caller -> He coughs at night. Two nights now. Not all night. A few times. And last night I heard a little whistle when he breathed out. A soft whistle.
Nurse -> Okay. A mild wheeze. What about during the day?
Caller -> Daytime he's okay. He ran around at recess. He came home and played with his cars. He's fine.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> His teacher said he did great in gym.
Nurse -> Is he breathing fast, or working hard to breathe?
Caller -> No. When he's sitting he's breathing normally. His belly isn't pulling in. His color is fine. He's eating. He told me about a fight at school over a pencil.
Nurse -> Ha. High drama.
Caller -> It was a pink pencil. With a feather.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. What medicines is he using right now?
Caller -> The rescue one. Albuterol. Two puffs with the spacer. I gave it four times yesterday. Once this afternoon, around three.
Nurse -> Albuterol, two puffs. Is that every four hours?
Caller -> The doctor said every four hours if he needs it. I gave it at bedtime, twice in the night when he coughed, and once at lunch. So that's four.
Nurse -> Okay. And does he have a daily one?
Caller -> Yes. The Flovent. Two puffs, twice a day. Morning and night. I gave him this morning's before school. And I will give tonight's soon.
Nurse -> Good. So Flovent is the daily one, and albuterol is the rescue one.
Caller -> Yes. The orange one and the blue one. I mix them up sometimes. I put a sticker on the orange one.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> A sticker is a great idea.
Caller -> My daughter picked the sticker. It's a unicorn.
Caller -> She has a sticker for everything. Even the cat.
Nurse -> Ha. That works. Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> June seventeenth. Twenty twenty. He turned six in June.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one one oh.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one one oh. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's right.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Can you walk me through how you give the puffs? I'd like to hear it.
Caller -> I shake it. I put it in the spacer. I hold the mask on his face. I press it. Then he breathes in, and I press the next one right away. Two puffs. Is that wrong?
Nurse -> Okay. Keep going.
Nurse -> You're doing most of it right. Two small changes. Give one puff at a time, not two together. Have him breathe in slowly for about ten seconds, and wait a minute before the next one.
Caller -> One puff at a time. Ten seconds. Wait a minute. Okay. I was rushing. He gets squirmy.
Nurse -> It's hard with a six year old. Count out loud with him. Make it a game.
Caller -> He is a wiggle worm. He tries to talk with the mask on.
Nurse -> Ha. That's normal.
Caller -> We can do that. We count to ten. He likes to count.
Nurse -> Perfect. And after the Flovent, have him rinse his mouth and spit. That prevents thrush.
Caller -> Rinse and spit. Okay. We do that, mostly. Sometimes he swallows. He thinks it's toothpaste.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Ha. Try water first.
Caller -> He loves to gargle. It's funny.
Nurse -> A gargle counts.
Nurse -> Good. Now, because he needed the rescue inhaler four times yesterday, I'd like to tell the team. They may want to adjust his plan. I'll send them a message tonight.
Caller -> Okay. Will they call me?
Nurse -> They might. Or I will.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow, and let you know what they say.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Thank you. What time?
Nurse -> Late morning.
Caller -> I'm home till one. Then I get his sister from school.
Nurse -> Noted.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> What should I watch for tonight?
Nurse -> Call 911 if his lips look blue, if he can't talk in full sentences, or if you see his ribs pulling in with each breath. Call us if he needs the rescue inhaler more often than every four hours.
Caller -> Blue lips. Can't talk. Ribs pulling. 911. More than every four hours, call you. I'll write that on the fridge.
Nurse -> Good. Keep the head of his bed up with an extra pillow.
Caller -> He has two already. He's a pillow hog.
Caller -> And a stuffed dinosaur. It's his night nurse, he says.
Nurse -> A good colleague.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Thank you, Ignacio. I feel better.
Caller -> I was worried I was doing it all wrong.
Nurse -> You weren't. You were close.
Nurse -> You're doing a good job. Good night.
Caller -> Good night.

transcript:
Nurse -> Quarry Hill Home Health, this is Priyanka.
Caller -> Hi, Priyanka. This is Nkechi Adeyemi. I'm a home health aide. I work with Mr. Gallagher. Rufus Gallagher. He's on the tube feedings. I need to order supplies and I have a question about the site.
Nurse -> Hi. Can you hear me okay?
Caller -> A little crackly. I'm in the kitchen. The signal is bad by the fridge. Let me move.
Nurse -> No problem.
Caller -> Better? I'm in the hallway now.
Nurse -> Much better.
Nurse -> Hi, Nkechi. Thank you for calling. How long have you worked with Mr. Gallagher?
Caller -> Since August. Three months. I come Monday to Friday, days. His wife does nights and weekends.
Nurse -> And how is the family doing with the schedule?
Caller -> We manage. It's a lot of shuffling but we manage.
Caller -> I started the week after his wife went back to nights.
Nurse -> That's a lot of coverage for one family.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's do supplies first. What's low?
Caller -> Sure. I made a list on my phone too. Just in case.
Nurse -> Perfect. Read it out when you're ready.
Caller -> The formula. The cans. There's three left in the pantry. He uses about two a day. So a day and a half. Maybe less, if he has a big day.
Nurse -> Three cans left. Okay. Is there more somewhere? A garage, a closet?
Caller -> I looked. I checked the closet and the basement. There's one case of the wrong one. The vanilla. He's on the plain one. So no. Three.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a priority. What else?
Caller -> I wrote everything down on the notepad so I wouldn't forget. Hold on, it's right here.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> The syringes. The big ones. Sixty milliliter. There's two left. We rinse them and reuse them, like you showed us. But one has a crack. The plunger sticks.
Nurse -> Okay. Two syringes, one of them cracked.
Caller -> I'd say one and a half. Ha. I'd throw the cracked one away.
Caller -> I put a piece of tape on it so nobody uses it.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Nurse -> Ha. Yes. Please do. How about the extension sets? The tubing that connects to the tube.
Caller -> One spare. In the bag. We use one a week. And the one in use is still good. So that's okay. But it's the last spare.
Nurse -> Okay. And the gauze? The little pads you put under the tube?
Caller -> Plenty of those. A whole box. And the tape. And the soap. It's the formula and the syringes. Mostly the formula.
Nurse -> Perfect. Who usually places the order?
Caller -> Usually it's on the schedule. But the schedule went out the window this month.
Nurse -> It happens.
Caller -> His wife does. Brenda. But she's been so busy. She works nights at a hospital. And with everything. She forgot to reorder. I told her yesterday I'd call.
Nurse -> That's very kind. We'll take care of it.
Caller -> Thank you. She is exhausted. I don't want her to feel bad.
Caller -> She hasn't slept more than four hours a night in weeks. She won't admit it.
Nurse -> It's a lot for any family.
Caller -> I tell her to nap when I'm here. She doesn't.
Nurse -> No, of course. It happens to everybody.
Caller -> I tell her, you take care of him, I'll take care of the paperwork.
Nurse -> That's a great team. Now, tell me about the site.
Caller -> Thank you. We try.
Caller -> There's some leaking. Around the tube. Where it goes in. A little yellowish fluid, on the gauze. I noticed it Tuesday. Then it was more this morning. The gauze was wet through. And the skin is pink. Not red. Pink. Around the tube.
Nurse -> Okay. Is the skin around it painful when you touch it?
Caller -> I should say, I'm not great at describing skin. I can send a picture if you want.
Nurse -> The agency doesn't allow pictures on personal phones. The nurse will see it.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I thought.
Caller -> He says it's tender. A little. He can talk, you know, but slowly. He said, it stings. When I cleaned it.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any swelling, warmth, or bad smell?
Caller -> A little puffy. Not much. No smell. Not warm. I put my hand on it. Same as the rest of his skin.
Nurse -> Good. Any fever?
Caller -> I use the ear thermometer. It's the good one. It beeps twice.
Caller -> No fever. I took it this morning and it was normal. His wife took it last night, and it was normal. He's not hot.
Nurse -> Any vomiting, or nausea, with the feedings?
Caller -> No. He's fine. He's tolerating the feeds. The last one was yesterday afternoon. No throwing up. No bloating. He burps a little. He's good.
Nurse -> Okay. Has the tube moved? Does it seem longer or shorter than before?
Caller -> It looks the same. I checked the number on it. It's at the same mark.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. How is he otherwise today?
Caller -> Good mood. He's watching the football replay. He types with his eyes. His device. He wrote, tell her I'm fine. Ha. He's a character.
Caller -> It's the same game he watched Sunday. He says he likes knowing how it ends.
Nurse -> Ha. I can relate.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell him hello from me.
Caller -> He's rolling his eyes at the screen. He's typing.
Nurse -> What does he say?
Caller -> He says you sound nice. He says to send a case of the good coffee too.
Nurse -> Ha. I can't help with that one.
Caller -> Hello from Priyanka. He's smiling. He says thank you.
Nurse -> Lovely. Okay. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> April twenty sixth. Nineteen sixty nine.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, oh one nine four.
Nurse -> Nine oh one, five five five, oh one nine four. Is that right?
Caller -> Yes. It's my work cell. They gave it to me.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll keep it on the order.
Nurse -> Great. Let me tell you what I'll do. I'll place an order with the supply company for formula, syringes, and extension sets.
Caller -> Good. How much formula?
Nurse -> The same as his standing order. I'll ask for an extra case, since you're low.
Caller -> I never know the exact number. Brenda keeps track of that.
Nurse -> I'll see what the chart says.
Caller -> That would be great. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll also arrange delivery tomorrow. Will someone be there?
Caller -> Yes. I'm here from eight to four. His wife is home after seven. Somebody's always here.
Nurse -> Perfect. The delivery should come tomorrow morning. If it doesn't, call me.
Caller -> Last time the driver rang the bell and left. We were in the back room.
Nurse -> I'll note to call before they leave it.
Caller -> That would help. Thanks.
Caller -> I will. Can they bring it to the side door? The front steps are hard for the delivery guy with the wheelchair ramp. It's blocked.
Nurse -> I'll add that to the note.
Caller -> Perfect. Side door. By the garage.
Caller -> There's a gravel path, tell them to watch their step.
Nurse -> I'm making a note.
Nurse -> Got it. I'm also going to send a message to the team about the leaking and the pink skin. I want them to take a look.
Caller -> Good. I wasn't sure if I should call about that. I didn't want to bother.
Nurse -> You're not bothering. This is exactly what to call about.
Caller -> Brenda tells me the same thing. I'm still polite.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep being polite.
Caller -> Okay. Good to know.
Caller -> I've been second guessing myself all week.
Nurse -> Next time, call sooner. We'd rather hear early.
Nurse -> And I'd like a nurse to come out tomorrow and check the site.
Caller -> Tomorrow? Great. Can they come in the morning? He's more awake in the morning. Afternoons he gets tired.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning. I can't promise, but I'll ask.
Caller -> That's fine. Thank you.
Caller -> If he's asleep, they can knock softly. He doesn't hear well when he's asleep.
Nurse -> Noted.
Nurse -> In the meantime, here's how to care for the site. Clean around the tube with mild soap and warm water, using a clean cloth. Pat it dry. Don't use peroxide or ointments. And put a dry gauze under the tube, and change it when it gets wet.
Caller -> Mild soap. Warm water. Pat dry. No peroxide. No ointment. Dry gauze, change when wet. Okay. I'm writing it. I use the pink notepad.
Nurse -> Good. Also, flush the tube with thirty milliliters of water before and after each feeding. That keeps it from clogging. And rinse the syringes in warm soapy water between uses, then let them air dry.
Caller -> Thirty before and after. Rinse in warm soapy water. Air dry. We do that. His wife does a thirty. I do a thirty. We're consistent.
Nurse -> That's great.
Caller -> I'm very careful. I was a nursing assistant at a hospital for six years before this.
Nurse -> I'm glad he has you.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot coming from a nurse.
Nurse -> It shows.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Last thing. Call us if he gets a fever, if he's vomiting, if the redness spreads, you see pus, the tube moves or falls out, or the formula won't go through.
Caller -> Wait, let me get a pen. This one is dead.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Ready.
Caller -> Fever. Vomiting. Redness spreading. Pus. Tube moves or falls out. Won't go through. Okay. If it falls out, don't I put anything back in? Call right away?
Nurse -> Call right away. And cover the opening with a clean gauze. Don't try to put it back yourself.
Caller -> Okay. I know. They taught us. I just want to make sure.
Nurse -> It's good to check.
Caller -> I'd rather ask twice than do it wrong once.
Nurse -> That's the right attitude.
Caller -> Is there a better way to hold the gauze? The tape pulls on his skin.
Nurse -> The nurse will look at that tomorrow too. There are other products.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll tell Brenda.
Nurse -> Tell her we're thinking of her.
Caller -> I will. She'll cry. Happy crying.
Nurse -> Anything else?
Caller -> One more. Can you tell the nurse to bring a new cushion for the wheelchair? The one he has is flat.
Nurse -> I'll mention it to the team. It may be a separate order.
Caller -> Okay. No rush. It's just a thought.
Nurse -> Thanks for telling me.
Caller -> Is it all right if I call again this week if I think of something?
Nurse -> Of course. Any time, day or night.
Caller -> Good. Thank you.
Caller -> I think that's it. Oh, wait. His wife said the delivery last time left the formula on the porch in the rain. Can they put it inside the screen door?
Nurse -> I'll add that too.
Caller -> Thank you so much. You made my day easier.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Nkechi. Thank you for taking such good care of him.
Caller -> I love my job. He's the best.
Nurse -> I can tell.
Caller -> Last week he made me laugh so hard I spilled the water.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully not on the formula.
Caller -> Just on my shoe.
Nurse -> It shows. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

Nurse -> Moss Landing Hospice, this is Beatrix.
Caller -> Hi, Beatrix. It's Annika Rhodes. I'm the daughter of Cordelia Fairweather. I just wanted to give you an update. Nothing urgent.
Nurse -> Hi, Annika. I'm so glad you called. How is your mom doing?
Caller -> I wasn't sure if it was worth a call.
Nurse -> It always is.
Caller -> She's okay. She's a little different this week. Sleepier. She naps most of the day. She wakes up for a bit around lunch and then goes back down.
Nurse -> Okay. Is that a change from last week?
Caller -> A little. Last week she was up in her chair most of the afternoon. This week she's mostly in bed. But she's comfortable. She seems peaceful.
Nurse -> That's good to hear.
Nurse -> Okay. How about her eating?
Caller -> Just a few bites. I make her scrambled eggs and she takes three or four bites. A little applesauce. She drinks a few sips of tea. That's about it. I know she's not hungry. I try not to push.
Nurse -> You're listening to her. That's right.
Nurse -> That's very common. How about pain? Does she seem uncomfortable?
Caller -> No. No pain that I can tell. She doesn't grimace. She's not moaning. No restlessness. She sleeps through the night. She just seems tired.
Nurse -> Good. That's what we want to hear.
Caller -> The grandkids came on Sunday. All five of them. She was awake for almost an hour. She held the baby. She knew everybody.
Nurse -> Oh, that's lovely.
Caller -> It was wonderful. I took a picture. She was smiling.
Caller -> She hates pictures. But she let me.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> I'm so glad you have that.
Caller -> Me too. My son brought his guitar and played her favorite song. She mouthed the words.
Nurse -> What song?
Caller -> Moon River. She's loved it since she was a girl.
Nurse -> A good one.
Caller -> We play it on the little speaker by her bed.
Caller -> My father used to hum it. He passed in two thousand ten. She still does it sometimes in her sleep.
Nurse -> That's very sweet.
Caller -> Okay. I'm tearing up. Sorry.
Caller -> It's been a long week.
Nurse -> Take a moment.
Nurse -> No need to apologize.
Nurse -> Let me get her chart up. Annika, what's your mom's date of birth?
Caller -> January thirtieth. Nineteen thirty eight. She'll be eighty nine in January. If she makes it.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. And what's a good number to reach you?
Caller -> You have it. It's in her chart. It's the same one. Use the number on file.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll use the number on file.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Have you noticed any changes in her breathing, her color, her hands or feet?
Caller -> Not really. She's breathing the same. Her hands are a little cool, but she's under a blanket. They've been like that for a while.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know.
Caller -> I keep a blanket on her feet. The wool one.
Caller -> Should I be worried about the sleeping?
Nurse -> It's a normal change as the body slows down. You're doing the right thing by being with her. I'd like a nurse to come see her Thursday. To check on her and see how you're doing.
Caller -> Thursday? That would be great. Morning or afternoon?
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning, and they'll call before they come.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll make coffee.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best way to welcome a nurse.
Caller -> I know. I learned from the last one. She drinks it black.
Nurse -> Smart.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> In the meantime, offer her small amounts of her favorite foods and sips of fluid, but don't force her to eat or drink. It's all right if she only takes a little.
Caller -> Small amounts. Favorites. Don't force. Okay. That's a relief. I was afraid I was doing something wrong.
Nurse -> You're not. You're doing so well.
Caller -> Thank you. I needed to hear that.
Nurse -> For her mouth, use a small swab dipped in water to moisten her lips and mouth. And put a little lip balm on, so her lips don't crack.
Caller -> A swab. Water. Lip balm. We have those pink swabs. The sponge ones. And the balm.
Nurse -> Perfect. Use them often.
Caller -> I keep them in a cup on the nightstand.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do it every time I check on her.
Nurse -> That's good.
Caller -> Is it okay if I sit with her at night? My husband says I should sleep.
Nurse -> It's okay. But try to rest too. Even a nap.
Caller -> I nap on the couch next to her bed. I have a pillow there already.
Nurse -> Good. You need rest too.
Caller -> My husband says that every day.
Nurse -> Perfect. Is there anything else on your mind?
Caller -> No. I think that's it. Just wanted to talk to someone who knows.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called. Anytime.
Caller -> Thank you, Beatrix. Have a good evening.
Nurse -> You too, Annika. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tamarack Home Health, this is Rosario.
Caller -> Hi, Rosario. This is Desmond Lockhart. I'm calling about my mother, Prudence Lockhart. I'm not sure if she took her insulin last night. It's the bedtime one.
Nurse -> Hi, Desmond. Is your mother with you right now?
Caller -> She's in the other room. She doesn't know I'm calling. Well, she knows. She rolled her eyes.
Nurse -> Ha. That's all right.
Nurse -> Hi, Desmond. Thank you for calling. Let's figure this out. Which insulin is it?
Caller -> Lantus. The pen. Twenty units at bedtime. Every night.
Nurse -> Okay. Lantus, twenty units, at bedtime. And what makes you unsure?
Caller -> Yes. It's the long acting one. She takes it at ten.
Caller -> So I stayed over last night. I was on the couch. And around ten, she said she was going to bed and she took her pen in the bedroom. This morning, she said, I took it, Desmond, don't fuss. But then I went in her room and the cap was on the nightstand. Not on the pen. And her log is empty for last night.
Nurse -> Take your time. Walk me through it.
Nurse -> Okay. So she says she took it, but the cap was off and the log was blank.
Caller -> No, wait. The cap was off the pen, on the nightstand. I mean, that's what she does when she takes it. She takes the cap off, leaves it. But she always writes it down. Always. The log is blank.
Nurse -> Okay. Does she ever forget to write it down?
Caller -> Sometimes. Maybe once a week. But not usually. She's very good with the log. She has a red pen.
Nurse -> Ha. A red pen. Good system.
Caller -> It's a system she started when my father was alive.
Nurse -> Have you asked her again this morning?
Caller -> I did. First she said yes. Then I said, are you sure, and she said, I think so. Then I said, did you feel the pen click, and she said, I don't remember. So now I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. That's very helpful. Is the pen with you? Can you look at the dial?
Caller -> I feel silly. It's one pen and I can't keep track of it.
Nurse -> It isn't silly. This is exactly the kind of thing to call about.
Caller -> Hang on. I'm going to get it. It's in the kitchen. I put it in the fridge, I think.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm stepping over the dog.
Nurse -> No hurry.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I have it. It's the purple one. There's a little window with a number. It says, um, it's blank. I mean, it says zero.
Nurse -> The dial reads zero. That's normal after a dose, or if it was never dialed. It doesn't tell us either way.
Caller -> Right. So no help.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. It would be nice if it kept a memory.
Nurse -> Right. Let's go through how she's doing. Did you check her sugar this morning?
Caller -> Yes. At seven. It was two hundred twelve.
Nurse -> Two hundred twelve. Is that high for her?
Caller -> It's higher than usual. She's normally around one thirty, one forty in the morning. So this is higher.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything unusual she ate yesterday?
Caller -> Dinner was spaghetti. With the bread. She had a second helping. And a cookie.
Nurse -> Okay. That could be part of it.
Nurse -> Okay. How is she feeling?
Caller -> She's okay. A little thirsty. She asked for a second glass of water at breakfast. That's not like her.
Nurse -> Any nausea, vomiting, belly pain?
Caller -> No. None of that. She ate her toast and her egg.
Caller -> She does the same thing every morning. Eggs, toast, coffee. Sometimes it's decaf.
Nurse -> Is she confused or unusually sleepy?
Caller -> No. She's sharp. She was doing the crossword while we were talking. She corrected my spelling.
Nurse -> Ha. Good. And has she had any other medicines this morning?
Caller -> I laid them out in the little tray. Seven compartments. Morning, noon, evening, bed.
Caller -> Her pills. She took them. I watched.
Nurse -> Okay. Desmond, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> July seventh. Nineteen fifty four.
Nurse -> And a number for you?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one four nine.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one four nine. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Caller -> I'll keep the volume up.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I don't know for sure if she took the dose, and neither do you. I can't tell you to give more, and I can't tell you to skip. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, and ask them what to do.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I just don't want to hurt her. If I give it and she already had it, that's a double dose.
Nurse -> Exactly. That's the concern. That's why please don't give an extra dose to make up for it. Wait for the clinician.
Caller -> Okay. I won't give anything. What if she goes high?
Nurse -> Good question.
Nurse -> That's what the clinician will weigh. I'll call you back within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll stay by the phone.
Caller -> I'm in the kitchen. The reception is good in here.
Nurse -> In the meantime, recheck her sugar in two hours. Write it down. And have her drink water.
Caller -> Two hours. Water. Write it down. Okay. That would be nine. I'll set an alarm.
Nurse -> That alarm is a good idea.
Caller -> My phone has a hundred alarms. One more won't hurt.
Nurse -> Good. If it keeps climbing, tell me when I call back.
Caller -> I'll write each number next to the time. On the back of the envelope.
Nurse -> That works.
Caller -> Will do.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to come out tomorrow, and go through the insulin routine with her. Maybe set up a better way to track it.
Caller -> That would be great. Honestly, I think she might be forgetting more. She's seventy two.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. The nurse can look at that, too.
Caller -> She would hate it if she knew I said that.
Nurse -> I understand. It's a hard thing to say about a parent.
Caller -> It really is.
Nurse -> It stays between us and the team.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Desmond, call 911 if she gets confused, has repeated vomiting, has trouble breathing, or if her meter just says high.
Caller -> Confused. Vomiting. Breathing. The meter says high. Okay. I'm writing it on the fridge whiteboard.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I take the pen away? Or leave it with her?
Nurse -> Leave it where it is. The clinician will say.
Caller -> I'll tape a note on it. Do not use. She will roll her eyes at that too.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine.
Caller -> Okay. I'll leave it in the fridge door. She'll look for it.
Nurse -> That's fine. Just don't have her give any until we call.
Caller -> Got it.
Nurse -> Is she nearby right now?
Caller -> I can see her through the doorway. She keeps looking over at me.
Nurse -> She can tell you're worried.
Caller -> Yes. She keeps asking if I'm okay.
Caller -> She's in the living room. Doing her puzzle.
Nurse -> Good. Keep an eye on her.
Caller -> She just asked me what I'm doing on the phone. I said work stuff.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I will. I took the day off.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Caller -> I figured. I'd rather be here.
Nurse -> Does she mind?
Caller -> She pretends to. She made me a sandwich, so I think she's happy.
Nurse -> Anything else you want to tell me?
Caller -> Not really. I just wanted to make sure I did the right thing by calling.
Nurse -> You did.
Caller -> No. I just feel bad. I should have been more careful.
Nurse -> You're being careful now. That's what counts.
Caller -> I try. My sister says I hover.
Nurse -> A little hovering is allowed today.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll page now. Talk to you soon.
Caller -> Okay. Thanks, Rosario.
Nurse -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Bayberry Home Health, this is Lucio.
Caller -> Hi, Lucio. This is Marisela Dunleavy. I'm a patient. I'm running low on my gabapenton and the pharmacy told me no refills. I need to talk to somebody.
Nurse -> Hi, Marisela. Thanks for calling. Let me get this straight. Your gabapentin, the nerve pain medicine?
Caller -> Sorry. I'm a little frazzled. I've been on hold with the pharmacy twice.
Nurse -> That's frustrating. Let's sort it out.
Caller -> Yes. The gabapenton. For my feet. I've been on it for two years.
Nurse -> Okay. Two years. That's a long time.
Caller -> Feels like longer.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the dose, and how often do you take it?
Caller -> Three hundred milligrams. Three times a day. Morning, afternoon, and bed. I took my morning one at eight.
Nurse -> Three hundred, three times a day. And how many pills do you have left?
Caller -> I counted last night. I have six. That's two days. Tomorrow and the day after. Then I run out.
Nurse -> Good that you counted.
Caller -> I count them every Sunday. It's a habit.
Nurse -> Okay. And what did the pharmacy say?
Caller -> I called this morning. The girl said there are no refills left on it. She said I need a new prescription from the doctor. She said it would take a couple of days. A couple of days. I don't have a couple of days.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> I understand. We'll see what we can do. Have you missed any doses lately?
Caller -> No. I'm very good. I take them. I have an alarm on my phone. I haven't missed one.
Nurse -> Good. That helps. How are your feet right now?
Caller -> Burning. The bottoms. Both of them. Like they're on a hot stove. It's about a five right now, because I took my pill. When it wears off it goes up.
Nurse -> Okay. A five out of ten. That's when you're on it.
Caller -> Right. I'm afraid of what it'll be like without it.
Caller -> Last time I was out for a day, I couldn't sleep. At all.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. We won't let that happen if we can help it.
Nurse -> That's a very reasonable worry. Let's not let it get there.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> What's your date of birth, so I can pull up the chart?
Caller -> October second. Nineteen sixty five.
Nurse -> Thank you. And the best number?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, oh one six nine.
Nurse -> Nine one eight, five five five, oh one six nine. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll send a refill request to your doctor's office today, marked as urgent, since you only have two days.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. That would be wonderful.
Nurse -> Of course.
Nurse -> I'll also call the pharmacy and confirm where the refill stands. They may already have a request in.
Caller -> They said they sent one. Last week. And they didn't hear back.
Nurse -> That's helpful to know. I'll mention that.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> I'll call you tomorrow to let you know where it stands.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time?
Nurse -> Around noon.
Caller -> Okay. I'll be home. I'm not going anywhere. With these feet.
Caller -> I can hear the phone from the couch. It's right next to me.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep taking your gabapentin three times a day, like you have been. Don't stop it suddenly, and don't stretch the doses to make it last. Stopping suddenly can cause problems.
Caller -> Don't stop it. Don't stretch it. Okay. I wasn't going to. But I was thinking about it. Taking two a day, to make it last.
Nurse -> Please don't do that. Take it as prescribed. If it comes down to the wire, call me.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you for telling me that.
Nurse -> Of course. Are you doing anything else for your feet? Soaks, socks?
Caller -> Cotton socks. And I keep them elevated. I have a heating pad but it makes it worse.
Nurse -> Okay. Skip the heating pad. Warm things can burn feet that can't feel it well.
Caller -> I know. I put it away. It's under the bed.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> It was my mother's. Fifty years old. It still works.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> My sister says I should try some cream. The capsaicin. Do you think that works?
Nurse -> Some people find it helps. Ask the doctor before you try it.
Caller -> I will. I'll ask at the appointment.
Nurse -> When is your next appointment?
Caller -> December. The ninth. I think.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> I wrote it on the calendar. With a star.
Caller -> I'm sorry to be a bother.
Nurse -> You're not a bother at all. This is what I'm here for.
Caller -> Thank you, Lucio. You've made me feel better already.
Nurse -> Good. Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Aspen Row Home Care, this is Yvette.
Caller -> Hi, Yvette. It's Tobias Underhill. I'm a caregiver for Genevieve Pomeroy. I think something's wrong at her house. I think her grandson is hurting her.
Nurse -> Tobias, thank you for calling. I'm listening. Are you with her right now?
Caller -> Thank you for picking up. I almost didn't call.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did.
Caller -> No. I'm in my car. I just left. I finished my shift at seven. I sat in the driveway for ten minutes before I called. I didn't want to leave her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she safe right now? Is the grandson there?
Caller -> He was there when I left. He's in the other room with the TV loud. She was in her recliner. She was okay. She was quiet.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there immediate danger? Do you think someone needs to go there right now?
Caller -> I don't think so. Not right this minute. I don't think he'd hurt her tonight. But I'm worried. That's why I'm calling.
Nurse -> Okay. Tell me what you saw.
Caller -> I have to say it in order or I'll lose my place. Is that okay?
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I was helping her change her shirt. She has a bruise. On her upper arm. The left one. It's purple and yellow. And it's shaped like, like fingers. Four marks on one side and one on the other. Like somebody grabbed her.
Nurse -> A bruise like fingermarks, on her left upper arm. Did she tell you how she got it?
Caller -> I asked. She said she bumped it on the door. But she wouldn't look at me. And the marks don't fit a door.
Nurse -> Did she fall?
Caller -> No. I asked that too. She said no. She said she didn't fall. She's very steady on her walker.
Nurse -> Okay. What else did you notice?
Caller -> I keep going over it in my head.
Caller -> When the grandson came in the kitchen, she flinched. I saw it. Her whole body went stiff. And he yelled at her. About the dinner. He said, why isn't this ready. In front of me. Like I wasn't there.
Nurse -> How did she respond?
Caller -> She said sorry. She said sorry, sweetheart. She kept apologizing. And she got quiet and went to her chair. She didn't talk to me for the rest of the shift.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else?
Caller -> Hold on. I'm checking the road. I'm still parked at the corner.
Caller -> He took her bank card. She told me. She said, he has my card, I don't know why. He said he'd pay the bills. And she says she has no money for her own groceries. I buy her oranges sometimes.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he live with her?
Caller -> I'd say that the house feels different since he moved in. Quieter.
Caller -> Yes. He moved in last spring. He's thirty four. I don't know what he does. He's there all day.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me all this. You did the right thing.
Caller -> I'm so worried. I didn't know if I should call you or the police.
Nurse -> You called the right place. I'm going to take this seriously, and the team will too.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Tobias, I need a few details. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> September eighteenth. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, oh one nine one.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, oh one nine one. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep it on.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what happens next. I'm going to send a message to the supervising team tonight about the bruise and what you observed. They'll decide how to proceed.
Caller -> Okay. Is she going to get in trouble?
Caller -> I just keep thinking she'll be scared if people show up.
Nurse -> No. She's not in trouble. Our job is to keep her safe.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> We'll be gentle with her.
Nurse -> I'm also putting in a referral to our social worker. They work with older adults who may be hurt or having money taken.
Caller -> Social worker. Okay. That's good. She needs somebody.
Nurse -> And I'd like a nurse to see her tomorrow. To look at the bruise, and to talk with her alone if possible.
Caller -> Alone. Good. Because when he's in the house she won't say anything.
Nurse -> I understand. The nurse will find a way.
Caller -> I'm there tomorrow at eight. Do you want me to stay when the nurse comes?
Nurse -> The team will contact you about that. For now, keep doing your regular shift.
Caller -> Okay. Will do.
Caller -> I'll act like nothing is wrong. I'm good at that. I was in theater in school.
Nurse -> Ha. That'll help.
Nurse -> Tobias, please don't confront the grandson. Stay calm, and treat everything as normal. Write down what you see and hear, with the date and time. And if she is ever in immediate danger, call 911 right away.
Caller -> Don't confront. Stay calm. Write it down. Call 911 if she's in danger. Okay. I have a notebook in the car. I'll write it tonight while it's fresh.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Caller -> I took a picture of the bruise. Is that okay? She said yes.
Nurse -> Don't send it from your phone. Keep it, and tell the team that you have it. They'll tell you what to do.
Caller -> Okay. I'll keep it safe. I won't show anyone.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Thank you for believing me.
Nurse -> Of course. Thank you for being such a good caregiver.
Caller -> I love her. She calls me her boy. She knits me a scarf every year.
Nurse -> She's lucky to have you.
Caller -> I hope she's okay tonight.
Nurse -> Me too. Call back if anything changes.
Caller -> I will. Thank you.

Nurse -> Maple Hollow Pediatric Home Care, this is Jerome.
Caller -> Hi, Jerome. This is Chiamaka Okonkwo. I'm calling about my son Tavish Okonkwo. He's seven. He's on an antibiotic for his ear and I have a question about whether he still needs it.
Nurse -> Hi, Chiamaka. Sure. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> Sorry about the time. I just got the kids settled.
Nurse -> No problem. The evening line is open until midnight.
Caller -> Good to know. I always forget that.
Caller -> So he was diagnosed Monday. A double ear infection. The doctor gave us amoxicillin, the liquid. It's day five. Today. And honestly he's fine. He's totally back to himself.
Nurse -> That's good news. Which day is it of how many?
Caller -> I wrote it on the calendar. With an X for every day. Tavish likes making the X.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a nice way to keep track.
Caller -> Five of ten. Ten days. That's what the bottle says. But he's playing soccer in the yard and he's eating dinner and he isn't complaining about his ear at all. So I'm wondering, do I really have to give the rest?
Nurse -> Good question. I'm glad you asked instead of just stopping. Let me ask a few things first.
Caller -> Okay. Sure.
Nurse -> I just want to make sure I give you the right answer.
Nurse -> What is the dose, and how often are you giving it?
Caller -> Seven and a half milliliters. Twice a day. Morning and night. I measure it with the little syringe that came with it.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. And what does the label say for the strength?
Caller -> Four hundred milligrams per five milliliters. That's what it says on the front. I don't know what that means exactly. I just follow the dose.
Nurse -> That's the concentration. It's how much medicine is in each five milliliters. So seven and a half milliliters is about six hundred milligrams in a dose. You're following it right.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. That helps. I always wondered.
Nurse -> It confuses a lot of people. Did he get this morning's dose?
Caller -> I thought I was the only one.
Nurse -> You're definitely not.
Caller -> Yes. At seven thirty. With his cereal. I gave it at seven thirty last night too. So he's on track.
Nurse -> Good. A regular schedule helps.
Caller -> It's the only time the house is calm. Before the bus.
Nurse -> Good. Now, how are the ears? You said he isn't complaining.
Caller -> He's been telling me about a video he saw. Something about a shark. I couldn't follow.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good sign. He's chatty.
Caller -> Right. The pain's gone. Mostly. At bedtime he tugs at the left one a little. Just tugging. He doesn't cry or anything. He did that the first night too. Maybe it's a habit.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to hear.
Nurse -> Okay. A little tugging at bedtime. Any fever?
Caller -> I took his temperature a few minutes ago. Ninety nine point one. Under the arm. He said he feels hot but it's not hot.
Nurse -> Ninety nine point one is not a fever. Any drainage from the ear? Fluid, pus, anything on the pillow?
Caller -> He said he felt hot. I think he just wants to stay up.
Nurse -> Ha. Probably.
Caller -> No. The pillow's clean. I checked it this morning. Nothing in the ear. He hasn't had a fever since Tuesday.
Nurse -> Good. Is he taking anything else for pain or fever?
Caller -> I also gave him a big glass of water at dinner. I'm trying to push fluids.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> The Motrin. The children's liquid. Five milliliters when he needs it. I gave it last night before bed. Just once. Not today.
Nurse -> Okay. Motrin, five milliliters, as needed, every six hours. Last given last night.
Caller -> Right. I haven't needed it today.
Caller -> He didn't even ask for it. I almost wish he would, so I'd know he's okay.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand that feeling.
Nurse -> That's a good sign. Let me get his chart. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Take your time. I'm on the couch. The house is finally quiet.
Caller -> March twenty second. Twenty nineteen.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, oh one one three.
Nurse -> Four oh four, five five five, oh one one three. Right?
Caller -> Oh, wait. It's my cell. The home phone is disconnected.
Nurse -> That's fine. The cell it is.
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay, now to your question. It's very natural to wonder. The answer is, yes, please finish all ten days.
Caller -> All ten. Even though he's better.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense. I just hate giving him medicine. He makes a face.
Nurse -> What does he do?
Caller -> He holds his nose and says, I'm being brave. Every time.
Nurse -> Ha. A brave guy.
Nurse -> Even though he's better. The medicine starts working in the first couple of days, so he feels fine. But the bacteria aren't all gone yet. If you stop now, the infection can come back, and it can be harder to treat.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't know that. My mother always said stop when they feel better. She said you save the rest for next time.
Nurse -> A lot of people grew up with that idea. But it's not right. Don't save leftovers.
Caller -> She also says to put onions in his socks.
Nurse -> Ha. I've heard that one too.
Caller -> I draw the line.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her. She'll argue. She's very opinionated.
Nurse -> Ha. Tell her the nurse said so.
Caller -> She respects anyone in scrubs. Even the pizza guy once.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I will. I'll blame you.
Nurse -> Please do.
Caller -> She's already texting me. She wants to know if he's wearing a hat.
Nurse -> Ha. Grandmothers.
Caller -> What if he forgets, or I miss one? Like if we're out late.
Nurse -> Give it as soon as you remember, then go back to your usual times. Don't double up.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> I'll put a reminder on my phone for the night dose. I always forget it when it's a late evening.
Nurse -> Let me go over the medicine with you so we're sure. Shake the bottle well before every dose. Measure seven and a half milliliters with the oral syringe, not a kitchen spoon. Keep the bottle in the refrigerator. And give it with food, about twelve hours apart.
Caller -> Shake. Syringe. Fridge. With food. Twelve hours. Yes. Do I have to refrigerate? I left it on the counter today.
Nurse -> Yes. It should be in the refrigerator. If it's been out for a few hours it's probably fine. Put it back now.
Caller -> I'm standing up. Going to the fridge. Hang on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. It's in the door, next to the milk.
Caller -> Okay. I'll do that as soon as we hang up. It's right next to me.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll wait.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Also, the syringe is stained pink. Is that okay?
Nurse -> It's fine. Rinse it with warm water after each use. And let it air dry.
Caller -> It was pink from the start. They gave us a free one with the bottle.
Caller -> Okay. I do rinse it. I just don't dry it well. I'll put it on a napkin.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Caller -> He gets a little loose in the stomach. A little soft. Is that from the medicine?
Nurse -> That can happen with this kind of antibiotic. Soft stools are common. It's something to mention if it's watery, or goes on after the course is done.
Caller -> Okay. It's soft. Not watery. Twice a day maybe. He thinks it's funny.
Nurse -> Ha. Seven year olds.
Caller -> He told his sister that his poop was a gift to the toilet.
Nurse -> Ha. Poetry.
Caller -> Everything's funny. Especially anything to do with bathrooms.
Nurse -> I know. I have a nephew.
Caller -> I can tell.
Caller -> How old is he?
Nurse -> Eight. He's obsessed with a game I can't pronounce.
Caller -> Ha. Mine too. It's like they all play the same thing.
Caller -> Then you understand.
Nurse -> Completely. Chiamaka, please keep checking his temperature if he feels warm. And write down each time you give the Motrin, with the time. That way you'll know when he can have the next one.
Caller -> Temperature if warm. Write down the Motrin and the time. Okay. I have a notebook by the fridge. A pink one.
Nurse -> Good. You'll be a pro by tomorrow.
Caller -> I hope so. I've been doing this for years and I still feel like I'm winging it.
Nurse -> Most parents do.
Caller -> I hope so. I'm so tired. I've had a cold myself. I've been coughing since Sunday.
Nurse -> I'm sorry to hear that. Get some rest if you can.
Caller -> I would love to. Two kids. A husband who works nights. You know.
Nurse -> I do. It's a lot.
Caller -> It is. But I'm okay. Thanks for asking.
Nurse -> You're welcome. I'd like to follow up with you after the weekend. I'll call you Friday to see how he's doing and make sure the doses are going well.
Caller -> Friday. Okay. What time?
Nurse -> Mid morning, around ten.
Caller -> I'll set an alarm so I don't miss your call. I have a thing with phones and the laundry.
Nurse -> Ha. Same.
Caller -> Ten works. I'll be home. The kids are at school then.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Is there anything I should look for before then?
Nurse -> Yes. Call us if he gets a fever, if the ear pain comes back, if you see any drainage from the ear, if he gets a rash, or if the loose stools get worse or last.
Caller -> Fever. Ear pain. Drainage. Rash. Stools get worse. Okay. Rash. Like hives?
Nurse -> Any rash, or itching, or swelling of the face or lips. If his lips swell or he has trouble breathing, call 911 right away.
Caller -> Okay. He's had amoxicillin before, when he was three. No reaction. But I'll watch.
Nurse -> That's good to know. Thank you.
Caller -> Is soccer okay? He wants to go to practice tomorrow.
Nurse -> Sure. Ask him how his ears feel first.
Nurse -> If he feels well and has no fever, that's fine.
Caller -> Okay. He'll be thrilled. He's been moping about missing the game Saturday.
Nurse -> Hopefully he can play it.
Caller -> He has his cleats by the door already. He sleeps with one of his shin guards.
Nurse -> That's dedication.
Caller -> Fingers crossed. His coach is very strict about attendance.
Nurse -> Ha. Hopefully he gets to play.
Nurse -> Ha. Soccer coaches.
Caller -> This one blows a whistle at everything. Even at snack time.
Caller -> Anything else I need to know?
Nurse -> I think we covered it. Call anytime if you have questions.
Caller -> Thank you, Jerome. You made me feel better. I was ready to quit the medicine tonight.
Nurse -> I'm glad you called first. Take care of yourself, too.
Caller -> Me too. I'll tell my husband when he gets home from work.
Nurse -> Please do. Good night to you both.
Caller -> I will. Good night.
Caller -> Thanks again. Sleep well.
Nurse -> Good night.

transcript:
Nurse -> Greywell Home Health, this is Dolores.
Caller -> Dolores, it's Rhoda Whitcombe. My husband Alistair Whitcombe. He can't breathe. He woke up gasping and he can't lie down. I don't know what to do.
Nurse -> Rhoda, take a breath. I'm right here with you.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm trying. I can't think.
Nurse -> Rhoda, I'm here. Is he awake? Can he talk to you?
Caller -> He's awake. He's sitting on the edge of the bed. He's, he's gulping air. Alistair, can you tell her? He can't talk. He can only say a word or two.
Nurse -> Okay. Keep him sitting up.
Caller -> Yes. He won't lie down. He keeps pushing me away.
Nurse -> Okay. When did this start?
Caller -> About half an hour ago. He woke up at two thirty with this terrible gasp. Like he was drowning. He sat straight up. He couldn't catch his breath. And it hasn't stopped.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Or maybe forty minutes. I looked at the clock when I woke up and then I forgot.
Nurse -> Rhoda, I'm going to ask you to do something in a moment. First, is he coughing anything up?
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Hurry.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Pink. It's pink and foamy. Like froth. He coughed it into a tissue. I'm looking at it. It's pink. It's like strawberry milkshake. Oh my God.
Nurse -> Okay. I hear you.
Caller -> I'm sorry I'm yelling. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Is there chest pain?
Caller -> Alistair, do you have chest pain? He's shaking his head. No. He says no. Just can't breathe.
Caller -> Alistair, tell her. Tell her. He's shaking his head again.
Nurse -> That's fine. Thank you.
Nurse -> Do you have the pulse oximeter, the finger clip?
Caller -> Yes. It's on the nightstand. Hold on. I put it on his finger. It's beeping. It says eighty four. Eighty four. That's low, isn't it?
Nurse -> Yes, that's low. Rhoda, I need you to call 911 right now. Hang up with me and call 911. Tell them he cannot breathe. Then call me back.
Caller -> What? Say that again. I'm sorry. Say it again.
Nurse -> Call 911 right now. Say your husband can't breathe.
Caller -> Right now? Right now? Okay. But wait. Wait, what's his pulse? It says one hundred eighteen. It went up. It was ninety this afternoon.
Caller -> I'm so sorry. I'm just scared.
Nurse -> I know. It's okay to be scared. Now call.
Nurse -> Rhoda. Rhoda, listen to me. That doesn't matter right now. Call 911. Please. This is an emergency.
Caller -> Okay. I'm sorry. Calling.
Caller -> Okay. I'm listening. I'm listening.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm calling. I'm hanging up. Wait, can you stay on the phone?
Nurse -> Don't hang up on me. Put me on speaker.
Caller -> Right. Right. Speaker. Where's the button? Here. Okay, you're on speaker.
Nurse -> I will stay on the line while you call 911 from another phone. Do you have a second phone?
Caller -> I have the cell. And the house phone. I'll use the house phone. It's in the kitchen.
Nurse -> No. Don't leave him. Use your cell. Put me on speaker, and put 911 on the cell.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm doing it. I'm dialing.
Caller -> Do I put the phone down? Where do I put it?
Nurse -> Put me on the bed next to you. Keep both hands free.
Caller -> Is nine one one the right number? Of course it is. Sorry.
Nurse -> It's the right number. Go ahead.
Nurse -> Good. Keep me on the speaker.
Caller -> It's ringing. It's ringing. Hello? Yes. My husband can't breathe. He has heart failure. We're at, oh. Alistair, what's the address? Forty one Larkin Road. Yes. Larkin. L A R K I N.
Nurse -> Good. Tell them his oxygen is eighty four.
Caller -> They want me to say it again. The address.
Nurse -> Say it clearly. Slowly.
Caller -> His oxygen is eighty four. He's coughing up pink foam. Yes. Yes, I'll stay on. Okay. They say stay on with them. They're sending an ambulance. They said ten minutes.
Nurse -> Good. Rhoda, stay with 911. I'll stay with you until they say you can hang up. Tell me when they've said it's all right to talk to me.
Caller -> They keep asking me questions. I can't answer and talk to you at the same time.
Nurse -> Answer them. I can wait.
Caller -> They said I can put them on speaker too. I'll put both. I have two phones.
Caller -> The dog is barking. Hold on. Sit! Sit, Biscuit! Sorry.
Nurse -> That's okay.
Nurse -> That works.
Caller -> Dolores, what do I do for him? What do I do right now?
Caller -> I feel so useless.
Nurse -> You're not useless. You're doing everything right.
Nurse -> Sit him upright, with his feet down on the floor. Not lying back. Keep him calm. Talk quietly to him. Unlock the front door for the crew. And don't give him anything to eat or drink.
Caller -> Upright. Feet down. Calm. Unlock the door. Nothing to eat or drink. Okay. Alistair, sit up. Feet on the floor. You're doing fine. It's okay, honey. Help is coming.
Nurse -> Good. Rhoda, is his oxygen machine on? The home oxygen?
Caller -> The what? Oh. The oxygen. Hold on, I'm thinking.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> He has the concentrator. It's in the living room. He's not wearing it right now. Should I get it?
Nurse -> Is the tubing long enough to reach the bedroom?
Caller -> No. It's too short. He'd have to walk to it. He can't walk.
Nurse -> Okay. Don't move him. The crew will bring oxygen.
Caller -> Dolores, I think I hear his breathing getting louder.
Nurse -> That's okay. Keep him upright. They're almost there.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Alistair, they're going to bring oxygen. Hold on.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. He's looking at me. He's scared. I'm scared.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> I've never seen him like this. Never. Not once in forty years.
Nurse -> I know. You're doing exactly the right thing. Stay with him. Hold his hand.
Caller -> I keep wanting to put him on the bed. But I won't.
Nurse -> Good. Sitting up is right.
Caller -> I'm holding it. It's wet. He's sweating. His hand is clammy.
Nurse -> That's okay. Keep holding it.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. Now, has he taken his medicines today? Especially his water pill?
Caller -> Medicines. Medicines. Why are you asking about medicines?
Nurse -> The crew will ask. I want you to be ready.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Caller -> He takes the furosemide. Forty milligrams. Every morning. He took it yesterday morning. Today he hasn't yet, because it's the middle of the night.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he miss any days this week?
Caller -> No. I give it to him. He's very regular. But he had pizza on Tuesday. And chips. He loves chips. I told him no.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful to know.
Caller -> I don't know why I'm telling you about the pizza.
Nurse -> It's all right. Whatever you remember helps.
Caller -> Is it because of the chips? Did I do something wrong?
Nurse -> No. Rhoda, no. This is not your fault. Please don't think that.
Caller -> He always said I worry too much. This time I didn't worry enough.
Nurse -> That isn't true.
Caller -> I should have taken the chips.
Nurse -> Rhoda. Rhoda. Stay with me here.
Caller -> I'm here. I'm here.
Nurse -> You didn't do anything wrong.
Caller -> Alistair, you're okay. The ambulance is coming. Okay. Okay. Sorry. What did you say?
Caller -> What time is it? Is it three? I can't see the clock.
Nurse -> It doesn't matter. Stay with him.
Nurse -> I said it's not your fault. Now, what's his date of birth? The crew will ask.
Caller -> December eighth. Nineteen fifty five.
Nurse -> And your number, in case we get cut off?
Caller -> Two one two, five five five, oh one eight seven.
Nurse -> Two one two, five five five, oh one eight seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'm using it. And the house phone for 911.
Nurse -> Okay. Now, can you gather his medicine list and his pill bottles into a bag? Quickly. And his oxygen tubing and the portable oxygen if you have it. Just put them near the door.
Caller -> I can't leave him. He's right here.
Nurse -> Don't leave him. Is there anything within arm's reach? A bag, or a basket?
Caller -> No. It's in the kitchen. The bag is in the kitchen.
Nurse -> Then wait. When the crew arrives, tell them to bring the bag. Or have a neighbor, someone.
Caller -> My son is on his way. He lives eight minutes away. I called him first. Before you. I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Good. What's his name?
Caller -> Cormac. He'll know what to bring.
Nurse -> That's all right. He can bring the bag.
Caller -> He's coming. He'll be here in a few minutes.
Nurse -> Good. Then you won't be alone with the crew.
Caller -> He's very calm. He's an electrician. He doesn't panic.
Nurse -> Good. Rhoda, I'm going to page our on-call clinician and tell them he is being taken to the hospital. I'll stay on with you.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Is he still sitting up? Still breathing?
Caller -> What? Yes. Sorry. Yes, he's sitting. Alistair, sit up.
Caller -> Yes. He's still gulping. He's sitting. His lips look a little blue. Is that bad? Dolores?
Nurse -> Tell 911 his lips are turning blue. Tell them now.
Caller -> His lips are turning blue. Yes. Yes, I told them. They say the ambulance is on the way. Almost there.
Caller -> They're asking if the front door is open. Alistair, is the door open? I'll open it. Hold on.
Nurse -> Open the door now if you can do it safely.
Caller -> I can see it from here. It's unlocked. I did it earlier.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him sitting up. Keep talking to him.
Caller -> I am. I am. I'm telling him about the garden. The tomatoes.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep telling him.
Caller -> Alistair, look at me. Look at me. Breathe. Breathe with me. In. Out. In. Out.
Nurse -> Good. Keep talking in a calm voice.
Nurse -> That's good. That's exactly right.
Caller -> My hands are shaking so much.
Nurse -> That's all right. Keep going.
Caller -> I hear something. I hear a siren. Dolores, I hear it. They're here.
Nurse -> Go to the door. Open it. Let them in.
Caller -> Is it all right to leave him? He's sitting.
Nurse -> Yes. The crew is outside. Go.
Caller -> Okay. I'm putting the phone down. I'm opening the door. They're in the driveway. They're here. They're here.
Nurse -> Good. Go. I'm here.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Caller -> They're coming in. Thank you. Thank you, Dolores.
Nurse -> Go ahead. Help them.
Caller -> They have a stretcher. They have oxygen. They're putting the mask on.
Nurse -> Rhoda, tell them everything you told me. His heart failure, the oxygen eighty four, the pink foam, the furosemide.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you. Thank you.
Nurse -> You did everything right. Go be with him.
Caller -> I will. I will. Thank you. I'm sorry I was so loud.
Nurse -> You were perfect.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Windward Home Health, this is Marguerite.
Caller -> Hi, Marguerite. It's Delphine Brockway. My husband is Ignatius Brockway. You were just here Tuesday. I'm calling with a few little things. Nothing terrible.
Nurse -> Hi. How are you holding up today?
Caller -> Oh, I'm fine. A little tired. The usual. How are you?
Nurse -> Doing well, thank you.
Nurse -> Hi, Delphine. Yes, I remember. How is Mr. Brockway doing?
Caller -> I told him I was calling and he said, tell her I'm fine. So that's his report.
Nurse -> Ha. Noted.
Caller -> I hope it's not too late in the day to call.
Nurse -> Not at all. The line is open.
Caller -> Good. I waited until he was down for his rest.
Caller -> He's holding steady. Mostly. A few little things. I wrote them on a list. Do you mind if I read it?
Nurse -> Please. Go ahead.
Caller -> Let me find my glasses. They're on my head. Of course they're on my head.
Nurse -> Ha. We all do that.
Caller -> Okay. Number one is the shaking. His tremor. It's worse in the late afternoon. Around four, five o'clock. The right hand mostly. He can't hold his tea. It spills.
Nurse -> Take it one at a time.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it worse than last week?
Caller -> Hold on. I'm checking my notes. I keep a journal.
Nurse -> That's very helpful.
Caller -> A little. Last week it was only at dinner. Now it starts around four. And he gets frustrated. He throws his hands up.
Nurse -> That's understandable. Let's talk about his medicines. Which ones is he taking for the Parkinson's?
Caller -> He's very proud. He doesn't like to ask for help.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> The Sinemet. One tablet. Three times a day. Eight, noon, and four. He took the noon one today. At twelve.
Nurse -> Okay. Sinemet, one tablet, three times a day. Eight, noon, and four. Does he take it with food?
Caller -> With breakfast. And lunch. Sometimes with a cracker. At four he has tea and a cookie.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll come back to that. What else is on your list?
Caller -> Okay. Just remind me. I'll forget.
Caller -> Number two. His sleep. He's having these dreams. Very vivid. He talks in his sleep. Yesterday he shouted, get the dog off the roof. We don't have a dog.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. That's quite a dream.
Caller -> He has strange dreams a lot lately. Last month it was a train.
Nurse -> Dreams can be odd at this stage.
Caller -> I laughed. But he was upset. He woke up sweating. He kept saying the dog was going to fall.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he seeing things when he's awake? Anything that isn't there?
Caller -> No. Not awake. Only the dreams. He knows where he is. He's sharp. He did the whole crossword this morning.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Number three?
Caller -> He gets embarrassed about it. He says he's going crazy.
Nurse -> He isn't. It's common. We'll talk to the doctor.
Caller -> Number three. Dizzy. When he stands up. He gets lightheaded. Just for a few seconds. He holds the counter. It passes. It happens about once a day.
Nurse -> Go on.
Caller -> Sorry, I keep getting ahead of myself. It's the list. I'm reading too fast.
Nurse -> Okay. Does he faint, or fall?
Caller -> He gets so annoyed when I hover.
Nurse -> It's a hard balance.
Caller -> No falls. Not since the spring. He's careful. He holds on. And I'm always right next to him.
Nurse -> Have you checked his blood pressure?
Caller -> I have. Just now, before I called. Sitting, it was one hundred fourteen over sixty eight.
Nurse -> One fourteen over sixty eight sitting. Did you check it standing?
Caller -> We bought the cuff at the drugstore. It beeps when it's done.
Nurse -> Those are fine. Just keep the arm at heart level.
Caller -> No. I didn't think of that. Should I?
Nurse -> The nurse will check it Monday, both ways. Let's hold that for now.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> I like knowing what the numbers mean. He doesn't. He just says, am I alive?
Nurse -> Ha. That's one way to read it.
Nurse -> What else is on your list?
Caller -> Number four. His bowels. They've been better. He's taking the Miralax. Not every day. When he needs it. He took it yesterday. One capful in juice.
Nurse -> Okay. Miralax, seventeen grams, as needed. Last yesterday. And is he going regularly?
Caller -> Every other day, about. Better than before. It's the prune juice and the walking. He walks the hallway ten times, twice a day.
Nurse -> That's wonderful.
Caller -> He counts in Latin sometimes. He was a teacher.
Nurse -> Oh, that's lovely.
Caller -> I'm very proud of him. He counts out loud. He's so competitive.
Nurse -> You should be. That kind of effort really matters.
Nurse -> That's a good habit. It keeps him focused.
Caller -> He gets to ten and starts over, just to be sure.
Nurse -> Ha. A man with a goal.
Caller -> Number five is just me. I'm tired. But that's not for you. That's for my sister.
Nurse -> Delphine, it is for me too. How are you doing?
Caller -> Oh. Well. Thank you for asking. Nobody asks.
Nurse -> I'm asking.
Caller -> I'm okay. I'm tired. I'm up twice a night with him. I nap in the afternoon.
Caller -> I don't mean to complain. We're lucky, honestly. It could be worse.
Nurse -> You're allowed to be tired.
Nurse -> That's a lot. Do you have help?
Caller -> My daughter comes Saturdays. And a neighbor brings dinner on Wednesdays. It's enough. I think.
Caller -> She brings the grandkids. They climb all over him. He loves it.
Nurse -> Good. Let's make sure you're taking care of yourself too.
Caller -> My daughter says the same. I tell her I'm fine.
Nurse -> Fine is a word we hear a lot.
Caller -> Ha.
Caller -> I'm trying. I joined a walking group. Tuesdays. It's women over seventy. We wear matching hats.
Nurse -> Ha. I love that.
Caller -> We have a group photo. I'll bring it Monday.
Nurse -> Please do. I'd love to see it.
Caller -> The hat is pink. It's very pink.
Nurse -> Perfect. Let me confirm Mr. Brockway's date of birth.
Caller -> I'm reading it back to myself now. Okay, I have it.
Caller -> Sure. I know that one by heart.
Caller -> June fourth. Nineteen fifty two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Seven oh four, five five five, oh one nine six.
Caller -> That's the house line. I forward it to my cell when I'm out.
Nurse -> Good to know.
Nurse -> Seven oh four, five five five, oh one nine six. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Same as always.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Great. Here's what I'll do. I'd like a nurse to come out Monday and see him. Check his blood pressure sitting and standing, and look at the tremor and the sleep.
Caller -> Monday. What time?
Caller -> I want to make sure I'm up and dressed before they come.
Nurse -> You'll have time.
Nurse -> Morning. I'll ask for ten.
Caller -> Ten is perfect. He's best in the morning. After his eight o'clock pill.
Caller -> By afternoon he's wiped out. Especially after four.
Nurse -> That matches what you told me.
Nurse -> Right. And I'm going to send a message to the team about the lightheadedness and the afternoon tremor. The doctor may want to look at the timing of his medicine.
Caller -> I was hoping you'd say that. I think the four o'clock one isn't lasting. And maybe he needs one earlier? I don't know. I'm not the doctor.
Nurse -> You're describing it exactly right. I'll put that in the message.
Caller -> Thank you. I've been rehearsing that all day in my head.
Nurse -> Of course.
Nurse -> It shows.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> For the dizziness, here are some tips. Have him sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before he stands. Rise slowly. And keep a hand on something steady, like the counter or the walker.
Caller -> Sit a minute. Rise slowly. Hold on. Okay. He does the hold on part. The sitting part he forgets. I'll remind him. Out loud. Every time.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> He rolls his eyes, but he does it. Eventually.
Nurse -> Ha. That's all we can ask.
Caller -> I'll write sit first in big letters.
Nurse -> That's great. Out loud works.
Caller -> I got it from the physical therapist. She said say it like you mean it.
Nurse -> She's right.
Caller -> I put a sticky note on the bathroom mirror too. It says, sit first.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Nurse -> About the Sinemet. Try to give it about thirty minutes before meals, with just a small sip of water. And keep the times as steady as you can each day.
Caller -> Thirty minutes before. Small sip. Same times. Okay. We usually give it right with the food. That might be the problem.
Caller -> Do I wake him up for the early one if he's sleeping in?
Nurse -> The nurse can help work out a plan for that on Monday.
Nurse -> It can matter. Protein in a meal can interfere with how it's absorbed. The nurse can go over this on Monday.
Caller -> I'll write that down. Protein. Hm. His lunch is usually a chicken sandwich.
Caller -> I'll have to look at what he eats. It's a lot of cheese.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll sort it out.
Nurse -> That's fine. We just might adjust the timing.
Caller -> Okay. I'm so glad I called.
Caller -> I almost didn't. I thought I was bothering you.
Nurse -> You're not bothering anybody.
Nurse -> Me too. And Delphine, call us if he falls, if he faints, if he starts seeing things when he's awake, if he has trouble swallowing, or if he goes two days without a bowel movement.
Caller -> Fall. Faint. Seeing things. Swallowing. Two days. Okay. I wrote it on the list.
Caller -> The list is on the fridge. Right next to his schedule.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> One last thing. He wants to know if he can go to our grandson's recital Friday. It's two hours. In a church.
Nurse -> Sounds lovely. If he feels well, I'd say yes. Bring his pill, and a seat on the aisle.
Caller -> He wants to wear his good jacket. It's a bit big on him now.
Nurse -> He'll look sharp.
Caller -> He's worried about the stairs. There are four steps up to the sanctuary.
Nurse -> Take your time and use the rail.
Caller -> On the aisle. Good thinking. In case he gets restless.
Nurse -> Exactly. And a water bottle.
Caller -> And a sweater. Churches are cold.
Nurse -> Smart.
Caller -> I'll pack it all. My grandson plays the trumpet. Badly. But with feeling.
Nurse -> Ha. That's the best kind.
Caller -> He practices in the garage. The neighbors hate it.
Nurse -> Ha. Supportive grandparents.
Caller -> It is. Thank you, Marguerite. You're a lifesaver.
Caller -> I feel much better. Honestly. It's good to say it out loud to someone.
Nurse -> That's what we're here for.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care. See you Monday.
Caller -> Please give my best to the rest of the team.
Nurse -> I will.
Caller -> See you Monday. Bye.
