transcript:
Nurse -> Brightwater Home Health, this is Ezekiel.
Caller -> Hi, Ezekiel. It's Imogen Trevino. I'm calling about my father, Osvaldo Trevino. I think my mother gave him the wrong pill and he's very sleepy.
Nurse -> Hi, Imogen. Okay. Let's slow down. Tell me what happened.
Caller -> Sorry. I drove over here and I'm still shaking.
Nurse -> It's all right. Take your time.
Caller -> So my dad takes clonidine for his blood pressure. Point one milligram. Twice a day. My mom does his pills. She got a new bottle from the pharmacy last week. She thought it was the clonidine. I looked at it this morning. It says clonazepam.
Nurse -> Clonazepam. Not clonidine. Let me make sure. Can you spell what's on the label?
Caller -> It's the little brown bottle. The label is faded.
Caller -> C L O N A Z E P A M. Clonazepam. Point five milligrams. It's a different pill. It's for anxiety, I think. My mom said it looked the same. Small, white.
Nurse -> They do have similar names, and they are easy to mix up. How many has he taken?
Caller -> I wish the pharmacy would put them on different shelves.
Nurse -> It's a fair thought.
Caller -> Two. One last night at bedtime, and one this morning around eight. She gave him one each time instead of the clonidine.
Nurse -> Clonazepam, point five milligrams, twice. Last night and this morning at eight. And he hasn't had his clonidine since?
Caller -> No. Not since the day before yesterday. I think. She started the new bottle last week. I'm not sure about the days. She gets confused.
Nurse -> Okay. How is he now?
Caller -> Hold on, I'll go look at him. Okay. He's still in the chair.
Caller -> He's really sleepy. He's in his recliner and he can barely keep his eyes open. When I talk to him he answers slowly. He said, what? Three times. It isn't like him. He's usually sharp.
Nurse -> Okay. Can he wake up when you talk to him, or shake his shoulder?
Caller -> Yes. He wakes up. But he goes right back. He's groggy. He said he feels like he's underwater.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Is he breathing normally? Any slow or shallow breathing?
Caller -> I think it's normal. He's snoring a little. His breathing is regular. His lips are fine. No, they're pink.
Nurse -> Good. That's helpful.
Nurse -> Good. Has he fallen, or hurt himself?
Caller -> No. He hasn't gotten up. He's been in the chair all morning.
Nurse -> Do you have a blood pressure cuff?
Caller -> I do. I just took it. Ninety eight over sixty. That's low for him. He's usually one forty.
Nurse -> Okay. Ninety eight over sixty. That's lower than usual.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you, Imogen. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, I should have said that earlier.
Nurse -> You're fine.
Caller -> March nineteenth. Nineteen forty six.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one one oh.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one one oh. Correct?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, and let them know about the wrong pill, his sleepiness, and the blood pressure.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Please hurry.
Nurse -> I will. I'd also like a nurse to come see him today.
Caller -> Today. Good. I'm here all afternoon. I came over as soon as I saw the bottle.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I called in to work. My boss understood.
Nurse -> Good. In the meantime, please don't give him any more clonazepam. Put both bottles together, the clonazepam and the clonidine, so the nurse can see them. And don't give his clonidine until the clinician says.
Caller -> No more clonazepam. Both bottles together. Wait on the clonidine. Okay. I'm putting them on the kitchen table. I'll put a note on the wrong one.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Caller -> I used a big red marker. WRONG. In capital letters.
Caller -> My mother is very upset. She's crying in the kitchen. She keeps saying she killed him.
Nurse -> Please tell her he is going to be okay. The medicine will wear off, and we are watching him closely. This is a very common mistake.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her. She's going to take it hard.
Nurse -> It's a common mix up. It's not her fault. The pharmacy labels are almost the same.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll hold her hand.
Caller -> She's making tea. She says it'll help. I let her.
Nurse -> That's good. It gives her something to do.
Nurse -> Imogen, call 911 if he becomes hard to wake, if his breathing gets slow, or if his lips turn bluish.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Slow breathing. Blue lips. 911. Okay. I'll check him every few minutes.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him in the chair, upright. Don't let him walk alone.
Caller -> I put a pillow behind him. He didn't complain.
Caller -> I won't. He tried to stand once. I put him back.
Nurse -> Good. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll keep watching. I have the phone in my lap.
Caller -> Is he going to be okay?
Nurse -> From what you tell me, I think so. He needs to be watched, and the clinician needs to weigh in. That's why we're paging.
Caller -> Okay. I'm going to sit by him.
Nurse -> That's right. I'll page now.
Caller -> Okay. I'll stay right here.
Caller -> Thank you, Ezekiel.
Nurse -> You're welcome. I'll be in touch.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Fernbrook Home Health, this is Tamsin.
Caller -> Hi, Tamsin. It's Beatriz Vasconcelos. I'm calling about my father, Lorenzo Vasconcelos. I need to order catheter supplies and I have a question about his urine.
Caller -> Sorry for calling this late, I know it's the evening line.
Nurse -> Hi, Beatriz. How is your father this evening?
Caller -> He's grumpy but fine. The cable is out and it's the end of the world.
Nurse -> Ha. I'll bet.
Nurse -> Hi, Beatriz. Sure. Let's start with the supplies. What are you running low on?
Caller -> Thank you. I made a list but I'm going to ramble.
Nurse -> Ramble away.
Caller -> The leg bags. The ones he wears during the day. There's two left in the box. And the big bags, the ones for overnight. There's one. One. I used the other one last night.
Nurse -> Two leg bags and one overnight bag.
Caller -> I wrote it on a sticky note so I wouldn't forget. It's on my hand now.
Nurse -> Ha. Old school.
Caller -> One overnight bag. Yes. I don't know how I let it get like this. I should have called last week.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> It's all right. How about the other supplies? Skin barrier cream, wipes, tape?
Caller -> I keep them in a bin in the closet. The bin is almost empty, actually.
Nurse -> Okay. We'll fill it.
Caller -> Plenty of those. I have three tubes of the cream. The wipes are fine. It's just the bags.
Nurse -> Okay. And when was the catheter changed last?
Caller -> I wrote that on the calendar. Hold on, let me look.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> He's mumbling something. Dad, I'm talking to the nurse. Yes. She says hi.
Nurse -> Hello, Mr. Vasconcelos.
Caller -> Yes. Three weeks ago, the Tuesday.
Caller -> Three weeks ago. The nurse changed it on a Tuesday. She said it's every four weeks.
Nurse -> Okay. Now tell me about the urine.
Caller -> I wasn't sure how to describe it. I kept looking at it. I think I know what normal looks like.
Nurse -> You do. Go ahead.
Caller -> That's the other thing. Today there's less in the bag. Usually by lunch it's about half full. Today it was barely a quarter at three o'clock. And it looks cloudy. Not clear like normal. Kind of milky.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any blood in it? Any bad smell?
Caller -> He had blood once, in the summer. I remember because I panicked. It was nothing.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me.
Caller -> No blood. I don't think there's a smell. Maybe a little. It's hard to tell. I'm not a good smeller. I had a cold last week.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he drinking much today?
Caller -> I try to put the glass in front of him. He pushes it away.
Nurse -> Ha. Stubborn.
Caller -> Not a lot. He's been lazy about it. He had coffee in the morning and half a glass of juice. That's it. He says he doesn't want to keep going to the bathroom, even though he doesn't have to go anymore. He forgets.
Nurse -> That might be part of it. How is he feeling in general?
Caller -> He's okay. He's cranky because he wants to watch the game and the cable is out.
Nurse -> Which game is it?
Caller -> The Sunday one. He's recording the replay on the other channel.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a crisis.
Caller -> He called the cable company four times. They put him on hold with music.
Nurse -> That's the worst.
Caller -> Big crisis. He's been yelling at the remote.
Nurse -> Does he have a fever? Chills? Belly pain?
Caller -> No fever. I checked. It was normal. No chills. And his belly's soft. I pressed gently and he didn't flinch. He said, stop poking.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring. Beatriz, I'd like his date of birth.
Caller -> I'm still a little worried. I just want to be sure.
Nurse -> That's fair.
Caller -> August twelfth. Nineteen forty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, oh one three six.
Nurse -> Two oh six, five five five, oh one three six. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll place an order with the supply company for leg bags and overnight drainage bags.
Caller -> Okay. I'm ready.
Nurse -> Great. I'll go through it step by step.
Nurse -> Anything else before I go?
Caller -> No, that's everything for tonight.
Caller -> Thank you. How many?
Nurse -> I'll order a month's worth. The chart has his standing amount.
Caller -> Perfect. That'll be a relief.
Caller -> I didn't want to run out in the middle of the night. It happened once before.
Nurse -> That's stressful. Let's avoid it.
Nurse -> I'll arrange delivery tomorrow. Will someone be home?
Caller -> Yes. I'm here. I took the week off. Anytime.
Nurse -> That's a great help to him.
Caller -> It's good to be here. Even if he yells at the remote.
Nurse -> Good. I'm also going to send a message to the team about the lower amount and the cloudy urine.
Caller -> Please. I was afraid to say it. I thought I was overreacting.
Nurse -> You're not. It's the right thing to report.
Caller -> Thank you for saying that. Dad hates when I fuss.
Nurse -> You're doing it right.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> And I'd like a nurse to see him tomorrow. To look at the catheter and the drainage.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Perfect. Morning?
Caller -> He's up early. Five thirty. Every day. The nurse can come whenever.
Nurse -> I'll write that down.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Great.
Nurse -> I'll make a note for the morning.
Nurse -> In the meantime, check that the bag is hanging lower than his bladder. Make sure the tubing isn't kinked, or caught under his leg. And empty the bag when it's about half full.
Caller -> Lower than the bladder. No kinks. Not under him. Empty at half. Okay. Wait. Let me check. He's in the recliner. Hold on.
Nurse -> Yes.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> The tubing. It's under his thigh. Folded a little. Is that it? That could be why it's less?
Nurse -> It could be. Straighten it and see if it drains.
Caller -> I'm moving his leg. Dad, lift your leg. Okay, I moved it. The tubing is straight now. I see urine going down. Yes. It's moving.
Nurse -> Good. That may have been it. Keep watching it for the next hour.
Caller -> I keep forgetting how heavy the bag gets. I'll check it more often.
Caller -> Okay. I will. Thank you. I feel silly.
Nurse -> No need.
Nurse -> Don't. It's an easy thing to miss.
Caller -> I laughed out loud when I saw it.
Nurse -> Ha. Honestly, it happens to everyone.
Caller -> It's always the dumb thing.
Nurse -> Ha. Often it is. Also, offer him water or other fluids through the day, as much as he'll take.
Caller -> Water. Okay. I'll make him tea. He likes the mint one.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Caller -> He drinks it with a straw. Two sips and he says that's enough.
Nurse -> A few sips count.
Caller -> Anything else?
Nurse -> Call us if he gets a fever or chills, belly pain, no urine in the bag for several hours, blood in the urine, or leaking around the catheter.
Caller -> Fever. Chills. Belly pain. No urine for hours. Blood. Leaking. Okay. I have a pen. Let me write it all.
Caller -> I put it in my phone notes too, just in case the paper gets lost.
Nurse -> Smart.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay, got it.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Fridge door. Under the magnet of the lighthouse.
Nurse -> Perfect. The nurse will see him tomorrow either way.
Caller -> I like that. Either way. It makes me feel better.
Nurse -> Good. That's the idea.
Caller -> Good. Thank you so much, Tamsin.
Caller -> I feel so much better having called.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> I'm going to make dinner now. Soup. He actually likes my soup.
Nurse -> Enjoy it.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Tidewater Home Health, this is Casimir.
Caller -> Hi, Casimir. It's Rafaela Ostrowski. I'm a patient. I just got home from the hospital last week. I'm on warfarin and I think I have two different doses and I don't know which is right.
Nurse -> Hi, Rafaela. Thanks for calling. Let's go through it. What does the bottle say?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm a little frazzled. I've been staring at these papers for an hour.
Nurse -> That's okay. Take a breath.
Caller -> The warfarin bottle says four milligrams. No, wait. Five. Five milligrams. Every evening. I'm sorry. I had it in my hand upside down. Five.
Nurse -> Five milligrams, every evening. And what does the discharge paper say?
Caller -> I have the paper right here. It's three pages stapled together.

Nurse -> Thank you. And a number for you?

Nurse -> Heron Point Hospice, this is Leocadia.
Caller -> Hi. It's Odette Delacroix. My father is Augustin Delacroix. I think we might have given him too much lorazepam tonight. Me and my brother both. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> Hi, Odette. You sound shaken. Take a breath.
Caller -> I'm trying. I'm trying. It's four in the morning and my brain is not working.
Nurse -> That's okay. I'm here.
Nurse -> Hi, Odette. Okay. Let's go through it together. First, how is he right now?
Caller -> I should have called an hour ago. I kept going back and forth on whether it was worth waking someone up.
Nurse -> It's always worth it. This is what the night line is for.
Caller -> He's asleep. He's really sleepy. But he wakes up. If I say his name, he opens his eyes and says, what? Then he goes back. He was restless before. Moaning, picking at the sheet. Now he's quiet.
Nurse -> Okay. Is anyone else in the room with him?
Caller -> Just me and Rene. My husband went home with the kids.
Caller -> I turned the light off. There's a little lamp in the corner. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's fine. Keep it dim.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he breathing comfortably?
Caller -> Hold on. Rene, come here. Come stand by him. Okay, Rene's here now.
Caller -> I think so. I'm counting. Hold on. I've got the watch. Twelve. Twelve breaths in a minute. It's slow, but it's even. No noise.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful. Keep counting a little later too.
Caller -> I will.
Caller -> Wait, let me start the timer. Okay. Counting. One. Two.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I'm walking. The kitchen is dark. Where is the light. Okay.
Nurse -> Twelve a minute. Any gurgling, rattling, pauses?
Caller -> No. No rattle. No gurgling. He's not struggling. His face is relaxed. His color is okay.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> His hands are warm. His feet are warm.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Now, tell me about the lorazepam. What's the dose, and how often can he have it?
Caller -> Point five milligrams. Under the tongue. Every four hours if he's restless. That's the comfort kit one. The little tablet.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It's the one the nurse showed us how to use. It melts. It's tiny.
Nurse -> Okay. And when did he get it tonight?
Caller -> I'm going to tell you exactly what I remember. Okay? Don't interrupt me.
Nurse -> I won't.
Caller -> That's the problem. I gave it around eight. I think. I put it under his tongue and he was fussing and I waited. And then my brother says he gave it around eight too. Rene! Did you give it? Rene says he gave it at eight fifteen.
Caller -> Rene, say it again. Say it so she can hear. He says eight fifteen. He's holding up his phone. He texted our aunt at eight twenty.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> He keeps shaking his head. He says he's sure. I'm sure too. We're both sure.
Nurse -> Take it slowly.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I'm jumbling it.
Nurse -> You're doing fine.
Nurse -> Okay. So you gave one at about eight, and your brother gave one at eight fifteen?
Caller -> I think so. Maybe. He says he gave it when I was in the bathroom. I didn't see him. And I said I gave it before the bathroom. So we could have both given it. Or only one of us. We don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. Did either of you write it on the log?
Caller -> No. That's the thing. Nothing on the log. We both forgot. Or we were going to write it later. I was going to. Rene says he was going to. The page is blank since six.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I feel so stupid. The nurse told us. She said write everything. And we didn't.
Nurse -> It's very easy to forget in the moment.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a pill count? Can you count how many tablets are in the kit?
Caller -> Hold on. I'll get the kit. It's in the kitchen. Rene, bring the kit. The little bag. Okay, he's bringing it.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay, it's here. It's a little bottle. The label says ten tablets. Let me count. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven. Wait. Rene, is it seven? He says seven.
Nurse -> Seven tablets. And how many were in the bottle when you started?
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I don't know exactly. The nurse said ten. And we gave one yesterday morning, I think. And one in the night. So that would be eight. Then seven would mean one tonight.
Nurse -> Or it could be that you started with nine, and two tonight. I can't tell from that.
Caller -> I wish I'd counted when they delivered it.
Nurse -> We'll make sure the nurse counts tonight.
Caller -> Right. Right. I can't either. That's what I'm afraid of.
Caller -> Rene says he's sure he gave one. I'm sure I gave one. So that's two. But maybe I gave it earlier. Maybe at seven forty five. Rene, what time was it?
Caller -> He doesn't know. He says the clock on the stove was blinking.
Nurse -> That's okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Let's keep going. What else has he gotten tonight? Any morphine?
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Yes. The morphine. Five milligrams. A quarter of the little syringe. I gave it at six. Rene watched me. We both agree on that one. It's written. I wrote that one.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for being so clear about that one.
Nurse -> Good. Morphine at six, and that's on the log. Odette, what's his date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, the nurse will want that too. Isn't it on the chart?
Nurse -> It is. I just need to confirm.
Caller -> Yes. I'm very careful with that one. It scares me.
Nurse -> That's understandable.
Caller -> December seventeenth. Nineteen forty.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, oh one eight eight.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, oh one eight eight. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great.
Caller -> It's on and the volume is all the way up.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, about the possible double dose and how sleepy he is.
Caller -> Please. I need a plan.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Am I going to get in trouble?
Nurse -> Take a moment if you need it.
Caller -> I keep thinking I did something terrible.
Nurse -> No. Not at all. This is a very common situation when two people are helping. You did the right thing, calling.
Caller -> I'm so relieved. I thought you'd be angry.
Nurse -> Not at all.
Caller -> I feel awful.
Nurse -> I know. But you're doing the right thing right now.
Caller -> Rene feels awful too. He's crying in the hallway.
Nurse -> I know. It's okay. I'd also like a nurse to come out tonight to see him.
Caller -> Tonight? Oh, thank God. When?
Caller -> I don't think I can do this alone. I keep thinking I'll make another mistake.
Nurse -> You're not alone. The nurse will be there soon.
Nurse -> As soon as someone is available.
Nurse -> I'll ask for as soon as possible. They'll call you before they come.
Caller -> Should I get anything ready? Towels? Water?
Nurse -> Just the log, the medicine bags, and the kit. Put them on the table.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll go sit by him now.
Caller -> Should I wake the nurse next door? She's a nurse, she's retired, she lives next door.
Nurse -> There's no need. We'll have our nurse there.
Caller -> Okay. I'll let her sleep.
Nurse -> That's kind of you.
Caller -> She had a long day too. Her knee has been bothering her.
Nurse -> In the meantime, please don't give any more lorazepam tonight, until the clinician calls you. And from now on, write the medicine, the dose, and the time on the log the moment you give it. Not later.
Caller -> No more tonight. Write it right away. Okay. Rene, did you hear that? He heard. He's nodding. We're going to put a pen on a string.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a great idea.
Caller -> Rene is going to find string. He just ran off.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> My mother used to do that with the grocery list.
Nurse -> It works.
Caller -> She also wrote the day on everything. Everything had a date on it. It drove my father crazy.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> What if he gets restless again? What do I do?
Nurse -> That's a good question.
Nurse -> Try comfort first. Keep the lights low. Speak softly. Gently turn him every couple of hours. And moisten his lips with a swab. If he gets restless, call me back, and we'll talk to the clinician about it.
Caller -> Lights low. Soft voice. Turn him. Swab. Call you. Okay. I have the swabs. The pink ones.
Caller -> They're in a cup on the dresser. I've been using them every hour.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Turn him how? Which side?
Nurse -> Either side. Use a pillow behind his back. Gently.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Good. And Odette, call us right away if he's hard to wake, if he's breathing fewer than ten times a minute, or if he starts gurgling or struggling to breathe.
Caller -> Okay. Say the second one again, I want to make sure I write it right.
Nurse -> Fewer than ten breaths in a minute.
Caller -> Fewer than ten. Okay.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Fewer than ten. Gurgling. Struggling. Okay. I have the watch. I'll count again in ten minutes.
Caller -> What if he's just deeply asleep? How do I tell the difference?
Nurse -> If he won't open his eyes to your voice or a gentle touch, call us.
Caller -> Okay. Got it.
Nurse -> Good. Count for a full minute.
Caller -> Okay. A full minute.
Caller -> A full minute. Okay.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It's hard to count and talk. Sorry.
Nurse -> You don't have to talk. I'll wait.
Nurse -> And keep the phone near you.
Caller -> It's in my pocket.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll page now.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for staying so calm. It helps.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Thank you. Leocadia?
Nurse -> I'm here.
Nurse -> Yes?
Caller -> Is he dying? Tonight? Is that what this is?
Nurse -> I don't think this is that. He's resting, and he's breathing comfortably. But we do want to watch him closely. The nurse can talk with you about what to expect.
Caller -> He's been so tired for weeks. I just keep wondering.
Nurse -> I know. The nurse will go over everything.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I just. I wanted to ask.
Caller -> We've been taking care of him for eight months. It's gone so fast. And so slow.
Nurse -> I know.
Nurse -> I'm glad you did. You can ask me anything.
Caller -> I'll write down my questions for the nurse. I have a lot of them.
Nurse -> Please do.
Caller -> Thank you. We'll wait for the call.
Nurse -> Sit with him. You're doing a good job.
Caller -> Rene is back with the string. He's tying a pen to the clipboard. Ha. It's very long.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> I'll page now. Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.
Nurse -> Bye, Odette.

Nurse -> Not yet. No reply is in the chart. I'll keep an eye out.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I figured.
Caller -> Okay. That's fine. She's still coughing. A dry cough. Three days now. It isn't terrible. She coughs a few times a day. More at night.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any fever?
Caller -> No fever. We have a thermometer. I took it this morning. Normal. And she's breathing fine. No wheezing. No short of breath. She did her puzzle at the table.
Nurse -> Good. Is she eating and drinking?
Caller -> Yes. She likes the soup I make. She's fussy, but she's eating.
Nurse -> What kind of soup?
Caller -> Chicken with little noodles. Her recipe, but I make it badly.
Nurse -> Ha. She still eats it.
Nurse -> Great. Mateus, what's her date of birth, so I can verify?
Caller -> May ninth. Nineteen thirty five. She'll be ninety one this year. Wait, she's already ninety one. Sorry.
Nurse -> Ha. Right. And your number?
Caller -> Sorry. Math is not my strong suit.
Caller -> Nine oh one, five five five, oh one four seven.
Nurse -> Nine oh one, five five five, oh one four seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my work cell. I answer it all day.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. Also, I see a nurse visit is planned Thursday.
Caller -> Thursday. Yes. They told me. Morning? I wrote it down.
Nurse -> The note says morning.
Caller -> Good. She's alert in the morning.
Nurse -> That helps.
Caller -> Good. Great. It's a lot. I'm glad everything is moving.
Caller -> I just want to make sure nothing falls through the cracks.
Nurse -> That's exactly why I'm checking.
Nurse -> It is moving. For the cough, you can offer her warm tea with honey. And an extra pillow so her head is up at night. A cool mist humidifier helps too.
Caller -> Tea with honey. Extra pillow. Humidifier. We have a humidifier from my aunt. It's in the garage. I'll bring it in.
Caller -> The humidifier is the kind with the little blue light. It's loud, but she likes it.
Nurse -> Perfect. And call us if she gets a fever, has trouble breathing, if she's coughing up colored mucus, or if she chokes when she drinks.
Caller -> Fever. Breathing. Colored. Choking. Okay. I'll text it to my cousin too.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> She'd kill me if she knew I was texting about her.
Caller -> She doesn't like to ask for things. My grandmother. She doesn't tell me when something hurts.
Nurse -> That's common. Keep asking. Watch her face.
Caller -> I try. She just says, I'm fine. Always fine.
Caller -> I do. She hides it. She's tough. She came here from Brazil when she was nineteen.
Nurse -> That's an incredible story.
Caller -> She talks about it more now. I record it on my phone.
Nurse -> What a gift.
Caller -> She taught herself English from the radio.
Nurse -> Wow.
Caller -> I'll tell her you said that. She'll love it.
Nurse -> Please do. Anything else?
Caller -> No, that's it. Thank you, Tobiah.
Nurse -> You're welcome, Mateus. Take care.
Caller -> You too. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Pelican Bay Home Health, this is Augustus.
Caller -> Hello? Is this the night line? I wasn't sure which number to call so I called the one on the fridge.
Nurse -> You've got the right place.
Caller -> Hi, Augustus. This is Philomena Radcliffe. I'm a patient. I'm calling because I think I'm confused about my insulin. Specifically the one I take at meals.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena. Is it okay that I call you Philomena?
Caller -> Phil is fine. Everyone says Phil.
Nurse -> Phil it is.
Nurse -> Hi, Philomena. Okay. Tell me what's confusing.
Caller -> I appreciate you picking up. I know it's late.
Nurse -> Never a problem.
Caller -> It's silly. I've done this for years. But tonight I froze.
Nurse -> It's not silly. Let's go slowly.
Caller -> Thank you for being patient. My last doctor made me feel stupid.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. This is complicated.
Caller -> I have two insulins. The Lantus, that's the long one. Twenty four units at bedtime. That I understand. I took it last night at ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Lantus, twenty four units, at bedtime. Last night at ten.
Caller -> Yes. And I use the purple pen for that one. The mealtime one is the orange pen. I got them mixed up once.
Nurse -> The colors help.
Caller -> Right. And then the other one is the Humalog. The mealtime one. I have a card. A sliding scale. You check your sugar, and the card tells you how many units.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Did you use the card tonight?
Caller -> I did. I keep it on the refrigerator, under a magnet shaped like a pineapple.
Nurse -> Ha. A fruit magnet is a fine place.
Caller -> I did. My sugar was two hundred eighty seven before dinner. I looked at the card, and the card says, hold on, let me find it. The row for two fifty to two ninety nine says four units. No. Six units. It's six. Sorry. I read the wrong row. Six.
Nurse -> Take your time with the card.
Caller -> It's laminated. It has a coffee ring on it. Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. So you took six units. And the row for two eighty seven is six.
Caller -> Yes. I'm fairly sure. I'm looking at the card now. It says two fifty to two ninety nine, six units. Yes. I took six.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Sorry. I'm squinting. The print is tiny.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Good. That's what the card says. So you did it right.
Caller -> I should go lie down, if it's all right. I'll keep the phone on.
Nurse -> That's fine. Rest, and I'll call.
Caller -> Thank you. I just needed someone to say it out loud.
Caller -> Oh. Okay. I wasn't sure. I second guessed myself. I was afraid I'd given too little, or too much.
Nurse -> Second guessing is natural when you're tired.
Caller -> I'd had a long day. My sister's car broke down and I drove forty minutes to get her.
Nurse -> It sounds like you gave the right amount. When did you take it?
Caller -> At about six. Right before I ate. My dinner was chicken and rice, and a salad. And a piece of cake. I had a little cake. It was my neighbor's birthday.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I'm trying to be good about the timing. The card says take it fifteen minutes before. I took it right before. Is that bad?
Nurse -> Fifteen minutes before is ideal, but it's not a disaster.
Nurse -> Ha. That could explain a high sugar.
Caller -> I know. I know. But it was a very small piece.
Nurse -> Ha. We all say that.
Caller -> Right. But the number before dinner was already high. It was high before I even had the cake. That's why I'm worried.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I wonder if I was sick. I felt fine. But the number says otherwise.
Nurse -> Okay. That's useful to know.
Nurse -> What was your sugar this morning?
Caller -> One forty two. Fasting. That's good for me. That's pretty normal.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I felt proud of that number. I wrote it in big letters.
Nurse -> How are you feeling?
Caller -> Honestly, a bit embarrassed. Calling at this hour.
Nurse -> Please don't be. This is exactly what the night line is for.
Caller -> Thirsty. A little. I've had three glasses of water since dinner. I keep going to the bathroom. But no stomach trouble. No nausea. No throwing up. And I'm thinking clearly, I think. You tell me. Ha.
Caller -> I keep the glass right here by the phone.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It's not a terrible thirst. It's more like my mouth is dry.
Nurse -> That fits with a higher sugar.
Nurse -> You sound very clear to me. Any blurry vision, headache?
Caller -> I made tea. Decaf. I'm trying to be good.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> No. No. Just thirsty. And tired. But I'm always tired at night.
Nurse -> Okay. Philomena, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> Oh, you need my date of birth? Sure.
Caller -> February twenty seventh. Nineteen sixty three.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Nine one eight, five five five, oh one two two.
Nurse -> Nine one eight, five five five, oh one two two. Right?
Caller -> That's my cell. The landline hasn't worked since the storm.
Nurse -> Cell it is.
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. I'd like to page the on-call clinician about the high numbers and about how you use the scale. I'm going to do that right now.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Okay. Is something wrong?
Caller -> Because if it's serious I'd rather know.
Nurse -> It isn't serious. I just want it looked at.
Nurse -> I don't think so. I want them to take a look at the pattern. You'll hear from me within the hour.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll stay up.
Caller -> I'll set a timer on the stove so I don't lose track.
Nurse -> If you don't hear from me, call back.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Caller -> I have a movie on. A bad one. It's perfect for waiting.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Good. I'd also like a nurse to come out tomorrow and watch you use the scale. So you feel sure about it.
Caller -> Oh, I'd love that. I'm a visual learner. I need someone to show me.
Nurse -> Then it's a good fit.
Caller -> My doctor just handed me the card and said good luck.
Nurse -> That's a lot to take in.
Nurse -> That's what we'll do.
Caller -> What time? I work Tuesdays and Thursdays. Tomorrow is Wednesday. I'm free.
Nurse -> Wonderful.
Caller -> I'll have coffee ready. Decaf. For the nurse.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you.
Nurse -> Perfect. They'll call before they come.
Caller -> Should I have my meter and my notebook ready?
Nurse -> Yes. And both pens.
Caller -> Both pens. Okay.
Caller -> Great.
Nurse -> They'll bring the new card too, if there is one.
Nurse -> Now, here's the main rule about the scale. Before every mealtime dose, check your sugar. Read the number against the card. Take only that dose. Don't add extra to catch up.
Caller -> Check. Read the card. Take only that. Don't add extra. Okay. I do that. I just had one moment of doubt.
Nurse -> That's it.
Caller -> I'm going to write that on a sticky note and stick it on the meter.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> That's normal. If you ever doubt, call us. Don't guess.
Caller -> I'll write that on the card. If in doubt, call.
Nurse -> That's a great note.
Caller -> Okay. I will.
Caller -> I mean it. I'll call if I'm unsure.
Nurse -> Good. Please do.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And check your sugar again at bedtime, and before breakfast. Write each number down. And keep drinking water.
Caller -> Bedtime. Before breakfast. Write it. Water. I have a little notebook. It's purple.
Caller -> I put stickers next to the numbers. Gold for good ones.
Nurse -> Ha. Whatever works.
Caller -> I got them at the dollar store. A hundred of them for two dollars.
Nurse -> A bargain.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I take extra tonight, to bring it down faster?
Nurse -> Good question to ask.
Nurse -> No. Please don't add any extra. Wait for the clinician to call you.
Caller -> Okay. I won't.
Nurse -> Thank you. That matters.
Nurse -> Also, I want you to know the signs of low sugar. If you get shaky, sweaty, or confused, drink half a cup of juice, and check again in fifteen minutes. And call 911 if you can't swallow or you're not responding.
Caller -> Shaky. Sweaty. Confused. Juice. Fifteen minutes. 911 if I can't swallow. Okay. I live alone. So I should keep my phone close.
Nurse -> Exactly.
Caller -> My daughter says I should get one of those necklace buttons. I keep saying no.
Nurse -> It's worth thinking about.
Nurse -> Yes. Keep it next to your bed.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'll charge it right now. It's at forty percent.
Caller -> It's always there. I have a little stand.
Nurse -> Good. Do you have juice in the house?
Caller -> Orange juice in the fridge. And glucose tablets in the drawer.
Nurse -> And do you have a way to get back up if you feel weak?
Caller -> I sit down first. Always. I learned that the hard way.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Caller -> And honey. If all else fails I can eat a spoonful of honey.
Nurse -> That works too.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Caller -> The little cartons. I buy them in bulk. They don't go bad.
Nurse -> Smart.
Nurse -> Perfect. You're well prepared.
Caller -> Thank you. Compliments are rare.
Nurse -> Ha. You earned it.
Caller -> I try. I've had diabetes eleven years. But I still get confused about the scale. The doctor changed the numbers in the fall.
Nurse -> That's a long time to manage this.
Caller -> It is. I've gotten better at it. The first year I cried every morning.
Nurse -> That can throw anybody off. The new card should be the only one you use.
Caller -> It really did. I'm still unlearning the old numbers.
Caller -> I threw the old one out. I think. Let me check the drawer. No. Wait. It's gone.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I have a daughter in Tulsa. She calls every night at nine. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> That's far.
Caller -> It is. But she calls and she visits at Thanksgiving.
Nurse -> That's nice. She can check in on you.
Caller -> She'll laugh when I tell her I called the night nurse.
Nurse -> Tell her she's welcome to call us too.
Caller -> She's a worrier. She gets it from me.
Caller -> She makes me text her a thumbs up every morning.
Nurse -> That's a nice habit.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Thank you for staying on the phone with me. It helps to hear a voice.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> My phone is at sixty percent so I can talk as long as you need.
Nurse -> We're nearly done.
Nurse -> Any time. That's what the night line is for.
Caller -> I'll remember that. Thank you.
Caller -> I feel better already. I'll wait for your call.
Caller -> I'll put the kettle on. It helps me think.
Nurse -> Sounds good.
Nurse -> Perfect. Talk soon.
Caller -> Good night, Augustus. Thank you again.
Nurse -> Good night, Phil.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Riverbend Hospice, this is Annabelle.
Caller -> Hello? Is this the hospice line? I'm Dwayne, from the assisted living.
Nurse -> You've reached it. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi. Annabelle. It's Dwayne Kowalczyk. I'm the L P N at Maple Court assisted living. I'm calling about one of our residents. Theodosia Marchetti. She's on your service. She's having hip pain and she's, she hasn't had a bowel movement in a while.
Nurse -> Hi, Dwayne. You're breaking up a little. Can you hear me?
Caller -> I can hear you. Sorry, the nurse's station is loud. Hold on, I'm going to the med room.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Better. The door closes in here.
Nurse -> Hi, Dwayne. Thanks for calling. Let me pull her up. Marchetti. M A R C H E T T I?
Caller -> That's it. Theodosia. She's in room, hold on, the cart's coming through. Excuse me. Room two fourteen.
Nurse -> Okay. Two fourteen.
Caller -> Yes. Down the hall from the activity room. You can hear bingo from there.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. Dwayne, tell me about the hip.
Caller -> She's had a rough week. She was doing so well before the fall.
Nurse -> I'm sorry to hear that.
Caller -> Okay. I have my notes here. I wrote them down before I called.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Caller -> She fell on, um, on Monday. Slid off the, off the edge of the bed in the night. We found her on the floor. Her left hip. She hasn't been the same. The pain's been, she says it's about a six. Six out of ten. When she moves. When she's lying still it's less.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'm listening.
Nurse -> A six when she moves. Did anyone evaluate her after the fall?
Caller -> Yes. And when she coughs, too. She says it grabs her.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Yes. The, the nurse practitioner came Tuesday. The X-ray was negative. No break. That's what they told us. And she went back to the, just rest and the, the pain medicine.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know. Which pain medicine is she on?
Caller -> Let me read it off the MAR so I get it right. It's in a binder, hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I can see her door from here. She's resting now.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> She was relieved. She was worried it was broken.
Nurse -> That's understandable.
Caller -> The oxycodon. Five milligrams. Every four hours as needed. It's on the, on the MAR. She got one at two.
Nurse -> Oxycodone, five milligrams, as needed, last at two.
Caller -> Yes. Right. At two o'clock. And before that at ten.
Nurse -> Okay. Ten and two.
Caller -> Yes. Right on schedule. She asks for it. She watches the clock.
Caller -> She told me she wishes she could just sleep through it.
Nurse -> I understand.
Nurse -> Okay. How does she do after the dose?
Caller -> Better. In about forty minutes the pain, she says it comes down to a three. A three. Then it comes back, up to a five, six. Around the, around the time of the next one.
Caller -> She says it feels like the edges get softer.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. So it wears off by the four hours.
Caller -> That's what I told the NP. She said to call hospice.
Nurse -> You did the right thing.
Caller -> Yes. Hold on. Hello, Mr. Abbott, I'll be with you in a minute. Sorry. That's a resident. He wants his paper.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Thank you. It's a busy shift. We're short one aide.
Caller -> I'm so sorry about the interruptions. It's a lot with the evening meds.
Nurse -> Of course.
Nurse -> I'm sorry to hear that.
Nurse -> No problem.
Caller -> Where were we. The oxycodon.
Nurse -> The pain medicine wears off. We'll come back to that. What about her bowels?
Caller -> Sorry, someone is calling my name from the hall. One second.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Back. Go on.
Caller -> No, no bowel movement. Four days. Since Friday. She's on the senna. Two tablets. Twice a day. She had them this morning.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Sorry, let me say that again. It's been four days. Four. She told me Sunday that nothing was happening.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Senna, two tablets, twice a day, and she took them this morning. Any belly pain, bloating, nausea?
Caller -> Her belly's soft. She says she's a little full. Not vomiting. She ate half her lunch. Some soup. She's drinking, but not great. Maybe four cups.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I pressed gently. She didn't wince. Excuse me, are you still there?
Nurse -> I'm here.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you tried anything else? Prune juice, fluids?
Caller -> She won't drink the prune juice. She says it tastes like feet. Ha. Excuse me. Did you say something? No, sorry, that was the, the call light.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> She says it tastes like feet. I've heard it three times today.
Nurse -> Fair.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Where was I. Yes. Prune juice, no. We tried warm water in the morning. She likes that.
Nurse -> That's all right.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she had any new swelling, bruising around the hip? Any more falls?
Caller -> I'll let the aide know to watch for it overnight.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> No. No new falls. We put the bed rail up. The, um, bed alarm. Swelling, I don't think so. It looks the same as Tuesday. Nothing new on the, on the skin.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> The aide checks on her every two hours. She's on the list now.
Nurse -> That's good.
Nurse -> Good. Dwayne, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> Do you want me to read it from the chart? Okay. Reading it.
Caller -> June fourteenth. Nineteen forty two.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And your number, for the callback?
Caller -> Four one four, five five five, oh one six zero.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, oh one six zero. Right?
Caller -> Yes. Same number as the main desk. Extension two.
Nurse -> Noted.
Caller -> Yes. It's the nurse's station. Ask for me. I'm here till eleven.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. And the best time?
Caller -> Anytime before eleven. I'm covering the whole floor tonight.
Caller -> Got it. Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'll send a message to the team about the pain and the constipation. I'd like them to look at a bowel regimen, and a scheduled pain plan.
Nurse -> Is there anything else you want me to include in the message?
Caller -> Tell them she asked about her rosary. It's in her other bag.
Nurse -> I'll mention it.
Caller -> Okay. That would be great. She's, I just, I don't want her hurting.
Caller -> I don't want her hurting. She's such a sweet lady. She calls me dear.
Nurse -> I understand.
Nurse -> I understand. I'll also call the pharmacy, and check her supply and the strength of the pain medicine.
Caller -> Yes. She's low. We have about, hold on, nine tablets left in the bubble pack.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Nine. Okay. I'll let them know.
Caller -> Thank you. I didn't want to run out on the weekend.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And I'd like a nurse to come out tomorrow to see her. To check the hip and her belly.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. What time?
Nurse -> Morning.
Caller -> Is the nurse a man or a woman? She prefers women for personal care.
Nurse -> I'll make a note of that.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Okay. She has therapy at ten. Can the nurse come before or after?
Nurse -> That's useful.
Nurse -> I'll note that. Therapy at ten.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> About the therapy, Dwayne. Give the pain medicine about thirty minutes before the therapist comes, or before a bath. And write the time down on the log each time.
Caller -> Thirty minutes before therapy. Write the time. Okay. We do that for the bath. Not for therapy. I'll tell the day shift.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Great.
Caller -> Thank you for staying on the phone with me. The line is bad tonight.
Nurse -> It's no trouble.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> One more thing before I hang up. Do I call this number if she gets worse overnight?
Nurse -> Yes. This line is staffed all night.
Caller -> I'll get back to the cart now. Mr. Abbott is still waiting for his paper.
Nurse -> Ha. Go ahead.
Caller -> Sorry. I keep getting interrupted. You've been so patient.
Nurse -> Not a problem at all.
Caller -> I wrote it all down on the whiteboard in the med room. In case the next shift asks.
Caller -> I'll make sure the day shift knows about the nurse coming.
Caller -> What else for the hip? Besides the, besides the medicine?
Nurse -> Good question. I'll give you a few things.
Nurse -> A pillow between her knees and under the hip when she's on her side. A warm pack, fifteen minutes at a time, not on bare skin. And offer her prune juice, or any fluids she will take.
Caller -> Pillow. Warm pack. Fifteen minutes. Fluids. Okay. We have those, the microwave ones. The rice ones.
Caller -> Excuse me. Mrs. Lindahl, I'll be right there. Sorry, call light.
Nurse -> No problem.
Nurse -> Those are fine. Test the temperature on your wrist first.
Caller -> Yes. I know. We burned a resident once with a heating pad. Never again.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> And call us if her pain goes over eight, if her leg looks shorter or turned, if you see new swelling, if she's vomiting, or if her belly is hard and swollen.
Caller -> Over eight. Leg shorter. Swelling. Vomiting. Hard belly. Okay. Got it. I'll tell the next shift too.
Caller -> Over eight. I wrote eight and underlined it.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Can I ask, is she, is this the, is she dying?

transcript:
Nurse -> Thornfield Home Health, this is Ludovica.
Caller -> Hi, Ludovica. It's Marjorie Abernethy. I'm calling about my husband, Cyrus Abernethy. I need some help with him in the evenings. This is killing me.
Nurse -> Hi, Marjorie. I'm glad you called. Tell me what's been going on.
Caller -> Sorry for calling so late. It's half past midnight. He's finally asleep.
Nurse -> It's no problem. The line is staffed.
Caller -> Every night around five o'clock he gets, I don't know, wound up. He paces. He asks me the same question. Where are we going? Where is my mother? Over and over. Forty times. I counted once. I'm going to lose my mind.
Nurse -> It sounds exhausting. How long has this been going on?
Caller -> It feels like years, but it's about three weeks.
Caller -> About three weeks. It was just once in a while. Now it's every night. And last night, he went to the front door. Twice. Once at ten and once at one in the morning. He had his hand on the knob. He said he had to go to work.
Nurse -> Did he go outside?
Caller -> I'd have had a heart attack. A figurative one. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Understood.
Caller -> No. No. I heard him. I was a light sleeper before this and now I'm a, a cat. I got up and talked him back to bed. Both times. He was fine. He just wanted to go to work. He retired in two thousand six.
Nurse -> Okay. Did he fall, or hurt himself, at any point?
Caller -> No falls. No injuries. He's steady on his feet. He hasn't hurt himself. Not a scratch.
Nurse -> I'm glad. Marjorie, how are you doing?
Caller -> Fine. No. Not fine. You asked, so I'll say it.
Caller -> Honestly? I'm dead on my feet. I haven't slept more than three hours in a row in weeks. It's just me. My daughter is in Seattle. I love him. But he's going to be the death of me. I mean that figuratively. I'm not, don't worry. I'm not going to do anything. I just want to sleep.
Nurse -> I understand. I'm glad you said that. Are you having any thoughts of hurting yourself or him?
Caller -> No. God, no. Never. I'm just tired. I just need a break. That's all. I'd never hurt him.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for telling me. It's a question I ask because the stress can be so heavy.
Caller -> I don't want you to think I'm a bad wife.
Nurse -> Not at all. I think you're a devoted one.
Caller -> I understand. No. I'm okay. Tired, but okay.
Nurse -> Let me get his chart. Marjorie, what is his date of birth?
Caller -> January twenty third. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six one five, five five five, oh one oh nine.
Nurse -> Six one five, five five five, oh one oh nine. Correct?
Caller -> Yes. It's the house phone and my cell. Same number.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to put in a referral to our social worker. They can talk with you about help at home, and respite, so you can rest.
Caller -> Respite. Oh. I'd love that. Is that a real thing? I thought that was just a word.
Nurse -> It's worth looking into.
Nurse -> It's a real thing. They can go through the options with you.
Caller -> Thank you. I'd cry if I weren't so tired.
Nurse -> Ha. It's okay to cry. I'll also send a message to the team about the evening agitation and the door. They may want to look at his routine and his medicines.
Caller -> I cry in the shower. It's the only private place.
Caller -> Please. I'm at my wit's end. That's an expression. I'm not at the end. I'm near it. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand the expression.
Caller -> I'm sorry. I keep making jokes. It's how I cope.
Nurse -> It's fine. I'll call you tomorrow to see how the night went.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time? I nap when he naps. Which is two to four.
Nurse -> Then I'll call at five. Is that a bad time, with the evening?
Caller -> It's the worst time. Call at noon. I'll be awake.
Nurse -> Noon it is.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll set a reminder.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> For the door, there are a few things that can help. Put a chime or an alarm on the front door, so you hear it. Keep the doors locked, with the key out of sight. And keep a light on in the hall at night.
Caller -> Chime. Lock. Key hidden. Light on. We have a door chime from the baby days. I'll find it. I think it's in the garage.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> A chime from the baby days. Perfect.
Caller -> I'm writing all this on the back of an envelope. I have no paper.
Nurse -> That works.
Caller -> My daughter will laugh.
Nurse -> For the evening, try keeping the afternoon quiet. Start winding down around five. Offer a snack, put on soft music, and answer his questions calmly, even the fortieth time.
Caller -> Wind down. Snack. Soft music. Calm answers. Okay. He likes Sinatra. I'll put on Sinatra.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Even the fortieth time. Ha. I'll try. I'll try not to scream.
Nurse -> It's okay to step into the next room for a minute if you need to.
Caller -> I do that. I go in the kitchen and count to ten.
Nurse -> That's smart.
Caller -> I learned it from a YouTube video. Counting to ten. Ha.
Nurse -> Whatever works.
Caller -> Thank you, Ludovica. Really. I feel less crazy now.
Nurse -> You're not crazy. You're doing an incredibly hard job.
Caller -> My neighbor says I should put him in a home. I don't want to.
Nurse -> The social worker can talk through all the options with you, no pressure.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Talk tomorrow.
Caller -> Goodnight.

transcript:
Nurse -> Alderwood Home Health, this is Magnus.
Caller -> Hello? Is this home health? I'm so sorry, I always call this number and get the machine.
Nurse -> You've got a person today. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Magnus. This is Evangelina Ruttledge. I'm a patient. My diabetes pill came from the mail order pharmacy and I think it's the wrong one.
Nurse -> Hi, Evangelina. Thanks for calling. Let's check it together. What are you supposed to be taking?
Caller -> Thank you for answering. I was about to call my daughter first, but I thought I should call you.
Nurse -> You made a good choice.
Caller -> Glipizide. Five milligrams. Twice a day. With breakfast and with dinner. I've taken it for six years.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Sorry, did I say that clearly?
Nurse -> Yes. Very clearly.
Nurse -> Okay. Glipizide, five milligrams, twice a day. And what does the new bottle say?
Caller -> It's the little white one. I've always taken it with food, so I don't get dizzy.
Nurse -> That's right.
Caller -> It says, hold on, I need my glasses. G L Y B U R I D E. Glyburide. No wait. Let me look again. Glipizide? No. Hm. It says glyburide. Yes. G L Y. Glyburide. Five milligrams.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> I'm going to write down what you said so I don't forget.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> They were on my head. Of course they were on my head. Ha. Okay.
Caller -> Thank you for being so kind. It means a lot.
Nurse -> Glyburide, five milligrams. Okay. Is it the same name on the bag the bottle came in?
Caller -> The paper in the bag says glipizide. The bottle says glyburide. They don't match. That's why I'm confused.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I read it three times. It says the right one. The bottle says something else. It's a mix up.
Nurse -> It sounds like it.
Nurse -> Good catch. Is the patient name on the bottle yours?
Caller -> Let me check the other side of the label too. Hold on.
Nurse -> Sure.
Caller -> Yes. Same name, same address. The doctor's name is right.
Caller -> Yes. Evangelina Ruttledge. My name. The doctor is right. The date is right. It's just the, the pill name.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Have you taken any pills from the new bottle?
Caller -> No. No. I haven't opened it. Well, I opened the lid and looked. But I haven't taken any. I took this morning's dose from my old bottle. I still have about two weeks left in it.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the right thing. How do the pills look? Are they the same as the old ones?
Caller -> What time is it, by the way? I lost track.
Nurse -> It's a little after ten.
Caller -> Oh good. I have time before pottery.
Caller -> I'll keep the log. I'm very neat about the log. It's got columns.
Caller -> I'll get a plastic bag. Hold on.
Nurse -> Sure.
Caller -> Okay. I have the bag. I'm putting the bottle in.
Caller -> Different. The old ones are small and white. The new ones are pink. Oval. That's how I knew something was off. I'm not good with names, but I know my pills.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That's a great way to catch it. Thank you for calling instead of just taking them.
Caller -> I'm stubborn, but not that stubborn.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good kind of stubborn.
Caller -> I've been taking them so long. I know the look of them like I know my own hands.
Caller -> I almost did. I'd taken the first ones out of the bottle. Then I thought, these look funny.
Nurse -> Where are those pills now?
Caller -> On the kitchen counter. In a little pile. I'll put them back in the bottle.
Nurse -> Okay. Please put them back in the bottle.
Caller -> Right. I'll do it right now. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. They're back in the bottle. I put the lid on tight.
Nurse -> Good. Don't take them.
Caller -> I won't. Not even by accident.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I put them in a sandwich bag too. Just in case. Double bagged.
Nurse -> That's thorough.
Caller -> I won't.
Nurse -> How are you feeling today? Have you checked your sugar?
Caller -> I did. This morning before breakfast. It was one eighteen. That's good for me.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I check it at six thirty every morning. I'm up with the birds.
Nurse -> That's a good habit.
Nurse -> One eighteen. Any shakiness, sweating, headache?
Caller -> No. None of that. I feel fine. I made oatmeal. I'm fine.
Nurse -> Good. Now let me ask. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> April eleventh. Nineteen fifty six.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one nine oh.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one nine oh. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll call the mail order pharmacy and tell them the bottle has the wrong pill in it. I'll ask them to send the right medicine.
Caller -> Oh, good. Thank you. Do you think they'll be nice about it? They're usually a recording.
Nurse -> I'll do my best.
Nurse -> I'll get a person. I'll stay on the line.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a message to the team so they know about the error.
Caller -> Okay. Good.
Caller -> Is it bad that I'm nervous? I know it's just a pill.
Nurse -> It's normal. You're careful, and that's good.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back today to let you know what the pharmacy says.
Caller -> Today. Okay. I'll be home. I have a pottery class at four, but I'll take the phone.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Pottery. Nice.
Caller -> We meet Thursdays too. Tomorrow I'll tell them the story.
Nurse -> Ha. A good story.
Caller -> I started after my husband passed. Two years ago. It gives me something to do with my hands.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Caller -> It's my favorite thing. I made a bowl. It's lopsided. It holds cereal.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a good bowl.
Caller -> It is.
Caller -> I'll bring you a mug. If I make a good one.
Nurse -> Ha. I'd like that. But I can't accept gifts.
Caller -> Oh. Rules. Of course.
Nurse -> Evangelina, in the meantime, please don't take any pills from the new bottle. Keep using the old bottle. And put the new one aside, in a bag, so the pharmacy can see it.
Caller -> Don't take the new ones. Use the old. Put the new in a bag. Okay. I'll put a sticky note on it that says wrong. In big letters.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> What if the old bottle runs out before they send the new one? I have two weeks, but still.
Nurse -> The pharmacy should send it well before that. And I'll make sure of it.
Caller -> Okay. I trust you.
Nurse -> I'll make sure.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel better.
Nurse -> Also, keep checking your sugar before meals and at bedtime. Call us if it's under seventy, or over three hundred.
Caller -> Before meals and at bedtime. Under seventy, over three hundred. I write them in the log. I'll keep doing that.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'm glad I looked. I could have taken the wrong pill for weeks.
Nurse -> This is why we check. You did it right.
Caller -> I appreciate that. I felt silly.
Nurse -> Don't. Nothing silly about it.
Caller -> My daughter's a pharmacist. She always says check the pills. I should call her.
Nurse -> That's helpful to have in the family.
Caller -> Most of the time. Sometimes she corrects my grammar too.
Nurse -> That's a good idea. She'll be proud.
Caller -> She works at a hospital in Denver. She'll probably call the mail order company herself.
Nurse -> Ha. Please let me handle it first.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her to wait.
Caller -> She will. Then she'll lecture me. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Anything else I should do?
Nurse -> Let me double check my notes.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm just sitting here with my tea.
Nurse -> I think that's it. Take care. I'll call you this afternoon.
Caller -> Thank you again. I mean it.
Caller -> Thank you, Magnus. Bye.

Nurse -> Little Fern Pediatric Home Care, this is Isadora.
Caller -> Isadora, it's Jacinda Castellano. My son Wrenley Castellano. He got into my mother's pills. The blood pressure ones. I think he swallowed some. I don't know how many.
Nurse -> Jacinda, slow down. I can hear you. Tell me one thing at a time.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm sorry. I'm shaking.
Nurse -> It's all right. I'm right here.
Nurse -> Jacinda, I'm here. Is he awake? Is he breathing normally?
Caller -> He's awake. He's right here. He's running around. He thinks it's a game. He's fine. He seems fine. Oh my God.
Nurse -> Good. Keep him where you can see him.
Caller -> He's in my arms now. He's squirming. He wants down.
Nurse -> Good. Hold him. Don't let him put anything in his mouth.
Caller -> I won't. I'm holding both his hands.
Nurse -> Okay. Take a breath. When did this happen?
Nurse -> Take your time. Who else is at home with you?
Caller -> Just my mother upstairs. She's asleep. My husband is working nights.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I'm breathing. I'm breathing. Sorry.
Caller -> About twenty minutes ago. I was in the kitchen. I heard the bottle shake. He was under the coffee table. The lid was off. There were pills on the rug. I found two on the rug.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It might be twenty five. I looked at the clock when I found him and then I lost track.
Nurse -> That's fine. About twenty minutes.
Nurse -> How many were in the bottle, do you know?
Caller -> I don't know. My mother takes one a day. She just filled it last week. I don't know. It was almost full. Maybe thirty. Now there are, I don't know, I'm counting. There are twenty seven. So three are gone? Two on the rug and, I don't know. He could have taken one. Or three. I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Take your time counting.
Caller -> I'm putting them on a napkin. One. Two. I keep losing count because he keeps grabbing.
Nurse -> Okay. What's the name of the medicine and the strength?
Caller -> I'm reading it. The label is tiny. Give me one second.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Amlodipine. Five milligrams. A tiny white pill. The label says amlodipine, five.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you. I've written that down.
Nurse -> Amlodipine, five milligrams. Does he have any symptoms? Is he sleepy, vomiting, acting strange?
Caller -> No. No. He's alert. He's laughing. He isn't throwing up. He's not sleepy. He just ate a snack. He's fine. Isn't he?
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> His hands are warm. His color is good. He's talking about dinosaurs.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> He may look fine right now, but with this medicine, the effects can come later. Jacinda, I need you to call 911 right now. Hang up and call. Tell them he swallowed up to three blood pressure pills.
Caller -> I know. I know. I just keep hoping.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> Nine one one? Right now? He looks fine.
Nurse -> Yes.
Caller -> Is this really necessary? I don't want to scare him.
Nurse -> It's the safest choice. He's not in trouble. We want to be careful.
Nurse -> Yes. Right now. It's the safest choice. Please call.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. My phone. Where is my phone. It's in my hand. I'm holding it.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm calling. I'm hanging up. Wait. Should I call poison control?
Nurse -> Go ahead. Ask.
Nurse -> Call 911 first. They will tell you what to do. I will page the on-call clinician.
Caller -> My mother is going to be so upset. She's asleep upstairs.
Nurse -> Don't worry about that now.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Before you hang up. Don't make him vomit. Don't give him anything to eat or drink. Keep the bottle and any pills you find, and take them with you. And stay with him.
Caller -> No vomiting. Nothing to eat or drink. Keep the bottle. Stay. Okay. I'm calling. Wrenley, come here. Come to Mama. Come.
Nurse -> Good. Go.
Caller -> I'm so scared.
Nurse -> I know. You're doing the right thing.
Caller -> I'm calling.
Nurse -> Quickly, so we have it in case you get cut off. What's his date of birth and your number?
Caller -> May eighteenth. Twenty twenty three. He's three. My number is four one four, five five five, oh one five seven.
Nurse -> Four one four, five five five, oh one five seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. I'll answer if you call back.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Okay. I'm calling now.
Nurse -> Keep your phone on afterward. I'll be paging the on-call clinician.
Nurse -> Go. After this, put all medicines up high, in a locked cabinet. We can talk about it later.
Caller -> Locked cabinet. Later. Okay. Wrenley, come to Mama. Come here. Come.
Nurse -> Stay calm for him. He'll follow your lead.
Nurse -> Stay with him. You're doing the right thing.
Caller -> Thank you. Thank you. I'm calling. Bye.

Nurse -> We're here all night.
Caller -> Hi, Winston. This is Genevieve Beaumarchais. My mother is Lucille Beaumarchais. I'm confused about her pain medicine and I want to be sure before I give anything tonight.
Nurse -> Hi, Genevieve. Is your mother comfortable at the moment?
Caller -> More or less. She's awake. I'll explain.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Hi, Genevieve. Thank you for calling instead of guessing. Could you spell the last name for me?
Caller -> Sure. Everyone struggles with it. B E A U M A R C H A I S. Beaumarchais. It's French.
Nurse -> Beautiful name.
Caller -> Thank you. We say it BOW mar shay. But nobody does.
Nurse -> I'll say it that way.
Nurse -> I'll get it right. Take it slow.
Caller -> The first time I ordered a pizza I spelled it and the guy hung up.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> B E A U M A R C H A I S. Got it. Is that Lucille, L U C I L L E?
Caller -> Yes. Two L's, then I L L E. It's my grandmother's name too.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> I'm named after my other grandmother. We have a lot of old names.
Nurse -> They're lovely names.
Nurse -> Thank you. Okay, tell me what's confusing you.
Caller -> I'll try to do it in order. I'm very tired.
Nurse -> There's no rush.
Caller -> So last week the nurse changed her pain medicine. She was on morphine, the liquid, and she's now on Dilaudid. Tablets. I can't keep them straight. The names sound alike.
Nurse -> I see the order change in the chart. Go on.
Nurse -> Okay. Which one is she supposed to be taking now?
Caller -> The Dilaudid. Two milligrams. Every four hours if she needs it. That's what the bottle says. The new bottle. I gave the last one at six tonight.
Nurse -> Dilaudid, two milligrams, as needed, every four hours. Last at six.
Caller -> Yes. And I wrote it on the log at six. The log is on the clipboard.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Right. And I still have the morphine. The old bottle. It's in the comfort kit. Right next to the new one. I almost grabbed the wrong one an hour ago, when she started to hurt. I stopped. I read it twice. I'm so glad I read it.
Nurse -> I understand.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I keep opening the kit and staring at the bottles like they'll tell me.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Good. That is exactly the right thing. Please don't give the morphine anymore. It was stopped last week.
Caller -> Thank you. I was shaking.
Nurse -> You did well.
Caller -> It's ten milligrams per, hold on, it's per five milliliters. The old one. I don't even know what it says. It says ten milligrams. It's the liquid. She hasn't had it in a week. Not since the day the nurse changed it.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's all very helpful. Why did they switch her, do you know?
Caller -> I hope I'm not rambling.
Nurse -> You're doing fine.
Caller -> Her kidneys. The doctor said the morphine could build up. The Dilaudid is easier on the kidneys, he said.
Caller -> That's what he said. I wrote it down. I always write things down.
Nurse -> Smart.
Nurse -> That's right. That's the reason for the change.
Nurse -> Right. That's correct. Okay. How is her pain right now?
Caller -> About a four. She said four when I asked. She's lying on her left side. She's moaning a little, but not terrible. She's, I think she wants to move but can't.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. Four out of ten. Would she like the next dose? It's been, what, about eight hours since six? No. It's been what, about nine now?
Caller -> Mom, do you want your medicine? She nodded. She nodded yes.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> It's almost three in the morning. So yes, nine hours. It's been a while. She's been sleeping most of the night. She woke up about twenty minutes ago.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> I can't sleep anyway. I sit in the chair next to her.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she itchy, or confused, or having any nausea?
Caller -> No itching. No nausea. She knows who I am. She asked about the dog. She said, where's Max? Max is on the foot of the bed. Ha. She's okay.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. Then yes, it is time. Give her one Dilaudid tablet, two milligrams, from the new bottle. Read the label to me first. What does it say?
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting up. The kit is on the dresser. Max is looking at me.
Nurse -> Ha. He's on duty.
Caller -> He hasn't left her side all night. Not once.
Nurse -> Dogs know.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Let me get it. The new one has a white cap. It says Lucille Beaumarchais. Hydromorphone. Dilaudid. Two milligrams. One tablet every four hours as needed. That's the one.
Caller -> I'm reading it with the flashlight on my phone.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the right one. Go ahead and give it.
Caller -> I double checked the strength on the side too. Two milligrams. Yes.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Caller -> Honestly it's nice just to hear a calm voice at night.
Caller -> I'm so glad. My heart is pounding.
Caller -> Okay. I'm giving it. Mom, open up. Under the tongue? Or swallow?
Caller -> Mom, here's your pill. Here's some water. Slow. Good.
Nurse -> Swallow, with a little water.
Caller -> She doesn't like pills. She says they taste like chalk.
Nurse -> A big sip helps.
Caller -> Okay. Mom, swallow. Good. She took it. She took it with water. Okay.
Nurse -> Good. Let her rest now.
Caller -> She's closing her eyes already.
Nurse -> Good. Please write the time on the log right now.
Caller -> I'm looking for the pen. It's on the string. My husband's idea.
Nurse -> Ha. Smart husband.
Caller -> It's two fifty eight. Writing two fifty eight. Done.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Great. Now, the other medicines. Is she on a bowel medicine?
Caller -> I have a list on the fridge. Hold on, I can read it.
Nurse -> That's okay. I have it.
Caller -> The senna. Two tablets at bedtime, every night. I gave it last night. I didn't tonight. She was asleep. Should I give it now?
Nurse -> Tomorrow evening is fine. Skip tonight. But don't double up tomorrow. Two tablets, one time.
Caller -> Okay. Skip tonight. Don't double up. Okay.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Right. One time tomorrow evening.
Caller -> One time. Got it.
Caller -> I put a note on the log. Skip tonight. Underlined.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Genevieve, I need her date of birth for the chart.
Caller -> Of course. She's eighty eight. Almost eighty nine. Birthday is in September, I'll say it properly.
Caller -> September thirtieth. Nineteen thirty eight.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one three one.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one three one. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll send a message to the team so they can take the old morphine out of the house and review her pain plan.
Caller -> Okay. Please. I'm ready.
Caller -> Thank you. I'd be so relieved. It's been sitting there like a trap.
Nurse -> I know.
Nurse -> I understand. And I'd like a nurse to come out tomorrow. To remove it properly, and to check on your mother.
Caller -> Should I save the other bottles for her to look at?
Nurse -> Yes. Keep everything on the dresser where it is.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time?
Caller -> Is it okay if my husband is here? He's her caregiver during the day.
Nurse -> Of course. The more the better.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll be here.
Caller -> I'll tell her the nurse is coming. She likes knowing who's coming.
Nurse -> That helps.
Nurse -> In the meantime, don't give the old morphine, even if you're in a rush. Put it in a separate bag, and mark it old, in big letters. And only give the new medicine at the dose on the label.
Caller -> Separate bag. Mark it old. Only the new one. Okay. I'm going to get a bag. And a marker. Hold on.
Nurse -> Yes.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. I have a paper bag. I'm writing OLD. And I'm putting the morphine in. Done. And I'm putting it in the closet. On the high shelf.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> That's perfect. And from now on, read the name on the label before every dose. Have a second person read it, if you can. And write the medicine, the dose, and the time on the log.
Caller -> I'll tell my husband. He'll feel better about it too.
Caller -> Read the label. Second person. Log it. Okay. My husband can check. He's asleep now but he can check in the morning.
Nurse -> That habit will protect her.
Nurse -> Good. Also, to help with comfort, reposition her with pillows, keep the room quiet, and offer sips of water or a warm drink if she wants.
Caller -> Pillows. Quiet. Warm drink. Okay. She likes warm milk. With honey.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> She likes the radio on low. Classical. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> Does she have a favorite mug?
Caller -> The blue one with the chip. She won't let me throw it out.
Nurse -> Ha. Keep the blue one.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Caller -> She used to make it for me when I couldn't sleep. Now I make it for her.
Nurse -> That's a lovely thing.
Caller -> I never thought I'd be the one making it.
Caller -> She's the best mother. I'm so lucky.
Caller -> She raised four of us in a two bedroom house. I don't know how.
Nurse -> That's remarkable.
Nurse -> I can hear it in your voice.
Nurse -> She's lucky to have you.
Caller -> Do you think she's in pain a lot? When she can't tell me?
Nurse -> That's a hard thing to wonder about.
Nurse -> I think you do a good job reading her face. And the new medicine should help. The team will talk with you about adjusting.
Caller -> I try. She squeezes my hand when it hurts. I know that squeeze.
Caller -> Okay. I'll ask the nurse tomorrow.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Is it all right if I ask about the dog?
Nurse -> You can ask anything.
Nurse -> Please do. Write your questions down.
Caller -> I've been doing that. I have a whole page.
Caller -> I put the dog on it. Is the dog okay on the bed? Max.
Nurse -> The team can answer that one tomorrow.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Thank you, Winston. I feel so much better.
Caller -> I might actually sleep for an hour now.
Nurse -> Please do. She's resting.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Call any time. Even at three in the morning.
Caller -> I'll put the number on the dresser mirror.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> I will. Good night. Or good morning. Ha.
Nurse -> Good morning. Take care.
Caller -> I'll call back if anything changes. Even a little.
Nurse -> Please do.
Caller -> You too, Winston. Thanks for everything.
