transcript:
Nurse -> Cascade Home Health, this is Elias.
Caller -> Hello? Hi. Is this the nurse line?
Nurse -> Yes, this is Elias. I'm a nurse. How can I help?
Caller -> Hi, Elias. It's Hadley Winterbourne. I'm a patient. I had my back surgery in September. I'm calling because the pain is getting worse and I'm not doing well.
Nurse -> Hi, Hadley. Thank you for calling. Is now a good time to talk?
Caller -> Yes. My sister is in the kitchen. I'm in the bedroom with the door shut.
Nurse -> Great. Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Take your time.
Nurse -> Hi, Hadley. I'm glad you called. Tell me what's going on.
Caller -> I've been working up to it all morning. I picked up the phone four times.
Nurse -> I'm glad the fifth time worked.
Caller -> The pain. It's a seven. All the time. It was a four, two weeks ago. Now it's a seven. In my lower back, down my left leg. The Tylenol isn't touching it.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's a lot to carry around.
Caller -> It is. I keep telling people I'm fine. I'm not fine.
Nurse -> A seven out of ten, and getting worse over two weeks. What are you taking for it?
Caller -> Tylenol. A thousand milligrams. Every eight hours if I need it. I took one this morning around nine. I've been taking it every time I can. It does nothing.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Tylenol, a thousand milligrams, as needed, every eight hours. Last at nine this morning.
Caller -> I wish it did more. I'd take anything at this point. Not anything. Sorry.
Nurse -> I know what you mean.
Caller -> Right. I'm not allowed to take more. I know.
Nurse -> That's the right thing to follow. Thank you for being careful.
Nurse -> How is your sleep?
Caller -> Terrible. I sleep two hours, maybe three. I lie there. I watch the clock. And I'm just. I'm low. I feel flat. I cry for no reason. I cried at a commercial yesterday. A dog food commercial.
Nurse -> That's exhausting.
Caller -> I've started to dread the night. The house gets so quiet.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That sounds really hard. How long has your mood been low?
Caller -> About two weeks. Since the pain got worse. Maybe longer. It's hard to say. Time is weird.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> Before that I was doing well. I was walking. I was knitting.
Nurse -> You've lost some of that.
Nurse -> Hadley, I'd like to ask you something directly, because I care about how you're doing. Are you having any thoughts about hurting yourself, or about not wanting to live?
Caller -> Um. Not exactly. I mean. Not like a plan. But I'll say this. I just wish I wouldn't wake up. Some mornings. I lie there and I think, I wish I just hadn't woken up.
Nurse -> Take your time. There's no wrong answer.
Nurse -> Thank you for telling me that. That took courage. I'm taking it seriously. Do you have a plan to hurt yourself or end your life?
Caller -> I've never said it out loud. I'm shaking.
Nurse -> It's okay. I'm right here. I'm not going anywhere.
Caller -> No. No plan. I don't want to do anything. I'm not going to do anything. I just wish it would stop. The pain. And the thinking. I'm so tired.
Nurse -> Thank you for being honest.
Caller -> I'm a teacher. I taught third grade for thirty years. I know about being honest.
Nurse -> It shows.
Nurse -> I hear that. Have you taken anything extra, or thought about taking a lot of your pills?
Caller -> I understand why you ask.
Caller -> No. I'd never. I've never thought about that. I have the Tylenol and that's it. And my sister took my other pills away. The prescription ones. She keeps them at her place.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there anything in the house that you might use to hurt yourself? Firearms? Large amounts of medicine?
Caller -> No guns. We never had guns. The medicine is just the Tylenol bottle. About twenty tablets. I counted. I've been counting.
Nurse -> I'm glad to hear it.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you for answering. Are you alone right now?
Caller -> Sorry. I keep thanking you.
Caller -> It's easier to say it over the phone than to someone's face.
Nurse -> A lot of people feel that way.
Caller -> I'm in my room. I shut the door.
Caller -> No. My sister Dorothea is here. She's staying with me. She's in the kitchen making soup. She has no idea I'm calling. She thinks I'm calling about the pain.
Nurse -> That's good that she's with you.
Caller -> She drove up from Tucson on Tuesday. She said she'd stay two weeks. She's been wonderful.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Nurse -> Would you be willing to tell her? Or let me talk with her?
Caller -> Maybe. Not right now. I don't want to scare her.
Nurse -> You won't be scaring her. She'll want to help.
Caller -> She lost her husband last year. I don't want to put this on her.
Nurse -> I understand that worry.
Nurse -> I understand. I'd like us to work on that together in a minute. First, I'd like to get a few details. What's your date of birth?
Caller -> Okay. Thank you for not rushing me.
Caller -> March eighth. Nineteen sixty four.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one seven six.
Nurse -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one seven six. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Hadley, here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, about the pain and what you told me. They need to know.
Caller -> Okay. Go ahead.
Caller -> Okay. Is that necessary?
Caller -> I just don't want to make a big deal.
Nurse -> It isn't a big deal. It's care.
Nurse -> Yes. I want you to have the right help. Your pain is not controlled, and you're feeling low. Those two things need attention today.
Nurse -> And I'll stay on the line as long as you like.
Caller -> I do want help. I think that's why I called.
Nurse -> That's a strong thing to say.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. You won't send the police, will you?
Nurse -> I understand why you're asking.
Nurse -> I'm not sending anyone to your door against your wishes. You've told me you have no plan, and you're safe right now. I'd like a nurse to come see you today.
Caller -> Today? Oh. Okay. That's, that would be good. I'd feel better with a person.
Caller -> I haven't seen a nurse since the staples came out.
Nurse -> It's time.
Nurse -> I'll ask for this afternoon. And I'll also put in a referral to our social worker. They can help with the low mood, and with managing the pain.
Caller -> Is it the same nurse as before? The one with the curly hair?
Nurse -> It may be. I'll find out.
Caller -> I've never seen a social worker. Is that like a therapist?
Nurse -> Many people haven't. They're kind and practical.
Nurse -> It's similar. They help people cope and find support. Many of our patients find them very helpful.
Caller -> Okay. I'm willing.
Nurse -> That's great.
Nurse -> I'll call you back within the hour, after I've talked to the clinician.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll be right here. I'm not going anywhere. I can't, with my back. Ha.
Caller -> Dorothea just called me from the kitchen. She wants to know if I want soup. I said yes.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Nurse -> If you need me before that, call right back.
Caller -> I will.
Nurse -> I appreciate your humor. It helps. Now, there's a crisis line you can call or text any time, day or night. It's nine eight eight. If the thoughts get stronger, or you think about acting on them, call or text it, call us, or call nine one one.
Caller -> It's how I survive, honestly. Humor and soup.
Nurse -> Both are good.
Caller -> Nine eight eight. I've seen that on TV. I'll save it in my phone. Right now.
Nurse -> It's free and it's there any time.
Nurse -> Go ahead. I'll wait.
Caller -> Hold on. Where's my phone. Oh. It's the one I'm talking on. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Use the one in your hand. Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Saved. Nine eight eight. Under C for crisis. Ha. I'm very organized.
Nurse -> Good. You can also text it if talking is hard.
Caller -> I didn't know you could text. That helps.
Nurse -> Perfect. And Hadley, please keep your sister with you today. And have her manage your medicines, so you don't have to.
Caller -> I'll text her the list too. She's good with lists.
Caller -> She'd never leave me alone anyway. She follows me to the bathroom door.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sister.
Caller -> Dorothea has the other pills at her house. The Tylenol I'll give to her. She can keep it in her purse.
Nurse -> That's a great idea.
Caller -> She's good at that. She was a bookkeeper.
Caller -> I'll tell her. I think I'll tell her. Let me think about how.
Nurse -> You're doing fine. Take your time.
Nurse -> You can say, I talked with the nurse, and I need your help today. That's enough.
Caller -> I need your help today. Okay. I can say that.
Nurse -> Exactly.
Nurse -> For the pain, in the meantime, a heating pad can help. Fifteen minutes at a time, with a cloth between it and your skin. Change position every hour, and take short, slow walks in the house.
Caller -> Heating pad, fifteen. Change position. Short walks. Okay. I can do those. I stopped walking. I was afraid it would hurt more.
Nurse -> Always with a cloth between it and your skin.
Nurse -> Slow and steady.
Caller -> I have a pad in the closet. Dorothea can plug it in for me.
Nurse -> Gentle walking usually helps. Just a few minutes.
Caller -> I have a cane. I haven't used it. Pride, I guess.
Caller -> It's in the umbrella stand. Next to an actual umbrella. Ha.
Nurse -> There's no shame in a cane.
Caller -> I'll walk to the mailbox. With Dorothea.
Nurse -> That sounds great.
Caller -> The mailbox is about forty steps. I counted once. When I could count steps.
Nurse -> Forty steps is a fine goal.
Caller -> Elias?
Nurse -> Yes?
Caller -> Thank you for not freaking out. I thought you'd freak out.
Caller -> My last nurse got that look. You know, the look. You didn't.
Nurse -> I'm just glad you told me.
Nurse -> It sounds like it was hard to say. I'm glad you said it. I'm not freaking out. I'm worried about you, and I want to help.
Caller -> It was. I've been carrying it for two weeks. It feels lighter already.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Caller -> I'm glad I called. I almost didn't.
Nurse -> So am I. You did something hard today.
Caller -> It didn't feel hard. It felt like drowning, and then it felt like someone held out a hand.
Nurse -> That's a good way to say it.
Nurse -> Me too. Let's talk soon. Go find your sister.
Caller -> I'll go find her now. I'll sit with her in the kitchen. She's making soup.
Caller -> I'm putting my slippers on. They're the purple ones.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Nurse -> The soup sounds good.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

Nurse -> Marigold Hospice, this is Rafferty.
Caller -> Hello? Is this the hospice? I can't tell if this is a recording.
Nurse -> No, I'm a real person. This is Rafferty.
Caller -> Hi, Rafferty. This is Winnifred Fontaine. My husband is Aurelio Fontaine. I have the sheet in front of me that the nurse left, the visit summary, and I want to read you some of it. I'm calling about his feet.
Nurse -> Hi, Winnifred. Sure. Tell me what's on your mind.
Caller -> Thank you for taking my call. I know you must be busy.
Nurse -> Not at all. Take your time.
Caller -> I'm sorry, I'm going to read a lot. I like to be thorough. I was a secretary for thirty years.
Nurse -> That's helpful. Go ahead.
Caller -> Okay. So the sheet says, patient name, Aurelio Fontaine. Date of birth, February sixteenth, nineteen forty six. No. Nineteen forty seven. It says nineteen forty seven. I think it's nineteen forty seven. I always say forty six, it's a habit.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> February sixteenth, nineteen forty seven. Thank you.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Yes. Sorry. I do that with his age too. I say seventy seven. He's seventy nine.
Caller -> We've been married fifty three years. I should know.
Nurse -> Fifty three. That's wonderful.
Nurse -> Ha. It happens.
Caller -> Yes. And then it says the team phone number is, hold on, I'll read it, one eight hundred, five five five, oh one one seven. And the after hours line is the same.
Nurse -> That's right. Thanks for confirming.
Nurse -> That's right. Go ahead.
Caller -> And then medications. It lists them. Lisinopril, ten milligrams, once a day. Atorvastatin, twenty, at bedtime. Metformin, five hundred, twice a day. Levothyroxine, seventy five micrograms, in the morning. And Tylenol, as needed.
Nurse -> Okay. That's his medication list. Are you having a question about his medicines?
Caller -> It's three pages with the schedule. I took a highlighter to it.
Caller -> I thought you might want to double check them.
Nurse -> It's very thorough of you.
Caller -> No, no. I'm just reading what's on the sheet. I thought you'd want to know I have it. Then it says the next appointment is Thursday, two o'clock, with the doctor. And Friday, the nurse visit. Is that the same as the one you're going to say?
Caller -> I like to keep everything in the same place. The sheet, the pillbox, the pen.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> I read the whole sheet every morning, with my coffee. I'm that kind of person.
Nurse -> The Friday visit, yes. We'll come back to that. What's the main thing on your mind?
Caller -> Okay. I'll try to get to the point.
Caller -> His feet. Sorry. I get to the point slowly. His feet are puffier this week. Both of them. The ankles, too. When he takes his socks off there are marks, from the elastic.
Nurse -> Okay. Puffier since when?
Caller -> I noticed it when I was helping him with his shoes. They felt tighter.
Nurse -> That's a good observation.
Caller -> Monday, I'd say. Maybe Sunday. It's not terrible. He can still wear his slippers. But it's more than last week.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Or it might have been Saturday. I don't have the exact day.
Nurse -> Is there any pain, redness, or sores on the feet?
Caller -> I'd have called right away if there were. The sheet says to call for that.
Nurse -> You're right.
Caller -> No pain. No redness. They're just puffy. A little shiny on top. I haven't seen any sores.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. And how is his breathing?
Caller -> He had a cold in October but it passed. He's been breathing fine since.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Normal. He's not short of breath. No chest pain. He told me yesterday he feels fine, just fat. Ha. He said his feet are fat.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. And how's his appetite?
Caller -> I make him a milkshake in the afternoon. With a little protein powder.
Nurse -> That's a nice touch.
Caller -> He used to love steak. Now he wants applesauce.
Nurse -> That's common.
Caller -> Fair. He eats breakfast. A couple of bites at lunch. He likes his pudding. He asked for pudding at four o'clock.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. Is he drinking?
Caller -> We keep a cup next to the chair. I refill it every hour.
Caller -> Yes. Water and juice. He likes the grape.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Winnifred, what number should we use to reach you?
Caller -> Oh, my phone number? Of course.
Caller -> You have it. It's on the sheet. It's the same number I always give. Use the number on file.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll use the number on file.
Caller -> Thank you. It never changes. We've had that number since nineteen eighty two.
Nurse -> That's a long time.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'd like a nurse to come out Friday and see him. To look at his feet and legs.
Caller -> Okay. Take your time.
Caller -> Friday. Yes. It's already on the sheet. Ha. See? I told you.
Nurse -> Right. I'm just confirming the details.
Nurse -> It is. I'll also send a message to the team about the puffier feet, so they can look at his plan before Friday.
Caller -> Good. Thank you. Will they change his medicines?
Nurse -> That's up to the team.
Nurse -> They'll look at everything. I can't say what they'll decide.
Caller -> I understand.
Caller -> I just like to know.
Nurse -> In the meantime, raise his feet on pillows when he sits or lies down. Keep his socks loose, no tight elastic. And look at the skin every day, for sore spots.
Caller -> Raise the feet on pillows. Loose socks. Check the skin. Okay. He has those thick socks. I'll cut the elastic. I have scissors.
Caller -> He doesn't like pillows. He says they make his back hurt.
Nurse -> A small one under the calves can work.

Nurse -> Or use a looser pair.
Caller -> I'll buy new ones. Or I'll take his cousin's. His cousin has the loose ones.
Caller -> His cousin Gus. He has feet like boats and wears the loosest socks in the family.
Nurse -> Ha. A good donor.
Nurse -> Soft cotton is best.
Nurse -> Ha. That works.
Caller -> Between us, the cousin is going to be annoyed.

Caller -> Anything else?
Caller -> He's been sleeping more in the afternoons. But he's always been a napper.

Caller -> Not that I can think of. I think the sheet covers everything.
Nurse -> It sounds like you've done great.
Caller -> I wanted to thank you for the sheet. It helps me feel organized.

Caller -> I'm putting the sheet back in the folder now. The folder is red.

Nurse -> Elm.
Caller -> Thank you. You've been a big help.
Caller -> I'll tell Aurelio I talked to you. He'll say, who? Ha.

Nurse -> You're welcome. See you Friday.
Caller -> Sorry for taking so long to get to the point.
Nurse -> You got there. It's all right.
Caller -> I'll make coffee. Thank you again, Rafferty.
Nurse -> Take care, Winnifred.

Nurse -> Lakeshore Home Health, this is Henrietta.
Caller -> Hello? Hello? Can you hear me? I'm sorry, I'm on the oxygen, it makes a hiss.
Nurse -> I can hear you. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi. Henrietta. This is Ottoline Pembrook. I'm a patient. I'm short of, I can't, I've been coughing and I'm short of breath.
Nurse -> Hi there. I'm listening.
Nurse -> Hi, Ortolan. Okay. Take your time. I'm here. Ortolan Pembrook, is that right?
Caller -> I wasn't sure if I should call at night. But it's not night. It's evening. I get confused.
Nurse -> Evening is fine. We're open.
Caller -> Thank you. Give me a second to catch my breath.
Nurse -> Take all the time you need.
Caller -> Okay. Okay. I'm back.
Nurse -> Take a slow breath with me.
Caller -> In. And out. Okay. Better.
Caller -> Is this, is it the pneumonia? Last time it was pneumonia.
Nurse -> I can't say. The clinician will help figure it out.
Nurse -> I'll be quick.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Close enough. Everybody says it wrong. I'm on the oxygen. It makes me, I talk slow.
Nurse -> Sorry if I got it wrong.
Caller -> It's all right. You sounded kind.
Nurse -> I'll do my best.
Caller -> It's Ottoline. Like a bottle. Doesn't matter. Go on.
Nurse -> That's fine. Tell me one thing at a time. What's going on?
Nurse -> I'm writing as you go.
Caller -> I can hear the pen. That's a comfort. Strange, but it is.
Caller -> Okay. I'll try. I've been practicing what to say. I wrote it on a card.
Nurse -> That's smart. Read it if you like.
Caller -> The cough. It's worse. Three days. Yellow stuff. Yellow phlegm. More than usual. And I'm winded. When I walk to the kitchen.
Caller -> I can hear it in the phone. Ha. You must think I sound like a seal.
Nurse -> I think you sound like someone who's working hard to breathe.
Caller -> It's not green. I looked. Just a pale yellow. Like butter.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I cough so hard I get dizzy. Then I have to sit down.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> A cough with yellow sputum for three days. And you're short of breath walking to the kitchen.
Caller -> Yes. That's right. The, the yellow is new. It used to be white.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Yes. And the, the bathroom. I have to stop. And sit. And, and rest. A minute. Then I'm okay.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Even getting dressed. I have to stop between the arms of a sweater.
Nurse -> That sounds tiring.
Nurse -> That's helpful to know.
Caller -> I'm embarrassed. I used to garden. Now I can't make it to the mailbox.
Nurse -> I'm sorry.
Nurse -> Okay. And at rest, sitting? Is your breathing comfortable?
Caller -> Give me, give me a moment. I'm thinking. I want to tell you right.
Nurse -> There's no rush.
Caller -> Pretty good. Sitting. Better. I'm talking in short, short sentences. I know. It's the, the cough.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> If I lie flat, I can't. So I sleep in the recliner.
Nurse -> That's a good setup.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That's okay. Do you have a thermometer? Have you checked your temperature?
Caller -> I do. I have two. One is broken. The other one is the good one.
Nurse -> The good one is fine.
Caller -> I did. An hour ago. Ninety nine point eight. It's a little high for me. I'm usually ninety eight.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> I use the ear one. It beeps when it's done.
Nurse -> Those are good.
Nurse -> Ninety nine point eight. And your oxygen? Do you have the finger clip?
Caller -> Yes. I'm wearing it. It says ninety two. On two liters. Normally it's ninety five. Ninety six.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I wait until the number stops jumping around. Then I read it.
Nurse -> That's the right way.
Nurse -> Ninety two on two liters. Okay. Any chest pain? Are your lips or fingers looking blue?
Caller -> It was ninety five this morning. I noticed it go down. That's why I called.
Nurse -> You did the right thing.
Caller -> No chest pain. No. My lips are pink. I looked in the mirror. And my fingers are fine. They're a little cold. They're always cold.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> My fingernails look okay too. Not blue.
Caller -> I check in the bathroom mirror. Every few hours. Like a ritual.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good. What medicines are you using right now?
Nurse -> Just the ones for this.
Caller -> I have the list. The pharmacy printed it. Hold on, it's on the table.
Nurse -> No rush.
Caller -> I can't reach it from here. I'll tell you from memory.
Caller -> The prednisone. Twenty milligrams. Every morning. This is day three. Of five. I took it this morning with my oatmeal.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I take it with the oatmeal. The doctor said it upsets my stomach otherwise.
Nurse -> That's smart.
Nurse -> Prednisone, twenty milligrams, a day. Day three of five. And anything for the breathing?
Caller -> Right. Five days. They gave me ten pills. I counted. Seven left.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> The neb. The, the albuterol. Two point five milligrams. In the nebulizer. I've used it three times today. The last one an hour ago.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Albuterol, two point five, in the nebulizer, three times today, and the last was an hour ago. Does it help?
Caller -> I count the minutes. Ten minutes per treatment. I set a timer.
Caller -> The little vials. They twist open. They smell like nothing.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Caller -> For a little while. Then the cough, it comes back. And the breathing.
Caller -> I'm so tired of coughing. My ribs are sore from it.
Nurse -> I'm sorry.
Nurse -> I understand.
Nurse -> Okay. Ortolan, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry. I know that. January. I always forget the year. It's the first thing to go.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> January ninth. Nineteen fifty four.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your phone number?
Caller -> Oh. My number. Of course. Let me think.
Caller -> Six four six, five five five, oh one five six.
Caller -> That's my cell. I keep it on the arm of the chair.
Nurse -> Six four six, five five five, oh one six five. Is that right?
Caller -> No. One five six. Oh one five six. Not six five.
Nurse -> Sorry about that.
Caller -> That's all right. Everyone mixes up those two.
Nurse -> Oh one five six. Thank you. Six four six, five five five, oh one five six.
Caller -> Yes. That's it.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Okay. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, about the cough and the shortness of breath.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I don't want to be a bother.
Nurse -> You're not a bother.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Do I need, do I need the hospital?
Nurse -> From what you've told me, I don't think you need the hospital right this minute. Your oxygen is ninety two, your lips are pink, and you can talk. But the clinician needs to look at this.
Caller -> Okay. Okay.
Nurse -> I'd like a nurse to come see you tomorrow. To listen to your lungs.
Caller -> The same one as last time? The one who was funny?
Nurse -> I'll ask. I can't promise.
Caller -> Tomorrow. What time?
Caller -> The neighbor boy mows my lawn on Saturdays. He might be there. He's seventeen. I'll tell the nurse not to mind him.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Morning, I'd expect.
Caller -> I'm up early. I don't sleep much. Any time is fine.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> I'm home. I'm always home.
Nurse -> Good. They'll call first.
Nurse -> And I'll call you back within two hours, after I've heard from the clinician.
Caller -> Two hours. Okay. I'll keep the phone, close. By the chair.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I have the book right here. Page ninety two. Ha. Same as the oxygen number. A coincidence.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I'll try to rest until you call. Is that okay?
Nurse -> That's a good plan.
Caller -> I'll sit by the window. In the good chair. It helps me breathe.
Nurse -> In the meantime, keep taking the prednisone with food each morning until it's finished. Use your nebulizer as needed, but not more often than every four hours.
Caller -> With food. Neb. Every four hours. Not more. Okay. I took the last one an hour ago. So the next one is, is four.
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> Right. Unless you feel much worse. Then call me.
Caller -> I'll try not to feel worse. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. Let's try.
Caller -> I will. I promise.
Nurse -> Thank you. That matters to me.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> Check your oxygen reading and your temperature every four hours. Keep the oxygen on two liters. And sit upright to breathe.
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting my pen.
Caller -> Every four hours. Two liters. Sit up. Okay. I write it down. In my book.
Caller -> I have a notebook next to the oxygen machine. I log the numbers.
Nurse -> Perfect. That'll help the nurse tomorrow.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Henrietta?
Nurse -> Yes?
Caller -> What if it, what if the number goes down?
Nurse -> I'm glad you asked.
Nurse -> Good question. Call nine one one if your lips turn blue, if you have severe trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or if your oxygen reading goes under eighty eight.
Caller -> Okay. Sorry. One more time slowly.
Nurse -> Blue lips, severe trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or under eighty eight.
Caller -> Got it. Thank you.
Caller -> Blue lips. Trouble. Chest pain. Confused. Under eighty eight. Okay. Eighty eight. I'm writing it. On the, on the fridge.
Nurse -> And the last one?
Caller -> Under eighty eight. Yes.
Nurse -> That's right.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I live alone. My sister is, she's an hour away. She can come.
Nurse -> Okay. That's good to know.
Nurse -> Would you like me to call her?
Caller -> She lives in Beaverton. She'd come in an hour. She always says to call.
Nurse -> Then please do, after we hang up.
Caller -> No. I will. After. After we talk.
Nurse -> Okay. Anything else you need?
Caller -> My granddaughter sent me a card today. She drew a dog.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Caller -> Not really. You've been a comfort. Thank you for calling it back so fast.
Nurse -> You're welcome.
Caller -> Let me think. I think that's all.
Caller -> No. Just, just my breath. Ha.
Caller -> Oh, and my cat is on the arm of the chair. She sits on my lap when I cough.
Nurse -> Ha. A good nurse.
Caller -> She purrs when I breathe in. I think she counts.
Nurse -> Cats are good company.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll work on it.
Caller -> You're very kind. Most of the nurses are in a rush.
Nurse -> I'm in no rush.
Caller -> Thank you. Bye.
Caller -> I'll let the sister know. She's going to scold me for waiting.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Ha. Then she cares.
Nurse -> Take care, Ortolan.
Caller -> You too. And thank you, Henrietta.

Nurse -> Hollow Creek Home Care, this is Dominic.
Caller -> Hi, Dominic. It's Rosamund Pyle. I'm the daughter of Beulah Strickland. I'm cleaning out her medicine cabinet and I have a question about her thyroid pill.
Nurse -> Hi, Rosamund. How are you today?
Caller -> A bit frazzled. I've been at it since nine. Cleaning cabinets is exhausting.
Nurse -> Ha. I believe it.
Nurse -> Hi, Rosamund. Thanks for calling. Go ahead. What did you find?
Caller -> I didn't know who else to ask. The pharmacist was on break.
Nurse -> We're happy to help.
Caller -> Two bottles of the levothyroxine. Seventy five micrograms. Same medicine, same strength. One is the new one from last month. The other one is old. I looked at the date. It expired two years ago.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> The old one is dusty. It was in the back of the drawer, behind the tape.
Nurse -> Ha. I know that drawer.
Nurse -> Two bottles, and one expired two years ago. Which one has she been taking?
Caller -> Yes. I even checked it twice. The date says twenty twenty four.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> The new one. I fill her pill box every Sunday from the new bottle. I'm sure about that. I never touched the old one. I don't know why she kept it.
Nurse -> That's a great system.
Caller -> I got the big box with the days and the times. It's purple.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. Is she still taking one a day?
Caller -> Yes. Once a day. In the morning. She took this morning's with her tea. At seven. I watched her.
Nurse -> Good. So she's on the right bottle. Did she ever take any from the old bottle, that you know of?
Caller -> I don't think so. But she's eighty eight. She could have. Her memory's not what it was. She puts things in odd places. I found her glasses in the freezer last week.
Caller -> I check her cabinet every week. I should have thrown it out then.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Has she had any new symptoms? Tiredness, fast heartbeat, anything unusual?
Caller -> I'm trying to think. She did mention she was tired. But she's tired every Tuesday after bridge club.
Nurse -> Ha. Bridge will do that.
Caller -> No. She's the same. She's cranky about the cold. She says the house is freezing. But that's every winter.
Nurse -> Okay. Good.
Nurse -> That's fine. Rosamund, I want to make sure I have her chart right. What's her date of birth?
Caller -> Of course. It's all in my head, but my head isn't reliable.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll check.
Caller -> August twenty third. Nineteen thirty eight. No. Twenty fourth. August twenty fourth. I always get that wrong. My own birthday is the twenty third.
Nurse -> August twenty fourth, nineteen thirty eight. Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Sorry about that. I'm better with my father's. He was born on Christmas.
Nurse -> That's easy to remember.
Caller -> Nine one nine, five five five, oh one eight one.
Nurse -> Nine one nine, five five five, oh one eight one. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Perfect. So, here's what I'd say. Use only the new bottle, the unexpired one. She takes it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, with water. And please don't combine the bottles or pour one into the other.
Caller -> Only the new one. Empty stomach. Water. Don't combine. Okay. I would never combine. But I wondered. I did wonder.
Caller -> She likes it with her tea though. Is a sip okay?
Nurse -> Plain water is best. Tea after about thirty minutes.
Caller -> Okay. I'll tell her.
Nurse -> It's a good thing to ask. Now, I'd also like to check with the pharmacy on when her next refill is due, so she doesn't run short.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. I never know when to call. The pharmacy is a mess on weekends.
Nurse -> That's what I'm here for.
Nurse -> I'll call them. They should be able to tell me the date.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll sleep better.
Caller -> Great.
Nurse -> For the old bottle, you have two options. You can take it to a pharmacy take-back box. Most pharmacies have one by the counter. Or you can mix the pills with used coffee grounds, seal them in a bag, and put them in the trash. Cross out the label first.
Caller -> Take-back box. Or coffee grounds. Cross out the label. Okay. I'll take it to the pharmacy. They have a box at the CVS on Pine. I go there Tuesdays.
Caller -> We don't drink much coffee. I'll have to buy some. For the grounds. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. The take-back box is easier.
Nurse -> That's perfect.
Caller -> I found six other old bottles. Some are from two thousand nineteen. Should I bring them all?
Nurse -> Yes. Bring them all. Don't keep old medicine in the house.
Caller -> I'll fill a grocery bag. It'll be heavy.
Nurse -> That's okay.
Caller -> I will. My father's pills are in there too. He passed in two thousand twenty. I never threw them out.
Nurse -> It's very common. It's good that you're clearing them out.
Caller -> I thought I was being silly keeping them. I kept thinking I'd need them. For what, I don't know.
Nurse -> You're not silly.
Caller -> It's hard. It's like a little time capsule. Every bottle has his name.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's a lot to go through.
Caller -> It is. But it needs to be done.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> Take your time with it.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm going to make a pile for Tuesday. I'll cross out the labels. It feels strange.
Nurse -> That sounds like a plan.
Nurse -> It does. Be gentle with yourself.
Caller -> Thank you, Dominic. That's kind.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Call anytime.
Caller -> I will. Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Kestrel Home Health, this is Lucinda.
Caller -> Hi. Is this home health? I'm calling about my wife. I'm sorry, I'm a little overwhelmed.
Nurse -> You're in the right place. Take a breath.
Caller -> Hi, Lucinda. This is Ambrose Plunkett. My wife is Genoveva Plunkett. She came home from the hospital yesterday and I'm trying to sort out her medicines. I have the discharge paper. The new Eliquis line is smudged and I don't know if it's five or two point five.
Nurse -> Hi, Ambrose. Okay. Let's go through the whole list together. I'm glad you called. Do you have the paper in front of you?
Caller -> I should say, I'm not good with medicine. I'm good with numbers. Not the same thing.
Nurse -> Ha. You're doing well.
Caller -> I wrote everything on a legal pad. Three pages. My handwriting is awful.
Nurse -> That's fine. We'll go slowly.
Caller -> I do. And the bottles. I laid them all out on the kitchen table. There are nine bottles. I counted.
Nurse -> Perfect. That's the best way to do it.
Caller -> I used the whole table. The dog is confused.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Nine. Okay. Let's start with the new ones. What did they start her on?
Caller -> I'm good at counting things. I was an accountant.
Nurse -> That'll help today.
Caller -> Okay. The new ones are in the white bag. The pharmacy bag.
Caller -> The metoprolol. Twenty five milligrams. Twice a day. That's new. She wasn't on it before. I gave her the morning one at eight.
Nurse -> Metoprolol, twenty five, twice a day, new. Last dose this morning. Good. Next?
Caller -> I wrote new next to it with a star. I'm using stars.
Nurse -> Stars are great.
Caller -> The Eliquis. It's the blood thinner. They stopped the old one, the warfarin. And started the Eliquis. Twice a day. That's the one with the smudge. It says twice a day, and then a number, and the number is smudged. It could be a five or a two and a half. I held it up to the light. I can't tell.
Nurse -> Mm hm. Go on.
Caller -> I have the little leaflet that came with it. It's in a language I don't understand. Medical.
Nurse -> Ha. Leaflets are like that.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there a number on the bottle?
Caller -> Let me read it from the label. Hold on. My glasses are in the other room.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Got them.
Caller -> The bottle says five milligrams. The label. But the paper might say two point five. I don't know. If it says two point five, then the bottle is wrong. Or the paper is wrong. I can't tell which.
Nurse -> That's exactly the kind of thing we need to confirm. Did you give her any Eliquis yet?
Caller -> I felt so stupid. I should be able to read my own wife's paper.
Nurse -> You're not stupid. The paper is smudged.
Caller -> Yes. One this morning at eight. The five milligram tablet from the bottle. And I was going to give another tonight at eight.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll come back to that. Let's keep going with the list. Now, the water pill.
Caller -> Okay. I'm sorry. I'm listening.
Caller -> The furosemide. It used to be forty. Now the paper says twenty. Once a day. In the morning. I gave her twenty this morning. I cut the old forty tablets in half. Was that right?
Nurse -> Twenty milligrams once a day. Cutting the forty in half would make twenty, if they're scored. Are the new bottles twenty milligram tablets?
Caller -> I used a pill cutter. She had one from before. It's the kind with the little blade.
Nurse -> Those are fine.
Caller -> There's a new bottle. Twenty. I'm using the new one. I threw the old halves back in the old bottle. It's confusing.
Nurse -> Okay. Good. The twenty milligram bottle is the one to use. Next?
Caller -> I'll put the old one in the stopped bag too. Is that right?
Nurse -> Yes. Good idea.
Caller -> The warfarin. Stopped. The paper says discontinue. I still have the bottle. She took her last one the night before she went into the hospital. That was Monday. Five milligrams, once a day.
Nurse -> Warfarin, five milligrams, stopped. Last dose Monday night. Good. Anything else stopped?
Caller -> It hurts to see the bottle. She took that for ten years.
Nurse -> I understand. It's a big change.
Caller -> The lisinopril. It says hold. Hold until the cardiology visit. Ten milligrams, once a day. She took her last one the day before the hospital. So that's on hold.
Nurse -> Lisinopril on hold. Okay. And the Tylenol?
Caller -> I just want to be sure it's on hold and not stopped forever.
Nurse -> The clinician will clarify that tomorrow.
Caller -> Yes. Tylenol. Five hundred. As needed. Every six hours. She had one yesterday evening for a headache. Just one.
Nurse -> Okay. One yesterday evening.
Nurse -> Okay. And how is she feeling?
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> She's asleep right now. She's in the recliner with a blanket. The dog is on her feet.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
Caller -> Tired. Very tired. She sleeps a lot. The hospital said that's normal. She's walking to the bathroom with the walker. She's a little pale. But she's eating.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> She's slept eleven hours a night since she got home. The hospital kept waking her.
Nurse -> Rest is good for her.
Nurse -> Okay. Is there any bleeding? Nosebleeds, bleeding gums, black stools, bruising?
Caller -> I check her skin every day. Her ankles, her arms. I'm looking for anything.
Caller -> No. Not that I've seen. No black stools. I asked her. She said no. And no bleeding from the incision. There's one small bruise on her arm, from the IV. That's old.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Ambrose, what's her date of birth?
Caller -> Of course. One second.
Caller -> May twenty seventh. Nineteen fifty two.
Caller -> She turned seventy four in May. We had a cake in the hospital. They sang.
Nurse -> What a nice memory.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one seven nine.
Nurse -> Five oh five, five five five, oh one seven nine. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house phone and my cell. Same number.
Caller -> I'll carry the cell with me. Even to the bathroom.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'm going to do about the Eliquis. I don't want you to guess. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now, to confirm the right dose from her discharge.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I was so afraid to guess.
Nurse -> Not guessing was the right call.
Nurse -> I'll also call the pharmacy, and ask what strength they dispensed and what the prescription says.
Caller -> Okay. They close at nine. It's twenty past eight.
Nurse -> I know. I'm moving fast.
Nurse -> Then I'll call them first, right away.
Caller -> I appreciate that. I'm a nervous wreck.
Nurse -> You're doing fine.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll call you back within the hour with an answer.
Caller -> What number will you call from? In case it shows as unknown.
Nurse -> It may show as private. Please answer anyway.
Caller -> I will. I'll answer everything tonight.
Caller -> Within the hour. Okay. I'll keep my phone on.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'll sit right next to it. With the dog.
Nurse -> In the meantime, please hold tonight's Eliquis dose until the clinician confirms it. Give the other medicines as listed. The metoprolol tonight, as scheduled.
Caller -> Okay. Can I ask why it's so complicated? The doctor said just two pills.
Nurse -> Switching blood thinners is a delicate change. The details matter.
Caller -> Hold tonight's Eliquis. Give the metoprolol. Okay. Wait. Won't she be unprotected, without the blood thinner?
Nurse -> That's a fair worry.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> A short delay while we confirm is safer than a wrong dose. The clinician will decide. I expect to reach them quickly.
Caller -> I understand. Thank you for explaining.
Caller -> Okay. I trust you. I just don't want her to have a stroke. She's had one TIA already. That's why she's on it.
Nurse -> I appreciate that.
Nurse -> I understand. We will not leave this hanging. I promise.
Caller -> Thank you. You have no idea how much that helps.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Next, take the warfarin and the lisinopril out of the pile. Put them in a separate bag marked stopped, and keep them away from the pill box.
Caller -> Wait. Let me get a bag first. A big one. Hold on.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Back.
Caller -> Okay. I'm reaching for them. They're by the sugar bowl.
Caller -> Got them. One has a blue cap. The other has a yellow one.
Nurse -> Perfect. Both go in the bag.
Caller -> And the old forty milligram bottle too? I forgot to ask.
Nurse -> Yes. All of the stopped ones.
Caller -> Separate bag. Marked stopped. Away from the pill box. Okay. I'll use a gallon bag. I'm writing STOPPED with a marker. Done. I'm putting it in the cabinet over the fridge.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> That's it.
Nurse -> That's perfect. I'd also like a nurse to come out tomorrow, to go over every bottle with you in person.
Caller -> Thank you. I'll feel better with someone in the house who knows.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Yes please. What time?
Caller -> Should I have the bottles in the same order? Or does it matter?
Nurse -> Leave them as they are. The nurse will sort them.
Nurse -> Morning. I'll ask for ten.
Caller -> Ten works.
Caller -> I'll make sure the dog is out of the room. She barks at the door.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you.
Nurse -> And Ambrose, call 911 right away if she has black or bloody stools, vomits blood, has a nosebleed that won't stop, falls and hits her head, or gets a sudden, severe headache.
Caller -> Black stools. Vomiting blood. Nosebleed. Head injury. Sudden headache. Okay. I'm writing it on the same bag. No, a different piece of paper.
Nurse -> Perfect. Keep that where you can see it.
Nurse -> Different paper is better.
Caller -> I put it on the fridge with the pineapple magnet.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Okay.
Nurse -> You've done a great job today. It's a lot of medicines to manage.
Caller -> I'm trying. My daughter is flying in tomorrow. She'll help.
Nurse -> That'll make a difference.
Caller -> Thank you. I've never done anything like this. She always handled her own pills. Now I'm the one.
Nurse -> I know. It's a lot, and you're handling it.
Nurse -> You're doing it carefully. Asking questions is the best thing.
Caller -> I'm learning. Slowly.
Nurse -> That's how everyone learns it.
Nurse -> I'll call the pharmacy now.
Caller -> Thank you, Lucinda. I'll wait for your call.
Nurse -> And Ambrose, you're doing a good job.
Caller -> Thank you. I didn't think I could do this. I'm still not sure.
Nurse -> You can.
Nurse -> Talk soon.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Larkin Street Home Care, this is Oswald.
Caller -> Hello? Is this Larkin Street? I'm new. I'm not sure I dialed right.
Nurse -> You did. This is Oswald, I'm a nurse here.
Caller -> Hi. Hi, this is Cornelius Blackwood. I'm an aide. I'm covering today for Odessa, she's on vacation. I'm at a client's house and I'm worried about him. I think his name is Mr. Haskins. Walter Haskins.
Nurse -> Hello, Cornelius. Where are you calling from?
Caller -> Thank you for picking up so fast.
Caller -> From the client's apartment. In the kitchen. He's in the living room. I'll keep my voice low.
Nurse -> Hi, Cornelius. Okay. Slow down. Walter Haskins. Do you have an address?
Caller -> Sorry. I'm talking fast. I always talk fast when I'm nervous.
Nurse -> It's okay. Take a breath.
Caller -> Yes. It's, hold on, it's on the sheet. Four oh seven, Alder Court. Apartment B.
Caller -> One second. I'm standing in the hallway so he doesn't hear me. It's very quiet in here.
Nurse -> Four oh seven Alder Court, B. Let me look. I have a Walter Haskell at that address. H A S K E L L. Is that him?
Nurse -> Thank you. Is there a doorbell or a keypad?
Caller -> The door was unlocked when I came. His daughter said she'd leave it open for me.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> Take your time. I'm looking at the door. It has a wreath on it. Fall leaves.
Caller -> Walking. The floorboards creak. Hold on.
Nurse -> Okay. I see it.
Caller -> Haskell. Haskins. It might be Haskell. I only saw it on the sheet once. I'm sorry. I didn't look closely. The sheet is, there's a coffee stain on it.
Nurse -> That's okay. Is he an older man? About eighty?
Caller -> I didn't mean to be unprepared. I only got this assignment last night.
Nurse -> That's not your fault.
Caller -> Yes. Yes. Eighty something. Gray hair, glasses. He has the big green chair. He has a cat named Biscuit.
Nurse -> Good. That helps me confirm.
Nurse -> Let's get him seen.
Caller -> And a mustache. He keeps trimming it, I think. It's neat.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. That matches the chart.
Caller -> He has a cardigan. The brown one with the leather buttons. He's very dapper.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> That sounds right. Okay. So tell me what's worrying you.
Caller -> He's not himself. At least, I think he's not. I don't really know what himself is. I've never met him. Odessa left me a note, but the note says nothing about, well, it says he likes tea and his show at three.
Nurse -> Mm hm. Go on.
Nurse -> Okay. What's different from what the note describes?
Caller -> He's quiet. Very quiet. The note said he's chatty. I said good morning and he just looked at me. Then he said, are you the new girl? Then nothing. He's been sitting in the chair since I got here at nine.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I've sat with other clients who were quiet. It felt different. This felt, flat.
Nurse -> Okay. That's a helpful description.
Caller -> I don't know if that helps. I'm not a nurse. I'm just an aide.
Nurse -> It helps a lot.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he eaten anything?
Caller -> Toast. At nine thirty. He ate half a piece. Then I made lunch at noon, a sandwich, and he didn't touch it. He said he's not hungry. He didn't want his tea either. And the note says he loves his tea.
Nurse -> Okay. And fluids?
Nurse -> Okay. Did he drink anything at all?
Caller -> A sip of water. Maybe two. When I handed it to him. Then he put it down.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I'll keep trying. I'll bring him water every few minutes.
Caller -> I offered juice, too. Apple. He shook his head.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. How does he look? Is his color okay?
Caller -> I don't know. He looks a little flushed? Maybe? I touched his forehead, quickly. It felt warm. But I don't know. My hands might be cold. I just came in from outside.
Nurse -> That's useful. Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Do you have a thermometer there?
Caller -> There's probably one. Everyone has one. I'll look after this.
Caller -> I haven't looked. I didn't want to go through his things.
Nurse -> You're being respectful. That's good.
Nurse -> That's okay. We'll come to that. Is he confused? Does he know where he is?
Caller -> I don't want to test him too much. He might feel embarrassed.
Nurse -> You can ask gently.
Caller -> I asked him what day it is. He said, Tuesday? It's Monday. Or is it? Hold on. What's today? It's Monday. I'm pretty sure. Yeah, Monday. He said Tuesday. But then he said it was a nice morning, and it's the afternoon.
Caller -> He's not usually forgetful, the note says. I assume.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Has he fallen? Has he complained of any pain?
Caller -> I didn't see a fall. I don't think so. He hasn't said anything hurts. But he doesn't say much. So I don't know.
Nurse -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he breathing normally?
Caller -> I think so. He's not gasping. He's just sitting. He's, I don't know, calm.
Caller -> I count his breaths sometimes. I count in my head. It's a habit from my mother.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I wasn't sure whether to call you or the agency's main number.
Nurse -> You reached the right line.
Nurse -> Does he know who you are?
Caller -> He asked if I'm the new girl. He called me Odessa once. Then he said no, not Odessa.
Caller -> I'm forty nine. Ha. New girl. I'll take it.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. Cornelius, you've done the right thing calling. Do you know his date of birth?
Caller -> I really appreciate you saying that. I haven't had many clients this fragile.
Nurse -> You're handling it well.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm sorry for all the rambling.
Nurse -> It's useful rambling.
Caller -> No. I wouldn't know that. It's probably on the sheet? Hold on. I'm looking. No. It just has his name and the address, and the emergency number, and what he likes. No birthday.
Caller -> Is that a problem? I feel like I should have known.
Nurse -> No. You aren't expected to.
Nurse -> That's fine. I'll find it. What's the best number to reach you?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one two eight.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one two eight. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell. It's the only phone I have.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to page the on-call clinician right now. I'll tell them what you saw and that we don't know his normal.
Caller -> Okay. I'm listening.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. Am I overreacting? I feel like I'm overreacting.
Nurse -> Take a breath.
Nurse -> No. You're not. You noticed a change. Even without knowing his baseline, quiet, not eating, not drinking, a little warm, and mixed up about the day is something we want to look at today.
Caller -> Okay. That makes me feel better. I was afraid you'd say, he's old, that's how they are.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Nurse -> No. I'd never say that.
Caller -> Good.
Nurse -> I'd also like a nurse to come see him today. I'll ask for as soon as possible.
Caller -> Today. Okay. Great. I'm here until five. Odessa's schedule says I leave at five.
Nurse -> Yes.
Nurse -> I'll make sure the schedule covers you.
Nurse -> You'll stay until the nurse arrives, if that's all right. I'll let your supervisor know.
Caller -> Yes. I'll stay. I don't have to be anywhere.
Nurse -> I'll make sure your supervisor knows.
Caller -> Thank you.
Caller -> I told my husband not to wait on dinner.
Nurse -> Thank you for staying.
Nurse -> Thank you. I'll call you back within thirty minutes after I've talked with the clinician.
Caller -> Thirty minutes. Okay. I'll keep my phone out.
Caller -> I'll sit with him in the living room. I won't leave him alone.
Nurse -> In the meantime, stay with him. See if you can find a thermometer, a bathroom cabinet is a good place. Take his temperature under his arm. Offer him sips of water. And write down what you see and the time.
Caller -> Okay. I'm already standing in the doorway watching him.
Caller -> Stay with him. Thermometer. Under the arm. Sips of water. Write it down with the time. Okay. I'm going to look in the bathroom. Hold on. I'm going to put you on the table.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Okay. Found one. It's the kind with the digital screen. It's in a little case. I'll go sit by him.
Caller -> It has a case with a little sticker. It says Walter on it in marker.
Nurse -> Good. That helps with the name.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll wait.
Caller -> Hold on. I'm putting him on his side a little. He's slumping.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Mr. Haskins? Mr. Haskins? Walter? I'm going to take your temperature. Under your arm. Is that okay? He nodded. He's lifting his arm. Okay. Okay. Wait for the beep.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> It beeped. One hundred point eight. Oh. That's high, isn't it?
Nurse -> That's a mild fever. I'll tell the clinician. Thank you for checking.
Caller -> Should I take his temperature again later?
Nurse -> Yes. In about an hour. Write both numbers down.
Caller -> Is mild a good word or a bad word?
Nurse -> It's a word that means it isn't dangerous on its own, but it matters with the other things you saw.
Caller -> Okay. That makes sense.
Caller -> Okay. Should I give him Tylenol?
Nurse -> It's a good question.
Nurse -> Please don't give anything until the clinician says. I'll call you back in thirty minutes.
Caller -> Understood. I'll keep it in my bag.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Okay. I won't. Sorry.
Nurse -> Cornelius, call 911 if he is hard to wake, can't answer simple questions, has trouble breathing, or falls.
Caller -> Hard to wake. Can't answer. Trouble breathing. Falls. 911. Okay. He's awake. He just looked at me. He said, hello, dear. That's good, right?
Caller -> I'll set an alarm to check on him every ten minutes. Just to make sure he's okay.
Nurse -> That's a good idea.
Nurse -> That's good. Keep talking to him.
Caller -> Biscuit just jumped on his lap. He's petting the cat.
Caller -> He's smiling a little. I think. It's hard to tell.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Caller -> I will. I'm going to tell him about my dog.
Caller -> I have a beagle named Pickle. He loves a good story.
Nurse -> Ha. He sounds fun.
Caller -> He's a menace. But a loving one.
Nurse -> Ha. A good name.
Nurse -> That sounds lovely.
Caller -> Thank you, Oswald. You've been really kind.
Nurse -> Of course. Hang in there.
Caller -> I'll text my husband that I'll be late. He'll understand.
Nurse -> You're doing a good job. Talk soon.
Caller -> I'm glad I called. I almost texted my supervisor instead.
Nurse -> The phone is better. Thank you.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Winterhaven Hospice, this is Leander.
Caller -> Hello? Is this the hospice? I called earlier and got a voicemail.
Nurse -> I'm sorry about that. You've got me now.
Caller -> Hi, Leander. This is Pilar Santoro. I'm the granddaughter of Hildegard Vanderwal. The hospital bed came yesterday and some of it is missing. And I found a red spot on her back.
Nurse -> Hi, Pilar. I'm glad you called. How is your grandmother right now?
Caller -> She's napping. She naps in the afternoons. I'll keep my voice down.
Nurse -> Hi, Pilar. I'm sorry about the missing pieces. Tell me what came and what didn't.
Caller -> Thank you. I didn't want to make a fuss, but my aunt said call.
Nurse -> Your aunt is right.
Caller -> The bed came. The frame, the motor, the remote. They put it together in her bedroom. But there are no side rails. The delivery man said they were on the next truck. That was yesterday at four.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> The delivery men were nice. They were quick. They just forgot half.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> The bed came without the rails. And the mattress?
Caller -> I should have checked the paperwork before the driver left. I signed it. I just wanted him gone.
Nurse -> That's very common.
Caller -> The mattress. They put her old mattress on it. The regular one. The paperwork says a pressure mattress. The special one that fills with air. It didn't come. He said it was backordered.
Nurse -> I see.
Caller -> It's an old one. It sags in the middle. I don't love it for her back.
Nurse -> Okay. So the bed is there, and the rails and the pressure mattress are not.
Caller -> Yes. It's a really nice bed. It goes up and down. She likes it. She calls it the elevator.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Yes. I've been calling the equipment company all morning. It goes to a menu. I pressed all the numbers.
Caller -> I was on hold for forty minutes. A song played the whole time. The same song.
Nurse -> That sounds maddening.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. We'll take care of it. Let me ask about your grandmother. You mentioned a red spot.
Caller -> Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear.
Caller -> Yes. This morning I was helping her change her gown. Her tailbone area, at the bottom of her spine. There's a red spot. About the size of a half dollar. It's not open. It's just red. And a little warm.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I was looking for a clean one and she turned and I saw it.
Nurse -> Okay. Is it open? Any drainage, blisters, broken skin?
Caller -> I looked closely. I took my glasses off and put them back on. Both ways, no blisters.
Caller -> No. It's not open. Just red. I pressed on it with my finger and it didn't turn white right away. Is that bad? I read that online.
Nurse -> That can be a sign of early pressure injury. I'm glad you caught it. Is she in pain there?
Caller -> I knew it. I read about it for an hour at two in the morning. I scared myself.
Nurse -> Reading at two in the morning will do that.
Caller -> She winces. A little. When I touch it. She doesn't say much. She's, she's ninety one. She says, it's fine, dear.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. Has she been staying in bed most of the day?
Caller -> She likes the bed more than the recliner. She says it's like a ship.
Nurse -> Ha. A cozy ship.
Caller -> Yes. Mostly. We sit her up for meals. She's mostly in bed.
Nurse -> Okay. That's helpful to know.
Nurse -> Okay. Pilar, I'd like her birth date for the order.
Caller -> Sure. I know that one. It's the same month as my sister's.
Caller -> October twelfth. Nineteen thirty five.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> She'll be ninety one in a month. No, wait. She's already ninety. Hmm. I'm not sure.
Nurse -> The date is what I need.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Two oh six, five five five, oh one seven nine.
Nurse -> Two oh six, five five five, oh one seven nine. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Caller -> I'll leave the ringer on. Even when I'm in the bathroom.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'll do. I'll place an order with the equipment company for the side rails and the pressure relieving mattress. I'll mark it urgent.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Please. I've been so worried.
Nurse -> I understand.
Nurse -> I'll also arrange delivery today. Will someone be at the house?
Caller -> Is it all right if the delivery man needs to use the side door? The front is blocked with her chair.
Nurse -> I'll add that to the note.
Nurse -> The company has a window between two and five usually.
Caller -> That works. I'll cancel my errands.
Caller -> Yes. Me. And my aunt. We're both here all day.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'll call the company myself and get a time.
Caller -> Sorry, one more thing. Can I move her mattress to the floor in the meantime?
Nurse -> No, please keep her in the bed at the lowest height.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> Thank you. I think they'll respond better to you than to me.
Nurse -> I'll do my best.
Caller -> Thank you, Leander.
Nurse -> Of course.
Nurse -> I'm also going to send a message to the team about the red spot. I'd like them to look at it, and add skin care to her plan.
Caller -> Please. I didn't know if I should be calling about it.
Nurse -> You should always call about skin.
Nurse -> Yes, you did the right thing. And I'd like a nurse to come see her tomorrow.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Good. Morning or afternoon?
Caller -> My aunt works afternoons. Morning is better for her.
Nurse -> I'll note that.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Caller -> Perfect.
Nurse -> In the meantime, here are a few things. Turn her every two hours, from one side to the other, with a pillow between her knees. Keep any weight off the red spot. Keep the skin clean and dry.
Caller -> Every two hours. Side to side. Pillow between the knees. Nothing on the spot. Clean and dry. Okay. I'm writing a chart. I'll put it on the wall.
Caller -> Should I wake her at night to turn her?
Nurse -> Yes, gently. Every two hours, day and night.
Caller -> Okay. We'll take shifts.
Caller -> We have to set an alarm. I'm terrible at remembering.
Nurse -> An alarm is a good idea.
Nurse -> That's a great idea. Also, until the rails arrive, keep the bed in its lowest position, and put pillows or rolled blankets along the open sides.
Caller -> Lowest position. Pillows on the sides. Okay. The remote is by her hand. Is that okay? She presses buttons.
Caller -> We have lots of pillows. Her friends brought them. Fourteen, I think.
Nurse -> Ha. That'll do.
Nurse -> Move the remote out of reach for now. Pressing it can raise the bed.
Caller -> She'll be so annoyed. She loves that remote.
Nurse -> Ha. Just for now.
Caller -> Oh. I didn't think of that. I'll put it on the dresser.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> Okay. Done. It's on the dresser.
Caller -> She tried to press the buttons earlier. She looked confused when nothing happened. Ha.
Nurse -> Ha. A sign of curiosity.
Nurse -> And call us if the skin opens, if it drains, if it turns purple or black, or if she seems to be in more pain.
Nurse -> I'll say it again if you need.
Caller -> No, I have it. Thank you.
Caller -> Opens. Drains. Purple or black. More pain. Okay. I'll look at it every time we turn her.
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Thank you for being so patient with me. I'm not good with this.
Caller -> I wasn't sure who to call. The agency number was on the bottom of the form.
Nurse -> That's the right number.
Nurse -> No problem at all.
Nurse -> You're doing great.
Caller -> I really appreciate it. She's my favorite person.
Nurse -> Anytime.
Nurse -> It shows.
Caller -> I'll tell her you said that. She'll say, who's Leander?
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Bye.

transcript:
Nurse -> Sparrow Hill Pediatric Home Nursing, this is Casper.
Caller -> Hello? Thank goodness. I wasn't sure anyone would pick up at this hour.
Nurse -> The night line is always staffed.
Caller -> Hi, Casper. It's Meenakshi Chaudhary. My son Ravi Chaudhary has a fever and I want to be sure I'm giving his medicines right.
Nurse -> Hi, Meenakshi. Let's go through it. How high is the fever?
Caller -> Hi. Thank you. I know you must be busy tonight.
Nurse -> Never too busy for a feverish four year old.
Caller -> I'm in the kitchen so I won't wake him. The couch is right around the corner.
Caller -> Thank you for calling back so fast. I only waited a minute.
Caller -> Okay. I wrote a few things down. I'm going to read them in a mess.
Nurse -> That's fine.
Caller -> One hundred two point three. I took it under his arm about twenty minutes ago. It was one oh three at nine. No. One hundred three at nine. It's coming down.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I used the digital one. It beeps three times. I held his arm down. He's wiggly.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> One hundred two point three now. Okay. How old is he, and about how much does he weigh?
Caller -> He's four. Forty pounds. About that. He had his checkup in September and he was forty one.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Caller -> I thought I should say so you can do the math. Is that right?
Nurse -> It is.
Nurse -> Okay. What have you given him so far?
Caller -> Two medicines. I know you're not supposed to give both. But the doctor said to alternate.
Nurse -> Alternating is fine if you space them.
Caller -> The Tylenol. The children's liquid. It says one sixty milligrams per five milliliters on the front. I gave seven and a half milliliters. Two hours ago. At eleven. No. It was ten forty. Two hours, almost.
Nurse -> Tylenol, seven and a half milliliters, about two hours ago. And what else?
Caller -> Yes. I measured it with the syringe. The one that came with the bottle.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'm sorry I'm so jumpy. He's never had a fever this high.
Nurse -> That's very understandable.
Caller -> The Motrin. The ibuprofen. The one with the hundred milligrams per five. Seven and a half milliliters. I gave it at, hold on. It was eleven. Yes. No. It was nine. It was before dinner. At nine tonight. No wait, that's not right either.
Nurse -> Take your time. When did you give the Motrin?
Caller -> I'm so scrambled. It's the middle of the night.
Nurse -> It's okay.
Caller -> Nine. Nine this evening. I'm sure. Because I gave it right after his bath. And then the Tylenol came later. I mixed up the order in my head. The Tylenol was ten forty. Wait. That would be after nine. Yes. So Motrin at nine, then Tylenol at ten forty. That's right.
Nurse -> Okay. Motrin at nine, then Tylenol at ten forty. Is that what you're sure of?
Caller -> Yes. Motrin first. Tylenol second. Nine and ten forty.
Caller -> Yes. I looked at the clock when I gave each one. I wrote them on the back of my hand. See? Ha. Not that you can see.
Nurse -> That habit is going to help.
Nurse -> Ha. Smart. Okay. How is he acting?
Caller -> I keep going in to check. Every five minutes. I'm wearing out the carpet.
Nurse -> Ha. That's what parents do.
Caller -> He's mostly lying down. He asked for his stuffed rabbit.
Nurse -> That's a good comfort.
Caller -> Tired. He's lying on the couch. He said his throat is a little sore. He's drinking water, a few sips at a time. He's watching his show. He's not crying.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he responding to you when you talk?
Caller -> Yes. He answers. He asked for his rabbit twice. He's with it.
Nurse -> Does he have a rash, a stiff neck, or any trouble breathing?
Caller -> I checked everything. Twice. I pulled up his shirt to look for a rash. He laughed. He's ticklish.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sign.
Caller -> No rash. I checked his belly. He can touch his chin to his chest. I made him. He did it. Breathing normal. He's not fast. No.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Good. What's his date of birth?
Caller -> Sorry, I'm happy to give it. It's July.
Caller -> He turned four in July. We had a dinosaur party. He still wants a dinosaur cake every day.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> July fourteenth. Twenty twenty two.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one nine eight.
Nurse -> Eight one six, five five five, oh one nine eight. Right?
Caller -> Yes.
Nurse -> Okay. Meenakshi, you've given the right amounts for his weight. Seven and a half milliliters of either of those is right for forty pounds. The important thing now is timing. You should wait at least six hours between doses of the same medicine.
Caller -> Oh good. I thought I'd made a mistake. Whew.
Nurse -> You didn't.
Caller -> Six hours for each one. So the Tylenol again after four forty in the morning. And the Motrin after three. Right?
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> The Motrin could be given again after three, yes. And the Tylenol, no sooner than four forty. And please don't give them both at the same minute. Write each dose and time on a sheet of paper.
Caller -> Write it on paper. Not my hand. Okay.
Nurse -> Ha. Paper is better.
Caller -> Okay. My handwriting is better on paper anyway.
Caller -> I'll tape it to the refrigerator. So my husband can see when he gets up.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> And then I'll draw a happy face on it for him to look at.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I have a notepad on the fridge.
Nurse -> Put the time and the amount for each dose.
Caller -> I'll do that. Two columns. One for each medicine.
Nurse -> Perfect. I'm going to send a message to the team about the fever, so they know.
Nurse -> Is there anything else you want to ask?
Caller -> I think that's all. I'm just glad someone is on the line.
Caller -> Okay. Should I tell my husband to call too?
Nurse -> He can call anytime.
Caller -> Is it okay if I wake him to give a dose, if he's asleep?
Nurse -> You don't need to wake him just for a dose. Let him sleep.
Caller -> Okay. That's a relief.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you.
Nurse -> I'll also call you back in about two hours, to see how he's doing and what the temperature is.
Caller -> Two hours. That would be one in the morning. Okay. I'll be up.
Nurse -> I'll watch the clock.
Nurse -> In the meantime, offer him small sips of water, diluted juice, or a popsicle, often. And dress him in light clothing. No heavy blankets.
Caller -> Sips. Juice. Popsicle. Light clothes. Okay. We have popsicles. The red ones. He loves them.
Caller -> The red ones. They stain everything. I put a towel down.
Nurse -> Ha. Smart.
Caller -> He's wearing his pajamas with the planets. They're cotton. Light.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Take him to the emergency room, or call 911, if he has a seizure, a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade when you press it, trouble breathing, or if he's hard to wake.
Caller -> I have the hospital on speed dial. I'm just saying.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Seizure. Stiff neck. Rash. Breathing. Hard to wake. Okay. I'm writing it on the notepad too.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Thank you, Casper. I was so nervous about getting the doses wrong.
Nurse -> You're welcome. You can call again if you're unsure.
Caller -> I will. I'm keeping this number by the phone.
Nurse -> You did a good job. You kept track.
Caller -> I try to be organized. It's the only way I survive two kids.
Nurse -> Two. That's a lot at midnight.
Caller -> Yes, the other one sleeps through everything.
Caller -> Thank you. It helps to have someone say that.
Caller -> I did. Ha. On my hand.
Nurse -> Talk in two hours.
Nurse -> And if anything changes before then, call right away.
Caller -> I will. Thank you.
Caller -> I'll answer on the first ring.
Caller -> Bye.
