transcript:
Nurse -> Pinewood Hospice, this is Tamara.
Caller -> Hello, Tamara. I hope this isn't a bad time. I can call back if it is.
Nurse -> It's a good time. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Tamara. It's Sunniva Lundgren. My father is Engelbert Lundgren. The comfort kit came yesterday and I'm scared of it. I want to understand every medicine in it before I need it.
Nurse -> Hi, Sunniva. I got your message about the kit. I'm glad you called.
Caller -> Thank you. I wasn't sure whether to bother you.
Nurse -> It's never a bother.
Nurse -> Hi, Sunniva. That's a wise thing to do. Let's go through them, one at a time. How is your father today?
Caller -> I couldn't sleep last night thinking about it.
Caller -> I made a list of questions. It's two pages long. My husband teased me.
Nurse -> Ha. Two pages is just right.
Caller -> Peaceful. Sleeping most of the day. He woke up for juice at ten and a few bites of pudding at noon. Then he went back to sleep. He doesn't seem to hurt. He isn't restless. His breathing is quiet.
Nurse -> Does he wake easily when you speak to him?
Caller -> Yes. He opens his eyes and smiles. Then he drifts off again.
Nurse -> That's a gentle pattern.
Caller -> He had a good morning. He asked about the weather.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I sit with him in the afternoon. I read to him. Mostly poetry. He used to be a teacher.
Nurse -> What a nice thing to do.
Nurse -> That's good. So none of the kit has been needed yet?
Caller -> Not yet. I keep waiting. Part of me hopes we never need it.
Nurse -> I understand.
Caller -> My brother says to just give something in advance. To be safe.
Nurse -> Please don't. Medicines are for symptoms, not for prevention here.
Caller -> Okay. That's what I wondered.
Nurse -> That's a natural feeling.
Caller -> No. I haven't opened it. It's in a plastic box on the dresser. There are six bottles and a little bag. I took them all out and lined them up, and I can't remember what the nurse said.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That's fine. Read me the first label.
Caller -> Okay. The box has a printed list on the lid but it's in tiny type.
Nurse -> We'll make the big one.
Caller -> Okay. It's small print. Let me turn on the lamp.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> I'm writing as fast as I can.
Caller -> There. Much better.
Caller -> The first one says morphine. Concentrate. Twenty milligrams per milliliter. It's in a brown bottle with a dropper. The label says five milligrams, which is zero point two five milliliters, under the tongue, every four hours as needed for pain or shortness of breath.
Nurse -> Right. That's a quarter of a milliliter. The syringe has a mark for it. It's for pain, or for the feeling of not getting enough air. Give it under the tongue, and it works within about twenty minutes.
Caller -> I have to say, that sounds like so little.
Nurse -> It's a small amount of a strong medicine. That's why the mark matters.
Caller -> A quarter of a milliliter. The line on the syringe. Okay. I'll show my husband. We've been calling it the little line. Ha.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect. What's next?
Caller -> Okay. I'm getting ahead of myself. I'll read each one slowly.
Caller -> I'll stick a note on the box with your name. In case my husband picks up.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> Next. Let me find it. It's the little tablets in the blister pack.
Caller -> The next one says lorazepam. Half a milligram. A tablet. Under the tongue. Every four hours as needed. For anxiety or restlessness.
Nurse -> Right. That one is for restlessness, anxiety, or agitation that comes from fear. Not for pain. A different symptom, a different medicine.
Caller -> Anxiety. Okay. He did get anxious in the hospital. Once.
Nurse -> Then you'll recognize it if it happens.
Caller -> I understand. I'll tell my husband that distinction. He's not very clear on it.
Nurse -> We'll go over it Thursday too.
Caller -> Different symptom, different medicine. Okay. I wrote that. And the next one says haloperidol. H A L O P E R I D O L. One milligram. Every six hours as needed. For nausea or agitation, or confusion that scares him.
Caller -> I like that. It's easy to remember.
Nurse -> That's the idea.
Nurse -> Right. Haloperidol, one milligram. That is for nausea, or for confusion or agitation that lorazepam doesn't settle. Some people call it Haldol.
Nurse -> Take it as it comes.
Caller -> It's a lot of syllables. I may just say the H one.
Nurse -> Ha. That's fine, as long as you read the label.
Caller -> Haldol. Yes. The nurse said Haldol. I didn't connect them. It's a long name. There's another one that sounds the same. Haloperidol and, no, that's the lorazepam. The names are all so alike. Haldol, Ativan. Ativan is the lorazepam, right?
Nurse -> Yes. Ativan is lorazepam. Haldol is haloperidol. Two different medicines, even though they can both help with agitation. That's why the labels matter.
Caller -> Ha. I'm going to need an index card for each one.
Caller -> I wish they'd put big letters on the front. The brand name is in a tiny font.
Nurse -> Good feedback. I'll pass it on.
Caller -> Okay. I'll write the brand names next to the real names. On a card.
Caller -> I'll use a red pen for the brand names and blue for the real names.
Nurse -> That should work well.
Nurse -> That's helpful.
Nurse -> Yes.
Nurse -> A card is a great idea. What's next?
Caller -> Atropine. Drops. One percent. Two drops under the tongue, every four hours as needed. For the, for secretions. The rattle. I think that's what they said. When it gets noisy.
Nurse -> Right. Atropine drops are for noisy, rattly breathing from secretions near the end. Two drops under the tongue. They dry the secretions. It's for the sound; it's mostly for the family's comfort, but it can help.
Caller -> I don't think I'm ready for that. I'm not sure I'll ever be ready.
Nurse -> It helps to know it's there if you need it.
Caller -> For the sound. Okay. That's a hard one to think about.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> I know.
Caller -> My mother died at home. I was twelve. Nobody explained anything. I want to do this right.
Nurse -> You're doing it right.
Caller -> Thank you for not rushing me.
Nurse -> Never.
Caller -> Okay. And then the little bag has the suppositories. Tylenol. Six hundred fifty milligrams. Every six hours as needed for fever or mild pain, if he can't swallow.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> Right. That's for fever, or mild pain, when he can't take anything by mouth. One suppository at a time. Not more than every six hours.
Caller -> We've been using the regular kind. The tablet. He took it fine until last week.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know.
Caller -> Is it hard to do? The suppositories?
Nurse -> The nurse will show you Thursday. It's easier than you think.
Caller -> One. Every six hours. Okay. I'm writing all of this.
Nurse -> Take your time. Sunniva, I'd like his date of birth for the chart.
Caller -> Sure. Let me just put down my pen.
Caller -> Sure. He'll be eighty two. He's eighty one now. No. Eighty four? Hold on, I always mess it up.
Nurse -> The date is what I need.
Caller -> July third. Nineteen forty one.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Eight oh eight, five five five, oh one oh five.
Nurse -> Eight oh eight, five five five, oh one oh five. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Caller -> I keep it charged now. I used to forget.
Nurse -> Good habit.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Perfect. Now, a few rules that hold for all of them. Use each medicine only for the symptom it's for. Give one at a time. Wait before you repeat it. And every time, write the medicine, the dose, and the time on the log.
Caller -> One at a time. Wait. Write it down. Okay. And what if two things happen at once? Like pain and restlessness?
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> Call me. We'll decide which to give first. Don't give two new things at once without talking to us.
Caller -> Okay. That removes a lot of pressure.
Nurse -> That's the idea. You don't have to be the nurse. You're the daughter.
Caller -> Thank you. That's exactly what I needed.
Caller -> Okay. Call you first. I like that rule.
Nurse -> Good. That's the rule for every family.
Nurse -> I'm also going to ask the team to send you a one page cheat sheet. Each medicine, what it's for, and how much. Large print.
Caller -> Oh, that would be so helpful. Large print. My husband's eyes are bad.
Nurse -> Large print it is.
Nurse -> I'll make sure of it.
Caller -> Thank you. We'll tape it inside the closet door.
Nurse -> I'll also have a nurse come out Thursday, to go over the kit with you in person.
Caller -> Thursday. Great. Can they show me the syringe? I haven't done it before.
Caller -> I get nervous with needles. Even without a needle. Ha.
Nurse -> Yes. They'll show you and watch you do it.
Caller -> Thank you.
Nurse -> About storage. Keep the kit together in one labeled box, away from other medicines, and out of reach of children and visitors.
Caller -> One box. Labeled. Away. We have grandchildren. Four of them. They come on weekends. I'll put it on the high shelf in my closet.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> My grandkids are curious. They open everything.
Nurse -> Ha. Then the closet shelf is perfect.
Nurse -> The closet shelf is good.
Caller -> I'll put a sign. KIT. So we don't forget where.
Nurse -> Ha. Good idea. And Sunniva, you can call any hour before giving anything, if you're unsure. And call if a medicine doesn't help within an hour.
Caller -> I'll tell my husband to bring the label maker from the garage. He loves that thing.
Nurse -> Ha. Perfect use for it.
Caller -> Any hour. Before. If it doesn't help in an hour. Okay. I'll put your number on the box.
Nurse -> Day or night.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Tamara, can I ask something? Will I know when to use them? I'm afraid I'll wait too long. Or give it too soon.
Nurse -> That's what the nurse and I will help with. If he shows you any sign of pain, restlessness, or trouble breathing, you can call me. We won't make you guess.
Caller -> Okay. That helps. I've been losing sleep over it.
Nurse -> Take care of yourself too.
Caller -> I'll try to nap this afternoon.
Nurse -> I understand. It's a lot of responsibility. You're doing great by asking.
Caller -> It is. I never thought I'd be the one.
Caller -> Thank you. I feel calmer already.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Caller -> It's nice to have someone to ask.
Nurse -> Good. Talk soon.
Caller -> I'll make the cards tonight. Thanks again, Tamara. Really.
Caller -> Bye.
Nurse -> Take care, Sunniva. Call any time.
Caller -> I will. Goodbye.

Nurse -> Dunmore Home Health, this is Evangeline.
Caller -> Hello? Good, you picked up. I always worry I'll get the machine.
Nurse -> Not today.
Caller -> Hello there. Is this Evangeline? I recognize your voice.
Nurse -> It is. Hi, Cassius.
Caller -> Hi, Evangeline. It's Cassius Whitlock. I'm one of your patients. The heel wound fella. I'm calling to check in and to ask about my appointment.
Nurse -> Hi, Cassius. Happy almost Thanksgiving.
Caller -> Same to you. I'm already thinking about the turkey. My wife brined it. In the bathtub.
Nurse -> Ha. That's commitment.
Nurse -> Hi, Cassius. Good to hear your voice. How is the heel?
Caller -> I was going to call yesterday but I got distracted by a football game. The kind where nobody scores.
Nurse -> Ha. Those are the longest ones.
Caller -> Thank you. I like talking to you. You never rush me.
Caller -> Better. Smaller. The nurse measured it last week, it was the size of a quarter. Now it's more like a dime. Very little drainage. The dressing is almost dry when I change it.
Caller -> She told me I was a model patient. I framed that.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I was thrilled. I took a picture of the paper ruler next to the heel. For my daughter. I know I'm not supposed to send it.
Nurse -> It's fine to keep for yourself.
Nurse -> Smaller is the best word I've heard all day.
Nurse -> I saw that in the notes.
Caller -> She's very precise. She uses a little paper ruler. She drew it on a clear sheet.
Nurse -> Ha. Yes, the tracing.
Nurse -> That's wonderful. Is there any redness around it, or any smell?
Caller -> I look every time I change the dressing. I don't want any surprises.
Caller -> No smell. I'd know. My wife says I have a nose like a bloodhound. And no redness. The skin around it is the same color as the rest. Pink, like a normal foot.
Caller -> She also says I could find a gas leak from two blocks away.
Nurse -> Useful skill.
Nurse -> Good. Any fever or chills?
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> My wife keeps asking me. Every morning. Fever? No. Chills? No. It's like a quiz.
Nurse -> Ha. She's thorough.
Caller -> No. I've been normal. Ninety eight. I don't have chills. I feel fine. I'm bored, mostly.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Ha. Bored is better than sick. Are you having any pain in the foot?
Nurse -> Do you have any hobbies to keep busy?
Caller -> I build model ships. Slowly. The glue gets everywhere.
Nurse -> Ha. A real craftsman.
Caller -> I've finished three puzzles. A thousand pieces each. The cat helped by sitting on them.
Nurse -> Ha. Good teamwork.
Caller -> A little. Maybe a two. In the evening it throbs a bit, after I've been up all day. Nothing like it was.
Caller -> Some nights I don't notice it at all. Tonight I did a little.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I prop it up on a pillow and watch the game. That usually helps.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Two out of ten in the evening. And your sugars?
Caller -> It's not constant. It's only when I've been up and about.
Caller -> This morning, fasting, one twenty eight. That's a good number for me. Yesterday it was one thirty five. The day before, one forty two. I'm trending down.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I write them down. I have a little book. My wife drew a graph.
Nurse -> A graph. Nice.
Nurse -> That is a good trend. And you're taking your metformin?
Nurse -> Keep it up. Keep writing the numbers down.
Caller -> I will. I even color code them. Green for good.
Nurse -> Ha. A green day.
Caller -> I'm trying. I walk the hallway in the boot. Ten laps.
Nurse -> That's good exercise.
Caller -> Yes. One thousand milligrams. Twice a day. With breakfast and dinner. I took this morning's with my eggs.
Caller -> I take it with food. I know you said that. I'm a good student.
Nurse -> You are.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Metformin, one thousand, twice a day. Any stomach upset?
Caller -> A little. Gas. But it's always been like that. My wife says I could power the house. Ha.
Nurse -> Okay. That's something to mention if it gets worse.
Nurse -> Ha. Okay. What about the boot? Are you wearing it?
Caller -> It squeaks, too. On the kitchen tile.
Nurse -> Ha. A noisy boot.
Caller -> I like to complain about it. It makes me feel better.
Nurse -> Complaining is therapeutic.
Caller -> Yes. I wear it whenever I'm up. Even to the bathroom at night. Although, I'll be honest, I'm so sick of this boot I could scream. It's hot. It's heavy. I clunk. My cat runs from me.
Nurse -> I know it's a pain.
Nurse -> Ha. I understand. But it's helping the heel heal, so keep it on.
Caller -> I know. I tell myself that every morning when I put it on.
Caller -> I know. I know. I'm not going to do anything silly. I'm just complaining. It's what retired men do.
Caller -> I just like to be dramatic. My wife says I should have been an actor.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> I know you're not. I just like checking.
Nurse -> Complaining is allowed. Cassius, what's your date of birth?
Caller -> I'll try to be less dramatic.
Nurse -> Don't change a thing.
Caller -> Thank you. I accept the license.
Caller -> June thirtieth. Nineteen fifty seven.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one oh nine.
Nurse -> Three oh three, five five five, oh one oh nine. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's the house phone. It rings on every floor.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll note it.
Caller -> It's an old phone system. My wife loves it. She says she can hear it from the garden.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Great. Now, your appointment. What's the question?
Caller -> I feel bad asking. I know you're busy.
Nurse -> It's no problem.
Caller -> The nurse is supposed to come Thursday. But Thursday is Thanksgiving. And my daughter is coming from Chicago. Can we move it? To Friday? Or even Monday?
Nurse -> Friday should be fine. Let me see. I'll move your nurse visit to Friday.
Caller -> Thank you for being flexible. I don't want to inconvenience anyone.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. Friday is great. What time? I'd like the morning, so I can nap in the afternoon.
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning. They'll call before they come.
Caller -> Morning. Great. The boot will be on.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I'll be here. I'll be in the boot.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> Perfect. I appreciate it. Hate to be a bother on a holiday.
Caller -> I'll keep the foot elevated while we watch the parade on TV Thursday.
Nurse -> That's a plan.
Caller -> One more thing. Is it okay if I shower? I've been sponge bathing around the boot.
Nurse -> Keep the dressing dry. A sponge bath is fine. The nurse can go over showering Friday.
Nurse -> Not a bother. Anything else?
Caller -> The list. Let me look. Number one was the appointment. Number two the strips.
Nurse -> Those two are done. What's next?
Caller -> Number three says: tell her thanks. Ha. That's it.
Caller -> Let me think. I wrote a list. Where is it. Oh. In my other pocket.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Yes, actually. A supply thing. I almost forgot.
Caller -> Yes. My test strips. I'm down to ten. I test twice a day. So that's five days. I called the pharmacy but the pharmacy said I need a new order.
Nurse -> Okay. I'll place an order with the supply company for glucose test strips.
Caller -> Thanks. I'd hate to run out on a holiday weekend.
Caller -> Oh, great. How long will that take?
Caller -> Two to three days is fine. I just don't want to be down to zero.
Nurse -> You won't be.
Caller -> Okay. That works. I have enough for five days.
Nurse -> Usually two or three days.
Caller -> Thank you. That's a load off. I was worried about running out during the holiday.
Caller -> I was dreading calling the pharmacy again. They always put me on hold.
Nurse -> Ha. We'll handle this one.
Nurse -> It's a good thing you called. I'm also going to send a message to the team that the heel is improving. They'll be pleased.
Caller -> I appreciate you saying so.
Caller -> I try to call early. My late father never did. He ran out of everything.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I hope so. I've been so good. I've been so good with the boot. I deserve a sticker.
Nurse -> You have been.
Nurse -> Ha. A gold star. I'll mention that in the message.
Caller -> I'm not even joking. I'd like a gold star.
Nurse -> You'll get one.
Caller -> Please do.
Nurse -> Let me remind you of a few things. Change the dressing as ordered. Keep the area clean and dry. And look at both feet every day.
Caller -> Change the dressing. Clean and dry. Look at both feet. Okay. I use a mirror. My wife holds it. It's a whole production.
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> Ha. A mirror is a great idea.
Nurse -> You can also use your phone camera.
Caller -> That's smart. I'll use that for the back of the heel.
Caller -> My wife hates holding it. She says my feet are ugly.
Nurse -> Ha. They're not.
Nurse -> And wear the boot whenever you're up, even for short trips.
Caller -> Even short trips. Yes, ma'am. Even to the kitchen. I'll wear it for Thanksgiving. Even for the pie.
Caller -> I put a note on the bathroom door. BOOT.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Especially at night, when it's dark.
Caller -> I leave the bathroom light on. And I keep the boot by the bed.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Especially for the pie.
Caller -> Ha.
Nurse -> Call us if you get a fever, if the redness spreads, if you notice a bad smell, more drainage, new pain, or a sugar over three hundred.
Caller -> Fever. Redness. Smell. Drainage. Pain. Over three hundred. Okay. I have the list on the fridge. It's a long list. But it's right there.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Evangeline, can I ask a silly question? What can I eat on Thursday? I mean, with my sugars.
Nurse -> Not silly. Enjoy the meal. Small portions. Watch the sweets. Maybe a small slice of pie. And check your sugar in the evening.
Caller -> I'm going to take a short walk after dinner. In the boot. Around the block.
Nurse -> Short and slow. That's good.
Caller -> I'm going to have a little of everything. Except the green bean thing with the fried onions.
Nurse -> Ha. That's a classic.
Caller -> A small slice. I can do that. My daughter makes a pecan pie that could win awards.
Nurse -> Then definitely a small slice, and savor it.
Caller -> Ha. I'll savor it. I'll count the pecans.
Nurse -> Enjoy every bite.
Caller -> I'll send you a picture of the pie. Oh. I can't. Never mind. I'll just remember it.
Nurse -> Ha. Thank you for the thought.
Nurse -> Ha. Have a wonderful holiday.
Caller -> We're expecting eleven people. The house will be loud.
Nurse -> Sounds wonderful.
Caller -> You too. Thank you for everything.
Nurse -> Take care, Cassius.
Caller -> Thanks again for everything. You and the whole team have been terrific.
Nurse -> It's our pleasure.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Eastbrook Hospice, this is Fabian.
Caller -> Hi. Hello? Can you hear me? I'm in the car.
Nurse -> I can hear you fine. Are you driving?
Caller -> Parked. In the grocery lot. I'll be quick.
Caller -> Hi, Fabian. It's Siobhan Quillfeather. My dad is Roderick Quillfeather. I'm just calling with a quick update. Nothing urgent.
Nurse -> Hi, Shavon. Thanks for calling. How's your dad?
Caller -> I wasn't sure it was worth calling. But I thought I'd rather say something.
Nurse -> It always is.
Caller -> Oh, thank you. How are you?
Nurse -> Doing well, thanks. Go ahead.
Caller -> He's good. Quiet. He sleeps a lot more than last week. He wakes up for a little while in the late morning, and then he naps until dinner.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> It's a gentle kind of sleeping. Not restless. He has his hand on the blanket.
Nurse -> That sounds peaceful.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he comfortable when he's awake?
Caller -> I ask him every few hours. Are you warm enough? Do you want the window open?
Nurse -> That's good attention.
Caller -> Yes. He smiles. He asks what's for dinner. He still has his sense of humor.
Caller -> Last night it was soup. He had three sips and said, delicious.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> That's wonderful, Shavon. Is he eating?
Caller -> Oh, yes. Sorry, I'm distracted. A cart almost hit my car.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Small amounts. Soft food. Pudding, yogurt, mashed potatoes. A few spoonfuls. He used to love steak. He says now he just wants something cold and soft.
Caller -> I put the pudding in a small cup. A big bowl overwhelms him.
Nurse -> Smart.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I make pudding from scratch. He says it's better than the store kind. Even though it's lumpy.
Nurse -> Ha. Lumpy is character.
Nurse -> That's very common. And pain? Any trouble breathing?
Caller -> I keep waiting to see. He says no every time I ask.
Caller -> None. No grimacing. No moaning. He's breathing quietly. No pain that I can tell, and I'm watching closely.
Caller -> He had a rough night last week. This week is better.
Nurse -> I'm glad.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I read his face more than his words. His face has always told me the truth.
Nurse -> That's a gift.
Nurse -> Good. I'm glad. Let me confirm his date of birth.
Caller -> Of course. Go ahead.
Caller -> December nineteenth. Nineteen forty four.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> He'll be eighty two in a few weeks. We're planning a little party. A quiet one.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> Thank you. And your number?
Caller -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one five one.
Nurse -> Six oh two, five five five, oh one five one. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> I'd better go in and shop before I forget what I came for.
Nurse -> Ha. Take care.
Nurse -> Okay, Shavon. I'd like a nurse to come see him Wednesday, to check in and see how you're all doing.
Caller -> That would be a relief. It's good to have someone look at him who knows what to look for.
Caller -> Wednesday. Good. What time?
Nurse -> I'll ask for the morning.
Nurse -> Morning. They'll call before they come.
Caller -> Perfect. I'll be here. My brother will too. He's driving in Tuesday night.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> That's nice. It's good to have family around.
Caller -> It is. He hasn't seen my brother since August. They'll talk about fishing.
Nurse -> Ha. A classic topic.
Caller -> And bad jokes. Mostly about my brother's boat.
Nurse -> Every family has one.
Caller -> Ours has three.
Caller -> It is. We're taking turns. I'm days, he'll be nights.
Nurse -> Sounds like a good plan.
Nurse -> Okay. For his mouth, use a small swab dipped in water to keep his lips and mouth moist, and put a little balm on his lips. Offer sips and soft foods like pudding or yogurt, but let him decide how much.
Caller -> Swab. Balm. Sips. Soft foods. Let him decide. Okay. We have those pink swabs. And the balm. It smells like cherry. He likes it.
Caller -> We also put on his favorite music. Sinatra. He hums.
Nurse -> That's lovely.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> He asked me yesterday if the Packers won. I told him they did. They didn't. But he was happy.
Nurse -> Ha. A kind fib.
Caller -> He doesn't remember the score anyway. He just likes hearing we won.
Caller -> I'll confess it when it doesn't matter.
Nurse -> And Shavon, call any time, day or night, with questions or if anything changes.
Caller -> Any time. Okay. I have the number on the fridge. Thank you, Fabian.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Take care.
Caller -> Bye.

Nurse -> Rowan Home Health, this is Ezra.
Caller -> Hello? Ezra? It's hard to hear myself think. I'll talk slowly.
Nurse -> Take your time.
Caller -> Hi, Ezra. It's Isolde Brannigan. I'm a patient. I finished my chemo cycle yesterday and I'm very nauseous. I want to check on my nausea medicine.
Nurse -> Hi, Isolde. I'm sorry you're feeling rough. Tell me what you've taken.
Caller -> Thank you. I'm lying on the couch with a bucket. Just in case.
Nurse -> Smart to keep one close.
Caller -> The ondansetron. The dissolving one. I took an eight milligram last night at about ten. No. Four. Four milligrams. The bottle says four. I always get that mixed up. It's the little tablet. Yes. Four.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> Ondansetron, four milligrams, last night at ten. Okay. How often are you allowed to take it?
Caller -> It's the one in the green box. My daughter wrote four on the lid.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Caller -> Every eight hours as needed. That's what the label says. I haven't taken any today. I'm almost eight hours. It's a little before six. No, it's noon. Hold on. I took it at ten last night so it's been fourteen hours. I haven't taken any today. I'm nervous about it.
Caller -> I wrote the times on a card. I do that every cycle. Ten at night, six in the morning.
Nurse -> Okay.
Nurse -> Okay. Fourteen hours. That's well past eight. Tell me how the nausea is.
Caller -> Sorry for the math. My head is foggy.
Nurse -> Totally fine.
Caller -> Moderate. It's there all the time. A rolling feeling. It's worse when I smell food. I vomited once this morning at seven. Just once. It was mostly water. And then I drank a little water, and it stayed down.
Nurse -> I'm sorry. That's miserable.
Caller -> It's okay. I've had worse. The first cycle was terrible.
Nurse -> It helps that you know what to expect.
Nurse -> Okay. One episode of vomiting. Are you keeping sips down?
Caller -> It was early. Seven. I haven't thrown up since.
Nurse -> That's a good sign.
Caller -> Yes. A few sips of water every ten minutes. And some ginger ale. It's flat. It stays down.
Nurse -> Good. Keep doing that.
Nurse -> Good. Any belly pain? Fever?
Caller -> I keep checking. I'm a champion checker.
Nurse -> Ha. Good.
Caller -> No pain. My stomach is just queasy. No fever. I took it a while ago and it was normal.

Nurse -> Okay.

Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he able to walk normally?
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Caller -> I watched him walk to the chair. I held his belt. He said, I'm not a toddler.
Nurse -> Ha.
Caller -> I helped him up. He stood, he held the sink. Then he walked to the chair with the walker. Slowly. He walks slowly anyway. I didn't see a limp.
Nurse -> Okay. Is he confused, sleepy, or vomiting? Any headache?
Caller -> He was joking with me about the dinosaur bandage.
Nurse -> Good sign.
Caller -> He knew exactly who I was. He knew the day. He argued with me about it. He didn't say he has a headache. No vomiting. He's had a piece of toast. I think he's fine. I'm not sure. I'm his son, I'm nervous.
Caller -> He even told me my shirt was inside out. It was.
Nurse -> Ha. A good sign.
Nurse -> That's a very reasonable thing to be. Tobin, what's his date of birth?
Caller -> Thank you. I've been awake since four.
Caller -> March fifth. Nineteen forty seven.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Five oh three, five five five, oh one oh seven.
Nurse -> Five oh three, five five five, oh one oh seven. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Caller -> I'll leave it on loud. Even though I'm working.
Nurse -> Good idea.
Nurse -> Great.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's what I'd like to do. I'd like a nurse to come see him today. To check his head, his elbow, and his hip and back. And to see how he walks.
Caller -> Okay. I'm ready.
Caller -> Today. Good. He'll complain. But good.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> I'll also send a message to the team about the possible fall. They'll want to know.
Caller -> Great.
Caller -> Okay. Thank you. I wasn't sure it was worth calling. If he really didn't fall, then it's nothing.

Caller -> I always think I'm bothering people.

Caller -> I've been telling myself he's fine. But I needed someone else to say it.

Nurse -> Great.

Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Should I be worried about his head? Even though he says no?

Nurse -> That's good.

Nurse -> That's helpful.
Caller -> My boss was fine with it. I told her it was family.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Thanks, Augusta. I'll feel better when the nurse comes.
Caller -> You've been really helpful. This was less scary than I expected.
Nurse -> I'm glad.

Caller -> Hello? Is this the nurse? I hope this is the right number. I've been rehearsing what to say.
Nurse -> It's the right number. Go ahead.
Caller -> Hi, Gideon. It's Anneke Strathmore. I'm Philippa Strathmore's daughter. I need to tell you something, and I want to say first that I didn't stop her blood pressure pill. I stopped the other one. The water pill. I probably shouldn't have.
Nurse -> Hi, Anneke. How are you?
Caller -> Nervous. I'll get to the point. It's about her pills.
Nurse -> Hi, Anneke. Thank you for telling me. Let's go through it. What is she taking?
Caller -> Thank you for answering. I wasn't sure about calling this late in the day.
Nurse -> It's fine. We take calls until nine.

Caller -> I feel nervous. I don't want to get in trouble.
Nurse -> You're not in trouble. Let's talk.
Caller -> She's on two. The amlodipine, five milligrams, once a day. That's the blood pressure one. I did not stop that one. I give it every morning. I gave it today.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I keep them in a pillbox, one of the big ones with the days. I fill it on Sundays.
Nurse -> That's great.

Nurse -> That's a good one.
Nurse -> Mm hm.
Nurse -> Okay. Has she fainted, or fallen?
Caller -> No. She hasn't fainted. She hasn't fallen. Not once. I'm always next to her.
Nurse -> Good. That's reassuring.
Caller -> I'm learning. Slowly. Thank you for being patient.
Nurse -> Good. Have you checked her blood pressure?
Caller -> This morning, before her pill. One forty two over eighty four. That's higher than it was in the hospital. But she hasn't had the water pill for three days.
Nurse -> Okay.
Caller -> I used the cuff the nurse showed me. It beeps when it's done. I did it twice. Same both times.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Okay. One forty two over eighty four. Thank you. I'm glad you checked. Anneke, what's your mom's date of birth?
Caller -> Her usual is one thirty something. So it's a bit up.
Nurse -> Okay. Good to know.
Caller -> I wrote it down right away. The number. And the time.
Nurse -> That's useful.
Caller -> Is that really high? I wasn't sure.
Nurse -> It's a little higher than we'd like, but not dangerous.
Caller -> Okay.
Caller -> October twenty seventh. Nineteen forty nine.
Nurse -> And your number?
Caller -> Four oh four, five five five, oh one seven three.
Nurse -> Four oh four, five five five, oh one seven three. Right?
Caller -> Yes. That's my cell.
Nurse -> Great. Thanks.
Caller -> I'll keep it with me all day. Even in the garden.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Caller -> Mom just asked who I'm talking to. I said the nurse. She said, tell him hello.
Nurse -> Hello, Mrs. Strathmore.
Caller -> She waved at the phone. She does that.
Nurse -> Ha. A friendly wave.
Caller -> Is there anything else I might be doing wrong that I don't know about?
Nurse -> Not from what you've described. You're being careful. Just keep checking with us.
Nurse -> Thanks.
Nurse -> Okay. Here's the honest answer. I'm glad you called, and I'm not upset. But you shouldn't stop a medicine without checking with us first. Stopping the water pill can raise her pressure, and the dizziness could have another cause.
Caller -> I'm bracing myself.
Nurse -> No need.
Caller -> Please. Be honest.
Nurse -> I will.
Caller -> I know. I know. I feel terrible. I didn't mean to do anything wrong.
Nurse -> It's okay. Let's focus on the next step.
Nurse -> You didn't do anything wrong on purpose. You were trying to help. What matters now is that the clinician knows. I'm going to send a message to the team right away, and ask whether to restart the water pill.
Caller -> Thank you. That means a lot.
Caller -> Okay. Please. Should I give it tonight? Or wait?

Caller -> I put the bottle in a drawer. Away from the pillbox. Just so I don't do it by habit.
Nurse -> That's a smart move.
Caller -> I will. I promise. I won't do anything.
Nurse -> Thank you.
Caller -> Wait. Don't restart. Keep the amlodipine. Okay. I will.
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> I'll call you back tomorrow to let you know what they say.
Caller -> Is it all right if I call you first if I hear back from anyone else?
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> Tomorrow. Okay. What time?
Caller -> I'll be here. I took the week off.
Nurse -> That helps.
Nurse -> Late morning.
Caller -> Eleven's perfect.
Caller -> Okay. That works. We have breakfast at eight and she naps at ten.
Nurse -> Then I'll call at eleven.
Caller -> Good. I'll be home with her.
Nurse -> In the meantime, check her blood pressure in the morning and the evening, sitting down. Write the numbers down. And have her stand up slowly.
Caller -> Sitting. Same arm. I remember that part.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Morning and evening. Sitting. Write it down. Stand up slowly. Okay. I have the cuff. And a notebook.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> I'll make a chart on graph paper. A friendly one.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> Perfect.
Nurse -> Call us if she faints, or falls, if her pressure goes over one hundred eighty, if she has a bad headache, or her legs swell up.
Caller -> Faints. Falls. Over one eighty. Bad headache. Swelling. Okay. I'll write that on the first page.
Nurse -> Right. Those are the ones to remember.
Caller -> I'll tape this to the fridge. Right at eye level.
Nurse -> Good.
Nurse -> Right.
Nurse -> Good.
Caller -> Thank you for not yelling at me.
Nurse -> Never. Mistakes like this are common.
Nurse -> Of course.
Caller -> My brother would have. He yells.
Nurse -> Ha.
Nurse -> I'd never. You did something very human. You reached out, which is what counts.
Caller -> I just love her. And I got scared.
Nurse -> That's what this is. Love and fear. It's normal.
Caller -> Thank you, Gideon.
Nurse -> You're doing right by her.
Caller -> I hope so. I try.
Nurse -> You're welcome. Talk tomorrow.
